## 144 — both of item 143's deferred targets retracted, and the spelling gap they uncovered

Item 143 left two measured targets "for a later pass": `SKIP 199990 LIMIT 10` at 658x native and
`ORDER BY a LIMIT 10` at 135x, both described as needing paging pushed into the walk. Neither
survives contact.

### SKIP: not a missing path, because a skipped row's projection is load-bearing

`applyProjection` pages lazily — `skip(n, …)` then `take(n)` — but `keyed` projects each row as
it is pulled, so `SKIP 199990` projects 199,990 rows and discards them. Moving the paging onto
the BINDINGS would make a skipped row cost no projection, which looks free because row position
depends only on the binding order.

It is not free. Both engines currently EVALUATE the discarded projections, and that is
observable:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) RETURN CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) AS a SKIP 3 LIMIT 2
    with the unparseable row at index 0 — OUTSIDE the returned window
    ts  RAISED E_INVALID_VALUE      native  RAISED E_INVALID_VALUE
```

So paging before projection would stop TS raising where native still raises — the same
raise-parity constraint that cost item 139 a measured 3.1x. What is left of the 658x is the
columnar-versus-boxed projection gap: native evaluates 200,000 projections in 0.2ms because it
does them a column at a time. Structural, like items 132/134/139.

### ORDER BY + LIMIT: already optimized, and my theory was wrong

I assumed the 139ms was projecting all 200,000 rows to keep ten. It is not: `orderNeedsOutput`
already drives a top-k over INPUT bindings that projects only the survivors. The proof is again
in the raise behaviour, and it is the opposite of the SKIP case:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) RETURN CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) AS a ORDER BY n.age LIMIT 2
    with the unparseable row sorting LAST
    ts  [{"a":1},{"a":2}]           native  [{"a":1},{"a":2}]      — no raise, both
```

Neither engine projects the non-survivors. The remaining cost is sort-key evaluation over
200,000 rows — the structural property read again.

### What the diagnosis DID find: an ORDER BY alias costs 1.7x its own expression

`aliasDefinition` substitutes `ORDER BY <alias>` with the expression the alias names, which is
what lets the top-k keep input bindings. It handles only "a plain column of an input variable",
so a COMPUTED alias declines, the sort reads an output column, the top-k is given up, and every
row is projected:

| query                                                 |       min |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | --------: |
| `RETURN n.age AS a ORDER BY a LIMIT 10` (plain alias) |      95.7 |
| `RETURN n.age AS a ORDER BY n.age LIMIT 10`           |      84.7 |
| **`RETURN n.age + 1 AS a ORDER BY a LIMIT 10`**       | **154.8** |
| `RETURN n.age + 1 AS a ORDER BY n.age + 1 LIMIT 10`   |      89.3 |
| `RETURN upper(n.name) AS a ORDER BY a LIMIT 10`       |     191.8 |

**1.7x for a pure spelling difference** — this repo's named bug class, in the exact shape the
spelling probe exists to catch, and the probe had no ORDER BY group at all.

The generalization is small (substitute any alias whose expression reads only INPUT variables,
which subsumes the two column cases) and, unusually, carries NO raise-parity risk on its own: the
substituted expression is still evaluated once per row as the sort key, so the change affects
only whether a row OBJECT is built.

**It cannot be done in one engine.** Measured, the two spellings differ in WHICH QUERIES RAISE,
and they differ the same way in native:

```text
  RETURN CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) AS a ORDER BY a LIMIT 2     ts RAISED   native RAISED
  RETURN CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) AS a ORDER BY n.age LIMIT 2 ts rows     native rows
```

Extending only TS would make it stop raising where native still raises. The TS comment claims to
mirror a Rust `alias_definition`, but no such symbol exists in the engine today (the Rust side
lowers to `OrderPage`), so the fix needs the native decision point located first. Left as a
two-engine change rather than half-done, and INSTRUMENTED instead: two new groups in the TS
spelling probe, one for the computed alias and one for the plain-column alias that already works.

```text
  ORDER BY alias vs its expression (item 144)
         16.65ms  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10
          9.69ms  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY n.k + 1 LIMIT 10
  ORDER BY plain-column alias vs its expression
          8.18ms  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10
          8.14ms  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10
```

1.72x on the probe's own fixture, matching the 1.73x at 200,000 rows, and flat for the plain
column — so the group localizes the defect to the substitution rather than to ordering. It sits
under the default 2x tolerance, so it documents rather than fails; `SPELL_TOL=1.5 bun run
spelling` flags it alongside the known inline-versus-clause node count.

Gates separately: full suite exit 0 (an `@lenke/sync` task failed once and nx labelled it flaky —
two further uncached runs exit 0, and item 140 verified the same task 5/5), `bun run lint` exit 0,
`fmt` then `fmt:check` 0, and the spelling probe clean at its default tolerance. No engine code
changed this item: the only edit is the probe's two new groups.

## 145 — a live cross-engine divergence, and item 144's conclusion corrected

Item 144 closed by calling the `ORDER BY <computed alias>` gap a two-engine change, on the
grounds that "the two spellings differ in WHICH QUERIES RAISE, and they differ the same way in
native". **That was wrong, and the way it was wrong is the finding.**

### The correction

Item 144's probe put the FAULTING expression in the sort key itself, so inlining it faulted
anyway and both engines raised — which looked like agreement. Put the faulting expression in a
DIFFERENT projected item and the engines part:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.age + 1 AS a, CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) AS b ORDER BY a LIMIT 2
    ts      RAISED                      <- projected every row, so `b` faulted on a row it
                                           never emits
    native  [{a:2,b:1},{a:3,b:2}]       <- projected only the two emitted rows

  …the same query with ORDER BY n.age + 1   returns those rows in BOTH
```

So this was a **live byte-identity violation**, not a shared design — and native is the
consistent engine: it inlines the alias into the sort-key scope, keeps the top-k over INPUT
bindings, and never projects a discarded row. The native fuzzer comment names the mechanism
(`try_late_materialize`) and records that this very deviation CLASS was found and fixed on that
side already; the TS side lagged for the computed-alias shape.

The fixture is what hid it. Mine had the fault and the sort key in one expression — the same
conflation that has cost this pass a measurement several times over.

### The fix

`aliasDefinition` substituted `ORDER BY <alias>` only for a direct `var`/`prop`. It now
substitutes ANY alias expression whose free names are all INPUT names (the two column cases are
subsumed: their free sets are `{name}` and `{variable}`). A shadowed name still declines, since
in the sort scope it would resolve to the output column and mean something else.

It cannot change WHICH expressions are evaluated per row — the substituted expression becomes
the sort key, evaluated for every row either way. What changes is that OTHER projected items
stop being evaluated for rows the top-k discards, which is exactly native's behaviour.

### Measured, interleaved, dist verified by BEHAVIOUR each round

| query (200,000 rows)                            | after₁ | before | after₂ |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -----: | -----: | -----: |
| `RETURN n.age + 1 AS a ORDER BY a LIMIT 10`     |   96.1 |  150.6 |   86.1 |
| `RETURN upper(n.name) AS a ORDER BY a LIMIT 10` |  110.5 |  173.4 |  115.4 |
| `ORDER BY n.age + 1` (CONTROL)                  |   85.5 |   88.1 |   86.3 |
| no ORDER BY (CONTROL)                           |    1.0 |    1.0 |    0.9 |

**1.75x**, and the alias spelling now costs what its expression spelling costs (86.1 against
86.3) — the spelling gap is closed, not merely narrowed. The dist was verified by BEHAVIOUR
rather than by grepping for the comment, which returns 0 because the bundler strips comments.

### The fuzzer missed it, and the first extension had no teeth

The differential fuzzer already generated `RETURN <expr> AS x … ORDER BY x`, so the shape was
reachable — but never with a LIMIT AND a second item that faults on exactly the discarded rows.
Widening the random band to emit both did NOT catch the reverted fix on three seeds: the fixture
is six vertices and `LIMIT 1-3` barely discards anything, so a random fallible expression faults
on the emitted rows too and both engines raise.

So two TARGETED queries were added, and every piece of them is load-bearing:

- `st` exists on vertices 1 and 3 ONLY, so `CAST(n.st AS INTEGER)` faults on those two and is
  NULL — not a fault — on the rest.
- `0 - n.n` is a COMPUTED alias, the substitution under test; a plain column shows nothing.
- ascending order puts n = 17, 13, 11 first (vertices with no `st`), leaving both faulting rows
  outside `LIMIT 3`.

Teeth verified: with the fix reverted, seeds 1, 7 and 42 all FAIL; with it in place all pass.
The widened random band is kept anyway — it can reach future variants — but the audit says
plainly that it is the targeted pair doing the work.

### A third confirmation about the spelling probe

The probe still PRINTS ~1.9x for this group. Isolated at the same `SPELL_N` the two spellings
are 6.66ms against 5.64 (1.18x), and at 200,000 rows they are 86.1 against 86.3. The probe runs
twenty-odd queries in one process, so each row's spread is inflated — items 141 and 143 found
the same thing. The probe's comment now says so: it is a FINDER, and a spread it prints is not a
settled delta.

Gates separately: 10 new tests, full suite exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check`
0, all seven fuzzers green on random seeds, spelling probe clean at its default tolerance. No
Rust changed — native was already correct.

## 146 — a raise-parity sweep over everything this pass added, and the sync flake diagnosed

Item 145 found a cross-engine divergence by separating the FAULT from the thing being
optimized. That technique generalizes to every fast path items 135-143 added, since each one
skips work for rows a query does not emit — so each could hide the same bug. This sweeps them.

### The arrangement, which is the whole trick

`st` is on v1 and v6 ONLY, so `CAST(n.st AS INTEGER)` faults on exactly those two and is NULL —
not a fault — everywhere else. v1 sorts FIRST by age and v6 LAST, so a `SKIP` drops the first
faulting row and a `LIMIT` drops the last. A query can therefore fault only on rows it
DISCARDS, which is the only way to tell two schedulings apart. Item 144 missed this by putting
the fault IN the sort key, where inlining faults anyway and both engines raise — which reads as
agreement.

### Result: 13 shapes, 0 divergences

Every fast path agrees with native, including the ones that had never been compared this way:
the DISTINCT walk (143), the fused hop projection (138), both grouped tallies (141/142), the
filtered node count (135), the far-hop walk (137) and the product count (136). Each evaluates
the fallible expression once per ELEMENT exactly as the general path does, so each raises, and
raises on both sides.

Two boundaries came out of it, neither previously pinned:

| shape                              | both engines |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------ |
| `ORDER BY a SKIP 2 LIMIT 2`        | rows         |
| `ORDER BY a SKIP 2` (unbounded)    | RAISE        |
| `SKIP 2` / `LIMIT 2` with no order | RAISE        |

So native's late-materialize fires for a BOUNDED top-k and not for an unbounded tail — the tail
has no candidate set to narrow. That is the line item 144 nearly optimized across.

### Committed as a test, not left as a probe

`packages/native/src/paged-projection-conformance.test.ts`, following `gql-conformance`'s idiom
(one NDJSON into both engines, compare the serialization OR the raised code, skip when the
native lib is absent). A fixed-shape test is the right tool here rather than more fuzzing: item
145 showed the random draw cannot reach this arrangement — a six-vertex fixture with `LIMIT 1-3`
barely discards anything, so a random fallible expression faults on the emitted rows too.

Teeth verified the only way available: with item 145's fix reverted the file FAILS, and with it
restored it passes. The other twelve shapes are regression guards rather than teeth — none of
them currently skips an evaluation, so no mutation can make them differ today. Said plainly
rather than claimed as coverage.

### The `@lenke/sync:test` flake, diagnosed after costing three ticks a re-run

It has appeared under `bun run test` in items 140, 144 and 146, each time passing on re-run and
each time labelled flaky by nx. **22 consecutive uncached runs in ISOLATION pass** (5 in item
140, 2 in item 144, 15 here), so it is not the test logic.

The cause is visible in the suite: `packages/sync/src/{engine,websocket,gremlin-write,reconnect,
reported-bugs}.test.ts` wait with `setTimeout(r, 1)` … `setTimeout(r, 10)` and then assert.
Under `run-many` those tests share a machine with twenty other projects, and a 1-2ms sleep stops
being long enough for the awaited work — so an assertion fires early. In isolation the same
sleep has the whole box and never misses.

Not fixed here: replacing timed waits with poll-until-condition across five files is test
infrastructure in a package this pass has not otherwise touched, and it deserves its own change
rather than being folded into a sweep. Recorded so the next red `run-many` is recognized in
seconds instead of re-investigated — and worth fixing, because a gate that is routinely red and
routinely re-run is a gate one learns to ignore.

Gates separately: 6 new tests, full suite exit 0 (one `@lenke/sync` flake as above), `bun run
lint` exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check` 0. No engine code changed — the sweep found nothing to fix.

## 147 — the write path, priced for the first time, and a copy that contradicted its own contract

Items 112-146 were all reads or ingest. This prices `SET`, sweeping the thing that matters for
it: the element's property WIDTH. One width cannot tell O(K) from O(K²), and this repo has been
caught by exactly that.

### The curve, and what it is NOT

2,000 nodes, one `SET n.p0 = 7` per node:

| width |     ts | ns/node | core only | native | ts/native |
| ----: | -----: | ------: | --------: | -----: | --------: |
|    64 |  3.5ms |    1747 |     2.2ms |  0.3ms |     12.3x |
|   128 |  5.7ms |    2828 |     3.9ms |  0.3ms |     21.9x |
|   256 | 44.7ms |   22338 |    42.7ms |  0.3ms |    171.8x |
|   512 | 91.6ms |   45790 |    91.7ms |  0.3ms |    327.9x |

Native is FLAT at 0.3ms across every width — it writes one columnar cell, so its `SET` is O(1)
in the element's width. And `core only` (the same write through `Vertex.setProperty`, no query)
tracks `ts` almost exactly, so none of this is the GQL executor.

**It is not O(K²), and checking mattered.** 128 → 256 is 2x the width and 7.2x the cost, which
looks like an exponent; but 256 → 512 is 2x the width and 1.76x the cost — linear again. So it is
linear with a CLIFF between 128 and 256, which is the JavaScript engine moving a wide object out
of fast properties into dictionary mode, not an algorithm. Reading the jump alone as O(K²) would
have sent me looking for a quadratic loop that is not there.

### Three O(K) passes per single-key write, one of them pure waste

`setProperty` builds `{ ...previous, [key]: value }` (O(K) spread), hands it to the commit funnel
which calls `normalizeProperties` (O(K)), and freezes the result (O(K)).

`normalizeProperties` lifts a tagged temporal (`{"@date": …}`) to its instance, and its contract
says _"Returns the same bag when nothing moved, so the common case costs one pass and no
allocation."_ **The code did not do that**: it allocated `out` and filled all K slots on every
call, then returned `bag` and threw the copy away. The copy is now built only once a value
actually moves — which is what the comment already claimed.

### Measured, interleaved, dist verified each round

|                         width | after₁ | before | after₂ |     ratio |
| ----------------------------: | -----: | -----: | -----: | --------: |
|                           512 |   67.4 |   91.6 |   64.6 | **1.42x** |
|                           256 |   36.4 |   44.7 |   33.0 | **1.35x** |
|                           128 |    3.9 |    5.7 |    4.1 |      1.4x |
| native (CONTROL, every width) |    0.3 |    0.3 |    0.3 |      flat |

The gain grows with width, as removing one of three O(K) passes should. ts/native at width 512
goes 327.9x → 219.6x.

### What remains is the design, not an oversight

The other two passes are inherent: the bag is immutable and frozen, so a single-key write must
build a new object (O(K)) and freeze it (O(K)). The freeze is what turns a stray
`v.properties.x = …` into a loud throw instead of silent index corruption — it is load-bearing,
not incidental. Native is O(1) only because it writes a columnar cell and has no bag at all.

So a wide-element write stays structurally behind, and the honest statement is the shape rather
than the ratio: **TS `SET` is O(width) per write; native is O(1).** For the wide-feature
workloads this matters to, that is the thing to know — the 1.42x is a third off a cost that is
still linear.

### Teeth: 5 mutants, all 5 caught

The lifted value never written; the copy seeded EMPTY (losing untouched keys); the ORIGINAL bag
mutated instead of copied; nothing ever lifted; and the copy returned even when empty-handed
(which loses the identity the optimization is). The identity assertion is the one that pins the
optimization itself — a copy would compare EQUAL and say nothing, so the test asserts `toBe`.

The lifting tests cover a tagged value first, last, several at once, and inside a list — the
last-position case because the copy is created on first move, so a late move has to be written
into the copy rather than the original.

Gates separately: 12 new tests, full suite exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check`
0, all seven fuzzers green on random seeds. No Rust changed.

## 148 — the same allocate-and-discard, one level down, where a map property cost 16µs a write

Item 147 fixed `normalizeProperties` building a copy it then threw away. That is a PATTERN, and
`normalizePropertyValue` had it twice more — so a write to an element carrying LIST or MAP
properties paid it per value, per write, however unrelated the write.

### Priced by sweeping the container's SIZE

2,000 nodes, one `setProperty('n', 7)` per node — a key the container is not even in:

| container size | plain only | + LIST prop |  + MAP prop | native |
| -------------: | ---------: | ----------: | ----------: | -----: |
|              0 |      339ns |       369ns |       778ns | 0.30ms |
|              8 |      330ns |       581ns |      2125ns | 0.28ms |
|             32 |      305ns |       612ns |      4995ns | 0.29ms |
|            128 |      232ns |      1160ns | **16322ns** | 0.28ms |

Native is flat at ~0.28ms whatever the element carries — the perfect control, since it writes one
columnar cell. The TS baseline is flat too, so the growth is entirely the container being
re-normalized: **a 128-entry map the write never touches cost 70x the whole baseline write.**

### Two instances, and the record one had no check at all

- **The list branch** used `value.map(...)`, allocating a whole new array on every call and
  discarding it whenever nothing moved — which is almost always, because a list that came OUT of
  the graph is already normalized.
- **The record branch** had no `changed` check whatsoever: `LenkeRecord.from([...value].map(…))`
  spread the record to pairs, mapped to fresh pairs, then deduped, **RE-SORTED** and
  reconstructed. Unconditionally. That re-sort is the 16µs.

Both are now lazy. The record rebuild also stops going back through `from`: it copies the `Map`
directly, because iteration order is already sorted and `set` on an existing key keeps its
position.

**That shortcut rests on every `LenkeRecord` being sorted, which was checked rather than
assumed.** The class is constructed in exactly two places in the whole repo — `LenkeRecord.from`,
which sorts, and the new copy, which copies an already-sorted one. The code says so, including
what breaks if a third site ever appears.

### Measured, interleaved, dist verified each round

| shape                        | after₁ | before | after₂ |     ratio |
| ---------------------------- | -----: | -----: | -----: | --------: |
| MAP prop, size 128           |   3.13 |  32.65 |   3.19 | **10.2x** |
| MAP prop, size 32            |   1.37 |   9.17 |   1.26 |  **7.3x** |
| LIST prop, size 128          |   1.39 |   2.17 |   1.41 |     1.55x |
| LIST prop, size 32           |   0.79 |   1.21 |   0.79 |     1.53x |
| plain only (CONTROL)         |   0.52 |   0.48 |   0.56 |      flat |
| native (CONTROL, all shapes) |  ~0.26 |  ~0.26 |  ~0.26 |      flat |

The map win grows with size because the re-sort it removes does; the list win is bounded by the
scan, which still has to visit every element to know nothing moved.

### Teeth: 9 mutants, all 9 caught

For each branch: the lifted value never written, the copy seeded EMPTY (losing untouched
entries), the ORIGINAL container mutated instead of copied, and nothing ever lifted. Plus the
record returning a copy when empty-handed, which loses the identity the optimization IS — that
one needs a `toBe` assertion, since a copy compares equal and says nothing.

The record tests carry the canonical-order invariant that bypassing `from`'s sort depends on: a
record built from `z, a, m` keeps `a, m, z` through a rebuild, including when the key that moves
is the LAST one (the copy already exists by then). Order is not cosmetic here — the codecs emit a
sorted object and the wire is byte-identical across engines.

Gates separately: 11 further tests (23 in the file), full suite exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0,
`fmt` then `fmt:check` 0, all seven fuzzers green on random seeds. No Rust changed.

## 149. The filtered node count ignored the property index — a regression item 135 introduced

`bun run bench:usage` has been printing this defect in plain sight, as a row whose two columns
are the same number:

```
read: keyed dedup lookup     ts(-) 731    ts(+) 727    engine(+) 111.7k
```

727 ops/s with an index on the key the query filters by, against 731 without one — while the
native engine more than doubles on the same index. Two identical columns is a stronger signal
than a slow one: a slow number can be an honest cost, but an index that changes nothing means
nothing is reading it. This is the repo's named bug class (equivalent spellings must cost the
same, historically 100-300x), in the form where the two "spellings" are the same query against
graphs that differ only in an index.

The query is

```
MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.score = $s AND u.active = true RETURN count(*) AS c
```

### It was mine, and the count shortcut was SLOWER than the path it replaced

Item 135 gave `buildNodeCount` a tally: when the start node carries constraints, walk the label
bucket and apply them through `inlineHolds`. That beat enumerating rows — but the general path
it bypassed **seeds from an index**, and the tally did not. Isolated, 20,000 users with `score`
indexed and 200 matches:

| shape                           | no index | indexed | ratio |
| ------------------------------- | -------: | ------: | ----: |
| `count(*)`                      |  0.93 ms | 0.91 ms |  1.0x |
| `count(*)` + a `LET` (declines) |  5.66 ms | 0.42 ms | 13.6x |
| `RETURN u.name` (no shortcut)   |  2.70 ms | 0.15 ms | 17.6x |

The middle row is the diagnosis in one line: adding a `LET` makes the shortcut DECLINE, and the
query gets 13.6x faster on an indexed graph. **A fast path that loses an index is a pessimization
whenever the index exists**, and it hid behind its own win on the unindexed graph, which is what
the probes and tests used.

### The fix: let the tally seek

`buildNodeCount` now takes the compiled start node and enumerates seed candidates with
`indexCandidates` — the general path's own enumerator, so the two agree on what is seekable and
the counts are O(1) estimates, making the choice free. It picks the smallest candidate and uses
it only when that candidate is narrower than the label bucket.

Two things the bucket scan got for free have to be paid for explicitly, and both are what the
tests target:

- **A seek returns vertices by VALUE, across every label.** The bucket path inherited the label
  from its seed; the seeded path has to apply `matchesLabel` per candidate. The check is guarded
  on `seeded !== undefined` rather than run unconditionally, so the common unindexed path is not
  taxed for it.
- **A seed hint is a NECESSARY condition lifted out of an AND-chain, so the seek is a SUPERSET.**
  Every candidate still goes through `inlineHolds`. This is the same soundness argument the
  general path rests on, not a new one.

`seedVertices` does the same choosing and was deliberately not used: it hides WHETHER it seeded,
and that is exactly the bit the label check needs.

### Measured, interleaved, min-of-three

Indexed column, isolated harness, `stash → build → probe → pop → build → probe`:

| shape                               | after₁ | before | after₂ |     ratio |
| ----------------------------------- | -----: | -----: | -----: | --------: |
| `score = $s`                        |   0.11 |   1.00 |   0.09 | **10.0x** |
| `score = $s AND active = true`      |   0.12 |   1.08 |   0.10 |  **9.8x** |
| `active = true AND score = $s`      |   0.10 |   1.07 |   0.08 | **10.5x** |
| `score = $s AND name = $n`          |   0.05 |   1.72 |   0.04 | **38.2x** |
| inline `{score: $s}` + `WHERE`      |      — |      — |      — | **16.3x** |
| inline `{score: $s, active: true}`  |      — |      — |      — | **13.2x** |
| `active = true`, no index (CONTROL) |   0.92 |   0.74 |   0.92 | see below |

The lift is **order-independent** — the swapped conjunction gets the same 10x — which is the
property the bug class is about. The two-seekable-conjunct row is the biggest because choosing
the smaller candidate (`name`, 1 row) beats taking the first one offered.

And the headline row moves: `read: keyed dedup lookup` ts(+) **727 → 20.5-20.9k ops/s across
three runs, 28x at the min**, against engine(+) 112.7k.

### The unseekable control: flat-to-20%-slower, and the cause is NOT the enumeration

A query whose key has no index now runs the candidate enumerator and finds nothing. Matched
runs put BEFORE at 0.675-0.901 ms and AFTER at 0.693-0.943 ms — **overlapping ranges**, so this
harness cannot separate the cost from its own noise, and the honest statement is flat to about
20% slower on a path that the seekable side pays back 10-38x. `bench:usage`'s own unindexed
column agrees: 731 → 705 / 676 / 709, within its own spread.

**REJECTED lever, recorded in the code**: guarding the enumeration behind a "does this graph
have ANY index?" check, so an unindexed graph skips it entirely. It needed a new `PropertyIndex`
accessor (`isIndexed` wants a key, `indexedKeys()` allocates) and bought NOTHING — 0.930 /
0.928 / 0.934 with it against 0.868 / 0.872 / 0.943 without. So whatever this path gives up is
closure layout, not the enumeration; this file has measured that twice before (items 119 and
141). The accessor was reverted rather than shipped for a reason that turned out to be wrong.

### Teeth: 13 tests, 2 of 3 mutants caught, the third survives by design

Every test asserts the indexed answer EQUALS the unindexed one, because that is the entire
contract: an index may change the cost and must never change the count.

| mutant                                     | result                 |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| drop the per-candidate `matchesLabel`      | caught — 10 of 13 fail |
| skip `preds` re-validation when seeded     | caught — 3 of 13 fail  |
| drop the "seek narrower than bucket" guard | **survives**           |

The third survives correctly and is not a gap: a wider seek is still a superset and `preds`
still re-validate it, so only the cost differs. It is a cost lever with no answer to assert,
and a timing threshold here would be flaky in CI.

The fixture is built to give the first mutant somewhere to fail: a second label (`Admin`)
carries the SAME indexed values, so a missing label check counts 12 where the answer is 6. The
second mutant needs the seek to be a strict superset, so `score = 7` selects 6 users of whom 2
are active. Also covered: conjunct order, both inline spellings, `$param`, `IN`, a range
predicate, an unindexed key, an UNLABELLED count (where the whole seek legitimately counts),
a value matching nothing, a key some vertices lack, and an index created BETWEEN two runs of
one query — the seek is chosen per execution, not at compile time.

Gates separately: 13 new tests, full suite exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check`
exit 0, all seven fuzzers green on random seeds. No Rust changed.

## 150. An uncorrelated MATCH filled its tail cache before yielding anything — 473x, and a live divergence

Two recorded targets for this pass were "`SKIP + LIMIT` 658x" and "`ORDER BY + LIMIT` 135x,
paging needs pushing into the walk". Reading the code first retired both: unordered `SKIP`/
`LIMIT` is already lazy (`take` short-circuits the projecting map) and `ORDER BY … LIMIT` already
has a bounded top-k that projects only the k rows it keeps. Re-deriving the numbers found
something else.

### The number that did not fit

| shape                |       ts |  native |        |
| -------------------- | -------: | ------: | -----: |
| full scan, 50k rows  | 18.53 ms | 6.16 ms |   3.0x |
| `LIMIT 10`, 10 rows  |  1.00 ms | 0.01 ms | 171.2x |
| `SKIP 1000 LIMIT 10` |  1.31 ms | 0.01 ms | 174.4x |

One millisecond to return TEN rows from a graph whose every row costs 18.53 ms. That is not
per-row work, and three checks placed it before anything was changed:

- **It is not the front end.** `prepare()` once and time only execution: parse+compile is
  0.012-0.18 ms, and `RETURN 1 AS one` executes in 0.0003 ms. The floor is inside the MATCH.
- **It is not the harness.** Amortized over 2000 calls in one timer, `LIMIT 1` is 0.598 ms
  against the per-call min of 0.535 — same number, so the per-call timer was not inflating an
  absolute floor the way a multi-query probe inflates spreads (items 141/143/145).
- **It is not O(N).** Sweeping 12,500 → 200,000 nodes leaves `LIMIT 1` flat at 0.4-0.9 ms while
  the full-scan control goes 3.18 → 77.7 ms. A cost that is flat in N but large is capped at
  something, which named the suspect: `TAIL_CACHE_CAP = 4096`.

### The defect

`hoistedMatch` caches an uncorrelated MATCH's tail so it is not rescanned per outer row (item
121). For the LEADING match of a query the incoming stream is ONE empty binding — so the cache
is built for a row that has no successor to reuse it, and `cacheTail` **collected up to 4096
bindings before the first one was yielded**. Over a bucket larger than the cap it then
overflowed, discarded all 4096, and re-matched from scratch.

So every `MATCH … LIMIT n` did a full `min(bucket, 4096)` match pass to produce its first row.

Confirmed with no code change at all, using the engine's own routing: `runMatch` sends
`clause.optional || clause.reads.size > 0` to a fully lazy `flatMap` and everything else to
`hoistedMatch`. The same query as plain `MATCH` and as `OPTIONAL MATCH` therefore runs the same
matcher over the same bucket and differs ONLY in whether the cache is built:

| amortized, ms      | N=1000 |   N=4096 |  N=20000 |
| ------------------ | -----: | -------: | -------: |
| `MATCH LIMIT 1`    | 0.1285 |   0.5327 |   0.5208 |
| `OPTIONAL LIMIT 1` | 0.0013 |   0.0009 |   0.0010 |
| ratio              |    99x | **592x** | **521x** |
| `MATCH` full       | 0.3002 |   1.5080 |   5.2667 |
| `OPTIONAL` full    | 0.2059 |   0.8682 |   4.7734 |

Three independent signatures in one table: the gap exists only under a LIMIT, it grows with N
up to the cap and then flattens, and the unlimited rows converge — so the cost is the EAGERNESS,
not the cache's bookkeeping.

### It was also a live cross-engine divergence

Eagerly filling the cache evaluates the clause on candidates a LIMIT never needs, and "which
queries raise" is part of byte-identity:

```
MATCH (u:User) WHERE CAST(u.st AS INTEGER) >= 1 RETURN u.name LIMIT 1
  ts:     RAISE E_INVALID_VALUE      <-- evaluated the cast on candidate 2
  native: 1 row                      <-- streams, stops at candidate 1
```

Fixed by the same change, and the `LIMIT 2` spelling still raises in BOTH — the item-145
direction, that a fix must not start skipping an evaluation the general path does make.

(The division spelling of this, `WHERE 1 / (u.st - 1) > 0 … LIMIT 1`, raises in both engines and
proves nothing: `u.st` is a string there, so the fault is on candidate ONE, which both engines
must evaluate. That is the item-144 mistake, avoided here only because the cast spelling was run
beside it.)

### The fix

`recordTail` replaces `cacheTail`: it yields the tail WHILE recording it, returning whether the
tail completed or overflowed the cap. The cache is now a free by-product of the first pass
instead of a pass of its own, and the first row comes out after one match. A consumer that stops
early abandons the generator mid-tail, so neither answer is reached and nothing is cached —
which is correct, because an abandoned tail is an incomplete one.

Applied at BOTH sites, because the same pattern was in both: `hoistedMatch`, and item 121's
multi-pattern tail in `visitRemaining` (there the first outer row streams and records, later
rows read the cache, and an overflow falls back to re-matching per row without revisiting the
first row's output).

**A regression caught on the way, and what it cost to fix.** The first version was 1.93x SLOWER
on a 20,000-row full scan (5.27 → 10.17 ms) with the `OPTIONAL MATCH` control flat. Cause: it
merged `new Map([...binding, ...row])` per row, where the old overflow path yielded the
matcher's bindings directly with no copy. For a leading MATCH the incoming binding is EMPTY, so
there is nothing to merge — the row now passes straight through, which is the same aliasing the
previous overflow path had. Later outer rows still read the cache through a copy.

### Measured, interleaved, amortized over 1000 calls, min-of-5

| shape                | before |  after |    ratio |
| -------------------- | -----: | -----: | -------: |
| `LIMIT 1`, N=20000   | 0.5208 | 0.0011 | **473x** |
| `LIMIT 1`, N=4096    | 0.5327 | 0.0007 | **761x** |
| `LIMIT 1`, N=1000    | 0.1285 | 0.0013 |  **99x** |
| `LIMIT 10`, N=20000  | 0.5221 | 0.0036 | **145x** |
| full scan, N=20000   | 5.2667 | 5.2250 |     flat |
| full scan, N=4096    | 1.5080 | 1.0434 |    1.45x |
| full scan, N=1000    | 0.3002 | 0.2122 |    1.41x |
| `OPTIONAL` (CONTROL) | 4.7734 | 4.8192 |     flat |

`MATCH` now tracks the `OPTIONAL MATCH` control at every size, which is the target — the two
should never have differed. The full scan at and below the cap gets 1.4x as a side effect: the
cache no longer makes a second pass of Map copies over rows it just produced.

### Retracted: the overflow retry is real in the code and immaterial in practice

On overflow `cacheTail` returned `undefined`, which left `cached` undefined — so the NEXT outer
row called it again, pulled another capful, and discarded it again. The comment on the cap
claims the waste is "bounded by the cap — once, not per outer row"; nothing recorded that it had
overflowed, so the claim was false.

**Measured, and it does not matter.** Reaching outer row 2 at all requires consuming every row
of an uncorrelated tail bigger than 4096, i.e. a product already large enough to be output-bound
— which is exactly what the rest of that comment argues. A probe sweeping 1/4/16/64 outer rows
showed no growth (1.79/0.92/1.59/0.74 ms) because the `LIMIT` is filled inside the FIRST outer
row and the others are never pulled. An `overflowed` flag is in anyway, since it is one boolean
and makes the comment true.

### An unrelated NATIVE finding, recorded not acted on

The same probe put native 13-30x BEHIND TS on a limited uncorrelated product:

```
MATCH (s:Tiny) MATCH (u:User) RETURN s.k LIMIT 1    ts 1.79 ms   native 23.33 ms
MATCH (s:Tiny) MATCH (u:User) RETURN s.k LIMIT 64   ts 0.74 ms   native 22.27 ms
```

Native appears to materialize the full cross product before applying the limit. Not pursued in
this item (this pass is the TS engine) and not yet diagnosed — it may be the
eager-materialize-before-a-blocking-op already open from the perf-fuzzer.

### Teeth: 12 tests, 4 of 6 mutants caught, 2 survive by design

| mutant                                            | result                    |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| never record — the cache stays empty              | caught: 4 here, 16 in gql |
| claim the tail completed even when it overflowed  | caught: the grouped test  |
| take the zero-copy path always (drop the binding) | caught: 2 here, 6 in gql  |
| multi-pattern: reuse the cache for the first row  | caught: 1 here, 1 in gql  |
| cap comparison off by one (`>= cap - 1`)          | **survives**              |
| never take the zero-copy path (copy every row)    | **survives**              |

Both survivors are answer-neutral cost levers and are recorded as such in the test file rather
than chased: treating an exactly-cap tail as overflow still returns the right rows (it
re-matches instead of reusing), and copying a row that need not be copied is always correct.
Neither has an answer to assert and a timing threshold would be flaky in CI.

**A test that looked like coverage and was not.** `count(*)` over independent patterns never
reaches this code — item 135's product-of-counts shortcut answers it from the two bucket sizes
without matching anything. The truncate-the-cache mutant left every `count(*)` assertion here
green and failed only the grouped one. The file now says so, so nobody reads those counts as
coverage.

The differential fuzzer gets the divergence as two TARGETED queries, because the random draw
cannot reach the arrangement: the fault has to land after the candidate that fills the limit,
and on that six-vertex fixture `st` lives on vertices 1 and 3 with vertex 1 FIRST in the bucket
— so every cast predicate faults on candidate one and reads as agreement. `1 / (n.n - 7)` puts
the zero on vertex 2 instead, and vertex 1 (n = 3) fills `LIMIT 1` first. Teeth verified by
reverting the fix and rebuilding: pre-fix TS raised there while native returned a row.

## 151. A keyless page over a cross product built the whole product first — 3680x (native)

Item 150 turned this up while measuring the TS engine and recorded it without acting: on a
LIMITed uncorrelated product, native was 13-30x BEHIND pure TS.

```
MATCH (s:Tiny) MATCH (u:User) RETURN s.k LIMIT 1    ts 1.79ms   native 23.33ms
```

### Diagnosis: three axes, each ruling something out

| shape                         |    before |
| ----------------------------- | --------: |
| 1 pattern, `LIMIT 1`          |  0.005 ms |
| 1 pattern, full (50,000 rows) |  6.690 ms |
| product, `LIMIT 1`            | 22.078 ms |
| product, `LIMIT 64`           | 21.973 ms |
| product, `LIMIT 5000`         | 22.172 ms |
| product `count(*)`            |  0.004 ms |

- **Early exit exists** — a single pattern answers `LIMIT 1` in 0.005 ms against a 6.690 ms full
  scan, so the limit IS pushed down somewhere. The Join is what lacks it.
- **The product's cost is FLAT IN THE LIMIT** (22.078 / 21.973 / 22.172 for 1 / 64 / 5000 rows),
  so the work is the product, not the rows emitted.
- **It tracks the product, not the output**: 3.2M → 22.1 ms, 640k → 2.7 ms. And `count(*)` over
  the same product is 0.004 ms, so the engine already knows both bucket sizes.

Pattern order and the comma spelling cost the same (21.0 / 21.5 ms), so there is no spelling bug
here — both spellings optimize to the same plan, as they should.

### Why it had no path

Native's executor is batch-at-a-time: `Plan::Join` pulls both sides whole and hash-joins them,
so there is nothing to "stream". The keyless-page path does have a cap — `pull_capped` for
row-preserving chains, then `pull_capped_stream` block-by-block — but `pull_capped` rejects
every row-MULTIPLYING operator, and `pull_capped_stream` needs `streaming_chain` to find ONE
scan root, which a join does not have. So the page built the product and sliced it.

### The fix: cap both sides of a cross product

`pull_capped` gains a `Plan::Join { on: [] }` arm that caps each side at `cap` and joins the two
capped sides. **Exact, not approximate.** `hash_join` emits LEFT-MAJOR (`i` over left rows
outer, `j` over the right's matches inner, both ascending), so output row `k` pairs left row
`k / R` with right row `k % R` for a right side of `R` rows. Both indices are below `cap` for
every `k < cap`, so neither cap can drop a row the window needs:

- `R <= cap` — the right cap does not bind, the right side is whole, the enumeration is the full
  one, and reaching output row `cap` needs only left row `cap / R`.
- `R > cap` — the right cap keeps `cap` rows, so left row 0 alone supplies `cap` output rows,
  and those are the product's first `cap`, because there every one of them pairs with left row 0
  too.

This does not lean on keyless page order being unspecified; it would hold even if that order
were part of the contract. The product of two capped sides can reach `cap * cap` rows, so it is
truncated to keep `pull_capped`'s "at most `cap` rows" promise — both current callers slice
anyway, but the next one might not.

**It went in the wrong place first.** The arm was added to the keyless-page dispatch in `pull`,
where the match is on `input.as_ref()` — and measured EXACTLY NOTHING, because the optimized
plan is `OrderPage → Project → Join`, so the input is a `Project`. Verified by dumping the plan
rather than guessing which guard declined. Moving it into `pull_capped` means the existing
`Project` arm recurses into it for free.

### Measured, min-of-seven, three fixture sizes

| shape (50,000 x 64 product)   | before | after |     ratio |
| ----------------------------- | -----: | ----: | --------: |
| product, `LIMIT 1`            | 22.078 | 0.006 | **3680x** |
| product, `LIMIT 64`           | 21.973 | 0.046 |  **478x** |
| product, `LIMIT 5000`         | 22.172 | 1.535 | **14.4x** |
| product reversed, `LIMIT 1`   | 21.011 | 0.004 | **5253x** |
| comma spelling, `LIMIT 1`     | 21.456 | 0.004 | **5364x** |
| 1 pattern `LIMIT 1` (CONTROL) |  0.005 | 0.005 |      flat |
| 1 pattern full (CONTROL)      |  6.690 | 6.554 |      flat |
| product `count(*)` (CONTROL)  |  0.004 | 0.004 |      flat |

The cost now SCALES with the limit (0.006 → 0.046 → 1.535) instead of being flat in it, which is
the shape the fix is supposed to produce. Native goes from 13-30x behind TS to ~300x ahead.

### Rows verified identical, not just counted

A row count cannot check this — a wrong pairing returns the right number. 33 windows across
three fixtures (`R < cap`, `R > cap`, and `R` straddling it, since the proof has two regimes
that take different branches) compared three ways: native paged vs native unpaged-then-sliced-in-JS
(what the engine did before), and native vs TS. All identical. SKIP windows included, because
the cap is `skip + limit` and a cap one too small drops the window's LAST row while every
LIMIT-only check still passes.

### Teeth: 6 tests, 4 of 6 mutants caught — and mutation found two TEST bugs

| mutant                               | result                        |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| left side pulled one row short       | caught — 4 failures           |
| right side pulled one row short      | caught — 4 failures           |
| join sides swapped                   | caught — 3 failures           |
| lineage dropped in the prefix gather | caught, after TWO test fixes  |
| never truncate the product           | **survives** — answer-neutral |
| `on.is_empty()` guard dropped        | **survives** — equivalent     |

The two survivors are honest:

- **Never truncating** is answer-neutral because both callers slice; it is contract hygiene, and
  the comment says so.
- **Dropping the `on.is_empty()` guard** leaves the whole suite green, and the reason is
  reachability, not a missing test: the cap also needs BOTH sides cap-safe, and the shared
  variable that makes `on` non-empty can only come from an EXPANSION — so a keyed join always
  has a Filter/Expand side and `pull_capped` declines there first. Confirmed by dumping the
  keyed-join plan. The guard stays as a stated precondition of the proof rather than a reachable
  branch, and the test says that instead of implying coverage it does not have.

**The lineage test was wrong twice, and only mutation showed it.** First it used
`MATCH p = (x:N)-[:E]->(y:N), (m:M)` — but an expansion is not cap-safe, so that query takes the
general path and exercised none of this. Rewritten with an edge-free single-node path
(`p = (x:N)`, a Join over two Scans) it STILL passed the mutant, because at `LIMIT 1` both sides
cap to one row, the product is exactly one row, `joined.rows() > cap` is false, and the
truncating branch — the only place the lineage is re-gathered — never runs. `LIMIT 3` on a 4x4
fixture makes a 9-row product that must be cut to 3, and then the mutant dies.

### A gate that was failing for the wrong reason

`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` exited 101 and `cargo fmt --check` exited 1 — not
findings: there is no `Cargo.toml` at the repo root, so neither command found a manifest. The

`packages/node`, and each needs its own `--manifest-path`. Worth knowing, because a non-zero exit
from a gate that never ran reads exactly like a gate that failed.

Gates separately: 6 new tests (921 engine tests pass), engine-core's 34 pass, clippy
`-D warnings` exit 0 per crate, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0 per crate, `rewrite_fuzz` green
including a 200,000-seed sweep, `fastpath_fuzz` green, the TS suite exit 0, all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green on random seeds. Mutation ran under `timeout 600` plus
`MemoryMax=16G MemorySwapMax=0`, with the cap proven to kill first (137 for an allocator bomb,

### The bench_all screen, and a 1.33x that was not real

328 numeric cells compared column-wise (the tables are multi-column, so matching a label to
"the last number on the line" pairs different columns with each other — the first attempt at
this comparison did exactly that and produced a meaningless 24-row diff). Six cells moved more
than 15%:

```
 1.33x  [query/shortest]  repeat-group head(b)     104072 -> 138646
 1.28x  [query/plan]      group + order + limit      1.85 ->    2.36
 1.18x  [query/shortest]  repeat-group control      69159 ->   81270
 1.17x  [algo/parallel]   pagerank                  16.93 ->   19.86
 1.17x  [algo/parallel]   pagerank                  24.67 ->   28.85

```

**Two of the six are in `query/plan (text -> plan, no exec)`** — PLANNING time, which a change
to an exec-side function cannot touch at all, one up 1.28x and one down 0.83x. They calibrate
this screen's noise at about ±28% on those rows, and nothing else exceeded it by much.

**The 1.33x is an artifact of `bench_all` itself.** Re-measured in an isolated harness
(`query_bench -- shortest`), min-of-three on each side:

| case                 | before (min of 3)     | after (min of 3)      |  ratio |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------- | -----: |
| repeat-group head(b) | 93305 / 95813 / 97439 | 95979 / 97608 / 91913 | 0.985x |
| repeat-group control | 73380 / 75515 / 75033 | 75838 / 78651 / 69859 | 0.952x |

Flat, marginally faster. Note that `bench_all` reported the AFTER figure for head(b) as 138646
while the isolated after-min is 91913 — the same case, 1.5x apart, because `bench_all` runs
every group in one process and the earlier groups leave the allocator and caches in a different
state. **`bench_all` is a screen, not a measurement**; this is the fourth time in this audit
that a multi-case probe has manufactured a spread an isolated harness then retracted (items

No row that the change functionally reaches moved, and the rows it cannot reach moved as much
