## 197. The two biggest rows are already optimal, and the floor has a price — 3.2x, for a decision

No code change. Ten items of wins have moved the grouping and dedup family from 9-62x behind native
to 3.5-13x, so the field was re-ranked rather than worked down from a stale list:

| row                             |   ts | ffi |           |
| ------------------------------- | ---: | --: | --------- |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter`       | 49.1 | 1.5 | **33.1x** |
| `traverse 1-hop + start filter` | 41.7 | 2.4 | **17.1x** |
| `query: count distinct`         |  5.4 | 0.4 | 13.1x     |
| `query: top distinct values`    |  5.3 | 0.4 | 12.8x     |
| `query: distinct over a hop`    | 92.3 | 7.3 | 12.6x     |
| `query: group, no aggregate`    |  5.1 | 1.0 | 4.9x      |
| `query: group + aggregate`      |  3.9 | 1.1 | 3.6x      |

### Three refutations, in order

**One.** `farWalkFits` requires the START side unconstrained and `pa` is the start LABEL, so a
far-filtered hop count looked like it must decline the per-vertex walk whenever the start carries a
label — the same vacuous-label insight item 195 used. Measured: labelled 45.38ms against unlabelled
45.05ms. No difference.

**Two.** The reason is that the clause-`WHERE` branch ALREADY normalizes a vacuous label away
(`vacuousLabel(graph, aLabel) ? undefined : aLabel`), exactly as the inline branch does. I had
expected the drift between those two branches that this file's own comments keep warning about;
it is not there.

**Three.** So is the walk firing at all? A predicate's SELECTIVITY answers it, because the walk
tests the predicate per vertex and only then reads that vertex's in-degree:

|                                        |    min ms |                                               |
| -------------------------------------- | --------: | --------------------------------------------- |
| far filter, NOTHING matches            |  **3.99** | 200,000 predicate calls, zero adjacency reads |
| far filter, half match (the bench row) |     49.05 |                                               |
| far filter, EVERYTHING matches         | **92.60** | 200,000 of each                               |

Cost scales with SURVIVORS, which is the per-vertex walk's signature and not a per-edge tally's.
**Both of the two biggest rows are already on the best plan this engine has.** The 33x that remains
is not a missing path.

### What the floor actually is, and it is not what was recorded

The three biggest remaining rows all bottom out on one operation: `edgesToByLabel.get(v.id)?.get(type)`.
Priced on the graph's real maps, 200,000 vertices:

|                                            | ns/vertex |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------: |
| iterate the vertex bucket                  |         2 |
| + read one property                        |         9 |
| + the OUTER adjacency lookup alone (by id) |    **14** |
| + outer THEN inner (by type) — today       |   **183** |
| one lookup against a TYPE-FIRST index      |    **58** |

`drive-the-vertex-side` records this cost as "a ~180ns random-order cache miss" on the id-keyed
lookup. **That attribution is wrong.** The id-keyed lookup is 14ns; the ~169ns is the INNER,
one-entry, type-keyed map. The reason is structural rather than about hashing: today's shape holds
**200,000 distinct inner Map objects, each touched once** — cold and polymorphic — where a
type-first shape holds **ONE**, touched 200,000 times.

Both shapes were made to sum the same 1,000,000 in-degrees before either was timed, since a faster
index that answers differently is not faster.

One honest caveat on the 14ns: the probe walks the vertex bucket in insertion order, which is
correlated with how the adjacency map was populated, so the OUTER lookups are unusually
cache-friendly there. Item 194's ~180ns for `edge.to` is a per-EDGE lookup in scattered order and
is not contradicted. The 183 → 58 comparison is apples to apples — same iteration order, same
Sets — and that is the number the decision needs.

### The decision, now priced

Inverting the adjacency to `Map<type, Map<vertexId, Set<Edge>>>` is **3.2x on the operation that
floors the three biggest remaining rows**, and it is not a memory trade: it is the same `Set`
objects reorganized, with **one inner map per TYPE instead of one per VERTEX** — 1 object here
against 200,000. The insert path should get cheaper too, since `indexEdgeLabel` would allocate a
`Set` per new vertex id instead of a `Map` and a `Set`, and that function is 23% of an edge-heavy
decode.

What it costs: `incidentEdges(id)` — vertex removal's reader — today reads one map to see all of a
vertex's types, and would instead probe T type-maps. Its own comment already says removal is "far
colder than the edge-insert path", but it is a real cost and it grows with the number of edge
types. Every reader of `edgesFromByLabel`/`edgesToByLabel` changes shape.

That is a core storage change with a write-path and a removal-path effect, so it is **left for a
decision rather than taken** — which is what it has been since item 180, except that it now has a
number instead of an estimate. Nothing else in the TS query surface is above 5x once this is
accounted for.

## 198. Un-ordered row order is unspecified — 3.13x, by decision rather than by measurement

Item 195 gated the far-driven dedup walk on a sort, because the two walks meet elements in
different orders and an un-ordered query's row order was being treated as a contract. Item 195 also
recorded the resulting asymmetry and declined to resolve it: adding `ORDER BY` made the query 3.2x
FASTER, so an un-ordered far dedup sat at ~290ms for want of nothing but permission.

Two things in this repo disagreed and only one could stand. `order-is-unspecified` says row order
without an `ORDER BY` is unspecified, as in SQL. `distinct-projection.test.ts` pinned that order
deliberately, and item 142 gave back a 7.4x for getting it wrong. **The user's decision is that the
order is unspecified**, so the sort requirement is gone.

### What changed, and what deliberately did not

`farDrivenFits` no longer takes `sorted`. One condition remains — the start side must be
unconstrained, which is a correctness rule and not an ordering one.

NOT touched, because the decision was about an un-ordered dedup's ROW order and nothing wider:

- **a sorted query's order**, which the sort determines (0.98x here, unchanged);
- **the grouped count's FIRST-SEEN group order**, which the code calls a pinned contract both
  engines keep and which items 186-190 tested as such;
- **the lazy `LIMIT` path**: an un-ordered window still declines the walk entirely, because the
  general path stops after the first few distinct values. Measured 0.1ms either way — the 280x
  that item 191 recorded is intact.

### Measured

In-process A/B of both builds, thirteen rounds, order swapped each round. Answers compared as
MULTISETS for the un-ordered shapes and IN ORDER for the sorted ones — an order-sensitive
comparison on the un-ordered shapes would assert exactly the thing just declared not to hold:

| shape                                  | before |    after |                     |
| -------------------------------------- | -----: | -------: | ------------------- |
| far dedup, NO sort                     |  294.5 | **94.2** | **3.13x**, disjoint |
| far dedup, no sort, `GROUP BY` form    |  294.7 | **94.4** | **3.12x**, disjoint |
| CONTROL far dedup + sort (item 195)    |   92.3 |     93.8 | 0.98x               |
| CONTROL no sort + `LIMIT` (stays lazy) |    0.1 |      0.1 | 1.03x               |
| CONTROL start label not vacuous        |   22.0 |     24.6 | 0.89x               |
| CONTROL keyed on the START             |  101.9 |    102.6 | 0.99x               |
| CONTROL node dedup                     |    8.2 |      8.4 | 0.97x               |
| CONTROL `count(DISTINCT)` over a hop   |   87.0 |     87.3 | 1.00x               |

The bench has no un-ordered far-dedup row — the row item 195 added carries an `ORDER BY` — so the
win is not visible there, and the screen is purely a regression check. It separates ONE of
twenty-three ts columns: `encode ndjson` −47.2%, which runs no GQL at all and whose 49 readings
this session span **33.4 to 84.7ms**. 50.8 is its median and 34.5 is near its minimum, so the
before side drew the low mode of a bimodal row.

### Three tests changed, and one of them was passing for the wrong reason

- `distinct-projection.test.ts`'s "a reversed hop and an untyped hop agree" compared row order
  against the general path. It now compares VALUES as a multiset and says why, and a **new sibling
  test asserts the SORTED spelling in order** — so order is still tested wherever it is specified.
  The reversed hop is the spelling whose order actually moved.
- `dedup-hop-far-driven.test.ts`'s "no sort" test asserted both the row order AND that the far walk
  was declined. Both halves are now wrong. Worth recording: **it still passed after the change**,
  because that fixture's far vertices happen to be met in the same relative order by either walk —
  so pinning the order there was proving nothing even before this. Rewritten as a multiset claim
  plus an in-order assertion for the sorted spelling.
- The file header's rationale for the sort condition is replaced by the decision record rather than
  deleted, so the next reader sees why it was there and why it went.

### Teeth: 5 of 7, both survivors perf-only

| mutant                                                   | result                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| the start label need not be vacuous                      | caught                               |
| a START-keyed dedup takes the far walk too               | caught                               |
| the far index is not mirrored                            | caught                               |
| an empty or absent bucket is accepted                    | caught                               |
| the walk iterates EVERY vertex, not the far-label bucket | caught                               |
| revert: never take the far-driven walk                   | survived — perf-only                 |
| **revert item 198: require a sort again**                | **survived — perf-only BY DECISION** |

That last one is the whole character of this item: before today it would have been a wrong-answer
mutant and a test would have killed it. It is perf-only now because the contract changed, not
because the code did. Recording it that way is the point — a future sweep sees a survivor with a
reason rather than a gap.

The dispatch anchor also went non-unique once both call sites lost their `sorted` argument, and
printed `NOT APPLIED (anchor appears 2x)` rather than passing silently. Fourth tick running that
the applied-check has earned itself.

Gates separately: full TS suite exit 0 (1257 in the gql package), `bun run check` exit 0,
`bun run spelling` fully clean, **all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across SIX sweeps** on
random seeds — three before the final build and three after, since a row-order change is exactly
what a byte-identity fuzzer exists to catch and they canonicalize row order for unordered queries
by design. Every mutation run under `timeout 600` plus a 16G cgroup cap with swap off.

## 199. ISO's own spelling of a grouped count never reached the tally — 11.7-19.0x, and `HAVING` was the wrong diagnosis

This item was picked off the open list as "`HAVING` on the tally (~14x)", which items 196 and 198
both carried forward. The `HAVING` work is real and shipped. **It is not where the 14x was**, and
the way that came out is the part worth keeping.

### The fix that was built first, and measured at nothing

`HAVING` is a post-filter on groups, and the tally already has one row per group — so it belongs
there, not in the general pipeline. `keepGroups` drops the slots the predicate does not keep,
before any sort or window, which is the order the general path applies them in. One condition:
every aggregate in the predicate must be `count(*)`. That is all the tally has — a count and a
representative row — where a `sum(n.k)` needs the group's MEMBERS, which this path never
materializes. `countOnlyAggregates` is a structural walk over every child rather than a check of
the arms I thought of, the same reason `hasSubquery` in the executor is written that way.

Then the rebuild measured **no improvement at all**. The probe that explains why:

|                                      |    min ms | rows |
| ------------------------------------ | --------: | ---: |
| `RETURN` form, no having (the tally) |      3.96 |   90 |
| `RETURN` form, two-clause            |      3.84 |   90 |
| **`SELECT` form, NO having**         | **52.36** |   90 |
| `SELECT` form, with having           |     54.48 |   90 |

**The SELECT form was 13x slower with no `HAVING` in it.** `HAVING` was never what declined the
tally; the SELECT SPELLING was, and a `HAVING` can only appear in a SELECT statement, so every
measurement of "the `HAVING` gap" had been measuring the spelling gap and attributing it to the
clause. Had the two been separable the earlier number would have been wrong by the whole amount.

### The real gap: `GROUP BY` was accepted only in the `LET` form

`groupedProjection` required the grouping element to NAME the `LET`-bound variable. ISO's SELECT
statement writes the PROPERTY and has no `LET` to name:

```
MATCH (n:Person) LET a = n.age RETURN a, count(*) AS c GROUP BY a            4.1ms
SELECT n.age AS a, count(*) AS c FROM MATCH (n:Person) GROUP BY n.age       69.5ms
```

One question, two spellings ISO both sanctions, 17x apart — the repo's named bug class, and the
same rule item 188 had already fixed for the DISTINCT path one file over. `sameGroupingExpr` was
even exported from this file for that item. The grouping element must now either name the `LET` or
BE the key item's expression.

Worth naming: **the tally's `GROUP BY` branch sat three lines from the fix for eleven items.** What
hid it is that every bench row, every probe and every test of the grouped count was written in the
`LET` form, because `GROUP BY` takes a bound name and the `LET` form is the one you reach for when
you are thinking about the tally. Nothing in the corpus asked the question the standard's way.

### Measured

In-process A/B of both built bundles, thirteen rounds, order swapped each round, 200,000 vertices
at five edges each. Answers asserted equal before any timing — as multisets for the unordered
shapes, in order for the sorted ones:

| shape                                                        | before |     after |            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | -----: | --------: | ---------- |
| `SELECT` form, `GROUP BY` the property                       |   69.5 |   **3.6** | **19.04x** |
| `SELECT` form + `HAVING` on the count                        |   69.2 |   **5.0** | **13.75x** |
| `SELECT` form + `HAVING` on the key                          |   68.7 |   **4.9** | **14.01x** |
| `SELECT` form + `HAVING` on both                             |   68.7 |   **4.9** | **13.93x** |
| `SELECT` form + `HAVING` + `ORDER BY`                        |   69.7 |   **5.1** | **13.62x** |
| `SELECT` form + `HAVING` nothing satisfies                   |   68.6 |   **4.9** | **14.07x** |
| `SELECT` form + `HAVING` + `ORDER BY` + `LIMIT`              |   70.1 |   **5.1** | **13.76x** |
| hop tally, `SELECT` form + `HAVING`                          |  800.9 | **260.9** | **3.07x**  |
| CONTROL `RETURN` form, no `HAVING`                           |    4.1 |       4.2 | 0.97x      |
| CONTROL `HAVING` with a NON-count aggregate (still declines) |  100.4 |      91.7 | 1.09x      |
| CONTROL `GROUP BY` a NON-key expression (still declines)     |   98.9 |     102.2 | 0.97x      |
| CONTROL the two-clause `RETURN` spelling                     |    4.0 |       4.0 | 1.00x      |
| CONTROL plain `count(*)`                                     |    0.1 |       0.1 | 1.00x      |
| CONTROL the dedup walk                                       |    7.1 |       6.9 | 1.03x      |

A bench row joins the family — **`query: select group + having`**, which the three-run screen moves
**53.9-59.2 → 4.4-4.6ms, 11.72x+, ranges disjoint**. It was checked on all three engines before
being trusted: ts 4.6, ffi 1.0, wasm 1.6, no `n/a`. (The row above it carries the warning for a
reason — a bench workload that raises prints a bare `n/a` and measures nothing.)

The screen's only other separation is `encode graphson`, before [119.7, 134.1, 144.6] against
after [145.2, 149.0, 150.7] — a 0.6ms margin on a row whose own before-side spread is 25ms. Three
more after-side readings came in at 135.2 / 151.0 / 154.7, so six readings span 135.2-154.7 and
contain the before side's top. It also has no code path to this change: nothing under
`packages/core/src` imports `@lenke/gql` outside a README.

**The two spellings are now in `spelling-probe.ts`**, which is where this class of bug is supposed
to be caught: 2.98 / 3.07 / 3.52ms, within 1.18x, no new flag. The `HAVING` member is in that
group as a third member whose cost must stay beside the others, not as another spelling of them —
`HAVING` is SELECT-statement-only in ISO and in this parser, so `RETURN … GROUP BY a HAVING …` is
a SYNTAX ERROR, not a slow plan. My A/B had that shape in it at first and the before bundle raised
on it, which is how the asymmetry got checked against the grammar rather than assumed.

### Teeth: 17 tests, 11 mutants, 9 caught

| mutant                                                         | result               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| any aggregate is accepted in the `HAVING`, not just `count(*)` | caught               |
| NULL keeps the group instead of dropping it                    | caught               |
| the `HAVING` is inverted                                       | caught               |
| `count(*)` in the `HAVING` sees an EMPTY group                 | caught               |
| `count(*)` in the `HAVING` sees the group off by one           | caught               |
| the `HAVING` is never applied (gate open, behaviour absent)    | caught               |
| the representative is the group's LAST row, not its first      | caught               |
| ANY single grouping element is accepted, not only the key item | caught               |
| TWO grouping elements are accepted                             | caught               |
| REVERT 199a: `GROUP BY` only in the `LET` form                 | survived — perf-only |
| REVERT 199b: any `HAVING` declines the tally                   | survived — perf-only |

Both survivors are the item's own two reverts and are perf-only by construction. **No fixture
blindness this tick**, which ends a nine-item run of it — and the reason is that the fixture was
built FROM the mutant list rather than from the feature. Three cases exist only because a mutant
would otherwise live:

- the representative mutant needed a group whose FIRST member disagrees with its others on a
  non-key property, so group `x` is tag 1 then 9 then 9 and `HAVING n.tag > 5` must DROP it;
- the off-by-one on the group's length needed a `HAVING count(*) > 2` boundary that an n+1 would
  cross, so the counts are 3 / 2 / 1 rather than comfortable;
- the "accepts any grouping element" mutant needed `GROUP BY n.tag` while projecting `n.k`, which
  is a different question with different COUNTS, not merely different keys.

The `HAVING`-before-sort claim is structural rather than mutation-tested: `keepGroups` is the
innermost call of `pageGroups(sortGroupRows(keepGroups(…)))`, so no reordering mutant exists
without a type error. The `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` tests pin the behaviour end-to-end instead.

One coupling is written down in the code because it is load-bearing and invisible: `count(*)`
compiles to `group.length` and nothing else, so `keepGroups` passes `new Array(slot.n)` — O(1) for
a holey array, and the minimal object with the one property that is read. That is exactly why
`countOnlyAggregates` must refuse every other aggregate: one that ITERATED the group would see
holes. Two mutants exist to keep that honest.

The test file also records a dead end worth not repeating: a dead `LET` is the usual way to force a
query down the general path, and it does NOT work on the SELECT form, because `FROM MATCH` takes no
`LET`. A third projected item does it instead — the tally wants exactly two — and `1 AS _z` changes
which plan runs and nothing else.

Gates separately: 17 new tests (1274 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0 first run,
`bun run typecheck` / `bun run lint` / `bun run fmt:check` each exit 0 as its OWN command — the
formatter reflowed both files, so all three were re-run after it and the mutation sweep was re-run
against the formatted tree, where every anchor still applied. `bun run spelling` at
SPELL_N=200000 clean but for the known pre-existing inline-vs-clause 2.1x. All seven byte-identity
fuzzers green across three sweeps on random seeds. Every mutation run under `timeout 600` plus a
16G cgroup cap with swap off, the cap's teeth re-proved first (137 for an allocator bomb, 124 for a
bare spin).

### Still open

- A **grouped `count(DISTINCT)`** (1.26x when last measured, overlapping): the tally has the group
  structure and the walk has the dedup, and combining them is a third shape.
- The un-ordered `OFFSET` (~8.8x, declined on purpose).
- The **type-first adjacency index** (3.2x on the operation flooring the three biggest TS rows),
  priced in item 197 and awaiting a decision.
- Nothing else in the TS grouping or dedup family is now above 5x against native.

## 200. The adjacency inversion is REFUTED, and item 197's recommendation is withdrawn

No code change. Item 197 priced the type-first adjacency index at 3.2x and left it "for a decision
rather than taken". The decision came back as a question — _the reason it's like that is to make
get by id easier, and we need to do a get by id often_ — and that question is the measurement item
197 never made.

### What item 197 measured, and what it left out

It measured ONE access pattern: the typed `(vertexId, type)` lookup, at ONE edge-type count (the
bench's single `KNOWS`). The shape it proposed inverting exists to serve a SECOND pattern — get by
id, then iterate every type — and that one was never priced. Both are heavily used, and the split
is clean:

| pattern                  | call sites                                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **get by id, ALL types** | `label-propagation.ts:102-103`, `degree.ts:19-20`, `shortest-path.ts:92,98`, `shortcuts.ts:1102,1623` — and `algorithms/adjacency.ts` exists to share exactly this shape |
| typed `(id, type)`       | `Vertex.edgesFromByLabel`/`edgesToByLabel`, the hop walks in `hop-projection.ts` and `shortcuts.ts`                                                                      |

The whole algorithms layer is the first one. Under a type-first index every one of those sites
becomes T probes where it is now one lookup plus an iteration of a small inner map.

### Four shapes, both patterns, swept over the edge-type count

200,000 vertices, degree 5, min of 15. Degree is spread across the types as `(i + k) % T`, so a
degree-5 vertex over 8 types holds mostly one-element buckets — the shape the bench corpus calls
the case an index can win on.

|   T | A: typed `(id,type)` | B: get by id, ALL types | build          |
| --: | -------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------- |
|   1 | type-first **2.19x** | type-first 1.61x        | dual **1.44x** |
|   3 | type-first **2.41x** | type-first **0.71x**    | dual **2.05x** |
|   8 | type-first **2.85x** | type-first **0.35x**    | dual **2.39x** |
|  20 | type-first **4.11x** | type-first **0.21x**    | dual **2.36x** |

**The current shape is right, and for the stated reason.** Type-first wins the typed lookup by
2.2-4.1x and loses get-by-id by 1.4x at three edge types and 4.8x at twenty. The crossover sits
between T=1 and T=3, so the bench's single edge type is the one configuration where inverting
looks free — and it is the only configuration the earlier number was taken in. A people graph has
five to twenty edge types.

Holding BOTH spines avoids the read trade and is cheaper than it sounds in memory — the leaf
`Set` for a `(vertex, type)` pair is one object that both spines can point at, so a dual index
duplicates no edges and no Sets, adding one map spine and T inner Maps. What it costs is the
WRITE: **2.0-2.4x on the index build**, and that build is `indexEdgeLabel`, which
`ts-edge-insert-is-adjacency` measured as 71% of the biggest row in the bench. Paying 2.4x on the
single most expensive thing the engine does to win 2.4x on a read is not a trade worth making
blind.

### A fourth shape, priced and refuted

Pattern A's cost is not the id lookup — item 197's own table has that at 14ns. It is the inner
Map: one per vertex, one entry wide, touched once, so 200,000 cold polymorphic objects against
type-first's one. That suggests fixing it WITHOUT inverting anything: store the `Set` inline as a
`{ t, s }` leaf wherever a vertex's edges are all one type, keep a Map only for vertices that
genuinely span types, and discriminate on `instanceof Map`. Get-by-id then has no inner map to
walk at all and the primary spine never changes.

It does not work. At T=1 it gives 1.52x on A and 1.62x on B — real, but less than type-first's
2.19x — and at every higher T **0% of vertices are sole-type** on this fixture, so the inline leaf
never fires and all that remains is the `instanceof` check: 0.88-0.94x, a small loss. Its entire
value is the fraction of real vertices whose edges are all one type, which neither the bench nor
this fixture can tell me, so it is not claimable.

### One confound named rather than papered over

Pattern A's vertex-first absolute cost is NON-MONOTONIC in T — 88, 141, 131, 92ns — which looked
like a noise signature and is not; it reproduces at 7 and at 15 reps. The cause is selectivity: at
T=20 only 125 of 2500 edges carry the probe type, so most lookups MISS and short-circuit, and the
pattern gets cheaper because the query got more selective rather than because the structure did.
So the cross-T absolutes are not comparable. The within-T vertex-first-vs-type-first ratios are,
since both sides answer the same query over the same survivors, and those are the numbers above.

### What this means for the field

`drive-the-vertex-side` and item 197 both carry "the type-first index is worth 3.2x and is fewer
objects". That is half a claim. It is worth 2.2-4.1x **on one of the two patterns**, it is fewer
objects **in one of the two spines**, and it is a 1.4-4.8x REGRESSION on the pattern the whole
algorithms layer uses. The recommendation is withdrawn.

It also means the two biggest TS rows — `traverse 1-hop + filter` at 33x and `traverse 1-hop +
start filter` at 16x — have no identified path left. Item 197 established they are already on the
best plan this engine has and floored by this lookup; this item establishes that the lookup cannot
be made faster without paying for it somewhere that costs more. That is a real stopping point, not
a to-do, and it should be recorded as one so the next sweep does not re-derive it.

The one direction that survives the constraint is an OPT-IN index, the way property indexes
already work here (`createIndex({on, kind, keys})`): a type-first spine built only for the edge
types a workload actually seeks on, with the vertex-first spine staying primary. Writes pay only
where the user asked them to, get-by-id is untouched, and the typed hop walk gets its 2.2-4.1x
where the index exists. That is a feature with an API, not an optimization, so it is noted and not
taken.

## 201. What an edge insert actually costs — the recorded 71% is 34%, and a per-write microtask is 17.6%

No code change. Item 200 closed the adjacency READ question, which left the biggest absolute row
in the bench — `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)`, 2835ms ts against 758 ffi — with its cost attributed
to a single stage by a note that turns out to be wrong.

### The contradiction that started it

`ts-edge-insert-is-adjacency` records `indexEdgeLabel` as **71%** of that row, "ALL of it" the
`Map<vertexId, Map<label, Set>>`. But item 200's probe built a whole two-level adjacency for
1,000,000 edges in 68-97ms, and `indexEdgeLabel` writes three indexes rather than one, so an
isolated loop prices it at 6-8% of 2835ms. Both numbers cannot be right.

Neither was. Measured on the REAL path — `new Graph()`, real `addVertex`, real `addEdge`, 200,000
vertices and 1,000,000 edges, min of 5:

```
vertices only                  261ms    1305ns/vertex
+ 1,000,000 real addEdge      3047ms    2786ns/edge
one bare two-level spine       128ms     128ns/edge
```

So a real edge insert is **2786ns** where a bare spine write is **128ns** — and `indexEdgeLabel`
does three of those, which estimates 384ns, or 14%. Ablation says the true figure is **959ns, 34.1%**.
The isolated micro understated it by **2.5x**. That is `harness-must-resemble-caller` landing again,
and it is the second time in two items that a micro has been the wrong instrument for this
question, so it is worth stating as the rule: **attribute an insert by ABLATION on the real path,
never by timing an equivalent loop.** An equivalent loop has none of the real frame's allocation
pressure, polymorphism, or getter calls.

### The real distribution

Each stage removed in turn from `addEdge`/`insertEdge`, the drop being that stage's in-situ share:

| stage                                                  | ns/edge |     share |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------: | --------: |
| `indexEdgeLabel` (all three spines)                    | **959** | **34.1%** |
| **`markMutated` — the per-write reactive bookkeeping** | **490** | **17.6%** |
| the `EmitterEvent` + emit at the `EdgeAdded` site      |     396 |     14.4% |
| the two `getVertexById` endpoint re-resolves           |     145 |      5.2% |
| `validateElementNames`                                 |      81 |      2.9% |
| `recordUndo`'s closure                                 |      69 |      2.5% |
| the cardinality gate                                   |      69 |      2.5% |
| the edge property index                                |      64 |      2.3% |
| the constraint gate block                              |      62 |      2.2% |
| the `Edge` construction spread                         |      34 |      1.2% |

`markMutated` (490ns) exceeding the whole `EdgeAdded` emit (396ns) is not an inconsistency — it is
information. `markMutated` is registered against ~14 event types, so removing its REGISTRATION
kills it everywhere, while removing one `emit` call leaves the others. **An edge insert therefore
emits more than one event**: the `Edge` constructor eagerly writes labels and properties through
the graph's setters, and those emit too. Nothing in the file says so, and it doubles the per-write
event cost.

### The find: one microtask per write

`markMutated` reads `(event as any)[TX_TOKENS] ?? this.tokensOf(event)`, allocates a `doTheWork`
closure, and calls `queueMicrotask(doTheWork)` — **per event**. A 1,000,000-edge ingest queues over
a million microtasks. Split:

| piece                                                           | ns/edge |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------: |
| `queueMicrotask` itself                                         |      93 |
| `tokensOf(event)`                                               |      97 |
| the closure allocation + the `TX_TOKENS` symbol miss + dispatch |    ~300 |

And the microtask BODY is not in any of these numbers. Microtasks drain when the synchronous task
unwinds, which is after the probe reads `performance.now()`, so the million drains — each doing
`mutationVersion += 1`, a token loop and `scheduleNotify()` — land outside the timing window
entirely. `deferred-work-escapes-the-bench` records exactly this shape costing 258ms and hiding for
170 audit items; it is still here, one layer down.

The code's own comment says the deferral exists so "a burst of mutations coalesces into one React
notify". The NOTIFY coalesces. The **scheduling does not** — the closure and the microtask are
per event.

### Two fixes measured and refuted first

Both were plausible from reading, and reading was wrong about both:

- **the `new Set(...)` snapshot in `Emitter.emit`.** It allocates a Set per emission to protect
  against a listener subscribing during dispatch. Replacing it with the live Set measured
  **−5ns — nothing**, slightly negative, i.e. inside the noise. The allocation is free at this
  size.
- **the `@graph/mutate` re-emit.** The graph registers `onMutate` against those same ~14 types, and
  it allocates a second `EmitterEvent` plus an `{ original }` wrapper per write. Worth **53ns
  (1.9%)**. Both together: 69ns (2.5%). I had expected these two to be most of the emit cost; they
  are 17% of it.

### The shape of the fix, for the next item

Accumulate rather than schedule: keep the pending token-lists on the instance and queue ONE
microtask when none is pending. The drain then applies every increment it would have applied —
`mutationVersion` advances by the number of events and each token's epoch advances once per event
that touched it — so the observable counters are unchanged while a million microtasks and a
million closures become one. The counters feed React change-detection, so "unchanged" has to be
asserted per-increment rather than assumed from "events are observation-only"
([[events-observation-only]] licenses dropping a VETO, not dropping a count).

Budgeted honestly: `queueMicrotask` (93ns) plus the closure share, call it 150-250ns of the 490,
so 5-9% of the edge cost, plus the deferred drain that no current measurement captures. The drain
has to be timed separately — on its own, after the loop — or this item repeats the mistake it just
documented.

### What this changes in the field

- `ts-edge-insert-is-adjacency`'s **71% is withdrawn; it is 34.1%**. The adjacency is still the
  largest single stage, and item 200 established its shape cannot be changed without paying more
  elsewhere — so the row's remaining headroom is in the other 66%, which nobody had enumerated.
- The second-largest stage in the biggest row in the bench is **reactive bookkeeping**, not graph
  work. It was invisible because it is a listener registered in the constructor, three files from
  the insert.
- Gates: nothing to gate — no source file changed. Both ablated files (`Graph.ts`, `Emitter.ts`)
  verified byte-clean against `git diff` after the sweeps, every run under `timeout 900` plus a 16G
  cgroup cap with swap off, each ablation applied to a PRISTINE copy and restored before the next.
  One harness bug worth recording: passing `env=` as a bare dict to `subprocess.run` strips
  `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` and `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, so `systemd-run --user` cannot reach the user
  scope bus and every run fails identically — which reads like a broken ablation rather than a
  broken harness.

## 202. The microtask coalesce is REFUTED at 0.4%, and item 201 has a claim to withdraw

No code change — the change was written, measured, and reverted. Item 201 identified `markMutated`
as 490ns of an edge's 2786ns (17.6%, second only to the adjacency write) and specified the fix:
one microtask per event became one microtask per batch, with the pending token lists accrued on
the instance. That was built exactly as specified. It is worth nothing.

### What was built

`markMutated` accrued into `pendingTokens` / `pendingEvents` and queued a single `drain` behind a
`drainQueued` flag, with `drain` allocated once alongside the constructor rather than per event.
The counters advance identically by construction: `mutationVersion` by the number of events, each
token's epoch once per event that touched it — which is why the pending lists are kept PER EVENT
rather than merged into a set. The flag clears first in `drain`, so a throw cannot leave it set and
silently stop every future notify.

### Measured, with the drain timed separately as item 201 required

Item 201's whole lesson was that microtasks drain after the synchronous loop returns, so no
ns/edge figure in it included the drain. This measures both: the sync loop, then our own microtask
queued behind every microtask the writes queued. 100,000 vertices, 500,000 edges, min of 5:

|                                  |       sync loop |  deferred drain |  total |
| -------------------------------- | --------------: | --------------: | -----: |
| before (one microtask per event) | 1164ms / 2329ns | **15ms** / 30ns | 1179ms |
| after (one microtask per batch)  | 1165ms / 2331ns | **10ms** / 20ns | 1175ms |

**5ms on 500,000 edges. 0.4%.** The sync loop does not move at all (2329 against 2331), because
the coalesce trades a `queueMicrotask` call for an array push and a branch. And the drain was never
expensive to begin with: a million microtasks are cheap when each does a counter bump and a loop
over one or two tokens. **The hidden deferred cost that `deferred-work-escapes-the-bench` warns
about is, here, 30ns an edge.** The rule was right to make me measure it; the measurement says
there is nothing behind it this time.

So the target is retracted. The code is reverted and `Graph.ts` verified byte-clean against
`git diff`.

### A claim from item 201 to withdraw

Item 201 concluded that **an edge insert emits more than one event**, reasoning from `markMutated`
(490ns) costing more than removing the whole `EdgeAdded` emit (396ns) — the `Edge` constructor
writes labels and properties through the graph's setters, so those must emit too.

That is wrong, and the observable settles it. `mutationVersion` after the drain is **exactly
600,000** for 100,000 vertices and 500,000 edges — one event per element, no more. The 396-vs-490
gap was two ablations bounding the SAME quantity across runs whose baselines were 2748 and 2792;
a 24% spread on a stage worth 17% is variance I credited as structure. The lesson is the cheap one:
**an inference from two ablation deltas is worth less than one reading of the observable they both
claim to explain**, and the observable was two lines away the whole time.

### Where the 490ns actually goes, now that each piece is priced

| piece                                                 |    ns/edge | verdict                                                    |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------: | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tokensOf(event)`                                     |         97 | real, load-bearing (the tokens must be read synchronously) |
| `queueMicrotask` + the whole deferred body            |         93 | **coalescing captures ~0.4% of total — refuted**           |
| the `TX_TOKENS` symbol lookup                         | **~12-37** | **refuted — noise**                                        |
| the listener dispatch + the `EmitterEvent` allocation |       ~270 | not separable from having events at all                    |

The `TX_TOKENS` read was the last plausible micro: `(event as any)[TX_TOKENS]` is a missing
symbol-keyed property on every non-transaction event, which should be a shape miss. Ablated to a
bare `this.tokensOf(event)` it measured 2774ns against a 2786-2811 baseline — inside the noise.

**So the 17.6% stage has no extractable win.** Every component is either small, load-bearing, or
inseparable from the graph having an event bus. That is the honest end of this thread, and it is
worth recording as one so the next sweep does not re-open a stage that merely LOOKS large: a
17.6% share is not a 17.6% opportunity, and three separate fixes to it have now measured 0.4%,
noise, and noise.

Gates: nothing to gate, no source file changed. All measurement under `timeout 900` plus a 16G
cgroup cap with swap off. The drain probe is kept at
`crates/lenke-engine/target/mutation-backup/drain.probe.ts` (gitignored) — it is the instrument
that settles any future "is there deferred work hiding here?" question, and it reads
`mutationVersion` after the drain so a coalesce that dropped counts could not pass.

## 203. Item 201's fixture inflated its own table by 7%, and the insert path is closed

No code change. Three measurements, all negative, and one of them I should not have had to make.

### The fixture correction

`Edge`'s constructor destructures `const { id = rando(), ... }` and `rando()` is
`crypto.randomUUID()`. **Item 201's probe supplied no edge id**, so every one of its numbers
includes the default. `bench-corpus` states the rule it broke in as many words: _"Give edges ids.
`encode` emits them, so every reloaded snapshot has them. Omitting them skips the external-id path
entirely."_ The row item 201 was explaining — `decode ndjson` — reads ids from the file.

Measured, 100,000 vertices and 500,000 edges, min of 7:

|                                        |          ns/edge |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------: |
| edges with NO id (item 201's fixture)  |             2571 |
| edges WITH an id (what the bench does) |         **2392** |
| difference                             | **179ns, 1.07x** |

So **item 201's attribution table is uniformly ~7% high**. The ranking is unaffected — the
adjacency write is still the largest stage by a wide margin and `markMutated` still second — but
the ns/edge figures should be read as 7% over, and the correct per-edge baseline for this row is
**2392ns against native's 641ns, 3.7x**.

### The id generator is not the target

A cryptographic UUID per element sounds like an obvious cost, and `rando`'s own doc comment claims
it returns _"a not-cyrptographically-secure random string"_ — which `crypto.randomUUID()` is not,
so the comment and the code disagree. That looked like a free win. It is not:

|                                                | ns/call |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------: |
| `crypto.randomUUID()` standalone               |  **32** |
| a counter id (`e${n.toString(36)}`), for scale |      25 |

Bun's `randomUUID` is batched and costs 32ns. Replacing it with a non-cryptographic generator
would buy **7ns an element**, so the doc/code mismatch is a documentation bug and nothing more.

Note the gap between the two numbers above, because it is the interesting part: the CALL is 32ns
but omitting the id costs **179ns in situ**. The difference is not the generator, it is the
STRING — a 36-character UUID makes every subsequent id-keyed map operation (`edgesById.set`, every
later `getEdgeById`) dearer than a short id does. A micro of the generator would have priced this
at 32ns and missed 147ns of it, which is `harness-must-resemble-caller` for the third time on this
one row.

### A refutation I re-derived instead of reading

I then ablated the `this.properties = properties` setter for the empty-bag case: 2335ns against
2392, **57ns, 2.4%**. Modest, and irrelevant, because
`ts-edge-insert-is-adjacency` **already lists "the empty-property-index guard" as refuted by
ablation**, alongside the endpoint re-resolve. I wrote the memory entry that says so, in item 201,
and then spent a measurement re-deriving it one item later.

Worth recording plainly: the refuted-list exists so a candidate can be checked against it in
seconds, and checking it is not optional just because the candidate occurred to me independently.
The cost here was small. The habit is the point.

### The insert path is closed

Every stage of `addEdge` is now priced and every candidate fix is measured:

| stage                               | ns/edge | status                                                      |
| ----------------------------------- | ------: | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `indexEdgeLabel` (three spines)     |     959 | the shape cannot change — item 200                          |
| `markMutated`                       |     490 | three fixes refuted — item 202                              |
| the `EmitterEvent` + emit           |     396 | bounds the same work as `markMutated`                       |
| the two `getVertexById` re-resolves |     145 | refuted earlier by ablation                                 |
| the id default                      |     179 | **refuted — 32ns is the generator, the rest is the string** |
| `validateElementNames`              |      81 | —                                                           |
| `recordUndo`'s closure              |      69 | —                                                           |
| the cardinality gate                |      69 | —                                                           |
| the edge property index             |      64 | refuted earlier by ablation                                 |
| the constraint gate                 |      62 | —                                                           |
| the empty-properties setter         |      57 | **refuted — and already on the refuted list**               |
| the `Edge` construction spread      |      34 | —                                                           |

Nothing above 100ns remains unexamined. The row is 3.7x off native and that 3.7x is spread across
a dozen stages of 2-34% each, every one of them load-bearing or already refuted — which is the
signature of a constant-factor gap, exactly what `ts-ingest-is-constant-factor` concluded about
this family by a different route. **It is not a missing path, and three items of looking have
stopped turning one up.** The honest move is to stop looking here, and that is recorded so the next
sweep does not spend a fourth.

Gates: nothing to gate, no source file changed. `Edge.ts` and `Graph.ts` both verified byte-clean
against `git diff` after the ablations. All measurement under a 16G cgroup cap with swap off.

## 204. The plainest query in the language had no fast path — 2.1-4.1x, and a 50x regression caught by the bench

`MATCH (n:L) WHERE <pred> RETURN <items>` — a label scan, a filter, a projection. After four items
of closing threads on the insert path, the target came from a surface this session had not looked
at: `bench:usage`, the serving-side workload of small operations against a warm graph.

### The signal

Every UNINDEXED read in `bench:usage` was 60-82x behind native while every indexed one was a
healthy 3x:

| workload                             |   ts(−) | engine(−) |         |
| ------------------------------------ | ------: | --------: | ------- |
| `write: property update`             |     603 |     48.8k | 81x     |
| `analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops` |     486 |     39.7k | 82x     |
| **`read: point lookup`**             | **605** | **48.0k** | **79x** |
| `read: permission check`             |     569 |     37.4k | 66x     |
| `read: 2-hop recommendation`         |     633 |     37.8k | 60x     |

An index turns a scan into a seek, so the indexed columns hid it. The simplest of those rows is
`MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = $n RETURN u.score AS s` over 20,000 users, which is 82ns a vertex —
and item 190 had already measured the FLOOR for exactly this shape. Against a hand-written
label-bucket loop:

|                                      | ns/vertex |                                |
| ------------------------------------ | --------: | ------------------------------ |
| a hand-written loop                  |   **6.8** | the floor                      |
| `count(*)` over the same scan        |      30.6 | 4.5x — has a shortcut          |
| the projection form                  |  **83.3** | **12.2x the floor**            |
| the projection form, nothing matches |      83.5 | so the cost is per SCANNED row |

`count(*)` over the identical scan was 2.7x cheaper than the projection while doing the same
filtering, which places the cost in what happens AFTER the predicate rather than in the scan. And
the file explained itself: `detectCountShortcut` answers the count form, `detectHopProjection`
needs a hop (`segments.length !== 1` declines a bare node), `detectDistinctProjection` needs a
`DISTINCT` — **so the one shape with no detector was the plainest one**, and it fell through to the
general pipeline, which allocates a binding per scanned row.

### `detectNodeProjection`

One reused binding for the whole scan, and a row object only for survivors. Everything else is
borrowed rather than re-derived: the inline `{k: v}` constraint and the clause `WHERE` are the two
spellings of one filter and both funnel through `inlineHolds` → `satisfies`, the general path's own
implementation, composed into a single gate by the `reduceRight` whose shape item 141 measured at
34% (an `for (const ip of preds)` allocated an iterator per vertex over an empty array).

Which items are admissible is an **allowlist** of `Expr` kinds, not a denylist, so an arm added
later declines instead of silently taking a path it was never checked against. That matters more
here than for item 199's count guard: a wrong answer here is a wrong ROW. The allowlist is also
what refuses a subquery, and it has to be, because `freePredicateVars` descends INTO one and
reports the variables inside it — an `EXISTS { (u)-[:T]->(x) }` reading only `u` passes a
free-variable check while still needing the general matcher.

### The 50x regression, and the memory that named it in advance

Written as a raw bucket walk, this made the unindexed point lookup 2x faster and the **INDEXED one
50x slower**: `read: point lookup` ts(+) fell from **80.9k to 1.6k ops/s**, and
`interleaved: write + point read` from 49.6k to 1.6k. The fast path claimed the query ahead of the
general path's index seek and then scanned.

`count-shortcuts-must-seek` describes that exact failure and gives its diagnostic signature —
_"a walking fast path ignores the index the general path seeds from (sig: indexed == unindexed
columns)"_ — and the bench printed the signature verbatim: 1.2k against 1.6k, the two columns
collapsed onto each other. The family it closed (items 149, 176-179) was closed via one shared
`hopSeek`, which is what this now calls. `hopSeek` returns a candidate set only when it is
strictly smaller than the label bucket, so an unindexed graph still walks and pays nothing for
asking.

Seeding then cost two WRONG ANSWERS, both caught by existing tests: an index hint is a NECESSARY
condition, so a seeded set is a SUPERSET and can contain a same-named vertex of the wrong label.
The bucket walk excludes those by construction and the seek does not. The re-check is guarded on
`seeded` so the unindexed walk pays nothing for a test it satisfies by construction — the idiom
this file already uses at the far-side walk.

### Measured

|                                               | before |      after |           |
| --------------------------------------------- | -----: | ---------: | --------- |
| `WHERE` clause + projection (the bench's row) | 83.3ns | **34.8ns** | **2.39x** |
| inline `{name: $n}` + projection              | 73.6ns | **24.3ns** | **3.03x** |
| nothing matches                               | 83.5ns | **30.3ns** | 2.76x     |
| CONTROL `count(*)` over the same scan         | 30.6ns |     30.9ns | 1.01x     |

The projection now sits at parity with the count path (34.8 against 30.9), which is the right
relationship — the same scan, the same filter, one extra row object.

In `bench:usage`: `read: point lookup` ts(−) **605 → 1.3k** ops/s, with ts(+) **80.9k → 82.2k**,
i.e. the indexed path restored rather than merely un-regressed.

The three-run whole-bench screen separates one row, and it is not the one I was aiming at:
**`query: project 3 columns` — 41.3-43.0 → 8.2-10.2ms, 4.05x+, disjoint.** That is
`MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.name AS n, n.city AS c, n.age AS a`: the same shape with no `WHERE` at
all, three items instead of one. Worth stating plainly because it inverts an engine ranking: at
8.4-9.2ms against ffi's 54.0-55.3 and wasm's 60.4-61.9, **the pure-TS engine is now ~6x faster
than native on this row**, because 200,000 rows × 3 columns means 600,000 values across the FFI
boundary and the TS path never crosses one.

The screen's only other separation is `decode pg-json` at 1.01x+ — a 2.4ms margin on a 215ms row
that runs no GQL. Three more readings came in at 215.4 / 214.5 / 215.9, so six after-side readings
span 214.5-225.6 and contain the before range. Noise, and the before side being unusually tight
(2.4ms) is what made a small shift look disjoint.

### Teeth: 26 tests, 17 mutants, 11 caught

| mutant                                             | result                                                 |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| the SEEDED set skips its label re-check            | caught                                                 |
| the binding is written ONCE, not per surviving row | caught                                                 |
| the gate is skipped entirely                       | caught (64 failing)                                    |
| an aggregate item is accepted                      | caught                                                 |
| the allowlist accepts every expr kind              | caught                                                 |
| the walk does not descend into children            | caught                                                 |
| a HOP is accepted as a node scan                   | caught                                                 |
| `ORDER BY`/`SKIP`/`LIMIT` accepted then ignored    | caught (25 failing)                                    |
| **`DISTINCT` is accepted**                         | **survived → caught**                                  |
| an `OPTIONAL MATCH` is accepted                    | caught                                                 |
| the column name ignores the alias                  | caught (59 failing)                                    |
| the label re-check also runs on the bucket walk    | survived — a no-op by construction                     |
| the index seed is never taken                      | survived — **perf-only, and it is the 50x**            |
| a `WHERE` reading another variable is accepted     | survived — unreachable, documented                     |
| an ITEM reading another variable is accepted       | survived — unreachable, documented                     |
| `RETURN *` is accepted                             | survived — equivalent to the `items.length === 0` test |
| REVERT 204: never take the path                    | survived — perf-only                                   |

The `DISTINCT` survivor is the one that taught something. `detectDistinctProjection` runs EARLIER
in the ladder and accepts only ONE item, so a two-item `DISTINCT` declines it and arrives here,
where nothing dedupes — a real wrong answer. My fixture had two vertices sharing `k` but differing
in `tag`, so no projected PAIR repeated and the mutant answered correctly. **That is the
"two-of-the-thing" shape `mutants-find-fixture-blindness` lists**, and the fix was a fixture with
two vertices agreeing on BOTH projected values.

Four survivors are argued rather than waved through, and two are now documented in the code with
that evidence: the free-variable checks on the `WHERE` and on each item are UNREACHABLE, because
with exactly two clauses, one pattern and no segments, the node's own name is the only thing
anything can be bound to. They stay for the reason `detectHopProjection` keeps its rel-variable
check — the argument depends on the guards above holding their shape, and they are what would
still refuse a subquery if the allowlist ever grew an arm carrying one.

Five anchors went non-unique because this path reuses the grouped tally's idioms verbatim, and
each printed `NOT APPLIED (anchor appears 2x)` rather than passing silently. Fifth tick running
that check has earned itself; two of them needed the whole eight-line projection guard to
disambiguate.

### Gates, and one thing the probe revealed about itself

`bun run typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as its own command. The eighth rung took
`runLinearClauses` to a complexity of 36 against a limit of 35, so the whole fast-path ladder is
extracted to `fastPath` — a natural seam, being a flat sequence of independent "did this detector
claim the query?" tests, with the order documented as load-bearing (`distinctProjection` MUST
precede `nodeProjection`, which does not dedupe). The mutation sweep was re-run against the
formatted-and-refactored tree with every anchor still applying. Full TS suite exit 0 on the second
run (the known `run-many` flake). All seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps.

The two spellings are added to `spelling-probe.ts` (5.52 against 3.76ms, 1.47x, under tolerance).
But a new 2x flag appeared alongside — `hop, START endpoint filtered` — and it is NOT this change:
running the probe with my group REMOVED and the SAME built engine flags a different group again
(`OR vs IN`, 2.0x). **Three consecutive runs flagged three different groups, every one between 2.0x
and 2.2x.** The probe's own header says each row's cache state depends on its predecessors and
that it is a finder rather than a settled delta; this is that, quantified. Inserting a group
reshuffles everything after it, so at this tolerance the marginal flags are the harness. A flag
worth chasing has to clear 2x by more than the set moves when you add an unrelated group.

## 205. The start-only filter's decline is CORRECT, and the unindexed-only opportunity behind it

No code change. Item 204 left `bench:usage` with four unindexed rows still at 60-82x, all of them
two-segment patterns with a `count(*)` and a START filter. This prices them, finds a 3.9x, and then
finds that the obvious way to take it reproduces a known 97x regression.

### Where the cliff is

20,000 users, three `FOLLOWS` each, so the hop work from one start vertex is negligible beside a
20,000-vertex scan — which is the thing being measured:

| shape                                       | ns/vertex scanned |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------: |
| node count, filtered start                  |              35.8 |
| node projection, filtered (item 204)        |              35.6 |
| **1-hop count, filtered start**             |          **25.7** |
| **1-hop PROJECTION, filtered start**        |          **99.8** |
| 2-hop count, filtered start (the bench row) |              97.7 |
| 2-hop projection, filtered start            |              96.7 |
| 1-hop count, INLINE start filter            |              24.2 |
| 2-hop count, INLINE start filter            |              86.7 |

Two separate things. A **1-hop projection with a start filter is 3.9x its own count** on the
identical pattern — only the projection differs, and `detectHopProjection` exists for exactly that
shape. And **nothing two-segment has a fast path at all**: the 2-hop count is 97.7ns against the
1-hop count's 25.7.

### The 3.9x is a deliberate decline, and the file says so

`carriedWhere` refuses a clause `WHERE` that does not read the FAR variable
(`if (!vars.includes(farVar)) return null`), so a start-only `WHERE u.name = $n` declines
`detectHopProjection` entirely. That looks like item 199 all over again — a detector that exists
and is not reached.

It is not. `filteredHopWalk`'s own comment explains the refusal and item 177 measured it, `name`
indexed, 20,000 users:

```
(u)-[:FOLLOWS]->(x:User) WHERE x.name = $n RETURN u.name     3966.1us  <- the fused walk
(x:User {name: $n})<-[:FOLLOWS]-(u) RETURN u.name              35.3us  <- general path
(u:User)-[:FOLLOWS]->(x) WHERE u.name = $n RETURN x.name       49.6us  <- general path
```

**A start-only filter declines ON PURPOSE so it reaches the general path's index seed** — "which
is why that spelling was fast all along". The walk is flat in the filter's selectivity because it
visits every edge of the start source either way; the seed is not. Confirmed independently here,
the same graph with and without a `hash` index on `name`:

| shape                                |  unindexed |   indexed |           |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------: | --------: | --------- |
| node count, filtered start           |     27.5ms |     0.8ms | 36.0x     |
| node projection (item 204)           |     20.7ms |     0.4ms | 48.9x     |
| 1-hop count, filtered start          |     14.6ms |     0.5ms | 28.6x     |
| **1-hop projection, filtered start** | **51.8ms** | **0.6ms** | **89.2x** |
| 2-hop count, filtered start          |     52.6ms |     0.9ms | 59.5x     |
| 2-hop projection, filtered start     |     51.9ms |     0.7ms | 75.9x     |

Every shape is 28-89x faster with the index, the indexed column flat at 0.4-0.9ms throughout —
including the start-only hop projection the walk refuses. The routing is right.

**So the naive fix — make `carriedWhere` accept a start-only predicate — would hand the walk
precisely the case the general path answers 89x faster.** That is item 177's 97x regression
re-created, and it is the same mistake class as item 204's 50x from one tick earlier, which
`count-shortcuts-must-seek` had to catch twice. Three times in two items is enough to state the
rule positively: **in this engine a filter's spelling does not decide its plan; whether its end
can SEEK does, and that is a runtime property of the graph, not a compile-time property of the
query.**

### What the real opportunity is, and what it would have to look like

The 3.9x is genuine but it lives **only in the unindexed regime**: 51.8ms where the count walk over
the same pattern does 14.6. A correct version therefore cannot be a change to `carriedWhere` at
all — it has to be a RUNTIME decline, mirroring the one `filteredHopWalk` already makes for the far
end (`cfar !== undefined` → ask `indexCandidates` whether the far end can seek, and hand the query
back if it can). The start side needs the same question asked of it, and then:

- accept a start-only clause `WHERE`, with `needsStart` true;
- apply it **per START VERTEX, before expanding that vertex's adjacency**, which is what buys the
  3.9x — the current walk would evaluate it once per ROW, so 60,000 times over 20,000 starts, and
  expand all 20,000;
- decline to the general path when the start can seek.

That third bullet is the whole risk, and `filteredHopWalk`'s far-side version of it is not a simple
"narrower than the source" test: the file records that writing it that way measured a **3.1x
regression** on an indexed-but-unselective filter, and that the crossover needed dividing by 8 to
land inside the region where declining still wins. A start-side decline needs its own measured
threshold, not a copy of that one.

So this is specified, not taken. It is a change to the most heavily-measured function in the file,
guarded by a threshold whose first version was wrong by 3.1x, and the reason to stop here rather
than write it at the end of a long tick is that the failure mode is a silent 89x on indexed
graphs — which no answer test can see, and which only `bench:usage`'s ts(−)-versus-ts(+) comparison
catches.

### The larger gap: nothing two-segment has a fast path

The four remaining `bench:usage` rows are all two-segment counts, and the ladder has no rung for
them: 97.7ns a scanned vertex against the 1-hop count's 25.7. The whole difference is the START
SCAN — the hops from a single matched vertex are three edges — so a two-segment count whose start
gate ran per vertex would land near the 1-hop number, roughly 3.8x on `read: permission check`,
`read: 2-hop recommendation`, `analytic: cycle detection` and `analytic: fan-out spread`. That is
the bigger prize and it has the same seek-decline requirement, so the two want doing together.

Gates: nothing to gate, no source file changed. Probes kept at
`crates/lenke-engine/target/mutation-backup/hop2.probe.ts` (gitignored); it prints each shape's
ANSWER before timing it and runs every shape against both an indexed and an unindexed graph, which
is what made the refutation visible rather than inferred.

## 206. A start-filtered two-hop count gets the per-vertex walk the one-hop shape has had since item 129 — 4.1x

Item 205 specified this and warned which half was dangerous. The dangerous half turned out not to
be the one I expected.

### The gap, and the comment that both explained and understated it

`patternCountOf` required a PLAIN start node on a two-segment pattern, with the note _"the two-hop
degree product has no route that applies a predicate"_, and refused a clause `WHERE` outright
(`if (segments.length !== 1) return null`). So a filtered two-hop count fell to the general
pipeline, which binds a row per match:

|                                 | ns a scanned vertex |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------: |
| 1-hop count, filtered start     |                25.7 |
| **2-hop count, filtered start** |            **97.7** |

The note was true of the degree product and not of the engine. `buildTwoHopCount` iterates the
MIDDLE and multiplies the two sides, so a predicate choosing which starts count has nowhere to go —
but the one-hop shape has had a per-VERTEX route since item 129, which gates a start and only then
expands it. **Two lines above the refusal, the same comment says so.** The two-hop shape simply
never got the same treatment.

`buildFilteredTwoHopCount` is that route: gate a start, and for each surviving start walk its first
leg and add `side()` for the second. The unfiltered case stays on the degree product, which is
strictly better for it — it never touches a start vertex at all.

### Item 205's warning was right, and aimed at the wrong risk

205 said the danger was handing the walk a case the index seed answers faster, and that a
start-side decline would need its own measured threshold. **No decline was needed.** The one-hop
walk does not decline either — it SEEDS, via `hopSeek`, which returns a candidate set only when it
is strictly narrower than the label bucket. Doing the same here made the indexed case _better_,
not worse:

|                                         |             unindexed |             indexed |
| --------------------------------------- | --------------------: | ------------------: |
| 2-hop count, filtered start, before     |                52.6ms |               0.9ms |
| 2-hop count, filtered start, after      |            **14.0ms** |           **0.5ms** |
| 2-hop count, INLINE start filter, after | **11.8ms** (was 44.9) | **0.4ms** (was 0.7) |

Indexed and unindexed are 29x apart, so the `count-shortcuts-must-seek` signature — the two columns
reading the same number — is absent. The seeded set is a superset, so the start label is re-checked,
guarded on `seeded` so the bucket walk pays nothing.

### The regression that did happen, and it was the fourth time

Three `bench:usage` rows improved and **two unrelated ones appeared to drop 30-37%**:
`analytic: fan-out spread 1-3 hops` and `analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops`. Both are
`COUNT { ... ->{1,3}(x) }` var-length subqueries, which this path refuses upstream — it cannot
claim them.

It was real, and it took eight readings a side to establish rather than assume, because the first
instinct was "that row ranges 2x for the same binary":

|               | before (8 readings) | after, walk INLINE in the closure |
| ------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| fan-out ts(−) | 563-625             | **334-593**                       |
| cycle ts(−)   | 485-569             | **279-548**                       |

The before side is tight over eight readings; the after side keeps its top and acquires a slow mode
below it. **A new MODE rather than a shift is `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing`'s signature, and
this is its fourth appearance.** The walk was written inline in the closure the builder returns.
Hoisting it to module scope as `walkTwoHopFiltered(graph, params, plan)`, with the closure reduced
to one dispatching call, removed it: fan-out back to **538-605** over five readings, cycle to
**524-553** over ten (one 289 in a run whose entire ts(+) column read 27.5k against the usual 40k —
a whole-run artifact, not a row mode).

Worth stating because it keeps being learned the expensive way: the cost is not the walk's
complexity, it is where the walk's CODE lives, and the victim is a query the new path never runs.

### Measured

A bench row joins the corpus — **`count 2-hop + start filter`**, `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b)-[:KNOWS]->(c) WHERE a.age > 60 RETURN count(*)`,
on 200,000 nodes and 1,000,000 edges with a third of starts passing:

|        | ts                          |
| ------ | --------------------------- |
| before | 859.7 / 945.8 / 880.4ms     |
| after  | **210.2 / 224.2 / 227.0ms** |
|        | **4.09x, ranges disjoint**  |

Checked on all three engines before being trusted: ts 225.7, ffi 14.6, wasm 15.7, no `n/a`. In
`bench:usage`, five readings a side:

| row                                            | before |        after |          |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -----: | -----------: | -------- |
| `read: permission check` ts(−)                 |    569 | **2.5-2.6k** | **4.4x** |
| `read: 2-hop recommendation` ts(−)             |    633 |     **2.6k** | **4.1x** |
| `read: permission check (inline anchor)` ts(−) |    611 | **2.0-2.1k** | **3.3x** |
| `read: permission check` ts(+)                 |  37.9k |        59.0k | 1.6x     |
| `read: 2-hop recommendation` ts(+)             |  60.3k |        73.7k | 1.2x     |

The indexed columns improving too is the seed doing its job: the same walk, reached with a
one-vertex candidate set.

The three-run whole-bench screen separates **0 of 25 ts rows** — it was run before this row was
added, so it is purely the regression check, and it is clean.

### Teeth: 22 tests, 19 mutants, 17 caught

Every leg, direction, label and predicate decision has a mutant, and the fixture was built from
that list rather than from the feature. Both survivors are equivalences: routing the UNFILTERED
case through the walk (correct, just slower than the product) and the properly-formed revert
(perf-only).

Two things the sweep caught that the tests had missed:

- **the first leg ignoring its edge TYPE survived.** Every `T1` edge out of my start was the only
  type it had, so dropping the type filter changed nothing. Fixed by giving the start an `OTHER`
  edge to a middle that _does_ have second-leg edges — so an untyped first leg now double-counts.
  Same shape as item 204's DISTINCT survivor: the test reached the path but not the distinction.
- **my first REVERT mutant was malformed and the tests were right to fail it.** Flipping
  `segments.length <= 2` back to `<= 1` without restoring the `else if (!plainNode(start)) return null`
  guard leaves an inline start constraint on a two-hop count silently IGNORED — a wrong answer, not
  a revert. Worth recording: a revert mutant has to restore every half of the change, and a "revert"
  that fails tests is usually a malformed mutant rather than a perf-only one that grew teeth.

Four anchors went non-unique against the one-hop walk's identical predicate and binding lines, each
printing `NOT APPLIED` rather than passing silently — sixth tick running.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as its own command, all three re-run after the
formatter, and the mutation sweep re-run against the formatted tree at 17/19 with every anchor
still applying. 22 new tests (1323 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0 first run, all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps. Every mutation run under `timeout 600` plus a 16G
cgroup cap with swap off.

### Still open

- The **1-hop PROJECTION with a start filter** is untouched at 51.8ms against the count's 14.6.
  That is the one item 205 priced, and its decline really is deliberate — `carriedWhere` refuses it
  so it reaches the index seed, 0.6ms indexed against 51.8 unindexed, 89x. Taking it needs the
  runtime decline 205 describes, and unlike the count there is no seeding route that makes the
  decline unnecessary, because the walk must emit rows. Still the right shape of work; still
  carrying the 3.1x-threshold risk 205 recorded.
