## 226. The Gremlin surface's two biggest gaps are a shared floor and a TinkerPop guarantee — both retracted

Ten items of this pass were GQL-only, so the Gremlin surface was the obvious unexplored ground.
**No code changed.** Both candidates it offered turned out to be closed already, for different
reasons, and both are recorded because the ratios are large enough that a later sweep would chase
them.

`bun run bench:gremlin`, 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges:

| traversal                 |     ts | native |    ts/nat |
| ------------------------- | -----: | -----: | --------: |
| `V().out().has().count()` | 53.7ms |   1.56 | **34.5x** |
| `V().has(age,gt).count()` |    7.8 |   0.34 |     22.9x |
| `V().out().values(age)`   |  267.6 |  30.75 |      8.7x |
| `V().out().count()`       |    0.0 |   0.60 |   tallied |

### The filtered hop count is a SHARED floor, not a Gremlin gap

34.5x is the biggest ratio in the table, and `filteredHopCount` already exists and already fires
(item 168 made it vertex-driven, 130.1 → 34.1ms). Priced against the GQL spelling of the same
question on one graph in one process:

|                                                                   |        |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | -----: |
| `V().out('KNOWS').has('age', gt(44)).count()`                     | 50.8ms |
| `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE x.age > 44 RETURN count(*)` | 51.9ms |

**Equal.** So the 34.5x is what BOTH surfaces pay against native, which makes it item 200's
adjacency-lookup floor rather than anything Gremlin is missing — a per-vertex `Map.get` on the id,
~180ns, the one the type-first index was refuted for. `V().has(age,gt).count()` is the same story
one shape down.

### The projection gap is a TinkerPop ordering guarantee, and here is the proof

`V().out().values(age)` is the biggest absolute TS row, and the GQL spelling of the same question —
walk 1,000,000 edges, read a far-endpoint property, emit 1,000,000 results — costs half as much
while doing strictly MORE work, because GQL builds a row object per result where Gremlin emits the
raw value:

|                                                    |         | per result |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------: | ---------: |
| `V().out('KNOWS').values('age')`                   | 292.7ms |      293ns |
| `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN x.age AS n` |   138.3 |      138ns |

`hopValuesShortcut` (item 170) is firing — 293ns/row is its documented 251ns/row plus noise — and
its own comment names the constraint. The measurement that settles it is three values wide:

    a1 -> x1,  a1 -> x2,  a2 -> x1       (x1.age = 10, x2.age = 20)

    GREMLIN  [10, 20, 10]    grouped by the START vertex
    GQL      [10, 10, 20]    grouped by the FAR vertex

GQL drives the FAR side, so it reads each far vertex's property ONCE PER VERTEX — 200,000 reads for
1,000,000 rows — where Gremlin must read it once per EDGE. At ~180ns for that random-order lookup
(item 164) a 5x reduction in reads is the whole 138-against-293. **GQL can do it because its row
order is unspecified; Gremlin cannot, because TinkerPop guarantees `V()`-then-adjacency order and
the differential fuzzer compares Gremlin results ORDERED.**

So the 2.12x is the price of a semantic guarantee, not a missing path. It is not closable in the TS
Gremlin engine without breaking the order its own fuzzer checks.

### What this says about the field

Two retractions in a row (223, 226). The count-shortcut family is now answered at one, two and
three segments across every filter position that has a once-per-element place to put a predicate,
and guarded by item 225's probe groups. The large remaining ratios are:

- **shared floors** — the per-vertex adjacency lookup (item 200) and the random-order property read
  (item 164), both of which the type-first index was measured and refuted for;
- **semantic constraints** — TinkerPop's traversal order here, and native's deliberate refusal to
  reverse on an unindexed predicate (item 223);
- **constant factors** — ingest, which item 203 closed as `JSON.parse` + alloc + freeze.

That is a different shape of field from where this pass started, and worth saying plainly rather
than continuing to turn over rows whose numbers are already explained.

### Gates

No code changed, so no bench screen and no mutation sweep — the position items 214, 223 and 225
took. `typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command; full suite exit 0 (1618
tests); all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.

### Still open

- `V().out().dedupe().count()` 3.9x and `V().groupCount(age)` 2.7x, both single-digit milliseconds
  in absolute terms.
- `E().count()` is the one row where TS BEATS native by a wide margin (0.0ms against 12.29). That is
  native leaving something on the table, not a TS win to bank, and it is outside this pass's remit —
  recorded because nothing else in the corpus points at it.

## 227. Every `query()` call re-parses its text — priced at scale, not built

`bun run bench:usage` had never been run in this pass. Its worst ts(+) row against the native
engine is `read: keyed dedup lookup` at 4.16x (26.9k ops/s against 111.8k), and decomposing it
found something underneath every row in that table rather than anything specific to it.

**No code changed.** This entry is the measurement, because the first version of it was a projection
and the projection was challenged — correctly.

### The finding

`query()` is `execute(parse(text, …), graph, params)`. There is no cache, so the same text is
re-lexed, re-parsed and re-compiled on every call. On a ONE-VERTEX graph the whole call is 9.13us
of which parse is 4.54 — i.e. almost all of it is fixed cost, which is what a one-vertex graph is
for.

### Why the one-vertex number was not enough

Projecting a saving from it assumed two things, neither measured: that the fixed cost is independent
of graph size and connectedness, and that cache maintenance is small against it. Both were
challenged and both needed numbers. `execute(preparsedAst)` is exactly what a cache would leave
behind, so `full - execute` is the real saving, measured per scale rather than inferred:

| scale               | `query()` | `parse` | `execute` |     saving |
| ------------------- | --------: | ------: | --------: | ---------: |
| 1 node, no edges    |    9.13us |    4.54 |      4.23 | 4.90 (54%) |
| 20k users, 1 edge   |     30.58 |    4.98 |     24.03 | 6.55 (21%) |
| 20k users, 5 edges  |     32.51 |    5.24 |     25.17 | 7.35 (23%) |
| 200k users, 5 edges |    950.46 |    8.34 |    958.43 | ~0 (noise) |

So **the relative saving collapses with execution cost** — 54% on a trivial query, 23% on this one
at 20k, nothing on a 200k scan. The challenge was right that a one-node projection does not carry.

### The serving shape, which is what the table is about

The row above scans. An INDEXED point lookup is the shape a serving workload actually runs, and
there the picture inverts — note `execute` is FLAT, because an index seek does not care how big the
graph is:

| scale               | `query()` | `execute` | saving |           |
| ------------------- | --------: | --------: | -----: | --------: |
| 20k users, 5 edges  |    8.63us |  **4.26** |   4.37 | **2.03x** |
| 200k users, 5 edges |     14.79 |  **4.27** |  10.52 | **3.46x** |

The saving GROWS with graph size (4.37 → 10.52us) because parse and compile allocate heavily and
allocation is slower against a larger heap, while the seek itself is constant. So for the workload
this bench exists to measure, caching is worth 2-3.5x and gets better at scale, not worse.

### Cache maintenance, measured rather than assumed

A `Map.get` on the 74-character query text: **3.7ns on a hit, 87.7ns on a miss** with a fresh key
each time. Against the 4,540ns of parse it replaces that is **0.08%**, so the concern that every
operation would pay for cache upkeep does not survive measurement. And on the expensive analytical
query, where the saving is ~1%, the maintenance is still 3.7ns — the change cannot make anything
slower in any measured shape.

### Connectedness

Tested at 20k users with 1 edge each against 5: saving 6.55us against 7.35. Essentially flat, which
is what one would expect of work that only reads the query TEXT — but it was worth confirming rather
than asserting, since it was one of the three things the projection assumed.

### An error this found in my own probe

The first pass measured the point lookup at 710us and called it the serving shape. It had indexed
`score` but not `name`, so it was full-scanning — the row where a cache matters most was the row I
had accidentally made expensive. Caught by the number being 50x the bench's own figure for the same
query, which is the check worth keeping: **when a probe disagrees with the standing bench by an
order of magnitude, the probe is wrong until proven otherwise.**

### Not built, and why

Caching changes memory retention for every consumer of `query()`, which is a policy decision with
an API dimension (a bounded internal LRU, or an explicit `prepare()` that callers opt into) rather
than a pure optimization. The numbers above are what that decision needs; the decision itself is
not mine to take unilaterally. Recorded here so it is priced and so the next sweep does not
re-derive it.

### Gates

No code changed, so no bench screen and no mutation sweep. `typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each
exit 0 as their own command; full suite exit 0 (1618 tests); all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.

### Also found in the same table, unpursued

- **A 1.34x spelling gap**: `MATCH (u:User {score: $s, active: true})` is 27.2us against the clause
  spelling's 36.4 for the same answer. That is item 224's cause in a third place — the clause
  conjunct pays a binding round-trip where the inline property is a direct read — and item 224's
  AND-chain restriction is why it was not simply extended: hoisting one conjunct of a clause `AND`
  would let it reject before the other evaluates, swallowing a raise.
- `write: 100 updates in one statement` is the one row where TS massively BEATS the native engine
  (710.4k ops/s against 135.8k). Not a TS win to bank — more likely the two engines are not doing
  the same work there, and it is worth a look before anyone cites that column.

## 228. A bounded parse cache — 1.5-2.6x across the serving surface, and the first version was 16% SLOWER

Item 227 priced the finding: `query()` is `execute(parse(text, …), graph, params)` with no cache, so
the same text is re-lexed, re-parsed and re-compiled on every call, and parse is roughly half of a
cheap indexed query. That entry deliberately stopped short of building, because caching changes
memory retention for every consumer. The decision came back: a bounded internal LRU.

### Safety first, because a cache over a mutable AST would be silently wrong

Reuse is sound only if a `Statement` is INERT. Three properties, verified before a line was
written rather than assumed:

|                                   |                                                            |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `execute` does not mutate the AST | `JSON.stringify` identical before and after                |
| parameters are not baked in       | same text, `$k = 0` then `1` then `0` → 4, 3, 4            |
| graph state is not baked in       | a cached statement sees a vertex added after it was parsed |

A cache over an AST that `execute` annotated would return stale answers on the SECOND call, and
every test that runs a query once would still pass. That is why these are tests and not notes.

### The cap is measured, and it decided the eviction policy

A retained `Statement` is **~2,064 bytes** (2,000 held statements cost 4,032 KB), so 64 entries is
~129 KB. The cap also settles LRU-vs-FIFO, because recency tracking is a `delete` plus a `set` per
hit and this runtime degrades on that as the map grows:

|  cap | `get` only (FIFO) | `get` + `delete` + `set` (LRU) | of the 4,540ns parse |
| ---: | ----------------: | -----------------------------: | -------------------: |
|   64 |             0.1ns |                     **57.2ns** |                 1.3% |
|  256 |              11.0 |                          191.5 |                 4.2% |
| 2000 |              11.4 |                         1179.0 |              **26%** |

So true LRU is affordable at 64 and would not have been at 2000 — at a larger cap the honest choice
would have been FIFO, which costs nothing per hit but keeps the wrong entries.

### The first version was 16% slower, and the challenge that found it

The projected saving came from a ONE-VERTEX graph, and the challenge was direct: does this hold at
200k nodes, does connectedness matter, and does cache upkeep slow every operation? Measuring
exactly that — four workloads spanning the cache's whole behaviour range — found a real regression:

| workload                             | before |          first version |
| ------------------------------------ | -----: | ---------------------: |
| ALL HITS, one text with bound params | 8.38us |    4.62 (1.81x faster) |
| **ALL MISSES, a value in the TEXT**  |   9.26 | **10.73 (16% SLOWER)** |
| working set 16 (fits the cap)        |  24.20 |          17.75 (1.36x) |
| **working set 256 (4x the cap)**     |  34.17 |  **36.90 (8% slower)** |

**The Map operations were not the cost.** The full miss path measures 202ns in isolation, against
1.47us observed. The cost is RETENTION: a parsed statement is ~2KB and used to die young, where a
cache keeps it alive across 64 more allocations — which tenures it and makes collecting it far more
expensive. **A cache that holds objects nothing will ask for again pays GC for the privilege.**

So a text is admitted on its SECOND sighting. The `seenOnce` filter holds TEXTS only — strings the
caller already has — so a single-use query retains nothing beyond its own key:

| workload        | before | with the admission filter |
| --------------- | -----: | ------------------------: |
| ALL HITS        | 8.16us |   **4.40 (1.86x faster)** |
| ALL MISSES      |   8.77 |    **8.91 (flat, 0.98x)** |
| working set 16  |  22.12 |             16.67 (1.33x) |
| working set 256 |  30.98 |   **30.99 (flat, 1.00x)** |

Both regressions gone, the hit path slightly better. The cost is a one-call warmup: a text is
parsed twice before it is cached, which against a hit path repeating thousands of times is not a
trade worth optimising away.

**A claim of mine that this corrected.** Item 227 said the change "cannot make anything slower in
any measured shape", on the strength of the 3.7ns `Map.get`. That was the lookup in isolation, not
the miss PATH, and it was wrong — the first version was 16% slower on a shape the projection had
not covered. The lesson is the familiar one in a new place: **measuring a component is not
measuring the change.**

### Measured

`bun run bench:usage`, the ts(+) column:

| row                                    | before |      after |           |              native |
| -------------------------------------- | -----: | ---------: | --------: | ------------------: |
| read: point lookup                     |  75.4k | **194.2k** | **2.58x** |              240.1k |
| read: permission check                 |  55.6k | **132.8k** |     2.39x | 111.8k — **beaten** |
| read: 2-hop recommendation             |  74.0k | **172.2k** |     2.33x | 158.1k — **beaten** |
| interleaved: write + traversal         |  40.0k |      89.8k |     2.25x |              102.9k |
| write: 100 updates in one transaction  |  98.0k |     213.1k |     2.17x |              239.7k |
| read: permission check (inline anchor) |  71.3k |     153.3k |     2.15x | 140.9k — **beaten** |
| write: property update                 |  95.7k |     186.8k |     1.95x |              226.8k |
| analytic: fan-out spread 1-3 hops      |  33.9k |      57.1k |     1.68x |              137.3k |
| read: keyed dedup lookup               |  26.9k |      42.4k |     1.58x |              111.4k |

1.5-2.6x across the surface, three rows now past the native engine, and the point lookup's gap to
native closed from 3.25x to 1.24x. The ts(-) columns barely move, which is right — those are
scan-dominated and the fixed cost is a rounding error against them.

The BULK bench gains too, which was not predicted: `query: group + aggregate` is 1.33x faster
in-process, because that bench also repeats each query text per rep. Its one slower flag, `query:
distinct over a reversed hop` at 1.05x+ on disjoint ranges, is refuted in-process at **1.03x** —
parse is ~5us against a 65ms query, 0.008%, so the cache cannot reach it.

### Teeth: 15 tests, 9 mutants, 4 caught — and why that number is the honest one

**A cache's failure modes are mostly not answer-observable**, so answer-comparing mutation has
little purchase here. The four caught are the ones that matter: ignoring `maxOperatorChain` on a
hit, never evicting, the admission filter never admitting, and the seen-once set never evicting.

Two of those needed work to become visible:

- **Boundedness was untestable.** Removing the eviction entirely changes no answer, so every test
  passed while the cache grew without limit — a memory leak no correctness suite can see, and
  boundedness is the property this design was chosen for. `parseCacheStats()` now exports size,
  seen and cap, and the bound is asserted across 500 distinct promoted texts.
- **Saturation hid the admission mutant.** The obvious assertion — single-use texts do not grow the
  statement cache — is true either way once the cache is at its cap, because "size unchanged" holds
  for both. Asserting on `seen` instead, which only the filter touches, catches it.

The five survivors are all retention-or-perf properties with answers unchanged: evicting the newest
instead of the oldest, leaving a promoted text in `seenOnce`, the chain-differs `delete`, a cap of
1, and bypassing the cache entirely. The admission filter's benefit is a PERF property, and its
only guard is the probe above — a timing assertion in the suite would be flaky, which is this
repo's standing position.

**A comment of mine that mutation corrected.** I had written that the chain-differs `delete`
"replaces rather than keeping a stale parse". It does not — `Map.set` already replaces. The delete
only moves the entry to the end so the replacement counts as recently used. Removing it changes no
answer, which is how the mutant exposed the wrong reason behind right code.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command. 15 new tests (1633 in the gql
package), full suite exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green, mutation re-run against the
formatted tree.

### Still open

- **The compile half.** This caches PARSE only, which is what the measured saving was
  (`full − execute(ast)`); `execute` still compiles its AST on every call, worth a further ~4.3us.
  Caching that needs a different seam and a check that no compile-time decision reads the graph —
  its own item, with its own measurement.
- A `prepare()` API for callers wanting explicit control, recorded as the follow-up it was offered
  as.
- `parseQuery` (the tooling export) stays uncached on purpose: it takes arbitrary tooling input,
  which is the shape an admission filter exists to keep out.

## 229. The compile half — a point lookup at 1.12M ops/s, and a 24% regression I invented

Item 228 cached PARSE and left `compile`, the other ~3.5us of a cheap query's fixed cost. `execute`
now memoises the compiled plan in a `WeakMap` keyed on the AST. Together the two caches take an
indexed point lookup from ~8.8us to ~0.8us.

### Why reuse is sound, checked before writing anything

`compile(query: Query): Plan` takes NO GRAPH — the type says a plan cannot depend on one. The
remaining risk was whether a plan bakes in anything about its parameters, and it does not:

|                              |                                                             |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| reuse with a different param | `$k = 1` then `2` → different, correct answers              |
| reuse with a MISSING param   | still raises `E_MISSING_PARAMETER`, as a fresh compile does |
| reuse across two graphs      | each graph answers for itself, interleaved                  |
| reuse after a mutation       | sees a vertex added after the plan was compiled             |

A plan that had baked in a parameter, a graph, or a validation decision would be wrong only on the
SECOND call, and every test that runs a query once would still pass. So these are tests.

### Measured

|                                      | parse cache only |  + plan cache |                           |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------: | ------------: | ------------------------: |
| ALL HITS, one text with bound params |     4.03-18.37us | **0.67-4.01** |       **6.02x, disjoint** |
| ALL MISSES, a fresh AST every call   |       8.41-50.63 |    8.67-49.49 | 0.97x, **ranges overlap** |

`bun run bench:usage`, ts(+), against the pre-228 baseline:

| row                                    | before |      after |           | native |
| -------------------------------------- | -----: | ---------: | --------: | -----: |
| read: point lookup                     |  75.4k |  **1.12M** | **14.9x** | 233.5k |
| read: 2-hop recommendation             |  74.0k | **552.7k** |      7.5x | 156.0k |
| interleaved: write + traversal         |  40.0k | **277.3k** |      6.9x | 102.5k |
| read: permission check                 |  55.6k | **380.1k** |      6.8x | 112.1k |
| interleaved: write + point read        |  50.5k |     289.0k |      5.7x | 112.1k |
| read: permission check (inline anchor) |  71.3k |     348.5k |      4.9x | 134.1k |
| write: 100 updates in one transaction  |  98.0k |     423.3k |      4.3x | 242.6k |
| analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops     |  34.5k |     127.0k |      3.7x | 140.9k |
| write: property update                 |  95.7k |     321.6k |      3.4x | 230.7k |

The bulk bench is flat — every row's range overlaps — which is right: 3.5us against a 100ms
traversal is nothing, and against the 3-4ms rows it is 0.1%.

### The regression I invented, and the harness that invented it

The first version was this same WeakMap. Measuring it against the one bench row that interpolates
values into the query TEXT — `INSERT (:Event {name: 'ev<i>', …})`, so every call is a fresh AST and
a guaranteed miss — read **9.69us against 12.67, 24% slower**. I took that as real, reasoned that
registering a weak entry carries GC bookkeeping paid on every miss for nothing, and redesigned:
the plan moved into item 228's parse-cache entry, compiled on promotion, so only a text that had
earned a cached AST got a cached plan. That measured 0.88x — still 12% slower.

**Then I checked the harness.** That workload inserts 4,000 vertices into a fresh graph per rep, so
the heap grows under the measurement:

    parse-only   7.13, 8.00, 11.14, 13.97, 21.02, 24.69, 28.99, 31.25 us
    + plan       8.92, 9.20, 10.80, 11.57, 18.07, 23.63, 27.35, 32.92

A 4.4x spread with the ranges almost entirely overlapping. **It cannot resolve a 20% effect, and I
had used it twice before looking at it.** Re-measured on a FIXED graph with varying query text —
the same all-miss question without the growth confound — the miss path is **0.97x with ranges
overlapping**. And the original WeakMap version, retested on that harness, is **0.99x, also
overlapping**.

So the regression never existed, the redesign was unnecessary, and it was reverted. The shipped
code is the three-line WeakMap: simpler, and it helps any caller holding a repeated AST rather than
only those going through `query`/`gql`.

This is item 228's lesson arriving in a new costume. There it was _measuring a component is not
measuring the change_ — a 3.7ns `Map.get` instead of the miss path. Here it is the other half:
**a measurement is only evidence if the harness can resolve the effect, and that is a property to
check BEFORE acting on the number, not after.** Both times the error pointed the same way — toward
believing a reading because it was convenient to act on.

### Teeth: 9 tests, 5 mutants, 3 caught

The dangerous one is caught: **consulting the cache before the read-only guard**. Transaction
control and the read-only check are properties of the graph and the moment, not of the statement,
so they sit in front of the cache; a mutant that lets a cached write plan skip them fails. Also
caught: returning a hit without checking there was one, and removing the tx-control short-circuit
so control statements get planned.

Of the two survivors, one is the expected perf-only (never storing the plan — the pre-229
behaviour). The other was **mis-written by me**: `planCache.set(stmt, compile(stmt))` stores a
second compile of the SAME statement, which is equivalent by construction rather than a different
statement. Recorded as a bad mutant, not as a finding.

The read-only test also needed rewriting before it meant anything. Its first version asserted that
`isReadOnlyTransaction()` returns a boolean — a test shaped like a test that checks nothing. The
real one warms the plan outside a transaction, then requires the same AST to be refused inside a
READ ONLY one, and requires the write not to have landed.

**Noticed in passing:** the READ ONLY flag SURVIVES a rolled-back transaction, so a write issued
afterwards is refused until `setTransactionReadOnly(false)` is called explicitly. The API is a
manual switch rather than something a transaction scopes, so this may be intended — recorded
rather than worked around silently, because a spurious refusal after an aborted transaction would
be an unpleasant surprise.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command (typecheck caught `parse`
returning `Statement` where `compile` wants `Query`). 9 new tests (1642 in the gql package), full
suite exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green. A crash in the generated mutation script —
it inherited item 224's double-mutant tail without its definition — left the tree CLEAN, because
item 224's own lesson had already moved the restore to before that block.

### Still open

- `read: keyed dedup lookup` is now the weakest serving row at 51.9k against native's 111.5k; its
  execution is a 200-candidate post-filter, not fixed cost, so the caches cannot help it.
- `interleaved: append + link` barely moved (57.9k → 61.2k): it writes, so its cost is the write
  path rather than query preparation.
- A `prepare()` API, still the offered follow-up for callers wanting explicit control.

## 230. An AND of equalities, and the clause spelling that cost 2.25x the inline one

`read: keyed dedup lookup` was the weakest ts(+) serving row after item 229, and item 229 had
recorded its cost as "a 200-candidate post-filter, not fixed cost, so the caches cannot reach it."
That was right about the caches and wrong about the post-filter being irreducible. The query is

    MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.score = $s AND u.active = true RETURN count(*) AS c

with `score` indexed and `active` not. It seeds from the index, walks 200 candidates and applies
the predicate to each — and it applied that predicate **2.25x more expensively than the same
question written inline**, which is this engine's named bug class sitting in the open on the most
ordinary filtered count there is.

### Diagnosis: both spellings reach the tally, so it is not a declined path

The first probe varied one axis at a time over the 200-candidate shape, timing both case orders
(item 182's position penalty):

|                                                                 |        µs |           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | --------: | --------- |
| THE ROW: `WHERE u.score = $s AND u.active = true`, `count(*)`   |     20.96 |           |
| the same answer as `(u:User {active: true}) WHERE u.score = $s` | **14.19** | **1.48x** |
| the same answer as `(u:User {score: $s, active: true})`         |     13.42 | 1.56x     |
| `WHERE u.score = $s` alone, `count(*)`                          |     14.89 |           |
| `WHERE u.score = $s` alone, 200 rows RETURNED                   |     19.06 |           |

Same answer, 66, from every spelling. The last two rows are what ruled out the obvious theory:
the clause-AND **count** (20.96) costs more than RETURNING 200 full rows for one conjunct (19.06),
so it is not that the shortcut declined and fell back to row building — `patternCountOf` carries a
clause `WHERE` for the node-only shape and has since item 135. The cost is per candidate.

200 candidates cannot resolve a per-candidate effect, so the second probe **held the scan fixed**
and made it big: the same 20,000-vertex label bucket with no index seek, varying only the spelling.

| spelling                                       | before |    after |                       |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -----: | -------: | --------------------- |
| clause `WHERE u.active = true`                 |   29.0 | **19.7** | 1.47x                 |
| inline `{active: true}`                        |   17.2 |     17.9 | control               |
| clause `WHERE u.active = $a`                   |   35.4 |     30.0 | param, declines       |
| inline `{active: $a}`                          |   21.0 |     21.9 | control               |
| clause `WHERE u.active = true AND u.score = 7` |   47.4 | **20.5** | **2.31x**             |
| inline `{active: true, score: 7}`              |   21.1 |     18.6 | control               |
| clause `AND`, one literal + one PARAM eq       |      — |     24.2 | the bench row's shape |
| clause `u.active = true AND u.score > 7`       |   49.7 |     50.3 | declines, control     |

ns per vertex, min of 14 readings each, both orders. Three inline controls and the declining
inequality case are flat; the two spellings the change reaches close to within 10% of inline.

### The cause, and why item 224 had left it

`satisfies` evaluates a compiled `where` through `compileExpr`, and the generic evaluator **reads
its element back out of the binding** — item 216's finding, now in a third place. Item 224 added
`eqProps` for exactly this: a `<ownVar>.<key> = <non-null literal>` predicate compiled to read the
element DIRECTLY. Two things kept it from reaching here:

1. **`compilePredicate` was called without `ownVar`** at the node-count tally's clause `WHERE`,
   because the argument was documented as being for an inline predicate only — where `inlineOf`
   has proved element-locality. But the tally proves exactly the same thing, three lines earlier,
   with `freePredicateVars`. One argument.
2. **`directEqProps` took exactly one comparison, never an AND-chain**, and item 224 wrote down
   why: `AND` here does not short-circuit (`compileExpr`'s `and` arm evaluates every item), while
   `eqProps` does, so hoisting one conjunct ahead of a sibling that RAISES would swallow the raise.

The second is a real constraint and the fix answers it rather than working around it: **admit an
AND-chain only when EVERY conjunct is `<ownVar>.<key> = <closed value>`.** A closed `=` cannot
raise in this engine — cross-type `=` is a no-match where `<=` throws, and `structuralEq` ends in
`===` — so when the whole chain is equalities there is nothing for a reordering to swallow. The
literal-valued conjuncts lift into `eqProps`; param-valued ones stay in `where` in their original
relative order. One conjunct of any other shape declines the whole chain, which is not caution: a
residual that CAN raise is precisely the case the paragraph above forbids.

Params stay behind because their value is unknown at compile time and `structuralEq(null, null)` is
TRUE where `=` is UNKNOWN — so `$p` resolving to null would match a stored null. Lifting them needs
a per-execution check on the resolved value; that is the open follow-up, and it is what the bench
row's remaining 24.2 ns a vertex is.

The same one-argument change went to the other four tally sites that had already proved locality
the same way: the two-hop MIDDLE clause predicate, the three-hop INTERIOR one, the grouped tally
and the keyed one.

### Measured: the row

`bun run bench:usage`, ts, three runs a side, the dist rebuilt and verified between sides:

| row                                | before               | after                 |                     |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------- |
| `read: keyed dedup lookup` ts(+)   | 59.0, 59.6, 61.0k    | **76.7, 76.8, 80.7k** | **1.30x, disjoint** |
| `read: keyed dedup lookup` ts(−)   | 1.1, 1.2, 1.3k       | **2.5, 2.5, 2.6k**    | **2.1x, disjoint**  |
| `read: point lookup` (control)     | 1.06, 1.09, 1.11M    | 1.15, 1.22, 1.45M     | control             |
| `read: permission check` (control) | 398.1, 398.2, 409.1k | 388.3, 398.5, 417.2k  | flat                |

The ts(−) column is the honest statement of the change: with no index the query walks all 20,000
vertices, so the per-vertex cost is the whole cost and the 2.1x matches the component measurement.
The indexed column gets 1.30x because only ~9 µs of its ~17 µs was predicate evaluation.

**A retraction of my own number.** Item 229 recorded this row at 51.9k. Measured on this box today
the before is 59.0-61.0k, so the gain is 1.30x and not the 1.52x the recorded figure would have
given. The recorded number came from a different session's run and I nearly reported against it;
measuring the before is the only reason the entry says 1.30x.

### The bulk screen flagged three rows, all refuted

`bun run bench`, ts, three runs a side, flagged `query: distinct + order by` (3.5-3.5 → 3.7-8.4 ms),
`query: top groups by count` (3.4-3.7 → 4.1-11.7) and `query: distinct over a reversed hop`
(65.3-72.8 → 69.3-92.1). None of the three has a `WHERE` clause or an inline property predicate, so
the diff's own logic cannot reach them — but that is not sufficient here, because this engine has
twice measured an unrelated query gaining a new slow mode purely because a module GREW (items 181
and 206), and this change adds ~60 lines to `executor.ts`. So the flag was priced.

Both BUILT bundles imported into one process, alternated round by round on one graph with the
side order swapped each round, answers asserted equal first:

|                                       | before    | after        |                |
| ------------------------------------- | --------- | ------------ | -------------- |
| FLAGGED distinct + order by           | 3.5-5.0   | 3.5-4.9 ms   | 0.99x, overlap |
| FLAGGED top groups by count           | 3.0-4.5   | 3.0-4.4      | 1.01x, overlap |
| FLAGGED distinct over a reversed hop  | 61.7-80.9 | 63.5-70.9    | 0.97x, overlap |
| control project 3 columns (unreached) | 11.5-23.9 | 11.5-23.5    | 1.00x          |
| control count distinct (unreached)    | 3.4-5.3   | 3.3-5.0      | 1.01x          |
| control AND of two eq (REACHED)       | 11.9-19.0 | **8.5-12.8** | 1.40x          |

All three refuted; the reached control moves, which is what says the harness could have seen an
effect if there were one. Three runs a side cannot resolve a 4 ms row — the same conclusion items
216 and 226 reached about the same screen.

`bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000`: **0 groups disagree on the answer, 0 groups over 2x.** The
item's own group was added to the probe — the clause AND against the inline form, the two
half-and-half spellings, and the reversed-operand form, which is the member that would catch a
mishandled flip in `asPropCompare` — and it spans 3.93-4.32 ms, a spread of 1.10x.

### Teeth: 15 tests, 11 mutants, and two surprises

8 of 11 behaved as predicted, including every mutant that half-applies a predicate: admitting any
operator rather than `=`, lifting a `null` literal, lifting params, DROPPING the residual so a
param conjunct is never applied. Three survive by construction and are labelled: keeping the whole
`where` as the residual (the same predicate twice), never lifting (the pre-230 behaviour), and
wrapping a lone residual in an `and` of one.

**Mutant 5 found fixture blindness in my own tests.** Dropping an inadmissible conjunct instead of
declining the chain survived, and the reason is that every chain in the fixture was made of
COMPARISONS — an inequality declines through the operator check and never reaches the branch that
decides what to do with a conjunct the rule cannot read. `WHERE n.k = 1 AND n.j IS NOT NULL` is not
a `compare` at all; three of five vertices have `k = 1` and only two of those have a `j`, so the
mutant answers 3 where the truth is 2. With that case the mutant is caught.

**The own-variable check could not be made observable, and the search for a shape that would is
the finding.** Removing it survives, which says only that it is redundant with the caller's
`freePredicateVars` guard; the discipline is then a DOUBLE mutant removing both. That survived too.
Rather than keep writing mutants, the guard was instrumented to print when it fires: **it never
fires across all 1,656 tests.** Probing shapes by hand found the one that reaches it — a correlated
`CALL (m) { MATCH (n:P) WHERE … }` body, whose count is a single-node pattern with a clause `WHERE`
reading the OUTER variable. That shape now has a test (it was uncovered either way, and
`WHERE m.k = 1` has the exact form `directEqProps` lifts, told apart only by the variable). But the
double mutant still answers correctly on it, so some third mechanism downstream makes the lift
unreachable. **I could not construct a distinguishing input; the check stays, labelled defensive.**
That is item 224's own conclusion about its param clause, reached the same way — by mutation rather
than by reading the code.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each run as their own command and exit 0 (lint caught a nested
ternary and a `prefer-optional-chain` on the first pass). 15 new tests, 1,656 in the gql package,
full suite exit 0. All seven byte-identity fuzzers green. The mutation sweep ran under
`timeout 900` plus a 16 G cgroup scope with `MemorySwapMax=0`, proven to kill first with an
allocator bomb (137) and a bare loop (124); pristine copies live under
`crates/lenke-engine/target/mutation-backup/`, and the harness restores BEFORE applying each
mutant rather than only after the loop.

### Still open

- **Lifting a PARAM-valued conjunct**, which is the bench row's remaining cost (24.2 against the
  all-literal 20.5 ns a vertex). It needs a once-per-execution check that the resolved value is not
  nullish, since `structuralEq(null, null)` is true where `=` is UNKNOWN. The check is cheap and
  the place for it is known; it was left out of this item to keep the semantics one question.
- **`compileNode` does not pass `ownVar` either**, so the GENERAL path's inline predicate still
  reads its element through the binding. `directEqProps` self-validates the variable, so this is
  safe on its face — but the general path is where byte-identity against native is measured, and it
  deserves its own measurement rather than riding along on this one.
- A nested `and` under an `and` (from parenthesisation) declines rather than flattening. A missed
  optimisation, not a wrong answer.

## 231. The spelling probe's oldest flag, closed by one argument — and one edit retracted for being unmeasured

After item 230 the `bun run spelling` probe had exactly one group still over its threshold, and it
had been there since item 204:

    MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 2 RETURN n.s AS s     6.70ms
    MATCH (n:P {k: 2})        RETURN n.s AS s     3.81      1.76x

A filtered node projection is the most common query shape there is, so this was the biggest
remaining known gap in the TS engine.

### Diagnosis, and the theory it killed

I expected the clause form to be building a row per vertex and filtering afterwards. The probe
said otherwise. Projecting ALL 200,000 rows unfiltered costs 9.37 ms and the clause-filtered
projection of 2,000 rows cost 9.64 — which fits that theory — but **the gap is flat in the number
of projected columns** (1 column 9.64, 3 columns 10.03; the inline twin 6.78 and 6.84), so it is
not row width. 200,000 × ~14 ns = 2.8 ms against a measured 2.86 ms gap: it is the predicate, read
through the BINDING, once per scanned vertex. Item 230's mechanism one level up.

Both spellings already reach `detectNodeProjection` — it carries a clause `WHERE` through
`nodeWhereOf` — so nothing had declined. And `nodeWhereOf`'s own comment named the reason, in a
note whose history it records as having been wrong twice before:

> `props` is EMPTY on both branches here … `compilePredicate(properties, where)` … does not lift
> equalities out of the `where`.

That was true when item 210 wrote it. Item 224 made it false by adding `eqProps`, and item 230
extended it to an AND-chain — **given `ownVar`**, which was not being passed. The free-variable
loop six lines above is exactly the proof that argument requires. One argument:

| 200,000 vertices, min of 10 readings, both case orders | before |    after |           |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -----: | -------: | --------- |
| clause `WHERE n.k = 2` → `n.s`                         |   9.64 | **6.03** | 1.60x     |
| inline `{k: 2}` → `n.s`                                |   6.78 |     6.06 | control   |
| clause → `n` (the element)                             |   9.99 | **5.97** | 1.67x     |
| clause → `n.k` (the filtered key)                      |   9.64 | **6.38** | 1.51x     |
| clause → 3 columns                                     |  10.03 | **6.32** | 1.59x     |
| no-filter control, 200,000 rows                        |   9.37 |    10.20 | unreached |

And the standing instrument, `bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000`, measured on the same box
either side of the change:

    a filtered node projection (item 204)   6.70 vs 3.81  (1.76x)  ->  3.91 vs 3.75  (1.04x)

**0 groups disagree on the answer, 0 groups over 2x.** That group is closed.

`bench:usage` is FLAT on every row, both columns, which is correct and worth stating: its fixture
indexes `name` and `score`, so a filtered read becomes a seek over a handful of candidates and the
per-vertex predicate cost is invisible. This change shows up where the scan is the work.

### An edit retracted

The same missing argument exists at `detectHopProjection`'s gate, where `whereReadsOnly` proves the
identical precondition. I made the same one-argument change there — and then could not measure it.

|                                                   |    ms |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ----: |
| hop, clause filter on the FAR end, with the edit  | 78.44 |
| hop, clause filter on the FAR end, **without** it | 79.18 |

Identical. The reason is arithmetic: that gate runs once per visited element, so even over a whole
200,000-vertex bucket it is ~2.8 ms against a shape that costs 79 — and the 2.57x gap that shape
_does_ have against its inline spelling therefore is not the gate. **So the edit was dropped.** It
was correct, it was free, and it bought nothing I could demonstrate; shipping it would have put an
unmeasured perf change in the history behind a measured one, which is how a plausible mechanism
becomes a believed one.

### Two findings the probe turned up, both bigger than what it fixed

Adding hop cases to price the retracted edit measured something else entirely, on 200,000 vertices
with one edge each:

|                                                           |         ms |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------: |
| `MATCH (f)<-[:E]-(a:P) RETURN DISTINCT f.t` — NO filter   |  **45.11** |
| the same with `WHERE a.k = 2` (2,000 of 200,000 vertices) | **348.14** |
| the same with inline `(a:P {k: 2})`                       |     295.92 |
| with the filter on the FAR end, clause `WHERE f.k = 2`    |      78.44 |
| with the filter on the FAR end, inline `(f {k: 2})`       |  **28.94** |

1. **A filter on the hop's START side makes the query 6.6-7.7x SLOWER than no filter at all.** A
   predicate selecting 1% of the starts should make this ~100x faster. Both spellings do it, so it
   is not a spelling gap — it is the shape.
2. **A clause filter on the FAR end is 2.57x its inline spelling** (78.44 against 28.94). That is a
   wider gap than the one this item closed, and the spelling probe has no group for it.

Neither is this item's; both are recorded as the next targets rather than folded in.

### Teeth: 10 tests, 5 mutants

The tests **assert the ROWS, not a count**, deliberately: a count cannot see which rows survived, so
a predicate selecting the wrong elements is invisible to it — the failure mode already recorded for
the `examples/` probes, which passed three times while the engine returned wrong rows. One case
projects three columns from the same element for the same reason a one-column fixture cannot
distinguish the right multiset of values from the right rows.

The one mutant caught is the informative one: **passing `ownVar` to the SUBQUERY branch as well
fails 6 tests.** `nodeWhereOf` routes a subquery-bearing predicate through `gatePredicate` so a
cheap conjunct is ordered ahead of the subquery, and the existing comment justified keeping that
discrimination by its 18% on the indexed point lookup. It is also answer-load-bearing, which the
comment did not claim and mutation showed.

The four survivors are all accounted for, and two of them are not findings:

- dropping `nodeVar` again is the pre-231 behaviour (perf-only, by construction);
- passing a WRONG own variable survives because `directEqProps` self-validates the variable — no
  conjunct matches it, so nothing lifts and the predicate stays with the general evaluator;
- removing the free-variable loop survives, and the file **already says so**: that check is
  documented as defensive, because with two clauses, one pattern and no segments `nodeVar` is the
  only bindable name. My "expected caught" was wrong, not the code — I had read the comment and
  predicted against it anyway;
- removing the `itemLocal` gate survives because it is a CONSERVATIVE decline. `ROW_LOCAL_KINDS`
  omits `isNull`, so `WHERE n.j IS NOT NULL` declines this fast path entirely; admitting it is
  answer-equivalent, since `compileExpr` handles `isNull` perfectly well. **A missed fast path, not
  a wrong answer** — and a third open item.

## 232. A one-hop projection drove the wrong end — 15x, and two fixture faults of my own first

Item 231's retracted edit left a hop finding behind, which I reported as "a filter on the START
side costs 6.6-7.7x the UNFILTERED hop — both spellings, so it is the shape, not a spelling gap."

**That was wrong, and so were the numbers under it.** Varying the arrow direction as its own axis
says it is a spelling gap after all, and the two fixtures I measured it on were each broken in a
way this file has a name for.

### Two fixture faults, found before the numbers were used

**Every vertex had the same label.** `orient` reverses a path when `endEst.count <
startEst.count`, both from label buckets — so a fixture where every vertex is `:P` makes the far
end's bucket the WHOLE GRAPH, the two estimates tie, and no reversal is possible. The 28x I
measured was partly an artefact of that, and it also mis-attributed the cause to the filter.
This is the recorded single-label trap, and it is the second time it has cost an item here.

**Then the selective-label cases returned 0 rows.** `:A` was `i % 10 === 0` and the filter was
`k = i % 100 = 2`, which no `:A` vertex can satisfy — so I was measuring empty-answer discovery,
the empty-predicate trap. Both are mine; both were caught on the probe rather than in an entry.

### The honest diagnosis

With a correct fixture (200,000 vertices, one edge each, `:A` on a tenth of them):

|                                                    |   rows |          ms |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -----: | ----------: |
| `MATCH (f)<-[:E]-(a:A) RETURN f.t` — **no filter** | 20,000 |   **130.2** |
| `MATCH (a:A)-[:E]->(f) RETURN f.t` — **no filter** | 20,000 |     **7.5** |
| the same pair with a filter on the `:A` end        |    200 | 129.9 / 0.5 |

**17.4x on the UNFILTERED question**, and that is the one that matters: with no predicate anywhere,
it rules out every predicate-based explanation at once — `orient`'s unindexed-predicate blindness,
and item 223's reversal WON'T-FIX, which was checked first precisely so as not to relitigate it.
Item 223 declines a SPECULATIVE reversal that trades a seed pre-filter for a post-filter on a
guessed selectivity. Nothing here is guessed.

Instrumenting the shortcut ladder settled where the cost is, rather than inferring it:

| query                                 | shortcut selected                  |
| ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `(a:A)-[:E]->(f) … RETURN f.t`        | `hopProjection`                    |
| `(f)<-[:E]-(a:A) … RETURN f.t`        | `hopProjection` — **the same one** |
| `(f)<-[:E]-(a:A) RETURN DISTINCT f.t` | `distinctProjection`               |
| the same with any filter              | **nothing** — general path         |

So the plain projection is not a declined path; it is one path, 17x apart on which end it drives.
`detectHopProjection` routes a projection that reads the START to `filteredHopWalk` (via
`needsStart`), and that walk always enumerated `candidateVertexSource(graph, startLabel)` — the
unlabelled 200,000 — resolving the far endpoint per edge to test the `:A` label. Its forward twin
reads the FAR end, takes the plain pair instead, and that pair's own dispatch happens to drive the
labelled side. Neither considered which end was cheaper.

### The change

`hopDrivesFar(graph, startLabel, farLabel)` — exported — is `candidateCount(far) <
candidateCount(start)`, and `farDrivenFilteredHopWalk` is the mirror it chooses: enumerate the far
candidates, resolve the START endpoint per edge.

**Why it is provable rather than an estimate**, which is the bar item 223 set: both walks visit the
same qualifying edges, so the EDGE term is identical and they differ only in how many vertices they
enumerate. Driving the smaller candidate set is cheaper by exactly that difference. (Usually by
more: driving the labelled side walks only the edges incident to that label.)

Three details that are not arbitrary:

- **STRICTLY smaller**, so a tie keeps the current side. The two walks meet rows in different
  orders and reordering an un-ordered projection for no gain is churn — and the tie case is
  exactly the single-label fixture above, which correctly does not move (193.2 → 198.2).
- **`candidateCount` scores a label it cannot seed from as the whole graph**, so the strict
  comparison ALSO establishes that the far label is seekable: a non-simple one can never be
  strictly less than the start's own count. The mirror keeps a defensive re-check anyway.
- **`farPred` is checked INSIDE the edge loop** although `far` is fixed for the whole loop and
  hoisting it would be free. Not free in RAISES: a far vertex reachable only from vertices that
  fail the START label is never reached by the start-driven walk, so a constraint that faults on it
  must not fault here. Mutation confirms the hoist raises and the test catches it.

It is one early return in the existing closure, and the mirror is its own closure built per
compile — item 159 measured 1.6x on the hot shape from a branch inside that inner loop, and 1.29x
from a shared module-scope walk whose call sites go polymorphic.

### Measured

| 200,000 vertices, `:A` on a tenth          | before |   after |                     |
| ------------------------------------------ | -----: | ------: | ------------------- |
| reversed, no filter (20,000 rows)          |  130.2 | **8.6** | **15.1x**           |
| reversed, filter on the far end (200 rows) |  129.9 | **7.8** | **16.7x**           |
| forward, no filter                         |    7.5 |     7.4 | control             |
| forward, filter on the start               |    0.5 |     0.5 | control             |
| EVERY vertex `:A`, reversed (the tie)      |  193.2 |   198.2 | correctly unchanged |

`bench:usage`: every row's range overlaps, before and after — right, since its fixture has no
one-hop projection with a selective far label.

The bulk screen flagged two disjoint rows, `traverse 1-hop project` (121.2-125.2 → 125.6-127.1,
1.03x SLOWER) and `distinct over a reversed hop` (68.7-71.6 → 64.4-67.6, 1.07x faster). 3% of a
125 ms row is 3.8 ms, which two bucket lookups cannot explain, so both were priced in-process —
answers compared as MULTISETS, because meeting rows from the other end is the whole point:

|                                           | before      | after          |                     |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------- | -------------- | ------------------- |
| FLAGGED traverse 1-hop project            | 143.2-156.4 | 142.0-164.8 ms | 1.01x, overlap      |
| FLAGGED distinct over a reversed hop      | 56.0-73.4   | 57.6-71.5      | 0.97x, overlap      |
| control reversed hop, far label (REACHED) | 118.4-151.5 | **15.6-21.8**  | **7.59x, disjoint** |
| control forward hop, start label          | 11.1-17.4   | 11.0-15.6      | 1.01x               |
| control project 3 columns                 | 8.7-13.7    | 8.8-12.9       | 0.99x               |

Both refuted, with a reached control that moves 7.59x so the harness is shown to resolve.

### Teeth: 12 tests, 9 mutants, 9 as predicted

**A drive side is answer-preserving**, so no row assertion can catch choosing the wrong one — a
mutant that never switches sides passes every result test. `hopDrivesFar` is therefore exported and
asserted directly, which is the escape items 172/173 found after 167/168 hit the same wall. All
four decision mutants are caught: never switching, always switching, switching on a tie, and
comparing the two counts the wrong way round.

The mirror itself IS answer-visible, and its mutants are caught by cross-spelling row comparisons:
reading the same adjacency index instead of the opposite one (18 failures), resolving the wrong
endpoint (17), dropping the start label (1). The tests project a column from EACH end for that
reason — a mirror that resolved the wrong endpoint returns the same number of rows with the two
values exchanged, which a one-column projection cannot see.

The one survivor is the defensive far-label re-check, which is defensive by construction and
labelled so.

Reserved words bit a fixture for the FOURTH time (`Right`). The standing rule — invent obvious
non-words — now has `Keepr` and `Skipr` to go with `Univ`, `LEGA`, `LEGM`, `LEGZ`.

### Still open

- **`bun run spelling` cannot guard this gap.** It compares answers with `JSON.stringify`, which is
  order-sensitive, so it cannot hold a group whose members legitimately differ in ROW ORDER — and
  the arrow-direction pair is exactly such a group. Giving it an opt-in unordered comparison is a
  change to its core check and wants its own item; the correctness guard meanwhile is
  `hop-drive-side.test.ts`, which compares as multisets.
- **`detectDistinctProjection` declines ANY filtered hop** — clause or inline, either direction —
  even though its shape already carries a `gatePred`. `distinctShape` requires the `WHERE` to read
  the same end the PROJECTION reads (`whereReadsOnly(where, keyedVar)`), so a filter on the other
  end declines. Worth 11-40x on the same fixture and needs the gate variable separated from the
  keyed variable.
- **A PRE-EXISTING raise divergence between two spellings**, found while building the raise test and
  confirmed against the unmodified build: an inline faulting `WHERE` on the pattern's START node
  raises where the same constraint on the FAR node does not, because the start's predicate is
  evaluated for every candidate while the far's is evaluated only for ends actually reached.
  `(n:Keepr)-[:E]->(t:Target WHERE trim(t.s) = 'x')` answers; `(t:Target WHERE trim(t.s) =
'x')<-[:E]-(n:Keepr)` raises `E_INVALID_VALUE`. Not this item's, and likely a native divergence
  too.

## 233. The same asymmetry in a dedup — and why item 232's criterion could not be reused

Item 232 recorded the next target as "`detectDistinctProjection` declines ANY filtered hop …
worth 11-40x". **That was wrong, and measuring it inverted the picture.** On 200,000 vertices with
`:Few` on a tenth:

|                                         | routing                       |        ms |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | --------: |
| `DISTINCT`, no filter, reversed         | **accepted** by the fast path | **111.4** |
| `DISTINCT`, no filter, forward          | accepted                      |   **8.9** |
| `DISTINCT`, filter on the other end     | **declined** → general path   |  4.7-29.1 |
| `DISTINCT`, filter on the PROJECTED end | accepted                      |     112.4 |

The cases it accepts are the slow ones, and declining is not the problem.

**The invalid comparison I nearly acted on** was 111.4 (accepted, UNFILTERED) against 29.1
(declined, FILTERED) — different queries, where the filter cuts 20,000 starts to 200. Forcing the
SAME queries both ways, with a temporary env gate on `detectDistinctProjection`, showed the fast
path and the general path cost the same on every hop-distinct row. **The gate was verified to
work** before that was believed: a NODE distinct is 3.5 ms with the fast path and 104.4 without,
30x. So the fast path is real — it saves ROW MATERIALIZATION, and a hop distinct materializes one
row per qualifying edge (20,000) where a node distinct materializes 200,000. Hence nothing to save
here, and the 111 vs 9 ms is item 232's drive-side asymmetry, in BOTH paths.

### Why the cheap criterion does not transfer, which is the point of the item

Item 232 compares two bucket SIZES and nothing else. It can, because a plain projection emits one
row per edge — so both walks visit the same qualifying edges, the edge term CANCELS, and only the
vertex count is left.

A dedup keyed on the START breaks at the first qualifying edge (`if (onStart) break`), so its edge
term is sublinear and workload-dependent. The adversarial case is not hypothetical: 100 far vertices
of degree 10,000 (1,000,000 incident edges) against 200,000 starts whose break fires on edge one
(200,000 edge visits). A bucket comparison switches into that and is **2.5x worse**. By item 223's
rule — fire only on a provable win — it must not.

So `dedupDrivesFar` MEASURES instead:

- `|S|` (`candidateCount(startLabel)`) is a LOWER BOUND on the start-driven walk: every start
  candidate costs a bucket lookup even with no edges.
- `|F| + E_F` is EXACTLY the far-driven walk — one lookup per far candidate plus one visit per
  incident edge. Each `E_F` term is an O(1) adjacency `size` read, and it is work the far-driven
  walk pays anyway.
- **The early exit is what makes the probe safe**, not tidy: it abandons as soon as the running cost
  reaches `|S|`, so the probe can never spend more than the walk it is deciding against. In the
  adversarial case it gives up after 200,000 increments and keeps the start-driven walk.
- The cheap `|F| < |S|` precondition runs first, so the probe is never paid where it cannot pay off
  — and, as in item 232, `candidateCount` scoring an unseekable label as the whole graph makes that
  comparison also establish the far label has a bucket to enumerate.

`walkFarSideResolvingStart` is the walk it chooses. Not `walkFarSide`, which offers the FAR element
and only asks whether its bucket exists — that answers "which far vertices are reached", the
`!onStart` question. This one answers "which START vertices reach a qualifying far vertex", so it
reads the edges, resolves the start, and applies the START LABEL there (the start-driven walk gets
that label implicitly from its enumeration).

`take` is offered the same start once per qualifying edge rather than once. Sound because it is
IDEMPOTENT for a dedup, and the extra calls are counted in the `E_F` term being compared. A gate is
likewise evaluated per edge rather than per vertex; it is pure, so the only observable is a raise,
which happens on the first evaluation either way.

### Measured

| 200,000 vertices, one edge each, `:Few` on a tenth | before |    after |             |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -----: | -------: | ----------- |
| `DISTINCT` reversed, START-keyed, narrow far end   |  115.0 |  **7.5** | **15.3x**   |
| `DISTINCT` reversed, filter on the projected end   |  114.6 |  **8.8** | **13.0x**   |
| `count(DISTINCT …)` reversed — the counting twin   |  114.0 |  **7.7** | **14.8x**   |
| `DISTINCT` forward (far-keyed)                     |   11.3 |     10.5 | control     |
| plain projection reversed (item 232)               |    9.4 |      9.1 | control     |
| **ADVERSARIAL: 10 hubs carrying every edge**       |   37.5 | **37.6** | **refused** |

The adversarial row is the one that matters most: the cost probe declines it and the walk is
unchanged, which is the behaviour a bucket comparison would not have.

**Neither standing bench can see this win**, and that is worth recording rather than hiding: the
bulk bench's `distinct over a hop` / `distinct over a reversed hop` rows label EVERY vertex
`:Person`, so `|F| = |S|` and the precondition refuses; `bench:usage` has no one-hop `DISTINCT` at
all. Both screens are therefore regression screens here, not confirmations — the same situation the
spelling probe was in for item 232.

The bulk screen's only disjoint row is `count 3-hop`, 1.03x FASTER, which the diff cannot reach.
`bench:usage` flagged `analytic: fan-out spread 1-3 hops` (124.6-133.3k → 113.6-121.9k ops/s, 1.08x
slower); its query is a QUANTIFIED pattern, which `distinctShape` declines on `segments.length > 1`,
so it was priced in-process rather than argued away — answers compared as multisets:

|                                         | before       | after           |                      |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------ | --------------- | -------------------- |
| FLAGGED fan-out spread 1-3 hops         | 0.747-3.553  | 0.678-1.738 ms  | 1.10x, overlap       |
| control reversed DISTINCT hop (REACHED) | 8.337-15.314 | **0.321-1.611** | **25.96x, disjoint** |
| control forward DISTINCT hop            | 0.381-0.592  | 0.213-1.020     | overlap              |
| control point lookup                    | 0.600-1.113  | 0.593-1.018     | 1.01x, overlap       |

### Teeth: 12 tests, 10 mutants, 10 caught

A drive side is answer-preserving, so `dedupDrivesFar` is exported and asserted directly. Every
guard is covered: never switching, dropping the cost probe for item 232's bucket comparison,
weakening the cost bound, dropping `!onStart`, dropping `!needsFar`, and inverting the cheap
precondition. The mirror's own mutants are caught by cross-spelling row comparisons — same index,
wrong endpoint, dropped start label.

**Two mutants corrected me rather than the code.**

`10 cost model drops the per-VERTEX term` I predicted would survive, on the grounds that a far side
narrow enough to win is dominated by its edge term. It was CAUGHT, and the case is instructive: 90
far candidates holding 30 edges costs 120 against a start side of 100, so edges alone would switch
into enumerating 90 vertices to find 30 edges. **The per-vertex term is load-bearing and my reason
for doubting it was wrong.**

`9 mirror drops the START label check` survived at first, and the cause was my fixture: every edge
targeted a `:Many`, so the start label rejected nothing, and the case that was supposed to
distinguish could not. Adding ONE `:Few`→`:Few` edge gives the label something to reject — and the
mirror only fires when the far side is narrower, so the test also has to put the narrow label on the
far end. Same shape as every other fixture-blindness entry: the test reached the path but not the
distinction.

### Still open

- The arrow-direction pair still has no guard in `bun run spelling`, for item 232's recorded reason:
  its answer check is `JSON.stringify`, which is order-sensitive, and these spellings legitimately
  differ in row order.
- `distinctShape` still requires the clause `WHERE` to read the same end the projection reads. That
  is now known NOT to be a performance gap — declining lands on a general path that costs the same —
  so it is a spelling-coverage question rather than a target.
- The pre-existing raise divergence from item 232 (an inline faulting `WHERE` on the START node
  raises where the same constraint on the FAR node does not) is untouched.

## 234. A floor measurement that killed two of three targets, and sized the third

A fresh surface: `bun run bench:gremlin`, which this session had not run. Three rows well behind
the native engine:

|                           |     ts | native |    ts/nat |
| ------------------------- | -----: | -----: | --------: |
| `V().has(age,gt).count()` | 7.9 ms |   0.34 | **23.1x** |
| `V().out().values(age)`   |  284.9 |  30.46 |      9.4x |
| `V().out().has().count()` |   50.3 |   1.55 | **32.6x** |

The temptation is to take the 32.6x. **The floor measurement says not to.** For each shape, what
does the same answer cost written by hand against the same indexes — the question item 204 asked,
and the only way to tell a recoverable overhead from a data layout TS cannot reach. All six rows in
ONE process, because two processes are not a comparison:

|                                   |        ms | ns a vertex |
| --------------------------------- | --------: | ----------: |
| ENGINE `V().has().count()`        |      7.65 |        38.2 |
| **floor** `V().has().count()`     |  **2.30** |    **11.5** |
| ENGINE `V().out().has().count()`  |     50.62 |       253.1 |
| **floor** same, vertex-driven     | **44.24** |       221.2 |
| floor same, index-driven          |     45.65 |       228.2 |
| floor scan only, no property read |      0.91 |         4.6 |

So:

- **`V().out().has().count()` is already AT its floor** — 50.62 against 44.24, 1.14x. Its count
  shortcut exists and already drives the far side (item 168); the 253ns a vertex is the
  string-keyed `index.get(v.id)` lookup, and a hand-written loop pays the same. The 32.6x gap to
  native is a DATA-LAYOUT difference. **Retracted**, and so is the index-driven variant I wrote to
  try to beat it (45.65 against 44.24, overlapping).
- **`V().has().count()` is 3.3x off its floor.** That is the target, and it is the whole of the
  row: 38.2ns a vertex where the tally is 11.5 and the bare scan 4.6.
- `V().out().values(age)` was left alone: its floor is an edge walk resolving 1,000,000 far
  endpoints, so most of the 9.4x is the same lookup, and the far-driven alternative would change
  emission ORDER rather than only cost.

### The change

`vertexStepCount` handled `hasLabel`, `out` and `in` — each a counter or bucket read — and returned
`undefined` for a `has`, so `V().has(k, pred).count()` ran the traverser pipeline: a traverser
allocated per vertex to be filtered and discarded. It now tallies.

**It declines when the index could seed, and that is the load-bearing condition rather than a
nicety.** `countShortcut` is consulted BEFORE `seedFromIndex` in `executor/index.ts`, so a tally
that scanned anyway would answer in O(V) where the general path's seed answers in O(matches) — a
fast path LOSING an index, which is item 149's failure and what
`count-shortcuts-must-seek` records. `seedForStep` is now exported for the purpose: its `count` is
an O(1) estimate and `build()` is never called, so asking costs nothing. **The tally therefore
fires exactly where the general path would have scanned, so it cannot be slower than what it
replaces.**

The decision turns on the PREDICATE and not just the key: an index on `age` does nothing for
`not(gt(44))`, so declining on "the key is indexed" alone would leave the pipeline doing a full
scan it does not need. That case has its own test.

Raise parity is free, and for a stronger reason than usual: `matches` is applied to every vertex in
`verticesById` order, which is exactly what `V()` emits and what the `has` step filters — the
evaluated set and its order are identical. (`matches` is total anyway; the ordering predicates
return false for a missing or incomparable value rather than throwing. The comment in
`filteredHopCount` claiming it can throw a cross-type error looks stale.)

### Measured

`bun run bench:gremlin`, three runs a side, rebuilt and verified between sides. Every row's
`answers` column reads `same` in all six runs:

| row                          | before        | after             |                    |
| ---------------------------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ------------------ |
| `V().has(age,gt).count()`    | 7.7, 7.9, 8.0 | **2.2, 2.2, 2.3** | **3.4x, disjoint** |
| `V().out().values(age)`      | 273.7-281.4   | 273.5-283.1       | overlap            |
| `V().out().has().count()`    | 49.6-50.2     | 47.1-51.5         | overlap            |
| `V().groupCount(age)`        | 7.3-7.6       | 7.3-7.6           | flat               |
| `V().out().dedupe().count()` | 6.9           | 6.9-7.1           | overlap            |
| the four counter rows        | 0.0           | 0.0               | flat               |

`ts/nat` on the changed row goes 23.1 → 6.6, and in-process the engine lands at 2.46ms against its
own 2.57ms floor — i.e. the row is now at the floor rather than merely nearer it.

**The GQL benches were not run as a before/after, and the reason is checkable rather than a
judgement**: `bench.ts`, `bench-usage.ts` and `spelling-probe.ts` contain zero references to
`@lenke/gremlin`, so they never load the changed module. That is stronger evidence than a
measurement of them would be. The full monorepo suite covers them for correctness.

### Teeth: 10 tests, 7 mutants, 7 caught

A count shortcut is ANSWER-PRESERVING, so the tests that matter assert the DECISION — `countShortcut`
is exported, and a mutant that simply never claims the shape passes every row assertion in the
package. All seven behave as predicted, including the two that matter most: **dropping the index
decline** (so the tally preempts a seek) and **inverting it** (claiming only the seekable case).

The row tests are built against the ways a tally goes wrong rather than the ways it goes right. The
fixture carries a vertex with NO `age` and one with a NULL `age`, so:

- a predicate matching nothing must answer 0 and not the vertex count;
- a predicate matching "everything" (`gt(-1)`) must answer 12 of 14 and not 14 — a one-sided
  fixture cannot see that;
- `not(gt(44))` must answer 7 and not 5, because a negated predicate IS true of a missing value.

### Still open

- `V().out().has().count()` at 33x native is a data-layout gap, recorded as such. The TS cost is the
  per-vertex `edgesToByLabel.get(v.id)` string-keyed lookup, which both the shortcut and a
  hand-written loop pay.
- `V().out().values(age)` at 8.6x. A far-driven version — iterate the far index, emit each
  vertex's value `degree` times — would skip 1,000,000 endpoint resolutions, but it changes
  EMISSION ORDER, which for a Gremlin `values()` is a different question from a count's. Needs the
  order contract settled first, probably against a TinkerPop console.
- `V().groupCount(age)` at 2.7x and `V().out().dedupe().count()` at 3.9x are the next smallest
  ratios and have had no floor measurement.

## 235. The Gremlin bench, fully floored: three rows retracted, one hypothesis refuted, one delta attributed

Item 234 floored two of `bench:gremlin`'s rows and left two without one. This finishes the survey.
No code changed; the result is that three of the four candidate rows are AT their floors and the
fourth's gap now has a cause.

All measurements in one process with the engine, 200,000 vertices and 1,000,000 edges:

|                                                     |         ms | ns a vertex |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------: | ----------: |
| ENGINE `V().groupCount(age)`                        |       6.93 |        34.7 |
| **floor** `V().groupCount(age)`                     |   **3.10** |    **15.5** |
| floor, raw-keyed Map                                |       3.14 |        15.7 |
| floor + one object allocated per vertex             |       3.06 |        15.3 |
| floor + the `hasOwn` guard `evalBy` applies         |       3.22 |        16.1 |
| floor + TWO generator layers                        |  **12.07** |    **60.4** |
| ENGINE `V().out().dedupe().count()`                 |       6.35 |        31.8 |
| **floor** `V().out().dedupe().count()`              |   **6.40** |        32.0 |
| floor, adjacency scan only                          |       1.76 |         8.8 |
| ENGINE `V().out().values(age)`                      |     285.74 |           — |
| **floor** `V().out().values(age)`                   | **245.79** |           — |
| floor, the same walk with the endpoint NOT resolved |  **95.47** |           — |

### Three retractions

**`V().out().dedupe().count()` is at its floor** — 6.35 against 6.40, and the engine is marginally
the faster of the two. `distinctHopCount` already does exactly what the hand-written loop does. Its
3.9x gap to the native engine is not an overhead. The floor itself decomposes: an adjacency scan
touching no bucket is 8.8ns a vertex, so **23ns of the 32 is the per-entry `byType.get('KNOWS')`
lookup.**

**`V().out().values(age)` is at its floor** — 285.74 against 245.79, 1.16x, and
`hopValuesShortcut` already answers it with one walk. The decomposition is the useful part:
the same walk with the endpoint NOT resolved is 95.47ms, so **the endpoint resolution is 150ms of
the 246 — 61% of the biggest row on this bench.** `Edge` stores its endpoints as string IDS
(`#from`/`#to`) and `edge.to` is a getter calling `getVertexById`, so every traversed edge pays a
string-keyed `Map` lookup.

**`V().out().has().count()`** was retracted in item 234 on the same grounds (50.62 against a 44.24
floor), where the per-vertex cost is `edgesToByLabel.get(v.id)`.

So **every remaining gap on this surface is one of two string-keyed lookups** — vertex-id-keyed
adjacency, or vertex-id-keyed vertex resolution — and both are a consequence of the TS core keying
its indexes by string id where the native engine uses dense integers. That is a core
data-representation question, not a shortcut, and it would touch byte-identity; it is recorded for a
deliberate decision rather than attempted here.

### A hypothesis of mine, refuted

I expected the `groupCount` delta to be the traverser allocated per element — one small object per
vertex that is filtered and discarded. **It costs nothing measurable: 15.3ns a vertex against the
floor's 15.5.** A short-lived object in a tight loop is free here. Worth keeping because it is the
natural guess and it is wrong, and because the same guess would be made about every step in this
pipeline.

Ruled out alongside it: the `hasOwn` guard `evalBy` applies (+0.6ns), a raw-keyed Map (items 192/193's
trick, which does not apply because this map is already raw-keyed — 15.7 against 15.5), `groupKey`
(two type checks for a number, since its object branch short-circuits), and the wrapper-object map
(90 buckets on this fixture).

### The delta that is left, attributed

**Two generator layers cost 60.4ns a vertex against the floor's 15.5** — and that is MORE than the
engine's own 34.7, so the engine pays somewhere between one layer and two. That is the whole of the
gap, and it is the same effect item 217 measured on the GQL side, where replacing one generator with
a direct iterator source was 1.6x on its own.

So `V().groupCount({by: k})` has **1.9-2.2x available** (34.7 → ~16), and the way to take it is the
one `countShortcut` already uses for `count()`: answer the shape without building the stream.
`vertexStepCount` gained exactly that treatment for `has` in item 234. The shortcut needs to decline
every `by` modulator except a plain property key, filter an absent key as `evalBy` does (NO_VALUE
takes no bucket), and key by `groupKey` so a non-primitive groups by value.

**The engine's row is NOISY where the floors are not** — four runs read 4.85, 6.93, 7.19 and 7.27ms
against floors stable at 3.06-3.14. So the ratio is 1.55-2.35x depending on the run, which is why
this entry states a range rather than the single number the first run suggested.

### Still open

- The `groupCount` shortcut above: attributed, sized, not built.
- **Endpoint resolution as a string-keyed lookup** is 61% of `values(age)` and the dominant term in
  two other rows. Dense integer ids in the TS core would address all three at once; it is a core
  change with byte-identity implications and wants an explicit decision.

## 236. The groupCount tally — built on item 235's attribution, not on a guess

Item 235 floored this row and attributed its gap by elimination. This takes it.

`g.V().groupCount().by(k)` ran the traverser pipeline; it now tallies the vertex set.

|                                                 |        ms | ns a vertex |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------: | ----------: |
| the traverser pipeline                          |      6.93 |        34.7 |
| a hand-written tally                            |      3.10 |        15.5 |
| the tally + one object per vertex               |      3.06 |        15.3 |
| the tally + the `hasOwn` guard `evalBy` applies |      3.22 |        16.1 |
| the tally + TWO generator layers                | **12.07** |    **60.4** |

The per-element traverser — the natural guess, and the one I made first — costs **nothing
measurable**. Nor does `hasOwn`, a raw-keyed Map (items 192/193's trick does not apply; this map is
already raw-keyed), `groupKey` (two type checks for a number) or the wrapper map (90 buckets). Two
generator layers cost more than the whole engine row, so the engine pays between one and two, and
the layering is the gap. Same effect as item 217 on the GQL side.

### Measured

`bun run bench:gremlin`, three runs a side, rebuilt and verified between sides. Every row's
`answers` column reads `same` in all six runs:

| row                          | before        | after             |                    |
| ---------------------------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ------------------ |
| `V().groupCount(age)`        | 6.6, 7.2, 7.3 | **2.9, 3.1, 3.4** | **2.3x, disjoint** |
| `V().has(age,gt).count()`    | 2.4-2.8       | 2.8               | overlap            |
| `V().out().values(age)`      | 277.4-280.9   | 280.5-283.3       | overlap            |
| `V().out().has().count()`    | 50.2-50.4     | 50.1-50.6         | overlap            |
| `V().out().dedupe().count()` | 7.0           | 7.0-7.1           | overlap            |
| the counter rows             | 0.0           | 0.0               | flat               |

`ts/nat` on the changed row goes 2.4-2.6 → **1.1-1.2**, so it is now at parity with the native
engine — which item 235 predicted, since the TS floor (3.10) already sat beside native's 2.75.

As in item 234, the GQL benches were not run as a before/after for a checkable reason: `bench.ts`,
`bench-usage.ts` and `spelling-probe.ts` contain no reference to `@lenke/gremlin`, so they never
load the changed module.

### The semantics live in ONE place
