`groupCountStep` and `groupCountShortcut` share `tallyGroupCount` and `groupCountResult`, extracted
for the purpose. Which of NO_VALUE, `groupKey`, and "the ORIGINAL key survives into the output" is
the rule here is exactly what two copies would drift on, and a shortcut that drifts is a wrong
answer. The `by` derivation is the same expression `dispatch` uses (`bys?.[0] ?? keyToBy(by)`), so
the legacy name and the modulator form resolve identically on both paths.

**NO INDEX INTERACTION**, unlike item 234's `has` tally: `seedFromIndex` needs a leading seedable
FILTER, and `groupCount` is not one — `seedRest` breaks on the first step and returns null either
way. There is no seek for this shortcut to preempt, because the question needs every vertex. The
shortcut also needs no `tracksPath` guard (unlike `hopValuesShortcut`): the plan is exactly `V()` +
`groupCount`, so it contains no path-consuming step, and a `groupCount` carries nothing forward.

Deliberately narrow: `by.kind === 'key'` only. A `traversal` by runs a sub-plan per element, a
`token`/`column` by projects something other than a property, and an `identity` by groups by the
ELEMENT — three different questions, all left to the step.

### Teeth: 10 tests, 8 mutants, 8 as predicted

A shortcut is answer-preserving, so the tests assert the DECISION (which shapes it claims) and the
EQUIVALENCE to the step it preempts. The step is no longer reachable for a claimed plan, so
equivalence is tested ACROSS paths: a three-step plan carrying a VACUOUS label is declined by the
shortcut and asks the identical question.

The one survivor is unwiring the shortcut — perf-only by construction, which is what the
differential asserts.

**Two findings worth keeping.**

**A leading extra step cannot distinguish an exact guard from a lax one.** My "declines anything
between the source and the aggregate" test passes either way, because with a leading step `steps[1]`
is not the `groupCount` and the shape declines for a second reason. The mutant that relaxes
`steps.length !== 2` to `< 2` survived until the test used a TRAILING step —
`V().groupCount().by('age').count()`, which the lax guard would answer as the Map while silently
dropping the `count()`. When a guard is a conjunction, a case that trips two clauses at once proves
nothing about either.

**Sharing the accumulator is what gives the differential its teeth.** Dropping the NO_VALUE filter
inside the SHARED helper is caught — because the shortcut filters an absent key with `hasOwn` before
calling it, so NO_VALUE reaches the helper only from the step, and the two paths then disagree.
Had the shortcut re-derived the filter, that mutation would have changed both paths identically and
the differential would have been blind to it.

The row tests are built against how a tally goes wrong rather than how it goes right. The fixture
carries a vertex with NO `age` and one with a NULL `age`, which are different outcomes — the first
takes no bucket, the second takes a `null` one — and a separate fixture carries two structurally
EQUAL but distinct objects, so a tally that used the raw value as its bucket key would give two
buckets where `groupKey` gives one.

### Still open

Unchanged from item 235: every remaining gap on this surface is a string-keyed lookup —
vertex-id-keyed adjacency (`V().out().has().count()`, `V().out().dedupe().count()`) or
vertex-id-keyed vertex resolution (61% of `V().out().values(age)`). Dense integer ids in the TS core
would address all three; it is a core change with byte-identity implications and wants an explicit
decision.

## 237. The var-length walk is 9.5x off its floor — and the bench hides it 200x

`bench:usage` run with BOTH engines for the first time this pass shows the TS GQL engine now WINS
most read rows — point lookup 4.9x, `100 updates in one statement` 6.8x, 2-hop recommendation 3.3x
— which is what items 228-233 bought. It loses on four. Two of those are the insert path, closed as
a constant factor by items 140 and 203, so they were not re-opened. The other two are the var-length
rows:

|                                      |  ts(+) | engine(+) |       |
| ------------------------------------ | -----: | --------: | ----- |
| `analytic: fan-out spread 1-3 hops`  | 118.5k |    140.6k | 0.84x |
| `analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops` | 106.0k |    144.8k | 0.73x |

### Where the cost is

Decomposed on the bench's own fixture (20,000 users, out-degree ONE, so a `->{1,3}` walk visits
about three vertices):

|                                                        |       µs |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -------: |
| the seeded start only                                  |     0.53 |
| one-hop count, NO subquery                             |     0.65 |
| `COUNT { one plain hop }`                              | **1.00** |
| `COUNT { ->{1,1} }` — the SAME answer as the plain hop | **2.47** |
| `COUNT { ->{1,3} }` (the row)                          |     5.65 |
| `EXISTS { ->{1,3} }`                                   |     2.85 |

The subquery WRAPPER is only 0.35 µs. A quantifier with ONE repetition costs 2.5x the identical
unquantified hop.

### The bench understates it by 200x

Both rows anchor on `u.name = $n`, which selects ONE outer row, and the subquery is CORRELATED — so
every per-execution cost is paid once and looks like a rounding error. Swapping the anchor for
`u.score = $s` (200 matching users) is the same question at 200 rows:

| 200 outer rows            |      total |  per row |
| ------------------------- | ---------: | -------: |
| no subquery               |    17.1 µs |    0.086 |
| `COUNT { one plain hop }` |      146.0 |     0.73 |
| `COUNT { ->{1,3} }`       | **1195.9** | **5.98** |

**Measure a correlated subquery at more than one outer row.** A single-row anchor hides a
per-execution cost completely, and both standing bench rows have one.

### The floor, and what it retracts

A hand-written TRAIL walk (the default mode — an edge may not repeat within a walk), depth 1..3,
counting ends, over the same 200 starts and answering the same 600:

|                                                     |     total |  per row |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------: | -------: |
| ENGINE `COUNT { ->{1,3} }`                          | 1563.3 µs | **7.82** |
| **floor**, 200 trail walks depth 1..3               | **164.2** | **0.82** |
| floor, mark `Set` hoisted out of the per-start call |     160.5 |     0.80 |
| ENGINE `COUNT { one plain hop }`                    |     159.0 |     0.80 |

**9.5x**, and the floor for the whole three-deep walk costs what the engine's UNQUANTIFIED one-hop
subquery costs. This is the largest recoverable gap this pass has found.

Hoisting the mark `Set` out of the per-start call buys **nothing** (160.5 against 164.2,
overlapping) — the third time this session that an allocation suspected of mattering has not (items
235, 236). Allocation is not the lever here.

**Also refuted before any code was written**: `trailEndsUnit` allocates `marks = new Set()`
unconditionally while `vertexMode` covers only `simple`/`acyclic`, which looked like waste for the
default mode — but the default mode is **TRAIL** (`pattern.mode ?? 'trail'`, four call sites), and
`hopCollides`/`hopMark` both use the set for trail. Not waste.

### Attributed: setup and per-rep, both large

The depth ladder at 200 outer rows separates the intercept from the slope:

|                                  |                                                                              per row |
| -------------------------------- | -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------: |
| plain hop, no quantifier         |                                                                              0.90 µs |
| `{1,1}`                          |                                                                             **3.64** |
| `{1,2}`                          |                                                                                 5.59 |
| `{1,3}`                          |                                                                                 6.82 |
| `{1,4}`                          | 5.91 — ranges OVERLAP `{1,3}`, so the trail restrictor stops the walk before depth 4 |
| the floor, whole depth-1..3 walk |                                                                             **0.76** |

- **~2.7 µs per EXECUTION of setup** (3.64 against the plain hop's 0.90), for a quantifier that is
  semantically one hop.
- **~1.2-2.0 µs per REPETITION** beyond the first.

Both terms are an order above the floor, which does the entire walk in 0.76.

### Candidates, and the tension in taking them

`trailEnds` delegates to `trailEndsUnit`, the general nested-unit matcher — group variables, per-rep
`WHERE`, path reconstruction, four path modes — and its own comment says that is deliberate: _"there
is ONE traversal implementation and no hand-tuned twin to drift."_ A flat fast path is exactly the
twin that comment rejects, and the comment was written without this measurement. 9.5x is the kind of
number this repo has accepted a guarded second path for before (`detectHopProjection`'s plain and
filtered pair; item 236's shortcut), but it has to be guarded and differentially tested rather than
argued.

Per-execution, in `trailEnds`/`trailEndsUnit`:

- **`trailEnds` rebuilds its `CUnit`** — `{ elems: [{ hop: { rel } }] }` — on every call, from data
  that is entirely compile-time.
- `resolve([...])` for the seed, the initial `Frame`, `expandFilteredArr`'s seed array, the
  `buildSteps` closure.

Per hop, in `resolve`:

- **A STRING KEY per work item**: `p.map(c => \`${unitId(c.unit)}:${c.rep}:${c.elem}\`).join(';')`,
  built to break min-0 epsilon cycles. For a FLAT unit there are no epsilon moves at all, so the
  visited set can never fire and the key is pure waste — the same shape as item 193's string-keyed
  group index, which was 3.0x there. It is only ~100-200 ns of the ~2.6 µs a hop, so it is a
  contributor and not the answer.
- Two array allocations and a `Set` per call, plus a cursor clone per move.

### ⚠️ Weak coverage in this area

Per item 214 and the corpus notes, **the differential fuzzer covers NO quantified or nested
groups.** A change here cannot lean on it, which is unusual for this engine — the fuzzers are
normally the safety net for exactly this kind of rewrite. Extending the fuzzer to emit quantified
patterns should come first, or the change needs a hand-built differential across modes, bounds,
per-rep `WHERE`, group variables and path variables.

### Not built

Diagnosis only. The prize is 9.5x on the two slowest serving reads, the attribution is specific, and
the implementation is a guarded second traversal path in the engine's most general matcher — which
wants its own item, with the fuzzer extended first.

## 238. The differential fuzzer's abbreviated-quantifier gap — and a fixture that made four path modes identical

Item 237 found a 9.5x on the var-length walk and stopped short of taking it, because the note said
the differential fuzzer covers no quantified patterns. **That note was over-broad and this item
corrects it:** the fuzzer has generated the GROUP form `((x)…){n,m}` since item 51, with per-rep
`WHERE`, direction pairs and a path variable. What it has never generated is the **abbreviated**
form `-[]->{n,m}` — and the two spellings take different code. A group builds a multi-hop unit;
the abbreviated form routes through `trailEnds`, which synthesises a one-hop unit of its own. So the
shape `bench:usage`'s two var-length rows actually use had no cross-engine comparison at all.

No path MODE was generated either, by either arm.

### The arm

`genAbbrevQuantified` emits seven hop spellings (both directions, both edge types, an edge
VARIABLE, and a per-HOP `WHERE` inside the brackets — distinct from the group arm's per-REPETITION
one), five bounded quantifiers including `{0,2}` and `{2,2}`, the four path modes plus an unspelled
default, four endpoints, and five result forms: `count(*)`, an unbounded `+`, two path-variable
forms (the only shapes that make `trailEnds` reconstruct the walk rather than yield bare ends) and
the endpoint projected rather than counted.

A mode is paired only with a BOUNDED quantifier. `WALK` with `+` has no restrictor, so over a cyclic
fixture it terminates only on the trail budget — and a resource limit is a poor thing to compare two
engines on. That choice earned itself later in this item.

### Its band was settled by measurement, after two wrong attempts

**First attempt: split the group arm 0.88-0.93 in half at 0.905.** The coverage floors caught it —
`sinkGenerated` fell below its threshold, because halving that arm halved every shape inside it.
That is exactly what those floors are for, and it is the second time this session a guard has
corrected me rather than the reverse.

**Second attempt: take 0.35 of the generic fallback's share**, which is the precedent the
subquery-item arm set. That gave only ~110 queries of 20,000 — too thin for 6 modes × 5 bounds.

**Settled: 1% taken from the group arm (0.88-0.89, leaving it 0.89-0.93).** Measured over seeds
1-3: **190-209 generated, 159-183 non-empty, 76-88 carrying a path variable.** The group arm keeps
~80% of its old rate and every one of its floors still clears — `perRep` 709-771 → 572-617 against
350, `sink` 358-400 → 288-320 against 200, `peel` 153-185 → 120-151 against 75. **None were
lowered**, which is the rule that file states for itself; the new ranges are recorded beside them.

The arm has its own counters and floors (`abbrevGenerated`, `abbrevNonEmpty`, `abbrevPath`, at
roughly half the measured minimum). Without them it could silently stop generating and the suite
would pass exactly as it does now — the failure items 115 and 125 both hit.

### Teeth, verified — and the two reasons the first verification lied

A generative test whose teeth were never checked is worse than no test, because it is believed. So
three mutants, each inside `trailEnds`, which ONLY the abbreviated form reaches:

|                                                                  |            |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| drop path reconstruction (`wantPath: false`)                     | **caught** |
| force `min` to 1, so `{0,n}` loses its zero-rep match            | **caught** |
| force WALK mode for bounded quantifiers, dropping the restrictor | **caught** |

**All three survived the first run**, and the cause was my harness: I passed `--no-build`, so the
mutants to `packages/gql/src/**` never reached the dist the fuzzer loads. That is the recorded
`fuzzers-read-built-dists` trap, walked into while verifying a fuzzer. With the rebuild in the loop,
two of the three were caught immediately.

**The third survived for a real reason: the fixture was ACYCLIC.** `trail` forbids repeating an
edge, `simple`/`acyclic` a vertex, `walk` nothing — and on a graph with no cycle none of those
restrictors can ever fire, so generating the four modes compared nothing. The fixture gained one
edge, `3 -> 1` on `E`, closing a cycle 1 → 2 → 3 → 1. The mutant is caught after it.

That edge also **improved every non-empty counter** rather than only the new one: `perRep` non-empty
277-296 → 304-314, `peelNonZero` 25-42 → 38-53. A cyclic fixture is simply a better one for a
traversal engine, and this file's history says the same about its second in-edge (item 51) and its
`:U` label (item 63).

A fourth observation worth keeping: with the cycle in place, forcing WALK mode for **unbounded**
`+` was caught by a TIMEOUT rather than by an answer — the walk ran to the trail budget. That is a
catch by this repo's rule, but not the one being tested for, so the mutant was narrowed to bounded
quantifiers and now diverges on an ANSWER. It also confirms the arm was right to keep `+` under the
default mode.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each as their own command, each exit 0. The complexity gate
intervened twice: adding the arm took the generator from 35 to 36, and extracting only the arm's
body did not help, because the BRANCH is the +1. Both quantified arms are now behind helpers —
`genAbbrevQuantified` and `genQuantifiedGroup`, the latter taking the `end === '(b)'` ternary out of
the generator with it — which brings it back to 35. The coverage numbers after that refactor are
IDENTICAL to before it (190/161/86 on seed 1), which is how I know the move changed nothing about
what is generated.

Full monorepo suite exit 0; all seven byte-identity fuzzers green; the differential fuzzer green on
seeds 1, 2 and 3 as well as on random seeds.

### What this unblocks

Item 237's 9.5x. The abbreviated form now has cross-engine coverage over four path modes, five
bounds, a per-hop predicate, an edge variable, path reconstruction and the `{0,n}` zero-rep — which
is the safety net a second traversal path in `trailEnds` needs, and the reason item 237 stopped.

## 239. A flat walk for the abbreviated quantifier — 1.4-1.5x on both rows, and the floor that promised 9.5x

Item 237 measured a 9.5x between the engine's var-length walk and a hand-written one, and item 238
built the fuzzer coverage the change needed. This takes it.

`trailEnds` answered the abbreviated `-[]->{n,m}` form through `trailEndsUnit`, the general
nested-unit matcher, on the stated grounds that _"there is ONE traversal implementation and no
hand-tuned twin to drift."_ It now takes a flat explicit-stack walk when no path is wanted, and
keeps the general matcher for `wantPath` and as the exported `trailEndsViaUnit`.

### What it actually bought, against what the floor promised

**1.64-2.13x, not 9.5x.** The same probe, before and after, at 200 outer rows:

| 200 outer rows                                         |   before |     after |                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -------: | --------: | --------------------- |
| `COUNT { ->{1,1} }`                                    | 391.7 µs | **238.7** | 1.64x, ranges overlap |
| `COUNT { ->{1,2} }`                                    |    615.6 | **361.9** | **1.70x, disjoint**   |
| `COUNT { ->{1,3} }`                                    |    844.3 | **484.5** | **1.74x, disjoint**   |
| `EXISTS { ->{2,4} }`                                   |    810.1 | **380.7** | **2.13x, disjoint**   |
| control: a PATH variable, which declines the fast path |   1565.2 |    1620.6 | overlap               |
| control: `COUNT { one plain hop }`, never quantified   |     55.9 |      54.3 | overlap               |

**Why the floor overstated it.** Item 238's floor was a direct recursive function: no generator, no
per-frame array, and nothing above it. The fast path is still a GENERATOR whose every emission suspends,
still calls `expandFilteredArr` (an array per frame), and is still reached through the subquery
pipeline that wraps it. So that floor priced _the walk_, not _the walk as this engine reaches it_ —
and the difference is the 3x still between them (2.42 µs a row against 0.82). That is the same error
shape as [[harness-must-resemble-caller]]'s: **a hand-written floor that skips the caller's protocol
overstates what is recoverable inside the callee.** I quoted 9.5x to the user and delivered 1.8x;
the gap is the protocol, and it is still on the table.

### On the two rows this was for

`bun run bench:usage`, ts(+), three runs a side:

| row                                  | before               | after                    |                     | native |
| ------------------------------------ | -------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------- | -----: |
| `analytic: fan-out spread 1-3 hops`  | 114.8, 122.1, 124.3k | **161.3, 171.1, 178.6k** | **1.38x, disjoint** | 140.6k |
| `analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops` | 103.3, 106.4, 125.3k | **184.2, 188.8, 192.3k** | **1.53x, disjoint** | 144.8k |

Both rows were the only read rows still losing to the native engine after item 233 (0.84x and
0.73x). **Both now beat it** — 1.15-1.27x and 1.27-1.33x.

The bulk `bench` screen, three runs a side: every row's range overlaps, no flags. It contains no
var-length row at all, so no gain was expected there either; it is a regression screen here.

### The rules it has to match, and how that is checked

For a one-hop unit every hop completes the top rep (`elem` reaches `elems.length` of 1), so after
hop `k` the rep count IS `k`: emit iff `k >= min && (max === null || k <= max)`, extend iff
`max === null || k < max`, and `min === 0` yields the empty walk at the seed first. `completesTop`
is therefore always true, which reduces `isClose` to SIMPLE mode returning to the seed. These were
read off `resolve` rather than reasoned about.

**THE EMISSION SEQUENCE IS THE CONTRACT**, not the set of ends — a caller may count, dedup or take
the first. `trailEndsViaUnit` is exported for that: the differential compares the two paths
element by element across **4 modes × 8 quantifiers × 3 hop spellings × 5 seeds**, on a fixture with
a cycle, a parallel edge (so TRAIL, which marks edges, and SIMPLE, which marks vertices, disagree)
and a self-loop. 37 tests, 486 assertions.

Three guards keep that comparison from being vacuous: walk must reach more than trail and trail more
than acyclic; simple must admit a return to the seed where acyclic does not; and `wantPath` must
still produce non-empty `verts`/`edges`.

### Teeth: 9 mutants, 9 caught — after one more test

Eight were caught by the sequence differential: emitting a rep too late or too few, never treating
a simple close as one, swapping the trail and simple marks, dropping the seed's own vertex mark,
omitting the min-0 empty walk, never unmarking on backtrack, and taking the fast path when a path is
wanted.

**The ninth needed a test that did not exist.** `extend one rep too far` (`rep < max` → `rep <= max`)
emits NOTHING extra — the emit test fails at `max + 1` — so the sequence is identical and the walk
merely descends one level further. The only observable is `steps`, because each hop is charged
against `graph.limits.trail`, and `resolve` offers a further repetition only when `rep < max`, so
the general matcher never reaches that depth. A pair of tests now pins it: a budget sweep requiring
both paths to raise at the same ceiling, plus a test that the smallest budget in the sweep is
actually reached — otherwise the sweep compares two successes and proves nothing.

### Three fixture and harness errors of mine, recorded

- **The group-form control ran for over ten minutes.** `COUNT { MATCH ((x)-[:FOLLOWS]->(y)){1,2} }`
  is UNANCHORED: for each of 200 outer rows it enumerates every 1-2 hop walk in a 20,000-vertex
  graph, about 8M walks a query. That is a different workload, not a control, and it was removed —
  the group form cannot reach the fast path anyway, since it enters at `trailEndsUnit`.
- **I compared two different probes.** The first "after" numbers were read against item 237's,
  measured by a differently-structured harness, and the tell was the plain-hop CONTROL moving 2.7x
  — a control that moves is a comparison that is not one. Redone same-probe.
- **`pkill -f` killed my own command.** Clearing the runaway took the shell chain with it, so a
  python edit in the same chain never ran; the `grep -c` afterwards is what caught it.

### Still open

- **~3x remains to item 238's floor** (2.42 µs a row against 0.82), and it is the protocol rather
  than the walk: the generator suspension per emission, `expandFilteredArr`'s array per frame, and
  the subquery pipeline above. A non-generator callback form of `trailEnds` is the obvious next
  step and would need every consumer changed.
- The GROUP form still goes through the general matcher for every case, which is correct — it is
  what the general matcher is for.

## 241. A ladder that attributed 64% of a gap to a function that turned out not to matter

Item 240 left four candidates unattributed for `read: keyed dedup lookup`'s 2.6x gap to its floor.
This priced them, attributed the gap, made the change the attribution pointed at, and then
**reverted it** — because the saving does not reach the query.

### The ladder

Each rung adds one mechanism to the floor, returns the SAME answer (66), and consumes its work —
item 216's rule, after an earlier ladder of mine read non-additively because its rungs did unequal
work. The real engine functions are imported rather than mimicked, since a mimic measures my idea
of them.

| rung                                                     |        µs |     delta |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | --------: | --------: |
| 1 floor: `idx.equals` + `labels.has` + property read     |      5.56 |         — |
| 2 + a per-candidate binding write                        |      6.36 |     +0.80 |
| 3 + the REAL `satisfies` with the row's own predicate    | **10.90** | **+4.54** |
| 4 + an indirect gate call per candidate                  |     11.37 |     +0.47 |
| 5 + the REAL `indexCandidates` enumeration and `build()` |     10.95 | **−0.42** |

So `satisfies` looked like **64% of the gap**, at ~23ns a candidate. `indexCandidates` — one of the
four suspects, and the one I would have guessed at — is **free**. Rung 5's 10.95 against the row's
12.62 accounts for nearly all of it, the remainder being the pipeline above.

### The change the attribution pointed at

`satisfies` iterates `pred.props` and `pred.eqProps` with `for…of`, which allocates an ITERATOR per
call **even when the array is empty** — and one of the two is empty on every call: a clause `WHERE`
leaves `props` empty and fills `eqProps`/`where`, an inline spelling does the reverse. It is called
once per candidate, so that is per element. The same shape as the grouped tally's, where
`for (const ip of preds)` over an empty array cost an unfiltered scan a consistent 34%.

Indexed loops instead. The ladder resolved it cleanly, controls flat:

| rung                     | before |    after |
| ------------------------ | -----: | -------: |
| 1 floor                  |   5.56 |     5.52 |
| 2 + binding write        |   6.36 |     6.37 |
| 3 + the REAL `satisfies` |  10.90 | **8.26** |
| 5 + `indexCandidates`    |  10.95 | **7.64** |

`satisfies`' own per-call cost fell **2.4x** (its delta over rung 2 went +4.54 → +1.89 µs), and
rung 5 fell 1.43x.

### And then it did not matter

`bench:usage`'s row did not move: 74.6-80.7k against 78.9k before. Its own probe — the one that had
matched the bench to within 0.1 µs — read 14.13 µs after against 12.69 before, with both controls
also up, which is a process-level shift inside a 14-28 µs spread rather than an effect.

So the in-process A/B, which is the instrument for exactly this case: both BUILT bundles in one
process, alternated round by round with the order swapped each round, answers asserted equal first,
400 calls a timing and 14 rounds a side.

|                                   | before      | after          |                    |
| --------------------------------- | ----------- | -------------- | ------------------ |
| THE ROW, keyed dedup              | 13.04-53.27 | 12.75-52.29 µs | **1.02x, overlap** |
| the inline spelling               | 12.80-53.50 | 14.29-60.52    | 0.90x, overlap     |
| control point lookup, 1 candidate | 0.65-2.85   | 0.71-2.28      | overlap            |
| control label count, O(1)         | 0.09-0.43   | 0.09-0.41      | overlap            |

**1.02x.** The mins are stable across 14 alternating rounds and would resolve a 25% effect on a
13 µs row; a 3.3 µs saving is 25%. It is not there.

**So the change was reverted**, by the standard item 231 set for its own retracted edit: correct,
free, and demonstrating nothing is not a reason to ship.

### The lesson, which is the item's real output

**A ladder that calls a function directly measures it in a context the engine never provides.** My
rungs called `satisfies` from a tight loop over a materialized candidate set. The engine calls it
through a gate closure, inside a tally closure, driven by a plan — and in that context the
allocation the ladder was pricing either does not happen the same way or is hidden behind the 200
cold vertex reads the row is actually bound by.

This is item 239's floor lesson with the ends swapped. There, a floor that skipped the CALLER's
protocol overstated what the callee could recover. Here, a ladder that skipped the caller's CALL
SITE attributed a gap to a callee that does not cost that in situ. Both say the same thing: **the
only decomposition that survives is one measured through the real call path, and the in-process A/B
of two builds is the only instrument here that measures that.** Reach for it before the ladder, not
after.

What is now known about this row, which is worth keeping: its 2.6x gap to the floor is **not** the
predicate content (item 240), **not** `indexCandidates` (free, measured), and **not** `satisfies`'
CPU work (2.4x cheaper with no effect). What remains is the 200 cold, random-order vertex reads the
floor also pays — which makes the floor's 4.90 µs suspicious in turn, since it reads the same
vertices in index order where the engine reads them through a materialized `Set`.

### Still open

- The row's gap is now attributable only to memory traffic and ordering, which is the same
  string-keyed-structure story as the Gremlin surface's remaining rows. Whether iteration ORDER over
  the candidate set explains the rest is the one untested hypothesis left.
- Items 140/203's insert-path constant factor remains the other two losing rows, unchanged.

## 242. A real cross-engine value divergence, found by item 238's own coverage

Item 238 added the abbreviated-quantifier arm to the differential fuzzer because item 237's change
needed a safety net. On a random-seed sweep it found a **value divergence** — which the fuzzer's own
message says no registry entry may excuse, because a value divergence is a bug in one of the
engines.

```
FUZZ_SEED=2419630540
MATCH p = SIMPLE (a:T)-[e:E WHERE e.w > 2]->{1,3}(b) RETURN size(nodes(p)) AS x ORDER BY x
  ts:     [{"x":2},{"x":2},{"x":2},{"x":3},{"x":3},{"x":3}]
  native: [{"x":2},{"x":2},{"x":2},{"x":3},{"x":3},{"x":3},{"x":4}]
```

**PRE-EXISTING, not caused by item 239.** It reproduces identically with the pre-239 matcher in
place, checked by building `ec5bd521^`'s `matching.ts` and re-running the seed. Item 239 routes
`wantPath === true` to the unchanged general matcher, so that is what the shape was always using.

### Which engine is wrong, and why

Projecting the endpoints names the extra row: `{startn: 2, endn: 2, len: 4}` — the path
**2 → 3 → 1 → 2**. On this fixture the only `1 → 2` edge is `e1`, whose `w` is **2**, and the
pattern's per-hop predicate is `e.w > 2`. So native traverses an edge its own per-hop predicate
excludes. **TS is right.**

Characterised across modes and bounds on a four-edge reduction of the fuzzer's fixture
(`1→2 w2`, `2→3 w5`, `1→3 w9`, `3→1 w7`):

|                                              | ts  | native |          |
| -------------------------------------------- | --- | ------ | -------- |
| `SIMPLE {1,3}` with `WHERE e.w > 2`          | 6   | **7**  | diverges |
| `SIMPLE {1,3}` with an inline `{w: 9}`       | 1   | **2**  | diverges |
| `SIMPLE {1,3}`, `count(*)` instead of a path | 6   | **7**  | diverges |
| `TRAIL {1,3}`                                | —   | —      | agree    |
| `WALK {1,2}`                                 | —   | —      | agree    |
| `ACYCLIC {1,3}`                              | —   | —      | agree    |
| default mode `{1,3}`                         | —   | —      | agree    |
| `SIMPLE {1,2}`                               | —   | —      | agree    |

So: **SIMPLE mode only, and only where the bound is wide enough to reach the close.** It shows with
a per-hop `WHERE` and with an inline property map, with and without a path variable. TRAIL agreeing
is the informative one — a trail walk would also want `2 → 3 → 1 → 2` (three distinct edges), and
native does not return it, which proves native applies the predicate correctly on an ORDINARY hop.

### Where it is

`crates/lenke-engine/src/exec/varlen.rs`, the `VarStep::Close` arm. It notes the step and emits
directly:

```rust
VarStep::Close => {
    sink.note_step();
    if len + 1 >= min && (len + 1).is_multiple_of(k) {
        node_stack.push(a.nbr);
        edge_stack.push(a.eid);
        sink.emit(row, node_stack, edge_stack);
        ...
    }
    continue;
}
```

The ordinary `VarStep::Go` arm falls through to `varlen_enter`, and the per-hop edge predicate is
applied neither in this loop (which checks only the edge LABEL and the self-loop drop) nor in
`varlen_enter` (which applies `body_filter` and `per_rep_pred`, different things). So the open
question for the fix is **where the per-hop predicate is applied on the Go path**, and the Close arm
needs the same check before it emits. The TS side applies it when materialising the adjacency
(`expandFilteredArr`), which is why its close cannot skip it — a closing hop is still a hop.

### CI is now intermittently red, deliberately

The shape is generated by item 238's arm at about 1% of 20,000 queries, and it reproduced on 1 of 6
random-seed sweeps locally. So `bun run fuzz` and CI will fail intermittently until the Rust fix
lands. That is the correct state: the repo's rule is that red is the to-do list, never a skip, and
the fuzzer explicitly refuses to let a registry entry excuse a value divergence. **It is not
suppressed and should not be.**

Deterministic replay: `FUZZ_SEED=2419630540 bun run fuzz differential`.

### Worth noting about the method

This is the second time in two items that coverage added for one purpose found a bug of a different
kind. Item 238's arm was built to protect item 239's fast path — a TS change — and what it caught
was a pre-existing NATIVE wrong answer in a shape neither engine's tests covered. The cost was one
band of generator share; the find is a wrong answer that had been shipping.

## 243. The native wrong answer item 242 found: a SIMPLE closing hop skipped its own predicate

Item 242 characterised a cross-engine value divergence and left the fix open with one question:
_where is the per-hop predicate applied on the `Go` path, and does the `Close` arm need the same
check?_ It is `varlen_enter`, and yes.

### The hole

`exec/varlen.rs`' walk classifies each hop through `varlen_step` into `Skip`, `Close` or `Go`.
`Go` pushes the node and edge and falls into `varlen_enter`, which is where `per_rep_pred` — the
per-repetition `WHERE`, and the lowering of an inline `-[e:R {w: 9}]->` too — is evaluated via
`rep_pred_ok`. **`Close` never calls `varlen_enter`.** It pushes, emits, pops, and continues: the
whole point of the arm is that a closed cycle does not descend. So the one hop that terminates a
SIMPLE path was the one hop no predicate ever saw.

That is why TRAIL agreeing was the informative half of item 242's characterisation. A trail may
revisit a node, so it never takes the `Close` arm at all — its closing hop is an ordinary `Go`,
gated normally. Only SIMPLE produces `Close`, and only GQL produces SIMPLE (`gql.rs:1234` is the
sole writer of `PathMode::Simple`).

The fix is three lines in each of the two drivers — the iterative `varlen_walk` and its
`#[cfg(test)]` recursive twin `varlen_dfs`, which the exec differential holds to byte-identity:
gate the emit on `per_rep_pred.is_none_or(|p| rep_pred_ok(p, store, node_stack, edge_stack, len + 1,
k))`, after the push, exactly as `varlen_enter` does it. `until_stop` and `body_filter` need no twin
here: both are Gremlin-only and `Close` is unreachable from Gremlin.

The fuzzer seed now passes:

```
FUZZ_SEED=2419630540 bun run fuzz differential      # 1 pass, abbrev=225/207/93
```

### What the fixture had to contain

Seven native tests, and the fixture is the whole of the work: a 3-cycle `a -> b -> c -> a` with
edge weights **9, 9, and 1** under `-[e:R WHERE e.w > 2]->{1,3}`. Every one of those four facts is
load-bearing, and dropping any one makes the test pass against the bug:

- a **cycle**, or there is no close;
- a bound that **reaches** it — `{1,2}` agreed with TS throughout, and has its own test saying so;
- a predicate that is **selective**, not vacuous;
- and the failing edge has to be **the closing one**. With weights 9/9/9 the close is legal and
  `a` must appear, which is the control test — without it, deleting the `Close` arm outright
  would also pass.

Then the same shape through every path that shares the walk, because each has its own sink: the
plain projection, the counting driver (`count(*)` = 2, not 3), a path variable (`size(nodes(p))`
never 4 — the fuzzer's own spelling), the inline `{w: 9}` spelling of the same constraint, and all
four path modes agreeing now that the close is gated.

### Mutation: 4 of 5 caught, and the survivor was the point

Built uncapped first, then each mutant under `timeout 900 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p
MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, restoring from the pristine copy before each. The cap was proven
to kill first: an allocator bomb at `MemoryMax=2G` exited **137**, a bare spin loop under `timeout
5` exited **124**.

| mutant                                                     | result                                           |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| 1 drop the gate on the iterative driver (the original bug) | caught, 5 of the new tests                       |
| 2 drop the gate on the recursive twin                      | **SURVIVED**                                     |
| 3 invert the gate on the iterative driver                  | caught, 6 (incl. the rewrite fuzzer)             |
| 4 price the rep one hop early (`len + 1` → `len`)          | caught, 12                                       |
| 5 invert the gate on the recursive twin                    | caught, 1 (`iterative_varlen_matches_recursive`) |

**Mutant 2 surviving while mutant 5 was caught names the blindness exactly.** Both touch the same
three lines of the same function. The twin is only ever exercised by
`iterative_varlen_matches_recursive`, the A/B that holds the two drivers to identical emission
sequences — and that sweep passed `None` for `per_rep_pred` in all 60 trials × 4 modes × 3
directions × 5 bounds. So: **dropping** a gate that is never armed changes nothing, while
**inverting** one does, because `is_some_and` on a `None` predicate returns false and suppresses
every close. The caught mutant was caught for a reason that had nothing to do with predicates.

Its doc comment said "the corpus + differential fuzzer cover the predicate hooks." That was the
belief under test, and item 242 is what it cost: the hole shipped, and the thing that eventually
found it was the cross-engine fuzzer, only after item 238 gave its fixture a cycle.

So the sweep now runs a **second** pass with a predicate armed — 40 trials over graphs whose edges
carry `w` in 0..4, predicate `w > 1` at mini-scope slot 1 (the repetition's first edge, valid for
every `k`), across the same mode/direction/bound/double-loop product. Two guards keep it honest: it
compares against `None` on the same shape and asserts the predicate **pruned at least one path**
somewhere, or it is two unfiltered walks being compared; and the selective weight is what makes
"applied" distinguishable from "dropped" at all. With it, mutant 2 is caught.

### Gates and screen

Unit tests 976 → 983 (7 new, plus the re-armed sweep inside an existing one). `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D
warnings`, `cargo fmt --check` and `bun run check` each as their own command. `bench_all` is a
regression screen here, not a target: the gate runs once per closing hop, which is at most once per
SIMPLE path, and no bench row holds a SIMPLE close.

### Still open, and adjacent

`exec/nested.rs` — the walker for a group unit with mixed hop directions — has **no `Close` concept
at all** (`nested.rs:261` simply skips any already-marked node). So I probed it rather than guess,
and it is **the same bug again, unfixed, and worse**: a 4-cycle `0->1->2->3->0` with a `1->3` chord,
`MATCH SIMPLE ((x)-[:R]->(m)<-[:R]-(y)){1,2} (z) RETURN z.n`:

```
ts:     0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3      (7 rows)
native: 1, 2                     (2 rows)
```

**TS is right, by hand.** One repetition is `x -out-> m <-in- y`. From `x = 0`: the only out-edge is
`0->1`, and `1`'s only in-edge is `0->1`, so `y = 0` — a closing repetition. From `x = 1`: `1->2`
closes (`y = 1`), `1->3` gives `y = 2` and closes at `y = 1`. From `x = 2`: `2->3` closes, and gives
`y = 1`. From `x = 3`: `3->0` closes. That is exactly TS's seven, and native's two are exactly the
**non-closing** pair. Native silently drops every closing repetition of a group pattern.

Same family as item 242, different walker, and it is a wrong ANSWER rather than a refusal — so it
needs its own item and its own fix, since `nested.rs` has no `VarStep` classification to extend.
The probe also turned up two loud refusals on the way: native rejects an edge property or a per-hop
`WHERE` **anywhere** on a subpath group (`edge properties / a per-hop WHERE on a subpath group are
not supported yet`), including the one-hop group `((x)-[e:R WHERE e.w <> 3]->(y)){1,4}` that TS
answers. Loud, so a different severity, but the same surface.

The differential fuzzer generates no group pattern with a cycle-closing bound at all, which is the
same coverage shape that hid item 242 — so that gap, not the walker, is the first thing to close.

## 244. The same close bug in the OTHER walker, in BOTH engines, and the coverage gap that hid it

Item 243 fixed the var-length closing hop and left one adjacent question: `exec/nested.rs` has no
`Close` concept at all, so can a SIMPLE **group** pattern close its cycle? I probed it rather than
guess, and the answer was two wrong answers — one in each engine — plus the reason neither had been
found.

### Native: every closing repetition silently dropped

`nested.rs:261` simply skipped any already-marked node, and the walk's own start is marked, so a
repetition ending back at the start was discarded. On a 4-cycle `0->1->2->3->0` with a `1->3` chord:

```
MATCH SIMPLE ((x)-[:R]->(m)<-[:R]-(y)){1,2} (z) RETURN z.n
  ts:     0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3   (7)        native: 1, 2   (2)
```

Native's two rows were exactly the **non-closing** pair. The fix gives `M` the walk's `start`, a
`simple` flag separate from `node_unique` (ACYCLIC must still forbid the close — that is the single
distinction between the two modes), and a `closed` flag: a hop onto the start is admitted although
the start is marked, and `closed` then bars every further hop. A close mid-unit therefore matches
nothing beyond itself and emits nothing, which is right — an interior repeat is forbidden — while a
close that completes the unit falls through to `outer_walk`'s ordinary boundary emit.

### TS: the same bug, found by an equivalence rather than by comparison

With native fixed, a 300-query sweep across 5 modes × 5 unit shapes × 3 quantifiers × 2 projections
over two fixtures left **10 divergences, all the nested sub-group shape, with native now returning
MORE than TS.** That is the moment to stop comparing engines and find a question with a
spelling-independent answer:

|            |   flat `{1,2}` |  `(({1,2})){1,1}` |  `(({1,1})){1,2}` |
| ---------- | -------------: | ----------------: | ----------------: |
| **SIMPLE** | ts 11 / nat 11 | **ts 6** / nat 11 | **ts 6** / nat 11 |
| ACYCLIC    |          6 / 6 |             6 / 6 |             6 / 6 |
| TRAIL      |        13 / 13 |           13 / 13 |           13 / 13 |
| WALK       |        14 / 14 |           14 / 14 |           14 / 14 |

One outer repetition of an inner 1..2-hop group **is** a flat 1..2-hop group. **TS answered the same
question 11 one way and 6 the other**, and the three other modes agreed across all three spellings —
so TS is wrong about one of its own two answers, no second engine required. (The 11 is also what the
fixture gives by hand: five of its paths close.)

The cause: `matching.ts` decided a close on the RAW cursor position —
`after.length === 1 && after[0].elem === after[0].unit.elems.length` — which is true only for a
**single-level** unit. One nesting level down the raw position sits at the INNERMOST unit's end with
the outer cursor still open, so a nested group closed on nothing. The right question is `resolve`'s
`completedOuter`, the post-epsilon-closure answer to "did an outer repetition just finish" — the
closure being exactly what pops finished inner reps up to the outer end. Resolved lazily, because
`nbr === from` is rare and `resolve` allocates; hoisting it above the collide check
unconditionally would run it for every rejected hop of every simple/acyclic walk, and no admitted
hop resolves twice.

300/300 agree afterwards.

### The coverage gap, which is the item's real output

`genQuantifiedGroup` generated **no path mode at all** — the mode existed only in the abbreviated
arm, so every group pattern this fuzzer ever produced ran under the default TRAIL, where there is no
close. And **nothing generated the nested sub-group shape**, not the fuzzer and not the corpus,
despite `nested.rs`' own doc comment calling it "the 2-level shape the corpus and fuzzer produce".

Both gaps are now closed, and both were verified by mutation rather than assumed:

- **A mode on the group arm** (bounded quantifiers only, the rule the abbreviated arm already
  records). Reverting the native fix is caught on every seed as a value divergence, 8-10 reports.
- **A nested sub-group unit.** Reverting the TS fix **SURVIVED** the moded arm — because its unit is
  always flat, so `after.length === 1` always held. With the nested arm it is caught on every seed.

### Four floors, and a floor met by the wrong queries

Adding the mode made three existing floors fail. That is the system working, and each one had a
different cause worth separating:

- **`hopFilter` 352-371 → 213-267, and the floor was never this shape's.** Its detector
  `/^MATCH \([ab]?[^)]*\)[-<]/` admitted the UNANCHORED GROUP form, because `MATCH ((x)-[e1:E]->…`
  satisfies it with `[^)]*` swallowing `(x`. So ~35% of that tally was group queries counted as
  one-hop filtered counts, and the drop was the pollution leaving. Tightened to `[^()]*`; the honest
  population is 117-158 / 108-141 over nine seeds, so the old `> 320` / `> 210` were **unreachable
  by the queries the counter is for**. Re-measured to 90/80. **A floor met by the wrong queries
  reads exactly like a floor met** — that is the lesson, and it is the counter's fault, not the
  floor's.
- **`peel` and `sink` were diluted, not polluted.** Their detectors keyed on `MATCH ((x)` and
  `MATCH (a:T)((x)`, which the mode prefix and the nested spelling both break. Teaching them the
  optional mode and the optional third `(` put both ABOVE their pre-change rates (sink 283-333
  against 288-320, peel 117-145 against 120-151) — the new arm contributes instead of diluting.
- **`perRep` genuinely shrinks** and is the only floor lowered: the nested spelling carries no
  per-repetition `WHERE` (one level down, `x`/`e1` are lists rather than scalars — a different
  question), so the shape loses its share of the arm. 352-422 / 215-243 against 572-617 / 304-359
  before; `> 350` cleared the minimum by **two queries**, which is not a floor. Now 260/150.
  **Lowering a floor is the last resort, after the detector has been checked** — here checking the
  detector saved two of the three.
- The new arm's own floors: `simpleGroup` 75-126 generated / 57-103 non-empty over nine seeds,
  floors 55/40.

The nested arm's share was settled by measurement in both directions. At 1 in 2 it halved
`perRep`/`sink`/`peel` at once; at 1 in 6 all three clear and mutation confirms it still catches.

### Mutation: 6 native, 3 TS

Native, each under `timeout 900 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`,
restoring from the pristine copy before each:

| mutant                                            | result                    |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| 1 no close at all (the original bug)              | caught, 4 tests           |
| 2 close under ACYCLIC too                         | caught, 3                 |
| 3 let a closed path keep hopping                  | caught, 3                 |
| 4 let a closed path start another outer rep       | **survived — equivalent** |
| 5 never clear `closed` on unwind                  | caught                    |
| 6 compare against the hop's source, not the start | caught                    |

Mutant 4 is equivalent and was predicted as such in the code comment: `do_hop` returns immediately
when `closed`, so the extra repetition matches nothing and the emit at the top of `outer_walk`
happens either way. The guard makes the termination structural rather than a consequence; it buys
no answer.

TS: reverting to the raw-position test is caught (4 of 5). Two survivors, and they named the same
untested consequence — **a close must not MARK its target.** The close bypasses `hopCollides`,
emits, and then deletes its mark, so marking an already-marked start makes `marks.add` a no-op and
the matching `marks.delete` **UNMARK the walk's own start**. A later mid-unit hop onto the start
(where `hopCollides` _is_ consulted) would then be admitted and the path would repeat the start as
an interior node. Constructed the distinguishing input rather than reasoning about it:

```
0->1, 1->0 (closes rep 1 at the unit end), 1->2 (completes rep 1 at 2),
2->0 (MID-unit of rep 2, must be refused), 0->3 (would complete rep 2 at 3)
```

`3` has no out-edge and nothing else reaches it, so an end of `3` means and only means that the walk
passed through `0` twice. `hopMark(mode, false, …)` returns `{n: 3}` under it and nothing else. Both
engines are now held to that fixture by a test each — native pushes and pops a `Vec` where a
duplicate is harmless, TS marks into a `Set` where it is not, so this is a divergence that the TS
data structure makes possible and the native one does not.

The second survivor, closing at a non-boundary, stays survived: when `emit` is false the branch
terminates either way, so the only observable is the `steps` budget — and see below.

### Still open

- **A trail-budget accounting difference, pre-existing and now written down.** Native's
  `varlen_step` classifies ANY `nbr == start` in SIMPLE as a `Close` and charges it a step; TS
  requires the boundary, so a non-boundary hop onto the start is rejected by `hopCollides` and
  charged nothing. The two budgets therefore differ by the number of such hops, observable only
  when `graph.limits.trail` is nearly exhausted. Not introduced here — the old `completesTop` had
  the same shape — but it is why the "close at a non-boundary" mutant survives, and a budget sweep
  is the test it would need.
- **Two loud refusals on the same surface**: native rejects an edge property or a per-hop `WHERE`
  **anywhere** on a subpath group (`edge properties / a per-hop WHERE on a subpath group are not
supported yet`), the one-hop `((x)-[e:R WHERE e.w <> 3]->(y)){1,4}` included, which TS answers.
  `nested.rs`' `do_hop` already evaluates `edge_pred_ok`, so the refusal is in the lowering rather
  than the walker — which makes it look cheaper to lift than it has been priced.
- `nested.rs`' doc comment claiming the corpus produces the 2-level shape is now true of the
  fuzzer. The GQL corpus still does not contain it.

## 245. The var-length walk's per-frame allocation is NOT the cost — refuted, with two probe errors on the way

Item 239 left ~3x between the flat var-length walk and item 238's floor, with three suspects and no
attribution: generator suspension per emission, `expandFilteredArr`'s array per frame, and the
subquery pipeline above. This priced the cheapest one, built it, measured it, and **retracted it**.
What ships is a one-line correctness hardening found while reading the same function.

### The target, and why it looked good

`expandFilteredArr` answers "this hop's neighbours" by running `expand`'s generator and allocating
**one `{ edge, node }` object per neighbour** into a fresh array. On the directed-single-label
no-predicate hop — `-[:KNOWS]->{1,3}`, the shape the two sensitive `bench:usage` rows use — the
filter is a no-op, so that whole structure is a **copy of a `Set` the graph already holds**:
`graph.edgesFromByLabel.get(v.id).get(name)`. Per frame: 1 generator + N objects + 1 array, to
reproduce something already in memory.

Built it as `isBucketHop` + a module-scope `flatFrame` (module scope, not a closure over the
generator's locals — items 181/206), with the frame holding `Edge[]` plus a parallel `nodes` array
only for the shapes whose far end differs per edge. One loop-invariant branch per step in place of
an allocation per step. All 1734 gql tests passed, item 239's 486-assertion emission-sequence
differential included.

### The first design was unsafe, and reading one clause would have missed it

The obvious version hands back a **live iterator** over the bucket instead of materialising. That is
wrong, and only one of the two write clauses shows why:

```
case 'set':    const arr = toArray(bindings); for (const b of arr) runSet(…)   // drains FIRST
case 'insert': bindings = toArray(map((b) => runInsert(graph, clause, b, params), bindings))
```

`set` and `remove` drain the row stream before writing — safe. **`insert` and `merge` run as
`toArray(map(…))`, so each write happens DURING the drain**, interleaved with the matcher feeding
it, and a JS `Set` iterator observes elements added during iteration. A live view would let
`MATCH (a)-[:R]->{1,3}(b) INSERT (x)-[:R]->(y)` traverse an edge the insert had just created. The
materialised snapshot is load-bearing, and checking `set` alone would have concluded the opposite.

### The measurement, and the probe error that preceded it

**The first probe measured a scan.** `MATCH (a:P {n: 1})-[:KNOWS]->{1,3}(b) RETURN count(*)` over
20,000 vertices with no index on `n` spends its time finding the seed: ~155 paths in 1.2 ms is
**7.7 µs a path**, which is nonsense for a 400 ns walk. Every row read 0.99-1.02x because the change
cannot reach a scan, and I nearly recorded that as the answer. The tell was the per-path arithmetic,
not the ratio — a flat result on a probe whose absolute number is implausible is a broken probe, not
a refutation.

Rebuilt on item 239's shape: a subquery walk per OUTER ROW, 200 outer rows, ~31,000 frames a query,
which amortises the one scan away and makes the walk 25x the scan-only control. In-process A/B of
both BUILT bundles, alternating round by round with the order swapped, answers asserted equal first,
12 rounds a side at 10 calls a timing:

| case                                   | before (µs) | after (µs)  |                     |
| -------------------------------------- | ----------- | ----------- | ------------------- |
| **sub-walk `{1,3}` ×200**              | 12595-22338 | 12288-18298 | **1.025x, overlap** |
| sub-walk `{1,2}` ×200                  | 3553-4250   | 3401-5372   | 1.045x, overlap     |
| sub-walk `{2,4}` ×60                   | 18834-24738 | 19932-23387 | 0.945x, overlap     |
| sub-walk predicated ×200 (general arm) | 18793-23935 | 19781-24521 | 0.950x, overlap     |
| control plain hop ×200                 | 1568-2914   | 1689-2463   | 0.928x, overlap     |
| control scan only                      | 531-1001    | 537-946     | 0.988x, overlap     |

**Nothing, in either direction.** And the decisive detail is the CONTROL: `control plain hop` — which
the change cannot reach — moved 0.928x, _further than any target row_. A control that moves further
than the effect means the instrument is reading process noise, so the two "regressions" at 0.945x
and 0.950x are not regressions either (item 183's rule, earned again).

**Retracted**, by item 231's standard: correct, free, and demonstrating nothing is not a reason to
ship.

### Why it was never going to be there, which is the useful part

The arithmetic says so after the fact and should have said so before: at ~400 ns a path, N
short-lived nursery objects at a few ns each cannot be a measurable share. What the frame _also_
does, per frame, is **two string-keyed Map lookups** — `edgesFromByLabel.get(v.id)` hashes the
vertex's string id, then `.get(label.name)` hashes the label — where native indexes an array by
integer id. That is the same cost that explained the three Gremlin rows closed as "structural" in
item 161 (a hash lookup inside the property read, not a layer of overhead), and the same shape as
item 186's string-keyed group index.

**So the next hypothesis for item 239's residual ~3x is the per-frame string hash, not the
allocation** — and it is not a local change: it wants an adjacency handle cached on the frame or
dense integer ids in the TS core, the latter being the decision already recorded as needing an
explicit call. Priced, not attempted.

### What ships: `relHasInlinePred`

Reading `expandFilteredArr` turned up a real latent wrong answer. Its predicate check was

```ts
const hasPred = rel.pred.props.length > 0 || rel.pred.where !== undefined;
```

while `satisfies` checks **three** fields: `props`, then `eqProps`, then `where`. A hop whose only
predicate had been lifted into `eqProps` would therefore be expanded **UNFILTERED**.

It is unreachable through the parser today — `compileRel` calls `compilePredicate` with no `ownVar`,
so `directEqProps` never lifts anything out of an edge's `WHERE`, and `eqProps` is always empty for
a rel. But item 230 is what added that lifting, and left `compileNode` not passing `ownVar` as an
open question; the day either does, this silently returns a superset. A skipped predicate filter
cannot be caught by a correctness test on a fixture lacking the spelling, and the fuzzer's edge
predicates are all `>` / `>=` — never the `=` against a literal that `eqProps` is for.

Now `relHasInlinePred(rel)`, reading all three, shared with the call that needed it. Three tests,
and the one that matters builds the `CRel` **by hand**, because the parser cannot produce the shape:
`eqProps: [{ key: 'w', value: () => 9 }]` (the value is a compiled closure, not a literal) must
filter 2 edges to 1. Mutation: removing the `eqProps` term fails 2 of the 3.

### Gates

gql suite 1734 → 1737. `bun run check` and `bun run fmt:check` as their own commands; all seven
fuzzers green. No bench row changes, and none should: the shipped change adds one `!== undefined`
and a `.length` to a check already on that path.

## 246. Re-deriving a rejected target, and the separation that makes it a different number

Item 245 closed by naming the per-frame **string-keyed Map lookup** as the next hypothesis for item
239's residual ~3x. This measured its ceiling before designing anything, found the target already on
the refuted list, and dropped it — but the measurement separates two things the earlier pricing
bundled, so the number is worth keeping.

### Two probes, and why the first one was not the answer

Both are deliberately UNSAFE upper-bound probes, not candidates: a process-lifetime `WeakMap` keyed
by the `Vertex` OBJECT, so a frame's adjacency reaches the bucket through one reference hash instead
of `edgesFromByLabel.get(v.id)` (a string hash) plus `.get(label.name)` (another).

- **Probe 1 cached the built array.** 1.145x / 1.142x / **1.216x disjoint**.
- **Probe 2 cached only the bucket REFERENCE**, rebuilding the array every frame exactly as HEAD
  does — same allocations, same generator, same N objects, only the two hashes gone. 1.089x /
  1.029x / **1.135x disjoint**.

Probe 1 is not an upper bound on "a cheaper lookup", because returning the same array on a hit also
skips **rebuilding adjacency for a REVISITED vertex** — and in a `{2,4}` walk over a degree-5 graph
vertices repeat constantly. Two different optimizations, one of them (memoising across visits) not
available safely at all. The separation says: the lookup is worth **1.09-1.14x** and the
rebuild-skip a further ~1.05-1.07x.

In-process A/B of both built bundles, order swapped each round, answers asserted equal first, 10
rounds a side. Controls flat on probe 2 (plain hop 0.985x) — though `control scan only` read 0.883x,
which is this instrument's noise floor and a reminder not to believe a single non-overlapping row
without a control that stays put.

### It was already priced, and the rejection stands

**Item 172 priced this exact mechanism and dropped it**: "an adjacency box (the items 161/162
treatment for `edgesFromByLabel`). The row lookup is only 14ns isolated (46ns in context), a cached
row reads 128ns against today's 174, and the dense-array ceiling is 97 — so **1.35x for a
cross-cutting cache with invalidation on `addEdge` and `removeEdge`. Bad trade, dropped.**"

My 1.09-1.14x end-to-end on the var-length walk is consistent with that 1.35x on the lookup alone —
the lookup is one part of a frame — so this is **corroboration on a path item 172 did not test, not
a reason to reopen it.** The invalidation cost is unchanged and so is the verdict.

And the bigger version of the same idea is **not rejected but awaiting a decision**: item 197 priced
inverting the adjacency to `Map<type, Map<vertexId, Set<Edge>>>` at **3.2x on the operation that
floors the three biggest remaining rows**, with its cost spelled out (`incidentEdges` probes T
type-maps instead of one; every reader of `edgesFromByLabel`/`edgesToByLabel` changes shape), and
left it "for a decision rather than taken — which is what it has been since item 180". Its own
closing line is the context for this item: _"Nothing else in the TS query surface is above 5x once
this is accounted for."_

### The lesson, which is why this entry exists at all

**Check the refuted list before measuring, and check it before DESIGNING.** I spent part of two
ticks on a mechanism this document had already priced twice — once as a rejection (172) and once as
a pending decision (197) — because item 245's conclusion named the mechanism from first principles
rather than from the audit. The rule already exists for benches
(`ts-edge-insert-is-adjacency`: "CHECK THE REFUTED LIST before measuring"); it applies to a
hypothesis the same way. A `grep` of this file for the data structure's name costs seconds and would
have gone straight to item 172.

What this item adds that was not there: the lookup and the rebuild are **separable**, and separately
they are 1.09-1.14x and ~1.06x. Anyone reopening the adjacency question should price those two
independently rather than measure a cache and attribute all of it to the hash.

No code changed.

## 247. The adjacency question is CLOSED, and item 197's "awaiting a decision" is what kept reopening it

The user has ruled out the type-first adjacency, for the reason item 200 already measured: it buys
the typed hop and **destroys lookup by id**. No code change, and no further measurement — this entry
exists to stop the question being re-raised a fourth time.

**Item 200 is the authority and it already closed this**, with the numbers:

> Type-first wins the typed lookup by 2.2-4.1x and loses get-by-id by 1.4x at three edge types and
> 4.8x at twenty. The crossover sits between T=1 and T=3, so the bench's single edge type is the one
> configuration where inverting looks free — and it is the only configuration the earlier number was
> taken in. A people graph has five to twenty edge types. **The current shape is right, and for the
> stated reason.**

Item 200 also priced and rejected the dual index (2.0-2.4x on `indexEdgeLabel`, the single most
expensive thing the engine does), and named the only surviving direction: an **OPT-IN** type-first
spine, the way property indexes already work — "a feature with an API, not an optimization, so it is
noted and not taken."

### What actually went wrong, which is a documentation bug

Item 197 priced the same structure at 3.2x and left it "for a decision rather than taken — which is
what it has been since item 180", and the later summary still lists "the type-first adjacency index
(3.2x…)" as open. **Item 200 then settled it and those earlier framings were never corrected**, so
the audit reads as though a 3.2x is sitting there awaiting permission. It is not. Both passages are
superseded by item 200; treat 197's number as the typed-hop half of a trade whose other half 200
measured.

I read 197, did not read 200, and raised a settled question. That is the SECOND time in this tick —
item 246 is the first, on the adjacency box — and both have the same shape: a hypothesis derived
from first principles, matching something this document had already priced, with the search skipped.
The rule from `ts-edge-insert-is-adjacency` is "CHECK THE REFUTED LIST before measuring"; the
correction is that **a "left for a decision" entry is not evidence the decision is open — grep
forward for the item that closed it.** An audit that only ever appends needs its stale openings
retracted in place, which is what this entry does.

### Where that leaves the TS surface

Item 197's closing line stands: nothing else in the TS query surface is above 5x. The three
`bench:usage` rows TS still loses are all previously-closed constant factors — `keyed dedup lookup`
82.2k against 111.7k (items 240/241; the residual is memory traffic and candidate iteration order),
`append node` 129.8k/323.5k and `interleaved append+link` 59.0k/172.6k (items 140/203; a 3.7x insert
constant factor whose single target is `addVertex`). So the loop's remaining headroom is native and
Gremlin, plus the two open cross-engine correctness items: the trail-budget accounting difference
(item 244) and native's refusal of an edge property or per-hop `WHERE` anywhere on a subpath group,
which TS answers and whose walker already evaluates `edge_pred_ok` — so that refusal is in the
lowering, not the walker.

## 248. A capability native refused and TS answered — and the lowering was already there

Item 244 left two loud refusals on its surface: native rejects an edge property or a per-hop
`WHERE` **anywhere** on a subpath group, the one-hop `((x)-[e:R WHERE e.w <> 3]->(y)){1,4}`
included, which TS answers. The note said the refusal looked like it was in the lowering rather
than the walker. It was, and nothing else was missing.

### Three facts that make it a three-line change

- `GElem::Hop` has carried `edge_pred: Option<Box<Expr>>` all along — "a PER-HOP edge filter
  (`-[e WHERE …]->` / inline `{k:v}`)".
- `nested.rs`' `do_hop` already evaluates it (`edge_pred_ok(epred, self.store, a.eid)`), and
  `parse_nested_group` already builds it via `edge_pred_from_rel`.
- The group's per-repetition `WHERE` already binds **node position `p` at mini-scope slot `2p` and
  edge position `p` at `2p + 1`** — so **hop `p`'s predicate IS a per-repetition conjunct at slot
  `2p + 1`**. The group needs no new evaluation machinery at all.

So `parse_subpath_group` collects each hop's predicate, built at `2 * edge_vars.len() + 1`, and
folds them into the per-rep predicate. `edge_pred_from_rel` becomes `edge_pred_at(rel, slot)` with
the old call delegating at slot 0 — **parameterising the slot rather than rewriting slots
afterwards**, which is what keeps a multi-hop unit correct without an expression walker.

### The measurement

A 300-query cross-engine sweep: 5 path modes × 10 unit shapes (k = 1, 2 and 3; a predicate on one
hop, on each hop, mixed `WHERE`/inline spellings, and alongside the group's own per-rep `WHERE`) ×
3 quantifiers × 2 projections.

```
before:  agree=0   diverge=300  nativeThrew=300
after:   agree=300 diverge=0    nativeThrew=0
```

### The guard that is not reachable, and says so

`parse_subpath_group` has two early returns for an inner-quantified body, **past the fold** — so a
collected predicate reaching one would be dropped SILENTLY. The `{m,m}` branch also rewrites
`edge_vars` so one parsed edge var stands for all `m` hops, which makes "which slot does this
address" ambiguous rather than merely unimplemented. It refuses loudly instead.

That guard appears unreachable: `((x)-[e:R WHERE e.w > 2]->{2,2}(y)){1,2}` is routed to the NESTED
parser (a `]` followed by a quantifier is what selects it), which has supported per-hop predicates
all along — verified against TS before writing it down (both answer 2 unfiltered / 1 filtered for
`{2,2}`, and 9 / 4 for `{1,2}`). **My first test asserted a refusal there and failed, because the
query answered.** The test now asserts the ANSWER, and the guard stays as the loud failure for a
spelling that may yet reach it.

### Tests and mutation

Native 989 → 994. The fixture is a weighted chain `0 -(w5)-> 1 -(w5)-> 2 -(w1)-> 3` where only the
last edge fails `w > 2`, so unfiltered is 5 and filtered is 3 — both asserted, because a predicate
that is dropped leaves the unfiltered number.

The load-bearing one is `each_group_hop_predicate_addresses_its_own_edge`: a two-hop unit whose two
qualifying repetitions have **different weights on each hop**, so "first hop light AND second hop
heavy" and its mirror select _different_ repetitions. A lowering that addressed every hop to slot 1
answers hop 1 correctly and tests hop 2 against hop 1's edge, and nothing else here distinguishes
that.

Six mutants under `timeout 900 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`,
restoring before each — all six caught:

| mutant                                               | caught by                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| 1 discard the collected predicates (the silent bug)  | 5 tests                     |
| 2 address every hop to slot 1                        | 1 — the test written for it |
| 3 off-by-one: the NODE slot instead of the edge slot | 4                           |
| 4 drop the group's own per-rep `WHERE` in the fold   | 5, incl. three pre-existing |
| 5 drop the hop predicates in the fold                | 5                           |
| 6 ignore the inline `{k: v}` props                   | 1                           |

### Fuzzer coverage, which is what found item 249

The group arm generated no per-hop predicate at all, so a hand-written probe found this gap rather
than the fuzzer — and a refusal against an answer IS a divergence here, so generating the shape is
all the guard needed. Added to both hop pools, including a predicate on the SECOND hop (the half
that needs its own slot). New counter `groupHopPred`, measured 415-454 generated / 261-294
non-empty over four seeds, floors 300/190.

**It found a TS wrong answer on its first run** — see item 249.

### A counter that moved the WRONG way

The new spellings inflated `perRep` from 352-422 to **486-527**, because its detector is
`q.includes('((x)') && q.includes(' WHERE ')` and a per-HOP `WHERE` lives inside the brackets. Same
over-matching item 246 caught in `hopFilter`, found this time by the number RISING: **a counter that
goes up when a spelling is added is as suspicious as one that falls.** Stripping `[...]` before the
test restores the honest band (352-398 / 197-231) and the new shape gets its own counter instead of
borrowing one.

## 249. The TS matcher evaluates only the OUTERMOST unit's WHERE — found by item 248's own coverage, on its first run

Item 248 added per-hop edge predicates to the fuzzer's group arm so the capability it had just given
native would stay covered. The arm failed immediately, on every seed, and not on the new capability:

```
MATCH (((x)-[e1:E WHERE e1.w > 2]->(y)){1,2}){1,2} RETURN count(*) AS x
  ts: 76    native: 12
MATCH (a:T)(((x)-[e1:E WHERE e1.w > 2]->(y)){1,2}){1,3}(b:U) RETURN b.n AS x, a.n AS t ORDER BY t, x
  ts: 20 rows    native: 7
```

### Which engine, settled without appealing to the other

The nested shape, native returning FEWER — the opposite direction from item 244, so not a repeat of
it. On a chain `0 -(w5)-> 1 -(w5)-> 2 -(w1)-> 3`, where only the last edge fails `w > 2`:

|                                | unfiltered |  `WHERE e.w > 2` |
| ------------------------------ | ---------: | ---------------: |
| flat `((x)-[e:E …]->(y)){1,2}` |      5 / 5 |        **3 / 3** |
| nested `(({1,1})){1,2}`        |      5 / 5 | **ts 5** / nat 3 |
| nested `(({1,2})){1,1}`        |      5 / 5 | **ts 5** / nat 3 |

One outer repetition of an inner 1..1-hop group IS a flat 1..1-hop group, so all three are the same
question — and 3 is the hand-derived answer (1-rep `0->1`, `1->2`; 2-rep `0->1->2`). **TS's "filtered"
answer is identical to its own UNFILTERED answer**, and its endpoints include `n: 3`, reachable only
across the forbidden edge. TS is wrong, and the equal-to-unfiltered number says exactly how: the
predicate is not being evaluated at all.

### The cause

`compileSubpathUnit` LIFTS a plain hop's inline `WHERE` to the repetition's unit predicate, and it
has to: `-[e:R WHERE e.w > x.n]->` references `x`, which is bound only when the rep completes. But
the matcher asks

```ts
const hasWhere = unit.where !== undefined;          // the unit it was HANDED
… if (completedOuter && hasWhere && !unitWherePasses(unit, …))
```

— the **outermost** unit only. A nested sub-unit's `where` is compiled, attached, and never read.
The compiler's own comment ("a NESTED hop's WHERE … STAYS on the `Sub`'s inner hop") describes the
quantified-hop case and does not cover a plain hop inside a nested sub-unit, which is the hole.

### The fix: narrow the lift, don't remove it

An **edge-only** predicate needs no lifting at all. Left on the hop, `expandFilteredArr` applies it
during expansion — correct at any nesting depth, and EARLIER than rep completion. So lift only when
the predicate reads something other than its own edge.

"Edge-only" is decided by an **ALLOWLIST**, not by `freePredicateVars`: that function does not
descend into a subquery (see `order-by-subquery-alias-collision`, which cost item 213), so it
reports the empty set for `EXISTS { … }` and would call a predicate edge-only that reads half the
row. Admitted: `prop`/`property_exists` **on the edge variable**, `lit`, `param`, `not`/`neg`,
`compare`, `arith`, `and`/`or`/`xor`, `list` — every one with its operands fully walked. Everything
else lifts as before.

An anonymous hop returns `false`: without a variable, a `WHERE` cannot be about its own edge.

All three spellings now answer 3, and the 300-query sweep from item 248 is unchanged at 300/300.

### Tests and mutation

Five TS tests. Four assert the equivalence and the endpoint set (`n: 3` present is the bug, not a
count being off). The fifth is the one that matters in the other direction: **a cross-variable
predicate must still be LIFTED.** `e.w > x.n` selects the same three repetitions as `w > 2` on this
fixture while being impossible to apply per hop, and its mirror `e.w < x.n` gives 1 — so the test
discriminates rather than just passing.

Three mutants, all caught:

| mutant                                          | result                           |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `edgeOnlyWhere` always false (the pre-fix lift) | caught, 2 of 5                   |
| `edgeOnlyWhere` always true (lift nothing)      | caught — the cross-variable test |
| drop the `e.variable === edgeVar` check         | caught — the cross-variable test |

The last two are caught by that single test, which is the point of having constructed it: the two
over-eager mutants are exactly the ones a nested-shape test cannot see.

### What it cost me, recorded

I ran the "revert the fix" mutant by copying the PRISTINE file over `executor.ts` — and had saved
only the pristine, not the fixed version, so the restore step had nothing to restore and the change
was gone. Reconstructed from the diff. The project rule says keep the pristine copy under `target/`;
the corollary for a mutant that is a straight REVERT is to **save the fixed copy too, before the
first mutant runs**, because there the pristine IS the mutant.

### Still open on this surface

`compileSubpathUnit` still attaches a `where` to a nested sub-unit when the predicate is the inner
subpath's own `WHERE` (`seg.subpathWhere` on the inner segment) rather than a lifted hop predicate.
That one is genuinely per-inner-repetition and cannot move to a hop, so the real fix for it is for
the matcher to evaluate an inner unit's `where` at inner-rep completion — a change in `resolve`'s
epsilon closure, which reports `completedOuter` but not which INNER units completed. No divergence
is known for it yet, and the fuzzer does not generate an inner subpath `WHERE`; that is the next
piece of coverage on this surface rather than a guess at a bug.

## 250. `scale/sweep`'s filtered count is not a regression screen — ANY native edit moves it ~8-10%

Item 248 is a parser-only change. `bench_all`'s `scale/sweep` row nevertheless showed `filter_us`
up 8-10% at all three sizes, and the loop's own instruction is to screen with `bench_all` confirmed
by min-of-three — so this had to be settled before shipping. It is the documented toll, and the
useful output is knowing the row cannot screen anything.

### Four measurements, each needed

**1. Single runs, which looked like noise.** `bench_all` before 74.2 / 304.8 / 764.6 against after
84.0 / 340.0 / 842.2. Consistent direction across three sizes, but one sample a side, and the two
prior `bench_all` runs already spanned 74.2-78.5 at 50k.

**2. Min-of-three, standalone — which compared the wrong things.** 90.3-92.9 against a `bench_all`
figure of 74-84. Standalone `scale_bench` and `bench_all` are different processes with different
allocator and cache state, so that comparison was apples to oranges and its "regression" was partly
the harness change.

**3. Like-for-like min-of-three, standalone both sides:** 83.3 / 341.3 / 841.0 against
90.3 / 368.8 / 924.9 — **disjoint at all three sizes.** Real, and `1hop_us` untouched.

**4. The two-binary alternating A/B** — both `scale_bench` binaries kept side by side, order swapped
each round, six rounds. Head 82.7-84.4 (after a cold first run of 91.9) against after 89.4-93.1 at
50k; 833.9-844.4 against 920.4-939.1 at 500k. Confirmed.

### And then the control, which is the whole point

`time_query` parses ONCE, outside the timed region, and `exec/tests.rs` is `#[cfg(test)]` — so
nothing in item 248 can execute during a filtered count. That leaves codegen layout, which needs a
control.

**My first control was no control at all**: a never-called private method. A private `fn` with no
callers is eliminated, so the binary was byte-identical to HEAD (`md5sum` would have said so had I
checked before trusting the flat result). **A null control has to be one the optimizer cannot
delete.**

The second control lengthens ONE ERROR STRING in `parse_subpath_group` — a real binary change,
zero behavioural effect for a filter scan:

| `filter_us` | HEAD        | item 248    | the null control |
| ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | ---------------- |
| 50k         | 82.7-85.9   | 89.4-93.1   | **92.0-95.1**    |
| 500k        | 840.8-846.4 | 920.4-939.1 | **925.2-934.4**  |

**The control reproduces the shift in full.** So the cost is not item 248's: **any edit to that
function moves this row ~8-10%.**

### What this is, and what it means for the screen

`pull-alignment-is-load-bearing` records that any edit to `exec::pull` costs the filtered-count
cluster 1.08-1.24x and never gains — "that's the toll, not a regression". The measured 1.08-1.10x
