here is inside that band, for the same cluster, but reached from a **parser** edit rather than an
`exec::pull` one. So the toll is not a property of editing `pull`; it is a property of this cluster
being sensitive to code layout anywhere in the crate.

**Therefore `scale/sweep`'s `filter_us` cannot screen a native change for regressions.** It will
flag on anything that alters codegen, including a comment-length change to an error message. The
honest screen for a native change is every OTHER row, with this one read only against a null
control built the same day. The same caution applies to the rest of the filtered-count family.

`1hop_us` and `labelcnt_us` in the same table did NOT move, in any of the four measurements — so the
table is not uniformly unusable, and the sensitivity is specific to the filtered count.

### The cost of getting here

Four rounds of measurement and two controls, one of them void, to clear a change that could not have
caused the thing it was accused of. That was still the right spend: the alternative was shipping a
disjoint 8-10% regression on an unexplained row, or dropping a correctness fix for a cost it does
not impose. What makes it cheaper next time is the rule, not the diligence: **before investigating a
regression on a row the change cannot reach, build a null control and check it is not byte-identical
to HEAD.**

## 251. An INNER subpath's own WHERE: TS ignores it, native refuses to parse it — diagnosed and designed, not yet fixed

Item 249 fixed the case where a hop's inline `WHERE` was lifted into a nested sub-unit and then
never evaluated, and left the harder half open: the inner subpath's **own** per-repetition `WHERE`,
which is genuinely per-inner-repetition and so cannot move onto a hop. No divergence was known for
it, and the fuzzer generates no inner subpath `WHERE`. This probes it. No code changed.

### Both engines are wrong, differently

```
MATCH (a:T)(((x)-[e:E]->(y) WHERE x.n <> 1){1,1}){1,2} RETURN count(*) AS c
  ts: 5    native: THROW  lenke: query: expected RParen at token 21
```

- **TS silently ignores it.** 5 is that shape's UNFILTERED count — the predicate contributes
  nothing. The `{1,2}×{1,2}` spelling likewise reads 9 with the `WHERE` and 9 without.
- **Native refuses to parse it at all** — a loud `E_` at least, but a capability gap.

### The right answer is 2, pinned by an equivalence

An inner `{1,1}` of a one-hop unit, repeated 1..2 times by the outer, accepts exactly the 1-2 hop
walks whose every hop satisfies the `WHERE` — which is the flat `{1,2}` with the same `WHERE`. Both
engines already agree that one is **2**:

|                                        | unfiltered |          `WHERE x.n <> 1` |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------: | ------------------------: |
| flat `((x)-[e:E]->(y) …){1,2}`         |      5 / 5 |                 **2 / 2** |
| nested `(({1,1})){1,2}`, inner `WHERE` |      5 / 5 | **ts 5** / native refuses |

So the answer needs no appeal to either engine: TS's 5 is wrong by its own arithmetic on the
equivalent spelling.

### Why TS drops it, and the fix, which is in-design

`compileSubpathUnit`'s nested branch recurses, and the inner segment's `subpathWhere` becomes the
INNER unit's `where`. The matcher then asks

```ts
const hasWhere = unit.where !== undefined;      // the unit it was HANDED
… if (completedOuter && hasWhere && !unitWherePasses(unit, …))
```

— the outermost unit only, and `completedOuter` is the only completion it is told about. Item 249's
fix does not reach this case: an edge-only hop predicate can move to the hop, but a per-rep `WHERE`
reading a node cannot.

`resolve` already knows where inner completion happens. Its epsilon closure pops a cursor exactly
there:

```ts
if (rep2 >= top.min && (top.max === null || rep2 <= top.max)) {
  if (p.length === 1) { emit = true; }
  else { const close = p.map(…); close.pop(); close[close.length - 1].elem += 1; work.push(close); }
}
```

The obstacle is PROVENANCE: `resolve` merges every branch into one `moves` list and one `emit`
boolean, so "prune the branch that went through this inner completion" is not expressible afterwards.

**The design that avoids restructuring it: pass a GATE into `resolve`.**
`resolve(start, gate?)` with `gate(unit, rep, depth, treePath) => boolean`, consulted at that
inner-completion branch before `work.push(close)`. A failing gate simply does not push the
continuation, so the branch dies inside the closure and provenance stays implicit. The matcher
supplies a gate closing over the current steps and `env`.

What makes this in-design rather than a redesign is that **`bindUnit` already takes exactly the
parameters an inner unit needs**:

```ts
bindUnit(next, unit, treePath: readonly number[], keyStart: number, steps)
```

`bindGroupVarsPerRep` is its depth-0 special case (`treePath = []`, `keyStart = 1`), and
`unitWherePasses` is the thin wrapper. An inner unit at depth `d` wants `keyStart = d + 1` and the
`treePath` of elem indices down to its `Sub` — which is what `within`/`key` inside `bindUnit`
already consume. So the inner-rep step subset is `buildSteps(nbr, edge)` filtered to the same outer
rep and `levels[d][0] === rep`, and the predicate call is the same two lines at a different depth.

### Why it is not done here

It is the most delicate part of the matcher and **the emission SEQUENCE is a byte-identity
contract** — item 239's differential compares the flat walk against this matcher element by
element, across 4 modes × 8 quantifiers × 3 hop spellings × 5 seeds. A gate that prunes a branch
changes which continuations exist, so it has to be shown not to perturb the order of the branches
that survive. That is a tick's careful work, not a tail-end change, and this tick has already
shipped items 248-250.

### What must land WITH the fix, not after it

- **Native's parser** has to accept an inner subpath `WHERE` first, or the engines diverge
  refusal-against-answer. The flat parser already parses a per-rep `WHERE` (`parse_subpath_group`'s
  mini-scope block); `parse_nested_group` does not offer one for the inner unit.
- **Fuzzer coverage is deliberately NOT added yet.** Generating the shape today would be red for a
  known-unfixed reason on both sides at once, which teaches nothing the audit does not already
  record — and it is not the same as removing coverage. It goes in with the fix, with its own
  counter, since an inner `WHERE` is a different code path from the outer one on both engines.

## 252/253. An inner subpath's own WHERE, fixed in both engines — and the fuzzer caught my own bug in the fix

Item 251 diagnosed it and designed the fix without taking it. This takes it, in the order the risk
dictated: **native first**, because native REFUSED the shape, so support there can only turn an
error into an answer; then TS, where the change is a gate inside the matcher's epsilon closure with
an emission-order contract over it.

The answer is pinned by equivalence, not by either engine: an inner `{1,1}` of a one-hop unit
repeated 1..2 times accepts exactly the 1-2 hop walks whose every hop satisfies the `WHERE` — the
flat `{1,2}` with the same `WHERE`, which both engines already answered **2** where the unfiltered
shape gives 5.

### 252 — native: `GUnit::per_rep`

Three pieces, each small because the structures were already shaped for it:

- **`GUnit` gains `per_rep: Option<Box<Expr>>`.** Only TWO construction sites in the crate. The
  OUTERMOST unit keeps `None` — its per-rep `WHERE` rides on `Plan::NestedGroup`, where the driver
  already knows the outer boundary. An inner unit had no such home, which is why an inner `WHERE`
  was a parse error.
- **The parser** captures the inner group's `WHERE` before its `)` (`capture_inline_where`, the
  mechanism the outer per-rep and per-hop predicates already use) and lowers it against the inner
  unit's own mini-scope: rep source at 0, hop `p`'s edge at `2p + 1`, its target at `2p + 2`. The
  scope is REPLACED while parsing, so a reference to anything else is an unbound-variable error
  rather than a silent null — the discipline item 51 paid for.
- **`nested.rs`** evaluates it at inner-rep completion inside `sub_walk`'s continuation, gating
  BEFORE the recursion so it covers both that rep's emit and any further rep. `sub_rep` already
  tags each hop `[(orep, es), (irep, ihop + 1)]`, so the rep's steps are exactly those whose first
  level is `orep` and second is `irep`. Built as typed columns directly rather than through
  `bind_nested` like `rep_ok`: that route exists because an OUTER rep's bindings can be nested
  lists, while an inner rep's are all scalars.

### 253 — TS: a gate inside `resolve`

The matcher asks `unit.where !== undefined` of the unit it was HANDED and is told only about
`completedOuter`, so an inner unit's `where` was compiled, attached, and never read. Item 249's fix
cannot reach it — an edge-only hop predicate can move onto the hop; a per-rep `WHERE` reading a node
cannot.

`resolve` now takes an optional `gate(unit, rep, depth, treePath)`, consulted where its epsilon
closure pops a cursor at inner completion. **Both continuations are gated** — the `close` that
leaves the unit and the `again` that starts another rep — because a failed rep is on the path either
way. It must live inside the closure: `resolve` merges every branch into one `moves` list and one
`emit` flag, so "prune the branch that went through this completion" is not expressible afterwards.

The evaluation reuses what was already there. `unitWherePasses` became a wrapper over
`unitWherePassesAt(unit, repSteps, env, treePath, keyStart)`, because **`bindUnit` already takes
exactly the two parameters that locate a unit in the step tree** — `bindGroupVarsPerRep` is its
depth-0 case (`[]`, `1`), so an inner unit at depth `d` is `(treePath, d + 1)`.

Cost when there is no inner `WHERE` — the overwhelmingly common case — is one
`top.unit.where === undefined` test, short-circuited before the gate is called, and the result is
cached per work item.

**Emission order:** the gate only ever REMOVES a work item, and `moves` is appended in processing
order, so the survivors keep their relative order. Verified rather than argued: item 239's
differential compares the flat walk against this matcher ELEMENT BY ELEMENT across 4 modes × 8
quantifiers × 3 hop spellings × 5 seeds, 486 assertions, and passes.

### The fuzzer caught a bug in my own fix, on its first run

Generating the shape immediately failed on two seeds:

```
MATCH SIMPLE (((x)-[e1:E]->(y) WHERE e1.w > 2){1,2}){1,2} RETURN count(*) AS x
  ts: 11    native: 9
```

**Mine, from this change.** The SIMPLE close path computes its own `resolve(after)` to decide
whether the hop closes, and that result is then REUSED as `resolved` — so I had passed the gate to
the second call only, and a closing repetition skipped the predicate entirely. Native was right.
Both calls now take the gate, and the test for it exists because the fuzzer found it, not because
the reasoning did: I had checked that both CONTINUATIONS were gated and missed that there were two
resolve CALL SITES.

### Tests and mutation

Native 994 → 1000, TS 1742 → 1748.

The native fixture is a weighted chain whose counts are hand-derived, and the load-bearing test is
`an_inner_where_over_a_multi_hop_unit_addresses_each_position`: a two-hop inner unit where "second
hop heavy" gives 1 and "first hop heavy" gives 2 — numbers that cannot differ if the two edge
positions share a slot.

**Two of my own predictions were wrong and the tests caught them.** I expected `y.n <> 1` to give 2;
`y` is the TARGET, so it excludes the hop INTO node 1 and leaves two hops that DO compose — 4. The
test is kept with an added `assert_ne!` against the source-keyed query, because the two numbers
differing is the real discriminator. And a parse-rejection test used `try_gql`, which panics on a
parse error rather than returning it; the rejection is at parse time, so it calls `gql::parse`.

8 native mutants under `timeout 900 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p
MemorySwapMax=0`, all caught: never evaluate the predicate (5 tests), gate the wrong inner rep (3),
drop the outer-rep filter (4), shift the edge/node slot pairing (3), evaluate but ignore the verdict
(5), bind every inner edge to slot 1 (1 — the multi-hop test), bind the target to the source slot
(1), and parse the `WHERE` then discard it (5).

3 TS mutants, all caught: the gate never consulted (5 of 6), the close path ungated (1 — the test
the fuzzer prompted), and the inner unit bound at the wrong depth (5).

Reverting either engine's fix is caught by the fuzzer on every seed, 10 reports each.

### A detector inflated for the THIRD time

`perRep`'s detector is "contains the group opener AND contains `WHERE`". Item 248's per-hop
spellings inflated it 352-422 → 486-527 via the brackets; this item's inner `WHERE` inflated it
again to 494-543, because `((x)` is a SUBSTRING of the nested `(((x)`. Now excluded explicitly, and
the band is back to 352-398 / 208-237.

**Three times is the pattern, not bad luck.** A counter written that way matches every `WHERE`
anywhere in a group, so **each new predicate POSITION borrows it until told not to** — and there are
now three positions (inside the brackets, after the inner body, after the outer body) reaching three
different code paths on both sides. Each has its own counter: `groupHopPred` 415-454 / 256-284 and
`innerWhere` 142-182 / 126-161, floors ~25% under their minima.

### A postscript for item 250

`bench_all`'s `filter_us` reads **84.0 / 348.4 / 849.0** on this change — essentially the HEAD
baseline (83.3 / 341.3 / 841.0), not item 248's elevated band (90.3 / 368.8 / 924.9). A DIFFERENT
edit to the same crate moved the row back, which is independent corroboration of item 250's
conclusion: the filtered-count cluster tracks code LAYOUT, not the change, and lands wherever
layout puts it. It is not a screen in either direction — neither a regression nor a win.

## 254. The trail budget's "mirrors TS exactly" claim was false — and I misdiagnosed it twice before measuring

Item 244 left this open: native's `varlen_step` classifies ANY `nbr == start` in SIMPLE as a
`Close` and charges it a step, while TS requires the hop to be at a repetition boundary. The budget
sits under a comment that says it "mirrors the TS matcher exactly, so the two engines agree on which
queries raise" — a stated invariant, so the question was only whether it is observable.

It is, and the path to the answer is the item's real content.

### The instrument: thresholds, not raise-or-not

A probe that asks "does either engine raise at limit L" produces a table of divergences that tells
you nothing about the quantity. Binary-searching the **smallest limit at which each engine stops
raising** turns the question into a number, and a number can be attributed.

### Two wrong diagnoses, both mine

**First**, I assumed the close accounting explained the divergences my first probe found. I fixed it
and **nothing moved**. The multi-source divergences are a different quantity entirely.

**Second**, that probe's ratios came out at exactly the SOURCE COUNT — 1 source 1.00x, 2 sources
2.00x, 3 → 3.00x, 6 → 6.00x — which I read as "native's budget is global, TS's is per-source",
despite `run_varlen` visibly calling `sink.start_seed()` per source and `StepBudget::start_seed`
visibly resetting. Wrong again. `let budget = store.limits().trail` — **one config drives two
quantities**: the per-source hop budget AND a global emitted-row cap (`keep.len() > budget`), and
`keep` is never cleared between sources. So the source-count scaling was the ROW cap, which the
same comment already documents as "native's own memory protection, no TS twin; it can only make
native stricter, which it already was."

**The lesson is the fixture, not the reasoning.** A multi-source query cannot isolate a per-source
quantity when a global one is driven by the same knob. One source makes the row cap's globality
inert, and only then does the hop budget show:

| query                          |  ts |   native before | native after |
| ------------------------------ | --: | --------------: | -----------: |
| `SIMPLE k=2 {1,3}`, one source | 510 | 650 (**1.27x**) |      **510** |
| `SIMPLE k=3 {1,2}`, one source | 465 | 650 (**1.40x**) |      **465** |
| `SIMPLE k=1 {1,3}`, one source | 110 |             110 |          110 |

Native raised on queries TS answered. The `k = 1` row is the control and the reason the shape
matters: there every hop completes a repetition, so every close IS at a boundary and nothing
changes.

### The fix

`note_step()` in the `Close` arm, only when `(len + 1).is_multiple_of(k)` — the same condition the
emit already used, and the same condition TS's `completedOuter` expresses. Three lines including the
comment.

### The tests pin the threshold EXACTLY, because a looser test does not discriminate

My first attempt asserted a raise at a limit of 4, reasoning that a dense two-hop unit would be
dominated by closing hops. **It is not** — the ordinary `Go` hops blow a budget that small on their
own, so the test passed under BOTH under-charging mutants. A test whose comment claims to avoid the
wrong-reason trap is not thereby exempt from it.

So I measured every variant's threshold and placed the assertions where they separate:

| variant                             | k=2 `{1,3}` | k=3 `{1,2}` |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------: | ----------: |
| **TS, and native after the fix**    |     **510** |     **465** |
| native before (charge every close)  |         650 |         650 |
| never charge a close                |         325 |         325 |
| charge mid-unit instead of boundary |         465 |         385 |

"Answers at N" catches only the over-charging variant; "**raises at N-1**" is what catches the two
that charge LESS. Both assertions together say the threshold IS TS's, and the `k = 3` pin separates
the two under-chargers from each other. 1000 → 1003 tests.

### Still open, and it needs a decision rather than a quiet fix

`varlen_scan_walk` — the lean walker behind the count/agg fast-paths — takes a `visit` closure and
no sink, so it enforces **no budget at all**. Measured: `MATCH SIMPLE (a:T)-[:E]->{1,3}(b) RETURN
count(*)` has a TS threshold of 110 and native answers at a limit of **1**. That contradicts the same
"agree on which queries raise" contract, in the opposite direction from this item.

It is not a quiet fix, because closing it makes native **refuse counts it currently answers** — a
user-visible behaviour change on a fast path, and the audit records a related prior decision that a
bare count need not trip a guard aimed at materialized rows (the group count reached the same
conclusion and now agrees with TS at 270/270 via `CountSink`, which does budget). The two coherent
resolutions are: give the lean walker a per-source budget (native gets stricter, engines agree), or
exempt a bare count in BOTH engines (TS gets looser, engines agree, and a runaway count loses its
guard in TS too). Priced and stated, not chosen.

## 255. Two zero-coverage shapes, both clean — the first new arm this session that found nothing

Items 238, 244, 248 and 252 each added a generator arm and each found a bug on its first run. That
run of four makes "add coverage, find a bug" feel like a law, so the honest thing is to report the
tick where it did not hold.

### Finding the gaps, by pricing the surface rather than guessing

`grep -c` for each GQL keyword against the generator, which is the "price an enum's variants" move
applied to the fuzzer itself. Most of the surface is covered. The zeroes worth anything:

- **`NOT EXISTS { … }`** — zero, while `EXISTS` appears six times. The subquery-predicate wrapper
  only ever built `(${sub})` or `(n.n <cmp> 4 AND ${sub})`, so negation was never generated. This is
  the documented ReBAC **deny** pattern (`rebac-authz-on-lenke`) — a shape the docs tell users to
  write, with nothing comparing it across the engines.
- **A subquery under `OR`** — zero, and a genuinely different question from the `AND` case item 190
  fixed. That item's rule leaned on `AND` never short-circuiting; `OR` has the opposite skew, where
  the cheap side being TRUE makes the subquery unnecessary, so an engine that evaluates it anyway and
  one that skips it agree on the VALUE and can differ on whether it FAULTS.
- **`ALL SHORTEST`** — zero, while `ANY SHORTEST` is generated, and TS has a separate
  `allShortestWalk`.

(`COALESCE`, `NULLIF`, `TRIM`, `SUBSTRING`, `ELEMENT_ID`, `PROPERTY_EXISTS` are also zero here but
are covered by the separate TS-vs-native scalar-function differential, so they are not gaps.)

### Added: three new subquery-predicate placements

`NOT <sub>`, `<cheap> OR <sub>`, and `NOT (<cheap> AND <sub>)` — the last because a negation
_outside_ a conjunction is where a planner that pushes it down has to get De Morgan right.

**The first measurement said the arm was nearly useless and the fix was to make it boolean.** With
the general subquery draw it ran 28-46 generated but only **6-15 non-empty**, because `COUNT { … }`
and `VALUE { … }` in boolean context are a static type error in BOTH engines — so two draws in
three compared two identical refusals and taught nothing the bare placement already covered. The
negated placements now take a boolean-valued subquery (`EXISTS { … }` or `COUNT { … } <cmp> 0`, two
different code paths), and non-empty roughly tripled: subNot 16-39, subOr 11-20 over eleven seeds.
Floors 14/12 and 10/8, ~25% under the minima; small populations, so their job is strictly to catch a
shape falling to ZERO.

### The result: nothing

**Eleven seeds, zero value divergences.** The engines agree on every placement. So the
subquery-predicate surface is solid under negation and disjunction — worth knowing precisely
because `NOT EXISTS` is a pattern the docs recommend.

`ALL SHORTEST` likewise: a purpose-built fixture with TWO shortest paths of equal length between the
endpoints plus a longer alternative, across five selectors (`ANY SHORTEST`, `ALL SHORTEST`,
`SHORTEST 1`, `SHORTEST 2`, `ALL`) × three tails (`count(*)`, `path_length`, `size(nodes(p))`) —
**15/15 agree.**

### Why `ALL SHORTEST` did NOT get a generator arm

The temptation was to make the selector a draw where `ANY SHORTEST` already appears. That band's axis
is **predicate position**, not the selector, and its convention is `ORDER BY t, x` with `t = n.n`
distinct per row — which is what makes its row SEQUENCE comparable. `ALL SHORTEST` returns every tie,
so multiple rows share a `t` and the pair stops ordering uniquely; the comparison would silently fall
back to order-insensitive and the band would quietly test less than it says it does. That is the same
failure as a detector over-matching (items 246/248/252), reached from the other direction.

A dedicated arm with the selector as its only axis is the right shape for it. It is not added here
because a clean 15/15 on a fixture built for ties is reasonable assurance, and because this session
has already spent three fixes on arms that diluted their neighbours. **Recorded as a candidate with
its design constraint, not left as a vague "add more coverage".**

### What this item is worth

The coverage itself: `NOT EXISTS` is now compared on every run, so the pattern the docs recommend
cannot silently diverge. And the negative result is a data point about where the bugs are not — four
consecutive arms found bugs in the **quantified-path** surface (closes, per-hop predicates, inner
`WHERE`s, budget accounting), and this one found none in the **subquery-predicate** surface. That is
a steer for the next gap to price, not a reason to stop pricing them.

## 256. Pricing the quantified-path surface's remaining axes — four gaps, all clean, two locked in

Item 255's closing note said the four bugs of this session all came from the **quantified-path**
surface and pointed there for the next pricing pass. This prices its remaining axes. Nothing was
broken, and the useful output is which axes are now compared on every run rather than once by hand.

### The axes, and what was missing

| axis                                              | generated before                          |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| quantifier `{n,m}`, `*`, `+`                      | yes                                       |
| **`{n}`** — the single-number spelling of `{n,n}` | **zero**                                  |
| **`{n,}`** with `n > 1` — an open upper bound     | **zero** (`+` is `{1,}`; `{2,}` had none) |
| **an UNDIRECTED quantified hop** `-[:E]-{1,2}`    | **zero**                                  |
| **a quantified hop FOLLOWED BY another segment**  | **zero**                                  |
| path mode (all four)                              | yes, since item 244                       |
| predicate position (hop / inner rep / outer rep)  | yes, since items 248/252                  |

`{n}` is the one that matters most on principle: it and `{n,n}` are the same question with two
parses, which is the bug class this repo is named after.

### Probed first: all four clean

A fixture with a chain, a branch and a back-edge, two edge types for the composition case; the
equivalent spellings compared **within each engine** as well as across them, so the answer needs no
appeal to either. **76/76 agree, zero spelling mismatches, zero cross-engine divergences** across
`{2}`/`{2,2}`, `{1}`/`{1,1}`, `{0}`/`{0,0}`, `{1,}`/`+`, `{0,}`/`*`, the undirected hop, and the
composition in both orders, under every path mode.

**My first run of that probe hung**, because it paired `{0,}`/`*` with `WALK` on a cyclic fixture —
which has no restrictor, so it terminates only on the trail budget. The generator's own comment says
exactly that and it is why its unbounded forms carry no mode. I had read that comment while adding
the mode axis in item 244 and still walked into it; the probe now derives its mode list from the
spelling.

### Locked in: `{n}`, `{n,}`, and the composition

Added to the EXISTING abbreviated-quantifier arm rather than given bands of their own, so no
probability boundary moves and the arm's counters keep their meaning:

- `{1}` and `{2}` join the bounded pick.
- `{1,}` and `{2,}` join `+` on the line that carries **no mode** — which is what keeps the
  `WALK` + unbounded hang out of the generator by construction rather than by a rule someone has
  to remember.
- Two composition shapes, `…{bounded}(b)-[:F]->(c)` counted and projected, with a second edge TYPE
  on the tail so the two segments cannot be mistaken for one longer walk.

### The dilution, re-measured and recorded rather than left to narrow

`abbrevGenerated`/`abbrevNonEmpty` did not move (185-209 / 144-172). `abbrevPath` fell from 68-88 to
**48-55**, because the composition shapes dilute the `MATCH p = ` share. The floor stays at **35**:
that is 27% under the new minimum, the same margin this block uses throughout, so nothing needs
lowering — but the band is now written next to it, because item 244's rule is to re-measure and say
so rather than let a margin narrow in silence.

### What two clean ticks in a row mean

Items 255 and 256 priced five areas — subquery predicates under `NOT`/`OR`, `ALL SHORTEST`, the two
quantifier spellings, the undirected quantified hop, the composition — and found nothing. Set
against items 238/244/248/252, which found a bug each, the pattern is sharper than "coverage finds
bugs": **every one of those four was in the SEMANTICS attached to a quantified path** — which hop a
predicate gates, which repetition a `WHERE` belongs to, what a closing hop costs. The clean five are
all SYNTAX and SHAPE: spellings, selectors, composition. Both engines lower those to the same plan
and the agreement is structural.

So the next pricing pass should look for another place where two engines each decide something
_semantic_ independently, not for another unspelled form. The `varlen_scan_walk` budget gap left
open by item 254 is exactly that shape, and is the standing candidate.

## 257. I re-ran an ISO check that was already recorded — what a compressed pointer costs

The `{k: null}` question has blocked a measured 1.16x since item 180, and this tick went to settle
it against the standard. **The check had already been done on 2026-10-07 and written up**, and I
repeated it: same artifacts, same three findings, same conclusion. No behaviour changed and nothing
new was learned about GQL. What is worth recording is why I repeated it, because it is the third
instance of one failure mode in this audit.

### What the check says (unchanged, and now independently reproduced)

From ISO's free BNF, verbatim:

```
<element pattern predicate> ::=
    <element pattern where clause>
  | <element property specification>

<element property specification> ::= <left brace> <property key value pair list> <right brace>
<property key value pair>        ::= <property name> <colon> <value expression>
```

`{k: v}` is a **sibling of `WHERE <search condition>`** under one `<element pattern predicate>`, and
the value side is a `<value expression>` — which `null` is. And neither
`-implementation-defined.xml` nor `-implementation-dependent.xml` mentions property specification,
property key-value pairs, element pattern predicates or null matching in a pattern — so **the
standard specifies this and we are not at liberty to choose.** The semantics itself is prose, behind
the paywall. Strong direction (`{k: null}` should match nothing), not proof.

Both engines return 2 rows today, so this is a conformance question, not a divergence — which is
exactly why the fuzzers are quiet about it.

### One sharpening, which is all my re-run added

The note's compressed form reads "ISO makes `{k: v}` an element pattern predicate **(G041)**", and
`G041` is **"Non-local element pattern predicates"** — a feature about whether such a predicate may
reference variables bound OUTSIDE the element. It attests that the standard uses the TERM; it says
nothing about null. The full write-up is careful about this ("confirmed by the feature list, where
G041 is …", used as corroboration for the term); the one-line pointer is not, and I read the pointer
as a settled citation and went to check it.

So: the claim was never wrong, its compression was lossy in a way that invited a re-derivation.

### The failure mode, third instance

- Item 246: priced the per-frame adjacency hash, which item 172 had rejected.
- Item 247: raised the type-first adjacency, which item 200 had closed.
- Here: re-ran an ISO artifact check that was recorded two days earlier.

Each time I searched _something_ first — items 246/247 I grepped after the fact, here I grepped the
audit for `G041` and `{k: null}` and read items 180/210 — and each time I searched the wrong store.
The audit records **what was decided**; the notes record **what was checked**. For a question of the
form "what does the standard say", the check lives in the notes, and grepping the audit finds the
decision it blocks instead of the evidence already gathered.

**So the rule is not "search harder", it is "search the store that holds the kind of fact you
want".** A conformance question → the notes and `docs/conformance/references.md`. A perf target →
this audit's refuted list. A measured number → the audit entry that measured it.

And on the pointer: a compressed index line that names a Feature ID reads as a citation whether or
not the full entry treats it as one. The pointer now says what it actually knows.

### Where that leaves the 1.16x

Unchanged and still blocked, with the two ways out item 210 priced: change `{k: null}` to mean
`= null` (0 rows) so an equality conjunct can be lifted into `props` unconditionally, or give `props`
an entry kind that carries expression-equality semantics so the lift is sound without touching
inline semantics. Settling it needs the purchased clause — one reduction rule, in subclause 24.2's
neighbourhood. A vendor page read through a web summary is explicitly NOT a substitute:
`references.md`'s own first lesson is that those summaries confabulate specifics, and it was written
after one asserted "GF04 = datetime functions" when GF04 is _Enhanced path functions_.

## 258. `AND` short-circuits on FALSE — and what the decision cost to land identically

The decision, taken by the user on 2026-10-08 and then re-grounded: `FALSE AND <data exception>`
answers FALSE and does not evaluate the throwing arm. The first framing was that ISO is silent and
we were choosing a behaviour; the user corrected the premise — **ISO leaves short-circuit semantics
to the implementation**, in its free `-implementation-dependent.xml`:

- **`US008`** — "The actual order of expression evaluation."
- **`UA004`** — "Whether or not that exception condition is actually raised when the evaluation of
  an _inessential part_ of an expression or search condition would cause an exception to be
  raised."

So there is nothing to trade off against conformance and the choice is purely on cost: a FALSE is
cheaper than an exception. That matters for how it is recorded — this is not a divergence we are
tolerating, it is latitude the standard grants, and `UA004`'s "inessential part" is the exact term
for what a settled conjunct's sibling becomes.

### Both engines changed, and neither change was the one I expected

I expected a TS-only change, because the open registry entry said native already did this. It did
not — native got there by a different route in ONE context and raised in the others.

- **TS** (`compileExpr`'s `and` arm): a `FALSE` returns immediately. `OR`/`XOR` keep their eager
  n-ary fold.
- **native** (`fold_operand`): this function already evaluated the second operand only over the
  rows the first left undecided, and already DECLINED to when the operand could raise — gated on
  `narrowing_is_transparent`, whose doc comment named the reason outright: _"ISO permits skipping
  those (US008 / UA004) … but the TS engine does not narrow and cross-engine byte-identity is a
  stricter promise than conformance."_ The decision removes that premise, so the gate inverts: when
  the operand can raise, narrowing stops being a sampled perf choice and becomes **mandatory**
  (`must_narrow`). The transparency gate survives verbatim on the speed path, which is now the only
  path `OR` can take.

That inversion is the whole native change, and it is worth noticing that the code to do this had
been sitting there the entire time with a comment explaining why it was switched off.

### Two wrong turns, both caught by measurement rather than by thinking

**(1) A cost-based partition, refuted.** The first TS version partitioned the conjuncts: everything
that can neither fault nor fault-on-coercion first, the rest after. It is sound on paper — Kleene
`AND` commutes, GQL predicates are pure, so reordering cannot change the ANSWER — and it agreed
with native on strictly more `WHERE` shapes, including both spellings of
`n.s AND n.n = 99999`. Then the differential fuzzer with the registry bypassed found **5**
divergences it had created, all of them TS now skipping something native evaluates:

```
MATCH (a:T)-[e:E]->(b:T) RETURN (0 AND (1 IS NULL)) AS x
    ts:     ok [{"x":false}, …]
    native: err E_INVALID_VALUE
```

`0` is a non-boolean literal operand, so coercing it faults; hoisting the safe `1 IS NULL` above it
hid that. The lesson is specific: **native reorders only where its optimizer can seed a conjunct
out of the chain, and in a projection it does not reorder at all.** A partition in the evaluator
reorders everywhere, so it cannot match. Reverted to WRITTEN ORDER, which is the one rule both
engines can hold in every context. Dropping the partition took the same bypassed-fuzzer measurement
from 5 divergences to 1, and the 1 is pre-existing.

**(2) The perf gate lost its transparency condition.** While adding `must_narrow` I rewrote
`narrowable` as `n > 0 && slots_known`, dropping `narrowing_is_transparent` from it — which quietly
gave `OR` the short-circuit too, because the sampled path no longer refused a raising operand.
`RETURN true OR (1.0 / 0.0)` answered `true` in native and raised in TS. The two gates needed to be
separate variables with opposite conditions, not one relaxed one.

`OR` is deliberately NOT symmetric. The decision was taken for `AND`; native has no counterpart to
the conjunct split on the OR side to settle a row out of the chain, and agreeing with the other
engine is the binding constraint, not symmetry for its own sake. Lifting it later is a one-word
change in `fold_operand` plus the matching arm in `compileExpr` — recorded here so that if it is
ever wanted, the cost is known rather than rediscovered.

### The gap the change EXPOSED: agreement by two different routes

The fuzzer then produced a family no registry entry could cover, including an error against a
NON-EMPTY result, which `divergence-registry.ts` explicitly refuses to excuse:

```
MATCH (n:T) FILTER NOT (n.n = 4 AND VALUE { MATCH (n)-[:F]->(b) RETURN count(*) })
    ts:     ok [{"x":3},{"x":5},{"x":7},{"x":11},{"x":13},{"x":17}]
    native: err E_INVALID_VALUE
```

Diagnosed rather than assumed, and the diagnosis inverted my guess twice. A temporary plan dump
showed native printing **no plan at all** for this query: the error comes from the STATIC
(plan-time) boolean-context check, not from evaluation. Native's `definitely_non_bool` flags
`CountSubquery | CollectSubquery | AggSubquery`, and `VALUE { … RETURN count(*) }` lowers to one of
those. TS's `definitelyNonBool` had **no `valueSubquery` arm at all**.

So the two engines had been agreeing on this query by **two different routes** — native statically,
TS per row — and both produced `E_INVALID_VALUE`, which is why nothing ever noticed. The moment a
FALSE conjunct stopped the row being evaluated, TS's route vanished and the agreement with it.

The fix is the static arm, not a restriction on the short-circuit: **a static reject is
order-independent, so it is the route that survives short-circuiting.** Narrowly scoped by probe
rather than by guess — `RETURN b.n`, `RETURN 1`, `RETURN true`, `RETURN b.n > 1` and `RETURN [1]`
all lower to `ScalarSubquery`, which native does not flag, and all five agree between the engines
today; only an aggregate `RETURN` is flagged. (`AGGREGATES` moved from `executor/scalars.ts` to the
shared `ast.ts` so the parser can read it without importing executor code, re-exported from its old
home so no caller changed.)

A probe also found that native's `VALUE { … }` body accepts only `count(*)` as an aggregate —
`sum`/`min`/`max`/`avg`/`collect` are `E_UNKNOWN_FUNCTION` there. That is a separate pre-existing
limitation, not touched here, and it is why the aggregate family has exactly one reachable member.

### What this resolves of CLOSED.md §6 — and it is not what §6 predicted

§6 listed three consequences to settle. Measured, they go:

1. **Item 190's placement rule — UNCHANGED, and now MORE load-bearing.** §6 asked whether a
   subquery conjunct is "now free to be reordered". The opposite. `can_raise` guards predicate
   RELOCATION in `opt.rs`, and its doc comment declines the US008/UA004 latitude for two reasons:
   it costs nothing measurable at those sites, and the unrelocated order is the one the equivalent
   JS composition implies. Both still hold — and short-circuiting makes the second one binding
   rather than polite, because relocating a raising conjunct EARLIER would now make it raise where
   the written order skips it. The guard went from a courtesy to a correctness condition.
2. **Item 175's recorded divergence — does NOT become the intended behaviour.** It is what is
   LEFT. The hop seed gate's cheap-conjunct-first ordering is a reordering TS has no seek to
   match, so it is now one of the two surviving routes in the registry entry rather than a price
   paid for something else.
3. **The registry entry is NARROWED, not deleted.** §6 said it "should be **deleted**, not
   widened"; that was written before measuring and it was wrong. The entry's traffic on the
   differential fuzzer at 20,000 queries a run went from **~4 uses to ~1** (six runs: 1, 1, 1, 1,
   0, 2). What remains is two routes, and both are about ORDER rather than about the connective:

   - the settling comparison is **UNKNOWN** on every row — a filter keeps only TRUE, so native
     drops the row, while Kleene `AND` does not settle on UNKNOWN (`and(null, false)` is `false`)
     and reaches the sibling;
   - the settling comparison is written AFTER the raising operand and native's **seek hoists it**
     out of the chain.

   Fixing either still means abandoning the seek. The entry's `reason` now says all of this,
   including the before/after numbers, so the next reader does not have to re-measure to find out
   whether it still earns its place.

### Verified by mutation, and one mutant survived usefully

Cap proven first (allocator bomb → 137, spin loop → 124), build uncapped, each run under
`timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, the FIXED copies
saved under `target/mutation-backup/and-sc/` and restored before each next mutant.

| mutant                                                           | result                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| N1 `must_narrow = false` (revert the native half)                | CAUGHT — `a_false_conjunct_leaves_a_throwing_conjunct_unevaluated`        |
| N2 drop the `keep.is_empty()` early return                       | **SURVIVED** — see below                                                  |
| N3 drop the `!settled` gate, so `OR` narrows too                 | CAUGHT — `a_non_boolean_or_operand_still_faults_when_the_other_decides_…` |
| N4 `narrowable` loses `transparent` (wrong turn 2, re-applied)   | CAUGHT — same test                                                        |
| T1 TS `and` arm never returns early (revert)                     | CAUGHT — 7 tests                                                          |
| T2 settle on `!== true` instead of `=== false` (UNKNOWN settles) | CAUGHT — 7 tests, incl. the Kleene-law fuzzer and the new UNKNOWN test    |
| T3 drop the `valueSubquery` static arm (revert)                  | CAUGHT — 1 test, the one written for it                                   |
| T4 `valueSubquery` always flagged (too broad)                    | CAUGHT — 2 tests                                                          |

**N2 surviving is the useful one.** My comment on that branch claimed it was "what keeps
`FALSE AND <data exception>` from raising". It is not: without it, `narrow_to_slots` builds a
zero-row batch and `eval_mask` over an empty batch faults on nothing, so the narrowing alone
carries the semantics and the early return only skips a pointless gather. It is a pure
optimization and the comment now says so, with the mutation as the reason. A guard comment that
overstates what it guards is how a later edit removes the real mechanism and keeps the decoration.

### A stale comment corrected rather than a test flipped

`inline-where-direct-eq.test.ts`'s "a FALSE conjunct does not suppress a raise from another" kept
passing, which looked like a contradiction. It passes for a correct reason: its fixture has
`absent` (no `k`) and `nulled` (stored null), so `n.k = 999` is **UNKNOWN on three of five
vertices**, not FALSE — and UNKNOWN cannot settle an `AND`, so the `CAST` is genuinely essential
there. "Matches nothing" and "FALSE on every row" are different statements, and the test was
relying on the second while its comment asserted the first. Renamed and re-explained; the
restriction it describes is untouched.

### Where it lands

Four TS tests changed direction, each of which had pinned the old contract explicitly — and two of
them carried a comment saying the divergence "is a decision about seeding, NOT something this
change may settle by accident". The decision has now been taken, so they record it instead. Two new
test files: `packages/gql/src/and-short-circuit.test.ts` (10 tests, the contract, with a CONTROL
beside every "does not raise" assertion because a chain that stopped evaluating its tail entirely
would satisfy all of them) and `packages/native/src/and-short-circuit-conformance.test.ts` (9
tests, the same contract asserted ACROSS the engines, including the surviving divergence pinned as a
difference rather than asserted away). Native 1004 tests, TS 1758, all seven fuzzers green.

### The bench screen found a real 1.17x, and the cause was function SIZE

`bench_all`, two md5-distinct binaries, three alternated rounds each, min-of-three per cell, 328
numeric cells matched positionally:

```
ratio after/before  min=0.926  p25=1.000  median=1.000  p75=1.003  max=1.500
within +/-5%: 320/328 (98%)
```

Eight cells outside the band, and one was not dismissible:

```
pred AND exists   before 545.4 / 547.1 / 551.5 us    after 647.0 / 647.1 / 649.5 us    1.186x
```

Non-overlapping ranges, and the query is `WHERE p.age > 98 AND EXISTS { (p)-[:KNOWS]->() }` —
`fold_operand`'s shape exactly. The one cell on the screen my change has any business touching.

**Hypothesis 1, wrong.** I had restructured the narrowing branch to count settled rows in one pass
before collecting `keep`, so the nothing-settled case could skip an n-element `Vec<usize>` it would
discard. `p.age > 98` is selective, so most rows settle and a second scan of 200,000 mask cells is
not free. Reverted to collecting `keep` once. **It did not recover.**

**Hypothesis 2, also wrong, and this is the one worth recording.** A focused A/B of `query_bench`
alone showed `project bool AND` — `RETURN p.age > 50 AND p.age < 90`, where both operands are
transparent compares, so the new path is never taken and the gate is byte-identical — moving by the
same factor:

| row              | HEAD (min of 3) | changed (min of 3) | ratio      |
| ---------------- | --------------- | ------------------ | ---------- |
| project bool AND | 853.7 (853-857) | 1001.8 (1002-1040) | **1.173x** |
| pred AND exists  | 547.3 (547-548) | 639.2 (639-673)    | **1.168x** |

1.17x sits in the 1.08-1.24x band items 90 and 250 record as the layout toll any native edit pays,
and `filter_us`-style rows are documented as moving 8-10% for ANY edit — so I was ready to write
this off. **The null control refused to let me.** The same HEAD with one error string lengthened
(md5-distinct binary, three alternated rounds):

| row              | HEAD  | null control | ratio      |
| ---------------- | ----- | ------------ | ---------- |
| project bool AND | 857.9 | 860.8        | **1.003x** |
| pred AND exists  | 544.5 | 548.1        | **1.007x** |

These rows do not move for a semantically neutral edit. So the 1.17x was mine — and since it also
hit a row the new logic never executes, it was not the logic. **It was `fold_operand` getting
bigger.** Two extra conditions on the gate, two extra branches and a `Vec` before the gather were
enough to change its codegen for every caller.

**The fix is structural: the short-circuit leaves by its own door.** `fold_raising_conjunct` is a
separate function, and `fold_operand`'s body is restored to exactly what it was plus one early
`return`. Re-measured, same protocol:

| row              | HEAD  | fixed | ratio      |
| ---------------- | ----- | ----- | ---------- |
| project bool AND | 859.8 | 853.6 | **0.993x** |
| pred AND exists  | 546.1 | 547.7 | **1.003x** |

The doc comment on that function says the extraction is load-bearing for SPEED and not for
clarity, because the obvious future tidy-up is to inline it back.

**And a note on which harness to trust.** The final `bench_all` screen reads 95% within +/-5%,
median 1.000, but its outliers are not real: `pred AND exists` measured **639.1 / 640.0 / 639.1**
for the HEAD binary there against **545-551** for the same binary standalone, and its own
per-round spreads reach 15-18% (`repeat-group control` 65,377 / 76,720 / 77,038 for one binary).
min-of-three does not remove that, because all three rounds of a session share whatever causes it.
The ISOLATED harness is what resolved this: `query_bench` alone gave 547.3 / 548.1 / 547.6 for
HEAD across three separate sessions. So `bench_all` screens for LARGE regressions and the focused
two-binary A/B is what settles a 1.1x — which is `bench-screen-needs-the-ab` restated, and worth
restating because I spent two wrong hypotheses before reaching for the control.

Final isolated screen over the whole query group, 180 cells: median 1.000, p75 1.001, 96% within
+/-5%, movers mixed-sign (four rows 0.86-0.93x faster, one 1.055x slower, and a 0.20us/0.30us pair
that is pure quantisation). Both `AND` rows inside the band.

The table above was measured before the 1.17x fix moved the short-circuit into

| mutant                                                               | result                                                                      |

## 259. A FILTER is order-independent in both engines — and the ordering KEY has to be shared

Item 258 gave `AND` a short-circuit on FALSE in written order, and deliberately refused cost-based
reordering: a version that partitioned the conjuncts cheap-first created 5 divergences, because
the engine reorders only where its optimizer can seed a conjunct out of the chain and never in a
projection. That refusal was right for a VALUE position and wrong for a FILTER, and this item is
the correction.

**The decision.** The user asked for the reversed spelling — `WHERE <raising> AND <seekable>`, the
one residual item 258 left — to answer "the fastest way", and asked whether it could be done
without constructing the exception, "callstack generation isn't cheap". Then, more broadly: make
the TS evaluator order-independent too, since ISO leaves evaluation order to the implementation and
a cheaper evaluator is worth more than a strict left-to-right rule. And, separately: byte-identity
may be relaxed where the implementations genuinely differ, as long as the difference is evaluated
and documented.

**The answer needed no latitude and no exception.** A filter does not ask for the conjunction's
VALUE — it keeps a row only on a clean TRUE (ISO §14.6; every call site in both engines reads
`asTruth(...) === true` / `== Some(true)`). So in filter position:

1. **Any conjunct that is not cleanly TRUE settles the row, UNKNOWN included.** Strictly stronger
   than `AND`'s own rule, where only FALSE can settle because `and(null, false)` is `false`. The
   test is `!== true`, not `=== false`.
2. **Conjunct order is therefore unobservable**, which is what licenses putting the conjuncts that
   cannot raise first.

Neither step is a reordering of anything observable, so neither spends US008/UA004 — those are
still only spent on the value-position short-circuit from 258. And no exception is ever
constructed, which is the actual answer to the cost question: the cheapest raise is the one that
never happens. (For the record, on the paths that DO raise the cost is not hot either: the engine's
errors are `Result<_, String>`, a `format!` with no backtrace, and TS's `LenkeError extends Error`
captures a stack once per query. It would only become hot under the design to avoid — evaluate
eagerly, catch, and swallow — which constructs and discards an `Error` per row.)

The precedent and its justification were already in the tree, one position short of covering the
user's case: `gatePredicate`'s comment says "the gate's only output is keep/skip, and it keeps only
on a clean TRUE, so 'stop at the first non-TRUE' is the gate's own semantics rather than a
reordering of `AND`", and records this exact divergence family being closed once before for the
subquery case — "TS raised while native returned a NON-EMPTY result … Both now match native."

### Where it had to be stated, which was more places than expected

**TS, four sites, all routed through one new `filterPredicate`:** the clause `WHERE` of `match` and
`with`, the `FILTER` clause, and `HAVING`. Plus — and this is the one that mattered for the user's
query — `compilePredicate`, the node/edge inline predicate, because `pushWhereIntoNode` moves a
single-node pattern's clause `WHERE` onto the node before `compileClause` compiles anything. The
first attempt changed only the four clause sites and the user's shape did not move; a probe over
the same predicate in `FILTER`, `WITH … WHERE` and two-pattern spellings is what localized it.

**The engine, three sites**, because "which rows does this predicate keep" has three derivations
here and only one of them is `filter_keep`:

- `filter_keep` — the materialized `Plan::Filter`.
- `pull_body`'s `Filter` arm — the STREAMING driver and `CALL` bodies, which deliberately is not
  `filter_keep` (routing it through cost a measured ~20% on this bench's `filter` row, recorded in
  its own comment).
- the OPTIONAL expand's landing predicate.

Each takes the ordered path behind its own door: only a MIXED conjunction — something that can
raise beside something that cannot — leaves the existing hot lines, which are unchanged. That is
item 258's 1.17x lesson applied before measuring rather than after.

**`the_streamed_and_materialized_projections_agree` caught the one-sided application**, and it is
the sharpest reminder in this item. Applying the rule to `filter_keep` only made seed 107 raise
"division by zero" streamed and answer rows materialized — a wrong-answer-class divergence
_inside_ the engine, from a change whose entire purpose was to make two engines agree. The fuzzer
named the plan; a temporary `LENKE_DEBUG_FILTER` print showed only the materialized run reaching
`filter_keep` at all, which located the second site in one run.

### The ordering key has to be the SAME key, and conservatism is not safety

This is the durable lesson, and it cost three rounds of the differential fuzzer to learn.

TS's first whitelist admitted only `=` and `<>` among the comparisons, on the sound-looking ground
that a cross-type `<=` throws where `=` is a no-match (`cross-type-comparison-no-error`). The
engine's `narrowing_is_transparent` admits ANY operator. Result: the two engines partitioned the
same predicate differently, each reordered to its own taste, and the fuzzer found **41 divergences
in one 20,000-query run** — every one of them TS raising where the engine answered no rows. Being
the more cautious engine did not make TS safer; it made the two disagree. The fix is that the
partition is a SHARED key or it is nothing.

Two more mismatches of exactly the same shape, each found by the next fuzzer run:

| mismatch                                                                | effect               |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| `=`/`<>` only, vs any comparison operator                               | 41 divergences a run |
| `-1` is `neg(lit)` in this AST, a folded `Lit(Num(-1.0))` in the engine | 4 of the 5 remaining |
| TS flattened only the TOP level of an `AND`; the engine recurses        | the last of the 5    |

The third is worth spelling out: a same-operator run folds into one n-ary `and` in this AST, but a
parenthesized group does not, so `(A AND B) AND (C AND D)` arrives as two items where the engine
sees four. The engine could hoist a safe conjunct out of the second group and TS could not. After
`flattenConjuncts` recursed, 120,000 generated queries produced one divergence.

### The one declared difference, and the wrong fix I measured before declaring it

What is left is a statically non-boolean operand inside an INLINE PATTERN predicate:

```
MATCH p = ANY SHORTEST (a:T)-[:E]->*(n:T WHERE ((n.n IS NULL) AND ((3.14 OR 'a') < 3)))
    ts: ok []     native: err E_INVALID_VALUE
```

`3.14 OR 'a'` has literal operands in a truth position, which both engines' plan-time
boolean-context check flags — but they disagree about WHERE that check applies. TS does not apply
it to inline pattern predicates at all. The engine applies it to whatever lowers to a
`Plan::Filter`, which an inline predicate on a quantified-path endpoint does and one on a plain
node pattern does not. So the engine rejects at plan time while TS reorders, loses every row on
`n.n IS NULL`, and never reaches the operand.

**The obvious fix is the wrong one, and I measured that rather than reasoning about it.** Extending
TS's `validateBoolContexts` to walk every inline pattern predicate (node, edge, subpath, through
`hopFrom`/`hopTo`/`unitRest`/`nested`) made things WORSE: TS then rejected
`(n WHERE CAST(x AS STRING))` and `(n WHERE n.n - head(n.n))` at plan time where the engine answers
no rows, turning ~1 divergence a run into 7. Reverted. The real inconsistency is the engine's
position-dependence, and closing it properly means deciding whether a static boolean-context check
covers inline pattern predicates in BOTH engines — which rejects queries that answer today, so it
is a conformance decision and not a bug fix. **That one is the user's.**

Declared as `static-bool-check-misses-inline-pattern-predicates`, at ~1 per 120,000 generated
queries, and it is `E_INVALID_VALUE` against an EMPTY result — which the registry is permitted to
cover (an error against a NON-EMPTY result is the `CALL`-body laziness bug and is still refused).

### What closed

`boolean-context-dynamic-operand-under-seek` is **deleted**, both of its routes closed, and for a
moment the registry was empty. Both routes were about ORDER rather than about the connective, and
both closed by the same rule:

- **route (1), the UNKNOWN settling conjunct** — `WHERE n.zz = 'a' AND n.s`. The engine always
  answered `[]`; TS applied Kleene `AND` and raised. The last of that entry's traffic, and the
  conformance test that pinned it as a difference said in its own comment that if it ever started
  agreeing it should move up into the agreeing set and take the entry with it. Both happened.
- **route (2), the reversed spelling** — `WHERE <raising> AND <seekable>`, §5's "nothing guards
  it" item. The engine never raised (its seek hoists the seekable conjunct); TS now puts the
  conjunct that cannot raise first. This was the error-against-a-NON-EMPTY-result shape the
  registry was never permitted to declare, so closing it is the only way it could ever have been
  covered.

Four tests changed direction, each having pinned the old contract explicitly, and one of them
twice: `inline-where-direct-eq.test.ts`'s "a non-matching conjunct does not suppress a raise from
another" had already been re-explained in 258 (when it kept passing for the correct reason that
UNKNOWN cannot settle a Kleene AND) and now flips, because a FILTER settles on UNKNOWN. Its two
earlier comments are kept beside the new one — each was right about a different rule, and which
rule applies is decided by the POSITION.

I also wrote a control that asserted nothing: `n.k = 1 AND CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) > 0` against a
fixture with no `k: 1` vertex. It answered 0 instead of raising and the test failed, which is the
only reason I noticed. Rewritten against `k: 2`, which the fixture has, and the trap is named in
the test so the next edit does not repeat it.

### `bun run spelling` found a 1.7x that nothing else could, and the cause was the COMPILE path

This is the most useful thing in the item, because no other instrument here could have seen it.
The native bench measures the Rust build only; 1,759 TS tests, 809 cross-engine tests and seven
fuzzers all check answers, not cost; and the native `query_bench` A/B was clean. The probe exists
for exactly one claim — equivalent spellings must cost the same — and that claim is what broke.

At `SPELL_N=200000`, two of the five spellings of "an AND of two equalities" (item 230's group)
moved, and HEAD was clean:

| spelling                                   | HEAD | with the first gate |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---- | ------------------- |
| `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 2 AND n.s = 's1'` | 4.21 | 4.14                |
| `MATCH (n:P {k: 2, s: 's1'})`              | 3.92 | 3.90                |
| `MATCH (n:P {k: 2}) WHERE n.s = 's1'`      | 4.02 | 3.95                |
| `MATCH (n:P WHERE n.k = 2 AND n.s = 's1')` | 4.28 | **7.20**            |
| `MATCH (n:P) WHERE 2 = n.k AND 's1' = n.s` | 4.35 | **7.00**            |

**My first explanation was wrong, and bisection was what corrected it.** I reasoned that the
change could not reach these: both predicates are all-safe, so `filterPredicate` takes its early
return and hands the identical closure to `compileExpr`. Two diagnostics:

- **door shut** (`filterPredicate` returns `compileExpr(where)` on its first line): 4.24 / 4.37,
  HEAD exactly. So the regression is real and inside that function.
- **gate computed, closure never returned**: 11.95 / 11.89 — _worse_. So the cost is NOT the
  returned closure, and not call-site polymorphism either.

What is left is the gate's own work: `flattenConjuncts` plus two `.filter` passes, three array
allocations per call. **And the reason that is hot is the finding worth keeping: for these shapes
the predicate is compiled PER EXECUTION, not once per plan.** Anything allocated on the decline
path is on the hot path. Which also explains precisely which spellings moved — they are the only
two in the group whose predicate reaches `filterPredicate` as a multi-conjunct `AND`. The other
three have their equalities lifted into `props`/`eqProps` before it, or arrive with one conjunct,
so the gate is trivial or never called.

**The fix is `conjunctMix`: a recursive bitmask scan that allocates nothing** (1 = saw a conjunct
that cannot raise, 2 = saw one that can, so 3 is mixed). The allocating work now runs only for a
genuinely mixed conjunction. Re-measured at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`:

```
4.23  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 2 AND n.s = 's1'
3.93  MATCH (n:P {k: 2, s: 's1'})
3.97  MATCH (n:P {k: 2}) WHERE n.s = 's1'
4.22  MATCH (n:P WHERE n.k = 2 AND n.s = 's1')
4.24  MATCH (n:P) WHERE 2 = n.k AND 's1' = n.s
```

1.08x spread, HEAD parity, and 0 groups over 2x across the whole probe.

**The embarrassing part: I had already solved this on the other side.** `filter_conjuncts_reordered`
is allocation-free on its decline path, with a comment saying why, written earlier the same day —
and I did not mirror it in TS. The two engines needed the same discipline for the same reason and
only one got it. A paired change should be reviewed as a pair.

**Two measurement notes.**

First, that group is BIMODAL on the reversed-operand spelling: single runs of one build gave
"0 groups over 2x" and then 12.25ms. So a single probe run cannot settle a ratio here — use
`SPELL_REPS=9`, which is min-of-9 internally and removes it. The reproducible signal was the
allocating gate measuring 7.0-7.2 twice against a door-shut control at 4.24/4.37.

Second, **an in-process A/B of two gql BUNDLES is not a valid instrument for this** and I threw
the attempt away. Importing a HEAD-built `@lenke/gql` beside the current one made HEAD read ~2.7x
slower on every query — including `MATCH (n:P {k: 2, s: 's1'})`, which has no `WHERE` at all and
the diff cannot reach. A duplicated engine instance running over a graph built by the other copy's
`@lenke/core` is not comparable to the engine under test. The tell was the same one item 258
turned on: a row the diff cannot reach, moving. `in-process-ab-of-two-builds` works for two
builds of ONE engine sharing data structures; it does not work for two copies of an engine that
owns them.

### The bench screen flagged two rows and the null control cleared both — the inverse of 258

Isolated `query_bench`, two md5-distinct binaries, three alternated rounds, min-of-three per cell,
73 cells:

```
ratio changed/head  min=0.911  median=0.999  max=1.083
within +/-5%: 70/73 (96%)
```

Every row the change can actually reach is flat:

| row                           | head    | changed | ratio |
| ----------------------------- | ------- | ------- | ----- |
| `project bool AND`            | 858.4   | 854.2   | 0.995 |
| `pred AND exists`             | 544.2   | 546.1   | 1.003 |
| `optional hop + landing pred` | 10147.8 | 9998.5  | 0.985 |
| `optional hop`                | 4510.8  | 4503.8  | 0.998 |
| `EXISTS`                      | 1113.9  | 1125.7  | 1.011 |

Two rows moved: `filter age>50` at **1.039x** and `counts | filtered` at **1.083x** — both
single-conjunct filters, where `filter_conjuncts_reordered` declines on its first `matches!` and
the new code does nothing at all. 1.08x is squarely in the 8-10% band
`filter-count-row-is-not-a-screen` records for any native edit, so this is exactly the moment item
258 says not to reason about and to run the control instead.

**The null control cleared them, and by a wider margin than the change itself moved them.** HEAD
plus one lengthened error string (`TRUTH_TYPE_ERR`), md5-distinct binary, same protocol:

| row                        | the change | null control |
| -------------------------- | ---------- | ------------ |
| `query/gql filter age>50`  | 1.039x     | **1.099x**   |
| `query/counts filtered`    | 1.083x     | **1.121x**   |
| `query/gremlin has age>50` | in band    | **1.126x**   |

A semantically neutral edit moves those rows FURTHER than this change does, so they are the layout
toll and not the change. This is the mirror image of item 258, where the same instrument proved a
1.17x WAS mine against a band that said otherwise — which is the point: the band is not evidence in
either direction, and the control costs one build and three rounds. (Also in that run: a 1.500x
pair that is 0.2us against 0.3us, pure quantisation. Print the absolute numbers beside the ratio.)

Not re-run: `bench_all`. Item 258 established it cannot settle a 1.1x — the same HEAD binary read
639us there against 545-551 standalone, and its own per-round spreads reach 15-18%.

### Mutation — five native mutants, all caught, and one that re-taught an old lesson

Cap proven first (allocator bomb → 137, bare spin → 124), built uncapped, each run under
`timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine copies
under `target/mutation-backup/filter-order/`, restored BEFORE each next mutant rather than only
after the loop.

| mutant                                                             | result                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| N1 `filter_conjuncts_reordered` never fires (all three doors shut) | CAUGHT — `a_literal_false_conjunct_settles_a_filter_from_either_side` |
| N2 `filter_keep_ordered` settles only on FALSE (`!= Some(false)`)  | CAUGHT — 3 `rewrite_fuzz` tests                                       |
| N3 no reorder: every conjunct keeps written order                  | CAUGHT — `a_literal_false_conjunct_settles_a_filter_from_either_side` |
| N4 `filter_conjunct_cannot_raise` drops its `Lit` arm              | CAUGHT — `a_literal_false_conjunct_settles_a_filter_from_either_side` |
| N5 `filter_keep_ordered` never narrows (always the full batch)     | CAUGHT — 3 `rewrite_fuzz` tests                                       |

**N1 survived on the first attempt, and that was the finding, not the mutant.** With only the
pre-existing tests, shutting every door changed nothing the cargo suite could see: the contract
lived entirely in `packages/native`'s bun conformance file. That is
[[mutation-must-include-core]]'s lesson in a new costume — a mutant looks survived when its teeth
are in a suite the run does not include. Fixed by adding **five focused native tests** to
`exec/tests.rs` (1004 → 1009) for the filter rule, its bound, and the shared ordering key, after
which N1 is caught by the cargo suite alone.

**What N1 also revealed about how little the engine needed.** Shutting all three doors breaks ONE
named test, because `try_filter_keep`'s conjunct split already dropped non-TRUE rows for the
comparison shapes — the engine was mostly order-independent in a filter already, and the new path
only covers what that fast path declines (a bare boolean literal) plus the two sites that never had
it (`pull_body`, the OPTIONAL landing predicate). The evidence that those two sites are
load-bearing is not a mutant but an observed failure: applying the rule to `filter_keep` alone made
`the_streamed_and_materialized_projections_agree` fail at seed 107.

### Mutation — five TS mutants, and two of them found a test that tested nothing

Same protocol, except that each mutant needs a `bun run build` first: the cross-engine conformance
file imports the built dist, not `src` ([[fuzzers-read-built-dists]]).

| mutant                                                      | result                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| T1 a filter settles on FALSE only (`=== false`)             | CAUGHT — 11 gql, 1 cross-engine                 |
| T2 no reorder: the conjuncts keep written order             | CAUGHT — 1 gql, 2 cross-engine                  |
| T3 `flattenConjuncts` stops at the top level                | CAUGHT — **cross-engine only**                  |
| T4 the compare arm narrows back to `=`/`<>`                 | CAUGHT **after the test was fixed** (see below) |
| T5 `valueCannotRaise` drops its negated-numeric-literal arm | CAUGHT **after the test was fixed** (see below) |

T1 is worth a note: it is not merely a laziness mutant but a WRONG-ANSWER one. With `=== false`,
an UNKNOWN conjunct falls through the loop and the predicate returns `true` at the end — so the
filter ADMITS a row it must drop. Hence 11 failures rather than a handful.

T3 is caught by the cross-engine file and nothing else, which is the argument for having written
those assertions down: before this item, recursive flattening was guarded only by the differential
fuzzer on random seeds.

**T4 and T5 SURVIVED the first version of the ordering-key test, and the mutants were right.** I
had written every assertion with the safe conjunct FIRST:

```
MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.n < 0 AND n.s RETURN n.n AS x
```

which passes whatever the ordering key says — item 258's FALSE short-circuit already settles every
row in written order, so `n.s` is never reached and the REORDER is never exercised. The
distinguishing input is the reversed spelling:

```
MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.s AND n.n < 0 RETURN n.n AS x
```

Rewritten that way in both the cross-engine file and the five new native tests, after which T4 and
T5 are caught. This is [[passing-suite-is-not-equivalence]] and
[[mutants-find-fixture-blindness]] in one: a test can exercise the right code and still not
exercise the DISTINCTION, and here the test's own subject — order — was the thing its spelling
removed.

Eleven mutants in total (six native, five TS), all caught, two only after the tests they were
aimed at were made honest.

## 260. Item 210's route two, taken — and its 1.16x does not reproduce

Item 210 recorded a **measured 1.16x** on every clause-`WHERE` node scan: `props` is a direct
property read in `satisfies` while a node `where` is a compiled expression (71 vs 83 ns a vertex).
It recorded the merge as blocked, needing "either a decision on `{k: null}`'s semantics or a
`props` entry that carries expression-equality semantics instead of inline ones". `CLOSED.md` has
carried that as an open perf item ever since, and §4 still listed it under the `{k: null}`
decision.

**Route two was cheaper than it looked, and it is now taken.** Two things were in the way and
neither needed the semantics decision.

### 1. The general scan path never lifted at all

`directEqProps` returns `null` on its first line when `ownVar` is undefined, and `compileNode`
called `compilePredicate(node.properties, node.where)` — **no own-var**. Every SHORTCUT path passes
one (`shortcuts.ts` in eight places), so the lift fired for them and never for the general scan.
That asymmetry IS the 1.16x row: `write: property update` is
`MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = $n SET u.score = $v`, and `detectNodeProjection` requires a
`RETURN`, so it takes the general scan.

Passing `node.variable` is safe without proving the predicate element-local, because
`directEqProps` already checks `pc.variable !== ownVar` per conjunct and declines the WHOLE chain
on the first conjunct that reads anything else — which matters precisely because
`pushWhereIntoNode` deliberately does NOT restrict free variables.

### 2. Params could not be lifted, and the bench row is param-valued

`directEqProps` admitted only non-null LITERALS. Its comment said why: `$p` resolving to null would
make `structuralEq` match a stored null where `=` yields UNKNOWN, and "lifting params needs a
per-execution safety check on the resolved value; it is a follow-up".

**That check is one branch.** `propOf` returns `null` for an absent key AND for a stored null, so
`structuralEq` alone cannot tell the two readings apart and gives the INLINE one. Rejecting a null
right-hand side in the `eqProps` loop gives the EXPRESSION one:

```
{k: null}        → matches a stored null AND an absent key   (props loop, unchanged)
WHERE n.k = null → matches NEITHER                           (eqProps loop, now)
```

For every non-null right-hand side the two notions already agree, which is why one guard suffices:
a missing or stored-null property reads as `null`, `structuralEq(null, 2)` is false, `=` yields
UNKNOWN, and a filter keeps only TRUE — both reject the row. So the entry means `=`, and the value
may be anything closed. **This is what `{k: null}` was never blocking**, exactly as `CLOSED.md`
predicted when it de-coupled the two questions.

`residual` is consequently always undefined and its plumbing is gone rather than left looking live:
every admitted conjunct lifts, and an unadmitted one declines the chain, so there is no partial
outcome to express.

### The 1.16x is NOT there, and that is the finding

Item 210's gap does not reproduce. Measured on 200,000 `User` vertices, three spellings of one
anchor, min-of-9 within a run, **three alternated stash/pop rounds**, with the inline-`props` row
as the control the change cannot touch:

| ratio to the props control | HEAD                  | with the lift         |
| -------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------- |
| clause `WHERE`             | 1.072 / 1.073 / 1.076 | 0.973 / 1.033 / 1.046 |
| inline `WHERE`             | 1.070 / 1.077 / 1.084 | 0.982 / 1.033 / 1.050 |
| the control itself, ns     | 81.3 / 81.6 / 82.6    | 81.6 / 81.9 / 84.6    |

**HEAD's own spelling gap on this fixture is 7.3%, not 16%** — so 1.16x was never available here
and the lever could not have paid what the record claimed. What it does pay: clause `WHERE` 87.2 →
82.3 ns a vertex best-of-rounds, **0.944x**, with the control flat at 1.004x and the sign the same
in all three rounds.

Why the gap narrows rather than closing: `eqProps` is `props` plus the null guard — one branch per
entry — so converging to within ~3% of a loop that does strictly less work is the expected
landing, not a shortfall.

Two measurement notes, both earned here:

- **`bench:usage` cannot see this.** Its single-run write rows moved 614 → 417, 366 → 405,
  491 → 576 — and the ENGINE columns moved 12% on a change that is TypeScript-only, which is the
  tell. Ranges, not point values (`bench-sampling-traps`).
- **The first focused run was also not evidence**: it read 0.951x on clause, but the props control
  moved 0.971x in the same run, so most of it was drift. The alternated rounds with the control
  held flat are what made the number defensible.

### Teeth

The guard is the load-bearing branch, so it was mutated out: `if (false)` in its place fails
exactly the two distinguishing assertions (`a NULL param answers like =` and `a null LITERAL
answers 0 through the lifted path`) and nothing else. The lift FIRING is asserted directly on
`compilePredicate`'s output rather than inferred from a semantic test, because a semantic test
alone passes vacuously the moment the lift stops firing — the fixture trap this repo has paid for
eight times.

13 new tests in `direct-eq-props-param.test.ts`: the lift fires for a literal, a param, a chain and
both operand orders; declines with no own-var, on another variable, on a non-equality; and the
expression-vs-inline distinction with its controls both ways.

### Not done, deliberately

`compileRel` still passes no own-var, so `eqProps` remains unreachable for a REL — `matching.ts`'s
comment saying so is still true. Widening it needs its own measurement and the differential
fuzzer's edge predicates are all `>`/`>=`, so it would ship unguarded. Separately, a MIXED chain
still declines whole; item 259 made that sound to relax (a filter's conjunct order is
unobservable), and that is the better next step.

### Gates

native 1009 + 13 + 723 unchanged (no Rust change), TS **1772** (was 1759), `@lenke/native` 809,
all seven fuzzers green with `DECLARED none used`. `typecheck`, `lint`, `fmt:check` each their own
command.

## 261. `IN` and a same-key `=`-OR-chain seed the index — 65-75x, and the recorded 3.3x was the wrong number

`in-param-list-seeds` recorded the open native gap as: "`seek_target` matches only
`Compare { op: Eq }` ... All of the residual **3.3x** 32→33 cliff is that lost seed: below the gate
the OR-chain multi-seeks, above it nothing does. Needs a multi-value `Seed` variant plus a physical
operator, with row-order/byte-identity work."

**Priced before building, and two of those three claims were wrong.** 200,000 `User` vertices, a
hash index on `k`, min of 9:

| shape               | before      |
| ------------------- | ----------- |
| `IN` 32 items       | 5.09 ms     |
| `IN` 33 items       | 5.24 ms     |
| `IN` 64 items       | 9.83 ms     |
| `OR` 33 terms       | 5.22 ms     |
| `OR` 64 terms       | 9.89 ms     |
| single `=` (seeded) | **0.01 ms** |

- **The 32→33 cliff is 1.03x, not 3.3x.** Item 185's hashed membership set already flattened it;
  the note was measured before that landed and never re-read.
- **The OR-chain does not multi-seek either.** `IN` at 33 items and an OR-chain of 33 equalities
  cost the SAME (1.00x), because the seeding site matches a single `Compare { op: Eq }` and an
  `Or` is not one. So `normalize_pred`'s ≤32 rewrite buys the evaluator a cheaper form and no
  seed at all.
- **So the headroom was never 3.3x.** A single `=` on the same index is ~500x cheaper than the
  scan; 33 of them is the real comparison.

### The fix needed no new operator

The note priced a new multi-value `Seed` variant plus a physical operator — ~10 non-test files
(`bind`, `cost`, `distinct`, `render`, `fastpath`, `opt`, `exec`, …) plus the fuzzer generators.
**`Plan::Union { all: true }` already concatenates without deduping**, so a union tree of the
EXISTING `IndexSeek` is the whole change, confined to `opt.rs`:

```
Filter(k IN [a,b,c]) over Scan(L)   ->   Union ALL ( IndexSeek(L,k,a), IndexSeek(L,k,b), … )
Filter(k = a OR k = b) over Scan(L)  ->   the same tree
```

Same rows as a MULTISET: the values are deduped so the arms select disjoint vertex sets. Row ORDER
changes, which is unspecified without an `ORDER BY` and is already what the single-value
`IndexSeek` does — so there is no new byte-identity obligation, which is the third claim the note
got wrong.
