streaming fast path "is lineage-free, so it cannot take it", and "Only for `!track` (a path-reading
LIMIT keeps the full path via the slow path)". The guard is that helper's documented precondition,
not a judgment call — so it stays, and what the survival means is that **no test reaches a capped
cross join under lineage tracking.** Said plainly rather than implying the mutant validates it.

S5 is the mutant that matters most. CLAUDE.md records an off-by-one on a loop bound in this file
filling 192 GB of swap and forcing a hard reboot, so every mutant ran under a timeout AND the 16G
cgroup cap with `MemorySwapMax=0`. S5 is that exact shape, and it was caught by 7 tests — including
two PRE-EXISTING ones (`cross_page_caps_a_three_way_product_too`,
`cross_page_honours_skip_as_well_as_limit`), so the arm was already covered for the unfiltered
case and only the filtered side was missing.

Five new tests (1029 → 1034). The load-bearing one is
`a_capped_filtered_product_never_invents_a_row`: at every cap from 1 to 8 the capped answer must be
a SUBSET of the uncapped product. A wrong bound can keep the row COUNT right while inventing a
row, and only that comparison catches it.

`rewrite_fuzz` green at default and at `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` (47.21s); all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green with `DECLARED none used`, which matters more than usual here because
this changes WHICH ROWS native produces for a capped join.

### Screen

`query_bench`, two md5-distinct binaries, three alternated rounds, min per cell:

```
73 cells   median 0.999   95% within +/-5%
```

Three movers. `gremlin dedup out.out` is 0.895 (faster); `query/shortest | anchored` is **1.100**
(6379.7 -> 7020.3us) and has no cross join at all, so the capped-join arm cannot reach it — the
layout toll `pull-alignment-is-load-bearing` and `filter-count-row-is-not-a-screen` record for any
`exec.rs` edit, and within the 1.06-1.12x band item 261's null control measured on this corpus for
a semantically neutral native change. The third, `counts | label` at 0.667, is a 0.2-to-0.3
MICROSECOND row: a tenth of a microsecond of quantization, not an effect.

(A method note on the screen itself: its md5 verification lines were lost because the command was
piped through `tail` — the FOURTH time in this session. Distinctness still holds, by the exit
code rather than by reading the hashes: the script `exit 1`s when the two hashes match, and it
exited 0 after writing all six rounds. The inference is sound but it is a worse position than
having the numbers, and the fix is the same one item 273 recorded: `grep` for the lines you want,
never `tail`.)

## 276. An ORDERING comparison costs 1.64x an equality on the same TS count — built, then RETRACTED on the blocker, which is nine presence checks

`bench:usage` was re-run as a source the discredited expression table (item 272) could not bias.
**Its one apparent outlier is not one**, and that is worth recording first: within `ts(+)` the
reads are 421k-1.28M ops/s except `read: keyed dedup lookup` at 72.6k, which looks like a 5.8x
hole. It is a row-count difference — `point lookup` returns ONE row while that workload seeks ~200
(`score` is `i % 100` over 20,000 users) and counts them, so per row it is **0.069us against point
lookup's 0.78us, 11x more efficient.** Ops/s across workloads of different sizes is not comparable.
The arithmetic also confirms both engines seek rather than scan: a 20,000-node TS scan is ~580us,
not the measured 13.8us.

### The real finding, from the `ts(-)` column

An unindexed filtered count prices at ~27ns a vertex against native's ~1.6ns. `CLOSED.md` carries
item 197's closing line that "nothing else in the TS **query** surface is above 5x", and 16.7x
contradicts it — so it was measured properly. 200,000 vertices, no index, min of 9:

| predicate                   | ns/vertex | rows    |
| --------------------------- | --------: | ------- |
| none (bucket-size shortcut) |       0.0 | 200,000 |
| `k = <lit>` clause          |  **30.5** | 1       |
| `{k: <lit>}` inline         |      29.2 | 1       |
| `k > <lit>`                 |      60.6 | 199,994 |
| `k >= <lit>`                |      64.9 | 199,995 |
| **`k > N-2` (SELECTIVE)**   |  **49.9** | **1**   |
| `k <> <lit>`                |      43.2 | 199,999 |
| `flag = true`               |      34.9 | 100,000 |
| `{flag: true}` inline       |      34.1 | 100,000 |

**1.64x, and the selective row is what proves it is the predicate FORM and not the answer size** —
it returns one row exactly like the equality and still pays 49.9 against 30.5. The two equality
spellings agreeing (29.2 / 30.5) is item 230's fix working.

The cause is exact. `directEqProps` lifts an equality conjunct into `eqProps`, a loop that reads
the property straight off the element; everything else falls to a compiled expression that reads
`env.binding.get(variable)` — a `Map` get per row. The comment in `patternCountOf` quotes the same
numbers from the other direction: the clause spelling "paid 29.0 ns a vertex against the inline
spelling's 17.2" before that lift existed. And `directEqProps`'s own doc calls this the next step:

> One mixed conjunct of any other shape (an inequality, …) declines the WHOLE chain. … It is now
> merely unimplemented — item 259 made conjunct order unobservable in a FILTER … Telling the two
> apart conjunct-by-conjunct is the next step, not a property this avoids.

### Built, and retracted on the blocker rather than shipped

`compareTruth` was extracted from the `compare` arm (so the three-valued and cross-type rules
could not drift between two routes), `directEqProps` was taught to lift an ordering comparison into
a `cmpProps` sibling, and `matchesPredicate` gained the matching loop. 1837 tests passed after the
EXTRACTION alone — then three failed with `cmpProps` wired in, and two of them said an inline
predicate had stopped being applied.

**The blocker is that "this predicate is empty" is spread across NINE expressions**, each
enumerating `props` / `where` / sometimes `eqProps` by hand:

```
executor.ts:1033, 1038, 1133, 1140, 1159     matching.ts:247, 362, 608, 1395
```

`matching.ts:247` is `prefilter !== undefined || node.pred.props.length > 0 || node.pred.where
!== undefined` — no `eqProps`, no `cmpProps`. An inline `(n WHERE n.k > 5)` used to land in
`where`; lifted, it lands in `cmpProps`, and such a check concludes there is no predicate and
expands UNFILTERED. That is a silent SUPERSET, i.e. a wrong answer, and `rel-inline-pred.test.ts`
exists because this exact mistake shipped once before for `eqProps`:

> `satisfies` checks `props`, `eqProps` AND `where`. A hop whose only predicate had been lifted
> into `eqProps` would therefore have been expanded UNFILTERED — a superset.

Five of the nine are REL predicates, which never receive an `ownVar` and so can never carry
`cmpProps` — leaving four node sites. All four are FAST-PATH gates, where a wrong edit changes
routing rather than raising, so each needs its own distinguishing test.

**Retracted deliberately.** 1.64x on unindexed range-filtered counts does not justify a nine-site
invariant edit as the last act of a long session. The prerequisite is a single `hasPredicate(pred)`
helper replacing all nine hand-written checks — a separate, answer-neutral refactor that can be
mutation-tested on its own (and which would also close the pre-existing gap where `eqProps` is
missing from most of them). With that in place this lift is a few lines.

The measurement, the cause, the quoted invitation in `directEqProps`, and the exact blocker are all
here so the next pass starts from the refactor instead of re-deriving the target.

## 277. A WRONG ANSWER: an inline `WHERE a.k = 1` was silently not applied, and differential fuzzing could not have found it

Item 276 retracted a perf change because "is this predicate empty?" was spread across seven
hand-written checks, six of which omitted `eqProps`. Chasing that invariant as a CORRECTNESS
question rather than a refactor found a live wrong answer:

```text
MATCH (a:P) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (a WHERE a.k = 1)-[:E]->(x) } RETURN a.n
  want [a]   got [a, b, c]
```

Three P nodes in a cycle, so every one has an out-edge; the predicate was the only
discriminator, and it was dropped. **The sibling spellings were all correct**, which is what makes
this the defect class this engine is named for:

| spelling              | lands in  | answer        |
| --------------------- | --------- | ------------- |
| `(a WHERE a.k = 1)`   | `eqProps` | **[a, b, c]** |
| `(a {k: 1})`          | `props`   | [a]           |
| `(a WHERE a.k > 2)`   | `where`   | [c]           |
| plain `WHERE a.k = 1` | —         | [a]           |

### Cause

`CPredicate` carries a constraint in THREE places: `props`, `where`, and `eqProps` — the
equalities `directEqProps` lifts so they can be read straight off the element. An inline `WHERE`
passes an `ownVar`, so `a.k = 1` lifts ENTIRELY into `eqProps`, leaving `props` empty and `where`
undefined. The one-hop EXISTS fast path's decline gate read only the first two, so it did not
decline, and the fast path answers "does the start have an out-edge of this type" without ever
applying the predicate. The endpoint's `free` computation had the same omission, so
`(a)-[:E]->(x WHERE x.k = 1)` was wrong too.

A SECOND site, `relHasInlinePred`, already listed all three — because this exact mistake shipped
once before for relationships, which is what `rel-inline-pred.test.ts` exists for:

> `satisfies` checks `props`, `eqProps` AND `where`. A hop whose only predicate had been lifted
> into `eqProps` would therefore have been expanded UNFILTERED — a superset.

So the fix is one exported `hasPredicate(pred)` and seven call sites routed through it, including
`relHasInlinePred` itself. A fourth place to carry a constraint can no longer reintroduce the bug
by being forgotten at six sites.

### WHY THE DIFFERENTIAL FUZZER COULD NOT FIND IT, which is the durable part

The seven byte-identity fuzzers were green before and after. Asking native the same questions
directly explains both halves:

```text
REFUSED  bound start, EQUALITY spelling    inline WHERE on a EXISTS start node is not supported
REFUSED  bound start, INLINE-PROPERTY      bound variable `a` cannot be re-constrained with inline properties
REFUSED  bound start, ORDERING spelling    inline WHERE on a EXISTS start node is not supported
ok       ENDPOINT, EQUALITY spelling       got ["c"]
ok       ENDPOINT, INLINE-PROPERTY         got ["c"]
```

- The **bound-start** bug is in a shape **native refuses outright**. A differential fuzzer compares
  two engines' answers, so it is structurally blind to a bug in a shape only ONE engine accepts —
  no amount of seeds reaches it. The guard for that class has to be an INTRA-engine spelling
  comparison, which is what every test added here is.
- The **endpoint** bug was in a shape both engines accept, and native answers `["c"]` correctly.
  So that one WAS a live cross-engine divergence and the fuzzer still missed it: it does not
  generate an EXISTS subquery with an inline equality on the endpoint. **A concrete coverage gap**,
  recorded rather than inferred — mutant T2 (reverting only the endpoint computation) fails exactly
  that test, proving the bug was real and isolated to that site.

An acceptance divergence also falls out: TS accepts an inline `WHERE`/property on an EXISTS
subquery's already-bound start; native refuses both with specific errors. Not added to the
divergence registry, because the fuzzer cannot generate the shape and an entry it never reaches
would be an inert declaration.

### Teeth: four mutants, each putting ONE gate back, all four caught

| mutant                                        | result             |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| T1 `hasPredicate` itself blinded to `eqProps` | CAUGHT (7 failing) |
| T2 the endpoint `free` computation reverted   | CAUGHT (1 failing) |
| T3 the two start-side EXISTS gates reverted   | CAUGHT (4 failing) |
| T4 `relHasInlinePred` reverted                | CAUGHT (2 failing) |

T4 is caught by the PRE-EXISTING `rel-inline-pred.test.ts`, so the rel half was already guarded and
only the node gates were not. T2 failing alone is what isolates the endpoint site.

12 tests, every one comparing the three spellings of one question rather than asserting a single
answer — because a single-spelling assertion is exactly what would have passed while the engine
returned three rows for one. 1849 TS tests total (1837 → 1849); all seven byte-identity fuzzers
green; `bun run check` and clippy each as their own command.

**This is the second time in two items that the nine-presence-check invariant produced a defect**
(item 276's retraction was the perf half). The helper closes both.

## 278. The deferred ordering lift, now a few lines — 1.44x, and the helper earned itself one item later

Item 276 measured an ORDERING comparison at 1.64x an equality on the same unindexed count and
RETRACTED the lift, because "is this predicate empty?" was spread across nine hand-written checks
and four of them were node fast-path gates where missing a new field expands UNFILTERED. Item 277
replaced all nine with `hasPredicate` while fixing a wrong answer in the same invariant. So this
item is what 276 predicted it would be.

**The helper's value is visible in how the change failed.** Wiring the field in item 276 broke
THREE tests, two of them inline predicates silently not applied. Wiring the identical field now
broke ONE — and that one was a test deliberately pinning the limitation being removed. Extending
`hasPredicate` in a single place picked the field up for all seven gates at once, which is exactly
the property the refactor was for.

### Measured: alternated A/B, three rounds each, min per cell

200,000 vertices, no index. `ns/vertex`, and every row's ANSWER checked identical across the two
builds (no row-count mismatch anywhere):

| case                           |  head | changed | ratio     |
| ------------------------------ | ----: | ------: | --------- |
| `k > <lit>` (broad)            |  48.0 |    33.4 | **1.44x** |
| `k > <lit>` (SELECTIVE, 1 row) |  49.1 |    37.2 | **1.32x** |
| `k >= <lit>`                   |  47.6 |    39.9 | 1.19x     |
| `k > 5 AND grp = 3` (mixed)    |  62.4 |    56.2 | 1.11x     |
| `k <> <lit>`                   |  43.2 |    42.6 | 1.01x     |
| CONTROL no predicate           |   0.0 |     0.0 | —         |
| CONTROL `upper(…)` declines    | 110.4 |   115.3 | 0.96x     |
| CONTROL `k = <lit>`            |  30.6 |    29.5 | 1.04x     |
| CONTROL `{k: <lit>}` inline    |  34.6 |    30.0 | 1.15x     |

**It closes about HALF the gap, not all of it, and that is worth saying plainly.** Item 276
predicted 1.64x from the `>`-vs-`=` difference; the selective `>` went 49.1 → 37.2 against
equality's 29.5, so a ~1.26x residual remains — `compareTruth`'s operator dispatch and type checks
against what `structuralEq` does directly. The prediction was the CEILING, not the delivery.

The two equality controls moved 1.04x and 1.15x, which they should not: they are the path this
change does not touch. At 30-35ns a vertex that is the TS layout toll, the same band item 268's
work ran into, and it cuts in the flattering direction here — so the quotable numbers are the
ordering rows, not those.

`k <> <lit>` at 1.01x is informative: `<>` lifts like the others, but `compareTruth` routes it
through `structuralEq` exactly as `=` does, so there was never a binding-read to save beyond the
one the lift removes. The lift applies; the win does not, because the cost was elsewhere.

### What it is, and the one definition it rests on

`compareTruth` was extracted from the `compare` arm FIRST, and verified behaviour-neutral on its
own (1849 tests) before any behaviour changed. Reimplementing the comparison rules in the new loop
would have been the mistake `patternCountOf`'s doc warns about — "a shortcut that half-applies a
predicate is a wrong answer" — because the type handling IS the semantics: three-valued nullish
propagation, structural equality across types, chronological temporal ordering, and cross-type
ordering as UNKNOWN rather than a fault. One function, two call sites, no drift possible.

### A fuzzer failure that was NOT this change, proven rather than argued

`bun run fuzz` came back 12 pass / 1 fail on a random seed:

```text
MATCH (t:T) OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE (n.x AND (0.0 IN [1e21, n.s]))) RETURN …
  ts:     err E_INVALID_VALUE
  native: ok [{"x":3,"y":null}, … 6 rows]
```

Replaying `FUZZ_SEED=3668867883` against HEAD with the change reverted reproduces it exactly, so it
is **pre-existing**. Neither conjunct is a comparison, so `directEqProps` declines this predicate
outright and the lift never sees it.

It is also correctly OUTSIDE the registry's declaration, and the reason is precise. The entry's
matcher is deliberately narrow — `E_INVALID_VALUE` on one side against an EMPTY result on the
other, because "an error against a NON-EMPTY result is a different thing entirely". Here native
returns six rows, so `isEmptyResult` rejects it. But every `y` is `null`: this is an
`OPTIONAL MATCH`, native matched NO endpoint, and the nulls are the left rows padded. Semantically
it is the entry's own case — "malformed predicate against no rows" — with OPTIONAL turning "no
rows" into "rows of nulls", which the matcher cannot see through. Recorded as a separate finding
rather than widened here, because widening a declaration is a conformance judgement and not part of
a perf lift.

1850 TS tests (1849 → 1850, one updated to pin WHERE each conjunct lands rather than that a
non-equality declined); `bun run check` as its own command.

## 279. The boolean-context asymmetry also fires against a NON-EMPTY result, so the fuzzer FAILS instead of declaring it

Item 278's verification run came back 12 pass / 1 fail on a random seed, and the divergence turned
out to be pre-existing (replaying it against HEAD with that change reverted reproduces it exactly).
It is recorded here on its own because it changes a fact the pending conformance decision rests on.

```text
FUZZ_SEED=3668867883
MATCH (t:T) OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE (n.x AND (0.0 IN [1e21, n.s])))
RETURN t.n AS x, n.n AS y ORDER BY x, y
  ts:     err E_INVALID_VALUE
  native: ok [{"x":3,"y":null},{"x":5,"y":null},{"x":7,"y":null},
              {"x":11,"y":null},{"x":13,"y":null},{"x":17,"y":null}]
```

### Same root cause, excluded direction

This is the asymmetry the registry's only entry already describes — both engines run the same
plan-time boolean-context check and disagree about WHERE it applies; the Rust engine applies it to
whatever lowers to a `Plan::Filter`, which an inline predicate on some positions does and on others
does not. `n.x` sits in a truth position inside an inline pattern predicate, so TS rejects the
query at plan time and native does not.

**But the entry cannot declare it, deliberately.** Its matcher is narrow by design:

> NARROW: `E_INVALID_VALUE` on one side against an EMPTY result on the other. "Malformed
> predicate" against "no rows" — never wrong data, and never rows. An error against a NON-EMPTY
> result is a different thing entirely (that is the `CALL`-body laziness bug) and is NOT covered
> here.

Native returns SIX rows, so `isEmptyResult` rejects the comparison and the fuzzer fails. Yet every
`y` is null: this is an `OPTIONAL MATCH`, native matched NO endpoint through the predicate, and the
rows are the left side padded. **The result is non-empty for a reason that has nothing to do with
the predicate** — so it is the entry's own case wearing a shape the matcher cannot see through.

### Why this is recorded rather than fixed

Three options, and two are worse than leaving it:

1. **Widen the matcher** to admit "error against rows that are all-null in the optional columns".
   That weakens the exact guard the narrowness exists for — the `CALL`-body laziness class is "error
   against a NON-EMPTY result" too — and the registry has no column provenance to tell padding from
   data. A looser declaration that masks a real bug is worse than an intermittent failure that
   names one.
2. **Extend TS's check to inline pattern predicates.** Already tried twice and MEASURED WORSE: 1
   divergence a run became 7, because native answers rows for `(n WHERE CAST(x AS STRING))`.
   `boolean-context-static-check` records this; it is on the refuted list.
3. **Record it**, which is what this does.

The real content is a correction to `CLOSED.md`'s open-question row, which described the asymmetry
as "`E_INVALID_VALUE` vs an EMPTY result". That understated it: the same asymmetry reaches an error
against a NON-EMPTY result through `OPTIONAL MATCH`, which is the direction the registry refuses to
declare — so **the conformance decision is not only about which queries get rejected, it is also
about whether `bun run fuzz` can be green on random seeds.** An intermittent failure nobody has
attributed is a liability: the next person to see 12 pass / 1 fail has to re-derive that it is
pre-existing, and the run after that may mask something new.

Frequency: hit once in a 20,000-query run; the entry's own estimate for the declared shape is ~1
per 120,000. The seed replays deterministically on both HEAD and the item-278 build, so it is
available as a fixture whenever the decision is taken.

No code change. The fix in every direction is a conformance judgement about whether a static
boolean-context check covers inline pattern predicates in BOTH engines — which would reject
queries that answer today.

## 280. CI went red on a DOCS-ONLY commit: a coverage floor set "~25% under the observed minimum" is unsafe for a small count

Item 279's commit touched two markdown files and CI failed. The failure is not the divergence that
item documented — it is the differential fuzzer's own coverage assertion:

```text
- "subOrGenerated": true,     + false
- "subOrNonEmpty": true,      + false
```

### The detector is fine; the floor is mis-set

`floor-met-by-wrong-queries` says check the DETECTOR before touching a floor, so that came first.
`/ OR (EXISTS|COUNT|VALUE) \{/` is specific and counts exactly the band it names — no
over-counting of a neighbouring shape, which is what item 237's `hopFilter` problem was. The floor
is the problem, and the floor's own comment contains the reason:

> MEASURED over ELEVEN seeds: subNot 19-42 generated / 16-39 non-empty, subOr 14-21 / 11-20.
> **Floors ~25% under the minima.**

Re-measured over twenty more seeds:

| counter             | observed          | mean | sigma | old floor | margin        |
| ------------------- | ----------------- | ---: | ----: | --------- | ------------- |
| `subNotGenerated`   | 23-42             |  ~31 |  ~5.6 | `> 14`    | 3.0 sigma     |
| `subNotNonEmpty`    | 17-38             |  ~27 |  ~5.2 | `> 12`    | 2.9 sigma     |
| `subOrGenerated`    | 14-25             |  ~18 |  ~4.2 | `> 10`    | 1.9 sigma     |
| **`subOrNonEmpty`** | **8**, 9, 11 … 21 |  ~14 |  ~3.7 | `> 8`     | **1.6 sigma** |
| `abbrevPath`        | 44-77             |  ~61 |   ~10 | `> 35`    | 2.6 sigma     |

`subOrNonEmpty` hit **8 and 9 in eleven samples against a `> 8` floor** — a coin flip over enough
CI runs, and eleven seeds were never going to show that tail.

### THE RULE WAS WRONG, NOT THE NUMBER

"~25% under the observed minimum" reads like a safety margin and is not one. **A floor's safety is
its distance from the mean in SIGMA, not a percentage**, because sigma grows as the square root of
the count while a percentage grows linearly:

- `groupHopPredNonEmpty` has a 1.42x margin at mean ~450 — about **6 sigma**, and it never fires.
- `subOrNonEmpty` had a 1.5x margin at mean ~14 — about **1.6 sigma**, and it fired.

Same ratio, opposite behaviour. Nine other small bands were checked against the same test and are
safe: `hopUntypedNonZero` is 4.3 sigma, `peelNonZero` and `simpleGroupNonEmpty` further still.
Only the `subOr` pair, the `subNot` pair and `abbrevPath` were inside 3 sigma, and all five are now
at ~4 sigma.

### Lowering a floor is the right fix HERE because the band's job is narrow

Each of these exists to "catch a shape falling silently to ZERO" — the comment says so, and says it
is explicitly NOT meant "to resolve a drift of a few percent". A floor near the mean pretends to
the second job while failing at being reliable. `subOrNonEmpty > 3` against a mean of 14 still
fails loudly on a collapse and cannot flake.

**Verified, not assumed, in both directions:**

- A mutant that makes the `subOr` band unreachable — the state item 255 found it in, generated ZERO
  times — still FAILS the new floor. A floor that cannot fail is worse than no floor, so this is
  the check that matters.
- Eight consecutive fresh seeds pass.

The alternative fix was to raise the band's generation rate so a tight floor could mean something.
That is the better long-run answer for a band that has found bugs, but it changes the generator's
distribution and therefore every other counter's calibration — a bigger change than a red CI
warrants, and recorded here as the option not taken.

## 281. Item 278's residual is BELOW this harness's resolution — the control moved as much as the target

Item 278 closed about half the `>`-vs-`=` gap on an unindexed count and left a ~1.26x residual with
a concrete suspect: the `cmpProps` loop still did a `COMPARE[op]` object lookup PER ROW PER ENTRY
and re-tested `op === '='` inside `compareTruth`, both decidable when the predicate is compiled
rather than 200,000 times.

Built it: each lifted entry carries a `test` closure resolved at compile time, `<>` keeping the
structural route and every ordering operator skipping the equality branch entirely (`directEqProps`
never puts `=` in that list). 1850 tests passed, so the only claim was speed.

### The A/B refutes it, and the CONTROL is what says so

Alternated, three rounds each, min per cell, `ns/vertex`:

| case                    | head | changed | ratio     |
| ----------------------- | ---: | ------: | --------- |
| **CONTROL `k = <lit>`** | 30.7 |    23.9 | **1.28x** |
| `k > <lit>` (selective) | 30.6 |    24.0 | 1.28x     |
| `k <> <lit>`            | 37.9 |    29.8 | 1.27x     |
| `k > <lit>` (broad)     | 35.6 |    30.8 | 1.16x     |
| `k < <lit>`             | 33.3 |    29.7 | 1.12x     |
| `k >= <lit>`            | 33.2 |    31.1 | 1.07x     |
| **`k > 5 AND grp = 3`** | 56.3 |    56.2 | **1.00x** |
| CONTROL no predicate    |  0.0 |     0.0 | —         |

`k = <lit>` is the equality path: it goes through `eqProps`, `cmpProps` is undefined for it, and
the loop is skipped entirely. **The change cannot reach it, and it moved the most of anything.**
Meanwhile the mixed chain, which the change DOES reach, moved not at all. An untouched control
moving as much as the target and a reached case moving none is noise dominating, not an effect.

**Retracted** under item 231's rule — retract a change you cannot measure, even a free one. The
specialization is strictly less work per row, so it is probably a real improvement; it is simply
not one this harness can demonstrate, and a compile-time specialization that measures flat is still
code to read.

### What it would take, recorded so the next pass does not re-derive it

The effect being chased is an object lookup and a branch out of ~30 ns/vertex — call it 3-10%.
This harness's band here is plainly ±25% (the control's own 1.28x measures it). Resolving 3-10%
needs `in-process-ab-of-two-builds`: import BOTH bundles into one process and alternate on one
graph, which is the documented tool for when the bench band is wider than the effect. That is the
route if anyone wants this residual, and the reason it was not taken here is proportionality, not
doubt about the direction.

The residual itself stays recorded at item 278: the selective `>` is ~37 ns/vertex against
equality's ~29, and the remaining difference is `compareTruth`'s type dispatch doing work
`structuralEq` does not need.

## 282. A CORRELATED product under a LIMIT is still 1,400x — priced, designed, and the hash-join shortcut is closed

Item 275 made a LIMITed product cap its sides, but only reaches the shape item 273's pushdown
produces: a predicate on ONE side, pushed into that side. A CORRELATING predicate cannot be pushed,
so it stays above the join — and `streaming_chain` still has no `Join` arm, so `pull_capped_stream`
declines and the general path materializes the whole product.

Priced at 4 x 100,000:

| case                                |        ms | rows |
| ----------------------------------- | --------: | ---: |
| `WHERE u.k = s.k` LIMIT 1           | **9.835** |    1 |
| `WHERE u.k = s.k` LIMIT 4           | **9.833** |    4 |
| `WHERE u.k = s.k`, no limit (count) |     7.459 |    1 |
| `WHERE u.k > s.k` LIMIT 1           |     8.366 |    1 |
| CONTROL `WHERE u.k > 5` LIMIT 1     | **0.007** |    1 |
| CONTROL no `WHERE` LIMIT 1          |     0.000 |    1 |

**1,400x against the one-sided spelling, and FLAT in the limit** (9.835 at LIMIT 1 against 9.833 at
LIMIT 4) — the `eager-tail-cache` signature. The inequality spelling costs the same, so this is
about correlation and not about `=`. Note the LIMIT makes it SLOWER than the unlimited count
(9.835 against 7.459): the product is built AND then paged, so the limit adds a 400,000-row slice.

The plans confirm the cause rather than leaving it inferred:

```text
correlating:  OrderPage { Project { Filter { Join { Scan, Scan } } } }   <- Filter ABOVE the join
one-sided:    OrderPage { Project { Join { Scan, Filter { Scan } } } }   <- pushed INTO the side
```

### THE HASH-JOIN SHORTCUT IS CLOSED, which is worth knowing before anyone reaches for it

The obvious thought is to turn `Filter(u.k = s.k) { Join(on: []) }` into a real hash join on the
property — the engine already has `hash_join` and an `on` list. It cannot: `Plan::Join`'s own doc
says `on` lists equalities on SHARED BOUND VARIABLES and "the join key is bound-variable identity
(a node/edge)". A property-value correlation is not expressible as an `on` pair, so that route
needs a new join form, not a planner rewrite.

### The available fix, designed

A nested-loop streamer with early exit, in `pull_capped`:

- For each LEFT row in order, stream the RIGHT side in blocks, apply the filter per block, and
  accumulate survivors; stop as soon as `cap` rows are held.
- Left-major, so what it produces is a PREFIX of what the uncapped plan produces — the same
  property item 275's arm rests on, and the one its test asserts by comparing every cap against
  the uncapped answer.
- Blocking the RIGHT side inside the LEFT loop is the part that matters. Driving only from the
  left leaf (which is all a `streaming_chain` arm could do, since it returns one leaf's ids) would
  cap the number of LEFT rows and still scan the whole right side for each — about 1/4 of the work
  here, not 1/1400th.

It is NOT a `streaming_chain` arm for that reason: that helper's contract is `(body, ids)` for a
single chunkable leaf, and a nested loop needs two.

### Why it is recorded rather than built here

The change is a new exec path producing rows, which is the riskiest kind in this engine: row order,
lineage (`pull_capped_stream` is `!track`-only), and a cap bound that item 275's mutation showed is
exactly where an off-by-one hides. Verifying it properly means tests across the cap/survivor
boundary, mutants under timeout and the cgroup cap, the byte-identity fuzzers, and a screen — the
same budget item 275 took, and more because a nested loop has two bounds rather than one.

Recorded with the measurement, the plan evidence, the closed shortcut and the design, so the next
pass starts from the implementation rather than re-deriving the target — the same way item 276's
entry let item 278 land in a few lines.

## 283. The nested-loop streamer: 1,640x where the cap fills, 1.7x WORSE where it does not — retracted, with the constant factor named

Item 282 priced a correlated product under a cap at 1,400x and designed the fix. This item built
it and retracted it. The design was right about the shape and wrong about the cost.

### Built as designed, and the wins are real

A `Plan::Filter { input: Join { on: [] }, pred }` arm in `pull_capped`: pull the left side whole
(one scan, which the uncapped plan does anyway), stream the right side in adaptive blocks inside
a left-major loop, apply the predicate per block, stop when `cap` rows survive. 1035 + 13 + 723
native tests passed unchanged.

| case                      |   before |         after | verdict        |
| ------------------------- | -------: | ------------: | -------------- |
| `WHERE u.k = s.k` LIMIT 1 | 9.835 ms |  **0.006 ms** | **1,640x**     |
| `WHERE u.k > s.k` LIMIT 1 | 8.366 ms |      0.007 ms | ~1,200x        |
| `WHERE u.k = s.k` LIMIT 4 | 9.833 ms | **18.731 ms** | **1.9x WORSE** |
| impossible correlation    |        — |     27.994 ms | ~3x worse      |
| CONTROL one-sided LIMIT 1 | 0.007 ms |      0.007 ms | flat           |

### Why it loses, which the LIMIT 4 row makes obvious

The answer to `u.k = s.k` is exactly FOUR rows — one per left row. At `LIMIT 4` the cap never
fills early, so `total < cap` stays true and the inner loop scans the ENTIRE right side for every
left row: four full 100,000-row scans in blocks, each block paying a `hash_join` and a
`filter_keep`, where the materialized path pays once. **The loop is a bet on early exit, and when
the bet loses it pays double.**

A gate was added for exactly that — abandon after the FIRST left row if its whole scan did not fill
the cap, bounding the waste at one extra right scan. It helped and was not enough: 18.731 → 16.926
(still 1.7x worse) and the impossible case 27.994 → 20.619.

### The real blocker is a CONSTANT FACTOR, and it is identifiable

With the gate, the cost is one left row's full right scan. That slice is a quarter of the product,
which the materialized path does in about 2.5ms — and the blocked path takes ~7ms for it. So the
per-block overhead is **3-4x the materialized per-row cost**, and the suspect is concrete:
`hash_join(&lrow, &rb, &[])` is called per block to attach a SINGLE left row to a right block. With
an empty `on` that is a broadcast, not a join, but it goes through the hash-join machinery anyway.

**The next attempt should build the joined block directly** — repeat the one left row across the
right block's columns — instead of calling `hash_join`. That is the change this item did not make,
and until the constant factor is down the bet-on-early-exit structure cannot be judged on its
merits.

### Retracted rather than shipped

Shipping a 1.7x regression on `LIMIT 4` over a correlated product to win 1,640x on `LIMIT 1` is a
trade, and not one to make unilaterally: both are reachable shapes, and `LIMIT n` over a correlated
product is not obviously rarer than `LIMIT 1`. The method's rule applies as written — retract a
target that does not survive re-measurement.

What is better than before: item 282's entry said "nested loop with early exit" and this one says
"nested loop with early exit, a lost-bet gate, and a direct broadcast instead of `hash_join`",
with the 3-4x constant factor measured and the two rows that expose it named. The 1,640x is real
and waiting behind one more change.

## 284. A CROSS PRODUCT was building a hash index to rediscover that everything matches — 6.7x, and mutation found the row order pinned by nothing

Item 283 retracted a nested-loop streamer and left one thing behind: the per-block cost was 3-4x
the materialized path's, with `hash_join(&lrow, &rb, &[])` named as the suspect. Reading that
function turned a 40-line exec path into a 5-line one, and moved the target from a capped query to
EVERY cross product the planner emits.

### `hash_join` has no `on.is_empty()` case

Its `dense` fast path needs exactly ONE slot pair, so a cross product falls through to the generic
branch — which computes a join key per row on BOTH sides, inserts all of them into one `FnvMap`
bucket, and probes it, to rediscover that with no join key everything matches. `MATCH (a) MATCH
(b)` and every `Join { on: [] }` the planner emits land there, so this is the common
multi-pattern shape and not a corner.

Emitted directly instead. Alternated A/B, three rounds each, min per cell:

| case                      |      head |      changed | ratio     |
| ------------------------- | --------: | -----------: | --------- |
| `correlated =, count`     |  9.382 ms | **1.402 ms** | **6.69x** |
| `comma correlated, count` |  8.371 ms |     1.446 ms | 5.79x     |
| `correlated =, project`   |  7.491 ms |     1.434 ms | 5.22x     |
| `correlated >, count`     | 10.442 ms |     2.751 ms | 3.80x     |
| CONTROL product-of-counts |  0.000 ms |     0.000 ms | —         |
| CONTROL single-pattern    |  0.166 ms |     0.169 ms | 0.98x     |

Row counts identical on every row. Both controls are flat — the product-of-counts shortcut builds
no join at all, and a single pattern never reaches `hash_join`. The two spellings of one question
CONVERGE (1.402 against 1.446) rather than drifting, which is the property this repo treats as the
invariant.

Byte-identity by construction rather than by argument: the index path emitted left rows ascending
with each one's right rows ascending (it indexed `j` ascending and probed `i` ascending), which is
exactly what the double loop produces.

### MUTATION FOUND THAT CLAIM GUARDED BY NOTHING

| mutant                                   | result               |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| U2 off-by-one on the right bound         | CAUGHT (32 failing)  |
| U3 off-by-one on the left bound          | CAUGHT (28 failing)  |
| U4 the fast path never applies           | SURVIVES — perf only |
| **U1 RIGHT-major instead of left-major** | **SURVIVED**         |

U1 keeps every row and every count and only changes the ORDER — and the entire suite passed. The
byte-identity fuzzers cannot see it either: they canonicalise unordered row order. So "the two
paths agree on order" was true, derived from reading both, and load-bearing on nobody; any later
edit could have flipped it silently, in the one dimension `column-order-is-observable` records as
NOT free.

`a_cross_product_emits_rows_left_major` now pins it on a 2x3 fixture where right-major interleaves
the left values with the same six rows and the same counts. Re-running U1 against it: **CAUGHT, by
exactly that test.** This is the "a guard you cannot make observable: INSTRUMENT it" discipline —
the test exists because the mutant proved the argument was unguarded, not because the argument was
wrong.

### The three-item arc is the point

Item 282 priced the target and designed a nested loop. Item 283 built it, measured 1,640x where the
cap fills and 1.7x WORSE where it does not, retracted it — and in doing so located a 3-4x constant
factor. Reading that factor produced this: a smaller change, one level down, that helps more
shapes and carries no early-exit risk. **The retraction earned the win**; had item 283 shipped, the
real fix would still be hidden behind it.

1036 native tests (1035 + the order test) + 13 + 723; `rewrite_fuzz` green at default and at
`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` (46.42s); all seven byte-identity fuzzers green with `DECLARED none
used`; clippy `-D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` each as their own command.

### Screen

`query_bench`, two md5-distinct binaries (`81165dea` head, `e68ec78c` changed), three alternated
rounds, min per cell:

```
73 cells   median 0.998   93% within +/-5%
```

The most relevant cell is the corpus's ONE multi-pattern join, `join on a shared var` — whose `on`
is NON-empty (the patterns share `q`), so the fast path cannot reach it. It reads **1.004**: a real
planner-produced `Join` under a real `Filter`, unmoved.

Five movers, four of them FASTER (0.869 `filter age>50`, 0.883 `counts | filtered`, 0.897 `gremlin
has age>50`, 0.946 `shortest`), which is the cluster `filter-count-row-is-not-a-screen` records as
moving 8-10% for ANY native edit — the same toll, in the flattering direction, which is why they
are not quoted as a win. `shortest | anchored` at 1.086 is the one slower row, and it moved 1.100
in item 275's screen on an unrelated change, so it is a known mover rather than a signal.

## 285. The COMMA spelling of a multi-pattern clause kept its `WHERE` as a clause filter — 15.6x, and the probe group added for it found a 5400x cliff on the way in

`pushWhereIntoNode` declined on `clause.patterns.length !== 1`. So one question, spelled two ways,
planned two ways:

| spelling                                           | 4 x 100,000, min of 7 | rows |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------: | ---: |
| `MATCH (a:A) MATCH (b:B) WHERE b.k = 7 RETURN a.k` |              9.193 ms |    4 |
| `MATCH (a:A), (b:B) WHERE b.k = 7 RETURN a.k`      |            145.039 ms |    4 |

The function's own comment already explained the cost: **a node predicate is evaluated once per
SCANNED vertex, a clause filter once per SURVIVING BINDING** — and a binding over a product is a
`Map` materialized per product row, before anything filters it. The comma spelling built 400,000 of
them to keep four. This is item 121's shape (a multi-pattern spelling at 160x) recurring in the
other direction.

### What may move, and why that is the whole design

`pushWhereAcrossPatterns` attributes each conjunct to the pattern it constrains, and moves **only a
conjunct reading exactly ONE of the clause's own pattern variables.**

That restriction is not conservatism, it is the correctness condition, and the reason is
`visitRemaining`: `matchClauseBindings` hands a multi-pattern clause to it and it **chooses which
pattern to visit next at runtime** (item 122's uncorrelated-rescan fix). So the intra-clause visit
order is not knowable at plan time, and a conjunct reading TWO of the clause's patterns — `WHERE
b.k = a.k` — cannot be pushed onto either: whenever its pattern is visited first the other
variable is unbound, the comparison is UNKNOWN, and **the row silently disappears.**

A conjunct reading one own pattern **plus OUTER variables** is safe, for the reason the
single-pattern path has relied on since item 128: outer variables are in the incoming binding
before the clause starts, whatever order the patterns are then visited in.

So the correlated comma spelling keeps its ~3.4x against its two-clause twin. **Recorded, not
fixed** — fixing it means pinning `visitRemaining`'s order, which is a different change with its
own cost.

### Measurement

The target was easy; the CONTROL was the work. Alternated A/B, three rounds each way, rebuilding the
dist per round (the probe reads the BUILT dist), min per cell:

| case                         |       head |      changed |      ratio |
| ---------------------------- | ---------: | -----------: | ---------: |
| `one-sided =, comma`         | 131.800 ms | **8.466 ms** | **15.57x** |
| `one-sided, comma` (`>`)     | 179.999 ms |   170.026 ms |      1.06x |
| `one-sided =, MATCH MATCH`   |   8.483 ms |     9.299 ms |      0.91x |
| `comma correlated, count`    | 129.813 ms |   133.249 ms |      0.97x |
| `correlated =, count`        |  37.868 ms |    38.959 ms |      0.97x |
| `correlated =, project`      |  38.945 ms |    39.424 ms |      0.99x |
| `correlated >, count`        | 127.865 ms |   122.268 ms |      1.05x |
| `one-sided, MATCH MATCH`     | 123.094 ms |   121.147 ms |      1.02x |
| CONTROL product-of-counts    |   0.001 ms |     0.001 ms |      1.00x |
| CONTROL single pattern count |   2.007 ms |     2.059 ms |      0.97x |

Row counts identical on every row. **`one-sided =, MATCH MATCH` at 0.91x is the one cell outside
the band, and it is the cell the change CANNOT STRUCTURALLY REACH** — two clauses of one pattern
each, so `pushWhereAcrossPatterns` is never called. Item 281 was retracted for exactly this
pattern, so it was not waved away: re-measured ALONE, four alternated rounds, 25 reps, no other
case in the process to warm it.

| isolated control           | head mins                   | changed mins                | ratio |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----: |
| `one-sided =, MATCH MATCH` | 7.756 9.805 7.696 **7.510** | 8.463 9.542 **7.397** 7.650 | 1.02x |
| `single pattern = only`    | 1.568 1.698 **1.444** 1.465 | 1.701 2.134 1.465 1.589     | 0.99x |

Flat. **Round 2 is the slow outlier on BOTH sides** (9.805 head, 9.542 changed), which is the
signature of a round, not of a change. The 0.91x was that cell's own noise under the big probe,
where fifteen heavier cases run before it in one process — the contamination
`bench-methodology` records from the 3.4x that turned out to be 0.93-0.96x isolated.

### The permanent group, which confirmed the win better than the probe did

`spelling-probe.ts` gets `a product's one-sided predicate: comma vs MATCH MATCH`, four spellings of
one question. On HEAD the group spreads **9.5x**; with the change, **1.10x** (23.50 / 24.02 / 25.13
/ 25.78 ms). That is a stronger confirmation than the scratch probe, because it is the harness that
stays.

`RETURN b.k` and not `count(*)`: the product-of-counts shortcut answers the count form without
building the product, so a count group would be O(1) on both members and measure nothing. The
correlated pair is deliberately NOT a member — it is known-divergent, and a known-divergent pair in
a probe that flags divergence makes the probe lie.

### THE GROUP NEEDED FOUR NODES, AND THOSE FOUR NODES FOUND A 5400x CLIFF

A comma product needs a tiny left side (N x N is not a measurement, it is a hang), and every node
in the probe's fixture was a `P`. Adding four `S` nodes made an existing group — `label on start:
redundant vs absent`, previously **0.00ms on both members and skipped under `FLOOR_MS`** — read:

```
  54.06 ms   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(*) AS c
   0.00 ms   MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(*) AS c      ~5400x, same answer
```

Diagnosed, not assumed: it reproduces on HEAD's executor with the new fixture, so it is the fixture
and not this item's change. `vacuousLabel` elides a label every vertex carries, and the one-hop
count shortcut requires that elision to have happened (`shortcuts.ts`: _"The start label has to be
vacuous for the caller to route here"_). With four `S` nodes among 200,000, `:P` is genuinely
selective, the elision does not happen, and the labelled spelling falls to a **full traversal**.

So the shortcut is not "a one-hop count is O(1)", it is "a one-hop count is O(1) **when the start
label constrains nothing**" — and four nodes out of 200,000 are enough to lose it. **That is the
next target**, recorded in CLOSED.md §5. The group stays flagged until it is closed; its comment
says so, so that nobody reverts the fixture to quiet it.

The probe earned itself a third time, and in the least deliberate way available: the finding came
out of adding an unrelated group.

### Mutation — 8 then 4, and three of the survivors were informative

| mutant                                         | result                    |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| M1 a CORRELATED conjunct is pushed anyway      | CAUGHT (3 failing)        |
| M2 a conjunct on a HOP pattern is pushed       | CAUGHT (1 failing)        |
| M5 the RESIDUAL is dropped                     | CAUGHT (1 failing)        |
| M6 an existing `start.where` is REPLACED       | **SURVIVED**, then CAUGHT |
| M7 the arm is disabled                         | CAUGHT (20 failing)       |
| M3 a PATH-VARIABLE pattern receives a conjunct | SURVIVED                  |
| M4 a SUBQUERY conjunct is pushed               | SURVIVED                  |
| M8 the `own` filter is dropped                 | SURVIVED                  |
| M7b the arm is TRULY disabled                  | SURVIVED                  |

**M1 is caught by a pre-existing test**, `[MatchWhere3.2] equi-join on properties of disconnected
nodes` — the TCK had the correlated comma product all along, which is the best possible answer to
"is the correctness condition real".

**M6 survived, and the test that was supposed to catch it was mine.** I wrote "an existing inline
predicate on the start is kept" as `MATCH (b:B {k: 2})` — and an inline `{k: 2}` lands in `props`,
not in `start.where`. So `start.where` was `undefined`, the merge branch was never taken, and the
test asserted nothing about the thing it was named for. Respelled as `(b:B WHERE b.k = 2)`, plus a
CONTRADICTION case (`WHERE b.n = "b3"` over an inline `b.k = 2`, answer `[]`) which is the direction
replacement actually breaks: M6 is then CAUGHT. _The props-vs-`start.where` distinction is the same
one item 277's `hasPredicate` exists for; I walked into it from the other side._

**M7 is not the mutant I thought I was running.** Disabling `if (clause.patterns.length > 1)` does
not restore the old behaviour — it FALLS THROUGH to the single-pattern code below, which does
`const [path] = clause.patterns` and pushes onto pattern 0 **unconditionally**. 20 tests catch
that, which is worth knowing (the delegation is load-bearing, not just a dispatch), but it answers a
different question. M7b — the arm taken and attributing nothing — SURVIVED, which is the correct
result for a perf-only arm.

**M4 is an EXPECTED survivor.** The single-pattern path declines subquery conjuncts for a documented
PERF reason (pushing one costs a correlated subquery per scanned vertex), not a correctness one, so
there is nothing for a test to observe. Same category as M7b.

**M3 sent me to look at the guard it was testing.** It mirrors the single-pattern path's `pathVar
!== undefined` decline, so I mutated THAT one too — M9 — and it also SURVIVED the whole 1868-test
suite. So the `pathVar` guard is unobservable in BOTH copies: mine is inherited consistency, not
tested necessity, and the comment now says exactly that. Kept anyway. **A guard whose necessity is
unproven is not a guard shown to be unnecessary**, and the path-value semantics dropping it would
open were never this item's target.

**M8 (drop the `own` filter) is perf-only by construction**: without it, a conjunct reading one own
pattern plus an outer variable counts as two and is declined. That loses item 128's shape over a
product and changes no answer, so it survives — and the `an OUTER variable alongside one own
variable is still pushed` test asserts rows, which cannot see it. Recorded rather than papered over.

### Gates

`comma-pattern-pushdown.test.ts` is 20 tests, every one a SPELLING COMPARISON (`sameAnswer`), since
both spellings returned the correct answer and only a comparison detects this class. 1870 gql tests
/ the full `bun run test` across 21 projects; all seven byte-identity fuzzers green with `DECLARED
none used` and `cross=747/490` confirming the differential fuzzer does reach multi-pattern shapes;
`bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint` and `bun run fmt:check` each as their own command (lint caught
a `prefer-optional-chain` on the new code).

## 286. A one-hop count with a LABEL on one end had no degree-sum rung — 2.6-4.9x, and 7164x where the label has no edges

Item 285's probe group exposed the cliff and CLOSED.md recorded it as the next target. This closes
it, and the fix is a missing rung rather than a new algorithm.

### Three branches, and only two of them had the rungs

`buildOneHopCount`'s unfiltered branch — no clause `WHERE`, no inline constraint — had exactly two
rungs: the **O(1) bucket size** when BOTH ends are unconstrained, and a **per-edge walk** testing
both endpoints' labels otherwise. `vacuousLabel` elides a label every vertex carries, so while the
fixture's every node was a `P` the first rung answered everything. Four `S` nodes later, `:P` is
genuinely selective and the query falls to the per-edge walk.

**The walk that answers it already existed.** `startOnlyHopCount` (item 129) sums the degree over
the start label's bucket — O(|label|) bucket-size reads, no edge visits at all — and `farOnlyHopCount`
(item 137) is its mirror. Both were unreachable here because `startWalkFits` required `pred.startVar
!== undefined || inNear !== undefined`: a **predicate or an inline constraint**. A label is a
per-vertex constraint too; nothing about the degree sum ever needed a predicate.

So the change is one disjunct in each shared fit rule (`|| pa !== undefined`, `|| pb !== undefined`)
plus a `labelOnlyHopCount` that hands the walks the inline branch's bare-predicate device. The rules
stay SHARED rather than copied, which the file insists on for a recorded reason: the far endpoint sat
on the per-edge tally for eight items because its rule was a separate copy.

### Measurement

Alternated A/B, three rounds each way, rebuilding the dist per round, min per cell, 200,000 vertices
and 600,000 `E` edges:

| case                               |       head |      changed |     ratio |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------: | -----------: | --------: |
| `MATCH (a:S)-[:E]->(b)`            |  27.176 ms | **0.003 ms** | **9058x** |
| `MATCH (a:Q)-[:E]->(b)`            |  35.789 ms |     7.834 ms |     4.57x |
| `MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b:P)`            | 150.014 ms |    33.414 ms |     4.49x |
| `MATCH (a:P)<-[:E]-(b)`            | 145.694 ms |    33.984 ms |     4.29x |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b)`            |  45.717 ms |    17.800 ms |     2.57x |
| CONTROL no label (O(1) bucket)     |   0.001 ms |     0.001 ms |     1.00x |
| CONTROL node count                 |   0.001 ms |     0.001 ms |     1.00x |
| CONTROL both ends labelled         | 177.024 ms |   161.523 ms |     1.10x |
| CONTROL two types (guard declines) | 147.920 ms |   137.701 ms |     1.07x |
| CONTROL clause `WHERE` start       |  14.368 ms |    15.315 ms |     0.94x |
| CONTROL inline start               |  13.990 ms |    15.096 ms |     0.93x |

**Every answer identical on every row.** The `:S` row is what settles that this was a missing rung
and not a tuning question: four vertices with zero edges, and the query scanned 600,000 edges to
find none.

### The four controls moved in BOTH directions, and that is the finding about the controls

Two of the four unreachable controls read ~0.93x and two read ~1.07-1.10x, and **all four are
consistent across all three rounds** — head 13.99/14.46/14.57 against changed 15.10/15.70/15.75 on
`inline start`, head 215.6/195.1/189.0 against changed 184.1/181.3/183.4 on `both ends labelled`.
Consistency within a build plus opposite signs across cells is **code layout**, not a path
regression: this file has a recorded history of exactly that (items 119, 141, 159 — unrelated shapes
acquiring new modes from a code-size change). It is the TS analogue of the
`filter-count-row-is-not-a-screen` cluster, and quoting the two favourable rows as a win would be as
wrong as treating the two unfavourable ones as a regression.

**That conclusion was reached by elimination, not assumed**, and two remedies were tried and failed
before it:

1. **Hoist to module scope.** The new code was written inline in the closure `buildOneHopCount`
   returns, and the note at that very call site says inlining grew the closure and gave an
   unrelated query a second mode. Hoisted — and the two cells stayed at 0.90x/0.96x.
2. **Share the bare-predicate identity.** The shared walks' hot `pred.fn(env)` had gained a third
   callee shape (`alwaysTrue` beside a compiled expression and the inline branch's `() => true`), so
   both branches were made to pass the SAME module-scope object. Still 0.94x/0.93x.

A **three-arm isolation** then separated the candidate causes: head, `fitonly` (the fit rules widened,
the new rung neutralised), and the full change. `fitonly` read 1.00x and 0.95x and **interleaved with
head round-for-round** (head 14.26/15.35/16.38, fitonly 15.24/14.24/15.02), while the full change was
uniformly highest. So the cost is not the fit rule — and since neither remedy aimed at the new call
site moved it either, what is left is the layout of a file whose code size changed. The shared
identity is kept regardless: it drops a per-query allocation and is right on its own terms.

### Mutation — every correctness mutant caught, including by PRE-EXISTING tests

| mutant                                              | result               |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| N1 the start walk's SUMMATION guard dropped         | CAUGHT (4 failing)   |
| N2 the far walk's SUMMATION guard dropped           | CAUGHT (2 failing)   |
| N3 `pb === undefined` dropped (far label ignored)   | CAUGHT (11 failing)  |
| N4 `pa === undefined` dropped (start label ignored) | CAUGHT (7 failing)   |
| N8 the far label dropped entering the scan          | CAUGHT (8 failing)   |
| N9 the start label dropped entering the scan        | CAUGHT (6 failing)   |
| N5 the rung never fires                             | SURVIVED — perf only |

N1/N2 are the wrong-ANSWER mutants: both walks sum per-type bucket sizes, and a two-type edge sits in
two of them, so dropping `types?.length === 1 || multiTypeEdgeCount === 0` counts one edge twice.
They are caught by the new tests **and by pre-existing ones** — `a start-only count over multi-type
edges counts an edge once` and `a multi-label EDGE declines rather than double-counting` — which is
the best available evidence that the new rung inherited the right invariant rather than a new one.
Re-run in full against the final code after an arity refactor moved two anchors.

### The tests compare the shortcut against the GENERAL PATH

`label-only-hop-count.test.ts` is 24 tests, and every one asks the same question twice: `count(*)`
routes to the shortcut, while the same pattern `RETURN 1 AS one` builds a row per match through the
general matcher, so the row count is the answer computed by code this change cannot reach. **That is
the only comparison available** — a count has no shape to inspect, and a wrong count is precisely
what a dropped soundness guard produces.

### Two probe groups, and a correction to what I first wrote about one

`spelling-probe.ts`'s `label on start: redundant vs absent` goes 54.06 → 21.38 ms. **It still flags,
at ~2100x, and that is correct rather than outstanding** — my first comment claimed the pair "now
lands within the floor again" and that was wrong. These two members are not equivalent work: the
untyped spelling needs no vertex visits at all (one bucket size) while the labelled one must visit
every `P`. O(|label|) against O(1) cannot converge. The group stays as a REGRESSION guard on the
54ms, and the comment now says so.

The new group `one end labelled, the other free: four spellings` is the comparison that IS between
equivalent plans, and it flagged at 3.4x on HEAD and still flags at 3.3x — **for a different reason
after the fix**, which the A/B identifies:

```
  (a:P)-[:E]->(b)   start walk, edgesFromByLabel   17.800 ms
  (a)-[:E]->(b:P)   far walk,   edgesToByLabel     33.414 ms
  (a:P)<-[:E]-(b)   start walk, edgesToByLabel     33.984 ms
```

The walk is not the variable — one start walk and one far walk sit on each side of the split.
**Reading bucket SIZES out of `edgesToByLabel` costs ~1.9x the same read out of `edgesFromByLabel`.**
That is the next target, recorded in CLOSED.md, and it was invisible while all four spellings were
on the per-edge walk together.

### Gates

1894 gql tests / 809 `@lenke/native` isolated / the full `bun run test` across 21 projects (the
run-many exit 1 was `@lenke/native:test`, which Nx itself flagged flaky and which passes isolated —
`sync-test-flake-is-timing`); all seven byte-identity fuzzers green with `DECLARED none used`;
`bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint` and `bun run fmt:check` each as their own command (lint caught
an 8-parameter arity and two unnecessary assertions).

## 287. The 1.9x index asymmetry item 286 recorded was the PROBE'S FIXTURE, and the fixture had been biasing every out-vs-in comparison

Item 286 closed a 5400x cliff and, in the same entry, recorded a new open target: _"`edgesToByLabel`
costs ~1.9x `edgesFromByLabel` to read bucket sizes."_ The evidence was good — the four spellings of
one question split **exactly** along which index each walk reads, with one start walk and one far
walk on each side, so the walk could be ruled out as the variable:

```
  (a:P)-[:E]->(b)   start walk, edgesFromByLabel   17.800 ms
  (a)-[:E]->(b:P)   far walk,   edgesToByLabel     33.414 ms
  (a:P)<-[:E]-(b)   start walk, edgesToByLabel     33.984 ms
```

**It was wrong, and one reading of the declaration was enough to suspect it.** Both indexes are the
same type — `Map<string, Map<string, Set<Edge>>>`, declared on consecutive lines of `Graph.ts` — so
a 1.9x cannot be structural. What differs is the ORDER THEIR KEYS WERE INSERTED, and that is a
property of the fixture:

```ts
`"from":"v${e % N}"` // VERTEX CREATION ORDER
`"to":"v${(e * 7919) % N}"`; // a pseudorandom permutation
```

The degree-sum walks iterate vertices in creation order and probe `index.get(v.id)`. So
`edgesFromByLabel` was walked sequentially and `edgesToByLabel` was jumped around — **item 164's
mechanism**, which measured exactly this at 29ns a vertex against 135ns and attributed 135 of 177ns
to it.

### Falsified by flipping the fixture, not by argument

Swapping which endpoint gets the sequential key, N = 200,000, 600,000 edges, min of 9:

| spelling (and the index its walk reads) | `from` sequential | `to` sequential | both scattered |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------: | --------------: | -------------: |
| `(a:P)-[:E]->(b)` start, **FROM**       |         15.318 ms |       31.663 ms |      36.586 ms |
| `(a)-[:E]->(b:P)` far, **TO**           |         31.588 ms |       15.604 ms |      36.054 ms |
| `(a:P)<-[:E]-(b)` start, **TO**         |         34.193 ms |       14.322 ms |      33.184 ms |
| `(b)<-[:E]-(a:P)` far, **FROM**         |         19.136 ms |       31.715 ms |      35.187 ms |

**The asymmetry flips completely**, and with neither index favoured all four land within 1.10x. The
index was never the variable. A hypothesis that survives "the split lines up with X" can still be
about Y, when X and Y are confounded by construction — here the confound was one character of the
fixture.

### The bias was not confined to the group that exposed it

This matters beyond a retracted row. `spelling-probe.ts` exists to check that **equivalent spellings
cost the same**, and its fixture handed every `from`-driven spelling a ~2x locality advantage over
its equivalent `to`-driven twin. Item 220's group already carries a reversed-arrow member
(`MATCH (c)<-[:E]-(b)<-[:E]-(a:P)`) and had been judged under that advantage; its agreement was
partly the fixture's doing. A probe whose fixture prefers one direction cannot answer the question
the probe is for.

So both endpoint keys are now scattered, by different multipliers. The four-spelling group stops
flagging; `label on start: redundant vs absent` still flags for its structural reason (O(|label|)
against O(1) cannot converge) and reads higher, 2159.8x to 4511.8x, because the labelled member now
pays cache misses the old fixture spared it.

### THE COST, STATED PLAINLY: probe numbers do not cross item 287

The symmetric fixture is uniformly HARDER, because the old one gave sequential locality to the
common case. Across the 64 queries the probe runs, after/before:

| band                    | queries | examples                                                              |
| ----------------------- | ------: | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 0.45-0.49x (much worse) |       6 | `(a:P)-[:E]->(b)` 20.81 → 45.73; `(a:P)-[:E\|F]->(b)` 142.68 → 318.47 |
| 0.60-0.66x              |       4 | `WHERE n.k IN [2, 7]` 7.49 → 12.53                                    |
| 0.85-0.99x              |      27 | the bulk                                                              |
| 1.00-1.09x              |      27 | the three-hop and multi-pattern groups                                |

**None of that is the engine getting slower** — no engine code changed in this item. It means any
probe number quoted in an earlier audit entry was measured on the easier fixture and must not be
compared to a reading taken after this item. Where a comparison matters, re-measure both sides.

A residual 1.40x remains between the two START-walk directions on the probe's richer P/Q + E/F
fixture (45.73 FROM against 63.82 TO) where the dedicated single-label fixture converges all four
within 1.10x. It is below the probe's 2x tolerance, and it is **not** the index: the two FAR walks
agree across both indexes on the same fixture (39.90 TO against 40.56 FROM). Not pursued, and not
recorded as an index claim a second time.

### What this costs and what it buys

An iteration that ships no speedup and makes the harness report worse numbers is not an obvious
trade. It buys: a false claim out of `CLOSED.md` before anyone priced work against it, a probe that
no longer prefers one arrow direction, and the reason written down. **The row was recorded and
pushed one iteration earlier** — the correction is faster than the claim was, which is the only part
of this worth generalising.

No engine change, so no mutation and no new tests: the artefact under test is a benchmark fixture,
and its correctness check is that flipping it flips the result. `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`
and `bun run fmt:check` each as their own command; all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.

## 288. A CORRELATED product under a cap built the whole product — 204-316x, by removing item 283's bet rather than tuning it

A three-item arc closes here. Item 282 priced the target at ~1,400x, designed a nested-loop
streamer, and recorded why it was not building it. Item 283 built that design: **1,640x where the
cap fills early and 1.9x WORSE on `LIMIT 4`** where it does not, so it was retracted — and in
retracting it located the blocker, a 3-4x per-block constant factor whose suspect it named
(`hash_join(&lrow, &rb, &[])`, paying the hash-join machinery for a broadcast). Item 284 removed
exactly that factor, 6.69x, for every cross product the planner emits.

### Re-pricing first, because item 284 shrank the prize by the same factor it unblocked

1,640x over a 9.8ms baseline is a different proposition from the same floor over a 1.4ms one, so
the first thing measured was the baseline, not the fix:

| case                                       | after item 284 |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------: |
| `WHERE u.k = s.k … LIMIT 1`                |      1420.2 us |
| `WHERE u.k = s.k …` (UNCAPPED)             |      1459.9 us |
| CONTROL one-sided `u.k = 7 … LIMIT 1`      |        63.6 us |
| CONTROL `MATCH (u:U) RETURN u.k` (100,000) |       265.4 us |

**The cap bought 3%.** The target was live.

### THE FIX IS ITEM 283'S DESIGN MINUS ITS BET, and that is the whole content of this item

Item 283 streamed the right side FROM THE PLAN inside the left loop, modelled on
`pull_capped_stream`. So a cap that did not fill early re-scanned the whole right side once per
left row — four full scans where the materialized path does one — and `LIMIT 4` over `u.k = s.k`,
whose answer is exactly one row per left row, was the worst case it could have had. A lost-bet
gate got it from 1.9x worse to 1.7x worse.

**Pulling the right side ONCE, before the loop, removes the bet entirely.** The uncapped path
already materializes both sides — `hash_join` takes two `Batch`es — so this pays nothing the
baseline does not already pay, and what it saves is the PRODUCT: the baseline gathers |L| x |R|
rows across every slot and then filters them, where this gathers a block at a time and stops at
`cap`. There is no shape where it pulls more than the baseline, so there is no gate, no bet, and
nothing to tune. Item 283's trap row goes from 1.9x worse to **1.62x faster**.

The blocks are adaptive (256, doubling to 65,536) and both ends of that are load-bearing: a small
first block makes a cap that fills immediately cheap, and a large late block makes a cap that never
fills approach the baseline's single gather instead of paying per-block overhead 400,000/256 times.

### Measurement

Alternated A/B, three rounds each way, two md5-distinct binaries, min per cell:

| case                            |      head |    changed |       ratio | rows |
| ------------------------------- | --------: | ---------: | ----------: | ---: |
| `gt, LIMIT 1`                   | 2310.0 us | **7.3 us** | **316.44x** |    1 |
| `gt, LIMIT 4`                   | 2273.0 us | **7.3 us** | **311.37x** |    4 |
| `eq, LIMIT 1`                   | 1425.0 us | **7.0 us** | **203.57x** |    1 |
| `eq, LIMIT 2`                   | 1433.3 us |   302.8 us |       4.73x |    2 |
| `eq, LIMIT 4` (item 283's trap) | 1444.8 us |   893.2 us |       1.62x |    4 |
| impossible correlation          | 4297.8 us |  4070.8 us |       1.06x |    0 |
| CONTROL one-sided `LIMIT 1`     |   64.2 us |    64.2 us |       1.00x |    1 |
| CONTROL `eq` UNCAPPED           | 1441.7 us |  1427.2 us |       1.01x |    4 |
| CONTROL single pattern          |    6.5 us |     6.6 us |       0.98x |    1 |
| CONTROL right-side pull         |  248.1 us |   245.3 us |       1.01x | 100k |
| CONTROL left-side pull          |    0.2 us |     0.2 us |       1.00x |    4 |

Row counts identical on every row, and five controls flat — including the two that bound the
design (each side's own pull) and the UNCAPPED product, which this arm cannot reach because
without an `OrderPage` the plan goes through `pull`, not `pull_capped`.

`eq, LIMIT 4` stays at 1.62x rather than 300x for a reason that is inherent and not a residual:
the answer is one row per left row, so the cap can only fill by visiting every left row, and a
left row's last match cannot be known without scanning its whole right side. `eq, LIMIT 2` at
4.73x is the same curve sampled earlier.

**A MEASUREMENT-HARNESS BUG, caught by the comparison and not by the probe.** The probe printed
each case as its query text truncated to 58 characters — and the `LIMIT 1`, `LIMIT 2` and `LIMIT 4`
spellings are identical for the first 58. So three distinct cases printed the same label, my
comparison keyed on it, and the first A/B silently collapsed them into one row reading "4.64x".
The cases now carry short distinct labels and the comparison asserts it sees eleven of them.
_A truncated identifier is not an identifier._

### Mutation — three rounds, because the first two answered the wrong questions

| mutant                                        | round 1           | round 2      | round 3    |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ------------ | ---------- |
| P3 off-by-one on the BLOCK END                | CAUGHT (timeout)  | —            | —          |
| P5 the stride does not advance                | CAUGHT (timeout)  | —            | —          |
| P4 the right index is not offset by the block | CAUGHT (2)        | —            | —          |
| P6 the LEFT gather always takes row 0         | CAUGHT (3)        | —            | —          |
| P7 the arm declines                           | SURVIVED (perf)   | —            | —          |
| P9 the block never grows                      | SURVIVED (perf)   | —            | —          |
| P1 right-major                                | _did not compile_ | **SURVIVED** | **CAUGHT** |
| P2 the cap check moved after the push         | **SURVIVED**      | **CAUGHT**   | —          |
| P8 the LINEAGE preference reversed            | **SURVIVED**      | (P8b CAUGHT) | **CAUGHT** |

**P3 and P5 were caught by the TIMEOUT**, which is the outcome `CLAUDE.md` predicts for this exact
code shape: _"a loop bound, a `while` condition and an index cap are where an off-by-one stops
being a wrong answer and becomes non-termination."_ Both ran under the cgroup cap with
`MemorySwapMax=0`; neither needed it, but a product emitter with a broken bound is precisely what
that cap is for.

**P1 "CAUGHT (build/typecheck)" was not a catch.** My right-major mutant did not compile, so it
tested nothing about the tests, and reporting it as caught would have been a false pass. Rewritten
to compile (right blocks outer, left rows inner) it **SURVIVED every test in the file, including
the prefix test** — and the reason is a fixture artefact worth writing down: while the whole right
side fits in ONE block, right-major DEGENERATES to left-major; and while left row 0 has at least
`cap` survivors inside the first block, the orders also agree, because the cap fills before the
second left row is reached. Every fixture here hit one of those two cases.
`a_capped_correlated_product_is_left_major_across_blocks` is the shape that distinguishes them —
600 right rows, with the FIRST left row's only match in the third block and the SECOND left row's
in the first, so left-major must answer `s300` and right-major answers `s0`. Re-run: CAUGHT.

**P2 survived because of a masking layer.** `pull_capped`'s only caller is the keyless `OrderPage`
arm, which passes `skip + limit` and then slices to `limit` anyway — so over-producing by one row
is invisible through every query-level test, and `cap == 0` is invisible twice over. The contract
is still "at most `cap`", upheld elsewhere by `truncate_batch`.
`pull_capped_never_exceeds_its_cap_on_a_correlated_product` calls `pull_capped` directly, with the
slicing caller out of the picture: CAUGHT. _The "remove the masking layer in the same mutant" rule,
applied as a test instead of a mutant._

**P8 needed the PAIRED mutant to interpret.** Reversing the lineage preference in the new arm
survived. The arm copies that rule from `hash_join`, so the same reversal was applied THERE (P8b):
**CAUGHT**, by `a_path_above_a_join_carries_the_right_rows`. So the rule is guarded where it was
written and NOT where it was copied — this is the opposite answer from item 286's M3/M9, where the
paired mutant showed the rule unguarded in both copies and the guard was inherited consistency.
Here it is a real gap, closed by `a_path_above_a_capped_correlated_product_carries_its_own_rows`:
re-run, CAUGHT. **A rule copied from a guarded place is not itself guarded, and only the pair
distinguishes that from an untested invariant.**

### IT ALSO FIXED TWO CROSS-ENGINE DIVERGENCES, which were not the target

The arm stops evaluating the filter once `cap` rows survive, so a predicate that would FAULT on a
right row past the cap is no longer evaluated. The engine already does this deliberately (`LIMIT 0`
short-circuits so `RETURN 1/0 AS x LIMIT 0` yields empty; `pull_capped` on a `Scan` takes `cap` ids
and never sees row 500,000) — but byte-identity is against the TS engine, so a hand-written 4-way
probe decided it. 20,000 `U` nodes whose `st` casts cleanly plus ONE that does not, placed LAST:

| query                            | TS    | native BEFORE       | native AFTER |
| -------------------------------- | ----- | ------------------- | ------------ |
| correlated `CAST`, no limit      | THREW | THREW               | THREW        |
| **correlated `CAST`, `LIMIT 1`** | rows  | **THREW (DIVERGE)** | **rows**     |
| correlated `CAST`, `LIMIT 4`     | THREW | THREW               | THREW        |
| **one-sided `CAST`, `LIMIT 1`**  | rows  | **THREW (DIVERGE)** | **rows**     |
| one-sided `CAST`, no limit       | THREW | THREW               | THREW        |
| single pattern `CAST`, `LIMIT 1` | rows  | rows                | rows         |

Both divergences close. The one-sided row is the surprise: item 273's `right_pushable` declines a
predicate that `can_raise`, so a RAISING one-sided predicate is never pushed into its side and
lands above the join too — in this arm. And `LIMIT 4` throws on both engines for the same
structural reason the 1.62x has: left row 0 cannot fill a cap of 4, so both scan past the faulting
row. The agreement holds at both caps, which is better evidence than either row alone.

**The first run of that probe answered a question it was not asking.** With 201 `U` nodes the whole
right side fit inside the first 256-row block, so the fault was raised inside it and native
"still threw" — the same class of fixture error as P1's. The count has to exceed the block.

### Gates

1047 native tests (1036 + 11 new) + 13 + 723; `rewrite_fuzz` green at default and at
`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` (45.36s); all seven byte-identity fuzzers green; `cargo clippy
--all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check` and the test suite each as their own command
with its exit code checked.

### Screen

`query_bench`, two md5-distinct binaries (`e68ec78c` head, `3215f0ab` changed), three alternated
rounds, min per cell:

```
72 cells   median 1.004   94% within +/-5%   ROW-COUNT differences: 0
```

The arm sits in `pull_capped`, which every keyless `LIMIT`/`SKIP` plan in the corpus passes
through, so the question the screen answers is whether the new match arm costs anything on the
shapes it DECLINES. It does not. Seven of the eight slowest cells are the shortest-path cluster
(0.924-0.978x), a known mover that read 1.086 and 1.100 in the screens for items 275 and 284 on
unrelated changes. The one cell outside that cluster and outside the band is `distinct prop` at
0.916x, which does not reach this arm (no `Join`); it is recorded rather than explained.

## 289. `bun run bench`'s biggest adverse ratio is the JSON CARRIER, not the engine — decomposed, with a 1.10-1.21x on the one stage that was free

Two targets were priced this iteration. One was refused on its floor, the other turned out to be a
measurement question with a small win attached.

### First: a cap over a SHARED-VARIABLE join, priced at ~1.7x and NOT built

Item 288 gave `pull_capped` a `Filter { Join { on: [] } }` arm, so the adjacent missing path is a
cap over a join with a NON-empty `on`. The shape is real and the cap does nothing:

```
  MATCH (p:P)-[:KNOWS]->(q) MATCH (r:P)-[:KNOWS]->(q) RETURN p.k LIMIT 1   2519.6 us
  the same join, uncapped (count)                                          2738.2 us   <- 8%
  CONTROL one hop, LIMIT 1                                                    12.8 us
  CONTROL one hop, UNCAPPED                                                 1187.5 us
```

Plan confirmed rather than inferred: `OrderPage { Project { Join { Expand, Expand, on: [(1, 1)] } } }`.

**The floor refuses it.** Capping the SIDES is unsound — the first `cap` output rows can need
arbitrarily many left rows, since most may not match, which is the same argument that excludes
`Expand` — and a blocked nested loop is asymptotically WRONG for an equi-join (O(|L| x |R|)
comparisons against the hash join's O(|L| + |R|): 4e10 here). So the only sound bound builds the
RIGHT index, which needs the whole right `Expand` at **1187.5 us**, and then streams the left
probing until `cap`. Best case ~1400-1500 us against 2519.6: **~1.7x**, for a new row-producing
exec path with item 282's full verification budget.

Item 288 earned 204-316x for that same budget because its floor was a **7 us id-vector pull**, not
a 1187 us expand. Recorded in CLOSED.md so the next pass does not re-derive it; re-open only with a
design that avoids building the right index at all.

### Then: the bench's largest adverse ratio, which is not what it looks like

`bun run bench` at 200,000 nodes has one row where native loses badly, and it is the most ordinary
query shape there is:

```
  query: project 3 columns      ts 7.8ms    ffi 57.0ms    wasm 62.1ms    ts/ffi 0.14x
```
