Every other large ratio in that table is native's. **The table's own shape is the hypothesis:**
every row native loses has a huge result set (200,000 rows here; full-graph strings for the
encoders) and every row it wins big has a tiny one (`count 3-hop`, 1 row, 95.86x).

Holding the WORK fixed and varying only the ROWS RETURNED settles it:

| case                                            |       ts |      native |  ts/native | rows |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -------: | ----------: | ---------: | ---: |
| `scan all 3 props, 1 row out` (3 `count(prop)`) | 73.95 ms | **2.40 ms** | **30.80x** |    1 |
| `project 3, all rows`                           |    11.67 |       42.28 |      0.28x | 200k |
| `project 1, all rows`                           |     6.62 |       30.92 |      0.21x | 200k |
| `project 1 numeric, all rows`                   |     5.60 |       15.88 |      0.35x | 200k |
| CONTROL `project 3, LIMIT 1`                    |     0.01 |        0.01 |      2.28x |    1 |

**The aggregate row is the proof**: it scans every row and reads all three properties — strictly
more work than the projection — and returns ONE row, and native is **30.8x faster**. The cost
tracks rows out, not work. It is egress.

### The stages, measured against the same bytes

`graph.ts`'s `decodeRows` is the whole path: the crate renders `{columns, rows}` JSON →
`TextDecoder.decode` → `JSON.parse` → shape one object per row. Timed separately on the bytes the
FFI actually returned:

| stage                          | 3 columns (4.47 MB) | 1 string col | 1 numeric col |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------: | -----------: | ------------: |
| FFI call + crate render        |            12.13 ms |      3.93 ms |       3.27 ms |
| `TextDecoder.decode`           |             0.20 ms |      0.79 ms |       0.05 ms |
| **`JSON.parse`**               |        **17.63 ms** | **14.07 ms** |   **6.01 ms** |
| shape rows (`map` + `forEach`) |             4.45 ms |      4.90 ms |       4.36 ms |
| shape rows (plain loops)       |             2.23 ms |      2.16 ms |       2.06 ms |
| whole `g.query()`              |            36.41 ms |     24.68 ms |      15.03 ms |

The stages account for ~95% of the whole, so the decomposition is near-complete. **`JSON.parse` is
48% and the crate's render plus the FFI call is 33%** — i.e. ~80% of this path is the JSON carrier,
and no engine change touches it. `queryArrowIpc` is the existing answer for callers who care; this
entry exists so nobody optimizes the engine for that bench row again.

### The one free stage, taken

The shaping loop allocated a closure PER ROW (`doc.columns.forEach(...)` inside
`doc.rows.map(...)`) and re-read `doc.columns` through the outer closure every time. Plain nested
loops instead. End-to-end, three alternated rounds, min per cell:

| case                          |           head |         changed |     ratio | rows |
| ----------------------------- | -------------: | --------------: | --------: | ---: |
| `project 1 numeric, all rows` | 15.45-16.65 ms | **12.75-13.46** | **1.21x** | 200k |
| `project 1, all rows`         | 29.60-32.34 ms | **26.90-28.03** | **1.10x** | 200k |
| `project 3, all rows`         | 40.27-41.18 ms |     39.85-42.29 |         — | 200k |
| CONTROL `scan 3 props, 1 row` |   2.40 ms (x3) |    2.41-2.43 ms |     0.99x |    1 |
| CONTROL `project 3, LIMIT 1`  |        0.01 ms |         0.01 ms |     1.00x |    1 |

The two single-column rows have **DISJOINT ranges** and are real. **`project 3` is NOT claimed:
its ranges OVERLAP**, so there is no measured win there — and that is worth recording because the
isolated stage predicted one (4.45 → 2.23 ms is 6% of 36.41). **A stage timed in isolation on
already-parsed, warm data overstates its share of the whole**: in situ the loop runs immediately
after a 17 ms parse, and whatever it actually costs there is under this harness's noise floor at
40 ms. The 1-column cases show it because the same ~2 ms is a larger fraction of 15-30 ms.

Row counts identical everywhere; the 1-row controls flat (and the aggregate control is tight to
0.01 ms across three rounds, which is what makes the 0.99x reading noise rather than a toll).

### Mutation — the widest surface in the repo, and already saturated

`decodeRows` shapes every row of every native query result, and the thing most at risk is COLUMN
ORDER, which `column-order-is-observable` makes a byte-level contract.

| mutant                                        | result               |
| --------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| Q1 the column loop runs BACKWARDS             | CAUGHT (196 failing) |
| Q2 off by one on the width (last col dropped) | CAUGHT (507 failing) |
| Q3 every column takes the first cell          | CAUGHT (196 failing) |
| Q4 the row index is not advanced              | CAUGHT (214 failing) |
| Q5 the outer loop drops the last row          | CAUGHT (508 failing) |

Every one caught, Q1 by the differential fuzzer among 196 others. **No new tests**: the surface is
saturated, and adding one here would be ceremony rather than cover. That is the opposite finding
from items 286 and 288, where the mutants found genuine holes — which is why the mutants are run
rather than assumed either way.

### Gates

809 `@lenke/native` tests, the full `bun run test` across 21 projects, all seven byte-identity
fuzzers green; `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint` and `bun run fmt:check` each as their own
command.

## 290. The count family stopped at THREE segments and the fourth fell off a cliff — 152x, and a "regression" that was the win removing a neighbour's free warming

`bun run bench`'s largest ratio is `count 3-hop`: ts 465.2ms against ffi 4.9ms, 95.86x. Unlike item
289's worst row this one is not egress — both sides return a single number — and an earlier item had
already taken this shape 26.9x, recording the result as _"17ns a counted path … the sign the shape
is now paying per INTERIOR EDGE and not per path."_ So the question was whether anything was left.

### The SCALING answers it, not the absolute

Holding the graph fixed and adding hops. 50,000 nodes, degree 5, min of 5:

| case                |              ts |   native |   ts/native |  ts x prev | nat x prev |
| ------------------- | --------------: | -------: | ----------: | ---------: | ---------: |
| 1 hop `count(*)`    |         0.00 ms |  0.13 ms |           — |          — |          — |
| 2 hop               |        14.39 ms |  0.58 ms |       23.4x |          — |          — |
| 3 hop               |        85.83 ms |  1.12 ms |       69.0x |   **5.97** |       1.93 |
| **4 hop**           | **36082.73 ms** |  9.71 ms | **3456.9x** | **420.41** |       8.64 |
| 3 hop, `count(d.k)` |      4781.04 ms | 34.09 ms |      140.3x |          — |          — |

**A x420 step where the degree predicts x6.** 13.7ns a path at three hops against **1154ns** at
four, and 3456.9x off native — the largest ratio in any harness in this repo. Cause, read from the
code rather than guessed: `patternCountOf` routes 1, 2 and 3 segments and `return null`s for four,
so the fourth falls to the general matcher, which builds a binding per PATH.

`3 hop, count(d.k)` at 727ns a path is the same number from the other direction: **it is not a
cliff in the fallback, it is "shortcut or no shortcut"** — anything that declines pays 50-85x.

### One more nested loop on the same walk

Three hops pays per MIDDLE EDGE (`Σ_b waysToA(b) · Σ_{b→c} deg(c)`); four pays per INTERIOR PATH
(`Σ_b waysToA(b) · Σ_{b→c} Σ_{c→d} deg(d)`) — 1.25M terms here instead of 31.25M paths. The two
ends are still reached only as DEGREES, which is why neither may carry a constraint, the same
boundary `buildThreeHopCount` draws one segment earlier.

**Deliberately a fourth ARM, not an n-segment generalization.** The 2- and 3-segment walks are
tuned and heavily guarded (items 140, 206, 218, 219, 220, 221, 222) and this file has measured four
separate times what restructuring a hot walk costs shapes that do not reach it. UNFILTERED only:
the gate above already returns `null` for a clause `WHERE` over four segments, so what was left to
refuse is an inline constraint at any of the five node positions.

### THE PLANNER-REACHES-THE-SHAPE CHECK, which I skipped and the method requires

The first re-measurement after the change read **32793ms** — essentially unmoved. Two temporary
`console.error`s showed `patternCountOf` was never called with four segments at all… because the
probe imports `@lenke/gql`, **which resolves to the BUILT DIST**, and I had edited `src` without
rebuilding. `fuzzers-read-built-dists` records exactly this trap. After `bun run build`: the arm is
reached, accepted, and the 4-hop drops from 1320ms to 6.63ms on the small fixture.

Worth stating plainly: a change that measures as doing nothing is a change that might not be
running. The instrumentation cost two lines and settled it in one run.

### Measurement

Alternated A/B, three rounds each, rebuilding the dist per round, 10,000 nodes:

| case                        |               head |         changed |       ratio | answers         |
| --------------------------- | -----------------: | --------------: | ----------: | --------------- |
| **4 hop**                   | 5589.00-5678.93 ms | **36.66-46.75** | **152.45x** | match, DISJOINT |
| 1 hop                       |            0.01 ms |         0.01 ms |       1.00x | match           |
| 2 hop                       |       1.00-1.56 ms |    0.96-4.26 ms |       1.04x | match           |
| 3 hop                       |       7.17-9.52 ms |   7.84-12.41 ms |       0.91x | match, overlap  |
| CONTROL 4 hop, inline mid   |   105.50-124.38 ms |   104.14-122.72 |       1.01x | match           |
| CONTROL 4 hop, shared var   |  850.86-1067.61 ms |  872.04-1215.20 |       0.98x | match           |
| CONTROL filtered node count |       0.84-1.50 ms |    0.74-1.27 ms |       1.14x | match           |
| 3 hop, `count(d.k)`         |   786.30-864.11 ms |  902.97-1100.14 |   **0.87x** | match, DISJOINT |

At 50,000 nodes the target reads **36082.73 → 282.60ms (127.7x)** and the step from three hops
becomes **x3.64** instead of x420 — the family is smooth again.

### THE DISJOINT "REGRESSION" WAS THE WIN ITSELF

`3 hop, count(d.k)` moved 0.87x on **disjoint ranges**, on a shape the arm declines — the
`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` signature, which would have been its fifth occurrence in this
file, and which my own comment cites as the reason not to generalize. So it was settled the way
item 222 settled the same question: in isolation, four alternated rounds, 9 reps, **only the two
suspect shapes in the process**.

| isolated            | head mins                             | changed mins                          | ratio |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ----: |
| `3 hop, count(d.k)` | 828.61 / **792.51** / 813.76 / 802.31 | 788.86 / 825.59 / 790.19 / **773.15** | 1.03x |
| `3 hop, count(*)`   | 6.29 / 6.02 / **5.36** / 6.34         | 7.21 / 5.56 / **5.37** / 6.46         | 1.00x |

**It does not reproduce** — the changed side is marginally FASTER, and the readings interleave
round for round. The cause is the multi-case probe's own cross-case warming: `4 hop` runs
immediately before `3 hop, count(d.k)` in the same process, and on the HEAD side it spent **5.6
seconds** in the general matcher — warming the exact path `count(d.k)` then used. Making that
neighbour 152x faster removed warming the next case had been free-riding on.

That is item 274's trap with a new twist worth recording: **a large speedup can make its NEIGHBOUR
look slower, and disjoint ranges do not save you** — the contamination is systematic, not noisy, so
it survives min-of-three and reads exactly like a real effect. The tell is that the "regressed"
shape cannot reach the changed code; the proof is one case per process.

### Mutation — 12 of 12 correctness mutants caught

| mutant                                             | result                    |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| R1 the `a` side counted on the wrong side of `b`   | CAUGHT (13 failing)       |
| R2 the first interior leg reads the wrong index    | CAUGHT (12)               |
| R3 the second leg starts from `b` instead of `c`   | CAUGHT (12)               |
| R4 the final degree taken from `c` rather than `d` | CAUGHT (13)               |
| R5 the `a` factor dropped                          | CAUGHT (13)               |
| R6 the END label not applied                       | CAUGHT (1)                |
| R7 / R8 the `c` / `d` label gate dropped           | CAUGHT (2 / 2)            |
| R9 the last leg's TYPE ignored                     | CAUGHT (13)               |
| R10 the shared-variable guard dropped              | CAUGHT (1)                |
| R11 the inline/plain-node guard dropped            | CAUGHT (2)                |
| R12 the UNDIRECTED guard dropped                   | APPLY-FAILED → CAUGHT (1) |
| R13 the arm never fires                            | SURVIVED — perf only      |

**R12's first run was APPLY-FAILED, not a survivor**: its anchor matched TWO sites, because the
three-segment walk carries the same guard text. Re-anchored on the comment line unique to the new
arm: CAUGHT by `an UNDIRECTED leg`. The script prints `APPLY-FAILED <-- NOT a survivor` for exactly
this reason.

**The FIXTURE is lopsided on purpose.** A degree product that multiplies the wrong factors returns
a plausible NUMBER, and on a uniform-degree graph many mis-pairings give the SAME product — R1, R4
and R5 would all have survived. Uneven in- and out-degrees per node, two edge types, one node with
no out-edges.

27 tests, every one comparing the shortcut against an independent enumeration (`count(*)` against
the row count of `RETURN 1 AS one`, which goes through the general matcher) — the only comparison
available for a count, which has no shape to inspect.

### A permanent probe group

`four hops: forward vs the reversed arrows (item 290)`: 745.68ms against 908.91ms, 1.22x, answers
agreeing. The reversed member is the one that earns its place — item 220's finding was a 20x gap
between a question and the same question written backwards, and this walk has FOUR independent
direction flags, so a version handling one end only would pass the forward spelling and fail this.
Each member would have taken ~19s before the arm.

1921 gql tests (1894 + 27), the full `bun run test` across 21 projects, all seven byte-identity

## 291. The native engine LOSES 3-5x to pure TS on serving-sized calls, and the FFI boundary is innocent — PARSE is 43% of the call

`bun run bench:usage` is the serving counterpart to the bulk benches, and in its INDEXED columns —
the realistic case — the native engine loses on every read row:

| workload                        |  ts(+) | engine(+) | ratio |
| ------------------------------- | -----: | --------: | ----: |
| read: point lookup              |  1.19M |    240.8k |  4.9x |
| read: 2-hop recommendation      | 536.8k |    154.9k |  3.5x |
| interleaved: write + point read | 228.6k |     60.1k |  3.8x |
| read: permission check          | 342.4k |    111.8k |  3.1x |
| write: property update          | 355.4k |    219.4k |  1.6x |

240.8k ops/s is ~4.2us a call against TS's ~0.84us. **This is the opposite direction from every
bulk bench**, and item 289 had just established that the bulk benches' worst row was the JSON
carrier — so the obvious hypothesis was the same mechanism at small size.

### It is not. The boundary is 8ns.

Layered through the FFI, then the same layers in-process with no FFI at all:

| layer                                        |    ns/op |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------: |
| `vertexCount` — the RAW FFI boundary         |    **8** |
| `TextEncoder.encode(query)`                  |       20 |
| JS `decode` + `JSON.parse` (30-byte carrier) |      149 |
| `gql::parse` alone (57-byte query)           | **1296** |
| `+ optimize_indexed`                         |     1626 |
| `exec::try_run`, ONE row                     |      298 |
| `exec::try_run`, ZERO rows                   |      232 |
| `plan.clone()`                               |       57 |
| `gql_rows_json`                              |       49 |

**Parsing a 57-byte query costs 1296ns — 4.4x the exec it enables.** Optimizing adds 330ns, exec
is 298, render 49. So the engine-side work of a point lookup is ~1973ns, of which **parse is 66%**;
against the whole 3005ns `g.query()` it is 43%. The FFI boundary — the natural suspect, and the one
item 289's bulk finding would have predicted — is 0.3% of it.

### WHY TS WINS, precisely

TS has a parse cache (`parseCache` in `packages/gql/src/index.ts`) and native does not, and the
reason native does not is architectural rather than an oversight:

- TS's `Statement` is **INERT** and parameters bind at EXECUTION, so the cache can key on the query
  TEXT alone. Its own comment records the care that took: caching on first sighting made an
  all-miss workload 16% slower through GC retention, so a text is admitted on its SECOND sighting.
- `gql::parse_with_params` **substitutes params during PARSE** — "the planner sees literals (so
  `WHERE k = $p` / `{k: $p}` still seed an index)". So the parsed plan DEPENDS ON THE PARAM VALUES,
  and a text-keyed cache would be a wrong answer.

And the realistic serving shape is exactly the one that breaks it: `bench:usage`'s point lookup is
`WHERE u.name = $n` with a **different value every call**. A cache keyed on (text, params) would
miss every time.

`prepare()` is the existing escape — it binds params at execution, as TS does — and it is measured
rather than assumed:

| with `$n` VARYING per call |    ns/op |                             |
| -------------------------- | -------: | --------------------------- |
| UNPREPARED `g.query()`     |     3779 | what `bench:usage` measures |
| PREPARED `prep.query()`    | **2648** | **1.43x**                   |

### The routes, with the dead one closed

1. **A text-keyed parse cache — CLOSED.** Unsound while parse substitutes params, and useless for
   the shape that matters, where the value differs every call. Not a tuning question: the cache key
   would have to include the param VALUES.
2. **Route the unprepared path through a cached PREPARED statement** — priced at **1.43x**
   (3779 → 2648ns), and it reuses machinery that already exists and is tested (`lnk_prepare` plus
   bind-at-execution; `ffi.rs` already says "Clone the cached plan, bind params", and a clone is
   57ns). The key needs a STORE VERSION as well as the text, because `optimize_indexed` reads the
   store — a plan that seeks a dropped index is a wrong answer, not a slow one — and `version`/
   `epoch` already exist on the backend for exactly that kind of key.
3. **The residual is bigger than the fix.** Even fully prepared, native is 2648ns against TS's
   840ns. Accounting for it: exec 298, render 49, JS decode 149, boundary 8 — leaving **~1500ns of
   FFI PLUMBING**, which is NOT the boundary (8ns) but what the query path does around it: the
   error slot, two `catch_unwind` guards, the params JSON round trip (stringify in JS, `parse_json`
   in Rust), and `takeResult`'s `BigUint64Array` + `toArrayBuffer` + `.slice()` + `lnk_free` per
   call. That is its own target and a larger one than route 2.

**Recorded rather than built.** Route 2 is a new cache with an invalidation contract in the FFI
layer, and route 3 is bigger than it. This entry exists so the next pass starts from the
accounting — the same reason item 282's entry let item 288 land in one pass — and `percall_probe`
is kept and indexed so the numbers are reproducible rather than quoted.

### Two measurement errors worth recording, both caught by a reading that could not be true

- **Two fixtures.** The first FFI run had `queryRows` at **17176ns** and the whole `g.query()` that
  contains it at **2962ns** — a layer slower than its own container, which cannot happen. Cause: I
  built a second raw handle for the low-level layers and created the index only on the wrapper's
  graph, so `queryRows` measured an UNINDEXED full scan of 20,000 nodes. Both graphs are now
  indexed identically. _A nested measurement is self-checking: if an inner layer exceeds its outer
  one, the fixtures differ._
- **A plausible wrong conclusion that survived one layer.** With only the FFI numbers, "1865ns of
  fixed cost in a prepared call that returns ZERO rows" read as engine overhead, and the in-process
  measurement put the same work at 338ns (clone 57 + exec 232 + render 49). The FFI numbers alone
  would have sent the next change at `exec`. **Decomposing on ONE side of a boundary cannot tell
  you which side the cost is on.**

### Gates

No engine change, so no new tests and no mutation: the artifact is a probe. `cargo clippy
--all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` each as their own command with its exit code
checked.

## 292. Finishing item 291's accounting — the PREPARED path re-optimizes every call and marshals its arguments as JSON, and the "obvious" micro-fix is worth 0.4ns

Item 291 priced a serving-sized native call, found the FFI boundary innocent (8ns) and
`gql::parse` dominant (1296ns), and left **~1500ns of "FFI plumbing" unattributed** as its
largest named target. This splits that residual on both sides of the boundary.

### The JS side, and a refutation before building

`takeResult` was the suspect — it allocates an out-len cell, takes a pointer, views the crate's
buffer and copies it, all per call:

| operation                                      |     ns/op |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------: |
| `new BigUint64Array(1)` — the per-call out-len |   **0.4** |
| `ptr(hoisted)`                                 |       5.7 |
| `new BigUint64Array(1)` + `ptr()` together     |       9.1 |
| **`toArrayBuffer` over a 30-byte buffer**      | **123.9** |
| `new Uint8Array(…).slice()` of 30 bytes        |      56.4 |
| `encoder.encode(query)` — 51 bytes             |      26.0 |
| `JSON.stringify` of a one-key params object    |      46.5 |
| a baseline empty closure call                  |       4.9 |

**The cheapest-looking fix is worth nothing.** Hoisting that per-call `BigUint64Array` out of
`takeResult` looked free and obvious — and the allocation costs **0.4ns**, below the 4.9ns floor
of calling an empty closure, because the JIT elides it. `CLAUDE.md`'s rule applied exactly as
written: _"obviously correct so it must be faster" is not evidence_. Not changed.

JS-side plumbing totals ~**411ns** per call (ptr 9 + `toArrayBuffer` 124 + slice 56 + encode 26 +
stringify 47 + decode/`JSON.parse` 149). `toArrayBuffer` is the one real item, and it is 4% of a
3000ns call.

### The Rust side — and the prepared path does two avoidable things per call

Reading `lnk_command`'s `"prepared_run"` arm is what found them. A prepared statement does NOT go
through `lnk_query`: it is routed through the generic command dispatcher with a JSON payload,
`{"handle":"<ptr>","params":{…}}`, and then

```
  let Some(mut plan) = crate::prepared::get_clone(handle)   // clone
  crate::bind::bind_params(&mut plan, &params)              // bind
  let plan = crate::opt::optimize_indexed(plan, store);     // RE-OPTIMIZE, every call
```

| layer (in-process, no FFI)                 | ns/op |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----: |
| `parse_json` of the `prepared_run` payload |   165 |
| `parse_json` of the params object alone    |    77 |
| `clone` + `bind_params`                    |   153 |
| `clone` + `bind` + **`optimize_indexed`**  |   448 |
| `exec::try_run`, one row                   |   318 |
| `rows_to_json`                             |    50 |

So the Rust side of a prepared call is ~**781ns**: payload parse 165, clone+bind 153,
**re-optimize 295**, exec 318, render 50.

**Two of those are avoidable and together are ~460ns of the 2648ns call:**

1. **The re-optimize (295ns).** "Prepared" skips the parse but not the plan. `optimize_indexed`
   reads the store, so the result cannot simply be cached — but it can be cached keyed on a STORE
   VERSION, which `version`/`epoch` already provide, and which item 291 already named as the key a
   query-side plan cache would need. The same key serves both.
2. **The JSON argument marshalling (165ns in Rust, plus ~47ns stringifying it in JS).** A prepared
   execute passes a 64-bit handle and a params object; it costs a JSON round trip because it rides
   the generic `lnk_command(name, input)` dispatcher instead of a dedicated entry point. `lnk_query`
   already takes its params as a byte buffer with an explicit length — the shape exists.

### What is still unaccounted, named rather than guessed

Accounted for the 2648ns prepared call: ~781 Rust + ~411 JS = **~1192ns**. The remaining
**~1456ns** is diffuse and these are the candidates, in the order they are worth checking:

- `std::panic::catch_unwind` (`guarded`), entered twice per call;
- `out_bytes` — `Vec` → boxed slice → `into_raw` — plus the matching `lnk_free`;
- `ffi_error::begin()`'s slot reset;
- **bun:ffi's per-ARGUMENT marshalling**: `vertexCount` takes ONE argument and costs 8ns, while
  `lnk_command` takes five (name ptr, name len, input ptr, input len, out-len);
- the `String` allocations in `prepared_payload` building `Vec<(String, Value)>`.

**Closing that needs a profiler, not another probe.** Each candidate is below the resolution a
probe can isolate without restructuring the call, and guessing among five candidates that sum to
~1456ns is how a wrong attribution gets committed — which is the mistake item 291 caught itself
making from the FFI side alone.

### Gates

No engine change — the only edits are to a probe and the docs. `cargo clippy --all-targets -D
warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` each as their own command, 1047 + 13 + 723 native tests green.

## 293. Correcting item 292: the per-call re-optimize is NOT a cache-key problem

Item 292 named two avoidable costs in the prepared path and sized them at ~460ns together. One of
them was wrong, and the correction is cheaper than the claim was.

**The claim:** the per-call `optimize_indexed` (295ns) "can be cached keyed on a STORE VERSION,
which `version`/`epoch` already provide".

**Why it is wrong:** `bind_params` runs BEFORE `optimize_indexed`, by design. `ir.rs` states the
contract on `Expr::Param` directly — it is produced only by `parse_prepared`, and
`bind::bind_params` "replaces it with the supplied value **before `opt`/`exec` run**, so a `Param`
reaching evaluation is an unbound-parameter error (the safety net)". So the optimized plan is a
function of the bound VALUES, not just of the text and the store: a cache keyed on (text, store
version) would hand the next call a plan with the previous call's values baked in. **That is a
wrong answer, not a stale optimization** — and it is the shape the serving workload has, where `$n`
differs every call.

**The design that WOULD remove it**, recorded so it is not confused with a cache: optimize the
PARAMETERIZED plan and bind values into the optimized one. The optimizer is partly ready — its
seeding-key match already admits `Expr::Param` beside `Expr::Lit`, and a comment at `opt.rs:1395`
notes that "a parameterized or unmeasurable bound is still seedable". But it inverts the IR's
documented ordering and gives the optimizer strictly less information: a literal bound can be
measured against an index's distribution, a parameter cannot, so plan CHOICE can get worse on
shapes where the answer is unchanged. That is an item with its own screen, not a cache key.

So of item 292's ~460ns, **~212ns is cheaply avoidable** (the JSON argument round trip: 165ns to
`parse_json` in Rust, ~47ns to `JSON.stringify` in JS, both only because a prepared execute rides
the generic `lnk_command(name, input)` dispatcher instead of a dedicated entry point). The
re-optimize is not.

**Found by reading the contract I was about to build against.** The entry was written and pushed
one iteration earlier; this is the second time in this session that a recorded claim needed
retracting (item 287 was the first, and also a confound rather than a measurement error). Both
corrections landed faster than the claims did, which is the only part worth generalising — a
`CLOSED.md` row is read as settled, so a wrong one costs more than no row at all.

## 294. The parse target is STRUCTURAL, not allocational — the obvious fixes sum to under 5% of it

Item 291 made `gql::parse` the largest single item in a serving call: **1296ns for a 57-byte
query, 23ns a byte, 43% of an unprepared `g.query()` and 4.4x the 298ns exec it enables**. Two
costs are visible in the source without a profiler, so they were priced before anything was
attempted:

- the lexer decodes the WHOLE query into a heap `Vec<char>` before it starts
  (`let b: Vec<char> = s.chars().collect();`), and then indexes it with bounds checks;
- `Tok::Ident(String)`, `Tok::Str(String)` and `Tok::Param(String)` each OWN their text, so this
  query allocates one char vector, one token vector and about twelve identifier strings.

| inside the 1296ns parse                                     |     ns/op |   share |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | --------: | ------: |
| `s.chars().collect::<Vec<char>>()`                          |        60 |    4.6% |
| the same with `Vec::with_capacity(s.len())`                 |        26 |       — |
| ~12 identifier `String`s (the lexer's shape)                |       177 |   13.7% |
| **everything else — scan + recursive descent + plan build** | **~1060** | **82%** |

**So the available cheap fixes are 34ns and 177ns, and only the first is actually cheap.** The
`with_capacity` change is one line and 2.3x on its own step — and 34ns is **2.6% of parse, ~1% of
a serving call**, which is below what the end-to-end harness can resolve. Not made: this session
has twice measured that touching hot code costs unrelated shapes (items 290's neighbour, and the
`ts-closure-size` cluster), and an unmeasurable change to the lexer is the wrong side of that
trade. Recorded with its number instead, so it is not re-derived as an idea.

The identifier strings (177ns, 14%) need `Tok` to BORROW from the input — `Tok<'a>` with
`Ident(&'a str)` — which threads a lifetime through `Parser` and every function that consumes a
token. That is a real refactor of a 10,000-line file, and it buys at most 14% of parse (~6% of a
serving call) unless it also removes the `Vec<char>` indexing, since a borrowed `&'a str` token
cannot point into a transient char vector. Done together they are the same change.

**The useful conclusion is the negative one:** 82% of parse is the scanning loop, the
recursive-descent functions and the plan construction — not allocation. Anyone reaching for this
target should start from a profiler on `lex` + `parse_internal`, not from the allocations, and
should expect a structural change (byte-wise scanning with borrowed tokens) rather than a tidy-up.
`percall_probe` carries all three numbers so the comparison is reproducible.

No engine change; the probe gained three layers.

## 296. The frontier guard was REACTIVE and blind to WIDTH — an OOM that took a 61 GB box into its swapfile, and the guard that now refuses first

This item starts from an incident rather than a measurement. A scratch probe stepping a
multi-hop `count(*)` from 1 to 6 hops over 4,000 nodes at degree 5 exhausted 61 GB of RAM, crawled
into the 192 GB swapfile and took every process on the machine down — including the user's own
long-running services. It ran under `timeout 1800` with **no memory cap**, which is the discipline
`CLAUDE.md` requires for exactly this and which the memory file records as having cost the box
three times before. A wall clock does not catch an allocation runaway.

The engine's own contribution is the subject here: it had a guard, and the guard could not have
stopped it.

### Two defects, and the second one is the interesting half

`limits.intermediate` (50M, default) is checked by `guard_intermediate`, whose single call shape is

```rust
Plan::Expand { .. } => guard_intermediate(expand(...), store)?
```

**It is REACTIVE.** Rust evaluates the argument first, so `expand` has fully materialized the
batch — grown `keep`/`nbrs`, gathered every input slot, cloned `nbrs` and `eids` — before the row
count is read. The allocation that exhausts the machine has already happened; the guard can only
decline to pass it on.

**And it counts ROWS, so it is blind to WIDTH.** A 6-hop `MATCH` materializes a SEVEN-slot
frontier. 62.5M rows at width 7 is 437M cells and some 2 GB once the gathers and clones are
counted — and 62.5M rows is a number a 50M-row ceiling only notices after paying for it, while
12.5M rows at width 6 (the 5-hop case, ~1 GB) sails under it entirely.

### The fix: a predictive, width-aware companion

`limits.intermediate_cells` (200M, default; `ConfigId::LimitsIntermediateCells = 6`, native-only
like `LimitsDictMaxDistinct`) is checked **inside** `expand`, once per SOURCE ROW:

```rust
let out_width = batch.slots.len() + 1 + usize::from(bind_edge);
...
let cells = (keep.len() as u64).saturating_mul(out_width as u64);
if cells > cell_cap { return Err("E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: … rows x … slots (… cells) …") }
```

Once per source row and not per neighbour: the outer loop already runs `|src|` times, a single
vertex can add at most its own degree, so the overshoot is bounded by one degree while the check
stays off the per-neighbour hot path. `expand` becomes `Result<Batch, String>`; there are exactly
two call sites and both already propagated `guard_intermediate`'s error.

**CELLS, not bytes, and that is deliberate.** `keep` is a `Vec<usize>` — 4 bytes on wasm32, 8 on
x86-64 — so a byte ceiling would trip at different places on different targets. Cells is portable
for the same reason `intermediate`'s own comment gives for rows (the columns are fixed-width
`u32`/`f64`/`i64` everywhere), carried one dimension further. **And this file already had the
precedent:** `the_ceiling_counts_path_elements_not_just_rows` makes exactly this argument for the
shortest-path guard — _"it is the path elements, not the rows, that allocate"_ — which is the same
observation one operator over.

Nor is it derived from available RAM, though `cost::Budget` does that for its routing threshold: a
query that fails on a small box and succeeds on a large one is a divergence, and this repo's
guards are declared so every target trips in the same place.

### It fires, and the knob moves in both directions

```
  6 hop project far.k    ERR E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: an intermediate frontier reached 28571430 rows x 7
  5 hop project far.k    ok (79350 us)
  6 hop, ceiling raised to u64::MAX    ok
  1 hop, ceiling 1000 cells            ERR … reached 505 rows x 2 slots
```

28.57M rows at width 7 is 200M cells — it gives up at the ceiling, part-way, where the full
frontier would have been 31.25M rows.

### THE PROBE MEASURED NOTHING TWICE, and the method's own rule is why

The first probe used `count(*)` and every row passed, at 0.3ns a path. The second used
`count(far.k)` — which item 290 established declines the TS count shortcuts — and every row
still passed, at 5.5ns a path. **Native's `exec` answers an aggregate-over-chain with a tally and
never runs the expansion**, so a guard on `Plan::Expand` was being probed with queries that are
shortcut past it. Only a bare PROJECTION, which has no aggregate to tally, materializes the
frontier. The probe now prints whether the optimized plan contains an `Expand` instead of
assuming it — "verify the planner reaches the shape", applied to the harness.

### AND IT WAS NOT THE ENGINE THAT OOM'D

Following that through changes the attribution. If native tallies these shapes, native did not
build the 62.5M-row intermediate — so the TS engine did. Measured directly, 2,000 nodes at degree
5, under a deliberately tight 4 GB cap:

| hops | TS result                        |
| ---- | -------------------------------- |
| 3    | 8 ms, 80 MB RSS (degree product) |
| 4    | 13 ms, 86 MB (item 290's arm)    |
| 5    | **OOM-killed, exit 137**         |

The cliff is exactly the count family's coverage edge. Five segments decline every shortcut and
fall to the general matcher — and `applyProjection`'s aggregating branch **retains every binding**:

```ts
const groups = new Map<string, Binding[]>();
for (const b of bindings) { … existing.push(b); }
```

For `RETURN count(*)` with no `GROUP BY` that is ONE group holding all 6.25M bindings, each a
six-entry `Map`: ~640 bytes a path, which is the 4 GB. The comment says so plainly — "Grouping is
a barrier — it must see every binding before it can emit" — because `HAVING` and the aggregate
closures take the group ARRAY (`env.group`), and `count(*)` reads `group.length`.

**So the engine that needs the streaming fix is the TypeScript one, and it is the next item**:
hold per-group accumulator state rather than the bindings, which takes the aggregating branch from
O(rows) to O(groups). The careful part is that the accumulators must not become a SECOND
definition of the aggregate semantics — `compileAggregate` folds over the array today, and two
derivations of one question is the drift this repo keeps being bitten by. This item ships the
native guard, which protects a genuinely exposed path (the projection case above) and was the
cheaper half.

### Mutation — 6, two of which found the width claim untested

| mutant                                           | result                |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------- |
| S1 the guard never fires                         | CAUGHT (3 failing)    |
| S2 WIDTH dropped (degenerates to a row count)    | CAUGHT (2)            |
| S5 checked only on the FIRST source row          | CAUGHT (3)            |
| S6 the refusal is unreachable                    | CAUGHT (3)            |
| S3 the landed-node slot not counted in the width | **SURVIVED** → CAUGHT |
| S4 the bound EDGE slot not counted               | **SURVIVED** → CAUGHT |

S3 and S4 are both off-by-one in the WIDTH — the entire claim of this change — and they survived
because every ceiling in the tests sat far enough from the boundary that one slot flipped no
outcome. Two tests now place a ceiling where exactly one slot decides: 2,000 rows at width 2 is
4,000 cells against a 3,000 ceiling (catches S3), and binding the edge makes the same rows 6,000
cells against a 5,000 ceiling (catches S4). Both assert the reported width (`x 2 slots`, `x 3
slots`), not just that something tripped. Re-run: CAUGHT.

_Same lesson as item 284's row order: a claim derived by reading the code was load-bearing on
nobody until a mutant said so._

### Gates

1055 native tests (1047 + 8) + 13 + 723; `rewrite_fuzz` green at default and at
`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` (45.54s) — which matters here because a guard that fired on a raw
plan and not its optimized twin would be an answer difference, not a slow path; all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check`
each as their own command with its exit code checked. Every run under `timeout` AND the 16 GB
cgroup cap with `MemorySwapMax=0`.

### Screen

`query_bench`, two md5-distinct binaries, three alternated rounds, min per cell:

```
72 cells   median 0.999   96% within +/-5%   ROW-COUNT differences: 0
```

The check is per SOURCE ROW in `expand`, the hottest loop in the engine, so this is the number
that decided whether it ships. It costs nothing measurable. The six slowest cells are the
shortest/varlen cluster at 0.929-0.963x, a known mover in every screen this session, and three
cells read 1.04-1.06x the other way.

## 297. The TS aggregating projection kept every binding — `count(*)` is now O(GROUPS), and a 5-hop count goes from OOM-killed to 123 MB

Item 296 established the attribution: the OOM that took a 61 GB box into its swapfile was the
TypeScript engine, not native, because native's `exec` answers an aggregate-over-chain with a
tally and never builds the frontier. This is the fix.

### The cause, in four lines of `applyProjection`

```ts
const groups = new Map<string, Binding[]>();
for (const b of bindings) { … existing.push(b); }
```

Every binding is retained, because the aggregate closures map over them (`env.group`) and
`HAVING` receives the array too. The comment says so deliberately — _"Grouping is a barrier — it
must see every binding before it can emit"_ — and for `RETURN count(*)` with no `GROUP BY` that
means ONE group holding every binding: 6.25M six-entry `Map`s, ~640 bytes a path.

Measured before, 2,000 nodes at degree 5, under a deliberately tight 4 GB cap:

| hops | before                           |
| ---- | -------------------------------- |
| 3    | 8 ms, 80 MB RSS (degree product) |
| 4    | 13 ms, 86 MB (item 290's arm)    |
| 5    | **OOM-killed, exit 137**         |

### `count(*)` is the one aggregate that reads only the group's SIZE

It compiles to `group.length` and nothing else. So when every aggregate in a projection is
`count(*)`, the other `n − 1` bindings are never read, and a counter plus one representative is
enough — O(groups) instead of O(rows). `compileProjection` decides it once:

```ts
const countedGroups =
  aggregating &&
  having === undefined &&
  projection.items.every((i) => everyAggregateIsCountStar(i.expr)) &&
  (projection.orderBy ?? []).every((o) => everyAggregateIsCountStar(o.expr));
```

`having` is **excluded rather than analysed**: it receives the group and may do anything with it,
and keeping the guarantee local is worth more than covering `HAVING count(*) > n`.

**ONE WALK, NOT TWO.** `hasAggregate` was a twenty-case structural descent, and the new question
needs the same descent. A second copy is exactly the drift this file keeps paying for, so the walk
became `collectAggregates(expr)` and both questions are expressed over it — `hasAggregate` is now
`collectAggregates(e).length > 0`, and `everyAggregateIsCountStar` is a predicate on the same
list. Mutation T11 (stop descending into `arith`) confirms the single walk is load-bearing for
both.

**THE LENGTH-ONLY VIEW IS A LIE, SO IT IS A LOUD ONE.** The counted bucket is replayed as a
`Proxy` over a length-1 array that reports the real `length`, so the rest of `applyProjection` is
untouched. A numeric index past 0 would otherwise read `undefined` — a plausible wrong answer of
precisely the kind this engine cannot detect — so the Proxy throws instead, naming the cause. It is
built once per GROUP, never per row, so it costs nothing that matters. `countedGroups` is the
guarantee; the Proxy is its backstop, not a substitute.

### The result: from fatal to bounded

Same fixture, same 4 GB cap:

| hops | before            | after                                        |
| ---- | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| 5    | **OOM-killed**    | **2,793 ms, 123 MB RSS**, answer 6,250,000   |
| 6    | took the box down | **14,090 ms, 127 MB RSS**, answer 31,250,000 |

The 6-hop case is the query from the incident. `heapUsed` moves 13 → 39 MB across it.

### IT IS A MEMORY FIX AND NOT A TIME ONE — the A/B says so

Three alternated rounds, dist rebuilt per round, min per cell at 200,000 rows:

| case                                  |   head | changed |                   ratio |
| ------------------------------------- | -----: | ------: | ----------------------: |
| counted, 8 groups                     | 3.4 ms |  3.4 ms |                   1.00x |
| counted, 1000 groups                  |    4.0 |     3.9 |                   1.03x |
| counted, N groups (worst case)        |   13.1 |    11.3 | 1.16x — **NOT claimed** |
| CONTROL retained (`sum`), 1000 groups |   80.3 |    82.2 |                   0.98x |
| CONTROL `collect_list`, 8 groups      |   59.3 |    61.9 |                   0.96x |
| CONTROL project, no aggregate         |    6.1 |     6.0 |                   1.02x |

**The 1.16x is not claimed: its rounds overlap badly** (head 19.1/13.1/19.0 against 20.6/11.3/11.3).
At 200,000 rows the retained arrays fit comfortably and both paths make one pass, so time-neutral
is the expected and the honest answer. What matters is that it costs nothing — the two controls
that keep their bindings either way read 0.98x and 0.96x.

**A first version of that probe was not an A/B at all.** It compared `count(*)` against
`count(*), sum(…)` and called the gap the counted path's benefit — but the retained query also
COMPUTES a sum, so the difference included work the counted path never had to do. It also reported
`process.memoryUsage().rss` per case in one process, where RSS only ever grows (386 → 982 MB
monotonically) and can attribute nothing. Both replaced: the same query before and after, and the
memory claim carried by the capped 5/6-hop runs above, which is where it is unambiguous.

### Mutation — 11, with one equivalent mutant worth naming

| mutant                                                  | result                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| T1 the counter never advances                           | CAUGHT (204 failing)      |
| T2 a new group starts at 0                              | CAUGHT (228)              |
| T3 the representative becomes the LATEST row            | CAUGHT (4)                |
| T4 every row lands in one bucket                        | CAUGHT (207)              |
| T5 counted buckets are never replayed                   | CAUGHT (243)              |
| T6 the view reports the array's length, not the group's | CAUGHT (204)              |
| T8 the gate accepts ANY aggregate                       | CAUGHT (40)               |
| T9 `count(expr)` accepted as `count(*)`                 | CAUGHT (5)                |
| T11 the collector stops descending into `arith`         | CAUGHT (1)                |
| T7 the streamed path never fires                        | SURVIVED — memory only    |
| T10 `!a.distinct` dropped from the gate                 | SURVIVED — **equivalent** |

**T10 is an equivalent mutant, not a gap, and that is provable rather than assumed:** it drops
`!a.distinct` while keeping `a.star`, so it can only matter if `count(DISTINCT *)` is expressible —
and it is `E_SYNTAX`. So `star && distinct` is unreachable today and the check is defence against a
future parser. That is a stronger result than item 286's `pathVar` guard, where the paired mutant
could only show the guard untested in both copies; here the unreachability is demonstrated.

T3 is the one caught by only four tests, and they are pre-existing: `GROUP BY with no aggregate is
DISTINCT > a projection that is NOT the grouping element keeps its representative row`. The
representative has to be the FIRST binding, and the suite already knew it.

### Gates

16 new tests, every one comparing the counted path against the retained one on the same question
(adding `sum` to a projection forces the retained path, and the `c` column must match) — the only
comparison available, because a counter that counts the wrong thing returns a plausible number.
1937 gql tests, the full `bun run test` across 21 projects, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green,
`bun run spelling` clean at `SPELL_N=200000` apart from the structural `label on start` pair item
286 explains; `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint` and `bun run fmt:check` each as their own
command. Every capped run under `timeout` AND `MemorySwapMax=0`.

### What is still O(rows)

`sum`/`min`/`max`/`avg`/`stddev` could each fold into bounded state too, but not from the per-block
OUTPUT value — `avg` needs `(sum, count)` and `stddev` the moments, so they need partial state
plumbed through `compileAggregate` rather than a counter beside it. `collect`/`collect_list` and
the percentiles genuinely need every value and never stream. The next step, if it is worth taking,
is an accumulator INTERFACE that the array path also folds through, so there is still one
definition of each aggregate's semantics; a second derivation is the thing to avoid.

## 298. The count family's cliff had MOVED, not closed — a sweep answers any depth, and it makes TS 5294x faster than native at eleven hops

Item 290 added a four-segment arm to the count family and its own note left the question open: was
that a fix, or had the cliff moved to five? **It moved.** The evidence is the RATE, not the time —
a degree product's cost per path FALLS as the path count grows, because the cost is a product of
degrees and the path count is not; the general matcher's is FLAT, because it builds a binding per
path. So the cliff shows as a rate that stops falling and jumps. 200 nodes of degree 5, min of 3:

| hops |     paths |      ms | ns/path |                                |
| ---- | --------: | ------: | ------: | ------------------------------ |
| 2    |     5,000 |    0.08 |    16.3 |                                |
| 3    |    25,000 |    0.22 |     8.7 |                                |
| 4    |   125,000 |    1.24 |     9.9 | the arms — rate flat           |
| 5    |   625,000 |  266.03 |   425.6 | **x43, and flat from here on** |
| 6    | 3,125,000 | 1353.82 |   433.2 |                                |

A fifth hand-written arm would have moved the cliff to six, so this one is the general case:
`longChainCount`, a forward sweep of per-position WAY COUNTS. `ways[v]` is how many ways position
`k` can be `v`; one pass per segment advances it; the last segment is a weighted sum of DEGREES
rather than a final pass, so it takes `side`'s bucket-size route and owes none of the three
per-edge costs item 218 removed. **O(hops x edges) in time and O(vertices) in memory**, where
enumerating is O(degree^hops) in both.

| hops | before     | after   | ratio     |
| ---- | ---------- | ------- | --------- |
| 5    | 266.03 ms  | 0.37 ms | **719x**  |
| 6    | 1353.82 ms | 0.52 ms | **2603x** |

### This is also the RUST result, and it is the larger one

The probe was extended to ask native the same questions, which is how the attribution came out
the opposite way round from item 290's. Native's `exec` tallies an aggregate-over-chain and never
materializes a frontier (item 296), so it does not OOM — but **tallying is still once per PATH**,
and its rate is flat at ~0.2-0.3 ns from four hops on. So native has the same exponential cliff,
in time, and no guard against it. Both engines agree on every answer at every depth:

| hops |         paths | ts ms | native ms | agree |
| ---- | ------------: | ----: | --------: | ----- |
| 7    |    15,625,000 |  0.68 |      3.35 | yes   |
| 8    |    78,125,000 |  0.35 |     21.03 | yes   |
| 9    |   390,625,000 |  0.38 |    103.11 | yes   |
| 10   | 1,953,125,000 |  0.43 |    457.59 | yes   |
| 11   | 9,765,625,000 |  0.42 |   2223.64 | yes   |

**TS is now 5294x faster than native at eleven hops**, counting 9.77 BILLION paths in 0.42 ms, and
the gap multiplies by 5 per hop. That inverts the standing "the Rust core is 1.5-4x pure-TS"
summary for this shape, and the Rust half — the same sweep in native's count path — is now priced
by a measurement rather than guessed at. It is a separate item because it is a separate engine
with its own fuzzers; what this one buys it is an ORACLE that did not exist before, since native's
current answer at 9.77e9 paths is independently derived from the sweep's.

### The oracle, which is the whole safety argument

A sweep that mis-attributes a weight returns a PLAUSIBLE NUMBER, so a test that asserts a
hand-computed count only proves the test and the code were written by the same person on the same
afternoon. The engine's own second route is the oracle: a clause `WHERE` over four or more
segments returns `null` from `detectCountShortcut`, so appending an always-true predicate that
READS a bound name forces the identical question onto the general matcher. `sweptAndWalked` asks
both and requires them equal, on 13 shapes — labels at every position including both ends,
all-reversed arrows, mixed directions, two edge types, the untyped abbreviated edge, and the
chains that die in the middle and at the end.

Labels ARE carried at every position, which the degree products cannot do: the sweep VISITS each
position, so there is a once-per-element place to test a label, where a product reaches its two
ends only as degrees.

### Mutation — 14, all CAUGHT, and three of them only after the tests were strengthened

| mutant                                           | result              |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------- |
| L1 the weight is dropped (counts predecessors)   | CAUGHT (14 failing) |
| L2 the way count is overwritten, not accumulated | CAUGHT (14)         |
| L3 every start contributes nothing               | CAUGHT (16)         |
| L4 the last leg stops multiplying by the degree  | CAUGHT (15)         |
| L5 the last leg drops the weight                 | CAUGHT (14)         |
| L6 one pass too many                             | CAUGHT (15)         |
| L7 the advance reads the wrong adjacency index   | CAUGHT (12)         |
| L8 the weight lands on the near end              | CAUGHT (12)         |
| L9 an interior label is never tested             | CAUGHT (2)          |
| L10 the shared-variable guard removed            | CAUGHT (1)          |
| L11 an inline node property ignored              | CAUGHT (1)          |
| L12 the `'both'` direction guard removed         | SURVIVED -> CAUGHT  |
| L13 the `plainRel` guard removed                 | SURVIVED -> CAUGHT  |
| L14 the start-label re-test removed              | SURVIVED -> CAUGHT  |

The three survivors are the useful part, and none was a gap in the code:

- **L12 and L13 survived an INEQUALITY.** `expect(both).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(out)` and
  `expect(quantified).toBeGreaterThan(0)` are both satisfied by the mutant: taking an undirected
  segment as whichever direction it was written makes the two counts EQUAL, and a quantified leg
  taken as a single hop still returns a positive number. Replaced with the exact measured values
  (420 against the baseline 204; 522 for `{1,2}`). **An inequality is not an assertion about a
  count — it is an assertion about an interval, and the mutant lives in the interval.**
- **L14 survived every single-label case, for a reason worth keeping.** `candidateVertexSource`
  narrows by `seedLabel`, and `seedLabel` on an `and` seeds ONE side and returns the other
  unchecked — so `:N&A` yields all 24 `N` vertices and the explicit `matchesLabel` re-test is what
  narrows them to the 8 that are also `A`. With `:A` the bucket is already exactly right and with
  `:N` the label is vacuous, so neither can tell the re-test from its absence. Only a conjunction
  whose seeded side is a SUPERSET does: 68 against the unnarrowed 204. The same reasoning applies
  to `or` and `not`, where `seedLabel` returns `null` and the source is every vertex in the graph.

`plainRel` also covers an inline RELATIONSHIP property, and nothing else does — there is no
relationship variable in `-[:E {d: 0}]->`, so the `s.rel.variable !== undefined` gate does not
reach it. Added as its own case (132).

One test defect worth recording separately: the fixture annotated its ids `string[]` when
`addVertex` returns a `Vertex`. **`bun test` strips types, so the suite was green while `tsc` was
red** — and the mutation harness reported all fourteen mutants `DID-NOT-TYPECHECK`, which is what
surfaced it. A mutation run whose every mutant fails the same way is reporting on the harness, not
the mutants.

### Regression — the control is the half of the dispatch the change cannot reach

Three ALTERNATED rounds, control against new, rebuilding between every side because `@lenke/*`
resolves to the built dist (item 290 lost a measurement to exactly that). Every row in `bench` is
four segments or fewer, so the new arm cannot reach any of them — which is the point, because
`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` has four times measured a new module-scope walk costing shapes
that never call it.

**32 ts rows at >=1.0ms: median 1.019, min 0.932, max 1.171, 19/32 within +/-5%.** The two rows
outside 10% both FAVOUR the new side and are `decode ndjson (nodes)` (1.117) and
`query: top groups by count` (1.171) — neither of which touches the count dispatch, so they
calibrate the floor rather than crediting the change. The worst reading, `encode graphson` at
0.932, is equally unreachable. Nothing stands out beyond a floor the repo already documents at
~10%.

`bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`: 0 groups disagree on the answer, 1 group over
2x — the structural `label on start: redundant vs absent` that item 286 explains. A **five-hop
forward-vs-reversed group was added**, per the rule that a new form gets its spellings there: 1040
against 1317 ms, 1.27x, the same forward/reverse asymmetry the four-hop group already shows and
well under the flag. That 1040 ms at 200,000 vertices / 600,000 edges is the sweep's own weak
point and worth naming: a `Map<string, number>` keyed by STRING vertex ids, which is most of the
per-edge cost. An index-keyed array is the obvious next move and is recorded, not attempted.

### Gates

22 new tests, 13 of them comparing the sweep against the general matcher on the same question.
1957 gql tests; the full `bun test` across 383 files shows 63 failures in `@lenke/sync`,
`@lenke/serialization` and `@lenke/native` that are the documented run-many timing flake — each
package green in isolation (176, 144 and 809 passing). All seven byte-identity fuzzers green,
though it is worth being explicit that the differential fuzzer **does not generate chains of five
or more segments**, so the new arm has no generated coverage; `chain-depth-probe.ts` (now
`bun run probe:depth`) is what stands in for it, and it is the cross-engine check that found the
native result above. `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, `bun run fmt:check` each as its own
command. Every capped run under `timeout` AND `MemorySwapMax=0`.

### What is deliberately NOT done

The two-, three- and four-segment walks are untouched. The sweep is asymptotically better than
both products — it does one pass per segment where `fourSegmentCount` iterates interior PAIRS —
and at five hops it already answers in 0.37 ms where the four-hop product takes 0.96 ms for a
fifth of the paths, which is a strong hint it would win at three and four too. That is a real
question with a real answer and it is a SEPARATE item, because those walks carry items 140, 206
and 218-222 between them and the cost of restructuring a hot walk in this file is the one thing
it has measured over and over.

## 299. The same cliff in NATIVE, and it was the larger one — 10.4x at four hops, 139.8x at six, 74,121x at eleven

Item 298 priced this by measurement rather than guess, and the attribution came out the opposite
way round from item 290's. Native's `exec` tallies an aggregate-over-chain and never materializes
a frontier (item 296), so it does not OOM where the TS engine did — but **tallying is still once
per PATH**, and its rate was flat at ~0.2-0.3 ns from four hops on. `try_3hop_product_count`
stopped at three; four and up fell through every arm in the `or_else` chain to enumerate-and-tally.

The fix is the generalization that arm stops one hop short of, and it is **the same identity**:
`try_3hop_product_count`'s `level1[b]` already IS a way-count vector, and its degree product is
the last two hops of a sweep written out by hand. `try_nhop_sweep_count` runs one pass per hop
with the last hop as a weighted sum of out-degrees, over **two reused buffers** — a fresh
`vec![0; nc]` per hop is the one cost here that would grow with the depth.

Native has an advantage the TS side does not: **node ids are dense `u32`, so the way counts are a
flat array and there is no hash at all.** That is precisely the cost item 298 recorded as the TS
sweep's open weak point (`Map<String, number>`).

### On the repo's own fixture — 200,000 nodes at degree 5, matched reps, three alternated rounds

| row   | control (min of 3 rounds) |     new | ratio      |                           |
| ----- | ------------------------: | ------: | ---------- | ------------------------- |
| 1-hop |                  484.2 us | 486.4us | 1.00x      | control — unreachable arm |
| 2-hop |                 3830.4 us | 3907 us | 0.98x      | control — unreachable arm |
| 4-hop |               67,249.5 us |  6465us | **10.4x**  |                           |
| 6-hop |            1,392,055.6 us |  9955us | **139.8x** |                           |

Ranges are DISJOINT on both wins (4-hop control 67,250-84,673 against new 6,465-6,539; 6-hop
control 1,392,056-1,478,110 against new 9,955-10,039) and OVERLAPPING on both controls, which is
the right shape: the controls are answered by arms this change cannot reach.

**The first reading of these two rows was not a valid A/B and is recorded rather than quietly
replaced:** it compared the control at `BENCH_REPS=3` against the new side at the default 7. A
min over fewer samples is greater than or equal to a min over more, so that can only ever
overstate the win — 10.3x and 144.0x became 10.4x and 139.8x once both sides used 3. The error
was small here and that is luck, not method.

### At depth, against the pure-TS sweep

`bun run probe:depth`, 200 nodes of degree 5. Native was 2223.64 ms at eleven hops and is now
0.03 ms — **74,121x** — and the two engines agree on every answer at every depth:

| hops |         paths | native before | native after | ts sweep |
| ---- | ------------: | ------------: | -----------: | -------: |
| 7    |    15,625,000 |       3.35 ms |      0.03 ms |  0.58 ms |
| 9    |   390,625,000 |     103.11 ms |      0.02 ms |  0.30 ms |
| 11   | 9,765,625,000 |    2223.64 ms |      0.03 ms |  0.39 ms |

That restores the expected engine ordering for this shape: item 298 left TS **5294x faster than
native** at eleven hops, which inverted the standing "the Rust core is 1.5-4x pure-TS" summary.
Native is now ~13x ahead of TS again, which is the hash difference above.

### The oracle, and why it is weaker now than it was an hour ago

Each test compares the sweep against the ENUMERATION, exactly as
`three_hop_product_count_matches_enumeration` does one hop earlier. A clause `WHERE` breaks the
peel (the base is no longer a bare `Scan`) and projecting a column instead of counting enumerates,
so both routes are reachable from one query shape. A fixed-length chain is a WALK — edges and
nodes may repeat — so there is no trail correction, which is what makes the two comparable.

**Worth being explicit about:** the cross-engine agreement in `probe:depth` is now sweep against
sweep, which is much weaker evidence than it was before this item. The strong, independent check
is the one item 298 captured — the TS sweep against native's ENUMERATION, at depths to eleven
hops and 9.77e9 paths, measured BEFORE this change existed. That reading is the reason this one
could be taken confidently, and it cannot be re-run now.

The fixture is IRREGULAR on purpose (degrees 1-4, two edge types, a self-loop and a back edge),
for the reason item 290's mutation run recorded: a uniform-degree graph hides a mis-weighted
sweep, because every wrong attribution lands on a bucket of the same size.

### Mutation — 15, 13 CAUGHT, and both survivors are provable

| mutant                                            | result                    |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| N1 the weight is dropped                          | CAUGHT (7 failing)        |
| N2 the way count is overwritten                   | CAUGHT (7)                |
| N3 every seed contributes nothing                 | CAUGHT (6)                |
| N4 the last hop stops multiplying by the degree   | CAUGHT (7)                |
| N5 the last hop drops the weight                  | CAUGHT (7)                |
| N6 one pass too many                              | CAUGHT (7)                |
| N7 one pass too few                               | CAUGHT (7)                |
| N8 the buffer is not cleared between passes       | CAUGHT (7)                |
| N9 the buffers are never swapped                  | CAUGHT (7)                |
| N10 the per-hop edge type ignored on the advance  | CAUGHT (6)                |
| N11 the per-hop edge type ignored on the last hop | CAUGHT (6)                |
| N13 the base label is ignored                     | CAUGHT (2)                |
| N14 `count(expr)`/`count(DISTINCT …)` as a tally  | CAUGHT (1)                |
| N15 the depth floor moves to 5                    | SURVIVED — perf only      |
| N12 the `is_alive` seed guard removed             | SURVIVED — **equivalent** |

**N12 is an equivalent mutant and that is provable, not assumed** — the same standard item 297's
T10 set. `Store::delete_node` does `std::mem::take(&mut self.out_adj[i])` and then detaches every
mirror entry from each neighbour's list, so a deleted node has **no out-edges and no in-edges**.
Seeding it with `ways = 1` therefore contributes nothing (the first pass iterates an empty
adjacency) and it can never be reached (no in-edges), and it is removed from every label bucket
besides. So `is_alive` in the seed cannot change an answer today. It is kept because
`try_3hop_product_count` has the same check and because "deletion clears adjacency" is an
invariant of the store rather than of this function. No test can distinguish it, and inventing one
would mean inventing a store state that `delete_node` does not produce.

N15 is the perf-only control and had to survive: moving the floor to 5 sends a 4-hop chain back to
enumeration, which is slower and still correct.

### Scope — narrower than the TS arm, deliberately

OUT-only and unfiltered, which `out_chain_depth` ENFORCES rather than assumes: a `Filter`, a bound
edge, a reversed hop or an `Any` direction all fail the peel, and the depth floor keeps one, two
and three hops on their own tuned arms. The pure-TS sweep carries mixed directions and per-position
labels; matching that here is a separate item, because every extra position this reaches is a
position the differential fuzzer does not currently generate — so the coverage would be the
hand-written tests alone.

### Gates

7 new Rust tests, every one against the enumeration. 1062 + 13 + 723 Rust tests green;
`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000 rewrite_fuzz` green in 46s; all seven byte-identity fuzzers green;
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`, `bun run check` each as its own
command (clippy caught a `useless_format` in the new tests). The mutation sweep built UNCAPPED and
ran each mutant under `timeout 900` + `MemoryMax=16G` + `MemorySwapMax=0`, restoring before each
next mutant, with the final md5 check confirming the tree came back.

**`query/gql` gained a `4-hop` and a `6-hop` case**, which is what defends this: the 6-hop shape is
3.1 BILLION walks over the standard fixture and cost 1.39 SECONDS enumerated. A regression there
does not look like a few percent, which is the property a bench row wants.

## 300. The sweep's own constant factor — 1.29-1.65x, and THREE of the four obvious explanations for it were wrong

Item 298 left this open in its own words: `longChainCount` costs 1040ms for five hops at 200,000
vertices / 600,000 edges, "far more than 5 passes over 600k edges should be", and named the
`Map<string, number>` way counts as the suspect. It also named `edgesOfTypes`' generator frame
(item 164's cost) as a second candidate. Both guesses were priced, and the useful result is how
much of this was NOT where it looked.

### Seven variants over the same real graph, same traversal, all required to agree on the answer

| variant                                               |    ms |    vs |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----: | ----: |
| `Map<string, number>` + `edgesOfTypes` — WHAT SHIPPED | 780.5 | 1.00x |
| the generator removed, Map kept                       | 704.2 | 1.11x |
| BOXED counters — one hash an edge instead of two      | 620.7 | 1.26x |
| a lazy dense index routed through helper CALLS        | 650.8 | 1.20x |
| a lazy dense index, every helper INLINED              | 370.2 | 2.11x |
| the same, with the bucket cache REMOVED               | 641.1 | 1.22x |
| an EAGER index over all V, scanning `0..n`            | 201.6 | 3.87x |
| a CSR of dense slots, no hash an edge                 | 119.0 | 6.56x |

All seven answered 48,600,000, which is the check that matters: a variant that reads a different
number is measuring a different loop.

**What that rules out.** The generator is worth 1.11x, so item 298's second candidate is not the
cost and `edgesOfTypes` keeps its multi-type `seen` logic rather than being duplicated inline.
`get`-plus-`set` versus `get` is worth 1.26x, so the FIRST candidate — "two string hashes an
edge" — is not the cost either. And routing the identical dense algorithm through
`intern`/`bump`/`widen` helpers threw away almost all of its win (1.20x against 2.11x), which is
`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` for the fifth time in this file: **the win was the tight
typed-array loop, and a function call per edge is enough to lose it.**

### The micro promised 2.30x and the engine delivered 1.27x, and that discrepancy was the find

The first in-situ A/B read 1.27x, not the 2.11-2.30x the inlined variant kept measuring. Rather
than average them, the micro was re-run with its per-slot bucket cache REMOVED: **641.1ms, 1.22x**
— agreeing with the engine almost exactly. So the micro had been caching `fwd.get(id)` per slot,
which it could only do because every one of ITS legs was `-[:E]->`, and the real function cannot,
because each leg reads its own direction's index.

**The 2.30x had never been available.** What that reframed, though, is the fix: the cache is sound
whenever every leg runs the SAME WAY, which is the common shape and the incident shape. `types`
need not match — `edgesOfTypes` still applies each leg's own types to the cached bucket map, and
each leg keeps its own label. Taking it turned 1.27x into 1.29-1.65x.

### In situ, three alternated rounds, one case per process

The two controls route to `threeSegmentCount` and `fourSegmentCount`, so the sweep cannot reach
them. One case per process because item 290 recorded a large speedup making its NEIGHBOUR read
0.87x slower purely by warming it.

| case                   | control |    new | ratio     |                                |
| ---------------------- | ------: | -----: | --------- | ------------------------------ |
| 3-hop **[CONTROL]**    |   250.1 |  255.4 | 0.98x     | flat                           |
| 4-hop **[CONTROL]**    |  1001.6 |  960.9 | 1.04x     | flat                           |
| 5-hop                  |   978.5 |  760.1 | **1.29x** | disjoint                       |
| 6-hop                  |  1479.2 |  894.5 | **1.65x** | disjoint                       |
| 7-hop reversed         |  1783.2 | 1395.0 | **1.28x** | disjoint                       |
| 6-hop MIXED directions |   965.4 |  906.6 | 1.06x     | the cache DECLINES — see below |

The mixed-direction row is the one that says what each half is worth: it takes the dense rewrite
and NOT the cache, and it moves 1.06x. **So the dense rewrite alone is near-neutral in situ, and
the adjacency cache is the win it enables.** Both halves are needed and neither is the headline on
its own.

Memory: both sides OOM-kill at `MemoryMax=1G` and both pass at 2G — an identical threshold, which
is dominated by the 200k/600k graph rather than by the sweep. The dense arrays are sized to the
REACHED set, not to the graph.

`bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`: the five-hop pair went 1040 → 783ms forward
and 1317 → 985 reversed, 0 groups disagree on the answer, and the one group over 2x is still the
structural `label on start` pair item 286 explains.

### A reading RETRACTED, with its numbers, because it did not survive re-measurement

Lint's `prefer-for-of` forced the hot pass from an indexed loop to `for...of`, and re-measuring
said that cost ~5%: 715.5 against 752.7ms at five hops, three alternated rounds, ranges DISJOINT
(715.5-729.4 against 752.7-773.4). That looked like grounds for a targeted disable, and it was
written as one. Putting the indexed spelling back read **760.1ms — no better than the `for...of`
it was supposed to beat.** The tell was in the raw rounds: the third round had moved every row on
that side (255 → 290, 961 → 1197).

**Disjoint ranges over three rounds are not proof when the whole SIDE moves.** The control has to
hold still too, and it did on the first reading and not on the second. The disable was reverted
and the rejected attempt left in the code with its numbers, per the standing rule, because the
shape of this one invites a re-attempt.

### Regression — the control is every bench row, none of which the sweep can reach

Three alternated rounds against HEAD, rebuilt between sides. **32 ts rows at >=1.0ms: median
1.003, 26/32 within +/-5%.** Four rows outside 10%, and the calibration is sitting in the list:
`encode graphson` moved 1.118 on its ts column AND **1.130 on its FFI column**, which runs Rust a
TS edit cannot reach — so this harness carries ~13% movement independent of the change.

`query: count distinct` (0.853) was the only QUERY row flagged, so it was ISOLATED rather than
argued away: one case per process, min of 9, three alternated rounds. It reads **1.16x FASTER on
the new side** (4.649 against 4.000ms) with overlapping ranges. It cannot reach `longChainCount`
anyway — `count(DISTINCT n.age)` over a bare node pattern has no segments — and the multi-case
reading was contamination.

### Mutation — 13, all CAUGHT, and three of them only by the MEMORY cap

`sweepChain` is a rewrite of the function item 298 mutated, so none of that evidence transfers —
the anchors it attacked no longer exist. A fresh set attacked the new mechanism: lazy slot
interning, the frontier-transition test, the per-slot cache and its uniformity guard.

| mutant                                               | result                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| M1 the cache is used even on a MIXED chain           | CAUGHT (1 failing)     |
| M2 the uniformity test becomes `some`                | CAUGHT (1)             |
| M3 the cache is not extended when interning mid-pass | CAUGHT (3)             |
| M4 the SEED does not extend the cache                | CAUGHT (17)            |
| M5 the frontier-transition test always fires         | **CAUGHT (OOM kill)**  |
| M6 the frontier-transition test never fires          | CAUGHT (18)            |
| M7 the way count is overwritten, not accumulated     | CAUGHT (18)            |
| M8 the weight is dropped                             | CAUGHT (18)            |
| M9 every seed contributes nothing                    | **CAUGHT (OOM kill)**  |
| M10 one pass too many                                | CAUGHT (19)            |
| M11 the grown buffer loses this pass's counts        | CAUGHT (1) — see below |
| M12 an interior label is never tested                | CAUGHT (3)             |
| M13 interning stops DEDUPLICATING                    | **CAUGHT (OOM kill)**  |

**M13 is the one worth the whole exercise, and it is not a wrong answer.** If interning stops
deduplicating, every reached vertex gets a fresh slot, the per-slot way counts never merge — and
`Σ over slots of (ways x degree)` is still exactly right. What it destroys is the BOUND: slots then
grow with the PATH count, which is the single thing this arm exists to prevent. **No assertion
about an answer can see that.** It was caught because the mutants run under `MemoryMax=4G` with
`MemorySwapMax=0`, and the same cap caught M5 and M9, where a frontier gains a push per edge and
never empties. The cgroup cap is not a safety belt here; for three of thirteen mutants it is the
only detector.

**M11 SURVIVED first, and the reason is a rule already in this repo.** It removes
`grownNext.set(next)`, so a buffer that doubles mid-pass loses the counts already written into it.
Every fixture in `long-chain-count.test.ts` reached at most 120 vertices against a 256-slot
starting capacity, so the doubling path was **dead code to the entire suite**. Fixed with a
deliberately shaped fixture: 3,000 vertices at degree 4 behind a TEN-vertex seed, so the frontier
goes 10 → 40 → 160 → 640 → 2560 and the grow fires in the MIDDLE of a pass with counts already in
the buffer. That is the only state that distinguishes the copy from its absence, and it is
`pull_capped`'s lesson verbatim: **when a loop has a block size, the fixture must exceed it,
twice.** Added in both directions, so the cached-adjacency route grows too.

### Gates

24 tests in `long-chain-count.test.ts` (2 new), 1961 gql tests, all seven byte-identity fuzzers,
`bun run probe:depth` still agreeing with native at every depth to 9.77e9 paths. `bun run lint`,
`bun run typecheck`, `bun run fmt:check` each as its own command. `chain-sweep-bench.ts` is now
`bun run bench:chain`, and it exists because `chain-depth-probe.ts` answers a DIFFERENT question —
depth needs a tiny graph to show the rate, a constant factor needs a big one to show itself.

### What is left, priced

The EAGER index's extra 1.76x over the lazy one is declined, not missed: it scans `0..V` and skips
zeros instead of tracking a frontier, which is faster while the frontier is SATURATED and costs
O(V) memory and O(V) hashes whatever the frontier's real size — so a selective start over a large
graph would pay for the whole graph. Keeping memory proportional to the REACHED set is the premise
of this arm (items 296-298), and taking both regimes would mean two sweeps, i.e. two definitions
of one thing. The CSR floor (6.56x) needs a dense adjacency the TS graph does not expose; native
already has exactly that, which is why its own sweep needs no hash at all (item 299).

## 301. Whether the sweep beats the degree products — a SPLIT verdict, 1.71x at four hops and 1.50x the wrong way at three

Items 298 and 300 both recorded this as open with a strong hint, and the hint pointed at one
answer for both depths: the sweep is O(hops x E) where `fourSegmentCount` iterates interior PAIRS,
and at five hops the sweep already answered in less absolute time than the four-hop product took
for a fifth of the paths. So the expectation was that it would win at three AND four.

**It wins at four and loses at three.** 200,000 vertices at degree 3, three alternated rounds,
one case per process, ranges disjoint on both:

| depth  | degree product |   sweep | verdict                |
| ------ | -------------: | ------: | ---------------------- |
| 3 hops |        250.1ms | 374.9ms | **the PRODUCT, 1.50x** |
| 4 hops |        980.2ms | 512.4ms | **the SWEEP, 1.91x**   |

The reason is the shape of each product, and it is the asymptotics — just not the ones the hint
assumed. `threeSegmentCount` pays per MIDDLE EDGE and multiplies two degree SIDES: that is O(E)
with no frontier materialized and no hashing anywhere, which is cheaper than three sweep passes
with a hash per edge. `fourSegmentCount` paid per INTERIOR PAIR, i.e. O(E x degree), which loses
to four O(E) passes. **The crossover sits exactly where a product stops being linear in the edge
count** — so it is one question with two answers, and taking the asymptotic argument on trust
