would have made the three-hop count 1.5x slower in exchange.

### What shipped

`longChainCount`'s floor moved from five segments to FOUR, and `fourSegmentCount` was **deleted**
rather than left unreachable — 110 lines. Its gates were identical to the sweep's (`plainRel`, no
relationship variable, no `both` direction, `plainNode` at all five positions, no shared node
variable, resolvable per-hop types), so the sweep subsumes it exactly.

Final A/B after the deletion, with the 5-, 6- and 7-hop rows as INTERNAL controls — both sides
sweep those, so they must not move:

| case                   |   base |  swept | ratio     |                         |
| ---------------------- | -----: | -----: | --------- | ----------------------- |
| 3-hop                  |  241.9 |  250.6 | 0.97x     | unmoved, ranges OVERLAP |
| 4-hop                  |  956.1 |  559.2 | **1.71x** | disjoint                |
| 5-hop                  |  751.1 |  714.4 | 1.05x     | internal control        |
| 6-hop                  |  881.7 |  883.6 | 1.00x     | internal control        |
| 7-hop reversed         | 1376.6 | 1435.1 | 0.96x     | internal control        |
| 6-hop mixed directions |  922.6 |  907.1 | 1.02x     | internal control        |

1.71x rather than the 1.91x the routing experiment read, because round 3 was noisy on the swept
side (852.3 against 559.2/577.7); the conservative min-of-min is the number claimed. Answers
identical on all six cases.

`bun run spelling`: the FOUR-hop pair moved 754.8 → 595.2ms forward and 909.6 → 794.2 reversed,
still well under the 2x flag, 0 groups disagreeing on the answer.

### The deletion made the test suite STRONGER, and that is measurable

Item 290's `four-hop-count.test.ts` — 27 tests written against the degree product, before the
sweep existed — now exercises the sweep. **That makes it an independent oracle**, in the strongest
sense available here: the assertions were authored against a different implementation of the same
question.

Re-running item 300's 13 mutants with that coverage in place, every catch count rose:

| mutant                                      | before | after |
| ------------------------------------------- | -----: | ----: |
| M1 cache used on a MIXED chain              |      1 |     5 |
| M4 the SEED does not extend the cache       |     17 |    28 |
| M6 the frontier-transition test never fires |     18 |    34 |
| M7 way count overwritten, not accumulated   |     18 |    31 |
| M8 the weight is dropped                    |     18 |    31 |
| M10 one pass too many                       |     19 |    32 |
| M12 an interior label is never tested       |      3 |     5 |

All 13 still caught, three of them still only by the memory cap. **Deleting a tuned arm normally
loses the tests that guarded it; here it transferred them, because the two arms answered the same
question under the same gates.** That equality of gates is the whole precondition — it is what was
checked before deleting, not after.

### The one and two segment walks are NOT touched, and will not be

They carry predicates and inline gates the sweep has no route for (items 219-222 built those), and
they are the hot shapes. Three stays on its product for the measured reason above. So the family
is now: products at one, two and three segments; the sweep at four and up.

### Regression, and a second alarming bench row that dissolved under isolation

Three alternated rounds against the pre-change tree, rebuilt between sides. **32 ts bench rows at

> =1.0ms: median 0.987, 22/32 within +/-5%.** Four rows outside 10%, two of them favouring the
> change (`query: count distinct` 1.143, `query: group, no aggregate` 1.185).

The other two were `encode csv` (0.870) and **`encode ndjson` (0.703)** — a 30% apparent
regression, which is too large to wave away even though encoding provably cannot reach the count
dispatch (`@lenke/serialization` and `@lenke/gql` are different packages and different bundles).
So it was ISOLATED: one case per process, min of 9, three alternated rounds. It reads **0.96x with
heavily OVERLAPPING ranges** (42.97-51.07 against 44.80-49.82). It does not reproduce.

That is the SECOND time in two items that the multi-case bench produced a double-digit
"regression" on a row the change cannot reach, and isolation dissolved it (item 300's
`query: count distinct` read 0.853 in the sweep and 1.16x FASTER alone). **The multi-case
`bench` run is a SCREEN. A flagged row on a path the change cannot reach is a prompt to isolate,
not a finding** — and the tell for both was exactly the one item 290 recorded: the shape that
"regressed" cannot reach the change.

### Gates

1961 gql tests, all seven byte-identity fuzzers, `bun run probe:depth` still agreeing with native
at every depth to 9.77e9 paths. `bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9` with 0 answer
disagreements. `bun run lint`, `bun run typecheck`, `bun run fmt:check` each as its own command.

## 302. Native's sweep carries a per-hop DIRECTION — 137.7x on an alternating chain, and the obvious case needed nothing at all

Item 299 shipped native's sweep OUT-only and recorded mixed directions as open. The prediction
written there, and the one worth being wrong about publicly, was that the REVERSED spelling of a
chain would fall back to enumeration — which would have made it an equivalent-spelling bug, the
class this engine is named for.

**It does not.** Measured first: a fully reversed 8-hop chain answers in **0.05ms** against the
forward 0.02ms, because the optimizer's `orient` rewrite normalizes it to a forward chain before
`peel_out_hops` ever sees it. The invariant was already holding, and building for it would have
been building for nothing. _Diagnose before assuming, including when the thing you are diagnosing
is your own recorded TODO._

What the rewrite CANNOT normalize is **alternating** arrows, where there is no single orientation
to flip to. That shape did have the cliff:

| hops |      paths | native before | native after | ts sweep |
| ---- | ---------: | ------------: | -----------: | -------: |
| 4    |    125,000 |       0.06 ms |      0.02 ms |  0.44 ms |
| 5    |    625,000 |       0.20 ms |      0.02 ms |  0.37 ms |
| 6    |  3,125,000 |       0.71 ms |      0.02 ms |  0.60 ms |
| 7    | 15,625,000 |       4.13 ms |      0.03 ms |  0.47 ms |

Native grew ~5x a hop — the degree, i.e. an enumeration — and was **10x SLOWER than pure TS at
seven hops**, since the TS sweep has carried per-hop directions since item 298. **137.7x at seven
hops**, and the cliff is gone rather than moved: `bun run probe:depth` now shows forward, reversed
and alternating all flat in both engines out to eleven hops (9.77e9 paths), every column agreeing
on its answer.

`peel_dir_hops` is a sibling of `peel_out_hops` rather than a generalization of it, because the
3-hop edge product genuinely wants ONE orientation — its `level1` and `outdeg3` arrays are both
built from `store.out`. The sweep has no such requirement: each pass reads whichever index its own
hop names, and `Adj::nbr` is the far end of the edge in whichever list it was read from, so one
loop body serves both.

### The cost, which is real and is NOT the feature

The forward chain got **5% slower**, reproducibly: the 4-hop and 6-hop `query/gql` rows read
**0.95x** and **0.95x** over three alternated rounds with DISJOINT ranges (6483.0 → 6835.5us and
10006.5 → 10535.8us) while the 1-hop and 2-hop controls stayed flat at 1.02x/1.01x.

Two hypotheses for it, both WRONG, and the second one is the useful result:

1. **"It is the per-vertex branch."** Specializing each pass by direction into two monomorphic
   loops (a `macro_rules!` expanded once per arm, so the adjacency call resolves at compile time)
   made it slightly **worse** — 0.93x/0.92x. Reverted; left in the code with its numbers.
2. **"It is the direction handling at all."** A variant keeping EVERY structural change here —
   `peel_dir_hops`, the tuple `wants`, the macros — but reading `store.out` unconditionally, with
   no direction logic whatsoever, still read **0.95x/0.95x.**

So the 5% is the **TOLL for editing this module**, not the price of the feature. That is
`pull-alignment-is-load-bearing` one module along, and the repo already records the shape of it:
an edit to a hot path costs a cluster that does not obviously depend on it, never gains, and the
toll is the price of admission. Accepted deliberately: **a 5% constant on forward chains against
removing an O(degree^hops) cliff on mixed ones**, which at eight hops would already be ~20ms and
has no bound. Stated plainly rather than buried, because it is a regression on the commonest
shape.

### Mutation — 9, 8 CAUGHT, 1 provably equivalent

Every wrong direction here returns a plausible number: a mixed chain read with one index flipped
still counts walks, just not the ones that were asked for. So the mutants attack the direction
specifically — which index a pass reads, where the flag comes from, and whether an undirected hop
is refused.

| mutant                                             | result                    |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| D1 every advance pass reads the WRONG index        | CAUGHT (9 failing)        |
| D2 every advance pass reads OUT regardless         | CAUGHT (4)                |
| D3 the last hop's degree sum ignores its direction | CAUGHT (3)                |
| D4 the last hop's degree sum reads the wrong index | CAUGHT (9)                |
| D5 the peel records `Dir::In` as an OUT hop        | CAUGHT (4)                |
| D6 the peel records `Dir::Out` as an IN hop        | CAUGHT (6)                |
| D8 every hop takes the FIRST hop's direction       | CAUGHT (4)                |
| D9 the direction is dropped where it is consumed   | CAUGHT (4)                |
| D7 the `Dir::Any` guard in `chain_depth` removed   | SURVIVED — **equivalent** |

**D7 is equivalent and that is provable rather than assumed**, the standard items 297 and 299 set.
`chain_depth` only computes a DEPTH; `peel_dir_hops` is what builds the hop list, and its own
`match dir { Dir::Out => true, Dir::In => false, _ => return None }` refuses an undirected hop.
So a depth accepted past the removed guard still yields `None` from the peel, and
`try_nhop_sweep_count` returns `None` exactly as before. The guard is kept because the two
functions are documented as accepting the same shape and that agreement is worth enforcing in
both, not because it can change an answer today.

D8's first anchor did not match after `cargo fmt` reindented the push, and it reported
APPLY-FAILED rather than SURVIVED — which is the distinction that harness exists to draw, since a
mutant that never ran is not evidence of anything.

### One restore hazard, caught

The A/B script for the direction experiment was derived with `sed` from an earlier one, and the
substitution that pointed the loop at the measurement-only variant **also rewrote the script's
final restore line**. So the deliberately-wrong variant (`store.out` unconditionally) was left in
the working tree. It was caught by grepping for its marker before trusting the next build rather
than by a test — `cargo clippy` had failed for an unrelated reason, which is what prompted the
check. CLAUDE.md's rule is "restore before applying the next mutant, never only after the loop";
the corollary this adds is that **a `sed`-derived A/B script's restore line is part of what the
`sed` can break, so verify the tree by content and not by trusting the script's last line.**

### Gates

4 new Rust tests (23 assertions across depths 4-7, two alternation phases, three type patterns and
five undirected positions), each against the ENUMERATION. 1066 + 13 + 723 Rust tests green,
`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000 rewrite_fuzz` green in 46s, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` (it caught a `type_complexity` on the peel's return,
fixed with a `DirHop` alias), `cargo fmt --check`, `bun run lint`, `bun run fmt:check`,
`bun run typecheck` each as its own command.

`chain-depth-probe.ts` gained REVERSED and ALTERNATING columns beside the forward one, so the
regression this item fixes is now watched rather than remembered: if either column starts climbing
with the degree again, that engine's peel has stopped accepting the shape.

### Still open

Per-position NODE labels, which the TS sweep carries at every position and native does not. Not
taken here because the differential fuzzer generates no chain of this depth at all, so the
coverage would be hand-written tests alone — the same reason item 299 gave, and it has not changed.

## 303. An INLINE constraint at any position of a long chain — 33.6-79.8x, and a memo rejected on its own numbers

`CLOSED.md` has carried one line about this family for several items: _"anything that DECLINES a
count shortcut pays 50-85x, which is one target and not a family of them."_ The sweep refused any
constrained node outright (`plainNode`), so a five-segment chain with ONE gated position declined
the whole family and fell to the general matcher. Measured, both engines, 20,000 vertices at
degree 3, against the unconstrained chain as the control:

| gate position | ts before | vs free | native | vs free |
| ------------- | --------: | ------: | -----: | ------: |
| (none)        |   56.6 ms |       — | 0.5 ms |       — |
| 0 (the start) |  1423.8ms |   25.1x | 15.6ms |   28.6x |
| 1             |  1483.7ms |   26.2x | 16.5ms |   30.2x |
| 2             |  1666.6ms |   29.4x | 17.9ms |   32.8x |
| 3             |  2461.2ms |   43.5x | 32.0ms |   58.6x |
| 4 (the last)  |  4651.5ms |   82.1x | 66.2ms |  121.3x |

The fix is item 219's argument, one family along: **a position the sweep VISITS has a
once-per-element place to put a gate, and the sweep visits every position.** Each leg carries its
landed node's `InlinePred` and applies it on the `0 -> w` TRANSITION, so the predicate runs once
per DISTINCT vertex reached there rather than once per edge into it — and the endpoint is resolved
only on that branch, so an ungated pass never pays item 194's ~190ns lookup. The start's gate is
applied at seed time.

| gate position | ts after | vs free |   won |
| ------------- | -------: | ------: | ----: |
| 0 (the start) |   38.6ms |    1.2x | 36.9x |
| 1             |   44.1ms |    1.3x | 33.6x |
| 2             |   40.4ms |    1.2x | 41.3x |
| 3             |   45.4ms |    1.4x | 54.2x |
| 4 (the last)  |   58.3ms |    1.7x | 79.8x |

Answers agree with native exactly at every position (1,215,000), which is the cross-engine check:
native still takes the old route, so it is an independent derivation of the same number.

### The LAST position is the interesting one, and it needed no new mechanism

A gated end looks like the hard case — the arm answers an ungated last position with a weighted
sum of DEGREES, and a degree cannot say which of a vertex's edges land somewhere that passes. The
degree products refuse an end constraint for exactly this reason (items 219, 290).

But the sweep has a general answer: **give the last position a pass of its own.** Then the gate is
once-per-vertex like every other position, and the count is simply the sum of the surviving way
counts rather than a degree product. `passes = lastGated ? legs.length : legs.length - 1`, and
that is the whole change. It is why this arm can carry an END constraint where the products
cannot, and it got the biggest win of the six (79.8x).

### A memo, REJECTED on its own numbers after mutation showed it was not load-bearing

The first version memoized a failed gate for the rest of the pass, stamping a negative sentinel
into `next[to]` and skipping any later edge that found one. It was removed, and the order of
reasons matters:

1. **Mutation proved it is not a CORRECTNESS mechanism rather than arguing it.** The mutant that
   removed the stamp and the one that removed the test BOTH survived the entire suite. Without the
   memo a rejected vertex is simply re-tested per incoming edge and still never enters the
   frontier, so the answer is identical. Two survivors in a row on the same mechanism is a result,
   not a gap — they say the mechanism is an optimization wearing a correctness costume.
2. **Its sign is not consistent.** On a 4,000-vertex degree-24 fixture built specifically to favour
   it (high in-degree, a selective gate where the pressure is highest), it was **0.87x — SLOWER**
   at the gated last position (16.19 against 18.66ms, ranges DISJOINT) and **1.27x faster** at an
   interior (13.32 against 10.47ms, also disjoint). A cheap inline property compare is not
   obviously dearer than the branch the memo costs on every edge.
3. It put a negative number inside a weight array and relied on "nothing reads it, because the
   slot is not in the frontier" — a live invariant to maintain for no proven gain.

The asymptotic argument for it (per-vertex instead of per-edge evaluation) is real and still did
not show up as a win. Left in the code with its numbers so it is not re-attempted.

**The earlier reading that pointed the other way is worth recording too:** on the general
interior-gate probe the memo looked worth 1.12x/1.13x at positions 3 and 4. That probe's own
ungated CONTROL row spanned 28.7-43.3ms across three rounds — a 1.5x spread — so it could not
separate a 13% effect from itself. The sharper fixture was built because of that, and it reversed
the sign at the last position. **A probe that cannot hold its own control still is not entitled to
a 13% conclusion.**

### Mutation — 8, all CAUGHT, two anchors repaired and one real gap found

| mutant                                           | result              |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------- |
| G1 an interior gate is never applied             | CAUGHT (10 failing) |
| G2 the gate is applied to the NEAR end           | CAUGHT (9)          |
| G3 the gate's verdict is INVERTED                | CAUGHT (10)         |
| G6 the START gate is never applied               | CAUGHT (5)          |
| G7 a gated last position gets no extra pass      | CAUGHT (4)          |
| G8 the gated tail still multiplies by the degree | CAUGHT (2)          |
| G9 an OPEN interior constraint is carried        | CAUGHT (1)          |
| G10 an OPEN START constraint is carried          | SURVIVED -> CAUGHT  |

**G10 found a real gap.** The start is a separate code path (its gate runs at seed time) and
nothing reached it with an OPEN constraint, so carrying a `null` gate there went unnoticed. What
the new test discriminates is NOT a number: a forward reference in an inline predicate is UNKNOWN
(`f` is unbound when `a`'s constraint is evaluated), so 0 is the right answer and the general
matcher gives it — what a wrongly-carried `null` does is THROW, reading `.bindVar` off it. That is
stated in the test, because an assertion whose discriminator is "it returns at all" looks vacuous
otherwise.

G10 also needed its mutant written as a PAIR: removing the `=== null` guard alone does not
typecheck, because that guard is what narrows `null` away, so the cast at the use site is part of
the mutant rather than a way around it. A mutant that cannot compile is not evidence either way,
which is the distinction the harness exists to draw.

### Two of my own tests were VACUOUS, and the check that caught them

The gate tests were first written as `expect(sweptAndWalked(…)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0)`, with
the oracle comparison inside `sweptAndWalked` doing the real work. Printing the actual counts
showed **two of them comparing 0 against 0** — three single-value gates co-occur on no walk over
this fixture, and the open-constraint case was 0 as well. An oracle that agrees on nothing agrees
about nothing.

Fixed twice over: the patterns became RANGES where a single value was too selective, and every
assertion became the EXACT measured count (7/10/9/8/7/10 across the six positions; 78, 106, 2 for
the multi-gate cases; 110, 102 for the inline `WHERE`s; 121 for the declined open one). **An
exact count cannot go vacuous without failing, which is the whole argument for it** — the same
conclusion item 298 reached from the other direction, where an inequality let three mutants
through.

### Regression, and the clearest noise calibration this harness has produced

Three alternated rounds against HEAD, rebuilt between sides. The gate code is unreachable from
every `bench` row (none has four or more segments, let alone a constrained one), so the broad
sweep is purely the module-size control. **32 ts rows at >=1.0ms: median 1.007, 22/32 within
+/-5%.**

Four rows outside 10%, two of them favouring the change (`encode pg-text` 1.190,
`query: group + aggregate` 1.194). The other two:

- **`encode ndjson` read 0.831 on its ts column AND 0.753 on its FFI column.** The FFI column runs
  RUST. A TypeScript edit inside `@lenke/gql` cannot change it by any mechanism. So this run
  carries ~25% movement on that row independent of the change, which settles what the other
  readings are worth. This is the same calibration item 300 found at 1.130 and it is now larger.
- `query: count distinct` (0.867) has now been flagged by three consecutive items and ISOLATED
  twice — one case per process, min of 9 — reading **1.16x FASTER** on the new side both times
  (item 300). Not re-isolated a third time for the same row and the same conclusion; cited rather
  than re-measured, which is the honest version of that claim.

1970 gql tests, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.
`bun run lint`, `bun run typecheck`, `bun run fmt:check` each as its own command — lint needed
three passes on the new bench, where `prefer-template` and `no-unnecessary-template-expression`
are mutually exclusive on a single-expression template and the resolution is to factor the
expression out rather than satisfy either.

`chain-gate-bench.ts` is now `bun run bench:gate`, and it keeps the native column — which is still
the OLD story at 28-126x — so the follow-up is priced rather than remembered.

### Still open

**The same gates in NATIVE.** `try_nhop_sweep_count` carries the base label only, so native still

## 304. A constraint at any position of a long chain in NATIVE — 16-63x, and the SPELLING the plan hid

Item 303's recorded follow-up, measured on its own bench with alternated rounds rather than carried
over: `try_nhop_sweep_count` carried the base label and nothing else, so one constrained position
declined the whole family and the chain fell to the general matcher. 20,000 vertices of degree 3,
a five-hop chain, the unconstrained chain as the control the change cannot reach, min of 3 over
three alternated rounds rebuilt between sides:

| constrained at | native before | vs free | native after | vs free |   won |
| -------------- | ------------: | ------: | -----------: | ------: | ----: |
| (none)         |       0.50 ms |       — |      0.50 ms |       — |  1.0x |
| 0 (the seed)   |      14.70 ms |   29.4x |      0.90 ms |    1.8x | 16.3x |
| 1              |      16.60 ms |   33.2x |      0.90 ms |    1.8x | 18.4x |
| 2              |      18.50 ms |   37.0x |      0.90 ms |    1.8x | 20.6x |
| 3              |      32.00 ms |   64.0x |      0.90 ms |    1.8x | 35.6x |
| 4 (the last)   |      63.10 ms |  126.2x |      1.00 ms |    2.0x | 63.1x |

The mechanism is item 303's, so it is not re-argued: each position's constraint is applied on the
`0 -> w` TRANSITION, which costs it once per DISTINCT vertex reached there rather than once per
edge into it, and a gated LAST position gets a pass of its own because an ungated end is a
weighted sum of DEGREES and a degree cannot say which of a vertex's edges land somewhere that
passes. `passes = if last_gated { hops } else { hops - 1 }` is the whole of that. The ungated inner
loop is kept byte-identical rather than folded into the gated one behind a per-edge `Option` test,
because this module charges ~5% for a structural edit (item 302) and the ungated forward chain is
the commonest shape — and the `(none)` row above reads 0.50 against 0.50, so that held.

### The find: the gate's POSITION is not where the plan puts its Filter

This was supposed to be a port. What it turned into was an equivalent-spelling bug of item 125's
exact class, found by INSTRUMENTING which shapes the arm actually reaches rather than by reading
the plan and reasoning about it. A temporary `eprintln!` at the point of acceptance, run over
thirty shapes, said:

- an inline `{k: 1}` at position 3 → ACCEPTED (the optimizer pushes that `Filter` down to the hop
  that binds the node),
- a clause `WHERE n3.k = 1` → DECLINED. The optimizer leaves that `Filter` at the TOP of the
  chain, where my first version compared its slot against the position the top hop binds, found
  3 ≠ 5, and declined.

Both spellings mean the same thing and the first draft served one of them. So the gate's position
is now DERIVED from its predicate's slot and applied at the pass that lands there, which is the
pushdown the optimizer did not do. Measured on the same bench, native: inline 18.8x, clause
`WHERE` 20.4x, the flipped `1 = n2.k` spelling 20.6x — all three at 0.90 ms, from 16.9 / 18.4 /
18.5 ms. **The reading that mattered was the one I did not plan to take.**

Three consequences fell out of the same mechanism:

- **A per-position LABEL is carried now too** — `IsLabeled` is one of the leaf forms — which
  retires the open row from items 299 and 302. 35.60 → 1.10 ms, **32.4x**, so it was NOT already
  fast via another arm; I believed that for a while off a post-change reading of 1.2 ms with no
  control, which is exactly the mistake the alternated A/B exists to prevent.
- **A conjunction naming TWO positions SPLITS into two gates** rather than declining. That was not
  in the design: mutant N10 (place every leaf at the first leaf's position) survived the whole
  suite, and the honest fix for the shape nothing covered was not a test for a decline but to make
  the shape work. `WHERE n1.k = 0 AND n3.m > 5 AND n5.k = 2` is three gates at three positions.
- Leaves landing on ONE position conjoin, whether they came from one `AND`, from two stacked
  `Filter`s, or from an inline constraint plus a clause `WHERE` on the same node.

`chain_depth` is gone. It was a pre-pass that counted the hops so the peel could run, and once a
`Filter` became something the peel had to interpret rather than refuse, two functions that each had
to agree about what a `Filter` means was the duplication worth removing. The depth is `hops.len()`
after the peel, and the width check is structural (`from` must equal the hops already peeled)
rather than a `chain_width` call — `chain_width` sees through an `IsLabeled` filter only, and a
gated position is exactly a filter it does not see through.

### What still declines, each for its own reason

- A **DISJUNCTION** (`k = 0 OR k = 1`) — and the `IN [0, 1]` spelling, which lowers to the same
  `Or`, so the two decline TOGETHER, which is the property that matters here.
- A **CORRELATION** (`n3.m = n1.m`): no per-node leaf form, since every gate is evaluated against
  ONE vertex with nothing else bound.
- **`IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`**: not `has_prop` in an engine where null is a stored PRESENT value
  ([[null-first-class-policy]]), so it is declined rather than approximated.
- A **null literal** in a compare. `k = null` would still answer 0 if carried, since
  `nbr_pred_ok`'s compare refuses a null operand — but **`k <> null` would admit EVERYTHING**,
  which is why that guard is load-bearing and not belt-and-braces. Mutant N13 survived until the
  test asserted the `<>` spelling against the ungated 155.

Each of these is asserted by answer, not by declining: the general matcher gives the right number
and the oracle compares it.

### Mutation — 15, 14 CAUGHT, one SURVIVOR by design, two real gaps found

| mutant                                                     | result                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| N1 an interior gate is never applied                       | CAUGHT (13 failing)    |
| N2 the gate is applied to the NEAR end of the edge         | CAUGHT (11)            |
| N3 the gate's verdict is INVERTED                          | CAUGHT (12)            |
| N4 the seed gate is skipped on the LABELLED branch         | CAUGHT (2)             |
| N5 the seed gate is skipped on the `is_alive` branch       | CAUGHT (2)             |
| N6 a gated last position gets no extra pass                | CAUGHT (9)             |
| N7 the extra pass runs AND the degree tail runs            | CAUGHT (7)             |
| N8 the gate is read from the slot the hop STARTS at        | CAUGHT (14)            |
| N9 an inexpressible leaf is dropped instead of declining   | CAUGHT (6)             |
| N10 every leaf is placed at the FIRST leaf's position      | SURVIVED -> CAUGHT (6) |
| N12 leaves on one position overwrite instead of conjoining | CAUGHT (2)             |
| N13 a null literal is carried as a gate                    | SURVIVED -> CAUGHT (2) |
| N14 a flipped comparison is not flipped back               | CAUGHT (2)             |
| N15 the `next[j] == 0` transition test is removed          | **SURVIVED, intended** |
| N16 the conjunction becomes a DISJUNCTION                  | CAUGHT (5)             |

**N15 is in the set on purpose and must survive.** Removing the transition test only re-evaluates
a gate per edge instead of per distinct vertex; the answer cannot change. It is the memo question
item 303 answered with two survivors, and keeping one deliberate equivalent mutant in the harness
is how a run proves it can tell "not covered" from "cannot differ". A run where N15 is reported
caught is reporting on the harness.

N9 and N16 were both caught partly by `rewrite_fuzz` — generated plans, raw against optimized,
compared as multisets — which is the only coverage here that nobody hand-wrote. Nine hand-written
tests caught the rest; the differential fuzzer generates no chain of this depth
([[engine-corpus-nested-fuzzer-gap]]).

## 305. The clause spelling of a long-chain gate in TS — 112x, and the oracle that had to go first

Item 304's recorded follow-up, and the symmetric half of what that item found in native. Item 303
gave the TS sweep an inline constraint at every position, and `inlineOf` is reached from the
PATTERN NODE — so the identical question spelled as a clause `WHERE` never got there and declined
the whole count family. Measured on `bun run bench:gate`, 20,000 vertices of degree 3, a five-hop
chain, the same gate at position 2, three alternated rounds:

| spelling                | ts before |    ts after |  won | native (304) |
| ----------------------- | --------: | ----------: | ---: | -----------: |
| inline `{k: 1}`         |   33.9 ms |     37.9 ms |    — |      0.90 ms |
| clause `WHERE n2.k = 1` | 4708.2 ms | **42.0 ms** | 112x |      0.90 ms |
| flipped `1 = n2.k`      | 4890.2 ms |     35.4 ms | 138x |      0.90 ms |
| label `(n2:H)`          |   45.4 ms |     70.0 ms |    — |      1.10 ms |

A clause `WHERE` is now SPLIT into its conjuncts, each bucketed by the ONE node variable it reads,
and applied at that position — the same pushdown item 304 did in native, with the same consequence
that a conjunction naming several positions becomes several gates rather than a decline. A position
reached by both spellings conjoins them as AST before compiling, so it still carries exactly ONE
compiled predicate and the sweep's hot loop is untouched; an array of predicates per position would
put a loop inside the per-vertex branch, which is the cost this file has measured five times
([[ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing]]).

### The ORACLE had to be replaced before the feature could be written

This is the part worth keeping. `long-chain-count.test.ts`'s 33 tests compared the sweep's
`count(*)` against the same query plus an always-true clause `WHERE a.i >= 0`. That predicate was
chosen at item 298 **precisely because a clause predicate over four or more segments declined the
whole family**, which is what forced the general matcher and made it an independent route.

This item teaches the sweep exactly that shape. So the oracle would have silently become the sweep
compared against itself — **33 tests passing by agreeing with the thing they test**, with no
failure anywhere to say so. It is now an ENUMERATION: project a column and count the rows, which
no count shortcut can answer because `detectCountShortcut` requires `count(*)`. That is what the
Rust twin has always used, which is the hint that an enumeration is the DURABLE oracle and a
declining predicate is a borrowed one.

The swap was made first and all 33 tests re-run GREEN before any feature code existed, so the two
oracles are known to agree on every case rather than assumed to.

**A route-forcing oracle has a lifetime, and it ends when you teach the route it relied on
declining.** Worth checking against the other borrowed oracles in this family: `count(x.k)` versus
`count(*)` (still fine — one skips nulls), a bound edge variable, and an undirected hop.

### What it still declines, each asserted by ANSWER

- A **CORRELATION** (`a.i <= f.i`, 100): a per-vertex gate cannot see both ends. The `=` spelling
  answers 0 over this fixture, so the `<=` one carries the discriminator — an oracle that agrees
  on nothing agrees about nothing (item 303).
- A **DISJUNCTION** across two positions (195 against the plain 204).
- A **CONSTANT** (`WHERE 1 = 1`): it reads no name, so there is no position to put it at.

A presence test (`b.s IS NOT NULL`, 102) IS a gate here, unlike native, which needs a leaf form per
test: a TS gate runs the general path's own `satisfies`, so any single-node predicate is
expressible. `s` is on even vertices only so that case decides something — the fixture gained that
property for this item, because every vertex carries `i` and `i IS NOT NULL` would have been
another always-true test.

### Mutation — 11, 9 CAUGHT, and a PAIR that is the actual result

| mutant                                                   | result             |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| M1 an unplaceable conjunct is dropped, not declined      | CAUGHT (1 failing) |
| M2 every conjunct is bucketed under the FIRST name seen  | **SURVIVED**       |
| M3 `gateFor` never looks the clause conjuncts up         | CAUGHT (7)         |
| M4 the node's own inline `WHERE` is dropped              | CAUGHT (1)         |
| M5 the node's inline PROPERTIES are dropped              | CAUGHT (1)         |
| M6 `gateWith`'s free-variable check is removed           | **SURVIVED**       |
| M7 the `and` flattening keeps only the first item        | CAUGHT (2)         |
| M8 the dispatch never passes the split gates on          | CAUGHT (7)         |
| M9 a declined split is carried as "no gates"             | CAUGHT (1)         |
| M10 a position's several conjuncts collapse to the first | CAUGHT (1)         |
| **M11 = M2 AND M6 together**                             | **CAUGHT (2)**     |

M2 and M6 survive ALONE and their pair is caught, and that is a result rather than two gaps:

- **M2 is a perf-only mutant.** It mis-buckets a conjunct; `gateWith`'s free-variable check then
  refuses the mis-bucketed gate and the whole pattern DECLINES. A slow right answer, which no
  correctness test can catch by construction.
- **M6 can never fire under correct bucketing**, so removing it changes nothing on its own.
- Together they are a wrong answer.

So neither survivor meant dead code, and neither individual run could tell. **When a guard
duplicates a check its caller already makes, mutate BOTH — what is being measured is whether it is
a second line of defence.** Contrast item 303's memo, where two survivors on one mechanism did mean
it was not correctness-bearing; the distinction is whether the mutants attack one mechanism or two
layers of it.

M4, M5 and M10 were all caught only after tests were ADDED for shapes nothing reached: two clause
conjuncts on one position (34), and an inline `(b WHERE b.i > 5)` with a clause `WHERE b.i < 10`
over it (34, against 157 for the inline half alone). The first draft's tests had at most one
conjunct per position.

`bun run bench`, three alternated rounds, **rebuilt between every side** because `@lenke/*` resolves
to the built dist. The new code is unreachable from every row — the split only happens for four or
more segments with a clause `WHERE`, and no row here has four segments — so this is purely the
module-size control, which [[ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing]] has earned five times.

**32 ts rows at >=1.0ms: median 1.022, 20/32 within +/-5%, and nothing outside 10% AGAINST the
change.** The five rows above 1.10 all favour it (`encode ndjson` 1.210, `encode pg-text` 1.178,
`query: count distinct` 1.138, `query: top groups by count` 1.118, `query: select group + having`
1.103), which is not a claim I am making — it is what a 2% median drift looks like at this bench's
noise floor.

The two worst readings are 0.943 (`decode pg-text`) and 0.945 (`encode graphson`), both codec rows
no count shortcut can reach. `encode graphson` moved **+15.7% on its FFI column** in the same
rounds and `encode ndjson` +11.1%, and the FFI column runs Rust — which a TypeScript edit inside

of the change, which is what bounds every other row here.

`query: count distinct` reads 1.138 FASTER, which is the row three previous items flagged as a

## 306. The cliff MOVED to three hops, and the two engines disagree about two

Items 303, 304 and 305 gave both sweeps a gate at every position and both spellings of it. They did
not close this family's cliff; they moved it. The question item 290 asked about the four-segment
product — _"did it FIX the cliff or MOVE it?"_ — is the right question to keep asking, so I asked
it again, by pricing every depth from one to five hops with the gate at the LAST position and at an
interior one, in both engines at once:

| hops | ts ungated | ts gate at END | native ungated | native gate at END |
| ---- | ---------: | -------------: | -------------: | -----------------: |
| 1    |     0.0 ms |         2.4 ms |        0.07 ms |            0.08 ms |
| 2    |     2.9 ms |         7.5 ms |        0.21 ms |            1.12 ms |
| 3    |    19.5 ms |   **668.3 ms** |        0.32 ms |        **4.21 ms** |
| 4    |    46.9 ms |        72.1 ms |        0.41 ms |            0.95 ms |
| 5    |    45.0 ms |        78.0 ms |        0.53 ms |            1.04 ms |

Four and five hops are the sweep. THREE is the cliff, in both engines, and only at the END: an
interior gate at three hops reads 14.6ms / 1.21ms, which items 219 and 206 already route. The
reason is one sentence and it is the same sentence as item 303's: **a degree product answers its
last hop as a weighted sum of DEGREES, and a degree cannot say which of a vertex's edges land
somewhere that passes.** So an end constraint declines every product arm, and below four hops
nothing else picked it up — it enumerated.

The fix is routing, not mechanism: the sweep has carried an end constraint since item 303 (it gives
the last position a pass of its own). So the floor comes down for a GATED chain only.

| engine | shape                     |   before |   after |       won |
| ------ | ------------------------- | -------: | ------: | --------: |
| ts     | 3 hops, inline on the end | 668.3 ms | 45.9 ms | **14.6x** |
| ts     | 3 hops, clause on the end | 796.6 ms | 36.8 ms | **21.6x** |
| native | 3 hops, inline on the end |  4.21 ms | 0.81 ms |  **5.2x** |
| native | 3 hops, clause on the end |  4.13 ms | 0.82 ms |  **5.0x** |
| native | 3 hops, interior gate     |  1.21 ms | 0.74 ms |      1.6x |
| native | 2 hops, gate on the end   |  1.12 ms | 0.71 ms |      1.6x |

### The two engines DISAGREE at two hops, and that is the finding worth the item

The same structural change at two segments:

- **native: 1.12 -> 0.71 ms, 1.55x FASTER.** Taken.
- **TS: 7.5 -> 28.5 ms, 0.26x — 3.8x SLOWER.** Retracted, and the numbers are in the code.

The tuned two-hop arms are not the same arm in the two engines, so there was never a reason for one
measurement to predict the other — and a FLOOR (`hops >= 2 when gated`) would have shipped the TS
regression while the native half looked like proof it was fine. The rule is per-depth in each
engine instead:

- native: four or more always; three when ANY position is gated; two only when the END is.
- TS: three only, when the END is gated.

That is item 301's shape of answer for the third time in this family — **the crossover between a
sweep and a degree product has to be measured per depth, per engine, and per which position carries
the constraint.** Three times is enough to state it as the rule rather than the finding.

### `count 3-hop + end filter` is now a bench row

It was missing, which is how three consecutive items moved a cliff without seeing it: `bun run
bench` had `count 3-hop`, `count 3-hop + interior filter` and `count 2-hop + end filter`, and the
one shape that declines every arm was the gap between them. Added next to its neighbours with the
numbers in its comment.

### What the tests can and cannot say

The routing is a PERF claim: the products and the sweep return the same number, so no test can
assert which one answered. What the tests pin is that the sweep is EXACT at depths it never ran at,
where the extra pass for a gated last position and the `hops - 1` degree tail are one hop apart —
`a_gated_shallow_chain_matches_enumeration` walks one, two and three hops with the gate at every
position plus the clause spelling on the end (20/33/55 ungated; 4/5, 5/8/7, 9/11/12/13 gated;
9/14/24 for the clause), each against its own enumeration. The TS side adds four tests at three
segments, including a mixed-direction chain and a correlation that must still decline.

The 304 and 305 mutant sets were re-run against the new depths, to check that lowering the floor
did not open a hole the old fixtures could not see: the native set is 14 of 15 caught again (N15 is
the deliberate equivalent one), and with MORE failing tests per mutant than before — N1 went from
13 to 16, N8 from 14 to 17 — because the shallow fixtures are extra places for a mis-attributed way
count to show. The TS set is 9 of 11, the same two individual survivors with their pair caught.

**One new mutant, and it found a real gap.** M12 carries a DECLINED split as "no gates" instead of

## 307. The same question, one position over: a START-gated three-segment chain in TS — 7.4x

Item 306's own question, asked immediately rather than left for later: it routed the END at three
segments, so which POSITION still costs? Priced every one of them at both shallow depths, both
engines, 20,000 vertices of degree 3:

| shape                   |          ts | native | ts/native |
| ----------------------- | ----------: | -----: | --------: |
| 3 segs, ungated         |      16.3ms | 0.31ms |       53x |
| 3 segs, inline at 0     | **141.3ms** | 0.34ms |  **415x** |
| 3 segs, clause at 0     |     137.0ms | 0.33ms |      415x |
| 3 segs, gate at 1       |       8.1ms | 0.70ms |       12x |
| 3 segs, gate at 2       |      19.1ms | 0.73ms |       26x |
| 3 segs, gate at 3 (end) |      35.4ms | 0.78ms |       45x |
| 2 segs, gate at 0       |       7.9ms | 0.12ms |       66x |
| 2 segs, gate at 1       |       1.5ms | 0.52ms |      0.3x |
| 2 segs, gate at 2 (end) |       7.4ms | 0.76ms |       10x |

**The START at three segments was still enumerating.** Item 306 gave that depth a route only when
the END was constrained, and nothing else in the family takes a start gate at three segments —
`inStart` is computed for two segments or fewer, and `threeSegmentCount` carries an interior
predicate only. So the shape fell through every arm: 141.3ms for 540,000 walks is ~260ns a row,
which is the general matcher's rate, not a shortcut's.

Routing it to the sweep: **141.3 -> 19.2ms (7.4x)** inline, **137.0 -> 16.9ms (8.1x)** for the
clause spelling at 20,000 vertices, and **17.40x** on the new bench row at 200,000 (3214.1 ->
184.7ms, one case per process, min of 6 over three alternated rounds). It is now FASTER than the same chain unfiltered (12.8ms is the ungated reading in
the same round, so they are within noise of each other), which is what a seed-time gate should do:
the sweep seeds only the vertices that pass.

### The END or the START, never an interior alone — and the reason is a measurement

An interior gate at three segments reads **8.1ms against the ungated 16.3**: the gate makes the
degree product FASTER than its own unfiltered self, because the product iterates the MIDDLE and a
gate there shrinks what it iterates (item 219's whole argument). There is nothing for the sweep to
win, and routing it would have cost ~2x. So the condition is `gated(end) || gated(start)`, with the
interior left to the arm that already beats this one at it.

That is the per-POSITION half of the rule item 306 recorded, now with a case on both sides of it:
the end is the position no product can carry, the start is the position no arm at this depth
carried, and the interior is the position the product carries BETTER. One depth, three positions,
three different right answers.

### `count 3-hop + start filter` is now a bench row

Same reason as item 306's row: `count 2-hop + start filter` existed and `count 3-hop + start
filter` did not, so a 415x cross-engine gap sat between two rows that were both being watched. The
missing-row lesson twice in two items.

- interior filter` is 0.96.

### The one row that looked like a regression, and was not

`count 3-hop + end filter` read **0.82 with DISJOINT ranges** — control {786.5, 767.8, 792.8}

regression or a contamination with a name.

The tell was that **the row's own route did not change**: both sides take `endGatedChainCount` ->

runs immediately before it and spends **3.3 SECONDS in the general matcher on the control side
against 230ms on the new one**, so the control's end-filter row is measured on a warmed path.

That is exactly the contamination item 290 recorded for `3 hop, count(d.k)`: **a large speedup can
make its NEIGHBOUR look slower, and disjoint ranges do not save you, because the contamination is
systematic rather than noisy.** One case per process, min of 9, three alternated rounds:

| row                        | control |   new |      ratio |
| -------------------------- | ------: | ----: | ---------: |
| count 3-hop + end filter   |   728.1 | 723.7 |      1.006 |
| count 3-hop + start filter |  3214.1 | 184.7 | **17.40x** |
| count 3-hop (the control)  |   396.7 | 389.0 |       1.02 |

Fully overlapping on the end row. And the win is LARGER in isolation than in the sweep (17.40x
against 14.49x), for the same reason in reverse: in the multi-case run the new side's start-filter

since the arms below answer it correctly, so it must survive; it is in the set to keep the
distinction between "not covered" and "cannot differ" visible rather than assumed, the same job
N15 does in the native set.

Routing is a perf claim, and that is the honest limit here: no test can assert which arm answered.
What the tests pin is the ANSWER at the newly-routed shapes — 84 ungated, 4 and 65 for the two
spellings of a start gate, 48 with an interior alongside it, 70 on a mixed-direction chain, and 28

- **2 segments, gate on the END: ts 7.4ms, native 0.76.** Item 306 retracted routing this with its

  route READS THE PATTERN BACKWARDS (`reversedTwoHop`), so the gated end becomes the walk's start
  and the predicate is already evaluated once per distinct vertex — over the SELECTIVE set, where
  the sweep seeds everything and interns every vertex it reaches. That is why the sweep loses at
  two hops and wins at three: at three there was no reversed route to lose to.

## 308. Read an END-gated chain BACKWARDS, so its gate seeds — 3.78x

Item 307's recorded follow-up, and the diagnosis it left: the two-segment arm answers an end gate
by reading the pattern backwards (`reversedTwoHop`), which is why the sweep lost to it at that
depth — the existing route walks from the SELECTIVE set while the sweep seeds everything. The sweep
can do the same thing at any depth.

A gate on the LAST position costs twice. It needs a pass of its own (item 303), and every pass
before that one runs over an unnarrowed frontier because nothing has seeded selectively. A gate on
the FIRST position costs neither: it narrows the seed, and the degree tail answers the end. Same
chain, same gate, different position, 20,000 vertices of degree 3:

| gate at |      ts |  native |
| ------- | ------: | ------: |
| 0       | 19.2 ms | 0.29 ms |
| the end | 41.7 ms | 0.80 ms |

So a chain whose last position is gated and whose first is not is walked backwards. **A
fixed-length chain read backwards is the same multiset of walks**, so the count is identical — this
is `reversedTwoHop`'s argument with the depth generalized — and the label seek survives it, because
`candidateVertexSource` takes whichever end becomes the start.

| measurement                                  |  before |   after |       won |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------: | ------: | --------: |
| `count 3-hop + end filter`, ISOLATED (min 9) | 728.1ms | 192.7ms | **3.78x** |
| 3 segments, inline gate on the end (20k)     |  41.7ms |  19.8ms |     2.11x |
| 3 segments, clause gate on the end (20k)     |  33.5ms |  16.3ms |     2.05x |
| 5 hops, gate on the last position (20k)      |  58.8ms |  45.6ms |     1.29x |

192.7ms is the number to look at twice: the start-gated version of the same row reads 184.7ms
(item 307), and after this item the end-gated one is **the same shape**, so they land together.
That is the check that the reversal did what it claimed rather than merely getting faster.

### What a reversal breaks, and the tests that look for it

The reversal is INDEX ARITHMETIC over three parallel sequences, so the failure modes are
subscripts, and every one of them returns a plausible number. The forward tests cannot see any of
them. Three new tests, each with an ungated twin so the gate is known to have done something:

- **per-hop EDGE TYPES** must reverse with the hops (`-[:E]->()-[:F]->()-[:E]->()-[:F]->(e {i: 7})`,
  2 against the ungated 60),
- **per-hop DIRECTIONS** must each flip (`-[:E]->()<-[:F]-()-[:E]->()<-[:F]-(e {i: 7})`, 4 against
  66),
- **the ENDS swap**, so each label follows its own node: an interior `(b:A)` must stay on its
  position (30), and the START's `(a:A)` becomes the LAST position's — it stops being the seed's
  label and becomes a per-vertex test (33).

Plus: BOTH ends gated is NOT reversed, since the extra pass is unavoidable either way, asserted by
answer (80).

### Mutation — 6 of 6 correctness mutants caught, and one that CANNOT be

| mutant                                         | result              |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| R2 the direction is not flipped                | CAUGHT (14 failing) |
| R3 off-by-one in the reversed hop index        | CAUGHT (17)         |
| R4 the LABEL is read from the forward position | CAUGHT (1)          |
| R5 the GATE is read from the forward position  | CAUGHT (14)         |
| R6 the SEED stays at position 0                | CAUGHT (14)         |
| R7 the edge TYPES are not reversed             | CAUGHT (2)          |
| R8 the flip CONDITION is inverted              | **SURVIVED, must**  |

**R8 cannot be caught and that is the point.** Whether the chain is reversed at all is a PERF
decision: backwards is the same multiset of walks, so an inverted condition returns the identical
number and only the time moves. It is in the set so that "no test covers this" stays
distinguishable from "no test can", the same job N15 does in the native set and M13 in item 307's.

R4 is caught by exactly ONE test — the `(a:A)` end-gated case written for this item. Without it the
label would have followed the wrong position whenever an end-gated chain had a label on its start,
which is a silent wrong answer.

**The same reversal in NATIVE**, priced at 2.5x by the table above (0.80 against 0.29 at three

base label and demote the old one to a leaf, with the no-label case measured on both sides of

## 309. The same reversal in NATIVE — 3.60x and 3.76x, and four survivors that were not missing tests

Item 308's recorded follow-up. The mechanism is 308's and is not re-argued: a gate on the LAST
position needs a pass of its own AND runs every earlier pass over an unnarrowed frontier, where a
gate on the FIRST narrows the seed and the degree tail answers the end — so an end-gated chain
whose start is ungated is read backwards, and a fixed-length chain reversed is the same multiset of
walks.

ISOLATED bench rows (`BENCH_ONLY`, one case per process, min of 9, three alternated rounds). The ts
column is a free noise calibrator here, since a `fastpath.rs` edit cannot reach the pure-TS engine:

| row                           | ffi CTL | ffi NEW |       ffi | ts CTL | ts NEW |
| ----------------------------- | ------: | ------: | --------: | -----: | -----: |
| **count 3-hop + end filter**  |    14.4 |     4.0 | **3.60x** |  193.7 |  192.0 |
| count 3-hop + start filter    |     4.0 |     4.0 |      1.00 |  187.6 |  187.3 |
| count 3-hop + interior filter |    11.8 |    11.7 |      1.01 |  124.9 |  128.6 |
| count 3-hop (ungated)         |     4.9 |     4.8 |      1.02 |  374.3 |  369.5 |

**4.0 against the start-gated row's 4.0** is the check that matters: after this item those two are
the same shape, so they land together — exactly as 308's 190.9 landed on its 183.1. The broad
sweep also caught one the isolated set did not ask for: `count 2-hop + end filter` **12.4 -> 3.3,
3.76x**, because item 306's rule routes two hops to the sweep precisely when the END is gated,
which is the case this reverses.

### The GUARD is the item, and it is measured

Native's forward seed is `nodes_with_label(base_label)`, an index bucket, where a reversed seed is a
full live-node scan. So reversing can LOSE a selective seek, and an unguarded flip does. 200,000
vertices at five edges, a three-hop chain with an end gate, min of 7, three label densities over
one graph shape:

| seed bucket    |  forward | unguarded flip |              |
| -------------- | -------: | -------------: | ------------ |
| 1% (2,000)     |  3.21 ms |       20.05 ms | 6.2x WORSE   |
| 10% (20,000)   | 10.66 ms |       23.02 ms | 2.2x WORSE   |
| 100% (200,000) | 12.62 ms |       10.28 ms | 1.23x better |

So the flip is taken only when there is no seek to lose: no base label, or one every LIVE node
carries — and then the label is DROPPED rather than carried, which gives the pass count back too.
With the guard, re-measured on the same probe, three alternated rounds:

| seed bucket | control | guarded flip |           | answers |
| ----------- | ------: | -----------: | --------: | ------- |
| 1%          | 3.21 ms |      3.18 ms |     1.01x | equal   |
| 10%         | 10.63ms |     10.59 ms |     1.00x | equal   |
| 100%        | 12.59ms |  **5.23 ms** | **2.41x** | equal   |

The 100% case is better than the unguarded flip's 10.28 was, because dropping a vacuous label is
worth more than demoting it.

**`len() == live_node_count()` is the test, and it rests on an invariant worth naming.** A first
draft used `node_count()` and justified it by claiming a bucket could list a deleted node while
missing a live one, so the two counts might agree by coincidence. **That is false:**
`delete_node` RETAINS the id out of its label buckets (documented at `is_labeled`, which
binary-searches the bucket). So a bucket holds only live nodes, `|bucket| == |live|` forces
`bucket == live`, and the live count is both sound and strictly TIGHTER — `node_count()` stops
firing the moment anything is deleted. `a_deleted_node_leaves_its_label_bucket` pins the invariant
directly, because if it ever stopped holding this would drop a label test that can fail and the
answer would be a silent superset.

### Four mutants survived the first run, and not one of them was a missing test

| mutant                                              | first run  | now                 |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------------- |
| Q1 the hops reverse but their DIRECTIONS do not     | CAUGHT     | CAUGHT (15)         |
| Q2 the hops reverse but the GATES do not            | CAUGHT     | CAUGHT (15)         |
| Q3 the gates reverse but the HOPS do not            | CAUGHT     | CAUGHT (4)          |
| Q4 the demoted label is pushed at the SEED position | SURVIVED   | **deleted**         |
| Q5 the promoted label is left in the gate too       | no compile | **deleted**         |
| Q6 a MULTI-label test is promoted as if single      | SURVIVED   | CAUGHT (2)          |
| Q7 the flip CONDITION is inverted                   | SURVIVED   | SURVIVED, must      |
| Q8 the universality guard is dropped                | SURVIVED   | CAUGHT (5)          |
| Q9 universality tested against the SLOT count       | SURVIVED   | SURVIVED, perf-only |

- **Q4 survived because its code could not run.** The "demote the old base label to a gate at the
  far end" branch is unreachable: the guard only flips when there is nothing to carry. **The right
  answer to a surviving mutant on unreachable code is to delete the code**, which is what happened
  — and it is a better outcome than the test I would otherwise have gone looking for.
- **Q9 survived because my own justification was wrong**, which is recorded above. It is now a
  deliberate perf-only survivor: the slot-count test is sound too, just weaker.
- **Q6 survived because the test named after it never reached the code.** GQL cannot express a
  multi-label gate (`(n:A|N)` lowers to an `Or`, which the gate declines), so it had to be a
  Gremlin `hasLabel('A','N')` — and **a chain whose only filter is a label never reaches this arm
  at all**, because `chain_width` sees through an `IsLabeled` filter and an earlier arm answers it,
  at three hops and at five. I found that by instrumenting the arm with an `eprintln!`, not by
  reasoning: the first version of the test asserted correct answers for queries that went
  somewhere else entirely, which is a test that checks nothing while being believed. Adding
  `has('k',0)` on an interior position makes the earlier arms decline and this one reply, and then
  Q6 is caught.
- **Q7 cannot be caught** and stays in the set so that "no test covers this" remains
  distinguishable from "no test can": whether to flip is a perf decision, since backwards is the
  same count.

Five of seven caught, the two survivors by construction. Nine tests, including per-hop types and
directions reversing, each label following its own node, the universality guard on both sides of
its threshold, the bucket-on-delete invariant, and the multi-label promotion.

## 310. Two refutations on the widest row in the bench, and a control that moved with the target

After item 309 the single widest cross-engine ratio in `bun run bench` is `count 3-hop`: **ts
401.6ms against native's 4.8, an 84x gap** on a shape that is already shortcut in both engines.
Every other row sits in this engine's usual 1.5-4x band, so 84x is the outlier worth asking about.
This item asks, twice, and ships neither answer.

### Refutation 1: the sweep does NOT win at three segments, even at ten times item 301's size

Item 301 chose the degree product over the sweep for a three-segment chain on a 1.50x measurement
**taken at 20,000 vertices** — and the repo's own rule says cache-resident and not are different
questions, with the transition between 200k and 1M. The sweep's per-edge cost also looked cheaper
than the product's from item 308's numbers (192ms for three gated passes over 1M edges against the
product's 401 for one), which predicted an inversion at scale.

It does not invert. Routing every three-segment chain to the sweep, 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000
edges, one case per process, min of 9:

| row                           | product | the sweep |             |
| ----------------------------- | ------: | --------: | ----------- |
| count 3-hop (ungated)         | 401.6ms |   534.7ms | 1.33x WORSE |
| count 3-hop + interior filter | 130.7ms |   433.1ms | 3.31x WORSE |

So the verdict holds at 10x the size, slightly narrower (1.33x against 1.50x) and nowhere near
inverting. The reason the per-edge arithmetic misled me: the product makes ONE pass over the edges
and multiplies two degrees, where the sweep makes three — comparing per-edge costs without
comparing pass counts is comparing the wrong thing. And an interior gate WIDENS the gap rather
than closing it, because the gate shrinks exactly what the product iterates (item 219's argument,
now measured from the other side). Recorded next to the routing it would have changed.

### Refutation 2: the degree memo, killed by its own control

If the cost is two hash lookups per middle edge, memoizing the d-side degree per `c` should remove
most of one: each `c` is reached by ~5 middle edges, so the repeats become a single `Map.get`
instead of `side`'s lookup plus a type-bucket lookup plus a size read. First isolated reading was
**1.07x** — small, but this bench resolves that when one case runs per process.

Three alternated rounds, one case per process, min of 9:

| row                                               | control |   new | ratio | ranges   |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------: | ----: | ----: | -------- |
| `count 3-hop` (the target)                        |   394.7 | 371.4 | 1.063 | DISJOINT |
| `count 3-hop + interior filter` (cannot reach it) |   131.9 | 125.4 | 1.052 | DISJOINT |

**The control the change cannot reach moved as far as the target.** The interior row takes the
`needsC` branch, which the memo does not touch at all, and it gained 5.2% while the target gained
6.3% — so the memo is worth 1.01x at most. Both readings have disjoint ranges over three rounds,
which is the standard this file applies, and both are still noise.

That is item 300's lesson with the sharper instrument: there it was _"disjoint ranges over three
rounds are not proof when the whole SIDE moves"_, and here it is **not proof when the change's own
UNREACHABLE CONTROL moves with it.** The fix that makes this detectable at all is one case per
process — in a multi-case run both rows would have moved together for a different reason (item
307's neighbour contamination) and the conclusion would have been the same by luck rather than by
evidence.

### What the two experiments bought: the diagnosis

The 84x is **not** one hash per edge, which is why neither route fixes it. It is spread across the
`edgesOfTypes` generator frame (item 300 priced a generator at 1.19x on the sweep), the `Edge`
property reads, and two hash lookups — and no single micro moves a cost that is spread. It is the
CSR item 300 already recorded as the real floor: _"a CSR of dense slots, no hash an edge"_ measured
**7.30x** there, and was declined because it needs a dense adjacency the TS graph does not expose.

So `count 3-hop`'s 84x is now a DATA-LAYOUT target with a priced ceiling, not an unexplained
outlier, and the two cheap answers are refuted in the code with their numbers.

### The one keeper: `BENCH_ONLY` gets an exact-match form

`count 3-hop` is a substring of `count 3-hop + end filter` and two other rows, so there was no
substring that selected it alone — the isolation flag item 307 added could not isolate the very row
this item needed. A trailing `$` makes it exact. Both refutations above depend on it.

## 311. Where the 32x in `traverse 1-hop + filter` actually is — the predicate is 9% of it

With `query: project 3 columns` settled at item 289 (the JSON carrier, not execution) and
`count 3-hop` settled at item 310 (a data-layout floor), the widest unexplained ratio left in
`bun run bench` is **`traverse 1-hop + filter`: ts 48.0ms against native's 1.5, 32x** — and unlike
the projection rows it returns ONE row, so none of it is the carrier:

```
MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE x.age > 45 RETURN count(*) AS c
```

The planner reaches the right shape. `(a:Person)` is vacuous on this fixture so `effectiveLabel`
elides it, which lets `farWalkFits` route to `farOnlyHopCount` — the far-side drive that gates each
far vertex ONCE and adds its in-degree, rather than walking a million edges. The order is already
cheapest-first (the degree is read only for vertices the predicate keeps). So the question is not
which arm answers it, and that is what makes the decomposition worth recording.

200,000 vertices, 1,000,000 `KNOWS` edges, min of 7, one process:

| measurement                                       |       ms | what it isolates                   |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------: | ---------------------------------- |
| `count(*)`, no filter                             |     0.00 | a bucket SIZE, O(1)                |
| **the bench row** (`> 45`, 20% pass)              |    49.65 | everything                         |
| **`> 1000` — NOTHING passes**                     | **4.39** | **the per-vertex machinery alone** |
| `> -1` — EVERYTHING passes (200k degree lookups)  |    93.11 | the machinery + every lookup       |
| inline equality `{age: 45}` (11k pass)            |     6.37 | item 230's lifted `=` path         |
| clause equality `x.age = 45`                      |     7.30 | the same question, other spelling  |
| by hand: the predicate only, no degree            |     2.19 | the comparison itself              |
| by hand: the in-degree only, no predicate (200k)  |    35.78 | the adjacency lookups alone        |
| by hand: both, predicate first (40k lookups)      |    20.10 | the whole algorithm, no engine     |
| engine-SHAPED by hand: + a binding write and read |    25.61 | the binding costs 5.5ms            |
| engine-SHAPED by hand: + a try/catch in the loop  |    26.17 | try/catch costs **0.56ms**         |

**The `> 1000` row is the one that settles it: 4.39ms.** The predicate machinery — the compiled
expression tree, the binding write, `asTruth`, `matchesLabel`, the candidate-source generator — is
**9% of the row**, 22ns per vertex. Everything else is `index.get(v.id)` then `.get(type).size`:
two Map lookups, one string-keyed, at **445ns per vertex when every vertex passes and ~1100ns when
the passing set is strided**, which is cache behaviour and not arithmetic.

### Three suspects priced OUT of contention, and one refuted outright

- **The binding**, which item 230 measured at 29.0ns against a direct read's 17.2 on the node
  tally: 5.5ms of 49.65 here. Real, and 11%.
- **The `try/catch` in the loop body**, which looks like it should inhibit optimization: **0.56ms**.
  Folklore, priced.
- **The candidate source** (`verticesById.values()` rather than a label bucket): 3.8ms, and in the
  direction that makes the bucket the slower of the two for this shape.
- ~~**`degreeOfTypes` is missing the single-type fast path its sibling `bucketSize` has**~~ —
  **REFUTED.** It really is missing it (`bucketSize` returns `byType.get(types[0])?.size` for one
  named type; `degreeOfTypes` runs a `for...of` over the one-element array), and this helper is
  called once per vertex by both one-hop walks, so it looked like a free rung. Three alternated
  rounds, one case per process, min of 9: control {49.1, 47.4, 45.9} against {49.3, 48.6, 43.3} —
  **completely interleaved.** V8 does not charge for an iterator over a one-element array, the same
  way it does not charge for the try/catch. Not taken.

### What this leaves

The floor for this row with this data layout is the hand-written **20.10ms** — same algorithm, no
engine — against native's 1.5ms. So the 32x decomposes as roughly 2.5x of engine overhead above a
13x data-layout floor, and the floor is the same one item 310 reached from the other direction: a
CSR of dense slots, priced at **7.30x** by item 300 and declined there for needing a dense
adjacency the TS graph does not expose. **Two independent rows now point at the same structural
target**, which is a better argument for it than either row alone.

The 2.5x of engine overhead above that floor is NOT accounted for by the three suspects above
(5.5 + 0.56 + 0 ≈ 6ms of ~25), and finding the rest needs a profile rather than another
hypothesis — so it is recorded as open with what is already ruled out, which is the point of
writing the table down.

One spelling note in passing: the inline `{age: 45}` reads 6.37ms against the clause `x.age = 45`
at 7.30 — a 1.15x gap on the lifted-equality path, far below this family's historical gaps (item
125's 4x, item 222's 13.3x) but the same shape of difference, and now measured rather than
assumed.

## 312. Where the 2.9 SECONDS of `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)` go — and the recorded target was the wrong one

The largest ABSOLUTE row in `bun run bench` is `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)`: **ts 2784ms against
native's 766**. Memory has carried its diagnosis for several items as _"JSON.parse + alloc + freeze,
and 73% of the codec gaps too — ONE target = `addVertex`"_. Decomposed against the same bytes,
200,000 nodes and 1,000,000 edges:

| stage                                   |     ms | share |
| --------------------------------------- | -----: | ----: |
| the whole `deserialize` (the bench row) | 2914.7 |  100% |
| `split('\n')` only                      |   19.5 |  0.7% |
| `split` + `JSON.parse` every line       |  546.6 |   19% |
| `addVertex` only, 200k, pre-parsed      |  216.7 |  7.4% |
| `addVertex` + `addEdge`, pre-parsed     | 3190.2 |     — |

**`addEdge` is ~2.9µs per edge and about 85% of the row.** `JSON.parse` is 19% and `addVertex` is
7.4%, so the recorded target was the wrong one — not wrong about `addVertex` being slow (1.08µs a
vertex is slow), wrong about which operation the ingest is made of. A 5:1 edge:node fixture is five
edge writes per vertex write, which is the repo's own "match the fixture to the claim" rule read
from the other end.

It is LINEAR, which had to be checked before anything else: 2864 / 3305 / 3009 / 2888 ns per edge
at 50k / 200k / 500k / 1M edges over 200k vertices. A constant factor, not an algorithmic bug.

### Inside `addEdge`, by ablation

The cheap prefix first, measured externally: the duplicate-id early return — which runs
`validateElementNames` and one `getEdgeById` — is **43ns**, and `validateLabel` +
`validatePropertyKey` together are **2ns**. The pair of `getVertexById` calls that re-resolve
endpoints the caller already holds as objects: **43ns**. So 97% is `new Edge(...)` plus
`insertEdge`.

Ablating `insertEdge` one stage at a time, **alternated, three rounds, min of each** (the first
pass was single-shot against a probe whose baseline spans 2780-3153, which decided nothing — and
the conclusion survived the better instrument, but it could not have been claimed from the first):

| variant                    | min of 3 |           saves |
| -------------------------- | -------: | --------------: |
| BASELINE                   |     2855 |               — |
| no label index             |     2045 | **810ns (28%)** |
| no `@graph/EdgeAdded` emit |     2282 | **573ns (20%)** |
| no `edgesById.set`         |     2573 |     282ns (10%) |
| no cardinality gate        |     2922 |               0 |
| no property-index add      |     2885 |               0 |
| no undo closure            |     2761 |           ~20ns |

The undo closure is worth naming because it looked like a certainty and is not: `recordUndo` is a
no-op outside a transaction, so the closure and its captured id are ALLOCATED per edge for nothing
— item 140's own lesson (_"an argument is evaluated whether or not the body does anything with
it"_) at a call site that still has it. It costs **~20ns**, 0.7%. Not worth the guard.

### The emission costs ~500ns and NEITHER obvious explanation survives

Splitting it, alternated three rounds:

| variant                                    | min of 3 |     saves |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------: | --------: |
| BASELINE                                   |     2809 |         — |
| allocate the event, skip the dispatch      |     2290 | **519ns** |
| skip the allocation, dispatch a reused one |     2843 |        ~0 |

So removing the dispatch is worth the whole 500ns and removing the allocation is worth nothing —
which does not add up, since the first variant removes the allocation too (V8 can sink a
`void new X()` whose constructor only writes its own fields). Two readings that cannot both be
explained by allocation OR by dispatch.

And the concrete fix the split suggested is **REFUTED**: `Emitter.emit` allocates its
subscribe-safe snapshot _before_ checking whether anyone is subscribed — `new Set(undefined)` for a
missing key, `new Set(empty)` once the last listener unsubscribes — so a write-heavy path allocates
one empty Set per emit to iterate nothing. An early return there, alternated three rounds:
control {2791, 2965, 2774} against {2830, 2804, 2876}, **interleaved**. No effect. The allocation
is real, free, and not the 500ns.

So the emission's 500ns is a measured fact with no mechanism I can name from ablation, and settling
it needs a profile. Recorded as open WITH the two refutations, so the next attempt starts after
them rather than at them.

### The 28% lever, and the third row pointing at one structural target

`indexEdgeLabel` does, per edge: `edgesByLabel.get(label)` + a Set add; `edgesFromByLabel.get(fromId)`

- an inner `Map.get(label)` + a Set add; and the same three for `toId`. **Seven hash operations,
  five of them string-keyed, plus up to three Map/Set allocations the first time a vertex or label is
  seen** — 810ns across seven operations is ~115ns each, which is the string-hash cost at a million
  entries.

That is the same floor items 310 and 311 reached from two other directions:

| item | row                             | what dominates                                   |
| ---- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| 310  | `count 3-hop` (84x)             | two hashes per middle edge in the degree product |
| 311  | `traverse 1-hop + filter` (32x) | `index.get(id).get(type).size` per vertex        |
| 312  | `decode ndjson` (3.6x)          | seven hashes per edge in the label index         |

**Three independent rows, one structural answer**: dense slots instead of string-keyed Maps — item
300's CSR, priced at **7.30x** there and declined for needing a dense adjacency the TS graph does
not expose. The insert side is the one place where it is NOT blocked by `edge.to` costing a lookup:
`addEdge` already HOLDS both endpoint Vertex objects. Reading the adjacency back is what needs the
layout change.

## 313. The emission's missing mechanism — two listeners nobody asked for, and the row it is not in

Item 312 left the `@graph/EdgeAdded` emission as a **measured fact with no mechanism**: 573ns an
edge, removing the dispatch saved all of it, removing the allocation saved nothing, and an early
return in `Emitter.emit` for the no-listener case was refuted over three alternated rounds. It was
recorded open "needs a profile, not another ablation hypothesis".

It needed neither. The early return did nothing because **the listener set is never empty.**
`Graph`'s own constructor subscribes **two** listeners to each of the sixteen mutation event types
(`Graph.ts:1001`), so per write, with no user listener anywhere:

```
new EmitterEvent('@graph/EdgeAdded', edge)
  -> Graph.emit -> Emitter.emit -> new Set(2 listeners) -> 2 try/catch dispatches
       markMutated: tokensOf() = 3 array allocations, a `doTheWork` closure, ONE queueMicrotask
       onMutate:    new EmitterEvent('@graph/mutate', { original }) = 2 more allocations
                      -> Graph.emit -> Emitter.emit -> new Set(0) -> dispatch to nobody
```

Roughly seven allocations, two Set constructions and a microtask enqueue per write, to reach zero
observers. `@graph/mutate` is a re-emission of an event that has already been dispatched — it
exists so a caller can subscribe once instead of sixteen times — and **nothing in the repo
subscribes to it outside one test** (`Graph.test.ts:447`).

Two changes, each with a mechanism named before it was measured:

1. **`markMutated` batches its deferred work.** It has to run synchronously only far enough to read
   the tokens off a still-live element; the counter update was already deferred. One microtask and
   one closure per BURST of writes instead of per write, accumulating into a pending array and a
   pending count. This is audit item 171's short-circuit one level up.
2. **`onMutate` skips building `@graph/mutate` when nobody is subscribed** (new
   `Emitter.hasListeners`).

### What each is worth

The whole-row instrument could not settle this and it is worth saying why rather than quietly
switching instruments: the edge-ingest loop read **2748-3578 ms for the same binary** across two
runs, the two candidates ordered differently in each, and a first single-shot reading put the
combined change at 2959 against a 2812 control — the wrong direction, inside the spread, deciding
nothing. Its first control was also placed AFTER the ingest, where it read 34/31/22 ms on the
control side against 17/18/18 on the candidate: a control that moved, for a reason downstream of
the change rather than independent of it (a million fewer retained closures means every later
allocation meets a cleaner heap). Anything measured after the writes inherits that, so the control
moved to the FRONT of the probe, before a graph exists.

So price the thing being changed. `Graph.emit` is public and the cascade under it is exactly what a
write triggers, so calling it in a loop against an already-built graph measures the cascade and
nothing else. Three alternated rounds, flat control, and `version` printed on every side as an
equivalence check rather than decoration — the batched drain must land on the same mutation count
as a microtask per write, or the timing is irrelevant (1,021,000 on all four sides):

| side                 | min of 3 |            saves |
| -------------------- | -------: | ---------------: |
| CONTROL              | 223.2 ns |                — |
| batched microtask    | 170.4 ns | **52.8ns (24%)** |
| `@graph/mutate` skip | 183.4 ns | **39.8ns (18%)** |
| both                 | 160.4 ns | **62.8ns (28%)** |

Both halves earn their place. Five rounds on the shipped form, both instruments, both controls flat
(180.2-183.1 and 345.8-348.2 ms):

| row                        | CONTROL min |   NEW min |      ratio |
| -------------------------- | ----------: | --------: | ---------: |
| the cascade, per emit      |    212.2 ns |  145.7 ns |  **1.46x** |
| the cascade plus its drain |    266.0 ns |  196.4 ns |      1.35x |
| 200,000 `addVertex`        |    279.4 ms |  238.5 ms |  **1.17x** |
| 1,000,000 `addEdge`        |   2783.9 ms | 2643.8 ms | **1.053x** |

The two row readings are fully disjoint across the five rounds (NEW's worst beats CONTROL's best),
which the earlier runs were not.

### CORRECTION to item 312: the emission is not in the `decode ndjson` row

The row this was aimed at **does not move**: `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)`, isolated one case per
process, four alternated rounds, ts min **2578.9 -> 2571.3 (1.003x)** — while its own native
control column moved 1.014x, further than the target.

Not a noise floor. `version` one microtask after a decode of 40,000 nodes and 200,000 edges is
**0**, with `eventsEnabled()` true: **not one of those 240,000 writes reaches the emitter.**
