`packages/serialization/src/ndjson/index.ts:173-201` wraps the whole load in `disableEvents()` /
`enableEvents()`, so `Emitter.emit` returns on `!this.enabled` and neither internal listener runs.

So item 312's table is valid for `addEdge` as an API call — which is what its probe measured — and
**invalid as a decomposition of that bench row, by the 20% the emission occupies in it.** The label
index (28%) and `edgesById.set` (10%) are in the row; the emission is not. Item 312 corrected its
predecessor for measuring the wrong operation and then attributed a probe's composition to a row;
the lesson is narrower than "match the fixture to the claim" — **a decomposition measured through a
different entry point than the row is a decomposition of the entry point.**

What the change does reach is every write made through the public API with events live: GQL and
Gremlin `INSERT`/`SET`, every host mutation, everything React sees. Bulk decode had already opted
out.

### Regressions

`bench:usage` is the serving counterpart and the row that matters is the interleaved write. Over
the whole table it showed nothing usable — ts medians 1.000x and 1.019x, but `write: append node`
read **0.738x on ts(-) and 1.569x on ts(+)**, the same row and the same change in opposite
directions, while the **native `wasm(-)` column, which no TypeScript change can reach, moved a
median 1.097x.** Every row there shares a warm graph and an allocator with the rows before it. So
`bench-usage.ts` gained the `BENCH_ONLY` selector `bench.ts` got at item 307 — and the row reads
130.0k isolated against 94.7k in the table, which is the instrument problem measured directly.

Isolated, three alternated rounds, `BENCH_BUDGET_MS=1500` (6x the default batch):

| column                              | CONTROL best | NEW best |
| ----------------------------------- | -----------: | -------: |
| ts(-)                               |       111.6k |   118.4k |
| ts(+)                               |       133.9k |   139.1k |
| engine(-) — the unreachable control |       352.1k |   353.1k |

No regression; marginally faster, within noise. At the default 250ms batch the same row was
bimodal and anti-correlated between its own two columns, summing to ~240k whichever way it split,
which is what the longer batch resolved.

### Teeth

`version` and `epoch(token)` are the public reactive surface — what `@lenke/react` polls to decide
whether to re-render — and had **no direct test**: the React tests cover them transitively, which
notices that reactivity is broken but not what the counters promise. Ten tests added
(`reactive-counters.test.ts`), all of which pass against the PRISTINE engine too, so they describe
the behaviour and not this implementation.

Nine mutants, under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0` because a drain
that re-queues itself is one edit away and an unbounded microtask chain neither allocates fast
enough to trip the cap nor terminates:

| mutant                                          | result                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| S1 `mutationVersion += pendingWrites` -> `+= 1` | caught (3)                                               |
| S2 the drain never clears its own flag          | caught (4)                                               |
| S3 `pendingTokens = []` -> `.length = 0`        | **SURVIVED — equivalent by design**                      |
| S4 deduplicate the burst's tokens through a Set | caught (2)                                               |
| S5 drop the `pendingWrites = 0` reset           | caught (2)                                               |
| S6 stop counting writes                         | caught (4)                                               |
| S7 never emit `@graph/mutate` at all            | caught (2)                                               |
| S8 `hasListeners` ignores an emptied bucket     | **SURVIVED — a lost optimization, never a wrong answer** |
| S9 never skip: always build the wrapper         | **SURVIVED — pure de-optimization of a correct path**    |

**S7 was originally a different mutant, and its survival is what fixed the code.** The guard was
first written as `txDepth === 0 && !hasListeners(...)`, on the reasoning that inside a transaction
the event is buffered and the subscriber list at buffer time is not the one that receives it at
commit. Dropping that condition survived — because `onMutate` never runs while buffering: inside a
transaction no listener is called at all, and `commitTransaction` zeroes `txDepth` BEFORE it
flushes (`Graph.ts:3814`). The condition was unreachable and its justifying comment was false, so
the surviving mutant was **adopted as the code** and S7 repointed at the guard's real correctness
mutant. Item 309's Q9 lesson, second occurrence: a survivor can mean the comment is wrong rather
than the test is.

### Answering the two questions this started from

- **Batching the undo closures** is not worth it, and the number is item 312's: `recordUndo`'s
  closure is allocated per write for nothing outside a transaction and is worth **~20ns, 0.7%**.
  Batching it into a compact op-record array would remove the allocation but add a dispatch
  switch, against 20ns. What was NOT measured, and is recorded open rather than claimed: inside a
  long transaction those closures are RETAINED until commit, so the question there is resident
  memory, not time.
- **The emitter stays.** Nothing here removes an event, changes a payload, or defers one that was
  synchronous; what is removed is a re-emission nobody subscribes to and sixteen-thousand-per-tick
  microtask scheduling behind a counter that was already deferred. React sees the same
  `version`/`epoch` numbers, one microtask boundary later at the latest, and
  `reactive-counters.test.ts` now pins that.

## 314. The rest of the emission — 2.32x more, and a guard declined before it was written

Item 313 removed ~140ns of the per-write emission. This item started by asking how much was left,
which needed a floor rather than an estimate: the ndjson decode disables events for its whole load,
so running the same ingest loop with `disableEvents()` is the engine with the cascade switched off.

| 1,000,000 `addEdge`, min of 3 |  ns/edge |
| ----------------------------- | -------: |
| events on, before item 313    |     2783 |
| events on, after item 313     |     2643 |
| **events off entirely**       | **2345** |

So the emission is **~438ns an edge**, item 313 took 138ns, and **~300ns was still there** — which
is a target with a number instead of a hunch.

### First, a guard declined at the ceiling

With events disabled a write still builds a `new EmitterEvent(...)` and passes it through
`Graph.emit` to `Emitter.emit`, which returns on `!this.enabled`: one allocation and two frames per
write, 1.2M times in the `decode ndjson` row, for an object nothing reads. The obvious fix is an
`eventsEnabled()` guard at the sixteen emit call sites.

**Priced at its ceiling first, and declined.** Deleting the two hot emit calls outright — not a
candidate, an upper bound — over three alternated rounds with a flat pre-write control: the edge
loop reads **2345.6 -> 2343.7 (1.001x)** and the vertex loop **193.9 -> 190.2**. V8 sinks the
allocation and inlines two early-returning frames, so the guard would buy nothing, cost sixteen
call sites, and add a condition to every write path. The repo's own standing note —
"obviously correct so it must be faster" is not evidence — at a cheaper price than usual: an
ablation that measures the ceiling costs one harness and settles the whole family.

### Then the 300ns, in two parts

1. **`tokensOf` allocated three arrays per write** for the topology case: `[...labels]`,
   `Object.keys(properties)`, then `[...labels, ...keys]` to join them. The caller that matters
   runs once per write and only iterated the result, so `pushTokens(event, out)` writes straight
   into item 313's pending array. `tokensOf` keeps its signature for the one caller that genuinely
   needs an array of its own (`Graph.emit` stores it on a buffered transaction event).
2. **`Emitter.emit` built a `new Set(...)` snapshot per emit.** It has to iterate a copy — a
   handler re-subscribing for its own event would otherwise loop forever — but item 313 established
   that the set it was copying holds the same two functions for the lifetime of a `Graph`. The
   snapshot is now cached per event type and invalidated by `on` / `once` / `detach`.

Priced separately, three alternated rounds on the direct cascade probe, flat control, `version`
identical at 1,021,000 on all four sides:

| side                | min of 3 |             saves |
| ------------------- | -------: | ----------------: |
| CONTROL (= 313)     | 164.2 ns |                 — |
| `pushTokens` only   | 127.1 ns |  **37.1ns (23%)** |
| snapshot cache only |  86.4 ns |  **77.8ns (47%)** |
| both                |  63.7 ns | **100.5ns (61%)** |

Five rounds on the shipped form, both controls flat (180.1-183.3 and 345.7-350.2 ms), every range
disjoint from its control's:

| row                   | CONTROL min |   NEW min |     ratio |            cumulative over 312 |
| --------------------- | ----------: | --------: | --------: | -----------------------------: |
| the cascade, per emit |    145.2 ns |   62.6 ns | **2.32x** |              **3.57x** (223.2) |
| 200,000 `addVertex`   |    234.7 ms |  196.0 ms |     1.20x | 1.43x (279.4 at 313's control) |
| 1,000,000 `addEdge`   |   2678.9 ms | 2393.5 ms | **1.12x** |             **1.16x** (2783.9) |

Against the events-off floor of 2345ns an edge, the emission now costs **~48ns of the ~438ns it
cost before item 313 — 89% of it is gone**, and what remains is close enough to the floor that the
next write-path item should look elsewhere.

### Teeth, and the mutant that found the missing test

A cache like this is the shape that passes a green suite and breaks on the fourth emit, so the
hazards were checked against the suite that already existed — and `Emitter.test.ts` turned out to
cover them properly: `once()` across three emits, subscribing mid-dispatch, and unsubscribing
another listener mid-dispatch _with a second emit afterwards_ to prove the removal took effect.
Four tests added for the hazards the cache itself introduces (emit-before-subscribe for both `on`
and `once`, per-type isolation, the last unsubscribe).

Nine mutants, under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0` — a mutant here
can loop forever by construction, since the snapshot is exactly what stops a handler re-subscribing
for its own event from recursing, and that loop allocates nothing, which is the case the memory cap
cannot catch and the timeout can:

| mutant                                          | result                              |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| T1 never invalidate on `on`                     | caught (2)                          |
| T2 never invalidate on unsubscribe              | caught (4)                          |
| T3 never invalidate on `once`                   | **SURVIVED at first — see below**   |
| T4 iterate the live set instead of the snapshot | caught (2)                          |
| T5 a fresh `Set` per emit (the old behaviour)   | **SURVIVED — equivalent by design** |
| T6 drop property keys from a topology event     | caught (5)                          |
| T7 drop labels from a topology event            | caught (8)                          |
| T8 `tokensOf` returns an empty array            | caught (1)                          |
| T9 invalidate even when nothing was removed     | **SURVIVED — de-optimization only** |

**T3 survived the first run and was a real gap.** Removing `once`'s invalidation on SUBSCRIBE still
fires-exactly-once correctly, because the wrapper's self-detach invalidates on the way out; what it
breaks is only `once` on a type that has already been emitted, where the cached empty list means
the listener never fires at all. The four tests added for the cache covered that case for `on` and
not for `once` — reading one off the other is exactly what a mutant is for. Test added, T3 caught,
and the asymmetry is written down next to it.

### Regressions

- **`decode ndjson (5 edges/node)`**: unchanged, and unreachable — it disables events, so neither
  `pushTokens` nor the snapshot runs. Four alternated rounds, ts 2550.6-2760.4 on the control side
  against 2626.7-2800.7, an 8% spread either way with a flat ffi column. Reported as a row whose
  instrument exceeds any effect it is being asked to show, which is the honest reading of an
  unreachable row that does not sit still.
- **`bench:usage write: append node`**, isolated, `BENCH_BUDGET_MS=1500`: **the direction flipped
  between two runs** — ts(-) read 117.9k -> 111.7k in one and 113.7k -> 117.6k in the next, with
  the native control column flat in both. Pooled over twelve readings the medians differ ~3% with
  heavily overlapping ranges on a column whose control side alone spans 117-140k. **No regression
  established, and none ruled out below ~10%** — stated that way rather than picking the run that
  agrees. There is also no mechanism for one: both changes strictly remove allocations and the
  cache adds a single `Map.get` per emit in their place.
- **`bench:usage interleaved: append + link`**, isolated, three alternated rounds: ts(-) 674 ->
  694, ts(+) 66.4k -> 64.8k, native columns flat. Within noise.

## 315. What a transaction RETAINS per write — the undo closures are 32% of it, and the number is exact

Item 312 priced `recordUndo`'s per-write closure at **20ns** and declined the guard. That answered
the wrong question for the case anyone would care about: outside a transaction the closure is
allocated and immediately dropped, but **inside one it is retained in `txUndo` until commit**. A
bulk load wrapped in a transaction holds one closure per write, each capturing an id, for the whole
load — and 20ns says nothing about that.

So measure the bytes. `Bun.gc(true)` then `heapUsed`, inside the transaction before commit drops
the log, against the same write count with no transaction at all:

| 200,000 `addVertex` |   inside | after commit | retained at peak |
| ------------------- | -------: | -----------: | ---------------: |
| no transaction      | 139.4 MB |     136.0 MB |           3.4 MB |
| **ONE transaction** | 189.9 MB |     135.8 MB |      **54.1 MB** |

**A transaction retains 270 bytes per write** — 54 MB at 200k, 270 MB at the million the bench
decodes. Ablating the three per-write accumulators one at a time, three rounds:

| what accumulates                     | MB / 200k | bytes/write |   share |
| ------------------------------------ | --------: | ----------: | ------: |
| buffered events + their token arrays |      26.7 |       133.5 |     49% |
| **the undo closures**                |  **17.5** |    **87.5** | **32%** |
| the touched-vertex set               |      10.0 |        50.0 |     19% |

Perfectly additive (54.2 against 54.1) and **byte-identical across all three rounds** — a
deterministic instrument, which after a session of 30%-spread timing rows is worth saying out loud:
when the quantity you care about is bytes, measure bytes. Three rounds here confirm determinism
rather than averaging noise out.

So the answer to "can we batch the undo closures": **yes, and it is worth 87.5 bytes a write — real,
and not the biggest piece.** Pricing the ceiling the way item 314 did, `no-undo-log` IS the ceiling:
87.5 B/write. A tagged compact log (an op-code array plus operand arrays, replacing eight distinct
closures) would capture maybe 55-60 of those 87.5, because the operands still have to live
somewhere — against a refactor across eight `recordUndo` call sites, each of which is a rollback
correctness path. **Priced and left open with the number**, not attempted blind.

## 316. One flat token buffer per transaction instead of one array per buffered event

The largest of the three — the event buffer at 133.5 bytes a write — had a piece that was pure
bookkeeping. Each buffered event carried its reactive tokens in an array hung off the event object
under a symbol key:

```ts
(event as any)[TX_TOKENS] = this.tokensOf(event);
this.txEvents.push(event);
```

That is one array allocation AND one hidden-class transition per buffered write. The tokens are
captured at buffer time for a real reason — a removal nulls the element's graph ref before commit
dispatches the event, so reading `labels` at the drain would throw — but **nothing needs them
grouped by event**: the drain bumps each occurrence once, in any order. So they go into one flat
`txTokens` array for the whole transaction, the event carries a bare marker, and commit hands the
buffer to the drain once after the flush.

Four places have to agree for that to be equivalent, which is the whole risk of the change:
buffer time pushes; `markMutated` contributes nothing for a marked event but still COUNTS the write
(`version` counts writes); commit hands the buffer over after the flush; and **both** rollback
paths discard it — an inner frame truncating to its savepoint mark, a full rollback clearing it.

| 200,000 `addVertex` in one transaction | retained at peak |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------: |
| CONTROL                                |          54.1 MB |
| NEW                                    |      **45.2 MB** |

**44.5 bytes a write, 16.5% of what a transaction retains**, byte-identical across three alternated
rounds. The non-transaction emit path is unchanged in time — 63.2 against 64.9 ns an emit, inside
the control side's own spread (74.5/63.2/64.2) — which is the point: this buys memory in the
transaction path and must not cost the hot path, and it does not.

### Teeth

Three tests added, all passing against the PRISTINE engine too, so they describe the behaviour and
not the implementation: a removal INSIDE a transaction (the case the early capture exists for — the
element is evicted before commit dispatches), an inner-frame rollback whose tokens must be dropped
while the outer frame's survive, and a rolled-back transaction followed by a committed one.

Eight mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`: seven caught,
one surviving by design (`=== undefined` against a truthiness test on a marker set to exactly
`true`).

Two are worth naming:

- **U8 looks equivalent and is not**, which is why it is in the set: commit clearing `txTokens`
  **in place** rather than replacing it, when the local it just took is the same array it is about
  to hand to the drain. Caught, 4 failing.
- **U7 survived the first run** — dropping the token-buffer clear from the full-rollback reset.
  Not an unreachable branch and not a false comment this time, but a test that could not see it:
  nothing is handed to the drain on a rollback at all, so the leaked tokens only become observable
  when the NEXT transaction commits and hands over a buffer still holding the discarded writes.
  "A rolled-back transaction advances nothing" passes with the bug in place. Test added, U7 caught.
  **Third distinct meaning of a survivor this session**, after 313's unreachable condition and
  314's symmetric-case gap: here the assertion was in the right place and one transaction too early.

## 317. `gql::parse` is allocational after all — 50 allocations for a 57-byte query, and 1.115x from two lines

`gql::parse` has been the largest open native target for a while: **1296-1334ns for a 57-byte
query, 43% of an unprepared serving call.** Item 294 priced the two costs visible in the source —
the lexer's `Vec<char>` pre-pass at 60ns and the ~12 owned identifier `String`s at 177ns — and
recorded the conclusion that the remaining ~82% is **"the scanning loop, the recursive descent and
the plan build"**, i.e. _"STRUCTURAL rather than allocational"_, with the next step as **"start from
a profiler on `lex`/`parse_internal`, not from the allocations."**

There is no profiler on this box. So the step had to be replaced rather than skipped, and what
replaced it says the recorded conclusion is wrong.

### First, split the 82%

`lex` is private and so is `Tok`, so a temporary `usize`-returning hook let an example time the
lexer alone without making either public (removed before commit; the harness restores a pristine
copy):

| phase                        |       ns | share |
| ---------------------------- | -------: | ----: |
| `lex` alone                  |      334 |   26% |
| the descent + the plan build |     1000 |   74% |
| **`gql::parse`**             | **1334** |  100% |

The entry had these as one lump. They are not: three quarters is after the lexer.

### Then eliminate the suspects, cheaply, before assuming any of them

Each of these cost one measurement and each came back too small to be the answer:

- **Keyword matching.** `peek_kw`/`eat_kw` are a `toks.get(pos)` plus a case-insensitive compare,
  and instrumenting them says the descent performs **74 comparisons for an 18-token query** (and
  62 for a 10-token one, so most of it is fixed: the parser tries a long list of alternatives
  regardless). That looks like the answer. Priced at its ceiling — 74 `eq_ignore_ascii_case` calls
  over the same operand shapes — it is **84ns**. So a keyword-classifying lexer (`Tok::Ident(String,
Kw)`, comparing an enum discriminant instead of a string) **cannot be worth more than 6.3% of
  parse**, for a refactor touching every keyword call site. **Declined at the ceiling**, item 314's
  lesson applied again.
- **`bump()` clones every token it consumes** — `self.toks.get(self.pos).cloned()` — which for
  `Tok::Ident(String)` is a heap allocation, and the parser backtracks in 12 places so it cannot
  simply move. A clean one-line cause for 20 allocations. Counted instead of believed: **5**.
  Hypothesis dropped.
- **The plan tree.** `plan.clone()` re-allocates the entire output: **9 allocations, 60ns.**

### Then count allocations, which is what the entry had ruled out

A counting global allocator, in its own binary because a counting allocator perturbs every other
case in the process (`examples/alloc_count_probe.rs`, kept — it answers one sharp question with a
bespoke fixture, which is what the corpus README says earns a standalone probe). **50 allocations
and 4187 bytes to parse 57 bytes.** A two-hop count: 80 and 7986.

A bucketed histogram said 32 were "≤8 bytes", which is not a fix. Resolving the small end to
**exact sizes** names them:

| allocation                                | count | what it is                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----: | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| exactly **8 bytes**, all inside `lex`     |    12 | one per identifier. `b[start..i].iter().collect()` reserves the char COUNT as a byte count, and Rust's first grow for a 1-byte element type is capacity 8 — so a 1-to-5-character identifier allocates 8 bytes. Already one allocation each. |
| **1B x10, 4B x4, 5-7B x5** in the descent |    20 | identifier `String` **clones**, at exact string lengths. **Ten are one byte: the variable name `u`, cloned ten times for a query that mentions it three.**                                                                                   |
| Vec growth reallocations                  |     7 | 3 for the char pre-pass, 4 for the token vector                                                                                                                                                                                              |

So parse **is** allocation-bound: ~31 of the 50 are in the descent, 22 of them transient (the final
plan is 9). At the ~16ns an identifier `String` that item 294 itself measured, the allocations
account for the gap its structural reading left unexplained. **The earlier conclusion came from
pricing the two allocation sources that were visible in the source and attributing the remainder to
a category** — the same error shape as item 312's, one level down: _a remainder is not evidence for
whatever you were going to say about it._

### What shipped: size the two vectors

Both were measured growing, so both get a capacity. `s.len()` is bytes — an exact fit for ASCII and
a safe over-reserve otherwise — and one token per 4 bytes is a close middle for GQL (the 57-byte
serving query lexes to 18 tokens); both vectors are transient, so an over-reserve costs a wider
memset and never a second allocation.

Four alternated rounds on `percall_probe`, whose `exec::try_run` and `parse_json` cases are in the
same process and cannot be reached by a change to the GQL lexer:

| row                        | CONTROL min | NEW min |      ratio |
| -------------------------- | ----------: | ------: | ---------: |
| `gql::parse` alone         |     1297 ns | 1163 ns | **1.115x** |
| parse + `optimize_indexed` |     1645 ns | 1497 ns |     1.099x |
| control: `exec::try_run`   |      298 ns |  292 ns |       flat |
| control: `parse_json`      |      165 ns |  166 ns |       flat |

Both target ranges are fully disjoint from their control's. Allocations **50 → 45**, bytes
**4187 → 2779** — a third of the bytes, because each growth copied the whole buffer.

On the corpus, `query_bench -- plan`, three alternated rounds — and this table carries its own
unreachable control, since the production Gremlin path has its own lexer and never calls
`gql::lex` (only `gremlin/tests.rs` references `gql::parse`):

| row                        | CONTROL min | NEW min |                          ratio |
| -------------------------- | ----------: | ------: | -----------------------------: |
| label scan                 |     0.83 us | 0.71 us |                     **1.169x** |
| 2-hop + filter             |     1.73 us | 1.51 us |                     **1.146x** |
| group + order + limit      |     1.67 us | 1.50 us |                         1.113x |
| **control: gremlin 2-hop** |     0.96 us | 1.03 us | 0.932x — moved the _other_ way |

**Item 294 declined the char vector's line alone at a measured 34ns and 2.6% of parse, and that
decline was correct for what it measured.** What it could not see is that the token vector
reallocates four times as well, because nothing had counted allocations. The pair is 134ns and
11.5%. A line priced in isolation and declined is not the same fact as the change it belongs to.

### Teeth

The change is two capacity hints and cannot alter behaviour, so the mutants worth running are not
"is the new code correct" but "would this suite notice if `lex` were broken at all" — a capacity
that silently truncated input would return a WRONG PARSE rather than an error. Five mutants, built
uncapped then run under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0` (a mutated
lexer can loop forever on a `while i < b.len()` whose index stops advancing, which allocates
nothing and so trips the timeout rather than the memory cap):

| mutant                                           | result                              |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| V1 the char pre-pass drops one character         | caught (495 failures)               |
| V2 the pre-pass is sized but never filled        | caught (495)                        |
| V3 `with_capacity(0)` — the pre-change behaviour | **SURVIVED — correct, just slower** |
| V4 a 4x over-reserved token vector               | **SURVIVED — wasteful, correct**    |
| V5 a truncating capacity _and_ a truncating fill | caught (493)                        |

V3 and V4 are capacity values: a test that failed on them would be asserting an implementation
detail. Their survival is what makes V1/V2/V5's 495 failures mean something.

Gates as separate commands: `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --manifest-path … --all-targets -- -D
warnings` (0), 724 Rust tests, all four `optimizing_preserves_*` optimizer-invariant fuzzers, and
all seven cross-engine byte-identity fuzzers on a freshly rebuilt wasm and `.so`.

### What is still open, now with a count instead of a category

The remaining target is the **20 identifier `String` clones in the descent, ten of them the same
one-byte name** — and `lex`'s 12, which only borrowing removes. Item 294's route (`Tok<'a>` with
`Ident(&'a str)`, which forces the `Vec<char>` indexing out at the same time, since a borrowed
token cannot point into a transient char vector) is confirmed from the other side: those 12 are
already one allocation each, so nothing short of borrowing touches them. But it only addresses the
lexer's 12 — **the descent's 20 clones are a separate change**, into the IR's owned `String`
fields, and that is where the larger half of the count is.

## 318. The native engine has no parse cache and the TypeScript one has had two since item 228 — priced at 2.38x and verified route-identical

Item 317 took 1.115x off `gql::parse` and left the remaining target as the descent's 20 identifier
clones. Before grinding that, one question the method demands and nobody had asked of this path:
**does a serving call even pay for parse, or is there a cache in front of it?**

There is not. `lnk_query` (`ffi.rs:628`) calls `gql::parse_with_params_limited` and then
`opt::optimize_indexed` **on every single call**, and a grep for `parse_cache` / `plan_cache` over
the whole crate finds nothing. Meanwhile the TypeScript engine has had **both** since audit items
228 (parse, 1.5-2.6x on the serving surface) and 229 (the compile half, point lookup to 1.12M
ops/s).

That is the explanation for a number this audit has carried since item 291 without a cause.
`bench:usage`, indexed point lookup: **ts 1.20M ops/s against the native engine's 239.9k** — the
pure-TypeScript engine beating the Rust one by 5x on a small-op row. From `percall_probe`:

| layer of a native serving call             |        ns |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------: |
| `gql::parse`                               |      1163 |
| `opt::optimize_indexed` on top             |       334 |
| `exec::try_run`, one row                   |      ~300 |
| **total**                                  | **~1797** |
| the prepared path: clone + bind + optimize |       456 |
| clone + `bind_params` alone                |       176 |

**83% of a native serving call is re-deriving a plan from text it has already seen**, and the
engine already contains the pieces that make it unnecessary — `parse_prepared` (params stay
symbolic as `Expr::Param`), `bind::bind_params`, and `prepared.rs`'s handle registry. A cache
holding the prepared plan turns ~1797ns into ~756ns: **a 2.38x ceiling on the serving path**, from
an existing probe's existing numbers.

### Verified before designed: does a cached plan change the route?

A cache must hold a plan parsed ONCE and reused with different parameter values, which means
parsing in PREPARED mode. Direct mode substitutes `$n` to `Expr::Lit` _during_ the parse, so the
optimizer sees a literal; prepared mode leaves `Expr::Param` for `bind_params` to fill. Those are
two different parses and the whole design turns on whether they converge:

```
optimize(parse_with_params(q, params))  ==  optimize(bind(parse_prepared(q), params))  ?
```

`examples/prepared_parity_probe.rs` asks it directly over fourteen shapes, against two stores — one
with no index and one with an index on the gated key, because a substituted literal could
plausibly seed an index that a bound param would not, and that difference is invisible without the
index present.

**Ten of fourteen are the identical optimized plan, in both stores** — including every seeding
shape: `u.name = $n`, the reversed `$n = u.name`, the inline `{name: $n}`, a range, an `IN` list, a
two-param AND, a param used twice, a two-hop with a param gate, and an aggregate with one. The
optimizer's output does not distinguish a bound param from a substituted literal.

Three carve-outs, and they are the design:

1. **A param in `LIMIT`/`SKIP`** — prepared mode refuses it, with the message it documents. The
   fallback is automatic: a prepared-parse error means "do not cache this text".
2. **A param in an INSERT value — prepared mode ACCEPTS it and plans it DIFFERENTLY.** This is the
   one that would have shipped quietly. Direct gives
   `Insert { nodes: [InsertNode { props: [("name", Str("new"))] }] }`, the literal path;
   prepared+bind gives `InsertFrom { input: Row, nodes: [InsertNodeExpr { .. }] }`, the general
   expression path. **Same answer, different operator** — a cache would route every parameterized
   INSERT off the fast literal path, a pure performance regression with no wrong answer to give it
   away. It needs an explicit carve-out, not an error-triggered fallback.
3. **An unbound param's message.** Direct returns `E_MISSING_PARAMETER: unbound parameter $nope`;
   `bind_params` returns a bare `unbound parameter $nope`. This looked like a shipped divergence
   between the two public paths and **it is not** — `ffi.rs:1116` sets the code itself for the
   prepared path rather than reading it off the message, so both agree at the boundary. Tracing
   that beat writing it up. It does mean a cache inside `lnk_query` must set the code explicitly:
   the direct arm there recovers it with `strip_prefix("E_MISSING_PARAMETER: ")`, which a
   bound-param error never carries.

### What the TypeScript twin already proved, and this must not relearn

Items 228/229 are not just precedent, they are the recorded trap list, and two of them are the
hard part of the implementation rather than the idea:

- **An admission filter is load-bearing, not a refinement.** A write-heavy workload sends unique
  text per call — `bench:usage`'s own append row is `INSERT (:Event {name: 'ev${i}'})` — so a cache
  that admits on first sighting fills with entries nothing will ask for again. Item 228's note:
  _"64 more allocations TENURES it. A cache that holds what nothing will ask for again pays GC for
  the privilege."_
- **Saturation hides an admission bug.** _"'Single-use texts do not grow the cache' is true either
  way once the cache sits at its cap. Assert on the filter's OWN counter (`seen`) instead."_ A test
  written the obvious way passes with the filter removed.

So the remaining work is bounded and its failure modes are already written down: a size-capped map
keyed on `(text, max_depth)` holding a prepared `Plan`, a two-strikes admission filter with its own
counter, the INSERT-with-params carve-out, prepared-refusal as a negative cache, and the explicit
error code on a bind failure. Nothing here needs a new measurement — it needs the implementation
and its mutants.

**Priced at 2.38x, route-verified on 10/14 shapes with three named carve-outs, not built.** Recorded
this way deliberately: the one carve-out that matters is invisible from the answer, and an
implementation that started from "prepared mode exists, use it" would have shipped it.

## 319. The native parse cache — 1.327x median on the serving surface, and two bugs the design did not anticipate

Item 318 priced this at a 2.38x ceiling and verified it route-identical on 10 of 14 shapes. This
builds it: `crate::parse_cache`, a bounded cache of PREPARED plans keyed on query text, wired into
both GQL arms of `lnk_query`.

The policy is item 228's TypeScript twin, deliberately, down to the cap of 64 — that one has
already been measured and mutation-tested, and its two decisions that look like refinements are the
ones that matter: **a text is admitted on its SECOND sighting**, and **the filter holds texts, not
plans**.

### Measured

`bench:usage`, three alternated rounds, `BENCH_BUDGET_MS=600`. The `ts` columns are the
pure-TypeScript engine in the same process — a control a change to the Rust FFI cannot reach:

| column         |     median |    min |    max |
| -------------- | ---------: | -----: | -----: |
| **engine(+)**  | **1.327x** | 0.959x | 1.547x |
| engine(-)      |     1.074x | 0.979x | 1.341x |
| control: ts(+) |     1.003x | 0.964x | 1.181x |
| control: ts(-) |     1.000x | 0.965x | 1.049x |

| row, `engine(+)`                   | CONTROL |    NEW |      ratio |
| ---------------------------------- | ------: | -----: | ---------: |
| analytic: fan-out spread 1-3 hops  |  149.0k | 230.5k | **1.547x** |
| analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops |       — |      — |     1.463x |
| read: point lookup                 |  259.8k | 363.6k | **1.400x** |
| interleaved: write + point read    |  125.1k | 171.4k | **1.370x** |
| interleaved: write + traversal     |       — |      — |     1.361x |
| 2-hop recommendation               |       — |      — |     1.354x |
| 100 updates in one transaction     |       — |      — |     1.327x |
| **write: append node** (all-miss)  |  378.8k | 363.3k |     0.959x |

The all-miss rows (`write: append node`, `interleaved: append + link`, whose text is interpolated
per call) read **0.959x and 0.966x** against a control column that itself spans 0.964-1.181x on
this harness, so the miss path's cost — one hash lookup and one ring scan — is at or below what
this instrument resolves. It was **0.883x** before the filter was fixed, and that WAS resolvable.

### The admission filter had to be rebuilt, and the bench said so

The first filter was item 228's shape transliterated: a `HashSet<String>` of texts seen once. That
made the all-miss row **0.883x** and turned three rows into regressions —
`interleaved: write + point read` **0.969x**, `write + traversal` **0.944x**. The cause is not the
one item 228 recorded. In TypeScript the string already exists and the cost being avoided is GC
retention of a ~2KB AST; **in Rust the allocation IS the cost**: an all-miss call paid
`text.to_string()` to insert and, once saturated, another `String` to clone the victim it evicted
— two allocations and four hashes of the query text, per call, to learn nothing.

So the filter became a fixed ring of query-text **hashes** (`[u64; CAP]` plus a cursor): no
allocation, nothing to evict, and a collision merely admits a text one sighting early, which is
harmless because correctness comes from the admission check and not from the filter. The refusal
set merged into the main map at the same time, so a miss costs ONE lookup instead of two.

| row, `engine(+)`                | allocating filter |  hash ring |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------: | ---------: |
| write: append node (all-miss)   |            0.883x | **0.986x** |
| interleaved: write + point read |            0.969x | **1.319x** |
| interleaved: write + traversal  |            0.944x | **1.312x** |

**Porting a policy is not porting its reasons.** The admission filter was right; its data structure
was right for a garbage-collected heap and wrong here.

### Admission VERIFIES rather than carving out

A text is admitted only if its prepared plan, bound to the parameters in hand, renders identically
to what the direct path produces; a text that fails is remembered as refused and always takes the
direct path. Item 318's INSERT divergence — prepared mode plans `InsertFrom`/`InsertNodeExpr` where
direct uses the literal `Insert`/`InsertNode`, same rows by a slower operator — excludes itself
rather than needing a rule, and so does any divergence a later change introduces. The comparison
costs one extra parse and two `Debug` renders on the call that admits a text, and nothing on a hit.

### The bug that check could NOT catch

`bun test packages/native` failed two GQL conformance differentials, and they are the item's most
useful output. **A now-function folds the host's `$__now` clock into the plan at PARSE time** —
`Expr::Lit(temporal_ctor(now, kind))` in `gql.rs` — so the plan of `RETURN current_date AS d` is
not a function of the query text at all, and a prepared parse (which runs with no params) folds it
to `Lit(Null)` with no `Expr::Param` left for `bind_params` to fill.

The equality check cannot see this, because **it compares ONE parameter set**. The conformance
suite's own sighting order is exactly the one that defeats it: `RETURN current_date AS d` is first
called with **no clock**, where both parses agree on `Lit(Null)` and the check is satisfied — so
the text is admitted with null baked in as the clock — and then called with a wired clock, which
hits that plan and reads the stale null.

Fixed as a refusal by SHAPE, not another comparison: `gql::text_may_read_clock`, a case-insensitive
substring scan for the five niladic now-functions, living next to `current_temporal_kind` which is
the authority on those names, and checked at admission only. It can over-report and cannot
under-report — a property named `current_date` costs its query a cache slot, where a missed
now-function serves a stale clock.

**The general lesson is about the verification, not the clock**: an admission gate that compares
one parameter set proves nothing about a parameter whose PRESENCE changes the plan. Item 318 tested
value-dependence (a short list, a 40-element one, NULL, cross-type) and found none, which was true
and did not cover this: `$__now` is not read as a value, it is read as a compile-time input.

### The other bug was mine, and the harness hid it

Before that, the **injection fuzzer** failed: `RETURN $p AS x` returned the admission call's value
for every later value. That was not a design flaw — it was mutant **W7** (`Some(bound)` for
`Some(prepared)`) living in my working tree, because I had piped the mutation harness into
`head -6`. SIGPIPE killed the script between applying W7 and the next restore, and **the harness's
own final content-verification never ran either**, since it is the last thing in the script.

`CLAUDE.md` already says _"restore before applying the next mutant, never only after the loop"_ —
and this harness does. It was still not enough, because the kill landed inside the window the rule
is about. Two additions: **never close a mutation harness's stdout early** (redirect to a file and
read the file; `tail` is safe, `head` is not), and **`git diff` before trusting the tree**, which is
what found it. The fuzzer caught it, but `cargo test` would have caught it first and I had rebuilt
the `.so` and gone straight to fuzzing.

### Teeth

Eleven tests (`parse_cache/tests.rs`) and eleven mutants under
`timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`:

| mutant                                                     | result                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| W1 admit on the FIRST sighting                             | caught                    |
| W2 admit WITHOUT verifying against the direct plan         | caught                    |
| W3 serve a cached plan under any expression-depth ceiling  | caught                    |
| W4 drop the `E_MISSING_PARAMETER` prefix on a bind failure | caught                    |
| W5 remember a FAILING parse                                | caught                    |
| W6 never evict                                             | caught                    |
| W7 store the BOUND plan                                    | caught                    |
| W8 `hash_of` without `\| 1`                                | **SURVIVED — equivalent** |
| W9 `CAP` 64 → 32                                           | **SURVIVED — equivalent** |
| W10 drop the clock refusal                                 | caught                    |
| W11 narrow the now-function list to one name               | caught                    |

Two tests were fixed because a mutant survived them first:

- **W3 survived** a `max_depth` test whose query was shallow enough that both ceilings accepted it,
  so both paths rendered the same plan whether or not the ceiling was checked. The fixture now
  asserts up front that the two ceilings DISAGREE about it — _"the fixture must EXCEED the shallow
  ceiling or this test proves nothing"_.
- **W9 was caught when it must be equivalent**: the filter-occupancy assertion hard-coded 40 where
  the ring holds `CAP`, so it failed on a tuning value. Now `40.min(cap)` — item 317's V3/V4
  principle, that a test which fails when a cap is retuned is asserting an implementation detail.

Gates as separate commands: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` (0),
`bun typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` (0), 1094 Rust tests, 809 `packages/native` tests including
the GQL conformance differential, and all seven cross-engine byte-identity fuzzers on a freshly
rebuilt wasm and `.so`.

Clippy also forced a decision worth recording: `large_enum_variant` on both enums, answered
differently. `Slot` boxes its admitted plan — the allocation is paid once per ADMITTED text, and it
keeps a `Refused` entry from carrying a plan-sized hole. `Lookup` does not, with the reason in the
code: it is a by-value return on the hot path, so boxing `Hit` would add an allocation to every
hit — the thing the module exists to make cheap — to save 248 bytes of stack that is about to be
dropped.

## 320. What the parse cache left behind — the serving path's new ledger, and two follow-ups refuted

Item 319 shipped the parse cache. The obvious next two steps are "cache the optimized plan as well"
(item 229's TypeScript twin did exactly that) and "make the optimizer cheaper". Both are refuted
here, each with a mechanism, before either was built.

### The new ledger

`percall_probe` gained the shipped entry point as a case, warmed first so it measures the HIT path
rather than an admission:

| layer of a native serving call |             before 319 |                                       after 319 |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------: | ----------------------------------------------: |
| the parse layer                | 1149 ns (`gql::parse`) | **144 ns** (`parse_cache::parse_for_run`, warm) |
| `opt::optimize_indexed` on top |                 334 ns |                                          334 ns |
| `exec::try_run`, one row       |                 307 ns |                                          307 ns |
| **a serving call**             |           **~1790 ns** |                                     **~785 ns** |

**7.98x on the parse layer and 2.28x on the call** — against item 318's predicted 2.38x ceiling,
which is as close as that prediction deserved to land.

Which moves the target: **`optimize_indexed` is now 43% of a serving call**, the largest single
layer, where before it was 19%.

### Refuted: caching the optimized plan (the obvious follow-up, and it would have been silent)

Item 229 cached the TypeScript engine's compiled plan, and its soundness argument is a type:
`compile(query: Query): Plan` **takes no graph**. The Rust analogue does not hold —
`optimize_indexed(plan, idx: &dyn IndexOracle)` takes the store, and takes it all the way down
(`fixpoint`, `orient_eligible`), so there is no store-independent prefix to split off.

That alone would only make a cached plan _stale_, which is answer-safe (the optimizer's fuzzed
invariant is that optimizing must not change the answer). The real obstacle is the ORDER. A cached
optimized plan must be optimized **before** binding, because the whole point is to reuse it across
parameter values — and **every seeding site in `opt.rs` matches `Expr::Lit(v)` and extracts a
concrete `Value`**, because `Plan::IndexSeek` holds a `Value` and not an `Expr`. `Expr::Param`
appears in the optimizer four times and is a non-seedable operand in all four.

Demonstrated rather than argued (`prepared_parity_probe`, second section), on a store with an index
on the gated key:

```
bind THEN optimize (what 319 does):
  Project { input: IndexSeek { label: Some("User"), key: "name", value: Str("name7") }, … }

optimize THEN bind (what a plan cache needs):
  Project { input: Filter { input: Scan { label: Some("User") },
                            pred: Compare { Eq, Prop{slot:0,key:"name"}, Lit(Str("name7")) } }, … }
```

A full label scan with a post-filter where the live path seeks. **This is the 100-300x class
`CLAUDE.md` names — "the planner recognized one spelling and scanned for another that meant exactly
the same thing… each cost 100-300x and each returned the correct answer, so no correctness test
could catch it"** — except the two spellings here are the same query before and after a cache. It
would have passed every test in the repo and shown up as a mysterious regression on an indexed
parameterized read.

So the optimize layer **cannot be cached across parameter values in this engine**, and the reason is
structural rather than a missing feature: index selection consumes the bound value.

### Refuted: the optimizer's fixpoint is not spinning

The other guess about 334ns is that `fixpoint` grinds — it loops up to 64 times, re-walking the
whole tree until a pass changes nothing. Instrumented (a temporary pass counter, removed before
commit), with the count and how many passes changed anything:

| query                                                  | passes | changed | wasted |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -----: | ------: | -----: |
| `MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = 'name7' RETURN u.score` |      2 |       1 |      1 |
| `MATCH (u:User) RETURN u.name AS n`                    |      1 |       0 |      1 |
| a two-hop `count(*)` with a start gate                 |      4 |       3 |      1 |
| `WHERE u.score > 2 RETURN count(*)`                    |      1 |       0 |      1 |

**Exactly one non-changing pass per fixpoint, which is the minimum a fixpoint can have** — the final
pass IS the proof of termination and cannot be skipped without a different algorithm. The serving
query costs two whole-tree passes, one of which is that proof. There is no loop to tighten: the
334ns is the cost of walking a ~60-variant plan tree once or twice, not of spinning.

(Worth noting in passing: `WHERE u.score > 2` on an unindexed key is rewritten by nothing at all —
one pass, zero changes.)

### Where this leaves the native serving path

~785ns, against ~1790 before: clone+bind 144, optimize 334, exec 307. Each remaining layer now has
a reason to be the size it is, and the two cheap structural moves are closed. What is left is
either narrower (the ~20 identifier clones item 317 counted, which are inside the 144 only on a
MISS now — a hit never parses) or much larger (a different optimizer organisation, which is not a
cache).

## 321. The adjacency box — 1.207x on `traverse 1-hop + filter`, and the first version optimized a function the row never calls

Three bench rows are bounded by string-keyed `Map` operations (items 310, 311, 312), and item 300
priced the structural answer — a CSR / dense adjacency — at **7.30x**, declining it for needing a
layout the TS graph does not expose. There is a cheaper intermediate nobody had priced: the
adjacency is keyed by the vertex's ID **string** at sites where the caller already holds the vertex
**object**.

### Priced first, over 200,000 vertices with a realistic id shape

| reaching a vertex's adjacency        | ns/vertex |          |
| ------------------------------------ | --------: | -------: |
| string key + inner label (**today**) |      59.7 |        — |
| object-keyed `Map` + inner label     |      30.5 |    1.96x |
| `WeakMap` + inner label              |      43.8 |    1.36x |
| **a cached reference + inner label** |  **16.1** | **3.7x** |
| string key alone                     |      11.0 |          |
| object key alone                     |       5.9 |          |
| a field read alone                   |       0.8 |          |

**Only a tenth of the 43.6ns difference is the hash.** The rest is locality: a field read reaches
the adjacency from a cache line the caller has already touched, where a string key hashes the
characters and then probes a 200,000-entry table. (A `WeakMap` is the worst of the three keyed
options and would have been the instinctive choice.)

So: `Vertex.adjFrom` / `adjTo`, lazily cached, **which is audit item 162's pattern** — `Vertex`
already caches its label box for exactly this reason, and the comment there says so. The
invalidation story comes with it: dropped by `evict` and by `set graph`, as `#box` and `#lbox` are.
Holding the reference is sound because the graph's outer entries are only ever `set`, never
deleted — `insertEdge` creates a vertex's inner map once and mutates it in place thereafter — and
`??=` caches only a box that EXISTS, so a zero-degree vertex re-reads and picks up its first edge
rather than remembering that it had none.

### The first version measured NOTHING, because it changed a function the row never calls

Pointed `Graph.outDegree` / `inDegree` / `findEdge` at the box, which is where item 311's
decomposition said the cost was (_"`index.get(v.id)` then `.get(type).size` — two Map lookups, one
string-keyed — at 445ns/vertex"_). Four alternated rounds: **48.2ms against 47.3ms, overlapping.**

The GQL shortcut does not call them. `shortcuts.ts` has its own local `degreeOfTypes(index.get(v.id),
types)` with its own string lookup, at four sites. **Item 311 had described the right line and I
changed a different function with the same shape** — the "verify the planner reaches the shape"
rule, applied to a helper rather than a plan.

With those four sites pointed at the box, four alternated rounds, one case per process:

| row (ts ms)               |  CONTROL |      NEW |                   ratio |
| ------------------------- | -------: | -------: | ----------------------: |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter` | **47.9** | **39.7** |              **1.207x** |
| control: the ffi column   |      1.5 |      1.5 |                    flat |
| `count 3-hop`             |      7.4 |      7.4 | flat (a different path) |

Ranges fully disjoint on the moving row, and the native column — unreachable from a TypeScript
change — flat at 1.5 on both sides. The gap to native narrows from **~32x to ~26x**.

`count 3-hop` is unmoved and that is the right result rather than a disappointment: item 310 located
its cost in the degree PRODUCT's two hashes per middle edge, which is a different code path and
still open.

### The two drives select OPPOSITE maps

`shortcuts.ts` has a near-side drive (`out ? edgesFromByLabel : edgesToByLabel`) and a far-side one
(`out ? edgesToByLabel : edgesFromByLabel`). Each site's `boxOf` had to mirror its own declaration;
reading it off the wrong one is a **wrong answer**, not a slow one. The edit was made by LINE with
the expected content asserted first, because the near declaration's text appears twice in the file
and a textual replace would have hit the wrong one — which it did, and the anchor check caught it
before anything was written.

### Teeth

Eight tests (`adjacency-box.test.ts`), every behavioural one passing against the PRISTINE engine
too, because a cache over graph-owned state is wrong only on the SECOND read and a suite that
builds a graph and queries it once would miss all of it. Five mutants under
`timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`:

| mutant                                          | result                            |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| X1 `evict` keeps the boxes                      | caught (2)                        |
| X2 `set graph` keeps the boxes                  | **SURVIVED at first — see below** |
| X3 `adjFrom` reads the IN-adjacency             | caught (56)                       |
| X4 the far-side drive reads the near side's box | caught (38)                       |
| X5 `??=` spelled as an explicit branch          | **SURVIVED — equivalent**         |

**X2's survival was the third occurrence this session of a symmetric-case gap.** `set graph` has no
internal caller, so it looked unreachable — but `label-box.test.ts:155` and `prop-box.test.ts:97`
both do exactly `v.graph = g2`, for `#lbox` and `#box`. The hazard was tested for two boxes and
read off for the third. Test added, mirroring the existing one; X2 caught.

Also worth recording: `expect(v.adjFrom).toBeUndefined()` **passes when the property does not exist
at all**, so on its own it is satisfied by an engine with no box. The positive case is asserted too.

### A pre-existing divergence found while regression-testing, and ruled out structurally

`bun run fuzz` came back **12/13 on roughly one run in three**, which memory records as this
suite's flake — but one in three is not one in thirty, so it was identified rather than counted.
The differential fuzzer prints a reproducing seed, and it reproduces deterministically:

```
FUZZ_SEED=1630169971
MATCH (t:T) OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE ((CASE WHEN ('' = null) THEN 'ää'
  WHEN ('' > 123456.789) THEN n.nan ELSE null END = split(duration('PT-2.5S'), -1))
  AND (n.s IS UNKNOWN))) RETURN t.n AS x, n.n AS y ORDER BY x, y

  ts:     err E_INVALID_VALUE
  native: ok [{"x":3,"y":null}, … six rows]
```

**It fails identically on CONTROL**, twice, so it is not item 321's. The fuzzer classifies it
itself: _"an evaluation-order difference, but no registry entry covers this shape"_ — the
raise-parity class of items 139/142/144/145, where one engine evaluates a sub-expression the other
short-circuits past. `split(duration('PT-2.5S'), -1)` is the raising operand.

Recorded as OPEN rather than fixed here: which engine is right is an ISO three-valued-logic
question, not a performance one, and it deserves its own item with the grammar in hand. **Replaying
the seed on both sides is what separated "my change broke the differential" from "main has a
reproducible divergence"** — counting failures would have told me neither.

## 322. The ordering key's fourth mismatch — `IS UNKNOWN`, and the fix was wrong in the other direction first

Item 321 found `bun run fuzz` red on roughly **one random seed in three** and ruled the divergence
out as pre-existing by replaying its seed on a control build. This settles it.

### Narrowing, which changed what the question was

The fuzzer's case is 200 bytes of `OPTIONAL MATCH` with a `CASE`, an `AND`, a cross-type compare
and a raising call. Bisected shape by shape, every piece agrees on its own:

| query                                      | both engines                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `split('a,b', -1)`                         | err `E_INVALID_VALUE` — the raising operand, and nothing to do with durations |
| `null = split('a,b', -1)`                  | err — a comparison evaluates both operands                                    |
| `(1 = 2) AND <raising>`                    | `false` — both short-circuit AND on FALSE, in written order (item 258)        |
| `<raising> AND (1 = 2)`                    | err — written order again                                                     |
| `WHERE <raising>` alone                    | agree                                                                         |
| **`WHERE <raising> AND (t.s IS UNKNOWN)`** | **ts err, native `ok []`**                                                    |

So the divergence needs a FILTER, an AND, and `IS UNKNOWN` as the second conjunct — and the
`OPTIONAL MATCH` in the fuzzer's case was incidental, contributing only the null-padding that
turned "no rows" into "rows with nulls".

### It is the fourth of a known class, not a new semantic question

`and-short-circuit-conformance.test.ts` already pins three of these, with the rule stated: _"A
filter reorders its conjuncts in BOTH engines, so the two must agree on WHICH conjuncts cannot
raise… A narrower key in one engine is not caution, it is disagreement."_ The earlier three were
ordered comparisons (41 divergences in one 20,000-query run), a negated numeric literal, and nested
parenthesized groups.

`truthCannotRaise` in `executor.ts` had the answer written in its own doc comment:

> "`isTruth` / `isTyped` / `isLabeled` are left out for now — they always yield a boolean, but
> their operands reach code this has not been checked against, and **a conservative omission costs
> only a missed reorder**."

That last clause is false, and this item is the bill. `IS UNKNOWN` lowers to
`{ kind: 'isTruth', truth: null }`, which falls to the switch's `default: return false`, while the
engine's `can_raise` admits the node — so TS kept written order and raised where the engine
reordered and dropped the row. **The tell was sitting next to it: `IS NULL`, which the key DOES
admit, agrees on the identical shape.**

### The fix was wrong in the other direction first

The first version returned `valueCannotRaise(e.expr)` for all three truth values, which **created
two NEW divergences**: `WHERE <raising> AND (n.n IS TRUE)` then answered no rows in TS while the
engine still raised. The engine admits only the `UNKNOWN` form — `IS TRUE`/`IS FALSE` lower to
something its `can_raise` calls raising — so the arm is `e.truth === null && valueCannotRaise(...)`.

**Being wider in one engine is the same mistake as being narrower**, which the comment I had just
written warned about while the code did it.

It was caught by measuring the test's expectations instead of reasoning them out: the first version
of the test asserted six outcomes from first principles and **got two of them wrong**. Whether the
safe conjunct SETTLES the row decides everything, and that is not obvious —

| conjunct             | truth for the fixture | settles a filter? | outcome    |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | ----------------- | ---------- |
| `n.n IS UNKNOWN`     | FALSE                 | yes               | `ok []`    |
| `n.zz IS UNKNOWN`    | TRUE                  | no                | both raise |
| `n.n IS NOT UNKNOWN` | TRUE                  | no                | both raise |

so three of the four new lines are controls for the arm rather than demonstrations of it.

### Why the recursion is VALUE-safety

Measured on both engines before choosing it: `t.s IS UNKNOWN` with a STRING `t.s` is **`false`, not
a fault** — a non-boolean operand is simply not that truth value, so the test INSPECTS rather than
coerces. What can still raise is the operand itself (`split('a,b', -1) IS UNKNOWN` raises in both).
That is exactly `valueCannotRaise`, and exactly what the neighbouring `isNull` arm already uses.

### `isTyped` and `isLabeled` stay out, now measured

The same comment left both out on the same cautious ground, so both were checked rather than
assumed — and both are correct to omit, for different reasons:

- `IS TYPED INTEGER` raises in BOTH engines with a raising sibling written first: it lowers to a
  cast, which `can_raise` calls raising, so neither engine hoists it.
- `IS LABELED P` raises in both because it is **TRUE** here — it settles nothing in a filter, so
  the raising sibling is essential whichever order they run in.

Admitting either would have been the mirror-image mistake a second time.

### Teeth

Five mutants on the one arm, under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`:

| mutant                                                   | result                            |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Y1 drop the arm (the bug)                                | caught                            |
| Y2 admit all three truth values (the first fix)          | caught                            |
| Y3 `== null` for `=== null` (`truth` is never undefined) | **SURVIVED — equivalent**         |
| Y4 recurse with `truthCannotRaise`                       | caught                            |
| Y5 ignore the operand entirely                           | **SURVIVED at first — see below** |

**Y5's survival needed a shape none of the other eleven assertions had.** Claiming `IS UNKNOWN` is
safe _regardless of its operand_ is invisible unless the test is written FIRST with a settling
sibling second: called safe, every conjunct is safe, so `filterPredicate` is not taken at all
(it declines an all-safe filter) and written order reaches the raising operand; called correctly,
the pair is MIXED, the sibling goes first and the row is dropped.
`WHERE (split('a,b', -1) IS UNKNOWN) AND n.n = 99` is `ok []` in both and `ERR` under Y5. Added,
with two controls: a sibling that MATCHES, and a sibling that is itself a non-settling
`IS UNKNOWN`.

### Verification

`bun run fuzz` was red on ~1 run in 3 and is now **10 consecutive clean runs**; the original seed
(`FUZZ_SEED=1630169971`) passes on replay. 4124 tests across core, emitter, gql, sync, native,
gremlin and mcp. The spelling probe at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9` reports **0 answer
disagreements**, its one over-2x group being the `label on start` guard `CLOSED.md` already records
as correct-not-outstanding (3312.2x here against 4160.8x on a control build — the same band).
Gates as separate commands: typecheck, lint, fmt:check all 0.

The registry's own doc comment claimed the opposite of what the code did — _"The TS engine has no
seek to match, but it does not need one: it reorders the conjuncts instead"_ sat next to
`executor.ts`'s _"WRITTEN ORDER, deliberately — no cost-based reordering"_. Both are true of
different paths (the filter reorders, the VALUE position does not), which is exactly the confusion
that let a key mismatch live in one of them.

## 323. The adjacency box cannot reach the 84x row, or the insert path — and the rule that says which rows it can reach

Item 321 took 1.207x off `traverse 1-hop + filter` with a cached per-vertex adjacency box. Two rows
look like the obvious next customers, and both are refuted here, each with a number.

### Where the box IS worth something, measured on its own

200,000 vertices and 1,000,000 edges, each edge visited once, over the real access shapes:

| route                                      | ns/edge |                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------: | ---------------- |
| A `id -> adjacency -> byType.size` (today) |   157.3 | —                |
| B `id -> Vertex -> box -> byType.size`     |   198.6 | **1.26x WORSE**  |
| C box with the Vertex **already held**     |    79.7 | **1.97x better** |
| D resolving the Vertex alone               |    22.3 |                  |

**B is worse than A plus D** (198.6 against ~102), which is the whole finding: touching two large
maps per edge thrashes more than either alone. The box is a 1.97x win and only when the caller
already holds the vertex — reaching it through an id is worse than not having it.

### Refuted: the ungated `count 3-hop` (84x, the widest ratio in the bench)

The three-segment degree product reads the d-side degree as `side(graph, e.toId, …)` — the edge's
stored ID string — and that is a measured choice, not an oversight: _"the `c` VERTEX has to be
resolved when anything reads it… with neither [label nor gate], the edge's stored ID is all the `d`
side needs (items 140, 218)"_. `Edge.to` is `getVertexById(this.#to)` with no cache of its own.

So this row holds no vertex, and acquiring one is route B: **1.26x worse**. Item 310's recorded
diagnosis stands and now has a mechanism rather than only a spread: the row cannot use the box at
all, and the CSR it priced at 7.30x remains the only lever.

### Refuted: the insert path, where the vertex IS in hand

`indexEdgeLabel` hashes `fromId`/`toId` into two 200,000-entry maps, and `addEdge` already resolves
both endpoints for `assertValidEdge` and throws them away (item 312 priced that pair at 43ns). So
threading them in costs nothing and should have turned four reads in five into field reads.

**The arm was reached exactly as designed** — instrumented rather than assumed, after item 321's
lesson: **80,000 box hits against 20,000 misses of 100,000 edges**, one miss per vertex at the
fixture's 5:1 ratio, since `??=` caches only a box that exists and the first edge is what creates
it.

It bought nothing. `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)`, isolated one case per process, four alternated
rounds: **CONTROL 2621.0-2756.6ms against NEW 2670.2-2707.7** — overlapping, and the min slightly
worse. The ffi column flat (776.0/779.9 against 767.3/770.5). Reverted, with the numbers recorded
next to `indexEdgeLabel` so the next attempt starts after it.

Why: a getter doing `??=` is not cheaper than a `Map.get` V8 has already optimized, and what
dominates `indexEdgeLabel` is the INNER per-label `Map`/`Set` work the box does not touch — item
312 priced the whole function at 810ns across seven hash operations, of which these two outer
lookups are two.

### The rule both refutations share

**A cache on an element pays when the element is REVISITED and the caller ALREADY HOLDS it.**

- `traverse 1-hop + filter` (item 321, 1.207x): the walk is driven from the vertex side and many
  edges share a far endpoint, so the box is warm and in hand. Both conditions.
- `count 3-hop` ungated: holds only an id, by a measured choice, and each middle edge is visited
  once. **Neither** condition — and route B shows that acquiring the vertex costs more than the
  box saves.
- the insert path: holds the vertex, but each vertex's box is cold for its first edge and the
  per-edge cost is not the outer hash. **One condition, and the wrong one.**

That is why item 321's win does not generalise, and it is cheaper to state than to rediscover: the
next three candidates can be sorted by those two questions before any code is written.

No behaviour change in this item — one comment, recording two refutations and the micro that
settled them. 4124 tests green; typecheck, lint and fmt:check as separate commands, all 0.

## 324. `edgesOfTypes` was a generator delegating to an iterator it could have returned — 1.253x on the 84x row

Picked from the current ratio table rather than from the last item's momentum. After items 321 and
323, `bun run bench`'s widest TypeScript ratios were `count 3-hop` **84.9x (413.8ms)** and the two
gated three-hop rows at **62.8x (258.9)** and **60.7x (244.6)**. The gated pair matters because
BOTH engines run the same algorithm there — the way-count sweep — so the gap is a per-edge
constant and not a missing path. Native answers those rows in 4.0-4.1ms, which is ~1.4ns an
edge-visit against TypeScript's ~86.

So the question was where 86ns goes, and two components were priced before anything was written.

| component of the sweep's per-edge cost       | ns/edge |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------: |
| `slotOf.get(farId)` — a string hash per edge |    27.2 |
| the `edgesOfTypes` generator frame           |     8.4 |
| everything else (getter, accumulate, loop)   |     ~50 |

**The hash was the bigger piece and is not what shipped**, for a reason worth recording: it prices
at 27.2ns rather than the ~115-157ns items 321/323 measured for a string-keyed `Map`, because
`e.toId` returns the same stored string object every time and V8 caches a hash on a string. The
fix for it is a dense ordinal per vertex, stored on the EDGE for both endpoints at insert — a real
layout change for a ceiling of ~1.44x on one row, so it is **priced and recorded, not built**.

### What shipped

`edgesOfTypes`' hot single-type path was `yield* byType.get(types[0]) ?? []` — a generator
delegating to an iterator it could simply have RETURNED, since a `Set<Edge>` is already an
`Iterable<Edge>`. Split into a returning fast path for the two single-bucket cases plus a generator
tail for the multi-bucket case, which genuinely wants to be lazy because it dedupes across buckets.

Priced in the sweep's own shape first — 200,000 frontier slots × ~5 edges × 3 passes, so 600,000
generator creations and 3,000,000 `next()` calls: **68.7ms against 43.4, 1.58x on that loop, 8.4ns
an edge.** The returning version measured at or _below_ the floor of iterating the Set with no call
at all (43.4 against 48.1), so the function call itself is free.

In situ, four alternated rounds, one case per process, with each line's ffi column as a control a
TypeScript change cannot reach:

| row (ts ms)                  | CONTROL min | NEW min |      ratio | ranges                                      |
| ---------------------------- | ----------: | ------: | ---------: | ------------------------------------------- |
| **`count 3-hop`**            |       397.6 |   317.4 | **1.253x** | [397.6-407.0] vs [317.4-335.2] — disjoint   |
| `count 3-hop + end filter`   |       198.4 |   167.8 | **1.182x** | [198.4-202.8] vs [167.8-173.1] — disjoint   |
| `count 3-hop + start filter` |       192.7 |   169.8 | **1.135x** | [192.7-201.9] vs [169.8-175.8] — disjoint   |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter`    |        39.9 |    39.4 |     1.013x | overlapping — flat                          |
| `query: distinct over a hop` |        53.7 |    53.6 |     1.002x | overlapping — flat                          |
| control: the ffi column      |             |         |       flat | 4.1/4.1, 4.0/4.0, 4.8/4.9, 1.5/1.5, 7.2/7.2 |

The two rows that do not walk many edges per result are flat in the same harness, which is the
control behaviour the change predicts rather than a disappointment.

### This corrects item 310

Item 310 refuted two routes to the 84x row and recorded the diagnosis: _"the 84x is not one hash
per edge… It is spread across the `edgesOfTypes` generator frame (priced at 1.19x on the sweep at
item 300), the `Edge` property reads, and two hash lookups — **and no micro moves a spread
cost**."_

The first of its three named components, removed on its own, moves the row **1.253x**. The spread
was real and the conclusion drawn from it was not: _a cost spread across three components is still
three components, and removing one of them removes one of them._ "No micro moves it" is a
prediction, and it was available to test for the price of one function split.

### A widened spelling group, stated rather than buried

`bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9` reports **0 answer disagreements** and two
groups over 2x. One is the `label on start` guard `CLOSED.md` already records as
correct-not-outstanding. The other is new to the list and this item put it there:

| `three hops: a vacuous start label vs none` (item 221) | before |      after |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -----: | ---------: |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)-[:E]->(d)`            | 518.41 |     537.92 |
| `MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)-[:E]->(d)`              | 277.16 | **203.25** |
| the ratio                                              |  1.87x |   **2.6x** |

The gap widened because the UNLABELLED member got **1.36x faster** and the labelled one did not —
both spellings should cost the same (a vacuous label is one every node carries), so this is item
221's pre-existing gap becoming more visible, not a new one. It is also a LEAD: the labelled
spelling evidently does not reach the single-type path that just got faster, which localises item
221 better than it has been. Recorded for its own item; the probe is a probe and its threshold is
relative.

### Teeth

Five mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`:

| mutant                                                            | result                                        |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Z1 the fast path returns the FIRST bucket, not the requested type | caught (51)                                   |
| Z2 the fast path returns empty                                    | caught (272)                                  |
| Z3 the untyped single-bucket case falls through to the generator  | **SURVIVED — a de-optimization, same answer** |
| Z4 the multi-bucket tail stops deduping                           | caught (21)                                   |
| Z5 a fresh `[]` instead of the shared `NO_EDGES`                  | **SURVIVED — equivalent**                     |

Z1 is the one worth naming: returning the wrong bucket is invisible whenever a vertex has only one
edge type, which the bench fixture does — it takes a MULTI-TYPE fixture to catch, and 51 tests have
one.

4124 tests green across core, emitter, gql, sync, native, gremlin and mcp; three clean full fuzzer
runs; typecheck, lint and fmt:check as separate commands, all 0.

## 325. Four vertices out of 200,004 cost a spelling 2.8x — and the probe group that should have caught it was testing something else

Item 324 widened `spelling-probe`'s `three hops: a vacuous start label vs none (item 221)` group
from 1.87x to 2.6x, by speeding up one member and not the other. That was reported honestly and
left as a lead. This is the lead, and the group turns out to have been measuring the wrong thing
since the fixture last changed.

### The group's premise was false

`vacuousLabel` is an EXACT equality — the label's bucket size against `vertexCount`:

```ts
expr?.kind === 'label' && (graph.verticesByLabel.get(expr.name)?.size ?? 0) === graph.vertexCount;
```

The probe's fixture gives every `v` node `:P`, and then adds **four `:S` nodes** for an unrelated
group (a comma product needs a tiny left side). Its comment reasons about them carefully and is
right about what it checks: _"They carry no edges, so the two groups that start an UNTYPED hop scan
see no extra rows."_ Right about the ROWS, and silent about vacuity — `|P| = N` against
`vertexCount = N + 4`, so **`:P` is not vacuous**, `effectiveLabel` cannot elide it, and the group
has been comparing a real label constraint against no label at all.

So its 1.87x was correct behaviour for a non-vacuous label, and item 324's 2.6x was correct
behaviour plus a genuine improvement to one member.

### What it costs, measured

Pointing the group at a label every vertex carries:

| `three hops`                                      | `:P` (non-vacuous) | a vacuous label |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -----------------: | --------------: |
| `MATCH (a:<label>)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)-[:E]->(d)` |          537.92 ms |   **190.91 ms** |
| `MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)-[:E]->(d)`         |          203.25 ms |       196.49 ms |
| the ratio                                         |           **2.6x** |       **1.03x** |

**Four vertices out of 200,004 cost the labelled spelling 2.8x.** That is the finding worth keeping,
and it is not a bug: eliding a label four vertices do not carry would change the answer. It is a
CLIFF — vacuity is all-or-nothing, so a single unlabelled node in a real graph defeats the elision
for every query anchored on that label, and the fall is from a bucket-size read to a per-edge label
check on the `a` side.

It also means the vacuous-label elision now has an end-to-end guard, which it did not have: with
the group pointed at `:P` the elision never fired, so nothing would have noticed it breaking.

### Fixed carefully, because the obvious fix silenced a deliberate guard

The first attempt gave the four `:S` nodes a `:P` as well. That restores `:P`'s vacuity and the
group reads 1.03x — and it also took `label on start: redundant vs absent` from 3225x to **under
the 1ms floor, not compared**. `CLOSED.md` records that group as _"CORRECT, not outstanding… It
