stays as a regression guard on the 54 ms; do not quiet it by reverting the fixture"_ — and its
2100-4160x has the same cause, so quieting it is exactly what that attempt did.

So the fixture gained a SEPARATE label (`:Univ`) that every vertex carries, including the `:S`
nodes, and only the vacuity group uses it. `:P` stays non-vacuous on purpose. Both groups now test
their own premise: the probe reports **0 answer disagreements, 0 groups under the floor, and one
group over 2x — the `label on start` guard, at 3225.6x.**

(`:All` was the first name tried and the engine refused it: _"`All` is a reserved word and can't be
used bare as a label name"_. Correct ISO behaviour, and a free confirmation that the reserved-word
check works.)

### Refuted along the way: `edgesOfTypes`' twin

Item 324's lesson was to grep for `yield*` as the first line of a branch. It found one:
`edgesMatching` in `graph-queries.ts` has the identical `yield* set` single-label fast path, on the
GENERAL traversal path that serves the rows the shortcuts decline — and the comment beside it
records item 119 measuring a generator layer at **~40ns in situ** against a micro's 8ns.

Counted before changing anything: **0 calls, across `traverse 1-hop project`,
`query: distinct over a hop`, `query: 2-hop subquery item` and `count 3-hop`.** `expand`'s own
single-type fast path (item 119) already bypasses `edgesMatching` for every caller that matters,
exactly as its comment claims. The candidate died for the price of a counter, before a line of it
was written — which is the whole value of instrumenting first.

`candidateVertices`' two `yield*` sites are likewise already done: item 164 added
`candidateVertexSource`, the returning twin, and the hot consumers use it.

No engine change in this item. The deliverable is an instrument that tests what it says, a cliff
with a number on it, and two candidates closed.

## 326. The adjacency's innermost `Set<Edge>` priced on three axes — the array wins two and a half of them, and the half is the whole problem

The adjacency is `Map<vertexId, Map<label, Set<Edge>>>`. An edge enters a given `(vertex, label)`
bucket exactly once, so the Set's dedup is never needed — it is paid on every insert and every
iteration. Nothing in `CLOSED.md` has priced replacing it with an array (item 200's type-first
inversion is a different question: which map is outermost, not what the innermost container is).

Three things change, and they do not point the same way, so all three were measured before anything
was written — 1,000,000 edges across 200,000 buckets of 5, the bench fixture's shape:

| axis                              | `Set<Edge>` |   array |                     |
| --------------------------------- | ----------: | ------: | ------------------- |
| INSERT, 1M edges                  |     45.8 ms |  6.4 ms | **7.13x**           |
| ITERATE, 3M visits (`for…of`)     |     29.2 ms |  4.6 ms | **6.37x**           |
| ITERATE, 3M visits (indexed loop) |     29.2 ms |  3.3 ms | **8.80x**           |
| REMOVE at **degree 5**            |      5.4 ms |  0.6 ms | **array 9x FASTER** |
| REMOVE at **degree 1000**         |      0.5 ms | 11.0 ms | **array 24x WORSE** |

The surprise is the fourth row: at degree 5 an `indexOf` over five elements beats a Set hash, so
the array wins all three axes at the fixtures' degree. The fifth row is the whole problem, and it
is not a fixture artifact — a people graph has vertices with thousands of edges, which is the
scale this engine is for.

### What it would be worth, and why that is not enough on its own

- **Insert.** `indexEdgeLabel` does THREE Set adds per edge (the label bucket, the from side, the
  to side). At 45.8ns each that is ~137ns of the 810ns item 312 priced for the whole function, so
  arrays take `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)` from ~2900 to ~2763 ns an edge — **about 1.05x** on
  the largest absolute row in the bench.
- **Iterate.** ~8.2ns an edge-visit saved. The way-count sweep makes 3M of them, so ~25ms of the
  ~170ms the gated three-hop rows now cost — **about 1.17x**, and it would compound with item 324.

So roughly 1.05x on ingest and 1.17x on the sweep rows: real, and not enough to justify a
wholesale swap that regresses high-degree removal 24x.

### The shape that would work, sized rather than built

A hybrid: an array up to a threshold, a Set above it. That is item 267's own pattern
(`IN_CHAIN_MAX = 32`, a measured line where one representation stops paying), and the thresholds
here are measured rather than guessed — the array is ahead at 5 and behind at 1000.

What makes it a real piece of work rather than a swap is the API surface, counted rather than
estimated: **21 sites type the innermost container as `Set<Edge>`** across `Graph.ts`,
`executor.ts`, `shortcuts.ts` and `graph-queries.ts`, and **12 of them read `.size`** — which a
hybrid has to provide, along with `has`, `delete` and iteration, without handing callers a wrapper
whose method calls give back what the container saved. (`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` is the
standing warning that an extra indirection on this engine's hot paths is not free.)

So: **priced, sized, and not built.** What would make it buildable is a decision about the
container's public shape — the measurement is done, and the remaining question is an API one, not
a performance one.

### Why the two obvious shortcuts do not exist

Neither win is available without changing the container. Iterating a `Set` as an array is not a
thing, and the insert saving is the `add` itself. There is no narrow slice of this to ship, which is
why this item ends with a table instead of a diff.

No behaviour change. The deliverable is the three-axis table, the degree-5-wins-removal result
that contradicts the obvious reading, and the 21/12 API count that says what the work actually is.

## 327. CORRECTION to item 326 — both removal rows measured locality, not degree, and the verdict changes

Item 326 priced the adjacency's innermost `Set<Edge>` against an array and reported removal as
**"array 9x FASTER at degree 5"** and **"array 24x WORSE at degree 1000"**. Both are wrong, and the
tell was in its own numbers: read per operation, `Set.has` came out at **27ns at degree 5 and 2.5ns
at degree 1000**. A hash set does not get ten times faster as it grows.

What got faster was the memory access. The degree-5 case probed **200,000 different buckets**, a
cache miss each; the degree-1000 case probed **one bucket**, hot throughout. The experiment varied
locality and degree together and attributed the result to degree.

### Re-measured with locality held constant

The same bucket count (2,000) and the same probe count (200,000) at every degree, probes scattered
across all buckets, the probed edge always present — which is the removal path's real case:

| degree | `Set.has` | `indexOf` |               |
| -----: | --------: | --------: | ------------- |
|      2 |    5.6 ns |    5.1 ns | array wins    |
|      4 |    5.9 ns |    5.7 ns | array wins    |
|  **8** |    7.2 ns |    7.3 ns | **crossover** |
|     16 |    7.8 ns |    9.1 ns | 1.18x         |
|     32 |    9.8 ns |   14.5 ns | 1.48x         |
|     64 |   10.6 ns |   21.6 ns | 2.04x         |
|    128 |   12.5 ns |   31.3 ns | 2.51x         |
|    512 |   21.2 ns |   89.5 ns | 4.22x         |
|   1000 |   13.6 ns |  100.8 ns | **7.41x**     |

So the crossover is at **degree ~8** — not "somewhere between 5 and 1000" — the high-degree penalty
is **7.4x rather than 24x**, and the array's low-degree advantage is **~1.03x rather than 9x**. Both
of item 326's removal figures exaggerated the contrast, in the same direction.

`Set.has` is not perfectly flat either (5.6ns at degree 2 against 21.2 at 512), but that growth is
cache pressure from touching more memory, not the hash — which is the same confound at a smaller
scale, and why the column is reported rather than summarised.

### The mechanism, stated plainly, because item 326 implied the opposite

A `Set`'s uniqueness check does **not** grow with size. `add`/`has`/`delete` hash the object and
probe a table: roughly constant whether the set holds 5 elements or 5 million. That is why item
326's insert (7.13x) and iterate (6.37-8.80x) results hold at _every_ degree — the Set loses there
always, because it pays a hash to enforce a uniqueness that cannot be violated, an edge entering a
`(vertex, label)` bucket exactly once.

What grows is the **array's** side, and only on removal: `indexOf` scans. The crossover is simply
"how many identity comparisons cost what one hash costs", and the answer here is about eight.

### The verdict changes, and in the array's favour

Item 326 concluded the trade was unattractive. With the real numbers it is better than that, for a
reason that has nothing to do with the crossover point:

**Removal happens at most once per edge. Iteration happens once per edge per query.** So the
threshold should be set by that ratio, not by where removal crosses over. At degree 128 an array is
2.51x worse on a once-per-edge operation and 6-9x better on a per-query one; a graph that is read
more than a handful of times comes out ahead.

The honest counter is degree SKEW: in a graph with a heavy tail, most EDGES live in high-degree
buckets, so a threshold at 8 would leave most edges on the Set path and give up most of the
insert/iterate win. A threshold of 64-128 keeps it, at a removal cost that is paid once.

That is a decision about expected read/write mix on real data, which is the user's to make and not
a measurement — so it is recorded here with the numbers it needs rather than chosen. Item 326's
API sizing stands: **21 sites type the container as `Set<Edge>`, 12 read `.size`.**

### The method note

This is the second time this session that a two-point comparison moved two variables at once — item
321's control moved with its target because it sat downstream of the change, and here degree moved
with locality. **Two points do not show a trend; they show a line through two points.** The sweep
above exists because a reader asked how the mechanism worked and the answer did not fit the
numbers.

## 328. Native's NDJSON decode is half serial, the recorded Amdahl bound was 25% optimistic, and the obvious candidate is free

Several items running, the TypeScript side has had the attention and the native serving path is near
its floor (item 320), so this tick asked the native corpus what ITS largest absolute cost is —
`bench_all`, the regression sweep, rather than a guess.

The answer is unambiguous and the corpus frames it itself. `ingest/ceiling (5 edges/node)`:

| 115.8 MiB | raw scan |    decode |     ratio |
| --------- | -------: | --------: | --------: |
|           |  9.10 ms | 717.56 ms | **78.9x** |

Nothing else in the corpus is within two orders of magnitude of that in absolute terms — the next
largest row is `query/gql project 3` at 5.4ms. So the native decode is the native target, and
`ingest/phases` splits decode from record-materialisation and teardown but never _within_ decode.

### The split, from data already in the corpus

`ingest/threads` measures the same decode at 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads: **729.08 / 555.59 / 460.24 /
411.51 ms**. Fitting `T(n) = P/n + S` gives the decomposition with no new measurement — and fitted
at every one of the six pairs rather than two, which is item 327's lesson applied the same day it
was learned:

| pair       | P (parallel) | S (serial) | ceiling |
| ---------- | -----------: | ---------: | ------: |
| n=1 vs n=2 |     347.0 ms |   382.1 ms |   1.91x |
| n=1 vs n=4 |     358.5 ms |   370.6 ms |   1.97x |
| n=1 vs n=8 |     362.9 ms |   366.1 ms |   1.99x |
| n=2 vs n=4 |     381.4 ms |   364.9 ms |   2.00x |
| n=2 vs n=8 |     384.2 ms |   363.5 ms |   2.01x |
| n=4 vs n=8 |     389.8 ms |   362.8 ms |   2.01x |

All six agree: **P = 347-390ms of parallel parse against S = 363-382ms of serial build, so the
serial half is 50-52% of a one-thread decode.**

### The recorded bound was 25% optimistic

`from_ndjson_threads`' own doc comment said _"Amdahl-bounded by the remaining serial insert at
~2.5x @ 8 threads (measured)"_. At today's serial fraction the ceiling is **1.91-2.01x**, so 2.5x
is not reachable — and the measured 1.77x is **88% of the real bound**, not 71% of an achievable
one. That reframes the parallel side from "underperforming" to "nearly done", and it is the kind of
stale number that sends someone after the wrong half. Corrected in place with the fit.

### The obvious candidate, killed by reading a type

Both serial loops clone every property value — `props.iter().map(|(k, v)| (k.as_str(), v.clone()))`
per node and `store.set_edge_prop(eid, k, v.clone())` per edge — and `staged` is destructured BY
VALUE, so both could consume instead of clone. At this fixture's scale that is ~2.4M clones (200k
nodes and 1M edges at two props each), which looks like a real slice of 370ms.

It is close to free. `GStr::clone` is a **16-byte struct copy** for an inline string (≤12 bytes,
which these are) and a **relaxed atomic increment** for a long one. No allocation either way. So
the clone-removal is worth single-digit milliseconds at most, and `Value`'s own doc comments say as
much about its `Arc`-boxed variants — _"so a per-row binding clone is a refcount bump"_.

Recorded because it is the first thing anyone will reach for, and because it cost one type lookup
rather than a measurement: **read the clone impl before pricing a clone.**

### What is left, sized

The serial build is ~370ms against a 9.10ms raw-scan floor, and it is already carefully built — bulk
mode deferring version/epoch upkeep, `add_node_bulk`'s single pass, pre-reserved adjacency from
resolved degrees, parallel endpoint resolution, and a recorded refutation of a parallel
counting-sort rebuild ("measured SLOWER — more passes over E, plus rayon overhead across 50k tiny
per-node tasks"). The remaining serial work is scattered adjacency writes whose ORDER is
load-bearing: eids are assigned in input order so the result is byte-identical at any thread count.

So the next move on it is not "parallelize the insert" — that is refuted and the ordering constraint
is real — but a decomposition of those 370ms into the store operations that make it up, which is
the probe this corpus does not have. Priced here as the target rather than attempted at the end of
a tick.

One behaviour-free change: the corrected comment. 1094 Rust tests green, clippy and `cargo fmt
--check` clean as separate commands.

## 329. Where native's 752ms decode actually goes — and 68ms of it is freeing records the parse never needed to own

Item 328 sized native's NDJSON decode as ~50/50 parallel parse against serial build, derived from
the corpus's existing threads sweep, and named the missing probe: a decomposition of the serial
half into store operations. This is it.

Instrumented at the parse/build boundary and at each serial stage (temporary timers behind
`LENKE_DECODE_PHASES`, removed before commit — `Instant::now()` panics under wasm), on the same
fixture `ingest/phases` uses for its `nodes+5edges x2 props` row: 200,000 nodes, 1,000,000 edges,
115.8 MiB. Round 1 discarded as cold; round 3 below.

### First, the fit was right

|              | item 328's Amdahl fit | measured directly |
| ------------ | --------------------- | ----------------- |
| parse        | 347-390 ms            | **370.5 ms**      |
| serial build | 363-382 ms            | **381.8 ms**      |

**Within 5%.** An `T(n) = P/n + S` fit over an existing thread-count sweep recovered the split
without instrumenting anything, which is worth knowing the next time a serial fraction is wanted.

### The decomposition

| stage                       |    ms |               share of the 752ms decode |
| --------------------------- | ----: | --------------------------------------: |
| **parse** (parallelizes)    | 370.5 |                                     49% |
| **serial build**            | 381.8 |                                     51% |
| · edge loop                 | 179.9 |                                     24% |
| · `resolve_endpoints`       |  98.1 | 13% (already parallel above one thread) |
| · **drop the staged edges** |  58.3 |                                **7.7%** |
| · node loop                 |  14.7 |                                         |
| · **drop the staged nodes** |   9.5 |                                    1.3% |
| · `rebuild_csr`             |   8.8 |                                         |
| · degrees + reserve         |   4.4 |                                         |
| · `materialize_ext`         |   4.0 |                                         |
| · `rebuild_edge_num`        |   3.8 |                                         |
| · `end_bulk`                |   0.0 |                                         |

The stages summed to ~282ms against a measured build of 355 on the first pass, and **the 73ms gap
was the only thing left in the function: dropping the staged records.** Timed explicitly it is
**67.8ms** — 9% of the whole decode, spent freeing memory, producing nothing.

### The target that falls out, priced

`EdgeRec` is `(String, String, Option<String>, Vec<String>, Vec<(String, Value)>)` and `NodeRec`
the same shape: every id, label and property KEY is a fresh `String`. A 1M-edge decode therefore
makes ~5M allocations in the parse and frees them again in the build.

- the **teardown** is measured in situ at **67.8ms**;
- the matching **build-up**, in a micro of the same record shapes, is **161.3ms** (213.03 owned
  against 51.75 borrowed, 4.12x on that loop — and the labels/props `Vec`s still allocate in both,
  so this is the `String` side only).

So borrowing is worth roughly **1.2-1.4x on the whole decode**, which is the largest native ingest
target identified. The in-situ half of that is firm; the 161ms is a micro, and this repo has
watched a micro both understate a layer 5x (item 119) and overstate a candidate to zero (items 321,
323), so it is recorded as indicative.

**And borrowing is actually available here, which it was not for the GQL lexer.** Items 294/317
could not borrow tokens because they would have pointed into a transient `Vec<char>`; here the
input `&str` outlives the entire decode, so `NodeRec<'a>`/`EdgeRec<'a>` holding `&'a str` is
straightforwardly sound. The `Value`s stay owned — they are parsed and typed, not substrings — and
the records are only shared immutably across staging workers, so the lifetime is `Send + Sync`
without further work. Recorded at the type definition, where anyone attempting it will land.

### What this closes

`resolve_endpoints` at 98ms looks like the second biggest serial stage and **is not a target**: it
is already parallel above one thread (the store is only read there), so it is 98ms at
`threads = 1` and a fraction of that in the configuration anyone running a large decode would use.
The edge loop's 180ms is the genuine serial floor, and the code already records a refutation of
parallelizing it.

No behaviour change: the instrumentation is removed, and what stays is the corrected
`from_ndjson_threads` comment plus the priced borrow target at `NodeRec`. 1094 Rust tests green,
all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green, clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands.

## 330. The staging parser allocated a `String` per JSON object KEY to compare it against a literal — 1.05-1.11x on the decode

Item 329 priced "borrow the staged records" at 1.2-1.4x and named `NodeRec`/`EdgeRec`. Reading the
code to build it found the target is NOT there, and is both smaller and much cheaper to reach.

### Three things the plan got wrong, found before writing any of it

1. **`record()` does not go through `Json` at all.** The staging path has its own streaming reader
   that writes fields directly into `Option<String>`, so the `json_string` clone at the heart of
   item 329's estimate (`Json::Str(s) => Ok(s.clone())`) is on a DIFFERENT path — the one `ffi.rs`,
   `schema_op.rs` and `exec/ddl.rs` use. Staging already moves rather than clones.
2. **A `Json<'a>` lifetime is a multi-tick refactor**, not a slice: 27 reference sites across three
   other modules. Starting it inside one tick would have left it half-verified.
3. **JSON strings cannot simply be slices** — an escaped string has to be unescaped into a buffer —
   so the borrow has to be a `Cow`, not a `&str`.

### What the waste actually is

`JsonParser::string()` already computed the escape-free slice and then called `.to_string()` on it;
its own comment said _"hand back the borrowed byte slice as ONE `String`"_. Two callers never
needed the `String`:

- **`record()` allocates one per JSON object KEY purely to `match key.as_str()` against literals,
  then drops it** — 4 per node line (`type`, `id`, `labels`, `properties`) and 6 per edge line.
- **a string property value** was allocated only to be copied into a `GStr` and dropped
  (`GStr::from(s.as_str())`).

On the corpus fixture (200k nodes, 1M edges) that is **~8M allocate-and-free pairs storing
nothing.** `string()` keeps its signature — now `self.string_cow()?.into_owned()` — so every other
caller is untouched, and the two wasteful ones take the borrowing twin. The `pairs()` property key
stays owned, because it IS stored.

### Measured

`ingest_bench`, three alternated rounds, min of each. Every row's ranges are disjoint:

| row (decode ms)         | CONTROL |    NEW |      ratio |
| ----------------------- | ------: | -----: | ---------: |
| `nodes+5edges x2 props` |  706.72 | 671.35 | **1.053x** |
| `nodes x1 prop`         |   71.53 |  64.42 | **1.110x** |
| `ingest/ceiling` decode |  718.07 | 658.96 | **1.090x** |

CONTROL spans [706.72, 734.52, 738.05] against NEW's [671.35, 672.55, 676.17] on the first row.

**And the per-allocation cost is 5-7ns, not the 25-40 assumed.** 35ms for ~8M alloc+free pairs on
the 5-edges row, 7.1ms for ~1M on the nodes row. So item 329's 1.2-1.4x estimate — built from a
micro that put the owned/borrowed gap at 161ms — **overstated it, for the same reason item 324's
hash priced at 27ns instead of 115**: an allocator with a hot free list and short-lived objects is
much cheaper than an isolated loop suggests. The measured win is 1.05-1.11x.

### Teeth

A `Cow` has exactly one interesting failure: taking the BORROWED path when the string needed
unescaping, which hands back a raw `\n` as two characters. Five mutants under
`timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`:

| mutant                                               | result                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| M1 borrow ALWAYS, even with escapes                  | caught (8)                                |
| M2 borrow `&b[run..i]` instead of `&b[start..i]`     | **SURVIVED — equivalent BY CONSTRUCTION** |
| M3 the object key compares the RAW slice             | caught (4)                                |
| M4 `string()` spelled with an explicit match         | **SURVIVED — equivalent**                 |
| M5 the property value materialises before the `GStr` | **SURVIVED — equivalent**                 |

**M2 was designed as a wrong-span mutant and is not one.** That return sits inside
`if buf.is_empty()`, and `run` is only advanced in the escape arm — so on the escape-free path
`run == start` always, and the two spans are provably the same slice. A survivor that turns out to
be equivalent is worth more than a caught one here: it says `run` is dead on that path.

Two tests added, and only one of them was a gap. The string-VALUE escape path was ALREADY covered
by `binary_round_trips_escaped_strings` (`"a\"b\nc\ttab\\end"`), which is why the new tests are the
KEY side: an escaped object key (`"id"` must still match `"id"`, reaching the match as a
`Cow::Owned`) and an escaped property key beside it (which stays owned, so it guards that borrowing
its neighbour disturbed nothing).

1096 Rust tests green, 809 `packages/native` tests, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green on a
rebuilt `.so`; clippy, `cargo fmt --check` and `bun fmt:check` clean as separate commands.

### What is left of item 329's target

The records themselves are still owned, and that is still worth something — but less than 1.2-1.4x,
since the 161ms micro that produced that figure has now been contradicted in situ by this change's
5-7ns-per-allocation result. The remaining pieces are the ids, labels and stored property keys,
which a `Cow` in `NodeRec`/`EdgeRec` would reach without the `Json<'a>` refactor at all — the
staging reader does not use `Json`. **Re-price it against this item's per-allocation number before
building it.**

## 331. A property write allocated its key three times and stored one — the two spares were a CDC record nobody was listening to and an `entry()` that owned before it looked

Item 330 closed with an instruction to itself: **re-price the staged-record borrow against this
item's per-allocation number before building it.** Item 329 had put that target at 1.2-1.4x of
native's decode from a micro, and item 330 then measured the real per-allocation cost in situ at
**5-7ns rather than 25-40**, so the estimate was built on a number known to be 5x high.

Re-pricing it needed an instrument, not a micro — the failure mode of the 161ms figure was that it
was a micro. So `alloc_count_probe` (item 317's counting global allocator) gained the decode. It
answered the pricing question and then found a better target on the way.

### The re-pricing

At 50,000 nodes x2 props with 5 edges/node, `from_ndjson` makes **3,050,033 allocations**, of which
**2,250,015 (73.8%) are 8 bytes or smaller** — the record ids, labels and property keys that
borrowing would remove. Scaled to the corpus's 200k/1M fixture that is ~9.0M, against item 329's
in-situ teardown of 67.8ms for ~11.4M frees (the 9.0M strings plus 2.4M `Vec`s), so the string share
of teardown is **~53ms**. Pairing that with an allocation side of the same order puts the borrow at
**~1.13-1.18x**, not 1.2-1.4x. It stays the largest native ingest target and it is still worth
building; the recorded estimate at `NodeRec` is now the counted one rather than the micro's.

### Attribution: what works and what does not

A bulk count says HOW MANY, not WHICH. Two methods were tried and only one survives, which is why
both are recorded in the probe:

- **Differencing small documents does not work.** Counting a 1-line, 2-line, 3-line … document and
  subtracting ought to give a per-line cost exactly. At that scale the store's own HashMap growth
  swamps the line, and the differences come out _negative_ in places (the 4-byte bucket went -2
  across adding a node). Removed, with the reason, so it is not tried a third time.
- **Varying one field of the fixture at 50k lines does work**, because growth amortizes to nothing
  and the bucket that moves by ~50k names itself. Node property keys (`k0`, 2 bytes) move the 2-3B
  bucket by exactly one per node per property. Node ids and labels (6 bytes) sit in 5-7B at two per
  node. And `"type":"node"` / `"type":"edge"` is the 4-byte row — **one allocation per line for a
  field a node never reads at all** (recorded as a follow-on; it is `string_cow`'s trick again).

### The finding the attribution produced

The bulk row showed **three 1-byte allocations per edge**, and the fixture has exactly one 1-byte
thing in it: the edge property key `w`. Widening that key to 2 and then 4 bytes moved **all three**
into the matching bucket together, so all three are the key. A node property key, by contrast,
allocates **once**. So the edge path allocated a key three times and stored one, and the node path's
own serving write does the same two spares — the decode just never reaches it, because
`add_node_bulk` bypasses `set_prop`.

Reading the three:

1. `Undo::RestoreEdgeCell { key: key.to_string() }` — already behind `self.undo.is_some()`, so free
   outside a transaction. **Not one of the three.**
2. `self.edge_props.entry(key.to_string())` — allocated on **every** set, including the
   overwhelmingly common one where the column already exists and the owned key is dropped
   immediately.
3. `self.record_change(Change::EdgeProp { key: key.to_string() })` — `record_change` takes the
   `Change` **by value**, so the key was allocated at the call site and then discarded by an
   `if let Some(ch) = &mut self.changes` that was `None`.

And the fix for (2) was already in this file, with a comment saying why: `bump_epoch` does
`get_mut` first and only pays for the key when the token is new — _"Avoid a String alloc when the
token is already tracked (the common case)."_ The idiom was known and three sites had not applied
it. That is what the grep-the-pattern-elsewhere step is for.

### The change

- `record_change_with(impl FnOnce() -> Change)` beside `record_change`, for the variants whose
  construction costs something. Four call sites: `set_prop`, `remove_prop`, `set_edge_prop`,
  `remove_edge_prop` — the three `Change` variants that carry an owned key.
- `apply_set_prop` and `set_edge_prop` look the key up before paying to own it. The create path
  costs a second lookup, which happens once per key for the store's life.

### Counted first, then measured

The count is the exact result and it needs no error bars. `nodes+5edges x2 props`:
**3,050,033 -> 2,550,034 allocations**, i.e. exactly **2 fewer per edge property write**, and the
1-byte bucket 150,002 -> 50,003 on the isolating fixture. **The nodes-only row is unchanged at
450,238** — a control the change cannot reach, for free, because the node bulk path does not call
`set_prop`.

Timing, **eleven alternated rounds** (seven ctl-first, four new-first, after the first order raised
a drift question), min of each:

| row                                   |   CONTROL |       NEW |        |
| ------------------------------------- | --------: | --------: | ------ |
| `ingest/phases nodes+5edges x2 props` | 661.07 ms | 629.03 ms | 1.051x |
| `storage/write SET p.age` (200k)      |  35.19 ms |  32.39 ms | 1.086x |
| `ingest/phases nodes x4 props` (ctl)  | 113.15 ms | 113.85 ms | flat   |
| `ingest/phases nodes x1 prop` (ctl)   |  63.81 ms |  65.20 ms | +2%    |

Both target rows are **fully disjoint across all eleven rounds** — every control value above every
new value. The two engine controls are flat to +2%.

**The +2% on `nodes x1 prop` is not this change, and the harness says so itself.** `recmat_ms` in
the same table is a `format!` loop inside the example binary that never calls the engine — a null
control by construction — and it reads **2-5% slower in the NEW binary in BOTH orders**, so it is
not run-order drift either. The engine is statically linked into these examples, so a store.rs edit
shifts every address in them; this is the same code-layout sensitivity already recorded for
`exec::pull`. Worth stating plainly: **the raw 1.05x on decode is smaller than this harness's own
null-control drift**, which is why the counted allocation reduction is the result being claimed and
the timing is the corroboration. The disjointness across eleven rounds, in both orders, with the
null control moving the _other_ way, is what makes it a flag rather than noise.

### Teeth

Four mutants, each applied to a restored pristine copy and run under `timeout 600` plus
`MemoryMax=16G MemorySwapMax=0`. All four caught:

| mutant                                                 | caught by                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| M1 the closure runs but its `Change` is never pushed   | 4 failures, incl. `commit_records_the_change_list_rollback_records_nothing` |
| M2 the column-creation guard inverted                  | **170** failures (the `expect` panics)                                      |
| M3 an edge property on an unseen key silently dropped  | 74 failures, edge-property and INSERT/MERGE tests                           |
| M4 the column created from `Null` instead of the value | **2** failures                                                              |

M1 is the one that mattered to design: it leaves the closure _called_ and discards only its result,
so it proves the pushed value is load-bearing rather than merely that something runs. M4's two
failures are the thin spot and are named here rather than smoothed over: **the created column's
SHAPE is guarded by exactly two assertions** (`set_null_no_longer_de_opts_the_column` and
`dict_max_distinct_knob_gates_high_cardinality_encoding`). They are the right two, and two is few.

1096 + 13 + 723 Rust tests green, 809 `packages/native` tests, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases
green; clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands.

**Still open, and now cheaper than it looked**: the `"type"` field's allocation per line (one per
node, one per edge, ~1.2M on the corpus fixture) is `string_cow`'s exact shape and needs no
lifetime work. The staged-record borrow re-prices to ~1.13-1.18x and remains the largest native
ingest target.

## 332. The staged records now borrow the input — 1.21-1.29x on native's decode, and both estimates of it were wrong

Items 329, 330 and 331 circled this target. 329 priced it at 1.2-1.4x from a micro. 330 showed the
micro's per-allocation cost was 5x high and told its successor to re-price. 331 did re-price it, by
counting the allocations rather than running a second micro, and came out **lower**: ~1.13-1.18x.

It is **1.21-1.29x**. So item 329's original range was right and the careful re-pricing was the one
that missed. That is the most useful thing in this entry and it is covered below.

### The change

`NodeRec`/`EdgeRec`/`StagedNdjson`/`Rec` gained a lifetime and hold `Cow<'a, str>` for every id,
label and property KEY. The `Value`s stay owned — they are parsed and typed, not substrings.
`Cow` rather than `&'a str` because two cases genuinely cannot borrow: a JSON string carrying an
escape (which must be unescaped into a buffer) and a numeric id (which is formatted). Both are
rare; both already existed as the owned arm of item 330's `string_cow`, so this change is mostly
_pointing the remaining callers at a function that was already there_ — `pairs`, `string_array` and
`id_as_string` each called `string()` only to own what `string_cow()` had already sliced.

Soundness is the easy half and item 329 had already established it: every decoder entry takes a
`&str` or `&[u8]` that outlives the whole decode, which is exactly what the GQL lexer could not say
(items 294/317, where a token would have pointed into a transient `Vec<char>`). The records are
shared immutably across staging workers, so the lifetime is `Send + Sync` with no further work.

**The binary codec had to come too, and wanted to.** `binary.rs` builds the same `StagedNdjson`, and
its `Reader<'a>::str` was doing _precisely_ what item 330 found on the JSON side: `take(n)` already
hands back `&'a [u8]`, and `str()` called `str::to_string` on the validated slice. The binary format
carries explicit lengths and no escapes, so there is no owned fallback at all there — it is a plain
`&'a str`. `value()` also did `GStr::from(self.str()?.as_str())`, allocating a `String` purely to
copy it into a `GStr`. The v2 constraint sections still own their strings (they feed structs that
want `String`, and a schema section is a handful of rows, not millions).

### Counted first

`alloc_count_probe`, at 50,000 nodes x2 props with 5 edges/node:

|                 | allocations |
| --------------- | ----------: |
| before item 331 |   3,050,033 |
| after item 331  |   2,550,034 |
| **after this**  | **800,034** |

**-68.6% against the previous commit**, and the small buckets are not reduced but _gone_: the ≤8
byte classes total **16 allocations** where they were 2,250,015. The nodes-only row drops
450,238 -> 200,238 the same way. The `"type":"node"` / `"type":"edge"` allocation item 331 left open
(one per LINE, for a field a node never reads) is included — it was the 4-byte bucket, and it is now
empty.

### Then measured

Five alternated rounds, orders 1/3/5 ctl-first and 2/4 new-first, min of each. **Every target range
is fully disjoint.**

| row                                   |   CONTROL |       NEW |            |
| ------------------------------------- | --------: | --------: | ---------- |
| `ingest/phases nodes x1 prop`         |  65.31 ms |  54.08 ms | **1.208x** |
| `ingest/phases nodes x4 props`        | 115.29 ms |  96.69 ms | **1.192x** |
| `ingest/phases nodes+5edges x2 props` | 633.18 ms | 500.44 ms | **1.265x** |
| `ingest/ceiling (5 edges/node)`       | 636.01 ms | 491.76 ms | **1.293x** |
| `value/codec flat scalars` decode     |  91.72 ms |  72.31 ms | **1.268x** |
| `value/codec meta record` decode      | 106.86 ms | 103.98 ms | 1.03x      |
| `value/codec flat scalars` ENCODE     |  30.14 ms |  30.37 ms | flat (ctl) |
| `ingest/phases recmat_ms`             |  37.14 ms |  36.84 ms | flat (ctl) |

Two controls, both flat: **encode** does not go through the staged records at all, and `recmat_ms`
is a `format!` loop inside the example binary that never calls the engine. The second one matters
because at item 331 it drifted 2-5% and put a 1.05x flag below its own noise floor; here it is
within 0.8%, so this effect needs no such argument. (`meta record` decode moves only 1.03x: a map
property's keys go to `GStr` through `make_record`, a path this change does not reach. Its _encode_
reads 1.09x faster, which nothing in this change can explain and is recorded as layout noise rather
than claimed.)

### Why the careful re-pricing was wrong, which is the transferable part

Item 331's arithmetic was: count the allocations the borrow removes (~9M at corpus scale), multiply
by the per-allocation cost item 330 measured **in situ** (5-7ns), get ~53ms of a 700ms decode,
conclude 1.13-1.18x. Every input to that was measured rather than assumed. It still came out low by
a factor of three, because the measured rate was the wrong rate:

- **item 330's allocations were short-lived and LIFO.** A key is parsed, compared to a literal and
  dropped before the next one is parsed. The allocator serves that off a hot free list: 5-7ns.
- **these are long-lived.** ~7M strings are held live across the entire parse and then freed in one
  bulk teardown after 300 MB of churn. That costs page faults on the way up and a cold pointer
  chase on the way down: **~19ns each** (132.7ms over the ~7M removed on the bench fixture).

So: **a per-allocation cost is not a constant of the allocator, it is a property of the
allocation's lifetime.** A count is still the right instrument — it has no noise floor and item 331
showed why that matters — but the rate it is multiplied by has to come from an allocation with the
same lifetime as the ones being counted. Both failed estimates of this target came from pairing a
good count with a rate borrowed from the wrong regime, 329's too high and 331's too low.

### Teeth

Four mutants, each on a restored pristine pair of files, built uncapped, tested under
`timeout 600` + `MemoryMax=16G MemorySwapMax=0`. All four caught:

| mutant                                                              | failures |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------: |
| M1 `string_cow`'s owned/escape arm bypassed (escapes come back raw) |        3 |
| M2 the binary reader borrows one byte short of the stored length    |        2 |
| M3 `record()` routes `to` into `from`, aliasing both endpoints      |       44 |
| M4 `string_array` drops the last label it borrowed                  |       83 |

M1 and M2 are the two that this change actually put weight on — every staged string now flows
through `string_cow`, and every binary string is now a slice of the caller's buffer — and they are
also the two with the fewest failures. **Named rather than smoothed over: the binary codec's string
length handling is guarded by exactly two assertions.** M3 and M4 are there because the rewrite was
mechanical across ~130 lines, and a mechanical rewrite's characteristic failure is a field that
ends up in the wrong slot; those have plenty of coverage.

1096 + 13 + 723 Rust tests green, 809 `packages/native` tests, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases
green (the binary codec is on both sides of that invariant, which is why they run here rather than
being skipped as Rust-only); clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands.

**What this leaves.** The staged records' `Vec`s still allocate — two per node and two per edge,
which is the ≤96 and ≤256 buckets, ~2.4M at corpus scale and now the largest remaining group in the
count. A `SmallVec`-shaped inline capacity of 1-2 would reach most of them, and the count says
exactly how many before anyone measures. The edge loop's 180ms serial floor and the input-order
constraint are unchanged (item 328).

## 333. Two arenas and a span instead of two Vecs per record — 1.07-1.26x more, a 50,000-node decode down to 271 allocations, and three mutants that survived because the fixture was uniform

Item 332 ended by naming the next lever from the count rather than from a guess: the staged records'
own `Vec`s, **616,488 of the 700,036 allocations** the decode still made. This is that, plus the
smaller sibling the same count exposed.

### Two changes, one theme: stop allocating a container per record

**(a) The `&[&str]` buffers in `build_store`'s node loop.** `lrefs` and `prefs` were declared inside
the loop, so each node heap-allocated two vectors whose entire life was one `add_node_bulk` call.
Hoisted above the loop and `clear()`ed — capacity survives, so after the first node they cost
nothing. **-100,000 allocations** (exactly 2 per node), counted.

**(b) The records' own `Vec`s, replaced by one arena per kind and a `Span`.** `StagedNdjson` gained
`labels: Vec<Cow<'a, str>>` and `props: Vec<(Cow<'a, str>, Value)>`, filled in line order;
`NodeRec` is now `(Cow, Span, Span)` and `EdgeRec` `(Cow, Cow, Option<Cow>, Span, Span)`, where
`Span` is `(u32, u32)`. Rust's first growth for a 24-to-56-byte element is capacity 4 and these hold
one or two, so the old shape allocated 96 or 224 bytes per record to store 24 or 56. `u32` because a
64-bit span would make the record larger than the `Vec` it replaced.

The parser grew `string_array_into` and `pairs_into` (append into a caller's arena, the
`Vec`-returning forms kept for the schema lines' `keys` and for a nested record VALUE, which has no
arena to append to). `binary.rs` got `str_list_into` / `props_into` the same way, so both decoders
still feed one `build_store`.

Two details that are easy to get wrong and are commented in place:

- **A repeated `labels` / `properties` key is last-wins**, which with a shared arena means rewinding
  to _this record's_ start, not the arena's front.
- **The parallel concat must rebase every span.** Each chunk stages into its own arenas, so its
  spans are chunk-relative; the offsets are read BEFORE the arenas are extended.

### Counted

`alloc_count_probe`, 50,000 nodes x2 props:

|          | nodes only | with 5 edges/node |
| -------- | ---------: | ----------------: |
| item 330 |    450,238 |         3,050,033 |
| item 331 |    450,238 |         2,550,034 |
| item 332 |    200,238 |           800,034 |
| **this** |    **271** |       **100,072** |

**A 50,000-node decode now makes 271 heap allocations in total** — the per-record cost is gone
rather than reduced. Across the four items the edge fixture is **30.5x fewer allocations**. What
remains at 100,072 is store structure (edge-property maps, adjacency growth), not per-record
transit.

### Measured

Five alternated rounds, 1/3/5 ctl-first and 2/4 new-first, min of each. Every target range disjoint.

| row                                   |   CONTROL |       NEW |            |
| ------------------------------------- | --------: | --------: | ---------- |
| `ingest/phases nodes x1 prop`         |  54.10 ms |  43.65 ms | **1.239x** |
| `ingest/phases nodes x4 props`        |  93.23 ms |  87.07 ms | **1.071x** |
| `ingest/phases nodes+5edges x2 props` | 502.49 ms | 401.70 ms | **1.251x** |
| `ingest/ceiling (5 edges/node)`       | 496.11 ms | 394.74 ms | **1.257x** |
| `ingest/threads @ 8`                  | 300.69 ms | 263.73 ms | **1.140x** |
| `value/codec flat scalars` decode     |  70.96 ms |  65.03 ms | **1.091x** |
| `value/codec meta record` decode      |  99.74 ms |  87.36 ms | **1.142x** |
| `ingest/phases recmat_ms`             |  35.67 ms |  34.83 ms | flat (ctl) |

The spread across rows is itself a check that the mechanism is the claimed one. **`x1 prop` gains
1.239x and `x4 props` only 1.071x**: the removed cost is per RECORD, so it amortizes over however
much content a record carries, and four properties dilute it. `threads @ 8` gains less than serial
(1.140x vs 1.251x) because the parse is the half that parallelizes, so making it cheaper leaves the
serial build a larger share — Amdahl, in the expected direction.

Cumulative on `nodes+5edges x2 props` across items 330-333: **706.72 -> 401.70 ms, 1.76x.**

### THREE MUTANTS SURVIVED, and the reason is the fixture

This is the part worth keeping. Five mutants, first run:

| mutant                                                | first run    | after the fix |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------- |
| M1 the LABELS span is not rebased on parallel concat  | **SURVIVED** | caught (1)    |
| M2 the PROPS span is not rebased                      | **SURVIVED** | caught (1)    |
| M3 `span_of` ignores the start, slices from the front | caught (82)  | caught (83)   |
| M4 the last-wins rewind truncates the whole arena     | **SURVIVED** | caught (1)    |
| M5 the binary reader's label span is one short        | caught (2)   | caught (2)    |

`decode_is_byte_identical_across_thread_counts` exists, compares 2/4/8/16 threads against serial,
and is exactly the test that should have caught M1 and M2. It did not, and the reason is that
**every node in its fixture carried the label `Person` and every edge an empty `properties`**:

- an unrebased span still lands on an _identical string_ when every string is identical, so the
  re-encode is byte-identical and the assertion passes;
- an **empty** span cannot be offset wrongly at all, so the props rebasing had no coverage from the
  edge side whatsoever.

This is precisely the fixture failure the repo guide warns about for the `examples/` probes — _"their
fixtures give every node the same label and ask for `count(*)`, and a planner rewrite that permutes
which slot holds which node is invisible to both"_ — found here in a **unit test**, which is where
the guide says correctness is supposed to live. Fixed by deriving each record's second label and
each edge's properties from its index, so a misread span produces a different answer. M4 had no test
at all (nothing in the suite feeds a duplicated key); added
`a_repeated_labels_or_properties_key_is_last_wins`, which also asserts the records on either side
keep their own labels — the thing a rewind to the arena's front would break.

**The generalisable rule**: a byte-identity test over a uniform fixture tests the plumbing and not
the addressing. Any change that makes a record's data reachable _by index_ rather than by ownership
needs a fixture where the index is recoverable from the data. Writing the mutants is what surfaced
it; the test had been green for its whole life and would have stayed green through a real rebasing
bug.

1097 + 13 + 723 Rust tests green, 809 `packages/native` tests, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases
green; clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands.

**What is left on this path.** The 100,072 remaining allocations are store structure rather than
decode transit, so the per-record ingest target is closed. The edge loop's 180ms serial floor
(item 328) and the input-order constraint are untouched, and `ingest/ceiling` now reads 394.74ms
against a 9.10ms raw-scan floor — still 43x, but down from 78.9x when item 328 opened this thread.

## 334. The TS engine built an undo closure on every write and threw it away — refuted on the write path, 1.3-1.9x on DELETE, and the harness that said "flat" could not have said otherwise

Four items on the native ingest path closed it (330-333), so this tick went to the TypeScript
engine, where memory names `addVertex` as THE ingest target. What it found there is the same shape
item 331 found in Rust, and a reader had asked about it directly: _"could we somehow batch the undo
changes to allocate fewer closures?"_

### The shape

`Graph.recordUndo(inverse)` **discards its argument unless `txDepth > 0 && !applyingUndo`** — it is
a no-op outside a transaction, which is the bulk-ingest case and the common one. All **eight** call
sites built the closure eagerly anyway, because the inverse is taken BY VALUE. Exactly
`record_change(Change::EdgeProp { key: key.to_string() })` at item 331, in a different language.

Two of the eight were worse than a closure. `removeVertex` and `removeEdge` capture the element's
state while it is still live:

```ts
const undoId = vertex.id;
const undoLabels = [...vertex.labels];
const undoProps = { ...vertex.properties };
```

so **a removal outside a transaction deep-copied the labels and every property** for a rollback
that could not happen. That copy is O(property width).

Added a private `undoWanted` getter (the same condition `recordUndo` tests) and gated all eight
sites on it; the two capture sites build one object when wanted and nothing when not.

**Answering the question as asked**: batching is not the fix and would not have helped. The
closures outside a transaction are not a cost to amortize, they are work with no reader — and
measured below, even removing them entirely does nothing on the write path. What _was_ worth
removing is the per-property copy standing next to them.

### Refuted on the write path, and said plainly

`decode ndjson (nodes)` is 200,000 `addVertex` calls — verified, `packages/serialization/
src/ndjson/index.ts:115` goes through it, so this is not item 321's mistake of optimising a
function the hot row never calls. Three alternated rounds, each side rebuilt (the bench reads the
built dist):

| row (ms, lower better)         | CONTROL (min) | NEW (min) |                         |
| ------------------------------ | ------------: | --------: | ----------------------- |
| `decode ndjson (nodes)`        |         242.2 |     236.6 | overlapping             |
| `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)` |        2594.6 |    2664.0 | overlapping, NEW slower |
| `query: count` (control)       |           3.0 |       3.2 | flat                    |

**Flat.** At 242ms for 200,000 nodes that is 1.2µs a vertex, and two closure allocations are not
findable in it. Every `bench:usage` row was flat too.

### AND THE HARNESS COULD NOT HAVE SAID OTHERWISE

Worth more than the flag it failed to produce. `bench:usage`'s `read: point lookup` is a row this
change cannot reach, and across three alternated rounds it read **685.4k, 911.4k, 1.16M ops/s — a
1.7x spread on an unreachable control.** So `bench:usage` cannot settle any question below about
2x, and the three rows I had been reading as "flat" were not evidence of flatness. Recorded because
the harness does not say this about itself and the next person to price a single-digit-percent
change there will read the same numbers.

### 1.3-1.9x on DELETE, with an in-table control

The write path was the wrong place to look: the removed copy is O(property WIDTH), and every
fixture in the repo gives a node three or four properties. The claim is about width, so the fixture
has to vary width. New permanent probe, `packages/native/delete-width-probe.ts`
(`bun run delete:width`), 20,000 nodes, min of 7:

| width | CTL `del_ns/node` | NEW `del_ns/node` |           | CTL in-txn | NEW in-txn | (control) |
| ----: | ----------------: | ----------------: | --------- | ---------: | ---------: | --------- |
|     4 |               362 |               273 | **1.33x** |        310 |        327 | flat      |
|    16 |               518 |               391 | **1.32x** |        670 |        640 | flat      |
|    64 |             1,334 |             1,031 | **1.29x** |      1,798 |      1,512 | flat      |
|   256 |            12,095 |             6,251 | **1.93x** |     14,634 |     14,339 | flat      |

**The in-transaction column is a control inside the same binary**, and it is the strongest evidence
here. Inside a transaction a rollback _can_ replay, so the capture is not dead and the copy is still
taken — and that column is unchanged at every width. Better still, the two columns' RELATIONSHIP
inverts: on CONTROL, delete-in-a-transaction and delete-outside-one cost nearly the same at width
256 (12,095 vs 14,634) because both copy; on NEW they differ **2.3x** (6,251 vs 14,339). That is the
mechanism's signature, not a timing coincidence.

A second permanent row went in on the way: `bench:usage` had **no delete workload at all**, so the
only delete number in the repo was the one this probe produced. Added
`write: append then delete node` (paired, so a time-boxed run does not shrink the graph toward
empty).

### Why the probe reads source instead of the dist

`delete-width-probe.ts` imports `../core/src/index.ts`, which trips the repo's own
`boundaries/no-cross-package-relative-import`. Disabled with a reason, and the rule's message names
this case — _"a source import that avoids a build step."_ It is a probe, not a fuzzer or a
cross-engine bench, so nothing about it is byte-identity sensitive and it has no reason to read a
dist. Going through `@lenke/core` puts a full `bun run build` between every edit and every
measurement: the A/B above cost six builds and about ten minutes, where the width sweep cost
seconds. That cost is exactly why the width sweep did not already exist.

### Verification

345 `packages/core`, 1990 `packages/gql`, 144 `packages/serialization`, 809 `packages/native`,
all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green. `lint`, `typecheck` and `fmt:check` each run as their own
command, each exit 0.

**A note on `bun test` from the repo root**: it reports 4639 pass / 63 fail. The identical
4639 / 63 comes back with this change reverted, so none of it is this item — it is the recorded
run-many flake in `@lenke/sync` / `@lenke/native` plus `packages/react`, whose failures are a
missing DOM (`document.body` undefined) when the suite is invoked outside nx. Checked rather than
assumed, because an unexplained 63 next to a change is indistinguishable from a caused one.

## 335. The transactional delete's property copy was never needed — 1.70x at width 256, and two mutants proved the change was resting on untested facts

Item 334 removed `removeVertex`/`removeEdge`'s state capture **outside** a transaction, where it was
dead. Its own probe then showed what was left: **inside** a transaction the capture is still taken
and is still O(property width) — 15,010 ns/node at width 256 against 6,251 outside. That is real
work for a rollback that genuinely might replay, so it looked like the floor.

It is not the floor, because the copy was never needed at all.

### Three facts, and the copy falls out

`{ ...vertex.properties }` exists to snapshot a bag that is about to become unreadable. But:

1. **the bag is `Object.freeze`d** — `#commitProperties` freezes every bag it stores;
2. **every write REPLACES `box.bag`** rather than mutating the bag, and the comment there says so:
   _"REPLACE the box's bag rather than the map entry … The bag itself stays frozen"_;
3. **`addVertex`'s constructor assigns through the public setter, which copies defensively** —
   `set properties` is `this.#commitProperties({ ...properties })`, with its own comment: _"the
   caller may keep a reference to `properties`, so copy defensively"_.

So a reference to the current bag already _is_ a stable snapshot, and the replay makes its own copy
when (and only when) it runs. `evict` does not clear `#box` either, so the bag outlives the vertex.
The capture becomes a field read.

The **labels** stay a copy: `commitElementLabels` replaces the box's `Set`, but the
add/remove-label funnel is a separate path I did not prove, and a label set is one or two entries —
O(1) in practice, and not worth the same argument. Recorded at the site so the asymmetry reads as a
decision rather than an oversight.

### Measured

`bun run delete:width`, three alternated rounds, min of each, `del_ns/node`:

| width | CTL in-txn | NEW in-txn |             | CTL plain | NEW plain | (control) |
| ----: | ---------: | ---------: | ----------- | --------: | --------: | --------- |
|     4 |        313 |        347 | overlapping |       234 |       241 | flat      |
|    16 |        456 |        517 | overlapping |       337 |       388 | flat      |
|    64 |      1,792 |      1,292 | **1.39x**   |       863 |       945 | flat      |
|   256 |     13,834 |      8,117 | **1.70x**   |     6,198 |     6,212 | flat      |

**The width-256 plain row is 6,198 vs 6,212 — flat to 0.2%**, which is the control this change
cannot reach: outside a transaction item 334 already skipped the capture, so that number must not
move, and it does not. At widths 4 and 16 the target is flat-to-slightly-worse, which is the
expected shape rather than a disappointment — a 4-key spread is nearly free, so there is nothing
to recover, and the within-side noise at those widths is ±30%. The effect appears exactly where the
mechanism says it should: at the widths where the copy is the cost.

### TWO MUTANTS SURVIVED, and both were facts this change depends on

Five mutants, each breaking one link in the argument above:

| mutant                                                         | first run    | after       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ----------- |
| M1 `#commitProperties` mutates the bag in place (fact 2)       | caught (48)  | caught (48) |
| M2 the constructor aliases the bag instead of copying (fact 3) | **SURVIVED** | caught (1)  |
| M3 a vertex rollback restores no properties                    | caught (4)   | caught (4)  |
| M4 `undoWanted` is always `false`                              | caught (16)  | caught (17) |
| M5 an **edge** rollback restores no properties                 | **SURVIVED** | caught (1)  |

M2 is the one that matters. **The defensive copy in `set properties` is the entire reason this
change is sound, and removing it broke no test.** It had a comment explaining itself and nothing
asserting it — which is exactly the state in which a later "the setter copies twice, let's drop
one" looks like free money. Added
`addVertex COPIES the properties it is given, so a caller cannot mutate graph state`.

M5 is narrower but the same kind: `rollback reverses edges, labels, and property removals too`
exists, and a rolled-back edge _removal_ still never had its properties checked. Added
`a rolled-back edge removal restores its PROPERTIES, not just its endpoints`.

**The generalisable point**: when a change's safety rests on behaviour elsewhere in the codebase,
mutate THAT behaviour, not just the lines you edited. Both survivors are in files this change does
not touch, and neither would have been found by mutating `removeVertex`. A comment asserting an
invariant is not a test of it, and three of this item's three facts were documented while only one
was guarded.

### Verification

347 `packages/core` (two new), 1990 `packages/gql`, 144 `packages/serialization`, 809
`packages/native`, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green. `lint`, `typecheck`, `fmt:check` and
`build` each run as their own command, each exit 0.

**What is left on the TS delete path.** At width 256 a transactional delete is now 8,117 ns/node
against 6,212 outside one, so ~1,900 ns of genuinely transactional work remains (the undo-log push,
`txTouched`, the deferred-check bookkeeping) and it is no longer dominated by a copy. The remaining
per-width cost in BOTH columns — 6,212 ns/node at width 256 against 273 at width 4 — is the
property de-index, which is a different target and a real one: it is ~23x the width-4 cost for 64x
the properties, so it is sub-linear but far from flat.

## 336. 93% of a wide TS delete was enumerating the element's property keys for the reactive token bump — 3.00x, after two candidate fixes that did nothing

Item 335 closed by naming the next target from its own probe: the per-width cost present in BOTH
delete columns, 6,212 ns/node at width 256 against 273 at width 4. It guessed the property
de-index. That guess was wrong and cost one grep to kill: `PropertyIndex.remove` iterates
`this.indexes` — the DECLARED indexes — not the element's properties, so with none declared (the
probe's case) it is O(0).

### Diagnosis, before any candidate

The only other O(width) thing in a removal is the reactive token bump: `pushTokens` pushes **one
token per property key** for `VertexAdded` / `VertexRemoved` / `EdgeAdded` / `EdgeRemoved`, because
a topology change really does alter the value set of every key the element carried.

Short-circuiting that one loop (a throwaway diagnostic, not a candidate):

| width | `del_ns/node` with it | without it |           |
| ----: | --------------------: | ---------: | --------- |
|     4 |                   273 |        250 | —         |
|    16 |                   391 |        266 | 1.47x     |
|    64 |                 1,031 |        280 | **3.68x** |
|   256 |                 6,212 |        421 | **14.8x** |

So it is not _a_ term, it is **93% of a width-256 delete** and essentially all of the
width-dependence. Worth stating because the number also bounds what any fix here can be worth.

### TWO CANDIDATES THAT MEASURED NOTHING, and what they ruled out

Both are recorded with numbers, next to nothing, because each is the obvious next move.

**`for...in` instead of `Object.keys`** — kills the intermediate array. Width 256: **6,617
ns/node against 6,212 baseline.** Slightly worse, inside noise. So the array allocation is not the
cost.

**`pendingTokens` as a `Map<token, times>` instead of a list.** The list keeps duplicates —
correctly, since the epoch numbers are observable and the file says they _"land on the same
numbers"_ as a per-write drain, and `epoch` is public API mirrored from the Rust core — so I kept
the counts exact and only changed the container, which caps it at the number of DISTINCT tokens
instead of one entry per (write x token): 5.12 MILLION strings in one microtask window at this
fixture. Three alternated rounds:

| width | list (min) | counts-map (min) |                  |
| ----: | ---------: | ---------------: | ---------------- |
|     4 |        267 |              236 | 1.13x better     |
|    16 |        318 |              290 | 1.10x better     |
|    64 |        907 |              751 | **1.21x better** |
|   256 |      6,221 |            8,344 | **1.34x WORSE**  |

A width-dependent trade with no winner, so not shippable — and it **refutes the mechanism I had
assumed**, that the cost was the pending array growing unboundedly. It is not: a structure that
never grows past 256 entries is slower at width 256.

**Then, to price the one lever I could not take**: a `Set<string>` (dedup) collapses 5.12M epoch
bumps to 256 but changes the counts, so it would be a cross-engine semantic decision rather than an
optimization. Measured anyway, to turn "a decision someone has to make" into a decision with a
number on it: **6,489 ns/node, no faster than the list.** So there is nothing to decide — dedup
buys nothing, because the per-token hash on the way in costs what the `Map.set` it saves costs.

Three structures, all within a trade of each other. The cost is not the receiver at all.

### What it actually is, and the fix

It is **key ENUMERATION over a wide bag**, which the engine holds in dictionary mode (the 128->256
cliff this repo already records for `SET`). `Object.keys` and `for...in` are equally slow there, and
neither can be avoided — but it can be done **once per bag instead of once per event**. The bag is
`Object.freeze`d and every write REPLACES `box.bag` rather than mutating it (items 335's facts), so
a key list is valid for exactly as long as the bag it came from.

`PropBox` gained `keys?: readonly string[]`, memoized through a new `propertyKeys` accessor on
`Vertex` and `Edge`, and cleared at the two sites that assign `bag`. An add and the matching remove
now enumerate once between them instead of twice.

**Memoized only above a width.** The memo RETAINS the key array where the old code threw it away —
about 8 bytes per property per element — and the measurements put the entire payoff at the wide
end. `WIDE_BAG = 64` is where the rows stop moving, so below it a graph would pay the memory and
get nothing.

### Measured

`bun run delete:width`, three alternated rounds (unthresholded, to measure the mechanism cleanly),
min of each:

| row                         |   CONTROL |       NEW |           |
| --------------------------- | --------: | --------: | --------- |
| width 256 delete            |     6,211 |     2,070 | **3.00x** |
| width 256 delete, in a txn  |     8,248 |     4,231 | **1.95x** |
| width 64 delete             |       897 |       879 | flat      |
| width 16 delete             |       337 |       389 | flat      |
| width 4 delete              |       272 |       261 | flat      |
| **width 256 ADD (control)** | 861.45 ms | 883.90 ms | +2.6%     |

**The add column is the control, and it is the one that proves the mechanism**: the add is the
event that COMPUTES the memo, so it cannot benefit, and it does not — it pays ~2.6% to retain the
array. Only the second enumeration is saved, which is exactly what a memo does. With the threshold
in place that cost drops to ~1% and the narrow rows return to baseline while width 256 keeps
2,444 / 3,896.

No regression where this runs below the threshold: the cross-engine TS `decode ndjson (nodes)` is
**236.0 -> 229.5 ms** and `(5 edges/node)` **2,578.5 -> 2,595.3**, both overlapping, with
`query: count` flat.

### Teeth

Five mutants. **M1 and M2 — the memo's invalidation, which is the entire invariant — SURVIVED.**

| mutant                                   | first run    | after      |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------ | ---------- |
| M1 a VERTEX write leaves the memo stale  | **SURVIVED** | caught (1) |
| M2 the same on EDGE                      | **SURVIVED** | caught (1) |
| M3 `propertyKeys` always empty           | caught (5)   | caught (6) |
| M4 only the first key reaches the epochs | caught (1)   | caught (3) |
| M5 the memo is never written (PERF-ONLY) | survived     | survived   |

M5 is the harness's own control: it is behaviour-preserving, so a survivor there is correct and
shows the other four are not just failing everything.

**And the threshold is why the gap existed.** Below `WIDE_BAG` nothing is cached, so a stale memo
is unobservable — every narrow fixture in the suite is blind to this _by construction_. The two
new tests in `reactive-counters.test.ts` therefore use an 80-property bag, add a key AFTER
creation, and assert that removing the element still bumps that key's epoch. With a stale memo it
does not, and a subscriber watching that key never learns the element went away.

That is the second item running where the surviving mutant pointed at a fixture rather than a
missing test (333's uniform labels, 335's untested dependency), and the third where writing the
mutants was the only thing that found it.

### Verification

349 `packages/core` (two new), 1990 `packages/gql`, 144 `packages/serialization`, 809
`packages/native`, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green. `lint`, `typecheck`, `fmt:check` and
`build` each as their own command, each exit 0.

**What is left.** At width 256 a delete is now 2,444 ns/node against 421 with the token loop gone
entirely, so ~2,000 ns of the bump remains — the pushes and the epoch `Map.set`s, which the three
container experiments above say is not reducible by changing the container. The remaining lever
would be enumerating _neither_ bag, which requires the epoch contract to stop being per-key, and
that is a cross-engine semantics question, not a perf one.

## 337. Item 333's arena concat grew six vectors from empty — 1.03-1.07x back on the threaded decode, and the Amdahl pairs disagreeing is what found it

Four items (330-333) took native's NDJSON decode 706.72 -> 401.70 ms, so every number in item
329's decomposition is stale. This tick re-derived it rather than reusing it, which is what found
a cost item 333 introduced and nobody measured.

### The tell: an Amdahl fit whose pairs stop agreeing

Item 328 fitted `T(n) = P/n + S` over the existing threads sweep at all six pairs — item 327's
lesson that two points are a line, not a trend — and **all six agreed**: P = 347-390 ms,
S = 363-382. That agreement is what made the fit trustworthy.

Re-run today on the same sweep (403.59 / 365.49 / 301.96 / 268.25 ms at 1/2/4/8):

| pair       | P (parallel) | S (serial) |
| ---------- | -----------: | ---------: |
| n=1 vs n=2 |      76.2 ms |   327.4 ms |
| n=1 vs n=4 |     135.5 ms |   268.1 ms |
| n=1 vs n=8 |     154.7 ms |   248.9 ms |
| n=2 vs n=4 |     254.1 ms |   238.4 ms |
| n=2 vs n=8 |     259.3 ms |   235.8 ms |
| n=4 vs n=8 |     269.7 ms |   234.5 ms |

**P ranges 76 to 270.** The model no longer fits, and the shape of the disagreement says why: every
pair involving `n=1` reports a much smaller P. That is the signature of a term that is **present
only when `threads > 1`** — work that scales with neither `n` nor `1/n`, so the two-parameter model
has nowhere to put it and smears it into P.

The 8-thread speedup had also fallen from item 328's **1.77x to 1.50x**, while the absolute time
improved from 411.51 to 268.25. Both are true, and reading only the absolute number is how the
regression stayed invisible: item 333's own A/B reported `threads @ 8` as one row (300.69 ->
263.73, 1.140x) and never looked at the ratio between its own columns.

### The cost

`stage_ndjson_threads` concatenates the per-chunk `StagedNdjson`s, and item 333 gave each of them
two arenas. All **six** vectors grew from empty with no reservation. Growing one to N by doubling
re-copies everything already in it at each step — about N extra element moves on top of the N that
belong there. On the corpus fixture that is 200k node records, 1M edge records, a 1.2M-entry label
arena and a 2.4M-entry property arena, so the concat was copying them roughly twice. **The serial
path never does any of it** (`threads <= 1` returns `stage_lines` directly), which is exactly why
it hid inside P.

Fixed by summing the parts' lengths first and `reserve_exact`ing all six, then `append`ing the
arenas rather than `extend`ing them. The ordering hazard item 333 introduced is unchanged and still
load-bearing: the span offsets are read BEFORE the arenas grow.

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, min of each:

| row                              | CONTROL |    NEW |            |
| -------------------------------- | ------: | -----: | ---------- |
| `ingest/threads` @ 2             |  359.84 | 349.39 | **1.030x** |
| `ingest/threads` @ 4             |  306.44 | 285.29 | **1.074x** |
| `ingest/threads` @ 8             |  261.72 | 246.20 | **1.063x** |
| `ingest/threads` @ 1 (control)   |  404.54 | 401.36 | flat       |
| `ingest/phases` serial decode    |  399.09 | 402.08 | flat       |
| `ingest/phases recmat_ms` (null) |   34.68 |  36.20 | +4%        |

All three target rows are disjoint across the three rounds. **`threads = 1` is the control the
change cannot reach** — that path never enters the concat at all — and it is flat, as is the serial
`ingest/phases` decode. The 8-thread speedup goes **1.546x -> 1.630x**.

`recmat_ms` is the `format!`-only null control, and it drifts +4% again, exactly as it did at item 331. Noted rather than explained: this harness's cross-build layout noise is real and about 4%, and
it is why the disjointness across rounds carries the claim rather than any single row.

### The residual, and the honest limit

Re-fitting on the new numbers, the pairs still disagree (P = 104 to 313 ms). So the
parallel-only term is **reduced, not removed** — what remains is the arena copy itself, which
`append` performs no matter how well reserved. That is the price of item 333's design: one
contiguous arena per kind is what made the serial decode 1.07-1.26x faster, and it is also work
only the threaded path does.

**The lever that would remove it, priced rather than built**: keep the per-chunk arenas and put a
chunk index in the `Span`, so nothing is merged. It costs a third `u32` per record (making `Span`
12 bytes, still smaller than the two `Vec`s it replaced) plus an indirection on every arena read in
`build_store`, and it trades a copy of 3.6M elements for a slightly more expensive read of each.
Worth doing only if the threaded decode becomes the dominant workload; recorded at the concat.

### Teeth

Four mutants, each on a restored pristine file, built uncapped, run under `timeout 600` +
`MemoryMax=16G MemorySwapMax=0`:

| mutant                                                  | result              |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| M1 the offsets are read AFTER the arenas grow           | caught (1)          |
| M2 the chunks are merged in REVERSE                     | caught (1)          |
| M3 a reservation sized from the wrong field (PERF-ONLY) | survived, correctly |
| M4 the LABELS span is not rebased (item 333's M1)       | caught (1)          |

All three correctness mutants are caught by exactly one test —
`decode_is_byte_identical_across_thread_counts`, the one item 333 had to fix because its uniform
fixture made it blind. **That test has now earned itself twice**, and M4 re-verifies that the fix
survived this rewrite rather than assuming it.

M3 is behaviour-preserving (a wrong reservation is slower, never wrong) and its survival is this
harness's control: without it, "3 of 4 caught" and "the suite fails everything" look the same.

1097 + 13 + 723 Rust tests green, 809 `packages/native`, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green;
clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands.

### What this says about the method

Item 328 wrote down that an Amdahl fit over an existing sweep recovers the serial fraction with no
instrumentation. The useful addition is the failure mode: **when the pairs stop agreeing, the fit is
not noisy — it is telling you the model is missing a term.** Here the disagreement was concentrated
in the pairs involving `n=1`, which localised the term to the threaded path before any code was
read. That is a free diagnostic on any sweep that already exists.

## 338. The two element-materializing rows read 2x the previous sweep, and it is the machine — a three-commit bisect, and why `bench_all`'s absolute numbers do not survive a session boundary

Seven items into this run, the right move was a fresh `bench_all` rather than another guess: it is
the regression sweep, and items 330-337 changed ingest enough that item 329's decomposition is
superseded. The sweep came back with two rows at roughly **double** the values recorded earlier in
this run:

| `query/perrow`     | earlier sweep | this sweep |       |
| ------------------ | ------------: | ---------: | ----- |
| `element p` (200k) |  249.8 ns/row |      516.5 | 2.07x |
| `element r` (1M)   |  179.9 ns/row |      374.9 | 2.08x |

Nothing else moved that way, and these are 100-375 ms rows, far too large for noise to double them.
A 2x on exactly the two rows that materialize an ELEMENT per row — the only rows in the corpus that
allocate 200k-1M `Value::Node` / `Value::Edge` — looks like a real regression with an obvious
suspect list.

### It is not any of the changes

Bisected rather than reasoned about: `query_bench` built at three commits spanning the entire run —
`c4aec4c9` (item 329, **before** any optimization in it), `8288aa11` (item 330) and `f793382c`
(item 337, HEAD) — and each run twice:

| commit                         | `element p` (us) |  `element r` (us) |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------: | ----------------: |
| `c4aec4c9` (item 329, pre-run) |  98,109 / 97,223 | 354,968 / 353,373 |
| `8288aa11` (item 330)          |  98,727 / 97,801 | 354,863 / 357,381 |
| `f793382c` (HEAD)              | 98,748 / 102,404 | 361,128 / 362,554 |

**All three agree**, including the one that predates every change. So the two rows are not a
regression from anything here; the earlier number is simply not reproducible on this machine today.

### What changed is the machine

At the time of this sweep the box carries tenants the earlier one did not: `uvicorn` at 4.8 GB
resident, `clickhouse-server` at 1.8 GB, 20 GB used of 61, **3.7 GB paged into swap**, load average
1.20. The two affected rows are precisely the allocation- and bandwidth-heavy ones, and the small
rows — `scalar p.age` at 1.7 ns/row, `count(*)` at 0.3 us, the whole `query/plan` group — are
unchanged, which is the pattern a memory-bandwidth competitor produces rather than a code change.

**So: do not chase it.** Recorded here with the bisect so the next sweep that shows 516 ns/row for
`element p` does not restart this.

### The methodological point, which is the reason this is an entry and not a shrug

The repo guide already says to know the noise floor and that anything under ~10% needs its own
isolated harness. This adds the other end of the scale: **a 2x gap between two `bench_all` runs
taken at different times can be entirely tenancy.** `bench_all` is a regression sweep for
_shape_ — which rows exist, which are orders of magnitude apart, which direction a change moves
them — and its absolute microseconds are only comparable **within one session, against an
alternated control**. Every flag in items 330-337 was measured that way, which is why none of them
depended on this.

A corollary worth having: the same sweep shows `value/codec` decode at **98.31 -> 64.25 ms** (flat
scalars) and **123.94 -> 84.66** (map records) across the same session boundary. Those are the
items 330-333 wins, and because the machine is now _slower_, they are if anything understated —
a cross-session comparison is unreliable in magnitude but its SIGN is still informative when the
tenancy bias points the other way.

No behaviour change and no code change: this item is the bisect and the conclusion.

**What the sweep did surface as a target**, read as shape rather than absolute time:
`algo/call` prices `degree` through GQL `CALL` at **13,870 us against 201 us direct — 69x
dispatch overhead**. That ratio is internal to one run, so tenancy cancels, and it is the largest
unexplained ratio in the corpus. Named here as the next thing to diagnose.

## 339. The corpus read 69x "CALL overhead" and 92% of it was returning the rows — 4.17x dispatch, 33.32x projection, and the projection is the same 518 ns/row two other rows already price

Item 338 closed by naming the largest unexplained RATIO in the corpus, deliberately a ratio because
a ratio internal to one run is immune to the machine tenancy that had just invalidated an absolute
comparison. `algo/call` priced `degree` through GQL `CALL` at **13,870 us against 201 us direct —
69x**, and its own comment claimed the comparison was fair: _"Same units as `direct` so the ratio is
honest."_

It was not honest, and reading the two sides was enough to see why before measuring anything.

- `direct` is `algo::degree(&store, Dir::Out, None, 1)`: it computes degrees into a `Vec` and
