  constructs **no row at all**.
- the `CALL` is `CALL degree() YIELD node, degree RETURN node, degree`: it runs the same procedure
  and then emits **50,000 rows, each carrying a NODE ELEMENT**.

So the ratio priced dispatch _plus_ a per-row materialization the direct call never performs, and
reported the sum as the procedure-call overhead.

### Split it and the number falls apart

Added a third measurement: the same procedure through the same query engine, **aggregating instead
of projecting**, so the two new ratios each mean one thing.

|                                                                |        us | ratio                        |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | --------: | ---------------------------- |
| `direct` (no rows)                                             |    186.38 | —                            |
| `counted` — `CALL degree() YIELD node, degree RETURN count(*)` |    777.62 | **dispatch 4.17x**           |
| `projected` — `… RETURN node, degree`                          | 25,907.47 | **projection 33.32x on top** |

**The real dispatch-and-plumbing cost of a named CALL is 4.17x, not 69x.** The other factor —
92% of the headline number — is returning the elements.

### And that cost is already in the corpus twice

25,907 us for 50,000 rows is **518 ns/row**. Item 338 measured `query/perrow`'s `element p` row, on
this same machine on the same afternoon, at **516.5 ns/row**. Those are the same number, so
`algo/call` was not measuring CALL at all in its dominant term: it was re-measuring element
materialization under a label that sent the reader to the procedure machinery. `query/perrow`
already prices that cost deliberately, with a `scalar p.age` row at 1.7 ns/row next to it to make
the contrast the point.

Fixed by reporting all three numbers and both ratios, with the reason in the code so the next
reader does not have to re-derive it. The README's by-question line changes from _"what does a CALL
cost"_ to _"a CALL's dispatch vs its projection"_, because those are different questions and the
old row answered neither.

### What this is an instance of

Item 338 had just finished arguing that `bench_all`'s absolute numbers do not survive a session
boundary and that ratios are the durable part. This is the complementary failure: **a ratio is only
as honest as the sameness of its two sides.** `counted / direct` and `projected / counted` are
sound because each pair differs in exactly one thing. `projected / direct` differed in two and
attributed both to the first.

The cheap test for it is the one that worked here: say out loud what each side does, and if the
sentences differ in more than one clause, the ratio needs a third measurement rather than an
explanation.

### What is left, and it is now the largest per-row cost in the engine

**Element materialization at ~518 ns/row** against `scalar p.age` at 1.7 ns/row in the same group.
It is the dominant term in `query/perrow element p` and `element r`, in `algo/call`'s projection,
and in anything that returns a node or an edge rather than a value from one. That is the next
target, and unlike the 69x it is a real one.

No behaviour change: the engine is untouched, the example gained a measurement and the README a
clearer question. Clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands; `fmt:check` 0.

## 340. The edge renderer never got the batch twin the node renderer has — 1.045x on the corpus's biggest row, 1.78x on a heterogeneous store, and the mutant that survived was a silently-wrong row

Item 339 named element materialization at ~518 ns/row as the next target. Before touching it, the
corpus comment and the existing isolated harness said this ground had been worked:
`exec::tests::element_render_cost` prices it in pieces and the bench records _"what remains is three
`Arc` allocations and a boxed `Value` per property, per row, by construction."_

So the first move was to make the pieces add up — item 329's rule that an unexplained remainder is a
stage you forgot. Running the existing harness: `node_result_value` whole is **224.9 ns/row** and its
named stages are `ext_id` 1.3 + `labels_of_refs` 36.5 + props 91.2 + field names 7.1 = **136.1**.
**An 88.8 ns remainder (39%)**, which reading the function places exactly: a `Vec<Value>` for the
labels list, and two `Arc::new` + two `Vec` for the nested and outer maps — the "by construction"
part, confirmed rather than assumed.

### The scaling the fixture cannot see

Reading the props loop found something the decomposition could not. It walks
`prop_keys_arc()` — **every distinct key in the STORE** — and filters by presence. So render cost is
**O(keys in the store), not O(properties on the element)**, and every fixture in the repo has four.

A heterogeneous graph is the realistic case: `Person` with name/email/dob beside `Company` with
domain/size/founded and a dozen other labels puts 50-200 distinct keys in one store while any
single node carries a handful. New sweep in the harness, node property count held FIXED at 4 and
only the number of OTHER keys varied:

| extra store keys |  full render | columns hoisted |
| ---------------: | -----------: | --------------: |
|                0 | 210.0 ns/row |            91.7 |
|               12 |        275.0 |           116.1 |
|               60 |        631.9 |           167.7 |
|              200 |      1,807.6 |           399.1 |

**7.99 ns per store key per row, and 1.54 with the column resolution hoisted** — so the
`store.column(k)` lookup is 81% of the scaling term. At 200 keys a `RETURN p` costs **8.6x** what
it costs at 4, for the same node.

### And the node path already had the fix

`render_nodes` hoists the column resolution for a whole batch, and its doc comment says so. Both
node egress sites (`col_into_values` and `render_col_into`) use it. **The edge path does not have a
batch renderer at all** — both `Col::Edges` arms called `edge_result_value` in a loop, and that
function hashes `edge_prop_map(k)` for every key on every row. The asymmetry is invisible in the
corpus because `element r`, its 1M-row case, has one edge key.

Added `render_edges`, the missing twin, and pointed both arms at it. Byte-identical by
construction: the same five fields in the same order, properties in `edge_prop_keys_arc()` (sorted)
order filtered to present, labels sorted, and the `u32::MAX` OPTIONAL-MATCH sentinel still NULL.

### Measured, both ways, because one number would have been misleading

**Query level**, three alternated rounds, min of each — the corpus fixture, one edge key:

| row                      | CONTROL |     NEW |            |
| ------------------------ | ------: | ------: | ---------- |
| `element r` (1M rows)    | 357,765 | 342,484 | **1.045x** |
| `element p` (control)    |  98,485 |  98,616 | flat       |
| `scalar p.age` (control) |   487.3 |   471.9 | flat       |

Fully disjoint on `element r` (ctl 357,765-359,387 against new 342,484-342,644). **`element p` is
the control that makes this legible**: nodes already went through the batched renderer, so this
change cannot reach them, and they do not move.

**Scaling**, both variants in ONE binary so there is no cross-build layout noise and no need for
alternated rounds:

| extra edge keys | per-edge | batched |             |
| --------------: | -------: | ------: | ----------- |
|               0 |    259.3 |   262.2 | 1.01x worse |
|              12 |    337.1 |   294.1 | **1.15x**   |
|              60 |    859.8 |   517.2 | **1.66x**   |
|             200 |  2,390.0 | 1,343.3 | **1.78x**   |

**10.65 ns per store key per row down to 5.41.** At zero extra keys the batch is 1.01x _slower_ —
the hoist is one pass that buys nothing when there is one key — and that is in the table rather than
rounded away. The residual 5.41 ns is `m.get(&eid)`, a hash per key per row, because edge properties
are per-key `HashMap`s where node properties are columns with a presence bitmap. That is the next
lever here and it is a representation change, not a loop.

### I made item 339's mistake one item later

The first draft of the scaling sweep had the per-edge variant DROP each rendered map while the
batched one returned a 200,000-element `Vec`. The batched row read **slower** at low key counts for
that reason alone — it was paying to retain the whole output. That is exactly item 339's finding,
_a ratio is only as honest as the sameness of its two sides_, walked into by the person who had
just written it down. Both sides now collect, and the note is in the harness rather than quietly
fixed, because the next person to add a variant there will be one `collect()` away from the same
thing.

### Teeth, and the one that mattered

| mutant                                             | first run    | after      |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ---------- |
| M1 the `u32::MAX` sentinel renders a map, not NULL | **SURVIVED** | caught (1) |
| M2 `from` and `to` swapped                         | caught (1)   | caught (1) |
| M3 the edge's labels are not sorted                | caught (1)   | caught (1) |
| M4 un-hoist the lookup (PERF-ONLY)                 | survived     | survived   |

**M1 is a silently-wrong row and nothing tested it.** `optional_match_binds_edge` exists and
returns `f.w` — a PROPERTY of the edge — so it never reaches the edge renderer, and the sentinel
check I had to carry across by hand was unguarded. Without it the renderer builds a map for edge
`u32::MAX`: `edge_ext_id` has no entry so it mints `"e4294967295"`, and `edge_endpoints` falls back
to `(0, 0)` — **a plausible-looking edge between two real nodes that does not exist.** Added
`a_missed_optional_edge_renders_null_not_a_map`, which returns `f` itself.

M4 is behaviour-preserving and its survival is the control, as at items 336, 337 and 339.

1098 + 13 + 723 Rust tests green (one new), 809 `packages/native`, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer
cases green — those matter here because this is an egress change on both sides of the invariant.
Clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands.

**Still open**: the 88.8 ns/row of `Arc` and `Vec` construction per rendered element, which is
structural; and the edge-property representation, where 5.41 ns per store key per row remains
because presence is a hash lookup rather than a bitmap.

## 341. The cross-engine bench had no row for the shape that dominates the native corpus — and the TS engine turns out not to materialize an element at all

Item 340 left the native element renderer at 492 ns/row in-process and asked what the TypeScript
engine does for the same shape. The answer was that nobody knew: `query/perrow` prices `RETURN p`
as the most expensive row in `bench_all`, and **the only place the two engines are compared had no
element-projection row at all.** Four added — a lazy and a forced-materialization pair for nodes and
for edges.

### The TS engine does not build the map

Checked before measuring, because the first number (ts 7.2 ms against ffi 209.4 — a 29x inversion
of the usual relationship) was too good to report without knowing what each side returned. Both
engines produce byte-identical output for `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n` — verified directly on a
two-node graph — but the TS engine returns a **live `Vertex` instance**:

```
constructor: Vertex      own keys: []      is plain: false      has toJSON: function
```

Zero own keys. It materializes nothing; the `{id, labels, properties}` map is built by whoever
serializes it, and if nobody does, never. The native engine builds it eagerly and then ships it over
the FFI/wasm boundary. **Same output, different time**, so the first row answers "how long until the
host HAS the rows" and not "what does producing the maps cost".

Hence the pairs. `materializeRows` applies `toJSON()` where it exists — the map on a live element,
absent on the native engine's plain object — so both sides are levelled without special-casing
either:

| 200,000 nodes                       |          ts |   ffi |  wasm |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------: | ----: | ----: |
| `project the element [ts lazy]`     |      7.1 ms | 204.7 | 138.8 |
| `project the element + materialize` | **49.6 ms** | 213.7 | 146.1 |

| 1,000,000 edges                  |            ts |    ffi |   wasm |
| -------------------------------- | ------------: | -----: | -----: |
| `project the edge [ts lazy]`     |      584.5 ms | 1346.3 |  932.9 |
| `project the edge + materialize` | **1086.6 ms** | 1389.1 | 1039.4 |

### What the difference between each pair says, which is the only carrier-free number here

**I nearly reported the ts-vs-ffi ratio as a finding. It is already closed.** Item 289 recorded that
the gap on _any_ row-returning query is the JSON carrier, not execution — _"the same fixture with
the same work and ONE row out is 30.8x the OTHER way (2.40ms against 73.95ms). Anyone chasing that
bench row should read `queryArrowIpc`, not the engine."_ My own new row reproduces it: `project 3
columns`, pure scalars, reads ts 12.9 against ffi 52.1.

So I checked `CLOSED.md` for "element render" and not for the carrier, which is precisely the
failure the repo guide names — _"Each pass searched something first and searched the wrong store."_
The four rows now carry a pointer to item 289 so the next reader does not spend a tick on it either.

What IS carrier-free is the difference **within** each engine's pair, since the carrier is identical
on both sides of it:

- **TS materialization costs 213 ns/row** (49.6 − 7.1 ms over 200,000 rows) — the whole of what it
  defers.
- **Native's in-process render is 492 ns/row** (item 340's isolated harness, no carrier).

So the native renderer is about **2.3x the TypeScript one at the same job**, measured in-process on
both sides. That is new, and it reframes item 340: its 1.045x was not nibbling at a floor — a
row-store doing the same work in less than half the time is evidence of real headroom, and it
points at the representation (native walks every key in the store and filters by presence; TS reads
a bag it already holds) rather than at the loop.

### Why the laziness is worth knowing in its own right

It is not a benchmark artifact, it is a product difference. A consumer that reads two fields off
fifty of a million returned elements pays TS nothing for the other 999,950 and pays the native
engine for all of them, twice — once to render, once to carry. The `[ts lazy]` rows are the honest
measurement of that, which is why they stay rather than being replaced by the forced pair.

No engine change: four bench rows, one helper, and a comment that stops three different
misreadings. `lint`, `typecheck` and `fmt:check` each run as their own command, each exit 0.

## 342. Pricing the presence representation before anyone refactors it — hoisting was 4.9x of the scaling term, packing the bits is 2.1x more, and a per-node key list is the only thing left

Item 341 ended with a number that said the native element renderer has headroom: pure-TS does the
same materialization in **213 ns/row** against native's **492**, in-process on both sides. Item 340
had already located the scaling term — the props loop walks every key in the STORE and filters by
presence, at 7.86 ns per store key per row — and named the representation rather than the loop.

This item prices the representation instead of changing it, because `Column`'s presence is
load-bearing well beyond rendering and the obvious fix turns out not to be the best one.

### What the representation actually is

`present: Vec<bool>` and `nulls: Vec<bool>` — **a BYTE per cell per vector**, with
`present_at(i) = present[i] || nulls[i]`. So a 200,000-row store with K columns keeps 400 KB x K of
presence, and rendering one element touches two bytes in each of K separate arrays.

That makes a packed bitset the obvious move: 8x less memory traffic, and `present || nulls` folds in
at build time. Obvious enough to be worth measuring rather than assuming.

### Three variants, one binary, 200,000 nodes with 4 properties each

The sweep varies only how many OTHER keys exist in the store. The packed variant's bitset is built
**outside** the timed closure deliberately: a per-batch build is O(K x N) and would show no win, and
the question is what a permanently-packed `Column` would be worth on the read side.

| extra store keys |  full render | columns hoisted | PACKED presence |
| ---------------: | -----------: | --------------: | --------------: |
|                0 | 220.6 ns/row |            89.8 |            90.5 |
|               12 |        289.5 |           116.9 |           102.9 |
|               60 |        643.5 |           167.4 |           145.4 |
|              200 |      1,791.8 |           408.0 |       **244.7** |

Per store key, which is the number that matters:

|                 | ns per store key per row |                                                                                                 |
| --------------- | -----------------------: | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| full render     |                 **7.86** | —                                                                                               |
| columns hoisted |                 **1.59** | **4.9x** of the scaling term, and already DONE (`render_nodes`, and `render_edges` at item 340) |
| packed presence |                 **0.77** | **2.1x more**                                                                                   |

At K=0 packed reads 90.5 against hoisted 89.8 — identical, so packing costs nothing when there is
nothing to skip. **The packed variant is checked against the byte-wise one for 1,000 rows before it
is timed**, because a fast path that skips work is indistinguishable from a fast one in a table of
microseconds.

### The recommendation, and why it is not the bigger number

Three rungs, now all priced:

1. **Hoist the column lookup** — 7.86 to 1.59 ns/key. Done.
2. **Pack presence into bits** — 1.59 to 0.77. A `Column` change: 1.67x on a K=200 render
   (408.0 to 244.7 ns/row), **and it reaches every other `present_at` caller** — filters, `count`,
   `IS NULL`, the seek paths — which this sweep does not measure and therefore understates.
3. **Skip the absent keys entirely** (a per-node key list or mask) — 0.77 to ~0, which at K=200
   would take 244.7 down toward the 90 ns/row floor: **another ~2.7x**, the largest single number
   here.

**Rung 2 is the recommendation despite rung 3 being bigger**, and the reason is maintenance rather
than magnitude. Packing is one representation change to a structure that already exists, with no
new invariant: nothing has to be kept in step, and every presence reader benefits. A per-node key
list is a new index that every `set_prop` / `remove_prop` must maintain correctly — the write path
items 331 and 335 were careful to keep cheap — and it would pay off only on element projection. If
rung 2 lands first, rung 3's remaining 2.7x can be judged against a much smaller base.

### What this item does NOT claim

The pricing is read-side only. Packing changes the codecs' view of a column and every `Vec<bool>`
site in `store.rs`, and none of that is measured here; the 1.67x is what the render scan would gain,
not what the change would cost to make. It is a target with a number on it, which is the thing this
repo asks for before a representation change, and explicitly not a plan.

Nor does it re-litigate the cross-engine comparison: item 289 settled that the ts-vs-ffi gap on any
row-returning query is the JSON carrier, and item 341's 213-vs-492 is the carrier-free pair.

No engine change. The three-way sweep and its cross-check stay in
`exec::tests::element_render_cost`, which is where this question already lived. 1098 Rust tests
green, clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands.

## 343. CORRECTION to item 342 — packing presence helps nothing but the render path, so the recommendation inverts

Item 342 priced three rungs on native's element render and recommended the middle one — packing
`Column`'s presence into a bitset — over the larger per-node-key-list win. The argument was not the
magnitude, it was breadth:

> Pack presence into bits … 1.67x on a K=200 render, **and it reaches every other `present_at`
> caller** — filters, `count`, `IS NULL`, the seek paths — which this sweep does not measure and
> therefore understates.

That clause is the entire reason for preferring the smaller win, and it was an assertion. Item 342
said so in its own text and shipped anyway. This item measures it.

### The clause is false

Those callers touch **one** column per row where the render path touches K. Same method as 342's
pricing — bitset built outside the timed closure, cross-checked against the byte-wise answer for
every row before timing:

| 200,000 rows, one column           |          bytes |  PACKED |               |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------: | ------: | ------------- |
| presence test only                 |     0.5 ns/row |     0.4 | 0.1 ns, noise |
| **presence test + read the value** | **3.3 ns/row** | **3.3** | **identical** |

The second row is the shape that matters — a filter, a `count`, a scalar projection all test
presence and then read. **The value read dominates completely and the presence representation does
not register.** Packing's 8x memory saving only pays when a row touches K columns, and that is the
element renderer and nothing else.

### So the recommendation inverts

| rung                 | win on element render | blast radius                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 2. pack presence     | **1.67x** at K=200    | `store.rs` (~90 `present[i]`/`push` sites) **plus** `exec.rs` and `exec/distinct.rs`, which borrow `present: &[bool]` out of the store into hot gather/filter paths — paths this item just showed it does not help |
| 3. per-node key list | **~2.7x** at K=200    | `set_prop` / `remove_prop`, the two functions items 331 and 335 already worked                                                                                                                                     |

**Rung 3 is the better change on every axis**: bigger win, smaller blast radius, and the one thing
against it — a new invariant on the write path — is confined to two functions, where rung 2's
cross-cutting edit reaches hot execution paths that gain nothing from it. Item 342's preference is
retracted.

The write-path cost is the thing to price next, and it is the same question items 331 and 335
answered for their own changes: a `set_prop` on an existing key must not pay for the index, only a
set of a key the node does not yet carry. That is a `contains`-then-insert on a small per-node
structure, which is the shape `bump_epoch` already uses in that file.

### The generalisable part

**"It also helps X" is a claim, not a bonus.** A recommendation that prefers a smaller measured win
on the strength of unmeasured breadth is resting on the unmeasured half. The tell was in item 342's
own sentence — _"which this sweep does not measure"_ — written as a caveat and then used as the
reason. One sweep, fifteen minutes, and the conclusion reverses.

It is also the second time in three items that the thing to check was the sameness or the scope of
a comparison rather than its arithmetic (item 339's two sides, item 341's carrier, this). The
arithmetic has not been wrong once; the framing has been wrong three times.

No engine change: the single-column pricing joins the render sweep in
`exec::tests::element_render_cost`, where the next person deciding this will find both halves
together. 1098 Rust tests green, clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands.

## 344. A 6.7x speedup in the wrong direction was a wrong answer: an element inside a map literal renders as its internal dense id

Looking for a shippable win among the per-row `render_cell` loops in `evaluator.rs`, the first step
was item 321's — check that a measured row reaches the code. So I priced the shapes those loops
serve, and one number made no sense:

| 200,000 nodes, native via ffi |             |
| ----------------------------- | ----------: |
| `RETURN p`                    |    232.9 ms |
| `RETURN {n: p} AS m`          | **34.6 ms** |
| `RETURN {a: p.age} AS m`      |     32.8 ms |
| `RETURN p.age`                |     13.1 ms |

Wrapping the element in a map literal — strictly more work — is **6.7x faster** than projecting it
bare, and indistinguishable from a map literal holding a scalar. A speedup in the wrong direction
is work not being done.

### It is not being done

```
MATCH (p:P) WHERE p.k = 1 RETURN {n: p} AS m
  native  [{"m":{"n":0}}]
  TS      [{"m":{"n":{"id":"a","labels":["P"],"properties":{"k":1}}}}]
```

`0` is the node's internal **dense id**. The engine's own `id` field is the EXTERNAL id, so this is
both a wrong value and an internal identifier leaking into user-visible output — and it is
**silent**: a plausible-looking number, no refusal, no warning.

### Scope, measured rather than assumed

| shape                        |                             |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `RETURN p`                   | correct, engines agree      |
| `RETURN [p]` (list)          | correct, engines agree      |
| `RETURN collect(p)`          | correct, engines agree      |
| **`RETURN {n: p}`**          | **DIFFERS** — `{"n":0}`     |
| **`RETURN {n: {inner: p}}`** | **DIFFERS** — `{"inner":0}` |
| **`RETURN {e: r}`** (edge)   | **DIFFERS** — `{"e":0}`     |

So it is the **map literal specifically**, for nodes and edges alike, at any nesting depth. Lists
and `collect` resolve correctly, which rules out the generic egress resolver — `resolve_elem` is
recursive over `List`/`Map`/`Record` and works.

### Three paths ruled out by reading, and where to look next

- `Expr::Slot(n)` evaluates to `batch.slot(n).clone()`, so a node variable stays a `Col::Nodes`.
- `render_cell` turns a `Col::Nodes` cell into the element map.
- `try_fused_maplit_json`'s non-scalar arm calls `render_cell` too.

None of the three explains a bare `0`, so the loss happens before egress: **the next place to look
is the plan** — whether the optimizer rewrites a MapLit entry that is a bare element variable into
a numeric read. Recorded rather than guessed at, because a blind fix in a path I had not pinned
down is how a silent wrong answer becomes two.

### Why it survived

The differential fuzzer — the one harness that compares the engines row-for-row — **has no coverage
of a map literal carrying an element.** That is the same nested-shape gap already recorded for
quantified groups. The bug and the gap are the same hole, which is the useful part: the fix should
include the generator case, or the next shape to go wrong here will also go unnoticed.

### What ships

`an_element_in_a_map_literal_renders_as_its_element_map`, `#[ignore]`d with the reason, asserting
the CORRECT behaviour so the fix has its assertion ready — it fails for the right reason today
(`cargo test -- --ignored`) and the default suite stays green at 1098 passed / 11 ignored. Its
check is deliberately shape-agnostic: no rendered value anywhere under a projected map literal may
be a bare number where an element was projected, so a partial fix cannot pass it.

Clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands. No behaviour change — this item is the
repro, the scope and the ruled-out paths.

**Note for the open-divergence list**: the three native divergences on record are all _loud
refusals_. This is a fourth and it is silent, which is strictly worse — nothing surfaces it to a
caller, and the leaked value is in range for a legitimate id.

## 345. FIXED — the record arm read `value_at` where the list arm reads `render_cell`, one line apart in the same `match`

Item 344 found that an element inside `{…}` rendered as its internal dense id, scoped it (records
only; lists and `collect` correct; nodes and edges alike; any depth), ruled out three paths by
reading, and stopped at "the next place to look is the plan". It was the plan — in the sense that
the plan named the arm.

### The plan named it

```
MATCH (p:P) RETURN {n: p} AS m
  RAW/OPT: Project { items: [("m", Record { fields: [("n", Slot(0))] })] }
MATCH (p:P) RETURN [p] AS l
  RAW/OPT: Project { items: [("l", List   { items:  [Slot(0)] })] }
```

`{…}` is `Expr::Record`, not `Expr::MapLit` — which is why item 344's reading of `MapLit` and its
fused JSON writer found nothing wrong with either. Both were innocent. The optimizer changes
nothing here, so the two arms sit side by side in one `match`:

```rust
Expr::List { items } => …  .map(|c| render_cell(c, i, store))      // element map
Expr::Record { fields } => … .map(|(k, c)| (k, c.value_at(i)))     // dense id
```

`value_at` on an element column yields the dense id as a `Num`. The `List` arm has always used
`render_cell` and carries the comment saying why — _"A VERTEX/EDGE element renders as its element
map (render_cell), consistent with a top-level one."_ The `Record` arm simply never got it. **One
line, eleven lines apart from the version that was right.**

Fixed by making `Record` do what `List` does. `resolve_elem` was already recursive over
`Record`, so nothing else needed touching.

### Verified across engines, not just in-process

All seven shapes now byte-identical between the native FFI build and the pure-TS engine, including
the three that diverged and a mixed record that was never tested:

|                                                 |                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `RETURN p` / `RETURN [p]` / `RETURN collect(p)` | agree (and did before)                            |
| `RETURN {n: p}`                                 | **agree** (was `{"n":0}`)                         |
| `RETURN {n: {inner: p}}`                        | **agree** (was `{"inner":0}`)                     |
| `RETURN {e: r}`                                 | **agree** (was `{"e":0}`)                         |
| `RETURN {a: p.k, n: p}`                         | **agree** — a scalar and an element in one record |

### The test, and two drafts of it that were wrong

Item 344 shipped the assertion `#[ignore]`d. Un-ignoring it took two corrections, both worth
recording because both are the same class of error as the bug:

1. It destructured the projected value as `Value::Map`. GQL's `{…}` is a `Value::Record`, and the
   `no_bare_ids` walk had no `Record` arm either — **so it was blind to exactly the nesting it
   existed to check.**
2. Rewritten, it forbade any `Num` anywhere under the projection. That also forbids a legitimate
   numeric PROPERTY, and it failed on the fixture's own `k: 1` _inside the element map it was
   supposed to be looking for_.

The shipped form follows the single-field record/map nesting down to the leaf and requires that
leaf to be an element map — a `Map` carrying an `id` key — descending into nothing else. A leaked
dense id is a `Num` and fails; a real property value is never reached.

**Teeth, verified rather than assumed**: reverting the one-line fix with the test in place turns it
red (`0 passed; 1 failed`). That is the whole mutation argument for a one-line change, and it was
run, not reasoned.

### What this says

Item 344's reading was careful and still looked at the wrong `match` arm for an hour, because the
surface syntax `{…}` reads as "map literal" and the AST calls it `Record`. **The plan dump settled
in one line what reading could not**, and it was available the whole time. For a "which code runs"
question, print the plan before reading the code — item 321's lesson in a different costume.

And the near-miss is worth stating plainly: the fix is one line, and the two drafts of its TEST were
each wrong in a way that would have let the bug through. A one-line fix does not imply a one-line
test.

1099 Rust tests green (the regression test now un-ignored and running), 13 fuzzer cases, 809
`packages/native`, 1990 `packages/gql`. Clippy and `cargo fmt --check` clean as separate commands.

**Still open from 344**: the differential fuzzer has no generator case for a record carrying an
element, which is why this survived. The fix closes the bug, not the hole.

## 346. Closing the hole, not the bug — the differential fuzzer can now generate a container carrying an element, and the first thing it found was a second divergence

Item 345 fixed the record arm. Item 344 had already named why it survived: **the differential
fuzzer — the one harness that compares the engines row-for-row — could not generate the shape.**
A fix that closes a bug and leaves the hole open is half the job.

### The hole, exactly

The generator's expression grammar is entirely scalar: every `genLeaf` is a literal, a temporal, a
stored-record path or a property read. Records (`{a: …, b: …}`) and lists (`[…, …]`) ARE generated
— so the hole was never "no containers", it was that **no container could ever hold an element.**
20,000 queries a run, and `{v: <vertex>}` was unreachable.

### The first attempt found a different bug, and had to be narrowed

The obvious fix is an element-valued leaf, so elements reach every container the grammar can build.
Done that way, the fuzzer went red within two runs — on something else:

```
MATCH (n:T) RETURN CAST([n, ''] AS STRING) AS x …
  ts:     "6,"
  native: "{\"id\":\"6\",\"labels\":[\"T\"],\"properties\":{…}},"
```

**The engines disagree about how an element STRINGIFIES**: TS casts it to its id, native to its
whole element map. A real value divergence — and the fuzzer's own message says a value divergence
is "a bug in one of them" which "no registry entry may excuse", so it cannot be parked.

It is also not this item's bug. Which engine is right is a `CAST` conformance question (ISO does not
obviously define a node-to-string cast at all, and "both should refuse" is a plausible answer that
changes behaviour for users), and deciding it inside a fuzzer-coverage change would be two
decisions in one commit. **Recorded as its own open divergence with the repro above** —
`FUZZ_SEED=4042405702` — and left for a conformance pass.

So the element case moved from the expression grammar to QUERY level: the existing hop-projection
family (`MATCH (a:T)-[e:E]->(b:T) RETURN …`) now draws a container-with-element a quarter of the
time, from eight shapes — `{v: a}`, `{v: a, w: b}`, `{v: e}`, `{v: {inner: a}}`, `{v: a, n: a.n}`,
`[a]`, `[a, b]`, `{v: a}.v`. Elements reach containers without reaching `CAST`, arithmetic or the
scalar functions.

Per this file's own convention — _"Only the CONTENT of this shape changed, not its probability
band, so no later boundary moved"_ — this is a content change to an existing band. No seed's family
assignment moves.

### Teeth, run twice

**Reverting item 345's one-line fix makes the fuzzer red immediately**, naming the family it was
blind to:

```
[seed …129] MATCH (a:T)-[e:E]->(b:T) RETURN {v: e} AS x
[seed …162] MATCH (a:T)-[e:E]->(b:T) RETURN {v: a} AS x
[seed …232] MATCH (a:T)-[e:E]->(b:T) RETURN {v: a, n: a.n} AS x
[seed …285] MATCH (a:T)-[e:E]->(b:T) RETURN {v: {inner: a}} AS x
```

Checked before the complexity refactor below and again after it (10 divergent seeds the second
time), because a refactor that quietly stops generating the shape would leave the hole open while
looking closed. Green over 13 consecutive runs with the fix in place.

### A gate that earned its keep

Adding the branch inline tipped `genQuery` from complexity 35 to 36 and `bun run lint` refused it.
Two attempts to satisfy it by extracting only the shape list still read 36 — a ternary is a decision
too — so the 25% split moved into the helper as well, leaving the band a single `return`. The gate
was right: `genQuery` is a 24-band `if` ladder and the correct place for a sub-choice is a named
function, not a 25th branch.

### Scope

No engine change — one generator family and its helper. All 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green,
`lint`, `typecheck` and `fmt:check` each exit 0 as separate commands.

**Still open**: the `CAST(<element> AS STRING)` divergence above, which is a conformance decision
and is now the only thing known to be reachable by an element-valued leaf. When it is settled, the
leaf can move from query level into `genLeaf` and the coverage widens from one family to the whole
grammar — that is the better end state, and this item is the half of it that does not need a
semantics call.

## 347. `CAST(<element> AS STRING)` is not an implementation choice — the free ISO artifacts close the easy escape without settling which engine is right

Item 346 found the engines disagree about how an element stringifies: `CAST([n, ''] AS STRING)`
gives `"6,"` in TS (the element's **id**) and the element's **whole map** in native. The tempting
resolution is "casting a node to a string is outside the standard, so pick one and document it as
implementation-defined." **The free artifacts say that escape is closed.**

### What the primary sources settle

**The syntax is legal.** From the BNF:

```
<cast specification> ::= CAST <left paren> <cast operand> AS <cast target> <right paren>
<cast operand>       ::= <value expression> | <null literal>
<cast target>        ::= <value type>
```

An element variable is a `<value expression>`, so nothing syntactic rejects this. Whether the
_type pair_ is castable lives in the prose, which is the paywalled part.

**It is not delegated.** The implementation-DEFINED artifact enumerates everything a conforming
implementation must choose and document. On casts it lists exactly one thing:

> The manner in which **lax casts** (and supporting type tests) are generated and included in the
> syntax transforms for the dynamic generation of **strict casts**.

That delegates the _generation mechanism_, not which pairs are castable. And the
implementation-DEPENDENT artifact — the list of things an implementation may do freely, with no
answer required — mentions casts not at all; its only entry near this area is the start datetime
for interval-to-scalar subtraction. **Those two files are the complete enumeration of permitted
freedom, and an element-to-string cast is in neither.** So two conforming implementations may not
disagree here, which means one of ours is wrong.

**And the error surface for "wrong" exists.** The conditions artifact carries `22G03` and `22G12`
_invalid value type_ for a wrongly-typed value reaching an operation, and the only cast-specific
code is `22018 invalid character value for cast` — a _character value that will not parse into the
target_, not a bad type pair. A bad pair is therefore not modelled as a data exception at all,
which is consistent with it being a static type rule.

### What they do not settle

Which answer is right. Neither engine's behaviour is attested anywhere free: TS exposes the
external id, native the whole element map, and **both are internal representations promoted to a
contract by accident.** The cast table is in the prose.

A web search for the type rules returned nothing usable — and is worth recording as a
reliability data point, because it also told me it _"found no source that uses 'lax' or 'strict'
for GQL casts, so I can't confirm those modes exist."_ They exist; the sentence quoted above is
from ISO's own artifact. **The primary source beat the summary again**, which is the warning
`references.md` opens with.

### So the decision, stated once

Three candidate answers, and this is a semantics choice rather than a measurement:

1. **Refuse** — `22G03 invalid value type`. The conservative option: nothing in the free artifacts
   says the cast exists, refusing can later be relaxed to whatever the prose says, and it breaks
   nobody who was relying on a behaviour the two engines never agreed on.
2. **The id** (TS's answer today) — plausible if GQL's cast table routes a reference value through
   its id, and the cheaper of the two.
3. **The element map** (native's answer today) — plausible if it routes through the element's
   serialized form, and consistent with how the engines render an element everywhere else.

**Not decided here, and deliberately not decided unilaterally**: all three change user-visible
behaviour in a shipped engine, and the repo already has firm, user-set policy on
refuse-versus-coerce for cross-type operations (the string-vs-temporal comparison rule). This item
narrows an open divergence to one question with the primary-source evidence attached, which is as
far as it can be taken without either the prose or an observed GA'd implementation.

Recorded in `docs/conformance/references.md` beside the artifact table, since the next person to
need "may we choose here?" should find the answer where the artifacts are described rather than in
an audit entry.

No code change. The divergence stays open and the fuzzer stays green, because item 346 deliberately
kept the element leaf out of `CAST`'s reach — when this is settled, that leaf moves into `genLeaf`
and the coverage widens from one family to the whole grammar.

## 348. Rung 3's write cost is free and its blast radius is five paths, not two — so both rungs park, and that is the third scope claim this thread got wrong

Item 343 retracted item 342's recommendation and preferred rung 3 (a per-node key list, ~2.7x on
element render) over rung 2 (packing presence, 1.67x), on these grounds:

> Rung 3: blast radius `set_prop`/`remove_prop`, the two functions items 331 and 335 already
> worked. **Rung 3 is better on every axis.**

Before building it, both halves of that got checked. One is better than claimed and one is worse.

### The write cost is free, and `Column::set` is why

`apply_set_prop` ends in `col.set(node as usize, value)`, and `Column::set` writes the slot's
`present[i]` / `nulls[i]` directly — it is already reading and writing exactly the bytes that say
whether the slot was occupied. **Having it return "this slot was previously absent" costs one byte
compare on a cache line it is writing anyway**, and the maintenance becomes one branch plus a push
on first set only.

So the thing item 343 flagged as rung 3's one drawback — a new invariant on the write path — is
close to free per write. That half is better than claimed.

### The blast radius is five paths, and two of them are the bulk fast paths

Enumerated rather than assumed. Every place that puts a value into a node-property column:

| site                                              |                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `apply_set_prop`                                  | the funnel — the one item 343 named                                                              |
| `apply_remove_prop`                               | must clear                                                                                       |
| `add_node_bulk`                                   | **bypasses the funnel by design** — "the single-pass fast path (no per-property hashmap lookup)" |
| `materialize` (`store.rs:393`, `col.set(i, val)`) | the `Builder` path, which is how every test fixture AND the NDJSON decode build a store          |
| `delete_node`                                     | must clear the row                                                                               |
| plus: a re-permute                                | adding a NEW key changes sorted key order, so every node's mask shifts                           |

Five write paths and a re-permute. And the two that are not the funnel are precisely the **bulk
paths written to skip per-property bookkeeping** — the ones items 330-333 spent four items making
fast. Maintaining a mask there either slows them or needs a wholesale rebuild at `end_bulk`, which
is the O(K x N) scan this whole rung exists to avoid, paid once per load. That is defensible but it
is not "two functions".

**A per-node mask is also where the memory lives**: 8 bytes a node for a `Vec<u64>` at K ≤ 64
(1.6 MB at 200k nodes, against the store's ~116 bytes an element), versus 24 + 8k for a
`Vec<Arc<str>>` per node — 11.2 MB on the same fixture, a ~28% increase in per-node footprint. The
mask is the right shape, and it brings the K > 64 fallback and the re-permute with it.

### Verdict: both rungs park, with the trigger written down

|                       | gain                                                                    | cost                                                                                                                           |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| rung 2, pack presence | 1.67x, render only (item 343 measured that its breadth claim was false) | ~90 sites in `store.rs` **plus** `exec.rs`/`exec/distinct.rs`, which borrow `present: &[bool]` into hot paths it does not help |
| rung 3, per-node mask | ~2.7x, render only                                                      | 5 write paths incl. both bulk fast paths, a re-permute on schema growth, a K > 64 fallback, 8 B/node                           |

Neither is small, and both buy **one shape**: rendering an element from a store with many distinct
property keys. That shape is real — a heterogeneous people-graph is 50-200 keys with a handful per
element — but **no row in the corpus measures it and no user has reported it.** Every fixture in the
repo has four keys, which is exactly why items 340-343 had to build the sweep to see the cost at
all.

So the trigger, stated so it is checkable rather than a feeling: **build one of these when a
measured workload renders elements from a store with more than ~60 distinct property keys.** Until
then the honest position is that a 2.7x on an unexercised shape does not justify touching five write
paths, and the sweep in `element_render_cost` is there to price it the day it matters.

### Three scope claims, three corrections — that is the pattern

- item 342 preferred rung 2 for **breadth** it had not measured → false (343).
- item 343 preferred rung 3 for a **blast radius** it had not enumerated → understated (this item).
- and 343's own closing line already named the shape of it: _"the arithmetic has not been wrong
  once; the framing has been wrong three times."_ This is the fourth.

Every one of these was a claim about SCOPE — how wide a benefit reaches, how wide a change reaches —
asserted in a sentence and refuted by fifteen minutes of checking. The measurements in this thread
have all held. **A scope claim is a measurement, and in this thread it is the only kind that has
ever been wrong.** The practical form: before preferring A to B on anything other than a measured
number, grep the thing you are claiming is narrow.

No code change. The verdict and the trigger go in `CLOSED.md`; the sweep that would price it stays
in `exec::tests::element_render_cost`.

## 349. A single-property SET normalized every property it was not changing — 1.39x to 2.66x by width, and the edge twin's normalization had no tests at all

The TS engine's `SET` has been recorded as O(property width) with three O(K) passes per write.
One of them is provably unnecessary, and the proof is an invariant items 335 and 336 already
established and tested.

### The redundant pass

`setProperty` commits `{ ...previous, [key]: value }` through `#commitProperties`, which calls
`normalizeProperties` — a walk of **every** key, calling `normalizePropertyValue` on each, to lift a
tagged temporal (`{"@date": …}`) to its instance. Item 147 had already made that walk
allocation-free, but it is still K calls on every write.

It cannot find anything on K−1 of those keys. A bag in the box **was normalized when it was
stored**, and item 335 established — and item 349's mutants re-check — that a stored bag is frozen
and REPLACED rather than mutated. So only the values a write _introduces_ can need lifting.

Split the funnel: `#commitNormalized` commits a bag whose values are already normalized, and
`#commitProperties` is now `#commitNormalized(normalizeProperties(bag))` for bags that came from
outside the graph. Four of the five write paths move to the cheap form:

| path                                  | what it introduces                                                |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `set properties` (public setter)      | the caller's whole bag → **normalizes everything, unchanged**     |
| `setProperty`                         | one value → `normalizePropertyValue(value)`                       |
| `setProperties`                       | its `props` → `normalizeProperties(props)`, O(\|props\|) not O(K) |
| `removeProperty` / `removeProperties` | **nothing** → no normalization at all                             |

The invariant is inductive and is the whole correctness argument: every path into the box
normalizes what it adds, so every stored bag is fully normalized.

### Measured

`bun run delete:width` gained a `set_ns/write` column — a single-property `setProperty` on an
element of the given width, which is the shape that matters, since an immutable bag means a
one-key write rebuilds the whole bag. Three alternated rounds, min of each:

| width |   CONTROL |   NEW |             |
| ----: | --------: | ----: | ----------- |
|     4 |    145 ns |   127 | overlapping |
|    16 |    327 ns |   235 | **1.39x**   |
|    64 |    820 ns |   308 | **2.66x**   |
|   256 | 16,321 ns | 7,914 | **2.06x**   |

Widths 16, 64 and 256 are fully disjoint across the rounds. **The delete column is the control**
and is flat.

2.66x from removing one of three passes is more than its share, and the shape says why: the pass was
not one walk but K calls to `normalizePropertyValue`, each with its own branching. That it peaks at
64 rather than 256 is also consistent — at 256 the spread and the freeze dominate more (the
dictionary-mode cliff this repo already records), so the removed pass is a smaller fraction of a
bigger number.

### Teeth, and the gap they found

Five mutants on the `Vertex` paths, one per link in the induction. **All four correctness mutants
caught** (the public setter skipping normalize, `setProperty` skipping it, `setProperties` skipping
it, and the bag no longer frozen), and the behaviour-preserving fifth — normalize twice — correctly
survived as the harness's control.

**Then the same two mutants on `Edge` both SURVIVED.** `Edge` carries its own copy of the entire
property funnel, and every normalization test in the suite drove `Vertex` only: stopping `Edge`
normalizing, on either the public setter or `setProperty`, broke no test. The vertex side had the
tests; the edge side had none.

That is the third time this session the node/edge asymmetry has bitten — item 340's edge renderer
never got the batch twin the node renderer had, and now the edge funnel never got the node funnel's
tests. **When a change touches `Vertex` and `Edge` together, mutate BOTH; the twins drift because
only one of them is ever in the fixture.** Added `an EDGE constructor lifts`, `an EDGE setProperty
lifts` and `an EDGE setProperties lifts`; both Edge mutants are caught now.

352 `packages/core` (three new), 1990 `packages/gql`, 144 `packages/serialization`, 809
`packages/native`, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green. `lint`, `typecheck`, `fmt:check` and
`build` each as their own command, each exit 0.

**What is left on this path**: two O(K) passes, and both are the representation rather than the
code — the spread, because the bag is immutable and shared, and `Object.freeze`, because K
properties must each be marked. A single-property write cannot be O(1) while a property bag is one
frozen object; that would need the columnar layout the native engine has, which is the TS engine's
largest open representation question and not this item's.

## 350. The "84x row" is the 26x row, and item 300's CSR has to be re-priced against that

`CLOSED.md` names `traverse 1-hop + filter` as "the 84x row" in several places, and item 300's CSR —
a dense adjacency for the TS engine — is recorded as "priced at **7.30x** and declined". Both
numbers are the basis on which the largest open TS data-layout change gets considered, and the
first thing this tick did was check them.

### Measured, three runs

`MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE x.age > 45 RETURN count(*) AS c`, 200,000 nodes at 5
edges/node:

| run |      ts | ffi | wasm |     ts/ffi |
| --- | ------: | --: | ---: | ---------: |
| 1   | 40.2 ms | 1.5 |  1.7 | **26.86x** |
| 2   | 38.4 ms | 1.5 |  1.7 | **25.51x** |
| 3   | 40.9 ms | 1.5 |  1.6 | **26.94x** |

**The gap is ~26x, not 84x.** Stable across three runs, same fixture and the same query the row has
always run. And a ratio inside one run is the comparison that survives — item 338's rule — so this
is comparable to the 84x, which was also a ratio.

### What accounts for it, and what does not

This session took two bites out of that row: item 321's adjacency box (**1.207x**) and item 324's
`edgesOfTypes` generator split (**1.253x**). Together 1.51x. The gap moved 84 → 26, which is 3.23x.

**So 2.14x of the improvement is unattributed**, and this item does not claim it. It could be
earlier items against the same three-component diagnosis, or the ffi column moving rather than the
ts one — 1.5 ms is close enough to the floor that a change on the native side would shrink the
ratio without TS improving at all. Attributing it would need the old absolute numbers, which item
338 has just finished explaining are not comparable across sessions. **What is defensible is the
current number, and that the old one should stop being quoted.**

### The consequence for the CSR

Item 300's 7.30x was priced against the 84x gap. Against 26x the case is materially weaker, and the
change is the same class item 348 just parked twice: a **representation** change — a dense,
integer-indexed adjacency the TS graph does not expose, because its vertices are keyed by string
id.

Item 321 already found the cheaper intermediate and said so at the time — _"a cheaper intermediate
than item 300's CSR"_ — and it, plus 324, is where 1.51x of the 3.23x came from. The pattern is
that the three-component diagnosis (generator frame, `Edge` property reads, two hash lookups) keeps
yielding to component-sized fixes, which is the opposite of what "it needs a CSR" predicted. Item
324 already recorded that reversal once: _"'No micro moves it' was a prediction and it was testable
for the price of one function split."_

So the CSR stays declined, now for a measured reason rather than an inherited one, and the two
remaining components are the next candidates at component size.

### One more thing the same run says

`count 1-hop [shortcut]` reads **ts 0.0 ms against ffi 0.5** — the pure-TS engine answers it from
an index while the native build pays the FFI carrier (item 289). Worth keeping next to the 26x,
because the two rows are the same graph and the same hop, and they point in opposite directions:
the TS engine is not uniformly behind, it is behind on _enumerating_ and ahead on _answering from
an index_.

### Scope

No code change. The stale figure is corrected where it is quoted, and the CSR's re-pricing goes
with it. **The point of `CLOSED.md` is that a list which lags is the failure it exists to prevent —
and this time the lag was inside it.**

## 351. The obvious next component is called zero times — `edge.to` is not on the 26x row at all

Item 350 re-priced the `traverse 1-hop + filter` gap at 26x, declined the CSR, and named the next
candidates: _"the two remaining components are the next candidates, at component size"_ — the
`Edge` property reads and the two hash lookups from item 310/324's three-component diagnosis.

The obvious one is `Edge`'s endpoint resolution:

```ts
get to(): Vertex { return this.#graph!.getVertexById(this.#to)!; }
```

A string-keyed `Map.get` per access, and `shortcuts.ts` says so at the hop site itself —
_"`edge.to` / `edge.from` resolve (a string-keyed `Map.get`, ~190ns — item 194)"_. It is also
exactly item 321's shape, which took 1.207x by caching a reference instead of a string-keyed
lookup. Everything pointed one way.

### The arithmetic did not fit, so I counted

The row runs 38-40 ms over 1,000,000 edges — **about 38 ns an edge, in total.** A single 190 ns
endpoint resolve cannot be inside that. Either the 190 ns is stale or the resolve is not happening,
and guessing which is how item 321 wasted a round.

Counted instead, with a temporary counter on both getters and the row's own query
(`MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE x.age > 45 RETURN count(*)`) over 100,000 edges:

```
edges=100000  edge.to=0  edge.from=0
```

**Zero.** Neither getter is called once. The hop path already works from `toId`/`fromId` and never
materializes the far vertex — `shortcuts.ts:1474` says it does, in a comment added for exactly this
reason: _"`toId` / `fromId` and skip resolving a whole vertex."_

### So the component list is stale, like the figure was

Item 350 corrected the 84x to 26x and left the component diagnosis inherited. It should not have:
**the endpoint-resolution component is already gone**, closed by whichever item added the
`toId`/`fromId` path, and the three-component diagnosis has been carrying a fourth-hand description
of a cost that no longer exists on this row.

What is left in the 38 ns an edge is **not known**, and this item does not invent a candidate for
it. A fresh decomposition is the next step — the same move item 329 made for native's decode, and
for the same reason: a stage list that does not add up is a stage list to redo, and this one has a
removed stage still in it.

### The cheap thing that saved a wasted round

One temporary counter on two getters, run once. It cost a few minutes and it refutes a target that
had: the code's own comment pricing it at 190 ns, a measured precedent (321) for exactly the fix, a
named place in a three-component diagnosis, and an entry in `CLOSED.md` pointing at it. Four
reasons to build it, and it is never called.

**The rule, which is item 321's with one more sharpening**: before optimising a function, check the
hot row CALLS it — and when a named cost and the row's total time disagree by 5x, that disagreement
is the measurement, not an inconvenience. 190 ns an edge inside 38 ns an edge was the tell, and it
was visible before any code was read.

No code change. The counter was temporary and is gone; the tree is verified clean and 352
`packages/core` tests pass.

## 352. The 26x row's remaining cost is LOCALITY — 2.9x per-edge degradation from size alone, which partly rehabilitates item 300's CSR

Item 351 refuted the obvious component and left the honest state: _"What is left in the 38 ns an edge
is not known, and this item does not invent a candidate for it. A fresh decomposition is the next
step."_ This is that decomposition, and it arrives somewhere neither 350 nor 351 expected.

### Two profiling traps first, both recorded because both cost a round

`bun --cpu-prof` is the repo's existing instrument (item 162 used it). It profiles the **whole
process**, which is the trap:

- **Attempt 1** built a 200k-node / 1M-edge fixture and ran 12 queries. The profile came back
  19.5% `indexEdgeLabel`, 15.6% `JSON.parse`, 9.2% `getVertexById`, 5.8% `#commitNormalized`,
  4.5% `validateLabel` — **every top frame is INGEST.** The fixture build swamped the region of
  interest and the profile said nothing about the query. Same family as items 339 and 341: what
  was measured was not what was claimed.
- **Attempt 2** shrank the fixture and ran 600 queries, and then the per-edge cost came out
  **5.6 ns** against the bench row's 38 — a 7x disagreement that is not noise. A tight repeat loop
  is a **different operating point** (warm steady state) from a bench harness's min-of-5, and
  profiling the wrong one answers a question nobody asked.

### The sweep, which is the finding

CLAUDE.md's first rule for a number like this is _"sweep the size — cache-resident and not are
different questions; the transition is between 200k and 1M elements."_ Same query
(`MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE x.age > 45 RETURN count(*)`), same code, every size given a
warm steady state so the comparison is across SIZE and not across JIT states:

|   nodes |     edges | best ms | **ns/edge** |
| ------: | --------: | ------: | ----------: |
|  20,000 |   100,000 |   0.558 |     **5.6** |
|  50,000 |   250,000 |   1.999 |     **8.0** |
| 100,000 |   500,000 |   7.075 |    **14.2** |
| 200,000 | 1,000,000 |  15.988 |    **16.0** |

**2.9x per-edge degradation from size alone.** Nothing algorithmic changes across those rows — it is
the same work per edge, costing three times as much because the data no longer fits. The native
engine over the same 1M edges is ~1.5 ns/edge and does not show this.

(These absolutes are a warmer operating point than the bench's 38 ns/edge, for the reason attempt 2
found. The SHAPE is the result, and it is internal to one run.)

### Which partly rehabilitates the CSR, and that is the third correction in this thread

Item 350 declined item 300's CSR because its 7.30x was priced against a stale 84x gap. Item 351
then found the named next component was never called, and observed that _"the three-component
diagnosis keeps yielding to component-sized fixes, which is the opposite of what 'it needs a CSR'
predicted."_

That observation now reads differently. The components that yielded — a generator frame (324), a
string-keyed adjacency lookup (321) — were **interpretation and hashing costs**, and they are gone.
What is left is **locality**, and locality is the one thing a component-sized fix cannot touch and a
dense adjacency precisely addresses. So item 300's _mechanism_ was right even though its _number_
was priced against a figure that no longer holds.

The honest form: **the CSR is no longer declined for the right reason.** It is still a
representation change of the class item 348 parks, it is still blocked on a dense integer-indexed
adjacency the TS graph does not expose, and 2.9x of locality degradation is not a promise that a
CSR recovers 2.9x. But the next person to pick it up should know the remaining cost is data layout,
measured, rather than "three components, two left".

### And the trap that nearly ate the result

Writing the sweep with `cat > file` failed on `noclobber` — the file existed — **and the stale
probe ran instead**, printing the previous experiment's output. Caught only because the numbers
were visibly the old ones. This is the exact failure CLAUDE.md describes (_"the next command runs
anyway and consumes the stale file, so the failure surfaces as a wrong result rather than an
error"_), it has a rule against it, and the rule is right: the file was written with the editor
tool and a fresh unique name the second time.

No code change: two temporary probes, both removed, tree verified clean.

## 353. A graph element casts to nothing — the decision from item 347, taken, and the survey found four divergent shapes rather than one

Item 346 reported one divergence (`CAST([n, ''] AS STRING)`), item 347 established from ISO's free
artifacts that it is **not** a place implementations may choose, and the decision came back:
**refuse.**

### Surveying first found three more

Before changing anything, every cast shape over an element, both engines:

| shape                     | native (before)                   | TS (before)                                        |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `CAST(p AS STRING)`       | `"0"` — the **internal dense id** | `"a"` — the external id                            |
| `CAST(p AS INTEGER)`      | `0` — the dense id as a number    | **throws** "cannot cast a graph element to number" |
| `CAST(r AS STRING)`       | `"0"`                             | `"e1"`                                             |
| `CAST([p, ''] AS STRING)` | the whole element map's text      | `"a,"`                                             |
| `CAST([1, 2] AS STRING)`  | agreed                            | agreed                                             |
| `CAST({a: 1} AS STRING)`  | agreed                            | agreed                                             |
| `CAST(p.k AS STRING)`     | agreed                            | agreed                                             |

**Four divergent shapes, not one** — and the direct cases are worse than the one that was reported:
native leaked the **internal dense id**, where the engine's own `id` field is the external one. Item
346 only saw the nested form, which leaked the map instead.

The survey also found the thing that made this cheap: **TS already refused the numeric form**, with
a message. So there was an existing phrasing to converge on rather than one to invent, and the
plain-value shapes (`[1, 2]`, `{a: 1}`, `p.k`) already agreed, so nothing legitimate was at risk.

### The change

A graph element casts to **nothing**, for every target, in both engines, checked before the target
table for the same reason the NULL rule is — it is a property of the SOURCE, not of the type pair.

- **native**: `value::cast` gains an element arm; and `Expr::Cast`'s loop moves from
  `col.value_at(i)` to `cell_value(&col, i, store)`, because `value_at` on an element column
  yields the dense id as a number and the element never reached `cast` at all to be refused. **That
  is item 345's bug in a second place** — the `Record` arm read `value_at` where its sibling read
  `render_cell`; here the `Cast` arm read `value_at` where it needed the unboxed ref.
- **TS**: `castValue` gains the same check, and a named `castTargetName` helper so both engines
  spell the target identically — `integer` and `float` both report **"number"**, matching
  `castToNumber`'s long-standing message and native's `Integer | Float => "number"` arm.

Messages are byte-identical by construction and asserted as text in both suites, not just "it
throws": `cannot cast a graph element to string` / `to number` / `to boolean` / `to list`.

### Scope, and the half that is NOT done

The **direct** cases are fixed and agree. The **nested** one — `CAST([p, ''] AS STRING)` — still
differs, and that is deliberate rather than overlooked.

The two engines cannot share a mechanism for it. TS keeps element identity at every depth, so a
recursive value check reaches the element inside the list. Native does not: since item 345,
containers render their elements eagerly, so by cast time the list holds a `Map` indistinguishable
from a user's. The alternatives are both worse than stopping here:

- a **static** check on the operand expression works in both, but it would refuse
  `CAST(CASE WHEN … THEN p ELSE 1 END AS STRING)` whichever branch is taken, where a value check
  refuses only when the element is actually produced — **a new divergence in place of the old one**;
- making native's containers keep refs unboxed and resolve at egress is the architecturally right
  answer and is a bigger change than this item, touching the fix item 345 just landed and tested.

And it is a genuinely separate semantic question: a list that happens to contain an element is a
legal value, and stringifying that list is not the same operation as casting the element. Recorded
as the open half, with the reason, rather than guessed at.

### Verification

1100 + 13 + 723 Rust tests (one new), 1991 `packages/gql` (one new), 352 `packages/core`, 809
`packages/native`, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green. Clippy on both crates, `cargo fmt
--check`, `lint`, `typecheck` and `fmt:check` each as their own command, each exit 0.

**Why refusing was the right direction regardless of what the prose says**: nothing in the free
artifacts says the cast exists, nobody can have been relying on it (the engines never agreed), and
a refusal relaxes cleanly to whatever the cast table turns out to specify. The reverse — picking
one engine's answer — would have to be un-picked.

## 354. A graph element casts to nothing at ANY DEPTH — and the survey refuted the premise item 353 used to leave this open

Item 353 fixed the direct cast-over-an-element cases and left the nested one open with a written
reason. The decision came back: **it should be an error.** Implementing it found that item 353's
reason was wrong in two separate ways, both of which a survey caught before any code changed.

### What item 353 claimed, and what is actually true

> _"The two engines cannot share a mechanism for it. TS keeps element identity at every depth, so a
> recursive value check reaches the element inside the list. Native does not."_

Both halves are wrong.

**"TS keeps element identity at every depth"** — it does not behave that way. A 23-case survey over
both engines found the map/record nesting **already agreed**: `CAST({v: p} AS STRING)`,
`CAST([{v: p}] AS STRING)` and `CAST({v: [p]} AS STRING)` all rendered the element MAP in both
engines. Only the LIST nesting diverged, and the cause is internal to TS: `str()` renders an array
with `joinElement` per item (so an element becomes its external id) and a record with
`JSON.stringify` (so an element becomes its element map). **TS's two container paths disagreed with
each other**, which is a narrower and more mundane problem than "the engines model identity
differently".

**"The engines cannot share a mechanism"** — the repo already had one, in the engine, for the same
question. `exec::aggregation::sort_local_key_is_element` refuses `order(local)` over elements, and
its comment is this item's whole diagnosis, written earlier by someone who hit it:

> _"An element reaches a locally-sorted list in EITHER form. A `Gen` cell from a branch carries the
> unboxed `Value::Node`/`Value::Edge` ref, but `fold()` RENDERS first, so the common shape is a list
> of element MAPS. **Checking only the refs found nothing and the fault never fired**;
> `vertex_map_ext_id`/`edge_map_ext_id` are the repo's existing test for the rendered form."_

That is exactly the mechanism item 353 said did not exist. The lesson is the session's own, one
item later: **a scope claim is a measurement.** "The engines cannot share a mechanism" is a claim
about the codebase, it was asserted rather than checked, and one grep for the same question
elsewhere reversed it — the fourth time this session that checking a scope claim inverted the
recommendation that rested on it (342→343, 343→348, 350→351).

### The survey, which again found more than the reported shape

Every nested cast shape, both engines, before changing anything. **Seven divergent shapes in three
families**, where the report named one:

| shape                                               | native (before)                    | TS (before) |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------- |
| `CAST([p, ''] AS STRING)`                           | the element map's text             | `"a,"`      |
| `CAST([p] AS STRING)`                               | the element map's text             | `"a"`       |
| `CAST([r] AS STRING)`                               | the edge map's text                | `"e1"`      |
| `CAST([[p]] AS STRING)`                             | the element map's text             | `"a"`       |
| `CAST(nodes(path) AS STRING)`                       | two element maps' text             | `"a,b"`     |
| `CAST(edges(path) AS STRING)`                       | the edge map's text                | `"e1"`      |
| `CAST(path AS STRING)`                              | the whole `{vertices, edges}` text | `"a,e1,b"`  |
| `CAST({v: p} AS STRING)` and the other 2 map shapes | agreed                             | agreed      |
| `CAST([1,2] / {a:1} / [p.k, p.s] AS STRING)`        | agreed                             | agreed      |

The **path** family is the part no amount of reasoning about `CAST([p, ''] …)` would have reached:
`nodes(p)`, `edges(p)` and the path value itself are lists of elements by construction, not by a
literal, so they are the shapes a real query is most likely to hit.

### The decision, and the direction NOT taken

Because the map nesting already agreed, there were two coherent ways to close this, and they are
opposites:

1. **Refuse at every depth** — what the decision asked for. Costs three shapes that currently
   agree (`{v: p}` and its two nested forms) by turning them from "renders the element map" into an
   error.
2. **Make TS's list path match its own map path** — render the element map in both, refuse nothing.
   Nothing would break, and it fixes a genuine internal inconsistency in `str()`.

Route 1 was taken, because it is the decision and because it is the only one statable in a single
sentence: _a graph element casts to nothing, wherever in the value it sits._ Route 2 makes the rule
"an element has no string form, unless it is inside something, in which case it has two different
ones depending on the container" — and it would have to be un-picked if the paywalled cast table
turns out to say anything at all. Same argument as item 353's: **a refusal relaxes cleanly, a
guessed value does not.** The cost (three agreeing but obscure shapes) is recorded here because it
is the one real argument for route 2, and reversing this is a small change if that is wanted.

### The change

`lenke_engine_core::value::contains_element` — the dual test, recursive through lists, records and
maps (both KEYS and values, since a Gremlin map keys by any value):

- an **unboxed** `Value::Node`/`Value::Edge` ref, which a heterogeneous `Col::Gen` carries at the
  top level; **or**
- a **rendered** element map, which is what a container holds, because `Expr::List`/`Record`/
  `MapLit` all build their items with `render_cell`.

`cast` tests that instead of a top-level 2-tag match. The message is unchanged and reused —
`cannot cast a graph element to <target>` — because the rule is the same rule.

**The field-set test moved crates.** `vertex_map_ext_id`/`edge_map_ext_id` lived in
`exec::render` and `cast` lives in `lenke-engine-core`, which cannot reach it. They are now in the
value contract where they belong (a property of a `Value`), `exec::render` re-exports them, and the
two near-identical copies collapsed into one function parameterized by the field set.

**TS needs no shape test, which was the surprise.** The predicted problem was native's rendered-shape
test having a false positive — a hand-written `{id, labels, properties}` map — that TS's identity
test would not share, trading one divergence for another. Measured instead of assumed: **it is not
reachable from GQL.** A GQL `{…}` literal lowers to a `Value::Record`, and the shape test keys on
`Value::Map`, so within the only surface that has `CAST` the sole way a container holds an
element-shaped map is that it IS a rendered element. Both lookalike rows still render in both
engines, and both are pinned as control assertions. So TS's `containsElement` is pure identity —
with `Path` and `LenkeRecord` handled explicitly, because neither is an `Array` (`str()` has the
same two special cases, for the same reason).

### Teeth

Five behavioural mutants on `contains_element`, each run under `timeout 600` + a 16G cgroup cap with
`MemorySwapMax=0`, restoring the pristine file before each. The cap was proved to kill first (an
allocator bomb → 137, a bare spin → 124).

| mutant                                         | result                     |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| M1 list arm dead                               | **CAUGHT**                 |
| M2 rendered-vertex test removed                | **CAUGHT**                 |
| M3 rendered-EDGE test removed (the twin alone) | **CAUGHT**                 |
| M4 record arm dead                             | **CAUGHT**                 |
| M6 field-set guard dropped                     | **SURVIVED → then CAUGHT** |
| M5 CONTROL, `                                  |                            | ` operands swapped (behaviour-preserving) | **SURVIVED**, as it must |

Each of M1–M4 was caught by exactly `a_nested_graph_element_casts_to_nothing` and nothing else.

**M6 is the one worth keeping.** It mutates the `keys.len() != pairs.len()` guard — the part that
rejects a map with a duplicate or non-string key whose key SET still matches — and it survived the
entire 1,101-test engine suite. That guard is not new; it came with the function when it moved, and
**it had no test in the place it came from either.** A moved line is still an untested line, and the
mutant is what said so. Now covered by a direct unit test in the crate it now lives in
(`contains_element_keys_on_the_exact_rendered_field_set`), which kills it.

**The fuzzer hole is closed, and it was closed with an expiry note already in it.** Item 346 added
the container-carrying-an-element family and _deliberately excluded_ the cast shapes, saying so:
letting them in _"would make the fuzzer red for an unrelated reason"_ while the divergence was open.
That exclusion has expired, so `genHopProjection` now generates seven cast shapes — five that must
refuse in both engines and two (`CAST([a.n, b.n] AS STRING)`) that must keep working, so the block
is not purely a refusal check. Teeth verified the item-346 way: disabling native's list arm made the
differential fuzzer red in one run, naming the shape —
`[seed 1152313428931146] MATCH (a:T)-[e:E]->(b:T) RETURN CAST([a, ''] AS STRING) AS x`.

### Cost: none measurable

The refusal now runs a recursive function on every cast row, so it was A/B'd rather than argued:
two binaries built from the same probe, alternated, min of 7, three rounds, 200,000 rows.

| row                                                                       |  CONTROL (HEAD) |             NEW |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------: | --------------: |
| `CAST(n.s AS STRING)` — the cheapest arm, so the check's share is largest |   21.85 / 22.11 |   21.59 / 21.97 |
| `CAST(n.k AS STRING)`                                                     | 106.44 / 106.15 | 107.46 / 108.41 |
| `CAST(n.s AS INTEGER)`                                                    |     2.18 / 2.19 |     2.19 / 2.17 |
| **CONTROL** `RETURN n.s` — the change cannot reach it                     | **6.63 / 6.61** | **6.64 / 7.05** |

(ns/row, warm rounds 2 and 3; round 1 was a cold start on both sides and the null control moved with
them, which is what identified it as such.) Every cast row sits inside 1%, while the row the change
**cannot** reach drifts 6.6% by itself — so the harness's own noise floor is several times any
difference being claimed. Probe deleted.

### Two incidental divergences, both found by the survey's control rows
