Neither is a cast-over-an-element question and neither is fixed here; both are recorded as open.

1. **Cast-failure messages differ in wording AND in type name.** `CAST([1,2] AS INTEGER)` →
   native `cannot cast list to number`, TS `cannot cast a list to number`; `CAST({a:1} AS INTEGER)`
   → native `cannot cast record to number`, TS `cannot cast **a map** to number`. Both raise
   `E_INVALID_VALUE`, and the differential fuzzer compares CODES, so it is blind to this whole
   class. Item 353 made the element messages byte-identical by hand; the rest of the cast table was
   never checked.
2. **`from` as a bare record-field name.** `RETURN {from: 1}` → native accepts it, TS rejects it as
   a reserved word (_"quote it as a delimited identifier with backticks"_). A parser divergence,
   found because an edge-element lookalike map needs a `from` key. Whether `from` is reserved in
   that position is an ISO BNF question, so it needs the grammar rather than a guess.

### Verification

1,101 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (one new), 35 `lenke-engine-core` (one new), 1,992
`packages/gql` (one new), 352 `packages/core`, 779 `packages/gremlin`, 809 `packages/native`, all 13
byte-identity fuzzer cases green. Gates each as its own command, each exit 0: clippy on both crates,
`cargo fmt --check` on both crates, `lint`, `typecheck`, `fmt:check`.

## 355. `side()` hashes an id its callers already hold a Vertex for — and using the box would be a REGRESSION on five of the six, because a memo taxes a visited-once element

`count 3-hop` is the widest cross-engine row left (`bun run bench`, this session: ts **330.3ms**
against ffi **4.9**, **67.6x**). Item 310 refuted the two cheap answers to it and left a
three-component diagnosis; item 324 removed the first component; items 350–352 corrected the
figure, refuted the second component on the _1-hop_ row and showed the residue there is locality.
This item decomposes the **3-hop** row itself, because its component list was inherited from a
different row and that is precisely the misattribution items 350/351 were about.

### What the row actually does per middle edge

The unfiltered shape takes `needsC === false`, so the inner loop is one line:

```ts
count += waysToA * side(graph, midOut ? e.toId : e.fromId, fromDOut, t3, dEff);
```

and with no `d` label, `side` takes its `far === undefined` path: **one `.get` into the
200,000-entry string-keyed `edgesFromByLabel`**, then one `.get` into a **1-entry** type map, then a
`.size`. So "two hash lookups" is right but **not symmetric** — and that asymmetry explains item
310's refuted memo, which replaced {one expensive hash + one cheap one} with {one equally expensive
hash} and bought ≤1.01x. It also means item 351's `edge.to` refutation does **not** transfer: this
path reads `e.toId`, a stored field, never resolving the vertex.

### The observation that looked like free money

**Six of `side`'s ten call sites already hold the `Vertex` object and pass its `id`**, which `side`
immediately hashes — while `Vertex.adjFrom` (item 321's box) is that same bucket already memoized on
the element. Item 323 refuted reaching the box _from an id_ (resolve + box, 1.26x worse), but its own
micro put the **vertex-already-in-hand** read at 1.97x, and nothing had tried that.

**Measured, and it inverts the recommendation.** 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, each variant in
its **own process on a fresh graph**, min of 3 alternated rounds, ns per iteration:

| variant                                   |  first pass |       warm |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------: | ---------: |
| vertex in hand, today (`v.id` → 200k map) |   **203.4** |      171.3 |
| vertex in hand, box (`v.adjFrom`)         |   **247.0** |      127.1 |
| edge, today (`e.toId` → 200k map)         |       259.0 |  **248.9** |
| edge, stored ref → box                    |       234.2 |  **187.9** |
| edge, resolve (`e.to` → box)              |       339.5 |      301.5 |
| CONTROL `v.id.length` / `e.toId.length`   | 11.0 / 16.3 | 3.4 / 10.1 |

The box is **1.21x WORSE on first touch** (247.0 against 203.4): it pays the same hash _and_ the
memo write. It is 1.35x better warm. **Five of the six sites visit each vertex exactly once per
query** — they are the hoisted per-`b` degree reads — so they would pay the cold cost and never
reach the warm win. On a freshly loaded graph that is a regression. Only the `c` position under
`needsC` is revisited (once per middle edge, ~in-degree times per vertex), where the blended cost is
~1.21x better. **One site, not six.**

The generalisable form: **a memo helps a revisited element and taxes a visited-once one, so "the
caller already holds the object" is not by itself a reason to read a memo on it.** This is the fifth
time this session that checking a scope claim reversed the recommendation resting on it (342→343,
343→348, 350→351, 353→354, and now this).

### The probe's own defect, which is the method note

The first version ran all five variants **in one process** and reported a "cold" number for each.
Every one of them was wrong for whichever variant ran later, because `adjFrom` **memoizes**: the
per-edge cases call `e.to.adjFrom` and so warm the box for all 200,000 vertices before the
per-vertex cases are timed. It read as "the box is faster even cold", which is the opposite of the
truth. Fixed by giving each variant its own process on a fresh graph.

**A ratio is only as honest as the sameness of its two sides**, and a memo makes ORDER OF
MEASUREMENT part of the two sides. The tell was that the cold and warm readings for the box were
implausibly close.

### What is priced and not built

An `Edge` holding a direct **reference** to its endpoint vertices is the one variant that _removes_
the lookup rather than relocating it: **1.32x warm / 1.11x cold** on the hottest read in the row,
~**1.18x** on the row. Declined, not from doubt about the number but because it needs a **new
invariant** — an endpoint reference must never outlive the endpoint _instance_, where items 140/218
deliberately store the id and both `evict()` and rollback replay swap instances for the same id.
~1.18x on one row does not buy that invariant, and the gap it leaves (67.6x → ~57x) is still the
CSR's.

**UNTRIED, and the only shape with no cold penalty and no new invariant**: _peek_ the box and hash
only on a miss, never writing it. Warm callers get 127.1, cold callers pay today's cost plus a field
read. It cannot be measured on this row — nothing warms the box on a fresh graph — so it needs a
mixed read/write workload (`bench:usage`), which is where item 321's boxes are already populated.
Recorded with a trigger rather than attempted.

### No code change

A `REJECTED, with its numbers` block beside `side()`, which is this file's existing convention for
exactly this (the item-310 and item-323 blocks sit a few lines away) and the repo's rule: record a
rejected optimization with its numbers next to the code it would have changed. Both probes deleted;
tree verified clean. 1,992 `packages/gql` and 352 `packages/core` tests pass; `lint`, `typecheck`
and `fmt:check` each exit 0.

## 356. Four codec decode rows had ZERO edges — and normalizing by bytes retracts both targets the un-normalized table suggested

Hunting the next target in `bun run bench`, two decode rows looked anomalous. Both retracted on
measurement, and the thing that made them look anomalous is a fixture hole worth more than either.

### The hole: the codec decode rows decode a nodes-only document

`decode pg-json` / `graphson` / `pg-text` / `csv` all take `setup: e.load(nodesDoc)` — **200,000
nodes and NO EDGES** — while `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)`, three lines above them in the same
table, decodes **1,200,000 elements**. Nothing said so.

Two consequences, and the first is the serious one:

- **Each codec's entire edge path was unmeasured, for all three engines** — endpoint resolution,
  edge-label indexing, the edge property bag. CLAUDE.md's rule is _"match the fixture to the claim:
  one edge per node is sparse, per-edge costs scale with the edge:node ratio"_. This is not a sparse
  fixture, it is **zero** edges per node, on rows named for a whole-graph decode.
- The adjacency of `decode graphson` (200,000 elements) to `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)`
  (1,200,000) **invites a comparison that is 6x off**, and I made it before checking the fixture.

Fixed by ADDING an edge-bearing twin per format rather than repointing the existing rows, so every
figure already recorded against the old row names stays comparable (item 341 added rows for the same
reason).

### What the new rows say

200,000 nodes at 5 edges/node = 1,200,000 elements. Bytes are of the same document each row decodes:

| format   |     MB | B/element |    ffi ms | ffi MB/ms | ffi ns/element |  ts ms | ts ns/element |
| -------- | -----: | --------: | --------: | --------: | -------------: | -----: | ------------: |
| ndjson   | 111.24 |      97.2 |     464.2 | **0.240** |            387 | 2902.4 |          2419 |
| pg-json  | 113.34 |      99.0 |     644.2 |     0.176 |            537 | 2675.3 |          2229 |
| graphson | 223.67 |     195.4 |    1199.9 |     0.186 |           1000 | 2954.5 |          2462 |
| pg-text  |  28.95 |      25.3 | **337.8** |     0.086 |        **282** | 3287.8 |          2740 |
| csv      |  32.66 |      28.5 |     372.9 |     0.088 |            311 | 3009.5 |          2508 |

**1. `decode graphson` is NOT slow — RETRACTED.** Un-normalized it reads 339.8ms against every other
format's ~80 on the nodes-only rows, a 4.2x outlier. Its document is **3.5x bigger** (410 B/element
against ndjson's 117 on that fixture) and its byte rate is **1.20x worse** (0.230 against 0.277
MB/ms). 3.5 × 1.2 = 4.2. There is nothing here to fix; it is a verbose format.

**2. Native's ndjson decode is NOT slower than pg-text's — RETRACTED, same shape.** Per element
ndjson (387) loses to pg-text (282) and csv (311), which looked like a target on the format that
matters most (ndjson is the snapshot channel, and items 328–333 optimized it specifically). **Per
byte ndjson is the FASTEST of the five** (0.240 MB/ms, 2.8x pg-text's 0.086). Its per-element
disadvantage is entirely that its document carries 3.8x more bytes per element.

**3. The per-byte ordering is the INVERSE of the per-element ordering.** Compact formats are slowest
per byte (pg-text 0.086, csv 0.088) and verbose ones fastest (ndjson 0.240). That is the signature of
a per-ELEMENT fixed cost — the graph build and the per-element dispatch — dominating wherever there
are few bytes to amortize it over. So **"ns/element" and "MB/ms" rank these five codecs in opposite
orders, and a decode claim has to say which unit it is in.**

**4. THE TS DECODE IS FORMAT-INDEPENDENT, and this is the useful result.** 2229–2740 ns/element
across five formats — a **1.23x spread** — where native spans 282–1000, a **3.55x spread**. Pure-TS
ingest is bound by the graph BUILD, not by any codec, and the figure agrees with the known cause:
item 312 measured `addEdge` at ~2.9µs an edge, and at a 5:1 ratio five of every six elements is an
edge. **So no codec work can make pure-TS ingest faster — the only target is `addEdge`**, which is
already the recorded one. A measured "where not to look".

**5. The widest decode ratios in the bench are now pg-text 9.73x and csv 8.07x**, where the table
previously showed 3.82x and 3.05x for those formats. Both were understated because the rows carried
no edges, and the edge path is where native's advantage is largest.

### Cost of the change

Four new rows, each a 1.2M-element encode in `setup` plus a 1.2M-element decode timed five times
across three engines. That is real wall clock added to every `bun run bench`; `BENCH_ONLY=decode`
(and its exact-match `$` form, item 310) isolates them. Taken deliberately: the alternative is four
codecs whose edge path nobody can see.

### No engine change

Bench coverage only. The probe that produced the byte counts is deleted — and its own first version
was wrong in the way this item is about: it encoded the EDGE-BEARING graph for all five formats and
so compared four of them against a document the bench never decodes. **Check which fixture a row
actually loads before normalizing it.** `lint`, `typecheck` and `fmt:check` each exit 0.

## 357. `addEdge`'s 810ns label index, finally SPLIT — the 1M-element Set is free, the two adjacency maps are all of it, and they are superadditive

Item 356 established that `addEdge` is the only lever on pure-TS ingest: the TS decode is
format-independent (2229–2740 ns/element across five codecs, a 1.23x spread, where native spans
3.55x), so the cost is the graph BUILD. Item 312 priced `indexEdgeLabel` at 810ns of a ~2.9µs edge
write and described it as "seven hash operations per edge, five string-keyed" — but never split that
810 across the **three** indexes the function maintains, so the figure could not be acted on.

### The instrument, which had to be built first

`bun run bench`'s decode rows cannot answer this. They include `JSON.parse` (19% of the row), and
they reach `@lenke/core` through `@lenke/serialization`, **which resolves to core's built DIST** — so
an A/B of core's SOURCE is not in effect at all, and every edit costs a full `bun run build` before
it can be measured. That is the stale-artifact trap in a new place, and it is why this decomposition
did not already exist.

`addedge-cost-probe.ts` (`bun run addedge:cost`) reads core's source, drives `addVertex` and
`addEdge` directly, and takes NODE ingest as the null control — nothing done to the edge path can
reach it. It reproduces both known baselines, which is the check that it measures the right thing:
**2743–3052 ns/edge** against item 312's ~2.9µs, and **898–1015 ns/node** against its ~1.08µs. Kept
permanently, like `delete-width-probe.ts`, because `addEdge` is now the named target and the next
A/B should cost seconds.

### The split

Ablating each index's update in turn — three alternated rounds, min of each, pristine restored
before every variant:

| variant                      | min ns/edge | range     | vs CONTROL                           |
| ---------------------------- | ----------: | --------- | ------------------------------------ |
| CONTROL                      |        2760 | 2760–2867 | —                                    |
| minus `edgesByLabel`         |        2592 | 2592–2748 | **overlaps — not measurable, ≤4%**   |
| minus `edgesFromByLabel`     |        2461 | 2461–2543 | −240 (8.9%), disjoint                |
| minus `edgesToByLabel`       |        2483 | 2483–2631 | −218 (8.1%), disjoint                |
| minus BOTH adjacency maps    |        2076 | 2076–2141 | **−684 (24.8%), disjoint**           |
| minus all three              |        1912 | 1912–2336 | −848 (30.7%), disjoint               |
| minus all three AND the loop |        1887 | 1887–2164 | indistinguishable from the row above |

**1. Item 312's 810ns is CONFIRMED in aggregate and now attributed.** 848ns here, 30.7% of the edge
write. The two per-vertex adjacency maps are essentially the whole of it.

**2. `edgesByLabel` is NOT MEASURABLE.** The index that holds a **1,000,000-element `Set`** per edge
type — the biggest container in the graph — cannot be distinguished from the control: its range
(2592–2748) overlaps the control's (2760–2867), and its apparent 109ns is 4%, inside the control's
own 3.9% repeatability. A `Set.add` into a million-entry Set is essentially free. **This retracts the
intuition that the big container is the expensive one** — the cost is in the two indexes with the
_small_ inner containers, because there are 400,000 of those.

**3. The per-label loop and the function call are FREE**, and this had to be checked before the
aggregate could be believed: with all three blocks removed, `indexEdgeLabel` is an empty function, so
the 848 could have been an artifact of ablating down to an empty callee that the JIT then inlines
away along with the loop. Removing the loop too lands at 1887 against 1912 — ranges overlapping
heavily, no effect. So the aggregate is real work, not a measurement artifact.

**4. The two adjacency maps are SUPERADDITIVE — 684ns together against 240+218 = 458 apart, a 226ns
shared term.** That is the finding that redirects the next step, because a shared term is not
reachable by fixing either index alone. Two mechanisms are consistent with it and **this item does
not separate them**:

- **~0.8 container allocations per edge.** Each index allocates one inner `Map` and one inner `Set`
  the first time it sees a given vertex id on that side: 200,000 of each per index at this fixture,
  so 800,000 objects for 1,000,000 edges. Removing one index leaves the other's allocation pressure
  in place; removing both removes it.
- **The cache cost of touching two 200,000-entry string-keyed Maps per edge**, which is item 323's
  own recorded observation in a different place: _"touching two large maps per edge thrashes more
  than either alone"_ — measured there as a read being worse than the sum of its parts.

**The experiment that would separate them**: merge the two adjacency maps into ONE (same number of
inner containers, one outer working set) against keeping two maps with no inner containers at all.
Named rather than run, because either direction is a representation change of the class item 348
parks, and the honest state is that the shared term exists and its mechanism is undetermined.

### What this does NOT license

A tagged single-label inner representation (store the `Set` directly, promote to a `Map` only on a
second label) would halve the 800,000 allocations and remove one hash level from every adjacency
READ as well. It is the obvious candidate and it is **not** taken here: `edgesFromByLabel` /
`edgesToByLabel` are read by `Vertex.adjFrom`, both engines' `graph-queries`, four algorithms, and
`shortcuts`' `side` / `bucketSize` / `edgesOfTypes` — a wide blast radius for a change whose own
price is bounded by the 226ns shared term plus whatever share of the 684 the allocations hold, which
is exactly the quantity this item could not separate. **Price the mechanism before paying for the
representation.**

### No engine change

A decomposition and a permanent instrument. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: `lint`,
`typecheck`, `fmt:check`; 352 `packages/core` tests pass, and the ablation harness restored the
pristine `Graph.ts` and verified it clean after every variant.

## 358. The inner-container allocation is NOT the cost — which refutes the representation change item 357 flagged, and retracts item 357's own superadditivity

Item 357 found the two adjacency maps cost 684ns together against 240+218 = 458 apart, named a
**226ns shared term**, listed two candidate mechanisms, and named the experiment that would separate
them. This is that experiment. **Neither mechanism survives, and the shared term does not either.**

### The two variants, chosen because they move the candidates in OPPOSITE directions

- **`no-inner-alloc`** — two outer maps kept (so the cache story is untouched), but the inner `Map`
  and `Set` are replaced by shared singletons, so **~800,000 allocations become 0** while every one
  of the 5 string-keyed `get`s and 3 `Set.add`s remains. If the shared term is allocation, this
  recovers it.
  _Priced caveat_: the shared Sets grow to 1,000,000 entries instead of ~5. Item 357 measured a
  1M-element `Set.add` as **not measurable** — that is exactly what `edgesByLabel` is — so the
  substitution is worth ~0 and does not confound the result.
- **`shared-outer`** — ONE outer map keyed by vertex id with `{f, t}` inner maps, so there is one
  working set instead of two **and allocation is made WORSE** (five objects per vertex instead of
  four). If the shared term is the cache cost of two large maps, this recovers it anyway.

Anchors (`control`, `minus-both`) were re-measured in the same run, because absolutes do not survive
a session boundary and only ratios inside one run are comparable (item 338).

### Round 1 — three alternated rounds, min of each

| variant                   | min ns/edge | range         |
| ------------------------- | ----------: | ------------- |
| control                   |        2757 | 2757–2943     |
| minus both adjacency maps |        2171 | 2171–2298     |
| `no-inner-alloc`          |        2498 | 2498–**2807** |
| `shared-outer`            |    **2821** | 2821–2990     |

`shared-outer` is **worse than the control**, so the two-large-maps cache story is out — merging the
working sets buys nothing and the extra object per vertex costs a little. `no-inner-alloc` showed
259ns at the min but its range **overlaps the control's**, which does not clear this repo's bar.

### Round 2 — the isolated A/B, five alternated rounds, min of five internal reps each

|                            | readings                     |      min | range |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------: | ----- |
| control                    | 2618, 2623, 2680, 2698, 2698 | **2618** | 3.1%  |
| `no-inner-alloc`           | 2637, 2505, 2533, 2490, 2509 | **2490** | 5.9%  |
| NULL CONTROL (node ingest) | 896 … 949                    |        — | 5.9%  |

**128ns, 4.9%** — with round 1 of five showing no effect at all (2637 against the control's 2618),
and the null control that the change cannot reach ranging **5.9% by itself**. The effect is at the
harness's noise floor.

### What this closes

**1. The inner-container allocation is not a target.** Removing _all_ ~800,000 of them is worth
≤128ns of a ~2600ns write, at the noise floor. **That was the entire motivation for a tagged
single-label inner representation** — store the `Set` directly and promote to a `Map` only on a
second label — which item 357 called "the obvious candidate" and declined on blast radius
(`Vertex.adjFrom`, both engines' `graph-queries`, four algorithms, three `shortcuts` helpers). Its
price is now measured rather than guessed, and it is ~free. **Refuted before it was built**, which
is the cheapest form this result could have taken.

**2. Item 357's 226ns shared term is RETRACTED.** Two mechanisms were consistent with it, this item
tested both, and neither reproduces: one is worse than the control, the other is at the noise floor.
226ns is 8% of this row and the harness's demonstrated repeatability is 3–6%, so the superadditivity
was never far enough above the floor to attribute. **A superadditivity is a difference of
differences, so it carries the noise of every term in it** — 357 treated it as a finding because
each individual ablation was disjoint from the control, but disjointness of the parts says nothing
about the residue after subtracting them. That is the lesson, and it is a sharper form of item 300's:
_disjoint ranges are not proof when the whole side moves_ becomes **disjoint ranges on the terms are
not proof about the remainder.**

**3. What the 586–684ns actually is: the string-keyed hash work itself.** Roughly 4 keyed `get`s, 2
`set`s and 2 `Set.add`s an edge, at ~75–100ns each on a 200,000-entry Map — which is item 312's own
~115ns-per-operation estimate arriving from a different direction. The only lever on that is the KEY
TYPE: a dense integer-indexed adjacency, item 300's, parked at item 348. **Every road in this area
keeps arriving there**, and this item is the fourth to do so (310, 350, 352, 358) — at some point
that is itself the finding.

### No engine change

The ablation harness restored the pristine `Graph.ts` and verified it clean after every variant.
`addedge-cost-probe.ts`'s header is corrected in the same commit, so the retracted superadditivity
is not left asserted in the file that produced it — a probe that keeps claiming a withdrawn finding
is worse than no probe. 352 `packages/core` tests pass; `lint`, `typecheck` and `fmt:check` each exit 0.

## 359. An unindexed dotted-path scan re-split its key once per NODE — 2.42x, and the bench row that found it was comparing two things at once

First native item since 333. `bench_all`'s `value/maps` section read

```
scalar age (flat)        368.7 us
scalar age (map graph)   379.0 us
map field meta.city    12145.3 us
```

which invites "a dotted map-field access costs 33x a scalar read". **The two sides of that ratio
differ in two things**, not one: a NUMERIC range on a flat column against a STRING equality through
a nested path. So the missing third measurement came first.

### Diagnosing it, with the third measurement and the plans

200,000 nodes, min of 7:

| case                                   |     best µs |
| -------------------------------------- | ----------: |
| A numeric flat `p.age > 50`            |       367.1 |
| B **string flat** `p.city = 'NYC'`     |   **271.3** |
| C string nested `p.meta.city = 'NYC'`  |     13126.8 |
| D **numeric nested** `p.meta.tier = 1` | **12812.4** |
| CONTROL numeric on the MAP graph       |       367.4 |

- **The string/numeric axis runs the OTHER way**: B is _faster_ than A (271 against 367), because a
  flat string equality lowers to an `IndexSeek` shape while the numeric range is a `Filter`. So the
  un-matched ratio **understated** the nested penalty — against the matched flat case it is **48x**,
  not 33x.
- **C and D are the same** (13127 against 12812), so it is not the string compare.
- **The CONTROL is identical to A** (367.4 against 367.1), so it is not the map's presence either —
  the section's own regression baseline (a map must not slow the flat columns) holds exactly.

The cost is the nested path and nothing else. The plans say which code runs — all three of B, C, D
lower to `IndexSeek`, differing only in the key (`"city"` against `"meta.city"` / `"meta.tier"`), so
with no index on this fixture **the 48x is the unindexed `IndexSeek` FALLBACK for a dotted key
against the same fallback for a flat one**: 1.36 ns/row columnar against 65.6 ns/row nested.

### The cause, one line

```rust
pub fn prop_path(&self, node: u32, dotted_key: &str) -> Value {
    let path: Vec<String> = dotted_key.split('.').map(String::from).collect();
    resolve_path(&self.prop(node, &path[0]), &path[1..])
}
```

called from the fallback's `filter` closure, **once per node**. For `meta.city` that is one `Vec`
plus two owned `String`s per row — **600,000 allocations to scan 200,000 nodes**, every one of them
recomputing the same constant. The split is a property of the KEY, not of the node.

This is the third time this session's family of items has found the same shape: item 331's property
write allocated its key three times and stored one; item 332's staging parser allocated a `String`
per JSON object key to compare it against a literal. **A key is constant across a scan; splitting,
parsing or owning it per row is the recurring bug.**

### The change

- `Store::prop_path_parts(node, parts: &[&str])` — the form a per-row loop should call. The
  fallback splits once before the iterator and calls it per row.
- `prop_path` keeps its signature and delegates, now collecting `&str` rather than owned `String`s —
  nothing there needed to own them.
- `resolve_path` becomes generic over `S: AsRef<str>`, so the index-maintenance callers keep passing
  their `Vec<String>` paths unchanged while the scan path passes borrowed segments.
- `resolve_path` gains a **one-segment arm**. Not a micro for its own sake: the general loop must
  `clone` its input before it can rebind `cur` in the loop body, which is an `Arc` bump and a drop
  per row for a value the one-level case never needs to own — and one level (`meta.city`) is the
  common shape.

### Measured

Two binaries from one probe, alternated, min of 3 rounds, 200,000 nodes:

| case                                       | CONTROL |        NEW |                     |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------: | ---------: | ------------------- |
| C string nested `meta.city=`               | 12001.9 | **4967.5** | **2.42x**, disjoint |
| D numeric nested `meta.tier=`              | 11732.0 | **4599.5** | **2.55x**, disjoint |
| B string FLAT — unreachable                |   249.5 |      250.4 | **1.00x**           |
| A numeric flat — unreachable               |   324.5 |      291.9 | 1.11x               |
| CONTROL numeric on map graph — unreachable |   334.9 |      299.7 | 1.12x               |

`bench_all`'s own row: **12145.3 → 4985.5 µs, 2.44x**, with both scalar rows in that section flat.

**An honest note on the controls.** B is a clean 1.00x, but A and the map-graph control — rows the
change cannot reach — both moved ~1.11x in the NEW direction. That is code layout, not the change:
this repo has the precedent recorded (`pull`'s alignment is load-bearing — any edit to `exec::pull`
costs the filtered-count cluster 1.08–1.24x, in that case adversely). So **the noise floor here is
~1.11x, not 1.00x**, and 2.42x clears it by a wide margin. Reported rather than banked.

No regressions across the rest of `bench_all`: `SET` 37.85→37.78 ms, 1-hop single-label 239.1→239.1,
seeded scan 273.7→256.9, every `algo/run` row within 2%, `scale/sweep` 1-hop flat and `filter_us`
~10% better. Nothing adverse beyond `scale/cdc` at +3.6%, inside its own band.

### Teeth

Four mutants under `timeout 600` + a 16G cgroup cap with `MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine restored before
each: descend the base property as a sub-field, the one-segment arm returning `Null`, the empty-path
arm returning `Null`, and splitting on the wrong separator. **All four CAUGHT** — by
`a_seek_with_no_index_skips_the_scan_only_when_the_schema_decides_it`,
`dotted_field_eq_seeds_index_both_spellings` and `dotted_path_index_maintained_through_mutations`.

**The control mutant earns its place twice here.** It deletes the new one-segment fast arm so a
single field falls through to the general loop — behaviour-preserving by construction — and it
**SURVIVED**, which is the assertion that the fast arm and the loop agree. A control that only shows
"the suite runs" is worth less than one that proves an equivalence the change depends on.

### And the harness is fixed so the trap cannot recur

`value/maps` gains the matched `string city (flat)` row. Without it the only available ratio was the
two-variable one, and the section invited a conclusion it could not support — item 356's lesson
applied to a different corpus. 14.9x of nested-path penalty remains after this fix (4990 against
247), which is the real, correctly-matched figure and is inherent to a boxed map value against a
typed column; a dotted-path INDEX already exists for workloads that need it (the plans show the seek
shape, and `query/seeded` measures 658x for an indexed equality).

### Verification

1,101 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests, 35 `lenke-engine-core`, `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000`
`rewrite_fuzz`, and all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green. Gates each as their own command, each
exit 0: clippy on both crates, `cargo fmt --check` on both, `lint`, `typecheck`, `fmt:check`.

## 360. The Gremlin lexer never got item 317's fix — 1.085x to 1.30x on parse, and the twin that drifted is a SURFACE LANGUAGE

Item 359's cause was a constant key re-split per row, so the method's next step is to grep the
pattern elsewhere. In the Rust engine every other `split('.')` turned out to be per-CALL, not
per-row — `create_index`, `drop_vertex_index`, `has_hash_index`, `index_lookup`,
`index_bucket_len` — so 359 fixed the only per-row instance and there is nothing to chase there.
(The TS engine has no `split('.')` at all.) What the grep found instead was a different drift.

### A correction, and how it was caught

I first reported `index_lookup` as having **no production caller** and therefore not worth
optimizing. That was wrong: the grep was truncated by `head` and I read the conclusion off an
incomplete list. `index_seek_ids` calls it at `exec.rs:3553`, and `exec/reverse.rs` three more
times. **A `head` on a `grep` whose output you are about to draw a negative conclusion from is the
same error as a fixture that cannot reach the shape** — the absence was in the pager, not the code.
Re-run without it: four production callers.

Priced anyway and declined: `index_lookup` and `index_bucket_len` each build a `Vec<String>` to
compare a path where their sibling `has_hash_index` already does it allocation-free
(`i.path.iter().map(String::as_str).eq(key.split('.'))`). That is ~2 allocations per seek, ~15ns
against a serving call's measured total, **~0.5%** — below any harness here. Recorded, not changed.

### Re-pricing the serving call first, which moved the target

`percall_probe` (item 291's instrument), re-run rather than quoted — item 261's rule:

| layer                                                  |   ns/op |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------: |
| `exec::try_run`, ONE row                               |     325 |
| `exec::try_run`, ZERO rows                             |     251 |
| **`parse_cache::parse_for_run`, WARM — the real path** | **160** |
| `gql::parse` alone (cold)                              |    1300 |
| parse + `optimize_indexed`                             |    1690 |
| `s.chars().collect::<Vec<char>>()`                     |      77 |
| the same, `with_capacity(s.len())`                     |  **28** |

**Item 291's "parse is 1296ns and 43% of the call" no longer describes the serving path** — the
parse cache (items 228/229) makes it 160ns warm. Carried numbers go stale in both directions.

The last two rows are an A/B the probe's author left in place as a candidate, and they point
somewhere specific.

### The finding: a fix landed on one of two parallel lexers

`gql::lex` pre-sizes both of its growing vectors, with item 317's reasoning in a comment above it
(_"audit item 317 counted the allocations of one `parse` and found the char pre-pass reallocating 3
times and the token vector 4 times, 7 of the 19 allocations the lexer makes"_), and item 317
measured that at **1297 → 1163 ns, 1.115x**.

`gremlin::lex` and `gremlin::math_lex` still opened with a bare `s.chars().collect()` and a bare
`Vec::new()` for the tokens. **The twin never got it.** This repo's recurring failure is exactly
this shape — items 333, 335 and 349 were all node/edge twins — and here the two twins are the two
**surface languages**, which `CLAUDE.md` describes as intentionally parallel. Parallel by design is
also parallel for drift.

### Settled by COUNT, because a count has no noise floor

`alloc_count_probe` gains three `gremlin::parse` cases. Allocations and bytes per parse:

| query                   | before            | after                 |
| ----------------------- | ----------------- | --------------------- |
| `has` + `values` (58 B) | 44 allocs, 3487 B | **39 allocs, 2535 B** |
| two-hop count           | 49 allocs, 3612 B | **44 allocs, 2648 B** |
| `g.V().count()` (13 B)  | 19 allocs, 1400 B | **15 allocs, 892 B**  |

Five allocations and ~27% of the bytes, exactly, with no noise floor to argue about.

**The divisor was chosen BY the count, not by analogy.** GQL reserves `s.len() / 4 + 8` tokens;
Gremlin is punctuation-dense (`g.V().count()` is 13 bytes and ~9 tokens), so `/4` under-reserves
and the vector grows anyway — which is the whole thing being fixed:

| divisor      | two-hop count                          |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| `/4` (GQL's) | 45 allocs, 3608 B — still reallocating |
| `/2`         | **44 allocs, 2648 B**                  |

The price of the wider reserve is ~480 bytes of memset on a short query (2535 against 2055 B) and
never a second allocation. Both numbers are in the code comment, so the next reader does not have to
take the divisor on faith.

### Clock backstop

Two binaries from one probe, alternated, min of 3 rounds of min-of-9:

| case                               | CONTROL |     NEW |                     |
| ---------------------------------- | ------: | ------: | ------------------- |
| gremlin `has` + `values`           |     812 | **725** | **1.12x**, disjoint |
| gremlin two-hop count              |     843 | **777** | 1.085x, disjoint    |
| gremlin `g.V().count()`            |     317 | **243** | **1.30x**, disjoint |
| CONTROL `gql::parse` — unreachable |    1180 |    1145 | 1.03x               |

1.12x lands on item 317's 1.115x for the same fix on the other lexer, which is the cross-check that
the twin behaves like its sibling. The tiny query gains most (1.30x) because the fixed overhead is a
larger share of it. The GQL control moves 1.03x — the floor.

### On teeth

**A capacity reserve cannot change behaviour, so mutation testing does not apply here** and is not
quietly skipped: there is no semantic to break, only a count to verify, which is what the allocation
counter did. The guard is that the whole suite and every byte-identity fuzzer stay green over a file
on the plan path — 1,101 + 13 + 723 Rust tests, 779 `packages/gremlin`, all 13 fuzzer cases.

### Verification

Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: clippy, `cargo fmt --check`. The `alloc_count_probe`
addition is permanent — the Gremlin lexer now has the same standing instrument its GQL twin has,
which is what would have caught this drift years earlier.

## 361. Gremlin had no parse cache — 3.74x to 5.43x on a repeated traversal, and the all-miss path had to be fixed before it was shippable

Item 360 found the Gremlin lexer had missed item 317's fix. This is the same drift one layer up:
`lnk_query`'s GQL arm has gone through a parse cache since item 318, and **its Gremlin arm called
`gremlin::parse` on every call.**

Priced before building. On a serving-sized traversal: parse ~735ns, `optimize_indexed` ~390,
against `exec::try_run`'s ~325 — so **~78% of the in-engine work was re-derived every call**, which
is the proportion item 318 cited for GQL (83%) as its reason for building the cache.

One thing checked first, because it would have been a bigger finding: the Gremlin arm does **not**
call `optimize_indexed` itself, which looked like Gremlin plans never being optimized at all. They
are — `exec::run_query` optimizes at its top, for both languages. No gap.

### Why this cache needs no admission CHECK, and when that expires

The GQL cache verifies each text against the direct parse, because a GQL plan is not a function of
its text alone: a parameter can be substituted during the parse, and a now-function folds the
host's `$__now` clock in (the GQL conformance differential caught exactly that). Neither applies
here:

- `gremlin::parse(query: &str) -> Result<Plan, String>` takes nothing but the text;
- its one limit, `MAX_TRAVERSAL_DEPTH`, is a compile-time constant;
- **the Gremlin ABI arm refuses parameters outright**, which is also what makes a clock fold
  impossible — `$__now` arrives as a PARAMETER, read from the params map inside `gql.rs`.

So the parse is a pure function of its text and the key is the text. That is an argument from a
signature, so it has an expiry, and it is written down with the test that enforces it: **if Gremlin
ever accepts parameters or grows a step that reads ambient state at parse time, this cache needs the
admission check its sibling has**, and `a_gremlin_parse_is_a_function_of_its_text` is what goes red
first.

### The all-miss path, which is where this nearly went wrong

First measurement, three alternated rounds:

|                             |  DIRECT |  CACHED |                 |
| --------------------------- | ------: | ------: | --------------- |
| `has` + `values`            |     679 | **154** | 4.41x           |
| two-hop count               |     765 | **145** | 5.28x           |
| `g.V().count()`             |     241 |  **69** | 3.49x           |
| **a FRESH text every call** | **379** | **438** | **1.16x WORSE** |

**That regression is the item, not a footnote, because of an asymmetry between the two languages:
Gremlin accepts no parameters, so a client varying a value must emit different TEXT every call** —
`has('name','name7')` against `has('name','name8')`. A value-varying serving workload is therefore
**all-miss by construction**, where GQL's equivalent is one cached text with bound params. Shipping
a cache that is 1.16x slower on the shape a parameterless language forces you into would have been
a regression dressed as a win.

The cost was the shared sighting filter: a ring answering `hashes.contains(&hash)`, a linear scan of
all 64 slots, on every miss. The Gremlin cache now has its own **direct-indexed** filter
(`hash % CAP`) — one load, one compare. A collision evicts another text's sighting and delays an
admission by one call, which is the same tolerance the ring already accepts (it admits a colliding
text one sighting early). GQL's filter is untouched: the ring is affordable there for a reason that
is about parameters, not about either cache.

After, three alternated rounds, min of each:

|                                    |    DIRECT |  CACHED |                               |
| ---------------------------------- | --------: | ------: | ----------------------------- |
| `has` + `values`                   |       735 | **156** | **4.71x**                     |
| two-hop count                      |       798 | **147** | **5.43x**                     |
| `g.V().count()`                    |       254 |  **68** | **3.74x**                     |
| a FRESH text every call            |       397 |     406 | **1.02x**, overlapping ranges |
| CONTROL `gql::parse` — unreachable | 1165–1190 |       — | flat                          |

### Teeth, and the control mutant doing its actual job

Five mutants under `timeout 600` + a 16G cgroup cap, pristine restored before each: answer from the
wrong key, admit on the first sighting, never evict, never forget a sighting, and a
behaviour-preserving control.

**The first run reported all five CAUGHT — including the control.** That is the control's entire
purpose and the only reason this was not mistaken for a clean result: every mutant had failed the
_same_ test, one that does not even exercise eviction. The suite was broken, by me.

The cause was the new filter: `a_single_sighting_does_not_admit_a_gremlin_traversal` asserted
`seen == 8` after eight sightings, and got 7 — **two of the eight texts hash to the same slot mod 64.** The direct-indexed filter was behaving exactly as designed; the assertion was about the ring's
internals. Rewritten to pin `note` and `forget` exactly with a SINGLE text, where nothing can
collide, and to assert the multi-text case on `size`, which no collision can move. Re-run: four
caught, control survived.

**And a second gap the mutants exposed.** `M1-wrong-key` — a lookup that ignores the key and returns
any stored plan — was initially caught only by the BOUNDEDNESS test, because the correctness test
cleared the cache per case and used one text, so returning "any stored plan" returned the right one.
A cache answering from the wrong key returns a wrong ANSWER; being caught by a bounds test is luck,
not coverage. The correctness test now also runs all eight shapes **interleaved**, three passes, so
every call is preceded by a call for a different text. M1 is now caught by both.

### Verification

1,106 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (five new), 35 `lenke-engine-core`, 809 `packages/native`, 779
`packages/gremlin`, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green — and the Gremlin fuzzer drives the FFI,
so it exercises this cache over hundreds of distinct generated traversals. Gates each as their own
command, each exit 0: clippy, `cargo fmt --check`.

## 362. The serving bench had no Gremlin rows — which is WHY 361's gap survived, and item 361 is worth 1.37x end-to-end, not 4.7x

Item 361 shipped a Gremlin parse cache measured at **4.71x on `gremlin::parse`**. That is a
measurement of a function, not of a call, and the loop's own rule is to really run the benchmarks.
Doing so produced three things: the coverage hole that explains the gap, the honest end-to-end
number, and a cross-language comparison nobody could make before.

### Why the gap survived 43 items

`bench:usage` is the serving harness — small operations against a warm graph, which is exactly
where per-call overhead shows. **Every one of its seventeen workloads is GQL. It had no Gremlin rows
at all.** The Gremlin ABI arm could go without a parse cache from item 318 to item 361 because
nothing was looking at the path where that costs anything.

`bench:gremlin` cannot substitute, and checking that first mattered: its rows execute over a
200,000-vertex / 1,000,000-edge graph, so its smallest rows print as `0.00`–`0.01 ms` and a ~600ns
per-call saving is far below their resolution. **A benchmark at the wrong size cannot see a per-call
effect however carefully it is run** — the same shape as item 356's nodes-only decode rows.

Fixed by ADDING rows, as item 356 did, so no recorded figure moves. The harness gains an optional
`gremlin` capability on `Engine` and a `needs` field on a workload; an engine without the capability
prints `-` rather than erroring per cell. **The pure-TS Gremlin engine legitimately has no text
entry** — its surface is a fluent builder (`g.V().out()`), so there is nothing to hand a string to.
That is a different surface, not a gap, which is why it is a `-` and not an `n/a`.

### The pair of rows is the point, and it comes from 361's own finding

**Gremlin accepts no parameters**, so a serving workload that varies a value must vary its TEXT —
which makes it all-miss against a text-keyed cache _by construction_. A GQL row varying `$n` is a
cache hit every time, because the value is a parameter and the text is constant. So two rows:

- **`gremlin read: point lookup`** — the value inlined per operation, a fresh text every call. The
  realistic serving shape, and all-miss.
- **`gremlin read: fixed count`** — the same text every call, warm hits. Where a parse cache helps,
  and the narrower case.

That asymmetry is about parameters, not about either engine, and putting both regimes in the
standing harness is what makes the cache's applicability visible rather than inferred.

### Item 361, measured end-to-end

A/B against a `.so` built with the cache bypassed at the one FFI call site — two rounds, ops/second:

| row                              |         CONTROL |                 NEW |            |
| -------------------------------- | --------------: | ------------------: | ---------- |
| `gremlin read: fixed count` (-)  | 626.1k / 618.2k | **842.8k / 831.9k** | **~1.37x** |
| `gremlin read: fixed count` (+)  | 606.7k / 623.7k | **833.4k / 877.6k** | **~1.37x** |
| `gremlin read: point lookup` (-) |   27.3k / 30.5k |       29.9k / 29.8k | neutral    |
| `gremlin read: point lookup` (+) | 307.6k / 314.0k |     309.6k / 306.9k | neutral    |

**So item 361 is worth 1.37x on a serving call, not 4.7x**, and nothing at all on the value-varying
shape. Both numbers follow from the parse-level pair it reported (4.71x on a hit, 1.02x on a miss) —
parse is only part of a call, and the translation from "4.7x on the function" to "1.37x on the call"
is the number a user would actually see. **Reporting the function's ratio as the change's value
would have overstated it 3.4x.** The item's own all-miss row predicted the neutral half exactly,
which is the cross-check that both measurements are of the same thing.

### What the new rows show that nothing could show before

Same question, both surface languages, indexed: **GQL 365.0k against Gremlin 317.2k — 0.87x.** Close
enough to be unremarkable, and now visible, which is the point: `CLAUDE.md`'s rule that equivalent
spellings must cost the same has a natural extension to the two LANGUAGES, and there was no
instrument for it.

**Unindexed it is 53.0k against 30.4k — Gremlin 0.57x of GQL, a 1.74x gap on the same question.**
Recorded as an open observation with its numbers, not diagnosed here: the parse difference cannot
explain it (at 30.4k ops/s an operation is 32.9µs, and the whole parse gap is ~575ns, 1.7%), so it
is in the plan or the execution and needs its own decomposition.

### No engine change

Harness coverage and a validation. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: `lint`,
`typecheck`, `fmt:check`. The seventeen existing rows are unchanged and read in their usual bands
(TS's indexed point lookup 1.20M against native's 365.0k remains item 291's recorded 3-5x serving
loss, untouched by this).

## 363. The Gremlin JSON egress scanned TWICE — a speculative probe ran the seed before the gates that reject it. 1.81x, and item 362's diagnosis was wrong

Item 362 measured a 1.74x cross-language gap on the same unindexed point lookup and recorded that
"it is in the plan or the execution and needs its own decomposition." **It was in neither.** This is
that decomposition; every candidate was eliminated by measurement rather than by reading.

### Eliminating four layers

| layer                                                   |           GQL |       Gremlin |               |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------: | ------------: | ------------- |
| `spelling_probe`, same question both languages          |       0.196ms |       0.192ms | **1.02x**     |
| `exec::try_run` on the optimized plans, 20k / 80k nodes | 15.4 / 61.7µs | 15.6 / 61.8µs | **identical** |
| `optimize_indexed` on the raw parse, 20k / 80k          | 0.29 / 0.30µs | 0.50 / 0.49µs | flat in N     |
| parse (GQL cached, Gremlin all-miss)                    |         160ns |        ~735ns | flat in N     |

So the engine accounts for **~0.8µs of CONSTANT difference** and nothing that scales — while a size
sweep of the serving bench showed the difference _growing_: 3.99 → 13.69 → 57.19µs at 5k/20k/80k
users, a steady **~0.7ns per scanned node**.

Two discriminators on the JS side finished the isolation:

- **`GQL inlined / GQL param` = 0.94x / 1.00x** — varying the TEXT costs GQL nothing, so the gap is
  not about parameters.
- **`GRM fixed / GQL param` = 1.31x / 1.79x** — with a FIXED Gremlin text, a pure cache hit with no
  parse at all, Gremlin is _still_ 1.79x. **So the parse, the cache and item 361 are all innocent.**

What remained was the one layer the in-process probe skipped: `exec::try_run` is not what the FFI
calls. GQL goes through `try_run_gql_json`, Gremlin through `try_run_gremlin_json`.

### The measurement that found it, and the control that proved it

| egress, 80k nodes                                   |                    µs |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------: |
| `try_run_gql_json` on the GQL plan                  |                  56.9 |
| `try_run_gremlin_json` on the Gremlin plan          | **115.1** → **2.00x** |
| **CONTROL: `try_run_gql_json` on the GREMLIN plan** |              **57.9** |

Exactly 2.00x at both sizes is the signature of a scan happening twice, and the control settles
whose fault it is: **the Gremlin plan is innocent** — its extra `Filter { PropertyExists }`, which
`values('score')` correctly requires (TinkerPop drops elements lacking the key where GQL yields
NULL), costs ~1.5%. The egress was scanning twice.

Ablating each of `try_run_gremlin_json_inner`'s five speculative probes in turn named it in one run:

```
baseline                            115.1 us
without try_fused_map_json          114.6
without try_fused_fold_json         112.4
without try_fused_maplit_json       113.6
without try_stream_gremlin_json      57.0   <-- the GQL egress's own 56.9
without try_stream_varlen_json      114.4
```

### The cause: a gate ordered after the work it exists to avoid

```rust
let (inner_body, ids) = streaming_chain(input, store)?;
if !single_hop_no_filter(&inner_body) { return None; }
if crate::cost::estimate(input, store).rows < min_rows { return None; }
```

**`streaming_chain` does not inspect a plan, it EXECUTES its seed** — on an `IndexSeek` it calls
`index_seek_ids`, which for an unindexed key scans the label and reads the keyed property of every
node. So every Gremlin read that reached this probe and then declined paid a complete scan for
nothing, and the fallback at the end of `try_run_gremlin_json_inner` scanned again.

The fix is to hoist the row-floor check above it. `cost::estimate` reads only `input` and the
store's O(1) counts, so it is free, and **reordering two independent pure early-returns cannot
change the function's result for any input** — only its time. GQL was never affected:
`try_stream_gremlin_json` has exactly one production caller.

### Measured

|                                                |               before |             after |                    |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------: | ----------------: | ------------------ |
| egress, 20k / 80k nodes                        |       28.5 / 115.1µs | **14.6 / 57.3µs** | 1.95x / 2.01x      |
| end-to-end through the FFI, 20k / 80k          | 1.74x / 1.95x of GQL | **1.01x / 1.00x** |                    |
| `bench:usage` `gremlin read: point lookup` (-) |          30.4k ops/s |         **55.0k** | **1.81x**          |
| `bench:usage` same row, indexed (+)            |               317.2k |            313.9k | flat, as predicted |

The indexed column staying flat is the cross-check: with an index the seed is O(1), so there was no
wasted scan to remove, and item 362's observation that the gap nearly vanished when indexed (0.87x)
was the clue that the cost scaled with the seed.

**It also inverts the comparison**: `gremlin read: point lookup` unindexed is now **55.0k against
GQL's 47.0k**, because a Gremlin cache hit is cheaper than GQL's parameter binding. The
cross-language gap this thread started from is closed and slightly reversed.

No regressions: every `bench:gremlin` row within noise (`V().out().values(age)` 31.50 → 31.48ms,
`V().out().has().count()` 1.53 → 1.55, `groupCount` 2.96 → 2.95) with all answers "same", and the
GQL serving rows unmoved. The near-zero gain on `V().out().values(age)` is itself consistent: there
the wasted seed was a 200k-id `Vec` copy, where the point lookup's was an O(N) property scan — **the
win is sized by how expensive the discarded seed was**, not by the query's total.

### Teeth

The change is a reorder of two pure guards, so there is no new semantic to mutate — but the
reachability of the streaming path is exactly what a reorder could break silently, and that is
already guarded. Forcing the gate to always decline fails **two** existing tests:
`streaming_json_sink_matches_materialized_bytes` (which `expect()`s the `Option`, so an unreachable
sink panics) and `streaming_gate_rejects_deep_and_value_filtered_chains`. Run as a mutant to confirm
those teeth rather than assumed.

### And the probe gap that let this hide

`spelling_probe` had cross-language groups for aggregates and projections but **none for a selective
property equality** — the commonest serving shape, and the only one where a seeding or egress
difference shows. Added, which is also how the plans were obtained: its verdict for the new group is
"plans differ but cost matches (1.02x)", which was the first clue that the plans were fine and
something outside them was not.

### Verification

1,106 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green, `bench:gremlin` and
`bench:usage` checked for regressions. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: clippy,
`cargo fmt --check`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `fmt:check`.

## 364. The same wasted-seed pattern grepped elsewhere — found once more, priced at 1.07x, and DECLINED. The cost is sized by the seed's share of the query

Item 363 fixed a speculative probe that executed its seed before the gates that reject it, worth
2.00x. The method's next step is to grep the pattern, which was done before anything else was
considered.

### Where it is NOT

`try_run_gremlin_json_inner`'s other four probes were already ablated at item 363 and cost 0–2µs of
115µs — they gate on plan SHAPE, which is free. `try_fused_map_json`, `try_fused_fold_json`,
`try_fused_maplit_json` and `try_stream_varlen_json` all begin with `let Plan::… else { return None }`
destructuring. So the pattern is not endemic; it is specific to a probe that needs a _frontier_ to
decide.

### Where it is

`try_stream_varlen_json`, which is called by **both** egress paths (so a win would be shared):

```rust
let vl_batch = pull(vl_in, store, false).ok()?;   // executes the var-length's INPUT
let endpoint_slot = vl_batch.slots.len();
if *slot != endpoint_slot { return None; }        // then declines
let Col::Nodes(src) = vl_batch.slot(*from) else { return None; };
```

Identical in shape to item 363's. Measured rather than assumed, which is the whole point of this
item.

### Priced

The declining shape is a quantified path projecting a variable other than the endpoint —
`MATCH p = (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,2}(b) RETURN a.name AS v` — since the probe only handles the
var-length ENDPOINT. 50,000 nodes at degree 3, GQL egress, probe present against ablated, three
alternated rounds of min-of-5:

|               | round 1 | round 2 | round 3 |       min |
| ------------- | ------: | ------: | ------: | --------: |
| probe PRESENT |   23.62 |   24.03 |   23.93 | **23.62** |
| probe ABLATED |   22.68 |   22.04 |   22.90 | **22.04** |

**1.07x, with disjoint ranges.** Real, reproducible — and **30x smaller than item 363's 2.00x for
the identical bug.**

### The generalization, which is the item

**The cost of a wasted speculative seed is sized by the seed's SHARE of the query.** In item 363 the
discarded seed was an unindexed scan that _was_ the whole query, so re-running it doubled the
work — exactly 2.00x. Here the discarded seed is the input of a var-length expansion that dominates
it, so the same bug is 6.7%. Finding a pattern is not the same as finding its price, and the second
instance of a 2x bug can be a rounding error.

This is also why item 363's near-zero gain on `V().out().values(age)` was consistent: there the
discarded seed was a 200k-id `Vec` copy rather than an O(N) property scan.

### Declined, with the reason and the trigger

The only cheap pre-check available is the existing static `chain_width(vl_in)`. Declining on it
would rest on an **unasserted invariant** — that `chain_width` equals the pulled slot count — and
getting that wrong does not produce a wrong answer, it silently loses the STREAMING path, which the
same run measured at roughly **1.20x on the accepted shape** (single round, so quoted loosely). A
1.07x gain against a 1.20x downside on a mis-set invariant is the wrong trade.

Recorded beside the code with its numbers, per the repo's rule, and with the trigger that would make
it safe: **if `chain_width` ever gains a test pinning it to the pulled width, this becomes a
three-line change.**

### No engine change

A `PRICED AND DECLINED` block beside the `pull`. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0:
clippy, `cargo fmt --check`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `fmt:check`; the Rust suite and all 13
byte-identity fuzzer cases green (nothing executable changed, and that is the claim being checked).

## 365. A fresh survey for a TS target: two candidates retracted by normalizing, and every remaining one is in a parked class — six decompositions now converge there

Items 360–364 were all native (two wins, a validation, a decline). The loop asks for both engines, and
the TS engine's last win was item 349, so this is a deliberate hunt for a TS target that is **not**
the parked dense-adjacency change. The result is that there isn't one, which took two retractions to
establish.

### The table, re-measured

`bun run bench`, ts against ffi. The widest TS ratios:

| row                              |      ts |     ffi |     ts/ffi |
| -------------------------------- | ------: | ------: | ---------: |
| `count 3-hop`                    |   335.0 |     4.9 |     68.88x |
| `count 3-hop + end filter`       |   222.5 |     4.2 |     52.98x |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter`        |    43.6 |     1.9 |     23.44x |
| **`query: count distinct`**      | **6.2** | **0.4** | **14.98x** |
| **`query: distinct + order by`** | **5.8** | **0.4** | **13.88x** |
| `decode pg-text (5 edges/node)`  |  3391.9 |   339.6 |      9.99x |
| `query: top distinct values`     |     3.8 |     0.4 |      9.21x |
| `query: distinct over a hop`     |    59.1 |     7.3 |      8.16x |

### Candidate 1: the DISTINCT family — RETRACTED

It looked like a clean intra-engine anomaly. On **native**, `count distinct` (0.4ms) is _faster_
than `group + aggregate` (1.1ms), as it should be — distinct is the simpler operation. On **TS** it is
_slower_ (6.2 against 5.2). An inversion on the same fixture, same question shape, is exactly the
signature worth chasing.

Normalizing per row kills it:

| TS row                |  ms | ns/row |
| --------------------- | --: | -----: |
| `count distinct`      | 6.2 | **31** |
| `distinct + order by` | 5.8 | **29** |
| `group + aggregate`   | 5.2 | **26** |
| `top distinct values` | 3.8 |     19 |

**DISTINCT is not anomalous against GROUP — they are both at the TS per-row floor**, within 1.2x of
each other, and the "inversion" is that 1.2x. The 14.98x ratio is produced by native doing the same
work at **2ns/row** with a vectorized typed-column scan, not by TS being unusually bad at DISTINCT.
Item 356's lesson in a third place: **the unit decides whether a row is an outlier.**

### Candidate 2: `encode graphson` — RETRACTED, same way

TS encodes GraphSON in 138.1ms against its own NDJSON encode at 42.8 — **3.2x**, where native's
ratio for the same pair is only 1.76x (72.1 against 41.0). A worse relative cost on one engine for
one format reads like a codec gap.

Per byte it inverts: GraphSON's document is **3.5x** the bytes (410 B/element against 117, measured
at item 356), so 3.2x the time for 3.5x the bytes makes TS's GraphSON encode slightly _faster_ per
byte than its NDJSON encode. Nothing to fix. (This row is also one the audit already flags as
high-variance — "its own session readings span 143-190" — so it was a weak candidate twice over.)

### What remains, and the convergence

Every other large TS figure is in a class already parked with measurements:

- the **hop/count family** (23–69x) — locality-bound, item 352 measured 2.9x per-edge degradation
  from size alone; the lever is the key type.
- the **decode rows** (3.1–3.4 SECONDS) — build-bound, item 356 showed the TS decode is
  format-INDEPENDENT (1.23x spread across five codecs against native's 3.55x), so no codec work can
  touch it and `addEdge` is the only lever; items 357/358 then split `addEdge`'s label index and
  found the residue is string-keyed hash work, with the inner-container allocation refuted at the
  noise floor.
- the **element-render rows** (685–1230ms) — parked twice at item 348, and item 289 established the
  JSON carrier dominates them.

**Six independent decompositions now terminate at the same dense integer-indexed adjacency** (310,
350, 352, 357, 358, and this survey). At some point that convergence is the finding: the TS engine's
remaining per-row cost is its string-keyed, pointer-chasing data layout, and every component-sized
fix in reach has been taken or refuted.

### The one unexplored non-CSR idea, named and not built

`count(DISTINCT k)` over an **indexed** `k` is answerable in O(1) from the index's key count rather
than by scanning every row — native's hash index is a `HashMap<Vec<u8>, Vec<u32>>` whose `len()` _is_
the distinct-value count, and the TS engine has the same shape. Neither engine does it, and the
200,000-row scan it would replace is the whole of these rows.

**Not built, because it is not sound as written**: index buckets retain deleted ids (the
`index_bucket_len` doc says so — "it may count a few tombstoned ids, which is fine for an estimate"),
so a value whose every holder has been deleted would still be counted and the answer would be
**wrong, not slow**. Making it exact needs bucket pruning on delete or a verification pass, and that
is a storage change with its own price. Recorded with the blocker rather than as a free win.

### No code change

A survey and two retractions. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: `lint`, `typecheck`,
`fmt:check`.

## 366. The dense adjacency is refuted ON DESIGN — and six converging decompositions were not evidence it was right

Item 365 reported that six independent decompositions (300, 310, 350, 352, 357, 358) terminate at
the same change — a dense integer-indexed adjacency for the TS graph — and treated that convergence
as the strongest case yet for building it. Put to the user as a decision, it came back refuted, with
a reason none of the six had considered:

> _"this would really hurt our ability to get something by an id. That's what the string keyed maps
> buy us"_

### Why that closes it

**The string-keyed adjacency buys O(1) access by EXTERNAL ID, and a dense layout does not remove the
hash — it relocates it.** Edges store external ids, by items 140/218's deliberate choice, so a dense
adjacency needs an ext→dense translation on every hop: exactly the string-keyed lookup the change
exists to eliminate, one level down. Paying off would require dense ids _throughout_, and then every
id-based entry point pays the translation at the boundary — for an API that is id-centric and whose
snapshots carry external ids (`encode` emits edge ids, so every reloaded snapshot has them).

### The methodological error, which is the part worth keeping

Each of the six items did its job: it eliminated the component-sized fixes in its row and named what
was left. The error was in the next step — **inferring that what was left must therefore be worth
doing.**

**A residue is a description of the cost, not a proposal.** Six routes arriving at the same residue
says the diagnosis is consistent; it says nothing about whether the implied change is sound. And the
convergence actively misled: each new arrival read as corroboration, when all six were measuring the
same thing (a traversal) and none was looking at the side that kills it (lookup by id). **Agreement
among measurements of the same shape is not independent evidence.**

Item 352 came closest to catching it — it rehabilitated the CSR's _mechanism_ ("locality is the one
thing a component-sized fix cannot touch") while noting "2.9x of locality degradation is not a
promise that a CSR recovers 2.9x". The missing question was not how much it recovers but what it
costs elsewhere, and a traversal benchmark cannot ask that.

### Consequence

The TS engine's per-row floor (26–31 ns/row, item 365) is **accepted, not pending**. Items 300 and
348's framing — "parked, blocked on a dense adjacency the TS graph does not expose" — should be read
as closed. Future TS work has to beat that floor another way or be about something else.

No code change.

## 367. Index buckets drop their emptied KEY, so the distinct-value count is exact — and the delete cost it was feared to carry is zero

Item 365 named an O(1) answer for `count(DISTINCT k)` over an indexed `k` — the hash index's key
count — and declined it as **unsound**: buckets were believed to retain deleted ids, so a value
whose holders were all gone would still be counted and the answer would be _wrong, not slow_. The
decision came back: prune buckets on delete.

### Diagnosing it first changed the size of the job

**The ids were already pruned.** `index_drop_node` has always done `bucket.retain(|&x| x != id)`, so
no bucket holds a deleted node. What survived was the **empty entry**: the key stayed in the map
with a zero-length `Vec`, so `map.len()` counted values no live node carries. The fix is three
lines, not a storage redesign — and `index_bucket_len`'s "may count a few tombstoned ids, which is
fine for an estimate" overstates what is actually stale.

So the change is: drop the map entry when its bucket empties, plus the accessor that makes the
count usable and a test that can see the difference at all.

### `index_distinct_count(key)`

`count(DISTINCT key)` in O(1) against a scan of every row, exact over live nodes carrying the
property. Deliberately recorded in its doc comment: a node WITHOUT the property is in no bucket (so
it does not count, matching `count` ignoring absent values), and a stored NULL has its own group key
and so counts as a distinct value — **which is the one thing a caller must handle, because SQL/ISO
`count(DISTINCT x)` excludes nulls.** That is a precondition for the shortcut, not for the
accessor.

### Teeth

Two tests, and every assertion in them is on a value whose holders are **all** deleted — the only
case where the pruning is observable. The twin is tested too, because a dotted index keys on a
descended value and every node/edge-shaped asymmetry in this repo was found by testing the twin
(items 333, 335, 349).

Verified by mutation rather than assumed: removing the `if bucket.is_empty() { … remove }` makes
both fail with exactly the predicted values — `left: Some(3), right: Some(2)` and
`left: Some(2), right: Some(1)`. The tests also pin that pruning did not break the LOOKUP: a seek
for a pruned value must answer `Some(empty)` and never `None`, since `None` means "no index" and
would silently route a query to a scan.

### The cost, which is the thing that was actually in question

Making every DELETE pay to make a cardinality query cheap is the wrong trade if the delete cost is
real, so it was measured before the change was kept. `bench:usage`'s `write: append then delete
node`, two `.so` builds differing only in the pruning, three alternated rounds, ops/second:

|                                             | round 1 | round 2 | round 3 |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------: | ------: | ------: |
| CONTROL, indexed (+)                        |  195.5k |  194.0k |  194.6k |
| NEW, indexed (+)                            |  192.5k |  197.6k |  192.0k |
| CONTROL, unindexed (-) — pruning CANNOT run |  204.2k |  199.8k |  205.4k |
| NEW, unindexed (-) — the null control       |  200.4k |  206.2k |  205.1k |

**Overlapping in both columns: no measurable cost.** The unindexed column is a real null control
here — with no index the pruning branch is unreachable — and it is flat, so the indexed column's
overlap is a measurement and not drift. The mechanism predicted this: one `is_empty()` per (index,
deleted node) pair and an occasional `remove`.

### What this does NOT yet deliver, and its preconditions

**No perf win yet.** This is the prerequisite: the accessor is now exact and free. The shortcut that
would use it — answering `count(DISTINCT n.k)` from the index instead of scanning — is a separate
item deliberately, because a fast path that is wrong is worse than one that is slow, and this one
has three preconditions that a planner has to check:

1. **NULLs.** `count(DISTINCT x)` excludes them; the index counts a stored NULL as a distinct value.
2. **The label.** `MATCH (n:Person) …` counts over `Person`, while the index is ANY-LABEL (its own
   doc says so). The shortcut is only valid with no label constraint, or a vacuous one.
3. **No other predicate**, for the obvious reason.

Written down here so the next item checks them rather than discovers them.

### Verification

1,108 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (two new), `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` `rewrite_fuzz`, and all
13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: clippy,
`cargo fmt --check`.

## 368. A NULL was indexed by ONE of the two builders, and item 367's pruning covered ONE of the two write paths — both found by a test written to confirm a claim

Item 367 shipped `index_distinct_count` and asserted in its doc comment that a stored NULL "counts
as a distinct value", recording that as a precondition a caller would have to subtract. Starting the
shortcut that would consume it, that claim got checked against `apply_set_prop`, which states the
opposite in its own comment:

> _"A NULL is never seek-indexed (`WHERE k = null` matches nothing), so it is excluded from both
> indexes"_

So the comment was corrected — and the test written to pin the correction **failed**, which is how
two separate bugs surfaced. **Item 367's claim was wrong about the policy and accidentally right
about the behaviour.**

### Bug 1: only one of the two index builders knew the policy

`create_index` indexed every present value including NULL. `create_range_index`, the twin builder
twenty lines below it, already does `if !v.is_null()`. So **skipping nulls is the established
policy and the hash builder was the one place that missed it** — the same twin asymmetry as items
333, 335, 349 and 360.

The consequence was that **an index's contents depended on write order relative to its creation**: a
null present at build time got a bucket, a null written afterwards did not. No seek could observe it
— `index_seek_ids` returns empty for a null value before consulting the index at all — but any
reader of the buckets themselves could, and item 367's distinct count is the first such reader. It
over-reported by one per null-holding value.

### Bug 2: item 367 pruned one of the two write paths

With the builder fixed, the test still failed on its last assertion: setting the last non-null value
to NULL left the count at 1. **Item 367 added the emptied-key pruning to `index_drop_node` (delete)
and missed `reindex_node` (set)** — a node whose indexed value CHANGES leaves its old value behind
with an empty bucket exactly as a deleted one did.

That is the same twin asymmetry again, one item old and mine. The pattern is not "node versus edge"
— it is **"this repo has two of most things, and a fix lands on the one you were looking at."**

### Teeth: the three fixes are guarded independently

Each mutant under `timeout 600` + a 16G cgroup cap, pristine restored before each:

| mutant                                               | result       | caught by                                |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| the BUILD path indexes nulls again                   | **CAUGHT**   | `a_null_is_not_a_distinct_indexed_value` |
| the SET path keeps its emptied key                   | **CAUGHT**   | `..._after_updates`, `a_null_...`        |
| the DELETE path keeps its emptied key (367's fix)    | **CAUGHT**   | `..._after_deletes` + the dotted twin    |
| CONTROL — `continue` replaced by an equivalent guard | **SURVIVED** | —                                        |

The separation is the point: no test covers two of the three, so each path is pinned by its own
assertions rather than by luck. The new `..._after_updates` test exists because the null test only
exercises set-to-NULL, which takes `reindex_node`'s `new: None` arm — a value-to-value update takes
the other arm, and that is the common case.

### Cost

Item 367 measured the DELETE path at no measurable cost; this adds work to every indexed UPDATE, so
that was measured the same way. `bench:usage` `write: property update`, two `.so` builds differing
only in the set-path pruning, three alternated rounds, ops/second:

|                                              | round 1 | round 2 | round 3 |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------: | ------: | ------: |
| CONTROL, indexed (+)                         |  300.9k |  300.2k |  304.4k |
| NEW, indexed (+)                             |  299.8k |  301.2k |  299.6k |
| CONTROL, unindexed (-) — pruning unreachable |   49.0k |   49.6k |   49.0k |
| NEW, unindexed (-) — the null control        |   47.7k |   50.3k |   50.1k |

Overlapping in both columns, with the unindexed column flat as a genuine null control. **No
measurable cost**, same as the delete path.

### Verification

1,110 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (two new, one corrected claim), all 13 byte-identity fuzzer
cases green. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: clippy, `cargo fmt --check`, `lint`,
`typecheck`, `fmt:check`.

## 369. `count(DISTINCT k)` from the index's key count — 1602x to 17434x, and two of its four gates are unreachable by construction

Items 367 and 368 made the hash index's key count exact and free. This is the shortcut that spends
it: `try_indexed_distinct_count` answers `count(DISTINCT n.k)` from `index_distinct_count` in O(1),
where `try_scan_distinct_count` below it does a vectorized typed-column scan of every live node.

### Verifying the preconditions rather than reasoning about them

Item 367 recorded three. Each was checked against the code or the engine's own answer:

1. **NULLs — dissolved.** `count(DISTINCT x)` excludes nulls and so does the index (since 368). Not
   argued: run over a fixture with a present null, an absent property and two real values, the
   existing answer and `index_distinct_count` are **both 2**. The paths agree, which is the only
   form of "sound" that matters for a fast path.
2. **The label — real, and testable in O(1).** A hash index is ANY-LABEL, so a labelled scan is
   answerable only when the label is **vacuous**. `nodes_with_label(l).len() == live_node_count()`
   is exact (label buckets are pruned on delete — `delete_node` "remove it from every label
   bucket") and O(1) (`live_node_count` is `node_count - deleted_count`, a maintained counter; the
   O(N) recount is `#[cfg(test)]`). A non-vacuous label declines to the scan.
3. **No other predicate** — the `Plan::Scan` pattern handles it.

### Measured

`bench_all`'s `query/seeded` section gains a cardinality block, beside the seek row because it is
the same shape of claim — same query, same answer, the only difference being whether the key is
indexed:

|                                          | scan µs | index µs |    speedup |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------: | -------: | ---------: |
| `count(DISTINCT p.name)` (200k distinct) |  4184.1 |  **0.2** | **17434x** |
| `count(DISTINCT p.age)` (90 distinct)    |   400.5 |  **0.2** |  **1602x** |
| **CONTROL `count(*)`**                   |     0.3 |      0.3 |   **1.0x** |

The high-cardinality key wins most because the scan's hash set grows to 200,000 entries where the
index already holds the answer. `count(*)` is already O(1) from the label bucket, so no index can
improve it — if that row ever shows a speedup, the section is measuring the fixture rather than the
shortcut.

### Teeth, and two gates that cannot be tested through a query

The correctness test is a **differential against the path it replaces**: the same store and query,
run with and without the index, must agree — across a present null, an absent property, a key
nothing has, a non-vacuous label, a non-distinct count and a grouped count.

| mutant                                                        | result                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| fire for ANY label, not just a vacuous one                    | **CAUGHT**                         |
| ignore `distinct` (answer `count(k)` with the distinct count) | **CAUGHT**                         |
| ignore GROUP BY keys                                          | **SURVIVED — provably equivalent** |
| CONTROL, `!=` rewritten as a negated `==`                     | **SURVIVED**, as it must           |

**The `distinct` and `keys` gates cannot be reached in a state where they matter, and that is worth
recording rather than papering over:**

- A non-distinct `count(plain_prop)` is claimed by `try_scan_count_prop` **earlier in the chain**,
  and a dotted argument lowers to `Expr::Field`, not `Expr::Prop`, so it never matches this
  pattern at all. The mutant was initially _not_ caught for exactly that reason.
- A GROUPED query's `Aggregate` input is `Project { input: Scan }`, never a bare `Scan`, because
