  **GROUP BY in this engine takes a bound name** so the `LET` always interposes a projection. The
  `Plan::Scan` pattern declines every grouped plan regardless of the `keys` gate — the same
  provable-equivalence category as item 288's T10.

Both gates stay, because **relying on the ORDER of a 32-entry fast-path chain for correctness is
what breaks when someone reorders it**, and because keeping the gates identical to
`try_scan_distinct_count`'s is what makes "the two never disagree about a shape" checkable by
reading. They are pinned by direct assertions on the function instead, the way
`try_scan_count_prop` tests its own dotted decline.

### Verification

1,111 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (one new), `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` `rewrite_fuzz`, all 13
byte-identity fuzzer cases green, `bench_all` checked (seeded 755.6x, `SET` 37.69ms, `value/maps`
in band). Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: clippy, `cargo fmt --check`, `lint`,
`typecheck`, `fmt:check`.

## 370. The RANGE index is the third twin with the same emptied-key bug — and here a stale key is a WRONG MINIMUM, not an inflated count

Items 367 and 368 fixed the hash index's emptied-key retention in the delete path and then the set
path. Grepping the pattern for the next index-answerable aggregate found it a third time, in
`range_remove`:

```rust
if let Some(bucket) = ix.map.get_mut(&OrdVal(value.clone())) {
    bucket.retain(|&x| x != node);          // the id goes
}                                           // ...the KEY stays
```

**One difference in this fix's favour**: both write paths route through `range_remove` (delete via
`index_drop_node`, set via `apply_set_prop`), so a single guard covers both — unlike the hash index,
where 367 and 368 had to fix two separate pieces of code.

**One difference against it.** A stale hash key only inflated a distinct COUNT. A stale range key is
an **ordered position**, so the `BTreeMap`'s first and last keys stop being the live minimum and
maximum. `range_lookup` is safe either way (an empty bucket contributes no ids, and deleted ids are
filtered), but any reader of the KEYS is not — and `min`/`max` answered from this index, which is
the next item, is exactly that reader.

Shipped with the accessor that makes it usable and observable: `range_min_max(key)`, the live
extremes in O(log n) against the O(live nodes) column scan `try_scan_num_agg` does.

### Teeth

`a_range_min_max_is_exact_after_deletes_and_updates` removes the current extreme at each step,
which is the only observable case: delete the minimum's holder, delete the maximum's, delete one of
two holders of a surviving value (nothing must move), then UPDATE the last holder away — the set
path, through the same `range_remove`, asserted rather than assumed to share the fix. Plus a SET to
NULL, since a null never enters a range index.

Mutation-verified: removing the guard fails it with the wrong-answer signature —
`left: "Some((Num(10.0), Num(99.0)))"` against `right: "Some((Num(50.0), Num(99.0)))"`. The
minimum stays at a **deleted node's value**.

### Cost — and the coverage gap that hid it

**No write-throughput benchmark creates a range index.** `bench:usage` indexes with
`kind: 'hash'`; range indexes appear only in `spelling_probe` and `simd_index_probe`. So anything
added to the range write path is invisible to the standard harnesses — the item-356 pattern a third
time, and the reason this was measured with a dedicated probe instead of inherited from 367/368's
hash result.

Worst case is a HIGH-cardinality key, where nearly every write empties its bucket and the prune
actually fires. 200,000 nodes, all values distinct, `set_prop` over a quarter of them, three
alternated rounds:

|         | round 1 | round 2 | round 3 |           min |
| ------- | ------: | ------: | ------: | ------------: |
| CONTROL |     242 |     243 |     241 | **241** ns/op |
| NEW     |     238 |     235 |     235 | **235** ns/op |

**Disjoint, and the pruning is marginally FASTER** — dropping the entry keeps the `BTreeMap` smaller,
so later `get_mut`s are cheaper. In a workload that empties buckets it pays for itself.

### ⚠️ An incidental finding worth its own item: a DELETE is ~33µs at 200,000 nodes

The same probe's delete column reads **33.2–33.8µs per `delete_node`** on a 200,000-node label with
no edges at all — three orders of magnitude above the set column's 235ns, and far too large to be
the range guard (which is why the set column had to carry the measurement).

It is **O(label size)**: `delete_node` removes the node from every label bucket, and a bucket is a
sorted `Vec`, so the removal is a memmove over the whole label. `bench:usage` cannot see it — its
fixture is 20,000 nodes, where the same cost is ~5µs and reads as ordinary per-op overhead. Not
diagnosed or fixed here; recorded with its numbers because a delete that scales with the label is a
real limit for any workload that churns.

### Verification

1,112 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (one new), all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases green. Gates each as
their own command, each exit 0: clippy, `cargo fmt --check`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `fmt:check`.

## 371. `min`/`max` from the range index — 2455x and 2567x, after the path sat DEAD because three other fast paths claim a bare `Scan`

Item 370 made the range index's extremes exact. This spends them: `try_indexed_min_max` answers
`min(k)` / `max(k)` from the `BTreeMap`'s first and last key in O(log n), where a column scan is
O(live nodes).

### The real work was proving the orders agree

`OrdVal`, the range index's key, compares by `value::cmp_total`. So does `min`/`max` (the repo's NaN
policy: predicates keep NaN unordered, but sort/min/max use a total order so the two engines stay
byte-identical). Reading two comparators is not evidence that they agree, so the differential test
carries the awkward shapes rather than the argument:

- a **mixed-type column** (strings AND numbers), which `Column::Num`'s fast path cannot serve, so
  only the general aggregate can — the shape where an order disagreement would show;
- a **NaN**, which the NDJSON fixture cannot express (ingest coerces it to null) and so is computed
  with `SET n.n = sin(1e400)`, the way the differential fuzzer has to;
- a present null, a key nothing carries, a non-vacuous label, and `min(DISTINCT …)`.

Each run with and without the range index, asserting the two answers match.

### Measured

|                          | scan µs | index µs |   speedup |
| ------------------------ | ------: | -------: | --------: |
| `min(p.age)`             |   711.9 |  **0.3** | **2455x** |
| `max(p.age)`             |   718.6 |  **0.3** | **2567x** |
| **CONTROL `avg(p.age)`** |   111.2 |    111.3 |  **1.0x** |
| **CONTROL `count(*)`**   |     0.3 |      0.3 |  **1.0x** |

`avg` is the right control for the range half: it needs every value, so no ordered index can serve
it. Three rounds, min 2455/2639/2638x and max 2567/2557/2651x.

### The thing worth keeping: the path shipped DEAD, twice

The first bench run read **1.0x** for both rows while every test passed. The shortcut was correct,
willing, and never called.

**THREE other fast paths can claim `min`/`max` over a bare `Scan`**, and the chain has 32 entries:

- `try_scan_multi_agg` — handles `Min | Max` with a `Prop` arg over a `Scan`.
- **`try_frontier_prop_agg`** — the one that actually caught it, and the non-obvious one: it gates on
  `chain_width(input)?`, and `chain_width` returns `Some(1)` for a bare `Scan` ("a seek, like a
  scan, seeds a single-slot frontier"). **A plain scan is a trivial frontier**, so a path named for
  frontiers claims a scan.
- the general aggregate, at the end.

Moving above `try_scan_multi_agg` was not enough — the second bench run still read 1.0x, because
`try_frontier_prop_agg` sits earlier still.

**And no test could have caught it.** The differential test compares answers with and without the
index, which passes trivially when both sides take the scan. The eligibility assertions call
`try_indexed_min_max` directly, which proves the function is _willing_, not that the dispatch
_reaches_ it. The instrument that found it was an `eprintln!` at function entry — item 267's "one
`eprintln` settled it", in a new place.

So the method's "verify the planner reaches the shape" needs a second half: **verify the DISPATCH
reaches the function.** A plan-shape check is necessary and not sufficient when 32 ordered
candidates can claim the same plan.

### Teeth

Mutants under `timeout 600` + a 16G cgroup cap: fire for any label → **CAUGHT**; swap the extremes
so `min` returns the maximum → **CAUGHT**; accept `distinct` → **CAUGHT**, and worth a note — it is
caught by the _eligibility_ assertion, not by a wrong answer, because `min(DISTINCT k) == min(k)`
and the answer is genuinely unaffected. The gate encodes a consistency decision (every sibling
declines `distinct`), and the test pins the decision rather than a correctness property. The
behaviour-preserving control survived.

Two of the four mutants initially failed to apply because the gate line is shared verbatim with
`try_frontier_prop_agg` — which is how that path was found in the first place.

### Verification

1,113 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (one new), `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` `rewrite_fuzz`, all 13
byte-identity fuzzer cases green, `bench_all` checked (`value/maps` and `algo/run` in band). Gates
each as their own command, each exit 0: clippy, `cargo fmt --check`, `lint`, `typecheck`,
`fmt:check`.

## 373. `SHORTEST k` over an unbounded quantifier had no trail bound — a 20-node graph took the machine down, and TS had been faulting correctly all along

Item 372 was going to be a dispatch-coverage audit: instrument all 26 chain entries, run the GQL
corpus scraped from the test sources, and count which fast paths are never reached (the question
item 371 raised — a path can sit dead for three releases because an earlier candidate claims its
plan). The corpus run **OOM'd the machine**, and the session with it.

The rerun had three bounds — a 120-node fixture, tight `set_limit` on `LimitsTrail` /
`LimitsIntermediate` / `LimitsIntermediateCells` / `LimitsRange`, and the cgroup cap. **It still
died, exit 137.** The cap worked; the limits did not. Progress tracing named one query out of 1,126:

```
MATCH p = SHORTEST 2 (x:N)-[:R]->*(y:N) RETURN cardinality(p) AS n
```

### It is not a scale problem

Isolated, it exhausts a **4 GB cap at n=20 — 20 nodes, 60 edges.** One feature at a time:

| query                    | result                           |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
| `SHORTEST 2 … ->*`       | **OOM**                          |
| `SHORTEST 2 … ->+`       | **OOM**                          |
| `SHORTEST 2 … ->{1,3}`   | OK, 556 rows                     |
| `SHORTEST 1 … ->*`       | OK, 381 rows                     |
| `ANY SHORTEST … ->*`     | OK, 381 rows                     |
| plain `->*`, no selector | correctly `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` |

The last row is the diagnosis. The **unbounded quantifier is already guarded** — the BFS path that
serves `Any` / `All` honours `limits.trail` and faults. `SHORTEST k` with `k >= 2` routes instead to
`shortest_k_path` → `collect_trails`, and goes around that guard entirely. `SHORTEST 1` and
`ANY SHORTEST` survive because they take the BFS path, not because they are smaller.

`collect_trails` recursively enumerates every edge-disjoint trail, `clone`ing the node and edge
stacks into `per_end` for each one. Its only bounds are `len == max` and no-edge-reuse — **both of
which bound DEPTH, and neither of which bounds the NUMBER of trails**, which is superexponential in
degree. With `*` or `+`, `max` is effectively the edge count, so there is no bound left at all.

### The guard, and why it is the same guard

`budget: &mut u64` threaded through the recursion, decremented per **recorded** trail (not per
visit), seeded by the caller from `store.limits().trail`, with the caller raising
`E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` when it returns at zero. Not a new knob — **the ceiling the BFS selectors
were already honouring**, now applied to the one traversal shape that had escaped it. An early
unwind drops the rest of the DFS once the budget is gone, since the caller is going to fault anyway.

### TS was right and native was out of step

The cross-engine check turned this from a crash into a **twin asymmetry**, which is the shape this
repo keeps producing (367, 368, 370 — "this repo has two of most things, and a fix lands on the one
you were looking at"). The pure-TS engine **already faults here**, `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`,
"Variable-length pattern exceeded the trail budget". Same code, so the fuzzers compare equal; native
was the only engine that could be killed by a 60-edge graph.

Worth stating plainly because it inverts the usual asymmetry cost: the divergence here was not a
wrong answer, it was **one engine terminating and the other not**. No differential fuzzer can find
that, because the run that would report it never finishes.

### Teeth

Mutants under `timeout 600` + a 16 GB cgroup cap, pristine restored before each:

- **M1, drop the decrement** (restore the bug) → **CAUGHT, rc=143**: the suite hung for the full ten
  minutes and `timeout` killed it. The honest demonstration — the mutant is caught by _not
  terminating_, which is exactly the failure mode, and the cap is what made running it safe.
- **M2, truncate silently** at budget instead of faulting → **CAUGHT** by the new test's
  `expect_err`. This is the wrong-answer variant: a quietly short result set.
- **M3, control** — remove only the early unwind, keeping the bound → **SURVIVED**, as intended. It
  is an optimization, not a bound, and nothing should pin it.

Regression test `a_shortest_k_over_an_unbounded_quantifier_faults_instead_of_exhausting_memory`: 20
nodes, `LimitsTrail = 5_000`, asserts the two runaway spellings fault **and** that the three
legitimate ones still return 381 / 556 / 381.

### No regression on the touched path

`bench_all -- query/shortest`, min of three alternated rounds each side, 599,998 rows (comfortably
inside the 1,000,000 default `trail`, so nothing legitimate newly faults):

| row                  | HEAD       | with the guard |              |
| -------------------- | ---------- | -------------- | ------------ |
| `shortest-k control` | 75102.4 µs | 73415.8 µs     | 1.02x faster |
| `shortest-k + path`  | 79833.6 µs | 81464.6 µs     | 1.02x slower |

Opposite directions at 2% is the noise floor reporting itself, which is the expected reading for one
`u64` decrement next to a `Vec` clone — but the decrement sits in the hot recursion, so it was
measured rather than argued.

### Verification

1,113 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (one new), `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` `rewrite_fuzz`, all 13
byte-identity fuzzer cases green via `bun run fuzz`. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0:
clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt`, `bun run check`.

**Item 372 remains open and is now runnable** — the corpus that killed it twice no longer has a
query that can.

## 374. The dispatch-coverage audit item 372 kept dying on — and the endpoint LABEL that cost a var-length aggregate 2.19x, or the whole query

Item 371 ended on "verify the DISPATCH reaches the function", which raises the obvious next
question: how many of the aggregate chain's entries are reachable at all? Item 372 tried to answer
it twice and **took the machine down both times**, because it ran a scraped corpus with no cap. It
also did not need to: `crates/lenke-engine/tests/gql_corpus` is **~1,200 curated cases with a
snapshot oracle**, a better instrument than the scrape, and under the cgroup cap it ran in **7.15
seconds**.

### What the chain actually does

All 28 entries instrumented with call/hit counters. **Every entry is CALLED** — so item 371's
shadowing is not chain-wide — but **10 of 28 never hit once**. A second probe handed each of those a
query written to its own documented gate, which is what separates "the corpus lacks the shape" from
"nothing can reach this":

| verdict                            | entries                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Alive, uncovered by the corpus** | `try_indexed_min_max`, `try_indexed_distinct_count`, `try_3hop_product_count`, `try_join_product_count` |
| **Benign shadowing**               | a 1-hop group count goes to `try_varlen_count` — item 47's documented flattening                        |
| **Declined for its own shape**     | the three var-length entries below                                                                      |

A finding in its own right: **the corpus builds no indexes at all**, so the two index fast paths
shipped in items 369 and 371 have zero corpus coverage. Their guard is their unit tests alone.

### The endpoint label

`try_varlen_agg` folds `sum`/`avg`/`min`/`max` during the var-length DFS. It is REACHED for
`-[:KNOWS]->{1,2}(b)` and DECLINED for `-[:KNOWS]->{1,2}(b:Person)`. Printing both optimized plans
(rather than guessing) shows the label adds exactly one wrapper:

```
Filter { input: VarLength{…}, pred: IsLabeled { slot: 1, labels: ["Person"] } }
```

and slot 1 is the endpoint slot the fast path **already requires** for its aggregate argument.

**The peel already existed.** `peel_endpoint_filter` is in the same file, and `try_varlen_count`
already calls it, under a comment reading "an endpoint filter sits ABOVE the hop, and declining on
it sent the count to the materializing path." It was applied to the count twin and to neither of
the others — 367, 368 and 370 again, where this repo has several of most things and a fix lands on
the one you were looking at.

### Two refuted implementations, and the fixture that was measuring the wrong thing

Peeling the filter is the easy half. What it costs to APPLY the predicate per reached endpoint is
what decides whether peeling wins, and the first two shapes were both **refused by measurement**:

| attempt                        | labelled sum @50k | vs not peeling at all |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------- | --------------------- |
| (no peel — HEAD)               | 22006 us          | —                     |
| `until_ok` per endpoint        | 40351 us          | **1.83x WORSE**       |
| same, label bucket hoisted out | 26940 us          | **1.22x WORSE**       |
| tautology + membership bitset  | **10416 us**      | 2.11x better          |

`until_ok`'s `IsLabeled` arm calls `store.is_labeled`, which is a label-string **hash** plus a
**binary search over that label's whole bucket** — per reached endpoint, and a `{1,2}` walk reaches
millions. The fold got cheaper and the filter got charged per row.

**The third shape came from reading what the general path already does**, and so did the discovery
that the benchmark was dishonest. `evaluator.rs` has both arms already: a label every LIVE node
carries is a **tautology** that tests nothing (E78), and otherwise a **membership bitset** built
once. The fixture was `social_store`, where every node is a `Person` — so the label is **vacuous**,
the general path short-circuits it to free, and I had been comparing a fold carrying a real test
against a filter that costs nothing. That is CLAUDE.md's every-node-has-the-same-label trap
arriving as a misleading PERFORMANCE number instead of a hidden wrong answer.

Two fixtures, because they answer different questions: UNIFORM (vacuous label — exercises the
tautology arm) and MIXED (half `Person`, half `Robot` — the label is selective and both sides must
genuinely test it).

### The numbers

Min of three alternated rounds. The CONTROL is a scan aggregate neither spelling routes through,
flat at ~28 us / ~109 us across every run.

| fixture              | HEAD                       | with the peel |               |
| -------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------- | ------------- |
| 50k uniform, `sum`   | 22778.8 us                 | 10115.9 us    | **2.25x**     |
| 50k uniform, `max`   | 21543.5 us                 | 11465.6 us    | **1.88x**     |
| 50k mixed, `sum`     | 21507.0 us                 | 14470.0 us    | **1.49x**     |
| 50k mixed, `max`     | 21232.2 us                 | 15191.6 us    | **1.40x**     |
| 200k x deg-5, either | **`E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`** | 61.6–90.3 ms  | **completes** |

The last row is the one that matters most. The labelled spelling did not merely cost more at 200k —
it **hit the trail ROW CAP that a fold never reaches** and raised where its twin returned an answer.
Two spellings of one query, the same answer available from both, and only one of them could finish.

On the uniform fixture `labelled / bare` is now **1.00x**: the tautology arm drops the test
entirely, so the labelled spelling becomes the bare one rather than merely approaching it.

**A regression the A/B caught before it shipped.** The BARE rows also drifted up ~1.11x, because the
first draft wrapped `emit` unconditionally and taxed the path with no endpoint filter to pay for it
— [[pull-alignment-is-load-bearing]]'s shape, except avoidable rather than a toll. The unguarded
walk now keeps exactly the sink it always had, and bare is back at parity (−2% to +5%, both
directions).

### Teeth

The fixture is the test. On a graph where every node carries the label, **every assertion passes
with the guard deleted** — so the test uses MIXED labels and hand-computed expectations, and pins
three spellings that disagree by construction (920 / 20 / 900).

It failed on its first run, and the engine was right: `min` over the Robot endpoints is 100, not 200. My arithmetic.

Mutants, pristine restored BEFORE each, under `timeout 600` + a 16G cap: guard is a no-op →
**CAUGHT**; tautology arm always taken, so a selective label tests nothing → **CAUGHT**; membership
test inverted → **CAUGHT**; the behaviour-preserving control (drop the unguarded fast lane — slower,
identical answers) → **SURVIVED**.

Re-proving the harness caught a setup error worth recording: the allocator bomb returned **143** at
the 60s timeout, which reads as the cap failing. Run directly instead of through an `sh` wrapper it
returns **137 in 0.16 s** — the wrapper was swallowing the kill. The spin loop returns 124. _Prove
the harness kills with the exact invocation you will use, not a near one._

### Still open

`try_varlen_distinct_count` and `try_varlen_distinctby_count` are the same family and still decline
their own shapes even unlabelled — not the endpoint-filter cause, so a separate question. And
`try_frontier_prop_agg` takes `max` but declines `sum`.

### Verification

1,115 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (one new), all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases via `bun run fuzz`,
`spelling_probe` reporting **"identical optimized plan → identical exec"** for the new group and no
perf cliffs overall. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: clippy `-D warnings`,
`cargo fmt`, `bun run check`.

Clippy earned its separate run here: it failed on the _temporary_ probes pulling the shared bench
harness in and tripping `dead_code`. The probes are deleted; the durable artifact is a
`spelling_probe` group for `(b:Person)` vs `WHERE 'Person' IN labels(b)` — equivalent on ANY graph,
unlike `(b)` vs `(b:Person)`, which coincide only when the label is vacuous.

## 375. A bare `Scan` is a trivial frontier, so the frontier path was answering scan `min`/`max` at 6.4x the columnar fold — and the test found a signed-zero divergence that turns out to be unobservable

Item 374's dispatch audit left three entries "declining their own shape". **Two of the three
retract**, and they are worth recording as retractions rather than quietly dropping:
`try_varlen_distinct_count` and `try_varlen_distinctby_count` decline a `{1,2}` trail because
`set_reachability_is_exact` permits a `Trail` only at `max <= 1` — BFS computes WALK reachability,
and a node reachable only by re-crossing an edge belongs to the walk set and not the trail set.
That is item 68, found by `fastpath_fuzz` at seed 3249. "Fixing" them would have re-introduced a
fuzzer-caught wrong answer; the probe was asking for the region the engine deliberately refuses.

### The third was real, and the control was worse than the target

`try_frontier_prop_agg` gates on `Min | Max`, so a frontier `sum` has no fast path — 2.02x at 50k,
2.51x at 200k. But the CONTROL row in that same measurement was 6.4x apart:

|            | 50k          | 200k         |
| ---------- | ------------ | ------------ |
| scan `sum` | 28.1 us      | 110.7 us     |
| scan `max` | **180.5 us** | **716.8 us** |

`try_scan_num_agg` gates on `Sum | Avg`. There was no single-aggregate columnar path for min/max at
all, so an unindexed scan `max` fell through to the frontier path — item 371's observation exactly:
`chain_width` returns `Some(1)` for a bare `Scan`, so **a path named for frontiers claims a scan.**
(Item 371's `try_indexed_min_max` covers this only when a range index exists; `social_store` has
none.) One theme behind both gaps: **the aggregate set is split across fast paths and each covers
only half of it** — `Sum|Avg` here, `Min|Max` there — so for any one shape, one half is fast and the
other falls through.

### The obvious fix was a net loss, and the dispatch probe is what showed it

Adding a `Sum` arm to `try_frontier_prop_agg` would also divert scan `sum` INTO it, because it sits
earlier in the chain than `try_scan_num_agg`: a 2.5x win on hops bought with a 6.4x regression on
scans. **Chain position is part of the change, not a detail after it.** So the order of work
inverts — extend `try_scan_num_agg` to `Min | Max` and move it above the frontier path first (safe
because it requires `Plan::Scan` EXACTLY, so it can only divert bare scans), and only then is a
frontier `Sum`/`Avg`/`Count` arm safe to add. The second half is not in this item.

Verified by instrumentation, not inference, before and after:

```
before:  scan max/min -> try_frontier_prop_agg
after:   scan max/min -> try_scan_num_agg
         1hop max     -> try_frontier_prop_agg   (unchanged — no real frontier diverted)
```

### The numbers, and a 9% tax that was real

| row                        | HEAD     | shared loop | split loops          |
| -------------------------- | -------- | ----------- | -------------------- |
| scan `sum` @50k (CONTROL)  | 28.1 us  | 30.7 us     | **28.2 us**          |
| scan `sum` @200k (CONTROL) | 111.3 us | 111.3 us    | **111.2 us**         |
| scan `max` @50k            | 180.6 us | 118.2 us    | **108.7 us — 1.66x** |
| scan `max` @200k           | 717.8 us | 417.7 us    | **428.7 us — 1.67x** |

The first draft shared one loop body behind an `is_extremum` test, and the `sum` control moved
**1.09x the wrong way at 50k** — a tax on the aggregate that was already fast, levied to pay for the
one being added, inside the loop whose whole point is that it auto-vectorizes. Splitting the folds
into separate loops put the control back at parity AND made `max` faster than the shared version:
**the branch was costing both folds, not just the one it was there for.** The same lesson as item
374's unguarded walk, one item later.

**The 1.66x is not the 6.4x the gap implied, and the ceiling is worth naming:** `sum` is a bare
accumulate that auto-vectorizes; min/max calls `cmp_num_total` per element through an `Option` and
does not. Closing that would mean exploiting NaN-sorts-last to recover a vectorizable plain
`min`/`max` — a hand-rolled reimplementation of the value contract, declined here, and `-0.0` is
exactly where it would have bitten.

### What the differential test found, and why it is NOT a bug

The test compares the new scan arm against the frontier path it was moved above, over the same node
set (a self-edge on every node), **by bits** — because `NaN != NaN` and `-0.0 == 0.0` under float
equality, so a plain comparison would pass on precisely the inputs the test exists for. It failed
on its first run:

```
signed zero/min: scan path gave Num(0.0), frontier path gave Num(-0.0)
```

`cmp_num_total` rates `-0.0` and `0.0` EQUAL, so each fold keeps whichever it visited FIRST, and the
two paths visit in different orders. The first conclusion was that the frontier path violated the
value model's "there is no negative zero". **That was wrong, and the test refuted it:** with the
values reversed, the scan path returns `-0.0` too. Both folds do, because they are the same fold.

The resolution is that it **cannot escape**. The JSON egress renders both as `0` — pinned by
`json.rs`'s own `(-0.0, "0")` case, matching `JSON.stringify(-0)` — so the sign bit never reaches a
result on either engine. The model's promise is kept at the boundary where it is observable, not in
the fold. No collapse was added: a change here would have been motion without an observable, in an
area the differential fuzzer already generates `-0.0` for and that has caused a native-vs-TS
divergence once before.

So the assertion is about the value being zero, with the reasoning recorded, and the sign is left
alone. **Filed separately:** a stored `-0.0` survives the write path (nothing collapses it on the
way in) and columnar reads never pass through `num_of`. Unobservable through JSON today; it would
become observable through any egress that preserves the sign.

### Teeth

Mutants under `timeout 600` + a 16G cap, pristine restored BEFORE each: min/max direction swapped →
**CAUGHT**; `cmp_num_total` replaced by a plain `partial_cmp`, so NaN stops being greatest →
**CAUGHT**; the `present` mask ignored → **SURVIVED at first**, and that was a real hole, not a
false alarm. An absent slot holds `0.0`, so the existing `[5, None, -2, None]` case answers `-2`/`5`
whether or not the mask is honoured — the mutation is invisible on data that straddles zero. Added
`[5, None, 3]` and `[-5, None, -3]`, where a stale `0.0` would win; **CAUGHT**. The
behaviour-preserving control (force the slow non-whole branch for every scan — identical answers,
more work) **SURVIVED**.

A fourth mutant is worth noting for what it would have shown: reverting the CHAIN MOVE alone leaves
every answer identical, so no test can catch it. That is why the move needed the dispatch probe.

### Verification

1,116 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (one new), all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases via `bun run fuzz`,
`spelling_probe` still reporting no perf cliffs. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0:
clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt`, `bun run check`.

### Still open

The frontier `Sum`/`Avg`/`Count` arm — 2.02x at 50k, 2.51x at 200k, now unblocked because bare
scans are diverted earlier in the chain. The bigger ABSOLUTE saving of the two gaps (~3.3 ms at 200k
against this item's ~0.3 ms), and the more characteristic query: aggregating over a traversal.

## 376. `count` is the one aggregate in the frontier family that is NOT order-dependent — 2.68x; `sum`/`avg` are refuted by a decision already in the code, and my dispatch probe had a blind spot

Item 375 left the frontier `Sum`/`Avg`/`Count` arm as the bigger of the two gaps: 2.02x at 50k,
2.51x at 200k, and ~3.3 ms of absolute saving against that item's ~0.3 ms. **Most of it is not
available, and the reason was already written on the function I was about to change.**

### Refuted before a line was written

`try_frontier_prop_agg`'s own doc comment:

> MIN/MAX only: they are order-INDEPENDENT, so collapsing the frontier to per-node multiplicity
> (which loses row order) is byte-identical; **SUM/AVG would change the summation order, so they
> stay on `try_frontier_aggregate`** (`frontier_ids`, which keeps order).

Floating-point addition is not associative, and collapsing a frontier to per-node counts destroys
row order, so a frontier `sum` cannot match the materializing path bit-for-bit. **The 2.5x is the
deliberate price of byte-identity, not a missing path.** Two items running, the value contract and
not the chain has set the ceiling.

It also showed that the first thing `counts.for_each(|v, _c| …)` does is discard the multiplicity —
correct for an extremum, which is blind to how often a node is reached, but a hop emits one row per
edge, so a `sum` would have to weight by `c`. That is the same order problem from the other end.

### A blind spot in my own instrumentation, worth recording

Item 375's dispatch probe reported `1hop sum` and `1hop count(prop)` as "(no fast path; general
aggregate)". **That was wrong, and it was my probe's fault:** `try_frontier_aggregate` sits in a
LATER `else if` branch, outside the 28-entry `or_else` chain I had instrumented. Its doc says
`frontier_ids` "is produced in the same row order the full batch would have", so both shapes
already had an order-preserving fast path. The gap I measured was order-preserving materialization
against the counts collapse — not "fast path vs none".

_An instrument that covers part of the dispatch reports absence where it only has no coverage._ Item
371's lesson needs this corollary: verify the instrument reaches every branch that can answer,
not just the chain you were reading.

### What survives, and why only this

`count(k)` is **integer** addition — order-independent, exactly the property `try_frontier_count`
already relies on to fold `count(*)` from the same multiplicities. So the collapse is byte-identical
for it, and for nothing else in the family. New `try_frontier_count_prop`, folding
`present`-masked multiplicities. Any column TYPE, unlike the numeric-only extremum fold, since a
count never reads the value.

|                      | HEAD (fd1ee917) | with the arm     |           |
| -------------------- | --------------- | ---------------- | --------- |
| `count(b.age)` @50k  | 824.2 us        | **377.7 us**     | **2.20x** |
| `count(b.age)` @200k | 4434.9 us       | **1657.1 us**    | **2.68x** |
| 1hop `max` (control) | 500.6 us        | 501.8 / 503.9 us | parity    |
| scan `sum` (control) | 27.8 us         | 28.4 / 28.2 us   | parity    |

It is now FASTER than `min`/`max` on the same shape (377.7 vs 501.8), which is the expected
ordering once stated: a count touches only the `present` mask, never the column values.

**The first fixed-build run read both controls ~10% high**, which would have been alarming; two
further runs put them at parity. The new entry sits AFTER the paths those rows take and cannot cost
them, and the re-runs agreed — ambient drift, confirmed rather than assumed.

### Chain position, a third time

My own item-375 reorder moved `try_frontier_prop_agg` ahead of `try_scan_count_prop`, so adding
`Count` to the frontier path would have **stolen bare-scan `count(prop)` from the path built for
it**. This went in as its own entry after the scan twin instead. The hazard that item 375 shipped a
fix for was live again one item later, in the region that item had just reordered.

### A gate that is unreachable, priced, and pinned

The new entry also declines a bare `Scan` explicitly. The M3 mutant — delete that decline —
**SURVIVED every behavioural test, as predicted**, because the chain already places
`try_scan_count_prop` first, so a bare `Scan` never arrives here. So I priced what the gate
protects: 25.6 vs 23.8 us (50k) and 93.0 vs 93.9 us (200k) with and without it — **noise in both
directions.** The gate buys nothing in speed and is about OWNERSHIP, kept because item 375 reordered
exactly this region. Pinned by a direct assertion, the practice item 369 established for its own
unreachable gates, and **that assertion then caught M3 (rc=101)** — turning a survivor into a
covered gate rather than leaving untested code in the tree.

### Teeth

Mutants under `timeout 600` + a 16G cap, pristine restored BEFORE each: multiplicity dropped (count
each node once rather than once per path) → **CAUGHT**, which is what the parallel-edge fixture
exists for — it answers 2 where the pattern yields 3, and a fixture without parallel edges cannot
tell the two apart; the `present` mask ignored → **CAUGHT**; the bare-`Scan` decline deleted →
**CAUGHT by the direct assertion** (survives everything else). The behaviour-preserving control →
**SURVIVED**.

The regression test's reference is **another path, not arithmetic I typed**: adding
`WHERE … IS NOT NULL` puts a `Filter` in the chain, so the general aggregate answers the same
question by a different route, and the two must agree.

### Verification

1,118 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (two new), all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases via `bun run fuzz`.
Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt`, `bun run check`.

## 377. A 5-hop `max` OOM-killed the TS engine where native answered in 38 ms — and the TIME was a different bug from the MEMORY

Items 375 and 376 were Rust-side, so this one went looking for the pure-TS engine. Two candidate
targets refuted first, both by the closed-work index, and both worth recording as refutations:

- **The TS spelling probe is healthy.** At the documented `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9` it reports
  0 answer disagreements, 0 under the floor, and exactly one group over 2x — at 3228x, which looks
  like a find and is a **deliberate guard**: `:P` is intentionally non-vacuous (four `:S` nodes out
  of 200,004), and `CLOSED.md` names the mistake in advance — _"the group this file records as
  'CORRECT, not outstanding… do not quiet it by reverting the fixture'"_. The separate vacuous
  `:Univ` group read 1.00x.
- **TS serving is at its accepted floor.** `bench:usage`'s `ts(-)` point lookup is 526us over
  20,000 users = **26.3 ns/node**, exactly the 26-31 ns/row floor item 365 settled as accepted, not
  pending. Also worth stating because it inverts the usual reading: **indexed TS is 2-3.6x FASTER
  than indexed native** (1.31M vs 362.5k ops/s) — a TS index hit is a `Map` lookup with no FFI
  boundary per operation.

My own memory note sent me at `addVertex` first; its index line still said "ONE target =
addVertex" while the note's body already carried two corrections (312 withdrew it at 7.4%; `addEdge`
is ~85%). Index line fixed.

### The target that survived

Every aggregate over a hop cost ~530 ms while PROJECTING the same 800,000 rows cost 14.6 ms — and
the hand-written floor for the same work (walk the edges, resolve the target, test the key) is
**24.5 ms**, so the engine was 22x above a reachable floor rather than at it. The denominator was
checked before it was trusted: `tsQuery` returns a materialized `Array` of 800,000 rows, not a lazy
sequence, which matters because 18 ns/row is faster than my own hand-written loop (the engine
iterates adjacency internally instead of through the public API).

`detectCountShortcut` gates on `!e.star`, so `count(*)` is 0.01 ms and `count(b.k)` is 530 ms. The
cause of the 530 ms, though, is in `applyProjection`, and item 297 had already found and documented
it for `count(*)`:

> `applyProjection`'s aggregating branch retains every binding so the aggregate closures can map
> over them … `count(*)` is the one aggregate that reads nothing but the group's SIZE

with the remaining work named precisely: _"Still O(rows): `sum`/`min`/`max`/`avg`/`stddev`
(foldable, but … they need partial state plumbed through `compileAggregate` — and the accumulator
must fold the array path too, or it becomes a second definition of the semantics)"_.

### It is a crash, not slowness — the same class as item 373, engines swapped

4.86M paths x ~640 bytes a path is ~3.1 GB, which predicts a fault. Verified under a 4 GB cap:

| 5-hop over 4,860,000 paths | pure-TS (HEAD)       | native      |
| -------------------------- | -------------------- | ----------- |
| `RETURN count(*)`          | 20 ms, 156 MB        | 589 us      |
| `RETURN sum(f.k)`          | **OOM-KILLED (137)** | **38.2 ms** |

Item 373 was native crashing where TS faulted correctly; this is TS crashing where native answers.
Neither is findable by a differential fuzzer, because the run that would report it never finishes.

**The first measurement of that said `rc=0`** — which was `tail`'s exit status, not the run's, the
exact pipeline trap CLAUDE.md documents for `clippy | grep`. Captured properly it is **137**. A
false negative that would have closed the item as "sum is fine".

### THE TIME AND THE MEMORY WERE TWO DIFFERENT BUGS

Fixing the retained bindings — the thing this item set out to do, and the thing that removes the
OOM — left the 1-hop timing **untouched at 534 ms** against 538. The measurement refused the
natural conclusion, so: a scalar aggregate has ZERO grouping keys, which means `soleKey` is
`undefined` and every row paid

```js
JSON.stringify(proj.groupKeys.map((fn) => valueKey(fn({ binding: b, params, graph }))));
```

— an array allocation and a stringify, per row, to produce the constant `'[]'` that the
empty-group line three lines below already writes literally. Hoisting it is where the time came
from, and it helps EVERY aggregate including the ones that still keep their bindings (`sum` moved
1.21x), which is itself the evidence that the two costs were independent.

### The numbers

Min of three alternated rounds, HEAD measured on the same machine state. The CONTROLS are the
PROJECTION of the same rows and `count(*)`, neither of which this change can reach:

| row                          | HEAD      | with the change |       |
| ---------------------------- | --------- | --------------- | ----- |
| scan `min`                   | 74.87 ms  | **43.57 ms**    | 1.72x |
| scan `max`                   | 67.23 ms  | **44.87 ms**    | 1.50x |
| scan `sum`                   | 73.18 ms  | **48.95 ms**    | 1.49x |
| scan `count(prop)`           | 64.59 ms  | **44.10 ms**    | 1.46x |
| 1hop `max`                   | 557.97 ms | **438.99 ms**   | 1.27x |
| 1hop `count(prop)`           | 561.45 ms | **446.42 ms**   | 1.26x |
| 1hop `sum`                   | 554.87 ms | **459.23 ms**   | 1.21x |
| 1hop `project b.k` (CONTROL) | 14.29 ms  | 14.60 ms        | flat  |
| `count(*)` (CONTROL)         | 0.01 ms   | 0.01 ms         | flat  |

And the 5-hop `max`: **OOM-killed → 3380 ms at 234 MB RSS.**

### Still open, with its cause named

The hop aggregate is still ~430 ms against a 14.6 ms projection. **It is not the aggregate
machinery**: `sum` improved by the same proportion despite never being folded, so the remainder is
shared by both paths and upstream of this change — the per-row `Binding` (`Map`) construction that
the projection path avoids by streaming values. Removing it needs a frontier-streaming aggregate
shortcut, the TS twin of `try_frontier_prop_agg`, which is a new shortcut and a separate item.
`sum`/`avg` are foldable too (`temporalSum` is already a left fold; `{mode, sawArray}` state
reproduces the `some(isTemporal)`-before-`some(isArray)` precedence, and the four awkward orderings
were checked to land on the same error) — also its own item, because getting that precedence subtly
wrong is a cross-engine divergence.

### Teeth

The DISTINCT spelling is a reference implementation reachable from the query language: `foldFor`
refuses `distinct`, and `max(DISTINCT x) === max(x)` for all x, so the test compares the folded path
against the retained one on the same question rather than against arithmetic I typed. `count(arg)`
has no such twin, so its reference is a filtered `count(*)`, which the match-level filter sends down
a different path.

One answer looked wrong and was not: a 5-hop `max` of `96` where `k = i % 100` suggested `99`. The
retained path agrees — the probe's LCG shares one `x` sequence across all sources, so the edge set
is structured and the reachable endpoints genuinely exclude the top few values.

Mutants, each with its OWN BUILD (a TS mutant that is not rebuilt looks caught while never having
run — the stale-dist trap, hit once earlier in this item when a fuzzer "passed" against a dist two
hours old; checking `stat` on src vs dist is what caught it): the fold's nullish skip dropped →
**CAUGHT**; extremum direction swapped → **CAUGHT**; all folds sharing accumulator slot 0 →
**CAUGHT**; `finish` reading the wrong slot → **CAUGHT**; the behaviour-preserving control (drop the
constant-key hoist — slower, identical answers) → **SURVIVED**.

### The complexity cap was right

`applyProjection` was already at its 35 limit; this change took it to 47. Extracting
`stepFolded`/`finishFolded` left it at 43, so the whole grouping block became `buildGroups`. That is
not appeasing a linter: the function now chooses between **three** bucket shapes — kept bindings,
counted groups (297), folded accumulators (377) — and was doing so alongside ordering, DISTINCT and
paging. Re-measured after the extraction: no cost (the scan rows came out slightly better).

### Verification

10 new tests, the full TS suite across 21 projects, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases via
`bun run fuzz`. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: `fmt`, `lint`, `typecheck`.

## 378. Item 377's cause CONFIRMED (not refuted, as I briefly recorded) — and deep offset pagination costs 499 ms to return ten rows, with a 500x trap in the obvious fix

Item 377 closed with the remaining ~430 ms attributed to "the per-row `Binding` (`Map`) construction
that the projection path avoids by streaming values". That was inferred from `sum` improving
identically while never being folded — real evidence, but it stopped at "shared and upstream". So it
was probed.

**The first probe looked like a refutation and was not.** `RETURN b.k` is 14.7 ms for 800,000 rows
while `RETURN b.k LIMIT 999999999` — the same rows — is 669 ms. I read that as "the cause is leaving
a lazy fast path, not Binding construction" and said so. Wrong: the discriminator is
`detectNodeProjection`, a SHORTCUT that streams values, and its gate is

```js
proj.distinct ||
  (proj.orderBy?.length ?? 0) > 0 ||
  proj.skip !== undefined ||
  proj.limit !== undefined;
```

So a `LIMIT` drops the query onto the generic path, which builds a `Binding` per row — **which is
exactly what item 377 said.** The probe found the mechanism; it did not contradict the cause. Item
377's entry stands unamended, and _this_ is the correction: I turned "my evidence stopped short of
the mechanism" into "my claim was wrong", which is an overcorrection, and a closed-work index that
records a retraction that never happened is as misleading as one that records a wrong cause.

### Deep pagination is the real shape; a shallow LIMIT is already fine

| shape                      | best          | rows    |
| -------------------------- | ------------- | ------- |
| `RETURN b.k` (shortcut)    | 14.72 ms      | 800,000 |
| `LIMIT 10`                 | **0.03 ms**   | 10      |
| `LIMIT 1000`               | 0.84 ms       | 1,000   |
| `SKIP 10 LIMIT 10`         | 0.03 ms       | 10      |
| **`SKIP 700000 LIMIT 10`** | **499.52 ms** | 10      |
| `LIMIT 999999999`          | 669.29 ms     | 800,000 |

`take` short-circuits, so a shallow page never pays — the 38x on `LIMIT 999999999` is real and
unrepresentative, and pricing the lever off it would have been pricing a query nobody writes. What
IS realistic is **offset pagination at depth: 499 ms to return ten rows**, because `skip` walks
700,010 rows through the generic path while the shortcut would stream the lot in 14.7 ms.

### OPEN AND PRICED — and the obvious fix is a 500x REGRESSION

`detectNodeProjection` returns `Row[]`: it materializes EVERY row. Letting it accept `skip`/`limit`
and slice would take `LIMIT 10` from **0.03 ms to ~15 ms — 500x worse on the common case** to win
33x on the rare one. **Do not simply widen the gate.** A sound fix needs either

- a cost decision rather than a gate flip — admit the shortcut only when `skip + limit` is large
  relative to the result (crossover on this fixture is around `skip` ≈ 24,000, since the lazy path
  costs ~620 ns a row against the shortcut's ~15 ms flat), which means a tuning constant and
  therefore a cardinality estimate on the TS side; or
- making the shortcut's production LAZY so `take` still short-circuits, which changes its `Row[]`
  contract.

Recorded rather than attempted: the measurement says the win is confined to deep offset pagination,
the naive version is a large regression on the shape everyone writes, and both sound fixes are
design changes rather than a gate edit.

### Also measured, for whoever prices the generic path next

`RETURN a.k, b.k` is 131 ms against the one-column 14.7 ms — reading a SECOND slot leaves the
shortcut too (it is a _node_ projection), so the 9x there is the same generic-path cost from another
direction, and a useful second data point on what that path charges per row.

## 379. A 1:1 endpoint move cannot change a COUNT — 15.2x on a bench row, after the target I went looking for turned out not to exist

`bench_all`'s `query/gremlin` section had `outE.outV` at 9111.8us against `out` at 608.6us. That
looked like TinkerPop's `IncidentToAdjacentStrategy` (`outE().inV()` → `out()`, `inE().outV()` →
`in()`, `bothE().otherV()` → `both()`) missing from the optimizer.

**That strategy is REFUTED — all three of its pairs are already equal**, both as traversals
(100076.0 vs 100279.1us) and as counts (116.9 vs 117.0us). `inV` and `otherV` are elided at
LOWERING: their plans are byte-identical to the bare `Expand`. There is nothing to win.

### Two of my own errors on the way, because each would otherwise read as insight

1. I sorted the whole `bench_all` log by time and compared rows I then explained away as
   cross-fixture. **They were in the same section with the same fixture** — my original comparison
   was right and my explanation of it was wrong.
2. My first probe measured the traversals WITHOUT `.count()`, read 1.00x, and nearly recorded
   "refuted — the traversals are identical." They ARE identical. **The gap was never in the
   traversal**; the bench rows are counts (`rows=1`), and stopping there would have filed a phantom
   refutation over a real gap.

### The real finding is simpler and more general

An endpoint move after an edge frontier is **1:1** — every edge has exactly one source — so a bare
`count(*)` over one can count the move's INPUT. `outE(L).outV().count()` and `outE(L).count()` are
the same number, and were 1720.9us against 118.4us. `outV` is the only spelling that reaches `exec`
as a plan node, which is why the special case was covered and the general argument was not.

An optimizer rewrite in `opt.rs`'s `Aggregate` arm, next to the existing `count(Slot)` → `count(*)`
canonicalization (which the comment there already calls "closing a spelling perf cliff") and
deliberately AFTER it, since that one is what admits this one.

### Three gates, none of them derivable from the rewrite alone

- **`bothV` is 1:TWO.** TinkerPop ground truth, run in a console rather than recalled, with a
  SELF-LOOP in the fixture because that is where endpoint steps diverge: over 4 edges
  `outE.bothV` = 8 and `bothE.bothV` = 16, while `outE.outV` / `outE.inV` / `outE.otherV` /
  `bothE.otherV` are all 4. Admitting `bothV` HALVES the answer.
- **`EdgeVertex` DROPS rows.** `exec` says "vertex/scalar from another arm) has no endpoint, so
  skip it" — so the step is 1:1 in TinkerPop's semantics and row-dropping in this implementation,
  and the elision needs an input that PROVABLY binds an edge. An `Expand { bind_edge: true }` whose
  own frontier is that slot is the conservative shape; no union arm can reach it. _The ground truth
  tells you what a step MEANS; it does not license eliding it over an arbitrary input._
- **Nothing may read the dropped slot**: no grouping keys (`groupCount().by('age')` reads the
  moved-to vertex) and every aggregate a bare non-DISTINCT `count(*)`.

### IT SHIPPED DEAD FIRST, and that is the part worth remembering

The first gate asked `plan_out_width(ev_in) == edge_slot + 1`. An `Expand { bind_edge: true }` lays
out `[source, EDGE, target]`, so with `edge_slot: 1` the width is **3** and the relation is
`edge_slot + 2`. The build was clean, 1,118 tests passed, and the benchmark read 1720.9us —
**unchanged**. A rewrite that declines every query is indistinguishable from one that is not there:
item 371's dead fast path, in a new place, caught only by re-measuring instead of trusting a green
build.

### The numbers

| row                                     | before         | after          |                                |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `outE().outV().count()` (probe)         | 1720.9us       | **117.9us**    | **14.6x**                      |
| `bench_all` `query/gremlin` `outE.outV` | 9111.8us       | **598.9us**    | **15.2x**                      |
| `out` / `out.out` (controls)            | 608.6 / 4142.1 | 603.2 / 3891.6 | flat                           |
| `outE.outV.values` (gate control)       | 14865.7        | 14126.5        | flat — correctly NOT rewritten |
| `values` (control)                      | 1298.1         | 1269.9         | flat                           |

### Teeth

Mutants under `timeout 600` + a 16G cap, pristine restored BEFORE each: admit `bothV` →
**CAUGHT**; drop the edge-bound-input gate → **CAUGHT**; revert the slot relation to `+ 1` →
**CAUGHT**, which is better than designed — I expected a dead rewrite to be invisible to tests, but
the test asserts the plan IS elided, so the failure mode that actually bit me is now guarded.

`all` → `any` on the aggregate check **SURVIVED, and is provably EQUIVALENT**: the two differ only
for a projection carrying 2+ aggregates, and no Gremlin shape produces that over an `EdgeVertex` —
`group().by().by(count())`, `groupCount()`, `project()`, `fold().count(local)` and `values().sum()`
all yield exactly one aggregate or none. Same category as item 297's T10.

**Investigating that survivor found an unpinned gate**: `groupCount().by('age')` keeps the move
because its key reads the moved-to vertex, and `keys.is_empty()` had no test. Now pinned, with
`dedup()` as the sharp case (it makes the move's OUTPUT determine the count) and a behavioural
check that distinct sources are genuinely fewer than edges, so the assertion is about answers and
not plan text.

### Verification

1,118 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests (one new), **`rewrite_fuzz` at `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000`** —
the right guard, since this is a plan rewrite and "optimizing must not change the answer" is exactly
its invariant — all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases, and `bench_all` compared row-by-row against the
pre-change sweep. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0: clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt`.

## 380. A sort under a bare `count(*)` looked like 17,000x and is a WRONG ANSWER — `order().by(k)` filters, and the console is the only reason I know

Item 379 closed on "grep the pattern elsewhere": its rule is that a row-count-preserving step can
be elided under a bare `count(*)`, and `EdgeVertex` is not the only such step. A SORT preserves row
count, so `order().by('age').count()` should be able to skip the sort entirely.

Measured at 100,000 vertices, and the gap is enormous:

| shape                             | best                                        |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `count()`                         | **0.3 us**                                  |
| `order().by('age').count()`       | **5097.8 us**                               |
| `order().by('age', desc).count()` | 5141.8 us                                   |
| `dedup().count()`                 | 438.1 us — not elidable, changes the count  |
| `values('age').count()`           | 522.4 us — not elidable, drops missing keys |
| `has('age', 30).count()`          | 72.6 us — not elidable, a filter            |

~17,000x, on a shape that is not a curiosity: every paginated UI issues a "total rows" query beside
its page query, reusing the same sorted builder with the tail swapped for a count. ORMs generate it.

I worked out the gates carefully from the IR. `OrderPage` carries `skip`/`limit` (a page DOES change
the count, so both must be absent) and `fault_on_element`, documented as "Gremlin `order()` over raw
graph ELEMENTS faults — TinkerPop throws" and **true for every Gremlin sort**; since a property value
can never BE an element, gating on the key shape (`SortKey.expr` a `Prop`/`Field`, never
`Expr::Slot`) provably cannot skip a fault. Three careful gates, and every one of them irrelevant.

### The console

```text
V.count                = 4
V.order.by(age).count  = 2     <-- the two keyless vertices are GONE
V.values(age).count    = 2
```

**`order().by('<key>')` DROPS elements lacking the key.** It is not a permutation, so it is not
row-count-preserving, and the premise under all three gates was false. The rewrite would have
answered **4 where the answer is 2** — a wrong answer with a 17,000x speedup attached, which is the
worst combination this engine can ship: fast, plausible, and silently incorrect.

My reasoning was specific and confident — a sort permutes rows, a permutation preserves cardinality
— and it was wrong about what the step IS. CLAUDE.md's rule that Gremlin semantics come from a
running console rather than from reasoning is the whole reason this is an audit entry and not a
commit. **It is the same shape as `values()`**, which this file already records TinkerPop dropping
keyless elements for; the lesson did not transfer because I was thinking about ordering, not about
projection.

### lenke conforms

|                             | TinkerPop | lenke |
| --------------------------- | --------- | ----- |
| `count()`                   | 4         | **4** |
| `order().by('age').count()` | 2         | **2** |
| `values('age').count()`     | 2         | **2** |

No divergence — which is the consolation prize, and worth having measured rather than assumed, since
a conformance bug here would have been the more important finding.

### A test, not a comment

The semantics are now pinned by
`a_gremlin_order_by_key_filters_and_so_cannot_be_elided_under_a_count`: the three TinkerPop numbers,
plus an assertion that the plan still CONTAINS `OrderPage` so a future fixture change cannot
silently disarm the count check.

**Its teeth were verified by writing the bug.** Applying the elision I had designed — a pure
`OrderPage` dropped under a bare `count(*)` — the test fails (rc=101). A test that merely asserts
today's behaviour is worth nothing if the change it exists to stop would still pass it.

### Still open, and cliff-shaped

The elision IS sound when the sort key is present on every live node — nothing is dropped, so the
sort really is a permutation. That needs an O(1) store-side present-count to gate on, and it is the
all-or-nothing vacuity cliff item 325 recorded for labels: "one unlabelled node in a real graph
defeats the elision for every query anchored on that label". A 17,000x that evaporates on one
missing property is a different proposition from a 17,000x, and it should be priced as such before
anyone builds it.

## 391. A property KEY was rebuilt per cell, copying its bytes and heap-allocating past 12 characters — 1.32x on element render, and my own fixture had hidden it

Item 342's ladder pointed at packing presence. Four ticks priced rung 3's write side (384), its
growth (385), its key-identity constraint (386), the cache design that dissolved it (387) and a
correction to that (388) — and then the target was re-measured before building, which redirected
everything:

- **389**: the K-slope reproduces at **2.16 ns/key**, not 342's 7.86, so rung 3 is worth 1.93x at
  K=200 and **1.08x at K=12** — and the **baseline is 466 ns/row and is not presence at all**
  (cheap numbers measured the same as 200k distinct strings).
- **390**: ablating that baseline, in-engine, one component at a time: **properties 221.1 ns (47%)**,
  the two `Value::Map` allocations **174.2 (37%)**, labels **57.2 (12%)**, the external-id lookup
  **~0** (ablating it measured 481.7 against 469.5 — free). Components sum to 452.5 of 469.5.
- **391**: 221 ns for FOUR properties is 55 ns each, and the values were plain numbers. The cost is
  the KEY.

### What the key cost

```rust
.map(|(k, c)| (Value::Str(Arc::clone(k).into()), c.read(i)))
```

`From<Arc<str>> for GStr` is `GStr::new(&s)` — it **copies the bytes**, inline up to
`INLINE_CAP = 12` and a **heap allocation with a refcount header** above it. So every cell paid an
`Arc` clone immediately dropped (two atomics) plus a copy or an allocation, to rebuild a key that is
identical for every node in the batch.

**MY FIXTURE HAD HIDDEN THE WORST OF IT.** Item 390's 55 ns/property used keys `"a".."d"` — all
inline, so it never touched the heap path. The length axis is the whole story:

| key_len    | inline? | before                | after                     |
| ---------- | ------- | --------------------- | ------------------------- |
| 1 / 8 / 12 | yes     | 478.4 / 480.3 / 465.6 | 446.0 / 441.6 / **436.8** |
| **13**     | NO      | **562.1**             | **448.2**                 |
| 20 / 40    | NO      | 597.1 / 593.9         | **453.4 / 445.1**         |

Crossing the cap cost **+96.5 ns/row (+24 ns per property)** and plateaued by 20 characters, so it
was the allocation and not the byte count. Real schemas are full of `employeeNumber` and
`departmentName`. _That is the uniform-label fixture mistake of item 374 in a new place: a fixture
that makes the measurement tidy by avoiding the case that matters._

### The change

Hoist the K key `Value`s out of the row loop and clone per cell — `GStr::clone` is one relaxed
`fetch_add` for a heap string and a 16-byte struct copy for an inline one, so it is a large win past
12 characters and neutral below.

**FOUR sites take it**, each checked rather than assumed: `render_nodes`, `render_edges` (its batch
twin, `maps` already resolved outside the loop), and the two `elementMap`/`valueMap` paths in
`evaluator.rs`, both inside `(0..n).map(|i| …)` with `node_cols` hoisted. **TWO sites deliberately
left alone**: `render.rs`'s single-element `edge_result_value`/`node_result_value` have no row loop
to hoist out of — the caller-level hoist IS `render_nodes`/`render_edges`, which exist (per their own
doc comment) because the per-element path was expensive.

### The numbers, and what the existing bench does NOT show

**Key length no longer matters**: 445-453 ns/row at 13-40 characters against 436.8 at 12.

`bench_all`, whose fixture uses `name`/`age`/`city`/`dept` — ALL INLINE: `element p`
**102630.0 → 93786.7 us (513.1 → 468.9 ns/row, 1.09x)**, `element r` 337100.6 → 330985.8 (337.1 →
331.0, 1.02x), `distinct node` 125517.2 → 120377.3. Controls flat: `project 3` 4702.8 → 4762.7 and
`count(*)` 0.3 → 0.3, neither touching an element.

So the honest headline is **1.09x on the bench and 1.32x with realistic key names** — the bench
cannot show the larger number because its keys are four characters long.

### Teeth

The risk is INDEXING: `key_vals[j]` pairing a value with the wrong key NAME is a silent wrong
answer, and `j` must index the unfiltered column list. Mutants under `timeout 900` + a 16G cap,
pristine restored BEFORE each: every value paired with the first key name, in nodes → **CAUGHT**;
off-by-one on the node index → **CAUGHT**; the same first-key error in the EDGE twin → **CAUGHT**;
off-by-one in the evaluator's `valueMap` path → **CAUGHT**. The behaviour-preserving control
**SURVIVED**. The existing 1,120-test suite already had teeth on key pairing; no new test was
needed, which is worth stating rather than adding one for form.

### Verification

1,120 + 13 + 723 Rust engine tests, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases via `bun run fuzz` — the
material check here, since the property map's contents and ORDER must be unchanged and all that
moved is when the key is constructed — and `bench_all` compared row by row. Gates each as their own
command, each exit 0: clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt`.

### What this leaves

Rung 3 is still unbuilt and still worth 1.93x at K=200 — but this took the realistic case without
touching storage. The remaining baseline is the two `Value::Map` allocations (174.2 ns/row, 37%) and
labels (57.2, 12%), neither of which this change reaches.

## 396. The edge twin of item 340's borrowing label accessor, six months late — 1.05x on edge render, and the length axis I predicted it would turn on is flat

Item 394 decomposed `render_edges` and put **60.2 ns/row (18%)** in labels. Item 395 then measured
the T axis and refuted the alarming-looking half of that: `etype_name`'s linear scan over every
edge type is **flat from 0 to 200 types**, so no reverse index is warranted. What was left is the
allocation path, and the fix was already written — on the other side of the store.

`labels_of_refs` (item 340) gives the NODE side its labels as `Vec<&str>`. The edge side only ever
had `edge_labels_of`, which clones a `String` per label out of `etype_ids` — for the caller to
immediately copy those same bytes again into a `GStr`. **Two of most things, and the fix landed on
the one I was looking at.** The list now reads 367/368/370, 374, 376, 391 and this.

New: `etype_name_ref` (the borrowing twin of `etype_name`) and `edge_labels_of_refs`, same order
(primary type first, then secondaries), callers still sort where they sorted. Eight call sites
moved: `render_edges` and `edge_result_value`, `json_out`'s streaming edge writer, the evaluator's
`labels(e)`, three per-edge `codec.rs` sinks and `binary.rs`. The owned `edge_labels_of` stays for
`codec.rs:176`, which needs a `Vec<String>` for a struct field. `codec.rs:536` loses a whole
allocation rather than half of one — it was building `Vec<String>` and then `Vec<&str>` from it.

### The numbers, and the prediction that was wrong

100,000 nodes at degree 5 (500,000 edges), min of three ALTERNATED rounds, each side rebuilt from a
snapshot of the other, OLD taken from `git checkout HEAD --` so the baseline is the committed tree.

| case                      | OLD (min of 3) | NEW (min of 3) |       | ranges                                   |
| ------------------------- | -------------: | -------------: | ----- | ---------------------------------------- |
| edge render, 5-char type  |          322.3 |      **306.6** | 1.05x | [322.3-332.8] vs [306.6-311.2], disjoint |
| edge render, 17-char type |          346.2 |      **333.4** | 1.04x | [346.2-350.5] vs [333.4-336.1], disjoint |
| CONTROL node render       |          149.1 |          147.9 | flat  | the change cannot reach it               |
| CONTROL edge count        |        311.8µs |        317.3µs | flat  | renders nothing                          |

`bench_all`'s `element r` reads **328.0 ns/row** against the 334.6-337.1 of items 391/394.

**I predicted this would turn on key length and it does not.** `GStr` inlines up to 12 bytes, so I
expected the 17-character type — above the cap, heap-allocating on BOTH the old and new path — to
show the larger saving. It shows the smaller one. The reason is that the saving is **one
malloc/free per label, not a copy of its bytes**: the old path allocated a `String` (always, at any
length) and then a `GStr` (only above 12); the new path allocates only the `GStr`. One allocation
disappears either way, and an allocation costs about what it costs regardless of size. The byte
copy I was counting is the cheap part. This is the same correction as 395 one item earlier — code
that reads worse than it measures — arriving from the opposite direction.

**13-16 ns/row of the 60.2 that 394 attributed to labels**, so a quarter of it, and short of the
20-30 I estimated. What remains in that 60 is the `Vec`, the sort, the surviving `GStr` per label
and the `Value::List` — all of which need a cached list to remove, which is item 393's unbuilt
forward node->labels cache in its edge form. At ~5% this is below the 10% the bench README says
needs its own isolated harness, which is why it got one: a dedicated probe, alternated, with two
controls, and disjoint ranges on every round rather than a mean.

### Teeth

The risks are COMPLETENESS (a multi-label edge losing its secondaries) and ORDER (the codecs write
these bytes, so a swap is a byte-identity break). Mutants under `timeout 900` and a 16G cap with
`MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine restored BEFORE each: drop the secondary labels -> **CAUGHT** (rc=101);
reverse the order, a no-op on single-label edges so it asks specifically whether anything covers a
multi-label edge's label order -> **CAUGHT**; drop the primary type -> **CAUGHT**. The
behaviour-preserving control (`Vec::with_capacity(1)`, same contents, same order) **SURVIVED**.

### Verification

The full Rust engine suite (exit 0), all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases via `bun run fuzz` — the
material check, since `codec.rs`, `ndjson.rs` and `binary.rs` are snapshot bytes — and `bench_all`
row by row. Artifact timestamps checked against the source edits rather than trusted: the runner
reported a 9/9 cache hit, which is exactly what a stale-artifact run looks like, and the `.so` and
the `.wasm` were both 3 minutes NEWER than the edits. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0:
clippy `-D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`.

## 397. `edge.from.id` round-trips an id the edge already holds through a `Map` — item 140 fixed one call site and the other 44 kept doing it. 1.78x connected components, 1.67x PageRank, 1.28x NDJSON encode

The TS/FFI bench says the TS engine renders a NODE element 3.4x FASTER than native (280 against
957 ns/row) and an EDGE element 1.10x SLOWER (1102 against 1002). Same engine, same operation,
opposite verdict — so the edge cost is not inherent to the TS engine, and its own node path is the
proof. Following that into `Edge.toJSON` found:

```ts
from: this.from.id,   // Map lookup -> Vertex -> read back the string it already holds
to: this.to.id,
```

and forty lines above it, `Edge.fromId`'s own doc comment, written by item 140:

> `from`/`to` resolve through `getVertexById`, so `edge.from.id` round-trips an id the edge already
> holds into a `Map` lookup and back to the same string … four `getVertexById` calls per edge,
> 4,000,000 to ingest a million.

**Item 140 applied that fix to `indexEdgeLabel` and nowhere else.** `grep` finds the round trip at
44 more sites: every graph algorithm's CSR-building loop (pagerank, centrality,
connected-components, strongly-connected-components, peer-pressure, neighbor-aggregate,
shortest-path), every serialization encoder (ndjson, pg-json, pg-text, graphson, csv, plus
`equality`), `Edge.toJSON`, both graph-clone paths, the transaction's `txTouched`, Gremlin's
`movement`/`projection` and `inspect`. Twice per edge in most of them.

Two sites deliberately left: `Graph.ts:1873-4` reads `params.from.id` where `params.from` is a
`Vertex`, not an edge — no round trip to remove.

### The cost of the round trip, priced before changing anything

200,000 nodes, 1,000,000 edges, alternated, min of seven. Controls: a loop touching only
`edge.id`, and one touching only the iterator.

| loop over 1,000,000 edges           |     best |  ns/edge |
| ----------------------------------- | -------: | -------: |
| `edge.from.id + edge.to.id` (today) | 89.65 ms | **89.7** |
| `edge.fromId + edge.toId`           | 14.26 ms | **14.3** |
| CONTROL `edge.id` only              |  7.57 ms |      7.6 |
| CONTROL iterate only                |  0.90 ms |      0.9 |

**6.3x on the accessor**, ~37 ns per round trip. That is an upper bound on what any caller can win,
not a result — which is the whole reason the end-to-end numbers below were measured separately.

### End to end

Alternated, min of three rounds at nine reps each, 50,000 nodes and 250,000 edges. The probe
imports `@lenke/core`'s SOURCE so a flip is a `cp` rather than an nx build.

| case                  |   OLD |       NEW |           | ranges                                      |
| --------------------- | ----: | --------: | --------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `connectedComponents` | 20.72 | **11.64** | **1.78x** | [20.7-21.0] vs [11.6-12.4], disjoint        |
| `pagerank(20)`        | 71.75 | **43.03** | **1.67x** | [71.8-73.5] vs [43.0-44.4], disjoint        |
| `encode ndjson`       | 79.61 | **62.25** | **1.28x** | [79.6-84.0] vs [62.3-66.9], disjoint        |
| `betweenness` (800n)  | 27.35 |     26.23 | 1.04x     | O(V*E) BFS dominates; CSR build is a sliver |
| CONTROL `degree`      |  9.21 |      9.28 | flat      | walks adjacency, never reads an endpoint id |

### Two measurement traps, either of which would have shipped a wrong number

**The algorithms return a PROMISE.** `defineAlgorithm` drains a generator and the result is
awaited. A first run of the probe timed only the synchronous prefix and reported `pagerank`,
`connectedComponents` and `degree` at **5.03 / 5.02 / 5.06 ms** — three unrelated algorithms
agreeing to two decimal places, which is what that failure looks like from the outside. Awaiting
turned `pagerank` into 44 ms.

**At three reps `encode ndjson` was noise.** It read 86.22 -> 62.24 with badly overlapping ranges
and one NEW round (88.56) WORSE than an OLD round (86.22). Nine reps separated it cleanly. A 1.39x
claim was available from the three-rep data and it would not have survived repetition — the exact
trap the bench README records.

### Teeth

The risk is DIRECTION: a transposed `fromId`/`toId` is a silent wrong answer that still produces
well-formed output — reversed edges in a CSR, reversed endpoints in a snapshot line. Mutants under
`timeout 1500` and a 16G cap with `MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine restored BEFORE each, every verdict
confirmed by re-running the mutant alone and reading WHICH tests failed:

- pagerank's two endpoint reads swapped -> **CAUGHT** by `pagerank > a sink outranks a source` and
  `mass is conserved`, plus the `CALL pagerank YIELD` conformance test.
- `Edge.toJSON` swapped -> **CAUGHT** by `a returned edge serializes to a rich {id, from, to, …}
object`, the rich-RETURN differential, and the 20,000-query cross-engine differential fuzzer.
- the NDJSON edge line swapped -> **CAUGHT** by five round-trip and shape tests including the
  shared cross-impl codec corpus.
- CONTROL (a behaviour-preserving temp binding) -> **SURVIVED**.

**The control's first run reported CAUGHT and that was a flake** — the known `@lenke/sync` /
`@lenke/native` timing flake under `run-many`. Re-run isolated it is rc=0. Worth recording because
a flake in a mutation harness reads as teeth: it makes every mutant look caught, including the one
whose whole job is to not be. The null control (the unmutated tree) was run separately and is green.

### Verification

Full TS suite across 39 tasks, all 13 byte-identity fuzzer cases via `bun run fuzz` — material
here, since five changed files emit snapshot bytes. Gates each as their own command, each exit 0:
`bun run fmt`, `bun run check` (typecheck + lint + fmt:check).

`bun run check` earned its place: it caught the one site where the receiver is not an `Edge`.
`ndjson`'s local `EdgeLike = VertexLike & { from: { id: string }; to: { id: string } }` is
structural, and both of its callers pass real edges from `graph.edges`, so the type was narrowed to
`{ fromId: string; toId: string }` rather than the site reverted.

### Method note

`Graph.ts` is 161 KB and **plain `grep` silently finds nothing in it** — the Unicode/binary-skip
trap. `grep -a` found `getVertexById`'s definition immediately. Any survey of this codebase that
did not pass `-a` has under-reported, this session's included.

## 398. `[...set]` is 1.79x `Array.from(set)` — 1.44x on an edge render, 1.22x on a vertex; and the sorted-labels invariant both `toJSON`s document had NO test

Item 397 came out of "the TS engine renders edges slowly". **That premise is wrong and this item
retracts it.** Timed directly, on the same graph, per element:

|                 | ns/element |
| --------------- | ---------: |
| `vertex.toJSON` |      133.5 |
| `edge.toJSON`   |   **94.7** |

An edge renders CHEAPER than a vertex. The bench's 1102 ns/row edge figure is the traversal and
the JSON carrier, not the render. Item 397's numbers stand on their own measurements; its framing
does not.

What the decomposition did show is that labels are most of what `toJSON` costs:

| piece of `edge.toJSON`         | ns/element |
| ------------------------------ | ---------: |
| `Array.from(labels).sort()`    |   **76.8** |
| - the `.labels` getter         |       16.2 |
| - `Array.from(Set)`            |       68.2 |
| - `.sort()`                    |         ~9 |
| ids (`id` + `fromId` + `toId`) |       24.1 |
| properties bag                 |       15.6 |
| CONTROL iterate                |        0.7 |

### Array.from vs spread, three independent runs

|                      |          |          |          |
| -------------------- | -------: | -------: | -------: |
| `Array.from(labels)` |     66.1 |     63.0 |     64.7 |
| `[...labels]`        | **35.8** | **35.2** | **36.2** |
| manual `push` loop   |     38.7 |     37.9 |     38.9 |

**1.79x, disjoint, and the manual loop is slower than spread.** Spread takes the engine's fast
path for an unmodified `Set` iterator; `Array.from` walks the generic iterator protocol. The
one-element `.sort()` is a no-op that still enters the sort machinery, so it is skipped below two
labels.

### End to end

Alternated, three rounds, 100,000 vertices and 500,000 edges:

|                        |   OLD |   NEW | min   | median    |
| ---------------------- | ----: | ----: | ----- | --------- |
| `edge.toJSON`          |  85.7 |  53.7 | 1.60x | **1.44x** |
| `vertex.toJSON`        | 125.0 | 102.0 | 1.23x | **1.22x** |
| CONTROL properties bag |  15.7 |  15.5 | —     | flat      |

**The median is the headline, not the min.** Round 3's NEW was a globally fast round — the CONTROL
also dropped, to 13.1 from its usual 15.6 — so min-of-three picks up that round's luck. The
min-of-three convention assumes the fast round is the uncontended one; when the control moves in
the same round it is measuring the machine. By median the control is flat and the change is 1.44x
and 1.22x.

### The invariant had no test, and that is the bigger finding

Both `toJSON`s carry a comment saying labels are sorted so the element "serializes byte-identically
to the native engine". Mutants, each **re-run in isolation** (see below):

- `Vertex.toJSON` never sorts at all -> **SURVIVED.** The whole suite passes.
- the guard off by one at `size > 2`, so a TWO-label element skips the sort -> **SURVIVED.**

So a documented byte-identity invariant was resting on nothing, and the guard this change
introduces sits exactly on the boundary that was least covered. `tojson-label-order.test.ts` now
pins it for both classes at two labels, three labels, one and none, plus the endpoint direction
item 397 touched. Teeth verified by re-applying both mutants: `if (false)` fails the two-label
tests, and `size > 2` fails **exactly** the two two-label cases while the three-label ones pass —
the boundary pinned precisely rather than approximately.

### The mutation harness was poisoning its own next run

Two verdicts in this session were wrong in the same way, and the cause is worth more than either.

`bun run test` restored a **cached build of the previous mutant**. After item 397's mutation run
the next full test run failed ten byte-identity tests with edge endpoints REVERSED — which is 397's
own M2 mutant, long after its source had been restored. The source read `from: this.fromId`
correctly and `git status` was clean. HEAD alone was green and a rebuilt run with the change
applied was green, which is what established that the tree was never the problem.
