`C project a.s` at 1M read 12.540/10.697/11.662 OLD against 17.365/17.747/17.505 NEW: disjoint,
consistent, and on a path this change cannot reach. At 200k and 50k it was flat, which is the clue.

Run in its OWN process (`PROBE_ONLY`), the same case measures **17.130/18.436/17.839 pristine
against 18.311/17.956/17.852 new** — identical, and ~17.8 ms on both sides.

So the projection's real cost is ~17.8 ms, and it is the **OLD full-bench figure that was wrong**:
the three string aggregates ahead of it each materialized 1M rows and left the allocator holding a
large warm arena, which the projection then reused. In NEW they allocate nothing, so the projection
pays for its own arena growth — which is its actual cost. Item 420 found contamination inflating a
control; this is the same mechanism **with the sign reversed**, flattering a baseline instead. The
rule is unchanged and now has both directions behind it: **isolate the control before writing down
a movement.**

### Teeth

`exec::tests::scan_string_min_max_agrees_with_the_frontier_path`, built on item 375's template:
every node carries a self-edge, so `(a)-[:E]->(b)` reaches each node exactly once and goes to
`try_frontier_prop_agg` while `(p:N)` goes to the new arm over the same set — so what is asserted is
that the two AGREE, not an expectation typed by hand. Cases: byte order (uppercase before
lowercase), a prefix against its extension, the empty string, non-ASCII, absent slots, all-absent,
duplicates, one row. `Value` has no `PartialEq` on purpose, so agreement is checked through
`value::cmp_total`.

The case worth naming: in the Dict arm an absent slot holds **code 0**, which names `dict[0]` — a
real string. So ignoring the `present` mask can only change the answer when `dict[0]` is not
otherwise among the scanned rows, which needs its first appearance to come from a node the scan does
not visit. The fixture puts `zzz` on a `:Q`, every `:N` value below it, and one `:N` with no value:
a fold reading `codes` without the mask answers `zzz`.

Six mutants, each on a restored copy under `timeout 300` + `MemoryMax=16G` `MemorySwapMax=0`, both
harness kills proved first (124, and 137 from a bomb that writes to its pages): ignore `present` in
the Dict arm, ignore it in the `Str` arm, flip the comparison in each arm, admit `Sum`/`Avg`, and
return the empty string instead of NULL for an empty set. **All six caught.**

A first version of the Dict case asserted `scan_is_cheap` on a 3-distinct-over-3-present fixture and
failed: the store takes the encoding only where it saves something, and three distinct values over
three rows is not that. The values now repeat, and the assertion stays — a fixture that silently
stops being dictionary-encoded would otherwise leave the arm untested while the test still passed.

### A named coverage gap: the fuzzer cannot reach the Dict arm

All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass. The differential fuzzer does generate this shape —
`genExpr` emits a bare `n.s` and line 1216 wraps `pick(r, AGG)` round it — so the `Str` arm is
covered. The `Dict` arm is NOT: its fixture has six `:T` nodes with six distinct `s` values, and
feeding exactly those into the store measures `dict=false`. So the dictionary path's cross-engine
parity rests on the unit test alone. Recorded rather than papered over; widening that fixture
touches a store shared by seven fuzzers and is its own item.

## 422 — fixing one spelling and not its siblings IS the asymmetry: the filtered-scan string min/max, 4.0-4.3x. The hop arm is priced and left, with the reason

Item 421 gave the bare-`Scan` `min`/`max` a columnar fold for `Column::Str` and `Column::Dict`.
The method's "grep the pattern elsewhere" step then says what to do next, and the answer was
uncomfortable: `Some(Column::Num { .. })` appears on **twelve** lines of `fastpath.rs` and
`aggregation.rs`, and two of them are the other two spellings of the question 421 just made 14.5x
faster. So 421 did not only close a gap — it opened a spelling asymmetry, which is the failure mode
this repo is named after.

Measured at 1,000,000 nodes over 97 distinct values, after 421 and before this:

```
                         string      numeric     the string gate's share
scan     max(a.s)       0.796ms      2.151ms     (421: folded)
FILTERED max(a.s)       7.412        2.326        3.2x
hop      max(b.s)      14.172        9.372        1.5x
```

The numeric column is the right denominator per spelling: the hop's own 9.372 ms says most of
its cost is the hop, not the string.

### What shipped

`try_filtered_scan_str_agg`, beside `try_filtered_scan_num_agg` in the chain (these two own the
`Filter(Scan)` shape between them; an arm below a path that claims the shape is dead, item 375).
Same two arms as 421 — `GStr::cmp` over survivors for `Str`, mark-codes-then-fold-the-dictionary
for `Dict` — over the survivor id list instead of the whole column. The survivor machinery is
byte-for-byte the numeric arm's, so both evaluate the predicate over the same rows in the same
order, which is what items 139/142 require of a fast path. The column type is checked BEFORE the
predicate is evaluated, so a declined shape does not pay for the filter twice.

Three alternated rounds, each side rebuilt, min of 5 within each:

```
                      OLD (3 rounds)            NEW (3 rounds)          ratio
filtered dict  50k  0.362 0.366 0.355      0.082 0.084 0.085          4.3x
filtered dict 200k  1.465 1.446 1.439      0.350 0.355 0.348          4.1x
filtered dict   1M  7.621 7.508 7.530      1.865 1.835 1.917          4.0x
C filtered numeric  2.358 2.348 2.335      2.367 2.359 2.340          flat
C scan dict (421)   0.805 0.812 0.805      0.808 0.818 0.813          flat
C hop dict (open)  14.258 14.317 14.343   14.350 14.354 14.217        flat
C project a.s      11.361 11.645 11.659   12.047 11.524 11.345        flat
```

The filtered dict fold now beats the filtered NUMERIC fold (1.865 against 2.367 at 1M), which is
the dictionary doing its job: 97 string comparisons where the numeric arm does a million `f64`
ones. And the hop control being flat across six runs is the evidence that arm is genuinely
untouched — the thing a fast path placed in the wrong chain position would quietly break.

### The hop arm is priced and deliberately left

`try_frontier_prop_agg` folds per-node path MULTIPLICITIES rather than rows. Item 376's rule about
which aggregates may do that — `count` yes because an integer count is order-independent,
`sum`/`avg` never — has to be re-read for a dictionary before extending it, and 1.5x on a path
whose own numeric cost is 9.4 ms is a smaller prize than the care it needs. A filtered scan has no
multiplicity (each survivor is one row), which is why it was the same fold over a different id list
and this one is not.

### Teeth, and the mutant that proved my fixture wrong

`exec::tests::filtered_scan_string_min_max_agrees_with_the_unfiltered_and_hop_spellings`. The hop
spelling is the oracle, and it is a good one precisely because this change cannot reach it: its
`Column::Num` gate sends a string to the general fold, so the same question over the same rows is
answered by code untouched here. Seven thresholds x min/max, including thresholds that keep
everything and nothing.

Six mutants under `timeout 300` + `MemoryMax=16G` `MemorySwapMax=0`, each on a restored copy, both
harness kills proved first (124, and 137 from a bomb that writes its pages). Five caught at once.
**M3 — dropping the `present` check in the Dict arm — SURVIVED**, and the reason was my fixture:
every absent slot it wrongly read named `dict[0]`, which was already among the survivors, so the
answer never changed. A survivor needs to be ABSENT and `dict[0]` needs to be excluded by the
filter for the bug to show. The leak fixture now has both — `zz` on the one row the predicate drops,
and one survivor carrying no `v` at all — and M3 fails with the assertion's own words, "an excluded
row's code leaked into a filtered max: got Str("zz")".

That is the second time in three items that a surviving mutant found something other than a missing
test: 420 refuted a comment, and this refuted a fixture that looked like it tested the leak and did
not. **A fixture built to exercise a guard has to be checked against the guard's removal, not just
written with it in mind.**

Gates separately: `cargo test` (1128 + 13 + 723), `rewrite_fuzz` at 50k seeds, `clippy -D warnings`
exit 0, `cargo fmt` clean, all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, `bun run check` exit 0. The Dict
arm's fuzzer coverage gap recorded at 421 applies here too, for the same reason and unchanged.

## 423 — the TS string comparator is REFUTED as a target at 12% of the query, the dictionary trick has NO TS twin, and item 420's throwaway explanation of its own number was wrong

Items 421/422 closed the native string aggregate with a dictionary. The obvious next move was the
TS twin, and item 420 had already written the lead-in: its string case gained only 1.6x where the
numeric one gained 3.2x, which 420 explained as "that cost is `compareValues`, which both paths pay
identically". Two things were wrong with that.

### There is no TS dictionary encoding, so 421's trick has no twin

`grep -rn dict packages/core/src/` returns nothing. The TS core stores properties as frozen JS
objects, not columns, so there is no `Column::Dict` analogue and no small distinct-value set to fold
over. (The "dictionary-mode cliff" in the session notes is V8's own object property storage flipping
at ~128 keys — an engine internal, not a lenke encoding.) The 14.5x half of 421 is native-only by
construction.

### What is left is the comparator, and it is 12% — not where the time goes

`compareValues(a, b)` for two strings runs 2x `isNullish`, 2x `typeRank`, a rank compare, 2x
`isTemporal`, 2x `Array.isArray`, 2x `instanceof LenkeRecord` and a rank-4 test before reaching
`compareCodePoints`. Every one of those is statically false for a string pair, and `min`/`max` pays
them once per row, so a specialization looked free and obvious.

Measured at 200,000 nodes, min of 3, **each case in its own process** (items 420/421: a control
sharing a process with anything that changed is not the same measurement):

```
scan max over a STRING     19.7 19.2 19.9    ~19.2ms
scan max over a NUMBER     17.1 18.0 16.2    ~16.2
scan count(a.s)            17.1 18.0 16.9    ~16.9   same rows, never reads a value
project a.s                15.7 12.9 12.8    ~12.8   the floor
```

String `max` minus `count` is **2.3 ms over 200,000 rows — 11 ns/row, 12% of the query.** Numeric
`max` minus `count` is NEGATIVE: the numeric comparison is free at this resolution. So the whole
prize for specializing the string comparator is 12% on the one shape that has it, against the
repo's own rule that anything under ~10% needs its own isolated harness and that "obviously correct
so it must be faster" is not evidence. Refuted before writing any code.

### And 420's explanation of its own number was wrong

420 reported its string case at 25.8 ms against a numeric 11.1 and explained the gap as the
comparator. The isolated numbers say the comparator is 12%, and the FULL-BENCH numbers here read
string 14.9 against numeric 18.0 — the opposite ordering, from the same binary, differing only in
what ran before each case in the process.

That is the third time this session the same mechanism has moved a number (420 inflated a control,
421 flattered a baseline, and here it reversed an ORDERING), and it is the first time it corrupted
a figure I then used to explain something. The rule earns a sharper form: **a ratio between two
cases in one process is not a ratio.** Either isolate both, or do not draw a mechanism from the gap.
420's audit entry and `CLOSED.md` line both carry the claim; the correction lives here rather than
being edited into them, which is how this file works.

### Noted for the next pass, not yet priced

`MATCH (a:P) RETURN a.s AS s ORDER BY s LIMIT 5` measured 62.0 ms against the projection's 12.8 —
310 ns/row for a five-row answer. `CProjection::orderNeedsOutput` exists so that `ORDER BY … LIMIT
n` can keep only the top-k input bindings, so the path is there; whether it fires on this shape is
the question, and it needs its own isolated measurement rather than this bench's.

## 424 — the TS top-k allocates three objects per input row to answer five; removing one bought 2.4% and was REJECTED. "It allocates per row" is not by itself a cost in this engine

Item 423 surfaced `MATCH (a:P) RETURN a.u AS s ORDER BY s LIMIT 5` at 62 ms against a 12.8 ms
projection. Isolated per process, nine reps, 200,000 rows:

```
ORDER BY u LIMIT 5        50.1ms      the target
ORDER BY u LIMIT 50       83.5
ORDER BY u LIMIT 5000     94.6
ORDER BY u (NO LIMIT)    485.1        the full sort
ORDER BY k LIMIT 5        51.5        numeric key, same cost
ORDER BY a.u LIMIT 5      54.3        the input-property spelling, same cost
max(a.u)                  20.7        same single pass, same comparator family
project a.u               13.6        the floor
count(*)                   0.0
```

**The top-k fires**: 50.1 against 485.1 unlimited is 9.7x, and the cost climbs with k (50 -> 84 ->
95), which a full sort's would not. The path is not missing; `orderNeedsOutput` is doing its job,
and the alias and input-property spellings agree to within noise, so there is no spelling
asymmetry either.

What is left is 50.1 ms against the `max` fold's 20.7 over the same rows with the same comparator
family — 145 ns/row for keeping five instead of one.

### The allocation theory, and its refutation

The top-k path allocates **three objects per input row**: the `{ b, keys }` wrapper and the
`orderBy.map(...)` key array at the call site in `applyProjection`, and `{ v, i }` inside
`boundedTopK`. The last is the worst of them on paper, because it is built BEFORE the
`less(e, heap[0])` test that throws it away — so 200,000 objects are allocated to keep five, which
is the same per-row allocation item 113 removed from the pass-through projection path.

Replaced with two parallel arrays (`vals`/`idxs`, swapped together, plus a `lessThanRoot` that
compares a candidate against the root without building an entry for it). Five alternated rounds,
nine reps, isolated per process:

```
pristine  50.5 49.6 54.2 49.9 50.1    median 50.1
new       48.3 48.9 49.6 48.8 50.8    median 48.9
```

**2.4%. Rejected**, under the repo's 10% floor. Recorded on `boundedTopK` itself, which is where
the next person will look.

The corollary is worth more than the change would have been: **"it allocates per row" is not by
itself a cost in this engine.** V8's young-generation bump allocation is near-free and the extra
array indirection costs back most of what removing it saves. The same arithmetic prices removing
the other two per-row allocations at roughly 5% — also under the floor — so the 145 ns/row is not
allocation and the whole theory is refuted rather than half-tested.

### And a measurement trap that nearly shipped the opposite conclusion

The first A/B read **58.0 -> 86.1 ms, a 1.48x REGRESSION**, and three alternated rounds then gave
pristine 55.3/54.6/95.0 against new 91.9/54.0/50.7. Both sides are **bimodal** at ~50 ms and
~90-95 ms, from the same two builds, so min-of-3 picks a mode rather than a cost. Nine reps
collapses the spread to the 2.4% above.

`ts-spelling-probe` already says this about this engine (it runs at `SPELL_REPS=9` for exactly this
reason) and I ran three anyway. Had the first round been believed, this item would have shipped a
revert of a change that is in fact 2% faster — or, worse, the reverse experiment would have
"confirmed" a 1.48x win. **A bimodal shape makes a min-of-three A/B a coin flip, and the tell is
that the two modes appear on BOTH sides.**

### Still open on this shape

50.1 ms against a 20.7 ms `max` fold, cause NOT identified. The remaining structural differences
are the generator layers between `bindings` and `boundedTopK`'s `for…of`, the per-row-per-key
`{ binding, params, graph }` env object that `s.fn(...)` takes (the aggregate fold allocates one
too, so it is not obviously the difference), and `compareSort`'s DESC/nulls wrapping around
`compareValues`. Priced at 145 ns/row, worth its own item, and to be measured at nine reps.

## 425 — the TS single-key top-k gets its own heap: 1.34-1.50x across six shapes. Item 424's refutation is what made this findable, and a surviving mutant showed my tie fixture tested nothing

Item 424 established what the `ORDER BY … LIMIT n` gap is NOT. The top-k fires (50.1 ms against
485.1 unlimited), the spellings agree, and removing the per-row allocation bought 2.4%. What it
left was a number: **182 ns/row of per-row machinery against the `max(a.u)` fold's 35 ns** over the
same rows with the same comparator family, with allocation accounting for ~6 ns of it.

So the cost is the machinery between `bindings` and the comparison, and for ONE sort key — the
overwhelmingly common spelling — all of it is avoidable:

- a `map` generator between `bindings` and the heap's `for…of`;
- a one-element `keys` array per row, and `a.keys[i]`/`b.keys[i]` index reads per comparison;
- `orderBy[i].descending` and `orderBy[i].nullsFirst` re-loaded on EVERY comparison inside the
  generic `cmp`, where they are loop-invariant for the whole query;
- `boundedTopK`'s `{ v, i }` entry, which 424 showed is the cheap part.

`applyProjection` now takes a specialized branch when `orderBy.length === 1`: parallel
`bindings`/`keys`/`index` arrays at most `cap` long, the sort flags destructured once, and an
eviction test that compares the candidate against the root without storing it anywhere.

Five alternated rounds, nine reps each (424's lesson — this shape is bimodal at three), isolated
per process:

```
                        OLD                          NEW                     ratio
order u LIMIT 5    51.7 52.1 47.1 49.6 48.6   39.1 35.1 34.6 37.1 37.4      1.34x
order u LIMIT 5000 95.9                       64.0                           1.50x
order u DESC LIMIT 5   50.4                   33.7                           1.50x
order u SKIP 10 LIMIT 5 50.1                  35.5                           1.41x
order k LIMIT 5    45.9 46.8 47.4             35.8 34.4 34.9                 1.34x
order a.u LIMIT 5  54.5 51.0 49.6             35.7 35.4 37.9                 1.43x
```

Controls, all three rounds, all flat with overlapping ranges: the TWO-KEY orders (`LIMIT 5` and
`LIMIT 5000`), which still run the generic heap and would catch a tax levied on it; the unlimited
sort (472.7/468.4/446.9 against 438.8/443.7/443.1); the `max` fold; the plain projection. Two of
those read as moved on a SINGLE round — `scan max u` 12.1 -> 16.7, a 1.38x on a path this change
cannot reach — and three rounds showed both flat. That is 424's bimodality again, and it is now
cheap to recognize.

The remaining gap to the `max` fold is 37 ms against 20.7, so roughly half of what 424 priced is
closed and the rest is still unattributed.

### Teeth, and the second fixture this session that tested nothing

`packages/gql/src/topk-single-key.test.ts`, 25 tests. The oracle is the same question with the sort
key written TWICE (`ORDER BY s, s`), which the `orderBy.length === 1` gate refuses, so the generic
heap answers it — and duplicating a key cannot change the order OR the tie structure, so both paths
fall to the arrival-index tiebreak on exactly the same rows. A test asserts the rewrite really
produced two keys, because otherwise every case would be comparing the new heap with itself.

Six mutants under `timeout 300` + `MemoryMax=16G` `MemorySwapMax=0`, each on a restored copy. Four
caught at once: capping at `LIMIT` instead of `SKIP + LIMIT`, ignoring `descending` in the eviction
test, paging before the sort instead of after, and never evicting.

**M1 — dropping the arrival-index tiebreak from `lessAt` — SURVIVED**, on a fixture built with
heavy ties specifically to catch it. The reason is worth keeping: with ties and no eviction, `up`
never swaps (every comparison is equal), so the heap array stays in arrival order, and a comparator
returning 0 everywhere leaves a stable sort alone. The tiebreak only becomes observable once
evictions have PERMUTED the array. Added a fixture that forces that — `d = [9,9,9,2,2,2,5,5,2]`
with `LIMIT 3`, so the three 9s fill the heap and each 2 evicts a root and sifts down — and
projected the arrival index so the order is visible in the answer. M1 now fails four tests.

**M2 — dropping the same tiebreak from the eviction test only — survives, and is provably
equivalent.** It is consulted only when the keys tie, and a candidate always arrives after
everything already in the heap, so `i < ix[0]` is false exactly where `c < 0` is. Documented on the
line rather than chased.

That is the second fixture this session that looked like it covered a guard and did not (422 was
the first, for the Dict `present` mask), and both were found the same way. **"I wrote the fixture
for this guard" is not evidence the fixture exercises it; removing the guard is.**

### What made this item possible

424 is why this one took one tick. It had already established the floor, the comparator, the
per-row cost, the fact that allocation is not it, and the nine-rep requirement — so this pass went
straight to the structural suspects with a measurement harness that could tell 1.34x from noise.
A refutation that records its numbers is not a dead end; it is the next item's instrument.

## 426 — a SKIP projects the rows it skips, in BOTH engines, against the engine's own stated rule. Found by an attribution probe, priced at 1.45x, and NOT changed

Item 425 left half its gap unattributed: 37 ms for `ORDER BY u LIMIT 5` against the `max(a.u)`
fold's 20.7 over the same rows. The attribution probe was two cases, and the second one was not
the question I asked.

```
ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 5        25.6 25.7 25.3    constant key: all ties, heap fills once, never evicts
ORDER BY u LIMIT 5        35.5 37.3 35.2    the real key and the real comparisons
SKIP 199995 LIMIT 5       48.8 50.0 51.3    the general stream, NO sort at all
```

Two things fall out. First the attribution: of the 35.5 ms, **25.6 is the general binding stream
plus the loop** — the key evaluation and 200,000 comparisons are the other ~10. So the rest of
425's gap is not the top-k's, it is the per-row `Binding` the general stream builds, which is item
377's long-standing item and not reachable from here. Also, the `max` fold is not a comparable
floor at all: since item 420 it runs on `detectNodeProjection`'s fused scan, a different
row-production path. **A floor measured on a different plan is not a floor.**

Second, and the reason this has its own item: **the unordered `SKIP` costs MORE than the sorted
top-k.** 48.8-51.3 ms against 35.5 — adding an `ORDER BY` makes the query **1.45x faster**. That is
the spelling asymmetry this repo is named after, and here it is not an oversight in the planner.

### Why, and why it is not an optimization

`applyProjection`'s generic tail maps every binding through `projectBinding` and pages the
PROJECTED rows. With a `SKIP` and no `ORDER BY` that projects all 200,000 to return five. The
ordered path does not: it keeps the top-k INPUT bindings and projects only the survivors, which is
exactly what item 145 built it to do.

So the obvious fix — page the bindings, then project — is a BEHAVIOUR change, because the
projection of a skipped row can fault. `skipcast_426` (committed) asks all four spellings of one
question over a fixture whose first node makes `CAST(a.s AS INTEGER)` fault:

```
RETURN CAST(a.s AS INTEGER) AS x                              FAULT   correct: row 0 is emitted
RETURN CAST(a.s AS INTEGER) AS x LIMIT 1                       FAULT   correct: row 0 is emitted
RETURN CAST(a.s AS INTEGER) AS x SKIP 1 LIMIT 1                FAULT   row 0 is NOT emitted
RETURN CAST(a.s AS INTEGER) AS x ORDER BY a.n SKIP 1 LIMIT 1   -> 1
```

The engine's own rule, written on the `LIMIT 0` branch, is **"project exactly the rows you emit"** —
`RETURN 1/(n.n - 7) AS x LIMIT 1` returns the first row rather than faulting on the second, in both
engines. The third line violates it and the fourth obeys it, so the two spellings disagree with
each other.

**Both engines agree on all four lines.** Checked natively, not assumed — same fixture, same four
queries, identical results including the `E_INVALID_VALUE` on line three. So this is a conformance
question against the engine's own stated rule, not a cross-engine divergence; making `SKIP` project
only what it emits would make TS diverge from native, which byte-identity forbids. It is the
project's decision, exactly as item 417's `inject`/`limit(0)` shape was, and for the same reason the
differential fuzzer could never have found it: **a differential fuzzer is structurally blind to a
bug both sides share.**

Nothing was changed. `skipcast_426` is committed so the next pass starts from a measurement, and
`examples/README.md` flags it as a conformance probe rather than a benchmark, to be run before
anyone touches paging in either engine.

### The route that WOULD be available inside the current semantics

A projection that cannot fault may be skipped unobservably, and the engine already has the shape of
that analysis (`rowLocal` / `itemLocal` decide whether an item reads only its own row). A
"cannot-fault" predicate is stricter — a bare property read and a variable reference cannot fault,
arithmetic over null yields null, but `CAST` can and so can the numeric-coercion paths — so it is a
conservative static check, not a rewrite. That is worth its own item at the 1.45x this measured; it
is not a change to make while the semantics question above is open, because the two fixes would
collide on exactly the rows that matter.

## 427 — a SKIP over a projection that cannot raise now skips the BINDINGS: 1.96-2.09x, landing on the floor 426 measured. Three mutants "survived" because the harness never applied them

Item 426 measured the cost of the current `SKIP` semantics (48.8-51.3 ms to return five rows out
of 200,000, MORE than the same query with an `ORDER BY`) and established that skipping
unconditionally is a behaviour change, because both engines fault on a skipped row's `CAST`. It
also named the route that is available inside those semantics: **a projection that cannot raise may
be skipped unobservably.**

### What shipped

`CProjection.cannotFault`, computed once at compile time from a deliberately tiny STRUCTURAL
allowlist — a bare variable reference, a single-level property read (`a.k`, which yields null for
an absent key) and a literal, plus `RETURN *`, which copies binding entries. A shape qualifies
because of what it IS, not because of an analysis of what it contains, so a new `Expr` arm cannot
be admitted by accident. Everything else is assumed to fault: `CAST` does, arithmetic over a
non-number does, a cross-type temporal comparison does, a function or subquery may.

`pagedFaultFreeRows` then skips the bindings and projects only the page, for an unordered,
non-distinct, non-aggregating projection with a positive `SKIP`.

Three alternated rounds, nine reps, isolated per process:

```
                           OLD                  NEW                ratio
skip fault-free     48.6 49.7 52.4       25.1 27.2 25.3           1.96x
skip, no LIMIT      52.5                 25.1                     2.09x
skip, two props     53.6                 25.6                     2.09x
skip, RETURN *      43.5                 25.3                     1.72x
C skip arith (refused)  52.3 56.8 59.0   57.8 54.5 52.4           flat
C skip DISTINCT (refused)  161.6         150.8                     flat
C order u LIMIT 5 (top-k)   36.3         36.0                     flat
C project u (no paging)      6.7          6.0                     flat
```

Every variant lands at **25.1-25.6 ms, which is exactly the 25.6 ms general-stream floor item 426
measured with a constant sort key** — so this is not a partial win, it is the whole of the
projection overhead removed. The best control is `RETURN a.k + 0 AS s SKIP …`: arithmetic, which
the allowlist refuses, so it still runs the generic tail and would catch a tax levied on it.

The invariant is pinned first in the test file, not last: `CAST(a.s AS INTEGER) AS x SKIP 1 LIMIT 1`
must still fault, because native does. Checked before and after.

Extracted into a module-scope helper rather than written inline, because the complexity cap
objected at **38 against a limit of 35** — the same cap that was right to object at item 377, and
the same answer: the branch's six conditions become one call. The hot loop is still one loop over
`bindings` and the helper is called once per query, so neither of item 159's effects applies.

### Three mutants "survived" because the harness never applied them

Six mutants, each on a restored copy under `timeout 300` + `MemoryMax=16G` `MemorySwapMax=0`. The
first pass reported M1 and M3 caught and **M2, M4, M5 and M6 SURVIVED** — and one line of harness
output, easy to scroll past, read `Can't open $F: No such file or directory`. A `$F` inside a
double-quoted `perl` block had been expanded by the shell before `perl` saw it, so that mutant was
never written to the file. A second pass that **compares the file against the pristine copy before
believing any verdict** found M4 and M5 had not applied either:

```
M1 gate always true        caught      THE invariant: a faulting projection gets skipped
M2 admit `arith`           caught      only after the fixture was fixed — see below
M3 drop the DISTINCT guard caught      pages before the dedup
M4 drop the ORDER BY guard caught      an ordered SKIP with no LIMIT pages unsorted
M5 LIMIT before SKIP       caught      the wrong page
M6 drop `!aggregating`     SURVIVED    provably equivalent
```

Item 398 recorded that a harness reporting a false CAUGHT reads as teeth. **This is the mirror: a
harness reporting a false SURVIVED reads as a missing test, and sends you to write one that was
never needed.** The applied-check is three lines (`cmp -s pristine current` → "NOT APPLIED") and it
belongs in every mutation script from here.

M6 is genuinely equivalent: every aggregate is an `Expr` of kind `func`, which the allowlist
refuses, so an aggregating projection cannot reach the branch. The guard stays and says so.

### And the third fixture this session that did not exercise its guard

M2 (admitting `arith` to the allowlist) survived even once applied. The test asserted that
`a.s + 1 AS x SKIP 1 LIMIT 1` throws — and it does, either way: `s` is a string on EVERY node, so
the arithmetic faults on whichever row is projected. The fixture could not tell "the skipped row
faulted" from "the emitted row faulted". Added `m`, a string on the first node and a number on all
the others, so the faulting row is exactly the row the SKIP steps over. M2 now fails.

Items 422 (the Dict `present` mask), 425 (the top-k tiebreak) and this one are three fixtures in
one session that looked like they exercised a guard and did not, all three found by removing the
guard. **The fixture has to make the guard's absence CHANGE AN ANSWER, and "I wrote it for this
guard" is not evidence that it does.**

## 428 — the native paging twin is REFUTED (it already pages lazily), and the measurement corrects item 427's own claim: that win is DEEP pages only

Item 427 closed a 1.96-2.09x on the TS side by skipping bindings where the projection cannot
raise. The method says to ask the same question of the other engine, so `skippage_428` asks it with
the unpaged projection as a ceiling and `count(*)` as a floor, at 1,000,000 nodes, min of 5:

```
T skip to the end (SKIP n-5 LIMIT 5)      2.556ms    5 rows
T skip, no limit                          2.579      5 rows
T skip, two props                         4.884      5 rows
T SHALLOW page (SKIP 100 LIMIT 20)        0.001     20 rows
C ordered top-k                           9.497      5 rows
C project all                            10.403  1,000,000 rows   the ceiling
C limit 5 only                            0.000      5 rows
C count(*)                                0.000      1 row
```

**Native has no gap.** The deep skip sits 4x BELOW the projection ceiling, and the shallow page —
what a paged UI actually asks — costs 0.001 ms, because the input stream is paged lazily. The 2.556
ms is the unavoidable walk of a million inputs, not the projection of skipped rows. The
width-dependence (2.556 for one property, 4.884 for two) is the input stream carrying two columns,
not per-row projection: if skipped rows were being projected, the figure would be at or above the
10.403 ms ceiling.

### The part that corrects item 427

If native's shallow page is free, the obvious next question is whether TS's ever was not. Measured
both sides of 427's change:

```
TS shallow page (SKIP 100 LIMIT 20)   pristine 0.2 0.2 ms    new 0.1 0.2 ms
```

**It was always cheap.** `skip` and `take` are lazy generators, so a shallow page stopped after
~120 bindings before item 427 as well. Item 427's targets were all `SKIP 199995` out of 200,000 —
every one of them a DEEP page — and its entry says "1.96-2.09x on four shapes" without saying so.

The scope is still worth having: offset pagination deep into a large set and export cursors are
real patterns, and the fix costs nothing on anything else. But the claim as written would let a
reader believe `SKIP 100 LIMIT 20` got 2x faster, and it did not. **A ratio is only as good as the
shape it was measured on, and "four shapes" that share a parameter value is one shape.** Recorded
here and in `CLOSED.md` beside 427's own line rather than edited into it, which is how this file
works.

### What the comparison DOES say

Walking a row costs native **2.6 ns** and TS about **125 ns** — 25.1 ms for 200,000 bindings
(item 426's constant-key floor, and item 427's landing point) against native's 2.556 ms for
1,000,000. That is a 48x gap on the plainest possible operation, and it is item 377's per-row
`Binding` priced on a third independent shape. No new target: 377 is open, named, and bigger than
anything paging-shaped.

## 429 — the chain sweep flipped for a GATE but never for a LABEL: 4.26x at four hops, 3.09x at five. Found by running the probe the repo mandates, which I had skipped through four planner changes

Five TS planner changes this session (409/410, 418, 420, 425, 427) and I had not run `bun run
spelling`, which this repo requires precisely when a predicate or projection form is added. Running
it at the documented `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9` reported `0 group(s) disagree on the ANSWER` and
one over-2x group that `CLOSED.md` already records as a deliberate guard — so by the probe's own
flags, nothing.

Two rows UNDER its 2x threshold were the find:

```
four hops: forward vs the reversed arrows (item 290)
   478.76ms  MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)-[:E]->(d)-[:E]->(x) RETURN count(*)
   710.86ms  MATCH (x)<-[:E]-(d)<-[:E]-(c)<-[:E]-(b)<-[:E]-(a:P) RETURN count(*)   1.49x
five hops (item 298)
   674.42ms  forward
   856.73ms  reversed                                                              1.27x
```

One question, two spellings, and the probe's threshold is 2x. **A probe's threshold is a budget for
what it will interrupt you about, not a claim that everything under it is fine** — the rows were
printed every time and nobody read them.

### The cause

`detectNhopSweepCount` already reads a chain backwards, and its own comment says why: a gate on the
last position needs a pass of its own and every pass before it runs over an unnarrowed frontier. But
the condition was `allGates[hops] !== undefined && allGates[0] === undefined` — gates only. A
**LABEL** on the last position narrows the seed exactly as a gate does, and it was invisible to the
test, so the reversed spelling seeded every vertex where the forward one seeded the `:P` bucket.

### What shipped

The flip is now decided PER CALL when neither end is gated and the end carries a label:
`candidateCount(graph, endLabel) < candidateCount(graph, startLabel)`. That is `hopDrivesFar`'s
question and its reasoning carries over — `candidateCount` returns the whole graph for a label it
cannot seed from, so the STRICT comparison also establishes the end label is seekable, and a tie
keeps the forward reading because the two orders intern vertices differently and churning that for
no gain is churn. Both leg arrays are built once at compile time and the per-call choice picks
between two ready objects; building legs inside the closure would put allocation on every call.

Three alternated rounds, nine reps, one shape per process, 200,000 vertices of degree 3 with `:P`
on a tenth:

```
                      OLD                      NEW                  ratio
rev 4 hops     806.9 779.8 776.4        183.8 182.4 183.2          4.26x
rev 5 hops     928.0 908.9 911.1        291.8 295.8 295.2          3.09x
rev 3 hops    1164.7 1113.2 1168.6     1138.1 1139.1 1121.3        flat
C fwd 4 hops   178.8                    181.5                      flat
C fwd 5 hops   292.3                    293.9                      flat
C rev, vacuous end label  501.3         490.3                      flat
C rev, no end label       503.3         495.6                      flat
C rev, end GATED (item 308)  225.6      224.7                      flat
C fwd, end gated  318.7 315.9 307.9     310.8 313.9 309.2          flat
C one hop forward          1.4           1.1                       flat
```

The reversed spelling now lands on the forward one (183.2 against 181.5; 295.2 against 293.9),
which is the actual claim: not "faster" but **the same cost for the same question**. Every control
is a shape the new rule must decline — a vacuous end label (where `candidateCount` ties), no end
label, and the gated cases item 308 already owns — and all are flat. `fwd end gated` read 1.13x
worse on a single round and was flat over three.

**The probe that found it now shows parity**: four hops 475.44 against 477.05, five hops 618.43
against 621.42.

### Teeth: the tests police the CONSTRUCTION, the measurement polices the DECISION

Reading a fixed-length chain backwards is answer-preserving by construction, so **no test can catch
a wrong decision** — and mutation proves it: making the comparison non-strict leaves all 15 tests
green. The 4.26x is the only evidence the flip fires. What tests CAN catch is a wrongly BUILT
reversal, and five mutants do:

```
M1 direction not negated        caught
M2 label on the wrong position  caught
M3 gate on the wrong position   caught
M4 leg ORDER not reversed       caught — after TWO fixture fixes
M5 seeds the wrong end          caught
M6 non-strict comparison        SURVIVED, equivalent by construction
```

M4 took three attempts and both failures were the fixture, not the mutant:

1. `:A` and `:D` had four vertices each, so `candidateCount` TIED and the strict comparison
   declined — the cases with labels at every position never exercised the reversal at all. Tiers
   are now different sizes with `:A` smallest. **A fixture for a cost-based decision has to make
   the decision FIRE, and that is a property of the data, not of the query text.**
2. The mixed-direction case read `out` flags false/true/false and the labelled one B/C/B — both
   PALINDROMIC, so reversing the leg order gave the identical sequence. Added non-palindromic
   cases.
3. And the real reason it kept surviving: every case was a **3-hop** chain, which does not reach
   this detector at all — `try_3hop_product_count` owns three segments, and the sweep starts at
   FOUR. A test for a 4+-hop path built entirely from 3-hop queries.

That is the fourth fixture this session that looked like it exercised a guard and did not (422,
425, 427), and the first where the reason was the _query_ being routed somewhere else entirely.
**Check which path answers your fixture, not just what it asserts.**

### Still open, found on the way

The reversed 3-hop chain costs **1113-1168 ms against the forward spelling's 346-348** — 3.3x, on
the same fixture and the same question, and this change does not touch it because
`try_3hop_product_count` owns that shape. Its own item: the 3-hop product has a different
structure from the sweep, so whether it can seed from the cheaper end is a separate question with
a separate answer.

## 430 — the 3-hop chain's end LABEL sent it to a degree product with nowhere to test it: 11.8x reversed, 3.67x forward, both spellings now on 95 ms

Item 429 left this measured and unreached: the reversed 3-hop chain cost 1113-1168 ms against the
forward spelling's 346-348, and 429's flip could not help because a 3-segment chain never reaches
the sweep — `try_3hop_product_count`'s TS twin, `threeSegmentCount`, owns three segments and the
sweep starts at FOUR.

### Diagnosis, which split into two effects

```
3 hops, reversed, `:P` at the far end    1112 ms
3 hops, reversed, NO label                296        <- so the label costs 3.8x
3 hops, forward,  NO label                174        <- and direction alone costs 1.70x
3 hops, reversed, vacuous `:Univ`         299        <- a vacuous label costs nothing, as expected
3 hops, reversed, end GATED               127        <- item 306 already routes this to the sweep
```

Two independent effects, and the measurement separated them rather than my assuming one. The label
is the big one, and `longChainCount`'s own doc had already written the cause down: "Labels are
carried at every position too: the sweep VISITS each one, so there is a once-per-element place to
test it, **which is what the end positions of the degree products lack.**" Item 306 acted on that
for a GATE — "AN END CONSTRAINT ON A SHORT CHAIN GOES TO THE SWEEP, because it is the one position
they cannot carry" — and left the LABEL case on the product, which then enumerated to test it.

### What shipped

`threeSegmentRoute` builds both routes and chooses per call: the sweep when either end narrows the
seed, the product when neither does.

```
                                              product      routed      ratio
MATCH (d)<-[:E]-(c)<-[:E]-(b)<-[:E]-(a:P)      1128.6 ms    96.0 ms     11.8x
MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)-[:E]->(d)       346.3       95.5         3.67x
C reversed, vacuous `:Univ` on both ends        301.0      298.4        flat
C reversed, end GATED (item 306)                127.5      126.7        flat
C 4 hops (item 429's path)                      183.4      185.8        flat
C 5 hops                                        296.0      298.5        flat
C one hop                                         1.3        1.1        flat
```

Three alternated rounds on the two targets, disjoint, identical answers. **Both spellings now land
on ~95 ms**, which is the claim — not "faster" but one cost for one question — and that is also
3.67x better than the previous BEST spelling, so this is not only a symmetry fix.

The sweep is not unconditionally better here: item 301 measured the product winning the unfiltered
shape, 250.1 against 374.9 ms. So a tie keeps the product, and because `candidateCount` returns the
whole graph for a label it cannot seed from, "nothing narrows" and "a label we cannot use" collapse
to the same answer — the one item 301 measured.

Extracted to a module-scope helper because the caller tripped BOTH the complexity cap (41/35) and
max-statements (81/80) — the same objection items 377 and 427 answered the same way.

### The no-label control, and why its first reading was wrong

`3 hops forward, no label` first read 176.7 -> 234.1, a 1.32x regression on a shape the guard
cannot reach (`labelled` is false when neither end has a label, so the branch returns the product
untouched). Three alternated rounds: pristine 172.0/180.1/244.0 against 233.7/226.3/168.0 — **both
sides bimodal at ~170 and ~230**, item 424's trap for the third time this session. Overlapping, not
a regression.

### Teeth: the same division of labour as 429, now with the mutants to prove it

Four mutants, each verified applied first (item 427's rule):

```
M1 always take the sweep        SURVIVED   equivalent — both routes are correct
M2 always take the product      SURVIVED   equivalent
M4 comparison INVERTED          SURVIVED   equivalent
M3 drop the interiorPred guard  caught     a clause `WHERE` is LOST on the way to the sweep
```

Three of four survive because they are route choices between two correct implementations, which no
answer can distinguish — so **the comparison is justified by the measurements and by nothing else**,
and that is now written on the function. The one mutant that changes an answer is the one that
loses a predicate, and it is caught.

The oracle is worth keeping: `count(*) + 0` is an aggregate nested in arithmetic, which every count
shortcut refuses, so the general matcher answers it — measured at **620.5 ms against the shortcut's
138.6** on the 200,000-vertex fixture, which is how we know it is a different route and not the
same one wearing a hat. Twelve routing shapes are compared against it, including both vacuous
spellings, an interior inline gate, an interior clause `WHERE`, an end gate and mixed directions.

### Still open

The **1.70x direction asymmetry with NO label anywhere** (reversed 296 ms against forward 174) is
untouched and is its own question: it is the product walking in-adjacency rather than out, with
nothing to narrow either end, so neither the label rule here nor item 429's flip applies. Whether
that is inherent to how in-edges are stored or another missing symmetry needs its own measurement.

## 431 — the no-label direction asymmetry is NOT locality and NOT a TS quirk: it concentrates at exactly the depth the degree PRODUCT owns, in both engines, and native's is 4.67x

Item 430 left this open: a 3-hop chain count with no label anywhere costs 296 ms reversed against
174 forward, on the same fixture, and neither item 429's flip nor 430's label rule applies. Three
hypotheses were available — adjacency locality, a TS implementation quirk, or something structural
— and `chain-layout-probe` (committed, `bun run probe:layout`) separates them by varying ONE thing.

Two graphs, same node count, same edge count, same degree, differing only in where each edge
points: SCATTER sends `i` to a xorshift target, so each node's `from` bucket fills sequentially
while the `to` buckets fill in scattered order; RING sends `i` to `(i + 1 + d) % N`, so node `j`'s
in-edges come from `j-1, j-2, j-3` and BOTH adjacencies are near-sequential. 200,000 nodes, degree
3, one shape per process, min of 5, both engines over one shared edge list:

```
layout   shape       ts ms          native ms       ts ratio   native ratio
scatter  2 hops   75.5 / 73.6      3.1 / 4.4         1.03x        1.42x
scatter  3 hops  170.3 / 289.3     3.3 / 15.4        1.70x        4.67x
scatter  4 hops  414.8 / 532.2     4.5 / 7.2         1.28x        1.60x
ring     2 hops   40.1 / 38.8      1.9 / 2.1         0.97x        1.11x
ring     3 hops   49.3 / 60.4      3.2 / 6.6         1.23x        2.06x
ring     4 hops  166.6 / 186.4     4.1 / 4.1         1.12x        1.00x
```

Three things fall out, and none of them is the hypothesis I started with.

**It is not locality.** The layout halves the magnitude everywhere — TS's 3-hop forward goes 170.3
to 49.3 for the identical query and the identical graph SIZE, which is a 3.5x that belongs entirely
to the data — but the 3-hop asymmetry SURVIVES it, 1.23x in TS and 2.06x in native. Locality
explains part of the cost and none of the shape.

**It is not a TS quirk.** Native has the same asymmetry and a BIGGER ratio: 4.67x against TS's 1.70x
on the scatter layout, 2.06x against 1.23x on the ring. Measured through the same probe over one
shared edge list, so the two cannot disagree about the fixture.

**It concentrates at THREE hops, in both engines.** 2 hops is 1.03x/1.42x and 4 hops is 1.28x/1.60x
(and 1.00x on the ring, perfectly symmetric), while 3 hops is 1.70x/4.67x. Three segments is the
ONLY depth answered by the degree PRODUCT — two hops has its own tuned walk (items 206, 218-222)
and four or more is the sweep (item 301) — so **the product is the direction-asymmetric operator**,
and the depth at which the asymmetry peaks is the depth it owns. That is a located target, not a
property of the data.

### What this corrects

Item 430 reported "1.68x already at TWO hops" and inferred a per-edge cost. That reading was **case
order**: all four shapes ran in one process behind a 1-hop warmup, which has a count shortcut and
so warms nothing, and the 2-hop pair SWAPPED which side was slower between two runs of the same
binary (40.9/68.6 one way, 68.8/42.8 the other). Isolated per process, 2 hops is 1.03x — no
asymmetry at all. Fourth occurrence of this mechanism this session (420, 421, 423) and the first
where it manufactured a _direction_ rather than a magnitude.

### Why this is its own probe

`chain-depth-probe` already sweeps depth to eleven hops in both engines and already has a
`reversed` spelling, so it was the obvious host — and it is the wrong one: 200 nodes at degree 5 is
entirely cache-resident, so it cannot show a locality effect, and the repo's own rule is that
cache-resident and not are different questions with the transition between 200k and 1M. Different
question, different size, different probe — and the depth probe stays small, which is what lets it
reach eleven hops.

### Next

Native's 3.3 -> 15.4 ms is the bigger ratio and the cheaper fix to verify, so the native degree
product is where this goes next. The TS side is the same question with a 1.70x prize and the same
diagnosis already in hand.

## 432 — the native 3-hop product was out-only because a COMMENT said its identity "really does want one orientation". It does not: 2.68x reversed, 3.41x mixed, and all eight direction combinations now take it

Item 431 located the chain direction asymmetry on the degree PRODUCT — the only depth native
answers that way — and priced native's at 4.67x, the bigger of the two engines. The cause is one
line in `peel_out_hops`:

```rust
let Plan::Expand { input, from, dir: Dir::Out, .. } = plan else { return None };
```

So a reversed chain declined the product outright and fell to the enumerate-and-tally path. And
the reason it was out-only was written down, on `try_nhop_sweep_count`'s own peel:

> A per-hop direction is also why this peel is its own function rather than a generalization of
> `peel_out_hops`: **the 3-hop product's identity really does want one orientation**, since its
> `level1`/`outdeg3` arrays are both built from `store.out`.

That is an observation about the CODE mistaken for one about the identity. The product is

```text
total = SUM over hop-2 edges (b - c) of   level1[b] x deg3(c)
```

and each of the three terms reads a DIFFERENT hop's adjacency — `level1` hop 1's, the middle loop
hop 2's, `deg3` hop 3's. Nothing ties them to each other, so each may independently be `out` or
`inc`. The two arrays both being built from `store.out` was a fact about which queries the peel
admitted, not a constraint. The comment is corrected in place.

### What shipped

`peel_dir_hops` replaces `peel_out_hops` (which had no other caller) and reports a direction per
hop; the product picks `store.out` or `store.inc` per level. `Dir::Both` still declines — one edge
can be walked two ways, so an undirected chain is not a chain of fixed steps.

Three alternated rounds, each side REBUILT with `--features capi`, min of 5, 200,000 nodes at
degree 3, scatter layout:

```
                       OLD (native)        NEW (native)      ratio
3 hops, all `in`     15.8 15.6 15.4      5.8 5.8 5.8        2.68x
3 hops, `-> <- ->`   14.0 14.0           4.1 4.1            3.41x
3 hops, `-> -> <-`    7.4  7.4  7.4      4.1 4.2 4.1        1.80x
C 3 hops, all `out`   3.4  3.4  3.4      3.3 3.5 3.3        flat
C 2 hops `in`         4.3  4.4           4.3 4.3            flat
C 2 hops `out`        3.0  3.1           3.1 3.1            flat
C 4 hops `in`         7.2  7.3           7.1 7.1            flat
C 4 hops `out`        4.6  4.6           4.5 4.6            flat
```

The mixed cases are a NEW capability, not a reordering: before this they declined the product
outright. And on the RING layout the reversed 3-hop is now 3.2 ms against the forward's 3.1 —
**symmetric**, which is exactly what item 431's ring control predicted: with the routing fixed, what
remains on the scatter layout (5.8 against 3.4) is the locality of reading `inc` buckets that were
filled in scattered order, and nothing else.

2 and 4 hops are flat because the product is 3-hop only; they are the controls that say so.

### The test compared the product with ITSELF, and all five mutants survived

First mutation run: **five of five SURVIVED**, against a test asserting that all 32 combinations
(8 directions x 4 label/type variants) agree with `count(*) + 0` — the oracle that worked for the
TS engine, where it is 620.5 ms against the shortcut's 138.6 and so demonstrably a different route.

An `eprintln` at the product's entry showed it firing **8 times per direction pattern** where 4 was
expected: `count(*) + 0` takes the product in NATIVE. So the oracle was the same path, the test
compared the product with itself, and nothing could fail. `count(d)` also fires it. `count(d.k)`
does not — and every node in the fixture carries `k`, so it counts the same rows.

With the real oracle, four of five are caught: hop 1, hop 2 or hop 3 forced to `out`, and the three
directions taken in the wrong order. The fifth — admitting `Dir::Both` — still survived, because
every hop in the 8-way loop is directed; four undirected shapes were added and it now fails
loudly (28 against 53).

**An oracle is a property of the ENGINE, not of the query text.** `count(*) + 0` is a different
route in one engine and the same route in the other, and I carried the TS result across without
checking. Item 371's rule is "verify the dispatch reaches the function"; this is its mirror —
**verify the oracle does NOT.** The trace that settles it is three lines and should be the first
thing written, not the last.

### Also: the `.so` trap, once

Four `cargo build --release` invocations without `--features capi` left
`target/release/liblenke_engine.so` with no FFI symbols, and the next probe run failed four times
with `exited with code 1`. `CLAUDE.md` records exactly this. The A/B script now builds every side
with the flag, and says why.

## 433 — the TS half of item 431 is REFUTED: its product already carried per-hop directions, so the TS engine was the reference native was missing. Both engines now converge on the same residual, which is the data

Item 432 fixed native's half of the chain direction asymmetry and left the TS half open with "same
diagnosis, same fix shape". That was a guess, and it was wrong.

`buildThreeHopCount` in `shortcuts.ts`:

```ts
const toAOut = s1.rel.direction === 'in';
const fromDOut = s3.rel.direction === 'out';
const midOut = s2.rel.direction === 'out';
...
const midIndex = midOut ? graph.edgesFromByLabel : graph.edgesToByLabel;
```

**Per-hop directions, already there** — one per leg, exactly the generalization item 432 had to
make in Rust. `longChainCount`'s own doc even says when: "the pure-TS sweep, which has carried
per-hop directions since item 298". So the TS product was never out-only and there is no missing
path on that side.

### What is left, measured on both engines

Three rounds each, one shape per process, 200,000 nodes at degree 3, after 432:

```
layout   shape       ts ms (3 rounds)        native ms      ts ratio   native ratio
scatter  3hop fwd   219.5 224.4 165.6        3.3 3.3 3.3
scatter  3hop rev   296.2 285.3 288.8        5.8 5.8 5.8     ~1.32x      1.76x
ring     3hop fwd    54.1  51.8  50.9        3.1 3.0 3.0
ring     3hop rev    59.8  59.2  58.1        3.1 3.1 3.1      1.14x      1.03x
```

**On the RING layout both engines are symmetric** — native 1.03x, TS 1.14x — and on SCATTER both
keep an asymmetry. So after 432 the residual in both is the same thing: reading `inc` buckets that
were filled in scattered order, which item 431's ring control isolated before either fix.

The TS ratio is quoted as "~1.32x" deliberately: its forward column reads 219.5/224.4/165.6, the
bimodality item 424 recorded, so anything between ~1.3x and ~1.75x is consistent with the data.
Native's column is 3.3/3.3/3.3 against 5.8/5.8/5.8 and needs no hedge — which is itself worth
noting, because the quiet engine is the one whose numbers can be trusted at this resolution.

### What this closes, and the part worth keeping

Item 431 found one asymmetry and it had **two different causes, one per engine**: native was
missing a path (fixed at 432) and TS never was. The symmetric-on-ring result is the evidence that
nothing is left but the layout, in both.

And the direction of the lesson is unusual enough to record: **the TS engine was the reference and
the Rust engine was behind it**, for twelve items' worth of time, and a comment on the Rust side
explained why the generalization was impossible while the TS side had been doing it since item 298.
The session's habit is to fix TS and then ask native the same question; here the question should
have gone the other way. **When one engine declines a shape the other accepts, the one that accepts
it is the specification** — not a second opinion to be confirmed.

Nothing changed in either engine.

## 434 — an instrument for item 433's lesson, and its first answer is a negative: no shape in 25 has native below the band once FFI EGRESS is taken out (58-94 ns a row, measured)

Item 433's finding was that the TS engine had carried a capability the Rust one declined, with a
comment on the Rust side explaining why it could not, and that twelve items passed before anyone
looked — because the habit is to fix TS and then ask native the same question. The instrument that
would have caught it in one run is to time the SAME shape on both engines and read the RATIO:
`CLAUDE.md` puts the normal band at "the Rust core is 1.5-4x pure-TS", a shortcut native has and TS
lacks pushes it far above (the 3-hop count runs 380x), so **the rows worth reading are the ones
where native is barely ahead or behind.**

`engine-gap-probe` (`bun run probe:gap`) does that over 25 shapes — counts, scan and hop
aggregates, projections, `ORDER BY … LIMIT`, a deep `SKIP`, DISTINCT, grouped counts, `EXISTS`, an
equality seek, a range, a 2-hop count, a var-length reach — at 50,000 nodes and degree 3, over one
shared edge list, with every answer compared.

### Three rows came in below the band, and all three are the harness

```
scan project  (5,000 rows)   ts 0.2 ms   native 0.53   0.5x
hop project  (15,000 rows)   ts 2.0      native 1.70   1.2x
node count       (1 row)     ts 0.0      native 0.00   0.5x
```

The first two look like exactly the find item 433 predicted. They are not. Three added rows do the
SAME scan work and differ only in how many rows leave the engine:

```
egress 1 row    MATCH (a:P) RETURN count(a.u)   native 0.01 ms
egress 5k num   MATCH (a:P) RETURN a.k          native 0.33      ->  58 ns a row
egress 5k str   MATCH (a:P) RETURN a.u          native 0.48      ->  94 ns a row
```

Native's scan is **0.01 ms** and everything above it is egress: crossing the FFI boundary and
building a JS object per row, which the TS engine never pays because it hands back objects it
already had. So a multi-row shape's ratio measures the harness, and the probe now marks those rows
`*` rather than inviting them to be read. The third row, `node count`, is a shortcut on both sides
reading 0.0 against 0.00 — a meaningless 0.5x, now marked `~` for "too fast to compare", because
presented unmarked it is a row someone would chase.

### What is left

Among the shapes whose ratio can be read, the lowest is **13.6x** (`varlen reach`) and the rest run
to 380x. **Nothing is below the 1.5-4x band**, so this shape set holds no native-missing-path
candidate of item 432's kind. A negative result, which is the useful kind here: the screen is cheap
and the next pass can extend the shape list rather than re-derive the method.

### What the egress number is worth on its own

58 ns a numeric row and 94 ns a string row is the FLOOR for any native query that returns many
rows, independent of how fast the query is — 5,000 rows cost 0.33 ms to hand over against 0.01 ms
to compute. That is the measurement behind `queryArrowIpc` existing at all, and the practical rule
it implies for this repo: **compare the two engines on AGGREGATE shapes, or through Arrow — never
on row-returning shapes through the object API**, because the row count then sets the result.

Also, for anyone reading the table: it runs every shape in ONE process, so the TS column carries
item 424's bimodality and a 30% difference in it means nothing. It is a screen. Any row it flags
gets a one-shape-per-process run before it is believed — which is how items 420, 421, 423 and 431
each went wrong in the other direction.

## 435 — `ANY SHORTEST` dropped the endpoint's LABEL in the native engine: a wrong answer, found by a perf screen, fixed by calling the helper that already existed

Item 434's gap screen covered 25 shapes and found no perf candidate. Extending it into the
families it had missed — undirected hops, self-joins, var-length, `ANY SHORTEST`, `CALL`, UNION,
CASE, coalesce, string functions, arithmetic predicates, `IN`, `IS NULL`, stddev, percentile — put
one row in the ANSWER-disagreement column:

```
shortest   ts 2537.7 ms   native 51.77   49.0x   NO
```

The screen compares answers because it costs nothing to, and that is the only reason this was
seen at all.

### What it was

```
MATCH ANY SHORTEST (a:P)-[:E]->{1,3}(b:P) RETURN b.i
  ts     [{bi:3}]                                  correct: only v3 is a reachable `:P`
  native [{bi:1},{bi:4},{bi:2},{bi:5},{bi:3}]       every reachable node
```

Native answered the labelled query as if the label were absent — its output for `(b:P)` is exactly
its output for `(b)`. The same pattern WITHOUT the selector filters correctly in both engines,
which is the oracle that says which answer is right. The lowering said so in as many words:

> // Endpoint node at slot 1: inline props filter it; **its label is ignored** (as
> // for any landing node in this subset).

And `landing_label_filter` — "The label predicate for a NON-seed node (a landing node — it has no
`Scan` to carry a seed label, so the WHOLE label constraint is a filter)" — is the helper for
exactly this case, and was never called. The fix is that call.

A post-filter is the right place as well as the right answer: `ShortestPath` emits one
representative per reachable target at its shortest distance, so dropping the non-matching targets
afterwards leaves each survivor at that same distance, which is what `ANY SHORTEST … (b:L)` asks
for. Restricting the BFS instead would compute the same set.

Verified against the TS engine as MULTISETS (row order is unspecified) at 50, 200 and 1,000 nodes
over five shapes including a grouped projection and a trailing `WHERE`: all agree. The two
remaining string-inequalities in the first check were row ORDER only — `[1,2,3,4,5]` against
`[1,4,2,5,3]` — which is this engine's documented policy, and comparing with `===` was my error,
not the engine's.

### Why nothing caught it

- **The differential fuzzer generates no quantified paths** — already recorded as a known gap, and
  this is what living in that gap costs.
- **Four hand-built reproducers agreed before the fix.** A diamond, a self-loop, a 2-cycle and a
  triangle all matched, because every node in them was `:P` — and a vacuous label is one you can
  drop for free. The bug needs a graph where only SOME nodes carry the endpoint label, which the
  50,000-node screen fixture had and my minimisations did not. I spent three rounds hunting a
  size threshold that did not exist.
- And the size sweep that "found" one was reading the same thing: it diverged at N=50 too, and the
  ratio tracked the `:P` fraction (1 in 10), which is what pointed at the label.

### Teeth, and the fixture lesson for the fifth time

Two mutants, each verified applied. Filtering **slot 0 instead of slot 1** is caught. Dropping the
**compound-label arm** (`vb_le`) survived at first — because the compound case I wrote was `:P|Q`,
and every node in the fixture is a `:P` or a `:Q`. `:P|R`, with no `:R` in the graph, must give the
same answer as `:P` alone; it now fails the mutant.

That is the fifth fixture this session that looked like it exercised a guard and did not (422, 425,
427, 429), and the shortest statement of the rule is the one this item earned: **every label and
predicate in a fixture must EXCLUDE something, or it tests nothing.** Vacuity is the common thread
in all five.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1130 + 13 + 723, `rewrite_fuzz` at 50k seeds, `clippy -D warnings` 0, `cargo fmt
--check` 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, `bun run check` 0. The fuzzers passing is worth
noting rather than assuming: this changes ANSWERS, and it changes them toward the TS engine, so
byte-identity could only improve — but "could only improve" is a prediction, and they were run.

## 436 — an aggregate nested inside a scalar function was a PARSE ERROR in native and an answer in TS: `peek_agg` looks at the item's first token

Item 434's screen reported one more thing beside item 435's wrong answer: `size(collect(a.k))`
failed on the native side with ``unknown function `collect` ``. The name was a red herring —
`collect(a.k)` on its own works in both engines. It is the NESTING that failed, and it failed for
every scalar function:

```
                              ts            native
abs(min(a.k))                 1             unknown function `min`
abs(min(a.k) - 10)            11            unknown function `min`
coalesce(max(a.k), 0)         1             unknown function `max`
size(collect(a.k))            3             unknown function `collect`
abs(count(*))                 3             expected an expression, got Some(Star)
max(a.k) + 1                  2             2                        <- works
```

### The cause, and why arithmetic was fine

The return-item parser asks `peek_agg()`, which looks at the item's **first token**:

```rust
let item = if let Some(func) = self.peek_agg() {
    …parse the aggregate; if an OPERATOR follows, re-parse with hoisting into an `AggExpr`…
} else {
    let e = self.expr()?;   // `abs(min(a.k))` lands here, and `min` is not a scalar function
    RetItem::Key(name, e)
};
```

So `max(a.k) + 1` works — it starts with an aggregate, and the operator sends it down the hoisting
path — while `abs(min(a.k))` starts with `abs` and never reaches hoisting at all. The machinery was
there; the switch was in the wrong place.

Hoisting is now enabled for every item and the result is an `AggExpr` only when something was
actually hoisted. For an item with no aggregate, `having_aggs` comes back empty and the item is a
plain `Key` — byte-for-byte what it was, which is the whole claim about the change being inert
where it does not apply.

All six spellings now agree with TS, including `abs(count(*))`, which had failed with a different
error and so was pinned separately. Two-deep nesting (`abs(coalesce(min(a.k), 0))`) agrees too.

### Teeth

`exec::tests::an_aggregate_nested_in_a_scalar_function_parses`, with `k` at -1, 0, 1 so `abs` has
something to do — a fixture whose minimum was already positive would let `abs` be dropped for
free, which is item 435's vacuity lesson applied before the fact for once.

Two mutants, each verified applied:

- **always return `AggExpr`**, even with no aggregates hoisted — caught. This is the one that
  matters: it would collapse every plain projection into one group, and the test asserts
  `MATCH (a:P) RETURN a.k` still returns a ROW PER NODE rather than a count of them.
- **drop the hoisting enable** — caught (back to the original error).

Controls in the test itself: `max(a.k) + 1` (the path that already worked), a bare `count(*)`, a
scalar function with no aggregate, and the row-per-node assertion.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1131 + 13 + 723, `rewrite_fuzz` at 50k seeds, `clippy -D warnings` 0, `cargo fmt` 0,
all seven byte-identity fuzzers, `bun run check` 0. This one touches the parser on EVERY return
item, so the full set is the point rather than a formality.

### What the screen has produced so far

Item 434's gap probe was built to find a perf asymmetry and has now found two correctness
divergences instead (435's dropped label, and this), and no perf candidate. **Comparing answers
while you time things costs nothing and has been worth more than the timings.** The screen's
remaining signal — CASE, coalesce and arithmetic predicates sitting at the bottom of the ratio band
at 2.3-5.2x — is still unexamined and is a perf question.

## 437 — a single arithmetic node in a filter costs 5.7x and a `coalesce` 21x, at IDENTICAL selectivity: the fused fast path matches a fixed list of `Expr` shapes and everything else materializes a column per node

Item 434's screen left one perf lead: CASE, coalesce and arithmetic predicates sat at 2.3-5.2x
against TS where everything else ran 13-380x. Those were three different query SHAPES, so the
screen could not say whether native is slow on them or TS is fast. `exprpred_437` asks it properly
— filtered `count(*)` over the same rows, with predicates differing only in the EXPRESSION, and
each pair chosen so the SELECTIVITY is identical:

```
                                     200,000       1,000,000     rows selected
a.k > 5                               0.365 ms      1.662 ms        90,908
a.k + 0 > 5                           2.087         9.902           90,908     5.7x / 6.0x
a.k * 1 > 5                           2.166        10.208           90,908     5.9x / 6.1x
abs(a.k) > 5                          2.169        10.212           90,908     5.9x / 6.1x
coalesce(a.k, 0) > 5                  7.815        37.636           90,908    21.4x / 22.6x
CASE WHEN a.k > 5 THEN true ELSE …    5.409        27.146           90,908    14.8x / 16.3x
a.k > 5 AND a.k < 100                 0.384         1.736           90,908     1.05x
a.k = 1                               0.187         0.843           18,182
NOT (a.k <> 1)                        0.186         0.848           18,182     1.00x
no predicate                          0.000         0.000
```

The row count is constant down each group, so **the gap is the expression and nothing else.** The
ratios hold at both sizes, which rules out a cache-residency effect.

### The mechanism, after two wrong guesses

`try_filter_keep` is a pattern matcher over `Expr` shapes — `Compare{Prop, Lit}` on a node or edge
column, `Not` of one (De Morgan'd), `And` of comparisons, a dict-column predicate — and each arm
reads the raw column in ONE fused pass and emits a keep-list, allocating no intermediate at all.
That is why `a.k > 5 AND a.k < 100` is free (1.05x) and `NOT (a.k <> 1)` is exactly its positive
form: both are in the list.

Everything else falls to `eval`, and I guessed twice about why that is slow before reading it:

- **Not a per-row tree walk.** `eval(expr, store, batch) -> Col` is COLUMNAR: it evaluates each
  expression node once over the whole batch.
- **Not boxing, either.** `Col` has typed `Num`/`Bool`/`Str` variants, `read_property` returns a
  raw `Col::Num` for a fully-present numeric column, and `arith_general` has a `(Col::Num, Col::Num)`
  raw-f64 arm. For this fixture all of that applies.

What is left is **materialization**: the general path builds one column per expression node —
`a.k` (200,000 f64), then `a.k + 0` (another), then the comparison (a `Col::Bool`), then the
keep-list — where the fast path makes a single pass and allocates nothing. Four passes and three
allocations against one pass and none is 5.7x, which is what was measured. `coalesce` is 21x
because it adds two more property columns and its per-cell path is not one of the typed arms.

### The fix, priced and not built

**Expression FUSION in the columnar evaluator** (or compiling an `Expr` to a closure, which is what
the TS engine does with `CompiledExpr` — item 433's lesson about which engine is the reference
applies here too). That is the real answer and it is a piece of work, not a tick; it is also the
deferred "eval-vs-columnar floor" question the bench README already records.

**A bounded partial is available and is the next tick's item**: add `Compare{Arith{Prop, Lit}, Lit}`
to `try_filter_keep`'s list, evaluating the arithmetic inline in the fused pass. That covers
`a.k * 2 > 10`, `a.k + 1 > 6`, `a.k / 2 < 3` — ordinary predicates, not the identity operations this
probe uses to hold selectivity fixed — at the 5.7x measured here. It is the same kind of arm
addition items 402 and 404 made to the seeding matcher.

What is NOT worth doing: constant folding. `a.k + 0 > 5` and `a.k * 1 > 5` fold to `a.k > 5` and
would make this probe's numbers vanish while buying nothing real, because `a.k * 2 > 10` cannot
fold soundly over floats. **The probe's cases are deliberately contrived to hold selectivity equal;
optimizing for the probe rather than the shape it stands in for would be measuring the instrument.**

## 438 — the fused arithmetic filter arm item 437 priced: 5.0x, landing on the plain comparison's cost, and the mutant that "fixes" a non-finite result is the one that would have diverged

Item 437 measured a single arithmetic node in a filter at 5.7x the equivalent plain comparison with
the selectivity held fixed, identified the cause as materialization (one column per expression
node, four passes and three allocations against one pass and none), named expression FUSION as the
real answer, and named this as the bounded partial: add the arithmetic shape to
`try_filter_keep`'s pattern list.

`try_filter_keep_arith` admits `<prop> <arith> <lit>  <cmp>  <lit>` — `a.k * 2 > 10`,
`5 - a.k >= 1`, `a.k + 1 <> 7` — in all three spellings (property either side of the arithmetic,
threshold either side of the comparison), evaluating the arithmetic inline in the keep pass.

Three alternated rounds, each side rebuilt, min of 5:

```
                        200,000                       1,000,000
                   OLD              NEW            OLD        NEW     ratio
a.k + 0 > 5     1.914/1.932/1.933  0.387/0.385/0.388   9.903   1.978   5.0x
a.k * 1 > 5     2.036/2.004/2.007  0.455/0.424/0.406  10.251   2.159   4.75x
C a.k > 5       0.330/0.333/0.333  0.299/0.304/0.301   1.690   1.558   flat
C a.k = 1       0.172 x3           0.173/0.175/0.174   0.854   0.857   flat
C NOT (a.k<>1)  0.171/0.172/0.172  0.170/0.173/0.174   0.853   0.858   flat
C abs(a.k) > 5  2.026/2.006/1.971  2.086/2.113/2.086  10.441  10.756   flat (declined)
C coalesce      7.099/6.950/6.928  7.077/7.230/7.049  38.358  38.562   flat (declined)
C case          4.828/4.958/4.948  4.895/4.975/6.159  27.602  28.262   flat (declined)
C two props     0.348/0.350/0.348  0.348/0.346/0.345   1.753   1.735   flat
```

The arithmetic cases now land ON the plain comparison (0.387 against 0.299), which is the claim:
the expression stopped costing anything beyond the pass it rides in. `abs`, `coalesce` and `CASE`
are the controls that matter most — the arm declines all three, and all three are flat, so nothing
was levied on the general path to pay for this.

### Semantics: three rules taken from the general path rather than from what looks right

- **No finiteness check on the result.** `arith_general`'s raw-f64 arm pushes `x + y` and does not
  test it, so an overflow to infinity is compared as infinity. The `Expr::Arith` doc says "any …
  non-finite operand OR result yields NULL", which describes the PER-CELL fallback, not the raw
  arm — and reading it as a general rule would have produced a divergence. The mutation run makes
  this concrete: **adding `if !y.is_finite() { continue; }` is CAUGHT**, and it is the change a
  careful reader of that doc would make.
- **A zero literal divisor DECLINES.** `arith_general` returns `Err("division by zero")`, and a
  fast path must not silently answer where the engine throws. `lit / a.k` declines outright,
  because the divisor is then a column and any row holding 0 would have to throw — which a
  keep-pass cannot express.
- **`present[i]` and the `u32::MAX` OPTIONAL-miss sentinel** are gated exactly as the plain
  comparison arm gates them.

### Teeth

`exec::tests::fused_arithmetic_filter_agrees_with_the_general_path`: **2,250 forms** — five
operators x five literals x six comparisons x five thresholds x three spellings — each compared
against the same predicate with a redundant `+ 0` wrapped round the arithmetic, whose outer operand
is an `Arith` rather than a `Prop` so the arm declines it and `eval` answers. Both sides throwing
counts as agreement, which is how the division-by-zero forms are compared. Plus explicit assertions
that `a.k / 0`, `a.k % 0` and `1 / a.k` still throw, and that `a.k * 2 > 1e308` keeps the one
overflowing row.

The fixture carries `1e308` for exactly one reason: without a value that large, `* 2` never
overflows and the finiteness divergence is unreachable — the vacuity lesson items 422/425/427/429/435
each paid for, applied in advance this time.

Four mutants, each verified applied: the division-by-zero decline, the operand order (so `5 - a.k`
is computed as `a.k - 5`), the `present` gate, and the finiteness guard. **All four caught.**

### What is still open

`abs`, `coalesce` and `CASE` are untouched at 5.9x, 21x and 15x. They are not more arm additions —
each would be another entry in a list that is always one spelling short, which is the argument
item 437 already made. The remaining answer is fusion (or compiling an `Expr` to a closure, which
is what the TS engine does), and that is unchanged by this item.

## 439 — the TS arithmetic-predicate gap is 1.91x, and the lift that would fix it COMPILES AND IS NEVER APPLIED. Reverted, because I measured before checking that it fires

Item 438 fixed the native filter's arithmetic gap (5.0x). Item 433's lesson is to ask the other
engine rather than assume which way a gap runs, so the same question went to TS — filtered
`count(*)`, same rows, predicates differing only in the expression, one shape per process, nine
reps (this engine is bimodal at three), selectivity held at 90,908 of 200,000:

```
a.k > 5                 5.21 ms
a.k + 0 > 5             9.96        1.91x
a.k * 1 > 5            10.33        1.98x
abs(a.k) > 5           14.30        2.74x
coalesce(a.k, 0) > 5   11.35        2.18x
a.k > 5 AND a.k < 100   5.50        1.06x   (free, as in native)
a.k = 1                 4.17
```

So TS has the same gap, much milder: **1.91x where native was 5.7x, and 2.18x where native was
21x.** The reason is the baseline, not the overhead — TS pays ~26 ns a row for the plain comparison
where native pays 1.65, so the same extra work is a far smaller fraction. The AND of two
comparisons being free in BOTH engines is the matching clue: lifting is what makes a comparison
cheap, and arithmetic falls off it in both.

### The fix that did not fire

TS's lift is `directEqProps`, which walks the AND-chain and requires every conjunct to be a bare
`<ownVar>.<key> <op> <const>`; anything else returns `null` for the WHOLE chain, so one arithmetic
conjunct costs the entire predicate its lifting. The symmetric fix is a `CArithProp` list — a
separate list, not a field on `CCmpProp`, which is the reasoning that type's own comment gives
about `eqProps` being the tuned path.

Built it: `asArithCompare` reading both operand orders and both comparison orders, carrying
