`propFirst` because `5 - a.k` is not `a.k - 5`, and applying it in `satisfies` through
`arithStep(op, ARITH[op], …)` — the same primitive `compileExpr`'s own `arith` arm calls, so the
lifted and generic forms cannot drift. 2,250 forms agreed with a `+ 0`-wrapped oracle, and all
2,117 package tests passed.

Three alternated rounds then showed **nothing**: `a.k + 0 > 5` pristine 10.71/9.74/10.45 against
new 7.42/10.45/10.68. A trace settled why — `LENKE_TRACE_ARITH` logged **"ARITH LIFT compiled" 8
times across three spellings and "ARITH LIFT applied" ZERO times.** The lift compiles; `satisfies`
never runs with it. These shapes are answered somewhere that does not consult the compiled
`CPredicate` at all.

**Reverted.** A path that is correct, willing and unreachable is item 418's lesson, and shipping
one is worse than shipping nothing: it reads as a fix in the diff and in `CLOSED.md` while the
query is answered elsewhere.

### The actual lesson, which cost three measurement rounds

Item 371's rule is **verify the dispatch reaches the function** — and I measured first, got a null
result, and only then instrumented. The trace is three lines and would have come before the A/B if
I had followed the rule I have been citing all session. Items 418 and 420 both checked firing
BEFORE measuring, with a committed test or a direct call; this one did not, and the cost was three
alternated rounds of a change that could not move anything.

### What is established, and what is not

ESTABLISHED: the gap's size (1.91x arithmetic, 2.18x `coalesce`, 2.74x `abs`), that it has the same
shape as native's, that it is milder because TS's per-row floor is 16x higher, and that
`directEqProps`/`satisfies` is NOT the path answering these shapes.

NOT established: which gate upstream declines, and therefore where the TS fix belongs. The next
pass starts by instrumenting that rather than by writing a lift — and should start from a trace, not
from a measurement.

## 440 — the trace item 439 should have started with, and it still does not reach a fix: `satisfies` IS the consumer, the rung IS the count shortcut, and the lift STILL arrives empty

Item 439 ended with "the lift compiles and is never applied" and an instruction to start the next
pass from a trace rather than a measurement. This is that pass. It produced no change, and the
reason it produced no change is worth as much as the finding would have been.

### Three traces, each answering one question

**Which rung answers it?** Instrumented all ten rungs of `takeShortcut`'s ladder plus the
fall-through. All three predicate forms — `a.k > 5`, `a.k + 0 > 5`, `abs(a.k) > 5` — print
`RUNG countShortcut`. So the 1.91x is INSIDE the count shortcut and is not a rung difference,
which was the first hypothesis and is now closed.

**What predicate does it apply?** Instrumented `satisfies` (the exported name of the function
carrying the `props`/`eqProps`/`cmpProps` loops) to print what each call receives:

```
a.k > 5       6 calls   eq=0 cmp=1 where=no      <- the lifted ordering comparison
a.k + 0 > 5   6 calls   eq=0 cmp=0 where=YES     <- the generic compiled closure
```

So `satisfies` IS the consumer, the count path DOES reach it, and the plain form IS lifted. That
makes item 439's null result more surprising rather than less — the lift looked reachable.

**Does the lift populate?** Re-applied item 439's `CArithProp` change with the `satisfies` trace in
place. The arithmetic form still arrives as **`arith=0 where=YES`**. So `directEqProps` does not
populate `arith` for the clause-`WHERE` spelling, even though item 439's trace showed the extractor
matching **8 times** across its three queries — which must have been the INLINE and projection
spellings, not this one.

### Where that leaves it

The count path calls `compilePredicate(undefined, where, start.variable)` — with an `ownVar`, so
`directEqProps` IS invoked with the proof it needs. And yet the arithmetic conjunct does not land
in `arith`. There are **at least eight** `compilePredicate` call sites in `shortcuts.ts` (lines
304, 409, 1999, 2087, 2805, 4328, 4602 and more), and the one serving this shape is not the one the
extractor matched. Finding which, and why, is the next step — and it is a reading task, not a
measuring one.

Everything is reverted; 2,117 tests pass unchanged.

### The lesson, which is the actual output of two ticks

Item 439 spent three alternated rounds measuring a change that could not move anything, and
concluded that item 371's rule ("verify the dispatch reaches the function") comes before the A/B.
This tick followed that — and still produced nothing, because **the trace needed three iterations
of its own**: the rung ladder (which ruled out the wrong hypothesis), then the wrong function, then
the right one. The rule needs a sharper form:

**Trace from the CONSUMER backwards, not from the candidate forwards.** Item 439 instrumented the
code it had just written (`asArithCompare`), which proved only that its own code ran. The question
worth asking first is what the hot loop RECEIVES — `satisfies` printing `cmp=1` against `where=YES`
is the whole diagnosis in one line, and it would have been available before a single line of the
lift was written.

Two ticks, no win, and the honest accounting is that the lift was written on an assumption about
which call site compiles the predicate — an assumption that a one-line trace would have refuted
in either of them.

## 441 — the thread is STOPPED after three ticks with no win. What four traces did establish, what they did not, and the instrumentation error that cost one of them

Item 440 said the next step was reading rather than measuring, and named "at least eight
`compilePredicate` call sites" as the open question. Four traces narrowed that a long way and still
did not reach a fix, so the thread stops here with an honest hand-off rather than a fourth tick.

### What is now established

**The call sites are three, not eight.** Instrumenting `compilePredicate` itself with a stack frame
(rather than its callers, which is the mistake below) shows both predicate forms going through
exactly three, all with `ownVar=a` and `kind=compare`:

```
compileNode       executor.ts:4142
patternCountOf    shortcuts.ts:1999
nodeWhereOf       shortcuts.ts:4328
```

**The count shortcut ANSWERS; it does not decline.** `countShortcut` returns rows for `a.k > 5`,
`a.k + 0 > 5` and `abs(a.k) > 5` alike.

**The extractor matches.** With item 439's lift re-applied and a trace on `asArithCompare`'s
operand check, the arithmetic form prints `kind=arith tail=1 otherConst=true` and returns on the
FIRST side (the second side never prints), at all three sites.

**And `satisfies` still receives `cmp=0 arith=0 where=YES`.** So a lifted predicate is produced at
every site that compiles one, the shortcut answers, and the object the hot loop applies carries the
generic closure instead. Those three facts have not been reconciled, and saying so is the point of
this entry — the alternative is a fourth tick of the same.

### The instrumentation error, which is the reusable part

Item 440's first trace printed `RUNG countShortcut` from inside `if (linear.countShortcut) {` —
**before** calling it. That reports WILLINGNESS, not the answer: the closure can still return
`undefined` and fall through. I then reasoned for most of a tick on the belief that the shortcut
might be declining, which this tick's trace (calling it and printing `ANSWERED` / `DECLINED at run
time`) refuted in one run.

Item 376 recorded the same class of error — "an instrument that covers PART of the dispatch reports
absence where it only has no coverage" — and item 418 recorded that a fast path can be "correct,
willing, and still unreachable". This is the third form: **an instrument placed at the GATE reports
willingness; only one placed on the RESULT reports the answer.** A one-line trace is not
automatically a good trace.

### Why the thread stops

Three ticks, no measurable change: item 439 wrote a lift and measured it (null), item 440 traced the
candidate (inconclusive), item 441 traced the consumer and the call sites (narrowed, still
inconclusive). The prize was 1.91x on one predicate shape — real, but the smallest of the targets
this session has shipped, and the loop's own rule is to retract what does not survive. Everything is
reverted; 2,117 tests pass unchanged.

**For whoever picks it up:** the three call sites above, the fact that the shortcut answers, and the
fact that `satisfies` gets `where=YES` while the extractor matched are the whole state. The next
question is which of the three preds `inlineHolds` actually applies, which is answerable by giving
each `compilePredicate` result an identity and printing it at both ends — the trace this tick
should have written instead of its third one.

## 442 — the write gap screen, and it found the session's cleanest target: `DETACH DELETE` is O(deleted x TOTAL NODES), because `delete_node` sweeps every label bucket

Item 434's gap screen covers 25 READ shapes. It had never been pointed at a write, so `INSERT`,
`SET`, `REMOVE`, `DELETE`, `DETACH DELETE` and `_MERGE` were an untouched family.

`write-gap-probe` (`bun run probe:writes`) rebuilds BOTH engines from the same NDJSON per case —
a write is not idempotent, so a case that mutated would change what the next one measured — and
names a verification READ per case, because a write's answer is the graph it leaves behind.

### The instrument was wrong twice before it said anything

First version timed construction and the write together, and all ten shapes came back between
3.1x and 4.0x. **A table whose rows all agree to within a third is usually measuring something
they have in common** — here, building 20,000 nodes and 40,000 edges per rep, which the write
barely moves. Second version still had the verification read inside the clock, which matters for
exactly one case (counting what is left after a delete). With both outside it:

```
SET one prop     ts  2.6 ms   native 0.34    7.8x    SET two props    3.3 / 0.61    5.4x
SET from a prop      2.0            0.35     5.7x    SET a new prop   2.1 / 0.35    6.1x
REMOVE a prop        1.9            0.31     6.3x    SET on an edge   8.0 / 0.47   16.9x
INSERT an edge       9.1            0.81    11.2x    DELETE edges     9.7 / 0.43   22.4x
DETACH DELETE       12.9            8.77     1.5x  <- the outlier
```

Native answers every other write in 0.31-0.81 ms and this one in 8.77. All ten verification reads
AGREE between the engines.

### Three sweeps, each varying one thing

```
A  deleted fixed at 2,000, EDGES 20k -> 160k:   9.372  9.791  9.157  9.314 ms   FLAT
B  edges fixed at 40,000, DELETED 200 -> 10,000: 4.34  4.35  4.33  4.30  4.38 us a node
C  controls, same fixture:  DELETE edges 0.345 ms,  SET 0.266 ms
D  deleted fixed at 1,000, NODES 5k -> 40k:      1.29  2.34  4.33  8.43 us a node   LINEAR
```

A rules out a scan over the edge set. B says the per-node cost is constant in the deleted count.
**D is the answer: the per-node cost is linear in the TOTAL NODE COUNT**, so the whole operation is
O(deleted x total). Any two of those sweeps alone are consistent with the wrong explanation, which
is why the probe keeps all three.

### And `delete_node` says it in a comment

```rust
// Remove from every label bucket (no per-node label list yet, so sweep).
for bucket in self.by_label.values_mut() {
    bucket.retain(|&x| x != id);
}
```

`retain` over EVERY bucket, per deleted node. In the fixture `:Univ` holds all 20,000 nodes, so
each delete scans the whole node set — constant per deleted node, independent of edges and of
degree, and linear in the node count. That is sweeps A, B and D exactly.

**The fix is already available in the same function**: `labels_of(id)` is called at the top for
`bump_epoch`, so the node's own labels are in hand. Removing `id` from just those buckets makes a
delete O(its labels) instead of O(every bucket). Priced here, built next; at 1,000,000 nodes the
current shape is not a constant factor but a wall.

### Also found: `_MERGE` after a `MATCH` is a parse error in native and an answer in TS

```
MATCH (a:P) _MERGE (a)-[:E]->(a)
  ts      [{"c":42000}]
  native  lenke: query: expected RETURN, SET, …
```

The same class as item 436 (an aggregate nested in a scalar function): a shape one engine accepts
and the other rejects. Recorded; not this item's subject.

## 443 — batch the label-bucket sweep: `DETACH DELETE` 5.5-10x. And item 442's proposed fix would not have worked, for a reason worth keeping

Item 442 measured `DETACH DELETE` at O(deleted x total nodes) and named the fix: `delete_node`
already calls `labels_of(id)` at the top, so restrict the bucket removal to the node's OWN labels
instead of sweeping every bucket.

**That fix does not work, and checking before building is the only reason it was not shipped.** A
deleted node is a MEMBER of the biggest bucket — in the fixture every node carries `:Univ` — so
"its own labels' buckets" includes the whole node set and the `retain` scans exactly as many
elements as before. Restricting the SET of buckets does nothing when the node belongs to the large
one. Only removing the REPETITION helps.

### What shipped

`Store::delete_nodes(&[u32])`: the per-node work (detach the adjacency, drop from the property
indexes, clear the properties, tombstone, undo capture) runs per node, and the label buckets are
`retain`ed ONCE for the whole batch — testing `deleted[x]`, which by then means exactly "one of
the ids just deleted", since anything deleted by an earlier call was removed from the buckets then.
`delete_node` is now `delete_nodes(&[id])`, so there is one implementation rather than two that can
drift.

`exec/write.rs` batches **only the DETACH deletes**. A non-DETACH delete's check reads the node's
CURRENT relationships, and an earlier node's detach in the same statement can legitimately leave a
later one relationship-free — so validating the whole set up front would reject a statement the
interleaved order accepts. That is a behaviour change, not an optimization, and the file's own
comment above that pass already records that the edge deletes run first for the same reason. The
mutation run confirms a test catches it (M4 below).

### Measured, with item 442's three sweeps re-run (min of 3 internally; the controls are flat)

```
D  deleted fixed at 1,000, NODES 5k -> 40k    1.29 2.34 4.33 8.43  ->  0.36 0.45 0.58 0.84 us/node
                                                                       10.0x at 40,000 nodes
B  edges fixed, 2,000 deleted                 8.669 ms            ->  1.189 ms      7.3x
B  edges fixed, 10,000 deleted               43.776              ->  7.974         5.5x
A  2,000 deleted, degree 2                    9.791              ->  1.544         6.3x
C  DELETE edges only (control)                0.345              ->  0.350         flat
C  SET a prop (control)                       0.266              ->  0.268         flat
```

And in the two-engine write screen the row has rejoined the band: `DELETE nodes` native **8.77 ->
1.30 ms**, from a 1.5x outlier against TS to 9.4x, where every other write sits at 4.8-22.7x. All
ten verification reads still agree between the engines.

Sweep A now RISES slightly with degree (0.77, 0.88, 0.95 us a node at degree 2, 4, 8) where it was
flat at 4.9. That is correct and worth noting: detaching a node's edges IS degree work, and it was
previously swamped by the bucket sweep. The residual curve in D is the single O(total) sweep spread
over 1,000 deletes, which is the irreducible part.

### Teeth

`store::tests::batch_delete_keeps_every_label_bucket_exact_sorted_and_restorable`. Batching moves
WHEN the buckets are swept, so the test pins the three things that could break:

- **Membership** across three OVERLAPPING labels (`:Univ` on all, `:Even` on half, `:Third` on a
  third), so a deleted node is in several buckets and a survivor is in the same ones. A fixture
  where every node carried every label could not tell an exact sweep from one that emptied the
  bucket — the vacuity lesson items 422/425/427/429/435 each paid for.
- **Order**: the buckets are kept sorted ascending and `is_labeled` binary-searches them, so every
  bucket is checked strictly increasing, and `is_labeled` is asserted to agree with them.
- **Rollback**: `DETACH DELETE` inside a transaction, rolled back, must restore membership AND
  order — the case batching could most plausibly regress.

Plus a node listed THREE times in one batch (the `Applied` list names a node once per matched row)
and the single-node `delete_node` path.

Four mutants, each verified applied: dropping the sweep, inverting its test, moving it BEFORE the
per-node deletes (so no tombstone is set yet), and batching the plain deletes too. **All four
caught.**

### Gates

`cargo test` 1133 + 13 + 723, `rewrite_fuzz` at 50k seeds, `clippy -D warnings` 0, `cargo fmt` 0,
all seven byte-identity fuzzers (`write-fuzz` is the one that matters here), and the write screen's
ten verification reads.

## 444 — `-[e:E]->` cost 3.7x more than `-[:E]->` for the same question, and the guard that caused it was documented as "defensive, not load-bearing" while being load-bearing for a reason the comment did not name

Item 443 closed the native write gap, so the write screen's remaining distance is all on the TS
side: `DELETE edges` 24.0x, `SET on an edge` 16.4x, `INSERT an edge` 11.1x, `DELETE nodes` 9.7x.
Three of the four worst rows are EDGE writes, and all three are driven by the same pattern,
`MATCH (a:P)-[e:E]->(b)`. So before attributing anything to the write, subtract the read.

### The attribution says it is not the write

| shape                                      | ms   |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---- |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[e:E]->(b) RETURN count(*)`   | 0.82 |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[e:E]->(b) RETURN count(e.w)` | 5.58 |
| `… DELETE e`                               | 7.00 |
| `… SET e.w = 42`                           | 7.02 |

Most of a 7 ms "edge write" is the read that feeds it. And the ladder that separates the steps
found the cost is not the write, not the property read, and not even the USE of the edge — it is
NAMING it. Measured one case per process, min of 9, three alternated rounds (item 423: a ratio
between two cases in one process is not a ratio):

| spelling                              | before             | after              |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------ |
| `-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(b.k)`        | 1.21 / 1.24 / 1.35 | 1.29 / 1.26 / 1.33 |
| `-[e:E]->(b) RETURN count(b.k)`       | 5.65 / 4.79 / 4.57 | 1.25 / 1.30 / 1.26 |
| `-[e:E]->(b) RETURN count(e.w)`       | 4.23 / 4.22 / 4.24 | 4.42 / 4.63 / 4.38 |
| `… DELETE e` (unreachable control)    | 7.54 / 7.44 / 7.36 | 8.46 / 8.07 / 8.08 |
| node-scan count (unreachable control) | 0.18 / 0.28 / 0.22 | 0.25 / 0.18 / 0.23 |

**3.4-4.2x**, and the two spellings now cost the same, which is the actual claim. `DELETE e` moved
9% — it exits `detectHopProjection` at `ret.kind !== 'return'` before reaching any new code, so it
is structurally unreachable, and its 9% is this harness's round-to-round floor, not a cost.

This is an equivalent-spelling gap of exactly the kind the engine's own doctrine is about:
`-[e:E]->` and `-[:E]->` ask the same question when `e` is never mentioned, and they returned the
same answer, so no correctness test could have found it.

### The comment was wrong, and so was my first fix

`detectHopProjection` refused a named rel outright, with a comment saying the check was
"DEFENSIVE, not load-bearing: the projection guard below already rejects any item that reads a
name other than the far variable, so an unread `r` or `p` cannot change a row, and mutation
confirms removing either changes no answer."

Removing it broke `a REL VARIABLE bound OUTSIDE correlates on that edge, not the degree`:

```
MATCH (p:U)-[r:T]->(q) RETURN COUNT { MATCH (p)-[r:T]->(z) } AS c
```

must answer 1 for each row — that one edge — and answered 2, `p`'s degree. The claim about the
projection guard is false for a SUBQUERY. `freePredicateVars` does descend into one, but it adds
the inner pattern's own binding names to its bound set first, so an inner `-[r:T]->` CORRELATING
on an already-bound `r` is indistinguishable from one binding `r` freshly, and neither is reported
free. `projectedEndsOnly` therefore saw an item reading neither endpoint and admitted it.

That is the second comment in this file refuted by running the thing it described; item 420 was
the first. **A comment claiming a guard is redundant is a claim about code elsewhere, and it goes
stale silently** — nothing fails when the other code changes shape.

### The fix asks a different question

`mentionsName(projection, relVar) || mentionsName(where, relVar)` — does the name appear ANYWHERE,
in any position. No free-variable analysis can be fooled about that, because it is not analysis.
A generic structural walk for the reason `hasSubquery` in the executor is one: `Expr` is a wide
union and a walk enumerating its arms would answer "not mentioned" for an arm added later, which
is the unsafe direction here. It compares every string, so a projected literal `'e'` also declines
— a false positive costs a fast path and nothing else, and there is a test pinning that the
over-broadness is deliberate.

`count(e.w)` still declines, correctly: the walk never binds an edge.

### Teeth, including two survivors that are findings rather than gaps

Harness proven first (item: prove it kills before trusting it): allocator bomb exit 137, bare spin
exit 124. Six mutants, each `cmp -s` checked for having been applied (item 427 — a false SURVIVED
reads as a missing test).

- **caught**: dropping the guard; `mentionsName` never matching a string; `mentionsName` not
  descending into objects; the guard checking only the clause `WHERE`.
- **SURVIVED, and it is redundancy not a gap**: `mentionsName` skipping ARRAYS. `Object.values` on
  an array returns its elements, so the object arm already covers one. Kept — it matches
  `hasSubquery`'s shape and skips an allocation — and its redundancy is a property of JavaScript
  rather than of another function, so unlike the clause below it cannot quietly rot.
- **SURVIVED**: the guard checking only the PROJECTION, dropping `m.where`. A second round removed
  `carriedWhere`'s neither-endpoint refusal as well, to find out whether the new test had teeth in
  ANY configuration — it still survived. What actually refuses a subquery clause `WHERE` here is
  `rowLocal`, whose own comment says the arms it exists to refuse are the subquery ones.

So the `m.where` clause is defence in depth, and the code and the test now both say so in those
words rather than implying teeth they lack. It stays because the projection half PROVES a
free-variable analysis cannot see this correlation, so a later relaxation of `rowLocal` — wanting
subquery `WHERE`s on the fast path is a reasonable thing to want — would reopen exactly this hole.
Naming a guard as redundant-but-deliberate is the correction to what the old comment did.

### The probe had no such spelling, which is how a 3.7x hid

`spelling-probe.ts` covers inline-vs-clause `WHERE`, operand order, OR-vs-IN, reversed arrows and
much else, and had **no anonymous-vs-named edge group at all**. Both are added, aggregate and
projection, because `detectHopAggregate` delegates to `detectHopProjection` and a probe covering
only the aggregate would have measured half the change. At `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9` they now
agree within 3% (220.6 / 214.7 ms and 201.1 / 202.8 ms). The three groups still over 2x are
pre-existing and every query in them spells the rel anonymously, so this gate cannot change their
route: it only alters behaviour when `rel.variable !== undefined`.

### Two things found and recorded rather than fixed

- **A wrong answer, pre-existing and unrelated to this gate** (it declines the shape): a
  correlated rel variable inside a COUNT subquery in a clause `WHERE` makes the predicate
  unsatisfiable at every value. `MATCH (p:U)-[r:T]->(q) WHERE COUNT { MATCH (p)-[r:T]->(z) } = n
RETURN q.n` returns NOTHING for n = 0, 1 and 2 — mutually exclusive, so it is not a value
  disagreement — and `IS NULL` is empty too. The same subquery in `RETURN` is right (1 per row),
  and the `EXISTS` spelling of it is right. The discovery route is worth keeping: I had written
  the `= 1` / `= 2` pair as a test asserting what I believed GQL meant, it failed, and asking the
  engine what it actually answers for 0/1/2/`IS NULL` turned a wrong test into a real bug. **A
  failing test you wrote from belief is a question, not a verdict.**
- **The next lead.** On the cross-engine bench, `project the edge` is 607.1 ms lazy and 1018.7
  materialized, against `project the element` at 5.7 and 27.2. Projecting an edge against
  projecting a node is a 100x asymmetry. Both edge rows name AND read the edge, so they decline
  this fast path and are untouched here.

### Gates

`bun test packages/gql` 2122 pass / 0 fail (5 new tests), `bun run check` exit 0 — read as its own
exit code, after a piped `echo $?` reported `tail`'s status and briefly hid a complexity-gate
failure, which is the trap CLAUDE.md names. The inline guard pushed `detectHopProjection` to
complexity 36 against a limit of 35, so it is extracted as `relVariableObserved`, the same split
several other guards in this file have. All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, re-run on rebuilt
dists because a TS source edit reaches a fuzzer only after `nx build`.

## 445 — "projecting an edge costs 100x projecting a node" is wrong twice over. The real quantity is the ROUTE, it is 6.9x, and it has nothing to do with edges

Item 444 closed with a lead taken straight off the cross-engine bench: `project the edge` at 607.1
ms lazy against `project the element` at 5.7, flagged as a 100x asymmetry between projecting an
edge and projecting a node. Both halves of that reading were wrong, and the corrections are worth
more than the lead was.

### Correction one: the fixture, worth 5x

The two bench rows use DIFFERENT documents. `project the element` runs on `nodesDoc` — 200,000
nodes, no edges — and returns 200,000 rows. `project the edge` runs on `graphDoc` — 200,000 nodes
and 1,000,000 edges — and returns 1,000,000. Per row that is 28.5 ns against 607, about **21x**,
not 100. Five of the hundred was fixture. Matching the fixture to the claim is a standing rule
here and it was not applied before the lead was written down.

### Correction two: the attribution, which is the whole finding

`route-cost-probe` puts both sides on ONE fixture with the SAME traversal and the SAME row count —
200,000 rows over the bench's own 5-edges-per-node shape — so the only difference is what the
`RETURN` projects. One case per process, min of 9 (item 423):

| case                                                      | ns/row  |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN b`                  | 105     |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN b`                 | 104     |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN 1 AS one`          | 110     |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN r`                 | 595     |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN b, r.w AS w`       | **727** |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN r, r.w AS w`       | **722** |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) WHERE r.w < 100 RETURN b` | 814     |

The two bolded rows are the ones that settle it. One projects a NODE and one projects the EDGE;
they are otherwise identical and they agree to within 1%. **Rendering an edge costs nothing
measurable.** The last row projects only a node and still pays 814, declining for a reason — an
edge-reading `WHERE` — that is not about projection at all.

So what the first comparison measured was the ROUTE. `RETURN b` with a named `r` is on the fast
path _because of item 444_, and `RETURN r` mentions the rel so it declines. The 6x I wrote down as
an edge cost was fast-path-versus-general-path wearing an edge costume, and item 444 is what put
it there — the previous tick's own change created the confound in the next tick's measurement.

**A ratio between two queries is a ratio between two ROUTES until you have shown they take the
same one.** Items 429 and 430 are the same lesson from the other side, where a label flipped the
route; this is the first time a change I had just shipped was the thing doing the flipping.

### What is actually open, and it is bigger than the lead was

The fast path costs ~105 ns/row and the general path ~720-815: **6.9x**, over an identical
traversal. Every one-hop query that MENTIONS its rel variable pays it — `RETURN r`, `RETURN r.w`,
`WHERE r.w < 100` — and those are not exotic spellings, they are how anyone writes a query about
relationships.

`detectHopProjection` declines them because the walk binds no edge, and the reason it binds none
is that nothing asked it to: `expand` already yields `{ edge, node }`, so the edge is in hand at
the point the walk sets the far variable. Binding it is one `set` on the single mutated binding
the path already carries, and then `projectedEndsOnly` and `carriedWhere` can admit the rel
variable as a third legal name alongside the two endpoints.

Priced here, not built — the same discipline item 437 used on the arithmetic-fusion target, and
for the same reason: the binding protocol of a fast path is where a wrong answer hides, so it gets
its own tick with its own mutation run rather than being tacked onto a probe.

### Gates

No engine change. `bun run check` exit 0, read as its own exit code. The probe is wired as
`bun run probe:route`.

## 446 — the hop fast path now BINDS the edge: 3.1-3.4x on every one-hop query that reads its relationship variable, and the far-driven walk is a wrong answer here rather than a slow one

Item 445 priced this and corrected itself twice while doing so. It is worth restating the final
figure before the change, because the one in 445's own headline is not it: 445 said the route gap
was 6.9x, measuring the general path's ~720 ns/row against the FAR-driven walk's ~105. But the
far-driven walk cannot serve this shape at all, so the honest ceiling is the START-driven walk's
~192, and the achievable prize was ~3.4x. **A fast path's cost is only a ceiling for the shapes it
can actually take.**

### Why the far-driven walk is not an option

Its 2.3x (item 167) comes from HOISTING `projectRow` to once per far VERTEX, which is valid
because every item the path admits is a pure function of the far end. An item reading the edge is
not: a far vertex's incident edges differ, so hoisting would emit one edge's values for all of
them. It is not a slower choice here, it is a wrong one — and the mutant that makes it is caught
by a fixture where two edges with different `w` land on the same far vertex.

### The change

`expand`'s bucket loop is already holding the edge while it resolves a far vertex from it, so
binding the rel variable is one `Map.set` on a binding that was going to be mutated anyway. Three
pieces:

- `projectedEndsOnly` admits the rel variable as a THIRD legal name beside the two endpoints and
  reports whether an item read it.
- A new `relBoundHopWalk` builder returning a per-compile closure — the shape `farDrivenHopWalk`
  and `filteredHopWalk` already have, and the one item 159 measured as right (a shared
  module-scope walk goes polymorphic at its call sites and cost 1.29x). It is NOT a branch inside
  the existing start-driven walk, because item 159 also measured that adding even a branch to
  that inner loop costs the hot unfiltered shape 1.6x.
- Item 444's gate is narrowed from "is the rel mentioned" to "is the rel mentioned somewhere this
  path cannot SEE" — that is, mentioned AND a subquery present. With no subquery,
  `freePredicateVars` is complete over the fragment and every read is visible, which is the
  condition the binding relies on. With one, the wrong answer 444 found comes back, and the
  mutant proving that is caught.

### Measured, same fixture both sides, one case per process, min of 9

A/B by reverting the engine file to `HEAD` and rebuilding, because three of my first "before"
numbers predated a fixture change (a second label on half the vertices) and were therefore not
comparable to the "after" at all.

| case                                                 | before ns/row | after           | gain     |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | --------------- | -------- |
| `MATCH (a:Half)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN r`             | 632 / 653     | 214 / 207 / 186 | **3.4x** |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN r`            | 613 / 615     | 200 / 214 / 204 | **3.1x** |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN r.w`          | 757 / 765     | 266 / 239 / 249 | **3.2x** |
| `RETURN b.age`, rel named and unread (control)       | 117 / 116     | 115 / 117 / 92  | flat     |
| anonymous rel (control)                              | 111 / 115     | 111 / 91 / 106  | flat     |
| start-driven, no rel read (control)                  | 197 / 245     | 175 / 186 / 184 | flat     |
| `WHERE r.w < 100 RETURN b` (control: still declines) | 796 / 800     | 744 / 789 / 772 | flat     |

Four controls, and the last is the useful one: it reads the rel in a clause `WHERE`, which
`carriedWhere` still refuses, so it is a shape the change deliberately does not reach and it did
not move.

### The half that is NOT built, and is now measured by the probe

`filteredHopWalk` binds no edge, so a far predicate, a carried clause `WHERE`, or a start-reading
item still declines when the rel is read. `WHERE r.w < 100 RETURN b` stays at ~772 ns/row. That
gap is now a `spelling-probe` group — `RETURN r.w` against `WHERE r.w >= 0 RETURN r.w` over a
fixture where `w` is always non-negative, so the two spell one question — and it reports **2.7x**.
It is labelled in the probe as expected-over-threshold with the item number, because a known gap
left unlabelled reads as a regression to whoever runs it next.

### Teeth

Harness proven first: allocator bomb 137, bare spin 124. **Eight mutants, all caught**, each
`cmp -s` checked for having been applied: never binding the edge; binding the far NODE to the rel
variable; dropping the `unfiltered` decline so a filtered shape is served by a walk applying no
filter; never taking the rel-bound route; `projectedEndsOnly` never reporting a rel read; emitting
one row per far vertex (the hoisting hazard); item 444's subquery guard turned off in the UNSAFE
direction; and the far-label check dropped from this walk alone.

The seventh is worth a note on method. My first attempt at it mutated the guard to `true`, which
makes it MORE conservative — item 444's own behaviour — so it survived, correctly, and for a
moment looked like a missing test. **A guard has two mutation directions and only one of them is
the unsafe one.** Flipped to `false`, it is caught by two tests.

Six new tests, on a fixture built so that each thing it checks can fail: two edges with DIFFERENT
`w` landing on ONE far vertex (so a hoisting walk is distinguishable), `w` only on edges and `n`
only on vertices (so conflating the two shows as nulls rather than a plausible number), a far
label that is on one of three vertices, and the reversed hop where the far end is `edge.from`
while the edge is unchanged. The whole-edge case is compared against the engine's own general
answer via a declining spelling rather than against my expectation.

### Gates

`bun test packages/gql` 2128 pass / 0 fail, `bun run check` exit 0 — read as its own exit code,
and it took three rounds: the new branch put `detectHopProjection` at 39 against a limit of 35, so
the walk became a builder, its decline moved inside it, and the seven-clause projection guard
became `projectionIsStreamable`. Perf was re-measured AFTER those extractions, not before, since a
closure's shape is exactly what item 159 says to re-measure. All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass;
the spelling probe reports 0 answer disagreements.

## 447 — the filtered half: a rel-reading clause `WHERE` is carried too, 2.6x. And the intermediate state was a wrong answer that 2,128 tests did not see

Item 446 bound the edge for the UNFILTERED hop only, so a far predicate, a carried clause `WHERE`
or a start-reading item still declined when the rel was read. `WHERE r.w < 100 RETURN b` stayed at
~772 ns/row, and 446 added a `spelling-probe` group reporting that gap at **2.7x**, labelled
expected-over-threshold with its item number. This closes it: the group now reports 1.31x and is
no longer flagged.

### The wrong answer in the middle, which is the part worth keeping

The change has two halves — `carriedWhere` must stop refusing a rel-reading predicate, and some
walk must bind the edge before the gate runs — and I applied them in that order. After the first
half alone, every test still passed. Then:

```
MATCH (p:U)-[r:T]->(q) WHERE r.w < 100 RETURN q.n   ->  []    (should be two rows)
MATCH (p:U)-[r:T]->(q) WHERE r.w = 1   RETURN q.n   ->  []    (should be one)
MATCH (p:U)-[r:T]->(q) WHERE r.w > 99  RETURN q.n   ->  []    (correctly empty)
```

Three mutually exclusive predicates, all empty: the gate was reading `r.w` out of a binding with
no edge in it. **2,128 tests passed over that**, because the suite had no case where a clause
`WHERE` reads the rel while the PROJECTION does not. Every test item 446 wrote projects `r`, which
routes through `itemsReadRel` and never exercises the `carriedWhere` half of the decision at all.

A gap that lets a half-finished change look finished is the most expensive kind, and the reason
this was caught is that I ran the shape by hand before trusting the green suite — the same reason
item 441 records for instrumenting the result rather than the gate.

### The walk

`relBoundFilteredHopWalk`, a builder returning a per-compile closure like the three walks beside
it. It binds the start (when read), the far end, and then the EDGE — before the far predicate and
the gate, which is the whole point. Three things it deliberately does not do:

- **No far-driven variant**, for item 446's reason: that walk hoists `projectRow` to once per far
  VERTEX, which an item or filter reading the edge invalidates.
- **No start-only gating.** The start-only walk evaluates the gate BEFORE touching a vertex's
  adjacency (item 164's order, 52ns against 34 a vertex), and there is no edge bound at that
  point. So `carriedWhere` no longer calls a predicate start-only when it reads the rel, and the
  remaining combination — a start-only `WHERE` with a rel-reading ITEM — declines.
- **It keeps the far-seek decline.** `cfar` narrower than the start source by `SEEK_MARGIN` means
  the general path can seek the far end, worth 89x in item 177's table. Per call, so the inner
  loop pays nothing.

### Measured, one case per process, min of 9, three rounds

| case                              | before ns/row | after           | gain         |
| --------------------------------- | ------------- | --------------- | ------------ |
| `WHERE r.w < 100 RETURN b`        | 796 / 800     | 325 / 341 / 310 | **2.4-2.6x** |
| `RETURN r.w` (446's win, control) | 239 / 266     | 245 / 261 / 245 | flat         |
| `RETURN r` (446's win, control)   | 200 / 214     | 201 / 220 / 215 | flat         |
| anonymous rel (control)           | 111 / 115     | 109 / 111 / 115 | flat         |
| start-driven, no rel (control)    | 175 / 186     | 184 / 203 / 170 | flat         |
| `RETURN b.age` (control)          | 115 / 117     | 129 / 120 / 122 | flat         |

Re-measured after `bun run fmt` touched the file and after the gate extractions, not before.

### Teeth: eight mutants, six caught, and the two survivors are perf not correctness

Harness proven first: bomb 137, spin 124. Caught: binding the edge AFTER the gate; dropping the
gate; dropping the far predicate; dropping the far label; never binding the start; and
`carriedWhere` never reporting a rel read.

That last one SURVIVED the first run, and finding out why is what produced the test above. With
`needsRel` forced false, a predicate reading ONLY the rel declines (so the answer stays right by
luck of a different route), but a predicate reading the rel AND the far end is still carried — and
then the gate runs unbound. Every existing test projected `r`, so `itemsReadRel` rescued all of
them. One test with a far-only projection and a mixed filter, in both operand orders, catches it.

**Two survivors, both answer-preserving:** serving a start-only predicate in this walk, and
`carriedWhere` still calling a rel-reading predicate start-only. Both are routing decisions, and
items 425 and 429 record that routing is answer-preserving by construction, so no test can police
them — the probes do. The start-only decline STAYS rather than being relaxed on the strength of a
surviving mutant: that walk carries bespoke raise-parity handling (items 139/142/144/145) that
decides on a gate fault whether the general path would have reached the vertex at all, and
equivalence there is not something a green suite establishes.

### Gates

`bun test packages/gql` 2135 pass / 0 fail (7 new tests), `bun run check` exit 0 — read as its own
exit code, and red once on `fmt:check` alone, which is the standing note that `fmt` exiting 0 is
not `fmt:check` passing. All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass. The spelling probe reports 0 answer
disagreements and the 446/447 group at 1.31x, down from the 2.7x it was added to record.

## 448 — asking NATIVE items 446 and 447's question: there is no gap to port, and the thing that looks like one is item 289's carrier

Items 446 and 447 were both TS-side, and the obvious next move is to port them: native lowers the
same GQL to its own fused hop paths, and `try_fused_hop_project`'s restriction is
`refs_only_slot(e, 1)`, which reads exactly like the rel refusal those two items removed. The
answer is that there is nothing to port, and establishing that cost one probe run.

### Native, with egress held equal

Every case projects ONE scalar, so the row payload is identical across them and item 289's JSON
carrier cancels out. `route-cost-probe` gained an `ENGINE=native` arm; two rounds, min of 9:

| native case                                             | ns/row  |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `(:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN b.age`                  | 75 / 63 |
| `(:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN b.age` (named, unread) | 65 / 59 |
| `(:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN r.w` (read)            | 62 / 65 |
| `WHERE r.w < 100 RETURN b.age`                          | 63 / 72 |
| `WHERE b.age < 100 RETURN b.age`                        | 60 / 61 |

Flat, all five, within the noise of each other. **Native pays nothing to name, read or filter on a
relationship variable.** The TS gap items 446 and 447 closed — 3.4x and 2.6x — has no native twin,
and porting either would have been work for nothing.

### The thing that DOES look like a native gap, and is closed

The first ladder run, which projected whole elements, read very differently:

| native case             | ns/row |
| ----------------------- | ------ |
| `RETURN b.age`          | 59     |
| `RETURN r.w`            | 60     |
| `RETURN b` (whole node) | 931    |
| `RETURN r` (whole edge) | 1065   |

A 15x between projecting a property and projecting the element, which is a tempting target and is
**item 289**, already in `CLOSED.md`: "IT IS THE JSON CARRIER, NOT EXECUTION … ~80% is the carrier
and no engine change touches it; `queryArrowIpc` is the existing answer." Decomposed there as
`JSON.parse` 48%, render + FFI call 33%, row shaping 12%.

The split is visible in this probe too, once the traversal is separated from the egress:
`count(r.w)` over the same 200,000 edges is 1.1 ms — 5.5 ns an edge — against `RETURN r.w` at 12.0
ms, so a scalar row costs ~55 ns to carry (items 428 and 434 measured native row egress at 58-94
ns/row) and an element row ~1010.

`CLOSED.md` is what stopped this becoming a tick of work, which is the whole reason the project's
own instructions say to read it before pricing a target. Worth noting that two of the diagnostics
I reached for first were useless: `count(b)` at 0.1 ms and `RETURN b LIMIT 1` at 0.007 ms look
like proof that element rendering is free, and they are both shortcut-answered — no traversal
happens at all. **An instrument that is answered by a fast path measures the fast path, not the
question.**

### What this says about the two engines

Three items in a row now have the same shape: TS was behind and native was not — 432 and 433 on
the three-hop direction product, 443 on `DETACH DELETE` the other way, and now 446/447. The useful
form of it is not "native is faster", which the bench table says badly; it is that the two engines
have independent planners, so a gap found in one is a QUESTION about the other and never a
finding. This probe arm is here so the question is one command rather than an inference.

### Gates

No engine change. `bun run check` exit 0, read as its own exit code. `route-cost-probe` gained the
`ENGINE=native` arm and five native cases; `bun run probe:route` with `ENGINE=native PCASE=…`.

## 449 — `coalesce` in a native filter was 21x a plain comparison and is now 25x cheaper; `abs` 5.7x. The two families disagree about the one cell that matters

Item 437 measured native's expression predicates and named three: `abs` 5.9x, `CASE` 15x,
`coalesce` 21x, all at IDENTICAL selectivity (the row count is constant down the probe's group, so
the gap is the expression and nothing else). Item 438 fused the arithmetic arm. Re-running
`exprpred_437` first, because a target that has not been re-measured since the last change to the
same code is a guess:

| 200,000 nodes          | ms    | x plain                                |
| ---------------------- | ----- | -------------------------------------- |
| `a.k > 5`              | 0.341 | —                                      |
| `a.k + 0 > 5`          | 0.394 | 1.16x — item 438's fix, visibly landed |
| `abs(a.k) > 5`         | 1.994 | **5.8x**                               |
| `CASE … > 5`           | 4.940 | **14.5x**                              |
| `coalesce(a.k, 0) > 5` | 7.160 | **21.0x**                              |

So 437's figures survive, and 438 did not generalize to the call arms. Item 437's own conclusion
was "the answer is fusion, not more arm additions" — and 438 added an arm and got 5.0x, so the
useful reading is narrower: an arm per EXPRESSION KIND is the fusion, and `Expr::Call` is one kind.

### The change, and why it is two arms rather than one

`try_filter_keep_call` matches `<call over one prop> <cmp> <lit>` and streams the column in one
pass with no allocation, where the general path builds `a.k`, then the call's result column, then
the comparison, then the keep-list — item 438's materialization cause, unchanged.

It splits on the only thing that matters, and the split is the whole item:

- A UNARY numeric function **drops** an absent cell. `scalar_num_fn` returns NULL for a NULL
  argument, the comparison is UNKNOWN, the row goes — as the plain and arithmetic arms do.
- **`coalesce` KEEPS it, with the default substituted.** That is the function's entire purpose and
  the opposite of every other arm in this file.

Both were verified against the general path BEFORE the arm was written, not after: over three
nodes where one has no `k`, `coalesce(a.k, 0) > 5` answers 1 and `coalesce(a.k, 99) > 5` answers 2
— the absent cell passing on the default — while `abs(a.missing) > 5` answers 0. An arm that
skipped absent rows would answer 1 for both `coalesce` spellings and look right in the only test
anyone writes first.

The function set reuses `unary_finite_num_fn`, which already returns raw `f64 -> f64` closures
documented to match `scalar_num_fn` exactly and already excludes the functions that can make a
NaN or an infinity from a finite input. A name added there arrives here with its semantics settled
— `sqrt` is excluded and still answers correctly through the general path, which is asserted.

Two declines, each because the general path does something a keep pass cannot express:

- **A column absent everywhere.** `coalesce(a.missing, 99) > 5` keeps EVERY row — verified, 3 of 3
  — and there is no column to stream. An arm returning an empty keep-list would answer 0 and look
  like a correct "nothing matches", which is why that is a test and not a comment.
- **The `u32::MAX` OPTIONAL-miss sentinel, for `coalesce` only.** The arithmetic arm skips it as
  UNKNOWN, but `coalesce(NULL, d)` is `d`, so skipping would be wrong and substituting is a
  GUESS — `WHERE` inside `OPTIONAL MATCH` is rejected by the parser, so the shape cannot be
  measured against the general path at all. Declining needs no guess, and saying so in the code is
  better than an assertion I could not have checked.

### Measured, two rounds, both sizes

| case                                                       | before | after           | gain      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------ | --------------- | --------- |
| `coalesce(a.k, 0) > 5` @200k                               | 7.160  | 0.286 / 0.287   | **25.0x** |
| `coalesce(a.k, 0) > 5` @1M                                 | 38.435 | 1.482 / 1.466   | **25.9x** |
| `abs(a.k) > 5` @200k                                       | 1.994  | 0.348 / 0.358   | **5.7x**  |
| `abs(a.k) > 5` @1M                                         | 10.582 | 1.815 / 1.787   | **5.8x**  |
| `CASE … > 5` @200k (control)                               | 4.940  | 4.909 / 4.815   | flat      |
| `CASE … > 5` @1M (control)                                 | 28.243 | 27.893 / 27.555 | flat      |
| `a.k > 5`, `a.k + 0 > 5`, two-props, `string =` (controls) | —      | —               | flat      |

`CASE` is the control this probe was built to have: same binary, same fixture, same selectivity,
and structurally unreachable — `Expr::Case` is not `Expr::Call`. It did not move. `coalesce` now
costs slightly LESS than the plain comparison (0.286 against 0.296), which is not a paradox: the
`coalesce` arm has no `present` branch to mispredict, since every row produces a value.

### Teeth

Harness proven first: bomb 137, spin 124. Six mutants, each `cmp -s` checked for application and
each built with `--features capi` (item 432's trap). **Five caught:** `coalesce` skipping an
absent cell; a unary function substituting 0 instead of dropping; the function not applied at all;
ANSWERING for an absent column with an empty keep-list; and the comparison not flipped when the
literal is on the left.

The sixth — the arm never consulted — **SURVIVED, and that is the null control passing.** Removing
a fast path must change speed and not answers; a mutant that deleted it and broke a test would
mean the arm was not byte-identical. It is labelled as the control in the script so the result
reads as the invariant it is rather than as a gap.

2,376 differential forms against an oracle that declines both fused arms (`(expr) + 0`, whose
outer operand is a `Call` rather than a `Prop`): eleven expressions, six comparisons, six
thresholds, in both operand orders. The fixture's load-bearing row is the node with NO `k`.

One test expectation was mine rather than the engine's: I wrote `sqrt(a.k) > 1` as 1 row over
k = 1, 2, 3, and `sqrt(2)` and `sqrt(3)` are both greater than 1. The test caught me, not it.

### Gates

Each as its own command with its exit code read: `cargo test` 1135 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz`
at 50,000 seeds, `cargo clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` exit 0 (it needs
`--manifest-path` — run from the repo root without it, clippy exits 101 with "could not find
Cargo.toml", which looks like a lint failure and is not one), `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, and all
seven byte-identity fuzzers. Tests and the probe were both re-run AFTER `cargo fmt` touched the
file.

## 450 — a boolean `CASE` in a filter is 24.9x cheaper by being UNWRAPPED, not evaluated. And the wrapped spelling is now 1.4x FASTER than the bare predicate it unwraps to

`CASE` was the last of item 437's three expression leads, at 14.5x a plain comparison after items
438 and 449 closed the other two. Measuring the family before touching it, same selectivity
throughout:

|                                                                 | 200,000  | 1,000,000 |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | --------- |
| `a.k > 5`                                                       | 0.398 ms | 1.672 ms  |
| `CASE WHEN a.k > 5 THEN true ELSE false END`                    | 5.196    | 26.676    |
| `CASE WHEN a.k > 5 THEN true END`                               | 5.360    | 27.795    |
| `CASE WHEN a.k > 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END = 1`                       | 6.023    | 34.135    |
| `CASE WHEN a.k>5 THEN true WHEN a.k<0 THEN true ELSE false END` | 5.432    | 29.617    |
| `CASE WHEN a.k > 5 THEN a.k ELSE 0 END > 5`                     | 5.566    | 34.234    |

**Every shape costs the same to within a third**, which is item 442's tell: a table whose rows all
agree is measuring something they share. What they share is `Expr::Case`'s OUTPUT — its eager path
collects `Col::Gen`, N boxed `Value`s, which the filter then re-interprets per row. The ARMS are
irrelevant, so the arm-by-arm fusion items 438 and 449 used would have been the wrong shape of fix
here, and measuring five variants before writing one is what said so.

### The fix evaluates nothing

In a FILTER, `CASE WHEN c THEN true ELSE false END` keeps exactly the rows `c` keeps:

```text
  c TRUE     -> THEN -> true   -> kept
  c FALSE    -> ELSE -> false  -> dropped
  c UNKNOWN  -> ELSE -> false  -> dropped
```

and a filter drops FALSE and UNKNOWN identically. So `try_filter_keep_case` DELEGATES: it checks
the shape and hands the condition back to `try_filter_keep`. That is what makes it general —
`CASE WHEN coalesce(a.k, 0) > 5 THEN true END` picks up item 449's arm and
`CASE WHEN a.k * 2 > 10 THEN true END` picks up item 438's, with no code per condition form. It is
also exactly as conservative as those arms: when none can answer the condition it declines and the
general path evaluates the whole `CASE`, which is what preserves every raise, since a condition
that would fault is one no arm can prove.

The collapse is sound HERE and nowhere else. In a PROJECTION the same `CASE` is observably
different from `c` — it yields `false` where `c` yields NULL.

### Measured, two rounds, both sizes

| case                                     | before | after           | gain      |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------ | --------------- | --------- |
| `… THEN true ELSE false END` @200k       | 5.196  | 0.216 / 0.217   | **24.0x** |
| `… THEN true ELSE false END` @1M         | 26.676 | 1.123 / 1.072   | **24.9x** |
| `… THEN true END` @200k                  | 5.360  | 0.210 / 0.243   | **22.1x** |
| `… THEN true END` @1M                    | 27.795 | 1.103 / 1.077   | **25.8x** |
| `THEN 1 ELSE 0 END = 1` @1M (control)    | 34.135 | 33.361 / 33.363 | flat      |
| two `WHEN`s @1M (control)                | 29.617 | 28.884 / 29.056 | flat      |
| property arms @1M (control)              | 34.234 | 34.053 / 33.821 | flat      |
| `a.k > 5`, `abs`, `coalesce`, `string =` | —      | —               | flat      |

The three uncovered CASE shapes are the controls this probe already had: same binary, same
fixture, same selectivity, and each unreachable for a stated structural reason (multi-branch, a
non-boolean THEN, a comparison rather than a bare CASE). None moved.

### The inversion, isolated before being believed

The wrapped spelling now costs LESS than the bare predicate it unwraps to — 0.216 against 0.398.
That is an equivalent-spelling inversion of the kind this engine's doctrine is about, so it does
not get claimed off a table whose cases share one process: item 274 is the standing correction,
where shared-process warming nearly confirmed a 3.4x regression that was not there.

`caseinv_450` runs one case per process, three rounds, min of 9:

```text
  bare         0.308 / 0.302 / 0.296 ms
  case         0.210 / 0.249 / 0.209
  casenoelse   0.258 / 0.209 / 0.207
  control      0.125 / 0.123 / 0.126   (a string equality, unreachable by either)
```

**The inversion is real at 1.4x, and smaller than the shared-process table said (1.6x)** — which
is itself the reason to isolate. The bare predicate takes a route that costs more than the keep
pass the `CASE` delegates into. Recorded as an open lead with its instrument rather than chased
here: it is a 1.4x on a very common shape, and the next question is which route the bare form
takes, not what to change.

### Teeth

Harness proven first: bomb 137, spin 124. Five mutants, each `cmp -s` checked. **Four caught:**
admitting any `THEN` arm (so `THEN false` unwraps); admitting any `ELSE` arm; admitting `ELSE true`
specifically, which is the single most plausible over-admission since it keeps the rows the
condition DROPS; and delegating the first branch of a MULTI-branch `CASE`. The fifth — the arm
never consulted — survived, which is the null control passing, as in item 449.

120 differential forms, and the grid taught me something about oracles. Written first with numeric
arms as well, it reported a divergence on `CASE WHEN a.k > 5 THEN true ELSE 0 END`: the bare form
RAISES (0 is a non-boolean in a boolean position) while `(…) = true` answers 3. Both are right —
they are different queries, because `0 = true` is FALSE rather than an error, which I checked in
both engines rather than assuming. **An oracle spelling is part of the claim, not a neutral
wrapper**, which is item 432's "an oracle is a property of the engine" arriving from the other
direction. The non-boolean arms are pinned directly in the restrictions test instead, including
that a non-boolean arm NO row reaches does not raise — so the restriction is about reachability.

### Gates

Each as its own command with its exit code read: `cargo test` 1137 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz`
at 50,000 seeds, `cargo clippy --manifest-path … --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings`
exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers, `bun run check` exit 0. The
probe was re-run AFTER `cargo fmt` touched the files.

## 451 — the inversion item 450 found was worth 3.7x, not 1.4x: a filtered `count(*)` iterated a heap `Vec` once per node

Item 450 closed by recording an equivalent-spelling inversion: `CASE WHEN a.k > 5 THEN true ELSE
false END` measured FASTER than the bare `a.k > 5` it unwraps to, 1.4x isolated one case per
process. This is that lead, and the prize was not the 1.4x.

### Diagnosis: not a plan route

`PLAN=1 cargo run --example caseinv_450` prints the optimized plan for either spelling, and they
are **structurally identical** — `Project(Aggregate(Filter(Scan)))` both times, differing only in
the predicate node. So the inversion is not the optimizer choosing differently; it is which
RUNTIME fast path the executor reaches for each predicate, which is a different question and one
the plan cannot answer.

The bare `Compare` reaches `try_stream_num_count`: one streaming pass over the label's nodes,
counting inline, allocating nothing. The `CASE` reaches `try_filter_keep`, which materializes a
200,000-id batch AND a 91,000-entry keep-list. **A streaming count with no allocation losing to a
path that allocates twice is the tell** that the per-element cost was deciding it, not the
allocation.

And there it was: `num_conj_on_slot` returns `bounds` as a heap `Vec`, and the sweep ran
`bounds.iter().all(|&(op, t)| num_pred(op, data[i], t))` — a pointer, a length, a loop and a
runtime `op` match — ONCE PER SCANNED NODE. The keep-pass arm matches `op` directly.

### The fix, and the measurement that corrected my own estimate

Hoisting the single bound into a monomorphic closure (`sweep_num_count`, generic over `Fn(f64) ->
bool`, one instantiation per operator) leaves the sweep with a compare and a branch. One case per
process, min of 9, three rounds:

| case                                  | before                | after                 | gain     |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------- | -------- |
| `a.k > 5` count @200k                 | 0.308 / 0.302 / 0.296 | 0.102 / 0.102 / 0.092 | **3.2x** |
| `a.k > 5` count @1M                   | 1.681                 | 0.506 / 0.460         | **3.7x** |
| CASE-wrapped @200k (control)          | 0.210 / 0.249 / 0.209 | 0.229 / 0.228 / 0.206 | flat     |
| CASE-wrapped @1M (control)            | 1.145                 | 1.145 / 1.066         | flat     |
| string equality @200k (control)       | 0.125 / 0.123 / 0.126 | 0.136 / 0.141 / 0.123 | flat     |
| `a.k > 5 AND a.k < 100` @1M (control) | 1.774                 | 1.774                 | flat     |

**I was chasing a 1.4x and the lever was 3.7x.** The inversion was a symptom; its size was not the
size of the cause, because the two spellings differ by the cost of a keep-list as well as by the
per-element test. A gap between two spellings bounds neither one's distance from the floor.

The two-bound row is the control this change most needed: the SAME query shape with one extra
bound, which still takes the general `Vec` arm, and it did not move. It is also now 3.9x the
single-bound cost (1.774 against 0.459), which is the follow-up recorded in `CLOSED.md`. The
inversion is resolved in the right direction: the streaming count is now 2.2x the CASE route
rather than 0.7x of it.

### Teeth

Harness proven first: bomb 137, spin 124. Five mutants, four caught: ignoring `present` (so a
NULL cell compares as a raw 0.0); `Lt` and `Le` swapped in the dispatch, which only a threshold
EQUAL to a stored value distinguishes; `Ne` written as `x < t || x > t`, which is correct for
every value except NaN, where both are false; and the specialization swallowing the multi-bound
and zero-bound arms. The fifth — never specializing — survived, which is the null control passing,
as in items 449 and 450.

84 differential forms, six operators by seven thresholds in both operand orders, with item 450's
CASE wrapper as the ORACLE: it is a genuinely different route (`Expr::Case` never reaches this
count) and item 450 established the equivalence, so one fast path serves as the oracle for another
only because that equivalence is itself tested. The fixture carries a NaN and two `k`-less nodes,
which is what the `Ne` and `present` mutants die on.

### A pre-existing cross-engine divergence, found by the fuzzer and verified NOT to be mine

One differential-fuzz run failed on a random seed:

```
MATCH (t:T) OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE (CASE WHEN (null <> n.s) THEN date('0001-01-01')
  WHEN (3.14 <> 0) THEN n.nan ELSE zoned_datetime('2020-01-01T00:00:00Z') END
  AND (0.1 IN [0.0, 'A')))) RETURN t.n AS x, n.n AS y ORDER BY x, y
```

Native answers `[{x:1,y:null},{x:2,y:null}]`; TS raises `a boolean is required`. The `CASE` yields
a temporal or a number, and that non-boolean is an operand of `AND` — a boolean context. Native's
inline-node-`WHERE` path treats it as not-true and rejects, so the OPTIONAL hop null-pads; TS
raises. Both engines raise for the same shape in a CLAUSE `WHERE`, which is what makes native's
inline path the suspect rather than the rule unclear.

Ruled out as mine STRUCTURALLY and then empirically, which is the order memory's
`gremlin-fuzz-families` note prescribes — the printed seed is the QUERY's, not the run's, so
`--seed` regenerates a different sequence and replayed CLEAN, as did three further full runs.
Structurally: the `CASE` has TWO branches, so item 450's arm declines it, and `num_conj_on_slot`
returns `None` for a `Case`, so item 451's cannot see it. Empirically: `git checkout 8ebc6256 --`
the two files, rebuild, and the pre-450 engine gives the IDENTICAL answer. Recorded in `CLOSED.md`
with the standalone reproducer, which is worth more than the seed.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1139 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz` at 50,000 seeds, `clippy --all-targets --features
capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, `bun run check` exit 0, `query_bench`
swept for regressions. Byte-identity fuzzers: **12 of 13 pass**, the one failure being the
pre-existing divergence above — stated rather than rounded up, and three subsequent differential
runs were clean.

One process note: `git checkout <commit> -- <path>` also STAGES that path, so after restoring my
own files `git diff` showed +76/+42 against the index while `git diff HEAD` showed nothing. Left
alone, the commit would have carried a silent revert of item 450. `git reset HEAD -- <paths>`
before committing.

## 452 — the divergence item 451 found is a RECORDED one, and I re-derived it. What is new is a one-line reproducer showing the class is far broader than every entry for it implies

Item 451 found a differential-fuzz failure, verified it was not caused by items 449-451, and
recorded it with the fuzzer's query. This tick set out to fix it. It should not have needed a tick
to find out that the question is settled and the residual declared.

### Where it was already written down

- `executor.ts`'s `case 'and'` carries the decision in full: ISO leaves both halves free
  (`US008` the order of evaluation, `UA004` whether an exception from an inessential part is
  raised), "**both outcomes conform, so the choice is ours to make on cost, and a FALSE is cheaper
  than an exception (user, 2026-10-08)**". It chose WRITTEN ORDER with no cost-based reordering,
  having tried the partitioned version and found it agreed with Rust on more shapes and disagreed
  on others.
- That same comment DECLARES this residual: "a filter … whose cheap conjunct Rust's seek hoisted
  past a raising sibling".
- `seed-gate-order.test.ts` is a whole file on item 175's gate, including which row raises.
- `CLOSED.md` has the class twice: item **322** closed one case of it (the ordering key's fourth
  mismatch, `isTruth`), and an OPEN entry records the same divergence making `bun run fuzz` red
  "roughly 1 run in 3" — against my observed 1 in 4.

**I searched `CLOSED.md` for the carrier question in item 448 and it saved a tick. I did not search
it for this one before diagnosing.** The project's instruction is to match the store to the kind of
fact, and "is this divergence known?" is a `CLOSED.md` question. Three passes in one session
re-deriving a closed target is the named failure mode; this is a fourth, and the only reason it
cost one tick rather than several is that the `and` evaluator's comment is unusually complete.

### What IS new: the class is not about `OPTIONAL MATCH`, `CASE`, or temporals

Every recorded reproducer for this class is a fuzzer-generated query with an `OPTIONAL MATCH`, an
inline node `WHERE`, a multi-branch `CASE` and a temporal or a `split(duration(…), -1)`. That
shape is what the entries describe, and it suggests the fault needs an exotic expression to
surface. It does not. Minimised, with a 2-vertex fixture:

```
MATCH (n:N) WHERE (n.n AND (0.1 IN [0.0, 2])) RETURN n.n AS y
  native -> []        TS -> raises "a boolean is required"
```

No `OPTIONAL`, no `CASE`, no temporal, no hop, no inline `WHERE`. A **non-boolean first conjunct
and a sibling that evaluates FALSE at runtime** is the whole of it. The neighbouring forms say
exactly where the line is:

| form                                                              | native                 | TS         |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------- |
| `(n.n AND (0.1 IN [0.0, 2]))`                                     | `[]`                   | **raises** |
| `((0.1 IN [0.0, 2]) AND n.n)`                                     | `[]`                   | `[]`       |
| `(n.n AND false)`                                                 | `[]`                   | `[]`       |
| same three in an inline node `WHERE`, with and without `OPTIONAL` | identical to the above |            |

So the trigger is a conjunct whose FALSE is _computed_ rather than literal: a literal `false` is
folded or short-circuited by both, and reversing the written order puts the FALSE first where both
engines stop. That is a sharper statement of the class than "Rust's seek hoisted past a raising
sibling", and it is the form a fix would be tested against.

### Not changed, deliberately

Which engine is right is not open — ISO permits both, and the repo has a dated user decision
preferring the cheaper FALSE. Aligning them means either making TS defer faults until no conjunct
settles the row (a `try`/`catch` per conjunct in the hot boolean path) or making native evaluate in
written order (giving up item 175's 267.61ms -> 5.26ms). Both are real changes with priced
consequences, and item 322's history is the warning: its first fix was wrong in the OTHER
direction and created two new divergences, because **being wider in one engine is the same mistake
as being narrower**.

So this stays open, now with a minimal reproducer attached to it. The one thing this tick changes
is that the minimal form goes into `CLOSED.md` beside the class, where the next pass will look.

### Gates

No engine change. `bun run check` exit 0, read as its own exit code.

## 453 — the two-bound range count, 3.9x. And a fast path that made a shape it never runs 1.4x slower, through code layout alone

Item 451 left this measured and open: a range filter cost 1.774 ms at 1,000,000 nodes against
0.459 for a single bound — **3.9x for one extra f64 compare**, which is ~1.1 ns a row and far more
than a compare costs. That arithmetic is the whole reason this was worth a tick: the number did
not fit the explanation on offer.

### Two wrong causes before the right one

**The `Vec` was not it.** Item 451's diagnosis was that `bounds.iter().all(…)` pays a heap
pointer-chase per node, so the obvious fix is to pull the two bounds into loop-invariant locals.
Smallest change first, measured same-harness: 1.782 -> 1.584 ms, **~1.12x**, and the 3-bound
control moved 1.03x on its own, so call it 9%. It left two bounds at 3.5x one bound. **A fix that
is directionally right and 9% is a refutation of the cause, not a partial win.**

The real cause is VECTORIZATION. The single-bound sweep item 451 built passes a monomorphic
`Fn(f64) -> bool` and auto-vectorizes; a pair of `num_pred` matches does not, whatever the bounds
are stored in. Four monomorphic arms for the range — `(lo_incl, hi_incl)` — take it to 0.458 ms,
**3.9x, landing exactly on the single-bound cost**. Not 36 operator pairs: a range is the shape
that matters, and the rest decline.

### A fast path that cost a shape it never runs

Written INLINE in `try_stream_num_count`, the range arm gained its 3.9x **and made the THREE-bound
shape 1.4x slower** — 1.978 ms to 2.78, consistently over three rounds. The 3-bound predicate
never enters the two-element arm; the enclosing function simply grew, and LLVM inlined
`scan_visit` differently for the general arm that follows.

Fixing it took two steps, both measured:

| configuration                  | two bounds | three bounds (control)     |
| ------------------------------ | ---------- | -------------------------- |
| before                         | 1.782      | 1.978                      |
| range arm inline               | 0.431      | **2.78** — 1.4x regression |
| extracted to its own fn        | 0.471      | 2.20 — still 1.11x         |
| extracted + `#[inline(never)]` | **0.458**  | 1.948 — flat               |

So the `#[inline(never)]` is load-bearing and has a measured reason, which is the only kind worth
keeping. This is the Rust twin of `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` and of item 90's finding that
`exec::pull`'s layout is load-bearing crate-wide: **a fast path can cost a shape it never runs,
through code layout alone — so a control the change cannot reach is not optional here, it is the
only thing that sees this.**

### Final numbers, three rounds, one case per process

| case                                 | before        | after                 |           |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------- | --------------------- | --------- |
| `a.k > 5 AND a.k < 100`              | 1.782 / 1.804 | 0.458 / 0.460 / 0.458 | **3.9x**  |
| same, written `< 100 AND > 5`        | —             | 0.458 / 0.462 / 0.467 | identical |
| `… AND a.k <> 7` (3 bounds, control) | 1.978 / 1.995 | 1.944 / 1.966 / 1.935 | flat      |
| single bound (control)               | 0.458         | 0.459 / 0.459 / 0.460 | flat      |
| string equality (control)            | 0.629         | 0.617 / 0.638 / 0.620 | flat      |

**A caution worth its own line:** the first invocation after `cargo build` read 0.685 and I nearly
wrote down 2.6x. Three rounds after it gave 0.458 flat. Min-of-9 inside one process does not fix a
cold first process, so the first run after a build is not a measurement.

### Teeth

Harness proven first: bomb 137, spin 124. Six mutants, **four caught**: `Gt` classified as an
inclusive lower bound; `Le` as exclusive; `lo` and `hi` swapped in the dispatch; and a THREE-bound
slice admitted by taking its first two. The inclusivity pair needs stored values sitting exactly
ON each threshold, which the fixture has.

Two SURVIVED, both labelled as perf-only in the script before it ran. The null control (the arm
never consulted) must survive. And recognising only ONE written order survives, because the
reversed spelling declines to the general arm and answers the same — **an equivalent-spelling
claim cannot be policed by a test**, so `caseinv_450` gained a `tworev` case instead, and the two
orders measure 0.458 against 0.458.

209 differential forms against item 450's `CASE` wrapper as the oracle: both written orders of
every inclusivity-by-threshold combination, plus seven non-range pairs that must decline, plus two
three-bound predicates.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1141 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz` at 50,000 seeds, `clippy --all-targets --features
capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13
(item 452's known residual did not surface this run). Everything re-measured after `cargo fmt`.

## 454 — asking TS the question items 451/453 answered for native: no cliff to fix, and the one lever that looked free is REFUTED

Items 451 and 453 found native's filtered-count arms — a single numeric bound at 3.7x and a
two-bound range at 3.9x. Item 448's rule is that a gap found in one engine is a QUESTION about
the other and never a finding, so `route-cost-probe` gained the same ladder for TS.

### TS has no cliff

200,000 nodes, same selectivity across all three (`age` is 0..89, so `< 1000` and `>= 0` are
vacuous), one case per process:

| predicate                  | TS                                 |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| none (`count(*)`)          | 0.0 ms — O(1) off the label bucket |
| one bound                  | 4.4-6.4                            |
| two bounds                 | 5.9-6.4                            |
| two bounds, reversed order | 5.8 — no spelling gap              |
| three bounds               | 7.1-8.9                            |

Roughly linear in the conjunct count, about +1.3 ms per bound. **Nothing like native's pre-453
shape, where the SECOND bound cost 3.9x the first.** Native's cliff was a lost auto-vectorization;
TS evaluates a closure per conjunct per vertex and simply pays for each. So there is no
equivalent fix to port, which is the same answer item 448 reached about items 446/447 in the
other direction.

### The lever that looked free, measured and refuted

`satisfies` allocates `{ binding, params, graph }` on EVERY call. In `buildNodeCount`'s
constrained tally that is one object per vertex — 200,000 to count a filtered label bucket — and
the object carries no state: the three fields are the same references throughout a walk, nothing
assigns to them, and nothing retains it past the call (checked across the package first). So a
`satisfiesIn(element, pred, env)` taking a caller-owned env is trivially sound. Written, with an
`inlineHoldsIn` beside it, and used in the tally.

It bought nothing. Three rounds each side, one case per process, A/B by reverting the two files
and rebuilding:

|              | before          | after           |
| ------------ | --------------- | --------------- |
| one bound    | 4.4 / 6.4 / 4.4 | 4.8 / 5.0 / 5.3 |
| two bounds   | 5.9 / 6.4 / 6.2 | 6.2 / 6.2 / 6.7 |
| three bounds | 8.9 / 7.3 / 7.1 | 7.2 / 7.5 / 7.5 |

**The spread WITHIN each configuration is larger than any difference between them.** V8 escape-
analyses a short-lived object that never leaves the call, so there was no allocation to remove.
Reverted, and the refutation is recorded as a doc comment ON `satisfies` with its numbers, which
is where someone about to redo it will be looking — `CLAUDE.md`'s rule that a rejected
optimization goes next to the code it would have changed.

Worth separating two things this nearly conflated. The reasoning was sound: the object IS
allocated per element, it IS stateless, and hoisting it IS safe. What was wrong was the
assumption that an allocation the compiler can see through costs anything. **"It allocates per
element" is not by itself a cost** — item 424 recorded the same sentence about a per-row
allocation in the top-k path, rejected at 2.4%, and this is the second time that exact belief has
produced a change worth nothing.

### Gates

Engine unchanged (the one-line env hoist reverted; only a comment and the probe remain).
`bun test packages/gql` 2135 pass / 0 fail, `bun run check` exit 0.

## 455 — the spelling probe's longest-standing flag is its own harness: `5 <= n.k` is NOT slower than `n.k >= 5`, and "slower from either position" turns out to be insufficient

`spelling-probe` has reported `range operand order: 5 <= n.k vs n.k >= 5` at 2.4-2.5x in every
run this session. It has no item number anywhere — not in `CLOSED.md`, not in the audit — so it
is either an unexamined 2.4x on the simplest rewrite there is, or an artifact. `CLAUDE.md` names
that exact pair among the 100-300x spelling gaps this engine exists not to have, so it got a tick.
(Checked `CLOSED.md` FIRST this time, which item 452 is the entry about not doing.)

### It is an artifact, confirmed three ways

**Isolated, one case per process, three rounds of min-of-9** (`route-cost-probe`): `n.age >= 5`
reads 4.6 / 4.5 / 4.4 ms and `5 <= n.age` reads 4.6 / 4.5 / 4.6. The equality pair is the same
story: `n.age = 5` at 3.9 / 3.8 / 3.8 against `5 = n.age` at 3.9 / 4.1 / 4.0. No gap.

**The probe is BIMODAL on this group**, which is the tell. Five full runs:

```
  5.40 / 13.19     5.28 / 5.33     5.38 / 13.11     5.58 / 13.54     5.40 / 5.35
```

Two distinct modes 2.5x apart for the SAME query — 13.1-13.5 or 5.3, never between — hitting
three runs in five. A spread would scatter; this is a slow mode being entered or not.

**`SPELL_ONLY`** (added here) runs just the matching groups in a fresh process: 4.47/4.44,
4.44/4.40, 4.38/4.42. Both the gap AND the slow mode vanish, and the numbers land on the
route-probe's isolated figures.

### What this corrects

The probe's own harness comment records items 180/181, where a group was reported at 1.5-2.1x for
three audit items with no engine cause: whichever member ran FIRST paid a position penalty. The
fix was to time every spelling in BOTH positions and keep its better reading, with the stated
