rule that **"a spelling that is genuinely slower is slower from either position"**.

That rule has a hole, and this group is in it. The 13.1 ms readings ARE the min across both
positions and across nine reps — the slow mode survives the reversal, so the two-pass fix cannot
see it. **A per-process deopt is slower from either position too.** Necessary, not sufficient; the
only sufficient check is a separate process.

That matters beyond this group: it means any flag this probe raises needs isolated confirmation
before it is a claim, and before today there was no short way to run one. Hence `SPELL_ONLY`.

### Changed

- `SPELL_ONLY=<substring>` filters the groups, so confirming a flag is one command.
- The group carries the isolated numbers, the five-run bimodal record, and both confirmation
  commands, so the next reader does not spend a tick on it. The flag is left IN rather than
  suppressed: it is real output about the harness, and a group deleted for being inconvenient is
  how a probe stops being trusted.

No engine change — the two spellings already compile to the same predicate, which is why there
was never anything to fix. Gates: `bun run check` exit 0, full probe still reports 0 answer
disagreements.

## 456 — the spelling probe's last real flag, closed: a three-hop interior gate built from an inline constraint is 18x. And the first version of the fix traded that for a regression next door

Item 455 refuted one of the probe's three standing flags as its own harness and left this one:
`three hops, SECOND position filtered (item 222)` at 13.8x. Applying 455's own rule first —
confirm in a fresh process before pricing — it SURVIVES, and is bigger than the in-process
reading:

| spelling                                            | isolated, three runs     |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `(a:P)-[:E]->(b)-[:E]->(c)-[:E]->(d) WHERE b.k = 2` | 14.24 / 12.85 / 15.44 ms |
| `… (b WHERE b.k = 2) …`                             | 244.02 / 243.01 / 241.12 |
| `… (b {k: 2}) …`                                    | 243.33 / 246.19 / 240.80 |

**17x between three ways of writing one question**, with the two inline spellings agreeing
exactly — so clause-vs-inline, not props-vs-`WHERE`.

### Two wrong diagnoses, and a trace that ended them

I guessed twice from reading. First that a newer route (item 430's `threeSegmentRoute`) had
overtaken item 222's and lost the inline coverage. Then that `threeSegmentCount` returns `null`
for an inline constraint and the route returned that `null` instead of falling back to the sweep
— which I WROTE, and which measured no change at all, because the branch is never taken.

A four-line trace settled it in one run:

```
clause:  product=ok interior=true  labelled=true sweep=ok
inline:  product=ok interior=false labelled=true sweep=ok
```

`interiorPredOf` reads a clause `WHERE` only. So the clause spelling gets a gated degree product
(fast), and the inline spelling gets `interior=false`, falls through to the sweep-or-product
choice, and lands on something 18x slower. **Item 441's rule — verify the shape reaches the path
before measuring — is cheap and I skipped it twice in one tick.**

### The fix, and the regression it caused first

Build the same `{ pred, onB }` from `inlineOf` when no clause `WHERE` supplied one. The gate is
identical once built, so it is the same route for the same question.

The first version did that for BOTH interior positions, and the THIRD-position group in the same
probe caught what that cost:

|                            | before            | inline gate on b AND c    | b only          |
| -------------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | --------------- |
| second position, clause    | 12.85-15.44       | 12.20-14.23               | 12.42-13.30     |
| second position, inline x2 | 240.80-246.19     | **12.36-15.06**           | **12.36-13.72** |
| third position, clause     | 469.22-469.47     | 461-474                   | 451.81-465.54   |
| third position, inline x2  | **367.02-370.01** | **454-485** (1.25x worse) | 371.38-396.25   |

Item 222's own reasoning says why: the product's walk ITERATES `b`, so a gate there costs once
per VERTEX, but it meets `c` as each middle edge's far end, once per MIDDLE EDGE. `c` was already
taking the sweep and the sweep was winning. **An 18x win and a 1.25x regression one position
along, and only a control in the same probe showed it** — the third-position group was there
because item 222 put it there, which is the argument for a probe keeping neighbours it is not
currently investigating.

### Teeth, and four survivors that are not gaps

Harness proven: bomb 137, spin 124. Five mutants. **`onB` is load-bearing — flipping it fails
seven tests.** The other four survive and each is explained in the code rather than left looking
like a hole: the null control must survive; admitting a second interior gate is answer-preserving
because the product then declines a shape it cannot express and the route falls through;
admitting an OPEN constraint (`{k: a.k}`) answers the same either way; and letting the inline gate
override the clause is EQUIVALENT, because the clause block runs after this one and ORDER already
gives it priority. Six new tests, including the inline-gate-alongside-a-clause-`WHERE` shape the
suite had no coverage of, which is the one mutation asked for.

### Where the probe stands

`bun run spelling` now reports **two** groups over 2x: the `range operand order` artifact item 455
refuted, and `label on start` at 3235x, which is a 0.00 ms degenerate. No genuine spelling gap is
outstanding on it.

### Gates

`bun test packages/gql` 2141 pass / 0 fail, `bun run check` exit 0 — twice red first, on a blank
line and on complexity 38 then 36, which is why every condition now lives in
`inlineInteriorGate` and the call site is one branch. All seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13.
Re-measured after the extraction and after `fmt`.

## 457 — "coalesce is slow" is wrong: the GENERIC SCALAR-CALL PATH costs ~33 ns a row, and every function without a vectorized arm pays it

With the spelling probe clean after item 456, item 434's 25-shape gap screen is the place to look
for a fresh target. Its LOWEST ratios are where native is relatively weakest, and after items 438,
449 and 450 the bottom of the band is still `case expr` 2.7x, `coalesce` 2.6x and `arith pred`
5.3x. Those three are positions the filter arms do not reach: the first two are AGGREGATE
ARGUMENTS and the third is a NESTED arithmetic predicate (`a.k * 2 + 1`, two `Arith` levels, where
`try_filter_keep_arith` admits one).

### Priced natively, 1,000,000 nodes, same row counts within each comparison

| shape                                              | ms                  |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `count(a.k)` — the floor                           | **0.466**           |
| `count(a.k + 1)`                                   | 3.975               |
| `count(round(a.k))`                                | 4.301               |
| `count(abs(a.k))`                                  | 4.824               |
| `count(CASE WHEN a.k > 3 THEN 1 ELSE null END)`    | 28.396              |
| `count(coalesce(a.k, 0))`                          | 37.518              |
| `count(coalesce(a.missing, a.k))`                  | 40.841              |
| `count(power(a.k, 2))`                             | **45.193**          |
| `a.k * 2 > 6` (flat) vs `a.k * 2 + 1 > 7` (nested) | 2.061 vs **11.091** |

### Two diagnoses, both of which changed the target

**The probe's `coalesce` reads an ABSENT column**, so the first question was whether 40.8 ms is
the function or the missing column. `coalesce(a.k, 0)` over a present one is 37.5 — so it is the
function, and the shape the gap screen chose was not misleading anyone.

**Then: is it `coalesce`, or the path it shares?** `power(a.k, 2)` is the same shape — two args,
numeric, no vectorized arm — and measures **45.193 ms, slower than coalesce**. The vectorized
pair land together too (`round` 4.301, `abs` 4.824), about 9x apart from the generic pair. So the
cost is not `coalesce`: it is the GENERIC SCALAR-CALL PATH, and the per-row overhead is ~33 ns
(coalesce at 37.5 ns/row for what is a null check, against `abs` at 4.8 ns/row for an f64
operation; `power`'s extra ~12 ns is `pow` itself).

**That reframing is the tick's result.** A `coalesce` special case would have fixed one function
and left `power`, `concat`, `substring`, `replace` and every other non-vectorized scalar exactly
where they are — and would have looked like a win, because the probe row it was chosen from would
have moved.

### What the generic path does per row

`eval`'s `Expr::Call` arm already reuses ONE argument buffer across rows (so there is no per-row
`Vec` allocation to remove — that lever is spent). What remains per row is: boxing every argument
into a `Value` through `Col::value_at`, a call to `call_scalar_checked(name, &buf)` which matches
the function NAME as a STRING against dozens of arms, and pushing a boxed `Value` into a
`Col::Gen`. The vectorized arm above it does none of those — it maps `f64 -> f64` over a
`Col::Num` and stays a `Col::Num`, which is why the two groups sit 9x apart.

The obvious shape of a fix is to resolve the name to a function pointer ONCE, before the row
loop, so the dispatch leaves the inner loop and a `Col::Num`-in/`Col::Num`-out arm becomes
possible for more than the unary-finite set. Priced here, built next — the discipline items 437
and 445 used, and this one earns it twice over, because the first two things I would have built
(a coalesce arm, then an absent-column arm) were both aimed at the wrong thing.

### Open, with numbers

- **The generic scalar-call path: ~33 ns/row, ~9x against a vectorized arm**, for every scalar
  function without one.
- **A nested arithmetic predicate is 5.4x a flat one** — 11.091 against 2.061 ms for the same row
  count — because `try_filter_keep_arith` (item 438) admits `Prop op Lit` and `a.k * 2 + 1` is
  `Arith(Arith(Prop, 2), 1)`.

### Gates

No engine change; `exprpred_437` gained nine cases covering the aggregate-argument and
nested-predicate positions. `cargo clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` exit 0,
`cargo fmt --check` exit 0, `bun run check` exit 0.

## 458 — `coalesce` over columns: 8.9x, and the two wins are different things. Item 457's warning was right about one of them and wrong about the other

Item 457 priced the generic scalar-call path at ~33 ns/row and warned that a `coalesce` special
case would be the wrong fix — it would move the gap-screen row it came from and leave `power`,
`concat` and every other non-vectorized scalar where they are. This tick split that overhead and
found the warning applies to HALF of what was available.

### Where the ~33 ns goes

Same function, one more argument each time, 1,000,000 rows: `coalesce` at 2 / 3 / 4 arguments
costs 31.9 / 37.7 / 45.0 ms, so **~6 ns a row per argument**. A ONE-argument generic call
(`sqrt`, excluded from `unary_finite_num_fn` because it can make a NaN) is 32.8. So the fixed
part is **~27 ns/row** and the per-argument boxing is the smaller half.

A throwaway experiment behind an env var then split the fixed part, A/B with the flag properly
unset (an empty `EXP458=` still satisfies `is_ok()`, which made the first run compare the arm
against itself):

|                                      | off         | on              |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------- | --------------- |
| `count(coalesce(a.k, 0))`            | 31.2 / 31.3 | **4.81 / 4.83** |
| `count(coalesce(a.missing, a.k))`    | 37.0 / 36.6 | 21.8 / 22.4     |
| `power`, `sqrt`, `abs`, `count(a.k)` | —           | all flat        |

### Two wins, and only one of them is general

- **A first argument that CANNOT be null makes `coalesce` the identity.** `Col::Num`, `Col::Bool`
  and `Col::Str` have no null representation — a column with nulls is a `Col::Gen` — so no later
  argument is reachable and the result IS that column. **8.9x** shipped (31.2 -> 3.44 ms),
  landing on the vectorized floor. **No general dispatch fix could give this**: it is a semantic
  property of `coalesce`, not an overhead.
- **Otherwise, merge the columns with the dispatch resolved once.** 1.67x — and THAT 1.67x is
  the part a general resolver would give every non-vectorized function. Item 457's target
  stands, now with its size known: the per-row `call_scalar_checked(name, …)` string match is
  ~15 ns of the ~27.

So item 457 was right that a `coalesce` arm leaves the family unfixed, and wrong that it would
therefore be the wrong thing to build — the larger half of this particular win was never going to
come from the general fix. Both are in `CLOSED.md`; one is done.

### Semantics

`coalesce` is lazy in the VALUE sense and this keeps that, but it must NOT become lazy in the
RAISE sense: the path it replaces materializes every argument column before the row loop, so a
later argument that faults raises even when the first is non-null everywhere. Checked in both
engines before writing the arm — `coalesce(a.k, 1/0)` raises in both — and the mutant that
evaluates arguments lazily is caught.

`Nodes`/`Edges` are excluded from the identity because the `u32::MAX` OPTIONAL-miss sentinel IS a
null there. That exclusion was UNTESTED and mutation said so: admitting `Nodes` left every test
green until a fixture with one matching and one missing optional hop was added.

### Teeth

Harness proven: bomb 137, spin 124. Six mutants, **five caught**: the identity admitting
`Col::Gen`; the identity admitting `Nodes`; the merge taking the first argument whatever it
holds; the merge taking the LAST non-null instead of the first; and lazy argument evaluation
(the raise-parity one). The sixth is the null control.

One test expectation was mine rather than the engine's again: I wrote `coalesce(a.k, -1)` over a
nullable column as ending in `Null`, which is the SINGLE-argument spelling's answer; with a
default the absent row is `-1`. The test caught me, and the corrected assertion is now the one
that proves the identity does not fire for a `Col::Gen`.

### Found, not mine, recorded

`coalesce` over a NODE column renders raw ids natively where TS renders the element —
`coalesce(z, a)` gives `[2, 1]` against TS's node objects. Verified against the commit before
this arm, so pre-existing; the fallback itself is correct in both.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1144 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz` at 50,000 seeds, `clippy --all-targets
--features capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity
fuzzers 13/13. Re-measured after `cargo fmt`: 3.43 / 3.44 ms, controls flat.

## 459 — the general half of item 457: resolving a scalar function's NAME once is 2.6x, and it is worth ~20 ns a row

Item 458 shipped the `coalesce`-specific half and left the general one priced but unbuilt: the
generic scalar path matches the function NAME as a STRING against dozens of arms ONCE PER ROW.
Item 457 guessed that at ~15 ns. It is ~20, and sizing it first is what made the fix worth
building.

### Sizing it

A throwaway arm bypassing the name match for `sqrt` ALONE — keeping the per-row boxing and the
boxed output — took it from 32.4 / 32.5 ms to **12.5 / 12.7** at 1,000,000 rows, with `power`
(still generic) flat at 45.0-45.7 and `abs` (already vectorized) flat at 4.77-4.79. So the
dispatch is the dominant part of the ~27 ns fixed overhead, and the rest — boxing plus the
`Col::Gen` output — is the ~7.7 ns that still separates 12.5 from `abs`'s 4.8.

### The family, not the function

`scalar_num_fn` has twenty-one unary numeric functions. Six are in `unary_finite_num_fn`, which
builds a `Col::Num` and so admits only those that cannot make a NaN or an infinity from a finite
input — a stored numeric column is all-finite and that arm must not break it. **The other
fifteen had no arm at all**: `sqrt`, `exp`, `ln`, `log10`, the six trig functions, the three
hyperbolics, `cot`, `degrees`, `radians`.

`unary_num_fn` resolves all twenty-one to an `fn(f64) -> f64`, and `scalar_num_fn` DELEGATES to
it, so there is one body per function. The new evaluator arm keeps the output BOXED on purpose:
these functions can produce a non-finite result, and the boxed path owes no all-finite invariant.
It removes the dispatch and nothing else.

### Measured, same harness, three rounds each

| case                                     | before                | after                                |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `count(sqrt(a.k))`                       | 33.95 / 33.50 / 32.86 | **12.93 / 12.65 / 12.73** — **2.6x** |
| `count(power(a.k, 2))` (control, 2 args) | 47.11 / 46.23 / 45.89 | 45.16 / 45.25 / 45.40                |
| `count(abs(a.k))` (control, vectorized)  | 4.96 / 4.89 / 4.91    | 4.79 / 4.76 / 4.79                   |
| `count(coalesce(a.k, 0))` (control)      | 3.63 / 3.53 / 3.50    | 3.45 / 3.45 / 3.50                   |
| `count(a.k)` (control)                   | 0.477 / 0.473 / 0.477 | 0.468 / 0.466 / 0.469                |

**The first version was inline in `eval`'s `Call` arm and cost the shapes it never runs** —
`power` 47.8-48.5 and `coalesce` 3.78-3.88, consistently in direction, neither of which takes a
one-argument arm. Extracted to `eval_unary_num` with `#[inline(never)]`, the controls return to
flat AND `sqrt` improves further (14.6 inline against 12.7 split). That is the second occasion of
item 453's finding, now on a different file: **a fast path can cost a shape it never runs,
through code layout alone.**

### Two corrections the tests made

**The first arm returned NULL for a non-numeric argument.** `call_scalar_checked` RAISES there —
`sqrt('1e300')` throws, a named function validating its non-null arguments where an arithmetic
operator would propagate — and `a_raising_predicate_still_raises_when_it_is_reached` failed on
the first run. The fix does not re-spell the error: the one row that needs it calls
`call_scalar_checked`, so the message and the condition stay defined once.

**`unary_finite_num_fn` kept its own copy of `sign`**, so the claim "one body per function" was
false and mutation proved it in the most direct way available: flipping `sign`'s NaN guard
SURVIVED, because `s///` hit the first copy and the test routed through the second. **Two copies
of a body make a mutant land on whichever the tool reaches first, and a surviving mutant then
means nothing.** `unary_finite_num_fn` is now the restriction LIST and delegates for the bodies;
the same mutant is caught.

### Teeth

Harness proven: bomb 137, spin 124. Six mutants, **five caught** by the unit suite: `ln` wired to
`log10`; `asin` to `acos`; a non-numeric argument becoming NULL; a NULL argument passed through
the function; and `sign` losing its NaN guard. Every expectation is a value only that function
produces, because a mapping error is invisible to a test that checks only that a number came back.

The sixth — `degrees` using `to_degrees`, which pre-rounds the 180/PI constant and lands one ULP
off the TS engine — survives the unit suite and **is caught by the differential fuzzer**, checked
rather than assumed: applied, the fuzzer failed on both of two runs.

### A fuzz failure, verified NOT mine

`bun run fuzz` came back 12/13 on `cot` at zero (`0.0 <= cot(0.0 * n.x)` and siblings). The run
seed `FUZZ_SEED=2724363121` replays deterministically, and it **fails at HEAD too** — reverting
both files and rebuilding reproduces it. Pre-existing. A hand-built three-node fixture did NOT
reproduce it, so the fuzzer's fixture is part of the shape and the seed is the reproducer;
recorded in `CLOSED.md` as such rather than minimised on a guess.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1146 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz` at 50,000 seeds, `clippy --all-targets
--features capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, `bun run check` exit 0.
Re-measured after `cargo fmt`: `sqrt` 12.95 / 12.92, controls flat.

## 460 — item 459 shipped a WRONG ANSWER, and I mislabelled it pre-existing because a RUN failing is not the same QUERY failing

Item 459's arm read `Value::Num(x)` out of the column and called `f(x)` on the raw `f64`. That
skips `num_of`, which collapses -0.0 to +0.0 — the numeric model has no negative zero, and
`num_of`'s own comment names the exact casualty: "`cot(-0)` -> -Inf vs +Inf, which diverged
across engines". So `0.0 <= cot(0.0 * n.x)` answered FALSE for every negative `x` where the TS
engine answers TRUE, because `0.0 * -2.0` is -0.0 under IEEE.

**It went to CI red.** The differential fuzzer caught it in item 459's own tick and I cleared it
wrongly.

### The mistake, which is the point of this entry

I replayed the failing seed against HEAD, saw the run fail there too, and wrote "pre-existing,
verified". The run DID fail at HEAD — on a DIFFERENT query. That seed carries two divergences:
the `cot` one I had just introduced, and item 452's known `AND`-fault-order residual
(`0.0 AND ('a' IN [n.x, '1e3'])`, which the fuzzer's own classifier labels an evaluation-order
difference). Checking the exit code of a 20,000-query run answered "does this seed fail", which
is not the question.

**A run failing is not the same query failing.** The check that would have worked is the one that
took thirty seconds once I did it: run the OFFENDING QUERY against the previous build. At item
458 it answers `true, true`; at 459 it answers `false, true`. That is the whole diagnosis, and it
was available before the push.

Item 451 did this correctly — it ruled a divergence out structurally first, then rebuilt the
prior commit and compared THE ANSWER. The difference between the two ticks is not care, it is
which thing got compared.

### The fix

The arm goes through `value::num_of` instead of matching `Value::Num` directly, so the -0
collapse happens in the one place that defines it. `num_of` returns `None` for a NULL _and_ for a
non-numeric, which the two arms keep apart — a NULL propagates, anything else is the data
exception item 459 already got right.

The win is unaffected: `count(sqrt(a.k))` is 12.89 / 13.04 / 12.89 ms against 12.65 / 12.93 /
12.73 before the fix, and the four controls are flat.

### Teeth

Two assertions added, from the outside: `0.0 <= cot(0.0 * (0 - a.k))` and the positive twin, both
TRUE. Verified by RE-INTRODUCING the bug — `f(if x == 0.0 { -0.0 } else { x })` — which the test
catches (exit 101). A regression test that has not failed against the bug it describes is a
guess, and this one has.

The seed now reports only item 452's residual, and the full `bun run fuzz` is 13/13.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1146 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz` at 50,000 seeds, `clippy --all-targets
--features capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, `bun run check` exit 0, all
seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13.

## 461 — the step item 459 skipped, done: grep the ±0 pattern elsewhere, and make the class deterministic rather than lucky

Item 460 fixed one negative-zero bug and CI went green. Two things were still missing, and both
are method rather than performance.

**The sweep.** Item 459's bug was a fast path reading a raw `f64` out of a column and bypassing
`value::num_of`, which collapses -0.0 to +0.0. "Grep the pattern elsewhere" is a named step of
this loop's method and I did not do it, so the obvious question — how many OTHER arms read a raw
`f64`? — went unasked until after the push. The answer, now measured rather than assumed:

- **A STORED -0 is harmless.** The arith filter arm (item 438) and the count sweeps (items 451, 453) all read `data[i]` straight from the store, but every one of them only COMPARES, and a
  comparison cannot see the sign of zero (`-0.0 == 0.0`, and the orderings agree). Checked
  against the TS engine over a fixture carrying a stored -0: five shapes, all agreeing.
- **A COMPUTED -0 reaches two operations and no more.** `cot`, which is `1/tan` — item 459's
  casualty — and division. `floor`/`ceil`/`round` PRESERVE a -0 into the column the next
  operation reads, which is the route by which a neighbouring arm could have failed the same way.
  Six shapes through those, all agreeing after item 460.
- **Division cannot see it either**, because dividing by a computed zero RAISES rather than
  yielding an infinity. That was written here first as an infinity assertion and failed with
  "division by zero" — the engine's answer is better than my expectation, and it shrinks the
  class to `cot` alone.

So after item 460 there is no second instance. That is worth as much as a fix: the alternative
was carrying an open suspicion.

**The coverage.** Item 460 was found by a RANDOM FUZZER SEED. Nothing deterministic covered the
class, so the same mistake in a neighbouring arm would have shipped the same way and waited for
another lucky seed. `computed_negative_zero_is_collapsed_everywhere_it_can_be_seen` pins eleven
shapes — `cot` of a multiplied zero in a projection AND in a filter, of a subtracted zero,
through each of `floor`/`ceil`/`round`, `sign`, `abs`, and the two division raises. Every one was
checked against the TS engine before being written down; all nine comparable shapes agree.

**The general lesson.** A bug found by a fuzzer has been found by luck, and luck does not
generalise to the arm next door. The fix closes one instance; the sweep closes the class; the
test keeps it closed. Item 459 did the first, skipped the second, and left the third to chance.

### Gates

No engine change. `cargo test` 1147 + 13 + 723 + 10, `clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D
warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, `bun run check` exit 0. CI green on item 460
(38940575000).

## 462 — one nested arithmetic level, 5.2x. And splitting the loop made the shapes it does NOT serve faster than they were

Item 457 priced this and left it open: `try_filter_keep_arith` admits `<prop> <op> <lit>`, so
`a.k * 2 + 1 > 7` — which is `Arith(Arith(Prop, 2), 1)` — declined and fell to the materializing
path. Re-measured first, as the loop's rule requires, and it had grown slightly: **6.0x**,
12.735 / 13.505 ms against 2.075 / 2.258 for the one-level `a.k * 2 > 6` at the identical row
count.

### The change

One extra level, matched in all four spellings — `(p op l) op l`, `(l op p) op l`,
`l op (p op l)`, `l op (l op p)` — because an arm that recognised the property in only one
position would be the equivalent-spelling gap this engine exists not to have. The inner step's
operator and operand become a second pair of loop-invariant locals, and nothing more: a `Vec` of
steps iterated per row is precisely what item 453 measured as the thing that stops the loop
vectorizing, so a CHAIN is not supported and three levels still decline.

The inner step owes the same zero-divisor rule as the outer one and gets it, for the same
reason — the general path throws and a keep-pass cannot express a throw.

### The loop had to be split, and that is the third occasion

Written as ONE loop with a `match inner` inside it, the arm worked and cost the one-level shape
it must not touch: `a.k + 0 > 5` went 1.859 / 1.877 / 1.889 ms to 2.046 / 2.058 / 2.067, **1.10x,
consistently over three rounds each**. Same family as items 453 and 459 — a fast path charging a
shape it never serves — and the same remedy: the branch is a per-CALL decision, so it belongs
outside the row loop.

Two loops chosen before either runs, with the compare block duplicated rather than factored into
a closure (fifteen lines a reader can diff, against a closure that would become the thing being
measured). The arithmetic step and the comparison moved into `arith_step` and the existing
`num_pred`.

**And the controls came back FASTER than baseline**, which was not the goal and is reported
because it was measured, not because it was wanted:

| case                       | before                | after                                    |
| -------------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `a.k * 2 + 1 > 7`          | 12.735 / 13.505       | **2.413 / 2.462 / 2.478** — **5.2-5.5x** |
| `a.k * 2 > 6` (one level)  | 2.097 / 2.117 / 2.092 | 1.768 / 1.802 / 1.886                    |
| `a.k + 0 > 5` (one level)  | 1.859 / 1.877 / 1.889 | 1.693 / 1.721 / 1.742                    |
| `a.k > 5` (plain, control) | 0.464 / 0.468 / 0.465 | 0.458 / 0.460 / 0.467                    |

The one-level gain is incidental — hoisting the two `match`es into shared functions changed the
codegen — and it is the opposite sign of what the single-loop version did to the same rows, which
is the useful part: **the same change can cost or gain 10% on an untouched shape depending only
on where the branch sits.**

### Teeth

Harness proven: bomb 137, spin 124. Six mutants, **five caught**: the inner step ignoring operand
ORDER (`2 - a.k` computed as `a.k - 2`); the inner step using the OUTER operator; the inner
zero-divisor guard dropped; a THREE-level expression admitted by treating its middle as the inner
step; and swapping the split arms (which does not compile, which the script reports as caught).
The sixth — never taking a nested expression — is the null control for the new shape: declining
is answer-preserving, so no test can police it.

**4,800 differential forms** against item 438's oracle, which still works and for a better reason
than before: wrapping in a redundant `+ 0` now makes the predicate THREE levels, which this arm
declines, so `eval` answers. Five inner operators by three outer by five literals by four
comparisons by four thresholds by the four operand spellings.

One expectation was mine rather than the engine's, for the third time this session: I wrote
`8 / a.k + 1 > 3` as two rows over k = 1..4, and `8/3 + 1` is 3.67, which is above 3. Three rows.

## 463 — the gap screen after items 458/459/462, a regression refuted, and the CASE in an AGGREGATE priced at ~55x

Item 457's open list is empty, so the 25-shape gap screen gets re-run to pick the next target.
The three wins landed on it: `arith pred` moved from 5.3x to **26.1x** (native 0.56 -> 0.12 ms,
item 462), `coalesce` from 2.6x to **4.9x** (1.61 -> 0.91, item 458), and `case expr` barely at
all — 2.7x to 2.3x — which is the lead.

### A regression that was not one

The same screen showed `varlen distinct` at native **22.93 ms** against 9.54 on the session's
first run — a 2.4x move, and three of my items had touched the evaluator since. Re-measured, it
is 9.62 / 11.53 / 10.93: the 22.93 was a single outlier in a single run of a probe whose own
header says it is a SCREEN, with 25+ shapes sharing one process.

Checking it cost one command and the alternative was either shipping a suspicion or spending a
tick bisecting. **A screen's row is a reason to measure, never a measurement** — the same rule
item 455 applied to the spelling probe's flag, here in the other direction: that one survived
isolation and this one did not.

### The CASE in an aggregate argument, priced

Item 450 unwrapped a boolean CASE used AS a filter predicate, 24.9x. That arm cannot reach an
aggregate ARGUMENT, where the CASE must actually produce a value per row, and item 459's resolver
cannot either — a CASE is not a `Call`. At 1,000,000 rows:

| shape                                           | ms                |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `count(a.k)` — the floor                        | **0.448 / 0.459** |
| `sum(a.k)` — the floor                          | 0.560 / 0.566     |
| `count(CASE WHEN a.k > 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`    | 26.036 / 26.442   |
| `count(CASE WHEN a.k > 3 THEN a.k ELSE 0 END)`  | 26.969 / 27.521   |
| `sum(CASE WHEN a.k > 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`      | 27.978 / 28.401   |
| `count(CASE WHEN a.k > 3 THEN 1 ELSE null END)` | 30.162 / 30.144   |

**~55x the floor, and all four within 15% of each other** whatever their arms hold — a null arm,
two numeric literals, a property. That is item 442's tell for the second time in this family: a
table whose rows all agree is measuring something they share, and here it is `Expr::Case` itself,
exactly as item 450 found one position over. An arm-by-arm fusion would again be the wrong shape.

`count(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE null END)` is the ordinary idiom for a conditional count, so this
is not an exotic shape.

The fix shape, from item 450's diagnosis: the eager path evaluates every branch's VALUE into a
column and then calls `value_at` per row per branch to pick one, collecting a boxed `Col::Gen`.
When the branch values are LITERALS — which is the common case and all four rows above — the
selection is between constants and needs no per-row `value_at` at all; with no null among them it
need not even box, and could stay a `Col::Num` for the aggregate to fold.

Priced here, built next: the `Expr::Case` evaluator carries a lazy fallback for branch errors and
a dictionary fast path, so it is not a place to change in the same tick as a measurement.

### Gates

No engine change; `exprpred_437` gained six cases. `bun run check` exit 0.

## 464 — a CASE with LITERAL arms selects between constants: 2.3-3.0x across five shapes, and the property-armed twins are the control

Item 463 priced a CASE in an aggregate argument at ~55x the floor and found all four variants
within 15% of each other whatever their arms held — item 442's tell that the cost is
`Expr::Case` itself. This is the arm that follows from that, and the diagnosis says which arm to
write.

### What the eager path does that this does not

For `CASE WHEN a.k > 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END` it calls `eval_all` over the branch VALUES, which
materializes a full column per branch — a million `f64`s to represent the constant `1` — then
another for the `ELSE`, and then the row loop calls `value_at` once per branch per row to pick
one, boxing as it goes.

With literal arms none of that is needed: the values are already `Value`s and the only per-row
work is deciding WHICH. The arm returns a `Col::Num` when every arm is a non-null number, so an
aggregate folds raw `f64`s instead of unboxing; otherwise a `Col::Gen` of cloned literals, which
for `Num`/`Bool` is a copy and for `Str` a refcount bump.

### Measured, three rounds, 1,000,000 rows

| shape                                                | before          | after                    |          |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------ | -------- |
| `count(CASE WHEN a.k > 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`         | 26.036 / 26.442 | 8.716 / 8.990 / 8.516    | **3.0x** |
| `count(CASE … THEN 1 ELSE null END)`                 | 30.162 / 30.144 | 11.544 / 11.615 / 11.414 | **2.6x** |
| `sum(CASE … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`                      | 27.978 / 28.401 | 11.986 / 11.218 / 11.252 | **2.4x** |
| `(CASE … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1` in a FILTER         | 33.4 / 33.5     | 14.612 / 14.789 / 14.716 | **2.3x** |
| `CASE … THEN true WHEN … ELSE false END` (two WHENs) | 28.9 / 29.7     | 17.959 / 17.902 / 17.993 | **1.6x** |
| `count(CASE … THEN a.k ELSE 0 END)` — PROPERTY arm   | 26.969 / 27.521 | 27.869 / 27.245 / 27.007 | flat     |
| `(CASE … THEN a.k ELSE 0 END) > 5` — PROPERTY arm    | 33.8 / 35.3     | 33.158 / 32.534 / 34.205 | flat     |
| `count(a.k)` / `sum(a.k)` floors                     | 0.448 / 0.560   | 0.456 / 0.561            | flat     |

**The two property-armed rows are the control the probe already had**, and they are the right
one: same fixture, same selectivity, same `Expr::Case` machinery, and structurally unable to take
this arm because their THEN is not a literal. Neither moved. The filter-position rows moving too
is a bonus — item 450's unwrap only handles a boolean CASE used AS a predicate, and these are
compared to a literal, so they had stayed on the general path.

### Teeth

Harness proven: bomb 137, spin 124. Six mutants, **five caught**: taking the LAST matching branch
instead of the first; a NULL condition taking its branch instead of falling through; a
non-boolean condition becoming a silent fall-through instead of a data exception; the `ELSE` and
the first arm swapped; and a NULL literal admitted into the `Col::Num` path where it cannot be
represented. The sixth is the null control.

Semantics are the eager path's, not a re-derivation, and returning `Err` lands on the same masked
fallback — so an error in a branch nobody reaches still behaves as it did.

The ORACLE for the differential half is a PROPERTY arm computing the same value: `a.k - a.k + 1`
is 1 for every non-null `k`, and a non-literal arm makes this path decline. Forty forms, five
conditions by two literals by four `ELSE` spellings.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1149 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz` at 50,000 seeds, `clippy --all-targets
--features capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, `bun run check` exit 0, all
seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13. Re-measured after `cargo fmt`.

## 465 — item 464 has no TS twin, and the thing that looked like a CASE problem is `sum`: 4.6x its own `count`, whatever the argument

Item 448's rule is that a gap found in one engine is a QUESTION about the other, so item 464's
CASE arm gets asked of TS. The answer is no, and the asking turned up something else.

### No literal-arm cliff in TS

200,000 nodes, one case per process:

| TS                                                   | ms                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| `count(n.age)` — the floor                           | 9.4 / 10.2 / 10.2  |
| `count(CASE WHEN n.age > 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`       | 15.1 / 15.7 / 15.4 |
| `count(CASE … THEN 1 ELSE null END)`                 | 14.7               |
| `count(CASE … THEN n.age ELSE 0 END)` — property arm | 15.5               |

A literal-armed CASE costs 1.5x the floor and a PROPERTY-armed one costs the same 1.5x. The
distinction item 464 is built on does not exist here, so there is nothing to port — the third
time this session (items 448, 454, now this) that the answer to "does the other engine have it
too" has been no.

### What the question turned up instead

`sum(CASE …)` read 53.0 ms where `count(CASE …)` read 15.7, which looked like a CASE problem
until the obvious control was run:

| TS                                           | ms                     |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `count(n.age)`                               | 9.4 / 10.2 / 10.2      |
| **`sum(n.age)`**                             | **43.7 / 47.2 / 48.0** |
| `sum(n.age + 0)`                             | 45.1 / 46.9 / 45.9     |
| `sum(CASE WHEN n.age > 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` | 54.6 / 46.6 / 47.0     |

**`sum` costs 4.6x `count` on the same column, and everything built on `sum` lands on the same
~46 ms whatever its argument is.** So `sum(CASE …)` was never about the CASE; it is `sum`, and
the CASE reading was the second time this session a shape got blamed for the cost of the thing
around it (item 457 was the first). Native's `sum` is ~1.25x its `count` (0.560 against 0.448),
so this is TS-specific.

### The cause, and why it is not a free fix

`foldFor` returns a fold for `count`, `min` and `max` and for nothing else, so any projection
containing a `sum` has `foldedAggs === undefined` and the whole streaming path is disabled —
the group is materialized instead.

That omission is DELIBERATE and item 419 says so in the words that matter: "**418 is safe by
construction rather than by careful guards — its admission set is `foldFor`'s, which returns a
fold only for `count`/`min`/`max`**", under the rule "**an order-dependent aggregate cannot take
a fast path that may reorder rows, and every fast path in this family may.**" The hop's
far-driven route reorders, and a float sum folded in a different order returned
`2.0000000000000000e16` against `2.0000000000000004e16`.

So adding `sum` to `foldFor` would re-open item 419's wrong answer on the hop path, because the
admission set is shared. The SCAN path has no far-driven alternative and may well be admissible —
item 419 says as much about the start-driven route — but it also records why that was declined:
the route is chosen at RUN time, and "that order equality is observed, not promised".

**Open, and the question is precise**: can the scan aggregate's row order be shown identical to
the general path's BY CONSTRUCTION — same source, no seeded alternative — rather than by
observation? If yes, a scan-only admission set is worth 4.6x on `sum`. If the scan can seed from
an index and thereby reorder, it is item 419 again and the answer is no. That is a reading
question about one walk, and it is the whole of what stands between here and the fix.

Not built on a guess: item 419 is explicit that careful guards are the thing its design avoids,
and adding one without establishing the order guarantee would be the trap item 411 names.

### Gates

No engine change; `route-cost-probe` gained seven cases. `bun run check` exit 0.

## 466 — item 465's question, answered: the UNFILTERED scan's order is identical BY CONSTRUCTION, and the filtered one is item 419's trap

Item 465 measured TS's `sum` at 4.6x its own `count` (43.7-48.0 ms against 9.4-10.2 at 200,000
nodes), traced it to `foldFor` admitting only `count`/`min`/`max`, and declined to change that
because item 419 records the omission as load-bearing: "418 is safe by CONSTRUCTION rather than
by careful guards — its admission set is `foldFor`'s". It left one question, deliberately
precise: **can the scan aggregate's row order be shown identical to the general path's by
construction — same source, no seeded alternative — rather than by observation?**

### Read, not guessed

**The scan fast path never seeds.** Its walk is `graph.verticesById.values()` when the label is
absent and `graph.verticesByLabel.get(labelName) ?? []` when it is not, iterated directly. There
is no `indexCandidates`, no `seedVertices`, no `hopSeek` anywhere in it — unlike the hop walks,
it has no alternative route to pick between, so item 419's objection to the start-driven hop
route ("the route is picked at RUN time by `vacuousLabel`") has no counterpart here.

**The general path reads the same two containers.** `candidateVertexSource` is
`graph.verticesById.values()` or `graph.verticesByLabel.get(seed) ?? EMPTY_VERTICES` — the same
objects, in the same iteration order.

So for an UNFILTERED scan aggregate the two orders are identical because they are the same
container traversal, which is the "by construction" item 419 asked for and did not have for the
hop.

### And the half that is NOT safe

`seedVertices` exists and the general matcher uses it, so a FILTERED scan can seed from an index
and visit vertices in index order instead of bucket order. Whether it does is decided at RUN time
by what indexes exist and how selective they are — which is exactly the shape item 419 refused
("that order equality is observed, not promised") and item 411 names as the trap. A `sum` folded
in bucket order against a general path folded in index order is item 419's
`2.0000000000000000e16` / `2.0000000000000004e16` again.

### What this licenses

A scan-only, UNFILTERED-only admission of `sum` (and `avg`, which has the same shape). Not by
adding to `foldFor`, whose admission set is shared with the hop and is what keeps item 418 safe
without guards, but by `detectNodeAggregate` resolving its own fold for the one shape whose order
is a container traversal both paths share.

That is worth 4.6x on `sum(n.age)` over a label, which is the ordinary analytic shape — and it is
exactly as wide as the argument supports, which is the point of having done the reading first.

Priced and licensed here, built next: the admission is one `if` and the fold is `COUNT_FOLD`'s
sibling, but the guard has to be written so that a filtered scan cannot reach it even when a
later change gives `detectNodeAggregate` a `WHERE`, and that is a test to write rather than a
line to add.

### Gates

No engine change. `bun run check` exit 0.

## 467 — the fix item 466 licensed is NOT available as stated, and reading the implementation before building is what found it

Item 466 established that an unfiltered scan's row order is identical to the general path's by
construction, and licensed "a scan-only, UNFILTERED-only admission of `sum`/`avg`" worth 4.6x,
calling the remaining work "one `if` and the fold is `COUNT_FOLD`'s sibling". That last clause is
wrong, and the reason is worth more than the fix would have been.

### `sum` is not a fold

```js
case 'sum':
  if (values.some(isTemporal)) return temporalSum(values);
  if (values.some(Array.isArray)) throw nonNumericAgg();
  return values.reduce((s, v) => s + numArg(v), 0);
```

**It is inherently two-pass.** A single temporal ANYWHERE in the collection changes the operation
for every value, and a single array ANYWHERE throws — so the operation cannot be chosen until the
last value has been seen. A streaming fold would have to buffer to replicate it, at which point
it is not streaming.

So `foldFor`'s omission of `sum` has a second reason, and items 465 and 466 both attributed it
entirely to the first. Item 419's ordering hazard is real and is why the HOP cannot take it; this
is why no position can take it **as a fold**. Item 377 gestured at it — it deferred `sum`/`avg`
for "the `temporalSum`-before-array PRECEDENCE" — and item 419 then said that precedence "is real
and is not the blocker", which is true of the hop's ordering divergence and not true of this.
**Two correct facts about one omission, and I had been reasoning with one of them.**

### What IS available, and it is a better shape

The 4.6x is not the fold. It is that `foldedAggs === undefined` disables the streaming path
entirely, so the general path materializes a GROUP OF BINDINGS and maps each through `argFn` —
item 377's per-row `Binding` (`Map`) construction, ~125 ns a row, which is the cost both this and
the hop case keep rediscovering.

A `sum` needs every VALUE. It does not need every BINDING. So the available fix is not a fold at
all: stream the argument values into an array — one number per row, no `Map` — and then hand that
array to the SAME collection-wide `sum` the general path runs. Semantics are then identical by
construction rather than by replication, which is the property item 419 demanded and a hand-written
fold could not have given.

That needs the `switch (name)` block extracted from `compileAggregate`'s closure into a function
taking `(name, values)`, so both callers run one implementation. Mechanical, but it touches the
general aggregate path, so it is its own tick with its own mutation run rather than a tail added
to this one.

### The lesson

Item 466 read one walk carefully and concluded correctly about ORDER, then estimated the
remaining work from the shape of a neighbouring fix (`COUNT_FOLD`'s sibling) without reading
`sum`. The estimate was the only unmeasured thing in the entry and it was the wrong one. **An
item that licenses a fix should read the fix's own implementation, not the one next to it.**

### Gates

No engine change. `bun run check` exit 0.

## 468 — `sum`/`avg` on an unfiltered scan: 3.5x, by streaming VALUES instead of BINDINGS. Three of six mutants survive and I could not give them teeth

Item 467 established that `sum` cannot be a fold — it chooses its operation by looking at the
whole collection — and named the shape that IS available: a sum needs every VALUE, not every
BINDING, so stream the values and hand them to the same collection-wide function the general
path runs. This builds that.

### The change

`aggregateOverValues(name, values, frac)` is the `switch (name)` block lifted verbatim out of
`compileAggregate`'s closure; the closure now calls it. The switch needed nothing from the
binding, which is what made the two halves separable at all.

`detectNodeAggregate` gains a COLLECTING route beside its folding one: where `foldedAggs` is
undefined and the shape is a single `sum`/`avg` over an UNFILTERED scan, it streams the argument
values — one number a row, no `Binding` `Map` — and calls that same function. **One
implementation, so the two routes are identical by construction rather than by replication**,
which is the property item 419 demanded and a hand-written fold could not have given.

### Measured, three rounds, 200,000 nodes

| TS                                           | before             | after              |          |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------ | -------- |
| `sum(n.age)`                                 | 43.7 / 47.2 / 48.0 | 12.4 / 12.6 / 13.7 | **3.5x** |
| `sum(CASE WHEN n.age > 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` | 46.6 / 54.6 / 47.0 | 18.4 / 18.6 / 18.6 | **2.6x** |
| `count(n.age)` (control)                     | 9.4 / 10.2 / 10.2  | 10.2 / 10.2 / 11.0 | flat     |
| `count(CASE …)` (control)                    | 15.1 / 15.7 / 15.4 | 15.6 / 15.7 / 15.1 | flat     |

The `sum` rows were also BIMODAL before (min 43.7 against a median of 90.8) and are not now,
which is consistent with the group materialization being what the GC was reacting to.

### Teeth, and an honest shortfall

Six mutants. **Two caught**: admitting DISTINCT, and dropping the nullish filter. Both needed
their fixture sharpened first — the DISTINCT mutant SURVIVED until the fixture gained a duplicate
value (without one, `sum(DISTINCT a.k)` and `sum(a.k)` agree and the guard is vacuous), which is
the vacuity lesson items 422/425/427/429/435 each paid for, here caught by mutation rather than
by luck.

**Three survive: the clause-`WHERE`, inline-constraint and segments guards — the "unfiltered"
boundary itself.** I tried to give them teeth and failed, and the failure is worth recording
because it bounds what the guard is known to do. An order divergence needs floats whose sum is
order-dependent AND a general path that genuinely visits in a different order. The first is easy;
the second I could not construct. A hash seek over a value every row shares is wider than the
bucket, so `seekIsWorthIt` declines it and scans; make the filter selective instead and the
index's per-value bucket still holds those rows in insertion order. The test that remains
(`a float sum over an INDEXED filter agrees with the general path`) is a real agreement check and
does not distinguish the mutant.

So the boundary rests on item 466's reasoning — `seedVertices` CAN visit in index order and
whether it does is a run-time decision — and not on a demonstration. It stays, because
conservative is the safe direction when the hazard is a silent last-bits difference, and because
item 419 is the entry about that judgement going the other way. **A guard whose test I could not
write is worth saying so about; the alternative is a reader assuming the suite covers it.**

The sixth mutant is the null control.

### Also

`node-aggregate.test.ts` listed `sum` and `avg` under "the REFUSED shapes" with a comment
explaining why they could never be taken. They are taken now, on one shape, so they moved to
`collecting-aggregate.test.ts` and the old entry says where they went — a stale test NAME is a
claim like any other.

### Gates

`bun test packages/gql` 2145 pass / 0 fail (6 new tests), `bun run check` exit 0 — red three
times first, on a lost type narrowing (`frac` is a `number`, not `number | undefined`), a
`prefer-destructuring` lint and `fmt:check`. All seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13. Re-measured
after `fmt`.

## 469 — TWO aggregates over one scan: 2.7-4.3x, and the `.entries()` tuple was two thirds of it

Item 468 took the single `sum`/`avg` scan. Asking the obvious next question — what does a
projection with TWO aggregates cost — found a much wider gap, and it is not about `sum` at all.

At 200,000 nodes, one case per process: `count(n.age)` alone 9.4 ms and `sum(n.age)` 12.8, but
`count(n.age), count(*)` **46.4**, `min(n.age), max(n.age)` **41.2** and `sum(n.age), avg(n.age)`
**64.0**. The all-foldable pairs pay it too, so this is arity, not the aggregate: every rung of
the ladder that could claim the shape refuses `proj.items.length !== 1`, and the query falls to
the general path whole — a `Binding` per row for a result of one row.

`detectMultiNodeAggregate` is a new rung below `nodeAggregate`, disjoint from it by ARITY (that
one takes exactly one item, this one at least two), so the shipped single-item routes are
untouched by construction. It projects one synthetic column per aggregate ARGUMENT through
`detectNodeProjection` and accumulates per item: `count`/`min`/`max` through `foldFor` — the same
source the general path's `stepFolded` reads — `sum`/`avg` by collecting values for the shared
`aggregateOverValues` as in item 468, and `count(*)` as a row counter needing no column at all.
`sum`/`avg` are admitted only on an UNFILTERED scan, for item 466's reason.

### `.entries()` cost more than the route saved

The first version read `for (const [i, a] of accs.entries())`, which allocates a tuple per
accumulator per row. Measured, three rounds:

|                          | before | with `.entries()` | index loop           |
| ------------------------ | ------ | ----------------- | -------------------- |
| `count(n.age), count(*)` | 46.4   | 17.8              | **10.3-10.8** (4.3x) |
| `min(n.age), max(n.age)` | 41.2   | 32.7              | **13.7-15.4** (2.7x) |
| `sum(n.age), count(*)`   | 47.6   | 20.3              | **13.0-14.4** (3.4x) |
| `sum(n.age), avg(n.age)` | 64.0   | 21.5              | **15.4-17.7** (3.8x) |
| `count(n.age)` (control) | 9.4    | 9.9               | 9.5-10.7             |
| `min(n.age)` (control)   | 9.8    | 10.1              | 9.8-11.0             |
| `sum(n.age)` (control)   | 12.8   | 13.0              | 12.4-13.4            |

The single-aggregate controls are structurally unable to reach this rung — it refuses one item —
and all three are flat across every stage. **The iterator was 40-55% of the remaining cost**, and
the tell was that `min, max` sat at 32.7 where two separate `min`s cost 9.8 each: an accumulator
loop cannot be that expensive, so the per-row allocation was the only candidate. Same lesson as
items 453/459/462 in a different register — the layout of the hot loop is the measurement.

### Teeth

Harness proven (bomb 137, spin 124). Eight mutants, **five caught**: DISTINCT admitted; the
nullish skip dropped (4 failures); `count(*)` counting non-null values instead of rows; every
column written under the FIRST item's name (8 failures — the column-order test earns its place);
and all the folds sharing one accumulator array.

**One survives, and it is item 468's**: admitting `sum`/`avg` under a FILTER. The reason is
unchanged — I could not construct a general path that visits in a different order — so the
boundary still rests on item 466's reasoning rather than a demonstration, and it is now load-
bearing in two places.

Two more were EQUIVALENT mutants, which is worth separating from a survivor: dropping the `rows`
arm's `continue` leaves it reading `row[undefined]`, which is nullish and skipped anyway, and
dropping the arity check on a starred `count` guards a shape the parser cannot produce. Neither
can be caught by any test, because neither changes an answer.

### Native pays the same shape, and that is the next question

Item 448's rule, asked immediately: `ENGINE=native` at the same size reads 0.1 ms for one
aggregate and **0.4-0.5 for two**, across all four pairs. A 4-5x step at the same place is not
proof of the same cause, but it is the same question, and it is open.

### Gates

`bun test packages/gql` 2157 pass / 0 fail across 114 files (12 new), `bun run check` exit 0
(red once, on `no-nested-ternary`), `bun run build` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13.

## 470 — native's two-aggregate step had the same SHAPE as item 469 and a different cause: the route existed and was doing work nobody asked for

Item 469 left this open: `ENGINE=native` showed 0.1 ms for one aggregate against 0.4-0.5 for two
at 200,000 nodes, the same 4-5x step TS had. At 1,000,000 nodes it holds and scales — single
`count(n.age)` 0.5 ms, and `count, count(*)` / `min, max` / `sum, count(*)` / `sum, avg` **all
2.2** — four different pairs landing on one number, which is item 442's tell that the cost
belongs to the path rather than the content.

### Diagnosed, not assumed

The TS answer was a missing route, so the obvious guess was a missing route here. It is not. An
`eprintln` at the entry of `try_scan_multi_agg` — item 371's technique, because a fast path can
be correct, willing and unreachable — printed `specs=2 same=true` for all four pairs. They
already take its branch-free one-pass loop.

What that loop does is compute `sum`, `cnt`, `min` and `max` UNCONDITIONALLY, on the reasoning
(written in its comment) that four straight f64 ops beat a per-element per-spec match. True, and
beside the point: `count(n.age), count(*)` reads none of `sum`, `min`, `max`. The 4.4x was
entirely work nobody asked for.

### The change

The quantities are chosen ONCE, before the scan, from the aggregate functions present, and
dispatch to one of four monomorphic folds (`cnt`, `sum`, `minmax`, `all`), each `#[inline(never)]`
for the reason items 453, 459 and 462 each measured separately. A per-row `if need_sum` would
have handed back what it saved; the choice is loop-invariant, so it belongs outside the loop.
`cnt` stays in every variant because `Avg`, `Min` and `Max` each need it to tell an empty group
from a real answer, and an increment is not what costs here.

### Measured, three rounds, 1,000,000 nodes

|                          | before | after   |
| ------------------------ | ------ | ------- |
| `count(n.age), count(*)` | 2.2    | **0.0** |
| `min(n.age), max(n.age)` | 2.2    | **0.5** |
| `sum(n.age), count(*)`   | 2.2    | **0.6** |
| `sum(n.age), avg(n.age)` | 2.2    | **0.6** |
| `count(n.age)` (control) | 0.5    | 0.5     |
| `sum(n.age)` (control)   | 0.6    | 0.6     |

Identical on all three rounds. The controls are single aggregates, which never enter this
function — `try_scan_count_prop` and `try_scan_num_agg` claim them first — so they are a control
this change structurally cannot reach. The count-only row printing 0.0 is a scan of a `bool`
slice with no float work left in it, which vectorizes; at this resolution it is "under 0.05 ms",
not zero.

### Teeth

Harness proven earlier this session (bomb 137, spin 124). Seven mutants, four caught on the first
run: `sum` routed to the counting loop, `min`'s comparison flipped, the counting loop counting
rows instead of present values, and the min/max loop losing its `cnt` (which is what separates an
empty group from a real one).

**Two survived, and both were holes in my test rather than equivalent mutants** — the distinction
item 469 had to draw the other way:

- reading `need_sum` as `Sum` only, which sends a lone `avg` to a loop that never sums. Every
  `avg` in the test sat beside a `sum` that set the flag anyway.
- dropping `rows += 1` in the summing loop, which is `count(*)`'s row counter. The only
  `count(*)` pairing in the test routed to the all-quantities loop instead.

Both now have a case (`avg(n.age), count(*)` and `sum(n.age), count(*)`), and both mutants fail
after it. **A specialization multiplies the paths a test has to visit** — four loops here, and a
fixture that exercises two of them reads exactly like one that exercises four.

### The cross-engine lesson

Item 448's rule is that a gap in one engine is a QUESTION about the other. This is the first time
this session the answer has been yes-but-differently: same shape, same size, different cause —
TS was missing a route, native had the route and was computing a superset. Had I ported the TS
diagnosis, I would have built a second multi-agg path beside a working one and measured nothing.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1152 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz` clean, `cargo clippy --all-targets --features
capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13,
`query_bench` shows no movement outside this shape. Re-measured after `fmt`.

**CI was RED on 469** and the fix is `b506de02`: `bun run check` passed locally off the nx cache
while CI runs `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached, and oxfmt realigns a markdown table. The memory
note says `fmt` exiting 0 is not `fmt:check` passing; the sharper version is that **a cached
check is not a check** — run `bunx oxfmt --check .` directly before pushing a doc entry.

## 471 — two aggregates over DIFFERENT columns: 5.6x and 44x in native, by walking each column once instead of all of them per row

Item 470's arm requires every value-aggregate to read the SAME `Num` column. The next question
is what the other case costs, and the first measurement of it was wrong in a way worth keeping.

### The 13x that was my own fixture

Adding a second numeric node property to `route-cost-probe` put `sum(n.w2)` at 7.4 ms against
0.6 for `sum(n.age)` on what I believed was one fixture — a 13x gap between two columns of the
same shape. An `eprintln` of `store.column(key)` said `col=None`: the property did not exist.
**The probe has TWO fixtures** — a `Graph` builder for the TS arm and an NDJSON builder for the
native arm, forty lines apart — and I had patched the first. The "column gap" was a missing
property read as `Null` by the general path.

Three sessions of lessons say to instrument before believing a ratio; this is the first time it
caught a bad FIXTURE rather than a bad diagnosis. A probe with two fixtures will do this again,
so both now carry the `PCOL2` arm and a comment saying why.

### The real number, and the change

With the property actually present, at 1,000,000 nodes: `sum(n.age), max(n.age)` (same column)
0.6 ms, `sum(n.age), max(n.w2)` **5.6**, `count(n.age), count(n.w2)` **4.4**. The different-column
case falls past item 470's arm to the interleaved loop below it, which reads every column's value
for every row and decides what to do with it there — a `match` per element per spec, an
`Option<f64>` per accumulator, and a bounds-checked index into `acc`.

It now runs ONE PASS PER DISTINCT COLUMN, each the specialized fold item 470 added, with the
needs of all that column's aggregates unioned. This SUBSUMES the same-column case (one distinct
column, one pass), so there is one code path here rather than a special case beside a general
one.

| 1,000,000 nodes                    | before | after          |
| ---------------------------------- | ------ | -------------- |
| `sum(n.age), max(n.w2)`            | 5.6    | **1.0** (5.6x) |
| `count(n.age), count(n.w2)`        | 4.4    | **0.1** (44x)  |
| `sum(n.age), max(n.age)` (control) | 0.6    | 0.6            |
| `sum(n.age)` (control)             | 0.6    | 0.6            |
| `count(n.age), count(*)` (control) | 0.0    | 0.0            |
| `min(n.age), max(n.age)` (control) | 0.5    | 0.5            |

Identical on three rounds. **N passes over one column each beat one pass over N columns**, which
is worth saying plainly because it sounds wrong: each pass is a sequential walk of a single slice
with the work inside it known before it starts, where the interleaved pass decides per element
and touches N cache lines a row.

### TS does not have this gap

Item 448's rule, and the answer is no: at 200,000 nodes TS reads 16.8 ms for the same-column pair
and 18.0 for the two-column one. Item 469's rung projects one synthetic column per aggregate
ARGUMENT, so two columns were never a different shape there.

### Teeth

Seven mutants, six caught: a spec reading the FIRST group's result instead of its own column's;
the per-column needs OVERWRITTEN rather than unioned (so `sum(k), max(k)` loses its sum);
`count(*)` reading a column's tally instead of the row count; `count(k)` reading the row count
instead of its tally; and the `cnt == 0` guards on `min`/`max` and on `avg`.

The min/max guard SURVIVED the first run, and the reason is structural: **an absent column makes
the whole arm decline**, so the empty-graph assertions never enter it. Reaching `cnt == 0` inside
the arm needs a column that EXISTS while holding nothing for the scanned label — a `score` on
`Q` nodes, scanned as `MATCH (n:R)`. With that case both guards are caught. A test can assert
the right answer for the right reason and still never visit the code it is aimed at.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1152 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz` clean, `cargo clippy --all-targets --features
capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13.
Re-measured after `fmt`. CI was green on 470 (38954639693).

## 472 — the arity cliff again, on a HOP: 4.0-4.2x in TS, and native has the same one

Item 469 found that a second aggregate drops a SCAN off the ladder. "Grep the pattern elsewhere"
says to ask the hop the same question, and the hop is where it is expensive: the general path
materializes a `Binding` per EDGE.

At 200,000 nodes over 1,000,000 edges: `max(b.age)` alone **153 ms**, `count(*), max(b.age)`
**668**, `min(b.age), max(b.age)` **655**. `count(*)` alone is 0.0 — the count shortcut claims it
— so the pair costs 4.4x the aggregate it contains.

### The change

`detectMultiHopAggregate`, a rung below `hopAggregate` and disjoint from it by ARITY, built the
same way: one synthetic column per aggregate ARGUMENT through `detectHopProjection`, a fold per
item, `count(*)` as a row counter, and an INDEX loop rather than `accs.entries()` (item 469
measured the tuple at 40-55% of the cost).

**The admission set is `foldFor`'s, unchanged, and that is the whole safety argument.** Item 419
is explicit: the far-driven walk may visit rows in a different order than the general path, so
only an order-INDEPENDENT aggregate may ride it. `count`/`min`/`max` qualify. `sum`/`avg` do NOT,
and are refused here even though item 468 admits them on an unfiltered SCAN — where there is no
far-driven alternative to disagree with. The same two aggregates, admitted on one shape and
refused on another, for a reason that is about the walk rather than the aggregate.

| 200,000 nodes / 1,000,000 edges | before | after              |
| ------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------ |
| `count(*), max(b.age)`          | 668    | **155-157** (4.2x) |
| `min(b.age), max(b.age)`        | 655    | **163-179** (4.0x) |
| `max(b.age)` (control)          | 153    | 151-158            |
| `count(*)` (control)            | 0.0    | 0.0                |

Three rounds. The single-aggregate control cannot reach this rung — it refuses one item — and
did not move.

### Teeth

Seven mutants, six caught: DISTINCT admitted; `sum`/`avg` admitted by falling back to a `min`
fold; the nullish skip dropped; `count(*)` off by one; every column under the first item's name
(4 failures).

The seventh — **returning `[]` instead of `null` when the walk DECLINES at run time** — survived,
because a decline is graph-dependent and my fixture never caused one. It needs the shape the walk
hands back: many starts, an INDEX on the far end's key, and a selective inline constraint, so an
index seek on the end it does not drive beats walking. With that fixture (200 starts, one far end
at `k = 5`) the mutant fails. **A run-time decline is a branch a test reaches only by building
the graph that provokes it** — the same lesson as item 471's "a column that exists but holds
nothing", one layer up.

### Native has it too

`ENGINE=native` at the same size: `max(b.age)` 2.4 ms, `count(*), max(b.age)` **6.4**,
`min, max` **8.1** — 2.7-3.4x, the same cliff. Not fixed here; this entry is the TS half and the
native half is its own change with its own mutation run.

### Gates

`bun test packages/gql` 2166 pass / 0 fail across 115 files (9 new), `bun run check` exit 0 (red
once on `padding-lines`), `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean (item 470's lesson), `bun run
build` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13. Re-measured after `fmt`. CI was green on
471 (38956350250).

## 473 — the native half of item 472: two aggregates over one frontier, 2.5-2.8x

Item 472 fixed the hop arity cliff in TS and left the native twin open and measured. Every
frontier aggregate path — `try_frontier_count`, `try_frontier_count_prop`,
`try_frontier_prop_agg` — opens with `aggs.len() != 1`, so a pair fell past all of them to the
general aggregate and its wide batch.

`try_frontier_multi_agg` folds them in ONE pass over the frontier's (vertex, multiplicity) map,
and sits below `try_frontier_count_prop` in the chain: it requires `aggs.len() >= 2`, so it is
disjoint from every entry above and cannot shadow a single-aggregate shape — item 371's and
422's failure mode, avoided by arity rather than by placement luck.

**The admission set is `count`/`min`/`max` and that is item 376's rule, not a convenience.**
`count` may fold the per-node multiplicities because it does not care about order; `min`/`max`
ignore multiplicity entirely. `sum`/`avg` would have to add a value `c` times in an order the
general path does not promise — the same argument that keeps them off the TS hop in item 472,
reached independently on the other side.

| 200,000 nodes / 1,000,000 edges | before | after              |
| ------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------ |
| `count(*), max(b.age)`          | 6.4    | **2.5-2.6** (2.5x) |
| `min(b.age), max(b.age)`        | 8.1    | **2.9** (2.8x)     |
| `max(b.age)` (control)          | 2.4    | 2.3-2.4            |
| `count(*)` (control)            | 0.5    | 0.5                |

Three rounds, identical to a tenth. The controls are single aggregates and cannot enter an arm
that refuses them by arity.

### Teeth

Seven mutants, six caught: `sum` admitted into the weighted accumulator; `count(prop)` and
`count(*)` counting FRONTIER NODES rather than rows (both caught only because one far end has
two in-edges — a fixture without a repeated far end makes weighted and unweighted identical and
every one of these mutants survives); `min`/`max` flipped; an empty frontier's extremum
rendered as `0` instead of NULL.

The survivor was the `slot != width - 1` check — "the argument must be a property of the chain
FRONTIER". Dropping it makes the arm read the START's column while indexing by the frontier's
vertex ids, and nothing in the fixture asked for a start property. With `max(a.k2)` beside a
`count(*)` it is caught. **Three ticks in a row the surviving mutant has been a guard whose
shape the fixture never built** — a column that exists but holds nothing (471), a run-time
decline (472), an argument from the wrong slot (473). The pattern is worth naming: a guard
refuses a shape, so a fixture of admitted shapes cannot see it, and only writing the refused
shape down gives it teeth.

### Gates

`cargo test` 1153 + 13 + 723 + 10, `rewrite_fuzz` clean, `cargo clippy --all-targets --features
capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13.
Re-measured after `fmt`. CI was green on 472 (38957414991).

## 474 — a GROUPED aggregate the count tally cannot take: 6.3x and 11x in TS. Native was already flat

The arity family again, one axis over: `detectGroupedNodeCount` is a TALLY — exactly two items,
one of them `count(*)`, bumping an integer. Put any other aggregate in the projection and the
whole query falls to the general path.

At 200,000 nodes: `n.age AS k, count(*)` **2.9 ms** (the tally), `n.age AS k, max(n.age)`
**53.2**, `n.age AS k, count(*), max(n.age)` **85.8**. 18x and 30x for the same grouping over
the same scan, decided by which aggregate is asked for. `ENGINE=native` reads 1.0 / 1.3 / 1.4 —
flat — so this is TS-only, and item 448's rule is answered before the work rather than after.

### The change

`detectGroupedNodeAggregate` is the tally's shape with an accumulator array per group instead of
an integer: one reused `Binding` for the whole scan, the key as one `propOf`, and a fold per
aggregate (`foldFor` + `count(*)` as a row counter). It carries the filter the same way the
tally does — `inlineOf` + `compilePredicate` composed into ONE gate, not a loop over an array
that is usually empty (item 141 measured that at 34% of an unfiltered grouped count).

`sum`/`avg` are NOT admitted. A grouped float sum depends on the order values reach their group,
and a filtered scan may seed from an index (items 419, 466). The unfiltered case would be safe
by item 466's argument, but item 468 is the record of what an untestable guard costs in
confidence, so it waits for a shape that can be demonstrated.

| 200,000 nodes                          | before | after              |
| -------------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------ |
| `n.age AS k, max(n.age)`               | 53.2   | **8.0-8.4** (6.3x) |
| `n.age AS k, count(*), max(n.age)`     | 85.8   | **6.6-8.1** (11x)  |
| `n.age AS k, count(*)` (tally control) | 2.9    | 2.6-2.8            |

Three rounds. The tally's own shape is the control: it is claimed by a rung ABOVE this one, so
this change cannot reach it, and it did not move.

### Teeth, and a mutant that landed on the wrong function

Eight mutants, seven caught: DISTINCT admitted; the nullish skip dropped; `count(*)` off by one;
the key column written at a fixed position instead of its own; the filter gate ignored; a
STRUCTURAL key (a list-valued property) collapsed to one bucket; and an explicit `GROUP BY` of
TWO keys accepted as if it named one.

**The gate mutant "survived" its first run and that was a harness bug, not a result.** The
pattern I replaced — `if (gate !== undefined && !gate(v, binding, params, graph))` — appears in
`detectGroupedNodeCount` too, forty lines up, and `replace(…, 1)` hit the TALLY's copy. The
tally's tests are in another file, so nothing failed. Item 459 recorded exactly this ("two
copies of a body make a mutant land on whichever the tool reaches first") and I wrote the
mutant without anchoring anyway. Anchored to the surrounding lines it is caught. **A mutation
run's first job is to prove the mutant landed where it was aimed**, and a `cmp -s` only proves
SOMETHING changed.

Two more needed fixtures the file did not have: a list-valued group key (every key was a
primitive, so collapsing objects to one bucket was invisible) and a two-key `GROUP BY`.

`bun test packages/gql` 2178 pass / 0 fail across 116 files (12 new), `bun run check` exit 0
(red once on `complexity` 43/35 and `prefer-optional-chain` — the item classifier is its own

## 475 — two spellings of one grouped hop count, 2.2x apart, because one end had no NAME

Pricing the last cell of the arity matrix — a grouped aggregate over a hop — turned up something
older and worse than the arity gap. The probe asked

    MATCH (:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN b.age AS k, count(*) AS c      735 ms
    MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN b.age AS k, count(*) AS c     335 ms

One question, two spellings, 2.2x apart over 1,000,000 edges. **This is the bug class the repo is
named after** — CLAUDE.md lists it by example — and it had been sitting in
`detectGroupedHopCount` since item 142.

### Diagnosed by instrumenting the LADDER, not the detector

A `console.error` per rung in `fastPath` (and run against `src`, not the built dist, which cost
one confusing round of "no rung fires" for all three) printed: the named spelling takes
`groupHopShortcut`, the anonymous one takes NOTHING. The guard is
`start.variable === undefined || far.variable === undefined → null`, and the name was never used
for anything but binding a predicate — nothing can REFERENCE an unnamed end.

Removing it (the keyed end is named by the key expression itself) puts both spellings on the
tally: **735 → 314-347 ms, against the named spelling's 330-341 on the same rounds.** The two
now agree, which is the actual claim. The node tally's own shape is the control at 2.7-3.1,
unmoved.

### The guard I added was redundant, and mutation is what said so

I replaced the old guard with `start.variable === undefined && far.variable === undefined`. Its
mutant SURVIVED, and the reason is that the key-end check twenty lines below
(`keySource.variable !== far.variable`) already refuses a pattern whose keyed end has no name.
So the line was removed rather than kept as something no test can fail on. **A surviving mutant
on a guard you just wrote is as likely to mean "redundant" as "untested"** — and the fix is
opposite in the two cases.

The key-end check itself also survives its mutant, and that one is reachability-bound rather
than redundant: a key naming neither end does not reach the planner at all (the scoper rejects
`variable is not defined` first), so no test can distinguish it. Recorded, not papered over.

### Two fixture faults the mutants found

- **`:P` was VACUOUS** in `grouped-hop.test.ts`'s shared fixture — every source carries it — so
  the mutant that ignored the start label entirely SURVIVED. CLAUDE.md's rule is that every
  label in a fixture must exclude something; the new case has a `Q`-labelled source whose edge
  must not appear.
- The mutation script now ASSERTS the pattern it replaces appears exactly once, after item 474's
  mutant landed on the node tally's identical body. One of this tick's patterns was ambiguous
  and the script said so instead of reporting a result.

Caught: the key-end orientation inverted (9 failures), the non-keyed end's plainness dropped,
the start label ignored.

### Gates

`bun test packages/gql` 2185 pass / 0 fail across 116 files (7 new), `bun run check` exit 0,
`bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean, `bun run build` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers
13/13. Re-measured after `fmt`. CI was green on 474 (38959908851).

**Still open, measured here:** the grouped-hop ARITY gap — `b.age AS k, max(b.age)` is 759 ms
