## 505 — `MATCH (a:L) MATCH (a)-[:T]->(x)` is the same query written twice, and TS charged 747.9 ms for the second spelling

Item 504's sweep found no new target in the cross-engine bench, so this tick priced two plan-level
enums nothing had: the SET operators and the left-outer hop. The left-outer lead turned out to be
a confound, and the control is the finding.

`MATCH (n:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN count(*)` costs 858 ms in TS against
native's 4.6, which looks like OPTIONAL. **It is not.** The fair control — item 445's rule, _a
ratio between two queries is a ratio between two routes until you have shown they take the same
one_ — is the same two clauses without OPTIONAL, and it costs **747.9 ms**. OPTIONAL is worth
~1.1x of that. What costs is the SPLIT.

| 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, one case per process | one clause     | two clauses    |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | -------------- |
| `RETURN count(*)`, ts                                    | 0.0 ms         | **747.9 ms**   |
| `RETURN x.age`, ts                                       | 157 ns/row     | **805 ns/row** |
| both, native                                             | 0.5 ms / 77 ns | 0.5 ms / 76 ns |

**Native costs the same for both spellings. TypeScript did not**, because every fast-path
detector reads ONE `match` clause, so the split form fell to the general row pipeline — the
equivalent-spelling class this repo treats as a defect regardless of the answer being right.

### A rewrite, not a rung

`fuseAnchorThenHop` runs before anything looks at the clause list and turns the pair into one
pattern, so all fifteen existing rungs apply with no rung knowing it happened.

|                                          | before                       | after                            |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| two-clause `count(*)`                    | 707.2 / 716.2 / 691.0 ms     | **0.0 / 0.0 / 0.0**              |
| two-clause projection                    | 816.0 / 806.2 / 798.1 ns/row | **146.3 / 155.6 / 147.8** (5.4x) |
| one-clause projection (control)          | 143.2 / 157.3 / 143.8        | 158.7 / 148.7 / 144.9            |
| OPTIONAL count (control — must NOT fuse) | 694.2 / 700.3 / 744.2 ms     | 726.4 / 714.9 / 710.0            |

Three alternated rounds. Both spellings now land on the same number, which is the claim.

### The probe group was proven against the bug

`spelling-probe` gained the pair, and against the PRISTINE engine it flags **20.2x**; after the
fix it does not flag at all. A group added after the fix has never seen the defect it exists for.

### Teeth, and two survivors that were MASKED BY EACH OTHER

Six mutants. Four fell at once: fusing an OPTIONAL clause (3 failures), fusing a re-constrained
start, fusing when both clauses carry a `WHERE`, and the null control staying clean.

**Two survived, and each was hidden by the other's guard.** Dropping the start-VARIABLE check
survived because the only test with a differing start also had a LABEL there, which the
re-constrained-start check refuses first. Dropping the anchor-has-no-SEGMENTS check survived
because its test shares no start variable, which the start-variable check refuses first. Two new
cases — a bare `MATCH (a:P) MATCH (b)-[:T]->(x)` cross product, and
`MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->(m) MATCH (a)-[:S]->(y)` where the anchor binds more than one variable — kill
both. _A guard whose mutant survives may be protected by a NEIGHBOURING guard rather than
untested, and the way to tell is a case that reaches it first._

Also measured and written into the test: an instrumented run counts **11 fusions** across the
file, exactly the two-clause cases — so a THIRD clause does not chain onto a fused one, because
the fused clause is no longer a bare node. The answer is right either way; widening the anchor to
"a pattern whose LAST node is the shared variable" is open.

## 506 — `MATCH (a)-[:T]->(a)` answered FOUR where two is right: every hop fast path ignored a repeated endpoint

Item 505 left a widening open — chaining a THIRD clause onto a fused pair. Implementing it
routed `MATCH (a:P) MATCH (a)-[:T]->(a)` into the one-clause spelling, and the two spellings
stopped agreeing. **The fusion was right and the one-clause spelling was wrong.**

A repeated node variable means ONE node, so `MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->(a)` matches the self-loops.
Probed against native on a fixture with two self-loops among four edges, **eight of ten shapes
diverged** and TS was wrong in every one:

|                                               | ts            | native       |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ------------ |
| `RETURN count(*)`                             | 4             | **2**        |
| `RETURN a.k`                                  | four rows     | **two**      |
| `RETURN a.k, count(*)`                        | `{1, 3}`      | **`{1, 1}`** |
| `RETURN max(a.k)`                             | 3             | **2**        |
| `<-[:T]-` / `-[:T]-` / unlabelled / named rel | 4 / 6 / 4 / 4 | **2** each   |

The two that AGREED are the two that already declined to the general matcher — a `DISTINCT`
projection and a filtered count — which is the tell: the general matcher has always been right,
and each hop fast path binds the far node over the start without checking that the name is the
same one.

### The fix is a whole-query gate, not fifteen audits

`repeatsNodeVariable` runs once per compile; when a pattern binds a node variable twice, the
detectors are handed an EMPTY clause list, which every one of them refuses on its first check. A
self-join takes the general matcher.

Conservative on purpose. **Item 487 fixed this same class one rung at a time for a repeated REL
variable, and the one-at-a-time fix is exactly what left this** — a rung that was never audited
for the hazard still has it. The cost is confined to patterns that are currently answered
wrongly, and the control says so: `count(*)` over a plain hop stays 0.0 ms and the projection
143.3-149.8 → 144.1-148.6 ns/row over three alternated rounds.

### Why nothing caught it

The differential fuzzer does not generate a one-hop pattern that repeats its endpoint, and the
GQL corpus has no such case. It was found by a REWRITE making two spellings of one question
disagree — the same mechanism item 499's spelling group exists for, arriving by accident instead
of by design. `packages/native/src/repeated-node-variable-conformance.test.ts` now pins fifteen
shapes across both engines, including the ordinary hop as the control that the gate must NOT
catch, and each one pins the ANSWER as well as the agreement, because two engines can agree on a
wrong one.

Two of my own hand values were wrong there and the engines corrected me: `(a)-[:T]->(x)-[:T]->(x)`
is three paths, not two, and the plain two-hop is five, not four.

### Teeth

Four mutants, three caught (the gate disabled, the repeat never reported, the START not counted
among the names); the null control is clean. Each is caught by the new differential file.

clean, `bun run build` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13. CI was green on 505.

**The widening that found this is NOT in this commit.** It is written and measured — the split

## 507 — the fusion anchor is any pattern whose LAST node carries the variable: 29.7x

Item 505 fused `MATCH (a:L) MATCH (a)-[:T]->(x)`, but only from a BARE-NODE anchor, so the fused
clause could never be an anchor itself and a third clause never chained. The anchor is now any
single pattern whose last node holds the shared variable, and the fused segments are the
concatenation.

| 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, min of 5                | before                       | after                 |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->(x) MATCH (x)-[:T]->(y) RETURN count(*)` | 2176.1 / 2238.2 / 2222.3 ms  | **74.0-74.5** (29.7x) |
| the same in three clauses                                   | 2211.4 / 2152.5 / 2205.8     | **73.7-75.9** (29.4x) |
| the one-clause spelling (control)                           | 74.4 / 74.2 / 74.4           | 74.2 / 74.3 / 74.2    |
| a one-hop projection (control)                              | 143.0 / 144.0 / 157.2 ns/row | 148.6 / 146.2 / 152.9 |

Three alternated rounds. The fused forms land ON the one-clause control, which is the claim.

### The guard that silently switched the whole rewrite off

The first version refused a pattern whose `selector` or `mode` was not `undefined`, reasoning
that a selector or a repetition restrictor describes the WHOLE path and must not be
concatenated. That reasoning is right and the test was wrong: **`parsePathPattern` writes
`selector: 'walk'` and `mode: 'trail'` onto every pattern it builds**, so the guard refused
everything and fusion stopped firing altogether — _including item 505's shipped case_.

Every test still passed, because a rewrite that declines is only slower. **The instrumented
count is what caught it: 11 fusions in its own test file before, 0 after, 14 after the fix.**
That number is now written into the test as an assertion-by-comment, because this is the second
time tonight an instrument caught something green tests could not (item 500 was the first).

### What the concatenation is allowed to do, checked rather than assumed

- **`trail` is the written default and is NOT enforced on a fixed-length pattern.** Verified in
  BOTH engines before relying on it: over a self-loop, `MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->(x)-[:T]->(y)` counts
  the path that reuses that one edge, and so does `WALK`, `TRAIL` and `SIMPLE` — all 2 where a
  trail restriction would answer 1. So concatenating two default patterns changes nothing.
- **A SELECTOR cannot sit on a fixed-length pattern at all** — `MATCH ANY SHORTEST (a)-[:T]->(x)
-[:T]->(y)` is a parse error ("support a single variable-length segment").
- **A VAR-LENGTH hop chains too**, and all four spellings of a `{1,2}` tail answer 6 on a
  three-cycle in both engines.

### Teeth

Five mutants, two caught: the segments concatenated BACKWARDS (3 failures) and the anchor's end
taken as its start (2). **`defaultPathShape` survives both its mutants and is equivalent TODAY** —
mode is not enforced on a fixed pattern and a selector cannot appear on one, so fusing under
either changes no answer. It is kept because the day mode _is_ enforced (a plausible conformance
fix) this rewrite becomes a wrong answer without it, and that reasoning is in the code.

## 508 — `OPTIONAL MATCH (u)-[:T]->(x:Q)` ignored the label in NATIVE, and returned rows whose `x` is not a `Q`

Pricing the native side of the left-outer hop found a 9x gap on `count(*)` (4.5 ms against 0.5
for the non-optional twin) — and writing the test for the fix found something worse in the arm
next to it.

`OPTIONAL MATCH (u)-[:T]->(x:Q)` **discarded the landing label**. `node_plain` returns the
label and the label EXPRESSION, and the optional lowering bound both to `_lbl2` / `_v2_le` and
used neither; inline properties and an inline `WHERE` became the `landing_pred` and the label
did not. So every neighbour matched:

```text
ts  [{"u":"a","x":"c"},            {"u":"b","x":null},{"u":"d","x":null}]
na  [{"u":"a","x":"b"},{"u":"a","x":"c"},{"u":"b","x":null},{"u":"d","x":null}]
```

`x` is bound to `b`, which is a `:P`. The count read 4 where TS has always said 3. Pre-existing —
verified by running the same test against the pristine build before writing a line of the fix,
which is how I know it is not mine.

The fix is three lines: the label goes through `landing_label_filter` into the same
`landing_pred` the props use, written FIRST because that is where it appears in the pattern.

### Teeth

Five mutants, four caught: the label dropped again, the bare label dropped, the label EXPRESSION
dropped, and the label applied to the source slot instead of the landing. The null control is
clean.

**The label-expression mutant SURVIVED the first run** — the suite had only bare `:Q`, and
`node_plain` hands back the compound form separately, so dropping `v2_le` changed nothing it
tested. Two cases (`x:!P`, `x:P|Q`) kill it. That is the third survivor this session caused by a
helper returning two things where the test exercised one.

A cross-engine probe over seven shapes now reads ALL SAME.

## 509 — `count(*)` over an OPTIONAL hop is a degree sum with a FLOOR: 7.6x

Item 508's held-back perf arm, landing now that the correctness fix it uncovered is its own

row — so `count(*)` is **Σ max(degree, 1)**, and `try_fused_count` now takes

| native, 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, min of 5           | before                    | after                      |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------- |

An unknown edge type is ZERO rows for a plain hop — and the SOURCE COUNT for an optional one,
because every source still null-fills. The arm inherited the plain hop's early return and
answered 0 where 3 is right; **this item's own test caught it before it shipped**, which is what
writing the test first is for. A landing predicate declines (it decides both which neighbours
count and whether the source null-fills).

Six mutants, four caught: the floor removed in the shallow arm, a landing predicate admitted,

## 510 — the TS side of the OPTIONAL-hop count: 17x

Item 509 gave the native engine Σ max(degree, 1) for a left-outer `count(*)`. TypeScript had no
rung for the shape at all — every detector refuses `optional` on its first check — so it fell to
the general row pipeline at **692-710 ms against native's 0.6**.

## 512 — a `LET` between the MATCH and the RETURN dropped the query off every rung: 8-11x, and `count(*)` to 0.0

Four unpriced plan enums measured in one pass (top-k, the list unwind, the `WITH`/`LET`
pipeline, the inline `CALL`). The `LET` one is an equivalent-spelling cliff and the smallest fix:

| ts, 200,000 vertices                          | with a `LET` | written directly          |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------- |
| `LET a = n.age RETURN a AS k`                 | **126.4 ms** | `RETURN n.age AS k` 13.7  |
| `LET a = n.age RETURN count(*)`               | **108.3 ms** | `RETURN count(*)` 0.0     |
| `LET a = n.age RETURN a, count(*) GROUP BY a` | 4.0          | the implicit spelling 5.0 |

Native pays 16.2 against 13.1 for the first pair, so this is the TS ladder's shape check and
nothing deeper — every node rung reads a TWO-clause shape, and `LET` is how this engine names an
expression (it is also the only way to key a `GROUP BY`, so the shape is idiomatic, not exotic).

`inlineTrailingLet` substitutes the expression into the projection that follows and drops the
clause, so the ladder sees the two-clause form. A rewrite, not a rung — item 505's pattern again.

|                                                    | before                  | after                 |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | --------------------- |
| `LET a = n.age RETURN a AS k`                      | 109.6 / 112.9 / 54.7 ms | **13.5 / 10.0 / 9.6** |
| `LET a = n.age RETURN count(*)`                    | 103.7 / 51.4 / 104.7    | **0.0 / 0.0 / 0.0**   |
| the direct projection (control)                    | 9.2 / 13.5 / 9.0        | 8.8 / 9.5 / 12.7      |
| the `GROUP BY` spelling (control — still declines) | 3.9 / 3.7 / 3.8         | 3.9 / 3.9 / 3.9       |

Three alternated rounds. **Both `LET` rows are BIMODAL before the change** (54.7 against 109.6,
51.4 against 103.7), so the honest claim is the conservative one: 8-11x against the common mode,
4x against the fast mode, and the count row to zero either way.

### Shallow on purpose

An item either IS the variable or does not mention it — so no expression tree is rewritten and no
nested binder (a `CASE`, a `LET … IN`, a subquery) can be entered by mistake. `a + 1` declines the
whole rewrite rather than being rebuilt. `GROUP BY` and `HAVING` decline because `GROUP BY` takes
a BOUND NAME, and `RETURN *` because the variable is one of its columns.

### Two things the existing suite and the mutants taught

**The COLUMN NAME is not the expression's.** An un-aliased `RETURN a` names its column after the
expression it evaluates, so the first version renamed `a` to `n.k` — caught immediately by
`DISTINCT over a LET-bound name`, which exists for that exact distinction. The rewrite now
carries the name it removes.

**"Cheap and pure" needs TOTAL, and only a faulting expression can show it.** Six mutants, five
caught; admitting ANY expression survived, because the declining case I had written was
`abs(n.k)` — total, so inlining it changes nothing. `CAST('abc' AS INTEGER)` and `1 / 0` both
throw, and a dropped `LET` would answer 3 instead: those two cases kill it. _Fourth survivor this
session that was a fixture coincidence rather than a missing assertion_ (505, 510, 511).

0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13, `bun run spelling` flags only item 325's deliberate

## 513 — a correlated inline `CALL` is its own `MATCH`: 900-1005 ms to 0.0

Item 512's widest leftover. `MATCH (n:P) CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN x } RETURN
count(*)` ran the body once per incoming row through the general matcher: **1005.2 / 909.1 /
902.4 ms** against the native engine's 6.2, and against **0.0** for the same question written as
one pattern.

`inlineCorrelatedCall` rewrites the clause to the `MATCH` it is equivalent to. Nothing else was
needed: item 507's fusion merges that `MATCH` into the preceding one, and the ladder answers it.

|                                                              | before                    | after               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN x }` + `count(*)` | 1005.2 / 909.1 / 902.4 ms | **0.0 / 0.0 / 0.0** |
| the plain hop count (control)                                | 0.0                       | 0.0                 |
| item 512's `LET` projection (control)                        | 14.4 / 10.5 / 13.0 ms     | 9.2 / 13.7 / 11.1   |

Three alternated rounds. **Three rewrites now compose** — `inlineTrailingLet` (512),
`inlineCorrelatedCall` (513), `fuseAnchorThenHop` (505/507) — and none of them added an
execution path.

### The condition whose violation is invisible

A body may introduce ONLY the names it returns. `CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:T]->(x)-[:S]->(y) RETURN
y }` hides `x`; inlining would leave it bound, which `RETURN *` and every later clause can see.
The set equality is what enforces that, and its mutant is caught by exactly one assertion — the
column list of a `RETURN *` after the call.

### Teeth, and a survivor that is a genuine equivalence

Five mutants, three caught: `OPTIONAL CALL` inlined (a left-outer join is not a join), the
leaked-name check dropped, and an ALIASED yield admitted. The null control is clean.

**Inlining an UNCORRELATED call (empty scope) survives, and it is equivalent** — a body with no
correlation yields the same rows for every outer row, so joining them IS the cross product a
second `MATCH` produces, and my test's answer could not differ. The guard stays because the
execution CONTRACT differs: the call runs its body once and reuses it, which may be the better
plan, so turning that into a cross product is a change with its own measurement rather than a
free one. Recorded at the guard.

## 516 — the `WITH` pipeline is the same cliff as the `LET`: 8-12x, and `count(*)` to 0.0

Item 512 inlined a trailing `LET`; the `WITH` spelling of the same renaming was never measured.
It is the same cliff, for the same reason — every node rung reads a TWO-clause shape:

| ts, 200,000 vertices              | with the clause | written directly | native |
| --------------------------------- | --------------- | ---------------- | ------ |
| `WITH n.age AS a RETURN a AS k`   | **124.0 ms**    | 13.7             | 17.7   |
| `WITH n.age AS a RETURN count(*)` | **112.0 ms**    | 0.0              | 0.6    |
| `WITH n AS m RETURN count(*)`     | **90.7 ms**     | 0.0              | 0.5    |

`boundExprs` now recognizes either binder and `inlineTrailingLet` substitutes both.

|                                       | before                  | after                 |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | --------------------- |
| `WITH n.age AS a RETURN count(*)`     | 112.6 / 109.5 / 46.0 ms | **0.0 / 0.0 / 0.0**   |
| `WITH n.age AS a RETURN a AS k`       | 115.9 / 112.7 / 51.9    | **13.9 / 10.5 / 9.6** |
| item 512's `LET` projection (control) | 14.6 / 14.2 / 15.4      | 14.1 / 10.1 / 10.5    |
| the direct projection (control)       | 14.7 / 10.0 / 15.0      | 13.6 / 13.9 / 14.8    |

Three alternated rounds, and **the `WITH` rows are bimodal like item 515's** (46.0 against 112.6),
so the claim is 8-12x against the common mode and ~5x against the fast one. Both land on the
direct spelling.

### `WITH` is not `LET`, in one way that matters

`LET` ADDS a binding; `WITH` REPLACES the row. So a `WITH` may carry SEVERAL items — a projection
evaluates every item against the INPUT row, so none can read another's alias — while the `LET`
arm takes exactly one. **Generalizing to multiple items broke the `LET` arm and an existing test
caught it**: `LET a = n.k, b = a` is legal and sequential, so collecting both into one
substitution map rewrote `b` to `a` with `a` no longer bound, and the column came back
`undefined`. `a later LET item may read an earlier one` exists for exactly that sequencing.

A `WITH` that FILTERS, dedupes, groups, orders, pages or AGGREGATES is a row boundary rather than
a renaming, and declines — four of those four are pinned, as is a faulting item (`1 / 0`,
`CAST('abc' AS INTEGER)`), which is the only thing that can distinguish the totality guard.

### Teeth

Five mutants, four caught: a `WITH … WHERE` admitted (2 failures), the row-boundary guards
dropped, the aggregate/cheap check dropped, and the single-item `LET` rule dropped (2) — that
last one is the bug above, re-introduced deliberately. The null control is clean.

### Also priced, and ALREADY fast

`SELECT count(*) AS c FROM MATCH (n:Person)` reads **0.0 ms** in TS and the hop form the same —
the ISO `SELECT` spelling lowers to the same clause list, so there was nothing to fix. Measured
rather than assumed, which is the only way to know a spelling is already converged.

## 517 — the four clause rewrites COMPOSE, and the test says so because the instrument does

Four rewrites now run on every TS query, in this order: `inlineTrailingLet` (a trailing
`LET`/`WITH` renaming, items 512 and 516), `inlineCorrelatedCall` (513), and `fuseAnchorThenHop`
(505, 507). Each was tested alone. Their COMPOSITION is a surface of its own — a rewrite can
expose a shape the next one accepts — and no item covered the combinations.

`rewrite-composition.test.ts` asks nine composed shapes twice: composed, and written directly,
compared as multisets. All nine agreed on the first run, which is exactly when a test is most
likely to be vacuous — so the instrumented count is what makes it evidence: across the file the
three rewrites fire **12 binder inlines, 10 CALL inlines and 26 fusions**, so the composed cases
really do pass through more than one.

What the nine cover: fusion then `LET`; fusion then `WITH`; `CALL` then fusion (including the
count, which only the fused form can shortcut); all three in one query; a `CALL` whose BODY is
itself two clauses, fused inside the body first; three `MATCH` clauses then a `WITH`; a rel
variable still bound after a fusion; and two cases where a rewrite must NOT hand the next stage
a shape it would answer wrongly —

- **the self-join gate** (506): fusion is what can PRODUCE `(a:P)-[:T]->(a)` out of two clauses,
  and every hop rung answers that wrongly. The gate runs on the REWRITTEN list, so it still
  catches it, and both spellings agree.
- **the OPTIONAL rungs** (510, 511): they read a three-clause shape whose middle is optional, and
  a fusion before it must leave that shape intact. It does.

The ORDER affects reach, not correctness: with fusion first, a `CALL` between two `MATCH`
clauses would block their merge — slower, not wrong.

## 518 — a PER-ROW `FOR` list is Σ its lengths: at least 5x, commonly ~32x

Item 515 took the constant list with one multiplication and left this one measured at 191.1 ms
against the native engine's 15.8. A list read from the row needs the anchors walked — but not a
row per element, which is what the general path was doing: 600,000 rows materialized to count
them.

ISO's unwind semantics ARE the arithmetic, and each case is a different number:

| the property holds          | contributes                                                            |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| a list                      | its length (an EMPTY list contributes 0 — the anchor's row disappears) |
| NULL, or the key is missing | 0                                                                      |
| any other scalar            | 1, because a non-list unwinds as a one-element list                    |

| ts, 200,000 vertices with three tags each          | before                | after                |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------- |
| `MATCH (n:Person) FOR t IN n.tags RETURN count(*)` | 82.9 / 72.6 / 83.2 ms | **2.5 / 2.3 / 16.3** |
| the constant `FOR` (control, item 515's rung)      | 0.0                   | 0.0                  |
| the plain node count (control)                     | 0.0                   | 0.0                  |

Three alternated rounds, and the third after-round is an outlier at 16.3 against 2.3-2.5 — so the
claim is **at least 5x, with the common mode ~32x**. It also beats native's 15.8 on this shape,
which is worth stating plainly rather than quietly: a bucket walk reading one property is a
cheaper question than the row pipeline either engine runs by default.

### Teeth

Six mutants, five caught: NULL counted as one, a scalar counted as zero, the length ignored, the
anchor LABEL ignored, and the null control clean.

**The anchor-variable check survives and is equivalent by construction**: with ONE lone-node
`MATCH` the anchor's variable is the only name in scope, so a property on anything else is an
unbound reference the compiler rejects before this runs — and a pattern WITH segments, where a
second name exists, is refused one line earlier. Recorded at the guard.

**One mutant was MISAPPLIED and the uniqueness assert caught it**: the bucket-iteration line is
character-identical to item 510's rung, so the pattern matched twice. Anchored on the property
read that follows it in this function. Items 474, 483, 494 and now 518: _two copies of a body is
the most reliable way to fool a mutation run in this repo_, and the assert is what keeps it from
reading as a survivor.

## 519 — the NATIVE unwind count, and a regression my own first version introduced

Item 518 gave the TS engine Σ the list lengths and in doing so made it FASTER than native on that
shape (2.3 against 15.8). Same arithmetic, other engine: `try_fused_count` now takes
`Plan::Unwind`.

| native, 200,000 vertices with three tags each      | before                | after                      |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `MATCH (n:Person) FOR t IN n.tags RETURN count(*)` | 16.5 / 16.9 / 16.5 ms | **9.9 / 8.7 / 8.5** (1.9x) |
| `FOR x IN [1,2,3]` (a ROW-INVARIANT list)          | 3.3 / 3.2 / 3.2       | **0.0 / 0.0 / 0.0**        |
| the plain node count (control)                     | 0.5                   | 0.5                        |

Three alternated rounds.

### The first version made the constant list 3.4x WORSE, and measuring both shapes is what caught it

The obvious arm evaluates the list per input row and sums. For a per-row list that is right and
1.9x. For a ROW-INVARIANT one it built 200,000 identical `Value::List`s to learn one length —
`FOR x IN [1,2,3]` went **3.4 ms to 11.6**, a 3.4x regression on a shape the arm had just
intercepted from a cheaper path.

The fix is to mirror the operator's own check: `unwind_rows` tests `slots_read(list)` and
evaluates an invariant list ONCE. The fast path now does the same, then multiplies. **A fast path
has to mirror the operator's invariance check, not just its element rule** — and the only reason
I saw it is that the probe case for the OTHER shape was in the same measurement pass. A control
that the change _can_ reach, measured because it was there.

### Teeth

Five mutants, four caught: the invariant branch ignoring the row count, NULL counted as one, a
scalar counted as zero, and a list's length ignored. The null control is clean.

The oracle is a declining twin inside the engine: `count(*) + 0` is an aggregate EXPRESSION, so
the arm refuses it and the general `unwind_rows` answers — every case is asked both ways and they
agree. ISO's rule is pinned case by case: a list contributes its LENGTH, an empty list 0, NULL or
a missing key 0, any other scalar 1, and `count(t)` (the elements, not the rows) is checked
separately as a different question.

### Gates

`cargo test --release` 1162 + 13 + 723 pass / 0 fail, `rewrite_fuzz` 10 pass, `cargo clippy
--all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt`, `bun test packages/native/src`
818 pass / 0 fail, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean, `bun run build` exit 0, all seven
byte-identity fuzzers 13/13. CI was green on 518.

The two engines now answer this shape at 8.5 (native) and 2.3 (ts) against 16.5 and 82.9 at the
start of the pair.

## 521 — a correlated subquery body's LABEL test: 10.5x, and it was a one-line spelling

Item 501 optimized the UNCORRELATED subquery body and left the correlated one explicitly open:
`opt` rewrites the plan it is handed and never descends into a `Plan` nested inside an `Expr`
(item 500), and a correlated body's `Plan::Row` leaf plus outer-slot references are a different
contract from a top-level plan — a seed rule would rewrite it into a shape `pull_body` cannot
evaluate. So the question was which part of `opt` a correlated body actually misses.

### Pricing the variants

Five correlated shapes at 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, native, `PR=5`. Every one egresses
200,000 rows, and `corrdeg` (the degree fast path from item 500) is the egress floor:

```text
  corrdeg      COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b) }                              11.3 ms   (the floor)
  corrfilt     COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b) WHERE b.age > 50 }             17.9
  corr2filt    …WHERE b.age > 50 AND b.age < 80       (TWO filters)     22.2
  corrlblonly  COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Half) }                         26.0
  corrlblfilt  COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Half) WHERE b.age > 50 }       186.1
```

The last row is the find, and the four above it are what make it a diagnosis rather than a guess.
186.1 is not the filter COUNT — two property filters cost 22.2. It is not the label test on its
own — that is 26.0, and only because the degree fast path intercepts it. It is the label test
**on the general path**, which the fast path reaches only when nothing else is in the body. The
top-level twin of the same query is 3.3 ms.

### The cause

GQL lowers `(b:L)` to `'L' IN labels(slot)`, which BUILDS a `Value::List` of the node's labels and
hashes a string PER ROW. `opt::normalize_pred` canonicalizes that to `Expr::IsLabeled`, which the
evaluator answers against the label buckets — a tautology short-circuit, a membership bitset, or a
binary search, and no per-row allocation. A correlated body never reaches `normalize_pred`, so it
kept the raw spelling.

This is the equivalent-spellings rule inside one engine: `(b:Half)` written at the top level and
the same `(b:Half)` written inside a `COUNT { … }` are the same question, and they cost 3.3 ms and
186.1 ms.

### The change

`canon_body_labels`, run on the body `correlated_subquery_body` returns — so `EXISTS`, `COUNT`,
`VALUE`'s `AggSubquery` and its `ScalarSubquery` all get it from one place. It walks only `Filter`
and `Expand`, reshapes nothing, and introduces no seed, so a body it declines is exactly the body
that ran before. The node gate is deliberately NARROWER than `opt::slot_is_node`, because the
contract is different: `Plan::Row` stands for the whole outer row, whose columns may be a number
or a list rather than a node. So an outer slot is never claimed, and a body slot is claimed only
on an exact endpoint match — both guards, so that an under-counted `row_width` still cannot land
on an outer column. A BOUND EDGE sits one slot below the endpoint and is refused, because its
label test means the edge's TYPE, which `IsLabeled` would answer wrongly.

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding between each:

```text
  corrlblfilt   before 187.1 / 192.4 / 187.5 ms   after 18.0 / 18.0 / 17.5
```

Disjoint, 10.5x. Net of the 11.3 ms egress floor the BODY went ~175 ms to ~7, so the body itself is
~25x. Controls, none of which the rewrite can reach (no label in the body, or already on the fast
path): `corrfilt` 17.9 → 18.2, `corrlblonly` 26.0 → 24.6, `corrdeg` 11.3 → 11.4, `correxists`
3.2 → 3.2.

### The TS engine does not have this bug

Measured before assuming the gap transfers: `corrlblfilt` 614.4 ms against `corrfilt` 669.4 — the
label is slightly CHEAPER there, not 10x dearer, so the TS engine answers a label test directly
and there is nothing to port. (It is 34x slower than native on this shape overall, which is a
different and much larger question: a correlated subquery costs ~3 µs an outer row there. Open.)

### Teeth

Six mutants, four caught, the null control clean, and two of the four only after the test was
strengthened — which is the point of running them. Caught: a bound edge claimed as a node, the
node gate removed entirely, the `Not` arm of the predicate walk dropped, and the walk not
recursing through an `Expand`.

The last two SURVIVED the first run, because every one of their cases still returned the right
answer — the two spellings are equivalent, so only the PLAN can say whether the rewrite fired. The
fix was to read the plan text in those cases: `!plan.contains("labels")` for the negated and
disjunctive forms, and for the two-hop body whose label filter sits BELOW a hop. **A rewrite that
is a pure canonicalization cannot be tested by its answers.**

The surviving mutant is the `slot < row_width` guard, and it is redundant TODAY: `body_width`
returns a width for every body shape the walk descends into, so an endpoint index is always
`>= row_width` and the exact-endpoint match already refuses outer slots. It is the defense against
`row_width` being wrong, which is the thing a future caller could get wrong — recorded here rather
than removed.

The edge refusal also asserts the plan still CONTAINS a raw `labels()` call, so the refusal is
about the slot and not about the edge test arriving as some other expression the walk never sees
(item 510's rule: a refusal test proves nothing if the shape it refuses happens to agree).

### Not done

The `spelling_probe` group this deserves needs a SECOND label in its fixture — every node there is
a `Person`, so a label test hits the tautology short-circuit and the group would measure nothing.
Adding one moves every other group's baseline, so it is its own change.

### Gates

`cargo test --release` 1163 + 13 + 723 pass / 0 fail, `rewrite_fuzz` 10 pass, `cargo clippy
--all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt`, `bun test packages/native/src`
818 pass / 0 fail, `bun run check` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached
clean, `bun run build` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13, `spelling_probe` no cliffs.
`query_bench` flat (`EXISTS` 1142.2 against 1131.2, `optional hop` 580.6 against 577.9, `join on a
shared var` 4911.1 against 4870.1). One native test failed in the first full run and passed
isolated and on re-run — the known run-many flake. CI was green on 520.

## 522 — the same bug in the OTHER correlated body: a `CALL` arm, 25x

Item 521's own rule, applied to itself: grep the pattern elsewhere. It patched
`correlated_subquery_body`, which `EXISTS`, `COUNT` and `VALUE` share — and there is a SECOND
correlated-body builder, `call_arm`, which nothing in 521 touched.

Measured first, at 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges:

```text
  CALL (x) { MATCH (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Half) WHERE b.age > 50 RETURN b }   171.4 ms
  CALL (x) { MATCH (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b)      WHERE b.age > 50 RETURN b }     8.1
  CALL (x) { MATCH (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b)                        RETURN b }     5.6
```

The identical shape, a wider ratio than 521's — 21x against 10x — because a CALL arm's body has
no degree fast path to fall back on, so the label test is paid on every row with nothing else to
amortize it.

### The change

One line: `canon_body_labels(body, outer_width + 1)` on what `call_arm` returns. That one place
covers the yielding form (`Plan::CallInline`), every `UNION` / `EXCEPT` / `INTERSECT` arm (each
goes through `call_arm`), and the scalar-aggregate form, which leaves `CallInline` entirely and
becomes a `CountSubquery` / `AggSubquery` in a projection.

The `+ 1` is the whole subtlety. A CALL arm's body is PROVENANCE-TAGGED — slot `outer_width` holds
the per-outer-row id — so its `Plan::Row` leaf stands for `outer_width + 1` columns, and the body's
own variables append from there. Off by one in either direction and the exact-endpoint match
silently never fires, with every answer still correct.

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding between each:

```text
  before 174.0 / 181.8 / 173.0 ms   after 6.9 / 7.0 / 6.7
```

Disjoint, 25x. Controls, neither reachable by the rewrite: the unlabelled arm 8.1 → 8.0, the bare
arm 5.6 → 5.5. And item 521's own shape (`corrlblfilt`) is unchanged at 17.5, which is the control
for the two changes not interfering.

### Teeth

Four mutants, three caught, the null control clean: the row width one too small (the provenance
column forgotten), one too large, and the call removed entirely. All three are caught by the plan
read rather than by an answer — `!plan.contains("labels")` — which is item 521's lesson applied
from the start rather than discovered again.

The test covers the yielding form, both aggregate forms (`count(*)` and `max`), a `UNION ALL`
tail, a label BETWEEN two hops inside the arm, and the bound-edge refusal with its
`plan.contains("labels")` companion assert.

### The TS engine, again measured rather than assumed

`callinlinelbl` 21.3 ms against `callinlinefilt` 39.9 — the labelled form is FASTER there, so no
cliff, nothing to port. Worth stating what that means across the pair: on this shape the TS engine
was 8x FASTER than native before the fix (21.3 against 174.0) and is now 3x slower (21.3 against
6.9). A cliff in one engine can hide behind a cross-engine ratio that looks like the usual
constant factor.

### Gates

`cargo test --release` 1164 + 13 + 723 pass / 0 fail, `rewrite_fuzz` 10 pass, `cargo clippy
--all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` exit 0, `cargo fmt`, `bun test packages/native/src`
818 pass / 0 fail, `bun run check` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached
clean, `bun run build` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13, `spelling_probe` no cliffs,
`query_bench` flat. CI was green on 521.

## 523 — what ELSE a correlated body misses: the label test was the only one

Items 521 and 522 fixed one of `opt::normalize_pred`'s rewrites inside a correlated body. The
obvious next question is whether the others cost anything there too, and the answer is no — which
is worth as much as the two fixes, because it closes the territory instead of leaving it as a
hunch.

`normalize_pred` does three other things, and each one has a spelling `opt` would have produced,
so the PAIR is the measurement. At 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, native:

```text
  WHERE b.age IN [11, 22, 33]                      20.0 ms
  WHERE b.age = 11 OR b.age = 22 OR b.age = 33     20.0      (what the IN rewrite produces)

  WHERE NOT b.age = 11                             19.4
  WHERE b.age <> 11                                19.3      (what the NOT rewrite produces)

  WHERE 50 < b.age                                 17.6
  WHERE b.age > 50                                 17.9      (what the operand-order rule produces)
```

Every pair is within the noise of the other. The `IN` one is the surprise, because the rewrite's
own comment records a nested `score IN […]` over a hop costing ~75x the vectorized OR — but that
was a TOP-LEVEL hop, where the filter runs over a wide batch and the boxed list value is
re-cloned per row. A correlated body runs per outer row over a batch the size of one vertex's
degree, so there is no vectorization to miss. **A rewrite's value is a property of the batch
width it runs at, not of the expression.**

So the label test was special, and it is worth being precise about why: it is the only one of the
four whose two spellings reach DIFFERENT EVALUATORS rather than the same evaluator with a
different tree. `IsLabeled` is bucket membership; `'L' IN labels(slot)` builds a list and hashes a
string. The other three are the same comparison either way.

### Gremlin has none of it

Checked structurally rather than by measuring, which is the right test for a "does this exist"
question: `IsLabeled` appears once in `gremlin.rs` (where `hasLabel` mints it) and the string
`"labels"` appears nowhere in it. Gremlin never emits the raw spelling, so none of its correlated
bodies — and it builds many, in `local()`, `where()`, `not()` and the degree paths — can have
this bug.

That closes the sweep: `correlated_subquery_body` (521), `call_arm` (522), Gremlin (nothing to
fix), and the other three rewrites (no cost).

### A new target, priced

The TS correlated-subquery ladder, same fixture, against native after 521/522:

```text
                                                      ts        native
  COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b) }                       100.6 ms     11.3     9x
  COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Half) }                  362.3        24.6    15x
  COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b) WHERE b.age > 50 }      745.6        18.2    41x
```

The third row is the MISSING path, and the first two say so: TS has a degree rung
(`degreeCountSubquery`) and it does carry a landing label, so the first two rows are walking the
adjacency box. The third declines on its first line — `if (expr.where !== undefined)` — and falls
back to materializing the body's bindings per outer row. A landing-predicate degree count is the
shape to build, and the two rows above it are its controls.

No engine change this tick. The probe cases are the deliverable alongside the numbers.

### Gates

`bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean, `bun run lint` exit 0, `bun run check` exit 0. CI was green
on 522.

## 524 — the TS landing-predicate degree count: 1.9x, and the spelling probe needs isolating too

Item 523 priced this: `degreeCountSubquery` declines on its FIRST line when the body carries a
`WHERE`, so `COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b) WHERE b.age > 50 }` fell back to materializing the body's
bindings once per outer row. The two rows above it in that pricing are what made it a diagnosis
rather than a guess — the rung exists and carries a landing label, so the third shape is not slow
everywhere, it is REFUSED.

`landingPredDegreeCount` walks the anchor's adjacency box and gates each neighbour instead. The
counting loop is `sideOfVertexGated`, at MODULE scope rather than inline in the returned closure —
item 268's finding is that a walk written inside a closure gives unrelated queries a new slow
mode, and this is the kind of change that would hit it.

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding the dists between each:

```text
  COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b) WHERE b.age > 50 }   before 661.6 / 649.2 / 637.3 ms
                                                  after 346.0 / 354.4 / 312.3
  COUNT { (x)-[:KNOWS]->(b) }  (control)         before  74.6 /  74.6 /  75.5
                                                  after  74.8 /  76.3 /  75.4
```

Disjoint, 1.9x. The control is the rung the change cannot reach — a body with no `WHERE` goes to
`degreeCountSubquery` as before, and `gated` is only built when that one returns null.

Against native's 18.2 ms this is still 19x (it was 36x), so the remaining cost is the per-neighbour
predicate evaluation itself — a compiled-expr call and a `Map.set` per edge. Recorded as what is
left rather than claimed as closed.

**The first measurement was wrong and the control is why I noticed.** The probe reads the BUILT
dist, so the first after-reading was the unchanged engine plus noise — 868.3 against 745.6, which
reads as a regression. `bun run build` first; `fuzzers-read-built-dists` applies to every TS
harness here, not only the fuzzers.

### Three-valued logic, pinned rather than assumed

A neighbour counts only on a clean TRUE, so a missing property leaves the comparison UNKNOWN and
the neighbour is not counted — and neither is it counted under the negation. The test pins that as
a partition (3 TRUE + 1 UNKNOWN + 0 FALSE over four neighbours), not as a complement, because a
missing value read as FALSE would satisfy a complement test and fail this one.

Every case is also asked with `AND x.n = x.n` appended — TRUE for every vertex in the fixture, but
it makes `freePredicateVars` return the outer name, so the rung refuses and the GENERAL PATH
answers the same question. A rung and the path it replaces must agree, and that twin is what says
so.

A cross-type comparison (`b.s < 1`, `b.s < date(…)`) is not a match in this engine and does not
throw; the first version of that test asserted a throw, on the NATIVE engine's behaviour. Corrected
to assert agreement with the general path, which is the observable claim, with a note that nothing
reachable from here faults so "a fault propagates" is stated rather than tested.

### Teeth

Seven mutants, four caught, the null control clean: UNKNOWN counted, the landing label ignored, an
already-bound landing admitted, and the hop direction ignored.

Two survivors, both explained, and one of them changed the code:

- **The self-join guard** (`hop.variable === startVar`) is redundant. If the landing names the
  anchor then the call site's `binding.has(inner[0])` is already true — the anchor had to be bound
  to get here — so the rung stands down there instead. Kept as the local statement of the
  invariant, with the redundancy recorded at the guard; M4 proves the check that does the work has
  teeth.
- **The no-subquery-in-the-predicate guard** survives because the hazard I wrote it for does not
  exist. The scratch binding is allocated per `countOf` CALL, not per rung, so a nested subquery
  that re-enters gets its own and reads the outer `b` out of the scratch map — which is exactly
  right. The guard is conservatism, and the comment now says that instead of claiming a
  re-entrancy bug. Widening it is a measurable change of its own and is left for one.

### The spelling probe's full run needs isolating too

`bun run spelling` flagged a group my change had not touched — "one end labelled, the other free"
at 2.1x, just over the 2x threshold, where the pristine build flagged none. Isolated with
`SPELL_ONLY`, that group is **1.04x on BOTH builds** (23.1-24.8 ms across four spellings, twice
each). Item 514's rule about `bun run bench` applies here as well: the probe runs every group in
one process, so a short group's spread is perturbed, and a full-run flag is a prompt to isolate
rather than a finding. The 5436.2x "label on start" flag is present on both builds and is the
known seeded-vs-scan group.

### Regression sweep

`bun run bench` read `count 3-hop` at 358.6 against 321.1 in the item 520 sweep. Isolated:
328.3 / 324.5 / 325.4, inside the 321-330 band this row has shown since item 514. So a LONG row is
not immune to sweep variance either, only less affected — qualifying item 514's wording. Everything
else flat or better (`subquery item` 27.8, `2-hop subquery item` 111.5, `distinct over a hop` 58.8,
`traverse 1-hop + filter` 43.6).

### Gates

`bun test packages/gql packages/core` 2737 pass / 0 fail (+11), `bun test packages/native/src` 818
pass / 0 fail, `bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached
clean, `bun run build` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13. CI was green on 523.

## 525 — a WRONG ANSWER in the one-hop EXISTS arm, found while chasing an 11% allocation

This tick went looking for item 524's pattern elsewhere — a per-edge binding allocation in a
correlated rung — and found a cross-engine wrong answer next to it. The perf result is the small
half.

### What the EXISTS rung does

`oneHopExists` (item 492) has two arms. A FREE endpoint — no label, no inline predicate, no
sub-`WHERE` — collapses the question to "does `x` have an edge of these types" and answers from a
bucket SIZE without visiting an edge. Anything else walks the adjacency and calls `matchNode` per
edge.

Priced at 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, ts against native:

```text
  EXISTS { (x)-[:E]->(b) }                        95.0 ms    1.3    the free arm
  EXISTS { (x)-[:E]->(b:Half) }                  277.6      15.2    label alone leaves it
  EXISTS { (x)-[:E]->(b) WHERE b.age > 1000 }    329.2       3.6    never matches: full walk
```

### The wrong answer

`shape.free` is a compile-time fact about the pattern TEXT. Boundness is a run-time fact, and the
arm never checked it — so an endpoint variable the outer row had already bound was IGNORED:

```text
  MATCH (x), (y) WHERE y.n = 3 AND EXISTS { (x)-[:T]->(y) }   ts: x = a AND d   native: a
  MATCH (x) WHERE EXISTS { (x)-[:T]->(x) }                    ts: every x       native: d
```

The second is the SELF-LOOP question, and `degreeCountSubquery` has carried exactly this check
since item 211 — its doc comment even spells out why ("`COUNT { (u)-[:T]->(u) }` counts
self-loops, not degree"). The EXISTS twin never got it. Both shapes returned the correct answer
from the native engine and no test covered either; the differential fuzzer does not generate an
EXISTS whose endpoint the outer row has bound (the same blind spot item 506's repeated node
variable fell into).

Fixed by gating the free arm on `far.variable === undefined || !binding.has(far.variable)` — the
run-time half of the same rule, next to the compile-time half. Pinned in
`bound-exists-endpoint-conformance.test.ts`, which asks both engines and pins the answer, with
`d` (a self-loop and nothing else) and `a` (two edges and no self-loop) as each other's
counterexample so an arm that confuses "has an edge" with "has THIS edge" cannot pass both.

**This is the fourth wrong answer this loop has found, and the fourth found by probing rather
than by a failing test.**

### The perf half: 1.11x, and the hypothesis was wrong

A LABEL-ONLY endpoint with no sub-`WHERE` now tests the label directly instead of calling
`matchNode`, which would do the same label test and then ALLOCATE a binding for an endpoint
variable nothing reads. `matchNode`'s other two parts are kept verbatim — the label, and
`consistent`, which is what makes a repeated endpoint mean identity.

```text
  EXISTS { (x)-[:E]->(b:Half) }   before 280.2 / 279.3 / 280.5 ms   after 257.9 / 248.6 / 250.7
  EXISTS { (x)-[:E]->(b) }        before  77.0 /  68.8 /  68.3      after  67.9 /  68.4 /  67.9
```

Disjoint, 1.11x, with the free arm flat — so the `binding.has` the fix adds to it costs nothing
measurable. But the hypothesis that motivated the change is REFUTED: the allocation is not the
2.9x gap between the two arms. It is 11% of it. The rest is the edge iteration itself — the
`edgesOfTypes` generator frame, the endpoint resolve and the label call, which are items 218 and
194's territory. Still 16x native on this shape.

**I nearly retracted a real win on a 5-rep reading.** At `PR=5` the after-number read 307.5
against a before of 277.6 and looked like a regression; at `PR=7` the same comparison is
280.2 → 257.9, disjoint over three rounds. The TS probe's bimodality (recorded for the spelling
probe at item 259) applies to this probe too.

### Teeth

Seven mutants, SIX caught, the null control clean: the free arm ungated, its gate inverted, the
label arm dropping `consistent`, the label arm dropping the label test, and the label arm
admitting either a sub-`WHERE` or an inline predicate. The last one is caught by an existing
suite (`an inline WHERE on the ENDPOINT of an EXISTS subquery`), and the sub-`WHERE` mutant is
caught by the differential fuzzer as well as the unit tests — which is the fuzzer earning its
place on a shape it does not generate directly.

`count 3-hop` read 397.0 in the shared sweep and 342.6 / 311.1 / 316.5 isolated, inside the
311-342 band it has shown for two ticks. No bench row uses `EXISTS`, so the sweep is a check on

## 526 — the fuzzer now generates the shape that hid two wrong answers

Four wrong answers have surfaced in this run of work and all four were found by probing, not by a
test. Two of them hid in the same place: a subquery whose endpoint names the variable the outer
row already bound.

```text
  item 506   every TS hop fast path bound the far node over the start without checking the name
             was the same one — `count(*)` read 4 where native read 2, over eight shapes.
  item 525   `oneHopExists`'s free-endpoint arm answered from a bucket SIZE, so
             `EXISTS { (x)-[:T]->(x) }` was true for every vertex with any edge.
```

Item 506's own note says why neither was reachable: _"the differential fuzzer does not generate a
one-hop pattern that repeats its endpoint."_ This closes that for the subquery body.
`subqueryBody` now draws a SELF arm — the endpoint is `n`, the outer variable — with no label,
because a bound variable may not be re-labelled inside a subquery body and native's rejection of
that is correct.

### The evidence it works, in three parts

A widening is a claim about what a generator can find, and all three parts are needed before the
claim means anything.

**1. The widened fuzzer catches item 525's bug: 6 of 6 seeds.** The bug re-introduced as a
one-line mutant (the free arm ungated), 20,000 queries a run.

**2. The PRE-widening fuzzer misses it: 0 of 6 seeds.** This is the part that makes the first one
a statement about the widening rather than about the suite. Without it, "the fuzzer catches it"
could have been true all along and the bug would have been a different kind of escape.

**3. Switching the SELF arm off fails the coverage floor.** `const self = r() < 0.2` → `false`
makes the run RED on `selfEndGenerated`, so the counter is a gate and not decoration — the same
check item 517 applied to a test that passed on its first run.

### The floor

Measured over NINE seeds of 20,000: generated 41-61 (mean ~49, sigma ~6.1), non-empty 29-43
(mean ~35, sigma ~4.9). Floors at `> 22` and `> 14`, ~4 sigma below the means — item 280's rule,
that the safety of a floor is its distance in SIGMA and not a percentage. A percentage applied to
a small count is what made `subOrNonEmpty` flake on a docs-only commit.

The NON-EMPTY floor is the one carrying weight: the fixture has to have self-loops for a row to
come back, and a generation-only counter would be satisfied by 20,000 empty answers agreeing.

### Still open, and named rather than implied

This covers the SUBQUERY body. Item 506's own shape is a TOP-LEVEL `MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->(a)`, and
the outer-pattern generator still does not produce a repeated endpoint — a separate widening, in
a different function, and the next one to do.

The RNG stream shifts for any seed that reaches `subqueryBody`, because the self arm draws. That
is what a generator widening does (item 214 did the same); `--seed` replay stays deterministic,
it just means something different than it did before this commit.

## 527 — the TOP-LEVEL repeated endpoint, and the fixture edge it needed

Item 526 closed the subquery half of this gap and named the other half: item 506's own shape is a
TOP-LEVEL `MATCH (a:T)-[:E]->(a)`, which the hop-family generator never produced. Seven shapes
now do — the one-hop forms in both directions, with and without a label, with a bound edge
variable and with a `WHERE`, plus the two two-hop forms that return to the START (a 2-cycle) and
to the MIDDLE (a self-loop on the second hop).

### The fixture had no self-loop

Which is why item 526's arm, measured on its own, was only half a test. On a fixture with no
self-loop `(a)-[:E]->(a)` is correctly EMPTY, so a fast path that OVER-counts there is caught —
item 525's bug was, 6 of 6 — but one that under-counts is not, and item 506's bug was an
over-count whose SIZE needs a real self-loop to show (`count(*)` read 4 against native's 2 on a
fixture with two).

Edge `e7` is that self-loop: `5 -[:F]-> 5`. On `F` and at vertex 5 deliberately — 5 is a leaf of
the F chain with no other out-edge, so the E cycle `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1` that the four PATH MODES
depend on is untouched and the quantified-walk shapes keep the structure they were measured
against. It is safe under every mode the generator pairs with an unbounded quantifier: trail
forbids repeating the EDGE so it is taken at most once, simple and acyclic forbid repeating the
vertex so it is refused outright, and walk is only ever generated with a bounded quantifier.

Confirmed in the counter: `selfHopNonEmpty` is 25-36 of 20,000, so these queries really do return
rows rather than agreeing on empty.

### The evidence, in four parts

**1. Item 506's bug, re-introduced (the whole-query `repeatsNodeVariable` gate forced to
`false`), is caught 5 of 5 seeds** by the widened fuzzer.

**2. The PRE-527 fuzzer — which already carries item 526's subquery arm — misses it 0 of 5.** So
the subquery widening was genuinely not enough, and this is not a claim the previous commit
already satisfied.

**3. Removing the WHOLE family fails the coverage floor.** The counter gates.

**4. Removing ONE of the seven shapes does NOT.** Recorded rather than fixed: the floor is a
FAMILY-level gate with a ~4 sigma margin, and one shape of seven sits inside that margin. A
per-shape floor would be nine more counters and would flake; what this floor protects against is
a collapse, which is the failure mode that has actually happened here (`subOrNonEmpty`, item
280).

### Floors re-measured, because a fixture change moves a count

Adding `e7` changed `selfEnd` from 41-61 to 40-57. Both families re-measured over NINE seeds of
20,000 with the new fixture:

```text
  selfEnd   generated 40-57 (mean ~51, sigma ~5.0)   non-empty 33-44 (mean ~39, sigma ~3.6)
  selfHop   generated 36-54 (mean ~42, sigma ~5.7)   non-empty 25-36 (mean ~29, sigma ~3.1)
```

Floors ~4 sigma below the means: `selfEnd > 22 / > 14` (unchanged, now a wider margin) and
`selfHop > 18 / > 15`.

## 528 — the TS `FOR` PROJECTION off the label bucket: 4.0-4.4x, and it now beats native

Items 515 and 518 gave the `count(*)` form of this shape the arithmetic. A projection has to emit
the rows, so there is no arithmetic to replace the walk with — which made it look like the cost
WAS the walk, and the third row below is what says otherwise:

```text
                                                     ts        native
  MATCH (n:Person) FOR t IN n.tags RETURN t AS t     92.7 ms    50.8
  MATCH (n:Person) FOR x IN [1,2,3] RETURN x AS x    97.4       40.1
  MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.age AS k   (no FOR)       9.5       11.0
```

Without a `FOR` the TS engine is FASTER than native. So the 2.0-2.4x is not a projection gap and
not an element-render gap — it is the per-element BINDING machinery, which the plain projection's
own rung never touches: `runFor` copies the whole binding into a `new Map` per element,
`elems.map` materializes an array of those per input row, and `mapToRow` walks the surviving map
again at the end. Three allocations an element, 162 ns a row against 48.

`detectForProjection` walks the label bucket and reuses ONE scratch binding across every element
of every anchor, because nothing retains it — `projectRow` reads it and returns a fresh `Row`.
The same trick as item 524's landing gate and sound for the same reason: the only consumer is
finished with the binding before the next element overwrites it. The walk itself lives in a
module-scope `forProjectionRows`, not inline in the returned closure (item 268's 4x hazard).

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding the dists between each:

```text
  FOR t IN n.tags  before  95.2 / 159.7 /  99.9 ms   after 25.2 / 23.7 / 24.0     ~4.0x
  FOR x IN [1,2,3] before  93.2 /  91.5 /  92.2      after 26.2 / 21.1 / 20.6     ~4.4x
  the plain projection (CONTROL)  9.8 / 10.7 / 11.7  after 10.9 / 10.7 /  9.6     flat
```

Disjoint. The control is the rung the change cannot reach — a query with no `FOR` clause never
reaches the detector at all — and it is also the row whose 9.5 against native's 11.0 was the
diagnosis, so it is doing two jobs.

**Both shapes now beat NATIVE** (24 and 21 against 50.8 and 40.1), which makes native's `FOR`
projection the open target on the other side. Recorded, not chased this tick.

### ISO's unwind rule, pinned case by case

A list contributes one row per element, an EMPTY list contributes none (the anchor's row
disappears), NULL or a missing key contributes none, and any other scalar contributes exactly one
— a non-list unwinds as a one-element list. The fixture has one vertex of each kind so the five
answers are five different numbers. `WITH ORDINALITY` and `WITH OFFSET` are pinned including the
fact that the ordinal RESTARTS per anchor, which is what distinguishes a per-anchor counter from
a global one.

Every case is asked twice: admitted, and with a `FILTER true` inserted — which keeps every row
but takes the clause count to four, so the rung declines and the general path answers the same
question. Compared as multisets, since row order without `ORDER BY` is unspecified.

### Teeth

Seven mutants, SEVEN caught, the null control clean: the ordinality kind swapped, NULL unwound as
a one-element list, a list NOT unwound, the landing label ignored, an aggregating projection
admitted (caught by item 518's own suite), `plainRowProjection` ignored, and the anchor bound only
once instead of per vertex.

One was MISAPPLIED on the first run and the uniqueness assert caught it: the label-bucket line is
character-identical across three rungs in this file, so the pattern matched three times.
Re-anchored on the line that follows it in this function. Items 474, 483, 494, 518 and now 528 —
**two copies of a body is still the most reliable way to fool a mutation run here**, and the
assert is the only reason it reads as a misapplication rather than as a survivor.

The free-name check on the projection items survives by construction rather than by test, and is
recorded at the guard: with ONE lone-node pattern the only names in scope are the anchor and the
`FOR` variable, so anything else is an unbound reference the compiler rejects before this runs.

## 529 — RETRACTION: native's `FOR` projection is not a target; item 528 read the carrier

Item 528 closed the TS `FOR` projection at 4.0-4.4x and ended by naming the other side as open:
_"Both shapes now beat NATIVE (24 and 21 against 50.8 and 40.1), which makes native's `FOR`
projection the open target on the other side."_ That sentence is wrong, and the first thing this
tick did was check it rather than act on it.

### The two instruments disagree, and one of them includes the boundary

```text
  route-cost-probe, ENGINE=native (FFI, 600,000 rows cross the boundary)
    FOR x IN [1,2,3] RETURN x      40.1 ms   =  67 ns/row
    FOR t IN n.tags  RETURN t      50.8      =  85 ns/row

  query_bench, IN PROCESS (same 600,000 rows, no boundary)
    for-in const project         8800.4 / 8944.3 us   =  14.7 / 14.9 ns/row

  query_bench, a ONE-COLUMN plain projection for scale
    project is null num           451.4 / 450.0 us    =   2.3 ns/row
    project absent cmp            789.4 / 851.8 us    =   4.0 / 4.3 ns/row
```

67 − 14.8 = **52 ns/row**, which lands inside the 58-94 ns/row native row egress this probe's own
header records (items 428, 434). So the 40.1 ms is the JSON CARRIER — closed at item 289 — and
comparing it against a TS number measured through the same carrier on a different code path says
nothing about the unwind.

**I made exactly the mistake CLOSED.md warns about two lines from where I was reading.** Item 341's
entry says it in capitals: _"⚠️ I NEARLY REPORTED THE ts-vs-ffi RATIO AS A FINDING. IT IS CLOSED AT
ITEM 289."_ Item 528's measurement was sound for the TS-vs-TS comparison it made — three alternated
rounds, one engine, one harness — and the ts-against-native sentence tacked on at the end was not
measured at all. **A number that is valid for the comparison you ran is not valid for the one you
mention in the last paragraph.**

### What IS left there, with its size

In process, the unwind projection is 14.8 ns/row against 2.3-4.3 for a one-column plain
projection — about 10 ns an element. `unwind_rows`' INVARIANT arm is already the good one: one
evaluation, one `Vec`, `reserve(n * k)`, and a `Value::clone` per element (item 519 built that).
The non-invariant arm calls `lists.value_at(i)`, which hands back an OWNED `Value::List` — a `Vec`
allocation per input row, 200,000 of them for a three-element `n.tags`.

That lever cannot be measured in process today: `query_bench`'s shared `social_store` has no list
property, and adding one would move every other row in the group off the baseline the audit
records — which is precisely the trap item 527 had to re-measure two coverage floors for. So the
honest state is: a named lever, an estimated ~18 ns/row from the FFI pair (85 − 67, through a
carrier that is itself ±36 ns/row, so the estimate is weak), and a fixture problem standing
between it and a real number.

## 530 — PRICING THE AGGREGATE ENUM: five of eleven had no rung (2.7-4.3x), and native PANICKED

Take a family, price every member against the same scan with the same argument, and the only
variable left is the member. ISO-GQL has eleven aggregate names; `nodeAggregate`'s rung admits
some subset of them, and which one is a question for the measurement rather than for reading the
guard. ts, 200,000 vertices:

```text
  ON the rung      count(n.age) 10.9   max 11.2   min 11.3   sum 13.6   avg 13.7
                   count(DISTINCT n.age) 3.0
  OFF the rung     stddev_pop 50.9   percentile_cont 56.8   percentile_disc 64.3
                   stddev_samp 69.9   collect 72.4
```

Native answers all eleven between 0.4 and 5.6 ms, so the gap was TS-only and as wide as 64x.

### THREE arity gates in one function, and only the third mattered

The first fix widened the MULTI-item gate and moved almost nothing: collect 72.4 → 45.0,
percentile_cont 56.8 → **62.1**, stddev_pop 50.9 → **64.5**. Diagnosing instead of pushing found
`unfilteredScanAgg`, the SINGLE-item gate, which runs ahead of it and refused everything but
`sum`/`avg`. Widening that one took collect to 11.5, stddev_pop to 13.5, stddev_samp to 13.4 —
and left both percentiles untouched, because a THIRD arity check (`aggNode.args.length !== 1`)
sits further down the same function and percentiles take two arguments.

**"Grep the pattern elsewhere" applies inside one function as readily as across a repo.** Three
guards, written at three times, each a plausible place to stop.

### The change

`VALUES_AGGREGATES` is a NAME SET, not five hand-written folds, and that is the point: every
member reaches `aggregateOverValues` — the one shared implementation the general path also calls
— so the rung changes where the values come from and nothing about the arithmetic or the order. A
second `sum` could not even be written correctly (the operation is chosen by looking at the whole
collection, item 467) and a second `stddev` would be a byte-identity hazard. `percentileFraction`
answers all three gates at once: `0` for a well-formed one-argument aggregate, the clamped
fraction for a well-formed percentile, `null` to refuse.

```text
  collect           before 50.4 / 60.5 / 45.4 ms   after 11.7 / 11.0 / 12.5    ~4.1x
  stddev_samp       before 52.4 / 50.9 / 51.9      after 12.7 / 11.8 / 12.0    ~4.3x
  percentile_cont   before 60.5 / 67.8 / 60.6      after 22.4 / 21.9 / 22.3    ~2.7x
  max      (CONTROL, the fold path)  10.4 / 11.2 / 11.4   after 11.0 / 12.0 / 11.1
  count(DISTINCT) (CONTROL, refused)  3.2 /  2.8 /  3.0   after  3.0 /  3.0 /  3.4
```

Three alternated rounds with a rebuild between each, disjoint, both controls flat.

### THE NATIVE ENGINE PANICKED, and the enum is what found it

Checking native for comparison, on the way to deciding whether the gap transfers:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) RETURN percentile_cont(n.age, 2) AS m
    thread panicked at src/exec/aggregation.rs:1018:48:
    index out of bounds: the len is 2 but the index is 2
```

`percentile_of` computes `rn = frac * (n - 1)` and indexes `nums[rn.ceil()]`. Nothing clamped
`frac`, so any fraction above 1 read past the end. The `disc` branch survived on its own
`.min(n - 1)`; the `cont` branch had no equivalent. It surfaces as `query evaluation panicked` —
**a crash, not an error**, which is a worse class than a wrong answer.

The TS engine clamps the fraction when it LOWERS the literal, so the fix is the same clamp at the
point of USE in native, where no caller can bypass it. Both engines now answer the maximum above
1 and the minimum below 0.

**Fifth defect this loop has found, and the fifth found by probing rather than by a test.** No
fuzzer generates a fraction outside [0, 1], and the two engines' percentile tests both used
in-range values.

### One divergence left, recorded rather than papered over

A NEGATIVE literal fraction: TS RAISES (`-1` is a unary-minus expression, not a literal token, so
`compileAggregate` refuses before reading a value) while native accepts it and clamps to the
minimum. ISO does not define the input and the panic was the part that needed fixing; folding
unary minus into a literal is a parser change with a wider blast radius than this item.

### Teeth

Five mutants plus two null controls; four caught, both controls clean. Caught: the native clamp
removed (the new Rust test fails on the panic), the native clamp's upper bound wrong, the TS
fraction dropped, and the TS fraction left unclamped.

The survivor is the TS non-literal-fraction refusal, and it is unreachable by construction:
`compileProjection` compiles the aggregate — and `compileAggregate` raises on a malformed
percentile — before any rung is consulted, so a malformed call never reaches the guard. Kept as
the local statement of the rule and recorded here.

Two test expectations of mine were WRONG and the twin caught both. `percentile_disc(x, 0.5)` over
four values is 20, not 30 (ISO's DISC is the smallest value whose cumulative distribution reaches
the fraction) — checked against native rather than argued. And `stddev_pop(x, 1)` does not throw
in EITHER engine: only the percentiles validate their arity, so a second argument is accepted and
ignored. The declining twin also caught a worse mistake: my first twin was `WHERE n.age >= 0`,
which is UNKNOWN for the vertex with no `age`, so it dropped a row and `collect(n.s)` came back
one element short. **A declining twin that asks a different question is worse than none, because
it reads as a divergence in the code under test.** `WHERE true` keeps every row and still turns
`unfilteredScan` off.

packages/core` 2755 pass / 0 fail (+5), `bun test packages/native/src` 822 pass / 0 fail (+1),

## 531 — the fuzzer generates an OUT-OF-RANGE percentile fraction, and the boundary surface is clean

Item 530's native panic reached main with a percentile arm already in the fuzzer. The arm picked
its fraction from `['0', '0.5', '1', '0.25']` — four in-range values — so the one thing that could
crash the `cont` branch was the one thing it never produced. Four out-of-range values added:
`1.0001`, `1.5`, `2`, `100`.

### Three-part evidence, again

**1. The widened fuzzer catches the panic: 4 of 4 seeds** (the clamp reverted as a one-line
mutant).
**2. The PRE-531 fuzzer misses it 0 of 4**, which is what makes the first part a statement about
the widening rather than about the suite.
**3. Removing the out-of-range values fails the coverage floor**, so the counter gates.

Floors from NINE seeds of 20,000: generated 156-200 (mean ~180, sigma ~12.6) → `> 128`;
non-empty 76-96 (mean ~90, sigma ~7.3) → `> 58`. ~4 sigma below the means, item 280's rule.

No NEGATIVE fraction, and that is a decision rather than an omission: `-1` is a unary-minus
EXPRESSION rather than a literal token, so TS raises `requires a numeric literal fraction` while
native accepts and clamps. That divergence is open and recorded at item 530, and generating it
would make the gate red for a known question instead of for a regression — the same reasoning
this file already applies to a named aggregate inside a `VALUE` body.

### The class, swept and clean

One float-derived index that panicked is a reason to look for the others, so:

**Every float-to-index conversion in the engine.** `ceil()/floor()/round()/trunc() as usize`
appears in exactly four places: the two percentile branches (now clamped), the `disc` branch's
own `.min(n - 1)`, and `opt.rs`'s seek-fraction cap, which derives from the live node count and
not from user input. Nothing else in the read path turns a float into an index.

**Fourteen boundary arguments, both engines, compared row for row.** `substring` past the end and
with an over-long length, a zero length, list indexing at 0 / 99 / on an empty list, `head` and
`last` of an empty list, string indexing, `round` with ±400 digits, division by zero, `power` with
a huge exponent, `log10(0)` and `sqrt(-1)`. **All fourteen agree**, and the only row that printed
as a difference is the division-by-zero ERROR PREFIX (`LenkeError: division by zero` against
`lenke: query: division by zero`), which is message text the fuzzer compares by code — not a
behaviour difference.

So the percentile was the one hole in that surface, not the first of many. Worth the twenty
minutes: the alternative was assuming either that it was isolated or that it was widespread.


SEVEN of eleven, a 4.3-4.9x gap, and on a much larger base than the scan's — the general path
materializes a `Binding` per EDGE. Native for scale: `max` 2.4 ms, `sum` 5.5, `percentile_cont`
10.0, `collect` 41.3, so the ts:native ratio runs from 17x to 123x.

Note that `sum` and `avg` are off the rung HERE while item 530's scan serves them. That is not an
oversight, and finding out why is the result of this tick.

### Why five of the seven must stay refused

`detectMultiHopAggregate`'s own doc records the rule, and it is item 419's: **the far-driven walk
may visit rows in a different order from the general path, so only an order-INDEPENDENT aggregate
may ride it.** `count`/`min`/`max` qualify. The rule is written for `sum`/`avg` explicitly —
_"refused here even though item 468 admits them on an unfiltered SCAN, where there is no
far-driven alternative"_.

So widening this rung the way item 530 widened the scan one would be WRONG, not slow:

- `sum`/`avg` — float addition is not associative, so a different order is a different last ulp,
  and byte-identity with native is a hard invariant.
- `collect`/`collect_list` — the ORDER IS THE ANSWER. A list is its sequence.
- `stddev_pop`/`stddev_samp` — one-pass moments, order-sensitive in the same way as `sum`.

**This is why the enum was worth pricing even where it cannot be fixed**: five of the seven rows
are a recorded design decision, and without reading item 419 they look exactly like five missing
fast paths worth 4.5x each.

### The two that CAN ride it, with their size

`percentile_cont` and `percentile_disc` SORT their values before using them, so the answer does
not depend on the order the values arrived in — the one property item 419's rule asks for.
Together that is **742.6 and 730.0 ms against the 155.8 the rung delivers**, about 4.7x, on a
shape whose native twin costs 10.0.

The NaN caveat, checked rather than waved past: a sort whose comparator maps incomparable values
to `Equal` is order-DEPENDENT when NaN is present. It cannot be here — the numeric model converts
a non-finite to `null` on ingest, so no stored property is NaN, and the probe in item 531 confirms
the expression surface agrees: `log10(0)`, `sqrt(-1)` and an overflowing `power` all yield `null`,
which the aggregate's non-null filter then drops.

PRICED, NOT BUILT. The admission needs an `argFn` that `foldedAggs` does not carry for a
non-foldable aggregate, so the argument has to be compiled for the synthetic projection the way
the SCAN path already does — a real edit with a real divergence risk, and the honest place to stop
this tick is with the number on it.
