## 533 — the percentile HOP rung: 4.0x, and a control that read as a regression and was not one

Item 532 priced the hop aggregate enum, found seven of eleven off the rung, and established from
item 419 that five of the seven must STAY off it — the hop walk may be far-driven, so only an
ORDER-INDEPENDENT aggregate may ride it. The two that qualify are the percentiles, because
`percentile_of` sorts its values before using them. This builds that.

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding the dists between each:

```text
  percentile_cont(b.age, 0.5)   before 753.2 / 748.8 / 740.2 ms   after 176.1 / 182.9 / 190.4
  percentile_disc(b.age, 0.5)   before 730.0                       after 205.7
  max(b.age)   (CONTROL, the fold path)  141.4 / 160.1 / 146.9     after 179.2 / 161.3 / 125.8
  sum(b.age)   (CONTROL, stays refused)  699.6 / 714.1 / 694.4     after 672.3 / 706.6 / 711.0
```

~4.0x on the target, disjoint. `sum` is the control that matters most here: it must stay on the
general path, and it does.

### THE CONTROL READ AS A REGRESSION AND IT WAS NOT ONE

The first version put the values-collect branch INSIDE the existing row loop — one extra test per
row. The fold control then read **125.7-127.5 ms before against 129.0-156.8 after, three
alternated rounds, non-overlapping at the bottom**, which is the signature of a real 1.02-1.23x
cost on a loop that runs once an edge; item 159 has measured that before.

So I split the loop in two, branched once per call, and re-ran. The split did NOT restore the
number (158.5), which is what prompted a second A/B instead of a third fix — and the second A/B
came back **141.4 / 160.1 / 146.9 against 179.2 / 161.3 / 125.8: overlapping and
non-monotonic.** The row is bimodal ACROSS BUILDS, 125-180 ms for the same source. Tick 532 had
measured the same pristine code at 155.8.

**Three alternated rounds can read disjoint by luck on a bimodal row.** The rule this session has
been applying — "confirm any flag with min-of-three alternated rounds" — is necessary and not
sufficient; what settled it was a second independent A/B after a change that should have fixed the
thing and did not. The loop split stays because one loop per path is clearer, and its comment now
says there is no perf claim attached rather than quoting the number that started it.

### Teeth

Six mutants including the null control; four caught, one explained survivor, the control clean.
Caught: the fraction ignored, the percentile NAME swapped (`disc` answered as `cont`), the nullish
filter removed, and `DISTINCT` admitted — the last two only after the tests were strengthened.

**The name check's mutant survives, and the explanation is the content.** Admitting `collect` on
the walk changes no answer on a four-node fixture with crossed edges (`s1 -> t2`, `s2 -> t1`),
because the walk only goes FAR-DRIVEN under conditions a fixture that small does not meet — so the
two routes agree and the order hazard never shows. That is exactly why item 419 is a RULE rather
than a test: the shape that would expose it depends on a planner CHOICE, not on the query. Recorded
at the guard.

Two test-harness problems found on the way, both worth keeping:

- `collect(b.age) + 0` cannot be a declining twin — arithmetic on a list raises. A second
  projection item declines instead (`proj.items.length !== 1`), and `detectMultiHopAggregate`
  refuses a non-foldable aggregate too, so the general path answers.
- `percentile_cont(DISTINCT b.age, 0.5)` over `[10, 10, 20]` is **15** while the non-DISTINCT form
  is 10 — the one case that separates a rung honouring DISTINCT from one ignoring it. `disc` gives
  10 either way, so a `disc`-only test would have passed the mutant.

### Also

`percentileFraction` moved from `shortcuts.ts` to `executor.ts` and is exported, so the scan rung
(item 530) and the hop rung share one implementation of "is this a well-formed percentile, and
what is its clamped fraction".

## 535 — a REDUNDANT LABEL costs 2.6x in TS, and the cause is a route change at the SECOND conjunct

Started from the one `bench:gremlin` row item 517 did not account for —
`V().has(age,gt).count()` at 28.3x native — and the first measurement sent the tick somewhere
else entirely. At 200,000 vertices all carrying `Person`, TS:

```text
  gremlin  V().has(age, gt(44)).count()                      2.55 ms
  gremlin  V().hasLabel('Person').has(age, gt(44)).count()   18.74       7.3x for the label
  gql      MATCH (n) WHERE n.age > 44 RETURN count(*)         4.51
  gql      MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.age > 44 RETURN count(*)  12.58       2.8x for the label
```

The label is carried by EVERY vertex, so both spellings do the same work: visit 200,000 vertices,
test one property. **Both surfaces charge several times more for the tautology.**

### Not the source, and not a per-conjunct cost

Two candidate explanations, both measured and both wrong:

**The label BUCKET is slower to iterate than the id map.** It is not: iterating
`verticesByLabel.get('Person')` (a 200,000-element `Set`) with the same age test costs **2.13 ms**
against **2.31** for `verticesById.values()`. The source is free; `candidateVertexSource` returns
the bucket directly.

**Each conjunct costs the same.** It does not — and this is the finding:

```text
  no label, 1 predicate                             4.51 ms    22.6 ns/row
  no label, 2 predicates                           11.86       59.3        +37 ns
  no label, 3 predicates                           12.66       63.3        + 4 ns
  label on EVERY node + 1 predicate                11.59       (= 2 preds)
  label on ONE THIRD  + 1 predicate                 4.72       (= 2 preds over 1/3 the rows)
```

One conjunct to two costs **+37 ns a row**; two to three costs **+4**. That is not a linear
per-predicate cost — it is a ROUTE CHANGE at the second conjunct, and a redundant label is what
silently turns a one-conjunct query into a two-conjunct one.

The selective-label row is what confirms it rather than leaving it as an inference: `(n:Third)` is
also a second conjunct and also on the slow route, but over a third of the rows — 11.59/3 ≈ 3.9,
measured 4.72. Same per-row cost, fewer rows. **So a label is not expensive; a SECOND CONJUNCT
is, and a label that excludes nothing pays for one without buying anything.**

### Where it probably is, stated as a hypothesis

`buildNodeCount(graph, label, preds)` applies its predicates through `inlineHolds` → `satisfies`
and handles a label plus predicates fine, so the count rung is not the thing refusing. The
suspect is the clause-`WHERE`-to-inline-predicate lifting (`pushWhereIntoNode` and the
`inlineOf`/`gateWith` family), which may lift ONE conjunct and decline a conjunction. **Not
confirmed** — located, not diagnosed, and the next tick's first job is to confirm it before
changing anything.

### Why this is worth a target

It is the repo's own bug class: two spellings of one question, one of them several times slower,
both correct. The TS spelling probe's only flagged group is `label on start: redundant vs absent`
— but that one is a HOP count where the two spellings are genuinely different work (O(1) bucket
size against O(|label|) degree summing), explicitly recorded as "no amount of further work closes
this pair". **This is a different shape with the same name**: a node-scan count where the work IS
the same, and the group that would have caught it does not exist.

Native pays nothing for the tautology, and already has the mechanism: `IsLabeled`'s evaluator
short-circuits when a label's bucket length equals the live node count (item E78).

No code change this tick. Numbers first.

`bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean, `bun run lint` exit 0, `bun run typecheck` exit 0. CI was

## 536 — CORRECTION to item 535: two of its three claims were MY OWN in-process contamination

Item 535's first job was named in its own text — _"the next tick's first job is to confirm it
before changing anything"_. Confirming it refuted most of it.

### What instrumenting found: the route is IDENTICAL

Instrumented `detectCountShortcut` and `buildNodeCount` and ran the four spellings. All four FIRE
the count rung, and all four reach `buildNodeCount` with **`preds=1, seeded=false`** — the same
builder, the same tally loop, the same number of predicates. There is no route change, and a
label does not add a conjunct. So the measured difference could not be coming from where item 535
said it was, and the next question was whether it was there at all.

### One case per process, and two claims disappear

```text
                                                  item 535 (one process)   isolated
  MATCH (n) WHERE n.age > 44 RETURN count(*)             4.51 ms              4.41
  MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.age > 44 RETURN count(*)     12.58                 4.40
  MATCH (n:Third)  WHERE n.age > 44 RETURN count(*)      4.72                 1.25
```

**A redundant label costs NOTHING in GQL: 4.40 against 4.41.** Item 535's 2.8x was contamination
— the labelled query ran third in a shared process and inherited a slow mode. The `:Third` row is
1.25 isolated, exactly a third of the rows at the same per-row cost, which is what the selective
case should look like and is not what 535 reported either.

The conjunct ladder, also one per process:

```text
  1 conjunct   4.39 ms   21.9 ns/row
  2 conjuncts  8.01      40.1          +18.2
  3 conjuncts  9.70      48.5          + 8.4
  4 conjuncts 11.39      57.0          + 8.5
```

So the marginal conjunct costs ~8.4 ns and the step from one to two carries ~10 ns extra — the
one-off cost of wrapping the predicate in an `and` node at all. **That is not the "route change at
the second conjunct" item 535 described**, whose +37-then-+4 shape was an artifact of the same
shared process. 1.83x for a second conjunct, uniform after it.

### What SURVIVES, and it is the Gremlin half

```text
  gremlin  V().has(age, gt(44)).count()                      3.37 ms
  gremlin  V().hasLabel('Person').has(age, gt(44)).count()   14.77       4.4x
  gremlin  V().hasLabel('Person').count()                     0.00       (bucket size)
```

Isolated, one case per process, on a fixture where every vertex carries `Person`. **Adding a step
that filters nothing costs 4.4x** — +57 ns a row for one extra per-element step, against the ~8.4
ns a marginal GQL conjunct costs. That is the real target, and it is Gremlin-only: the GQL engine
charges nothing for the same redundancy.

### The lesson, which is about me and not the engine

I measured a comparison with an ad-hoc in-process `bun -e` loop after this session had recorded
the same trap three times: `bun run bench`'s short rows (514), the spelling probe's groups (524),
`bench:usage`'s ops/sec rows (534). **A min-of-nine inside one process is not isolation**, and the
route-cost probe exists precisely because one case per process is the only form that works here.
Item 535's numbers were taken the one way this repo has written down four times as unreliable.

What saved it was not caution but the next step in the method: _diagnose before assuming_. The
instrumentation said the route was identical, and a measurement that cannot be explained by the
code is a measurement to re-take.

## 537 — a Gremlin filter CHAIN now tallies: 4.0x, and a step that filters nothing was the tell

Item 536 left one surviving finding from 535: Gremlin charges several times more for a
`hasLabel` that excludes nothing. Diagnosing it found the actual rule, which is not about labels
at all.

### The diagnosis: a per-STEP pipeline cost, and a shortcut that takes only one step

Isolated, one case per process, 200,000 vertices all carrying `Person`:

```text
  V().has(age, gt(44)).count()                      2.37 ms   11.9 ns a vertex
  V().has().has().count()                           6.25      31.2
  V().has().has().has().count()                     8.01      40.1
  V().hasLabel('Person').has(age, gt(44)).count()  19.27      96.4
  V().hasLabel().hasLabel().has().count()          25.83     129.1
```

`countShortcut`'s `vertexStepCount` is documented as _"the ONE intermediate step whose count is a
bucket size"_ — it answers `V()` plus one step. Two steps reach the `mid.length === 2` arm, which
holds the HOP counts and declines a pair of filters, so the whole query ran the traverser
pipeline. Item 234 had already measured what that costs: _"3.3x of that row is the pipeline, not
the predicate — a traverser allocated per vertex to be filtered and discarded"_, 38.2 ns a vertex
against a hand-written tally's 11.5.

So the rule is **~40-50 ns a vertex PER STEP**, and a redundant `hasLabel` is expensive only
because it is a second step. The GQL engine charges nothing for the same redundancy (item 536:
4.40 ms against 4.41), which is what made this the surface that was behind rather than a shared
floor.

### The change

`filterChainCount` takes ANY chain of vertex filters — `hasLabel` and `has`, in any order, any
length — and tallies it. A `hasLabel` naming exactly ONE label becomes the SOURCE (its bucket), so
the tally is O(bucket) rather than O(V); a multi-label test stays a predicate, because a vertex may
sit in several of those buckets and `labelledCount` declines it for the same reason.

Every admitted step is a TOTAL predicate — `matches` returns false for a missing or incomparable
value rather than throwing, and a label test cannot fault — so evaluating all of them over every
vertex of the source raises exactly what the pipeline raises, and the conjunction's order is
unobservable. That is `propertyCount`'s own argument, and it is why this can tally rather than
having to mirror the pipeline's short-circuit. It inherits `propertyCount`'s index rule too:
decline when any `has` could seed, because `countShortcut` runs before `seedFromIndex` and a tally
that scanned anyway would lose the index (item 149).

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding between each:

```text
  V().hasLabel('Person').has(age, gt(44)).count()   before 19.33 / 19.38 / 12.97   after 3.27 / 3.38 / 3.33
  V().has().has().count()                           before  6.83 /  7.20 /  6.49   after 3.43 / 3.62 / 3.52
  V().has().count()  (CONTROL, the one-step arm)    before  2.22 /  2.36 /  2.31   after 2.40 / 2.35 / 2.25
```

Disjoint on both targets — **4.0x** and **1.9x** — with the single-step arm flat, which is the
control the change cannot reach.

### The bench had no row for it, and now does

`bench:gremlin`'s nine rows contain no filter chain, which is why a 4-6x gap sat there unseen.
Two rows added — `V().hasLabel().has().count()` and `V().has().has().count()` — and the first is
an EQUIVALENT-SPELLING guard as much as a perf row: on that fixture every vertex is a `Person`, so
it asks the same question as `V().has().count()` and must stay close to it. They read 6.1 and 6.2
there against 3.3 and 3.5 isolated, because that harness runs every row in one process; the
isolated numbers are the ones above.

### Teeth

Seven mutants including the null control; four caught, two explained survivors, the control clean.
Caught: the index decline removed, a MULTI-label test allowed to seed a single bucket (which
answers 0 where 7 is right), the property tests disjoined, and the label test negated.

The two survivors are answer-preserving and recorded at the guard: re-testing the label that
already seeded the bucket is redundant work for the same count, and admitting a ONE-step chain
would duplicate `vertexStepCount` rather than contradict it. `mid.length < 2` stays so the
single-step arm keeps its own cheaper answer.

The existing suite had a test asserting this shape DECLINES (`declines a shape that is not a bare
V().has().count()`), which is exactly the kind of test a widening must replace rather than delete:
it now asserts the claim AND the answer, against the pipeline's own, with a non-zero sibling —
because `0` is the correct answer for the first case and a tally that always answered 0 would pass
it.

## 538 — a single-label `hasLabel` now SEEDS its bucket: 2.4-2.5x, on every terminal

Item 537 fixed the `count()` terminal with a tally. Grepping the pattern elsewhere found the same
per-step tax on every OTHER terminal, where a tally cannot help because rows have to be emitted.
Isolated, one case per process, 200,000 vertices all carrying `Person`:

```text
  V().has(age, gt(44)).values('age')                      17.58 ms
  V().hasLabel('Person').has(age, gt(44)).values('age')   29.69      +12.1
  V().has().groupCount(by: age)                            6.45
  V().hasLabel().has().groupCount(by: age)                13.94      + 7.5
  V().has().dedupe().count()                              14.15
  V().hasLabel().has().dedupe().count()                   28.01      +13.9
```

### The gap

`hasLabel` has always been a `COMMUTING_FILTER` in `index-seed.ts` — reorderable, re-appliable,
droppable when something else consumes it — but **nothing made it a SOURCE**. `seedRest` picks the
most selective candidate among the leading filters and only `seedForStep` produced one, which
reads the PROPERTY index. So `V().hasLabel(L)` swept `verticesById` and filtered per element, at
~40-70 ns a vertex for the step alone (item 537's ladder).

The GQL engine has had the label bucket as a source since the beginning — `candidateVertexSource`
is three lines — which is why item 536 measured GQL charging nothing for a redundant label.

### The change

`labelSeed` makes a single-label `hasLabel(L)` a seed candidate: `count` is the bucket's size,
`build` returns the bucket, and `removable` is true because the bucket IS exactly the elements
carrying the label. It then competes with the property seeds on selectivity, so a `name` seek with
one match still beats a 200,000-element label bucket — which is what keeps this from taking an
index away (item 149's failure).

Multi-label declines: `hasLabel(a, b)` keeps an element carrying EITHER and an element may carry
both, so the union is neither a bucket nor a sum — the same reason `labelledCount` declines it. A
label nothing carries seeds the EMPTY set rather than declining, because declining would leave a
scan that rejects every element.

**On ORDER.** Seeding emits the bucket's order rather than the id map's. That is not a contract:
TinkerPop leaves `g.V()`'s order unspecified, this repo treats an unordered result's order as
WON'T-FIX, and the cross-engine Gremlin fuzzer compares such results as MULTISETS (`deepSort`,
skipped only when the plan has an explicit `order()`). The property seeds beside this one have
always reordered the source the same way. Checked before building, not after.

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding between each:

```text
  V().hasLabel().has().values('age')            before 30.25 / 30.04 / 30.80   after 12.74 / 12.96 / 12.91
  V().hasLabel().has().dedupe().count()         before 27.00 / 28.29 / 27.75   after 11.21 / 10.62 / 12.24
  V().has().values('age')  (CONTROL, no label)  before 17.63 /  9.97 / 11.35   after 10.63 / 17.62 / 17.54
```

2.4x and 2.5x, disjoint. The control — a traversal with no label, which the seed cannot apply to —
is **overlapping and non-monotonic in both directions** (9.97-17.63 either side), the bimodality
item 533 recorded. Flat, and the right conclusion is that it says nothing either way rather than
that it improved.

Both targets now BEAT their unlabelled twins (12.9 against 17.6, 11.2 against 14.2), because the
seed replaces the id-map sweep with a bucket iteration as well as removing the step.

### Teeth

Six behavioural mutants and a null control; **all six caught, the control clean** — but three of
them only after the tests were strengthened. The first run caught the multi-label seed (which
answers wrongly) and a zeroed `count` (which steals the choice from a better property seek), and
MISSED the other three because they are answer-PRESERVING: keeping the consumed step is redundant
work, declining a missing label leaves a scan that rejects everything, and never seeding at all is
just the old behaviour.

So the new tests assert the DECISION — the step is dropped, the empty bucket is still a seed, a
multi-label does not seed, a selective property seek still wins, an edge source has no bucket.
That is the same reason the count-shortcut tests are written that way, and it is what turns a
perf-only change into one a mutant cannot pass.

### Benches

`bench:gremlin` had no row for either shape. Three now: the two from item 537 plus
`V().hasLabel().has().values(age)`, the row-returning twin, which is the only one of the three
this item's fix reaches. `V().hasLabel().has().count()` also improved in-sweep (6.1 → 3.9 on one
run), since the seed removes the step before the chain tally is consulted.

## 539 — the START-filtered hop count: 6.2x, and the worst spelling cliff this surface had

Item 538's seed made a leading `hasLabel` free for a filter CHAIN. Grepping once more found the
shape where it was not nearly enough. 100,000 vertices / 500,000 edges, one case per process:

```text
  V().out('KNOWS').count()                         0.00 ms   the edge bucket's size, O(1)
  V().hasLabel('Person').out('KNOWS').count()     95.34      500,000 traversers
  V().has(age, gt(44)).out('KNOWS').count()       49.97
```

Every vertex carries `Person`, so the first two ask the SAME question — and one is an O(1) read
while the other is a 95 ms walk. `vertexStepCount` answers `V().out(T).count()` from the edge
bucket and `filteredHopCount` answers a filter AFTER the hop; a filter BEFORE one had no arm at
all. The GQL surface has had the start-filtered hop count since item 206.

### The change

`startFilteredHopCount` answers it as Σ the hop-degree of the starts that survive the filters —
the same argument `adjacentCount` makes (`out(T)` emits one traverser per traversed EDGE),
restricted to a subset of the starts. A COUNT is order-free, so nothing observable moves.

Three conditions, each buying something specific:

- **`both` is refused**, because it walks out-edges then in-edges and a self-loop is incident
  twice — `vertexStepCount`'s own exclusion.
- **Multi-type `out(a, b)` needs `adjacentCount`'s guard**: summing the buckets would count an
  edge carrying both types twice while the walk yields it once.
- **RAISE PARITY shapes the source.** `matches` can throw (a cross-type comparison, mirroring
  TinkerPop's `ClassCastException`), and the pipeline evaluates each filter only on what the
  EARLIER filters passed. So the filters are applied in written order with a short circuit, and
  the label bucket may be the source only when its `hasLabel` is FIRST — where the bucket is
  exactly that step's survivors. A `has` ahead of a `hasLabel` is therefore evaluated over every
  vertex, which is what the pipeline does.

### Reading the box, not hashing the id

The first version read `graph.edgesFromByLabel.get(v.id)` per surviving start and measured 22.13 /
16.25 / 12.51 ms on the three shapes. The vertex's OWN adjacency box gives 16.25 / 1.99 / 10.68 —
the GQL twin has read the box since items 162 and 321, and a string-keyed `Map.get` on a
100,000-entry map is ~190 ns (item 194). **The number in that comment was wrong when first
written** — I put "5.9 ms" in it before measuring and corrected it to the three measured pairs;
a fabricated figure in a comment is the thing this session has spent two ticks undoing.

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding between each:

```text
  V().hasLabel('Person').out('KNOWS').count()   before 95.34 / 97.43 / 97.80 ms   after 15.81 / 14.61 / 15.80
  V().has(age, gt(44)).out('KNOWS').count()     before 49.97 / 48.61 / 49.48      after 10.03 / 10.02 /  9.76
  V().out('KNOWS').count()  (CONTROL, O(1))     before  0.00                      after  0.00
```

**6.2x** and **5.0x**, disjoint. The control is the O(1) arm this cannot reach, and it stays 0.00.

### Teeth

Six behavioural mutants and a null control; **five caught, one explained survivor**. Caught:
`both` admitted, the hop direction ignored, the filters disjoined, the index decline removed, and
a MULTI-label allowed to seed a single bucket — that last one drops every vertex carrying only the
second label, and the test that catches it asks both orders so it cannot pass by luck of which
label comes first.

Two of the five were caught only after the tests were extended, which is the same pattern as item
538: a decision-only guard (the index decline) and a wrong-answer case the fixture did not reach
(multi-label). The survivor is answer-preserving — not slicing the seeded `hasLabel` out of `rest`
re-tests a label the bucket already guarantees — and is recorded at the guard.

The two mutants whose anchors a later narrowing refactor touched were **re-run against the final
text**, because a mutation result recorded against code that no longer exists is not a result.

### Benches

Two rows added: `V().hasLabel().out().count()` and `V().has().out().count()`. The first is the
equivalent-spelling guard against `V().out().count()` directly above it — the pair that was 0.00
against 95.34.

## 540 — a VACUOUS `hasLabel` is dropped from the plan: up to 48x, and it reaches every shortcut

Items 537-539 added three arms for a leading filter: a chain tally, a label seed, a start-filtered
hop count. Grepping once more found the shape none of them reached, and the reason they each had
to be written separately.

```text
  V().out('KNOWS').values('age')                         65.24 ms
  V().hasLabel('Person').out('KNOWS').values('age')     134.40      2.1x
  V().out('KNOWS').dedupe().count()                       3.39
  V().hasLabel('Person').out('KNOWS').dedupe().count()  102.63     30.3x
```

### The real rule, which the three previous items were each a special case of

**Every shortcut in `run` matches a plan PREFIX that starts at the source.** `countShortcut` wants
`V()` plus one or two steps; `hopValuesShortcut` wants exactly `V().out(T).values(k)`;
`groupCountShortcut` wants `V().groupCount()`. A leading `hasLabel` is one step too many for all
of them, so it does not merely cost its own per-element test — **it drops the whole query onto the
traverser pipeline**. That is why a redundant label was worth 4x on a count, 2x on `values`, and
30x on `dedupe().count()`: the numbers are not about labels, they are about which shortcut each
shape lost.

Item 538's index seed does remove the step, and verifying that directly is what located this:
`seedFromIndex` returns `steps=["out","values"]` for the labelled plan, so the step IS gone — but
only AFTER the shortcuts have declined, because the seed runs below them.

So the fix is to remove it from the plan FIRST rather than to add a label-aware arm per shortcut.
`dropVacuousLabels` drops a single-label `hasLabel(L)` whose bucket holds every live element — the
plan-level form of the tautology short-circuit native's `IsLabeled` evaluator has (item E78).

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding between each:

```text
  V().hasLabel().out().values('age')          before 207.31 / 203.63 / 218.04 ms   after 120.36 / 127.56 / 122.33
  V().hasLabel().out().dedupe().count()       before 156.80 / 167.91 / 156.82      after   3.28 /   3.29 /   3.27
  V().out().values('age')  (CONTROL)          before 115.60 / 113.79 / 123.60      after 113.49 / 119.36 / 125.67
```

1.7x and **48x**, disjoint, with the no-label control overlapping. (This A/B used an all-`KNOWS`
fixture, so its absolute numbers differ from the mixed-type pricing above; the control is on the
same fixture.)

`bench:gremlin` shows it reaching the earlier rows too: `V().hasLabel().has().count()` 5.8 → 2.4,
`V().has().has().count()` 6.2 → 3.5, `V().hasLabel().has().values(age)` 17.4 → 12.1, and
**`V().hasLabel().out().count()` 37.4 → 0.0** — identical to the unlabelled row directly above it,
which is what that equivalent-spelling pair was added for.

### Teeth, and what the survivors say

Six behavioural mutants and a null control. **One caught, five survived** — and the analysis is
the deliverable rather than a reason to manufacture tests:

- `bucket.size === total` — CAUGHT, 15 failures. The only load-bearing condition: without it every
  label is dropped and the filters stop filtering.
- the single-label restriction — survives, and is sound to relax: if `labels[0]`'s bucket is the
  whole set then so is the UNION. Kept because "a vacuous union" is a different test.
- the LEADING-run restriction — survives. A vacuous VERTEX label is in fact droppable after a hop
  too, since the endpoints are a subset of the vertices. Kept because that reasoning depends on
  the stream still holding vertices, which this function does not check.
- the `tracksPath` gate — survives. A filter appends nothing to a path in either engine.
- the edge-bucket branch — survives, because the vertex map simply misses on an edge-type name.
  Correct by accident rather than by the lookup, so the branch stays.
- skipping the empty graph — survives; every query over one answers empty anyway.

**I did not add tests to catch the five.** They change no answer, and a test written to fail a
harmless mutant would assert an implementation choice as if it were a contract. Recorded at the
guard instead, which is what makes the next reader able to relax any of them deliberately.

The one load-bearing mutant was **re-run against the final text** after a `prefer-optional-chain`
fix moved its anchor — item 539's rule.

## 542 — the EDGE source seeds its type bucket: 3.7x on a count, and NOTHING on `values`

Item 538 shipped the vertex label seed and left the edge half out — its own test asserted "an EDGE
source has no label bucket to seed from" as a limitation. Closing it, with the honest split in the
result.

### Priced

500,000 edges, half of them `KNOWS`, one case per process:

```text
  E().has(w, gt(3)).count()                      35.66 ms
  E().hasLabel('KNOWS').has(w, gt(3)).count()    62.65
  E().values('w')                                47.43   (500,000 rows)
  E().hasLabel('KNOWS').values('w')              64.58   (250,000 rows — HALF the rows, MORE time)
```

A type's bucket is exactly the edges carrying it, so a single-label `hasLabel(T)` is removable for
the same reason as the vertex side. The multi-type hazard belongs to SUMMING buckets
(`adjacentCount`'s guard), not to reading ONE: a two-type edge sits in both buckets and
`hasLabel(T)` keeps it either way, so one bucket is still exact.

### Measured, and one of the two shapes did not move

Three alternated rounds, rebuilding between each:

```text
  E().hasLabel('KNOWS').has(w, gt(3)).count()   before 64.61 / 67.53 / 62.50 ms   after 17.21 / 16.88 / 17.50
  E().hasLabel('KNOWS').values('w')             before 52.09 / 52.82 / 61.73      after 54.83 / 51.73 / 52.48
  E().has(w, gt(3)).count()  (CONTROL)          before 34.22 / 34.96 / 42.28      after 34.32 / 35.32 / 34.59
```

**3.7x on the count. Nothing on `values` — overlapping, both ways.** The single reading that
suggested otherwise (64.58 → 51.76) was noise, and three alternated rounds are what said so. I do
not have an explanation for why halving the source does not help that shape and am not going to
invent one; it is recorded as measured, and the control confirms the harness was working.

### The test it replaced was testing nothing

The limitation test asked for `hasLabel('knows')` — lowercase — and this fixture's edge types are
`KNOWS` and `CREATED`. So it asserted "no seed" against a label **no edge carries**, which could
not have seeded anything whatever the code did. Replacing it (item 537's rule: a widening replaces
such a test rather than deleting it) is what surfaced that, because the replacement failed on an
empty stream until the case was fixed.

Labels are case-sensitive here, as TinkerPop's are. The new test pins both real types (2 `KNOWS`,
4 `CREATED`), the empty seed for a type nothing carries, and the multi-type decline.

### Teeth

Three mutants, two caught, the null control clean: the VERTEX bucket used for an edge source
(which seeds EMPTY, because a vertex-label map misses on an edge-type name — 5 failures) and the
seed reverted (caught by the new test's claim assertion).

## 543 — why the seeded `values` shape did not move: one hypothesis refuted, part of it explained

Item 542 recorded its own unexplained result — the edge label seed gave 3.7x on a count and
nothing on `values` — and said so rather than narrating a reason. This is the follow-up.

### The seed IS firing

`seedFromIndex(traversal(E(), hasLabel('KNOWS'), values('w')))` returns `steps=["values"]`: the
step is consumed and the source is the 250,000-element bucket instead of 500,000 edges. So the
question is not whether the seed applies.

### The penalty scales with how SPARSE the bucket is

```text
  E().values('w')                                        101 ns a row   500,000 rows
  E().hasLabel('KNOWS').values('w')  every edge KNOWS      95            500,000  (item 540 drops it)
  E().hasLabel('KNOWS').values('w')  99% of edges         123            495,000  SEEDED
  E().hasLabel('KNOWS').values('w')  50% of edges         206            250,000  SEEDED
```

The all-KNOWS row is the control that matters: with the label vacuous, item 540 removes it and the
per-row cost is the normal source's. Seeded, the per-row cost is 1.27x at a 99% bucket and **2.0x
at a 50% one** — so halving the element count doubles the cost of each, and the TOTAL is a wash
(51.57 ms for 250,000 rows against 51.88 for 500,000). That is the whole of item 542's null result.

### The obvious fix is REFUTED

`seedRest` built its traverser stream as an inline IIFE generator over a closure, where
`sourceFromIds` is the same loop as a module-scope generator function — and this repo has a
recorded rule about exactly that (item 268, `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing`: a walk inline in a
closure gives unrelated queries a new slow mode, so hoist it). Hoisting it to `seededStream`
changed **nothing**: 206 → 217 ns a row.

So the hoist was reverted rather than shipped. It is a refactor whose only justification would
have been the number it did not produce, and the comment I had written for it quoted that number
as if it had. **Shipping that comment would have been the same mistake item 539 corrected and item
536 was about.**

### What IS explained, and what is not

Raw iteration of the same elements, nine reps:

```text
  all edges, ARRAY, 500,000      17 ns an element
  KNOWS Set, 250,000             31            1.8x the array
  KNOWS as an ARRAY, 250,000     20            so the subset's ORDER costs ~3 ns
```

So `Set` iteration costs ~11 ns an element more than an array of the same elements in the same
order, and the subset's scattered order costs ~3 more. Together ~14 ns of the ~105 ns-a-row gap.
**A seventh of it, and the remaining ~90 ns is unlocated.** Written down as a partial result
because a partial measurement recorded as one is useful and a partial measurement reported as a
cause is not.

### What this means for the seeds

A bucket seed trades ELEMENT COUNT for LOCALITY, and whether that trade wins depends on what the
steps after the source cost per element. Item 542's count form wins 3.7x because a `has` test plus
a tally per element dwarfs the access penalty; the `values` form breaks even because projecting one
property does not. That is a rule worth having before the next seed is added: **a seed is not
free, and its benefit is not the ratio of the counts.**

No code change. The deliverable is a refuted hypothesis, a measured explanation of one seventh of
the gap, and the rule above.

## 544 — DISTINCT and ORDER BY over a ONE-ROW count: 29.78 and 34.53 ms to 0.00

Item 540's structural rule — every shortcut matches a plan prefix, so one extra thing in front of
it drops the whole query — has a GQL twin: the ladder's detectors match clause lists and
projections, so one extra PROJECTION CLAUSE does the same. Pricing the vacuous ones, 200,000
vertices, one case per process:

```text
  MATCH (n:Person) RETURN count(*) AS c                     0.00 ms
  …RETURN count(*) AS c LIMIT 1                             0.00      (already handled, item 125)
  …RETURN count(*) AS c SKIP 0                              0.00
  …LET z = 1 RETURN count(*) AS c                           0.00      (inlined, items 512/516)
  …WHERE true RETURN count(*) AS c                          1.79
  …RETURN DISTINCT count(*) AS c                           29.78
  …RETURN count(*) AS c ORDER BY c                         34.53
  …FILTER true RETURN count(*) AS c                        32.91
```

### The argument was already in the file

`detectCountShortcut` explains why SKIP/LIMIT are NOT refused: _"an un-grouped `count(*)` with one
item is exactly ONE row, so a page over it is arithmetic on a one-element list — and refusing it
made `LIMIT 1`, which cannot change the answer, cost 380x"_. **DISTINCT and ORDER BY are
identities on one row for exactly the same reason**, and both were being refused two lines above
that comment. One row cannot be deduplicated away from itself and cannot be reordered.

Neither spelling is contrived, which is what makes this worth doing rather than a curiosity:
ordering by the count you just asked for, or writing `DISTINCT` out of habit, is what a reader
does. `FILTER true` is contrived and is left where it is.

### The one real condition

ORDER BY is admitted only for a sort key that is a plain reference to the OUTPUT column, because
any other expression could FAULT while being evaluated for the sort and a shortcut that skipped
the sort would skip the fault with it. `ORDER BY 1 / 0` raises on the general path and must keep
raising — it does, and the test pins it against the same query without the ORDER BY as the control,
so the throw is attributable to the key rather than to the count.

```text
  RETURN DISTINCT count(*) AS c              29.78 → 0.00
  RETURN count(*) AS c ORDER BY c            34.53 → 0.00
  RETURN count(*) AS c ORDER BY c DESC             → 0.00
  RETURN DISTINCT count(*) AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 1 → 0.00
```

Every admitted case is also asked with `FILTER true` inserted, which keeps every row and declines
the shortcut, so the general path answers the same question — and `ORDER BY c LIMIT 0` still
returns nothing, which is `pageOneRow`'s existing behaviour.

### Checked against native, and an unrelated divergence found

All four admitted shapes agree with the native engine, including `ORDER BY c LIMIT 0` → `[]` and
`ORDER BY 1 / 0` → both raise.

One row DIVERGES and it is **not** this change: `MATCH (n:P) RETURN count(*) AS c ORDER BY c + 0`
answers `[{"c":2}]` in TS and RAISES in native. Verified against the pristine build before saying
so — the shortcut declines that key either way, so both answers come from the paths they always
came from. Recorded as open.

### Teeth

Three mutants and a null control; two caught, the control clean. Caught: any ORDER BY key admitted
(the faulting-key test), and the gate inverted. The surviving mutant drops the NAME comparison, and
it is equivalent by construction: an aggregating projection's ORDER BY resolves against the OUTPUT
columns and there is exactly one here, so any valid `var` key already IS that column. Recorded at
the guard.

## 545 — the same one-row identity on FOUR aggregate rungs: up to 4.8x, and three identical guards

Item 544 did the count rung. The four aggregate rungs refuse DISTINCT and ORDER BY for the same
wrong reason, and an un-grouped aggregate projection delivers exactly one row whatever the
aggregate is. Priced at 200,000 vertices / 400,000 edges, one case per process:

```text
  MATCH (n:Person) RETURN max(n.age) AS m                   12.28 ms
  …RETURN DISTINCT max(n.age) AS m                          38.02      3.1x
  …RETURN max(n.age) AS m ORDER BY m                        37.06      3.0x
  MATCH (:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN max(b.age) AS m      90.71
  …RETURN DISTINCT max(b.age) AS m                         385.64      4.3x
  …RETURN max(b.age) AS m ORDER BY m                       428.73      4.7x
```

After, all six at the baseline: 12.14 / 12.32 / 12.58 and 90.75 / 91.53 / 89.98. **Up to 4.8x**, on
`detectNodeAggregate`, `detectMultiNodeAggregate`, `detectHopAggregate` and
`detectMultiHopAggregate`, all through one shared `sortsOnOutputOnly`.

### THREE IDENTICAL GUARDS, two of which must NOT be patched

The multi-item node guard's text appears **three times** in `shortcuts.ts` — and the other two are
`detectGroupedNodeAggregate` and `detectGroupedHopAggregate`, which produce MANY rows, where
neither clause is an identity. Patching by text would have collapsed a grouped result.

The uniqueness assert caught it (`site2` counted 3, not 1) and the fix was to anchor each
replacement on the COMMENT above its guard. Items 474, 483, 494, 518, 528 and now 545 — **two
copies of a body is the most reliable way to fool a bulk edit in this repo, and this is the first
time the duplicate was a guard that had to keep its old behaviour rather than one that wanted the
same change.** The test file now pins the grouped shapes at three rows, so a future bulk edit that
reaches them fails.

### Checked against native, ten shapes

All ten agree, including both multi-item forms, `ORDER BY 1 / 0` (both raise) and the GROUPED
`RETURN n.n AS k, count(*) AS c ORDER BY k` → three rows in the right order, which is what says the
grouped rungs still decline.

### Teeth

Three mutants and a null control; one caught, the control clean. Caught: any sort key admitted,
which the faulting-key test catches on both the single- and multi-item rungs.

Two survivors, both answer-preserving and recorded at the guard: dropping the NAME check is
equivalent by construction (an aggregating projection's ORDER BY resolves against the output
columns, so any valid `var` key already names one), and emptying the name set only makes the rungs
DECLINE — slower, not wrong. Only `kind === 'var'` is load-bearing, which is the same conclusion

## 548 — a trailing `FILTER` folds into the MATCH before it: 3.5-8.6x, and a divergence closed

`FILTER <pred>` is ISO's clause-level predicate statement (§14.6), and after a non-optional MATCH
it asks exactly what a clause `WHERE` on that MATCH asks. Only the `WHERE` spelling reached the
ladder: every detector matches a clause LIST, and a `FILTER` is one clause too many. This is item
540's structural rule — a shortcut matches a PREFIX, so one extra thing in front drops the whole
query onto the general pipeline — restated on the GQL clause list rather than the Gremlin step
list.

### The price

200,000 vertices / 200,000 edges, one case per process, min of three, before and after on the same
fixture:

| query                                                                  | before   | after     | WHERE control (before/after) |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | --------- | ---------------------------- |
| `MATCH (n:Person) FILTER n.age > 44 RETURN count(*) AS c`              | 41.72 ms | **11.33** | 10.73 / 11.12                |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b) FILTER b.age > 44 RETURN count(*) AS c` | 278.94   | **32.29** | 33.63 / 32.63                |
| `MATCH (n:Person) FILTER n.age > 44 RETURN max(n.age) AS m`            | 43.26    | **12.23** | 12.20 / 12.42                |

3.7x, 8.6x and 3.5x, each landing on its own `WHERE` twin. The control the change cannot reach —
`MATCH (n:Person) RETURN count(*) AS c`, no FILTER anywhere — is 0.00 both ways.

### Native never had it

Checked FIRST, because the alternative is porting a fix to an engine that does not need it (item
546's lesson):

```text
MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.age > 44 RETURN count(*)              0.20 ms
MATCH (n:Person) FILTER n.age > 44 RETURN count(*)             0.18
MATCH (:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b) WHERE b.age > 44 RETURN count(*) 0.88
MATCH (:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b) FILTER b.age > 44 RETURN count(*) 0.91
MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.age > 44 RETURN max(n.age)            0.51
MATCH (n:Person) FILTER n.age > 44 RETURN max(n.age)           0.51
```

And `spelling_probe` now says why in a form a timing cannot: _identical optimized plan → identical
exec_. The two new Rust groups are a regression guard on that, not a target.

### The one refusal that is about semantics

`OPTIONAL MATCH … FILTER p` is **not** `OPTIONAL MATCH … WHERE p`. A clause `WHERE` on an optional
is evaluated INSIDE it, so a start with no match still yields its null-filled row; a `FILTER` after
it drops that row. On the two-`:P` fixture the pair reads 1 and 2, and the test pins both halves so
a future widening of the fold fails rather than silently collapses an optional. (Native rejects
`WHERE` inside an `OPTIONAL MATCH` outright — "not supported yet" — so the two spellings are not
even both available there; the conformance test asserts that refusal instead of comparing.)

The predicate's free variables are deliberately **unrestricted**, for item 128's reason: a node
predicate is evaluated against the INCOMING binding, which already holds every earlier clause's
variables, so an outer reference resolves in the pattern exactly as it did in the filter. Two
`FILTER`s in a row fold onto the same MATCH, in written order.

### A divergence CLOSED, not caused

The faulting-predicate test failed on the first run, and the diagnosis is worth more than the fix:

```text
                                   before 548      native
WHERE 1 / 0 > 0 AND n.n > 9        [{"c":0}]       [{"c":0}]
WHERE n.n > 9 AND 1 / 0 > 0        [{"c":0}]       [{"c":0}]
WHERE 1 / 0 > 0 FILTER n.n > 9     THREW           [{"c":0}]
WHERE 1 / 0 > 0                    THREW           THREW
```

A partitioned clause `WHERE` short-circuits on the FALSE conjunct and never reaches the faulting
one — pre-existing, in BOTH engines, in BOTH written orders, and consistent with item 259 (a
FILTER keeps only clean TRUE, so order is free in the predicate position). Folding makes the
`FILTER` spelling the `AND` spelling, which is the entire claim of the change, and the TS answer
becomes native's. Verified against the pristine build before writing it down. A faulting predicate
with nothing to short-circuit against still raises on both spellings, which is what says the fault
was not simply discarded.

### Teeth

Five mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`,
each asserted to match exactly once, pristine restored before each:

| mutant                           | result               |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| M1 fold across an `OPTIONAL`     | **caught** (1 fail)  |
| M2 conjoin order swapped         | survived — explained |
| M3 fold onto any previous clause | **caught** (1 fail)  |
| M4 `hasAggregate` guard dropped  | survived — explained |
| M5 null control                  | clean                |

M2 is the predicate position, where order is unobservable (item 259) — the conjuncts are
partitioned and only clean TRUE survives, so no test can distinguish the two orders and inventing
one would be inventing a contract. M4 is defensive: with the guard dropped,
`FILTER count(*) > 1` and `FILTER sum(n.n) > 1` answer **identically** to the guarded build, so
nothing distinguishes it either; it is kept by analogy with `inlineTrailingLet`'s same guard, and
recorded as such rather than claimed as load-bearing.

## 549 — a vacuous `ORDER BY` / `OFFSET 0` STATEMENT in front of the projection: 126.60 → 0.00 (TS half)

Item 548 folded a trailing `FILTER`. The same question asked of the rest of the clause enum found a
second, bigger instance immediately: ISO's `<order by and page statement>` is a
`primitiveQueryStatement` (§14.10), so `ORDER BY` / `OFFSET` / `LIMIT` can stand as a pipeline step
of its own BEFORE the projection — and there it is one extra clause in front of every detector.

### Pricing the enum

The read-side clause variants that can sit between a MATCH and a RETURN are `with`, `filter`,
`page`, `let`, `for`, `callNamed` and `callInline`. `let` was items 512/516, `callInline` is
`inlineCorrelatedCall`, `filter` was item 548 — so `page` was the biggest MISSING one, priced at
200,000 vertices / 200,000 edges, one case per process:

```text
                                                        TS         native
MATCH (n:Person) RETURN count(*)                        0.00 ms    0.01 ms
MATCH (n:Person) OFFSET 0 RETURN count(*)              83.00       0.57
MATCH (n:Person) ORDER BY n.age RETURN count(*)       126.60      10.07
MATCH (n:Person) ORDER BY n.age OFFSET 0 RETURN …     142.82       —
MATCH (n:Person) ORDER BY n.age RETURN max(n.age)     194.35      10.30
MATCH (n:Person) ORDER BY n.age RETURN collect(…)     241.16       —
```

`OFFSET 0` with no `LIMIT` keeps every row whatever follows. An `ORDER BY` with no page cannot move
a projection that is ONE order-free row. Both are identities, and both cost two orders of magnitude.
**Native has the cliff too** (0.01 → 10.07), which is the difference from item 546: there is a real
Rust twin to build, tracked as the next item rather than claimed here.

After, same fixture: `OFFSET 0` **0.00**, `ORDER BY … count(*)` **0.00**, `ORDER BY … max(n.age)`
**15.61**, `collect` unchanged at 218 (refused, as it must be), `ORDER BY … LIMIT 10` unchanged at
78 and still answering 10. The control the change cannot reach — the same count with no page
clause — is 0.00 both ways.

### The four refusals

Each is a test case and each is a caught mutant:

- **a `LIMIT`, or an `OFFSET` that is not literally 0**, changes which rows reach the projection.
  `OFFSET 1 RETURN count(*)` reads 1 against 2; `ORDER BY n.n LIMIT 1 RETURN max(n.n)` reads 1 and
  `DESC LIMIT 1` reads 3, so the sort is load-bearing under a limit.
- **an order-DEPENDENT aggregate.** `ORDER BY n.n RETURN collect(n.n)` is `[1,2,3]` and `DESC` is
  `[3,2,1]`. `sum`/`avg`/`stddev` are refused with it: order-free in arithmetic, not in floating
  point, and byte-identity with native pins the summation order.
- **a projection that is not one row.** Every item must CARRY an aggregate, because an item without
  one is an implicit GROUP BY key — many rows, whose order the statement sets. `RETURN *` and an
  explicit `GROUP BY` are refused for the same reason.
- **a faulting sort key.** `ORDER BY 1 / 0` RAISES in both engines; dropping the sort would swallow
  it. Only a bare variable or ONE property read may be dropped, and both are fault-free: `n.missing`
  is null, and `LET z = 1 … ORDER BY z.n` answers in both engines rather than raising — probed
  rather than assumed.

### Teeth

Six mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`,
each asserted to match exactly once, pristine restored before each:

| mutant                                    | result               |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| M1 a `LIMIT` allowed                      | **caught**           |
| M2 any `OFFSET` allowed                   | **caught**           |
| M3 the one-row check dropped              | **caught** (2 fails) |
| M4 the fault-free-key check dropped       | **caught**           |
| M5 `collect`/`sum` admitted as order-free | **caught**           |
| M6 null control                           | clean                |

Five of five caught and no survivors — the first batch this session with none to explain, which is
what four independent refusals with four independent tests buys.

## 550 — the native twin of 549: a vacuous sort under a scalar aggregate, 10.10 ms → 0.01

Item 549 shipped the TS half and said the Rust twin was real work rather than a check that finds
nothing. It was. Two arms in `opt::apply_local`, measured pristine-against-change on one fixture of
200,000 vertices / 200,000 edges, one case per process:

| query                                                          | before   | after    | ratio |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | ----- |
| `MATCH (n:Person) ORDER BY n.age RETURN count(*)`              | 10.10 ms | **0.01** | 1010x |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b) ORDER BY b.age RETURN count(*)` | 11.68    | **0.50** | 23x   |
| `MATCH (n:Person) ORDER BY n.age RETURN max(n.age)`            | 10.35    | **0.44** | 23x   |
| `MATCH (n:Person) OFFSET 0 RETURN count(*)`                    | 0.56     | **0.01** | 56x   |

Three controls the change must NOT reach, all flat: `ORDER BY n.age RETURN collect(n.age)` 16.97 →
17.03 (refused), `ORDER BY n.age LIMIT 10 RETURN count(*)` 2.11 → 2.08 and still answering 10
(refused), and the plain `RETURN count(*)` 0.01 both ways.

### The two arms

`Aggregate { input: OrderPage, keys: [], aggs }` → `Aggregate { input: <the page's input> }`, under
four conditions, and the keyless-page arm `OrderPage { keys: [], skip: None|Some(0), limit: None }`
→ its input, which needs no condition on its consumer because it is an identity for anything.

The conditions are item 549's, restated against the IR: the aggregate must be KEYLESS (with group
keys the group ORDER is first-seen, which the sort sets), every `Agg` must be order-free
(`agg_is_order_free`: `Count`/`Min`/`Max` and the two percentiles — `Collect`'s own doc comment says
it folds "in the group's row order, so a preceding sort carries through", and `Sum`/`Avg`/the
stddevs are refused because byte-identity pins the summation order), the page must keep every row
(`page_keeps_every_row`), and no sort key may raise.

### The existing test that failed, and what it was really guarding

`exec::tests::a_gremlin_order_by_key_filters_and_so_cannot_be_elided_under_a_count` failed on the
first build — and the diagnosis is the item. Its three NUMERIC assertions passed; only its
structural `plan.contains("OrderPage")` failed, on this plan:

```text
Aggregate { input: Filter { input: Scan { label: Some("P") },
                            pred: PropertyExists { slot: 0, key: "age" } },
            keys: [], aggs: [Count] }
```

The `order().by('k')` row-drop — TinkerPop removes a traverser whose key is absent — lives in a
SEPARATE `Filter(PropertyExists)` that the Gremlin lowering emits before the page (`by_absent_gates`
→ `key_present_gate`). It survives any rewrite of the page, so the count stayed 2 and the semantics
the test exists for were never at risk.

The real reason to decline a Gremlin page is different and was not what the test named: `exec::order`
RAISES for a sort key that resolves to a graph element when `fault_on_element` is set — the runtime
backstop for a mixed/branch frontier the parser could not classify (`both(...).inject(1).order()`).
Eliding the page would swallow that fault. So the guard is `!fault_on_element`, which takes GQL
pages only (GQL `ORDER BY <element>` sorts by external id and cannot fault), the old test passes
unchanged, and its structural assert stays as the regression guard it is. A new test records the
distinction so the next reader does not re-derive it.

### Teeth

Seven mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p
MemorySwapMax=0`, built uncapped first, each asserted to match exactly once, pristine restored
before each:

| mutant                                      | result                | caught by                              |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| M1 the order-free check dropped             | **caught**            | the new opt test                       |
| M2 `page_keeps_every_row` dropped           | **caught** (5 fails)  | the new test **and `rewrite_fuzz` ×3** |
| M3 the keyless check dropped                | **caught**            | the new opt test                       |
| M4 the `can_raise` check dropped            | **caught**            | the new opt test                       |
| M5 a Gremlin page allowed                   | **caught** (2 fails)  | the OLD Gremlin test, and the new one  |
| M6 the keyless-page drop made unconditional | **caught** (18 fails) | the cross-page cap cluster             |
| M7 null control                             | clean                 | —                                      |

M2 is the one worth recording: `opt::rewrite_fuzz::optimizing_preserves_rows_{without,with}_indexes`
and `_across_shapes` all caught it, which is the first DIRECT evidence this session that the

## 551 — the four order-sensitive hop aggregates ride the START-driven walk: 2.1-2.6x

Item 532 priced the hop-aggregate enum and found seven of eleven off the rung, five of them
CORRECTLY under item 419's rule: the walk may be FAR-DRIVEN, so it can visit rows in a different
order from the general path, and only an order-INDEPENDENT aggregate may ride it. It concluded that
widening the rung "would be WRONG, not slow". Item 533 then took the one sound half (the
percentiles, which sort their values).

**The rule is right and the conclusion was too broad.** It is a property of ONE of the walks, not
of the rung.

### The hazard, reproduced

`hopPercentile`'s own comment said admitting `collect` "changes no answer on a four-node fixture …
because the walk only goes FAR-DRIVEN under conditions a fixture that small does not meet". That
is true of a fixture with a start LABEL and false without one. Nine rows are enough:

```text
MATCH (a)-[:K]->(b) RETURN b.age AS k      ts [0,0,1,2,2,3,4,5]   native [5,2,3,4,0,0,2,1]
MATCH (a:P)-[:K]->(b) RETURN b.age AS k    ts [5,2,3,4,0,0,2,1]   native [5,2,3,4,0,0,2,1]
```

Row order without an `ORDER BY` is unspecified (item 198), so the first line is legal for a
PROJECTION — and fatal for a fold whose answer is that order. The second line is the finding: with
the start label non-vacuous the walk is start-driven and its order is the general path's, which is
native's. So the admission condition is the WALK, not the aggregate.

### The change

`detectHopProjection` takes a third parameter `forceStartDriven`, consulted at both of its
far-driven decision points (the plain far-end-only walk's `vacuousLabel` test and
`filteredHopWalk`'s `hopDrivesFar`). The aggregate rung passes it for the six order-sensitive
names, which `hopPercentile` now admits alongside the percentiles — they go down the same
non-foldable `values` path, which already applies the general path's `nonNull` rule.

An UNDIRECTED hop is refused outright: `hopAggregateWalks` serves it as two walks (all out-rows,
then all in-rows) where the general path interleaves them per start vertex, so the order differs by
construction and no flag can fix it.

### The numbers

ts, 200,000 vertices / 200,000 edges, one case per process, alternated rounds:

| aggregate           | pristine           | after               | ratio    |
| ------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- | -------- |
| `sum(b.age)`        | 307.28 / 290.36 ms | **124.24 / 132.63** | 2.3-2.5x |
| `avg(b.age)`        | 327.67             | **125.26**          | 2.6x     |
| `collect(b.age)`    | 291.70 / 308.78    | **123.93 / 128.89** | 2.3-2.5x |
| `stddev_pop(b.age)` | 268.67             | **125.25**          | 2.1x     |

Three controls the widening must not reach: `max(b.age)` 91.00/101.30 against 87.71/79.01,
`percentile_cont(b.age, 0.5)` 136.10/109.48 against 108.97/107.75 — the 136.10 was the outlier and
the two bands overlap, which is the expected answer since a percentile is order-INDEPENDENT and
still takes the far-driven walk — and `count(*)` 0.01 both ways.

### Teeth, and the guard that survived

Five mutants under the cap, each asserted to match exactly once, pristine restored before each:

| mutant                             | first run  | after the second fixture |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------ |
| M1 the flag not passed to the walk | **caught** | caught (2 fails)         |
| M2 the plain walk ignores it       | **caught** | caught                   |
| M3 the FILTERED walk ignores it    | survived   | **caught**               |
| M4 the undirected form allowed     | **caught** | caught                   |
| M5 null control                    | clean      | clean                    |

M3 is the item's second finding. `filteredHopWalk` has its own far-driven branch, chosen by
`hopDrivesFar` when the far side enumerates fewer vertices — and nothing in the first fixture
reaches it, so the guard looked redundant. It is not: with it removed, over 40 `:P` sources and 3
`:R` far vertices,

```text
MATCH (a:P)-[:K]->(b:R) RETURN collect(a.age)
  mutant  [0.6, 1.5, 2.4, 3.3, …]              the start values grouped by far vertex
  native  [0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.8999999999999999, …] start order
```

A second fixture (an aggregate over the START variable, which is what routes through that walk)
gives the guard teeth. _A mutant that survives because nothing looks is a missing test; this is the
second time this session that distinction paid._

### Cross-engine

52 assertions, every one comparing TS against native as a SEQUENCE rather than a multiset — the
last ulp and the list order are exactly what the byte-identity invariant is about. The fixture is
built so a far-driven walk would reorder it: crossed edges, non-integral ages so a reordered `sum`
shows in the last ulp, three `:Q` nodes to make `:P` selective, and a far vertex with NO `age` so
the `nonNull` rule shows (nine rows fold eight values).

Item 551 widened the single-aggregate hop rung. `detectMultiHopAggregate` had the same gap for the
same reason — its admission set is `foldFor`'s, so every item needed a streaming fold and any
projection carrying one of the six order-sensitive names fell to the general path. Priced at
200,000 vertices / 200,000 edges, one case per process, two rounds after:

| projection                           | before    | after               | ratio    |
| ------------------------------------ | --------- | ------------------- | -------- |
| `count(*) AS c, sum(b.age) AS m`     | 313.32 ms | **126.92 / 130.72** | 2.4-2.5x |
| `sum(b.age) AS s, avg(b.age) AS a`   | 360.59    | **137.34 / 138.14** | 2.6x     |
| `collect(b.age) AS l, count(*) AS c` | 320.79    | **117.98 / 131.26** | 2.4-2.7x |

### A control that read as a 1.5x regression and was not

`max(b.age), min(b.age)` — all-foldable, all-extrema, nothing this change can reach — read **149.49
ms** on its first measurement against a pristine 101.32. That is the shape of a real regression: a
hot two-accumulator row loop that just acquired a branch.

Three repeats gave **102.60 / 99.99 / 99.46**. A one-off, and it is recorded because the honest
version of this entry is the one that says so: a single reading of a control is not a control. The
other foldable control, `count(*), max(b.age)`, read 92.75 before and 89.67 / 89.71 / 92.40 / 92.57
after.

### The change

A third `HopAcc` variant, `values`, which collects the column's non-null values and finishes
through the same `aggregateOverValues` the general path runs — the array path the single-aggregate
twin's non-foldable branch already used. `orderSensitive` is the OR over the items, and it both
forces the start-driven walk and refuses an undirected hop, exactly as in 551.

The two PERCENTILES come along for free here: they were refused by the fold requirement, they read
no row order, and so they need no forcing. `count(*), percentile_cont(b.age, 0.5)` now takes the
rung at 139.20 ms.

`detectMultiHopAggregate` crossed the complexity gate at 40 against a limit of 35, so the per-item
admission is extracted to `hopAccFor`, which reads nothing from the loop but the column index. The
extraction was measured, not assumed: the three wins read 130.72 / 138.14 / 131.26 after it against
126.92 / 137.34 / 117.98 before, and the two controls 92.40 / 100.04.

## 553 — the grouped-scan rung collects the non-foldable aggregates: 8.1-11.5x

This one was written down as a target, with its closing condition, inside the function it is about.
`detectGroupedNodeAggregate`'s doc comment:

> The admission set is `foldFor`'s plus `count(*)`. `sum`/`avg` are NOT admitted: a grouped sum over
> floats depends on the order values reach their group, and a FILTERED scan may seed from an index
> (items 419, 466, 468). The unfiltered case would be safe by the item-466 argument, but a grouped
> path that takes `sum` only when unfiltered is a guard with no test — item 468 recorded how that
> goes — so it waits for a shape that can be demonstrated.

### The demonstration

A range index on `age`, ten `:P` nodes in two `tag` groups with ages interleaved:

```text
WHERE n.age >= 5 RETURN n.tag AS k, collect(n.age)       no index  [7,5,9] / [8,6]
                                                         indexed   [5,7,9] / [6,8]
WHERE n.age + 0 >= 5 RETURN n.tag AS k, collect(n.age)   indexed   [7,5,9] / [8,6]
RETURN n.tag AS k, collect(n.age)                        either    [0,4,8,2,6] / [7,1,5,9,3]
```

Line 1 is the hazard: the seek visits in index order, so the values reach their group in a different
order. Line 2 is the control that isolates it — the same predicate written so it cannot seed is
unchanged by the index, so the cause is the SEED and not the filter. Line 3 is the licence: an
unfiltered grouped collect is index-independent.

And every one of those answers is **the same in both engines**, including the reordered one. That
matters twice: it means the reordering is a real contract rather than a TS artifact, and it means
there was no pre-existing divergence hiding here (which was worth checking before trusting the
demonstration).

### The numbers

ts, 200,000 vertices, one case per process, pristine against the change:

| projection                                | before    | after     | ratio |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------- | --------- | ----- |
| `n.age AS k, sum(n.age)`                  | 105.77 ms | **9.22**  | 11.5x |
| `n.age AS k, collect(n.age)`              | 100.84    | **9.73**  | 10.4x |
| `n.age AS k, percentile_cont(n.age, 0.5)` | 111.27    | **13.69** | 8.1x  |

Three controls: the two rungs the change does not touch, `n.age AS k, count(*)` 6.42 → 4.04 and
`n.age AS k, max(n.age)` 9.84 → 9.28, and the REFUSAL, `WHERE n.age > 1 … sum(n.age)` 174.67 →
163.75 — still on the general path, as it must be.

A third `GroupAcc` variant, `values`, collects per group and finishes through the same
`aggregateOverValues` the general path runs. The percentiles ride the same flag although they sort
their values and would be safe either way: a second condition for one name is a guard with no test,
which is the mistake this item exists to avoid repeating.

### Native has no twin

Checked before looking for one — the hop-aggregate enum on the native engine, 200,000 vertices /
200,000 edges: `count(*)` 0.56 ms, `sum` 1.35, `avg` 1.36, `stddev_pop` 1.35, `max` 1.74, `min`
1.77, `percentile_cont` 2.02, `count(DISTINCT)` 2.03, `collect` 8.46. No cliff, and `collect`'s
8.46 is the cost of materializing a 200,000-element list rather than a missing path.

### Teeth

Six mutants under the cap, each asserted to match exactly once:

| mutant                                       | result               |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| M1 a FILTERED scan admitted                  | **caught** (2 fails) |
| M2 the HOP rung admitted through the flag    | **caught**           |
| M3 the null skip removed                     | **caught** (8 fails) |
| M4 the percentile fraction zeroed            | **caught**           |
| M5 `refsOnlyVar` narrowed back to folds only | survived — explained |
| M6 null control                              | clean                |

M5's survivor is recorded at the guard rather than tested around: while the flag confines the
collected accumulators to the SCAN rung, the group key and the aggregate necessarily read the one
variable, so no shape distinguishes the two spellings. It stays because it becomes load-bearing the

One mutant was MISAPPLIED before the run even started and the uniqueness assert caught it: the
grouped SCAN and grouped HOP rungs share their result loop character for character, so the `finish`
edit matched twice. Here the right answer was to patch BOTH deliberately — the hop rung passes
`unfiltered: false`, so its `values` branch is unreachable, and keeping the two copies identical is

## 554 — the grouped-HOP rung too: 2.4-2.5x, a wrong claim corrected, and a divergence found

### The correction first

Item 553 left this rung open and wrote the reason at the call site: _"its walk has a far-driven
alternative that visits rows in a different order (item 419), so an order-sensitive fold there needs
the forcing items 551/552 gave the un-grouped hop rungs, not this flag."_

That was a guess from item 419's rule rather than a reading of the loop, and it was wrong. The
grouped hop rung's walk is:

```ts
for (const v of candidateVertexSource(graph, startLabel)) {
  for (const step of expand(graph, v, adjacency)) {
```

No far-driven branch anywhere — unlike `detectHopProjection`, which has two. Its visit order is the
start side's, which is the general path's, so item 553's flag is exactly the right instrument and no
forcing is needed. _The lesson is the one items 535/536 recorded: a rule that applies to one rung is
not a property of every rung that looks like it, and reading the loop costs less than the detour._

The undirected form needs no refusal either, for the same reason: this walk takes `both` through a
single `expand`, where items 551/552 had to decline it because `hopAggregateWalks` serves it as two
passes.

### The numbers

ts, 200,000 vertices / 200,000 edges, one case per process, pristine against the change:

| projection                                | before    | after      | ratio |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------- | ---------- | ----- |
| `b.age AS k, sum(b.age)`                  | 461.01 ms | **191.52** | 2.4x  |
| `b.age AS k, collect(b.age)`              | 467.25    | **192.49** | 2.4x  |
| `b.age AS k, percentile_cont(b.age, 0.5)` | 471.90    | **192.39** | 2.5x  |

Three controls: `b.age AS k, count(*)` 161.12 → 162.10 and `b.age AS k, max(b.age)` 182.73 → 177.38
(the rungs the change does not touch), and the REFUSAL `WHERE b.age > 1 … sum(b.age)` 487.81 →
451.26, still on the general path.

### A pre-existing DIVERGENCE, found while giving the guard teeth

The seed guard's mutant survived, so I built the shape that should catch it — and found something
else. Ten `:P` nodes, one `:K` edge each, a range index on `age`:

```text
MATCH (a)-[:K]->(b) WHERE b.age >= 5 RETURN b.tag AS k, collect(b.age) AS m
  no index    ts [7,9,5] / [8,6]    native [7,9,5] / [8,6]    agree
  indexed     ts [5,7,9] / [6,8]    native [7,9,5] / [8,6]    DIVERGE

MATCH (a)-[:K]->(b) WHERE a.age >= 5 RETURN a.tag AS k, collect(a.age) AS m
  no index    ts [7,5,9]            native [7,5,9]            agree
  indexed     ts [5,7,9]            native [5,7,9]            agree
```

TS seeds the FAR end of a hop from the index and native does not. **Verified against the pristine
build before this item**, so it is pre-existing; the START-end filter agreeing in both
configurations is what locates it in the far-end seed specifically, and the no-index rows are what
say the two engines otherwise walk the same order.

Not fixed here, and recorded as open: the fix is a decision about which engine's seeding is right,
which is a planner question and not a rung condition. The byte-identity fuzzers do not generate a
grouped collect over an indexed graph, which is why this sat unseen.

### Teeth

Five mutants under the cap:

| mutant                                  | result                          |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| M1 the seed guard dropped               | survived, then **caught**       |
| M2 the flag turned off                  | survived — a PERFORMANCE mutant |
| M3 the null skip removed                | **caught** (5 fails)            |
| M4 `refsOnlyVar` narrowed back to folds | **caught**                      |
| M5 null control                         | clean                           |

M1 is the interesting one. It survived because the only shape where the guard matters is the
DIVERGING shape above, so a cross-engine `agree()` cannot be its oracle. The test is now against
**the general path in the same engine** — the invariant that actually applies to a rung, since a
rung exists to answer what the general path answers faster. With the guard removed the rung answers
its own scan order `[7,9,5]` where the TS general path answers `[5,7,9]`, and that is caught.

M2 is recorded as uncatchable rather than as a gap: turning the flag off makes the rung decline, the
general path answers identically, and only the clock changes. A test for it would be a timing
assertion, which is what `spelling_probe` is for.

M4 is the payoff on item 553's recorded survivor: widening `refsOnlyVar` to cover the collected
accumulators was undistinguishable on the scan rung and is load-bearing here, where the key is one
end of the hop and an aggregate can read the other. That entry predicted exactly this.
