## 555 — two fuzzer coverage floors were chasing the distribution's tail (CI red, no divergence)

CI failed on item 553, and the first thing to establish was whether it was a divergence. It was not:

```text
✗ differential fuzz: TS gql engine vs Rust engine > 20000 random queries render byte-identically
  - "hopUntypedGenerated": true
  + "hopUntypedGenerated": false
```

A COVERAGE assertion, not a comparison. `hopUntypedNonZero` (floor 20) passed while
`hopUntypedGenerated` (floor 28) failed, so the count was 21-28 with the two counters within a few
of each other.

### Why it cannot be the engine

`tally(cov, q, ts)` runs on every generated query, and the `hopUntyped` arm reads only the query
TEXT (`/-\[e?\]-/` against a one-hop filtered-count pattern). The `nonEmpty` flag it also takes
can move with the engine; the `Generated` counter cannot. So nothing in items 549-553 could have
affected it, and the candidates were the seed and the floor.

### The measurement

Twelve seeds, small and large, on the build that went red:

```text
hopFilter   102/78  122/98  124/103  125/104  127/104  127/106
            131/107 131/110 133/115  140/115  145/113  167/146
hopUntyped   34/27   37/33   37/33    38/31    39/38    40/35
             40/37   42/38   45/42    46/40    46/43    50/46
```

Eight further `hopUntyped` seeds (37, 40, 41, 44, 45, 48, 51, 55) only widened the top.

Minima **102/78** and **34/27**, against floors of 90/80 and 28/20. Three of the four sat 8-18%
under their own observed minimum — and `hopFilterNonZero`'s floor of 80 sat ABOVE its minimum of
78, which it proved by failing on seed 2718281828 while I was verifying the `hopUntyped` fix. _Two
flaky floors, the second found only because the first fix had to be re-verified across seeds rather
than on one._

### The fix, and why this margin

Lowered to `hopFilterGenerated > 60`, `hopFilterNonZero > 45`, `hopUntypedGenerated > 20`,
`hopUntypedNonZero > 12` — about 40% under the observed minima, and the file's own comment says why
that is the right margin:

> Their job is to catch a shape silently falling to ZERO, which is what happened twice (items 115,
> 125).

A floor tight enough to flag a 25% dip is a floor that flags the weather. The counters' purpose is
zero-detection, and 40% of headroom serves it while leaving the tail alone.

### Teeth — the part a lowered floor needs most

A floor that no longer catches what it exists for is worse than no floor. Two mutants under the cap,
each breaking one counter's regex so its tally falls to ZERO:

| mutant                         | result              |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------- |
| Z1 `hopUntyped` driven to zero | **caught** (exit 1) |
| Z2 `hopFilter` driven to zero  | **caught** (exit 1) |

Then verified green on five seeds including both that had failed: 2718281828, 55555, 7, 1357911, 999999999.

### Gates

`bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean.

## 556 — the GQL fuzzer's grouped arm never collected; and an INDEXED pass retracted after measurement

Item 554 found a WITHIN-GROUP order divergence by hand, and the memory note after it said the gap
was that the fuzzers never build an index. This tick went after both. One half survived measurement
and one did not.

### What survived: the grouped arm now collects

The generator's grouped-aggregate band emitted exactly one shape,
`MATCH (n:T) LET k = <expr> RETURN k, count(*) AS c GROUP BY k ORDER BY k, c`. A count cannot see
the order values reach their group, so the entire class item 554 belongs to was unreachable — and
`collect_list` appeared in the `AGG` list but only on the scan arm.

Half the band now collects, and **every choice in it was forced by a mutation run against the
engine** rather than designed up front. Each is a condition the TS grouped-scan rung imposes, and I
learned each by watching a mutant survive:

| round | mutant survived because                                                         | fix                                    |
| ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| 1     | the collected property `n` is DENSE, so no null reached the accumulator         | collect the sparse `st` half the time  |
| 2     | a `LET`-keyed group DECLINES the rung (it needs a property of the matched node) | emit implicit grouping by `n.s`        |
| 3     | the rung refuses a projection that SORTS (items 190, 199)                       | drop the `ORDER BY` from that spelling |

With all three, the null mutant (`if (isNullish(value))` → `if (false)` in the grouped `values`
accumulator) is **caught on seeds 7, 1 and 55555**. Before them it survived every seed.

_The lesson is the generator's, not the engine's: a generated shape that DECLINES the rung it was
written for reads exactly like one that takes it. Only a mutant distinguishes them._

One mutant still survives and is recorded at the helper rather than worked around: reversing the
within-group order changes nothing, because `s`, `st` and `n` are distinct on all three fixture
vertices, so no group ever holds two rows and a reversed one-element list is the same list. Catching
it needs a fixture with a repeated key, which is a fixture change.

The arm is extracted to `genGrouped` because the extra spellings put `genQuery` at complexity 38
against a limit of 35.

### What was RETRACTED: the indexed pass

Built as described: a second graph pair, range indexes on `n` and `x`, a hash index on `s`, both
engines given identical indexes (the invariant is TS-indexed against native-indexed — an index MAY
legitimately change an order-sensitive aggregate's row order, as item 553 measured in both engines,
so "the index changed nothing" is not the claim). Then I measured whether it reached anything:

| fixture                              | answers differing from the unindexed plan |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| 3-vertex `NDJSON`, NaN setup missing | 128/5000                                  |
| 3-vertex `NDJSON`, NaN setup applied | **0**/5000                                |
| purpose-built 400-vertex fixture     | **0**/5000                                |

The first row is the useful one. 128 looked like real reach — until a mutant that removed index
creation ENTIRELY still scored 128. The differences were the two computed NaNs that the original
pair carries from its `SET` setup and the new pair did not. _A reach counter measuring the wrong
difference reads exactly like one measuring the right difference._

With the fixtures made identical, the index changes NO answer the generator produces. A direct probe
says why: on a 400-vertex graph a seek does change a grouped `collect` over a FILTERED source
(`[34,32,24,…]` scanning against `[24,24,24,…]` seeking) — but it leaves the plain projections and
counts the generator emits untouched. The shapes an index perturbs are exactly the ones the
generator does not write.

So the pass was 5,000 repetitions of the pass above it. Reverted, with its 400-vertex fixture and
the `compareOne` extraction that existed only to feed it. Shipping it would have been a test that
proves nothing while looking exactly like one that does — items 115 and 125's failure, which this
file's own floors exist to prevent.

**What closing the gap actually needs**, recorded so the next attempt starts here: a generated shape
that is BOTH order-sensitive AND filtered on an indexed property, plus a fixture with repeated group
keys. The grouped-collect arm above is the first half of it.

### Gates

`bun test packages/native/src` 850 pass / 0 fail, six seeds of the differential fuzzer green (7, 1,
55555, 2718281828, 987654321, 1357911), `bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0,
`bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean, all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13. CI was green on 555.

## 557 — a one-hop VALUE-subquery aggregate: 2.0x, and four divergences the enum turned up

### Pricing the enum

The correlated-subquery surface, 200,000 vertices / 200,000 edges, one case per process:

```text
RETURN COUNT { MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) }                           25.25 ms
RETURN EXISTS { MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) }                          26.42
RETURN VALUE { MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN count(*) }           27.07
RETURN VALUE { … RETURN avg(x.age) }                              154.73
RETURN VALUE { … RETURN sum(x.age) }                              155.16
RETURN VALUE { … RETURN max(x.age) }                              161.03
RETURN VALUE { … RETURN min(x.age) }                              170.50
CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN count(*) } RETURN count(*)  278.56
```

One rung, four misses. `count(*)` rides the degree path (item 499); the others materialized the
whole match set per outer row. Native: 4.67 / 5.77 / 5.48 for count/max/sum, flat — the gap is
TS-only.

### The rung

`hopValueAggregate` streams the anchor's adjacency through `sideOfVertexGated` with ONE scratch
binding and ONE value array per outer row, then hands the values to the same
`aggregateOverValues` the general path calls — so the two routes cannot drift on a nullish rule or
on what an empty group returns (`max` null, `sum` 0). The admission mirrors
`landingPredDegreeCount`'s: one segment, a plain unlabelled anchor, a landing variable that is not
the anchor, a `WHERE` reading only the landing, and an ARGUMENT reading only the landing.

Alternated rounds: max 161.03 / 165.30 → 81.19 / 80.12, sum 155.16 / 188.64 → 78.53 / 81.34, min
170.50 → 86.30, avg 154.73 → 78.82. The `count(*)` control 27.07 / 25.57 → 25.90 / 24.46.

### FOUR divergences, found by pricing the enum

Probing the enum against native turned up four shapes where the engines disagree, none of them
caused by this work:

```text
VALUE { MATCH (n)-[:T]->(x) RETURN collect(x.n) }       ts [[2,5],[],[5],[]]   native THROWS
VALUE { … RETURN collect_list(x.n) }                    ts same                native THROWS
VALUE { … RETURN stddev_pop(x.n) }                      ts answers             native THROWS
VALUE { … RETURN count(x.n) }                           ts [2,0,1,0]           native THROWS
```

Native's message is `RETURN CollectList(…) is not supported in …` — a loud refusal, so the
dangerous class (a wrong answer) is not involved. **All four are excluded from the rung**, and the
reason is worth stating because it is not a correctness one: optimizing a shape the two engines
disagree about only makes the divergent answer arrive faster, and it would then be the faster answer
that has to be unpicked when the divergence is settled. The test pins both sides.

`count(<arg>)` was admitted in the first draft and the conformance probe caught it — which is why

## 558 — an OPTIONAL hop under a null-blind aggregate is just a hop: 3.8-5.2x

### Pricing the enum

Item 557 ended on the `CALL (n) { … }` route at 278 ms. Pricing its neighbours first turned up a
bigger number next door:

```text
MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.age > 60 RETURN count(*)                              11.18 ms
MATCH (n:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE n.age > 60 RETURN count(*)                20.74
MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.age > 60 CALL (n) { … RETURN count(*) } RETURN count(*)  318.32
MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.age > 60 OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN count(*)  414.43
```

and the OPTIONAL family split cleanly once asked properly:

```text
                                                               TS        native
MATCH (n:P) OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[:T]->(x) RETURN count(*)         8.12 ms   0.66 ms
...with a clause WHERE on the first MATCH                      191.69      —
...RETURN count(x)                                             410.12      1.30
...RETURN max(x.age)                                           475.90      1.52
```

`count(*)` rides item 546's rung; everything else fell to the general path, 315x and 313x off
native.

### The identity

An optional match contributes ONE null-filled row per start with no match. Every aggregate here
drops nullish values before folding (the general path's `nonNull`, which `aggregateOverValues` is
handed), so those rows change nothing — except `count(*)`, which counts ROWS. So an un-grouped
projection whose aggregates all take an ARGUMENT cannot tell the two forms apart, and
`unoptionalizeForAggregate` flips the flag so the existing hop-aggregate rungs apply.

| query                         | before          | after      | ratio    |
| ----------------------------- | --------------- | ---------- | -------- |
| `… RETURN count(x)`           | 410.12 ms       | **78.84**  | 5.2x     |
| `… RETURN max(x.age)`         | 457.60 / 475.90 | **91.36**  | 5.0-5.2x |
| `… RETURN sum(x.age)`         | 494.60          | **131.65** | 3.8x     |
| `… RETURN count(*)` (control) | 7.79            | 7.81       | —        |

### The fixture is the test

`b` and `z` have no out-edge, so the null-filled row exists and is observable. **On a fixture where
every start matches, the optional and non-optional forms are indistinguishable** — the whole
rewrite would look correct for the wrong reason, which is the trap item 557's M2 fell into one tick
earlier with a coinciding maximum.

Thirteen shapes answer identically to the PRISTINE build, including the one native cannot be asked
(`WHERE` inside an `OPTIONAL MATCH`, which it rejects outright). Every admitted shape is ALSO asked
without the `OPTIONAL` in the test and must match, which is the equivalence the rewrite claims
rather than an assertion about its output.

Three refusals, each pinned by the number it protects:

- `count(*)` reads **5** where the non-optional form reads 3.
- a grouped `RETURN n.n AS k, max(x.n)` keeps **four** groups (two with null aggregates) where the
  non-optional form keeps two.
- a projection with no aggregate keeps **five** rows against three.

### Teeth

Five mutants under the cap:

| mutant                               | result                |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------- |
| M1 a star count admitted             | **caught** (12 fails) |
| M2 `groupBy`/`having` checks dropped | survived — redundant  |
| M3 a non-aggregate item admitted     | **caught** (23 fails) |
| M4 `!proj.star` dropped              | survived — redundant  |
| M5 null control                      | clean                 |

The two survivors are redundant and kept deliberately: `!proj.star` is implied by
`items.length > 0` (a bare `RETURN *` projects no items) and `groupBy`/`having` by
`items.every(hasAggregate)` (a GROUP BY key must appear as a non-aggregate item, and `RETURN` never
sets `having` — only `SELECT` does). Both stay because the implication runs through another part of
the projection rather than through anything local, which is the same reason `detectHopAggregate`
keeps its own `groupKeys` check.

M2 was MISAPPLIED on its first attempt and the uniqueness assert caught it: the guard's text is
near-identical to item 549's `oneOrderFreeRow`, so the pattern matched twice. Items 474, 483, 494,
518, 528, 545, 546, 552, 553 and now 558 — **ten times in this session**, and every one of them was
caught by the same two-line assert.

then **9992.3 / 12052.8 / 10737.0** on three repeats, min inside the band. It is a RUST row and this

## 559 — a FILTERED anchor on the optional-hop count: up to 27x, three spellings, and a second value divergence

### The cliff

Item 558's enum left one row unexplained: adding a clause `WHERE` to a query already on the
optional-hop count rung cost 191.69 ms against 8.12. The cause is one line —
`detectOptionalHopCount` refused `m.where` outright — and the arithmetic says it did not need to:
the rung computes Σ max(1, degree) over the anchors, so a filter changes WHICH anchors are summed
and leaves `sideOfVertex` untouched.

Then the equivalent-spelling question, which is the part worth doing: are the filter's SIBLINGS
admitted? They were not — `plainNode(anchor.start)` refused both inline forms. 200,000 vertices /
200,000 edges, one case per process:

| query                                                               | before  | after     | ratio     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | --------- | --------- |
| `MATCH (n:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN count(*)` | 7.65 ms | 10.03     | control   |
| `… WHERE n.age > 60`                                                | 191.17  | **22.50** | 8.5x      |
| `MATCH (n:Person {tag: 'x'}) …`                                     | 391.04  | **14.49** | **27.0x** |
| `MATCH (n:Person WHERE n.age > 60) …`                               | 214.24  | **22.58** | 9.5x      |

The inline property map was the worst of the three, which is the shape of every index-seeding bug
this repo records: one spelling recognised, another scanned, same answer.

### A SECOND value divergence, found while building a mutant

The `inlineOf`-refusal mutant needed a shape the rung declines, and the obvious one turned up
something else:

```text
MATCH (n:P {t: null})       RETURN count(*)   ts 1   native 1   agree
MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.t = n.t RETURN count(*)   ts 1   native 1   agree
MATCH (n:P {t: n.t})        RETURN count(*)   ts 2   native 1   DIVERGE
MATCH (n:P {t: n.missing})  RETURN count(*)   ts 1   native 0   DIVERGE
```

The two agreeing rows are what make this precise rather than a guess. Both engines read a LITERAL
inline null as an IS NULL test (item 260's decision) and a clause-`WHERE` comparison against null as
UNKNOWN. **The divergence is an inline property whose value EXPRESSION evaluates to null at run
time**: TS takes the IS NULL route, native the `= null` route, so a node with the key absent
matches in one engine and not the other.

Verified against the PRISTINE build, so it predates the item that found it. It is in the DANGEROUS
class — different rows, not a refusal — and it is the second such divergence open, beside item
554's far-end hop seed. Which engine is right is an ISO question about whether the IS NULL rule
attaches to the literal or to the evaluated value; recorded rather than guessed.

### Teeth

Six mutants under the cap:

| mutant                                        | result                    |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| M1 the gate not applied                       | **caught** (6 fails)      |
| M2 an outer-variable `WHERE` admitted         | survived — unreachable    |
| M3 the `inlineOf` refusal dropped             | survived, then **caught** |
| M4 the two gates composed in reverse order    | survived, then **caught** |
| M5 the floor applied to a filtered-out anchor | **caught** (5 fails)      |
| M6 null control                               | clean                     |

M2 is unreachable rather than untested: a clause `WHERE` naming another variable is rejected before
the rung ever sees it, by both engines (`variable 'y' is not defined` / `unknown variable 'y'`).

**M3 and M4 both needed a second attempt, for the same reason, and it is the lesson of the tick:
the first discriminator produced the same number on both sides of the bug.**

- M4: `{t: 'zz'} WHERE 1 / 0 > 0` faults under one composition order and short-circuits under the
  other. My first attempt used a filter that KEPT some anchor, so both orders faulted.
- M3: `{t: n.t}` answers 5 whether the gate is applied or dropped, because TS's inline IS NULL rule
  keeps the property-less anchor either way. `{t: n.missing}` separates them — the value is null for
  every anchor, so the gate keeps only `z` (degree 0, floor 1) where no gate counts all four.

That is twice in two ticks (item 558's fixture, item 557's M2) that a case which looked
discriminating was not, and each time the only thing that said so was a surviving mutant.

```text
...WHERE n.age > 60                                               52.75     14.3x
```

## 561 — VERIFICATION: items 548-560 sweep clean, and a reproducible Gremlin-fuzzer FALSE RED

Thirteen items since item 547's sweep: five GQL clause rewrites (548, 549, 558), the native twin
(550), five aggregate-rung widenings (551, 552, 553, 554, 557), two filtered-anchor widenings (559,
560), one fuzzer floor re-measurement (555) and one retraction (556).

### The sweep

Seven harnesses, both spelling probes, the Rust suite, and `rewrite_fuzz` at 200,000 seeds.
**Everything in band and nothing needed isolating** — the first sweep this session where no row
read up:

```text
bun run bench      count 3-hop 327.3 (311-342), traverse 1-hop + start filter 33.2 (best
                   recorded, band 37-41), count 2-hop + end filter 97.1 (best), subquery item
                   28.1, 2-hop subquery item 111.4, traverse 1-hop project 131.5
bench:usage        point lookup ts(+) 1.29M (best recorded), 100 updates in one statement 968.0k,
                   keyed dedup 77.3k, interleaved write + traversal 219.4k
bench:gremlin      all 14 rows answer "same"; V().hasLabel().out().count() still 0.0
query_bench        optional hop 580.6, + miss 63.6, + landing pred 9825.8, 1-hop 506.1/539.8,
                   for-in const x3 15.5, varlen count 863.6
spelling_probe     Rust: NO PERF CLIFFS. TS: 0 answer disagreements, only the documented
                   `label on start` regression guard over 2x
rewrite_fuzz       LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000 clean
cargo test         1167 pass / 0 fail; clippy --all-targets -D warnings and cargo fmt exit 0
```

### The finding: `orderOverPaths` asked about the FIRST `order(`

CI went red on item 560, and the failure was a Gremlin-fuzzer divergence that **replays** — seed
4026198038:

```text
g.V().label().order().by(desc).path().order().by(desc).fold()
  ts:     [3, 5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 13]   (by label desc, then id asc)
  native: [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 13, 1]   (by id desc, as strings)
```

Same seven paths, different order. The suite's own rule already covers this — _"a path-stream
`order()` is unspecified (sorting paths-of-elements has no total order)"_ — and `unordered` already
reads `|| orderOverPaths(text)`. The bug is in that predicate:

```ts
const o = text.indexOf('order('); // the FIRST order
return o >= 0 && p < o; // p = the first path()/tree()
```

With TWO orders and a `path()` between them, the first `order(` sits BEFORE the path, so `p < o` is
false and the function answers "not over paths" — while the SECOND order is over a path stream all
the same. `lastIndexOf` is the whole fix: if ANY `order(` follows a `path()`, the stream being
sorted is a path stream.

### Attribution, established rather than assumed

`git show 8864f198:` for all four GQL files I have touched since (executor.ts, shortcuts.ts,
hop-projection.ts, clauses.ts), rebuild, replay the seed: **it fails identically**. So none of items
548-560 caused it. It is also not the known 1-in-30 Gremlin residual, which replays CLEAN — this one
replays dirty, which is what made it worth chasing rather than re-running.

### Teeth — a relaxed comparison has to be shown still to catch things

Four mutants on the native side of the comparison, five seeds each:

| mutant                                                   | result         |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| Z1b drop a row on a path-order query                     | **caught** 2/5 |
| Z2 mangle a value on a path-order query                  | **caught** 1/3 |
| Z3 reverse each path's elements, path-order queries ONLY | **not caught** |
| Z4 reverse each path's elements, ANY query               | **caught** 5/5 |

Coverage measured rather than guessed: **4-9 of 400 queries per run** are `orderOverPaths`, so the
relaxation touches ~1.5% of comparisons.

Z3 and Z4 together are the honest account of what it costs. `deepSort` canonicalizes WITHIN a row
as well as between rows — deliberately, for the `coalesce(...).path()` case its own comment records
— so those 4-9 queries lose their within-path element-order check. **That contract is still covered
on every path query without an `order()`**, which is the large majority, and Z4 proves it at 5/5.
Z1b and Z2 show the row CONTENTS are still compared for the relaxed shapes.

_An alternative was to skip path-order queries outright, as the slice case does. That would have
lost Z1b and Z2 as well, so the multiset compare is the better trade — and this is the second time
this session that the choice between "skip" and "compare more weakly" came down to which mutants
survive each._

## 562 — the CALL-with-aggregate-body route: a 24.9x target priced, the rewrite RETRACTED

### Pricing it

Item 558 left `CALL (n) { … }` at 278 ms as "the largest number still on the board". Asked properly
at 200,000 vertices / 200,000 edges, one case per process:

```text
CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN count(*) AS c } RETURN sum(c)      760.86 ms
CALL (n) { … RETURN count(*) AS c } RETURN count(*)                          691.35
CALL (n) { … RETURN x.age AS a } RETURN count(*)   (pass-through body)       576.33
RETURN sum(COUNT { MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) })                                 30.56
MATCH (n:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN count(*)                                 0.01
```

Rows 1 and 4 are the same question: Σ over `n` of its degree. **24.9x**, which is the widest
equivalent-spelling gap left in the GQL surface.

The reason the two differ is structural. An un-grouped aggregate body yields exactly ONE row per
outer row — null or 0 over an empty match, never nothing — so the lateral join neither drops nor
multiplies rows and the call is a per-row scalar, i.e. a `VALUE {}` subquery. That has rungs (items
499, 557); the CALL route has none. `inlineCorrelatedCall` handles the OTHER body shape (a
pass-through yielding pattern variables, rewritten to a plain MATCH) and correctly refuses this one.

**The equivalence was verified against native on six shapes before any code was written**, including
what an unmatched start contributes (`c: 0` for a count, `m: null` for a max) — both engines agree
on all six, and the hand-written `LET c = VALUE { … }` spelling agrees too.

### The rewrite, and why it was retracted

`inlineAggregateCall` turned the call into `LET c = VALUE { MATCH … RETURN <agg> }`, composing with
`inlineTrailingLet` and item 557's rung. It worked: **760.86 → 68.43 ms, 11.1x**, with the
pass-through control flat (576.33 → 568.72) and the `sum(COUNT{})` control flat (30.56 → 31.41).

Then the conformance probe:

```text
CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:T]->(x) RETURN count(*) AS c } RETURN sum(c) AS t, count(*) AS r
  rewritten                      {t: 6, r: 3}   WRONG
  native                         {t: 2, r: 3}
  the hand-written LET spelling  {t: 2, r: 3}
  `sum(COUNT{…})` spelling       {t: 2, r: 3}
```

6 is one node's degree of 2 counted three times — the per-row scalar computed once and reused. A
ONE-item outer projection is correct (`RETURN sum(c)` → 200,000 on the big fixture, `RETURN max(m)`
→ 2 on the unit one); a TWO-item outer projection is wrong.

Two things I checked before giving up on it:

- **It is not the inlining.** Moving `inlineAggregateCall` OUTSIDE `inlineTrailingLet`, so the `LET`
  survives as a clause and is evaluated per row, gives the same wrong answer.
- **It is not the equivalence.** The hand-written `LET c = VALUE { … } RETURN sum(c), count(*)`
  answers 2. So the generated clause differs from the parsed one in some way I did not locate —
  `memoizeIfUncorrelated` reusing a first-row value is the hypothesis the numbers fit, but I did
  not confirm it, and an unconfirmed hypothesis is not a reason to ship.

**Reverted, tree verified back to the baseline** (all three spellings agree again, both suites green).

_Had I measured only the one-item shape, this would have shipped a wrong answer with an 11x
headline._ Both earlier CALL probes this session — item 557's enum and item 558's — used a single
outer item, which is why the first measurement looked clean. The second item in a projection is now
in the probe.

### A fifth subquery-body divergence, found in the same probe

```text
CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:T]->(x) RETURN count(*) AS c, max(x.n) AS m } RETURN n.n AS k, c, m
  ts      [{k:1,c:2,m:2}, {k:2,c:0,m:null}, {k:null,c:0,m:null}]
  native  THROWS  "an aggregating RETURN inside …"
```

TWO aggregate items in a CALL body. Same family as item 557's four, same class (a loud refusal, so
not a wrong answer), and the reason the retracted rewrite admitted only ONE aggregate item.

### What a future attempt should do first

Find why a GENERATED `let` clause binding a correlated `valueSubquery` is evaluated once while the
PARSED one is evaluated per row. The two ASTs look identical at the shape level, so the difference
is in something keyed off them — the correlation analysis behind `memoizeIfUncorrelated` is the
place to look, and the repro is a single query.

### Gates

`bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun test packages/gql packages/core` 2784 pass / 0 fail, `bun test
packages/native/src` 876 pass / 0 fail — the reverted tree, unchanged from item 561. CI was green on 561.

## 563 — item 562's CALL rewrite, fixed: a MANUFACTURED subquery node must be marked correlated

### The cause, which generalises past this rewrite

Item 562 retracted `inlineAggregateCall` because a two-item outer projection answered 6 where the
answer is 2. The diagnosis took one grep:

```ts
const markIfCorrelated = (expr, scope) => { … correlatedSubqueries.add(expr) … };
```

`correlatedSubqueries` is a `WeakSet` keyed by AST-node IDENTITY, and `markIfCorrelated` is called
from SCOPE CHECKING — a pass over the PARSED tree. A rewrite that MANUFACTURES a subquery node runs
after it, so the new node is never in the set, and `memoizeIfUncorrelated` then computes the
per-row scalar once and reuses it for every row.

The node is correlated by construction: this rewrite fires only when `c.scope` is non-empty, i.e.
the call imports outer names. So the fix is one `correlatedSubqueries.add(sub)`, and it is a
statement of that fact rather than an analysis.

**The obligation is general.** Any future rewrite that manufactures an
`exists`/`countSubquery`/`valueSubquery` node inherits it, and nothing in the type system says so —
which is why it is written at the rewrite and recorded here.

### The measurement was wrong too, for the same reason the bug hid

Item 562 reported 760.86 → 68.43 ms, 11.1x. That fixture had ONE edge per node, where Σ(degree)
over N rows and (the first row's degree × N) are the SAME NUMBER — so the memoized answer looked
correct AND the memoization looked like the win. Re-measured at 200,000 vertices with degree
`i % 4` (300,000 edges), alternated rounds:

| query                                                 | pristine           | after               | ratio    |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- | -------- |
| `CALL (n) { … RETURN count(*) AS c } RETURN sum(c)`   | 779.58 / 769.30 ms | **491.96 / 510.91** | 1.5x     |
| `CALL (n) { … RETURN max(x.age) AS m } RETURN max(m)` | 779.69 / 801.46    | **268.32 / 387.63** | 2.1-2.9x |
| `RETURN sum(COUNT { … })` (control)                   | 52.45              | 53.75 / 52.06       | flat     |

**The real win is 1.5-2.9x.** The other 7x of item 562's headline was the bug running less work
than the query asked for. _A uniform fixture hid a wrong answer AND inflated its speedup, in the
same number — that is the third coinciding-fixture trap in six ticks (557's maximum, 558's matched
starts, this)._

The control spelling is still ~9x faster than the rewritten CALL, so this closes part of the 24.9x
gap and the rest stays open: the `LET`-bound subquery is evaluated per row through
`compileValueSubquery`, where `sum(COUNT{…})` reaches the degree path directly.

### Teeth

Six mutants under the cap:

| mutant                                              | result               |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| M1 the correlation marking dropped                  | **caught** (9 fails) |
| M2 two aggregate items admitted                     | **caught**           |
| M3 a pass-through body admitted                     | **caught** (6 fails) |
| M4 an `OPTIONAL CALL` admitted                      | survived — no-op     |
| M5 an alias colliding with a body variable admitted | survived — no-op     |
| M6 null control                                     | clean                |

M1 is the regression guard for this whole item and it fails nine tests, which is what a
per-row-scalar bug should look like once a non-uniform fixture exists to see it.

Both survivors were probed rather than argued: an `OPTIONAL CALL` over an aggregate body answers
identically to the plain one (the body always yields its row, so the left-outer fill never
happens), and an alias that shadows a body pattern variable changes nothing because the call hides
body variables either way. Both guards stay as statements of intent; admitting the OPTIONAL form
is a small opportunity left unmeasured.

One mutant was MISAPPLIED and the uniqueness assert caught it: the guard's first line is
character-identical to `inlineCorrelatedCall`'s. **Eleventh time this session.**

## 564 — mirroring the PARSER'S normalization: a further 3.2x, a sixth divergence, and an inert rewrite reverted

### The remaining gap had one cause

Item 563 left the rewritten CALL at 491-510 ms against the `sum(COUNT{…})` spelling's 52. Measuring
the intermediate spellings decomposed it exactly (200,000 vertices / 300,000 edges, one case per
process):

```text
CALL (n) { … RETURN count(*) AS c } RETURN sum(c)          504.16 ms
LET c = VALUE { … RETURN count(*) } RETURN sum(c)          151.30
LET c = COUNT { … } RETURN sum(c)                          151.90
RETURN sum(VALUE { … RETURN count(*) })                     51.99
RETURN sum(COUNT { … })                                     51.43
```

Two separate factors: **3.3x** between the rewritten CALL and the hand-written `LET`, and **2.9x**
between a `LET` clause and the same subquery inline in the projection.

The first has a one-line cause. `parseValueSubquery`:

```ts
if (
  patterns.length >= 1 &&
  ret.kind === 'func' &&
  ret.name === 'count' &&
  ret.star &&
  !ret.distinct
) {
  return { kind: 'countSubquery', patterns, where };
}
```

The parser NORMALIZES `VALUE { … RETURN count(*) }` into a `countSubquery` — item 499's lowering
onto the degree path — and item 563's rewrite manufactured the `valueSubquery` form, so it never
reached it. _Item 563's lesson was that a manufactured node misses an identity-keyed WeakSet; this
is the same lesson about a normalization the parser applies on the way in._

Mirroring the parser's conditions, alternated rounds:

| query                                               | before             | after               |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- |
| `CALL (n) { … RETURN count(*) AS c } RETURN sum(c)` | 504.16 / 498.10 ms | **159.49 / 156.85** |
| the hand-written `LET` spelling, for comparison     | 149.91             | —                   |
| `RETURN sum(COUNT { … })` (control)                 | 52.13              | 41.22 / 52.98       |

3.2x, landing on the hand-written spelling — which is the check that the mirroring is faithful
rather than merely faster.

### Teeth

Four mutants under the cap: `star` dropped, `distinct` dropped, always-`countSubquery`, and a null
control. The third is caught (3 fails) and the control is clean.

**`star` survived its first run**, and the fixture is why: with no REACHED property-less neighbour,
`count(x.n)` and the degree are the same number. A second fixture — `a` with two neighbours, one
of which has no `n` — separates them (1 against 2) and catches it. _Fourth coinciding-fixture trap
in this run of ticks (557's maximum, 558's matched starts, 563's uniform degree, this)._

`distinct` is unreachable beside `star`: `count(DISTINCT *)` is a parse error, so the pair can
never both be true. The parser's own comment records the same redundancy about its copy, which is
what says this is a property of the grammar rather than of either implementation.

### A SIXTH divergence, the third in the dangerous class

Found while building that second fixture:

```text
CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:T]->(x) RETURN count(x.n) AS c } RETURN n.n AS k, c
  ts      [{k:1,c:1}, {k:2,c:0}, {k:null,c:0}]     counts the NON-NULL values
  native  [{k:1,c:2}, {k:2,c:0}, {k:null,c:0}]     counts the ROWS

MATCH (n:P)-[:T]->(x) RETURN count(x.n)             ts 1   native 1   AGREE
```

The agreeing line is what makes it precise: without the CALL the two engines agree, so the
divergence is the CALL-BODY position rather than `count`. Verified identical on the pre-563 build,
so pre-existing. Both sides are pinned in the test.

### Tried and REVERTED in the same tick

The second factor — a `LET` clause costing 2.9x the inline subquery — looked like a widening of
`inlineTrailingLet`: admit a subquery binding when the projection reads the name EXACTLY ONCE (so
the evaluation count is unchanged; zero reads would swallow a fault, two would double the work).

It is **inert**. `inlineTrailingLet`'s `subst` is all-or-nothing — it substitutes only where an
item IS the bound name, and refuses any expression that MENTIONS it — so `RETURN sum(c)` never
inlines however the admission is widened. The apparent 151.90 → 112.21 did not survive an
alternated round: **110.21 pristine against 161.67 after**, the ordering reversed. Reverted.

Closing that 2.9x needs a STRUCTURAL substitution (replacing the `var` node inside an expression
tree) rather than a wider admission, and the evaluation-count argument above is the condition it
would have to satisfy. Recorded as open with the blocker named.

## 565 — `inlineTrailingLet` substitutes into a FUNCTION ARGUMENT: the CALL route reaches parity

### Why item 564's attempt was inert

Item 564 widened `boundExprs` to admit a subquery binding and measured no change. The reason is one
function:

```ts
const subst = (e: Expr): Expr | null => {
  if (e.kind === 'var') { … }                 // the item IS the name → substitute
  const free = freePredicateVars(e);
  return [...bound.keys()].some((n) => free.has(n)) ? null : e;   // mentions it → REFUSE
};
```

All-or-nothing. `RETURN sum(c)` mentions `c` without being `c`, so it refused however the admission
widened — which is why the measurement moved by nothing and why the apparent 151.90 → 112.21 turned
out to be the row's bimodality.

### Both halves together

`boundExprs` admits the subquery AND `subst` replaces a bound name in a function-ARGUMENT position.
200,000 vertices / 300,000 edges, one case per process:

| spelling                                                       | before                      | after                          |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `LET c = COUNT { MATCH (n)-[:KNOWS]->(x) } RETURN sum(c)`      | 114.06 / 170.48 / 173.33 ms | **53.46**                      |
| `CALL (n) { … RETURN count(*) AS c } RETURN sum(c)`            | 156.85 / 159.49             | **52.93**                      |
| `RETURN sum(COUNT { … })` (the target all along)               | 50.14 / 52.78 / 52.18       | 52.87                          |
| `LET a = n.age RETURN sum(a)` (a CHEAP binding, same widening) | —                           | 22.28 against the inline 20.03 |

Three spellings of one question, one cost. **End to end across items 563, 564 and 565 the CALL
route goes 779 → 53 ms, 14.7x**, and the remaining difference from the hand-written spelling is
inside the noise band.

### The two conditions

**Exactly ONE read**, counted across the projection's items AND its ORDER BY keys. A cheap, total
expression can be inlined any number of times; a subquery cannot:

- read TWICE and substituted twice, the work doubles;
- read ZERO times, the binder's evaluation disappears — **and with it any fault it raises**. A
  faulting zero-read binder throws in BOTH engines today (`LET c = COUNT { … WHERE 1 / 0 > 0 }
RETURN count(*)`), which is exactly what the `> 1` mutant stops doing.

**ONE LEVEL.** Arguments are replaced where they are bare names and the result is re-checked for a
surviving mention, so `sum(c + 1)` refuses and keeps the clause. This is deliberately not an
exhaustive walk over the 40-arm `Expr` union: a missed arm there would drop the binder while a
reference to its name survived, which is a wrong answer rather than a slow one.

### Teeth

Six mutants under the cap:

| mutant                                     | result                    |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- |
| M1 the once-read guard dropped             | survived, then **caught** |
| M2 zero reads admitted (`> 1` for `!== 1`) | survived, then **caught** |
| M3 a deep reference admitted               | **caught**                |
| M4 a non-`func` expression admitted        | **caught** (4 fails)      |
| M5 ORDER BY reads not counted              | survived — cost-only      |
| M6 null control                            | clean                     |

M1 and M2 both needed the FAULTING zero-read test, and the reason is the same one this session
keeps relearning: every other consequence of those mutants is a double evaluation, which produces
the same answer. A disappearing FAULT is the only observable, so the test had to contain one.

M5 is cost-only and recorded at the guard: under-counting ORDER BY reads can only admit a case
where an item reads once and a sort key reads again, and substituting both gives two evaluations of
the same subquery — slower, never different.

(band 26-32); `2-hop subquery item` 112.9, `group + aggregate` 4.0.

## 566 — VERIFICATION: two enums priced, NO cliff in either

Items 548-565 worked the GQL clause list, the aggregate rungs and the subquery routes. This tick
asked whether the two surfaces NOT yet priced this session hide a cliff. Neither does, and the
negative result is the deliverable — `CLOSED.md` exists so the next pass does not re-derive it.

### Predicate forms on a scan count

200,000 vertices, one case per process, every form the parser accepts in that position:

```text
n.age = 44            10.49 ms      n.age IS NOT NULL      10.24
n.age >= 44           11.94         n.age IS NULL          11.45
n.age > 44            12.26         n.age <> 44            13.42
n.age IN [1, 2, 3]    15.69         NOT n.age > 44         15.96
n.age > 44 OR n.age < 2  18.46      n.age > 44 XOR n.tag = 'x'  18.71
n.tag STARTS WITH 'x' 32.21         n.tag CONTAINS 'x'     32.51
```

A 3.1x spread end to end, rising smoothly. The string predicates are the dear end at ~161 ns a row
against the numeric comparisons' ~61 — predicate dispatch over a string, not a different route.
No form falls off its rung, which is what the equivalent-spelling probe already asserts for the
pairs it covers and this extends to the whole list.

### Aggregate arguments on a scan

```text
count(n.age)   14.96 ms     count(abs(n.age))   26.39
max(n.age)     15.88        max(abs(n.age))     32.02      max(n.age + 1)  18.94
sum(n.age)     19.70        sum(abs(n.age))     32.87
```

A computed argument costs 1.7-2x a bare property, which LOOKS like a rung refusing one — and
`max(n.age + 1)` at 18.94 is what says it is not. Arithmetic rides the same path nearly free; the
difference is the FUNCTION CALL. A twelve-name sweep (`upper`, `lower`, `trim`, `size`, `left`,
`substring`, `abs`, `floor`, `round`, `sqrt`, `coalesce`, `||`) lands in one 25-50 ms band with no
outlier, which is the shape of a dispatch cost rather than a missing path.

### The ceiling, measured

| query                                         | TS       | native   | ratio |
| --------------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | ----- |
| `WHERE n.age > 44 RETURN count(*)`            | 12.26 ms | **0.15** | 82x   |
| `WHERE n.tag STARTS WITH 'x' RETURN count(*)` | 32.21    | **0.13** | 248x  |
| `RETURN max(n.age)`                           | 15.88    | **0.43** | 37x   |
| `RETURN count(abs(n.age))`                    | 26.39    | **0.82** | 32x   |
| `RETURN count(substring(n.tag, 0, 1))`        | 50.39    | **1.60** | 31x   |

61 ns a row against 0.75. **A data-layout difference, not overhead**: the TS rung walks vertex
objects and calls a closure per row where native scans a typed column with no per-row dispatch at
all. Item 234 reached the same conclusion from the Gremlin side and withdrew two targets on it;
this is the GQL scan's version of the same ceiling.

_A 248x ratio is exactly the kind of number that looks like a missing fast path and is not._ The
rung is already taken; what is left is the layout, which is a different project from anything this
loop has been doing.

## 567 — NATIVE: an OPTIONAL hop's landing LABEL kept the slow spelling — 19.5x

Sixteen of the last eighteen items were TypeScript. This priced the NATIVE optional-hop enum, which
is where the loop had not looked.

### The enum

200,000 vertices / 350,000 edges, one case per process:

```text
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:KNOWS]->(q)                    0.64 ms
MATCH (p:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(q:Person)               0.26        non-optional, with a label
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:KNOWS]->(q WHERE q.age > 50)   3.67
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:KNOWS]->(q:Nope)              44.67
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:KNOWS]->(q:Person)            46.25        72x the first
```

Two spellings of ONE landing filter — a label and a predicate — differing by 12x, and the
non-optional row showing a label costs nothing when a plain `Filter` carries it. That pair is what
located the problem in the POSITION rather than in the test.

### The cause

`normalize_pred` canonicalizes GQL's `'L' IN labels(slot)` into `IsLabeled`, the node that the
tautology short-circuit and the membership bitset both read — three implementations, chosen by a
cost estimate. Grepping its call sites:

```text
opt.rs:1048   Plan::Filter { input, pred } => { … normalize_pred(pred, &i) … }
```

**One site.** Everything else that carries a predicate keeps whatever spelling the front end
emitted, and `OptionalExpand::landing_pred` is one of those: `gql.rs` builds it from the landing
label via `landing_label_filter`, and it reached the evaluator as a `labels()` CALL whose result is
a materialized list per candidate.

### The fix

Normalize the landing predicate in `map_children`'s `OptionalExpand` arm. Two details:

- the landing slot is the one this node APPENDS, so the predicate is normalized against the
  REBUILT node rather than against its input;
- `slot_is_node` had no `OptionalExpand` arm, so it fell through to `_ => false` and the
  canonicalization would have declined anyway. The arm mirrors `Expand`'s, including that a bound
  edge sits one slot before the landing node.

| measurement                                            | before           | after               |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------- | ------------------- |
| `query_bench` `optional hop + landing label` (new row) | 173,141.9 µs     | **8,877.7** (19.5x) |
| `query_bench` `optional hop + landing pred` (control)  | 10,112.6         | 11,381.3            |
| probe `(q:Person)`                                     | 46.25 / 58.05 ms | **5.65 / 6.46**     |
| probe `(q:Nope)`                                       | 44.67 / 45.25    | **2.67 / 2.71**     |
| probe `(q WHERE q.age > 50)` (control)                 | 3.82 / 3.67      | 3.67 / 4.34         |
| probe plain optional (control)                         | 0.62 / 0.64      | 0.60 / 0.75         |

The two spellings now sit within 1.3x of each other on the bench fixture instead of 17x, and the
bench carries both rows side by side so a regression in either shows as a gap.

### Teeth

Four mutants under the cap:

| mutant                                | result                    |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| M1 no normalization                   | **caught**                |
| M2 normalize against the INPUT plan   | did not compile           |
| M3 `slot_is_node` ignores `bind_edge` | survived, then **caught** |
| M4 null control                       | clean                     |

M3 is the instructive one. Declining to canonicalize is ANSWER-PRESERVING — it is only slower — so
no assertion about rows could catch it. The test asserts the PLAN instead: `IsLabeled { slot: 2` for
the bound-edge spelling, where the landing node sits one slot after the edge. _A perf-only guard
needs a structural assertion; this is the second time this session (item 550's Gremlin page was the
first)._

The dangerous direction of that mutant — treating an EDGE slot as a node and reading node labels
for it — is what `slot_is_node`'s own doc warns about for the `Filter` case. It is unreachable
here: an edge label test would have to come from a trailing `WHERE` inside the `OPTIONAL MATCH`,
which this engine rejects outright.

## 568 — grepping item 567's pattern: it does not repeat; and the quantified-group count priced

### The grep, which is the step item 567 earned

`normalize_pred` had one call site. Item 567 added the second. The question is whether the other
predicate-bearing plan positions need it too — `ir.rs` has three:

- **`Hop.edge_pred`** and **`ShortestPath.edge_pred`** — both over an EDGE. Canonicalizing a label
  test there would be WRONG, and `slot_is_node`'s own doc says why: an edge's `IS LABELED` lowers
  to the same `In(Lit, labels(slot))` form but means its TYPE, which `IsLabeled` (node labels)
  answers wrongly.
- **`RepeatGroup.per_rep_pred`** — over the rep's mini-scope. A label there would be worth
  normalizing, except that a label inside a quantified group is REJECTED by this engine:
  `MATCH (a:P)((x)-[e:T]->(y:P)){1,2}` → _"a label/property/WHERE …"_.

So the pattern does not repeat, and that is the finding. _Item 567's fix was the whole of it._

### What the same probe found instead

60,000 vertices / 180,000 edges, one case per process, both engines:

| query                                                           | native    | TS         |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | ---------- |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->{1,2}(y) RETURN count(*)` (abbreviated)      | 1.07 ms   | 421.35 ms  |
| `MATCH (a:P)((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2} RETURN count(*)` (group)      | 1.06      | **786.15** |
| `MATCH (a:P)((x)-[:T]->(y)){1,2} RETURN count(*)` (no edge var) | —         | 769.55     |
| `… ((x)-[e:T]->(y) WHERE y.age > 50){1,2} …`                    | **34.21** | 672.79     |
| `… ((x)-[e:T]->(y) WHERE e.w > 5){1,2} …`                       | **42.59** | 654.86     |
| `… {1,1}` with the same target predicate                        | 15.04     | —          |

Answers agree throughout (719,998 unfiltered; 171,883 and 159,981 filtered).

**Target 1 — TS, an equivalent-spelling gap of 1.87x.** The group spelling costs 786.15 where the
abbreviated one costs 421.35, for one question. The native optimizer already closes this:
`drop_unread_group_binds` turns a group whose per-rep bindings nothing reads into a plain
var-length hop, and its doc records the measurement (a bare `count(*)` over a group went
64,655µs → 606µs there). TS has no equivalent.

**Target 2 — NATIVE, 32-40x from a per-rep predicate.** The unfiltered count rides the way-count
sweep at 1.5 ns a row; any per-rep predicate drops it to the general group executor at ~200 ns a
row, even though the filtered query produces FEWER rows. A sweep that prunes its frontier per rep
is the shape of the fix.

### Why neither is built in this tick

**The differential fuzzer generates no quantified or nested group.** That is already recorded as a
coverage gap, and it means the net that caught item 562's wrong answer and item 561's harness bug
is not watching this shape at all. Both changes would need their own tests built first, and a
quantified-path rewrite is the worst place in the engine to be the first thing to touch a shape
nothing fuzzes.

> **CORRECTION (item 569).** The paragraph above is WRONG, and the way it went wrong is the
> lesson. The GQL differential fuzzer generates quantified groups in quantity — one run prints
> `perRep=352/222 abbrev=185/160/50 simpleGroup=75/55 groupHopPred=416/256 innerWhere=142/129`
> of 20,000, each with a coverage FLOOR. I read a one-line memory summary ("the differential
> fuzzer covers NO quantified/nested groups") and did not open the note, whose own body corrects
> it: groups have been generated since item 51 and the ABBREVIATED form was added at item 238.
> The blocker I recorded did not exist. Item 569 builds the TS target the fuzzer was supposedly
> not watching, and the summary line has been fixed.

The TS target carries a second, named hazard. Item 444's note in `hop-projection.ts` records that
a NAMED but UNMENTIONED variable cannot be cleared by free-variable analysis: `freePredicateVars`
adds a subquery's own pattern names to its bound set, so an inner `-[r:T]->` that CORRELATES on an
already-bound `r` is indistinguishable from one binding it freshly — and removing a guard on that
basis produced a wrong answer (2 where the answer is 1). A group-binding elision inherits that
exactly and must refuse any query containing a subquery outright rather than trust the analysis.

Recorded with the numbers and the traps so the next attempt starts from the measurement.

## Item 569 — a quantified hop's UNREAD group bindings, 2.10x, and a seventh divergence found by its own test

Item 568 priced this and declined to build it, on a blocker that **did not exist**. The
correction is inserted above item 568's entry; the short version is that the GQL differential
fuzzer generates quantified groups in quantity (`perRep=414/240 abbrev=211/187/63
simpleGroup=99/74 groupHopPred=442/272 innerWhere=162/142` in the run below), each with a
coverage floor, and I had read a one-line memory summary instead of opening the note whose own
body corrects it. The lesson is item 568's, not this one's: a blocker is a claim, and a claim
gets checked at the source.

### The gap

`((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2}` and `-[:T]->{1,2}(y)` are one question. The group spelling compiles to a
repetition UNIT that materializes a per-rep LIST for every inner variable it names; when nothing
downstream reads those lists, that work is pure. The native optimizer has elided it since
`drop_unread_group_binds`; TS had no equivalent.

### The rewrite

`dropUnreadGroupBinds`, composed into `compileLinear` ahead of `unoptionalizeForAggregate`. It
collects every expression anything downstream could read — the projection's items, its ORDER BY
keys, its GROUP BY and HAVING, and the MATCH's own WHERE — takes their free variables, and for
each segment whose unit is ONE plain hop drops `hopFrom`/`hopTo` and the edge variable when none
of the three is mentioned.

Narrow on purpose. A subquery ANYWHERE in those expressions refuses the rewrite outright, which
is item 444's trap and not conservatism: `freePredicateVars` adds a subquery's own pattern names
to its bound set, so an inner `-[e:T]->` that CORRELATES on an already-bound `e` is
indistinguishable from one binding it freshly. With no subquery present, "mentioned" is exactly
what a free-variable walk reports.

### Measured, three alternated rounds, 60,000 vertices / 180,000 edges, one case per process

```
                                                    before             after
```

### Teeth: six mutants under the cap, five caught, control clean

Two survived the first run, and both are instructive.

**M1 (the subquery guard removed)** survived because my subquery case read an OUTER variable.
Item 444's trap needs the inner pattern to REBIND the name:
`COUNT { MATCH (p:P)-[e:T]->(q) }` beside an outer group-bound `e`. TS correlates it against the
per-rep LIST and answers `d=0`; eliding the outer binding makes the inner `e` fresh and answers
`d=3`. With that case added, M1 is caught. **Sixth coinciding-fixture trap in this run of ticks**
— and the first where the coincidence was in the QUERY rather than the data.

**M5 (the MATCH's WHERE not collected) still survives, and the reason is the divergence below.**
A group binding read from a clause WHERE is already null in TS, so eliding it does not change the
count — the guard is correct and becomes load-bearing the moment the divergence is fixed, but it
has no observable today. Recorded rather than papered over: a survivor with a known cause is a
different thing from one nobody looked at.

A harness note worth keeping: the mutation script restored the source after the last mutant but
did not REBUILD, so the next test run read a dist still holding M6. It looked like a new failure
and was the previous mutant. These tests read built dists (`fuzzers-read-built-dists`); a restore
that does not rebuild is not a restore.

### A SEVENTH cross-engine divergence, found by this item's own conformance test

A group binding read from anywhere but the projection's item list is NULL in TS and the per-rep
list in native:

```
WHERE size(e) > 1              ts [{c:0}]   nv [{c:3}]    and the same for x and y
WHERE e IS NULL                ts [{c:6}]   nv [{c:0}]    which is what says it is NULL
FILTER size(e) > 1             ts [{c:0}]   nv [{c:3}]    a separate clause, so not the seed gate
ORDER BY size(e) DESC, k       ts [{k:1},{k:1}]  nv [{k:1},{k:2}]
RETURN size(e)                 ts and nv AGREE            the projection resolves it correctly
```

`bindGroupVarsFlat` does put the lists in the binding Map, so the fault is in how a clause-level
expression resolves the name, not in the matching. Silent wrong rows, so it belongs to the
dangerous VALUE class. Verified pre-existing: it reproduces on HEAD with the rewrite reverted and
the package rebuilt. **Not fixed here** — a correctness fix is its own item, and folding it into
a perf change would make neither reviewable.

An EIGHTH, smaller one fell out of the M1 case: a subquery whose inner pattern rebinds a
group-bound name is `E_SYNTAX` in native and answers in TS. Error against rows, so the narrower
class.

## Item 570 — a per-rep predicate is a BODY FILTER spelled differently, and the algebra can fold it: 17.6x

Item 568's second target, the one it left open. `((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2} RETURN count(*)` costs
1.06ms and the same query with a per-repetition `WHERE` costs 34-42, even though the filtered
query produces FEWER rows.

### Diagnosed, not assumed — and the control is what did it

`WHERE true` costs **49.95ms for the same 719,998 answer as the 1.05ms unfiltered query**. A
predicate that rejects nothing and reads nothing pays the whole penalty, so the cost is the
ROUTE, not the predicate's work. And 719,998 paths in 1.05ms is 1.5ns a path, which no DFS does:
the unfiltered count is answered by `try_varlen_count`'s ALGEBRAIC branch, degree arithmetic in
O(V+E), while any `per_rep_pred` falls to enumeration.

`try_group_count` already carries a `per_rep_pred`, so this was never a missing route. It was the
wrong one.

### The coincidence of two definitions

`rep_pred_ok` builds the rep's mini-scope as node `2p` / edge `2p+1`, so at `k = 1` **slot 2 is
the hop target** (slot 0 is the rep's source, 1 its edge, `2k+1` the path source).
`VarLength::body_filter` is documented as "a predicate on the HOP TARGET, applied at each landing
past the source; a target that fails is PRUNED". At `k = 1` the per-rep check fires at
`len > 0 && len.is_multiple_of(1)` — every landing past the source. Same predicate, same points,
same prune.

So a per-rep predicate reading NOTHING BUT slot 2 is a body filter, and `opt` now flattens it:
`refs_only_slot(p, 2)` guards it (exhaustive over `Expr`, no catch-all) and `remap_slot` retargets
it onto the endpoint. Then the algebra folds it in as a second mask beside the endpoint one — two
masks, because they apply in different places: a 2-hop path `s -> y -> z` needs
`body(y) && body(z) && end(z)`, a 1-hop needs `body(y) && end(y)`, and the zero-length path has no
landing at all so only `end(s)` touches it.

### What the fuzzer caught, which is the item's real lesson

The first version flattened in EVERY mode and `optimizing_preserves_rows_*` failed on all three
seeds immediately (seed 19386, `mode: Simple`). In Simple mode a hop back to the start is a
`Close` step that emits WITHOUT passing through `varlen_enter`; the walker gates it with an
explicit second `rep_pred_ok` call and has no body-filter twin there — because a body filter was
Gremlin-only and Gremlin never sets Simple. The code says so in a comment I had read and not
connected. Flattening a Simple per-rep predicate re-introduced item 242's wrong answer through a
new door.

Restricted to TRAIL/WALK, which costs nothing: the algebra only runs for those two anyway.
ACYCLIC never reaches `Close` and would be safe, but would buy only the cheaper evaluator on an
unmeasured shape, so it is left out deliberately.

### Measured, three alternated rounds, 60,000 vertices / 180,000 edges, one case per process

```
                                               before                after
((x)-[e:T]->(y) WHERE y.age > 50){1,2}    34.79/35.09/36.27    1.98/2.01/1.98   17.6x
((x)-[e:T]->(y) WHERE e.w > 5){1,2}       38.96/38.63/40.91   37.30/37.99/37.88 refused
((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2}                      1.05/1.06/1.06      1.17/1.16/1.16   control
SIMPLE … WHERE y.age > 50 …               36.19/34.14/35.82   33.95/34.08/35.66 control
```

Three controls the change cannot reach — the edge-reading predicate (mini-scope slot 1, refused),
the unfiltered count, and the excluded Simple mode. All flat.

**One honest wrinkle:** the unfiltered row reads 1.05-1.06 before and 1.16-1.17 after, consistently
across all three rounds. That is ~10%, which is exactly where this repo's noise floor sits, on a
1ms total measured min-of-5 — and a plausible mechanism exists (one `body()` call per edge in the
2-hop loop, ~360k calls). Reported rather than argued away. `query_bench` and `bun run bench` show
nothing broader moved, and `spelling_probe` reports NO PERF CLIFFS.

`query_bench` gains the pair: `quantified hop + per-rep target WHERE` 10,820us against
`quantified hop + per-rep EDGE WHERE (refused)` 117,888us — the refusal measured beside the win,
so a regression that silently admits the edge form shows as the second row collapsing onto the
first with a changed answer.

A 225-query cross-engine sweep over mode x bound x predicate-position: 0 divergent.

### Teeth: eight mutants under the cap, seven caught, one proved DEAD

Four of the first seven survived, and the cause is worth more than the fix. **The algebra never
ran in the unit tests.** It is gated on `src.len() * avg_deg.powi(max) > 2 * (nodes + edges)`, and
the three-node fixture gives 8.3 against 16 — so the plan assertions passed while the arithmetic
they were supposed to protect was never executed. A second test with 40 nodes at out-degree 4
(640 against 400) checks RAW AGAINST OPTIMIZED over ten shapes, and three of the four are then
caught.

The fourth, `body(s)` in the trail correction, is UNKILLABLE: the arm is already inside
`body(a.nbr)` with `a.nbr == s`, so the term is provably true there. Dead, not untested — removed
rather than pinned. A ninth mutant deleting the whole trail correction is caught by three existing
tests, which is what says that correction is covered at all.

## Item 571 — a clause WHERE made TS walk a DIFFERENT PATTERN: four wrong answers from one dropped field

Item 569 found that a quantified group's per-rep bindings read as NULL from a clause expression,
pinned both engines' answers and deferred the fix. This is that fix, and the bug is considerably
worse than 569 recorded.

### The cause is one line

```ts
segments: patterns[i].segments.map((s) => ({ rel: s.rel, node: attach(s.node) })),
```

The MATCH compiler's seed-hint loop — which runs **only when the clause has a WHERE** — rebuilt
each segment by listing its fields. `CSegment` is `{ rel; node; unit? }`, so `unit`, the compiled
repetition unit, was dropped. One occurrence; a spread fixes it.

### Why that is not just a missing binding

`walkSegments` reads `unit` to CHOOSE ITS WALKER: `trailEndsUnit` repeats the compiled unit, and
the `undefined` branch is `trailEnds`, the abbreviated single-edge walk. So a clause WHERE did not
blank the group lists — it made TS walk the wrong pattern, and lose the per-repetition filter with
it. Four distinct wrong answers against native, on a 4-node fixture:

```
((x)-[:T]->(m)<-[:T]-(y)){1,2}      WHERE a.n > 0    ts 8   nv 2
((x)-[e:T]->(y) WHERE y.n > 1){1,2} WHERE a.n > 0    ts 8   nv 5   per-rep filter LOST
((x)-[:T]->(m)-[:T]->(y)){1,2}      WHERE a.n > 0    ts 8   nv 5
((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2}               WHERE size(e)>1  ts 0   nv 4
```

Each of those WITHOUT the clause WHERE agreed. **`WHERE a.n > 0` rejects nothing on that fixture,
and adding it changed the answer from 2 to 8.**

Why item 569 saw only the null bindings: for a `k = 1` unit the abbreviated walk and the unit walk
agree on the COUNT, so the damage there was confined to the bindings. `k > 1` is where the row
count itself goes wrong.

### The cost, three alternated rounds, 40,000 vertices / 120,000 edges

```
                                               before                  after
((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2} WHERE size(e) > 1   253.79  answer 0       577.46  answer 359998
((x)-[:T]->(m)-[:T]->(y)){1,2} WHERE …    257.00  answer 469270  4320.69 answer 3518711
((x)-[:T]->(m)-[:T]->(y)){1,2}            4111/4278/4375         4364/4453/4362   control
((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2}                      247.69                 238.45          control
```

The third row is the control that settles it: that pattern ALWAYS cost ~4.3s, with or without the
clause WHERE, so the "after" figures are simply the correct cost. Read the other way round: a
clause WHERE was an accidental **17x speedup that returned the wrong answer** — which is this
repo's equivalent-spelling rule exactly, two spellings of one question differing 17x because one
of them was wrong.

So this item makes two shapes slower and is still unambiguously right. The k=1 shapes, which are
the common ones, are unchanged (247.69 against 238.45), partly because item 569's
`dropUnreadGroupBinds` legitimately removes the unit there when nothing reads the bindings — the
same end state the bug reached by accident.

### THE COVERAGE GAP, which matters as much as the fix

Four wrong answers went past all seven byte-identity fuzzers. The reason: the differential
fuzzer's quantified-group arm emitted `RETURN count(*)` and a projection and **never a clause
`WHERE` after the pattern** — the one position that runs the broken loop. Three WHERE positions
existed in that arm (per-hop inside the brackets, per-repetition after the unit) and this third
one did not.

Added, with `groupClauseWhere=280-329/173-200` of 20,000 and floors at half of measured. Two
details the file's own comments predicted:

- **It is a MODIFIER, not two more entries in `forms`.** As its own form it took `unanchored`
  from one of three to one of five, and `unanchored` is the only spelling that reaches native's
  counting sink — `sinkGenerated` fell to 162 and its floor failed. The floor did exactly its job.
- **It is excluded from `perRepGenerated`.** That detector is "group opener AND contains WHERE",
  and the file warns that three predicate positions have borrowed the counter already; this is the
  fourth, and `CLAUSE_WHERE` is subtracted before the per-rep test rather than left to inflate it.

The detector moved to its own function because `tallyGroupShapes` sits on the complexity gate —
inline it read 36 against a maximum of 35. Third split in this file for that reason.

### Teeth: three mutants under the cap, all three caught

- reverting the spread to the field list → the conformance test
- the fuzzer's clause WHERE replaced with empty strings → the new `groupClauseWhereGenerated` floor
- the clause WHERE restored as its own `forms` entry → `sinkGenerated`, the dilution floor

The new test carries its own 4-node fixture, because the shared 3-node one has in-degree 1
everywhere and answers ZERO for a reversed unit — a coinciding fixture where right and wrong both
round to nothing.

## Item 572 — a per-rep predicate is ONE TRAVERSAL: 16.9-20.6x, and the right abstraction was the finding

Item 570 closed the TARGET-only per-repetition predicate by flattening it onto
`VarLength::body_filter` and folding it into the degree algebra as a node mask. It left the edge
case open. Pricing the rest of the position enum first, 60,000 vertices / 180,000 edges:

```
WHERE y.age > 50               2.00 ms   done at 570 (node mask)
WHERE e.w > 5                 37.29      the EDGE
WHERE x.age > 50              32.61      the rep SOURCE
WHERE y.age > 50 AND e.w > 5  43.81      both at once
[e:T WHERE e.w > 5] inline    37.39      same cost, so the spellings are consistent
WHERE a.age > 50              rejected   "unknown variable" from a SUBPATH where
```

**The `AND` row is what settled the design.** A node mask beside an edge mask cannot express
`y.age > 50 AND e.w > 5` — the predicate does not factor into them. But at `k = 1` a per-rep
predicate is a function of exactly `(x, e, y)`, which is ONE EDGE TRAVERSAL, and the algebra only
runs for `Dir::Out`, where an edge id fixes all three. So a single mask indexed by edge id carries
a target test, an edge test, a source test and any conjunction of them. One abstraction, four rows.

### What was built

- `traversal_pass_mask` in `exec/varlen.rs`, the edge twin of `node_pass_mask`: blocks of 4096
  edges, each evaluated with slot 0 = source, 1 = edge, 2 = target.
- The degree algebra EXTRACTED from `try_varlen_count` into `try_degree_algebra`, taking three
  independent filters — `end_pred` (the path's last node), `body` (every landing, item 570) and
  `trav` (one traversal, this item). They apply at different places, which is why they are three:
  a 2-hop `s -> y -> z` over edges `a`, `b` is counted when
  `trav(a) && body(y) && trav(b) && body(z) && end(z)`.
- `try_group_count`'s `RepeatGroup` arm now attempts it, so the EDGE and SOURCE cases reach a
  closed form without the `opt` flatten they cannot use.

### Measured, three alternated rounds, one case per process

```
                                       before                 after
WHERE e.w > 5                    37.94/38.70/37.49     1.80/1.88/1.82   20.6x
WHERE x.age > 50                 32.38/32.41/32.77     1.71/1.72/1.73   18.9x
WHERE y.age > 50 AND e.w > 5     44.12/44.30/46.20     2.61/2.64/2.63   16.9x
-[e:T WHERE a.age > 50]->{1,2}   32.27/31.99/33.50    32.21/32.63/33.03 control
SIMPLE … WHERE e.w > 5           42.68/38.40/37.56    37.30/37.67/37.56 control
((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2}             1.20/1.16/1.15       0.84/0.89/0.84   control
```

Answers identical throughout. Two controls flat and one improved. A 425-query cross-engine sweep
over mode x bound x 14 predicate positions: 0 divergent — **on a 60-node / 242-edge fixture,
chosen so `est_paths` is 960 against the algebra's threshold of 600.** The first version of that
sweep used 6 nodes and 9 edges, where the figure is 13.5 against 30 and the closed form never
runs; a clean sweep over that proves nothing. Item 570 learned this by having four mutants
survive, and it nearly cost the same twice.

### THE GUARD THAT MATTERS: slot 3

`max_slot(p) <= 2` is the test, and the excluded case is real rather than theoretical.
`-[e:T WHERE a.age > 50]->{1,2}(y)` — an inline bracket `WHERE` on an abbreviated var-length hop
referencing the OUTER ANCHOR — parses, lowers to a `k = 1` RepeatGroup, and puts the anchor at
mini-scope slot `2k+1`. That is not a function of one traversal (the anchor varies per path) and
the mask's mini-batch has only three columns, so admitting it reads a column that is not there.
The mutant widening the bound to `<= 3` survived the whole suite until a case for it existed.

Subqueries are excluded outright. `max_slot` already reports `outer_width - 1` for one, but
relying on that is fragile, and a correlated subquery run once per EDGE IN THE STORE would cost
more than the enumeration being replaced.

### Teeth: eight mutants under the cap, seven caught, one unkillable

Three survived the first run and each had its own cause.

- **The slot bound (above).** A missing test, now written.
- **Swallowing the mask's `Err`** survived because of a COINCIDING FIXTURE — sixth in this run of
  ticks. I had set the edge weights to `eid % 4` and the predicate was `<= 5`, so it rejected
  nothing and the filtered and unfiltered counts were identical. `% 10` separates them.
- **Defaulting an endpoint-less edge** is unkillable: the loop runs over `0..edge_count`, so
  `edge_endpoints` cannot return `None`. Documented as an invariant guard rather than pinned.

The fault-fallback test needed two corrections of its own, and the second is a finding.
`e.w + 1 <= 5` on a string does NOT raise — it is null — so the first version was vacuous. And a
per-repetition predicate NEVER raises whatever is in it: `rep_pred_ok` ends in
`.unwrap_or(false)`, "a false / null / faulting predicate fails the rep". The mask is built with
`filter_keep`, which does raise, so the same value is poison there and inert in the walk. The test
now proves the fault through the non-group spelling, which is the evaluator the mask actually uses.

### A NINTH cross-engine divergence, found by that test

```
MATCH (a:Q)((x)-[e:T]->(y) WHERE CAST(e.w AS INTEGER) <= 5){1,2} RETURN count(*)
  ts      ERR E_INVALID_VALUE
  native  [{c:1}]            the fault fails the rep, and the walk continues

MATCH (a:Q)-[e:T]->(y) WHERE CAST(e.w AS INTEGER) <= 5 RETURN count(*)   BOTH raise
```

The agreeing line makes it precise: the divergence is the PER-REP POSITION, where native's
`rep_pred_ok` swallows a fault and TS propagates it. Verified pre-existing on the pre-572 build.
Error against rows, so the narrower class. Recorded, not fixed.

### The one position still enumerating

`query_bench` gains a third row for it, so it stays visible:
`quantified hop + per-rep PATH-SOURCE WHERE` at 304,725us against the target row's 7,978 — 38x,
and the biggest remaining gap in this family. It is not a traversal question but a per-SOURCE-ROW
one: the anchor is constant along a path, so the predicate is a seed filter. A different lever,
and deliberately not taken here.

The 570 row's label was also corrected: `per-rep EDGE WHERE (refused)` is no longer refused, and
its 117,888us is now 20,006. It stays beside the target row because the two reach the closed form
by DIFFERENT routes — a node mask via `opt`, a traversal mask via `try_group_count` — and on that
fixture the edge mask is the dearer of the two (350,000 edges to ask about against 200,000 nodes).
