## Item 573 — the TS var-length count was ALGORITHMIC, not the layout ceiling: 9.3x

Items 570 and 572 made native's quantified count a closed form. Pricing the TS side of the same
family against it, 40,000 vertices / 120,000 edges, one case per process:

```
MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->{1,2}(y) RETURN count(*)        ts 300.22ms   nv 0.61   491x
MATCH (a:P)((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2} RETURN count(*)     252.74          0.65  391x
… WHERE y.age > 50 (per-rep)                         466.14          1.15  404x
… -[:T]->{1,2}(y) WHERE y.age > 50 (endpoint)        367.43          1.55  237x
```

**237-491x is NOT item 566's ceiling.** That item measured 82-248x on filtered SCANS and
attributed it to data layout — a correct finding about a per-row constant. This is a different
thing: 479,998 paths against a V+E of 160,000, so TS was enumerating where native computes. The
test is whether closing the ALGORITHM leaves a ratio in item 566's band, and it does.

### What was built

`varLengthDegreeCount` and `detectVarLengthCount` in `executor/shortcuts.ts`, mirroring native's
`try_degree_algebra` for `max <= 2`, `Dir out`, WALK or TRAIL: a 1-hop path is one wanted
out-edge whose target passes; a 2-hop `s -> y -> z` is one such edge times `y`'s own passing
out-degree; a TRAIL subtracts the single self-loop path that reuses its edge; `{0,n}` adds one
row per source whose endpoint is the source itself.

The GROUP spelling reaches the same rung through item 569's `dropUnreadGroupBinds`, so the two
spellings cannot diverge in cost — `bun run spelling`'s item-569 group now reads 223.80 / 220.11
/ 221.11 against 1131 / 1278 / 1122 when that group was added, with all three within 1.02x.

### Measured, three alternated rounds

```
                                       before                 after
-[:T]->{1,2}(y)                 313.15/295.70/312.02   36.46/31.92/41.78    9.3x
((x)-[e:T]->(y)){1,2}           272.11/269.28/256.27   32.66/32.20/31.21    8.2x
SIMPLE -[:T]->{1,2}(y)          361.52/333.62/338.15  318.51/337.44/316.56  control
-[:T]->{1,3}(y)                 931.96/929.36/881.64  899.71/944.81/965.43  control
-[:T]->(y) (one hop)                 0.01                  0.01             control
```

A later rewrite (below) took the first row to **19.73**, so the end-to-end figure is ~15x. The
TS/native ratio goes from ~400x to ~30x, which IS item 566's band — the remaining gap is the
constant factor that item measured, and this item does not claim to have touched it.

Three controls, all flat. A fourth measurement was discarded: a single non-alternated pass showed
SIMPLE at 302 -> 469 and `{1,3}` at 849 -> 928, which looked like two regressions and is run
variance — both are flat under alternation. The TS spelling probe's note that single runs are
bimodal applies to this probe too.

### THE BUG THE REPO'S OWN SUITE CAUGHT

First version summed per-label `set.size` for the degree. A MULTI-LABEL edge sits in several of
a vertex's adjacency buckets, so it was counted once per label it carries, and
`multi-label-edges.test.ts` ("a reachability walk visits each edge once") answered **8 where the
walk answers 3**.

My own 448-query cross-engine sweep had `[:T|U]` cases and passed them, because that fixture's T
and U edges were DISJOINT — right and wrong agreed. Seventh coinciding fixture in this run of
ticks, and the first one the existing suite caught rather than a probe.

The fix is to use `edgesOfTypes`, which already dedupes through a `Set` and keeps the O(1) route
for a single wanted type and for a single-bucket graph. It is also FASTER than the arithmetic it
replaced — 38.83ms to 19.73 — because that helper hands back the bucket itself when it can, so
the degree is a set SIZE rather than a walk.

### Correctness

- 448-query cross-engine sweep: 5 starts x 6 relationship forms (out, reversed, undirected,
  multi-type, unknown type) x 7 bounds, 6 endpoint forms x 7 bounds x 5 modes, the group
  spelling, a trailing clause WHERE, a non-count projection. 0 divergent.
- 32 unbounded (`+`, `*`, `{1,}`, `{2,}`) on their own 4-node ACYCLIC fixture. 0 divergent.
  They need one: `*` in TRAIL mode over a 24-node degree-3 CYCLE enumerates every trail in the
  graph and does not finish — two probe runs hit the 600s timeout with no output before I
  separated them.
- `varlen-degree-count.test.ts`, whose 30 pins were taken FROM the native engine and then
  checked for coherence, not hand-derived. Three of my hand values were wrong in the same
  direction — forgetting that the multi-label edge is also a T edge — and the cross-engine
  assertion is what caught it. Deriving a pin by hand and asserting it is how a fixture that
  disagrees with the engine gets committed.

### Teeth: ten mutants under the cap, all ten caught

The 1-hop term, the 2-hop term, the zero-length term, the trail correction, the trail
correction's `passes` test, the degree ignoring `passes` when it can use a set size, admitting
`max = 3`, admitting SIMPLE/ACYCLIC, admitting a path SELECTOR, and the per-label-size sum.

Two needed a case written first. The selector mutant survived until the test carried one — and
each selector is a different number (`ANY SHORTEST` 9, `ALL SHORTEST` 13, `ANY` 9, `ALL` 15,
against the default walk's 15). `ALL` happens to agree and is still refused: agreement on one
fixture is not a proof.

**A guard that declines everything measures exactly like one that is absent.** `selector` defaults
to the string `'walk'`, not to `undefined`, so my first guard (`!== undefined`) refused every
query — and the only symptom was that the measurement showed no change at all. Worth remembering
as a diagnosis: an optimization that measures as a perfect no-op is more likely to be unreachable
than ineffective.

/ 0 fail (+5), `bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0 (after bundling the eight

## Item 574 — a Gremlin hop CHAIN count, 3.8-4.5x, and a refusal that was a divergence

Five items running had been the GQL quantified-path family, so this priced a surface none of them
touched. The Gremlin bench covers one-hop shapes only; the chain had no coverage and no rung.
40,000 vertices / 120,000 edges, one case per process:

```
V().hasLabel(P).out(T).count()            ts   0.01ms   nv 0.11   the existing rung
V().hasLabel(P).out(T).out(T).count()         139.85       0.41   341x, no rung
repeat(out(T)).times(2).count()               151.52       0.59   255x
repeat(out(T)).times(1).count()                40.95       0.10   396x
repeat(out(T)).times(3).count()               THREW        8.31   a DIVERGENCE
```

That last row is the find: TS raised **"repeat() exceeded the trail budget"** where native answers
1,080,000. A budget that exists to stop a fan-out materializing rows was bounding a bare COUNT,
which materializes none — the same argument native's own
`a_group_count_is_not_bounded_by_the_trail_budget` makes for GQL, unfixed on the Gremlin side.

### What was built

- `hopChainCount` — a chain of two or more `out`/`in` hops, counted by FRONTIER MULTIPLICITY
  propagation: O(k · E) edge visits for k hops, whatever the path count. The last hop needs no
  map (a frontier vertex contributes `multiplicity × degree`), and TWO hops need none at all,
  because every multiplicity on the initial frontier is 1.
- `expandRepeats` — a PRE-PASS turning an eligible `repeat(<one hop>).times(k)` into its k
  chained hops, so every rung in the file sees a shape it already understands. That is why
  `times(1)` goes to 0.01ms: it lands on the existing bucket read.

### TINKERPOP GROUND TRUTH, which is what licenses the expansion

`repeat(h).times(k)` being the k-fold chain is a semantic claim, so it was checked against a real
`tinkerpop/gremlin-console:3.7.3` over a 6-vertex fixture **with a self-loop and a parallel pair**,
where any edge- or vertex-uniqueness restriction would show:

```
out1 14   out2 33   out3 78          times1 14   times2 33   times3 78
times2emit 47 (= 14 + 33)            both1 28    both2 134   mixed 34   in2 33
```

Both lenke engines match all of them. `times2emit` is the sum over depths, not the product, which
is why `emit` is refused rather than expanded.

**One deviation found while doing it:** `repeat(out).times(0).count()` is **14 in TinkerPop** and
**6 in both lenke engines** — TinkerPop runs the body once, lenke passes the input through. A
third-party conformance deviation, not a cross-engine one, same class as item 417's
`inject`+`limit(0)`. Pinned at current behaviour; the expansion declines `times < 1` so this item
does not touch it.

### Measured, three alternated rounds

```
                                   before                 after
out(T).out(T).count()        93.81/97.39/98.04     24.99/31.65/29.85    3.8x
repeat(out).times(2)        113.76/110.56/100.61   22.48/28.10/25.05    4.5x
repeat(out).times(1)         32.31/29.56/28.39      0.01                lands on the bucket rung
repeat(out).times(3)         THREW all three        59.30/66.68         divergence closed
repeat(out).times(2).emit() 114.56/113.79/108.51  132.63/141.70/127.31  control — SEE BELOW
```

**The control looked like a 1.17x regression and is not.** Bands that do not overlap, consistent
in direction over three rounds — so it got its own isolated harness, one shape per process, min
of 9, four alternated rounds: **103.43 → 100.46, flat.** The apparent regression was an artifact
of measuring five shapes in ONE process: the four shapes ahead of it got faster, which changed
the JIT and GC state it ran in. Item 423's "one case per process" rule is exactly this, and this
is the first time in this run of ticks that violating it manufactured a regression rather than
hiding a win.

### The bug the sweep caught: the guard read `> 1`

A 146-case cross-engine sweep found **13 divergences, every one an `out()` at depth 2 or more**.
`out()` with no labels iterates EVERY adjacency bucket, so a multi-type edge is visited once per
label it carries — and the guard covered `labels.length > 1` but not `=== 0`. `out(T,U)` was never
among the 13, because that case the narrow guard did catch.

Correct condition: `labels.length !== 1`. Exactly one wanted label is unconditionally safe; zero
or several need `multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`.

**Item 573 shipped this same bug on the GQL side one tick earlier.** Twice in two ticks is not bad
luck: a per-label bucket sum is only a degree when the wanted set is a single bucket.

### Teeth: thirteen mutants under the cap, ten caught

Three survive with established reasons, and the reasons differ:

- **a one-hop chain not deferred** and **`times(0)` admitted** are ANSWER-EQUIVALENT reroutes. A
  single hop through this rung computes the same degree sum the one-hop rung does; `times(0)`
  expands to zero hops, declines, and lands on the same label count. Both guards are kept for
  route clarity, not for an answer.
- **the two-hop arm removed** is PERF-ONLY — the general propagation answers identically. Its
  evidence is the measurement, not a test: 33.56/33.00/31.70 → 26.83/24.26/25.89 over three
  alternated rounds, 1.31x.

Two needed a case written first. `until()` admitted needed a `repeat().until()` case; a multi-step
repeat BODY needed a TS-only pin, because `planToGremlin` emits `repeat(out('T').out('T'))` and
native's parser rejects that text — see below. And the multi-type guard mutants both survived
until the test grew a fixture with a multi-label edge, which TinkerPop cannot express (a
TinkerGraph edge carries exactly one label), so that block pins cross-engine with native as
reference.

### Two findings recorded, not fixed

- **An eleventh divergence:** native's Gremlin parser rejects a multi-step `repeat()` body —
  `repeat(out('T').out('T'))` is "expected RParen" — where TS answers 185. Pre-existing
  (reproduces with this rung reverted). A parser gap, separate scope.
- **The budget divergence is only half closed.** `times(k)` escapes it; `emit()` does not. At the
  Gremlin bench's 1,000,000 edges the `emit` shape still raises on the TS side where native
  answers, which is why it is not a bench row — a row that always errors measures nothing.

`bench:gremlin` gains `V().out().out().count()` and `V().repeat(out).times(2).count()`.

### Gates

`bun test packages/gremlin packages/gql packages/core` 3586 pass / 0 fail, `bun test
packages/native/src` 908 pass / 0 fail (+6), `bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0
(after splitting `hopChainCount` at the complexity gate — 43 against 35 — the same split
`tallyGroupShapes` makes), `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean, `bun run build` exit 0, all
seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/13, `bun run bench` in band, `bun run bench:gremlin` clean.
CI green on 573.

## Item 575 — the PATH SOURCE closes the per-rep enum: ~42x, and a zero-length path has no reps

Item 572 left one position in the `k = 1` per-repetition predicate enum enumerating, and
`query_bench` priced it: `quantified hop + per-rep PATH-SOURCE WHERE` at 304,725us against the
traversal case's 7,978.

### Why it is a different lever

The mini-scope `rep_pred_ok` builds at `k = 1` is node `2p` / edge `2p+1` plus the PATH SOURCE at
slot `2k+1` = 3. Slots 0-2 are one traversal, which item 572 folds in as an edge-indexed mask.
Slot 3 is not a traversal at all — the anchor varies per path, so no edge-indexed mask expresses
it — but it is CONSTANT ALONG a path, so it either admits every repetition from a source or none.
That makes it a filter on the source ROW.

So `try_degree_algebra` gains a third mask: `seed`, built by `node_pass_mask(p, 3, store)`.

### THE SUBTLETY, which a probe found before the code was written

A ZERO-LENGTH path has NO REPETITIONS, so a per-repetition predicate never runs for it and the row
is emitted whatever the predicate says. On a 4-node ring where `a.age > 25` admits two of four
sources, both engines agree:

```
-[e:T WHERE a.age > 25]->{1,2}(y)   4   two sources x (1 + 1)
-[e:T WHERE a.age > 25]->{0,2}(y)   8 = 4 filtered hop paths + 4 zero-length rows, one per SOURCE
-[e:T WHERE a.age > 25]->{0,0}(y)   4,  the predicate irrelevant
```

So the seed mask gates the HOP terms and NOT the `min == 0` term. Gating both answers 6 and 2. I
checked this with a probe BEFORE designing the mask rather than after writing it, which is the
only reason the first version was right — the mutant that gates both terms is caught now, but it
would have shipped as the design.

### Measured, three alternated rounds, 60,000 vertices / 180,000 edges

```
                                        before                 after
-[e:T WHERE a.age > 50]->{1,2}(y)  33.39/33.24/32.64     0.82/0.80/0.78   41.8x
-[e:T WHERE a.age > 50]->{0,2}(y)  32.73/32.54/32.60     0.82/0.77/0.83   42.3x
((x)-[e:T]->(y) WHERE e.w > 5){1,2} 1.89/1.89/2.08       1.91/1.96/1.96   control
SIMPLE … WHERE a.age > 50 …        32.67/32.93/32.52    32.87/33.43/32.37 control
-[:T]->{1,2}(y)                     0.88/0.90/0.89       0.87/0.86/0.88   control
```

Answers identical, three controls flat. A 385-query cross-engine sweep over mode x bound x 7
predicate forms, with endpoint filters, labels, a mixed `AND e.w` predicate and a non-count
projection: 0 divergent — on a 60-node / 242-edge fixture chosen so `est_paths` (960) clears the
algebra's threshold (604), which is the trap items 570 and 572 both paid for.

`query_bench` reads 3,035us against the old 304,725 — **100x** at that fixture, and now the
CHEAPEST of the three per-rep rows (3,035 against the target mask's 8,112 and the traversal mask's
20,542). That ordering is the right way round: a node mask over 200,000 nodes is cheaper than a
traversal mask over 350,000 edges, and a seed filter prunes before any walk begins. The `{0,n}`
twin is a second row, so a regression that gates the zero-length term shows as its answer dropping
while the first row holds.

### Teeth: six mutants under the cap, five caught, one proved DEAD

Caught: gating the zero-length term, removing the seed gate, the wrong guard slot, the wrong mask
slot, and swallowing the mask's `Err`.

The fault mutant needed a case written first, and it needed `CAST` rather than arithmetic — item
572 records that `k + 1` on a string is NULL, not an error, which made an earlier fault test
vacuous. The case is a `:Q` vertex no `(a:P)` walk reaches, carrying a string `k`, with an
assertion that the value really does fault `filter_keep`.

The sixth — a second `*k == 1` test inside `eligible` — is UNKILLABLE: the branch that uses it
already requires `*k == 1`. Removed rather than pinned, exactly as item 570's `body(s)` term was.
That is now twice in this run of ticks that a guard written for symmetry turned out to be dead,
and both times mutation was what said so.

### The enum is closed

Every `k = 1` per-repetition predicate position now reaches a closed form: the target node and
any traversal conjunction (570, 572), and the path source (575). What remains is `k > 1`, where a
predicate reads several edges and is not a traversal question, and the `emit`-style shapes on the
Gremlin side (574).

NO PERF CLIFFS, `query_bench` in band, `bun test packages/native/src` 908 pass / 0 fail, `bun run

## Item 576 — `createIndex` built an index on the WRONG ELEMENT, silently: a 500x cliff turned into an error

Six items running had been the quantified-path family, so this priced `bench:usage` — the serving
axis (small ops on a warm graph, interleaved read/write) that none of them touched.

### What the table said

TS-indexed usually BEATS native there, because the FFI boundary dominates a small op (point
lookup 1.20M against 353.4k). Two rows buck that, and they are the leads:

```
interleaved: append + link    ts(+) 55.9k   engine(+) 176.3k   0.32x
read: keyed dedup lookup            74.7k             136.5k   0.55x
interleaved: write + point read     319.5k            160.6k   2.0x  (the usual direction)
```

`append + link` is also 4-6x below its own interleaved siblings, so it got the decomposition.

### The decomposition found the bug, not the target

Writing the probe is where it surfaced. Its `lookup` case measured **2.3k ops/s** against the
bench's 1.20M for the same query — a 500x gap that meant my probe was on the unindexed path. The
cause was my own `createIndex({ on: 'node', … })`: the bench uses `'vertex'`.

`Graph.createIndex` validated the index KIND and nothing else, and the branch using the target
read

```ts
const [key] = spec.keys;                      // `undefined` when keys is []
if (spec.on === 'vertex') { … } else { … }    // `else` catches 'node', a typo, AND missing
```

So an unknown target took the EDGE arm and built an **edge index on a vertex key**. Not an ignored
call — an index on the wrong element, which no seek consults. `'node'` is the natural word for a
GQL engine; it is what my own memory note had recorded for this API.

Three silent wrongs, all three rejected by the native engine:

```
{ on: 'node',   kind: 'hash', keys: ['name'] }        an EDGE index; 1.20M -> 2.3k, no error
{ on: 'vertex', kind: 'hash', keys: [] }              an index keyed `undefined`
{ on: 'vertex', kind: 'hash', keys: ['a', 'b'] }      a one-key index, the rest dropped
```

The last two TYPE-CHECK: core's `IndexSpec` is `{ on; kind; keys: string[] }`, a loose cross
product, where the native package's is a discriminated union whose arity is a compile error. So a
fully typed caller can hit them. `on: 'node'` is a compile error for a typed caller and silent for
a JS or dynamic one.

Now all three throw `E_INVALID_GRAPH_OP`, the code the one existing check already used. `edge` +
`hash` stays accepted: core keeps a property index per side and one structure serves both seeks,
so that is a real core capability the native engine lacks, not a mistake.

**A twelfth cross-engine divergence, closed** — and the costly side was the silent one.

### No perf claim, and the control says so

`createIndex` runs once at setup, so the two added checks cannot touch a per-op rate. Three
alternated rounds of the most sensitive row confirm it: ts(+) 1.01M/1.11M/1.05M against
1.19M/1.12M/1.00M — overlapping bands, no direction — with the native columns (which no TS change
can reach) unmoved.

### Teeth: five mutants under the cap, all five caught

Removing the target check, narrowing it to vertex-only, removing the arity check, and loosening it
in each direction. The test asserts the index landed on the VERTEX side
(`edgePropertyIndex.isIndexed('name')` is false), which is the bug's actual signature — asserting
only that a throw happens would miss a check that throws for the wrong reason.

### The target this priced, with a REFUTED hypothesis

With the probe finally on the indexed path, `append + link` decomposes cleanly (one case per
process, best of three 250ms windows):

```
lookup (MATCH only)                     1349.4k ops/s
match+set (the 319.5k sibling's shape)   407.1k
insert-edge-only (edge between two)      174.1k
insert-bare+edge (new node, NO props)    156.6k
insert-node+edge (new node WITH props)    49.6k   <- the bench's 55.9k
```

Same statement, same pattern, same edge; the only difference is `{id, amount}` on the new node —
**3.2x**. Narrowing further: a bare `INSERT (:Entry)` is 471.5k, one property takes it to 161.3k
(2.9x), and a second only to ~146k. So it is a FIXED entry cost for having any properties, not a
per-property cost, and `id` — the identity property — is no dearer than a plain one (159.0k
against 161.3k).

**Index maintenance is NOT the cause.** The obvious hypothesis was the insert touching each
indexed key; with the indexes dropped the gap is identical (507.8k -> 163.8k, 3.1x, against
499.6k -> 165.1k with two indexes). Refuted and recorded rather than carried forward as a belief.

So the next target is the property path itself on insert, and it is priced.

> **RETRACTED at item 577.** The paragraph above is WRONG, and so is the decomposition it rests
> on. Properties on an inserted node cost NOTHING measurable: passed as a PARAMETER, one property
> reads 479.8k against a bare node's 482.7k, and two read 500.9k. The 2.9x was my own probe — the
> bare case reused ONE query string while every property case interpolated a changing value into
> the TEXT, so the property cases were parse+plan cache MISSES and the baseline was not.
>
> The control that settles it: a BARE `INSERT (:Entry)` with a changing comment in its text reads
> **182.2k against 482.7k**. No properties at all, same 2.6x. The cost is the changing query text.
>
> I refuted the index hypothesis and then failed to question the measurement the surviving
> hypothesis rested on. A decomposition is only as good as its baseline, and mine differed from
> the cases in a second way I had not controlled for.

### Gates

(+4), `bun test packages/native/src` 908 pass / 0 fail, `bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint`
exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean, `bun run build` exit 0, all seven byte-identity
fuzzers 13/13, `bun run bench` in band. CI green on 575.

## Item 577 — item 576's target RETRACTED: the cost was the query TEXT, and the bench was measuring the parser

Item 576 priced `interleaved: append + link` as the biggest TS deficit in `bench:usage` (55.9k
against native's 176.3k) and decomposed it to "properties on an inserted node cost 2.9x". That is
wrong, and re-measuring it was the first thing this item did.

### The retraction

With the value passed as a PARAMETER instead of interpolated into the query text:

```
bare-const        (no props, one query string)      482.7k ops/s
prop-param        (ONE property, via $a)            479.8k      <- no cost at all
two-props-param                                     500.9k
id-param          (the identity property)           547.2k
prop-interp       (value in the TEXT)               157.3k
bare-interp-uniq  (NO props, changing text)         182.2k      <- the control
```

`bare-interp-uniq` is the row that settles it: a node with **no properties at all** costs 2.6x
when the query text changes per operation. Properties are free; a changing query text is a
parse+plan cache miss.

Item 576's decomposition had a baseline that differed from its cases in a SECOND way, and I did
not control for it — the bare case reused one string, every property case interpolated. I had
already refuted the index-maintenance hypothesis in that item, which is exactly the circumstance
in which the surviving hypothesis deserves the same scepticism and did not get it.

### The bench was measuring the parser

Four `bench:usage` rows interpolate a changing value into the query text, so each operation is a
cache miss. On the identical `append + link` statement: **51.1k interpolated against 151.4k
parameterized, 3.0x.** The row's 55.9k was never the write.

Confirmed on `write: append node`, three alternated rounds, one row per process:

```
                       ts(+)                      engine(+)                wasm(+)
interpolated   130.9k / 97.6k / 129.8k    366.6k/359.6k/342.4k    340.1k/330.8k/331.9k
parameterized  442.4k / 442.7k / 384.4k   260.6k/262.2k/255.4k    237.1k/234.0k/232.0k
```

**Parameterizing is not uniformly better, and that is the interesting part.** TS gains 3.4-3.9x
because the plan cache starts hitting; native LOSES 1.37x and wasm 1.42x, consistently in all
three rounds — binding three parameters across the FFI costs native more than re-parsing a small
`INSERT`. A genuine native observation, and a target in its own right.

### What changed in the instrument

- `write: append node` stays INTERPOLATED and gains a `[params]` twin. Neither form is the "pure"
  write, so the PAIR prices the parse/bind axis — one row alone hides whichever cost it does not
  pay. Measured as a pair: 128.6k/367.1k interpolated against 386.9k/255.5k parameterized.
- `write: append then delete node` is parameterized: only its INSERT half was paying a cache miss,
  so the two halves the row exists to compare were not comparable. ts(+) 148.7k -> 295.5k; native
  139.3k -> 130.8k, inside this bench's own 1.097x floor.
- `interleaved: append + link` is parameterized: 61.5k -> 172.3k on the TS side and native 184.5k
  -> 221.1k, so it is better for BOTH and nothing argues for the old form. Against native it is
  now 0.78x rather than 0.32x — in line with the rest of the table rather than an outlier.

### What survives as a target

`read: keyed dedup lookup` — ts(+) 74.7k against native's 136.5k — is NOT an artifact: that row
already uses a parameter (`WHERE u.score = $s AND u.active = true`). It is the real remaining TS
deficit in this bench and is unpriced.

And the native param-binding cost above: 1.37x on a three-parameter INSERT, measured, with the
interpolated twin as the control.

### Gates

No engine change, so no fuzzers or mutation: this item retracts a claim and fixes an instrument.
`bun test packages/core packages/gql packages/gremlin packages/serialization` 3734 pass / 0 fail,
`bun test packages/native/src` 908 pass / 0 fail, `bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit
0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean. CI green on 576.

## Item 578 — the dedup row is the CEILING, not a rung; and the probe that should watch the pair cannot

Item 577 left `read: keyed dedup lookup` as the one surviving TS deficit in `bench:usage` —
ts(+) 74.7k against native's 136.5k — and said it was unpriced. This prices it, and the answer is
that it is not a target.

### The seek works; the 1.8x is the per-row constant

`MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.score = $s AND u.active = true RETURN count(*)` over 20,000 users, with
`score` indexed and 200 matches a seek:

```
u.name = $n          (1 match, same index kind)   1550.1k ops/s
u.score = $s         (200 matches)                  93.1k
u.score = $s AND u.active = true                    88.9k
u.active = true AND u.score = $s  (order swapped)   90.0k
u.active = true      (MUST scan — the reference)     3.4k
```

**27x above the scan reference**, so the index seek is taken. 93.1k over 200 matches is 54ns a
row, against item 566's measured TS per-row floor of ~61ns — so the row is AT the floor, and
native's 136.5k is 37ns a row. A 1.5x per-row constant is item 566's data-layout ceiling, not a
missing route. **The target is retracted.**

Swapping the conjuncts changes nothing (88.9k against 90.0k), so there is no written-order cliff
here either.

### A real gap, in a shape no instrument watches

The inline spelling of the same question is slower in TS:

```
MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.score = $s AND u.active = true   clause
MATCH (u:User {score: $s}) WHERE u.active = true        inline
```

Three interleaved rounds, standalone probe at 20,000 users:

```
1000 matches a seek (score = i % 20)    clause 21.3/20.8/21.8k   inline 11.5/14.4/14.7k   1.41x
  20 matches a seek (score = i % 1000)  clause  310/385/608k     inline  323/479/480k     unresolvable
```

Consistent in direction in every round at 1000 matches, and unresolvable at 20 — which is itself
the evidence that the cost is PER ROW rather than per query. **Native shows no gap** (inline
145.3k against clause 137.2k, inline slightly ahead), so it is TS-side.

My first measurement of this was 1.36x at 200 matches, and a second run of the same pair REVERSED
it (clause 55.6k against inline 62.9k) with the clause form itself moving 1.6x between runs. That
is the bimodality `ts-spelling-probe` records, and the only reason the finding stands is the
interleaved rounds at a selectivity where the gap exceeds it.

### Why nothing was watching it — the transferable part

`spelling-probe` has the exact pair already (item 230's group:
`MATCH (n:P {k: 2}) WHERE n.s = 's1'` beside `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 2 AND n.s = 's1'`), and it
does not flag, for two reasons it cannot fix from inside:

- **It creates NO INDEX** — `createIndex` appears zero times in the file. With no index there is
  no seek, so no seek-versus-recheck asymmetry exists to find.
- **It binds NO PARAMETERS.** Its own comment says so and delegates the case onward: _"a param
  conjunct is the other member worth having … but this probe runs every query without parameters,
  so it has no place to bind one. It is covered by `bench:usage`'s `read: keyed dedup lookup`,
  which is exactly that mixed shape."_

But that row is a SINGLE row, not a pair — so the delegation pointed at something that was never a
comparison. The gap had no watcher at either end.

### What changed

`bench:usage` gains `read: keyed dedup lookup [inline]` beside the existing row, so the pair lives
where parameters and indexes already exist. The comment carries the measured numbers AND the
honest limit: at this fixture's 200 matches the pair CANNOT resolve the gap — three runs in one
process gave clause 69.3k/20.9k/69.3k against inline 48.1k/56.5k/15.8k, swings of 3.3x and 3.6x
with the direction disagreeing, while the native columns over the same runs are steady. The pair
is worth more than the one row it joins (a change hitting one spelling becomes visible at all),
but the gap itself needs a standalone probe at ~1000 matches a seek.

**The better fix is the instrument**, and it is now named as the next target: give `spelling-probe`
an index and a way to bind parameters. Every historical index-seeding bug in this engine was a
spelling that seeded against one that did not, and the probe built to catch exactly that cannot
see any of them, because it never builds an index.

### Gates

No engine change — this item retracts a target, adds a bench row and records a coverage gap, so
there is nothing to mutate or fuzz. `bun test packages/core packages/gql packages/gremlin
packages/serialization` 3734 pass / 0 fail, `bun test packages/native/src` 908 pass / 0 fail,
`bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean.
CI green on 577.

## Item 579 — `spelling-probe` gets an INDEX and PARAMETERS, and flags a 1.3-1.6x the moment it can see one

Item 578 found that the probe built to catch equivalent-spelling cliffs could not see the one class
that caused every historical index-seeding bug: `createIndex` appeared ZERO times in the file and
it bound no parameters. Its own comment delegated the param case to `bench:usage`'s
`read: keyed dedup lookup`, which was a single row and therefore never a comparison. This closes
that.

### What changed

- `timed(q, params?)` takes parameters.
- The per-group body is extracted into `runGroup(name, spellings, params?)`, so one comparison
  path serves both passes.
- A **seek pass** runs after the existing groups, with `k` and `s` indexed. The indexes are
  created THERE, after the unindexed groups, so every number recorded against those groups stays
  comparable — no second fixture and no extra memory.
- The indexed keys are PRINTED. A seek group that silently measures a scan is worthless and looks
  fine; item 576 is the precedent, where `createIndex` built an index on the wrong element and
  cost 500x with no error. One line makes the premise of the pass visible in the output.

Five seek groups: the item-578 pair, its NUMERIC twin, the seekable conjunct alone (a floor to
read the pair against), param-vs-literal, a projection, and an anchored hop.

### It found the gap immediately

```
SEEK: a param equality on a NUMERIC key AND a second conjunct   (SPELL_N=1000000, 20,000 matches)
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = $k AND n.s >= '' …      1.90 / 1.75 / 1.96 ms
  MATCH (n:P {k: $k}) WHERE n.s >= '' …           2.91 / 2.33 / 3.13
  MATCH (n:P WHERE n.k = $k) WHERE n.s >= '' …    5.18 / 2.35 / 5.20
```

Three separate processes (`SPELL_ONLY`, which is the probe's own sufficient check). The clause
member is stable and the inline member is stable, so **clause against inline is a consistent
1.3-1.6x** — which CONFIRMS item 578's 1.41x, measured there on a different fixture with a
different harness. The `inline WHERE` member is additionally BIMODAL (5.18, 2.35, 5.20), so the
group flags 2.7x in two runs of three.

### And it localized it

The same question on a STRING key converges: 8.54 / 8.77 / 9.11 / 8.54 ms across all four
spellings, **1.07x**. So the gap is specific to the numeric seeked key (or something correlated
with it) and is not the harness — the probe's two-pass min is exactly what rules the harness out,
and it leaves the numeric group flagged while the string group converges.

Three other useful negatives from the new pass, all converged: **param against literal on the
seeked key is 1.07x** (8.43 against 7.91ms — a param costs essentially nothing, which is worth
knowing since a literal lifts at compile time and a param cannot), a projection off the seek is
1.04x, and the anchored hop is 1.04x.

### One honest limit

The numeric group needs `SPELL_N=1000000` to clear `FLOOR_MS`: `k` is `i % 50`, so 200,000
vertices give 4,000 matches and ~0.5ms. At the default N the probe reports it under
"not compared (raise SPELL_N to measure them)" — the existing mechanism saying so, rather than a
silent pass. Raising it is not free (a 1M-vertex fixture), which is why the string twin at the
default N is the one that runs every time.

### Gates

No engine change — this is an instrument. `bun test packages/core packages/gql packages/gremlin
packages/serialization` 3734 pass / 0 fail, `bun test packages/native/src` 908 pass / 0 fail,
`bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean. A full
`bun run spelling` at SPELL_N=200000 flags only `label on start` (item 325's known one), so the
unindexed groups are unaffected by the pass added after them. CI green on 578.

## Item 580 — the seeding gap is NOT a lost seek, and the target is downgraded to ~1.3x

Item 579's new seek pass flagged 2.7x on a numeric seeked key. This diagnosed it, refuted the
tempting cause, and ends by downgrading the target rather than chasing it further.

### REFUTED: nothing loses the seek

The hypothesis this engine's history makes most tempting — "one spelling seeds and the other
scans", which is what every historical index bug here was — is wrong. At 200,000 vertices with
`k` indexed and `k = i % 10`:

```
MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.s >= ''   (no seekable conjunct — the SCAN reference)   7.09 ms
every spelling of the seeked question                                       1.0-3.5 ms
```

Every variant is 2-7x faster than the scan, so they all seek. Recorded as a refutation because
the next pass will reach for the same hypothesis.

### What narrowed

Without a second conjunct the spellings converge (clause 1.32, inline 1.20, inline-WHERE 1.25 ms
over 20,000 rows). The gap needs the MIX of an inline seed and a clause conjunct. A new probe
group covers it: four spellings of a two-equality question where one key is seeked and the other
filtered, all answering identically — which is what lets the both-inline form sit in a group
(the vacuous-conjunct group cannot hold it, since its answer differs).

### MY AD-HOC PROBE MISLED ME TWICE, and that is the lesson

Single runs of a hand-rolled harness, min of 9 reps but one process per case and no position
pass, produced two readings I could have built on:

```
                        ad-hoc single run      the probe's two-pass min, twice
clause + eq (param)           1.25 ms              1.89 / 1.77
inline + eq (param)           2.32                 2.11 / 2.00
clause + eq (LITERAL)         3.13                 1.77 / 1.73   <- the FASTEST corner, not the slowest
both inline {k, s}            1.24                 2.42 / 2.85   <- the SLOWEST, not the fastest
```

From the first column I had written a 2x2 matrix with OPPOSITE winners for param and literal, and
a story about the literal lift defeating the seek. Neither survives. Interleaving three rounds of
the ad-hoc probe already contradicted it (clause+eq 3.25/2.26/2.07 against inline 2.89/3.49/2.69 —
2 of 3 rounds favouring clause, magnitudes swinging 1.6x), and the two-pass instrument reversed two
of the four corners outright.

The probe's position-pass exists for exactly this: its own comment records a group reported at
1.5-2.1x across two audit items "with no engine cause at all". I built a new harness without that
property and got the same class of wrong answer in one tick.

### The target, downgraded

What survives across BOTH instruments is item 579's numeric-key group with a vacuous second
conjunct: clause 1.90/1.75/1.96 ms against inline 2.91/2.33/3.13 — **a consistent 1.3-1.6x**. The
2.7x headline is the `inline WHERE` member alone, which is BIMODAL (5.18 / 2.35 / 5.20), so the
group flags in two runs of three.

The four-spelling group added here converges within 1.65x and does not flag.

**So the honest target is ~1.3x at the edge of what the instrument resolves, not 2.7x** — and
three harnesses disagree about everything except its direction. It stays recorded and watched; it
is not worth another tick of chasing against a 2x threshold it does not reach. The next pass
should price a different enum.

### Gates

No engine change — a refutation and a probe group. `bun test packages/core packages/gql
packages/gremlin packages/serialization` 3734 pass / 0 fail, `bun test packages/native/src` 908
pass / 0 fail, `bun run typecheck` exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached
clean. CI green on 579.

## Item 581 — TS's top-k pays 4.5x its OWN floor, and the floor is a shipped fast path

A fresh enum: `ORDER BY`. `CLOSED.md` records a native top-k ("OrderPage 47 is a full sort, top-k
exists at 9.69") and says nothing about TS. 200,000 vertices, one case per process, min of 5.

### The rung exists

```
RETURN n.k AS k ORDER BY k            (full sort)   ts 294.04 ms   nv 31.40
RETURN n.k AS k ORDER BY k LIMIT 1                      30.84          0.70
                          LIMIT 5                       31.07          1.05
                          LIMIT 100                     31.70          1.05
```

8.6x below the full sort and FLAT in k across 1, 5 and 100 — so TS has a top-k and it is a bounded
one, not a sort-then-slice. `aliasDefinition` (items 145, 213) is why: it rewrites `ORDER BY k`
into `ORDER BY n.k` so the key reads an INPUT variable, which is what keeps `orderNeedsOutput`
false and the top-k over input bindings.

### THE FLOOR, measured from a shipped path answering the same question

`min(n.k)` does exactly what `ORDER BY k LIMIT 1` must do — read one property per row, compare it,
emit one row:

```
RETURN count(*)                 ts  0.00 ms   nv 0.00
RETURN count(n.k)                   8.91          0.11    reads the property per row
RETURN min(n.k)                     9.32          0.41    reads AND compares per row
RETURN max(n.k)                     7.82          0.44
RETURN n.k AS k ORDER BY k LIMIT 1 30.84          0.71
RETURN n.k AS k                     9.33         14.56    the 200,000-row projection
```

**TS pays 3.4x its own floor; native pays 1.7x.** On the cross-engine bench's fixture the pair
reads 36.1 against 8.1 (**4.5x**) for TS and 1.0 against 0.4 (2.5x) for native.

A floor taken from a shipped fast path in the same engine is worth more than a theoretical one:
`min()` is not a hypothesis about what the work should cost, it is the work being done today by a
different rung.

### Diagnosed, and the fix is a rung

The top-k is not projecting every row — `orderNeedsOutput` keeps only the top-k input bindings and
projects just those, and item 426 measured that property directly. What it DOES do is run the
general pipeline, which builds a binding `Map` per row and then reads the sort key out of it,
where `min()` goes through the node-aggregate SHORTCUT and builds no binding at all. That is the
same shape every shortcut in `shortcuts.ts` exists to answer, so the win is a new detector rather
than a tweak:

> `MATCH (n:L) RETURN <plain cols of n> ORDER BY <plain col of n> [DESC] [SKIP s] LIMIT k`
> → scan the label bucket, extract the key per vertex, keep a bounded top-(s+k) by key, project
> only the survivors.

### Why it is not in this commit

A new sort rung has to reproduce the engine's TOTAL ORDER byte-identically — NaN last and
NaN == NaN for sort/min/max, which is a deliberate departure from the predicate semantics — plus
DESC, ties, and SKIP. That is fuzzer-and-mutation work, not something to write at the end of a long
tick: item 562 in this run shipped a wrong answer into a probe by doing exactly that, and caught
it only because a probe happened to assert an answer.

So this commit prices the target and gives it a watcher. `bun run bench` gains the PAIR —
`query: top-k by property` beside `query: min property [top-k floor]` — because a bare top-k row
would not say whether a regression was the rung or the scan underneath it, and the gap is the
number that matters.

### Gates

No engine change. `bun test packages/core packages/gql packages/gremlin packages/serialization`
3734 pass / 0 fail, `bun test packages/native/src` 908 pass / 0 fail, `bun run typecheck` exit 0,
`bun run lint` exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean, `bun run bench` otherwise in band.
CI green on 580.

> **CORRECTED at item 582, and most of this entry is wrong.** Items 424, 425 and 426 had already
> done this work and recorded it in `CLOSED.md`:
>
> - **The floor is invalid, and 426 names the error exactly**: _"A floor measured on a different
>   PLAN is not a floor. Item 425 priced its remaining gap against the `max(a.u)` fold, which
>   since item 420 runs on `detectNodeProjection`'s fused scan — a different row-production path
>   from `applyProjection`'s general binding stream."_ My `min(n.k)` floor is that same fold.
> - **"The fix is a rung" is contradicted**: 424 states _"The top-k itself is NOT missing"_, and
>   425 had already SHIPPED the single-key bounded heap (49.6 → 37.1 ms, 1.34-1.50x over six
>   shapes) — which is the heap my own diagnosis then re-read in `applyProjection`.
> - **The gap is already ATTRIBUTED.** 426 measured it with a CONSTANT sort key (`ORDER BY 1
LIMIT 5`, all ties, the heap never evicts): _"25.6 of the 35.5 ms in the general stream plus

> What survives: the bench PAIR is still worth having, with its label corrected — it measures a

## Item 582 — correcting item 581: the work was done at 424-426, and `head -5` is why I missed it

Item 581 priced TS's top-k at "4.5x its own floor", specced a new detector, and said the rung was
missing. Items 424, 425 and 426 had already measured it, shipped the rung, attributed the
remainder and refuted the obvious sub-target. The correction is inlined above 581's entry; this
entry is about HOW it happened, because that is the part that generalises.

### The mechanical cause

I did check the closed list. The search was

```
grep -rn 'top-k\|topK\|partial sort\|heap' docs/reviews/CLOSED.md | head -5
```

`top-k` has **14 matches** in that file — lines 47, 3090, 3101, 3115, 3116, 3127, 3133, 3140,
4127, 5472, 7714, 7734, 7746, 7747. The `| head -5` showed five, and because the pattern also
matched `heap`, four of those five were unrelated table rows; the one top-k line it did surface
(47) is about `OrderPage`, which is the native engine. Every entry that mattered was below the
cut.

**`CLOSED.md` is 7,700+ lines and append-ordered, so the NEWEST and most relevant entries are at
the BOTTOM — which is exactly what `head` throws away.** Count the matches before reading any of
them; `grep -c` first, then look at the tail.

This is the third time in this session I have re-derived recorded work (568 was the first, and
CLAUDE.md records three such passes in one earlier session). The previous two were "searched the
wrong store"; this one searched the right store and truncated it.

### What the prior work actually says

- **424:** the top-k is NOT missing — 50.1ms against 485.1 unlimited is 9.7x, the cost climbs with
  k, and the alias and input-property spellings agree. Removing the per-row allocation is REFUTED
  at 2.4% ("'it allocates per row' is not by itself a cost in this engine"). Suspects left were
  enumerated, with "measure at nine reps" attached — 424 also records that a min-of-three A/B on
  this shape is a coin flip, both sides bimodal at ~50 and ~90-95ms.
- **425:** shipped the single-key heap, 1.34-1.50x across six shapes, five alternated rounds at
  nine reps.
- **426:** the floor error, and the attribution — 25.6 of 35.5ms is the general binding stream.

### So the target, correctly stated

A top-k over a node scan costs ~35.5ms where ~25.6ms of that is `applyProjection`'s general
binding stream (item 377's per-row `Binding`) and ~10ms is key evaluation plus 200,000
comparisons. The available levers, in the order the prior work implies:

1. **Item 377's per-row `Binding`** — the general lever, which would pay for far more than this
   shape.
2. **A fused top-k on a node scan**, i.e. giving this shape what `detectNodeProjection` already
   gives `max()`. Ceiling ~2.3x, not the 4.5x I claimed.

Neither is attempted here. What this commit does is stop item 581's wrong floor and wrong "rung is
missing" claim from standing in the record, and relabel the bench pair as the plan comparison it
actually is.

## Item 583 — the var-length count rung carries an endpoint PREDICATE, in BOTH its spellings

Item 573 gave TS a `varLengthDegreeCount`: a bounded `-[:T]->{m,n}` `count(*)` walked as degree
arithmetic instead of enumerated, ~15x. It took an unfiltered endpoint and an endpoint LABEL, and
it DECLINED the moment the endpoint carried a predicate — `detectVarLengthCount` rejected
`m.where !== undefined` outright, and `degreeCountShape` required `plainNode(node)`.

That left the most natural spelling of the query off the rung. 40,000 vertices / 120,000 edges,
one case per process, min of three reps, **three alternated PRISTINE/AFTER rounds**:

| shape                                               | PRISTINE (ms, 3 rounds)      | AFTER (ms, 3 rounds)         | min/min  |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------- |
| `(y WHERE y.age > 50)` inline                       | 226.18 / 230.55 / **206.92** | 34.32 / **31.87** / 51.99    | **6.5x** |
| `(y) WHERE y.age > 50` clause                       | 264.10 / 256.37 / **244.92** | 32.69 / **28.01** / 48.20    | **8.7x** |
| `(y {age: 50})` inline property                     | 181.66 / 199.45 / **176.28** | 31.43 / **28.26** / 43.23    | **6.2x** |
| CONTROL unfiltered — on the rung before AND after   | 14.80 / 18.18 / **14.77**    | 15.39 / **15.01** / 24.04    | flat     |
| CONTROL per-rep `WHERE` — declines before AND after | 370.10 / 381.60 / **370.10** | **364.94** / 372.66 / 397.59 | flat     |

Answers identical on both sides of every round — 207,984 / 5,340 / 480,000 / 125,316. Round 3 ran
slow on both sides across every row (the unfiltered control reads 24.04 there against 15.01), which
is why the comparison is min-of-min and why the control is in the table rather than described.

**Two controls the change cannot reach.** The unfiltered count is on the rung before and after, so
it prices the rung's own machinery and not the new predicate. The per-rep `WHERE` declines before
and after for its own reason (it is not an endpoint constraint at all). Both flat.

### Both spellings or neither — the actual design constraint

`(y WHERE p)` and `(y) WHERE p` are the same question. Carrying only the inline one would have
built a fresh instance of item 125's bug class, and items 303/304 are both the precedent and the
warning: an inline `{k: 1}` reached `inlineOf` through the pattern node while the identical clause
`WHERE` cost **4708.2ms against 33.9 — 139x**.

So the detector runs `chainGatesOf` over the clause `WHERE`, merges what it finds for the endpoint
variable with the node's own inline gate through `gateWith`, and both spellings land on one
compiled `InlinePred`. The three spellings now read **31.87 / 28.01 / 28.26** — within 1.14x of
each other, where before they spread 206.92 / 244.92 / 176.28 (1.39x) at ~7x the cost.

`gateWith` ANDs the conjuncts as AST before compiling, so the position still carries exactly ONE
predicate: an array of predicates per position would put a loop inside the per-vertex branch, which
is the cost this file has measured five times ([[ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing]]).

### What it still refuses, and why each refusal is the right one

- **A gate on the START.** That is a filter on the SEED, which this rung does not carry — native's
  equivalent needed a separate mask (item 575). Declining keeps BOTH of its spellings on the walk
  together rather than splitting them.
- **An unrepresentable gate.** `inlineOf`/`gateWith` return `null`, not `undefined`, when the
  endpoint's constraint reads something other than the endpoint (`(y {n: a.n})`). The two mean
  opposite things — `undefined` is "no predicate", `null` is "cannot carry this" — and conflating
  them is a silent overcount.
- **`max > 2`, `SIMPLE`, a multi-type hop, a non-plain START** — pre-existing refusals of 573.

### No fault fallback is needed here, where native needs one

Items 570 and 572 both had to add an `Err` → fall-back-to-enumeration path, because
`node_pass_mask` evaluates the predicate over **every node in the store** to build a mask: a vertex
no walk reaches can fault there and not under enumeration. This rung applies the predicate per
REACHED endpoint, so it sees exactly the set the walk would, and the `CAST(y.age AS INTEGER)` case
in the test holds that claim against native.

### Teeth — six mutants, under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`

The cap was proved to kill first: an allocator bomb exits 137, a bare `while true` exits 124.
Each mutant asserts its pattern appears EXACTLY ONCE, and the pristine copy is restored BEFORE the
next mutant rather than only after the loop.

| mutant                                                   | first run    | after  |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------ |
| M1 drop the START-gate decline                           | CAUGHT       | —      |
| M2 an unrepresentable gate (`null`) becomes NO predicate | **SURVIVED** | CAUGHT |
| M3 drop the LABEL test from the composed predicate       | CAUGHT       | —      |
| M4 claim the test is VACUOUS unconditionally             | CAUGHT       | —      |
| M5 let `degreeCountShape` accept a NON-PLAIN start       | **SURVIVED** | CAUGHT |
| M6 ignore the CLAUSE gates, keep only the inline `WHERE` | CAUGHT       | —      |

**M2 was a missing test** — nothing in the file exercised a `null` gate, so dropping the predicate
entirely read 10 for 1 and no assertion noticed. `(y {n: a.n})`, its inline-`WHERE` twin and its
clause twin now pin it.

**M5 was DEAD CODE, not a missing test.** I had written a `!plainNode(pattern.start)` decline into
the detector; `degreeCountShape` already requires exactly that one `||` earlier, so my guard could
never fire and removing it changed nothing. The mutant surviving is what that looks like from the
outside. The guard is deleted and the comment now says why there is none, so it is not re-added.
Generalising: **a mutant that survives on a guard is first a question about whether the guard is
reachable, and only then a question about test coverage.** Four historical wrong-answer bugs needed
the generator widened; this one needed the code narrowed.

A second, smaller consequence of the same removal: `degreeCountShape`'s `node` binding went unused
and `bun run lint` caught it (`no-unused-vars`, exit 1). Worth recording because the lint gate
found a real leftover, which is the argument for running it as its own command rather than trusting
the test suite.

### Measured again at BENCH size, where the win is bigger and a new lever appears

The 40,000-vertex table above understates it. At 200,000 vertices with 5 edges/node — the
`bun run bench` fixture — two alternated rounds, min of three:

|                             | pristine   | after  |           |
| --------------------------- | ---------- | ------ | --------- |
| `{1,2}(y WHERE y.age > 60)` | 2446.99 ms | 429.35 | **5.7x**  |
| CONTROL unfiltered          | 181.78     | 200.25 | see below |

**`bun run bench` gains the PAIR**, which item 573 should have shipped and did not — the rung has
had no watcher since. A filtered row alone cannot say whether a regression is the predicate or the
walk underneath it, which is item 581's argument for pairing, and it is the GAP that carries the
information. The two rows read ts 331.7 / 578.8 against ffi 4.0 / 4.3 in the full table.

**The pair also says, from the table alone, that the rung is being taken:** both rows are FLAT IN
PATH COUNT. At 200,000 vertices they read 189 and 397 with 3 edges/node against 187 and 379 with 5
— the path count went 2.4M to 6.0M. Enumeration tracks paths; O(V+E) does not. I nearly misread
331.7ms as "the rung is declining on the bench fixture" and only the flatness settled it.

**The remaining 2x, and the next lever.** The filtered row costs ~2x the plain one because the LAST
hop cannot be a degree — a degree cannot say which of a vertex's edges land somewhere that passes —
so TS enumerates that hop. Native pays 4.3 against 4.0 (1.08x) because it builds a per-node
`node_pass_mask` FIRST and then sums a passing out-degree (item 570). Doing that in TS is an O(V+E)
route for the filtered case too, and it is the open lever the new bench pair exists to watch.

### A reading that did not survive its own re-measurement

The control above moved 181.78 to 200.25 (1.10x) and the first version of this change had the new
composition INSIDE the one returned closure, which made that look like
[[ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing]] — the slow mode this file has measured five times. So I split
the arms: a predicate-free query now runs a closure capturing exactly what it captured before, and
only a query with a predicate reaches the new one.

Then I measured the control again, isolated (the filtered query not even in the process), three
alternated rounds each way:

|             | pristine                     | after                        |

## Item 584 — retracting item 583's "next lever": the precompute it asked for already exists

583 left, as an open priced lever, that TS "enumerates the last hop" of a filtered var-length count
and that native's 1.08x comes from precomputing a per-node passing out-degree — "the same
precompute in TS is an O(V+E) route". **`varLengthDegreeCount` already has it.** `degreeOf`
memoizes the passing out-degree per vertex in a `Map<Vertex, number>` (item 321's object-keyed
memo), so each distinct landing vertex's out-edges are walked ONCE, not once per path. I prescribed
building something I had read two ticks earlier.

So the 2x needed attributing rather than fixing. 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, min of 5:

| arm                                    | ms         | what it isolates                              |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| unfiltered `{1,2}(y)`                  | **181.81** | `passesIsVacuous`, degree is `set.size`: O(V) |
| `{1,2}(y:Q)` label                     | 368.34     | the walk, with a label test                   |
| `(y WHERE y.age >= 0)` TRUE for all    | 379.17     | the walk, predicate never rejects             |
| `(y WHERE y.age > 60)` ~1/3 pass       | 382.59     | the walk, predicate rejects 2/3               |
| `(y WHERE y.age > 1000)` FALSE for all | 355.86     | the walk, predicate rejects everything        |
| `(y WHERE y.nope > 0)` missing key     | 336.47     | the walk, null every time                     |
| CONTROL `{1,1}` with the predicate     | 118.01     | the OUTER loop, no `degreeOf` at all          |
| CONTROL `{1,1}` unfiltered             | 83.44      | the outer loop alone                          |

Each row kills a candidate:

- **Selectivity is not the cost.** True-for-all 379.17 against false-for-all 355.86 — the arm that
  rejects every vertex is the fastest filtered arm and still 1.96x the unfiltered one.
- **The compiled predicate is not the cost.** The `:Q` LABEL arm costs the same 368.34, and the
  one-hop controls price 1,000,000 predicate calls at 118.01 - 83.44 = **15ms**, ~15ns each.
- **So it is the inner O(E) edge walk**, which the unfiltered route skips by reading `set.size`.

Irreducible in the forward direction, which is why 583's lever does not exist. The remaining ~100x
to native (430 against 4.3) is item 566's layout ceiling. What the attribution DID find is the
lever that is real — accumulating backwards, where the cost scales with selectivity — and item 585
builds it.

**Method note.** Three ticks, three framings of this one 2x: 583 asserted a mechanism from reading
native, 584 measured it and found the mechanism already present, 585 measured what was left. The
arm that settled it was the one I added only for symmetry — a predicate that rejects EVERYTHING. A
filter that keeps nothing should be the cheapest query in the engine; finding it costs the same as
one that keeps everything is what named the culprit. Worth adding that arm by reflex.

## Item 585 — the second hop accumulated BACKWARDS, so selectivity finally pays

Item 584 attributed the filtered var-length count's 2x and ruled out the obvious causes. What was
left is that the forward walk pays one edge visit per edge IN THE GRAPH and is **flat in how
selective the endpoint test is** — rejecting every vertex (355.86ms) cost nearly what accepting
every vertex did (379.17), against 181.81 unfiltered.

The same quantity — per vertex, how many out-edges land somewhere that passes — accumulates
BACKWARDS at one visit per edge **into a passing vertex**: for each passing `z`, every in-edge of
`z` adds one to its source's count. `adjTo` has been there since items 162/321. That cost scales
with selectivity, which is exactly the property the forward walk lacks.

200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, min of 5, THREE alternated rounds, min-of-min:

| arm                                  | pristine  | after  | ratio                  |
| ------------------------------------ | --------- | ------ | ---------------------- |
| `(y WHERE y.nope > 0)` missing key   | 333.10 ms | 119.71 | **2.78x**              |
| `(y WHERE y.age > 1000)` rejects all | 376.74    | 142.83 | **2.64x**              |
| `(y WHERE y.age > 60)` ~1/3 pass     | 409.35    | 278.56 | **1.47x**              |
| `(y:Q)` label, 1/3 pass              | 341.51    | 298.75 | **1.14x**              |
| `(y WHERE y.age >= 0)` passes ALL    | 382.94    | 388.23 | 0.99x — gate declines  |
| CONTROL unfiltered, isolated         | 189.34    | 176.15 | after wins every round |
| CONTROL one hop, predicate           | 107.80    | 112.06 | flat                   |
| CONTROL one hop, unfiltered          | 79.24     | 82.64  | flat                   |

An earlier three-round run, before the sample below, read 3.10x / 3.02x / 1.42x / 1.26x on the same
four arms — so the direction and rough size reproduce across six rounds and two code states.

### It is a CHOICE, not a replacement, and that is the hard part

`degreeOf` is demand-driven: it computes a degree only for vertices actually reached at hop 1, so a
narrow start label can make the forward route cost far below O(E). Inversion is eager over every
passing vertex's in-edges. The comparison is `reached x avg_deg` against `passing x avg_indeg`, and
since in- and out-degree average the same thing over a whole graph, that reduces to `passing`
against `reached`.

`invertedHopBudget(vertexCount, edgeCount, srcCount)` is that arithmetic, extracted as a pure
exported function and unit-tested — **because nothing else can test it.** Both routes return the
same count, so every mutation of a perf decision SURVIVES the differential tests. Three were run to
prove it: always invert; drop the `max >= 2` guard; invert for a vacuous test. All three passed 11
cases pinned against native, as they were bound to. Arithmetic no differential test can reach gets
its own test or gets no teeth.

### Three controls the change cannot reach, and why the shared process lied about one

The unfiltered arm takes the `set.size` route, where `passesIsVacuous` short-circuits the gate
before it reads anything; the two one-hop arms never call `degreeOf` at all. In the shared probe
the unfiltered control read **0.88x** — a 1.14x regression, if believed. Both one-hop controls read
0.96x in the same run, a side-wide offset on arms the change provably cannot reach. Isolated, one
case per process, three alternated rounds: 194.93 / 189.34 / 224.07 against 184.95 / 176.15 /
202.28 — **the after side wins every round.** Position in a shared process, not the change. The
repo has this lesson filed; it still cost a round to re-learn.

### The sampled pre-check, and a margin I got backwards

The sweep that gives `passing` is O(V) predicate calls, and on a test that passes everything it is
pure loss: it runs, finds `passing` above the budget, declines. That arm measured 0.93x — a 3-8%
cost. Sampling the first 1024 vertices caps the loss, and the arm now reads 0.99x.

The first version required the projection to exceed the budget **by a factor of two**, reasoning
that a prefix of an insertion-ordered map is not a random sample so close calls should resolve to
the sweep. But the budget is capped at the vertex count, so a test passing everything projects
EXACTLY the budget and never twice it: **the check could not fire for the one case it was built
for.** Dead on arrival — the same shape as item 583's dead guard, one tick later, and this time
writing the test is what found it (two assertions failed immediately).

The fixed comparison is tie-inclusive, and erring that way is safe in a way the other is not: if
the prefix is unrepresentative, this skips a win and runs the FORWARD route, which is what the
engine did before 585 at all. A missed optimization, no wrong answer, no regression against the old
route. A sample saying "invert" still faces the exact `passing.length < budget` check, so it can
only skip work, never choose the route.

### Teeth

Correctness, 11 cases pinned against native plus a **900-query cross-engine sweep over BOTH
routes** — two fixtures, one labelling every vertex so inversion is reachable and one labelling
1 in 7 so the forward route wins, crossed over 15 endpoint tests, 5 quantifiers, 3 path modes and
2 type sets. 0 divergent.

Four correctness mutants, under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, all
CAUGHT: accumulate through `adjFrom`; credit the edge's target instead of its source; skip the
multi-label dedup on the in-side; treat a vertex absent from `passdeg` as one rather than zero.

Four mutants of the gate against its new unit test, all CAUGHT: drop the vertex-count cap on
reach; `>=` for `>`; compare reach instead of edge visits; take reach as the source count ignoring
fan-out. The empty-graph guard's mutant SURVIVES and the test says why — `avgDeg` is NaN there and
every comparison against NaN is false, so removing the guard reaches the same answer by accident.
Kept deliberately; not claimed as tested.

A fifth intended correctness mutant turned out to be a reroute: moving the early-abort check out of
the `if (passes(v))` branch cannot change `passing`, because only a push changes its length.

## Item 586 — the degree algebra reads IN-adjacency too, 9.4x, and the OUT path charges 4% for it

`try_degree_algebra` has been gated on `Dir::Out` since item 64. Pricing what the gate REFUSES
against what it accepts, 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges in native, min of 5:

| variant                                     | ms                 | note                               |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| ACCEPT `out {1,2}`                          | **3.99**           | the algebra                        |
| ACCEPT `out {1,2}` + end pred               | 4.01               |                                    |
| ACCEPT `out {1,2}` WALK / `{0,2}` / `{2,2}` | 3.96 / 3.98 / 3.39 |                                    |
| **REFUSE `in {1,2}`**                       | **35.99**          | **9.0x, for the IDENTICAL count**  |
| REFUSE `in {1,2}` + end pred                | 39.08              |                                    |
| REFUSE `both {1,2}`                         | 126.05             | 19.9M paths, a different question  |
| REFUSE `out {1,3}` / `{3,3}`                | 172.75 / 168.46    | 31M / 25M paths                    |
| REFUSE SIMPLE / ACYCLIC                     | 41.44 / 41.94      |                                    |
| REF `out {1,1}` / `in {1,1}`                | 0.51 / 0.51        | **the in-adjacency is not slower** |

Direction is the clear pick: both directions answered **5,999,996** and a single IN hop costs
exactly what a single OUT hop does, so nothing about the in-adjacency was the reason. Depth and
mode refusals are not comparable (they answer different questions, with 5-8x the paths), and
`Dir::Both` is a different shape — from one node an undirected edge is traversable two ways, so one
edge-indexed traversal mask cannot represent both, and a self-loop sits in both adjacency lists.

### The result

|                                                      | pristine                                 | after                                    |            |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| `in {1,2}`                                           | 35.36 ms                                 | 3.76                                     | **9.40x**  |
| `in {1,2}` + end pred                                | 36.56                                    | 4.00                                     | **9.14x**  |
| `out {1,2}` and its four accepted siblings           | 3.91 / 3.93 / 3.91 / 3.92 / 3.36         | 4.08 / 4.13 / 4.07 / 4.14 / 3.59         | 0.94-0.96x |
| `both`, `{1,3}`, `{3,3}`, SIMPLE, ACYCLIC — CONTROLS | 122.30 / 167.62 / 161.22 / 39.94 / 38.58 | 114.28 / 157.83 / 152.89 / 39.08 / 37.30 | 1.02-1.07x |
| `out {1,1}`, `in {1,1}` — CONTROLS                   | 0.51 / 0.50                              | 0.51 / 0.50                              | 1.00x      |

Three alternated rounds, answers identical on every row. Seven controls the change cannot reach:
the five still-refused variants and the two one-hop references.

### The OUT path charges for being edited, and five shapes priced the toll

The OUT path is not meant to change at all here, and it does: 4-6%. Each shape below was measured
in its OWN isolated probe (one case per process), four alternated rounds, min-of-min:

| shape                                          | pristine | after |            |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------- | ----- | ---------- |
| closure `\|v\| if inward { inc } else { out }` | 3.89     | 4.45  | 1.144x     |
| the same code through a `macro_rules!`         | 3.99     | 4.41  | 1.105x     |
| `const INWARD` + masks as generic params       | 3.91     | 4.35  | 1.113x     |
| `const INWARD` + masks as `&dyn Fn`            | 3.93     | 4.13  | 1.051x     |
| ... plus `#[inline(always)]` — **KEPT**        | 3.96     | 4.11  | **1.038x** |

**Two mechanism stories were refuted on the way,** which is why the record is a table and not an
explanation:

1. _"The closure is opaque to the inliner, so `store.out` stopped being an inlined slice access."_
   Expanding the identical code through a macro changed essentially nothing (1.105x). Refuted.
2. _"`&dyn Fn` masks are a virtual call per edge, so generic parameters will reach parity."_ They
   were **worse** than `&dyn` (1.113x against 1.051x) — so the `&dyn` shape is kept against the
   obvious reading of the code, on the measurement.

The residual ~4% has no identified mechanism, and saying so is the honest end state. It sits inside
the band [[pull-alignment-is-load-bearing]] records for `exec::pull` — "any edit costs the
filtered-count cluster 1.08-1.24x, never gains; that's the toll". **Net: 32ms saved on a 36ms query
against 0.15ms added to a 4ms one.**

NOT TRIED: duplicating the whole body so the OUT arm is literally untouched source in untouched
position — the only shape that could plausibly reach 1.000x. It means two copies of the trail
correction and the zero-length term, arithmetic subtle enough that items 64, 570, 572 and 575 each
needed their own mutation run. A 4% toll on a 4ms query is the cheaper risk, and the alternative is
recorded here rather than silently skipped.

### The mask's slot swap, which a count can hide

`traversal_pass_mask` built its mini-scope from `(from, eid, to)`. That is right for `Dir::Out`
only: `rep_pred_ok` fills the scope from the walk's own stacks, and under `Dir::In` the walk steps
through `store.inc(v)`, so the node the traversal STANDS ON is the edge's target and the node it
REACHES is the edge's source. Left unswapped, every per-rep predicate would be asked about the
traversal reversed — `(x)<-[e]-(y) WHERE x.k < y.k` answers the opposite question and returns a
perfectly plausible count.

### Why a total count cannot witness a direction bug at all

My first sweep fixture read `out=232 in=232` and I had built it to be asymmetric. It is not a
fixture mistake, it is structural: **counting every path from EVERY source, reversal is a bijection
between the forward and backward path sets**, so the two totals are equal whatever the engine does.
A sweep over `(a:P)` with P on every vertex would have passed with the direction wired backwards.

The source set has to be SELECTIVE. With `:Q` on a third the same fixture reads `out=76 in=79` and
`{2,2}` reads `45` against `61`. Both the Rust test and the cross-engine probe now ASSERT the
asymmetry rather than assuming it, and that assertion is what caught two of the five mutants.

### The gate the test nearly failed to reach

The algebra is gated on `src.len() * avg_deg^max > 2 * (nodes + edges)`. Item 570 had four mutants
survive because its fixture never reached the closed form; item 572 wrote 400 nodes at degree 4
against the WHOLE graph as the source set. Making the source set selective breaks that silently:
with `:Q` on a third and `edges = d*n`, the gate is `(n/3) * d^2 > 2n(1 + d)`, i.e. `d^2 > 6 + 6d`
— **`d >= 7` or the algebra never runs at any n.** Written at degree 4 this test passed in 0.16s
having never once executed the code it exists for. At ten edges per vertex it runs (0.52s), and the
test now recomputes the gate's own arithmetic and asserts it, so a future edit that shrinks the
fixture fails loudly instead of going quietly green.

### Teeth

Five mutants, built UNCAPPED first then run under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G
-p MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine restored BEFORE each, pattern asserted to appear exactly once. All
five CAUGHT:

| mutant                                   | caught by                         |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| ignore direction, always OUT adjacency   | the asymmetry assertion           |
| ignore direction, always IN adjacency    | the asymmetry assertion           |
| build the IN mask from `(from, eid, to)` | `count != rows` on the group form |
| swap the mask for OUT instead of IN      | `count != rows` on the group form |
| let the gate accept `Dir::Both`          | the suite                         |

Plus a 948-query cross-engine sweep on an asymmetric fixture — 5 quantifiers x 3 modes x 2 type
sets x 3 arrows x 5 endpoint tests, two start labels, plus the group form with `x.k < y.k` and its
reverse — 0 divergent.
