## Item 587 — a WALK counts by LEVELS at any depth, 9.7-23.6x, and the fuzzer found a crash

The algebra was bounded at `max <= 2` since item 64, and the bound is the TRAIL correction: at two
hops there is exactly ONE way to reuse an edge (a self-loop taken twice) and the closed form
subtracts it; at three there are several interacting ways and no single term.

A WALK forbids nothing, so its count obeys a recurrence instead:

    u_0(v) = 1 if the endpoint test passes v, else 0
    u_j(v) = sum over admissible traversals v -> y of u_{j-1}(y)

and the answer is `sum over sources s, over j in min..=max, of u_j(s)` — one pass over the graph per
level, O(max * (V + E)). Specialize it to max = 2 by hand and it is `degree_algebra_total` term for
term, which is the correctness argument for the mask placement: `u_1(s)` is the filtered out-degree
and `u_2(s)` the sum of neighbours' filtered out-degrees.

**WALK is the GREMLIN mode.** `repeat()` lowers to `PathMode::Walk` ("Gremlin allows revisiting
edges", gremlin.rs), so depth past 2 is the common Gremlin shape rather than a niche ISO spelling.
That is what made this worth doing instead of the TRAIL inclusion-exclusion.

### The result

200,000 vertices / 600,000 edges, min of 5, three alternated rounds, answers identical on every row:

| variant                                  | pristine | after |            |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------- | ----- | ---------- |
| WALK `{1,3}`                             | 38.87 ms | 3.97  | **9.79x**  |
| WALK `{3,3}`                             | 38.47    | 3.47  | **11.09x** |
| WALK `{0,3}`                             | 39.66    | 4.10  | **9.67x**  |
| WALK `{1,4}`                             | 104.44   | 5.01  | **20.85x** |
| WALK `{4,4}`                             | 105.83   | 4.75  | **22.28x** |
| WALK `{1,3}` + end pred                  | 47.75    | 3.85  | **12.40x** |
| WALK IN `{1,3}`                          | 39.86    | 3.91  | **10.19x** |
| `g.V().repeat(out()).times(3).count()`   | 38.73    | 3.46  | **11.19x** |
| `g.V().repeat(out()).times(4).count()`   | 103.40   | 4.39  | **23.55x** |
| `repeat(out()).emit().times(3).count()`  | 39.15    | 3.72  | **10.52x** |
| TRAIL `{1,3}` — CONTROL, still refused   | 49.15    | 51.40 | 0.96x      |
| WALK `{1,2}` — CONTROL, untouched route  | 2.75     | 2.84  | 0.97x      |
| TRAIL `{1,2}` — CONTROL, untouched route | 2.79     | 2.75  | 1.01x      |
| `repeat(out()).times(2)` — CONTROL       | 2.50     | 2.42  | 1.03x      |

The depth grows the win, which is the recurrence's signature: enumeration tracks paths and the
recurrence tracks levels. **The three readings of the untouched depth-2 route point OPPOSITE ways**
(0.97x, 1.01x, 1.03x), which is noise around 1.00 rather than item 586's consistent toll — and that
is why `max <= 2` keeps the closed form it has always had, byte for byte, instead of being folded
into the recurrence.

On a smaller, denser fixture (2,000 vertices at degree 4) depth 8 reads **627ms against 1ms**, both
answering 174,760,000.

### The optimizer fuzzer found a CRASH, at 200,000 seeds and not at the default

`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000 cargo test rewrite_fuzz` failed with an index-out-of-bounds where the
default sweep passed. Instrumenting the index gave the answer immediately:

    DIAG src id 4294967295 >= u.len() 24 (nc) len=31 min=1 max=3

`4294967295` is `u32::MAX` — **the NULL sentinel a Nodes column uses.** A plan whose source slot
holds a null node reaches the recurrence, and the recurrence indexes `u[s]` for every source at
every level, where the closed form only ever indexed by a NEIGHBOUR id (always real). The
pre-existing route survives a null source for that reason, plus `is_none_or` short-circuiting the
masks when there is no predicate.

Fixed by testing the bound BEFORE asking `seed_fn`, since that would index its own mask with the
same sentinel, and treating a null source as contributing no hop paths — which is what it has: a
null node has no adjacency. The same guard is on the zero-length term, where a null source would
have the ENDPOINT mask asked about a node that does not exist; enumeration evaluates that predicate
on NULL and keeps no row, so excluding it is the matching answer.

**Three mutants of the guards, and only one has teeth.** Dropping it entirely is CAUGHT by
`rewrite_fuzz` at 200,000 seeds — the fuzzer that found it. Testing the sentinel AFTER `seed_fn`,
and dropping the guard on the zero-length term, both SURVIVE: the fuzzer's case had no seed
predicate and `min = 1`, so each needs a null source simultaneously with a seed mask, or with
`min = 0`. I tried to reach those from the surface through `OPTIONAL MATCH` feeding a var-length
hop and the shape is `E_SYNTAX`, so they are kept as explicitly DEFENSIVE bounds checks rather than
claimed as covered. Unlike item 583's dead guard, nothing here proves them unreachable — the
fuzzer's generator simply does not produce the combination, and a bounds check against a crash under
that uncertainty is not the same as a decline that implies protection it does not give.

### Overflow refuses rather than wrapping, and inherits a PRE-EXISTING hang

This is the one route whose counts can genuinely exceed u64: an unbounded `repeat()` caps at 100
levels and a degree-4 graph passes 1.8e19 around level 32. The step uses `checked_add`, and a `None`
falls through to enumeration.

**That fallback does not terminate, and it did not before this change either.** Both builds were
run at `WALK {1,45}` on a 2,000-vertex degree-4 fixture under a 60-second budget and BOTH timed out,
while depth 8 answered on both. The mechanism is worth recording: a bare `count(*)` DFS-counts paths
without materializing rows, so the trail ROW cap never bounds it. Pre-existing, open, and not made
worse here — the route now answers exactly wherever u64 holds and inherits the old behaviour past
that. The alternative was `wrapping_add`, i.e. a wrong answer that looks like a right one.

### Teeth

Ten mutants beyond the three above, built UNCAPPED first then run under `timeout 600 systemd-run
-p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine restored BEFORE each. All CAUGHT: level 0 ignores the
endpoint test; drop the body filter; drop the traversal mask; collect levels strictly above min; one
level short; never advance the level vector; let a TRAIL take the recurrence (caught by a
trail-count-below-walk-count assertion); drop the seed gate; gate the zero-length term by the seed
predicate.

The last two SURVIVED at first, for a reason worth keeping: every other per-rep predicate in the
test reads `x`, `y` or `e`, so `seed` was `None` throughout and both mutants were no-ops. A
predicate on the hop's OUTER ANCHOR is a different slot (`2k+1`, item 575) and needed its own case

zero-length term as un-seed-gated.

`a_deep_walk_counts_what_enumeration_counts` checks count against materialized ROWS at every depth
from 1 to 5, which also pins the two routes against each other, and asserts the gate's own
arithmetic — at depth 3 over the whole graph that is `d^3 > 3(1 + d)`, so **degree 3 is the minimum
and degree 2 never reaches the recurrence**. Third instance of item 570's trap in three ticks.

Item 587 shipped the level recurrence in native, and the bench watcher it added then priced the TS

path. This is the twin, and it is the same arithmetic:

    u_0(v) = 1 if the endpoint test passes v, else 0
    u_j(v) = sum over wanted out-edges v -> y of u_{j-1}(y)

Specialize it to max = 2 by hand and it is `varLengthDegreeCount` term for term: `u_1(s)` is the

TS is still 115x native here, and the residual is the data layout rather than the algorithm:

depth 3 and more as depth grows. Not attempted here.

## Item 589 — the level route reads a flattened CSR, 1.6-3.7x, and the attribution was measured

Item 588 left TS at 115x native on a deep WALK count and ASSERTED the cause was
`Map<Vertex, number>` read once per edge per level. That was an estimate. Measuring it first is
what made this tick cheap, and it changed the design twice.

60,000 vertices / 180,000 edges, min of 5:

|                                       | ms                 |                                                 |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| cost is LINEAR IN DEPTH               | 23.83 per level    | intercept 3.12                                  |
| walk the adjacency only               | 3.34               |                                                 |
| ... + one `Map.get` per edge          | 19.05              | so the map is **15.71 of the 23.83**            |
| ... + `Map.get` INDEX then dense read | 19.52              | **going through a map for an index is as slow** |
| one `Map.set` per vertex              | 2.30               |                                                 |
| BUILD a CSR once (E map lookups)      | 18.28              | one level's worth, paid once                    |
| dense read from the built CSR         | **0.10 per level** |                                                 |
| dense write per vertex                | 0.18               |                                                 |

The third row is the one that fixed the design: resolving an index _through_ a map per edge costs
the same as the map lookup it replaces, so the neighbour indices have to be PRECOMPUTED, not looked
up. A `Float64Array` holds exactly what the map held — a JS number is an f64, summed in the same
adjacency order — so this is a layout change and not a semantic one.

### The result, one case per process, three alternated rounds

| quantifier                     | map (588) | CSR (589) |           |
| ------------------------------ | --------- | --------- | --------- |
| `{1,3}`                        | 63.46 ms  | 32.97     | **1.92x** |
| `{3,3}`                        | 61.86     | 38.18     | **1.62x** |
| `{1,4}`                        | 89.16     | 36.03     | **2.47x** |
| `{1,6}`                        | 134.25    | 36.14     | **3.71x** |
| `{1,2}` — CONTROL, closed form | 37.37     | 34.48     | 1.08x     |

**The route is now FLAT in depth** (33 / 38 / 36 / 36) where the map version scaled with it — which
is the shape the attribution predicted. The `{1,2}` control moved 1.08x on code neither side
touches, so the noise floor on this harness is ~8% and the wins are clear of it.

`bun run bench`'s watcher reads **619.9 -> 348.3ms**, so 1.78x on the bench's own fixture, and
TS/native goes 115x -> 62.8x. Across items 587-589 that row is **8362.9 -> 348.3, 24x**.

### Two measurements that corrected me mid-tick

**1. `{3,3}` cheaper than `{1,4}`, which is impossible.** The first A/B ran all cases in one
process and read `{3,3}` at 1.02x while `{1,4}` read 2.90x — depth 4 cannot cost less than depth 3
doing strictly more work. It was JIT warmup landing on whichever case ran first. One case per
process gave the coherent table above. Fourth tick running where a shared process lied.

**2. The CSR was 58ms flat, not the ~23ms the micro-benchmark implied.** Built as a `number[]` with
`push` and then `Int32Array.from`, the build cost ~55ms instead of ~20 — boxing, array growth, then
a full copy. Preallocating to `graph.edgeCount` and filling in ONE pass fixed it (the wanted-type
filter can only keep fewer edges than the graph has, so the bound is safe and the slack is never
read). That is the difference between the 1.36x the first version measured and the 1.92x here.

### Teeth

Nine mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine restored
BEFORE each. Seven CAUGHT immediately: offsets lag by one vertex; the level reads the SOURCE index
instead of the neighbour; the level buffers are not swapped; collect levels strictly above min; one
level short; level 0 ignores the endpoint test; the zero-length term ignores the endpoint test.

**Two survived, and both were the COINCIDING FIXTURE — eighth and ninth in this run of ticks.**

- **"the last CSR offset is not closed"** survived because the main fixture's last-inserted vertex
  is `iso`, which has no out-edges, so a short final offset drops nothing.
- **"source indices resolved as list POSITION"** (`srcIdx[i] = i`) survived because `:P` covers
  every vertex in insertion order, making the wrong formula accidentally right.

A second fixture breaks both: its last-inserted vertex carries two out-edges, and its start label
sits on the 2nd, 5th and 6th vertices so the source set is NOT an insertion-order prefix. Both
mutants are CAUGHT against it, and the pins are hand-checked as well as taken from native — the
T out-degrees are 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2 with `:Q` on three vertices, so `{1,2}` from the Q set is
5 + 3 + 4 = 12 and `{3,3}` is 3 + 2 + 3 = 8.

A 6300-query cross-engine sweep over depths 1-6 and five modes: 0 divergent.

`bun run lint` wants `for...of` over the source-index array. That goes through the iterator protocol

## Item 590 — a two-hop Gremlin count from every vertex is a DEGREE INNER PRODUCT, 6.4-7.1x

A fresh enum: `bun run bench:gremlin`, where `V().out().out().count()` read **ts 351.9ms against
native 2.80 — 125.8x**, the largest gap in that bench, with `repeat(out).times(2)` at 85.7x.

### Diagnosing first refuted my opening assumption

Item 574 shipped `hopChainCount` for exactly this shape, so I assumed the rung was declining.
Asking `countShortcut` directly — it is exported, which the tests already rely on — said otherwise:

```text
  out(K) x2   claims 1000000   exec 52.03   shortcut-only 56.98 ms
```

The rung CLAIMS the shape, returns the right answer, and `exec` ~ `shortcut-only`, so it is the
thing running. **The arithmetic itself cost 57ms**, and there was no missing route to build. Reading
it showed why: the two-hop arm walks every edge and asks each TARGET for its degree, so a vertex's
degree is recomputed once per in-edge rather than once.

### Attribution, which made this an ALGEBRAIC change rather than the layout one I expected

40,000 vertices / 200,000 edges, min of 5:

|                                               | ms        |                                |
| --------------------------------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------ |
| walk both levels of adjacency, nothing else   | 9.14      |                                |
| + per-edge target bucket `.get(label).size`   | **61.80** | what it did                    |
| + per-edge `Map.get` on a memoized degree map | 42.07     | only 1.5x — **not** the fix    |
| build a flattened CSR of neighbour indices    | 37.65     | item 589's trick: no help here |
| ... then the dense read through it            | 0.11      |                                |
| **the inner product, degree passes included** | **7.73**  | **8.0x**                       |

Summing over ALL sources, every traversal of the first hop arrives at some `w`, and the number of
ways to arrive is a DEGREE of `w`:

    count = sum over w of arrivals(w) * departures(w)

where each factor is the degree on whichever side its hop traverses — an `out` hop arrives along
`w`'s IN-edges and departs along its OUT-edges, an `in` hop mirrors that. One pass over vertices,
two bucket reads each, no edge walk at all.

I came into this tick expecting to reapply item 589's CSR. The attribution says the CSR would have
bought **nothing here** (37.65ms to build against 61.80 for the whole current arm), and the memoized
degree map — the obvious fix from reading the code — only 1.5x. Measuring the candidates before
writing one is what found the 8x.

### Why self-loops and parallel edges need no special case

That is what makes the identity exact rather than approximate. A self-loop at `w` is one of its
in-edges and one of its out-edges, and it contributes to `arrivals` and `departures` exactly as the
walk visits it once in each role. Parallel edges are separate members of both degrees. A multi-label
edge is counted once because `degreeOfTypes` dedupes, and the upstream guard already refuses a
zero-or-many-label hop on a graph with multi-type edges (item 574's own 13-divergence lesson).

### The result

200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, one case per process, three alternated rounds:

| case                                                  | before    | after  |           |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | --------- | ------ | --------- |
| `out(T).out(T).count()`                               | 370.76 ms | 57.81  | **6.41x** |
| `in(T).in(T).count()`                                 | 368.79    | 57.60  | **6.40x** |
| `out(T).in(T).count()`                                | 325.38    | 45.64  | **7.13x** |
| `repeat(out(T)).times(2).count()`                     | 410.39    | 57.51  | **7.14x** |
| `hasLabel(Person)` + two hops (vacuous label dropped) | 366.84    | 57.36  | **6.40x** |
| `out(T).count()` — CONTROL, one hop                   | 0.01      | 0.01   | 1.00x     |
| three hops — CONTROL, multiplicity-map arm            | 689.75    | 669.88 | 1.03x     |
| `has(age>44)` + two hops — CONTROL, keeps the walk    | 176.93    | 182.54 | 0.97x     |

`bun run bench:gremlin` reads `V().out().out().count()` at **55.9 against 351.9**, ts/native from
125.8x to **20.3x**, and `repeat(out).times(2)` from 85.7x to 15.3x. Every other row unchanged.

### Teeth, and a fixture that could not tell three of four directions apart

Nine mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine restored
BEFORE each. Six CAUGHT immediately: arrivals from the departure side; departures from the arrival
side; both factors on the first hop's direction; add instead of multiply; the identity used for a
FILTERED source; the identity used for three hops.

**Three survived, all coverage gaps:**

- **departures using `h0`'s labels**, and **arrivals using `h1`'s**, because every case put the SAME
  label on both hops. `out(T).out(U)` is 0 and `out(U).out(T)` is 2, so mixed labels separate them.
- **`unfiltered` defined as `!canSeed`** rather than "no filter steps". A `has` filter is not
  seedable, so `canSeed` is false for it and the mutant would take the identity on a filtered
  source. My test had a `hasLabel` filter but no `has` one.

All three are CAUGHT with the added cases. Separately, the cross-engine probe's first fixture read
`out/out=130 in/in=130 out/in=192 in/out=130` — **three of the four direction pairs coincided**, so
it could not have caught a swapped degree side at all. `out/out` and `in/in` must ALWAYS agree (both
are `sum(indeg*outdeg)`, and multiplication commutes), but the others are separable: two hubs in the
fixture pull them to 35 / 35 / 73 / 59, and the test ASSERTS three distinct values rather than
assuming them. Item 586's lesson, third application.

36 traversals across four direction pairs and four label sets against native: 0 divergent. Pins are
native's and hand-checked — the T out-degrees sum to 23, and `sum(indeg*outdeg)` is
2+9+8+2+4+4+1+3+2 = 35.

No TinkerPop run is attached because no SEMANTIC question is open: item 574 established from a real
console that `repeat(h).times(k)` IS the k-fold chain, and `out().out()` was never ambiguous. What
changed is which arithmetic computes an already-settled answer.

TS is 20.3x native here, down from 125.8x. The remaining 57ms is two bucket reads per vertex at

## Item 591 — the vertex's own adjacency box, not a hash of its id, 1.26-1.31x

`V().out(T).has(k,pred).count()` was the largest remaining ratio in `bun run bench:gremlin` — ts
53.0ms against native 1.53, **34.6x**.

### What was already there, and the inconsistency inside one file

The vertex-driven inversion exists (item 168): rather than one predicate test per EDGE, it tests
each far VERTEX once and adds its whole degree. So the algorithm was not the problem. What it did
was reach the adjacency through `graph.edgesToByLabel.get(v.id)` — **a map keyed on the id STRING**
— while `startFilteredHopCount`, three functions below in the same file, has read `v.adjFrom`

the box since items 162 and 321". One rung in this file learned the lesson; its neighbour never did.

that bench at 307.6ms.

`distinctHopCount` was left alone deliberately: it iterates the index's VALUES with no vertex
object in hand, so there is no box to read.

### My micro-benchmark over-promised by 1.4x, which this very file warns about

The attribution probe measured the pieces at 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges:

|                                           | ms                |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| iterate `graph.vertices`, nothing else    | 0.35              |
| + `edgesToByLabel.get(v.id)`              | 41.54             |
| + `v.adjTo` instead                       | 30.50             |
| `get(v.id)` + a property read and compare | 32.86             |
| `v.adjTo` + a property read and compare   | **18.29 — 1.80x** |

The real change measures **1.26x**, not 1.80x. My probe inlined `byType.get('KNOWS')?.size` and
`typeof age === 'number' && age > 44` where the shipped code calls `degreeOfTypes(byType, labels)`
and `matches(pred, value)` — helper calls that dominate, so removing the id lookup is a smaller
share of the whole.

`hop-values.ts` carries this exact warning at the top of the function I edited: _"My first probe
inlined what the shipped code has to call, and over-promised by 1.5x — `harness-must-resemble-caller`,
again."_ I read that comment while making this change and still repeated the mistake, by a nearly
identical factor. The attribution was still worth having — it is what ruled out the algorithm and
located the cost — but the RATIO from a probe that skips the callees is not the ratio you ship.

### Teeth

A layout change cannot be caught by a differential test on its own terms — both routes read the same
adjacency — so the mutants target the thing that CAN go wrong: the SIDE. Five under
`timeout 600 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine restored BEFORE each.

Four CAUGHT at once: either site reading the wrong side, and `filteredHopCount` ignoring direction.

**One survived**, and it was the coinciding fixture again: `hop-values` always reading `adjFrom` is
correct for `out` and wrong for `in`, and `hop-values.test.ts`'s `in_('E').values('age')` expects
`[10, 10]` — which the mutant also produces. Correct, `b` and `c` are each reached from `a` (age
10); mutated, `a`'s two out-edges each yield `a`'s OWN age. Same answer by luck.

A second fixture breaks it: `d` has an out-edge into `a`, so `a` has an in-neighbour whose age
differs from its own, and the two answers are `[40, 10, 10]` against `[10, 10, 40]` — different in
order and in content. The test asserts the out and in answers DIFFER, so it cannot quietly coincide
again. Both the survivor and its mirror are then CAUGHT.

40 cross-engine traversals over four label sets, both directions, counts AND ordered streams:
0 divergent. The ordered comparison matters here — `values()` is a stream and Gremlin order is a
contract, and this change touches the loop that produces it.

### Still open on these rows

`V().out().has().count()` is 27.6x native: what is left is `degreeOfTypes` plus `matches` per
vertex, which the attribution above prices at ~18ms of the 42. `V().out().values(age)` is 8.5x and
dominated by per-EDGE work (a property read and a yield per edge), where the id lookup was only
ever one per vertex — which is why that row moved 1.07x and not more. The same id-keyed pattern
survives at **12 more sites in `packages/gql/src/executor/hop-projection.ts` and one in
`executor.ts`**; each needs its own check that a vertex object is in hand, and its own measurement.

## Item 592 — the same lesson at 14 GQL sites, 1.2-1.4x, and four harness faults on the way

Item 591 surveyed the id-keyed adjacency pattern and left 14 sites unchanged across
`packages/gql/src/executor/hop-projection.ts` and `executor.ts`. All 14 have a VERTEX OBJECT in
hand and reach the adjacency through `index.get(v.id)` — a map keyed on the id STRING — where the
vertex carries its own `adjFrom` / `adjTo` box.

### Reading item 159 before changing anything, and reading it CORRECTLY

`hop-projection.ts` warns that each walk "indexes one of `edgesFromByLabel` / `edgesToByLabel`
through a captured `out: boolean`, and item 159 measured a branch in that inner loop at 1.6x on the
hot directed shape". Taken at face value that forbids this change: replacing `index.get(v.id)` with
`(out ? v.adjFrom : v.adjTo)` puts a branch back.

It does not, and the distinction is the whole justification. Item 159's branch was in the INNER
loop — per EDGE. These lookups are in the OUTER loop — per VERTEX, once per start, with the inner
loop iterating the bucket it returns. That is exactly item 591's shape, where the branch replaced a
string-keyed lookup and still won 1.26-1.31x. **`distinctHopCount` in the Gremlin file remains
excluded for the real reason: it iterates the index's VALUES with no vertex object at all.**

### The result

200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges, one case per process, FOUR independent runs with the side order
alternated (see below for why the ordering had to become a variable):

| case                                | id map       | box         | ratio by run                   |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------ | ----------- | ------------------------------ |
| `(a)-[:KNOWS]->(x:Q) RETURN x.name` | 27.6-33.1 ms | 16.6-21.2   | **1.42 / 1.53 / 1.69 / 1.78x** |
| `(a:P)<-[:KNOWS]-(x) RETURN x.name` | 68.1-74.7    | 47.6-51.1   | **1.40 / 1.43 / 1.46 / 1.46x** |
| `(a:P)-[r:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN r.w`   | 172.6-203.4  | 143.4-152.9 | **1.20 / 1.26 / 1.33 / 1.39x** |
| `(a:P)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN x.name` | 98.4-113.7   | 76.2-93.2   | **1.21 / 1.22 / 1.25 / 1.34x** |
| `count(*)` over one hop — CONTROL   | 0.01         | 0.01        | 1.00x every run                |

**Reported as ranges, not points, and the reason is in the controls below.** The tightest row
(reversed `<-[:KNOWS]-` projection) reproduces inside 1.40-1.46x across four runs and both
orderings; the loosest spans 1.42-1.78x.

`bun run bench`, an independent harness, moves the same way against item 589's recorded values:

| row                                          | before      | after              |
| -------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------ |
| `traverse 1-hop project`                     | 128.7 ms    | **105.9**          |
| `query: distinct over a hop`                 | 62.0        | **46.3**           |
| `traverse 1-hop project + start filter`      | 111.8       | **102.4**          |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter` / `+ start filter` | 43.9 / 37.3 | 43.4 / 37.1 — flat |
| `count 2-hop + mid filter`                   | 41.9        | 41.4 — flat        |

The flat rows are the ones that take a COUNT shortcut rather than a projection walk, which is the
expected split: this change touches the walks that build rows.

### Correctness: byte-identical ORDERED output, which is the strongest available evidence

A layout change must move nothing, including row ORDER. 321 queries over three edge-type sets,
three arrow directions, five start/far label combinations and six projection shapes, run on both
builds and diffed as text: **byte-identical across all 321.** So `v.adjFrom.get(T)` is the same
`Set` object the index yields, with the same iteration order — not merely the same membership.

Against native the same 321 compare equal as MULTISETS. They do NOT compare equal ordered, and that
is correct rather than a divergence: GQL row order without `ORDER BY` is unspecified in this engine
([[order-is-unspecified]]), the same stance SQL takes. Comparing ordered would have asserted a
contract that does not exist — my first sweep did exactly that and reported 19 false divergences.
Gremlin is the opposite, which is why item 591's sweep DID compare ordered.

### Teeth: 14 per-site mutants, 0 survivors

Each rewritten site had its adjacency SIDE swapped, one site at a time, under
`timeout 900 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`. **All 14 CAUGHT.** Per-site and not
a global swap deliberately: a global swap is caught by whichever site happens to be covered and
says nothing about the others. This is the first change in several ticks that needed no new test —
the existing suite already reaches every one of these walks.

### FOUR harness faults, which is the part worth carrying forward

1. **The side ORDER was a hidden variable.** The first A/B ran `pristine, after` within every
   round, so `after` always ran second and benefited from any warming. Reversing it moved
   `hop-far-label` from 1.69x to 1.53x — within the noise, but the bias was systematic. The driver
   now alternates the order per round.

2. **A control that materializes 200,000 rows is not a control.** `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.name`
   reads 1.10x, then 1.51x, then **0.58x** across runs — on code this change cannot reach
   (`outNeighbors`, a one-hop helper a no-hop query never calls). It is GC-dominated and swings
   5.91-13.62ms. Replaced with a filtered node COUNT, which still drifts 1.17x; the only
   rock-steady control is the one-hop `count(*)` shortcut at exactly 1.00x in every run. **This
   machine's run-to-run drift on medium-weight TS queries is up to ±50%**, which is why the table
   above gives ranges and rests on reproducibility across runs rather than one min-of-min.

3. **zsh does not word-split an unquoted variable.** `order="p592 a592"; for side in $order` ran
   ONCE with a two-word value; the `cp` failed silently and the probe measured whatever was in the
   tree. The run printed four plausible lines and meant nothing. The A/B driver is Python now.

4. **A `cp` of the pristine copy over the working tree, before the AFTER copy was saved, LOST the
   edits.** `git diff --stat` came back empty and the rewrite had to be redone from scratch. The
   mutation discipline already says "restore before applying the next mutant"; the same hazard
   exists in an A/B harness, and the rule it needs is: **save the AFTER copy in the same breath as
   making the edit, before any script that can install a pristine one.**

## Item 593 — three candidate targets, three refusals, and a micro-probe that mispriced again

No change ships from this tick beyond a recorded refutation. All three candidates were killed by
reading or by measuring, and two of them were killed by work that already existed.

### 1. `query: project 3 columns`, native 7x SLOWER than TS — ALREADY CLOSED at item 289

`bun run bench` reads this row ts 8.6ms against ffi 60.5. The native engine looked like the
problem, and the corpus prices the engine side directly: `query_bench -- perrow` gives
`string p.name` **1.42ms** and `scalar p.age` **0.485ms** over the same 200,000 rows, so a
three-column projection is ~3ms of engine time against 60.5 through the FFI.

That decomposition is already in `packages/native/src/graph.ts`, written at item 289: the path is
**48% `JSON.parse`** (17.63ms for a 4.47MB carrier), **33% the crate's render plus the FFI call**,
12% row shaping — "that 7.3x is the JSON CARRIER, not execution... Anyone chasing that bench row
should read `queryArrowIpc`, not the engine."

Worth noting what MISLED me toward it: `percall_probe`'s header says "the natural suspect (the FFI
boundary) is innocent: a `vertexCount` round trip is **8ns**". True, and about a SCALAR round trip.
It says nothing about 200,000 rows, where the carrier is the whole cost. A boundary measured at one
row does not price a boundary at a million.

### 2. Native Gremlin `values()` against native GQL projection — NOT A GAP

`query_bench -- gremlin` reads `values` at **1350us** where `perrow`'s `scalar p.age` is **485us**
over the same store, which looked like 2.8x between the two surfaces of one engine. Reading the
cases refuted it:

- the Gremlin case is `g.V().values('name').count()` — it ends in `count()`, so ONE row comes out;
- `scalar p.age` is `MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.age`, which materializes 200,000 rows;
- one reads a STRING and the other a NUMBER, and `perrow` prices those at 7.1 against 2.4 ns/row.

Normalized, Gremlin is 6.75 ns/row against GQL's 7.1 for the same string column **while building no
rows at all**. There is no gap. Two different mismatches at once — row count and column type — and
either alone would have invented the 2.8x. This is the "match the fixture to the claim" trap with
the fixture being someone else's bench case.

### 3. Hoisting the per-vertex invariants out of `filteredHopCount` — REFUTED at 1.01-1.05x

Item 591 left this row priced at 27.6x native with the remainder attributed to `degreeOfTypes` plus
`matches` per vertex. The loop calls `degreeOfTypes(byType, hop.labels)` — which branches on
`labels.length` and then walks the array — plus two property reads off `filter`, once per vertex,
none of which varies per vertex. Hoisting `labels[0]` into a constant, inlining the single-type
degree as `byType.get(only)?.size ?? 0`, and destructuring `{ key, pred }` above the loop:

| case                                                               | before   | after |            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- | ----- | ---------- |
| `out(K).has(age,gt(44)).count()`                                   | 41.59 ms | 41.17 | 1.01x      |
| `in(K).has(age,gt(44)).count()`                                    | 39.09    | 37.76 | 1.04x      |
| `out(K).has(age,gt(500)).count()`                                  | 41.43    | 40.89 | 1.01x      |
| `out(K).has(city,'c7').count()`                                    | 43.67    | 41.48 | 1.05x      |
| five CONTROLS — hop count, dedupe, start-filtered, two-hop, values |          |       | 1.00-1.01x |

Four alternated rounds, order reversed on alternate rounds, one case per process. Everything inside
this box's noise floor, so the call and the array walk are ~1-5% of the row. **Reverted**, with the
numbers recorded beside the loop so it is not re-attempted.

### The estimate that sent me there was wrong, and this is the second tick running

I reasoned: item 591's probe measured an INLINED equivalent of this loop at 18.29ms, the real row is
42.2ms, therefore the calls the probe skipped cost ~24ms. The A/B says they cost ~1-5%. **The 24ms
is not in the loop body at all** — the probe is simply not this code, and the difference lives in
the plan dispatch and whatever the probe's isolated loop let the JIT do.

Item 591's own entry says the same thing from the other direction (its probe over-promised 1.80x
against a real 1.26x), and `hop-values.ts` has carried that warning since item 170. So the rule
earns a sharper form: **a micro-probe can locate a cost and must not be used to size one.** Item
589's attribution was still decisive — it ruled out the algorithm and found that an index lookup
through a map costs the same as the map lookup it replaces — but every ratio that shipped in these
ticks came from an A/B of the real code.

### What this says about the row that is still 27.6x

The ORDER is already optimal: without an index on the key, every vertex with a matching edge must
be tested, and `seedForStep` already hands the indexed case to the index path. What remains is a JS
property read and a predicate dispatch per vertex against native's columnar read — item 566's
layout ceiling, not a missing route. Recorded as such rather than left looking like an open lever.

## Item 594 — the two-hop `COUNT { }` subquery's 17.5x is a STRING-KEYED LOOKUP PER FIRST-HOP EDGE

A new family: `bun run bench` reads `query: 2-hop subquery item` at ts 113.5ms against native 6.5
(**17.5x**), while its one-hop sibling is 30.9 against 4.8 (6.4x). Something costs 3.7x more for one
extra hop, and `degreeCountSubquery` already answers both — it accepts up to THREE segments.

### The code had already asked the question, and already half-answered it

`degreeCountSubquery`'s return type says: _"Present only for the shapes that can read the anchor's
box — the one-hop degree. The two-hop side still resolves mid-vertices by id, which is a different
question."_ That reads like an open lever, and after items 591/592 closed the id-keyed pattern at 15
other sites it looked like the obvious next one.

**It is not reachable, and the reason is in `Edge`:**

```ts
get to(): Vertex {
  return this.#graph!.getVertexById(this.#to)!;
}
```

An `Edge` stores endpoint IDS. `e.to` is a GETTER that performs a string-keyed lookup. So at a
first-hop landing there is no vertex object in hand, and "read the box instead" would pay the very
lookup it is trying to avoid. `twoHopSide`'s unlabelled branch says this already — "the loop was
resolving it (`e.to`, a string-keyed `Map.get`) only to hand `mid.id` straight back to another
`Map.get` — two lookups an edge where one does" — and its LABELLED branch records the box read
tried and **measured flat** (369.9 / 384.4 / 367.7 against 384.1 / 364.2 / 372.0).

So items 591/592's lever does not generalize, and the boundary is sharp: it applies wherever a
VERTEX OBJECT is already in hand, and nowhere else. `distinctHopCount` was excluded for the same
reason (it iterates the index's values); this is excluded because edges hold ids.

### Measured, so the claim is not just the comment restated

200,000 vertices at degree 5, varying ONLY the anchor set so first-hop edges vary with it:

| shape                        | ms     | first-hop edges   | ns/edge |
| ---------------------------- | ------ | ----------------- | ------- |
| 2-hop, all anchors           | 206.97 | 1,000,000         | **207** |
| 2-hop, ~2/3                  | 149.20 | 655,555           | 228     |
| 2-hop, ~1/3 (the bench row)  | 81.66  | 322,220           | 253     |
| 2-hop, ~1/10                 | 35.80  | 100,000           | 358     |
| 1-hop, all anchors           | 32.64  | 1,000,000 counted | **33**  |
| 2-hop, LABELLED middle, ~1/3 | 138.11 | 322,220           | 429     |

Linear in first-hop edges — the ns/edge climb at small anchor sets is the 200,000-vertex anchor scan
amortized over fewer edges. The two-hop pays **~174 ns/edge over the one-hop**, and item 194's
figure for a string-keyed `Map.get` is **~190 ns**. That is the whole gap, arrived at from a second
direction. The labelled middle at 429 ns/edge is consistent too: it resolves the vertex as well.

### The memo that looks like the fix, and is not

Each mid vertex is visited ~5 times at this degree (1,000,000 first-hop edges over 200,000 mids), so
a per-query memo on the mid id would collapse 4 of every 5 inner lookups. But a `Map<string, number>`
get is the SAME ~190 ns as the adjacency get it replaces, so the memo saves only the inner per-type
read — about 24ms of 207, under this box's noise floor. Not attempted, and recorded so it is not
attempted later on the strength of the 5x revisit count alone.

**Making this cheaper means giving the core graph dense vertex indices instead of string ids** — the
same conclusion item 289 reached about the JSON carrier, from the other end of the engine. That is
an architectural change, not a rung, and it is now written next to the type that raised it.

### Gates

3746 pass / 0 fail, `bun test packages/native/src` 925 pass / 0 fail, `bun run typecheck` exit 0,
`bun run lint` exit 0, `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean, `bun run fuzz` 13 pass / 0 fail across

## Item 595 — cache the edge's resolved ENDPOINTS, 2.4-2.6x, and three reps invented two regressions

Items 591/592 closed the id-keyed adjacency lookup wherever a VERTEX OBJECT was in hand, and item
594 found the boundary: an `Edge` stores endpoint IDS, so `e.to` is a getter that calls
`getVertexById` — a string-keyed `Map.get`, ~190ns at bench size. The hot executors resolve an
endpoint from an edge at **56 sites**, many once per edge in a loop. This caches the resolution.

### Why a cached REFERENCE is safe here, where `#box` needed a stable container

`Edge` already caches `#box` and `#lbox`, but those are safe for a reason that does not transfer: a
box is a container the graph mutates in place, so the cache cannot go stale. A vertex REFERENCE can,
if the object for an id is ever replaced. Four paths have to hold, and all four do:

- **`addVertex` with an existing id RETURNS the existing vertex** — `if (params.id && this.getVertexById(params.id)) return this.getVertexById(params.id)!`. It never replaces the object.
- **`removeVertex` cascades to the incident edges**, so no edge outlives its endpoint.
- **A rollback re-adds the vertex FIRST and then its edges**, both as fresh objects, so no edge object observes a replaced endpoint.
- **`set graph` drops the cache** alongside `#box`/`#lbox`, which is what a graph MOVE needs.

Cost: two references per edge, so ~16MB on a 1,000,000-edge graph, and only for edges whose
endpoints are actually read — the fields stay `undefined` until then. `fromId`/`toId` remain correct
where only the id is wanted (item 140) and allocate nothing.

### THREE REPS INVENTED TWO REGRESSIONS, and a null control proved the harness rather than the change

This is the part worth carrying forward. At min-of-3, one case per process, order alternated:

| case                           | before    | after  | at 3 reps | at 9 reps |
| ------------------------------ | --------- | ------ | --------- | --------- |
| two-column hop projection      | 193.70 ms | 73.24  | 2.16x     | **2.64x** |
| Gremlin `out(K).values(age)`   | 121.76    | 48.08  | 2.28x     | **2.53x** |
| hop projection + far filter    | 144.24    | 60.52  | 1.90x     | **2.38x** |
| labelled-middle `COUNT { }`    | 127.88    | 104.89 | 1.33x     | **1.22x** |
| one-column hop projection      | 71.59     | 62.06  | **0.82x** | **1.15x** |
| `COUNT { }` one hop — CONTROL  | 11.56     | 11.84  | **0.77x** | **0.98x** |
| node-only projection — CONTROL | 5.73      | 5.23   | 0.96x     | **1.10x** |

Two rows read as REGRESSIONS at three reps — including a control that touches no edges at all — and
both dissolved at nine. The deciding instrument was a **NULL CONTROL**: the same two fields added to
`Edge` but never read or written, so the only thing that changes is the size of every edge. It read
**1.40x FASTER** on the node-only projection and 1.17x faster on the two-column one — speedups a
dead field cannot cause. That is what established the swing as the harness, not object growth and not
the cache, and it is why the rep count went up instead of the change being abandoned.

The failing rows share a property: they materialize many rows, so they are GC-dominated. Item 592
hit the same thing (`ctl-project-nohop` reading 1.10x, then 1.51x, then 0.58x) and replaced the
control; the better fix is **nine reps on any allocation-heavy row**, which this tick measured
converging where three did not.

### Independent confirmation from the repo's own benches

| row                                               | recorded    | now                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `traverse 1-hop project + start filter`           | 102.4 ms    | **68.4** (1.50x)                                 |
| `V().out().values(age)` (ts)                      | 273.3       | **167.7** (1.63x), ts/native 8.5x -> 5.6x        |
| `query: 2-hop subquery item`                      | 113.5       | **95.7**                                         |
| `traverse 1-hop project`                          | 105.9       | 100.2                                            |
| `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)`                    | 3120.2      | 2918.7 — ingest uses `fromId`/`toId`, unaffected |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter`, `query: subquery item` | 43.4 / 30.9 | 44.2 / 29.6 — flat                               |

### Teeth, and the mutant that found the hazard I had reasoned about

Five mutants under `timeout 900 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`. Crossing the two
slots, resolving `from` from the `to` id, and returning the cache without resolving it are all
CAUGHT. One is an answer-equivalent reroute (never cache, always resolve) and survives by
construction.

**The fifth — deleting the invalidation from `set graph` — SURVIVED all 4,671 tests across 347
files.** Nothing in the suite moved an edge between graphs and then read its endpoints, which is
exactly the stale-reference hazard the soundness argument turns on.
`packages/core/src/core/edge-endpoint-cache.test.ts` now pins it, in the style of its neighbour
`adjacency-box.test.ts` ("a cache over graph-owned state is wrong only on the SECOND read"): it
populates the cache against one graph, moves the edge to a second graph holding DIFFERENT vertex
objects under the same ids, and asserts the endpoints come back from the new graph. The ids are
identical either way, so the assertion has to read a PROPERTY to tell them apart — an id-level check
would pass against the stale objects. Both that mutant and a one-sided variant are now CAUGHT, and
two more tests pin the `addVertex`-returns-existing and `removeVertex`-cascades paths.

## 596 — the parse cache REFUSED every parameterized INSERT, and bind is where the fix goes

`bench:usage` has a pair of write rows that should differ only in how the value arrives, and the
parameterized one was losing by 23%:

| row                            | before      | after      | vs the literal twin |
| ------------------------------ | ----------- | ---------- | ------------------- |
| `write: append node` (literal) | 363.4k op/s | 369.8k     | —                   |
| `write: append node [params]`  | 280.4k      | **326.5k** | 0.77x -> **0.88x**  |

Binding a value is supposed to be the CHEAP way to repeat a write — it is the one case where the
text is identical every time. Items 228/229 built a cache of prepared plans precisely so
a repeated text stops re-parsing, and the parameterized write is the most repeatable text there is.

### It was being refused, and the module header said so

`parse_cache`'s admission check (`prepared_equivalent`) admits a text only if its PREPARED plan,
bound to the parameters in hand, renders identically to what the DIRECT path produces. Item 318
surveyed twenty shapes for divergences and found two: a parameter in `LIMIT`/`SKIP`, and

> a parameter in an INSERT value, where prepared mode ACCEPTS it and plans
> `InsertFrom`/`InsertNodeExpr` instead of the literal `Insert`/`InsertNode` path — the same rows by
> a slower operator, with no wrong answer to give it away.

and recorded it as benign because "the INSERT case excludes itself." For CORRECTNESS that is right.
What self-exclusion also means is that the text is remembered as REFUSED forever: every call
re-parses, and then pays parameter marshalling on top of what the interpolated form already pays.
That is the whole of the 23% deficit. The cost was sitting in a comment that read as a
reassurance.

### Why the divergence exists, and why it is removable

`gql.rs` already lowers `InsertFrom { input: Row }` to `Plan::Insert` when every property is a
literal — but it runs during the parse, while `$n` is still an `Expr::Param`, so a parameterized
INSERT fails the literal test. `bind::bind_plan`'s `InsertFrom` arm has just made those same
templates literal. The lowering simply needs to run again afterwards. `lower_insert_literal` moved
from `gql.rs` to `ir.rs` as `pub(crate)` so both callers share one definition rather than the bind
side growing a second copy that can drift.

### THE PLACEMENT WAS WRONG FIRST, and the probe said it was right

I put the re-lowering in `opt.rs`, where answer-preserving rewrites live. `prepared_parity_probe`
flipped from "DIFFERENT PLAN — a cache would change the route" to "SAME plan", so it looked done.
It was not: **the admission check compares UNOPTIMIZED plans**, so a rewrite in the optimizer runs
strictly too late to be seen by it. The cache went on refusing the text while the probe reported
agreement. `stats().refused` is what showed it (`refused=1` with the probe green), and that is the
instrument to reach for — the probe answers "do the two routes end up at the same plan", which is
not the question the cache asks.

In `bind` it has to sit AFTER the match rather than inside the `InsertFrom` arm: the arm holds
`&mut` borrows of the plan's own fields and cannot assign through `plan` while they live. The
replacement is computed first so the immutable borrow ends before the assignment.

### Measured

Three alternated rounds, order reversed per round, one `bench:usage` process per side, `cargo build
--features capi` per side because the TS harness dlopens the `.so`:

| row                                  | before | after  | ratio     |
| ------------------------------------ | ------ | ------ | --------- |
| `write: append node [params]`        | 280.4k | 326.5k | **1.16x** |
| `write: append then delete node`     | 145.8k | 154.6k | 1.06x     |

Exactly one row clears the noise floor and it is the targeted one. The thirteen READ and
non-parameterized rows are controls the change cannot reach — a re-lowering that only fires on
`Plan::InsertFrom { input: Row }` has nothing to do on any of them — and they span 0.96x-1.02x,
which is this box's floor. `write: append then delete node` at 1.06x is the one row that is
arguably reachable and is not claimed: it sits inside that same spread.

The write rows are the only ones the change can reach; every read row is the control, and they sit
inside the noise floor.

### Teeth, and a mutant that was NOT what it looked like

Three mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p
MemorySwapMax=0`:

| mutant                                     | result                          |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------- |
| B2 invert the `Plan::Row` guard            | CAUGHT                          |
| B3 drop the re-lowering entirely           | CAUGHT                          |
| B1 drop the `matches!(**input, Plan::Row)` | **SURVIVED twice**, then CAUGHT |

B1 is the dangerous-looking one: without the guard, a `MATCH … INSERT` with literal properties
collapses to `Plan::Insert` and would insert ONCE instead of once per matched row. It survived.

The first explanation I reached for was that my fixture did not have the shape — `FOR x IN [1,2,3]
INSERT (:N {v: x})` has a SLOT property and `INSERT (:N {v: duration('PT1S')})` has a CALL
property, so `lower_insert_literal` refuses both on its own and the guard was never what stopped
them. That was a real fixture fault (the coinciding-fixture trap again), so I added
`MATCH (u:User) INSERT (:Audit {kind: 'seen'})` — input rows, every property a literal, nothing
else to refuse it. **It still survived.** Rather than guess a third time I dumped the plans, and
the shape was exactly as assumed.

The answer is in the test HELPERS, and it changes what the guard is:

`direct_of` calls `parse_with_params_limited`, the UNBOUND direct parse, which no re-lowering
touches. So dropping the guard does not hand a collapsed plan back to the caller. It makes the
bound prepared plan disagree with the direct one, `prepared_equivalent` REFUSES the text, and every
call falls through to the direct path. The rows are right; what is lost is the cache slot.

**So the `Plan::Row` guard is a PERF guard whose correctness backstop is the admission check** —
which is the property the cache was built to have, now demonstrated by a mutant instead of argued
in a comment. A test can only observe admission, so
`a_row_driven_insert_keeps_the_per_row_operator` now sights the `MATCH … INSERT` twice and asserts
`stats().refused` is unchanged and `stats().size == 1`. B1 is CAUGHT there.

Two things generalize. First: **a surviving guard mutant is a question about what is observable,
not only about reachability.** I checked reachability twice (fixture shape, then the plan dump) and
both times the fixture was fine; the gap was that the assertion compared two values the mutant
moves together. Second: the pre-existing test asserting that a parameterized INSERT is REFUSED had
to be REVERSED, not deleted — it was pinning the carve-out as a contract, and the replacement
(`a_parameterized_insert_is_cached_now_that_bind_re_lowers_it`) pins the new one, including that a
different parameter value still returns the right rows through the cached plan.

## 597 — the native serving wrapper's per-call constants, 1.1-1.32x on every `bench:usage` row

Item 596's A/B table made something plain that had been attributed and left: on `bench:usage` the
native engine LOSES to pure TS on most serving rows (`read: point lookup` ts 1.21M against the
engine's 379k). Item 319 priced that as the FFI boundary — "TS-indexed usually BEATS native on that
bench (FFI dominates a small op)".

**That attribution is wrong, and its own probe says so.** `percall_probe`'s header records the raw
boundary at 7ns, and a `vertexCount` round trip measures 11ns today. A boundary that costs 11ns
cannot dominate a 2640ns call. Item 289's rule applies in reverse here: a boundary measured at a
million rows does not price one at a single row, and this row returns ONE.

### Decomposed by stage instead

`g.query` is three stages — `compileGql` -> `backend.queryRows` -> `decodeRows`. Timed separately,
through the same backend the bench uses:

| layer                                          | ns/op |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----- |
| `g.query(Q, {n})` — the bench row              | 2328  |
| `g.query(QLIT)` — constant text, no params     | 1621  |
| `g.query('RETURN 1 AS s')` — the wrapper FLOOR | 1152  |
| `backend.queryRows(Q, params)` — no wrapper    | 1725  |
| `backend.queryRows('RETURN 1 AS s')`           | 847   |
| raw boundary (`vertexCount`)                   | 11    |

So ~300ns is JS wrapper work on EVERY call, and the 847ns backend floor is itself mostly not the
boundary. Two levers, each located by micro-probe and then built against the real code (item 593's
rule: a probe may LOCATE a cost and must not SIZE one).

### Lever A — read the JSON carrier with a `CString`

`takeResult` does `toArrayBuffer` + `new Uint8Array` + `.slice()`, and then the caller does a
`TextDecoder.decode`. bun:ffi's `CString` decodes UTF-8 straight from the pointer in one step:

| reading a 30-byte JSON carrier from a pointer       | ns/op |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ----- |
| `toArrayBuffer`+`slice` -> `decode` -> `JSON.parse` | 381.6 |
| `CString(p, 0, len)` -> `JSON.parse`                | 132.8 |
| `CString` read alone                                | 22.6  |
| `JSON.parse` floor (string already in hand)         | 112.4 |

`toArrayBuffer` ALONE is 109.5ns. On a 3414-byte carrier the saving is 369ns, so this is a per-call
constant that does not turn into a tax on large results.

`EngineAbi` gains an OPTIONAL `queryText`; `Backend` gains `queryJson`/`gremlinText`, which prefer
it and otherwise decode `abi.query`'s bytes. The byte forms stay exactly as they were — ~20 test
call sites and `present-null-bench` want bytes, and widening `queryRows`' return type to
`Uint8Array | string` would have broken every one of them for no gain. The wasm backend implements
no `queryText` and takes the fallback.

**THE EXPLICIT LENGTH IS LOAD-BEARING.** The crate's buffer is not NUL-terminated, so the
zero-terminated form scans past the payload into whatever the allocator left there. Verified
against a buffer deliberately filled with non-NUL garbage immediately after the payload: ASCII,
2/3/4-byte UTF-8, an empty result, and a LITERAL NUL mid-payload, which the length form does not
truncate.

### Lever B — the replacer in `stringifyParams` was UNREACHABLE

It passed `JSON.stringify` a replacer purely to reject a `bigint`, and a replacer puts the whole
serialization on its slow path: **181.2ns against 58.7** for a one-key params object.
`Object.entries` -> `for..in` is another 50.8 -> 15.0.

Unreachable by exhaustion over what `assertParamModel` admits above it: a null/string/boolean/number
holds no bigint; a top-level bigint is thrown THERE, with a better message than the replacer's; a
flat list is recursed into, so a bigint element is thrown too; a tagged-temporal object must have
exactly one key whose value is a STRING, so a bigint field falls through to that function's final
throw; a `Temporal` is a class instance and `temporal.ts` contains the token `bigint` zero times;
and `undefined`/function/symbol encode to nothing. And if a future `Temporal` field ever held one,
`JSON.stringify` throws a `TypeError` of its own accord — the failure is loud, not silent.

### Measured

In-probe, with `backend.queryRows` as a control built into the same probe (it stays on the byte
route, so the change cannot reach it):

| layer                            | before | lever A | both |
| -------------------------------- | ------ | ------- | ---- |
| `g.query(Q, {n})`                | 2328   | 2087    | 1818 |
| `g.query(QLIT)`                  | 1621   | 1360    | 1346 |
| `g.query('RETURN 1 AS s')` floor | 1152   | 888     | 881  |
| `backend.queryRows(QLIT)` CTRL   | 1329   | 1355    | 1281 |
| `backend.queryRows(floor)` CTRL  | 847    | 858     | 815  |

Then `bench:usage`, three alternated rounds, order reversed per round, one process per side:

| row                                   | before | after  | ratio     | ts before | ts after | ts    |
| ------------------------------------- | ------ | ------ | --------- | --------- | -------- | ----- |
| `write: 100 updates in one tx`        | 341.8k | 450.7k | **1.32x** | 443.9k    | 438.9k   | 0.99x |
| `read: point lookup`                  | 377.5k | 495.5k | **1.31x** | 1.20M     | 1.16M    | 0.97x |
| `write: append node [params]`         | 320.5k | 418.8k | **1.31x** | 524.5k    | 513.4k   | 0.98x |
| `interleaved: write + traversal`      | 142.9k | 185.3k | **1.30x** | 231.8k    | 241.7k   | 1.04x |
| `write: property update`              | 309.5k | 395.1k | **1.28x** | 350.9k    | 373.6k   | 1.06x |
| `interleaved: write + point read`     | 167.6k | 214.1k | **1.28x** | 329.1k    | 333.2k   | 1.01x |
| `interleaved: append + link`          | 225.5k | 288.5k | **1.28x** | 199.4k    | 200.4k   | 1.01x |
| `analytic: fan-out spread 1-3 hops`   | 248.1k | 311.3k | **1.25x** | 191.0k    | 195.2k   | 1.02x |
| `analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops`  | 216.2k | 259.7k | **1.20x** | 218.4k    | 225.9k   | 1.03x |
| `read: permission check (inline)`     | 185.1k | 217.8k | **1.18x** | 438.8k    | 473.6k   | 1.08x |
| `write: append node`                  | 374.3k | 442.4k | **1.18x** | 88.9k     | 93.8k    | 1.06x |
| `read: 2-hop recommendation`          | 220.6k | 256.8k | **1.16x** | 543.0k    | 561.3k   | 1.03x |
| `read: permission check`              | 147.4k | 165.7k | **1.12x** | 486.0k    | 483.9k   | 1.00x |
| `write: append then delete node`      | 152.6k | 170.2k | **1.12x** | 527.7k    | 522.7k   | 0.99x |
| `read: keyed dedup lookup [inline]`   | 144.3k | 158.1k | 1.10x     | 54.5k     | 58.6k    | 1.08x |
| `read: keyed dedup lookup`            | 139.6k | 150.8k | 1.08x     | 75.2k     | 77.3k    | 1.03x |
| `write: 100 updates in one statement` | 795.5k | 830.8k | 1.04x     | 1.14M     | 1.08M    | 0.95x |

**EVERY ROW MOVING IS THE SITUATION THAT NEEDS A CONTROL, AND THE FIRST RUN THREW ITS CONTROL
AWAY.** This change is in the native wrapper only, so the `ts` column is a control it cannot reach
— measured in the SAME processes, on the same fixture, in the same rounds. The driver's first
version recorded `ts` as one max across both sides, which cannot answer whether TS moved too; a
uniform gain is then indistinguishable from machine drift. Carried per side, `ts` reads 0.95x-1.08x
centred on 1.01x while the engine column reads 1.04x-1.32x. Two independent three-round runs agree
within 0.04x on every row.

The `ts` spread also prices the FLOOR at about +/-6%, so `write: 100 updates in one statement`
(1.04x) is AT it and is not claimed. Its shape is the right one anyway: it is the only row that
makes one FFI call per ~100 counted operations, so a per-call constant is amortized ~100x, and it
gains least. The cheapest calls gain most. That ordering is what a per-call constant predicts, and
it is the strongest evidence here after the control.

### Teeth

Six mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`.
The harness was proved to kill FIRST: a bare spin loop exits 124, an allocator bomb under a 1G cap
terminated well inside its window.

| mutant                                              | result                    |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `CString` with no explicit length (zero-terminated) | CAUGHT (277 fail)         |
| length `len - 1`                                    | CAUGHT (550 fail)         |
| length `len + 1`                                    | CAUGHT (544 fail)         |
| `stringifyParams` validates nothing                 | CAUGHT (9 fail)           |
| `parseJson` ignores a string payload                | CAUGHT (554 fail)         |
| **`queryJson` ignores `abi.queryText`**             | **SURVIVED**, then CAUGHT |

The survivor is a ROUTE CHOICE: both routes return the same string, so it is answer-equivalent and
all 925 tests passed. This is the shape `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` records — and there is no
arithmetic here to extract as a pure function, because the decision is a capability check. So the
test observes WHICH ROUTE RAN: `buildEngineBackend` over a fake `EngineAbi` that counts calls,
asserting `queryJson`/`gremlinText` take `queryText` when it exists, that the byte forms stay on
`abi.query`, and that the fallback returns the identical answer by the other route — which is
exactly why the result cannot catch it. Re-run: CAUGHT.

Two tests, not one, because the claims are different. The route-choice test needs no transport. The
other, `the text carrier matches the byte carrier, including multi-byte UTF-8`, runs inside the
existing both-transports suite and asserts the text form EQUALS the byte form — so the FFI
`CString` read and the wasm `TextDecoder` read are held to each other as well as to the expected
value. It covers 2/3/4-byte UTF-8, a multi-byte PARAMETER value, an empty result (length 0, where a
zero-terminated read has nothing to stop it), and a long carrier. Neither claim is visible on an
ASCII payload, which is what every other test in that file uses.

## 598 — the parameter cost RETRACTED as a target, and the one piece worth taking (~30ns)

Item 597's decomposition left a number unexplained: through the FFI, `backend.queryRows` with one
parameter costs 1760ns against 1281 without — **479ns for one small parameter**. That looked like
the next lever.

### The bigger candidate was already refuted, and CLOSED.md said so

Before pricing it I checked `CLOSED.md`, which is what it is for. `optimize_indexed` runs on EVERY
serving call (`exec::run_query` calls it; the native parse cache holds the UNOPTIMIZED plan), worth
~350ns, and the TS engine has had a plan cache since item 229 — so "native has no plan cache" reads
like the obvious missing path. **Item 293 refuted it a commit after item 292 proposed it:**
`bind_params` runs BEFORE `optimize_indexed` by design, so an optimized plan has THAT CALL'S
parameter values baked into it. A `(text, store-version)` key would serve stale values — a wrong
answer, not a slow one. Not re-derived. (The design that would remove it is to optimize the
PARAMETERIZED plan and bind into the optimized one, which inverts the documented IR contract and
hands the optimizer less information. Still its own item, still not a cache key.)

### The 479ns does not have a lever in it

It decomposes into five pieces, none of them individually above `bench:usage`'s floor:

| piece                                                            | ns   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---- |
| JS: building the params object + `JSON.stringify` (value varies) | ~130 |
| Rust: `ndjson::parse_json` of the params object                  | 67   |
| Rust: `params_from_obj` (clones the key `String`, converts)      | ~60  |
| JS: `encoder.encode(params)`                                     | ~20  |
| Rust: `bind_params`' lookup table                                | ~30  |
| accounted                                                        | ~307 |

The remainder is bun:ffi's per-ARGUMENT marshalling — `lnk_query` takes eight arguments where
`vertexCount` takes one — which item 292 already recorded as needing a profiler rather than another
probe. **So the 479ns is retracted as a single target.** What is left is the one piece that is a
clean change.

### `bind_params` built a `HashMap` per call, for one parameter

```rust
let map: HashMap<&str, &Value> = params.iter().map(|(k, v)| (k.as_str(), v)).collect();
```

A heap allocation plus a SipHash-1-3 insert per parameter and a SipHash per `$name` occurrence —
and there is exactly ONE lookup site (`bind_expr`'s `Expr::Param` arm), so the table bought nothing
but its own construction.

The question worth asking is not whether a scan wins at one parameter but **where it stops
winning**, since a scan is O(P) per lookup against the map's O(1). `examples/bind_probe.rs` sweeps
both axes:

| params x lookups | hashmap ns | scan ns | ratio  |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ------- | ------ |
| 1 x 1            | 32.9       | 2.0     | 16.2x  |
| 2 x 16           | 171.9      | 43.5    | 4.0x   |
| 4 x 4            | 94.1       | 18.8    | 5.0x   |
| 8 x 16           | 238.9      | 137.5   | 1.7x   |
| 16 x 1           | 204.8      | 2.0     | 101.0x |
| 32 x 16          | 526.8      | 153.1   | 3.4x   |

**There is no crossover in the range** — the map's BUILD cost dominates throughout, and at 32
parameters it is 386.7ns before a single lookup. (The param-less row reads 0.2ns against 0.0: the
optimizer removes both, so that row says nothing and is not a 3672x anything.)

### Honestly sized, and the bench is used only to certify no harm

The realistic shape is one parameter used once: **32.2 -> 2.0ns**. `percall_probe` confirms it on
the real function rather than a stand-in — `clone + bind_params` **147 -> 119ns** — which is the
same ~30ns from a second instrument.

~30ns of a ~2030ns serving call is ~1.5%, and item 597 priced this bench's floor at ~±6% from the
ts column's spread. So `bench:usage` CANNOT resolve this change, and a three-round alternated run
was done as a REGRESSION CHECK: engine 0.96x-1.08x scattered around 1.00, worst row 0.96x.

**The control makes the point better than the engine column does.** In that same run the ts column
— which a Rust bind change cannot touch at all — spans **0.82x-1.16x**, WIDER than the engine
column's 0.96x-1.08x. When the control's spread exceeds the effect, the bench is not an instrument
for the effect; it is only evidence of no harm. The win is claimed from `bind_probe` and
`percall_probe`, and no bench row is claimed.

### Teeth, and both mutants were about READING THE NAME

| mutant                                         | result            |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| forward scan (first-wins instead of last-wins) | CAUGHT (new test) |
| `find(                                         | _                 | true)` — ignore the name entirely | **SURVIVED**, then CAUGHT |

**`.rev()` is not a style choice, and the first mutant is why.** A repeated parameter name is
LAST-WINS: `HashMap::collect` gave that for free, and a forward scan is FIRST-wins — the same rows
by a different value, with nothing in the suite to notice. Last-wins is this codebase's convention
for any repeated JSON key (item 333 pins it for `labels`/`properties`, and its own comment records
that the mutant truncating to 0 survived until that test existed, "because nothing else in the
suite feeds a duplicated key"). It is REACHABLE: `Json::Obj` is a `Vec<(String, Json)>` whose
parser pushes, so `params_from_obj` can hand `bind_params` two entries under one name.
`g.query(text, obj)` cannot produce one — a JS object has no duplicates — but `lnk_query` takes the
params as a raw JSON string, so any ABI caller can.
`a_repeated_parameter_name_is_last_wins` was written AGAINST THE OLD CODE FIRST, so it pins
existing behaviour rather than describing the refactor.

**The second mutant is the sharper one.** `find(|_| true)` matches any key, so with the reverse
scan it returns the LAST parameter for every `$name` — and it survived all 1,177 tests. Every bind
test supplies one parameter, or two whose values are interchangeable, so nothing noticed the lookup
had stopped reading the name at all. **A one-parameter fixture cannot witness a name-blind lookup**,
the same shape as item 586's total count that could not witness a direction bug.
`two_parameters_bind_to_their_own_names` supplies two whose values are deliberately NOT
interchangeable — alice is 30 and bob is 25, so crossing the bindings matches nobody — and asserts
both the matching pair and the crossed pair. Re-run: CAUGHT.

That is the real yield of this item. The perf change is 30ns; the two tests close a silent
wrong-answer path and a coverage hole that had been open across every parameter test in the file.

`bun test packages/core packages/gql packages/gremlin packages/serialization` 3750 pass / 0 fail,
