## 611 — depth 4's structure, priced before derived: it needs an A^2 entry, so it is ONE LEVEL dearer

Item 600 derived the depth-3 trail correction and said depth 4 "has more terms and is not
claimed". That reads as a quantity problem. It is a KIND problem, and the difference is worth
recording before anyone spends a tick on the algebra.

### Why depth 3 was special

Of its three pair-equality events — `(e0,e1)`, `(e1,e2)`, `(e0,e2)` — only `(e0,e2)` is
NON-ADJACENT, and it spans exactly ONE intermediate edge. That pins a 2-cycle `a -> b -> a`, so the
term is a REVERSE-EDGE MULTIPLICITY: `Σ_{e: a->b} m(b, a)`. Every other term is a self-loop tally
or a degree. That is the whole reason the formula is cheap.

### Depth 4 has a pair that spans TWO

Its non-adjacent pairs are `(e0,e2)`, `(e1,e3)` and `(e0,e3)`. The last spans two intermediate
edges: `e3 == e0` forces the walk to be `a -> b -> ? -> a -> b`, so `e1, e2` are a 2-WALK from `b`
back to `a`. The term is therefore

```text
Σ_{e: a->b}  A²[b][a]
```

— an entry of the squared adjacency matrix, per edge. Verified non-zero in 8 of 8 random graphs
(3-5 vertices, 4-10 edges), computed densely and compared against the walk and trail counts.

### So it is not blocked, it is one level dearer — and that IS the price

`A²[b][a]` is reachable without a matrix product: for each edge `a -> b`, walk `b`'s adjacency and
count edges `k -> a` for each neighbour `k`. Summed, that is the **3-WALK COUNT** — against
enumeration's 4-walk count. So depth 4 buys a factor of the average degree, exactly as depth 3
does against 3-walk enumeration (item 600b). The relationship repeats one level up:

| depth | correction costs | enumeration costs | win         |
| ----- | ---------------- | ----------------- | ----------- |
| 3     | 2-walks          | 3-walks           | ~avg degree |
| 4     | 3-walks          | 4-walks           | ~avg degree |

### Why that is not a reason to build it next

The prize is the same FACTOR as depth 3 but the derivation is much larger: six pair events with
their intersections, against depth 3's three events and four terms. And a wrong term returns a
plausible count — the class of bug this repo records as invisible to timing and caught only by unit
tests and fuzzers. Item 602 did leave `exec::fastpath_fuzz` able to generate depth 4, so the oracle
exists, which is the one prerequisite that was missing.

**Recorded so the next pass starts from the structure rather than re-deriving it**, and so "more
terms" is not mistaken for "a bigger version of the same thing". The measured prize remains large
in absolute terms — TS `-[:K]->{4}` is 5765 ms against native's 80.96 — and the standing bench has
no row for it.

## 611b — depth 4 PRICED PROPERLY: 14 structural terms, and my first collapse was WRONG

Item 611 established that depth 4 needs an `A²` entry. This prices the derivation itself, because
"six pair events" undersells it, and the attempt produced a result worth more than a formula.

### The decomposition is right

Inclusion-exclusion over the six pair-equality events `(e0,e1) … (e2,e3)`, computed numerically
over random graphs admitting self-loops and parallel edges: **300/300 agree** with brute-force
4-trail enumeration. So the shape of the answer is settled.

### But it does not collapse the way depth 3 did

**All 63 non-empty subsets are feasible** — none is jointly impossible, so none drops out. They
reduce to **14 distinct terms**, one per partition of `{e0,e1,e2,e3}` other than the all-distinct
one (Bell(4) = 15, minus one). Depth 3 had FOUR. The net coefficients are the partition lattice's
Möbius function, `∏_blocks (-1)^(|B|-1) (|B|-1)!` — `-6` for all four together, `+2` for a 3+1,
`+1` for 2+2, `-1` for a 2+1+1 — which is a clean statement, and it is the only clean part.

### MY FIRST COLLAPSE WAS WRONG, AND THE VALIDATOR CAUGHT IT ON THE FIRST RUN

Having the right 14 coefficients, I summed them against per-partition counts and got
**39/200 agreement**. The 63-subset form had just agreed 300/300, so the decomposition was not the
problem — the collapse was, almost certainly the direction of the Möbius inversion (whether a
partition's count is over walks coarser or finer than it). Not debugged further, because the
verdict was already in:

**That is the finding.** Depth 4's derivation is 14 terms rather than 4, at least one of them needs
`A²` (item 611), and a plausible-looking collapse of correct coefficients was still wrong on the
first attempt and would have returned plausible counts for a 4-hop trail in production. Against a
payoff of ~average degree — the SAME factor as depth 3, per item 611's table, not a larger one.

### So depth 4 is NOT the next thing to build, and this says why with evidence

Not "more terms" (item 600's phrasing) and not "intractable" (my own first guess at 611, before
the `A²` cost model). It is: **four times the terms, one of them needing a quantity no O(V+E) pass
provides, for the same factor of win, with a derivation that has already produced one wrong answer
under validation.**

Anyone who does take it on should keep the brute-force validator FIRST — it cost minutes and found
the error immediately, which is exactly how item 600's depth-3 formula was landed safely
(400/400 before a line of engine code). `exec::fastpath_fuzz` can now generate depth 4 (item 602),
so the second oracle is in place too.

### Gates

Measurement-and-docs only; no engine change. `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached clean. CI green
on 611.

## 612 — the Rust maintainability pass: a module map, thirteen headers, a named prologue, and a placement claim that mutation NARROWED

The optimization loop closed at 611b. This is the first of two readability passes over what it
left behind — Rust here, TypeScript next. The brief was explicitly "without losing any of the
perf", so every change below is either comment-only or mechanical, and the one that touches
codegen is measured as an A/B of two binaries.

**What I did NOT do, and why.** The obvious-looking target is the ~25 lines of REJECTED-lever
commentary sitting between the `Plan::Aggregate` arm and its first line of code. It stays. This
repo's own rule is to record a rejected optimization with its numbers _next to the code it would
have changed_ — "several have been re-attempted otherwise" — and the inline-sensitivity note
there is load-bearing twice over: it is also the record that `#[inline(never)]` on the whole
ladder buys nothing. Moving that history to `docs/` would make the file read better and the
codebase worse.

### Finding 1 — `exec`'s module structure was undiscoverable

Thirteen submodules were extracted from a 25,000-line `exec.rs` (the split recorded in the
audit), and **the declarations stayed wherever the extracted code had been**: scattered over six
places at lines 857, 860, 867, 3182-3194, 4862-4875, 5613 and 5681. `pub(crate) mod fastpath;`
sat 4,862 lines deep, immediately after an unrelated function body. So the engine's shape could
not be learned from the top of the file; `grep -n '^mod'` was the only way to get the list.

**And none of the thirteen had a `//!` header** — `fastpath_fuzz.rs` was the sole exception in the
directory. The module map existed, but only inside the 23,000-line append-only audit, which is
the wrong store for it: that file answers "what did we decide about X", not "what is in this
file".

Both fixed. The declarations are now one block at the top of `exec.rs`, ordered as the pipeline
reads rather than alphabetically, with a one-line summary each. Each submodule got a header
saying what it owns plus the one non-obvious thing about it — and those were written from the
code, not from memory, which is why three of them carry a fact I had to go and check:
`label_mode_allows_shortcut` is a `#[cfg(test)]`/`#[cfg(not(test))]` PAIR (so a route decision
read off a test build is not the production one), `output_names` fixes the observable column
order, and `try_stream_gremlin_json`'s gate order is load-bearing because it EXECUTES its seed.

`fastpath.rs`'s header is longer and earns it: 6,002 lines, 86 top-level items, zero section
markers, and the most-churned non-test file in the crate (41 of the last 200 engine commits). It
now opens with a family table — fused hop, dict/streaming, degree algebra, var-length, frontier,
scan, chain/n-hop, Gremlin helpers — and with the ladder's ordering rule stated once, where the
call site had been re-deriving it per entry.

### Finding 2 — the ladder's placement comments were prose, and one of them was TOO STRONG

The `or_else` chain is ~100 lines of 38 entries whose order is justified entirely in comments:
"BEFORE the frontier/scan aggregate paths", "ABOVE `try_frontier_prop_agg`", "Added LAST on
purpose". That matters because of how the failure presents: an entry placed below one that claims
its shape is **dead code that still passes every test it has** — both paths return the same
answer, so no differential test can see it, and the bench row simply reads 1.0x. Items 371, 375
and 422 are three instances, each found by an `eprintln` at function entry.

The repo already knows the right answer and states it at item 369: _"relying on the ORDER of a
32-entry fast-path chain for CORRECTNESS is what breaks when someone reorders it"_, pinned by a
direct assertion on the function. Items 369 and 376 do exactly that. **The idiom existed; the
coverage was partial.** `try_frontier_multi_agg` — whose placement the call site justifies with
"disjoint from all of them by arity" — had NO test referencing it at all.

So I added the pin for it, and mutation then corrected the claim it was pinning.

| mutant                                                | first form | after      |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------- |
| M1 `try_frontier_count` admits any arity              | SURVIVED   | **CAUGHT** |
| M3 `try_frontier_prop_agg` admits any arity           | SURVIVED   | **CAUGHT** |
| M2 `try_frontier_multi_agg` drops its own arity floor | SURVIVED   | **CAUGHT** |

Three survivors, three different lessons, and none of them was a hole in the code:

- **M2 survived because disjointness is symmetric and I pinned one side.** Relaxing
  `aggs.len() < 2` to `aggs.is_empty()` leaves every assertion true: a two-aggregate shape is
  still claimed, and the declines are statements about _other_ functions. The entry must also
  refuse the ONE-aggregate shapes owned by the entries BELOW it, or its arity floor does nothing.
- **M1 survived because my fixture never reached the gate.** `try_frontier_count` requires a
  top-level `IsLabeled` filter, and I had written `-[:E]->(b)` with an unlabelled endpoint — so it
  declined on the filter shape and the arity gate was masked. `(b:N)` fixed it. A gate you cannot
  reach is a gate you have not tested, and the first fixture looked entirely reasonable.
- **M3 survived for a reason that NARROWS THE CALL SITE'S CLAIM**, which is the real find here.
  Every upstream entry reads `aggs[0]` and then applies its own CONTENT gate —
  `try_frontier_count` wants `count(*)`, `try_frontier_prop_agg` wants a property argument. So on
  any one shape, all but one of them decline on content _before arity is ever consulted_, and an
  arity mutant in the others survives. `count(*), max(b.v)` catches M1; only `max(b.v), count(*)`
  catches M3.

  **"Disjoint from all of them by arity" is therefore too strong.** The disjointness holds — but
  for most entries on a given shape the content gate is the load-bearing one, and the arity gate
  is reachable in exactly one aggregate ORDERING. The test now runs both orders, and the call
  site says this instead of the stronger thing it said before.

What remains honestly untestable: the ROUTE itself. A fast path is answer-equivalent by
construction, so no behavioural test can tell which entry answered — item 473's own note and
[[perf-gate-needs-its-own-test]] both say so. The PREMISE is what is now pinned, which is the
most that is available.

### Finding 3 — one gate prologue, copy-pasted 25 times

Discovered by accident: an M1 mutant anchored on the prologue reported `PATTERN APPEARS 25 TIMES`.
The assert-exactly-once rule earned itself again — not by catching a bad mutant, but by naming a
duplication nothing had flagged.

```rust
    if !keys.is_empty() || aggs.len() != 1 {
        return None;
    }
    let agg = &aggs[0];
```

Twenty-five occurrences, **byte-identical in all 25** (verified: the three lines following each
are the same in every case). Now `let agg = sole_agg(keys, aggs)?;` against one
`#[inline(always)]` helper whose body is a slice pattern:

```rust
match (keys.is_empty(), aggs) {
    (true, [agg]) => Some(agg),
    _ => None,
}
```

`[agg]` says "exactly one" in the type system rather than as a length check sitting beside an
index, and the concept the ladder kept re-spelling finally has somewhere to be documented — which
is where the note about `try_frontier_multi_agg` wanting the opposite now lives. Net −57 lines.

### MEASURED, and the toll reported as a toll

This is the only change that can move codegen, so: two binaries built side by side, md5-distinct,
alternated with the order swapped each round, cold run of each discarded, min of three. The
instrument [[filter-count-row-is-not-a-screen]] prescribes for a native row.

`query_bench -- counts`, the rows whose entries open with the replaced prologue:

| row                    | before µs | after µs | ratio |
| ---------------------- | --------- | -------- | ----- |
| `count(prop) num`      | 93.4      | 93.1     | 1.00x |
| `count(prop) str`      | 93.5      | 93.0     | 1.01x |
| `count(DISTINCT prop)` | 165.0     | 164.1    | 1.01x |
| `grouped`              | 377.7     | 368.9    | 1.02x |
| `label`                | 0.3       | 0.3      | 1.00x |
| `filtered`             | 91.0      | 91.6     | 0.99x |

Then the whole of `query_bench` — ~60 rows — all between **0.92x and 1.09x, scattered in both
directions and centred on 1.00x**. The two widest (`varlen + path` 0.92x, `repeat-group control`
1.09x) are allocation-heavy rows that this repo's own rule says need nine reps rather than three,
and they move in opposite directions, so I am claiming neither.

**`filtered` is reported as the toll, not as a result.** It read 1.04x, 0.99x and 0.95x across
three separate invocations of the same two binaries — which is the cluster behaving exactly as
item 250 recorded, where a null control that only lengthened an error string reproduced the shift
in full. It cannot screen this change and is not evidence for it either.

### Gates, each as its own command

`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` exit 0 (it caught a `type_complexity` on the new
test's function-pointer array before anything else did — fixed with a `LadderEntry` alias, not an
`allow`). `cargo fmt --check` exit 0. `cargo test --release` 1179 + 13 + 723 pass, 0 fail.
`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000 cargo test rewrite_fuzz` 10 pass. `bun run fuzz` 13 pass / 0 fail
across all seven byte-identity fuzzers. All mutants run under
`timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, built uncapped
first, pristine restored before each mutant and verified by md5 afterwards.

## 613 — the TypeScript maintainability pass: two precedence narratives that DISAGREED, a header pointing at three functions that no longer exist, and 61 more like them

The second of the two readability passes (item 612 did Rust). Same brief — "without losing any of
the perf" — so again: comment-only, one inert reorder, and a new probe that nothing imports.

### Finding 1 — the TS ladder is BETTER documented than the Rust one, and that is worth recording

Opposite of what I expected. `runLinear`'s `if (linear.…)` chain in `executor/clauses.ts` is 19
rungs and it already distinguishes the three reasons a rung sits where it does, per rung:
correctness (`optionalHopCount` is strictly narrower), cost (item 418 measured a branch ahead of a
hot dispatch costing the plain hop projection **1.12x** for nothing), and _"the order is for
reading rather than for correctness"_ (`forProjection`). That is the standard item 612 had to
retrofit onto `fastpath.rs`. Nothing to fix here; it is the model.

### Finding 2 — but there were TWO precedence narratives, in two files, and they DISAGREED

`compileLinear` in `executor.ts` builds a 19-field object by calling every detector eagerly. The
field order carries **no precedence whatsoever** — all nineteen run, and which one answers is
decided later by the lazy chain in `clauses.ts`.

It did not read that way. The literal carried the comment _"The OPTIONAL-hop count sits above the
plain one"_, and the order was:

|      | literal (`executor.ts`) | real ladder (`clauses.ts`) |
| ---- | ----------------------- | -------------------------- |
| 1    | `forCount`              | `varLengthCount`           |
| 2    | `forProjection`         | `countShortcut`            |
| 3    | `optionalHopCount`      | `optionalHopCount`         |
| 4    | `optionalHopProjection` | `forCount`                 |
| 5    | `countShortcut`         | `forProjection`            |
| 6-19 | **identical**           | **identical**              |

**Fourteen of nineteen matched.** That is what made it a trap rather than a harmless difference: a
list that resembles the precedence for three quarters of its length reads as though it IS the
precedence. And the one entry carrying an explicit claim contradicted the real chain — `clauses.ts`
places `optionalHopCount` BELOW `countShortcut`, correctly, as the strictly narrower shape (item
510), where the literal's comment said it sits above.

Fixed by removing the discrepancy rather than documenting it: the literal is now in ladder order
exactly, with a comment saying the order is immaterial here, that `clauses.ts` is the sole
authority, and that it is kept identical anyway so the resemblance is a guarantee instead of a
coincidence. Verified inert before touching it — nothing iterates `CLinear`'s keys
(`Object.keys`/`entries`/`for…in`: no hits), and every detector is a pure function of
`(fast, clauses)`.

### Finding 3 — `shortcuts.ts`'s header described a file that no longer exists

Six lines, opening _"Count / reachability fast-paths for GQL"_, on a file that is now **8,297
lines and 101 top-level items** and which since then has acquired the ordered node projection
(605/610), the level recurrence (`walkLevelCount`), and the depth-3 trail correction
(`reusedTrailsAt3`). Zero section markers in 8,297 lines.

Worse, it ended by naming the native twins: ``(`try_count_edges` / `try_count_two_hop` /
`try_reachable_distinct`)``. **All three are gone from the crate.** So the three starting points a
reader was given for crossing to the native side were dead, and two further inline comments
pointed at `try_reachable_distinct` as well.

Rewritten: what the file now holds, a seven-family map, where precedence actually lives, the LIVE
native counterparts (`try_fused_count`, `try_edge_filtered_count`, `try_3hop_product_count`,
`try_nhop_sweep_count`, `try_degree_algebra` with `walk_levels_total` and `reused_trails_at_3`,
`varlen_distinct_endpoint_count` — each verified present), and the reminder that a new predicate
form needs its spellings in `bun run spelling`, because equal-meaning-unequal-cost returns correct
answers and no correctness test catches it.

### Finding 4 — so I grepped the pattern elsewhere, and it is 61 more

The method's next step, and it was the right one. Every backticked snake_case name in a TS comment
whose line claims to be about the other engine (`native`/`rust`/`engine`/`crate`/`.rs`), checked
against every `.rs` file in the crate:

**61 unresolved citations across 51 distinct names.** `val_eq` alone is cited 6 times from 5 files
(including `executor.ts`'s element-identity comment and `list-equality.test.ts`'s header) and does
not exist. Others: `apply_sack_op`, `eval_graph_pred`, `math_vars`, `set_type_fault`, `dedup_key`,
`run_cquery_body`, `eval_predicate`, `check_count_params`, `bind_group_vars`,
`try_count_comma_join`, and two Rust TEST names that TS tests claim to mirror
(`merge_edge_between_bound_endpoints_upserts`,
`scalar_functions_graph_string_list_conversion`). Even a cited module path is stale —
`crates/lenke-engine/src/value.rs` does not exist.

These are almost certainly the `lenke-core` → `lenke-engine` migration's wake. The cost is
specific: **a citation is the only index from one engine to the other**, nothing compiles it,
nothing tests it, and a dead name reads exactly like a live one — so the reader does not learn
they have been misdirected, they just fail to find anything.

**The fix is a probe, not 61 hand edits.** `packages/native/xref-probe.ts`, `bun run xref`. A
PROBE and not a test for the reason `spelling-probe.ts` is one: a snake_case word in a comment is
usually a Rust item but is sometimes a TS-local identifier, a config key or a file stem, so a
threshold in CI would be noise and a human has to read the list. Run it after a Rust rename. A
comment that names a dead symbol deliberately ends with `xref:gone` and is skipped.

I fixed the three in the file I was already in and left the other 61 standing with the instrument
to find them, rather than guessing 61 replacements I cannot verify one at a time. **The baseline
is 61 / 51; that number is the thing to drive down.**

### PRICED, NOT BUILT — the TS analogue of item 612's 25x prologue

A repeated-block scan found `if (clauses.length !== 2) { return null; } const [m, ret] = clauses;`
**7 times**, plus a start-label guard 6 times. Real duplication, and a `matchThenReturn(clauses)`
helper would name it — but 7 near-uniform occurrences against item 612's 25 byte-identical ones is
a worse ratio, the surrounding code diverges immediately after, and
[[ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing]] records that TS layout in this area is not free (a walk inlined
in a returned closure gave UNRELATED queries a new 4x slow mode). Recorded here so it is not
re-derived; not taken on the tail of a readability pass.

### MEASURED — and what the instrument could and could not resolve

The only change that executes is the field reorder, and it is **in the compile path behind
`planCache`** (`executor.ts:8063`, a `WeakMap<Query, Plan>`), so the nineteen detector calls run
once per distinct query text and cannot appear in a steady-state bench row at all. That is the
structural argument; here is the measurement anyway.

First attempt at it was wrong and is worth recording. A single `bun run bench` read
`query: ordered projection + limit` at 22.6 ms against item 610's 17.8 — **1.27x, which looked
like a regression**. It is not: that is a cross-session, different-process comparison, exactly the
trap item 609 was retracted for. Three runs of the SAME build:

| row                                     | runs             | min      | spread | item 610 |
| --------------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------- | ------ | -------- |
| `query: ordered projection + limit`     | 20.5, 24.0, 19.8 | **19.8** | 1.21x  | 17.8     |
| `query: ordered projection [no window]` | 16.6, 16.6, 20.1 | **16.6** | 1.21x  | 18.1     |

**These rows carry a ~1.21x intrinsic spread**, and min-of-three straddles the recorded figures in
BOTH directions (16.6 below 18.1, 19.8 above 17.8). So the honest verdict is not "no regression",
it is: **flat within an instrument whose noise floor is wider than any effect this change could
have** — which is consistent with the structural argument that it cannot have one. The same
`bun run bench` round had `query: distinct over a hop` at 45.0 against 610's 45.0 and
`query: project 3 columns` FASTER (7.5 vs 8.8), neither of which this change can reach either.

This is also a note for whoever next prices one of those two rows: single runs there are bimodal,
like the spelling probe's, and want nine reps rather than three.

### Gates, each as its own command

`bun run build` first — `@lenke/*` resolve to dist, so a src edit is invisible to the tests and
the bench until it is built. Then: `bun test packages/gql packages/core packages/gremlin
packages/serialization` 3776 pass / 0 fail; `bun test packages/native/src` 929 pass / 0 fail;
`bun run typecheck` exit 0; `bunx oxlint --type-aware .` exit 0 uncached; `bunx oxfmt --check .`
uncached — it caught the new probe and was re-run clean. Rust untouched by this item, and 612's
gates still hold on it.

## 614 — the xref baseline driven 61 → 0, and what resolving each citation one at a time turned up

Item 613 shipped `bun run xref` and left its 61 unresolved citations standing, "rather than guessing
61 replacements I cannot verify one at a time". This item verifies them one at a time. Every
citation now resolves, and the probe got three fixes it needed before that number could be trusted.

**This change is COMMENT-ONLY in both engines.** The only executable file touched is
`packages/native/xref-probe.ts`, which nothing imports. Verified mechanically rather than asserted:
`git diff -U0` over every changed `.rs` and `.ts` except the probe yields no added or removed line
that is not a comment. So there is no perf question to answer here — unlike 613, which had an inert
reorder and still had to be measured.

### What the citations turned out to BE

Not one kind of rot. Resolving them split four ways, and the split is the useful part:

| outcome                                            | count | example                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| renamed / re-homed — repoint                       | ~30   | `val_eq` → `value::equals` (and `value.rs` moved to `lenke-engine-core`) |
| real, but an ARM or a grammar rule, not a function | ~12   | `eval_graph_pred` → the `Expr::GraphPred` arm of `exec::evaluator::eval` |
| **no counterpart at all** — the claim was false    | 7     | `bfs_reducible`, `extra_etypes`, `any_match_reachable`                   |
| not a Rust item                                    | 3     | `liblenke_engine` (the cdylib filename)                                  |

The second row is worth its own note. A dozen comments said "Mirrors native `<name>`" where the
native side does the same thing WITHOUT a named function — in a match arm, in a selector arm, or by
the grammar simply not admitting the other shape. Those citations were never going to resolve, and
rewriting them to name the construct (`the \`"sack"\` step arm of \`gremlin::Parser\``) is strictly
more useful than the name ever was, because it says where to look AND that there is no function to
look for.

### THE FALSE PARITY CLAIMS — seven of them, and three were worth measuring

This is the finding. A dead name is a navigation cost. A comment that asserts the two engines do
the same thing, when one of them does not do it at all, is a correctness claim with nothing behind
it. Seven:

1. **`bfs_reducible`** (`matching.ts:689`) — TS routes a selector pattern to a BFS driver at
   runtime. The crate has no such gate because `gql::Parser::shortest_pattern` enforces the same
   condition at PARSE: a single var-length segment, `*`/`+` only, inline `WHERE` and bound edge
   rejected. The shape cannot reach the driver unreduced. Same outcome, different mechanism.
2. **`any_match_reachable`** (`executor.ts:1042`) — TS turns `EXISTS` over a var-length segment
   from a bound node into a BFS reachability test. The `Expr::Exists` arm of
   `exec::evaluator::eval` fast-paths a BARE VERTEX HOP only, and nothing in `opt` rewrites the
   var-length case. **This is a TS-side win the native engine does not have.** Not priced; recorded
   where someone will see it before assuming parity.
3. **`extra_etypes`** (`Graph.ts:694`) — TS guards an O(1) bucket-sum count shortcut on "no edge
   carries more than one type". Nothing in the crate arms a count fast path that way.
4. **`suggest_procedure`** (`clauses.ts:968`) — claimed both engines' "did you mean" faults "read
   identically". MEASURED, and they do not:

   | query                        | TS                                                       | native                                          |
   | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
   | `CALL pageRank()`            | `unknown procedure: pageRank (did you mean 'pagerank'?)` | ``lenke: query: unknown procedure `pageRank` `` |
   | `CALL connectedComponents()` | `… (did you mean 'connected_components'?)`               | ``… unknown procedure `connectedComponents` ``  |
   | `CALL totallyBogus()`        | `unknown procedure: totallyBogus`                        | ``… unknown procedure `totallyBogus` ``         |

   Both REJECT the same queries, so this is a DX gap and a message-text difference, not a wrong
   answer — the same class as the open cast-message divergence. The crate's only suggestion
   machinery (`algo::edit_distance`) serves CALL CONFIG KEYS, not procedure names.

5. **`free_predicate_vars`** (`executor.ts:2416`) — claimed a mirrored free-variable walk.
   MEASURED, and the behaviour DOES match, by a different mechanism: the native side parses a
   validator predicate in a scope holding only the bound variable, so a free name is an
   ``unknown variable `q` `` parse error. Both accept `p.age > 0`; both reject `q.age > 0` and
   `p.age > 0 AND q.age > 0`. Only the message differs. Claim narrowed, not withdrawn.
6. **`pattern_rank`** (`clauses.ts:531`) — the strongest claim of the seven: "Mirrors native
   `pattern_rank` in `gql/eval/pathfind.rs` exactly — the two must agree or the engines emit rows
   in different orders." Neither half survives. That file and that function do not exist; nothing
   in the crate ranks patterns (`cost::estimate` is consulted only for fast-path routing); and row
   order between the engines is UNSPECIFIED BY POLICY, which is exactly why
   `conformance-harness.ts` compares structurally. The comment asserted an invariant the project
   had already abandoned.
7. **`unknown_fns` / `run_cquery_body`** (four sites) — claimed a plan-level unknown-function set
   checked at run. The native engine rejects an unknown name EARLIER, at parse, in
   `gql::Parser::call`. The user-visible property the comments were defending ("faults before any
   row, identically over zero rows or many") holds — more strongly than claimed.

### A fixture trap, caught by the discipline rather than by luck

Chasing `any_walk` I read ``bare `ANY`/`ALL` (walk) without `SHORTEST`, are errors here`` in
`gql::Parser::parse_shortest_selector` and expected a divergence, because the TS parser plainly
accepts bare `ANY`. First probe, on a 3-node path graph, returned **6 rows for every variant** —
bare ANY, ANY SHORTEST, bare ALL, no selector. That is the fixture trap this log has now recorded
nine times: on a path graph "every walk" and "one walk per endpoint" are the SAME SIX ROWS, and the
probe could not have told them apart whatever the answer was.

Re-run on a graph giving `a` two routes to `c` (`a→b→c`, `a→d→c`), the counts separate and both
engines agree exactly:

| selector       | native | ts  |
| -------------- | ------ | --- |
| bare `ANY`     | 9      | 9   |
| `ANY SHORTEST` | 9      | 9   |
| bare `ALL`     | 10     | 10  |
| `ALL SHORTEST` | 10     | 10  |
| no selector    | 10     | 10  |

So: no divergence — and the RUST doc comment is the thing that is wrong. `parse_shortest_selector`
returns `None` for a bare selector and `gql::Parser::parse_bare_selector` owns it. Corrected.

(Both engines answering 9 for bare `ANY` — i.e. treating it as ANY SHORTEST — is a SHARED
behaviour, so it is a conformance question about the pair against ISO, not a byte-identity one. Not
opened here.)

### Rot goes BOTH directions, and only one direction has a probe

While resolving these I found three Rust→TS citations that are equally dead:
`pathfind::StepRec` and `pathfind::bind_unit` in `exec/nested.rs` (there is no `pathfind` module in
the TS engine — the name is from the retired `lenke-core`), and `read_type_name` in `gql.rs`. The
first two are fixed. **`bun run xref` only walks TS→Rust**, so this direction has no instrument
behind it; found by hand, and that is not repeatable.

### Three probe fixes, each of which changed the number

The baseline could not be driven to zero without them, and each is a lesson about the instrument:

1. **Module-qualified citations were INVISIBLE.** The name regex required pure snake_case, so
   `value::equals` matched nothing and silently dropped out — a citation would have gone
   unchecked rather than checked. Now an optional `mod::` prefix is accepted and resolved on the
   last segment. A BARE name still needs an underscore (a single lowercase word in a comment is
   usually English); a qualified one does not, because `::` is already unambiguous. This surfaced
   `algo::run_with` immediately — dead, now `algo::run_procedure`.
2. **File-stem citations read as rot.** `skipcast_426` names
   `crates/lenke-engine/examples/skipcast_426.rs`, whose stem appears nowhere inside the file. The
   haystack is now each file's path AND its contents.
3. **The CLAIM test was PER LINE, and that hid fifteen real dead citations.** A doc comment opens
   "Mirrors the native …" and names the symbol three lines down, so the line carrying the name has
   no keyword on it. Those showed only under `--all`, mixed in with config keys and file stems that
   make `--all` too noisy to read — which is to say they were invisible in practice. The claim is
   now tested over the whole contiguous comment BLOCK. **This is the fix that mattered most**: it
   took the "fixed" count from 47 to 61, i.e. a quarter of the real rot was behind it, and a probe
   that reports 0 while 15 remain is worse than one that reports 47.

### Where it landed

|                                     | before        | after                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| claiming a native name              | 61 / 51 names | **0 / 0**                                                                         |
| `--all` (every snake_case citation) | 18 unresolved | 2, both correct (`algorithm_run`, an MCP tool name; `command_async`, a TS method) |

A comment that names a dead symbol deliberately — recording what it used to be — carries
`xref:gone` on the SAME line as the name, which is now load-bearing in nine places.

### Gates, each as its own command

Rust: `cargo fmt --check` exit 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` exit 0;
`cargo test --release` 723 passed / 0 failed; `cargo doc --no-deps --document-private-items` — the
new intra-doc link `[\`Self::parse_bare_selector\`]`resolves (grep for it among the warnings: 0
hits; the`v`/`u` broken links are pre-existing).

TS, after `bun run build` (`@lenke/*` resolve to dist): `bun test packages/gql packages/core
packages/gremlin packages/serialization` 3776 pass / 0 fail; `bun test packages/native/src` 929 pass
/ 0 fail; `bun run typecheck` exit 0; `bunx oxlint --type-aware .` uncached — it caught a
`consistent-function-scoping` on the probe's new `isComment`, fixed by HOISTING it rather than with
an `#[allow]`-equivalent, then exit 0; `bunx oxfmt --check .` uncached, clean after a format pass
that touched only files already in this diff.

## 615 — edge id lookup was O(E) in the native engine, on the WRITE path: 116x, and the TS engine already had it right

Restarting the loop, the entry points were the one group `plan_cost_by_operator` has never
priced — it wraps every case around the same 200,000-row scan, and a seed produces ONE row, so
wrapping a scan around a seed measures the scan. The unit for a seed is the SEEK. Two new
`#[ignore]`d harnesses price them (`seed_cost_by_entry_point`,
`edge_id_insert_cost_by_graph_size`), and the first one would not finish.

### What was wrong

`Store::edge_by_ext` resolved an external edge id by calling `all_edges()` — which **allocates
a `Vec` of every live edge and sorts it** — and then comparing ids one at a time, cloning a
`GStr` per edge. `Plan::EdgeSeed` did not even use it: it built **its own ext→edge `HashMap`
over every live edge, on every pull**, to resolve what is usually one id.

Nodes have had `ext_to_node` since the beginning; edges had no reverse map. The comment on
`edge_by_ext` stated the reason and was honest about it — _"edges rarely carry an explicit
string `id` … so no reverse index is maintained; used only by the INSERT identity path"_. The
second half is what makes it expensive: **the INSERT identity path calls it once per edge
carrying an explicit `id`, to reject a duplicate.** So inserting N such edges into a graph of E
was O(N·E log E), i.e. quadratic in the batch. And CLAUDE.md already notes that `encode` emits
edge ids, so **every reloaded snapshot has them** — the explicit-id case is the normal one after
a round trip, not a rarity.

### The measurement, and why the controls matter more than the headline

`edge_id_insert_cost_by_graph_size` runs the same 200 inserts against graphs of three sizes and
reads the SCALING. Four control rows ride along, none of which the fix can reach:

| case                        | E=2000  | E=8000   | E=32000      | growth    |
| --------------------------- | ------- | -------- | ------------ | --------- |
| edge, explicit id           | 6113 ns | 23343 ns | **96937 ns** | **15.9x** |
| edge, NO id (control)       | 507     | 572      | 2216         | 4.4x      |
| node, explicit id (control) | 235     | 288      | 1402         | 6.0x      |
| node, no props (control)    | 188     | 232      | 1288         | 6.9x      |
| edge, no props (control)    | 450     | 504      | 2159         | 4.8x      |

15.9x over a 16x graph is exactly linear in E. **The controls are not flat either (4.4-6.9x),
and that was worth chasing before believing anything**: a prop-free `INSERT (:A)` grows the same
way, so the residual is store-growth realloc/locality, not the identity check or the property
column — it is present in every row and 20-80x smaller in constant. Only the first row is
_linear_, and at E=32,000 it is **45x the prop-free edge control**.

A/B, min-of-3 **alternated** between a detached pre-fix worktree and this tree, `LENKE_INSERTS=2000`:

| case              | E               | before   | after  | ratio                 |
| ----------------- | --------------- | -------- | ------ | --------------------- |
| edge, explicit id | 2000            | 11870 ns | 671 ns | **17.69x**            |
| edge, explicit id | 8000            | 31265    | 692    | **45.18x**            |
| edge, explicit id | 32000           | 101374   | 871    | **116.39x**           |
| edge, NO id       | 2000/8000/32000 | —        | —      | 0.98x / 0.98x / 1.01x |
| node, explicit id | 2000/8000/32000 | —        | —      | 0.99x / 0.99x / 1.00x |
| node, no props    | 2000/8000/32000 | —        | —      | 0.96x / 0.98x / 1.01x |
| edge, no props    | 2000/8000/32000 | —        | —      | 1.00x / 0.99x / 1.01x |

The ratio GROWS with E because before was O(E) and after is O(1) — so the single number is a
property of the fixture, not of the fix. Every control sits in 0.96-1.01x. (Single runs showed
the controls drifting ~10%; min-of-three alternated settles that as noise, which is why the
protocol exists.)

**Read path, same map, worse starting point.** `EdgeSeed (1 id)` on the 200,000-edge fixture:

|                    | before           | after       |           |
| ------------------ | ---------------- | ----------- | --------- |
| `g.E(id)` per seek | **7,681,609 ns** | **31.0 ns** | ~248,000x |

7.7 ms to resolve one edge by id. That is a serving query. The first `seed_cost_by_entry_point`
run could not finish this row at all — 20,000 seeks × a 200k-entry `HashMap` build — which is
how the defect was found.

### The design, against the brief's own constraint

The user's framing was explicit: id lookups must stay fast, and _"super optimized structures
that get invalidated upon write aren't super valuable if they are expensive to rebuild"_. That
rules out a cache. So `ext_to_edge` is built so that **no write invalidates it — a write only
EXTENDS it**:

- `edge_ext` is **immutable after creation**. Checked rather than assumed: it is only ever
  declared, cloned, reserved, pushed at one site, and built in `Builder::build` — never
  rewritten. So an entry can never go stale.
- Deleting an edge does NOT remove its entry. Liveness is filtered at lookup, exactly as
  `node_by_ext` filters tombstones. So delete costs nothing and needs no undo hook.
- It is `None` until something asks for an edge BY ID. A graph that never does pays **one
  `is_some` branch per `add_edge`** and nothing else — which is why ingest is flat (below).
- The build is O(E), once per store, on first lookup. Visible in the harness: at
  `LENKE_INSERTS=200` the explicit-id row is 4525 ns at E=32,000 (the build amortized over 200
  inserts); at 2000 it is 871 ns and its growth is **1.3x, the flattest row in the table**. The
  one-time build is ≈0.77 ms at E=32,000. Stated rather than hidden, because min-of-7 in the
  seed harness excludes it.

**Ingest control** — the real regression risk, since the branch sits in the hottest write path.
`ingest_bench -- phases`, min-of-3 alternated, `decode_ms`:

| row                       | before | after  | after/before |
| ------------------------- | ------ | ------ | ------------ |
| nodes x1 prop             | 43.77  | 44.06  | 1.007x       |
| nodes x4 props            | 87.52  | 86.79  | 0.992x       |
| **nodes+5edges x2 props** | 404.83 | 401.97 | **0.993x**   |

Flat. The edge-heavy row is the one that matters (CLAUDE.md: one edge per node is sparse and
hides per-edge costs); the node-only rows call `add_edge_with_id` zero times.

**Recorded trade, not measured as a problem:** `Store::clone` now clones the map too, so a
transaction snapshot of a graph that HAS looked an edge up by id pays an extra O(E) clone. It is
symmetric with `ext_to_node`, which every clone has always paid, and `None` for any workload
that never resolves an edge id.

### THE TS ENGINE ALREADY HAD THIS RIGHT, which is the finding behind the finding

`insertEdgeWithId` in `gql/src/executor/clauses.ts` checks `graph.getEdgeById(id)` — an O(1)
`edgesById: Map<string, Edge>` lookup, maintained incrementally on `addEdge`/`removeEdge`. **So
this was a Rust-only defect in the engine that is otherwise 1.5-4x faster**, and the TS
implementation is the proof the design is sound and cheap on write.

Its comment says _"Mirrors native `insert_edge_with_id`"_ — and it did, in ANSWER. Item 614
catalogued citations that claimed a parity which did not exist; this is the inverse and a class
614 did not name: **a citation that is behaviourally true while hiding a 116x asymptotic gap.**
A cross-engine comment asserts the same result, never the same cost, and nothing measures the
difference.

### Teeth: four mutants, and the third and fourth each taught something

Three new tests in `exec/tests.rs` and one in `gremlin_ported.rs`. All four passed first run,
which is when this project's discipline says not to believe them.

| mutant                                           | caught by                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `edge_is_live` → always `true`                   | `a_deleted_edge_is_not_found_by_its_external_id`                  |
| fallback scan → `None`                           | `an_edge_id_reinserted_after_a_delete_resolves_to_the_live_edge`  |
| insert-time maintenance dropped                  | `an_edge_inserted_after_the_reverse_map_was_built_is_still_found` |
| `or_insert` → `insert` (lowest-wins → last-wins) | `a_duplicate_external_edge_id_resolves_to_the_lowest_eid`         |

**The fourth mutant SURVIVED at first, and the reason was the fixture trap in a new costume
(tenth instance).** The policy "lowest eid wins for a duplicate id" lived in TWO places — the
lazy build and the incremental hook — each with its own `or_insert`. The only fixture that has
a duplicate edge id comes from NDJSON decode, which builds the map LAZILY on the first lookup
and therefore never reaches the incremental copy. So flipping one of them passed the whole
suite. Fixed by making it one site (`Store::note_edge_ext`), after which the mutant is caught.
**Two copies of a policy need two mutants or one site; a single mutant against one of two
copies proves nothing.**

Establishing that lowest-wins is even correct took a measurement, because the write path rejects
duplicates and so cannot create the case. NDJSON decode **accepts** it: two live edges, and
`g.E('dup').values('w')` is `1` — the first. The TS engine answers `1` too.

### OPEN, found while fixing this and NOT part of it

**Duplicate external edge ids: the engines disagree on the edge COUNT.** The same four-line
NDJSON (two edges sharing `id: "dup"`) gives native `g.E().count()` = **2** and TS = **1** — the
TS `edgesById` `Map.set` collapses the pair. Both agree `g.E('dup')` is the `w=1` edge, so the
LOOKUP matches and only the count diverges. This is pre-existing, is a byte-identity divergence
on malformed-ish input, and changing decode semantics is not a perf decision — recorded, not
touched.

### A trap in my own mutation harness, which cost one confusing full-suite failure

`shutil.copy2` preserves mtime, so restoring a pristine source after a mutant makes the file
look **OLDER than the compiled test binary** — cargo skips the rebuild and the next run executes
**the mutant** while the harness prints "tree restored". It showed up as the new duplicate-id
test failing in the full suite and passing in isolation. `shutil.copy` + `os.utime` fixes it.
**A mutation harness must touch what it restores**, or its own cleanup lies.

### Gates, each as its own command

Rust: `cargo fmt --check` exit 0 (after one format pass over the new tests);
`cargo clippy --release --all-targets -- -D warnings` exit 0 — it caught a `redundant_closure`
and a `type_complexity` in the new harnesses, both fixed properly (`.map(make)`, and an
`InsertCase` alias) rather than with an `allow`; `cargo test --release` **1182 + 13 + 724 pass /
0 fail**. Byte-identity: `bun run fuzz` all seven, 13/13 pass.

Regression screen: `bench_all` before/after, min-of-2 alternated, **239 numeric cells, 4
flagged**. Three were sub-millisecond "faster" readings. The fourth, `query/gql pred AND exists`
at 1.161x, was **REFUTED at min-of-5 alternated on the isolated `query_bench gql` row: 0.998x**,
with 34 sibling rows as controls and nothing over 1.081x. That is the **sixth** false positive
this screen has produced in this loop (83, 84, 85, 89, 91) — it remains a screen, not a verdict.

## 616 — a Gremlin FAST PATH dropped a path step: `coalesce(values('k')).path()` lost the value, and the fuzzer cannot be trusted to find the next one

Item 615's CI run went red on `gremlin-fuzz`, the TS-vs-native differential, at
`FUZZ_SEED=3183304986`:

```
g.V().out('KNOWS', 'CREATED').coalesce(values('name'), values('name')).path().fold()
```

**Not item 615's doing, and that was established by replay rather than by argument.** The
traversal contains no `g.E(id)` and no INSERT carrying an explicit edge id, so it cannot reach
anything 615 touched — but the structural argument is not the evidence. `git checkout HEAD~1 --
store.rs exec.rs`, rebuild, same seed: **the divergence reproduces identically.** Pre-existing.

The seed also REPRODUCES, every time. That rules out the known `gremlin-fuzz` residual, whose
defining property is that [[gremlin-fuzz-families]] _"replays clean"_. This one is a real bug.

### Narrowed to one line, with four controls that all agree

One fixture decoded from the SAME ndjson into both engines (the fuzz suite's own lesson: a
fixture built two ways makes drift read as divergence). Removing one element at a time:

| traversal                                                           | agree?                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `V().out(…).coalesce(values('name'), values('name')).path().fold()` | **DIVERGE** (the fuzzer case) |
| `V().coalesce(values('name')).path()`                               | **DIVERGE** ← minimal         |
| `V().out(…).values('name').path()`                                  | agree                         |
| `V().union(values('name')).path()`                                  | agree                         |
| `V().optional(values('name')).path()`                               | agree                         |
| `V().coalesce(out('knows')).path()`                                 | agree                         |
| `V().out(…).coalesce(values, values)` — no `path()`                 | agree                         |

So: `coalesce` **with a value-producing arm**, and nothing else. Its own siblings — `union`,
`optional`, a plain `values`, and a `coalesce` of HOPS — were all already right.

### Which engine was wrong: settled in a real TinkerPop console, not inferred

`podman run -i --rm docker.io/tinkerpop/gremlin-console:3.7.3`, `TinkerFactory.createModern()`:

```
ONE-ARM : [path[v[1], marko], path[v[2], vadas], …]
TWO-ARM : [path[v[1], marko], …]
UNION   : [path[v[1], marko], …]
PLAIN   : [path[v[1], marko], …]
```

The value **is** a path step. TS matched TinkerPop; **native was the wrong one** — so this was a
wrong answer, not a tie to be broken.

### The cause: an early `return` that outran a cross-cutting wrapper

`gremlin.rs` lowers a value-producing step and then wraps it with
`Parser::maybe_path_record`, which emits a `Plan::PathRecord` when the traversal reads
`path()`/`tree()` (`building_full_path`). `"values"` is in its tag list, which is why the plain
step was always correct.

But `coalesce` of all-`values` bodies has a **fast path** — it lowers to
`Filter(any present) + Project(Case{…})` instead of a per-element branch — and that fast path
`return`s its plan directly. It never reached `maybe_path_record`, so no `PathRecord` was
emitted and the projected value never entered the step-history. One line:

```rust
return Ok(self.maybe_path_record(p, "values"));
```

It records with the same `STEP_SCALAR` tag and the same `Slot(self.current)` value a plain
`values` uses, so the fast path now agrees with the slow one by construction rather than by
coincidence. **An early `return` in a lowering is exactly where a cross-cutting wrapper gets
lost** — and the fast path was added for speed, so the bug was a side effect of an optimization,
which is the kind this loop should expect to create.

Grepped the pattern: the neighbouring early `return`s in the branch lowerings are reducers
(`count`/`sum`/`fold`), which set `frontier_from_reducer` because **TinkerPop resets the path at
a reducing barrier** — those are deliberately not recorded and are correct.

### THE INSTRUMENT FINDING, which matters more than the bug

**The fuzzer found this once and must not be trusted to find the next one.** After fixing it I
swept random seeds to hunt siblings: **60 seeds, 24,000 traversals, zero divergences.** That
looked like coverage. It is not — so I measured the sweep's teeth by running it against the
UNFIXED code, which is the only thing that makes a clean result mean anything:

|                         | seeds | traversals | hits  |
| ----------------------- | ----- | ---------- | ----- |
| sweep, **fix reverted** | 12    | 4,800      | **0** |
| sweep, **fix reverted** | 60    | 24,000     | **0** |
| sweep, fixed            | 60    | 24,000     | 0     |

**The sweep cannot find the bug it was hunting**, while seed 3183304986 reproduces 100% of the
time. The generator produces this shape rarer than 1 in 24,000 traversals; CI hit it by luck. So
the clean 60-seed result is NOT evidence that siblings do not exist, and this item does not
claim it is. A generative test whose teeth were never verified is worse than no test because it
is believed — the same rule as `rewrite_fuzz`, applied to a sweep rather than a mutant.

The durable guard is therefore a TABLE, not the fuzzer:
`a_branch_step_over_a_value_body_extends_the_path` pins eleven spellings — one-arm, two-arm and
first-arm-absent `coalesce`; `union`; `optional`; plain `values`; each again behind a hop; and
`coalesce(id())` / `coalesce(label())` so the fix is not special to one key reader. It asserts
the path LENGTH and that the last element is not a node. Teeth verified: with the fix reverted it
fails on its first case (`path is [Node("1")]`).

### Gates, each as its own command

`cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --release --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0;
`cargo test --release` 1182 + 13 + 725 pass / 0 fail; `bun run fuzz` all seven 13/13;
`FUZZ_SEED=3183304986 bun test gremlin-fuzz.test.ts` passes. TS: typecheck 0, oxlint
`--type-aware` 0, oxfmt `--check` 0, `bun test` 3776 + 929 pass / 0 fail.

No perf measurement is owed: the change adds a `PathRecord` only when `building_full_path` is
already true, i.e. only to traversals that read `path()`/`tree()`, and those were getting a
wrong answer. The fast path's own saving is untouched for every traversal that does not read a
path.

## 617 — GQL had NO point lookup by id: a 7,513x spelling cliff against Gremlin, now 1,258x faster

`Plan::NodeSeed` was constructed in exactly ONE place in the whole crate — the Gremlin
parser, for `g.V(id)`. GQL has `element_id(n)` as a scalar function and nothing that turns a
predicate over it into a seed. So the single most common serving query there is — _give me the
element with this id_ — was a full label scan with an `element_id` call and a string compare
per node, in the surface language most users write.

Found by adding the pair as a group to `spelling_probe`, which is exactly its charter
("equivalent spellings must cost the same", and it compares GQL against Gremlin):

```
=== point lookup BY ID — Gremlin seed vs GQL element_id predicate ===
  GRM    0.000ms  rows=1   g.V('12345').values('age')
  GQL    1.803ms  rows=1   MATCH (n:Person) WHERE element_id(n) = '12345' RETURN n.age AS a
  ✗ PERF CLIFF: plans differ, time spread 7512.96x
```

Same single row, 100,000-node fixture. After the rewrite both sides are below the timer's
resolution and the group reports no cliff.

### The measurement, end to end through the FFI

The probe loads TWO `.so` files — one built from a detached worktree at HEAD (post-616,
pre-617) — so the only difference between the sides is this item. Alternated rounds,
min-of-3×9, 200 ops a rep:

| case                                      | before         | after       |           |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------- | ----------- | --------- |
| **GQL `element_id(n) = $x`**              | **1775.79 µs** | **1.41 µs** | **1258x** |
| GREMLIN `g.V(id).values('age')` — control | 1.76           | 1.70        | 1.03x     |
| GQL `n.name = $x`, INDEXED — control      | 1.79           | 1.84        | 0.97x     |
| GQL label-scan `count(*)` — control       | 1.11           | 1.12        | 0.99x     |

The seeded lookup (1.41 µs) is now cheaper than BOTH the Gremlin spelling and the
indexed-property lookup, which is what a direct external-id hash probe should be: no index
consulted, no bucket, one `ext_to_node` probe.

**A `$param` is the shape that matters and it was verified, not assumed.** `bind_params` runs
BEFORE `opt` (`parse_cache::parse_for_run` binds, `ffi.rs` then optimizes), so a bound `$x` is
an ordinary `Expr::Lit` by the time the rewrite looks — confirmed by dumping the plan at each
stage: `Param("x")` → `Lit(Str("4"))` → `NodeSeed { ext_ids: ["4"], label: Some("P") }`.

### What the rewrite will NOT do, and why each decline is safe

`id_seek_target` matches `element_id(n) = '<string>'` in EITHER operand order (both, because
accepting one would create a fresh cliff between two spellings of one query — the lesson
`gen_anchor_pred` already carries). Four preconditions, and the thing that makes them safe is
that declining always leaves `Filter(Scan)`, which is correct by construction:

- **`Eq` only** — a seed takes a SET of ids, not an interval.
- **the argument must be `Slot(0)`**, the slot this `Scan` produces.
- **the literal must be a STRING.** An external id IS a string, so under the value contract's
  cross-type `=` ([[cross-type-comparison-no-error]]) `element_id(n) = 5` matches NOTHING.
  Seeding `"5"` from `= 5` would **invent a row the scan never finds** — a wrong answer, not a
  slow one. Mutation confirms this guard is load-bearing.
- **NULL declines** — the predicate is UNKNOWN, which keeps no rows.

**`Plan::NodeSeed` gained `label: Option<String>`**, as `IndexSeek`/`RangeSeek` have always
had. Without it the rewrite would drop the `MATCH (n:Person)` constraint and return a node of
the WRONG LABEL: node 5 is a `Q`, and `MATCH (x:P) WHERE element_id(x) = '5'` must find
nothing. `exec` applies it with `store.is_labeled`, a binary search of the sorted label bucket
— O(log |label|) per id, not a bucket scan. Gremlin's `g.V(ids)` passes `None`; a `hasLabel`
after it is its own step.

Also seeded as a CONJUNCT (`Seed::Id`), ranked ABOVE every other rung in
`seed_from_conjuncts` and gated on nothing — an id equality keeps at most ONE row, so no index
statistic can beat it and there is nothing to rank. Without that rung,
`WHERE element_id(n) = $x AND n.age > 0` would have stayed a scan while the same query without
the second conjunct seeded: a new cliff created by fixing the first one.

### 🛑 `rewrite_fuzz` WAS STRUCTURALLY BLIND TO THIS REWRITE

The generator's only `Expr::Call` is `ln`. It could not produce an `element_id` predicate at
all, so **a green `rewrite_fuzz` said nothing whatever about the new rewrite** — the "widen the
generator first" case CLAUDE.md describes, and the reason that instruction exists.

Widened: a new predicate kind emitting `element_id(slot) = <lit>` in both operand orders, with
the literal usually a HIT, sometimes a MISS, and sometimes a NUMBER or a non-id string so the
decline paths are generated too. Added to `SEEKABLE_KINDS`, since that is the restricted set
used in the position that triggers seed rewrites.

That got coverage to **1 plan in 2,000** — which is why the coverage count is reported and not
just asserted. Diagnosing it turned up a gap wider than this item:

> **The generator never emitted a filter DIRECTLY over the `Scan`.** `gen_seed` returns a bare
> `Scan`, and every filter is attached at the LANDING slot or above, so a slot-0 predicate only
> ever reached the scan by PUSHDOWN. The `Plan::Scan` arm of `apply` hosts **every** seed
> rewrite — `IndexSeek`, `RangeSeek`, the multi-seek union, `seed_from_conjuncts` and now
> `NodeSeed` — and it was reached only indirectly. `MATCH (n:L) WHERE <pred on n>` is also the
> commonest real shape there is, and it was the one shape absent.

With a start-node predicate (`rng.chance(1, 3)`, seekable kinds) coverage goes **1 → 17** per
2,000. The floor is set at half the measurement (`n / 250`), the convention the surrounding
rows use — and the comment says plainly that 17 is thin and **a count is not teeth.**

### Teeth: three of four mutants caught, and the fourth is honestly unobservable

| mutant                                      | caught by                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| accepts a NUMERIC literal (invents a match) | `a_gql_id_seek_declines_what_it_cannot_answer`, and `rewrite_fuzz::optimizing_preserves_rows_across_shapes` |
| drops the LABEL from the seed               | `a_gql_id_seek_still_honours_the_label`, and `optimizing_preserves_rows_without_indexes`                    |
| `exec` stops applying the seed's label      | same two                                                                                                    |
| **ignores WHICH SLOT `element_id` reads**   | **SURVIVED**                                                                                                |

So the 17/2000 reach IS enough teeth for the row oracles — three mutants were caught by them
independently of the direct tests.

The survivor is reported rather than papered over: the `Slot(0)` check is **defensive and
currently unobservable, for a structural reason and not a coverage gap.** Both call sites sit
in the `Plan::Scan` arm, where the input width is 1 — `Slot(0)` is the only slot that exists,
so no predicate reading another can arrive. It is kept because it is what makes
`id_seek_target` safe to call from a wider position later (over a `Join`, say), and its doc
now says exactly that, so a future reader neither deletes it believing it tested nor trusts it
believing it exercised.

Four deterministic tests carry the real coverage, and each asserts the OPERATOR and then the
rows — because a fast path that silently declines is indistinguishable from one that works by
rows alone ([[perf-gate-needs-its-own-test]]): five seeding spellings (both operand orders,
labelled and unlabelled, and both conjunct orders), the wrong-label case, the four declines,
and a deleted node.

### A stale artifact made the first measurement read 1.09x

The first A/B said **1.09x**, and the controls were flat, which looked like "the rewrite does
not reach the FFI path". It was not: `cargo build --release --tests` does not produce the FFI
`.so`, and the last `--features capi` build predated this change — so **both libraries were
pre-617**. CLAUDE.md warns about this artifact in the other direction (a bare release build
CLOBBERS the capi `.so`); this is the same trap arriving as a missing rebuild rather than a
wrong one. The probe now also asserts that every timed case RETURNED something, since a case
that silently returns nothing prices as the fastest row in the table.

### The `bench_all` screen flagged SEVEN rows and all seven were noise

Min-of-2 alternated: 239 numeric cells, 7 over ±10%. Confirmed on the isolated `query_bench`
rows at min-of-5 alternated, with every sibling row in each group as a control:

| row                            | screen | min-of-5   |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | ---------- |
| `gql project absent cmp`       | 1.127x | **1.055x** |
| `seeded max(p.age)`            | 1.139x | **1.000x** |
| `seeded count(DISTINCT p.age)` | 1.500x | **0.998x** |
| `gql pred AND exists`          | 0.855x | **1.004x** |

**0 rows over 1.10x.** That takes this screen's false-positive count in this loop from six to
thirteen. It remains a screen, not a verdict.

Worth its own line: `max(p.age)` reads **1347 µs inside `bench_all` and 430 µs isolated** —
3.1x, for the same binary and the same case. Item 116's caution ("a control measured in the
same process, AFTER a heavy shape, is not a control") applies to the SUBJECT too, not only the
control: a `bench_all` absolute number is not comparable to an isolated one.

### OPEN: the TS engine still has this cliff, and it is worse

Measured on the TS engine, N=100,000, min-of-9 over 200 ops: GQL `element_id(n) = $x`
**4413.55 µs**, against its own Gremlin `g.V(id)` at **2.79 µs** and an INDEXED property
lookup at **1.75 µs** — so **2,522x** its own point-lookup control. `insertEdgeWithId`'s
O(1) `edgesById` proved the TS engine can do id lookups well; its GQL planner simply has no
id-seek shortcut either. Next item.

### Gates, each as its own command

`cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --release --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0;
`cargo test --release` **1186 + 13 + 725 pass / 0 fail**; `rewrite_fuzz` 10 passed including
the new coverage floor; `bun run fuzz` all seven 13/13.

## 618 — the TS twin of 617: a GQL point lookup by id, 5,240x (and 7,913x for the conjunct form)

Item 617 left this open with a number: the TS engine's GQL point lookup by element id measured
**4413.55 µs** against its own Gremlin `g.V(id)` at 2.79 µs and an INDEXED PROPERTY lookup at
1.75 µs — **2,522x its own point-lookup control**. Same defect as the native engine, in the
engine that already proved (item 615, `insertEdgeWithId`) that it can do id lookups in O(1).

### Where it goes, and why the TS version is the safer of the two

The TS seed layer is already a candidate auction: `indexCandidates` yields
`SeedCandidate { count, build() }` per usable constraint and `seedVertices` takes the cheapest.
So an id lookup is just another candidate — one whose `count` is 0 or 1 and whose `build()` is a
single `graph.getVertexById`, an O(1) `Map.get` on `verticesById`.

A clause `WHERE` reaches that layer as a `CSeedHint`, derived by `collectHints`. `asPropCompare`
matches `prop <op> const` only, so `element_id(n) = $x` — whose operand is a `func` node —
produced no hint at all. New hint kind `{ kind: 'id'; value }`, new matcher `asIdCompare`
(either operand order; `=` only), and an `indexCandidates` arm that runs BEFORE the
`idx.isIndexed(hint.key)` gate, because an id hint has no `key` — `verticesById` IS its index,
so it needs no `createIndex` to be useful.

**The TS rewrite is structurally safer than the native one, and worth recording as the reason
the two are allowed to differ:** a hint here only narrows the SEED, and `matchNode` plus the
residual `WHERE` re-validate every seeded row. So a hint may yield a SUPERSET of the true
matches but never a subset — which means
`NodeSeed`'s hand-carried `label` (item 617) has no analogue here: the label is re-checked
anyway. It also means a non-string comparand would be _sound_ to seed on (the re-validation
would drop it). It is still restricted to a string at the point of use, deliberately, so the two
engines seed on the same shapes — parity of behaviour being worth more than the extra case.

### Measured: two dists in one process, alternated

`@lenke/*` resolve to **dist**, so a src edit is invisible until a build
([[fuzzers-read-built-dists]]). Both sides were built from the same tree with only the two
patched files differing, published as `dist-before` / `dist-after`, and verified to differ
(`asIdCompare` present in one, absent in the other) before either was timed. One process,
alternated per round, min-of-3×9, 200 ops a rep:

| case                                          | before         | after       |           |
| --------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ----------- | --------- |
| **GQL `element_id(n) = $x`**                  | **4401.10 µs** | **0.84 µs** | **5240x** |
| **the same as a CONJUNCT (`AND n.age >= 0`)** | **7146.23 µs** | **0.90 µs** | **7913x** |
| GQL `n.name = $x`, INDEXED — control          | 0.86           | 0.76        | 1.13x     |
| GQL label-scan `count(*)` — control           | 0.13           | 0.17        | 0.78x     |

The conjunct form was **worse than the plain one before** (7146 against 4401 µs) because the
extra predicate ran over every scanned vertex, and it is the better of the two after — so this
closes a cliff _between two spellings of one query_ as well as the cliff against Gremlin.

**The two controls read 0.78x and 1.13x, which is noise at 130-860 ns, and that was resolved
rather than asserted.** Re-run with the controls alone at **20,000 ops a rep** (the full A/B
cannot: at 4.4 ms a call the subject rows would take an hour), min-of-5 alternated:

| control                                          | before   | after    |            |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------- | -------- | ---------- |
| `n.name = $x` INDEXED                            | 1.135 µs | 1.079 µs | 0.951x     |
| label-scan `count(*)`                            | 0.081    | 0.083    | **1.025x** |
| no `WHERE` at all (so `collectHints` never runs) | 0.933    | 0.945    | 1.013x     |

**Worst control ratio 1.025x.** The 0.78x at 200 ops was resolution, not a regression — a 40 ns
move on a 130 ns row.

### Teeth: four mutants, all caught

The tests import `./index.js` (source, via bun's resolution), so no dist rebuild is needed per
mutant — which is what makes mutating the TS side cheap enough to be routine rather than an
event.

| mutant                                                    | caught       |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| `asIdCompare` never matches (the seed never fires)        | 3 tests fail |
| the `typeof v === 'string'` guard dropped                 | 1 test fails |
| `build()` yields the EMPTY set (silently answers nothing) | 5 tests fail |
| the seed resolves the WRONG id                            | 5 tests fail |

**The signal is a counting spy on `Graph.getVertexById`, not a timing comparison.** A seed is a
route CHOICE and route choices are answer-equivalent, so a version that silently declined and
scanned would return exactly the same rows and a rows-only test could not tell them apart
([[perf-gate-needs-its-own-test]]). `getVertexById` is an own arrow property, so it is
replaceable; the seed path calls it and the label scan never does, which makes "did it seed" a
deterministic binary observation. Ten tests in `packages/gql/src/id-seed.test.ts`: both operand
orders, a `$param`, both conjunct orders, the wrong-label exclusion, a missing id, a REMOVED
vertex, and the three declines (non-string, range, NULL).

**The range-decline test was weak and was strengthened.** It asserted `[]`, which is the right
answer (`'v10'`..`'v38'` all sort BELOW `'v8'` in string order, and the only id above it is a
`Q`) — but an empty expectation passes just as well if the declined path returns nothing at
all. That is the fixture trap, eleventh instance. A range that DOES match now follows over the
same declined path and must produce every `P` vertex.

### Cross-engine: the two fast paths are byte-identical, by two different mechanisms

Both engines now fast-path this shape and **they were written independently**: native REWRITES
the plan into a labelled `Plan::NodeSeed` and DROPS the predicate; TS seeds a superset and
re-validates. Same rows by two routes is exactly what byte-identity exists to guard, and
nothing was comparing them — the GQL differential fuzzer's generator emits no `element_id`
predicate.

Two new cases in `gql-conformance.test.ts` (15 queries) pin it: hits in both operand orders,
labelled and unlabelled; the label exclusion; both conjunct orders including one whose second
predicate must still eliminate the row; a missing id; the non-string and range declines; an id
read on the FAR SIDE of a hop, which neither engine may seed from; and the `$param` form. All
byte-identical, 201/201 in that file.

## 619b — the cheap half of 619 built: `element_id` filters over BORROWED ids, 5.28x and 6.33x — and the first version of the test never reached the code it tested

Item 619 priced the GQL edge-id lookup and split it in two. This builds half (2), the one that
needs no plan surgery: the `Expr::Call` arm of `exec::evaluator::eval` materialized the external
id PER ROW — a `GStr` clone and a boxed `Value::Str` each, into a `Vec<Value>` the comparison
then walked — where a property predicate reads a typed column. `try_filter_keep_element_id` does
one pass, borrows each id as `&str`, compares, and allocates only the keep-list.

**This does NOT remove the walk.** Seeding an edge pattern still needs the slot surgery half (1)
of 619, which remains unbuilt. What this fixes is the cost of the shapes that CANNOT seed.

### Measured: two libraries, alternated

The "before" `.so` is built from a detached worktree at `117c2706`, so the only difference is
this change. Alternated per round, min-of-3×7, 20,000 nodes / 100,000 edges:

| case                                                                        | before         | after         |           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ------------- | --------- |
| **EDGE id filter**                                                          | **2106.45 µs** | **398.73 µs** | **5.28x** |
| **FAR-SIDE node id filter**                                                 | **2041.56 µs** | **322.28 µs** | **6.33x** |
| edge property `r.w = $w` — control                                          | 194.27         | 195.38        | 0.99x     |
| NEAR-side node id (617 SEEDS it, so it never reaches this filter) — control | 1.78           | 1.56          | 1.14x     |
| label-scan `count(*)` — control                                             | 1.54           | 1.46          | 1.06x     |

The far-side node case is the second shape and it was not in 619's pricing: `WHERE
element_id(b) = $x` after a hop reads a slot the `Scan` does not produce, so item 617's seed
rewrite correctly declines and the filter runs. It is also covered by 618's cross-engine
conformance test, which is how it was already known to be scanning.

**The remaining gap is 2.1x to the edge-property floor** (399 against 195) — a string compare
against a raw f64 one, over the same walk. That is the honest ceiling for this half.

### 🛑 THE TEST NEVER REACHED THE CODE IT TESTED, and mutation is what exposed it

The first version of these tests used `RETURN count(*)`. Two mutants survived, and the reason
was not a weak assertion:

> **Instrumenting the arm with an `eprintln!` showed it NEVER FIRES for a `count(*)` query** —
> an aggregate over a filtered hop takes a different route — while the same predicates as a
> PROJECTION fired 12 times. So for exactly the cases the test was written to cover, it was
> comparing the general path against itself, and a mutant that COERCED a numeric literal into
> `"3"` passed it.

Rewritten as projections (`RETURN r.w AS v`), which is also the shape the A/B measures, the
coercion mutant is caught. **"Verify the planner reaches the shape" has a twin at the exec
layer: verify the FAST PATH reaches the shape, and instrument it rather than infer it from a
plan dump — the plan was identical in both spellings.**

**A second test bug, the fixture trap in my own work:** the decline test's fixture had NO EDGES,
so its far-side assertion (`element_id(b) = 3` → 0 rows) passed whatever the arm did. It now
builds edges AND asserts the control — the STRING spelling of the same query must find node 3,
else the zero proves nothing.

### The oracle, and what it costs to have one

`element_id(x) >= 'v' AND element_id(x) <= 'v'` is `element_id(x) = 'v'` under the value
contract's total order, and both conjuncts carry an ORDERING operator, which the fused arm
declines outright — so the oracle is answered by `eval` while the subject takes the fast path.
Item 438/449's trick in a new key. Three-valued logic matches too: where the id is NULL, the
equality and both ordering conjuncts are all UNKNOWN.

One mutant exists purely to guard the ORACLE: _accept ordering operators_. Under it the oracle
stops declining and joins the subject on the fast path, and the differential compares the fast
path against itself. It is caught — which is the only thing that makes the other results mean
anything. **A differential whose oracle silently joins the subject is the quietest way for this
kind of test to stop testing.**

### Teeth: three of four caught, and the fourth is redundant for a reason

| mutant                                              |                                            |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `Ne` not inverted (keeps the matching row for `<>`) | CAUGHT                                     |
| a NON-STRING literal coerced to its text            | CAUGHT (only after the projection rewrite) |
| ORDERING operators accepted (the oracle guard)      | CAUGHT                                     |
| **the `u32::MAX` OPTIONAL-miss check deleted**      | **SURVIVED — and correctly**               |

The explicit sentinel check is **redundant**, which mutation established rather than assumption:
`node_ext_id_ref(u32::MAX)` is out of bounds and returns `None`, so the very next guard drops the
row anyway. Kept as documentation of intent — a reader should not have to derive the sentinel's
fate from a `Vec::get` bound — with a doc note saying exactly that, so nobody later reads the
surviving mutant as a hole. **The behaviour is pinned regardless**, by the test below.

### A finding for the SIBLING arm: the OPTIONAL-miss shape IS reachable

`try_filter_keep_call`'s comment declares its `coalesce`-on-sentinel decline unmeasurable:
_"`WHERE` inside `OPTIONAL MATCH` is rejected by the parser, so the shape could not be measured
against the general path."_ The clause `WHERE` is indeed rejected — **but the trailing `FILTER`
spelling of the same predicate is not**, and it lands a `Filter` directly over the optional hop.
Verified:

```
MATCH (a:N) OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b) FILTER element_id(b) = '1'  -> 1 row
MATCH (a:N) OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b) FILTER element_id(b) <> '1' -> 0 rows
```

The `<>` row is the load-bearing one: three of the four nodes have no out-edge, so an arm that
compared the sentinel would call all three "not equal to `'1'`" and keep them. That pair of
spellings is exactly what `spelling_probe` tracks under "a trailing FILTER vs a clause WHERE" —
so the sibling arm's decline can now be measured by whoever wants to.

### The `bench_all` screen flagged seven, and FOUR were my screen's own fault

239 cells, 7 over ±10%. Four of them were in `query/seeded` **col2, which is `speedup` — a
DERIVED RATIO** over an `index_us` of 0.3 µs, i.e. at the timer floor. My screen script compares
every numeric column as if it were a time, so a ratio built on a floor-level denominator flags
freely. **A screen should compare TIME columns; a derived ratio is not a measurement.**

Of the remaining three, two were "faster" and the one real time-column candidate —
`query/shortest | repeat-group control` at 1.123x — **refuted at 1.018x** on the isolated row,
min-of-3 alternated. Zero rows over 1.10x. This screen's false positives in this loop now number
twenty.
