walk, not derived from an accumulator, so it is a separate arm), and two aggregates over DIFFERENT
columns so the per-accumulator argument functions are genuinely distinct. This is item 651's blind
spot one site over, which suggests the lesson is about aggregate closures generally rather than
about either site.

**One survivor was MY MUTANT'S FAULT.** `count(*) via undefined instead of the kind check` is
EQUIVALENT: routing a `rows` acc through `undefined` makes `isNullish` skip it on the very next
`continue` — the identical outcome by a different route, so no test could catch it. Replaced by one
that deletes the `rows` guard outright (the `rows` variant has no `argFn` field at all, so
`a.argFn(env)` is a runtime `TypeError`), which is **CAUGHT**. The guard is load-bearing, not
decorative.

So all three survivor kinds appeared in two items: **inert** (651's collect-path guards,
unreachable), **equivalent** (this mutant, which did not mutate), and a real **test gap** (the
label recheck). A bare count conflates all three.

### Regression verification

- 2564 `packages/gql` tests pass, 0 fail (3 new).
- All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, including the TS-vs-native differential.
- `bun run lint` 0, `bun run check` (typecheck + lint + fmt:check) 0.

## 653 — deduplicating identical aggregate ARGUMENTS: REFUTED for the common case, priced with no code written

**REFUTED (TypeScript), nothing built.** Item 652 found that `max(n.w), min(n.w)` evaluates `n.w`
twice per vertex and recorded a CSE over identical argument expressions as open. It does not
survive pricing.

### The price, taken WITHOUT writing the optimization

`max(n.w), count(*)` is structurally what the CSE turns `max(n.w), min(n.w)` into: it holds the
accumulator count at TWO and varies only the number of argument evaluations, because item 652
measured the `rows` arm as free (`three` landed on top of `two`). 200,000 vertices, min of three
alternated rounds:

|                                          | min                                             |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `max(n.w), min(n.w)` — TWO evaluations   | **6.13 ms**                                     |
| `max(n.w), count(*)` — ONE evaluation    | 6.46                                            |
| grouped twin, two against one evaluation | 8.06 against 7.76 (3.9%, under the noise floor) |

**Two evaluations is FASTER than one.** A bare property read off an already-bound vertex is the
cheapest expression in the language, and evaluating it twice costs less than any machinery to
avoid it. Worse than merely not helping: since the saving is zero, an always-dedup would add an
extra loop level to the shape people actually write — a REGRESSION.

### Both halves of the enum, because `n.w` is the cheap extreme

Stopping at the convenient answer would have missed the live variant. With an EXPENSIVE shared
argument the same pair does separate:

|                                                                  | min                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `max(abs(n.w) * 2 + 1), min(abs(n.w) * 2 + 1)` — TWO evaluations | 27.23 ms (stable: 27.23 / 28.14 / 28.34) |
| `max(abs(n.w) * 2 + 1), count(*)` — ONE evaluation               | 20.85 typical                            |

About **1.31x**, and real. But capturing it needs a cost model to decide whether an argument is
expensive, because applying the CSE unconditionally loses the cheap case above — and the cheap
case is the common one. That is substantial apparatus for
`max(<non-trivial expr>), min(<the same expr>)`, so it is **not built**.

### Why this is recorded rather than left as a note

Both halves are written into `detectMultiNodeAggregate`'s walk, next to the code they would have
changed. This session has already hit the cost of not doing that twice in one family: a header
advertising 18-30x for grouped `sum`/`avg` that re-measured at **1.23x**, and three comments
reading "PRICED AND NOT BUILT" / "NOT FIXED" for a lever that was built in both engines (item
650). A target priced from the wrong floor, or left unpriced, gets re-derived.

### The aggregate family is now covered end to end

`detectNodeAggregate` (651), `detectMultiNodeAggregate` (652), `detectGroupedNodeAggregate` and
`detectHopAggregate` all fold during their walk; the last two already did (the hop rung at 155.8 ms
against the general path's 742.6, item 418). No materializing aggregate path remains.

## 654 — `CAST(x AS STRING)` stops allocating three times per row: 1.24x, and the remaining cost is `{:e}`'s fmt machinery

**FIXED (native).** Found by running the `expression_cost_by_kind` enum harness and taking its
largest row. `Cast to STRING` read **92.67 ns/row, 103x** the cheapest useful read (`Prop (Num)`
at 0.90) — the biggest row in the table, and the only large one with no caveat beside it: `In`
(45.96) is labelled planner-unreachable, `Call upper` (41.45) is per-distinct-value on a dict
column, `Call contains` (33.65) takes `typed_strsearch_mask` as a filter. That harness's header
records two earlier passes misreading it as a predicate-cost table; this row is a projection cost
and `CAST` is a projection.

### The result, and the honest shape of it

|                             | ns/row    |                   |
| --------------------------- | --------- | ----------------- |
| before                      | 92.67     | 103x `Prop (Num)` |
| after the stack-buffer port | 77.93     | 1.19x             |
| after `js_number_gstr`      | **74.83** | **1.24x total**   |

Controls flat at every step: `Prop (Num)` 0.90 → 0.95, `Call upper` 41.45 → 41.65, `List [p,p]`
28.98 → 28.94.

**🛑 THE DIAGNOSIS OVER-PROMISED.** `js_number` did THREE heap allocations per call — a
`format!("{:e}", …)`, a `mant.chars().filter(…).collect::<String>()`, and the output
`String::new()` — which looked like most of 92.67. Removing all three bought 1.24x. What actually
dominates is `write!("{:e}", …)`: still Rust's full `fmt` machinery even when it targets a stack
buffer. Removing THAT needs a shortest-round-trip float formatter (Ryu/dragonbox), and this crate
is deliberately dependency-free ("None — std-only"), so hand-writing one is out of proportion to
what is left. **74.83 is the floor under std**, recorded so the row is not re-targeted.

### The fix was a PORT, not an invention

`lenke-codec::jsonfmt::push_js_number` has had exactly this stack-buffer shape all along — a
`Scratch` buffer for the `{:e}` step, a stack `[0u8; 24]` for the digits, zero allocations. The
two crates are both std-only and INDEPENDENT (neither depends on the other), so the fast version
could not be called from here; the duplication already existed and this makes both copies fast.

`write_js_number` is now generic over `std::fmt::Write`, which is what lets `js_number_gstr`
format into a stack buffer and hand `GStr::new` a `&str` — `GStr`'s 12-byte INLINE capacity then
takes almost every number with no allocation at all. `value::cast` used to call
`GStr::from(js_number(x))`: an owned `String` per row, copied into the `GStr` and dropped.

### Verified against the code it replaced, not against a table

The original allocating algorithm is kept VERBATIM as a test reference, and ~8,000 values are
swept through both: every ECMA-262 branch, both sides of the `n > 21` and `n <= -6` boundaries,
one/two/three-digit exponents (`push_u32`'s loop), `f64::MAX`, `5e-324`, `f64::MIN_POSITIVE`, both
signs, plus a deterministic mantissa/exponent sweep. The existing 12-case table could not have
established that. This function backs `CAST`, `to_string` AND JSON egress, so a formatting
divergence is a wrong answer in three surfaces at once, not a slow one.

### ⚠️ A cross-crate byte-identity invariant had NO test

`lenke-codec` carries its own independent copy of this formatter. **This copy backs JSON and
`CAST`/`to_string`; the codec's backs CSV and pg-text.** If they drift, one engine spells the same
number two ways depending on the egress format — a byte-identity bug ACROSS formats, which no
single format's test can see. The duplication predates this item; the test does not.

### Grepping the call sites found a free one

`json_fmt::write_number` — the JSON egress path — did `out.push_str(&js_number(x))`, allocating an
owned `String` purely to copy it into the output buffer and drop it. Once per NON-INTEGER number
in every serialized result (the integer-valued fast path above it bypasses `js_number` entirely,
so the reach is narrower than it first looks). Now it writes straight through.

### Regression verification

- 1203 + 13 + 725 native tests pass, 0 fail — including `results_json_numbers`, the test that
  would catch a divergence on the JSON path, and 2 new parity tests.
- All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, including the TS-vs-native differential.
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` 0 on both crates; `cargo fmt --check` 0.

## 655 — every generic scalar `Call` pays a 16 ns string-DISPATCH toll; two obvious causes killed first

**PRICED, not built (native).** Item 654 took the largest row of `expression_cost_by_kind`; this
takes the next one and finds the cost is not where the row's name suggests.

### The decomposition

|                                  | ns/row    |                                                 |
| -------------------------------- | --------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `Prop (Str)`                     | 1.04      | just reading the column                         |
| `Call abs`                       | 2.02      | a TYPED fast path; never reaches the dispatcher |
| **`Call pi` (NILADIC)**          | **16.14** | **DISPATCH ONLY — no argument at all**          |
| `Call char_length` (one Str arg) | 26.93     | ≈ 16 dispatch + ~9 argument + ~2 work           |
| `Call upper`                     | 41.54     | ≈ 16 dispatch + ~9 argument + ~16 string        |
| `Call lower`                     | 42.34     |                                                 |

`pi()` takes no argument, so it does no `value_at`, no boxing and no string production: its 16.14
ns is the per-row trip through `call_scalar_checked`, whose dispatch is a `matches!` over 6 names
followed by a match with **~89 string arms**. `abs` at 2.02 is the control — a fast-pathed
function bypasses the dispatcher entirely, so the toll is not inherent to making a call.

**The `Call` rows of that table are not comparable to the others until this is subtracted.**

### 🛑 Two obvious causes, both killed before any code was written

- **`upper`'s `String` allocation.** `str_map` does `Value::Str(f(s).into())`, so `to_uppercase()`
  allocates and `GStr` copies it — item 654's exact shape, one row down. It is at most ~16 of
  41.54 ns, and the dispatch above it is just as big. Going straight at it would have bought a
  fraction of what is there.
- **A `Vec<Value>` of arguments per row.** **Already fixed**, and documented at the call site:
  `buf` is reused across rows. Reading before writing is the only reason this was not "fixed" a
  second time — exactly the failure item 650 found in three stale comments.

The decisive instrument was the NILADIC row. Comparing `upper` against `char_length` could show
that string production was not the whole cost, but only a call with NO argument separates dispatch
from argument handling.

### What the lever is, and why it is not taken here

Resolve the function name ONCE PER BATCH instead of once per row: ~16 ns off `char_length`
(2.4x), `upper` (1.7x), `contains` (1.9x) and every other generic call — a whole-family win rather
than one row.

Not built, deliberately. It means restructuring 89 string arms into a function-pointer table, and
a wrong mapping there is a WRONG ANSWER rather than a slow one. Every cheap shortcut considered —
an integer match, a per-batch cache, a captured closure — still needs the name-to-behaviour
mapping written out once per function, so there is no partial version worth landing. Priced here
so the decision is made with the number in hand rather than from the shape of the code.

The three new harness rows (`char_length`, `lower`, `pi`) are the durable artifact: they keep the
decomposition reproducible, and the header now carries it so the `Call` rows cannot be re-read as
whole-function costs.

## 656 — hoisting a scalar function's argument checks per batch: BUILT, MEASURED FLAT, REVERTED — and it corrects item 655

**REFUTED (native), reverted.** Item 655 priced a 16 ns/row toll on every generic scalar `Call`
and named "resolve the function name once per batch" as the family's biggest lever, projecting
2.4x on `char_length`. **That attribution was wrong, and this is the measurement that says so.**

### What was built

`call_scalar_checked` re-derives its argument checks per row, and every one is a function of
`name` alone — constant for the batch: a 6-name temporal test, a 27-name numeric list, a ~20-arm
`(str_pos, num_pos)` match, then `reverse|size|cardinality`, `concat`, and `to_boolean`. For
`upper` that is roughly 70 string comparisons per row before dispatch even begins.

A `ScalarPlan` struct computed once per batch, with every list moved VERBATIM so behaviour was
preserved by construction, and `call_scalar_checked` kept as a thin wrapper so other callers were
untouched. It compiled, clippy was clean.

### The result: flat

|                | before | after |
| -------------- | ------ | ----- |
| `upper`        | 41.54  | 41.48 |
| `char_length`  | 27.01  | 26.57 |
| `lower`        | 42.34  | 44.43 |
| `contains`     | 33.65  | 32.89 |
| `pi` (niladic) | 16.13  | 15.76 |

Stable across rounds. **For `pi` this removed ~38 string comparisons per row and bought ~2%.**

**Why:** rustc compiles those `matches!` lists into length-and-prefix switches that branch-predict
perfectly, so the comparisons are nearly free. The 89-arm dispatch is not the cost either — `pi`
is its SIXTH arm and still cost 16 ns.

### 🛑 The actual error: a spike read too coarsely

The lever came from spiking `call_scalar` (the same dispatch with NO checks) against
`call_scalar_checked`: 9 ns/row cheaper, stable over three alternated rounds. That number is
right. **Attributing it to the name tests was not** — `call_scalar` skips the name tests AND the
per-row value loops AND the `Result` plumbing, and I assigned the whole saving to the part I had
been reading.

**A spike bounds the TOTAL available; it does not say which component holds it.** The fix would
have been a spike that removed ONLY the name tests. Three successive attributions of this same
16 ns — 89-arm dispatch (655), then the name tests (656) — each came from reading code rather
than isolating a component, and each was wrong.

### What is left, stated narrowly

The 16 ns is real and the 9 ns ceiling is real. Both obvious mechanisms are refuted. What remains
unmeasured is the **non-inlined call** and the **per-row `Result`/`Value` construction**. Anyone
re-targeting this should isolate one component at a time rather than removing all of them at once.

The harness header now carries this correction in place of item 655's projection, so the table
cannot send the next reader at the dispatch again.

## 657 — the 69x on multi-hop COUNT is the TS adjacency LAYOUT; the engine is already AT its floor

**REFUTED (TypeScript), nothing built.** The cross-engine bench's largest ratio is not a target.

### The screen, and why it looked like one

`bun run bench` at 200,000 vertices / 5 edges per node flags the whole multi-hop count family:

|                                          | ts (ms) | native | ratio      |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------- | ------ | ---------- |
| `count 3-hop`                            | 328.8   | 4.8    | **69.05x** |
| `count var-length 1-2 hops + end filter` | 274.1   | 4.4    | 62.68x     |
| `count var-length 1-2 hops`              | 221.7   | 4.2    | 53.36x     |
| `count 3-hop + end filter`               | 205.8   | 4.0    | 51.25x     |
| `count 3-hop + start filter`             | 197.6   | 4.0    | 49.28x     |

And the TS engine HAS dedicated routes here — a degree product for a three-segment chain and a
way-count sweep — so a 69x suggested the shortcut was not firing.

### Step 1: the route DOES fire, established structurally rather than from timing

`threeSegmentRoute`'s gate: the bench's `(a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b)-[:KNOWS]->(c)-[:KNOWS]->(d)` has
a label on the start and no interior predicate, so `labelled` is true and the gate reaches the
product-vs-sweep comparison. TS is already on its dedicated path; 328.8 ms is what that path costs.

So the question was never "is the shortcut reached" but "is 328 ms the floor".

### Step 2: the floor says the engine is already at it

A hand-written loop over the SAME indexes (`edgesFromByLabel` / `edgesToByLabel`), computing the
same count by the same degree-product identity:

|                                                                         | ms                        |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| **SUB-FLOOR** — touch every middle edge, read one degree, NO arithmetic | **314.2**                 |
| **FLOOR** — hand-written degree product                                 | **332.4 / 332.3 / 319.0** |
| **ENGINE**                                                              | **327.2 / 321.2 / 321.2** |

Both produce **25,000,000**, which is what validates the floor's identity rather than leaving it a
plausible-looking loop. The engine is at the floor and in two of three rounds marginally FASTER
than the hand-written version. **There is no route overhead to remove.**

### What the 69x actually is

The sub-floor is the whole story: merely WALKING 1M middle edges and reading one `Set.size` costs
**314 ns per middle edge**. TS adjacency is `Map<id, Map<label, Set<Edge>>>` — two string-keyed
`Map` lookups plus `Set` iteration per edge. Native does the same traversal at ~4.8 ns per middle
edge off columnar arrays.

So the only real lever is the adjacency REPRESENTATION — CSR-style arrays in `packages/core`
instead of nested maps of sets. That is a redesign of the TS core's data structures, not an
optimization of `shortcuts.ts`, and nothing smaller can move this family.

### 🛑 Why the floor was measured BEFORE any attempt

**Item 234 retracted two of three TS targets once a per-shape floor was measured** — the big ratio
was data layout, not engine overhead. This is the third. Had the floor been skipped, the next
several ticks would have gone into `shortcuts.ts`, which is also exactly where the closure-size
lesson records an edit giving UNRELATED queries a new 4x slow mode. The floor cost one probe.

**Do not re-target the multi-hop count routes on the strength of a cross-engine ratio.** The ratio
is real and the routes are already optimal given the layout underneath them.

## 658 — the native engine is 11x FASTER than TS on a 3-scalar projection; the bench row is the JSON EGRESS

**DIAGNOSED (native), nothing built.** `bun run bench`'s `query: project 3 columns` is one of the
few rows where native looks slower than TS — ts 7.9 ms against ffi 57.8 and wasm 65.9, a 7.3x the
wrong way. It is not the engine, and it is not even mostly the serializer.

### The split, 200,000 rows, min of five, repeated

`MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.name AS n, n.city AS c, n.age AS a` on the bench's own `nodesDoc`
shape (`name` unique per row so no dict column; `city` constant):

| stage                                                                | ms                     | ns/row             |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------ |
| `pull` — engine only, NO egress                                      | **0.7 / 0.7 / 0.7**    | 3.6 / 3.6 / 3.7    |
| `try_run_gql_json` — engine + egress, what `lnk_query` actually runs | 12.3                   | 61.4               |
| **egress** (combined − pull)                                         | **11.6 / 11.7 / 11.5** | 57.8 / 58.5 / 57.5 |

JSON output: **6,666,694 bytes** — 6.7 MB of text for 600,000 scalars.

**So the native ENGINE answers this in 0.7 ms, which is 11x faster than TS's ENTIRE 7.9 ms.** The
bench's 57.8 ms decomposes as ~0.7 engine + ~11.6 Rust-side JSON + **~45 ms of FFI transfer and
JS-side parsing** of that 6.7 MB. TS wins the row because it never serializes at all — it builds
JS objects directly in-process.

### Why this was measured as a SPLIT rather than attacked

The ffi and wasm columns sitting close together (57.8 / 65.9) looks like a cost shared by both
bridges, which it is. But "shared by both bridges" does not say whether the engine, the serializer
or the transfer holds it — **decomposing one side of a boundary cannot tell you which side the
cost is on** (item 291). Timing `gql_rows_json` alone would also have understated it, since
building the row view the serializer needs is part of the cost; so the egress half is measured as
`combined − pull` through the real `try_run_gql_json`, the same function the FFI calls.

### What this does and does not leave open

- **The engine is not a target on this shape.** 3.6 ns/row for three property reads plus row
  assembly is consistent with `expression_cost_by_kind`'s `Prop (Str)` at 1.03 ns/row. There is
  nothing here to win.
- **The serializer is near its floor.** 6.7 MB in 11.6 ms is ~575 MB/s with escaping, ~19 ns per
  emitted scalar. Item 654 already removed the per-number allocation from this exact path, and
  this measurement is POST that fix.
- **The real lever is the result FORMAT, and it already exists.** `queryArrowIpc` / `toArrowIPC`
  give a columnar binary egress. Routing bulk scalar results through it instead of JSON text would
  remove both the 11.6 ms and the ~45 ms of transfer-and-parse. But that is an API choice about
  what `lnk_query` returns, not a perf tweak, and `lnk_query`'s JSON contract is what every
  current caller depends on.

**Do not read this row as a native engine deficiency.** It is the price of handing results across
a process boundary as text, and the engine underneath is an order of magnitude ahead of TS.

## 659 — item 657's floor finding does NOT generalize: on a filtered traversal the TS engine beats the naive floor by 3.6x

**CORRECTION to a generalization I was about to make.** Item 657 showed the TS multi-hop COUNT
family sitting exactly at the adjacency floor, so the 33-69x cross-engine ratios there are the
layout. The obvious next step was to declare the rest of the TS traversal ratios the same thing —
`traverse 1-hop + filter` at 27.2x, `2-hop subquery item` at 13.1x. **Measured instead, and it is
not true.**

### `traverse 1-hop + filter`, 200,000 vertices / 5 edges per node

`MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE x.age > 45 RETURN count(*)`:

|                                                             | ms                     | answer  |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------- |
| SUB-FLOOR — walk the edges, touch each target, NO predicate | 123.0                  | —       |
| FLOOR — by hand: walk + read `age` + test                   | 146.6 / 153.7 / 146.0  | 488,840 |
| **ENGINE**                                                  | **40.7 / 41.0 / 42.5** | 488,840 |

Both answers agree at 488,840, so the floor computes the right thing — it is simply **3.6x SLOWER
than the engine**, and slower than the bare walk.

### 🛑 The lesson: a floor built from the OBVIOUS algorithm can sit ABOVE the engine

My floor assumed the only way to answer this is to walk every `KNOWS` edge and test the landed
vertex's property. The engine does something better — seeding from the `age` index, or reading a
property column, rather than visiting each target. So the floor measured a DIFFERENT, worse
algorithm and proves nothing about whether the engine is optimal.

This cuts both ways and is the part worth remembering:

- A floor ABOVE the engine does not vindicate the engine. It only means my loop was worse.
- A floor AT the engine (item 657) is informative ONLY because the floor there was the engine's
  own algorithm — a degree product, which is what the route actually computes.

**So "measure the floor first" is right, but the floor has to be the floor of the engine's OWN
algorithm, not of the first one that comes to mind.** Item 657's count floor qualified by luck of
construction; this one did not.

### What this leaves

The 27.2x on `traverse 1-hop + filter` is **unexplained and still open.** It is NOT refuted as
layout — the engine is already 3.6x better than the layout's naive cost, so the remaining gap to
native's 1.5 ms is something else. Pricing it properly needs the floor of whatever route the
engine actually takes, which means identifying that route first (as item 657 did structurally for
`threeSegmentRoute`) rather than guessing at an algorithm.

Do not carry item 657's conclusion across to the traversal rows. One family was measured; the
other was not.

## 660 — the RIGHT floor finds 1.65x on `traverse 1-hop + filter`, which item 659's wrong floor had hidden

**PRICED (TypeScript), open.** Item 659 established that a floor built from the obvious algorithm
can sit ABOVE the engine and then proves nothing. This is that correction applied: build the floor
from the engine's OWN algorithm and the same row yields a real, measurable gap.

### Identifying the route first, from the code

`buildOneHopCount` is a **degree-sum walk** — iterate a vertex bucket, apply the per-vertex
constraint once, add that vertex's degree — with the far-side spelling driving from the FAR end
(its own header records the rungs and their measurements, 44.7 → 18.0 ms and 156.8 → 35.8 ms).

That explains item 659's result exactly: the engine tests `age` once per VERTEX (200,000) where
the naive floor read it once per EDGE (1,000,000). Five times fewer tests, 3.6x observed. The
naive floor was a worse algorithm, not a bound.

### The right floor: the engine's own algorithm by hand

`MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE x.age > 45 RETURN count(*)`, 200,000 vertices / 5 edges per
node, min of three alternated rounds:

|                                                          | ms                     | answer    |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | --------- |
| SUB-FLOOR — degree-sum, NO predicate (every vertex)      | 34.6                   | 1,000,000 |
| **FLOOR — degree-sum, far-driven, predicate per vertex** | **25.6 / 24.6 / 24.4** | 488,840   |
| **ENGINE**                                               | **40.3 / 41.4 / 40.4** | 488,840   |

**The engine is 1.65x above its own algorithm's floor** (40.3 against 24.4), and both agree at
488,840.

A check that the floor is doing the right thing rather than something accidentally cheap: the
floor WITH the predicate (24.4) beats the sub-floor WITHOUT it (34.6), because the predicate skips
~51% of vertices and so skips their degree lookups too. A floor that ignored the predicate would
have been both wrong and slower.

### Why this matters beyond the number

Item 659's naive floor said "the engine is 3.6x better than walking every edge", which is true and
useless. The right floor says "the engine is 1.65x above the cost of the algorithm it actually
runs", which is actionable. **Same row, same engine, opposite conclusions — the difference is
entirely which algorithm the floor implements.**

So the 27.2x cross-engine ratio on this row decomposes as: ~1.65x the engine leaves on the table
against its own route, and the rest the adjacency layout (item 657) — `Map<id, Map<label,
Set<Edge>>>` at ~314 ns per edge touched.

### Not built

1.65x is real and above the noise floor, but the gap is inside `buildOneHopCount`'s walk, and that
function's own header records a 0.95-0.96x regression on two spellings merely from writing the
walk inline in the returned closure instead of at module scope. An edit there needs the full
spelling probe and `bench:usage`, not a tick. Priced here so the next attempt starts from 24.4 ms
as the target rather than from a cross-engine ratio.

## 661 — the Gremlin surface screened: every row triaged, and `V().out().has().count()` proves both languages share one route

**SCREENED (both engines), nothing built.** `bun run bench:gremlin` at 200,000 vertices /
1,000,000 edges, min of 5. **All 17 rows answer `same`** — no correctness divergence anywhere on
the surface.

### The biggest ratio is a route already priced, and the number proves the design claim

|                                    | ts        | native | ts/nat |
| ---------------------------------- | --------- | ------ | ------ |
| `V().out().has().count()`          | **41.7**  | 1.50   | 27.9x  |
| `V().hasLabel().has().count()`     | 2.6       | 0.10   | 26.5x  |
| `V().has(age,gt).count()`          | 2.3       | 0.10   | 23.3x  |
| `V().out().out().count()`          | 53.2      | 2.75   | 19.4x  |
| `V().repeat(out).times(2).count()` | 53.2      | 3.71   | 14.3x  |
| `V().out().values(age).order()`    | **509.1** | 79.92  | 6.4x   |
| `V().out().values(age)`            | 168.1     | 30.15  | 5.6x   |

`V().out().has().count()` reads **41.7 ms — the same figure as GQL's `traverse 1-hop + filter`**,
which item 660 priced at 1.65x above its own algorithm's floor. Same route, same cost, so that
pricing covers this row too. **That identical number is also direct evidence for the repo's
central design claim**: both surface languages lower to one path, so a cost found on one is the
same cost on the other. Nothing extra to do on the Gremlin side of it.

`V().repeat(out).times(2).count()` matching `V().out().out().count()` at 53.2 ms is consistent
with item 574's settled finding that `repeat().times(k)` IS the k-fold chain.

The two small-absolute rows (2.6 and 2.3 ms) carry large ratios but are under the floor where a
ratio means anything — the same hazard item 124 recorded and the spelling probe's `FLOOR_MS` exists
to suppress.

### The biggest ABSOLUTE cost is `order()`, and it is refuted on the code's own record

`V().out().values(age).order()` at 509.1 ms against an un-ordered twin of 168.1 — so the sort adds
**341 ms in TS against 50 ms native**. A typed-array numeric sort would be far faster, and that is
exactly what cannot be done:

- `ordered-rows.ts` states it directly: _"`compareSort` is deliberately untouched: it is the one
  comparator, byte-identical to the Rust `compare_sort`, and a second derivation of 'which row
  sorts first' is the one thing byte-identity cannot survive."_
- A typed-array sort is also **not stable**, and tie order under `ORDER BY` is **observable
  between the engines** (item 605 measured both agreeing over a 60-row fixture with 20 ties per
  group). `Array.prototype.sort` is stable, which is load-bearing.
- The surrounding multi-key loop was already attempted: **measured 1.00-1.02x against the
  pre-change dist, alternated in one process, and reverted** — it also cost three array
  allocations per sort call.

So the obvious fix is the one explicitly ruled out, and the adjacent one has been tried and
reverted. **Not a target.**

### State of the screen

Both cross-engine screens are now fully triaged. Every large ratio has an attributed cause:
the adjacency layout (657), JSON egress with the engine 11x ahead (658), TS ingest closed by prior
work, `buildOneHopCount` at 1.65x above its floor (660), and `order()` blocked by byte-identity
(this item). **No row in either screen is an unexplained target.**

## 662 — native `DETACH DELETE` of one node is ~3x slower than TS's, and the harness comment pointed at the wrong baseline

**PRICED (native), open.** `bench:usage` is the SERVING regime — small operations against a warm
graph — and neither bulk screen covers it. Memory is explicit that bulk throughput and
per-operation cost are different questions and a change can help one while hurting the other, so
this is a separate surface, not a re-run.

### The row, and why it is the interesting one

Native WINS `write: append node` by ~3.5x but LOSES `write: append then delete node` by ~2.5x,
consistently across both index conditions. Append is fine; the delete is where it goes backwards.
It is the only write in the table where native loses.

### 🛑 The harness's own comment points at the wrong baseline

The row says "read it against `write: append node` to isolate the delete". That subtraction
produces a PAIR CHEAPER THAN ITS OWN FIRST HALF, which is what prompted checking instead of
publishing:

- `write: append node` inserts THREE properties with a **changing query text** — a parse+plan
  cache MISS every operation. The file's own note records TS at 3.4-3.9x faster once
  parameterized.
- `write: append then delete node` inserts TWO properties, **parameterized** — a cache hit.

So the comparable baseline is `write: append node [params]`. The comment is now corrected in place,
including the `units: 2` reminder (the reported figure is units/sec, so an iteration is two).

### The price, one process, correct baseline

`BENCH_ONLY=append`, 20,000 users, 250 ms batches, best of 3:

|           | append [params] | pair / iter | **DELETE**             |
| --------- | --------------- | ----------- | ---------------------- |
| ts(+)     | 2.09 µs         | 4.83 µs     | **2.74 µs**            |
| engine(+) | 2.51 µs         | 11.74 µs    | **9.23 µs** (~3.4x TS) |
| ts(−)     | 2.34 µs         | 5.52 µs     | 3.18 µs                |
| engine(−) | 2.37 µs         | 11.24 µs    | 8.87 µs (~2.8x TS)     |
| wasm(+)   | 3.16 µs         | 16.56 µs    | ~13.4 µs               |

Stable in both index conditions, and **append is at parity** (2.51 against 2.09) — so this is the
delete specifically, not writes generally.

The insert halves still differ by one property (3 vs 2), which inflates the baseline and therefore
**understates** the delete. Conservative, which is the direction a recorded number should err.

### Why a subtraction at all

A delete-only loop empties the graph, which is why the harness pairs them — and on an unindexed
`MATCH (t:Tmp) WHERE t.name = $n` a shrinking bucket makes each delete progressively cheaper, so a
bespoke delete-only probe would be biased in a direction I would then have to characterize. The
same-process subtraction removes cross-run variance, which was the real weakness of the first
estimate, and the residual bias is known and conservative.

### Open

~3x on a single-node `DETACH DELETE`, native, in the serving regime. Not yet diagnosed: the
candidates are the detach scan over adjacency, the tombstone/`deleted` bookkeeping, and the
commit-time constraint recheck that item "write cost / deferred checks" already found dominating
`SET`. Diagnose before assuming — this session has mis-attributed three costs by reading code
instead of isolating a component.

## 663 — a single-node delete was O(total nodes); now O(1), 501x at 200,000 nodes, and native overtakes TS

**FIXED (native).** Item 662 priced a single-node `DETACH DELETE` at ~9.2 µs native against TS's
~2.7 and left it undiagnosed. The cause is algorithmic, not a constant factor.

### The mechanism

`Store::delete_nodes` closed with a sweep over EVERY label bucket:

```rust
for bucket in self.by_label.values_mut() {
    bucket.retain(|&x| !deleted[x as usize]);
}
```

Right for a batch, degenerate for a batch of one: deleting a single `Tmp` node rewrote the
20,000-entry `User` bucket too — with a scattered `deleted[]` probe per element — even though the
victim was never in it. A node belongs only to its own labels' buckets.

### Confirmed O(V) by a size sweep BEFORE any edit

The hypothesis came from reading the code, and this session has mis-attributed three costs that
way (655, 656, and 659's floor). A size sweep settles it without further reading, with DEGREE held
at zero so adjacency cannot be the variable:

| nodes   | before     | ns per node | after     |          |
| ------- | ---------- | ----------- | --------- | -------- |
| 1,000   | 0.410 µs   | 0.410       | 0.110 µs  | 3.7x     |
| 10,000  | 3.350      | 0.335       | 0.120     | 27.9x    |
| 50,000  | 16.340     | 0.327       | 0.120     | 136x     |
| 200,000 | **65.180** | 0.326       | **0.130** | **501x** |

The before column's ns-per-node is **flat at ~0.33** — the signature of O(V). After, the cost is
flat in µs across a 200x range in node count, and ns-per-node collapses to 0.0006. **The
complexity is gone, which matters more than the 501x: the old cost grew with the graph.**

### The fix, and why the threshold is load-bearing in both directions

For a batch of ≤8, only `retain` on buckets a victim actually belongs to — membership is a binary
search, which the sorted buckets already support (`labels_of` relies on it).

The threshold is not cosmetic. The guard costs O(labels × ids × log n), so on a large batch it is
pure waste atop a sweep that would touch nearly every bucket anyway — and **item 443 recorded that
per-node bucket removal made a BATCH delete O(deleted × total)**. Small batches take the targeted
path; everything else keeps the sweep that item earned.

### End to end on the serving path

`bench:usage`, `BENCH_ONLY=append`, 20,000 users:

|                                | before | after      |           |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | ---------- | --------- |
| `append then delete` engine(+) | 170.4k | **383.6k** | **2.25x** |
| engine(−)                      | 177.9k | 408.1k     | 2.29x     |
| wasm(+)                        | 120.8k | 246.0k     | 2.04x     |

Isolated against the parameterized baseline (item 662's correction), the **delete itself goes
9.23 → 2.78 µs, 3.3x** — and **native now slightly beats TS** (2.78 against 3.20) where it was
3.4x behind. Controls flat: `append node` 415.2k → 418.2k, `append node [params]` 397.8k →
412.3k, `interleaved: append + link` 287.8k → 291.4k, all inside the bench's own 1.097x floor.

### Mutation: 3/5, and a fixture subtlety found the one gap

A wrong guard here is a STALE TOMBSTONE — a deleted node still matching `MATCH (n:Label)`, a wrong
answer, not a slow one. Three correctness mutants, all now caught; two perf mutants labelled
answer-equivalent in advance, both survive.

The first run was 2/5. "Checks only the FIRST id" survived — and **not** for want of a batch test.
`batch_delete_keeps_every_label_bucket_exact_sorted_and_restorable` deletes `[0, 3, 6, 9]`, and
victim `0` carries EVERY label in that fixture, so a mutant reading only `ids[0]` still touched
every bucket. **The membership test is observable only when a bucket holds a LATER victim and not
the first.** `a_batch_delete_cleans_a_bucket_only_a_later_victim_is_in` uses DISJOINT labels (`A`
holds node 0, `B` holds node 1), with a survivor in each bucket so an over-eager sweep fails too,
and checks from both the bucket's side and the node's own `labels_of`.

One mutant was **mislabelled by me**: "the threshold admits every batch" is answer-equivalent (the
targeted path is correct at any size, only slower), so surviving was right. Corrected in the
script so the next run does not read it as a gap.

### Verification

1223 + 13 + 726 native tests pass, 0 fail (1 new). All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, including
`write-fuzz`, which drives deletes against the TS engine. clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` 0;
`cargo fmt --check` 0.

## 664 — rolling back an insert was O(inserted x total nodes); now O(inserted), 892x at 200,000 nodes

**FIXED (native).** Item 663's "grep the pattern elsewhere" step, applied to the TECHNIQUE rather
than the symptom, and the second site is worse than the first.

### The mechanism

`pop_last_node` — the undo of `add_node` — removed one id by scanning every label bucket in full:

```rust
for b in self.by_label.values_mut() { b.retain(|&x| x != id); }
```

So rolling back a transaction that inserted N nodes was **O(N × V)**. No bench row covers the
rollback path, which is why it had gone unnoticed.

### Confirmed quadratic by a size sweep BEFORE any edit

Same discriminator as item 663: hold the INSERT COUNT fixed at 200 and vary only the graph size.

| existing nodes | before       | µs per inserted | after     |          |
| -------------- | ------------ | --------------- | --------- | -------- |
| 1,000          | 51.270 µs    | 0.2564          | 7.510 µs  | 6.8x     |
| 10,000         | 384.790      | 1.9240          | 7.900     | 48.7x    |
| 50,000         | 1838.130     | 9.1906          | 8.030     | 229x     |
| 200,000        | **7371.781** | 36.8589         | **8.260** | **892x** |

The before column's µs-per-inserted tracks the node count — the signature of the quadratic. After,
the total is flat across a 200x range and per-inserted is constant at ~0.04 µs, so the rollback is
O(inserted).

### The fix needed no threshold, unlike item 663

`pop_last_node` removes the HIGHEST id, and the buckets are sorted ascending — `add_node` appends,
and `has_label`'s binary search already depends on that order. So if the id is in a bucket at all
it is necessarily the LAST element: `if b.last() == Some(&id) { b.pop(); }`.

**The guard is conservative by construction.** It pops only when the last element IS that id, so
it can never remove the wrong one; a violated sort order would leave a stale entry — the pre-fix
behaviour — rather than corrupt the bucket. A `debug_assert!` pins the assumption (last or
absent), and the **debug** suite was run so the assert is actually compiled in: 1204 tests pass.
Verifying an invariant in a release build where `debug_assert!` is a no-op would have proved
nothing.

### 🛑 Mutation found the CORRUPTION case untested, hidden behind the same fixture blind spot

First run 2/4. The survivor was the worst mutant: an **unconditional** `b.pop()`, which removes the
actual last element from buckets the inserted node was never in. Inserting a `B` node and rolling
back would silently evict an unrelated `A` node from its bucket — **data loss in another label**,
not a stale tombstone.

It survived because **every existing rollback test inserts a node carrying the same label as the
nodes already present**, so every bucket contains the new id and popping unconditionally happens
to be right. The `first()`-instead-of-`last()` mutant WAS caught, so the hole was specific.

`rolling_back_an_insert_leaves_an_unrelated_label_bucket_intact` needs two properties to be able
to fail, and both are in the test's own reasoning: an unrelated label whose bucket does not contain
the newcomer, and TWO members in it — with one member the bucket empties either way and the
assertion could not tell the mutant from the fix. Re-run: **3/4, every correctness mutant caught,
only the equivalence probe (the old full-scan `retain`) surviving as labelled in advance.**

**The general rule, now seen twice in two items:** a fixture where the subject is the ONLY
candidate cannot test a guard that SELECTS among candidates. Item 663's batch test had a victim
carrying every label; this one had inserts sharing the existing label.

### Verification

1226 + 13 + 726 native tests pass, 0 fail (1 new); the DEBUG suite passes with the `debug_assert!`
active. All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, with the `.so` rebuilt `--features capi`. clippy
`--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `cargo fmt --check` 0.

## 665 — the bucket-sweep pattern hunt is EXHAUSTED: every other `retain` in the store is correctly scoped

**SCREENED (native), nothing to fix.** Items 663 and 664 each found a label-bucket operation that
was O(total nodes) where it should have been O(1). This is the systematic follow-through, so the
pattern is not re-grepped a third time.

All 13 `retain` sites in `store.rs`, classified:

| site                                           | scope                       | verdict             |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `delete_nodes` label sweep                     | was O(V)                    | **FIXED, item 663** |
| `pop_last_node` label sweep                    | was O(V)                    | **FIXED, item 664** |
| index buckets (`indexes[j].map`, two sites)    | nodes sharing ONE key value | correctly scoped    |
| range buckets (`ranges`)                       | nodes sharing ONE key value | correctly scoped    |
| `in_adj` / `out_adj` detach (four sites)       | O(degree)                   | correctly scoped    |
| invariants / indexes / ranges / snapshot paths | small config lists          | not per-node        |

**Why the index buckets are not the same bug.** They retain over a bucket keyed by a specific
VALUE, so the scope is "nodes sharing this key", not every node. A low-cardinality key does make
that bucket large — on `bench:usage`'s `score` index it is ~1,000 of 20,000 — but no asymptotic
win is available: the bucket is a `Vec`, so removing one id costs a scan or a memmove either way.
Changing that needs a different data structure, not a guard.

**`min_label_map` is also sound**, though it looks like an O(V) rebuild. It is cached keyed on
`node_count`, has exactly one caller (`element_label` over a large node frontier), and its key is
safe because labels are IMMUTABLE after creation in both surface languages — so a stale entry can
only describe a deleted node, which cannot appear in a frontier.

### The shape worth remembering

Both real bugs had the same signature: **a per-element operation reaching for a structure indexed
by something other than the element.** `delete_nodes` and `pop_last_node` both touched EVERY label
bucket to remove ONE node, when a node belongs only to its own labels' buckets. The index and
adjacency sites do not, because they are already keyed by the thing being changed.

## 666 — the TS engine does NOT have items 663/664's bug: its delete is already O(1) in the node count

**SCREENED (TypeScript), nothing to fix.** Items 663 and 664 found two O(total-nodes) label-bucket
operations in the NATIVE store. The standing instruction covers both engines, so the same
instrument was pointed at TS rather than assuming the asymmetry ran one way.

### The sweep: hold the operation count fixed, vary the graph size

`MATCH (t:Tmp) WHERE t.seq = $s DETACH DELETE t`, 200 deletes, min per delete, ONE SIZE PER
PROCESS (a shrinking graph inside one process would also shrink the bucket being measured).
Degree is held at ZERO, the same control the native harness used, and the victims carry their own
`Tmp` label so the big `User` bucket is the one a native-style sweep would have touched needlessly.

| nodes   | µs per delete |
| ------- | ------------- |
| 1,000   | 6.150         |
| 10,000  | 4.890         |
| 50,000  | 5.410         |
| 200,000 | 4.660         |

**Flat across a 200x range**, with no trend — if anything slightly faster at the top, which is
noise. TS removes a node from its label set in constant time; it never sweeps the other buckets.

### Why this is worth recording rather than assuming

The native bug was invisible at one size: item 662 measured native's delete at ~9.2 µs and TS's at
~2.7 and read it as a 3.4x CONSTANT FACTOR. It was a complexity class, and only the size sweep
separated them. The same reasoning applies in reverse here — TS's ~3-6 µs at one size says nothing
about its slope, so the sweep is the only thing that distinguishes "already fine" from "the same
bug, not yet painful".

### ⚠️ Do not compare these LEVELS to the native figures

Three different instruments are in play and only the SLOPE is comparable:

- this harness times the whole query (parse/plan cache, the `MATCH` seek, then the delete),
- item 663's native sweep timed `Store::delete_nodes` alone (0.130 µs at 200,000 post-fix),
- `bench:usage` subtracts an insert baseline under warm 250 ms batches (TS 3.20 µs, native 2.78
  post-fix).

Reading across them would manufacture a ratio out of instrument differences, which is the
unmatched-A/B error in a new costume.

### State of the write path

Native's single-node delete (663) and insert rollback (664) are now O(1); the pattern hunt across
all 13 `retain` sites is exhausted (665); and TS has neither bug. **No known O(V)-per-operation
cost remains on either engine's write path.**

## 667 — the rest of the write surface is O(1) in the node count; the write-path sweep is COMPLETE

**SCREENED (native), nothing to fix.** Items 663 and 664 each found an O(total-nodes) write cost,
and **neither was visible in any bench row** — a bench measures one graph size, so a complexity
class hides inside what looks like a constant factor. (Item 662 read native's delete as a "3.4x
constant factor"; it was O(V).) This applies the discriminator to the remaining write surface in
one table, so the question is answered per operation instead of re-asked per item.

### Hold the operation count fixed, vary the graph size

200 operations each, min per operation, degree held at zero or one so adjacency is never the
variable:

| operation            | 1,000    | 10,000 | 50,000 | 200,000 |
| -------------------- | -------- | ------ | ------ | ------- |
| `set_prop`           | 0.030 µs | 0.030  | 0.030  | 0.030   |
| `add_edge`           | 0.080    | 0.080  | 0.080  | 0.100   |
| `delete_edge`        | 0.030    | 0.030  | 0.030  | 0.030   |
| `add_node` (CONTROL) | 0.090    | 0.100  | 0.110  | 0.100   |

**Flat in TIME across a 200x range**, with ns-per-node falling proportionally — the signature of
O(1), and the exact inverse of item 663's flat 0.33 ns/node and item 664's rising µs/inserted.

`add_node` is the control: it appends, so it cannot scale with the node count, and a rising figure
there would have meant the harness itself was size-dependent rather than the operation.

`set_prop` holding at a constant 30 ns is also a **regression check** on the earlier "write cost /
deferred checks" work, which found `SET` scaling with row width from a commit-time constraint
recheck — with no constraint registered the skip still holds.

### Scope, stated so the table is not over-read

These are STORE-level calls. A full query adds parse/plan and the `MATCH` that finds the target,
and item 666's note about mixing instruments applies — do not compare these numbers to
`bench:usage` figures or to item 666's whole-query TS sweep. The complexity question is answered
at the store level because that is where both bugs lived.

### The write path is closed

|                                                      |                                          |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| native single-node delete                            | O(V) → O(1), **501x** at 200k (663)      |
| native insert rollback                               | O(N×V) → O(N), **892x** at 200k (664)    |
| all 13 `retain` sites classified                     | two fixed, eleven correctly scoped (665) |
| TS delete                                            | already O(1), bug was native-only (666)  |
| `set_prop` / `add_edge` / `delete_edge` / `add_node` | all O(1) (this item)                     |

**No known O(V)-per-operation cost remains on either engine's write path**, and the harness that
would find a new one is now in the tree rather than reconstructed from scratch next time.

## 668 — the read path has no complexity bug, and the point-lookup spellings agree at EVERY graph size

**SCREENED (native), nothing to fix.** The write-path sweep (663, 664, 667) asked "does this scale
with the node count?" and found two complexity bugs no bench row could see. The read path had
never been asked, and the question is sharper there: **a read returning k rows from a graph of V
nodes should cost O(k) if it seeks and O(V) if it scans**, so a seeking shape whose cost RISES
with V is a planner failing to reach the shape it should.

### Result size held at one row; only the graph grows

| read                               | 1,000     | 10,000     | 50,000     | 200,000     |
| ---------------------------------- | --------- | ---------- | ---------- | ----------- |
| point lookup, indexed numeric      | 0.230 µs  | 0.210      | 0.220      | 0.230       |
| point lookup, indexed string       | 0.200     | 0.220      | 0.210      | 0.210       |
| point lookup, INLINE spelling      | 0.220     | 0.210      | 0.220      | 0.220       |
| `count(*)` over the label          | 0.260     | 0.270      | 0.270      | 0.260       |
| **scan all, one column (CONTROL)** | **1.150** | **10.390** | **52.260** | **210.030** |

Every seeking shape is flat across a 200x range. `count(*)` is O(1) off the label bucket's size.

### ⚠️ The control is what makes the flatness mean anything

An unfiltered scan is O(V) by definition, and it rises **exactly linearly** — 182x for 200x the
nodes, with ns-per-node pinned at ~1.05. Had it stayed flat, the harness could not see scaling at
all and no other row's flatness would have been evidence of anything.

This session needed that lesson twice: `expression_cost_by_kind` read five rows at its own floor
with `WHERE true` as the SLOWEST of them until a positive control (`upper`, 56.85 ns/row against a
1.74 floor) proved the instrument had resolution.

### The second finding: equivalent spellings agree at every SIZE, not just one

The three point-lookup spellings — clause-numeric, clause-string, and **inline** — agree within
noise at every graph size (0.230 / 0.200 / 0.220 at 1,000; 0.230 / 0.210 / 0.220 at 200,000).

That is this repo's central invariant — two spellings of one question must cost the same — checked
on an axis it has never been checked on. `spelling_probe` and `bun run spelling` both compare
spellings at ONE fixed size, so a divergence that only appeared as the graph grew (one spelling
seeking, another scanning) would have been invisible to them. It does not exist here.

### State of the complexity sweep

| path                                                 | verdict                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| native single-node delete                            | O(V) → O(1), 501x at 200k (663)           |
| native insert rollback                               | O(N×V) → O(N), 892x at 200k (664)         |
| all 13 store `retain` sites                          | two fixed, eleven correctly scoped (665)  |
| TS delete                                            | already O(1) (666)                        |
| `set_prop` / `add_edge` / `delete_edge` / `add_node` | all O(1) (667)                            |
| point lookups (3 spellings), `count(*)`              | all O(1); scan control linear (this item) |

**Both the read and write paths are now swept for complexity**, and both harnesses
(`write_cost_by_graph_size`, `read_cost_by_graph_size`) are in the tree, so the next pass runs one
command instead of rebuilding the instrument.
