| **scan all, one column (CONTROL)** | **75.590** | **613.860** | **1568.731** | **5256.750** |

Every seeking shape is flat across a 200x range — slightly FASTER at the top, which is JIT, not a
trend. **TS seeks are O(1) in the node count**, as native's are (668). No complexity bug on either
engine's read path.

### ⚠️ The control rises, but its SLOPE is confounded — recorded rather than presented as clean

The scan grows 69.5x for 200x the nodes, not 200x, because its per-row cost FALLS from 75.6 to
26.3 ns as the graph grows: 9 reps over 200,000 rows is 1.8M row-builds and fully JIT-optimised,
where 9 over 1,000 is 9,000 and is not. So the control confirms the instrument can see scaling —
which is its job, and the reason the flat rows mean anything — but its 69.5x is NOT a clean O(V)
measurement and must not be quoted as one.

Native's equivalent control rose 182x with ns-per-node pinned at ~1.05 (668), because a compiled
engine has no warm-up of this kind. **The same control behaves differently on the two engines, and
that difference is the JIT, not the algorithm.**

### Item 579's clause-vs-inline gap reproduces — and does NOT worsen with scale

The INLINE spelling is consistently faster than the numeric clause spelling: **3.81-4.16 against
5.33-7.44, about 1.4x, at every size.** That is item 579's recorded finding (it flagged 1.3-1.6x
clause-vs-inline on a numeric seeked key, with the string twin converging), and this adds the
missing axis:

**The gap is a CONSTANT FACTOR, not a complexity divergence.** Had one spelling been seeking while
the other scanned, the ratio would have grown with the graph — 1.4x at 1,000 nodes would have
become ~280x at 200,000. It is 1.4x at both ends. So both spellings seek; one simply pays more
per operation.

That reframes the target: it is per-operation overhead in the clause path, bounded and not
scale-dependent, which is a much weaker reason to touch the planner than a divergence would have
been.

### State of the complexity sweep

Both paths, both engines, now swept: native write (663, 664, 667), native read (668), TS write
(666), TS read (this item). **No known cost scales with the graph where it should not**, on either
engine, read or write.

## 670 — deleting a node costs O(its NEIGHBOUR's degree): 28.74 µs to delete one leaf of a 50,000-degree hub

**PRICED (native), open — and the obvious fix is BLOCKED by byte-identity.**

The complexity sweep (663, 664, 667, 668, 669) varied the NODE COUNT with degree pinned at zero or
one. Degree is a separate axis, and `delete_node_inner` has a shape that makes it interesting:

```rust
for a in &out { self.in_adj[a.nbr as usize].retain(|m| m.eid != a.eid); }
```

Removing ONE mirror entry scans that neighbour's whole adjacency. So a delete costs O(sum of its
neighbours' degrees), not O(its own degree) — and the sharp case is a LEAF of a hub.

### Node count held CONSTANT at 60,000; only the hub's degree varies

| hub degree | µs per leaf delete | ns per D |
| ---------- | ------------------ | -------- |
| 100        | 0.160              | 1.6000   |
| 1,000      | 0.680              | 0.6800   |
| 10,000     | 5.890              | 0.5890   |
| 50,000     | **28.740**         | 0.5748   |

**ns-per-D flat from 1,000 upward — O(D) in the NEIGHBOUR's degree**, for a victim of degree 1.
The padding holds the node count fixed so the axis already swept cannot leak in.

**This is the hub shape real people-graphs have**: one requisition with 50,000 applications, one
company with thousands of employees. Deleting a single application costs 28.74 µs and grows
linearly with the requisition's size — a per-operation cost set by the hub, not by the row.

### 🛑 `swap_remove` would make it O(1) and is NOT available

The adjacency IS already sorted by eid (edges append, eids ascend), so a binary search could find
the entry in O(log D) and `swap_remove` would drop it in O(1). **But `out_adj` ORDER IS
LOAD-BEARING for byte-identity.** The CSR index and the per-type partitions are built in
`out_adj` order — the store's own comments state that a CSR slice is "byte-identical to" that
order, and that a type-grouped concat "would not preserve" it. Reordering adjacency changes
traversal order, which changes row order, which breaks the TS/native invariant.

So removal must keep order, which means a memmove: still O(D) in the worst case.

### 🛑 CORRECTION (item 671): the binary-search route is NOT available either

This section first said `binary_search_by_key` + `Vec::remove` "preserves order and replaces
`retain`'s full predicate scan", implying it was available and merely position-dependent. **It is
not available at all, and leaving that written would have invited an incorrect fix.**

A binary search needs the adjacency sorted by eid. It usually is — edges append and eids ascend —
but **`Undo::RestoreEdge` does `push(adj)`**, appending a restored entry to the END regardless of
its eid. Within one transaction:

```text
[10, 20]  ->  delete edge 10  ->  [20]  ->  add edge 30  ->  [20, 30]
rollback, replayed in REVERSE: undo the add -> [20], then restore edge 10 -> [20, 10]
```

The list is now unsorted. A binary search over it could MISS the entry and leave a dangling mirror
on the neighbour — corruption, not slowness.

So **both** candidate fixes are refuted, for different reasons:

| fix                                                      | why not                                                                                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `swap_remove` after finding the entry — O(1)             | `out_adj` ORDER is load-bearing for byte-identity (CSR slices and per-type partitions are built in it) |
| `binary_search_by_key` + `Vec::remove` — O(log D + tail) | the list is NOT reliably eid-sorted; `Undo::RestoreEdge` appends out of order                          |

A linear find is what correctness requires, and `retain` already is one. **The O(neighbour-degree)
cost is inherent to the current adjacency representation**, not an oversight — moving it needs a
different structure (an eid-keyed index per node, or a tombstone-and-compact scheme), which is a
design change with its own byte-identity surface.

### The position measurement, kept because it is the baseline a future attempt needs

The baseline is **flat across position** — one leaf per store, rebuilt per repetition so no earlier
delete shifts the position being asked for:

| position of the victim | hub degree | µs per op |
| ---------------------- | ---------- | --------- |
| FIRST (oldest edge)    | 50,000     | 36.310    |
| MIDDLE                 | 50,000     | 35.390    |
| LAST (newest)          | 50,000     | 34.250    |

A 6% spread, which is what `retain` should give: it scans all D wherever the entry sits. Any future
attempt has a position-matched baseline to compare against, so the comparison cannot become an
unmatched A/B.

## 672 — TS's hub-leaf delete is O(1) where native's is O(hub degree): a crossover, and a fixture error that inverted the answer

**SCREENED (both engines).** Item 670 found native deleting a degree-1 leaf of a hub in O(hub
degree) — 28.74 µs at D=50,000 — because removing the mirror entry scans the neighbour's adjacency
`Vec`, with both candidate fixes refuted (item 671). TS stores adjacency as
`Map<id, Map<label, Set<Edge>>>`, and a `Set` delete is O(1), so the prediction was that TS stays
flat where native rises.

### 🛑 The first run said the opposite, and the fixture was why

Without an index, `MATCH (l:Leaf) WHERE l.k = $k DETACH DELETE l` is a LABEL SCAN over all D
leaves. So each iteration measured **find-then-delete**, while item 670's native harness called
`store.delete_nodes(&[victim])` with no match at all. That run read **1394.71 µs at D=50,000
against native's 28.74 and "showed" TS 48x slower** — almost all of it the scan.

Scan-plus-delete against delete-only is the **unmatched A/B this session has twice written up as
an error** (items 662 and 666) and then committed anyway, in its own probe. The index makes the
match a seek and the comparison about the delete.

### With the seek index: TS is flat, native is linear

| hub degree | TS µs     | ns/D  | native µs (670) |                    |
| ---------- | --------- | ----- | --------------- | ------------------ |
| 100        | 9.720     | 97.2  | 0.160           | native 61x faster  |
| 1,000      | 9.450     | 9.45  | 0.680           | native 14x         |
| 10,000     | 9.940     | 0.994 | 5.890           | native 1.7x        |
| 50,000     | **9.400** | 0.188 | **28.740**      | **TS 3.1x faster** |

**TS flat across a 500x range in hub degree.** The prediction was right; only the first fixture
was wrong.

### The crossover is real in DIRECTION; its position is NOT established here

Native wins at low degree on constant factors; TS wins at high degree on complexity. But TS's
9.4 µs includes the whole query (parse/plan cache, the seek, then the delete) while native's 28.74
is `delete_nodes` alone — **the slopes are comparable, the levels are not.** Native's full-query
figure would be higher, moving the crossover left; nothing here pins where.

Quoting "the crossover is at D≈15,000" from this table would repeat the error the first run already
made once.

### Why this strengthens item 670 rather than just annotating it

670 concluded the O(neighbour-degree) cost is "inherent to the current adjacency representation"
and that moving it needs a different structure. **This shows the alternative structure demonstrably
avoids the cost** — TS's `Set` pays nothing per edge removed, for the same mirrored adjacency and
the same logical operation. So the native cost is a consequence of choosing `Vec` (which the CSR
build and per-type partitions need for ORDER), not of mirroring. That raises the value of an
eid-keyed per-node index, and bounds what it would buy: everything above the crossover.

## 673 — enabling the edge-type index makes a hub-leaf delete 8.3x WORSE, and this fix IS available

**FOUND (native), fix identified.** Item 670 measured a hub-leaf delete with the opt-in edge-type
index OFF (its default). With it ON:

|                               | µs per hub-leaf delete, D=50,000 |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| edge-type index off (CONTROL) | 34.200                           |
| **edge-type index ON**        | **283.410**                      |

**8.3x.** Same fixture, same victim position, the index the only variable.

### The mechanism

`delete_node_inner` calls `reindex_node_etypes` for the victim AND EVERY NEIGHBOUR:

```rust
if self.edge_type_index {
    self.reindex_node_etypes(id);
    for a in out.iter().chain(inc.iter()) {
        if a.nbr != id { self.reindex_node_etypes(a.nbr); }
    }
}
```

and that function **rebuilds a node's whole type map from scratch** — iterating both adjacency
lists and allocating a fresh `Vec` per edge type:

```rust
let mut om: U32Map<Vec<Adj>> = U32Map::default();
for a in &self.out_adj[i] { om.entry(a.etype).or_default().push(*a); }
```

So deleting one leaf reindexes the hub in full: O(hub degree), twice over, with allocation churn —
to reflect the removal of ONE entry.

### Why this one matters

The index is OPT-IN, and its whole purpose is to make type-filtered hops seek a per-node bucket
instead of scanning the adjacency (`create_edge_type_index`'s doc points at `examples/expand_bench`
for that side). **So a user turns it on for read speed and silently pays 8.3x on hub deletes** —
exactly the shape a people-graph has, where deleting one application from a 50,000-application
requisition is a routine write.

The READ side of that trade is benchmarked. The WRITE side never was.

### 🛑 Unlike items 670/671, the fix IS available

Remove the one entry from the relevant type bucket instead of rebuilding both maps:

```text
out_type_idx[nbr][etype].retain(|a| a.eid != eid)
```

- **Order is preserved.** `retain` keeps relative order, so the "buckets are filled in
  out_adj/in_adj order" property — the thing that blocks `swap_remove` in item 670 and makes CSR
  slices byte-identical — is untouched.
- **It needs no sortedness**, so item 671's refutation (a restored edge appends out of eid order)
  does not apply either.
- **It removes the allocations**, which a full rebuild pays per edge type per neighbour.

Still O(bucket) for a single-type hub, where bucket == degree — so no asymptotic win there — but
it drops a second O(D) pass, both map rebuilds and the allocation churn. For a MULTI-type hub it
is O(bucket) instead of O(degree), which is a real asymptotic improvement in the number of types.

Not yet implemented; priced here so the next step starts from 283.41 µs against a 34.20 µs floor.

## 674 — the hub-leaf delete regression is FIXED: drop one type-bucket entry instead of rebuilding, 5.35x

**SHIPPED (native).** Item 673 measured an 8.3x penalty on a hub-leaf delete from enabling the
opt-in edge-type index, and identified the fix. Implemented:

| hub-leaf delete, D=50,000     | µs per op  |
| ----------------------------- | ---------- |
| edge-type index off (CONTROL) | 32.500     |
| index ON, before (item 673)   | 283.410    |
| **index ON, after**           | **52.970** |

**5.35x.** The index-on penalty over the no-index floor falls from **8.3x to 1.63x**; the residual
is item 670's mirror scan, which is irreducible without an eid-keyed adjacency.

**The control is what carries this.** Both arms are measured in ONE process by the same harness, so
the comparison is internal: the index-OFF arm, which the change cannot reach, moved 34.200 → 32.500
(5%, inside the floor) while the subject moved 5.35x. That ratio is the evidence — no cross-binary
alternation needed, and it is a stronger claim than two numbers from two builds.

### The change

`delete_node_inner` called `reindex_node_etypes` for the victim and EVERY neighbour, rebuilding each
one's whole type map — both directions, a fresh `Vec` per etype — to reflect ONE removed entry. It
now drops that one entry:

```text
drop_etype_entry(nbr, is_out, etype, eid)  ->  bucket.retain(|a| a.eid != eid)
```

plus clearing the victim's own two maps directly (its adjacency was already taken, so there is
nothing to rebuild from).

### Why it is byte-identical, not merely answer-equal

A bucket is **the subsequence of the adjacency carrying that etype, in adjacency order**. `retain`
preserves relative order on BOTH sides, and the mirror detach is itself a `retain` — so removing by
eid leaves exactly what a full rebuild would produce.

Checked, not assumed: the only readers are `out_typed` / `in_typed`, which look up ONE key and never
iterate the map, so the hash-table order a rebuild reshuffles is unobservable. (An emptied key is
removed anyway, to keep the structure identical to a rebuild's; `map_or(&[], …)` cannot tell an
absent key from an empty bucket, so that part is housekeeping.)

This extends a technique the file already used: `add_edge`'s hot path has done the incremental
APPEND since the index was introduced. Only the removal side rebuilt.

Item 671's objection — a restored edge appends out of eid order — does not apply, because no reader
binary-searches a bucket.

### 🛑 Mutation 6/7, and the hole was in MY OWN TEST

The existing `edge_type_index_tracks_delete` does delete with the index on, but **every bucket it
asserts on ends up EMPTY**, so a mutant clearing the whole bucket passes it — and its `out_ids`
helper SORTS, so bucket order, which is the entire correctness argument here, was invisible to the
whole suite.

So `deleting_a_node_drops_one_type_bucket_entry_per_edge_and_keeps_the_order` reads buckets RAW,
with a same-etype survivor on both sides of the hub.

**First run 5/7 — and the survivor was the mutant the new test existed to kill.** `swap_remove`
instead of `retain` (right contents, wrong order) passed, because the fixture's bucket was `[1,2,3]`
with the victim at index 1: `swap_remove` pulls the LAST element into the gap and yields `[1,3]`,
identical to `retain`. The test's own comment named that trap — "only by luck; with the victim in
the middle of a longer bucket it would not" — and the fixture was built the way the comment warns
against, so the order assertion was decorative.

Widened to five entries, where `retain` leaves `[1,3,4,5]` and `swap_remove` leaves `[1,5,3,4]`.
Re-run **6/7**: every correctness mutant caught (whole-bucket clear, drop-nothing, retain inverted,
swap_remove/order, direction swapped, victim's own buckets left populated), with only the
housekeeping mutant surviving as labelled in advance.

That survivor mattered: a `swap_remove` variant is FASTER than `retain` and silently wrong in
traversal order — exactly the class the byte-identity invariant exists to stop. The 5.35x stands on
`retain` specifically.

**The fixture rule, now for the THIRD time in this session** (items 663, 664, 674): _a fixture where
the subject is the only candidate cannot test a guard that selects among candidates._ 674 adds a
corollary — **a fixture where two algorithms coincide cannot distinguish them**, and writing the
warning down is not the same as acting on it.

### Open after this

The symmetric undo path (`Undo::RestoreNode`) still rebuilds, and the same argument applies: a
restore PUSHES the mirror to the end of the neighbour's adjacency, so a rebuild puts it at the end
of the bucket, which an incremental push matches. Not yet measured — next.

## 675 — the SAME rebuild in `delete_edge`, on the hotter path: 13.28x penalty, now 1.75x

**SHIPPED (native).** Item 674's "grep the pattern elsewhere" step. `delete_edge` had the identical
bug and is the hotter of the two paths — it is also what `Undo::AddEdge` rolls back through, so
rolling back an `add_edge` paid it as well.

### Alternated A/B, 3 rounds each, rebuilt between every round

| arm    | index off (CONTROL) | index ON | ON/off     |
| ------ | ------------------- | -------- | ---------- |
| BEFORE | 18.690              | 248.230  | **13.28x** |
| AFTER  | 18.660              | 32.720   | **1.75x**  |

**Subject 7.59x; control flat at 1.002x.**

**The alternation was load-bearing, and not for the usual reason.** The win was never in doubt — the
harness measures both arms in ONE process, so that ratio is internal. The open question was the
CONTROL: the fix captures the etype inside the `retain` closure, and that closure runs on BOTH
paths, index or no index, so a regression there would hit every user who never enabled the index.
Two numbers from two builds cannot answer it.

And the un-alternated pair was simply wrong. Single builds gave the control 13.940 then 10.420 —
which would have supported a 9.3x claim — while six alternated rounds pin it at 18.66-18.69 every
time. The real figure is 7.59x. **A control that appears to IMPROVE by 1.34x is not good news, it is
a measurement that has not converged.**

### The change

Same shape as item 674: drop the one entry instead of rebuilding both endpoints' whole maps. The
etype is captured off the adjacency entry as the existing `retain` drops it, so there is no second
scan and no `edge_etype` lookup; `None` means the eid was absent at both endpoints, i.e. the
documented no-op.

All FOUR (endpoint, direction) combinations are updated, because the method is deliberately
direction-agnostic — "safe to call with the endpoints in either order" — and `drop_etype_entry` is a
no-op where the eid is absent. A self-loop makes two of the four redundant no-ops.

Note this one could not change the COMPLEXITY: `delete_edge` already spends four O(degree) `retain`s
on the flat adjacency, so O(degree) is the floor. The 7.59x is the two map rebuilds and their
per-etype allocations coming off the top of it.

### Mutation 5/6

`drop_etype_entry` itself was mutated at item 674 (6/7); these target the NEW code — the etype
capture and the four-way dispatch. Caught: only endpoint `u` updated, only the OUT direction
updated, the captured etype off by one (wrong bucket), and the etype never captured. The old full
rebuild survives as the labelled equivalence probe — correct, just 7.6x slower.

**One of those catches was worthless as first written and was re-run.** "The etype is never
captured" was done by dropping `mut`, so it CAUGHT at the build step — the compiler refusing an
assignment in the closure, which is no evidence the TESTS detect a stale entry. Re-run as a
compiling variant (`dropped_etype.filter(|_| false)`, so the capture happens and the drop is
skipped): caught by the tests, exit 101. A build failure counts as caught for a mutant that cannot
exist, but it must not be read as oracle coverage of the behaviour it was aimed at.

`delete_edge`'s existing index test had **both** of item 674's blind spots: `edge_type_index_tracks_delete`
asserts only on buckets that end up EMPTY, through a SORTING helper. So
`deleting_an_edge_drops_one_type_bucket_entry_and_keeps_the_order` reads raw, with a five-entry
bucket and the victim at index 1 (where `retain` and `swap_remove` part company), and exercises the
swapped-endpoint call the doc comment promises works.

### Open after this

Both rollback paths still rebuild: `Undo::RestoreEdge` (store.rs:5109) and `Undo::RestoreNode`
(5149/5157). A restore PUSHES the mirror to the end of the neighbour's adjacency, so a rebuild puts
it at the end of the bucket, which an incremental push matches — the same argument. Not yet
measured. `create_edge_type_index` (3414) rebuilds legitimately and stays.

## 676 — the index turned an O(1) rollback into O(hub degree): 326x, and the complexity is gone

**SHIPPED (native).** The last two sites of items 674/675's pattern, and the biggest — because here
the rebuild was not a constant factor on an already-linear path, it WAS the whole cost.

### A size sweep settles the class, rather than inferring it from the code

Operation held fixed (roll back ONE edge delete), hub degree varied. **Flat in µs means O(1); flat
in ns-per-D means O(D)** — the discriminator from items 663/664.

| hub degree | off, µs | off, ns/D | ON before, µs | ON before, ns/D | **ON after, µs** | ON after, ns/D |
| ---------- | ------- | --------- | ------------- | --------------- | ---------------- | -------------- |
| 1,000      | 0.040   | 0.0400    | 2.150         | 2.1500          | 0.050            | 0.0500         |
| 10,000     | 0.050   | 0.0050    | 18.110        | 1.8110          | 0.080            | 0.0080         |
| 50,000     | 0.100   | 0.0020    | 93.560        | 1.8712          | 0.420            | 0.0084         |
| 200,000    | 0.290   | 0.0014    | **329.460**   | 1.6473          | **1.010**        | 0.0050         |

Before: ns-per-D flat at ~1.65-2.15 ⇒ **O(D)**. After: ns-per-D collapses ⇒ **O(1)**, the same shape
as the index-off control, which was O(1) throughout. **326x at D=200,000** (a re-measurement after
the mutation run gave 0.900 µs, so 326-366x; the sub-µs values sit near the timer floor, so the
COMPLEXITY SHAPE is the claim and the ratio is quoted conservatively).

Rolling back a hub-LEAF node delete: 84.490 → 0.570 µs, **148x**.

### Why this one is 326x where items 674/675 were 7-8x

`delete_edge` and `delete_node` already spend O(degree) on the flat adjacency, so there the rebuild
was a constant factor on top of a linear floor. **A restore is a PUSH**, so its floor is O(1) and
the rebuild was the entire cost. Same bug, three sites, and the size sweep is what distinguishes
"expensive" from "asymptotically wrong".

### The change

`push_etype_entry` — the restore counterpart of 674's `drop_etype_entry`. `Undo::RestoreEdge` pushes
each entry onto the adjacency and onto its bucket in the SAME order; `Undo::RestoreNode` pushes each
neighbour's regained mirror, and still rebuilds **id itself**, whose entire adjacency is assigned
wholesale there — that rebuild is O(its own degree), which is its own data and unavoidable.

### 🛑 Rollback does NOT restore adjacency ORDER, and the test had to be written to that

The forward delete removes the entry from the middle and the restore pushes it back at the END, so
after rolling back the delete of `0 -> 2` the adjacency is `[1, 3, 4, 5, 2]` — and the bucket must
mirror THAT, not the original `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. Asserting the pre-delete order would have been
asserting a property the engine does not have. This is pre-existing behaviour, unrelated to the fix,
but it is what makes the incremental push correct: an entry appended to the adjacency belongs at the
end of its etype's bucket.

### Mutation 6/7 — and the fixture rule bit for the FOURTH time

`edge_type_index_survives_rollback` could not see any of this: one- and two-entry buckets read
through the SORTING `out_ids` helper. So
`rolling_back_a_delete_leaves_each_type_bucket_mirroring_the_adjacency` reads raw, over both rollback
paths, asserting bucket-mirrors-adjacency at every node.

**First run 5/7, with an unlabelled correctness mutant surviving:** "RestoreNode skips the
neighbours' bucket pushes". It survived because it was **INERT, not equivalent** — it mutates the
`for a in &out` loop, which handles the victim's OUTGOING edges and their mirrors in neighbours' IN
buckets, and the fixture gave the victim only an INCOMING edge, so that branch never executed.

A survivor count cannot tell inert from equivalent; only reading why each one survived can. That is
the argument for labelling expectations in advance and investigating every mismatch.

Added `2 -> 3` so the victim has an outgoing edge, plus an explicit assertion that node 3's IN bucket
regains the mirror in adjacency order. Re-run **6/7**: all six correctness mutants caught (push
nothing, wrong direction, push twice, FRONT-INSERT order, skip the neighbour pushes, drop id's own
rebuild), with only the labelled equivalence probe surviving — a rebuild after a correct push is
idempotent.

The front-insert mutant dying is what licenses the order argument the whole fix rests on.

### The edge-type index's write side, now priced end to end

It is OPT-IN, enabled for type-filtered hop speed (`examples/expand_bench`), and its write side had
never been measured at all:

| path                       | penalty before                   | after          |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------- |
| hub-leaf node delete (674) | 8.3x                             | 1.63x          |
| hub edge delete (675)      | 13.28x                           | 1.75x          |
| **rollback (676)**         | **O(1) → O(D), 1136x at D=200k** | **O(1), 3.6x** |

`create_edge_type_index` (store.rs:3414) rebuilds legitimately and stays; it is the only remaining
`reindex_node_etypes` caller besides `RestoreNode`'s own-node rebuild.

## 677 — an interval index made an UNRELATED rollback O(V): 15.2 ms at 200k nodes, now O(1)

**SHIPPED (native).** Items 674-676 priced the edge-type index's write side. Asking the same
question of the OTHER opt-in index found the largest regression of the session.

| nodes   | off, µs | off ns/node | ON before, µs | ON before ns/node | **ON after, µs** | after ns/node |
| ------- | ------- | ----------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ---------------- | ------------- |
| 1,000   | 0.060   | 0.0600      | 78.200        | 78.2000           | 0.070            | 0.0700        |
| 10,000  | 0.090   | 0.0090      | 863.090       | 86.3090           | 0.090            | 0.0090        |

sets a NODE property, which an index over EDGE props cannot see.

### The rebuild is right; paying it unconditionally is not

`rollback` calls `rebuild_interval` — both per-node axis vectors reallocated, then every node
reindexed — whenever the index exists. The comment there explains why, and it is sound: the interval
index depends on edge PROPS as well as adjacency, restored in an order per-record maintenance cannot
safely track.

So the fix does NOT attempt incremental maintenance. It asks whether the transaction could have
reached the index at all, by scanning the undo log — **O(the transaction), not O(the graph)** — and
skips only when every record is provably unreachable: a node property, a label, or an edge property
under a key the index is not built on. The `match` is exhaustive with no wildcard, so a future
`Undo` variant forces the rebuild until someone proves it safe.

`rollback_to` had the same unconditional rebuild and matters more: it is per FAILED STATEMENT, so a
long transaction paid a whole-graph rebuild per failure.

### 🛑 Mutation 5/8, two unlabelled survivors, and they were DIFFERENT things

The mutants here are asymmetric, which is the reason this needed its own tests: **skipping too much
is a stale index and a wrong answer; skipping too little is merely slow and invisible to every
correctness and differential suite.** Three perf-direction mutants were labelled expected-survivors.

First run 4/8 with two UNLABELLED survivors. Counting them would have said "two gaps"; reading them
said one gap and one of my own false claims.

**1. Adjacency changes never count — a REAL gap, the exact mirror of one already fixed.**
`interval_index_survives_rollback` writes interval properties AND changes adjacency, so the gate
answers yes from the PROPERTY records alone; a version ignoring adjacency entirely passes it. Added
`rolling_back_an_adjacency_only_change_still_fixes_the_interval_index`, whose transaction writes no
properties at all, over both an edge delete and a node delete. (`Undo::RestoreEdge` and
`RestoreNode` really do depend on the rebuild; `Undo::AddEdge` routes through `delete_edge` and
maintains the index itself.)

**2. A reverted schema op no longer forces the rebuild — MY LABEL WAS WRONG, not the suite.** The
comment I had written claimed this was load-bearing because `restore_schema` can recreate an index
the tx dropped. It can — but `create_interval_index` reindexes every node, so the index is already
correct when it returns, and the other branch clears it to `None`. The flag cannot change an answer.
Kept as insurance, because the skip silently depends on that coupling and a lazier `restore_schema`
would leave the index empty — but the comment now says it is insurance that mutation showed to be
non-load-bearing, and the mutant is relabelled so the next run does not re-litigate it.

Re-run **5/8**: every stale-index mutant caught (gate always false, edge-prop never counts,
adjacency never counts, last-record-only, `rollback_to` never rebuilds), with exactly the three
labelled perf/insurance survivors.

Two new tests exist only because the gate is a decision no answer depends on in the common case:
one whose only interval-relevant record is a PROPERTY change, and one where an irrelevant write
comes LAST, pinning that the gate asks "did ANY record reach the index" rather than "did the last
one" — a cheaper-looking check that passed every other test in the file.

### Both opt-in indexes, write side, now priced end to end

| path                                   | before                   | after         |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------- |
| edge-type: hub-leaf node delete (674)  | 8.3x                     | 1.63x         |
| edge-type: hub edge delete (675)       | 13.28x                   | 1.75x         |
| edge-type: rollback (676)              | O(1) → O(D), 1136x       | O(1), 3.6x    |
| **interval: unrelated rollback (677)** | **O(1) → O(V), 26,241x** | **O(1), ~1x** |

Still unpriced: `rebuild_interval` on the FORWARD path — `remove_edge_prop` on an interval key
(store.rs:4533) rebuilds the whole graph per removal. Same function, different caller, not yet
measured.

## 678 — `remove_edge_prop` rebuilt the WHOLE interval index; its twin `set_edge_prop` already did not

**SHIPPED (native).** The cleanest find of the run, because the fix already existed in the file
twelve lines away.

| nodes   | off, µs | off ns/node | ON before, µs | ON before ns/node | **ON after, µs** | after ns/node |
| ------- | ------- | ----------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ---------------- | ------------- |
| 1,000   | 0.040   | 0.0400      | 22.030        | 22.0300           | 0.190            | 0.1900        |
| 10,000  | 0.040   | 0.0040      | 271.450       | 27.1450           | 0.280            | 0.0280        |
| 50,000  | 0.050   | 0.0010      | 1397.920      | 27.9584           | 0.320            | 0.0064        |
| 200,000 | 0.090   | 0.0004      | **4813.790**  | 24.0690           | **0.470**        | 0.0024        |

**4.8 ms to remove ONE edge property**, from an edge whose source had out-degree 4 — 53,486x the
control. ns-per-node flat at 22-28 ⇒ **O(V)**; after, it collapses ⇒ O(source degree). **8,023x** at
D=200,000. The fixture holds the source's out-degree at 4 and grows only the graph, so anything that
scales is scaling with the GRAPH, not the edge's fan-out.

### One of a pair got the fix

`set_edge_prop` reindexes only the edge's source node for an interval-axis write, with a comment
explaining why that is sufficient: the index is out-edge / source-partitioned, so `by_lo[node]`
holds only NODE's out-edges. `remove_edge_prop` called `rebuild_interval` — O(V+E) — for the same
key on the same index. Removing an axis takes the edge OUT, which is exactly as local as moving it.

This is what "grep the pattern elsewhere" is for: the expensive version survived next to the cheap
one because nothing distinguished them.

### 🛑 `remove_edge_prop` had NO interval coverage at all

`interval_index_tracks_writes` exercises `set_edge_prop` and `delete_edge` and stops there. That
absence is why a whole-graph rebuild could sit beside a local reindex indefinitely — both return the
same answers.

`removing_an_interval_axis_drops_the_edge_from_the_index` pins the real contract: an edge is indexed
only when BOTH axes are present and numeric (`reindex_node_interval` requires it, and so does the
brute-force oracle), so removing either drops it from both; siblings off the same source are
untouched; restoring the axis re-indexes it; and the lo axis behaves like the hi axis.

### Mutation 3/4, after two SKIPS that were the guard working

First run reported 1/4 — but two mutants were **SKIPPED, not survived**: their anchor, the bare
`if let Some((from, _)) = self.edge_endpoints(eid) { self.reindex_node_interval(from); }`, now
appears TWICE in `store.rs`, because matching `set_edge_prop` is the entire point of the fix. The
exactly-once assertion refused both rather than mutating the wrong twin and reporting the result as
if it were this one.

Re-anchored on the comment unique to `remove_edge_prop`: **3/4**, every correctness mutant caught
(reindex dropped, TARGET reindexed instead of SOURCE, interval-key guard inverted), with the old
whole-graph rebuild surviving as the labelled equivalence probe.

A skip and a survivor look alike in a tally and mean opposite things. Worth keeping the two
distinguishable in the output.

### The two opt-in indexes' write side, complete

| path                                  | before                   | after                               |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| edge-type: hub-leaf node delete (674) | 8.3x                     | 1.63x                               |
| edge-type: hub edge delete (675)      | 13.28x                   | 1.75x                               |
| edge-type: rollback (676)             | O(1) → O(D), 1136x       | O(1), 3.6x                          |
| interval: unrelated rollback (677)    | O(1) → O(V), 26,241x     | O(1), ~1x                           |
| **interval: remove an axis (678)**    | **O(1) → O(V), 53,486x** | **O(source degree), 8,023x faster** |

**Four of the five were COMPLEXITY regressions, not constant factors** — which is why a benchmark at
one graph size would have missed every one of them, and why the size sweep is the instrument that
found them. `rebuild_interval` now has exactly one caller that is not a schema op or a rollback, and
none on a per-write path.

## 679 — the TS engine does NOT share items 676-678's bug (measured, not assumed)

**NO CHANGE (TypeScript).** Items 676-678 were all one shape: an index maintained by rebuilding the
whole structure on a path whose own cost is O(1) or O(degree). The question for the other engine is
whether it does the same thing.

Reading `Graph.ts` says no, and for a specific reason: `#restoreSchemaSnapshot` returns early unless
a SCHEMA op ran in the transaction, so a plain data rollback never touches the property indexes —
the data undos maintain them. That is exactly the guard the Rust interval path lacked.

**Swept rather than trusted.** Operation held fixed (roll back one unrelated property SET), graph
size varied:

| vertices | index off (CONTROL) | index ON | ON ns/vertex |
| -------- | ------------------- | -------- | ------------ |
| 1,000    | 4.210 µs            | 3.300 µs | 3.3000       |
| 10,000   | 2.520               | 2.470    | 0.2470       |
| 50,000   | 1.710               | 1.990    | 0.0398       |
| 200,000  | 1.800               | 1.570    | 0.0078       |

ns-per-vertex collapses by 540x across a 200x size range ⇒ **O(1)**, and the index sits inside the
control's noise at every size. No bug here.

**A caveat on the instrument, stated because it would otherwise read as a win:** the absolute times
FALL as the graph grows (4.21 → 1.80 µs), which is JIT warmup across the sweep, not a graph effect.
So the controlled comparison is index-on vs index-off WITHIN a size; the cross-size signal is the
ns-per-vertex collapse. A sweep whose absolute numbers improve with N is reporting warmup, and on
this engine a sweep needs per-size warmup or a discarded first size to be read any other way. (The
Rust sweeps are not exposed to this — no JIT.)

Recorded as a comment beside `#restoreSchemaSnapshot` with the numbers, per the standing rule that a
rejected target lives next to the code it would have changed, and saying explicitly that the early
return is load-bearing and the path is already flat.

### What this says about the five Rust items

It is evidence the Rust fixes were corrections to Rust, not a shared design flaw: the TS engine had
the right discipline — maintain incrementally, rebuild only when identity changes — and the Rust
engine had it in `set_edge_prop` and `add_edge` but not in their twins. Three of the five fixes just
extended a technique already present in the same file.

## 680 — ONE adjacency write permanently demotes every later read, and the penalty is SELECTIVITY not 2x

**DIAGNOSED (native), fix named with its blocker. No code change.** Tonight's lever — grep every
`rebuild_*` caller and ask what the host path costs — applied to the CSR read overlay.

`rebuild_csr` runs at LOAD only (`Builder::build`, the codec and ndjson readers) and nowhere else
outside tests. Every adjacency write calls `invalidate_csr`, which just clears `csr_fresh`; the
readers (`out_typed_csr`, `out_typed_flat`, `out`/`inc`) then return `None` and fall back to the
per-node `Vec`s. **Nothing re-arms it.**

### It is not a cost of interleaving — it is permanent

Same query three times: fresh, after one `add_edge`, then again with no further writes.

| nodes   | fresh (CONTROL) | after ONE add_edge | the NEXT read    | `rebuild_csr` itself |
| ------- | --------------- | ------------------ | ---------------- | -------------------- |
| 1,000   | 3.960 µs        | 7.170 (1.81x)      | 7.190 (1.82x)    | 23.240               |
| 10,000  | 34.930          | 68.250 (1.95x)     | 67.930 (1.94x)   | 247.660              |
| 50,000  | 172.330         | 343.511 (1.99x)    | 342.290 (1.99x)  | 1331.840             |
| 200,000 | 700.400         | 1468.769 (2.10x)   | 1482.030 (2.12x) | 8789.789             |

The third column equals the second at every size, so the loss is for the rest of the session, not a
one-off. **CLAUDE.md's "interleaving a write with a traversal costs ~2.5x the traversal alone"
describes the wrong thing** — corrected there in this commit.

### 🛑 The mechanism is SELECTIVITY, and guessing would have set the wrong fix

Two mechanisms predicted different things: locality (one packed array vs per-node `Vec` chasing)
predicts a roughly CONSTANT penalty; selectivity (`out_typed_flat` scans only the type's partition,
the fallback walks every edge and filters) predicts it tracks the edge:type ratio. Holding the graph
at 50k nodes and varying only what fraction of edges carry the queried type — every node gets
`share` out-edges of which exactly ONE is type E, so the TOTAL edge count moves but the ANSWER does
not:

| 1 in N carry type E | fresh µs | stale µs | penalty    |
| ------------------- | -------- | -------- | ---------- |
| 2                   | 177.610  | 348.220  | 1.96x      |
| 4                   | 178.390  | 372.530  | 2.09x      |
| 10                  | 170.061  | 497.610  | 2.93x      |
| 50                  | 165.850  | 3991.659 | **24.07x** |

**Selectivity.** The fresh arm is FLAT (177.6 → 165.9) across a 25x change in total edges, because
it only ever scans type E's partition — always V edges. The stale arm grows with the total. So the
penalty is unbounded as the type gets rarer, and a many-edge-type graph (the realistic people-graph
shape: HELD, APPLIED_TO, REPORTS_TO, INTERVIEWED …) pays proportionally more. "~2x" was an artifact
of the first fixture's 1-in-2 type mix.

### Why no fix landed, and what the amortization says

A lazy rebuild on read is the obvious move, and the numbers say when it pays: penalty-per-read vs
rebuild cost amortizes after **~7 reads** (1k), 7.4 (10k), 7.8 (50k), **11.4** (200k) — strikingly
stable. But:

- **That threshold is per QUERY SHAPE, not universal.** This query scans the whole graph, the shape
  the CSR helps most. A point lookup's penalty is near zero, so a read-counting policy tuned here
  would rebuild (8.8 ms at 200k) for workloads that gain nothing. The policy would have to weigh the
  WORK of the fallback reads, not count them — and that bookkeeping sits on the hot read path, where
  item 540's alignment finding and the TS closure-size finding both show incidental additions cost
  1.08-4x on their own.
- **Rebuilding on `commit` is worse, not better.** It fits "write burst then many reads", but a loop
  of one-write transactions would pay a full O(V × ntypes + E) rebuild per commit — 8.8 ms each at
  200k.
- The readers take `&self`, so any lazy rebuild needs interior mutability (the struct already uses a
  `RwLock` for `edge_prop_keys_cache`, so it is possible, not free).

**The narrower fix the diagnosis actually points at:** the selective-type scan needs only a GLOBAL
per-type edge list, not the whole CSR — appendable O(1) on `add_edge` and O(partition) on delete,
i.e. maintainable incrementally exactly as items 674-676 made the edge-type index's buckets
maintainable. That would make the fresh/stale distinction vanish for this shape without any rebuild
policy. Not costed yet; the maintenance price needs measuring before it is proposed.

Also note `build_typed`'s inner `for t in &mut typed` pushes an offset for EVERY node × EVERY etype,
so `rebuild_csr` is O(V × ntypes + E), not O(V + E) — which is why the rebuild column climbs from
5.87x of a read at 1k to 12.55x at 200k.

## 681 — RETRACTED: the "8.5x one-hop spelling gap" was my harness skipping the optimizer

**NO BUG. The engine is correct and the probe was wrong.** Recorded because the wrong number was
convincing and the trap is reusable.

### What I measured, and why it was meaningless

Item 680 left `MATCH (a)-[:E]->() RETURN count(*)` walking a 50,000-edge partition where the answer
is a length, so I went looking for an O(1) count. `try_degree_algebra` answers a hop count from
degree sums without enumerating, but it is reached from `try_varlen_count` — the QUANTIFIED shape —
so I compared the plain hop against `->{1,1}`:

| one-hop count(*), 50k-edge type | fresh        | stale    | answer |
| ------------------------------- | ------------ | -------- | ------ |
| plain `(a)-[:E]->()`            | 172.200 µs   | 523.900  | 50000  |
| quantified `->{1,1}`            | **1465.470** | 1409.610 | 50000  |

8.5x for an identical answer — the equivalent-spelling class CLAUDE.md calls the serious one. The
hypothesis was also backwards (I predicted the quantified form would be FASTER), which should have
been the first warning.

**`exec::run(plan, store)` executes the plan AS GIVEN. It does not optimize.** So that table compares
a raw `VarLength` against a raw `Expand` — a plan the engine never runs, because `opt.rs:1018`
already collapses a one-hop `VarLength` with no `until`/`body_filter` under WALK/TRAIL into an
`Expand`. Dumping both plans settles it: they optimize to the byte-identical
`Project{Aggregate{Expand{Scan}}}`.

Re-measured on the optimized plans:

| one-hop count(*), optimized | fresh      | stale   |
| --------------------------- | ---------- | ------- |
| plain `(a)-[:E]->()`        | 174.250 µs | 510.980 |
| quantified `->{1,1}`        | 179.970    | 502.730 |

3.3% apart fresh, 1.6% stale. **They cost the same because they ARE the same plan** — which is the
engine's whole claim about surface syntax, working.

### 🛑 The trap, which is the reusable part

**A bench that parses a query and hands it to `run` measures the RAW plan.** For a simple shape raw
and optimized coincide and nothing goes wrong; for anything the optimizer rewrites, the bench
reports a plan that never executes. The failure is silent and the number looks like a finding.

Checked how far it spread (`grep the pattern elsewhere`): of 287 `crate::gql::parse(` sites in
`exec/tests.rs`, the only TIMING benches running an unoptimized plan were item 680's two probes.
Both now call `optimize` — that query's raw and optimized plans are identical, so **680's numbers
are unaffected** (re-run under the fix: penalties 1.78/1.91/1.94/2.58x and the selectivity trend
1.97/2.08/2.83/31.47x, matching the original 1.81/1.95/1.99/2.10 and 1.96/2.09/2.93/24.07 — so that
last row is 24-31x run to run, not a point value). Everything else that parses raw is a CORRECTNESS
test, where running the unoptimized plan is deliberate and valuable: it exercises `exec` on shapes
the optimizer would otherwise rewrite away. **The rule is about timing benches, not about tests.**

### What is kept

`plain_vs_quantified_hop_count` stays, restructured as a spelling-equivalence guard in
`spelling_probe`'s shape: it asserts the two spellings optimize to the IDENTICAL plan (the real
signal) and then times both (the backstop). A `plain_vs_quantified_hop_plans` dump prints RAW vs
OPTIMIZED for both, which is what makes this trap visible in one command next time.

The O(1) count idea is NOT refuted — a no-filter typed hop count over a universal source really is
`out_typed_flat(w).len()`, and the engine really does walk it at ~3.4 ns/edge. That target is still
open; item 681 simply never tested it. See item 680 for the staleness half.

## 682 — the unfiltered typed-hop count had NO fast path at all: 601x, answered from a size

**SHIPPED (native).** Item 681 named this target and never tested it. It is real.

| one-hop count(*), 50k-edge type | before     | after     |
| ------------------------------- | ---------- | --------- |
| plain `(a)-[:E]->()`            | 174.250 µs | **0.290** |
| quantified `->{1,1}`            | 179.970    | **0.290** |

**601x.** Both spellings land on it identically — item 681's plan-equality result paying off: they
optimize to the same `Expand`, so one fast path serves both and no second code path was needed.
Stale stays ~550 µs, because the gate declines and falls back.

### Verified which path handles it rather than guessing

`exec.rs` says it outright: _"A fast path can be correct, willing, and still unreachable; an
`eprintln` at function entry is what shows it, not a test."_ Instrumenting all seven `try_*_count`
entries showed **every one entered and declined** (36 hits each = 9 reps × 2 spellings × 2 states).
So the shape fell through to the general materializing aggregate, walking 50,000 edges at 3.4 ns/edge
to return what is a length. `try_frontier_count` requires a top-level `IsLabeled` filter and says
"the bare-chain counts already have their own fast-paths" — this one did not.

Precedent in the same function: **item 412** fixed `E().count()` building and SORTING a million ids
to return a length (`live_edge_count`). This is that fix one level up, the hop twin of
`try_scan_count`'s `EdgeScan` arm.

### Every gate is a way the size and the path count come apart

- **`Dir::Out` only** — there is no `in_typed_flat`, and `Both` double-traverses an undirected
  self-loop (which `double_loops` selects; that flag has no effect on a directed hop, so it is
  deliberately not consulted).
- **Exactly ONE edge type** — a `want` list needs a sum, and an edge carrying two of the wanted
  types would be counted twice where the walk counts it once.
- **No multi-label edges** — `Adj.etype` holds the PRIMARY type only; secondaries live in
  `edge_extra`, so the partition misses an edge whose SECONDARY type is `T` and the size would
  UNDERCOUNT. `for_each_nbr` makes the same choice (the fuzzer's `configure_adjacency` documents
  it as state 3: a multi-label edge forces the flat scan plus the secondary-label probe).
- **Unlabelled whole-graph `Scan` source**, no `bind_edge`, no `DISTINCT`.
- **A fresh CSR overlay** — which is also what keeps it correct across deletes: any adjacency write
  invalidates the overlay, so a fresh partition can never hold a detached edge (item 680).

### The test compares a SIZE against a WALK on the same store

`set_csr_enabled(false)` drops the overlay, so `out_typed_flat` returns `None`, the fast path
declines and the general aggregate walks. That is the only honest way to test a path that returns a
count WITHOUT looking at the edges it counts. 13 shapes (every gate, plus two hops and a filter
above the hop), on a fixture with several types, a self-loop, PARALLEL edges and a deleted node —
plus a second store where an edge is primary `F` / secondary `E`, so `-[:E]->` must find SIX, not
five.

### 🛑 Mutation 5/6, and one "catch" was not mine

Caught: the size off by one (which is what proves the happy shape REACHES the fast path, rather than
the test comparing two walks), the multi-label gate, the direction gate, the unlabelled-source gate,
the single-type gate. The `bind_edge` gate survives as labelled — binding the edge adds a slot, not a
row, so the count is unchanged.

**The single-type catch came from a DIFFERENT test in the suite, not from mine.** Re-running that
mutant against `typed_hop_count_from_size_agrees` alone: it PASSED. My shape list had no edge-type
disjunction, so taking the first of the list was invisible to it. Added
`MATCH (a)-[:E|F]->() RETURN count(*)`; that mutant now dies against this test directly (exit 101).

A full-suite oracle attributes every catch to "the suite". It is worth re-running a mutant against
the ONE test you wrote, because "5/6 caught" and "my test has teeth" are different claims.

## 683 — a VACUOUS `{1,1}` QUANTIFIER costs the TS engine 2238x for an identical answer

**FOUND (TypeScript), fix gated and not yet implemented.** Item 682 added the O(1) typed-hop count
to the native engine. Asking whether TS needed the same thing answered no — and found something
worse next to it.

### First, the negative result: TS already had the O(1) rung

`shortcuts.ts` says so ("the O(1) bucket size when BOTH ends are unconstrained"), but its figure is
from a 200k/600k fixture and item 682's is from 50k/50k, so the two were not comparable as written.
Measured on item 682's OWN fixture (50,000 vertices, 10 out-edges each, exactly one of type E):

| TS, 50k nodes / 50k E of 500k edges  | µs           | answer |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------ | ------ |
| `MATCH (a)-[:E]->() RETURN count(*)` | 1.600        | 50000  |
| `MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b) …`              | 1.670        | 50000  |
| `MATCH (a:N)-[:E]->() …`             | 1.930        | 50000  |
| **`MATCH (a)-[:E]->{1,1}() …`**      | **3580.920** | 50000  |

So TS has had it all along and the native engine was the one walking. **Item 682 closed a cross-engine
asymmetry, and native now LEADS on this shape: 0.290 µs against TS's 1.600, where before it was
174.250 against 1.600 — a 109x deficit became a 5.5x lead.** (The mirror of item 679, where TS had
the rollback discipline Rust lacked.)

### 🛑 Then the bug: `->{1,1}` is 2238x the plain spelling

`{1,1}` is ONE repetition. With no edge variable and the default `trail` mode it asks exactly what a
plain hop asks, and both answer 50000. But the quantifier carries the segment past every gate that
bails on `segments.some((s) => s.rel.quantifier)` (e.g. `matching.ts:451`), so the plain spelling
takes the O(1) `edgesByLabel` bucket size while `{1,1}` enumerates.

**This is the bug class CLAUDE.md calls the serious one** — same answer, different price, invisible
to every correctness test. The native engine normalizes it away in the OPTIMIZER (`opt.rs`: a
one-hop `VarLength` with no `until`/`body_filter` under WALK/TRAIL becomes an `Expand`), which is
why the same two spellings sit within 3.3% there (item 681). TS has no `ir::Plan` to canonicalize,
so it needs the equivalent normalization in its planner.

### Added to the TS spelling probe, which had no quantifier group at all

```text
       6950.3x  a vacuous {1,1} quantifier vs a plain hop
                      0.00ms  MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(*) AS c
                     69.50ms  MATCH (a)-[:E]->{1,1}(b) RETURN count(*) AS c
          4.0x  a vacuous {1,1} quantifier vs a plain hop, labelled start
                     24.69ms  MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(*) AS c
                     99.27ms  MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->{1,1}(b) RETURN count(*) AS c
```

0 groups disagree on the ANSWER, so this is purely cost. **Quote the 2238x, not the 6950x:** the
fast arm there is AT the timer floor (0.00 ms), so that ratio is floor-limited and the probe
divides by `max(fastest, 0.01)`. The 50k measurement has both arms above the timer's resolution.
(The filtered `SPELL_ONLY` invocation also runs no null control, which the probe says plainly — at
0.00 vs 69.50 ms the instrument is not the question, but the gating control did not run.)

**BOTH ENDS UNLABELLED is load-bearing in that group.** With `(a:P)` the plain spelling cannot use
the bucket size either (it takes the degree-sum walk), so both members walk and the spread is only
4x. The first version of the group used `:P` and under-reported the gap by three orders of
magnitude. The labelled twin is kept, because it isolates the enumeration overhead alone.

### The fix's gates, each measured rather than assumed

A normalization may drop a `{1,1}` only when:

- **`min === 1 && max === 1`.**
- **No edge variable.** Verified: with one, the quantified form binds a LIST (`e: [{…}]`) where the
  plain form binds a SCALAR (`e: {…}`). Dropping the quantifier would change the result's type.
- **Mode is the default, `walk`, or `trail` — never `simple`/`acyclic`.** `acyclic` forbids any
  repeated NODE, so at one hop it drops a self-loop the plain spelling keeps. (`edges(p)` is a list
  under both spellings, so a path variable is not by itself a blocker; a self-loop count is 2 under
  both at the default mode.)
- **No non-`walk` selector, and not a nested group** (`hopFrom`/`hopTo`/`innerQ` absent).

Worth noting that lenke's default mode is `trail`, not ISO's nominal `walk` — the ast comment
explains why ("unusable unbounded") — so the common case is inside the safe set.

Not implemented this tick: the normalization point has to be chosen so that every downstream gate
sees the simplified AST, and that wants its own differential + mutation run rather than being
bolted on at the end of a measurement tick.

### The gates, and which are measured

- `min === 1 && max === 1`.
- **No edge variable** — measured: under a quantifier it binds a LIST, without one a SCALAR.
- **Mode default/`walk`/`trail`, never `simple`/`acyclic`** — measured: `ACYCLIC (x)-[:T]->{1,1}(y)`

- **`walk` selector only**, **no group/nested**, and the redundant `subpathWhere`.

## 686 — the depth-4 trail cost model, CONFIRMED empirically before deriving anything (~78x in TS)

**PRICING. No engine change.** Item 685 priced depth 4 at 234x the depth-3 row. Before deriving
6-event inclusion-exclusion, this applies 600b's own correction — _"a complexity claim about a graph
algorithm is a claim about the ADJACENCY REPRESENTATION"_ — and checks the cost model, because a
refuted model would make the derivation moot.

### What depth 4 actually requires

A 4-walk `(e0,e1,e2,e3)` is a trail when all four edges are distinct, so **six** equality events
must be excluded, against depth 3's three. Each has a structure forced by the walk:

| event                     | gap | what it forces                                  |
| ------------------------- | --- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `e0=e1`, `e1=e2`, `e2=e3` | 0   | the repeated edge is a SELF-LOOP                |
| `e0=e2`, `e1=e3`          | 1   | a REVERSE edge between the pair                 |
| **`e0=e3`**               | 2   | a **2-WALK** from `head(e0)` back to `tail(e0)` |

`e0=e3` is the dominant term: it needs 2-walk counts between an ORDERED PAIR, per edge. The
adjacency is in edge-insertion order with no index, so that is `Σ_{e: a→b} Σ_{c: b→c} deg(c)` — the
**3-walk count**. (At depth 3 the analogous term `c02` needed only `m(b,s)`, costing the 2-walk
count, which is what 600b corrected the model for. Depth 4 is one level worse, as expected.)

So the shortcut trades ~W4 path-steps for ~W3 probes: a factor of ~`deg`, in WORK.

### Measured: enumeration is ~deg per level, and probes are ~15x cheaper than paths

20,000 vertices, degree 5, TS:

| depth | TRAIL ms | answer     | vs prev   |
| ----- | -------- | ---------- | --------- |
| 2     | 20.3     | 499,996    | —         |
| 3     | 14.5     | 2,499,936  | 0.72x     |
| 4     | 5628.7   | 12,499,368 | **388x**  |
| 5     | 28900.8  | 62,493,832 | **5.13x** |

- **Depth 5 / depth 4 = 5.13x ≈ deg.** Enumeration costs ~`deg` per extra level — 600b's model,
  measured instead of asserted.
- **Depth 4 / depth 3 = 388x** is the cliff: depth 3 is on the closed-form rung (601) and depth 4
  enumerates.

**The estimate comes from two MEASURED constants, not an assumed one** (600b's and 602's shared
lesson, where an assumed ns-per-probe made the depth-3 estimate conservative by ~2x):

- the depth-3 closed form: ~500k probes in 14.5 ms → **~29 ns/probe**
- depth-4 enumeration: ~12.5M paths in 5628.7 ms → **~450 ns/path**

Probes are ~15x cheaper than paths here, so a depth-4 formula at ~2.5M probes lands near **72 ms
against 5628.7 — roughly 78x in TS**, well above the ~5x a work-ratio-only reading would predict.
That asymmetry is the same one 600b identified and 601 confirmed at 40.79x.

### Two reading notes

- **The depth-2 row is SLOWER than depth 3 (20.3 vs 14.5 ms), and that is JIT WARMUP, not an
  anomaly** — depth 2 ran first in the sweep. Both are on rungs. This is item 679's caveat about JS
  sweeps catching its author: the cross-size signal on these engines is never the absolute time of
  the first row.
- Depth 4's 5628.7 ms here against item 685's 3365.6 ms on the bench's own fixture is a different
  graph (this generator's edges are `(i*7+d*13+1) % V`), so the two are not the same row. The
  RATIOS within each run are what carry.

### Go-ahead, with the derivation still outstanding

The cost model survives, so the project is worth doing, and the estimate is now grounded rather than
asserted. What remains is the derivation itself: 6 events means up to 63 intersections, most empty or
collapsing, and 600 declined to derive them for exactly that reason.

A cleaner decomposition than raw inclusion-exclusion, worth trying first:
`T4 = Σ_{e0: a→b} ( t3(b) − u3(b, e0) )`, where `t3` is the per-source depth-3 trail count the
engines ALREADY compute and `u3(b, e0)` counts 3-trails from `b` that use `e0` — which splits into
three small cases by the position of `e0`. That reuses the validated depth-3 machinery instead of
restating it, and isolates the expensive ordered-pair term in one place.

Validation instrument is ready: 601's brute force over randomized graphs (400/400 at depth 3) and
`fastpath_fuzz`, which can see depth 4 since 602. **Item 685's fixture hazard applies** — pick a
fixture where the depth-3 WALK and depth-4 TRAIL differ, and assert that they do.

## 687 — the depth-4 trail DECOMPOSITION, derived and validated 500/500 (not yet wired)

**DERIVATION + VALIDATION. No engine change.** Item 600 declined to derive depth 4 because
inclusion-exclusion over its six equality events needs up to 63 intersections. This avoids that
entirely by reducing depth 4 to the depth-3 count the engines ALREADY compute, plus one correction.

### The identity

```text
T4 = Σ over e0 (an edge a → b) of [ t3(b) − u3(b, e0) ]
```

- `t3(b)` = 3-trails starting at `b` — the per-source depth-3 count from items 600/601/602.
- `u3(b, e0)` = 3-trails starting at `b` that USE the edge `e0`.

Every 4-trail is an edge `e0` followed by a 3-trail from `b` that avoids `e0`, and conversely — so
the identity is exact, not an approximation.

### `u3`, the novel part, in three DISJOINT cases

A trail uses each edge at most once, so `e0` occupies exactly ONE position of the 3-trail
`(f0, f1, f2)`. The cases therefore simply ADD — no intersection terms at all, which is what
replaces the 63-term expansion:

| case      | requires                                                                            | count                                                                                  |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `f0 = e0` | the trail starts at `b` and `e0` leaves `b`, i.e. **`a == b`** (a self-loop at `b`) | 2-trails from `b` avoiding `e0`                                                        |
| `f1 = e0` | `f0` leaves `b` and LANDS ON `a`; then `f2` leaves `head(e0) = b`                   | `Σ_{f0: b→a, f0≠e0} #{f2 ∈ out(b) : f2 ∉ {f0, e0}}`                                    |
| `f2 = e0` | `(f0, f1)` is a 2-trail from `b` to `a`, neither being `e0`                         | `#{(f0,f1) : f0 ∈ out(b), f1 ∈ out(head f0), head(f1) = a, f0 ≠ f1, f0 ≠ e0, f1 ≠ e0}` |

The `f2 = e0` case is the expensive one — a 2-trail count between the ORDERED PAIR `(b, a)`, per
edge — exactly the term item 686 priced at ~W3 probes. The other two are degree-local.

### Validated against brute force, with the oracle's teeth checked

A self-contained prototype (no engine imports, so the oracle shares no code with the subject):
enumerate every 4-walk, keep those with four distinct edges, compare against the decomposition.

- **500/500 graphs agree**, 3-9 vertices, 2-17 edges.
- The generator produced the cases that matter and SAYS so: **452** graphs with self-loops, **313**
  with parallel edges, **229** with reverse pairs. (Parallel edges are what break a naive version,
  per item 600.)
- **Each `u3` case was instrumented and all three fired** — 8804 / 6389 / 5847 hits. A case that
  never fires is a case the run did not test, however many graphs agreed; this is the "correct,
  willing, and unreachable" check applied to the formula's own branches rather than to a fast path.
- **Mutation 6/6.** Caught: the `a == b` self-loop guard dropped; case `f2` omitted; case `f1`
  forgetting to exclude `e0` from `f2`; case `f2` forgetting to exclude `e0` from `f1`; case `f1`
  dropping the landing test; and `t3` taken at the TAIL instead of the head. The two
  forgot-to-exclude mutants are the ones a hand-check would most likely miss.

`t3` is brute-forced in the prototype ON PURPOSE, so that any disagreement is attributable to the
`u3` case analysis — the part nobody had written down. Substituting the engines' validated closed
form for `t3` is an implementation step, not a correctness question.

### Why this shape matters beyond depth 4

The identity is **recursive**: `T(k+1) = Σ_{e0} [ t_k(head) − u_k(head, e0) ]`, and `u_k` splits
into `k` disjoint cases by position. So depth 5 would need `u4`, which is four cases rather than a
2^10 expansion. Depth 4's cost is dominated by one ordered-pair term; whether depth 5 stays
tractable depends on what `u4`'s analogous terms need from the adjacency, which is item 686's rule
("a complexity claim is a claim about the representation") and should be checked before promising
anything.

### What is left to wire, and the hazards already known

1. A per-source `t3(v)` — both engines compute depth-3 trails, but whether `t3` is exposed PER
   SOURCE or only as a total needs checking; the identity needs per-source.
2. The ordered-pair 2-trail count for case `f2`, which is the ~W3 term and the only piece that is
   not degree-local.
3. **Item 685's fixture hazard**: on a fixture where the depth-3 WALK and depth-4 TRAIL coincide
   (both 35 on that six-vertex graph), a test cannot distinguish a correct depth-4 trail from an
   off-by-one computing a depth-3 walk. Assert they differ.
4. **Item 602's oracle warning**: once BOTH engines run the same formula, the byte-identity fuzzers
   only prove they agree, and would pass on a shared wrong answer. The brute-force oracle above is
   what has to carry it, so it belongs in the repo as a test when the formula lands — not left in a
   scratchpad.

## 688 — item 687's identity is IMPLEMENTABLE: both engines already expose `t3` per source

**STRUCTURAL CHECK. No engine change.** Item 687's identity needs `t3` PER SOURCE, and item 687
listed that as prerequisite 1 with a question mark. Answered: **both engines have it**, and the cost
now resolves against the actual code rather than against a model.

### Rust

The depth-3 machinery is NOT in `degree_algebra_total` — that function handles depth ≤ 2 only (a
1-hop term plus `outdeg[nbr]`, minus the one self-loop reuse). The depth-3 trail lives in
`walk_levels_total` + `reused_trails_at_3`, and both halves are per-source:

- `walk_levels_total` keeps `u: Vec<u64>` indexed BY NODE and swaps it per level, so after `len`
  iterations `u[s]` is the number of `len`-walks **from `s`**.
- `reused_trails_at_3(s, …)` takes one vertex and returns the edge-reusing 3-walk count for it,
  off precomputed `Trail3Tables { pass, self_loops, pass_deg }`.

So `t3(s) = u[s] − reused_trails_at_3(s)`, per source, with no new machinery.

### TypeScript

Same shape, built by item 601: `reusedTrailsAt3(v, off, nbr, pass, selfLoops, passDeg)` is
per-vertex, over a CSR of `Int32Array` offsets and neighbours, with `u` a per-vertex `Float64Array`.

### What that does to the cost

The identity's FIRST term is `Σ_{e0: a→b} t3(b) = Σ_b in(b) · t3(b)` — a weighted sum over a
per-vertex vector, so an **O(V) pass** once the vectors exist. And `reused_trails_at_3` is called
once per VERTEX rather than once per edge, costing `Σ_b W2(b) = W2` overall — the same order as the
existing depth-3 work, not a new asymptote.

The SECOND term `Σ_{e0} u3(b, e0)` is per-EDGE, and its `f2 = e0` case needs the 2-trail count
between an ORDERED PAIR. **Checked in both engines: neither adjacency is sorted by neighbour.**

- Rust: edge-insertion order (`rebuild_csr` does `extend_from_slice` with no sort — 600b).
- TS: `nbr[at] = idx.get(e.to)` filled in `edgesOf(order[i])` order, no sort anywhere in that file.

So there is no binary search to reach for in either, and the term costs ~W3 in both — item 686's
price holds, now verified against the representation instead of inferred from it.

### One asymmetry worth knowing before choosing the sorted-adjacency option

600b noted the term IS recoverable to O(V+E) by radix-sorting each adjacency segment, "its own
decision". That decision is NOT symmetric across the engines:

- Rust's CSR is a PERSISTENT overlay (`rebuild_csr` at load), so sorted segments would be built
  once and amortized over every later query — though item 680 showed one adjacency write discards
  the whole overlay, so the amortization is only as good as the write rate.
- **TS builds its CSR per QUERY**, inside the detector (the comment there prices the build at ~20ms
  against per-level work of 0.3ms). A sort would be paid on every execution, so the trade is much
  worse on the engine that stands to win the most (item 686: ~78x in TS).

So if the ordered-pair term is ever made O(V+E), the two engines want different answers, and TS
probably wants the scan.

### Prerequisites, updated

1. ~~A per-source `t3(v)`~~ — **SATISFIED in both engines**, as above.
2. The ordered-pair 2-trail count for case `f2` — still the only non-degree-local piece, ~W3,
   unsorted in both.
3. Item 685's fixture hazard (depth-3 WALK and depth-4 TRAIL must differ on the test fixture).
4. Item 602's oracle warning (once both engines share the formula, byte-identity proves only
   agreement; item 687's brute force must move into the repo as a test).

## 689 — the depth-4 trail CLOSED FORM, validated 600/600 and measured at 197x (blueprint, not yet wired)

**DERIVATION COMPLETE. No engine change.** Item 687 proved the decomposition with `t3` brute-forced.
This replaces every piece with the closed form an engine would compute, so the result is a
blueprint rather than an identity.

### The formula, in full

With no predicates (`pass[x] = 1`, `pass_deg[v] = outdeg(v)`), writing `L(v)` for self-loops at `v`,
`od(v)` for out-degree, `m(u,v)` for the edge multiplicity of the ordered pair, and `walk_k(v)` for
the level recurrence both engines already keep per vertex:

```text
reused3(v) = L(v)·od(v) + Σ_{e: v→b} [ L(b) + m(b,v) ] − 2·L(v)
t3(v)      = walk3(v) − reused3(v)                      ← what 601/602 already ship, per source

T4 = Σ_{e0: a→b} [ t3(b) − u3(b, e0) ]

u3(b, e0) = case0 + case1 + case2        (DISJOINT — e0 sits in exactly one position)

  case0  (f0 = e0, only when a == b, i.e. e0 is a self-loop at b):
         walk2(b) − L(b)·od(b) + (L(b)−1)·(od(b)−2)
  case1  (f1 = e0):
         a == b ?  (L(b)−1)·(od(b)−2)  :  m(b,a)·(od(b)−1)
  case2  (f2 = e0):
         Σ_{f0: b→c, f0 ≠ e0} [ m(c,a) − [b=c=a] − [c=a ∧ b=a] ]
```

The two `(L(b)−1)·(od(b)−2)` terms are not a copy-paste: in case0 the `−1` drops `e0` from the
self-loops available to `f1` and the `−2` drops both `f1` and `e0` from `f2`'s choices; case1
reaches the same product by a different route (`f0` a self-loop ≠ `e0`, then `f2` excluding `f0`
and `e0`). Mutation distinguishes them.

### Validated, with the oracle's teeth checked

|                                 | agreement   |
| ------------------------------- | ----------- |
| depth-3 closed form, PER SOURCE | **600/600** |
| depth-4 closed form             | **600/600** |

Generator: 549 graphs with self-loops, 377 with parallel edges, 262 with reverse pairs.

**The depth-3 line is a free cross-check of the SHIPPED arithmetic** — `reused_trails_at_3`
transcribed and brute-forced per source. It had never been checked against brute force per
_source_; item 600 validated the total.

**Mutation 8/8**, all by the brute-force oracle: case0's `L−1` and `od−2`, case1's self-loop
branch, both of case2's coincidence corrections, case2's `f0 ≠ e0` skip, and in `reused3` the
all-three-equal add-back (`−2L` → `−L`) and **the reverse-edge term as a BOOLEAN instead of a
count** — which is precisely the error item 600's comment warns about ("two parallel `v → b` edges
make `e0, b→v, e2` a valid trail"). The two `reused3` mutants are caught by the depth-3 AND depth-4
checks, so depth 4 inherits depth 3's correctness rather than masking it.

### 🛑 Measured at 197x, and item 686's estimate was CONSERVATIVE by 2.5x

On the shape item 686 measured (20,000 vertices, degree 5, 100,000 edges), where the engine
enumerating read 5628.7 ms:

|                                           | ms       |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------- |
| tables — O(V+E) plus the ordered-pair map | 10.9     |
| the depth-4 formula                       | 17.7     |
| **total**                                 | **28.6** |

**197x**, in an unoptimised prototype using a JS `Map`. And the answer is **12,499,368** — exactly
what the engine answers by enumeration on that fixture, which is a far stronger correctness signal
than the small random graphs.

**Why 686 under-estimated at ~78x:** it priced case2 at ~W3 probes because it assumed SCANNING `b`'s
adjacency to find `m(b,a)` — neither engine's adjacency being sorted (item 688). But the formula
does not have to use the adjacency: an ordered-pair hash map built in O(E) — 600b's "auxiliary O(E)
structure, its own decision" — makes `m(c,a)` an O(1) lookup, and case2 drops to
`Σ_b in(b)·od(b) = W2` lookups. Measured here: W2 = 500,000 against W3 = 2,500,000.

**This is the THIRD time in this lineage an assumed cost model came in conservative against a
measurement** — 600b corrected 600's "unbounded" to "~average degree", 602 then beat 600b's ~4-8x
with 11.45x, and now 686's ~78x against a measured 197x. The recurring lesson is 602's own:
_an estimate from an assumed constant is worse than a measurement_. The direction is consistently
pessimistic, which is the direction that does not look like a mistake.

### What is left

Engine integration only — the algebra is done and measured. Both engines already expose `t3` per
source (688); what is new is the ordered-pair map and the three `u3` cases. Carry forward:

  a persistent overlay, TS rebuilds per query, so the build cost lands differently.
- item 685's fixture hazard: depth-3 WALK and depth-4 TRAIL must DIFFER on the test fixture.
- item 602's oracle warning: once both engines share the formula, byte-identity proves only that

  it is the only thing that would catch a shared wrong answer.

ENUMERATION.

exactly what a total cannot see. Items 687-689 build directly on the per-source value.

`trail-count-bruteforce.test.ts` closes both: depths 1-3, TRAIL and WALK, exact depths and ranges,
with and without an endpoint predicate, over 60 randomized multigraphs — plus a per-source test on a
fixture whose per-source counts are deliberately UNEQUAL, so a mix-up between sources shows. 909
assertions.

The generator asserts it produced what the trail terms exist for (self-loops, parallel edges,
reverse pairs) and that the trail and walk answers actually DIVERGE somewhere — otherwise a green run
would be reporting on the generator rather than the engine.

### 🛑 Mutation found two gaps in the oracle, each diagnosable to a missing fixture DIMENSION

First run **4/6**, and neither survivor was an equivalence:

- **"the LEVEL-2 correction is dropped"** survived because the test queried only EXACT depths.

  item 602's "a correction applied once for the whole range answers `{3,3}` correctly and `{1,3}`
  wrongly", from the testing side.

refused since item 583). Re-run **7/7**, including a new mutant on the `pass[b] === 0`

| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------ |
| all-three-equal add-back `−2x` → `−1x`               | CAUGHT |
| the reverse-edge term as a BOOLEAN, not a count      | CAUGHT |
| the `e1 == e2` self-loop-at-the-landing term dropped | CAUGHT |
| the `e0 == e1` term on the RAW out-degree            | CAUGHT |

| the LEVEL-3 correction dropped                       | CAUGHT |

Each survivor was a fixture DIMENSION the test did not vary: the endpoint mask, and the depth range.
Neither is exotic — both are in the route's own contract — and the formula's terms for them were
unguarded. **A randomized generator does not help with a dimension it holds constant**, however
many trials it runs; 60 graphs of exact-depth unfiltered queries are 60 samples of one corner.

## 691 — item 690's per-source test was validating the WRONG ROUTE, and depth 4 is now pinned

**TEST ONLY. No engine change.** Two things: the oracle reaches depth 4, and a flaw in what item 690
committed one tick earlier is fixed with a measured before/after.

### 🛑 The flaw: `plainNode` allows a label but NOT a property

Item 690's per-source test queried `MATCH (a {n: 3})-[:K]->{3}(y)`. That is an inline PROPERTY, so
`plainNode(pattern.start)` is false, `degreeCountShape` refuses, and the query answers through the
general ENUMERATING path. **The test validated the right numbers through the wrong route — the
closed form it exists to check was never running.**

This is "a fast path can be correct, willing, and still unreachable" (exec.rs) applied to a TEST
rather than to a fast path, and it is the same shape as item 371's dead `try_indexed_min_max`: the
unit test passed while the route was unreachable.

**Measured, not inferred.** The same level-3 mutant (`total -= 0 * reusedTrailsAt3(…)`) run against
the per-source test alone:

| test form                 | start plain?     | vs the mutant  |
| ------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------- |
| `(a {n: v})` — item 690's | no (property)    | _**SURVIVED**_ |
| `(a:V{v})` — fixed        | yes (label only) | **CAUGHT**     |

The fix gives every vertex its own label (`V0`, `V1`, …) alongside the shared `P`, so one source can
be selected while the start pattern stays plain. Item 689's gap — the depth-3 correction never
brute-forced PER SOURCE — is only now actually closed.

**Why item 690's mutation run did not reveal this:** it ran the whole FILE, and the first test (60
randomized graphs with a plain `(a)` start) catches all seven mutants on its own. The per-source
test contributed nothing and the tally could not show it. That is item 682's lesson at one more
level of resolution: a per-FILE oracle attributes every catch to the file, exactly as a per-SUITE
oracle attributes it to the suite. **Run the mutant against the one TEST whose claim you are
making**, with `-t`.

### Depth 4 pinned

`[4, 4]`, `[1, 4]` and `[2, 4]` added to the depth table. These PASS immediately and are meant to:
the detector refuses `max > 3` for a trail, so depth 4 takes the general enumerating path, which is
correct and slow. The answers are pinned now so the oracle is already in place when the depth-4
closed form (687-689) lands.

(Last tick's note said the depth-4 test "should fail before the implementation lands". That was
wrong — the fallback is correct, so there is nothing to fail. A guard, not a red test.)

1,449 assertions, 2,945 TS tests pass, lint and check 0.
