## 714 — the second store has an index now: `closed-levers.ts`, and it failed its own motivating case first

**TOOLING (both engines). One annotation added to the Gremlin lowering; no behaviour change.**

Items 710, 712 and 713 were each spent on a target that turned out to be closed, and 713 found the
mechanism: CLAUDE.md names TWO stores for refutations —

- "has this lever been tried?" → `CLOSED.md`, then the audit item it cites;
- "Record rejected optimizations with their numbers, **next to the code they would have changed**."

— and only the first had an index. `CLOSED.md` has two (`open-markers.ts` plus its own tables); the
source had none, while holding **47 refutation markers across 830 files**. Item 713's miss was not
carelessness and not the wrong pattern: it was the wrong STORE, and the store that held the answer
could not be searched as a whole.

### `docs/reviews/closed-levers.ts`

```text
bun docs/reviews/closed-levers.ts                  # the whole index
bun docs/reviews/closed-levers.ts inline props     # "has this been tried?" in one command
bun docs/reviews/closed-levers.ts --orphans        # markers carrying no item number
```

It scans `packages/` and `crates/` for the vocabulary this repo actually uses — `REJECTED`,
`REVERTED`, `REFUTED`, `WITHDRAWN`, `NOT BUILT`, `WAS TRIED`, `DECLINED ON`, `🛑` — gathered by
grepping for each form rather than guessed, and prints `item · file:line · the marker`.

**COMMENTS ONLY**, because `REJECTED` in code is an identifier or a string and including those made
the first run 40% noise. And it does NOT decide whether a hit is a rejected OPTIMIZATION:
`store.rs` says "REJECTED if `key` backs a unique constraint", which is API behaviour, and a script
that tried to tell them apart would become one more thing to distrust — the same choice
`open-markers.ts` makes, for the same reason.

### It failed the one case it was built for, which is why this item has numbers

The first version returned **ZERO hits for `inline props`** — the marker it exists to surface. That
marker reads inline `` `props` ``, and the backticks broke a literal match. Items 694/695 made the
same mistake one store over, and 695's own note says it: _a sweep is only as good as its pattern._

Two fixes, both found by testing the instrument against its motivating case rather than by reading
it:

- **fold to bare words** before matching, on both the text and the needle, so punctuation and
  backticks cannot hide a term;
- **search the whole COMMENT BLOCK**, not the matched line. A lever's subject is usually named a
  line or two below the word `REJECTED`. This also raised the count of markers whose item number
  could be extracted from **15 to 27**, because the number sits below the marker as often as on it.

With both, `inline props` returns item 644's marker, which is what cost three ticks.

### And it immediately found a gap in my own previous item

`closed-levers.ts unroll` reported **nothing** — because item 711's refutation went into `CLOSED.md`
and the audit and NOT to the call site, which is the half of CLAUDE.md's rule I skipped one tick
earlier. `flush_repeat` now carries it: what was tried, the 3.76-against-2.69 it was chasing, that
it converged to 2.59, that a `VarLength` walk is governed by `limits.trail` while a chain of
`Expand`s is not, and which test caught it.

**20 of the 47 markers still cite no item**, which `--orphans` lists. Those are the ones a reader
cannot follow up, and annotating them is a standing piece of work rather than something to do in
one pass.

### What this does not do

It does not replace `CLOSED.md`. A lever refuted in an audit item and never annotated at the call
site is invisible here — item 711 was exactly that until this item, and the empty-result message
says so in those words rather than letting silence read as "never tried".

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run check` 0.

## 715 — the mirror detach, with the one route 670/671 did not refute: 1.58x on the oldest edge

**FIXED (native).** Item 670 priced a hub-leaf delete at O(the NEIGHBOUR's degree) and item 671
refuted both candidate fixes with a table:

| fix                               | why not                                                   |
| --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `swap_remove` — O(1)              | `out_adj` ORDER is load-bearing for byte-identity         |
| `binary_search_by_key` + `remove` | the list is NOT reliably eid-sorted (`Undo::RestoreEdge`) |

Both entries are about getting to the element FASTER. Neither is about the `retain` itself, and
671's own sentence names what is left: _"A linear find is what correctness requires, and `retain`
already is one."_ A linear find that is not `retain` was unrefuted — screened through both stores
first, which is what item 714 built `closed-levers.ts` for.

```rust
// before
self.in_adj[a.nbr as usize].retain(|m| m.eid != a.eid);

// after
if let Some(at) = adj.iter().position(|m| m.eid == a.eid) {
    adj.remove(at);
}
```

Same complexity, same order, no sortedness assumption. `retain` compares all D entries and shifts
survivors one at a time; this stops comparing at the match and moves the tail with one `ptr::copy`.

### The win is POSITION-dependent, and the baseline table already said so

Before measuring I predicted a modest win, reasoning from the harness's own position table (`LAST`
32.39 against `FIRST` 41.77 — with `retain` the scan is always full D, so that spread is the
SHIFT). The prediction was right about the mechanism and wrong about the shape: the win is large at
the front and nil at the back.

Three alternated rounds, min per arm, the repo's own `delete_cost_by_neighbour_degree`:

| row                        | BEFORE | AFTER | ratio     |
| -------------------------- | -----: | ----: | --------- |
| victim FIRST (oldest edge) |  38.31 | 24.22 | **1.58x** |
| victim MIDDLE              |  34.11 | 26.89 | **1.27x** |
| victim LAST (newest)       |  29.98 | 28.75 | 1.04x     |
| D=100 CONTROL              |   0.17 |  0.16 | 1.06x     |
| D=1,000 CONTROL            |   0.68 |  0.67 | 1.01x     |
| index ON CONTROL           |  51.52 | 49.70 | 1.04x     |
| D=50,000 aggregate         |  29.07 | 28.25 | 1.03x     |

The model fits exactly. For a victim at index `i` of `D`: `retain` pays D compares plus a
one-at-a-time shift of the D−i survivors; this pays i compares plus a vectorized move of the same
D−i. At `i = 0` that removes every compare and vectorizes the whole move (1.58x); at `i = D−1`
the two are the same work (1.04x, inside the controls' own 1.01-1.06x drift).

**So the honest headline is the FIRST row, not the aggregate.** The bench's own `leaf (degree 1)`
row moves 1.03x because its victim sits near the end of the hub's adjacency. The case that gains is
deleting the OLDEST edge of a hub — which is FIFO expiry, the shape a people-graph actually runs
(archive the oldest applications, drop the oldest events), and the reason this is worth shipping
rather than a curiosity.

### Mutation 3/3, and one of them re-examines 671's refusal

Labelled before running. Caught: the match inverted (removes a wrong entry), and the out-side
detach loop never running (a dangling mirror).

The third was labelled **UNCERTAIN on purpose**: `swap_remove` is precisely the change 671 refused
on byte-identity grounds, and if it SURVIVED the suite then that refusal had no test behind it. It
is **CAUGHT (exit 101)**. So 671 was right and is now demonstrated rather than argued — which is
worth more than my own two mutants, because it is the claim a future attempt would lean on.

Two earlier anchors refused (one matched twice, one needed a helper to compile) and nothing wrong
was written either time.

### The invariant the change rests on is now a test

`retain` removes EVERY entry with that eid; `position` + `remove` removes the first. They differ
only if a duplicate mirror can exist. `mirror_entries_are_unique_per_direction` asserts no node's
adjacency holds one eid twice, in either direction, over parallel edges both ways plus a self-loop,
and — the case worth covering — **after a rolled-back transaction**, because `Undo::RestoreEdge`
re-appends an entry and that is the mechanism 671 found leaves the list unsorted. Unsorted is fine
for a linear find; duplicated would not be.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1216 + 13 +
725 pass, 0 fail (1216 is the new test); all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass — required rather than
formal, since this touches adjacency order, which is exactly what that invariant covers.

## 716 — the same pattern in the PROPERTY INDEX, three sites: 5.52x on a 50,000-node bucket

**FIXED (native), and one O(1) follow-up priced with the reason it is not taken here.**

"Grep the pattern elsewhere" is a step in the method, and item 715's `retain`-removes-one shape has
four more instances in `store.rs`. The TS twin needs nothing — item 672 already recorded that TS's
hub-leaf delete is O(1) because its adjacency is a `Set`. The native ones that matter are the
PROPERTY INDEX buckets:

- `apply_set_prop` — the node leaves its old value's bucket;
- `index_drop_node` — the delete path;
- the RANGE index twin.

A bucket holds every node sharing one value, so for the shape an index is usually created for — a
LOW-CARDINALITY property like `status`, `stage`, `tenant` — the bucket is a large fraction of the
graph and a single `SET` scans all of it.

### Confirmed O(bucket) before any edit, with the node count pinned

`index_set_cost_by_bucket_size`, 60,000 nodes in every store so the axis swept at items 663-669
cannot leak in; only how many share the victim's value varies:

| bucket | µs per op | ns per B   |
| -----: | --------: | ---------- |
|    100 |     0.309 | 3.0940     |
|  1,000 |     0.346 | 0.3456     |
| 10,000 |     2.023 | 0.2023     |
| 50,000 |     9.460 | **0.1892** |

ns-per-B flat from 1,000 upward is O(B), and the cost rises 30x on bucket size alone.

### The alternated A/B

Three rounds, min per arm. `B=100` is the control the change cannot help — with a hundred entries
there is nothing to stop scanning early for.

| row           | BEFORE | AFTER | ratio     |
| ------------- | -----: | ----: | --------- |
| B=100 CONTROL |   0.23 |  0.20 | 1.10x     |
| B=1,000       |   0.35 |  0.20 | **1.73x** |
| B=10,000      |   2.06 |  0.49 | **4.21x** |
| B=50,000      |   9.60 |  1.74 | **5.52x** |

Bigger than 715's 1.58x, and for a reason: there the victim sat near the END of the hub's adjacency
(so `retain` had little to shift), while a bucket's victim is wherever the node was inserted — here
near the front, which is the case where stopping the scan at the match saves the most. Still O(B);
the constant is ~5x smaller.

### Mutation 2/3 CAUGHT — and the survivor is the interesting one

Caught: the SET-path match inverted (prunes a wrong node), and the DELETE-path removal skipped (a
dead node left in the bucket).

**`swap_remove` SURVIVED — the exact opposite of item 715, where it was CAUGHT.** There, `out_adj`
order is load-bearing because the CSR and the per-type partitions are built from it, and a test
proved it. Here nothing pins bucket order: not the 1,217-test Rust suite, and not the seven
byte-identity fuzzers, which I ran against the mutant specifically to find out.

That is worth **O(1) instead of O(B)** — the whole remaining cost of this path — and it is NOT
taken here, deliberately:

- **Two silent oracles may mean "unobservable" or may mean "untested",** and this repo has the
  rule for exactly that: a survivor can be equivalent, inert, a skip, or a TEST GAP, and a tally
  cannot tell them apart. Both readings are live.
- The policy side points at "available": row order for an unordered query is recorded as
  unspecified, WON'T-FIX, compare-as-multisets. But bucket order drives the order a SEEK emits
  rows in, so taking it changes what an unsorted query returns FIRST — observable to a user even
  where the contract says unspecified, and a contract question is the user's call rather than a
  tuning decision.

So: **PRICED AND OPEN** — `swap_remove` at these three sites, worth the O(B) term, blocked on
whether seek order off a bucket is contractually free. Recorded at the call site too, so
`closed-levers.ts` finds it.

### The invariant the change rests on is a test

`retain` dropped every entry equal to the node; this drops the first. They differ only if a bucket
can hold a node twice. `a_seek_returns_each_node_once_after_every_index_write_path` asserts it
through the SEEK rather than by reaching into the bucket — a duplicate entry is only a defect
because it would emit a duplicate ROW, and the observable form needs no new accessor on `Store`.
It covers the build, a `SET` out, a `SET` back, a rolled-back transaction, and a delete. Items
367/368/349 are three instances of one index-pruning asymmetry found one at a time, which is why
this is asserted rather than reasoned.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1217 + 13 +
725 pass, 0 fail; all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass — load-bearing here, since an index feeds
seek order.

## 717 — `delete_edge` scanned a hub's adjacency up to SIX times for one eid: 1.99x, and the pattern sweep is done

**FIXED (native).** The last instances of items 715/716's shape, and the hottest: `delete_edge` is
the ordinary single-edge delete, not a node teardown.

It ran, for each of the two endpoints and each of the two directions:

```rust
if logging {
    removed.extend(adj.iter().filter(|a| a.eid == eid).map(|a| (node, true, *a)));
}
adj.retain(|a| { if a.eid == eid { dropped_etype = Some(a.etype); false } else { true } });
```

That is **four full scans without a transaction and six with one** — a `filter` pass to capture the
undo entry and a `retain` pass to drop it — each running to the end of a hub's 50,000 entries for
an eid that occurs once. One `position` now does both jobs: it stops at the match, the entry is
read before removal, and `remove` moves the tail with a single `ptr::copy`. `drop_etype_entry`'s
bucket (item 674's own function) gets the same treatment, where the bucket is the node's degree in
that one type.

### The alternated A/B

Three rounds, min per arm. The NODE-delete rows are the controls: item 715 already converted that
path, so both arms share it and it must not move.

| row                          | BEFORE | AFTER | ratio     |
| ---------------------------- | -----: | ----: | --------- |
| edge delete, index OFF       |  19.22 |  9.64 | **1.99x** |
| edge delete, index ON        |  51.91 | 46.29 | 1.12x     |
| node delete D=100 CONTROL    |   0.16 |  0.17 | 0.94x     |
| node delete D=50,000 CONTROL |  25.09 | 24.93 | 1.01x     |

**With the edge-type index ON it is only 1.12x**, and that is the honest reading: the scan was
roughly half of the un-indexed delete and is a small share of the indexed one, where the four
`drop_etype_entry` calls and the bucket work dominate — items 674/675's territory, already fixed
there and not revisited here.

### Mutation 3/4, and the survivor is INERT rather than a gap

Caught: the match inverted (drops a wrong edge); the captured `etype` dropped (the type index keeps
a dead eid); and `swap_remove`, which item 715 predicted would be caught here because the CSR is
built in `out_adj` order — it is, which is the second confirmation of that claim on a second path.

The survivor was labelled UNCERTAIN in advance: recording the undo entry even outside a
transaction. It is **inert, and I can say which rather than leaving it ambiguous** — `removed` is
consumed only under `if let Some(log) = &mut self.undo`, and `logging` IS `self.undo.is_some()`, so
without a transaction the vector is built and dropped unread. The `logging` guard is a perf guard,
not a correctness one, which is the same call item 601 and `ordered-rows.ts` make about their own
answer-equivalent guards.

### The sweep of this pattern is complete

Four items, one shape — `retain` used to remove a single known element from a long list:

| site                                    | item | result                                          |
| --------------------------------------- | ---- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| adjacency mirror detach (node delete)   | 715  | 1.58x on the oldest edge                        |
| property index buckets, three sites     | 716  | 5.52x at a 50,000-node bucket                   |
| `delete_edge`, four scans + type bucket | 717  | 1.99x un-indexed                                |
| TS adjacency                            | 672  | already O(1) — a `Set`, nothing to do           |
| TS property index                       | —    | a B-tree using `splice`; already position-based |

The remaining `retain`s in `store.rs` are the batch sweeps (`delete_nodes` over label buckets,
correct for a batch and the subject of item 663) and small config lists — invariants, index
descriptors — where the list is a handful of entries.

`cargo clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1217 + 13 +
725 pass, 0 fail; all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, which this needs rather than merely

## 718 — the 715-717 cluster did NOT regress the serving regime, and the row that looked like it cannot measure the cluster at all

**VERIFICATION (native). No engine change; one harness row annotated.**

Items 715/716/717 all changed WRITE paths, measured in the bulk and complexity harnesses. Memory is
explicit that bulk throughput and per-operation cost are different questions and a change can help
one while hurting the other, so the cluster owed `bench:usage` a check.

### The flag, and what alternation did to it

`write: append then delete node`, engine(-): **446.2k ops/s before the cluster, 407.7k after** —
~9% down, on the one row in the table that deletes anything. Read across processes, which is where
this session has been wrong four times.

Three alternated rounds, BEFORE = the store as of pre-715, AFTER = post-717, rebuilt between every
arm, max per arm (these are rates):

| row                          | BEFORE |  AFTER | ratio |
| ---------------------------- | -----: | -----: | ----- |
| **append then delete**       | 449.1k | 431.7k | 0.96x |
| append node CONTROL          | 460.2k | 447.4k | 0.97x |
| append node [params] CONTROL | 456.4k | 458.8k | 1.01x |
| read: point lookup CONTROL   |  56.1k |  55.5k | 0.99x |

**The control moved as far as the subject.** The 9% was harness variance between processes; there
is no regression. Item 310's rule, and the fifth time in this session a cross-process reading has

The victim is the `Tmp` node the same iteration just inserted, so it has **no edges**: the mirror
detach loop runs zero times and `delete_edge` is never called. Item 715's 1.58x and 717's 1.99x are
both unreachable from it — the row prices parse, bind and tombstone.

**And this fixture should not grow a hub to fix that.** It is deliberately small and warm
("measures per-operation cost, not cache behaviour"), and its largest in-degree is a Team at 100
MEMBER_OF edges — a degree items 715 and 716 both measured INSIDE the control band (1.06x and
1.10x at D=100). The degree axis belongs to `delete_cost_by_neighbour_degree` and
`edge_delete_cost_by_index`, which pin the node count and sweep degree to 50,000. Bolting a

So the row is annotated instead, with both halves: that it prices a degree-ZERO delete and cannot
show those items, and that the cluster was checked for a regression here and did not cause one. A

## 719 — label propagation's tiebreak CLONED an id per comparison: 1.39x, and mutation found the untested rule

**FIXED (native).** A new area — the algorithm bench, which neither bulk screen covers — picked by
reading `algo_bench` for an impossible ordering, the technique that produced items 699 and 700.

### The ordering

| algorithm           |    ms | per iteration |
| ------------------- | ----: | ------------: |
| `pagerank(20)`      | 12.90 |         0.645 |
| `label_prop(10)`    | 33.62 |     **3.360** |
| `peer_pressure(10)` | 50.97 |         5.097 |

Both PageRank and label propagation are "visit every edge, combine per node" over the same 50,000
vertices, and LP costs **5.2x per iteration**. LP's tally is already the right shape — a dense
counter reset through a touched-list, so O(degree) and not O(n) — which is what made the gap worth
looking at rather than explaining.

### The cause: the tiebreak, and why it runs far more often than it looks

```rust
Some((bl, bc)) => c > bc || (c == bc && store.node_ext_id(lbl) < store.node_ext_id(bl)),
```

`node_ext_id` is `self.node_ext.get(id).cloned()` — a `GStr` clone, twice per comparison. And
`&&` means it only runs on a TIE, which looks rare until you notice the degrees: in a social graph
most neighbours contribute a DISTINCT label with count 1, so after the first candidate nearly every
comparison IS a tie. The clone was on the hot path, not the cold one.

`node_ext_id_ref` already existed, documented as "skipping the `GStr` clone" — the same asymmetry
item 703 found between the CSV encoder and its pg-text sibling. `GStr::cmp` is
`as_bytes().cmp(..)` and `str`'s ordering is the same byte order, so the tiebreak is unchanged by
construction.

### The alternated A/B

Three rounds, min per arm. Four controls from the same table and the same process, none of which
compares an external id — `pagerank` is the useful one, being the other edge-sweep shape.

| row                    | BEFORE |  AFTER | ratio     |
| ---------------------- | -----: | -----: | --------- |
| `label_prop(10)`       |  33.64 |  24.13 | **1.39x** |
| `peer_pressure(10)`    |  50.64 |  43.54 | **1.16x** |
| `degree` CONTROL       |   0.19 |   0.19 | 1.00x     |
| `wcc` CONTROL          |   0.92 |   0.92 | 1.00x     |
| `pagerank(20)` CONTROL |  12.68 |  12.70 | 1.00x     |
| `betweenness` CONTROL  | 258.90 | 263.20 | 0.98x     |

The controls are as flat as this harness gets, which is what makes 1.39x and 1.16x readable.

### Mutation found a test gap in the rule the comment calls deliberate

Two of three caught: the LP tiebreak direction flipped, and peer-pressure's. **The third
SURVIVED — replacing `node_ext_id_ref(lbl) < node_ext_id_ref(bl)` with `lbl < bl`**, comparing the
DENSE id instead of the external one.

`lp_winner`'s own comment says external is deliberate: _"Ties are broken by the SMALLEST
external-id string (matching the TS engine's `vid.text` comparison, not the dense id, so
multi-digit ids agree too)"_. Nothing tested it, and this is the fixture rule once more: **the two
orders are identical for single-digit ids, which is every fixture the suite had.** A Builder mints
the dense id AS A STRING, so the divergence starts at ELEVEN nodes — as strings `"10" < "2"`, as
numbers `2 < 10`.

`the_label_tiebreak_uses_the_external_id_string_not_the_dense_id` builds twelve nodes where node 11
touches only 2 and 10, making its vote a clean two-way tie that the tiebreak alone decides: label
`10` under the external-id rule, `2` under a dense-id one. It asserts the premise (`"10" < "2"`) as
well as the outcome, so a future reader need not re-derive why the fixture is eleven nodes wide.
With it, **all three mutants are caught**.

That gap mattered: which label wins is a cross-engine invariant (the TS engine compares `vid.text`),
so a dense-id tiebreak would be a silent divergence on any graph with ten or more nodes and a tie —
and the algo fuzzer did not catch it either.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1218 + 13 +
725 pass, 0 fail (1218 is the new test); all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, including the algo
one that compares these results against the TS engine.

## 720 — the snapshot encoder cloned to lend: ~1.05x, a new bench row, and a DATA-LOSS gap nothing caught

**FIXED (native).** Item 719's cloning-accessor pattern, grepped across the engine as the method
asks. Most hits are fine — `codec.rs`, `render.rs` and `exec/write.rs` all CONSUME the owned value,
so the clone is real work. One subsystem clones only to lend: `binary::to_binary`, the FFI snapshot
encoder (`lnk_*` exposes it, so it is a user-reachable egress path).

```rust
w.str(&store.node_ext_id(id).unwrap_or_default());   // 1 per node
let labels = store.labels_of(id);                     // a Vec<String> per node
w.opt_str(store.edge_ext_id(*eid).as_deref());        // 1 per edge
w.str(&store.node_ext_id(*from).unwrap_or_default()); // 2 more per edge
```

Every one is handed straight to `w.str`, which takes `&str`. **And the asymmetry is inside the same
function**: the edge loop already called `edge_labels_of_refs` while the node loop called
`labels_of` — borrowed on one side, cloned on the other, which is what made this visible.

### It had no bench, so it got one

`to_binary` was not in any harness. Item 705's `ingest/codecs` case is the right home — its question
is "what does each ENCODE format cost, per byte?" and this is an encode format:

```
format                      encode_ms        MiB       MiB/ms
binary                          90.05      73.67        0.818
ndjson                         137.54     115.82        0.842
pg-json                        127.64     117.92        0.924
pg-text                        131.51      33.15        0.252
graphson                       164.75     237.68        1.443
csv                            259.68      36.47        0.140
```

### The A/B, and the number I am actually claiming

Three alternated rounds, min per arm, the five text formats as controls:

| format           | BEFORE |  AFTER | ratio     |
| ---------------- | -----: | -----: | --------- |
| **binary**       |  91.19 |  82.96 | 1.10x     |
| ndjson CONTROL   | 134.67 | 134.58 | 1.00x     |
| pg-json CONTROL  | 122.62 | 126.58 | 0.97x     |
| pg-text CONTROL  | 124.77 | 124.27 | 1.00x     |
| graphson CONTROL | 157.32 | 156.16 | 1.01x     |
| csv CONTROL      | 253.79 | 244.68 | **1.04x** |

**1.10x is not the honest figure.** `csv` cannot be reached by a change in `binary.rs`, and its arms
separated by rank too (AFTER max 250.90 < BEFORE min 253.79) at 1.04x — so there is arm-to-arm
drift. Normalising binary against csv within each round gives BEFORE 0.359 / 0.352 / 0.365 against
AFTER 0.348 / 0.331 / 0.348 — still disjoint, at **~1.05x**. That is the claim: a real ~5%, not the
10% the raw column shows. Item 310's rule, applied to my own result before quoting it.

### Mutation found silent DATA LOSS on an FFI path

Two of four caught immediately (the wrong node's id written; the from/to endpoints swapped). Two
survived, and they are different things:

**`w.opt_str(None)` for EVERY edge — losing every edge's external id — SURVIVED the whole suite.**
Verified by hand against the test that should catch it rather than trusted from a tally (item 713's
lesson): `binary_round_trips_via_ndjson_equality` compares `to_ndjson(&back)` with
`to_ndjson(&st)`, and **the NDJSON writer MINTS an id where one is absent**, so it fills the gap on
both sides. A round trip cannot see a defect its own inverse repairs — item 705's finding in a
second place, and here it hides data loss on a path reachable through `lnk_*`.

`a_binary_round_trip_keeps_edge_ids_and_label_order` reads the edge id off the store, with a
fixture id (`my-edge`) that a minted dense-id string cannot coincide with. With it the mutant is
**CAUGHT**.

**The label-order survivor is EQUIVALENT, not a gap**, and that distinction is measured too:
reversing the written order still survives, because `from_binary` inserts labels into the label
BUCKETS and `labels_of_refs` sorts on the way out, so the stream's order is unobservable by
construction. The test's label assertion pins the READ — that a reload presents canonical order —
and says so rather than claiming a catch it does not make.

The code comment was corrected in the same pass: it credited `binary_round_trips_*` with pinning
the bytes, which mutation had just shown to be false.

## 721 — reading a node's labels is O(the graph's DISTINCT LABEL COUNT), an axis no fixture sweeps: 3.4x from 1 label to 40

**PRICED (native), open — and the contained fix I tried alongside it measured NULL and was
reverted.** The harness is the item's product.

Item 720's grep carried on into the TS core, and the asymmetry runs the OTHER way this time. TS
holds a per-element label box, cached on the vertex — an O(1) read. Native DERIVES a node's labels:

```rust
pub fn labels_of_refs(&self, id: u32) -> Vec<&str> {
    self.by_label.iter().filter(|(_, ids)| ids.binary_search(&id).is_ok()) ...
}
```

A binary search in EVERY label bucket, per node. `delete_node`'s own comment says why — _"no
per-node label list yet, so sweep"_ — and item 442 recorded that for the delete path. What nobody
had priced is the READ path, and it is everywhere: `render.rs`, `json_out.rs` (three sites),
`evaluator.rs`, `codec.rs`, `binary.rs`.

### Why no harness could see it

**Every bench fixture in this repo gives each node ONE label** (`Person`). At L = 1 the sweep is a
single binary search, so the cost is invisible — the fixture rule, and the fifth time this session
a fixture could not reach its subject. A people graph has ten or twenty labels (Person, Candidate,
Employee, Requisition, Application, Team), and each multiplies this.

`label_read_cost_by_label_count` pins the node count at 20,000 and the row count at 500, and varies
only the number of DISTINCT labels in the graph. Each node carries `Hit` plus one other, so a
node's own label count stays at 2 and the axis is purely how many buckets the sweep visits:

| distinct labels | `exec::run` µs | JSON carrier µs |
| --------------: | -------------: | --------------: |
|               1 |          50.89 |           92.13 |
|               4 |          60.77 |           99.60 |
|              10 |          77.97 |          117.02 |
|              20 |         121.56 |          160.41 |
|              40 |         171.56 |          208.45 |

**3.4x on the same 500 rows**, linear in the label count past a fixed floor, on both the row and
the JSON path. Nothing about the query changed.

### The contained fix: BUILT, MEASURED NULL, REVERTED

Three sites in `json_out.rs` read `store.labels_of(id).first()` — which builds a `Vec<String>`,
cloning every label the node has, SORTS it, and takes the smallest. A `min_label_ref` doing the same
sweep with `.min()` over `&str` is byte-identical (sorting then indexing 0 IS the minimum) and
allocates nothing.

Three alternated rounds, with a CONTROL in the same table and process: the `exec::run` column
renders through `render.rs`, which the change does not touch.

| distinct labels | JSON ratio | run ratio (CONTROL) |
| --------------: | ---------: | ------------------: |
|               1 |      0.98x |               0.97x |
|               4 |      1.03x |               1.01x |
|              10 |      1.03x |               1.01x |
|              20 |      1.04x |               1.03x |
|              40 |      1.01x |               1.02x |

**The control tracks the subject at every point.** Reverted, and the reason is arithmetic rather
than mystery: the fixture gives each node TWO labels, so the change removes 2 allocations against
40 binary searches — a twentieth of the work at L = 40, under any floor this harness has. A fixture
with many labels PER NODE would price it differently, and that axis is untested; this item does not
claim it either way.

### What the real fix is, and what it costs

A per-node label list, which is what TS has. It makes the read O(the node's own labels) instead of
O(the graph's), and it is a STORAGE change rather than a tuning one:

- `by_label` stays — it is the label-scan index and nothing here replaces it;
- the new list wants label IDs, so it needs a label dictionary (the store already has
  `etype_ids` for edge types, so the shape exists);
- four write paths maintain it (node creation, add label, remove label, delete node);
- **byte-identity surface:** labels are returned in canonical sorted order today, and a
  per-node list must preserve exactly that, which is the part to get wrong.

Priced at the table above and left open with that sketch, deliberately not attempted in the same
tick as its measurement — items 686 and 689 are the precedent (derive, validate, then wire in its
own item).

--all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1219 + 13 + 725 pass, 0
fail; the reverted arm is the committed tree, so item 720's fuzzer run still stands for it.

## 722 — item 721's accessor already existed, and the fix it was reaching for is already built one file over

**CORRECTION + LOCATED (native). No engine change; two call sites annotated.**

This tick set out to build item 721's per-node label list. Reading every `by_label` mutation point
first — because a missed one is a wrong answer, not a slow path — turned up two things that change
what the work is.

### 1. `min_label_ref` was a re-invention. `min_label_name` was already there

Item 721 added a `min_label_ref` accessor for the three `labels_of(id).first()` sites. The store
already has, body for body:

```rust
pub fn min_label_name(&self, id: u32) -> Option<&str> {
    self.by_label.iter().filter(|(_, ids)| ids.binary_search(&id).is_ok())
        .map(|(l, _)| l.as_str()).min()
}
```

— with a doc that states its own purpose: _"without allocating/sorting the whole label list the way
`labels_of(id).first()` did"_. So the API I wrote was a duplicate, and its own documentation
already named the call sites it was for.

721's revert was on perf grounds and happened to save a duplicate API from being committed. **The
duplicate is the part worth recording**: I grepped `CLOSED.md`, the audit and `closed-levers.ts`
before that tick, and none of them covers "does this accessor already exist" — that question is
answered by reading the store's own API surface, which I did not do.

### 2. The real fix is `min_label_map`, and `evaluator.rs` already chooses it correctly

The store also has a whole-store inversion: `(names, code_of)` built in one pass, **cached on
`node_count`**, O(total membership) to build and then O(1) a row. Its doc says plainly that
"callers processing a large node frontier use this instead of the per-node probe".

Exactly one caller does — `evaluator.rs`, for the Gremlin `label()` step — and it already carries
the threshold this question needs, with the reasoning attached:

```rust
if n >= store.node_count() / 4 {
    let map = store.min_label_map();   // O(total membership) + O(1)/row
```

> _"Small frontiers keep the per-node path — inverting the whole store would cost more than a
> handful of probes."_

**The JSON render path has the same cost and neither of the better routes.** It uses `labels_of(id)
.first()` — the worst of the three — at three sites. That is why item 721's substitution measured
NULL: it swapped one per-node probe for another per-node probe, when the lever is the map.

### Why it is not wired in this tick

`write_node_stub(out, store, v)` and its two siblings are per-ELEMENT helpers. They see one node,
not a row count, so they cannot apply the evaluator's `n >= node_count() / 4` gate — using the map
means plumbing it through the render path, and picking a threshold without a frontier size to
measure against is exactly the guess item 721 said not to make in the same tick as the
measurement.

And the hazard is real and named: on a cache MISS the map costs O(total membership), charged to
however many rows the query returns. A one-row query against a mutating store misses every time —
`bench:usage`'s `interleaved: write + point read` is where that would surface, and any attempt owes
that row an alternated check.

**Priced from item 721's own harness**: the JSON column is 92.13 µs for 500 rows at one distinct

## 723 — item 721's null was UNREACHABILITY, not "the sweep dominates", and that repairs two records

**CORRECTION (native). No engine change.** This tick went to plumb item 722's `min_label_map`
through the render path and found, by checking reachability first, that both of the preceding items
had the wrong file.

### The check that should have run at 721

Item 721 changed three `labels_of(id).first()` sites in `json_out.rs`, measured a null against a
tracking control, and explained it: _"the fixture gives each node TWO labels, so the change removes
2 allocations against 40 binary searches."_ That explanation is wrong.

Those three sites live in `try_fused_map_json`, which is called from **`try_run_gremlin_json_inner`**.
The harness measured **`try_run_gql_json`**, which goes `try_stream_varlen_json` →
`gql_rows_json(try_run_inner(..))` and never enters that function. **The modified code did not run.**

Item 700's rule is the one that catches this — _instrumenting one function tells you it did not
run; it does not tell you what ran instead_ — and it is the fifth time this session that
"does the change reach the shape?" has been the question that mattered. I applied it to the engine's
code repeatedly and not to my own change.

### Which accessor serves which path, measured by reading the dispatch

| path                                | label call                                         | what it needs             |
| ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| GQL `RETURN n` (what 721 measured)  | `labels_of_refs` (render.rs 331, 412)              | **ALL** labels, as a List |
| GQL/Gremlin single `label()` render | `labels_of(id).into_iter().next()` (render.rs 278) | the MINIMUM               |
| Gremlin `elementMap` / `valueMap`   | `labels_of(id).first()` ×3 (json_out.rs)           | the MINIMUM               |
| Gremlin `label()` over a frontier   | `min_label_map` — already correct                  | the MINIMUM               |

So item 721's 3.4x — 92.13 µs for 500 rows at one distinct label against 208.45 at forty — is real
and lives in **`labels_of_refs` on the GQL render path**. And `min_label_map` cannot serve it: the
map yields one label per node, while `RETURN n` emits the whole list.

### What that does to item 722

722 concluded "the real fix is `min_label_map`". For the min-label SITES that stands, and its other
findings stand — `min_label_name` really was a duplicate of what 721 added, and the evaluator really
does hold the only correct threshold. But the emphasis was wrong for the column 721 measured: 722's
own last paragraph says the per-node list "also serves `labels_of_refs`, which wants ALL labels",
and that is the part that matters for the 3.4x rather than the aside it was written as.

### State of the label question, as precisely as it can now be put

- **`labels_of_refs` on the GQL render path** — the 3.4x, O(the graph's distinct labels) per row,
  fixed only by a **per-node label list** (item 721's sketch: a label dictionary, four write paths,
  and the canonical sorted order as its byte-identity surface).
- **the four min-label sites** — fixable with `min_label_map` plus the evaluator's frontier gate,
  which needs plumbing through per-element helpers that see no row count (item 722).
- **`min_label_name`** — the existing no-allocation per-node probe, strictly better than
  `labels_of(..).first()` at the same complexity, and NOT measurably better on any harness yet
  pointed at a path that reaches it.

Three items on one question, and what each tick actually bought: 721 the measurement and the
harness, 722 the existing-API survey, 723 the reachability map. The lever is unchanged and
unattempted; what is gone is the chance of attempting it in the wrong file, which both earlier ticks
were set up to do.

Gates: no code change to gate beyond the records. `cargo fmt` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## 724 — the per-node label list, built: 4.37x at forty labels, and the complexity is GONE

**FIXED (native).** Items 721-723 measured, surveyed and located; this builds it. The three ticks
before it were not overhead — 723's reachability map is the only reason this one edited the right
file.

### The change

`by_label` (label → sorted ids) STAYS; it is the label-scan seed. Added alongside it:

```rust
node_labels: Vec<Vec<u32>>,   // node id -> label ids
label_names: Vec<String>,     // append-only dictionary
label_id: FnvMap<String, u32>,
```

`labels_of_refs` now indexes the forward map and resolves names, instead of probing EVERY bucket
with a binary search. `labels_of` is its owned twin.

**The forward map is NOT kept sorted.** `labels_of_refs` sorts the resolved NAMES, which is the
canonical order its callers rely on — sorting ids would order by intern sequence, and that is the
byte-identity surface item 721 named as the part to get wrong.

### Eight write paths, and the test that found the one I missed

Two node inserts, the sink insert, `add_label`, `remove_label`, the batch delete sweep,
`pop_last_node`, and `Builder::build`'s one-pass inversion. The undo pair needed nothing — it
routes through `apply_add_label` / `apply_remove_label`.

`the_forward_label_map_agrees_with_the_bucket_sweep` compares the new reader against the old sweep,
kept as a `#[cfg(test)]` oracle, over build / add / repeated add / remove / add_node / delete /
rolled-back transaction. **It failed on its first real run**: "after delete_nodes: node 1
disagrees". `delete_nodes` has a `TARGETED_MAX = 8` fast path that RETURNS before the sweep, and my
clear was after the branch — so a small-batch delete left a dead node holding its labels. The clear
is now above the branch.

**Note what order that happened in.** The test passed BEFORE the readers were switched, because it
was then comparing the sweep with itself — the "two gates covering one shape" trap. It only became
an oracle once `labels_of_refs` stopped being the sweep, and that is when it caught the bug.

### The measurement, and a control label I had to correct

`label_read_cost_by_label_count` (item 721), node count pinned at 20,000, 500 rows, varying only
the graph's distinct label count. Three alternated rounds, both files swapped per arm:

| distinct labels | rows before | after | ratio     | JSON before | after | ratio     |
| --------------: | ----------: | ----: | --------- | ----------: | ----: | --------- |
|               1 |       50.60 | 38.31 | 1.32x     |       95.49 | 79.54 | 1.20x     |
|               4 |       63.67 | 38.10 | 1.67x     |      107.44 | 78.24 | 1.37x     |
|              10 |       80.71 | 36.44 | 2.21x     |      125.94 | 76.28 | 1.65x     |
|              20 |      125.78 | 39.20 | 3.21x     |      167.47 | 81.62 | 2.05x     |
|              40 |      174.06 | 39.87 | **4.37x** |      214.17 | 81.94 | **2.61x** |

**The complexity is gone**: 38.31 → 39.87 across a fortyfold change in label count, where it was
50.60 → 174.06. The win scales with the axis, which is what a complexity fix looks like.

**Item 721 used the `rows` column as a CONTROL for a `json_out.rs` change. It is not one here** —
this change is in `store.rs`, which both columns reach, so neither is a control. The real control
had to come from outside: label-FREE algorithms, measured on both arms, read `degree` 0.95x, `wcc`
1.03x, `pagerank(20)` 0.94x, `label_prop(10)` 0.99x — flat, so nothing outside the label read moved.
Saying "control" about a column that the change reaches is the error that cost items 721 and 722,
and it was avoided here only by checking which files each column touches.

### Mutation 4/4

A node insert forgetting the forward map; `forward_remove_label` as a no-op; the delete clear
removed; and `labels_of_refs` no longer sorting, which is the byte-identity claim. All caught, by
the agreement test plus the suite.

### What is left

`min_label_map` and the four min-label sites (item 722) are untouched and still open — this fixes
the ALL-labels read, which is where 721's 3.4x lived. And `by_label` is now maintained alongside a
forward map, so the two can drift; the agreement test is what stands between that and a wrong
answer, which is why it compares the readers rather than asserting on internals.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1220 + 13 + 725 pass, 0 fail
(1220 includes the new agreement test); all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass — required rather than
formal, since labels are rendered into results and their ORDER is part of the bytes.

**VERIFICATION (native). No code change.** A storage change touches every render path, so item 724
owed the bulk sweep a check.

`bun run bench`'s `traverse 1-hop project` read **ffi 98.8 and 102.2 after 724, against 71.3 and
74.2 before** — a 1.3x regression on a row that renders ELEMENTS, which is exactly where the change
lives. `traverse 1-hop project + start filter` was up too (27.1 against 19.7).

### What the in-process harness says

`query_bench -- perrow` prices a row by what it returns, in one process with no JSON carrier — the

| row                     |    BEFORE |     AFTER | ratio     |
| ----------------------- | --------: | --------: | --------- |
| `element p` (node)      |  95,532.3 |  84,757.6 | **1.13x** |
| `element r` (edge)      | 332,568.4 | 333,405.2 | 1.00x     |
| `scalar p.age` CONTROL  |     482.7 |     489.3 | 0.99x     |
| `string p.name` CONTROL |   1,323.4 |   1,352.6 | 0.98x     |

**Faster, not slower** — and on the single-label fixture, which is the hardest case for 724 (its own

**That is the SIXTH cross-process reading this session that did not survive alternation** (items

Edges never had the problem. `edge_labels_of_refs` reads `edge_etype[eid]` — a direct index — plus

That is item 720's shape one level up: there, the same function borrowed on one side and cloned on
the other; here, the same store answered "what labels does this element carry" in O(1) for edges
and O(the graph's distinct labels) for nodes. **Both were found by asking why a pair that should
match did not** — and `element r` at 332 ns/row is still the most expensive row in that table, now

## 726 — three bench rows project an ABSENT property, and the "sort is faster than no sort" row is why anyone noticed

**DIAGNOSED (both engines). One lever built and REVERTED; three bench rows annotated.**

### The impossible ordering, and what it actually was

The sweep read native `traverse 1-hop project` at **102.2 ms** and the SAME query with `ORDER BY n`
at **76.4** — sorting a million rows making a query 1.34x faster. The technique that found items
699 and 700, pointed at the next row.

It does not reproduce. In isolation, both list positions, min of 7: **69.3 unordered against 70.7
ordered** — flat, not inverted. **That is the seventh cross-process reading this session not to
survive an isolated re-measurement** (697, 699, 711, 718, 720, 725, this).

### But the probe found something real, by getting the fixture wrong first

My first probe gave nodes a `name` and read 86.4 unordered against **187.3** ordered — a normal
2.17x for a sort. The bench reads flat. The difference is the fixture: **`graphDoc`'s nodes carry
only `age`, so `x.name` is ABSENT on every one of them.**

So three bench rows — `traverse 1-hop project`, `+ order by`, and `+ start filter` — project a
million NULLS. They price the hop, the row plumbing and an absent-property read; they do not price
a property read. And `+ order by` sorts a million IDENTICAL keys, which is why its sort term is
near zero in native and why the pair looked inverted under noise.

### The lever that followed, and why it is reverted

If every key compares equal, a STABLE sort is the identity, so it can be skipped — and with an
early exit the check costs one comparison on mixed data. Built in `sortRowsByColumns`, byte-identity
argued from stability, using `compareSort` itself so "equal" means what the sort means.

| row                           | BEFORE | AFTER | ratio     |
| ----------------------------- | -----: | ----: | --------- |
| absent key, `ORDER BY`        |  249.9 | 238.8 | 1.05x     |
| absent key, unordered CONTROL |   96.5 |  95.7 | 1.01x     |
| 90 distinct CONTROL           |  297.5 | 280.5 | 1.06x     |
| all distinct CONTROL          |  372.3 | 316.0 | **1.18x** |

**A control moved further than the subject**, so the 1.05x is not a result. Reverted.

### And the reason is a correction to my own hypothesis for this tick

I assumed TS's ~155 ms premium on the ordered row WAS the comparisons — a million-key sort at ~20M
comparator calls. **Instrumentation says otherwise**: the short-circuit fires
(`sortRowsByColumns n=1000000 allEqual=true`, verified rather than inferred), the sort is genuinely
skipped, and the query still costs 250.8 against the unordered 95.7.

So the premium is **MATERIALIZATION**, not sorting: the unordered projection streams lazily (the
bench's own `[ts lazy]` rows say so) while `ORDER BY` must hold all 1,000,000 rows. Skipping the
comparisons leaves that untouched. Half of a 1.34x-looking mystery was noise and the other half was
a cost I had mis-attributed before measuring.

**Note what the instrumentation was for.** Items 721-723 were spent on a change that never ran, so
this time I checked reachability when the numbers disappointed — and the answer was the opposite of
that case: the code DID run, which is what made "then the sort is not the cost" the only reading
left. Both outcomes need the same check.

### What is recorded where

The three bench rows now carry the fixture warning and the measured decomposition, with the reason
they are NOT repointed at `age`: every figure recorded against those row names would stop being
comparable, which is the call item 356 made about `decode ndjson`'s fixture. The all-equal lever is
left unbuilt with its numbers, since the next reader's instinct will be the same as mine.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run check` 0. The only committed source edit is a bench comment.

## 727 — item 726's premium is the START-DRIVEN WALK, not materialization, and it is refuted at 698

**DIAGNOSED (TypeScript). No engine change; one constraint annotated.** Item 726 left a question:
TS's `ORDER BY` on a million-row hop projection costs ~155 ms over the unordered twin, and 726
proved the SORT is not it (the all-equal short-circuit fires and the premium stays). 726's answer
was "materialization". That is wrong too.

### Instrumented, not reasoned

Both queries take the SAME route — the hop projection — and the ordered one takes its sort:

```
--- unordered     PROBE727 hop sort gate: sorts=none
--- ORDER BY n    PROBE727 hop sort gate: sorts=taken
```

So there is no route change and no extra materialization: both build and realise 250,000 rows. What
the sort changes is one flag:

```ts
startDriven: forceStartDriven || sorts !== undefined,
```

**A sort forces the START-DRIVEN walk.** The far-driven walk is cheaper and cannot be used, for a
reason `ordered-rows.ts` already states: it REORDERS rows deliberately, `Array.prototype.sort` is
stable, so tie order would change — and tie order is observable between the engines (item 605
measured both agreeing over a fixture with 20 ties per group). The forcing is a correctness
constraint, not an oversight.

### Which lands on refuted ground

That cost IS the sorted-hop target. Item 697 re-priced it and **item 698 refuted it**, by building
the floor items 659/660 ask for — the unordered query PLUS a bare sort of its own rows:

| degree 1                             | ms       |
| ------------------------------------ | -------- |
| unordered (200,000 rows)             | 38.3     |
| a bare sort of the engine's OWN rows | 10.0     |
| **honest floor**                     | **48.3** |
| `ORDER BY k`                         | **41.8** |

**0.86x of the floor** — the engine sorts more cheaply than materialising and sorting separately.
At degree 3 a 1.58x gap remains, against 2.94x if the unordered row is the reference.

**And that is exactly the error I walked into from the other side.** Item 726 compared `ORDER BY`
against the UNORDERED row and called the difference a premium to be explained. 698's own note says
the unordered reference overstates by ~1.9x because sorting genuinely costs something. I cited
659/660's floor rule twice in this session and then used the wrong reference anyway.

### What was actually missing, and is now there

Neither `CLOSED.md` nor `closed-levers.ts` could have stopped this: the constraint lives in an
unmarked boolean expression in `hop-projection.ts`, and 697/698 are recorded under "sorted hop",
which is not what a reader staring at `startDriven` would search. The expression now carries the
marker — what forces it, why the cheaper walk is unavailable, that it is refuted at 698, and the
honest floor with its numbers. `closed-levers.ts startDriven` finds it and cites 698.

That is the third time this session the fix has been an annotation rather than code (714 built the
index, 723 mapped accessors to paths, this marks a constraint), and each one is a tick that will not
be spent again.

### The chain, so item 726's question is closed rather than left open

| hypothesis                       | status                                                          |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the sort's comparisons           | REFUTED at 726 — short-circuit fires, premium stays             |
| materialization                  | REFUTED here — both arms realise the same rows                  |
| a route change off the shortcut  | REFUTED here — instrumented, both take the hop route            |
| **the forced start-driven walk** | **CONFIRMED, and refuted as a target at 698 against its floor** |

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run check` 0. The only edit is a comment; the instrumentation was reverted from the pristine
copy and the tree verified before writing this.

## 728 — the bench corpus is now fully screened, and the one flaw found was in my own instrument

**SCREENING + TOOLING. No engine change.** Three surfaces were checked and all three are closed or
clean; the actionable finding is a citation bug in `closed-levers.ts`, which three items have
relied on.

### `value_bench` — the biggest unscreened ratio, and it is closed

`map field meta.city` reads **5064.4 µs against flat `string city`'s 255.2 — 19.8x**, the largest
ratio on any surface this session had not looked at. **Closed at item 382**, which measured the

flat side is fast because `Column::Str` is DICTIONARY-encoded, so a string equality is a
vectorizable `u32` code compare. The map side is a boxed `Record` with a string-keyed field lookup.
Closing it means SHREDDING nested fields into columns, Parquet-style — a storage feature with a
snapshot-format consequence.

**The two-store screen worked exactly as designed here**, and in the direction opposite to item
713's: `closed-levers.ts map field` returned nothing and its own empty-result message says "that is

### `storage_bench` and `scale_bench` — clean

- `storage/write`: a bulk `SET p.age` over 200,000 nodes at **25.21 ms**, 126 ns an element.
- `storage/multilabel`: a second label on every edge costs **2.5 → 9.3 bytes/edge** and **242.9 →

**Every group binary in the corpus has now been read this session** — `ingest`, `query`, `storage`,
`value`, `algo`, `scale` — plus the three standalone probes, the Gremlin surface (661), the serving
regime (662/718), and the spelling probe (712).

### The real finding: `closed-levers.ts` cited whatever the prose mentioned first

Item 727 annotated a constraint whose marker is about item **698**, and the tool printed **605** —
because it took the first `item NNN` match in the comment block, and the prose opened by referring
to 605. I "fixed" it by reordering the sentence to suit the tool, which is the wrong way round: a
citation that depends on prose order is one a reader cannot trust, and I would not have noticed had
the two numbers not both been familiar.

The rule is now explicit: a number on the MARKER'S OWN LINE wins, the block is the fallback, and a
block citing several items prints `698+` — the `+` is the part that matters, because it tells the
reader there is more in the block than the one number. The 605 case would have printed `605+`.

**This is the hazard the tool exists to prevent, in the tool.** Item 714 built it after three items
were spent on closed targets; it has now had its own first mis-citation found and fixed by use.
20 of 51 markers still cite no item at all (`--orphans`), which remains standing work.

`no-nested-ternary` fix); `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0. No engine source changed.

## 729 — the deep sweeps are clean AND the fuzzers have teeth for this session's storage changes, which is the part worth proving

**VERIFICATION. No code change.** Four storage changes shipped this session — 715 (the adjacency
mirror detach), 716 (the index buckets), 717 (`delete_edge`), 724 (the forward label map) — each
with a default-seed fuzzer run. CLAUDE.md asks for more than that on a storage change, and two
things were missing.

### The deeper sweeps

| sweep                                        | result                   |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000 … rewrite_fuzz` | 10 pass, 0 fail (42.3 s) |
| all seven byte-identity fuzzers, seed 11     | 13 pass, 0 fail          |
| … seed 2026                                  | 13 pass, 0 fail          |
| … seed 77731                                 | 13 pass, 0 fail          |

So the optimizer invariant and the cross-engine invariant both hold past the default seeds.

### But green is not evidence until the teeth are checked

CLAUDE.md is blunt about this — _"a generative test whose teeth were never verified is worse than no
test, because it is believed"_ — and my mutation runs this session all used the UNIT SUITE as the
oracle. Whether the FUZZERS catch a storage defect was never tested, so "all seven pass" was
carrying more weight than it had earned.

Mutant: `forward_remove_label` as a no-op, so a removed label keeps appearing in every render. It is
the mutant item 724's agreement test already catches; the question here is whether the fuzzers catch
it INDEPENDENTLY.

**They do.** Fuzzers alone, unit suite not run: **12 pass, 1 fail** —

```
(fail) differential fuzz: write path (TS engine vs Rust engine)
       > 400 random write sequences agree on rows and graph state
```

The write-path differential generates label mutations and compares TS against Rust on rows AND graph
state, so item 724's forward map is covered by two independent oracles: the agreement test inside
the store, and the cross-engine differential from outside. The mutant was reverted from the pristine
copy and the suite re-run (13 pass, 0 fail) before this was written.

### What that settles, and what it does not

It settles that the four storage changes sit under a generative guard with demonstrated teeth, which
is what "without regressions" needs in order to mean anything on a storage change. It does NOT
generalise to every defect shape — one caught mutant proves coverage of one shape, which is the same
caution item 690 recorded about its own oracle. What is now known rather than assumed: **a wrong
per-node label reaches the differential fuzzer**, and that was the structural change with the widest
blast radius of the four.

Gates: no code change to gate. `cargo build --features capi` 0 on the restored tree; `git status`
clean of source edits.

## 730 — the orphan list was over-reporting by half, and a wrong citation would be worse than none

**TOOLING. No engine change; three doc clauses reworded.** `closed-levers.ts --orphans` reported 20
markers that a reader cannot follow up. Triaged one by one, it was reporting three different things
and only half of them were the thing.

| what it reported                  | count | what it is                                         |
| --------------------------------- | ----: | -------------------------------------------------- |
| cites an item                     |    31 | followable                                         |
| cites a DATE or an `E<n>` run tag |     7 | **also followable** — "REJECTED (2026-09-27, E80)" |
| not a lever at all                |     3 | "REJECTED **if** `key` backs a unique constraint"  |
| genuinely unreferenced            |    10 | the real list                                      |

### Two fixes, each at the right level

**The date/run-tag reference is a reference.** `--orphans` counted only `item NNN`, so seven markers
that say "REJECTED (2026-09-17, E68/E69)" were in a to-do list they do not belong in. A flag that
over-reports gets ignored, which is the one failure mode a to-do list cannot survive. The reference
test now accepts a date or an `E<n>` tag.

**The three non-levers were fixed in the PROSE, not in the script.** They said "REJECTED if `key`
backs a unique constraint", meaning the API REFUSES a call — the same word for a different thing.
Teaching the script to tell a lever from a behaviour clause is exactly the judging it refuses to do
(`open-markers.ts` makes the same choice), so instead they now say **REFUSED**, and the tool's doc
records the convention: `REJECTED`/`REVERTED`/`REFUTED` mean "this optimization was tried and did
not work"; a function that turns a call away is _refused_. Three sites, and the false positives are
gone without the script guessing.

**20 → 10, and every remaining entry is a genuine unreferenced lever.**

### Why the remaining ten are left alone

I tried to attribute one: `exec.rs:6149` ("tie. REJECTED, all measured NEUTRAL at 200k", with three
sub-levers each carrying its own numbers). `CLOSED.md` has no match for its phrasing, so attributing
it means a content search through a 23,000-line append-only log, not a grep.

**And a guessed citation would be worse than no citation.** An orphan says "read the comment"; a
wrong item number says "read item 412", and the reader who does has been sent somewhere that does
not discuss it — which is precisely the failure items 721-723 cost three ticks to, in the form of a
comment pointing at the wrong pair. So the ten stay orphaned, honestly, and the list is now short
enough to be worked through one at a time by someone with the session context to do it right.

Note what each remaining marker still gives a reader even unattributed: the lever, the direction it
failed in, and usually its numbers. The missing part is only the audit entry.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1220 + 13 + 725 pass, 0
fail; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0.
