## 751 — a filtered query slower than its unfiltered parent is NOT automatically a bug: the filter removed the closed form

**NEGATIVE RESULT. No change. The finding is a limit on the heuristic that produced items 748 and 749.** Those two came from reading a sweep for an ordering impossible on its face. Applied to the TS
side of the same family, it produces a candidate that looks at least as strong and is not a defect
at all.

### The apparent anomaly

TS, isolated, 200,000 vertices:

| row                          |       ts |
| ---------------------------- | -------: |
| `count 2-hop` (ungated)      | **72.8** |
| `count 2-hop + start filter` | **89.9** |
| `count 2-hop + mid filter`   |     42.3 |
| `count 2-hop + end filter`   |     99.8 |

A start filter narrows the sources to ~39% — strictly fewer — and costs **1.23x MORE than no filter
at all**, and 2.1x more than a mid filter. On its face that is 748's shape: less work, more time.

### Reachability first, and it ruled out the obvious answer

A throw in `walkSegments` (the general matcher): **all four rows answer** — none falls off the
shortcut family, so this is not shortcut-versus-general. A throw in `longChainCount`: the **3-hop**
row reaches it and none of the 2-hop rows do, so two hops has its own route.

### The cause: the filter does not shrink the problem, it changes the algorithm

Two documented routes, and the file states the reason plainly:

- `buildTwoHopCount` iterates the **MIDDLE** and multiplies the two sides — `Σ_b indeg(b) ×
outdeg(b)`. It never traverses an edge; two degree lookups per middle vertex answer the whole
  count.
- `buildFilteredTwoHopCount` drives from the **START**, because _"once a predicate selects which
  `a`s count, the start side's factor is no longer a plain degree"_. Gate a vertex, then expand it.

So the operation counts run the other way from the input sizes. Ungated: ~400k degree lookups, zero
edge visits. Start-gated: ~200k predicate calls, ~390k edge visits, ~390k lookups — **more total
work on 61% fewer sources**, because the degree product is unavailable once the start side is
conditional.

The gated route is also already the better of its options: item 206 built it precisely because the
filtered shape fell to the general pipeline at 97.7 ns a scanned vertex against the one-hop walk's
25.7.

### 🛑 What this costs the heuristic, which is the part worth keeping

"An ordering impossible on its face" is a good detector — it found a 4.12x and a 1.53x in the two
items before this one. This is its failure mode, and it is specific: **a filter can remove a closed
form.** When it does, the filtered query is legitimately dearer than its unfiltered parent, and the
comparison that looked impossible was never valid, because the two rows are not the same algorithm
with different inputs.

So the refined rule: before treating `filtered > unfiltered` as a defect, ask whether the unfiltered
case has a route the filtered one cannot take. Where the answer is no — items 748 and 749, where
`count 2-hop + start filter` and the 3-hop ran the SAME sweep with the same gates — the ordering
really is impossible and the defect is real. Where the answer is yes, as here, there is nothing to
fix.

Noted too: the mid filter at 42.3 is the fastest of the four and cheaper than ungated, which is the
reverse again. That one IS consistent with work done — a mid gate prunes the frontier between the
hops, which is the one position where a predicate removes work from the remaining pass rather than
adding a pass of its own. It needed no separate investigation once the start case was understood.

### What was checked and left alone

No code changed. Both probed files were restored and `git status` is clean of source edits; the
throws were temporary. `count 2-hop` and the three filtered rows all already exist as bench rows
(the ungated one added at item 749), so the family stays measurable without anything new.

Gates: no change to gate. `bun run build` 0 on the restored tree.

## 752 — `bench:usage`'s two index columns are not independent: the second is warmer, and on a parse-dominated row that beats the effect being measured

**DIAGNOSED AND PROVED; the cheap fix was tried and did NOT survive, so nothing ships but the
warning.** The serving benchmark holds the largest cross-engine ratios in the repo, so items
739/740's rule — re-run the harness that priced it — pointed here.

### The impossible reading

| row                           |     ts(-) |      ts(+) | engine(-) | engine(+) |
| ----------------------------- | --------: | ---------: | --------: | --------: |
| `write: append node`          | **88.7k** | **135.0k** |    463.7k |    427.5k |
| `write: append node [params]` |    548.0k |     410.0k |    462.6k |    417.4k |

**Indexing makes TS's plain append 1.52x FASTER.** It cannot: an index adds maintenance to a write,
which is what native shows (8% cost) and what the parameterized twin shows (1.34x cost). Isolated
and repeated, the ordering held 3/3: ts(-) 77.2/90.5/106.5k against ts(+) 97.1/137.6/134.7k.

### The cause, proved by reversing it

`rate` warms with ONE operation — the pilot that sizes the batch, which is a different job and is
labelled "Warm" in the source — and `[false, true].map(…)` runs both columns in ONE process,
unindexed first. The interpolated append is parse-dominated (6x its parameterized twin), so by the
time `(+)` runs, the `(-)` cell has executed that path thousands of times.

**Reversing the column order moved the advantage with the ORDER, not with the index:**

| order    | measured FIRST    | measured SECOND        |
| -------- | ----------------- | ---------------------- |
| original | unindexed 77-106k | indexed **97-137k**    |
| reversed | indexed 94-105k   | unindexed **128-145k** |

That is decisive. The difference is tier-up, and `best of BATCHES` cannot see it because every
batch of the first column is colder than every batch of the second.

### 🛑 Three fixes tried; the cheap one does not hold

| fix                               | result                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 600-op warmup before both columns | converged ISOLATED (131.8 vs 131.6) but **not** in the full matrix (112.7 vs 138.7)                                                                                                         |
| 3000-op warmup                    | **corrected the SIGN** — ts(-) 111.2k against ts(+) 88.7k, indexed slower, which is what index maintenance should look like — but minutes of extra wall clock, and only one round completed |
| discard each cell's FIRST BATCH   | **INCONSISTENT**: 1.54x, 0.98x, 1.11x over three rounds                                                                                                                                     |

The third was the one I expected to ship: it costs one 250ms box a cell instead of thousands of
operations, and at ~100k ops/s a discarded batch is ~25,000 warm operations, far above the 3,000
that worked. It still does not reliably remove the bias, and **a fix whose benefit cannot be
demonstrated is the thing items 726 and 737 were reverted for.** So the harness is back at HEAD.

What the three together do show: the unindexed arm is the unstable one (77-133k across every run
this item made) while the indexed arm is steady (127-138k). That is consistent with warming as the
mechanism — sometimes the first column warms enough inside its own batches and sometimes it does
not — and it is why one round of any arm proves nothing here.

### What this costs the record

**Every `(-)` vs `(+)` figure in `bench:usage` was taken under this bias**, including the recorded
claim that TS's indexed column WINS. Where the columns differ by orders of magnitude the index
effect obviously dominates — `read: point lookup` is 2.2k against 927.3k, and no amount of tier-up
explains 400x. Where they sit within ~1.5x the comparison is confounded, and `write: append node` is
the case that was.

A second casualty: that row's own comment says it "carries an INDEXED key deliberately" so the
columns differ and indexes do not "look free on writes". With the bias removed at a 3000-op warmup
the honest reading is ts(-) 111.2k against ts(+) 88.7k — so the row CAN show the cost, but only
under a warmup the harness does not perform.

**So the rule until someone fixes it: read `(-)` against `(+)` only from an isolated run of that
row, and only on a row whose columns differ by more than ~1.5x.** The corrected full matrix is in
this item for the rows where that holds.

Gates: `bun run check` 0 on the reverted tree; `git status` clean. No change shipped.

## 753 — `bench.ts` has the SAME one-call warmup and is not affected, and the reason is the unit size

**AUDIT. One comment added; no behaviour change.** Item 752 found `bench:usage`'s index columns
confounded by tier-up. `bench.ts`'s `best()` warms with a single call too — `f(); // warm` — and it
is the instrument every A/B this session has been measured on, so whether it shares the defect is
not an idle question.

### It does not, and the discriminator is measurable

`BENCH_REPS=1` (the warm call plus ONE timed run) against the default min-of-5:

| row                                    | REPS=1 | min of 5 | residual |
| -------------------------------------- | -----: | -------: | -------: |
| `count 3-hop`                          |  353.3 |    312.5 |    1.13x |
| `query: project the element [ts lazy]` |    7.9 |      6.6 |    1.20x |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter`              |   44.6 |     40.9 |    1.09x |

So one warm call leaves **9-20%** in the first timed run — not nothing. Two things make it harmless
where the same pattern was fatal in `bench-usage`:

1. **The unit is a whole query over the fixture**, not one small operation. One call of `count
3-hop` runs the entire pipeline over 200,000 vertices; one call of `INSERT (:Event …)` does
   almost nothing. The same line of code is a real warmup in one harness and a no-op in the other.
2. **The min discards it, and every column pays it identically.** Each engine gets its own warm call
   and its own min, so an engine-vs-engine ratio is not a warmth comparison. `bench-usage`'s bias
   was _between_ the two cells being compared and its best-of-batches could not reach across them.

That second point is the one that matters, and it is why **every alternated A/B in this session
stands**: each arm ran in its own process with its own warm call and its own min-of-5, so the two
arms were at the same warmth by construction. The defect at 752 required comparing two columns
measured at _different_ warmth inside one process, which an alternated per-build A/B never does.

### The generalisable rule

A one-call warmup is adequate or not depending on **how much work one call does**, and a warming
bias only distorts a comparison when the two things compared sit at **different warmth**. Both
halves have to hold before a residual matters: `bench.ts` has a 9-20% residual and sound
comparisons; `bench-usage` has a 26-52% residual and unsound ones.

The note is in `bench.ts` rather than only here, because the live risk is someone reading item 752
and "fixing" this file — or, worse, discounting the session's measurements on the strength of 752.

### What stays open from 752

Why a discarded first batch (5,000 operations for a `grows` row, since those are fixed-count rather
than time-boxed) warms _less reliably_ than 3,000 explicit operations is still unexplained. The
difference in setup is that the explicit warmup ran once on its own graph before both columns, while
a discarded batch runs inside each column on a freshly loaded graph — so a graph-shaped inline cache
is the obvious suspect and is not evidence. Left open rather than guessed, which is item 734's
standing lesson.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0.
Comment only.

## 754 — `bench:usage` rates do not COMPOSE across rows: the interleaved pair is 1.34-1.56x faster than its own two halves

**NEGATIVE RESULT, short. No change.** A third limit on this harness, found while looking for an
engine target in it, and recorded because the inference it invites — "interleaving is free" — is one
a reader would otherwise draw from the matrix.

### The contradiction

Three rows run byte-identical queries on identical keys:

| row                               | query                                                  |  ts(+) |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | -----: |
| `read: point lookup`              | `MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = $n RETURN u.score AS s` | 927.3k |
| `write: property update`          | `MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = $n SET u.score = $v`    | 293.6k |
| `interleaved: write + point read` | **both of the above, in sequence**                     | 347.3k |

Neither declares `units`, so the interleaved row reports PAIRS per second. One pair therefore costs
**2.88 µs**, while its two halves cost **1.08 + 3.41 = 4.48 µs** measured alone — the pair is
**1.56x faster than the sum of its own parts.** Using the warmest write figure this item produced
(360.0k at a 1000 ms box) the gap narrows to 1.34x and does not close.

### What it is not

- **Not different work.** The query texts are identical and the keys are the same distribution
  (`user${i % GRAPH}`, the read offset by one).
- **Not laziness.** `@lenke/gql`'s `query` returns `R[]`, so `void e.query(..)` materializes; the
  unindexed read row's 455 µs an operation is real work.
- **Not index degradation under repeated writes.** That was the hypothesis — the standalone write
  row performs ~2x more writes per box than the interleaved one, and `score` IS indexed, so
  degradation would depress exactly the row that looks depressed. The box sweep refutes it: longer
  boxes are FASTER, not slower (276.2k at 50 ms, 328.8k at 250 ms, 360.0k at 1000 ms), which is
  warming again and the opposite of degradation.

### What it is, and the rule

The rows are independently warmed cells, each with its own pilot and its own batches, and the matrix
is built to span five orders of magnitude rather than to support arithmetic between cells. **So a
rate from one row may not be composed with a rate from another**, and the interleaved rows cannot be
read as "the pair costs its parts plus a penalty".

Why the pair comes out FASTER rather than merely incomparable is unexplained, and is left that way:
the box sweep shows the per-cell rate is a function of how many operations the cell got through, and
the interleaved cell gets through half as many of each query — which predicts it should be SLOWER,
not faster. So the mechanism is not simply warming either. Item 734's lesson applies: a measured gap
with no cause beats a guessed cause.

**Together with items 752 and 753 this closes what `bench:usage` supports**: not `(-)` against `(+)`
on a row whose columns are within ~1.5x (752), and not one row's rate against another's (754). What
it does support is one engine against another within a single cell, which is what its biggest
recorded figures are, and which nothing here disturbs.

Gates: no change to gate. `git status` clean.

## 755 — I re-priced frontier `sum`, which `CLOSED.md` forbids by name; the figure is 34x and the search terms are the fix

**RE-PRICED REFUTED GROUND. No change but the index.** Item 419 ends with: _"the native frontier
`sum` is refuted and `CLOSED.md` says in as many words: **do not re-price frontier `sum` as a
target**."_ I priced it anyway. The useful parts are the number, which is larger than the one on
record, and the reason my search did not find the refutation.

### What the measurement said

`AggFn` looked like an enum with an uncovered variant — 38 `AggFn::Count` mentions in `fastpath.rs`
against 54 for Sum/Min/Max/Avg, so the coverage question was which _shapes_ each reaches. In-process,
200,000 vertices of degree 5, identical 3-chain, varying only the aggregate:

| query                             |        ms |
| --------------------------------- | --------: |
| `count(*)`                        |       4.7 |
| `count(d.age)`                    |       4.7 |
| `min(d.age)`                      |       5.2 |
| **`sum(d.age)`**                  | **177.3** |
| **`avg(d.age)`**                  | **178.3** |
| 1-hop `sum(x.age)` (for contrast) |       5.5 |

**34x between `min` and `sum` on the same shape**, and the 1-hop sum is fast, so it is specifically
the multi-hop case. It also looked implementable: the sweep already builds `ways[]`, so
`Σ ways[d] × age(d)` is one weighted pass.

### Why it is refused, which the code says twice

- `try_frontier_multi_agg`: _"`count` folds the per-node multiplicities because it does not care
  about order, and `min`/`max` ignore multiplicity entirely. `sum`/`avg` would have to add a value
  `c` times in an order the general path does not promise."_
- `try_frontier_prop_agg`: _"SUM/AVG would change the summation order."_

Floating-point addition is not associative and byte-identity is a hard invariant, so
`Σ ways[d] × age(d)` is not the same f64 as the general path's path-order addition. The weighted
pass I had in mind is precisely the thing that breaks it. Items 376 and 419 settled this on both
engines.

The hazard note I _did_ find first pointed the other way and nearly misled me: _"DO NOT add `Sum` to
`try_frontier_prop_agg` while it sits earlier in the chain"_ reads as a PRECEDENCE problem, and item
375 has since moved `try_scan_num_agg` above it (verified: `exec.rs` 1663 before 1671), so that
precondition is now inverted and the note looks satisfied. It is not the blocker. The blocker is one
level up and unaffected by ordering.

### 🛑 The figure that is new, and worth having anyway

`CLOSED.md` prices this decision at **2.5x on hops** — a one-hop figure. On a 3-chain it is **34x**
(177.3 against 5.2). That is not a reason to reopen it: the contract is the contract, and
`order-is-unspecified` plus the summation-order rule are load-bearing. But a reasoned decline is
worth more with its true price attached, the same point item 743 made about `Dir::Both`, and 2.5x
understates what byte-identity costs here by an order of magnitude.

### What actually failed: my search terms, not the record

I checked `CLOSED.md` before implementing — correctly — and grepped `weighted sweep`, `chain sum`,
`sum over a chain`, `multi-hop sum`. All empty. The record's vocabulary is **"frontier"**, and a
measurement does not suggest that word: the thing I measured was a 3-hop CHAIN, and only the code
calls its endpoint set a frontier.

What found it was the CODE's doc chain — `try_frontier_prop_agg`'s note → item 376 → item 419 —
reached by grepping `AggFn::Sum` in `fastpath.rs`. **For "has this lever been tried", the fast path's
own doc comment is the better index than `CLOSED.md` keywords**, because the comment sits on the gate
you are about to change and cannot be missed by vocabulary.

So this item adds the missing terms deliberately — **chain sum, multi-hop sum, 3-chain sum,
sum(d.age) over a chain, weighted sweep** — so the next grep in any of them lands here and then on
376/419.

Gates: no code change. `git status` clean; the probe example was deleted.

## 756 — `count(DISTINCT y)` over `->{1,2}` ERRORS where its `MATCH WALK` twin answers in 0.5 ms, and the gate is stricter than its own argument

**MEASURED. No change — the widening it suggests needs a correctness proof this item does not
have.** Item 374 left a note that `try_varlen_distinct_count` and `try_varlen_distinctby_count`
"decline their own shapes even unlabelled". Following the method that worked at item 755 — read the
fast path's own doc before measuring — explains it, and measuring it turns up something sharper than
slowness.

### What the gate says, and what it does

The path answers `count(DISTINCT endpoint)` by multi-source BFS in O(V+E) instead of enumerating
every path. Its TRAIL region is `max <= 1`, and item 68 (`fastpath_fuzz`, seed 3249) is why: on two
nodes and one edge, `(x)-[:R]-{2,3}(y)` returns NO rows as a trail — length 2 needs two distinct
edges — while the BFS walks `a -> b -> a` and reports 2.

**TRAIL is the DEFAULT mode.** So the shape a user writes declines, and only an explicit
`MATCH WALK` reaches the fast path. That is the whole of item 374's note.

### The cliff, at 50,000 vertices of degree 5

| query                                                     | result                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,2}(y) … count(DISTINCT y)` | **E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED** (27.8 ms to fail) |
| `MATCH WALK (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,2}(y) … same`         | **0.5 ms** → 49,657                        |
| `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,1}(y) … same`              | 0.5 ms → 49,657                            |
| `MATCH WALK … ->{1,3}(y) … same`                          | 0.7 ms → 49,657                            |
| `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,3}(y) … same`              | **E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED**                   |

This is not a perf gap, it is a **failure**: the default spelling blows the 1,000,000-row trail
limit on a graph of 50,000 nodes, while one keyword makes it sub-millisecond. `{1,1}` answers because
`max <= 1` is inside the safe region, which confirms the mechanism from the outside.

Every spelling that answers agrees on **49,657**, so on this fixture the trail and walk
distinct-endpoint sets coincide — which is what makes the next section tempting and is not proof of
anything.

### 🛑 The gate is stricter than the argument in its own doc, and I could not close the gap

The doc argues: _"a node with ANY walk of length `L ≤ max` has shortest distance ≤ L, so a `min ≤ 1`
reachability is the same set whether paths are walks or trails (the shortest path is simple, reusing
no edge)"_ — a **`min <= 1`** condition. The gate then implements **`max <= 1`**, which is far
narrower, and item 68's counterexample had `min = 2`, so `min <= 1` would already have excluded it.

That looks like a free widening worth the cliff above. **I am not making it**, because trying to
construct the correctness argument produced a case I cannot dismiss: undirected `x—y`, one edge,
`{1,3}` from `x`. A WALK of length 2 reaches `x` itself, so the walk endpoint set is `{x, y}`; the
set of nodes at shortest distance in `1..=3` is `{y}`, since `x` is at distance 0. If the BFS
computes the latter — which is what the doc says it computes — then it and the true WALK answer
differ at `min = 1`, and the equivalence the doc asserts does not hold in the direction that matters.

Either my reading of the BFS is wrong or the doc's argument is loose. Settling it needs the actual
BFS read line by line plus a `fastpath_fuzz` run over that fixture shape, which is more than this
item did. So: **a candidate widening with a measured 0.5 ms-against-failure payoff, blocked on a
semantics question, with the exact fixture to test first written down.**

### Why the note said "even unlabelled"

Item 373/374's family note says a fix here "needs a MIXED fixture to be measured honestly and a
mixed fixture to be TESTED at all". That is true of the LABEL-filtered variants and is a separate
blocker: `social_store` gives every node `["Person"]` and every edge `"KNOWS"`, so a label or type
test excludes nothing (item 721's trap). None of the figures above depend on a label, which is why
they could be taken at all.

Gates: no code change. `git status` clean; the probe example was deleted.

## 757 — the widening item 756 floated is REFUTED on two nodes and one edge, and the doc that suggested it is now a test

**REFUTED AND PINNED. Doc corrected, one test added; no behaviour change.** Item 756 measured a real
cliff — `count(DISTINCT y)` over `->{1,2}` fails with `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` at 50,000 vertices while
its `MATCH WALK` twin answers in 0.5 ms — and floated widening the fast path's trail region from
`max <= 1` to `min <= 1` on the strength of the fast path's own doc. It left the semantics question
open with the fixture to test first. This tests it.

### My reading of the BFS was wrong; the doc's argument was wrong too, differently

756 suspected the BFS computed shortest distance, which would make it wrong for WALK as well.
Reading it line by line: the `min <= 1` arm sets `reached[nbr] = true` on **every encounter** and
uses `visited` only to gate RE-EXPANSION, and the `min >= 2` arm walks level sets. Both admit a node
arrived at by a walk longer than its shortest path, which is exactly WALK semantics. **The code is
right and the doc's "nodes at shortest distance" phrasing was the loose part.**

That relocated the question rather than answering it, and the answer is a counterexample. Two nodes,
one edge, `(x:S)-[:R]-{1,3}(y)`:

| spelling        | distinct endpoints | rows |
| --------------- | -----------------: | ---: |
| `MATCH WALK`    |              **2** |    3 |
| default (TRAIL) |              **1** |    1 |
| both at `{1,1}` |                  1 |    — |

A WALK returns to the source by re-crossing the single edge; a TRAIL cannot. So the source is a walk
endpoint and not a trail one, and the sets differ at `min = 1`.

**The doc's argument fails on exactly one word.** It said walk and trail reachability coincide for
`min <= 1` because "the shortest path is simple, reusing no edge" — true, but the shortest path is an
admissible answer only when its length is **`>= min`**, and for a SOURCE on a cycle that length is
**0**. Item 68's counterexample had `min = 2` and so looked like the only hazard; this one has
`min = 1` and `max = 3`.

So `max <= 1` is the trail region and the gate was right all along: at one hop no edge can be
reused, which the same fixture confirms (both spellings answer 1 at `{1,1}`).

### The guard is a test, not the corrected comment

The widening produces a **wrong answer** (2 against 1), not a slow one, so a comment cannot refuse
it. `a_trail_distinct_endpoint_count_is_not_the_walks_at_min_one` pins both halves — that the two
spellings DIFFER at `{1,3}` and AGREE at `{1,1}` — and **the mutation is the widening itself**:
`PathMode::Trail => max <= 1` relaxed to `true` fails that test and nothing else in 1,223. Verified,
not assumed.

That is the mirror of `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`: a route choice is answer-equivalent and needs a
perf A/B, while a SEMANTICS choice needs a pinned answer. This one is the second kind, and item 756
had correctly declined to make it without one.

### What remains true from 756

The cliff is real and unaddressed: the DEFAULT spelling of a distinct-endpoint count over a
var-length hop enumerates and can exhaust the trail limit, where the `WALK` spelling is
sub-millisecond. What is now settled is that the cheap fix is not available — a trail-correct
distinct-endpoint count past one hop needs per-path edge sets, which is not a BFS, as the fast
path's own doc says. Anyone revisiting it should price the general path instead of widening the
gate.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` **1223** + 13 + 725 pass, 0
fail; `fastpath_fuzz` 1 pass; the seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun
run check` 0.

**RE-PRICED AND SIZED. No change — the refactor is 52 match arms and is not being half-done at a
tick boundary.** Five consecutive candidates this stretch turned out already closed (751, 755, 756,
757, and the `element_id` ordering below), so this tick enumerated the open set instead of sampling
it, using the index that has actually worked: **the code's own doc comments**, not `CLOSED.md`

| hop `max(b.s)` on a string/dict column (**422**) | 14.172 against 9.372, **1.5x**                                 | deliberately left: it folds path MULTIPLICITIES, and item 376's `count` yes / `sum` never rule must be re-read for a dictionary first                                                    |

Three, across both engines. That is the strongest evidence yet for what item 731 claimed and 739/740
corrected: the reachable space really is worked out, and the remainder is contract-blocked,
multi-tick, or rare.

### Item 457's target re-priced, because a price can die (739)

| shape                                | ns/row now | item 457 |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------: | -------: |
| `count(a.age)` — the floor           |       0.46 |     0.47 |
| `count(abs(a.age))` VECTORIZED       |       4.11 |      4.8 |
| `count(round(a.age))` VECTORIZED     |       4.75 |      4.3 |
| **`count(power(a.age, 2))` GENERIC** |  **43.45** | **45.2** |
| `count(coalesce(a.age, 0))`          |   **3.22** |     37.5 |

**The generic overhead stands at 43.45 ns/row**, and `coalesce` has since dropped **11.6x** — which
is the item at `CLOSED.md`:4218 shipping two coalesce-specific wins (the identity, 8.9x, and the
dispatch resolved once, 1.67x). So the function-specific work landed and the GENERAL resolver did

would give every non-vectorized function. So item 457's target stands with its size now known: the
per-row `call_scalar_checked(name, …)` string match is ~15 ns of the ~27 ns fixed overhead."_

`power` is now the shape that exposes it, since `coalesce` no longer does. Subtracting `pow`'s own
~12 ns leaves ~31 ns of fixed overhead on `power`, of which ~15 is the name match — so hoisting it

### The work, sized rather than guessed

The string match is not in `call_scalar_checked` (134 lines, 5 grouped arms over 55 names — mostly
null/arity pre-checks). It delegates at its last line to **`call_scalar(name, args)`: 388 lines, 52
string match arms.** So the change is:

1. an enum of 52 variants,
2. `resolve(name) -> Option<ScalarId>` called ONCE per `Expr::Call`, not per row,
3. 52 arm patterns changed from a string to a variant, with `name` still threaded through for the
   error messages that interpolate it,
4. the evaluator's `Expr::Call` arm resolving before the row loop.

Mechanical, no semantics, no contract exposure — but 52 arms is not a thing to leave half-converted
at a tick boundary, and a typo in one arm is a silently wrong function. It gets its own tick with

## 759 — the two-argument numerics are vectorized: `power` 3.33x, `mod` 3.55x. And item 457's PREMISE is refuted — the name dispatch is worth ZERO

**SHIPPED, and it closes item 457 by refuting it rather than by doing it.** Item 758 sized 457's
resolver hoist at 52 match arms and handed it this tick. I built the whole thing, measured it, and
it bought nothing — which is what found the real lever sitting next to it.

### The refactor, built and rejected

The hoist as 758 specified it: a `ScalarId` enum of one variant per ARM (50, not 52 — the 92 names
the library accepts collapse to 50 arms), `resolve_scalar(name) -> Option<ScalarId>` called once per
`Expr::Call`, all 50 arm patterns converted from string literals to variants, the five pre-check
passes in `call_scalar_checked` re-keyed on the id, and the evaluator resolving above the row loop.
The arm BODIES were untouched: the conversion was driven from a script that scans the match with a
depth tracker and replaces only the pattern text, asserting it finds exactly 50 arms and 92 names
with no name in two of them. It compiled on the first build and all 1,223 tests passed.

**It measured zero.** `count(power(a.age, 2))` at 200,000 rows: **43.45 ns/row before (item 758's
figure), 44.04 after.** Controls flat.

And the hoisted code IS the measured path — checked positively (items 721-723), not inferred:
deleting `"power"` from `resolve_scalar`'s arm makes the probe's assertion fire with
`returned Num(0.0)`. So the 44 ns is real and the name match is not in it.

**Reverted.** A 300-line mechanical refactor that buys nothing is review surface for nothing; the
copy is in the scratchpad and the numbers are here.

### What that refutes, which is bigger than item 457

Item 457 priced "the per-row `call_scalar_checked(name, …)` string match" at ~15 of ~27 ns.
Item 459 then sized it at **~20 ns a row** by bypassing the generic path for `sqrt`
(32.4 -> 12.5 ms at 1,000,000 rows) and both it and item 458 credit their wins — which are real —
to "matching the function NAME as a STRING against dozens of arms".

That attribution is wrong. Those bypasses removed the whole generic per-row path: the `Vec<Value>`
argument buffer rebuilt per row, both operands read back out of it, the boxed output. **The name
match is a length switch over a handful of candidates and costs ~0.** rustc does not compile a
50-arm string match the way the comments assume.

So three audit items and two code comments named the string dispatch as the cost, and the one
experiment that isolates it says it is free. The wins stand; the explanation does not.

### The real lever, which the refutation pointed at

`count(nullif(a.age, 7))` — a function that does nothing but two null checks and a clone — cost
**28 ns a row**. That is the generic path's fixed cost with no arithmetic in it, and it is where
`power` was. Items 458 and 459 took `coalesce` and the twenty-one UNARY numerics out of it. The
**two-argument numerics were still in it**: `power`, `log`, `mod`, `atan2`.

`binary_num_fn(name) -> Option<fn(f64, f64) -> f64>` and `eval_binary_num` are the binary twins of
459's pair, plus a typed-slice arm: when both operand columns are `Col::Num`, read the `f64` slices
and skip two `Value` boxings a row.

**Min of three ALTERNATED rounds, two saved binaries so no rebuild sits between arms** (200,000
rows, reps 9):

| shape                                     | before | after |     ratio |
| ----------------------------------------- | -----: | ----: | --------: |
| `count(power(a.age, 2))`                  |  42.88 | 12.88 | **3.33x** |
| `count(power(a.age, a.age))` two slots    |  43.77 | 13.78 | **3.18x** |
| `count(mod(a.age, 7))`                    |  34.91 |  9.83 | **3.55x** |
| CONTROL `count(abs(a.age))` vectorized    |   4.03 |  4.05 |     1.00x |
| CONTROL `count(round(a.age))` vectorized  |   4.53 |  4.55 |     1.00x |
| CONTROL `count(coalesce(a.age, 0))`       |   3.10 |  3.15 |     0.98x |
| CONTROL `count(nullif(a.age, 7))` generic |  28.37 | 28.48 |     1.00x |
| CONTROL `count(a.age)` the floor          |   0.51 |  0.55 |     0.93x |

Five controls. `abs`/`round` are vectorized and cannot enter this dispatch at all; `nullif` is
generic and two-argument but not numeric, so it is the control that isolates "two-argument" from
"numeric"; the floor has no `Expr::Call`. Its 0.93x is 0.04 ns on a sub-nanosecond row.

The typed-slice arm is 18.92 -> 12.95 of that (same round, controls flat), and it is NOT the
broadcast of the literal: `power(a.age, a.age)`, two real slot columns, measures the same as
`power(a.age, 2)`. What is left above the floor is `powf` itself — `mod`, the cheap operation in
the family, lands at 9.83 against a vectorized unary floor of ~4.5.

### The regression sweep, and the flag it retracted

`query_bench` and `value_bench` built from both arms and compared row by row. **95 comparable
query rows**; the only non-noise flag was `query/perrow | element p` at **1.12x** (83,070 ->
92,764 us), which is the layout-shift shape the project notes already describe for `exec::pull`.
Three ALTERNATED rounds of that case retract it: **1.00x** (before 83,109 / 84,166 / 85,288
against after 83,384 / 84,628 / 85,146 — the ranges interleave), with `element r` 1.01x and
`count(*)` 1.00x beside it. `scalar p.age` reads 1.07x with overlapping ranges, inside the ~10%
noise floor. The other six flags in the single-run sweep were all 0.40 -> 0.30 on sub-nanosecond
rows. `value_bench`'s six rows are flat over two alternated rounds (1.00x, 1.00x, 1.01x, 1.00x,
1.00x; the sixth, the map-graph scalar twin, was flat in the single-run pass).

A first version of that sweep script reported "0 comparable rows" for both groups and exited 0 —
a vacuous pass, which is item 746's defect in a new instrument. It now refuses to pass on too few
rows, and the second failure it reported ("only 6 rows" for `value_bench`) was its own threshold
and not the parser: that group really does emit six.

### Teeth, labelled in advance

Three mutants, each under `timeout 600` + a 16G cgroup cap with swap off. The cap was proved to
kill first: an allocator bomb dies on SIGKILL, a bare spin loop on 124.

| mutant                                 | predicted | got           |                                                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------- | --------- | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| operands swapped in the typed arm      | FAIL      | FAIL, 4 tests | as predicted — incl. `signed_zero_folds_in_atan2`                                               |
| the typed arm deleted                  | SURVIVE   | SURVIVE       | as predicted: a route choice is answer-equivalent, so its guard is the A/B above and not a test |
| `zero_folded` replaced by the identity | FAIL      | **SURVIVE**   | **not as predicted**                                                                            |

The third is the one worth reading. `atan2` is the only function here whose result can see the sign
of a zero operand, and `broadcast` turns a `-0.0` literal into a `Col::Num`, so the fold looked
reachable. A panic probe says both `atan2` tests DO reach the typed arm — and the mutant still
survives, because the `-0.0` is already gone: the parser folds it in a literal and ingest folds it
in a stored property, which `a_negative_zero_literal_beside_a_column_still_folds_in_atan2` now
pins END TO END with a literal operand, a column operand, and a stored `-0.0`. So the fold is
**unreachable and kept anyway**, as a statement of the rule, on the precedent of `round`'s
`!is_finite()` digit-count guard — and the code comment now says which it is. A survivor is
EQUIVALENT, a SKIP, an INERT path or a GAP, and the difference is only visible if you go and look.

### Not done

`nullif` at 28 ns is the next instance of the same shape, and so is every other non-vectorized
generic function. The lever is not the dispatch — it is the per-row `Vec<Value>` argument buffer
and the boxed output column, for which the general fix is a two-argument vectorized form keyed on
the ARGUMENT kinds rather than a per-function arm. Nobody should re-derive the dispatch price: it
is zero, measured twice here.

## 760 — the TS twin of 759: a scalar CALL cost 35-43 ns a row over the floor, flat across every family. Numerics now 1.93-2.24x

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 759 found the native engine's generic scalar-call cost and
refuted the explanation everyone had been using for it. This asks the same question of the pure-TS
engine, and the answer is the same shape with one part INVERTED.

### The price, and what makes it the machinery rather than the function

200,000 vertices, min of 9, `count(a.age)` as the floor (it has no `Expr::Call` at all):

| shape                     | ns/row | over the floor |
| ------------------------- | -----: | -------------: |
| `count(a.age)` FLOOR      |  20.93 |              — |
| `count(abs(a.age))` unary |  63.27 |          42.34 |
| `count(power(a.age, 2))`  |  64.18 |          43.25 |
| `count(mod(a.age, 7))`    |  58.76 |          37.84 |
| `count(nullif(a.age, 7))` |  55.78 |          34.85 |
| `count(upper(a.name))`    |  85.36 |          64.43 |

**A call more than triples the cost of a row, and it is flat across unary, binary, generic and
string.** The giveaway is that `nullif` — which `callScalar` reaches only after missing
`UNARY_NUM`, `UNARY_STR` and `BINARY_NUM` — is CHEAPER than `abs`, which hits the first table it
tries. So it is not dispatch depth. The per-row work that does not vary by function is: a fresh
argument ARRAY from `args.map((f) => f(env))`, three dictionary misses inside
`assertScalarArgTypes`, the walk down the dispatch chain, and a read of `env.graph.limits`.

**Where it INVERTS 759.** In Rust, hoisting the name match alone measured exactly zero, because
rustc compiles a 50-arm string match to a length switch. A JS `Record` lookup on a megamorphic
string key is not that, and neither is a per-row array allocation. Same question, same shape of
answer — "it is the machinery" — but the native half of the machinery that is free is the half
that costs here. Do not carry either conclusion across without measuring.

### The change

`unaryNumCall(f, a)` and `binaryNumCall(f, a, b)` in `executor/scalars.ts`, resolved in
`compileFunc` while the QUERY compiles. Both are **module-scope factories**, not closures built
inside `compileFunc`: a walk inlined into a returned closure gave unrelated queries a new slow mode
once already (the TS closure-size finding), and this is the same hazard.

`SCALAR_NEEDS_ARG_ASSERT` is the gate. The specialized path skips `assertScalarArgTypes`, so it
refuses any name whose arguments that function validates by POSITION — and the set is BUILT from
the same three tables the assert reads (`STR_ARG_POSITIONS`, `NUM_ARG_POSITIONS`, `POLY_STR_LIST`),
so adding a position there cannot leave it stale. No member of `UNARY_NUM`/`BINARY_NUM` is in it
today; the gate is there so that adding one does not have to be noticed.

### The A/B, and the bias its first version had

Both dists in ONE process, alternated round by round — item 628's shape, because a separate process
carries its own JIT state and thermal history. Each arm asserted to BE the code it claims before
any timing (`binaryNumCall` present in post, absent in pre), per item 747's rule.

| shape                             |   pre |  post |     ratio |
| --------------------------------- | ----: | ----: | --------: |
| `count(abs(a.age))`               | 51.98 | 25.16 | **2.07x** |
| `count(sqrt(a.age))`              | 48.90 | 24.94 | **1.96x** |
| `count(power(a.age, 2))`          | 47.60 | 24.68 | **1.93x** |
| `count(mod(a.age, 7))`            | 53.64 | 23.98 | **2.24x** |
| `count(atan2(a.age, 2))`          | 54.08 | 32.58 |     1.66x |
| CONTROL `count(nullif(a.age, 7))` | 63.39 | 54.56 |     1.16x |
| CONTROL `count(upper(a.name))`    | 80.10 | 82.43 |     0.97x |
| CONTROL `count(round(a.age, 1))`  | 66.82 | 61.98 |     1.08x |
| CONTROL `count(a.age)`, no Call   | 19.87 | 20.14 |     0.99x |

Four controls, each unreachable for a different reason: `nullif` is generic AND two-argument (so it
isolates "two-argument" from "numeric"), `upper` is the string family and is gated out,
`round(x, d)` is two-argument numeric but lives in `callScalar`'s switch rather than in
`BINARY_NUM`, and the floor has no `Expr::Call`.

**The first version of this probe ran the arms in a fixed order and its own unreachable controls
read 1.13x and 1.16x.** That is a warming bias: with a fixed order the second arm always runs on a
warmer cache and a hotter JIT, which is item 753's rule applied in the other direction — a warming
bias distorts only when the compared things sit at different warmth, and a fixed order puts them
there by construction. Swapping the order every round cancels it (floor 0.99x, `upper` 0.97x).
The residual 1.16x on `nullif` is probably real and in the change's favour: in the post dist only
four function shapes ever flow through `callScalar`, so its inline caches are less polluted.

### Teeth: the fuzzers caught what 2,586 unit tests did not

Four mutants, labelled in advance, each rebuilt into the dist first (a mutant only in `src` is a
mutant that never ran) and each run under `timeout` + a 16G cgroup cap with swap off.

| mutant                                     | predicted | gql tests | fuzzers  |                          |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------- | --------- | -------- | ------------------------ |
| binary operands swapped                    | FAIL      | FAIL      | FAIL     | as predicted             |
| binary 2nd arg's null guard dropped        | FAIL      | **pass**  | **FAIL** | as predicted             |
| unary null guard dropped                   | FAIL      | FAIL      | FAIL     | as predicted             |
| the `SCALAR_NEEDS_ARG_ASSERT` gate emptied | SURVIVE   | pass      | pass     | as predicted, EQUIVALENT |

The second row is the one to keep: **a null second argument to a binary numeric function throwing
instead of propagating passes all 2,586 unit tests and is caught only by the byte-identity
fuzzers.** That also answers the question a green suite cannot — whether the fuzzers REACH the new
path. They do. The fourth is equivalent by construction (no numeric function is in the assert
tables), which is why it was predicted to survive rather than read as a gap.

### One instrument note

The pre-change dist was copied to `packages/gql/dist-pre760` so Node resolution could still find
`@lenke/*` through the workspace root — and `bun run check` then FAILED with 40 lint errors inside
it, because the ignore list names `dist` and not that. The gate was reporting my scratch directory,
not my change. Worth knowing before chasing it: a built artifact parked under a non-ignored name
breaks the lint gate in a way that reads like the change broke it.

### The sweep

`bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`, which is the right regression pass for a
change to the TS COMPILER: the hazard is not the changed query but closure shape giving unrelated
ones a new slow mode. **0 groups disagree on the ANSWER**, and the two groups over 2x are both
recorded as CORRECT rather than outstanding — `label on start: redundant vs absent` (item 325 says
so in as many words) and `a product's one-sided predicate: comma vs MATCH MATCH` (item 285). The
in-process controls are the other half of this: `upper` at 0.97x and the no-`Expr::Call` floor at
0.99x ARE unrelated queries running beside the change.

### Not done

`upper` at 64 ns over the floor is now the most expensive row here, and the string family is gated
out because `assertScalarArgTypes` validates its argument positions. Folding that assert INTO a
specialized closure is the same change one layer harder: the `dataException` messages are
byte-identical cross-engine, so the fold has to reproduce them exactly. `nullif` and the rest of
the generic path still allocate the per-row argument array — removing that needs `callScalar`'s
signature to stop taking an array, which is a wider change than this one.

## 761 — the one-argument STRING family: `char_length` 2.03x, `lower` 1.64x, `upper` 1.49x. The cost that remains is the `toUpperCase`, not the engine

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 760 specialized the numeric families and left the string family on
the general path, because `assertScalarArgTypes` validates its argument POSITIONS and the
specialized path skips that pass. This one does not skip it — it moves the check INTO the closure.

### The row that separates machinery from work

`upper` was the most expensive row 760 left behind, at ~64 ns over the floor. But it also
allocates a new string per row, so that figure is machinery PLUS real work. `char_length` is the
row that splits them: gated out for exactly the same reason, and it returns a NUMBER, so it
allocates nothing.

| shape                                | ns/row | over its floor |
| ------------------------------------ | -----: | -------------: |
| `count(a.name)` STRING FLOOR         |  18.67 |              — |
| `count(char_length(a.name))`         |  53.86 |      **35.19** |
| `count(upper(a.name))`               |  65.16 |          46.49 |
| `count(lower(a.name))`               |  62.60 |          43.93 |
| `count(starts_with(a.name, 'name'))` |  80.90 |          62.23 |
| `count(abs(a.age))` after 760        |  24.94 |           5.13 |

**35.19 ns is machinery — the same figure item 760 measured for the numerics — and only ~11 ns of
`upper`'s 46 is the `toUpperCase` itself.** That 11 ns is not available to any change here, which
is why `upper` improves less than `char_length` does and why the headline on this family is
smaller than the raw row suggested.

### The change, and why it needs its own factory

`unaryStrCall(name, f, a)` rather than a reuse of `unaryNumCall`: this family IS argument-checked
by position, so the check moves into the closure instead of being skipped. `SCALAR_ASSERTS_STR0_ONLY`
admits only names whose ENTIRE positional check is "position 0 is a string" — `left`/`right`/
`substring` also check a numeric position, and `reverse`/`size`/`cardinality` accept a list and
raise a different message. It is derived from the same three tables the assert reads, so a new
position cannot leave it stale.

`str()` is not called on the argument: its type has just been proven to be `string`, and `str`'s
fallback for one is `String(v)`, which is identity on a primitive.

### A duplicated contract string, and the doc comment that claimed a test it did not have

The first version spelled the `dataException` message a second time inside the new closure, with a
comment saying _"A test pins the two spellings together."_ **It did not. Nothing pinned that text
anywhere** — `grep` finds it in exactly two places, this engine and `exec::scalar.rs`, and the only
`upper` test asserted `toThrow()` with no argument.

So: one `requiresStringMessage(name)` helper, used by the positional assert AND the specialized
closure, and a test that pins the exact text through BOTH paths — `upper(1)` (specialized at
compile time) and `replace(1, 'a', 'b')` (general, three string positions). The message is a
cross-engine contract, matching native's `call_scalar_checked`, so a drift between the two TS paths
would have been invisible to every test that existed.

### The A/B, and the flag it retracted

Both dists in one process, order swapped every round, each arm asserted to BE the code it claims.
THREE runs:

| shape                                 | ratio (3 runs)          |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `count(char_length(a.name))`          | **2.03 / 2.19 / 2.21x** |
| `count(lower(a.name))`                | **1.64 / 1.82 / 1.81x** |
| `count(upper(a.name))`                | **1.49 / 1.65 / 1.58x** |
| CONTROL `count(starts_with(…))`       | 1.08 / 1.10 / 1.03x     |

`byte_length` is the sharpest control here: the gate ADMITS it, but it is not in `UNARY_STR` (it

**The single-process probe had flagged `starts_with` at 1.26x SLOWER** — a control this change

## 762 — skipping the positional argument assert is worth NOTHING, and the harness that said otherwise was measuring itself. 760/761 re-confirmed on a fixed instrument

**REFUTED, REVERTED, and the instrument it was measured on is now characterized.** The change
was built, measured three ways, and is not in the tree. What this tick actually produced is a
correction to how every TS A/B in this session was read.

### The target, and the diagnosis that looked right

Items 760/761 left the general path paying ~35 ns a row for machinery. The decomposition pointed
at the positional assert: `starts_with` — two arguments WITH two asserted positions — cost 62 ns
a row over the string floor, while `nullif` — two arguments with NO asserted position — cost 35,
and `starts_with`'s own work is one `String.prototype.startsWith`. `assertScalarArgTypes` does
three dictionary lookups on a megamorphic string key per row (two `Record`s and a `Set`), and for
most functions all three MISS.

So: `callScalarUnasserted`, the assert-free half, with the compiler picking it once per
`Expr::Call` for any name the existing `SCALAR_NEEDS_ARG_ASSERT` gate does not contain — the same
split as the native engine's `call_scalar_checked` / `call_scalar_id` pair.

### What it measured, and the three readings that killed it

| instrument                                  | `nullif` | `round(x, d)` | `to_integer` | verdict         |
| ------------------------------------------- | -------: | ------------: | -----------: | --------------- |
| in-process, multi-shape, min-of-9           |    1.09x |         1.03x |        1.07x | inside noise    |
| one shape/process, median-of-plateau, run 1 |    1.25x |         0.97x |        1.07x | inconsistent    |
| the same, run 2                             |    1.06x |     **0.90x** |    **0.89x** | two rows SLOWER |

Three rows that take the IDENTICAL code path do not agree in sign. **The assert is not a
measurable cost.** Same shape of result as item 457: a dispatch cost that reads large in a
decomposition and vanishes when you remove it.

### The harness was flattering the change — on rows it could not reach

The in-process two-dist A/B (both dists in one process, order alternated) reported this for 762:

| row                                             |      ratio | can the change reach it?              |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ---------: | ------------------------------------- |
| `nullif` / `round` / `to_integer` — the TARGETS | 1.03-1.09x | yes                                   |
| CONTROL `starts_with`                           |  **1.56x** | **no** — keeps `callScalar` unchanged |
| CONTROL `byte_length`                           |  **1.47x** | **no**                                |
| CONTROL `substring`                             |  **1.23x** | **no**                                |

The controls moved four times as much as the targets, in the change's favour, which is impossible
as a per-row effect. The cause is the harness: in the PRE arm all nine query shapes funnel through
one `callScalar` call site; in the POST arm some of them are routed elsewhere, so the site left
behind is less polymorphic and its inline caches are cleaner. **A multi-shape in-process A/B
therefore cannot be trusted for any change that REDISTRIBUTES call sites** — which is every change
items 760, 761 and 762 made.

That also corrects item 760's own note. It read `nullif` at 1.16x on a row the change could not
reach and said the residual was "probably real and in the change's favour … its inline caches are
less polluted". The mechanism was right; calling it a real win was not. Here the same mechanism
produced 1.5x on rows nothing had touched.

### And `min` was the wrong estimator, in a way that was hiding the win

The per-rep series, 14 reps, one shape per process, `count(abs(a.age))`:

```
pre-760   128.8 87.0 98.4 98.9 90.7 83.9 80.3 85.9 83.4 83.8 87.0 89.4 83.5 51.9   -> min 51.9
post-761   58.8 32.4 25.4 24.8 17.7 17.0 17.1 16.9 18.1 16.6 16.5 16.9 21.4 22.2   -> min 16.5
```

**The pre arm plateaus at ~84 and produces ONE rep at 51.9, which is what `min` reports.** The post
arm is flat from rep 5 on, so `min` is a fair summary of it. The two arms were being estimated
differently, and the estimator was understating the gap — the opposite direction from the usual
worry about `min`.

`nullif` is worse: `119.1 96.1 126.8 49.3 44.9 45.9 60.6 83.1 82.5 82.9 81.7 81.6 78.7 78.3` —
it oscillates between a ~45 mode and a ~82 mode WITHIN one process. The general path is bimodal;
the no-`Expr::Call` floor (13.5-19.3) and the specialized closures (16.5-17.1) are not. The
difference is the per-row allocation: the general closure builds a fresh argument array for every
row, which is 200,000 arrays a rep, and the plateau is what that costs once the heap is working.
**Removing the bimodality is a second, qualitative benefit of 760/761 that none of the ratios
state.**

### The instrument that works, and what it says about 760/761

One shape per process (so no other shape pollutes the dispatch), 14 reps, the first three dropped
as warm-up (they are visibly the JIT tiering: 128 → 98 → 90), the MEDIAN of the rest, and the min
of that across three order-alternated rounds:

| shape                              | pre-760 | post-761 |     ratio |
| ---------------------------------- | ------: | -------: | --------: |
| `count(abs(a.age))` (760)          |   48.80 |    17.90 | **2.73x** |
| `count(char_length(a.name))` (761) |   49.00 |    19.60 | **2.50x** |
| `count(upper(a.name))` (761)       |   67.40 |    50.30 | **1.34x** |
| CONTROL `count(nullif(a.age, 7))`  |   53.40 |    54.20 |     0.99x |
| CONTROL `count(a.age)`, no Call    |   14.40 |    15.20 |     0.95x |

**Both controls land inside 5%, which no earlier instrument in this session managed.** And items
760 and 761 CONFIRM: `abs` 2.07x in-process against 2.73x isolated, `char_length` 2.03-2.21x
against 2.50x, `upper` 1.49-1.65x against 1.34x. So those entries' numbers were the right size and
in the right direction — the harness bias and the estimator bias pushed in opposite directions and

### Not done

The general path's ~35 ns is still there and the assert is not it. What remains in that closure is
the per-row argument ARRAY, the walk down `callScalar`'s dispatch chain, and a read of
`env.graph.limits`. The array is the one the bimodality points at, and the native engine's fix for
the same thing was to reuse ONE buffer across rows — which is safe there because Rust makes
retention explicit. Here `args` flows into `callExtendedScalar` and from there into
`callTemporalFn`, `callStringListFn` and `callListSetFn`, so a reused buffer needs all three
audited for retention first; an aliasing bug of that kind would be invisible to every test. That
audit is the next tick's work, not a guess to ship.

## 763 — ONE argument buffer instead of one per row: `nullif` 1.39-1.55x, `starts_with` 1.32-1.34x, and it is the lever 762's bimodality pointed at

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 762 refuted the assert as the general path's cost and left two
things behind: a per-row argument ARRAY, and the observation that this path is BIMODAL while the
specialized closures are flat. This is the fix the second of those pointed at.

### The audit that had to come first

The native engine's `Expr::Call` arm already reuses one `Vec` across rows and says why. Doing the
same in TypeScript is only safe if nothing retains the array — and in Rust that question answers
itself, while here it had to be checked. Every use of `args` at or below `callScalar`:

- `callScalar` itself: `const [a, b] = args`, `args.length`, `args.find(…)` for `coalesce` (which
  returns an ELEMENT), and `callExtendedScalar(name, args, limits)`.
- `callExtendedScalar`: `const [a, b] = args`, then forwards to the dispatchers.
- `callTemporalFn`: `args[0]`, `const [x, y] = args`.
- `callStringListFn`: `const [a, b] = args`, `args[1]`, `args[2]`.
- `callListSetFn`: `args[2]`.

**Nothing returns the array, stores it, or closes over it.** Re-entrancy cannot alias it either:
the buffer belongs to ONE compiled `Expr::Call`, and a nested call (`nullif(nullif(x, 7), 8)`) is
a different node with its own buffer — a node cannot appear inside its own argument subtree, so
the same buffer is never being filled twice at once. That reasoning is in the factory's doc
comment, because a future arm that DOES retain `args` turns this into a use-after-free in slow
motion: the value handed back would be rewritten on the next row, and a single-row result would
still look right.

### Measured on item 762's instrument, twice

One shape per PROCESS, 14 reps, first three dropped as warm-up, median of the rest, min across
three order-alternated rounds.

| shape                                            |    read 1 |    read 2 | ns saved |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------: | --------: | -------: |
| `count(nullif(a.age, 7))` 2 args                 | **1.55x** | **1.39x** |  21 / 15 |
| `count(starts_with(a.name, 'name'))` 2 args      | **1.32x** | **1.34x** |  17 / 18 |
| `count(byte_length(a.name))` 1 arg               |     1.15x | **1.32x** |  14 / 27 |
| `count(substring(a.name, 2))` 2 args             |     1.07x |     1.11x |  11 / 16 |
| `count(replace(a.name, 'name', 'x'))` 3 args     |     1.10x |     1.07x |  14 / 10 |
| CONTROL `count(abs(a.age))` specialized          |     0.95x |     0.99x |        — |
| CONTROL `count(char_length(a.name))` specialized |     1.01x |     0.99x |        — |
| CONTROL `count(a.age)`, no Call                  |     1.00x |     1.00x |        — |

**The saving is a near-constant 10-27 ns, so the RATIO falls as the function's own work rises** —
`substring` and `replace` have expensive bodies and move least, `nullif` does almost nothing and
moves most. That is the shape removing one allocation per row should have, and it is why the
headline figure depends entirely on which function you quote. The three controls are specialized
paths that never enter this factory; they do not move.

### Teeth, labelled in advance

| mutant                                                    | predicted | gql tests | fuzzers |                          |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | --------- | ------- | ------------------------ |
| the last slot left STALE (`i < n - 1`)                    | FAIL      | FAIL      | FAIL    | as predicted             |
| the buffer hoisted to MODULE scope (shared by every call) | FAIL      | FAIL      | FAIL    | as predicted             |
| allocate per row again                                    | SURVIVE   | pass      | pass    | as predicted, EQUIVALENT |

The first two are the point. A stale slot is the exact failure mode a future retention bug would
have, and **the shared-buffer mutant is the aliasing bug the doc comment warns about** — it is
caught, so nested general calls already have coverage and there is no gap to fill. The third is
answer-equivalent by construction, so its guard is the A/B above and not a test.

### What this says about the earlier figures

Item 762 established that the general path swings between a ~45 ns and a ~82 ns mode inside one
process while specialized closures sit flat, and guessed the per-row array was the cause. This
confirms it: removing the array is worth 10-27 ns a row, which is the right size for the gap
between those two modes.

## 764 — dispatch DEPTH is free (the deepest call is the cheapest), and `coalesce` was paying for a per-row CLOSURE instead

**REFUTATION PLUS A SMALL SHIPPED WIN.** Item 763 left the dispatch chain as the last suspect in
the general path and noted that the two precedents point opposite ways: item 457 refuted the name
dispatch as a cost in the NATIVE engine, while item 760's table specialization in TypeScript was
most of a 2x. Neither gets to stand in for a measurement, so this measured it.

### Depth is the discriminator, and it runs backwards

For a general name the chain is: three positional-assert lookups (refuted at 762), then
`UNARY_NUM`, `UNARY_STR`, `BINARY_NUM`, `in NUM_CONSTANTS`, `TRIM_FNS.has`, then a ~30-case
switch, and only then the seven extended dispatchers. So pick names at different depths and see.
200,000 vertices, 14 reps, first three dropped, median of the plateau (item 762's estimator):

| shape                   | depth                                     | ns/row | over floor |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | -----: | ---------: |
| `count(a.age)`          | no Call at all                            |  21.21 |          — |
| `coalesce(a.age, 0)`    | switch case **1**                         |  59.49 |  **38.28** |
| `nullif(a.age, 7)`      | switch case 2                             |  48.06 |      26.86 |
| `nullif(a.age, a.age2)` | switch case 2, two SLOTS                  |  51.16 |      29.95 |
| `to_integer(a.age)`     | later in the switch                       |  53.81 |      32.60 |
| `_is_nan(a.age)`        | **past every table AND the whole switch** |  38.97 |  **17.76** |
| `abs(a.age)`            | specialized at compile time (760)         |  24.73 |       3.52 |

**The deepest path in the library is the CHEAPEST general call, and the shallowest is the dearest.**
Depth is anti-correlated with cost, so the chain is free — a `Record` miss on a monomorphic
per-closure name is a few hundred picoseconds, not nanoseconds. The target is dead, and it dies
with a control: `abs` at 3.52 shows what the row costs when the whole general path is skipped.

### What the ordering actually pointed at

If depth is not the variable, the body is. `coalesce`'s was
`args.find((x) => !isNullish(x)) ?? null` — **a fresh closure allocated on every row**, which is
why the function resolved in the switch's first case was the most expensive one in the library.
Replaced with a plain loop, extracted as `firstNonNullish` because inlining it put `callScalar` at
complexity 36 against a limit of 35. `coalesce` is now the CHEAPEST general call (17.73 over the
floor, below `_is_nan`'s 20.33).

### Two instruments, two answers, and both are reported

| instrument                              |       `coalesce(a.age, 0)` | `coalesce(a.missing, a.age)` |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------------------: | ---------------------------: |
| 7 shapes in ONE process (the 764 probe) | **1.53x** (59.49 -> 38.97) |                            — |
| one shape per process, read 1           |                      1.06x |                        1.24x |
| one shape per process, read 2           |                      1.18x |                        1.02x |

Controls across both isolated reads: `nullif` 0.95/1.02x, `_is_nan` 1.04/1.04x, `to_integer`
1.01/0.98x, `abs` 0.96/1.02x, the no-Call floor 1.01/0.98x.

**No single number is available here and the honest answer is the range.** Isolated, the effect is
roughly 5-20%; in a mixed-shape process it is 1.53x. Both are real measurements of different
situations: a monomorphic call site lets V8 escape-analyze that closure away, while a megamorphic
`callScalar` in a mixed workload does not. Item 762's redistribution bias does NOT apply — this
change moves no call sites, and the same functions flow through the same sites in both arms — so
the mixed-process figure is not an artifact in the way 762's controls were. A real workload has
many shapes, so the larger figure is the more representative one; the smaller is the one I can
defend with clean controls.

### Teeth, and a gap the mutation found

| mutant                                | predicted | gql tests BEFORE | fuzzers |                          |
| ------------------------------------- | --------- | ---------------- | ------- | ------------------------ |
| returns `args[0]` regardless of null  | FAIL      | **pass**         | FAIL    | as predicted             |
| falls out as `undefined`, not `null`  | FAIL      | **pass**         | FAIL    | as predicted             |
| back to `find` with its per-row arrow | SURVIVE   | pass             | pass    | as predicted, EQUIVALENT |

**Both wrong-answer mutants passed all 2,586 unit tests.** `coalesce` had no VALUE test anywhere —
only two arity tests in `gql.test.ts` asserting `not.toThrow()`. The byte-identity fuzzers caught
both, which is the right backstop, but a fuzzer localizes nothing. So there is now a value test
pinning `coalesce(null, 5)`, `coalesce(1, 2)` and `coalesce(null, null)` — the last asserting NULL
rather than `undefined`, which only an in-engine assertion can tell apart because both render as
null at JSON egress. **Its teeth were verified, not assumed: both mutants now FAIL the unit suite
where they previously passed.**

### An interrupted mutation run, and why the rule exists

The first run aborted on a non-unique anchor (`return null;\n};` appears twice in the file) at
mutant 2 — after mutant 1 had been built into the dist. The assert fires before the write, so
`src` was pristine, but **the DIST still carried mutant 1**, and the dist is what the tests and
fuzzers read. CLAUDE.md's rule is "restore before applying the next mutant, never only after the
loop"; the TS corollary is that restoring the source is not enough, because the artifact is a
build step away. Rebuilt and verified by grep before continuing.

### The sweep, and an instrument slip in reading it

`bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`: **0 groups disagree on the ANSWER**, and two
groups over 2x — `label on start` (item 325) and `a product's one-sided predicate` (item 285), the
pre-existing pair. Item 763's third flag (`one end labelled`, 2.03x) is absent again, which is
what `CLOSED.md` predicts for a group straddling a 2.0x threshold.

**The first reading of this gate was unusable and nearly went unnoticed.** The probe was piped
through `tail -8`, which cut the `disagree on the ANSWER` line — the one thing in that output that
is not a perf heuristic. Only the flag summary survived, so the run could say nothing about
correctness. Re-run with a `grep` that keeps it. The lesson generalizes past this probe: when a
tool's output ends with a summary, `tail` silently drops the part that matters most.

### Not done

Same pattern, not priced: the list set-ops allocate a closure per ELEMENT —
`a.some((w) => structuralEq(w, b))` at four sites, plus the dedup helper. They capture `b`, so
they need a loop rather than a hoist, and the fixture here has no lists, so they are recorded
rather than fixed blind.

The structural question left open is better posed now: `abs` (specialized) costs 3.52 ns over the
floor and `_is_nan` (the cheapest general call) costs 17.76. That ~14 ns gap is not the assert
(762), not the chain (this item) and not the argument array (763). What is left is that the
specialized closure is tiny and monomorphic while `callScalar` is a ~100-line megamorphic function
that cannot inline into the aggregate loop. If that is right, the fix is a compile-time resolution
to a small handler per name — the TS shape of the refactor item 457 refuted natively, which is
exactly why it needs its own measurement rather than either precedent.

## 765 — the one-argument STRING family vectorized in NATIVE: `char_length` 2.47x, `upper` 1.89x. The GStr clone was a red herring and the ASCII fast path is refuted

**SHIPPED (Rust).** Six TypeScript ticks in a row (760-764) left the native engine untouched, so
this is the Rust side of the same question — and it is item 459's numeric pair applied to strings,
which is a precedent that transferred cleanly where 457's did not.

### The hypothesis I started with, and the fixture built to test it

`Col::value_at` is `Col::Str(v) => Value::Str(v[i].clone())`, and `GStr` inlines up to
`INLINE_CAP = 12` bytes: at 12 bytes a clone is a 16-byte memcpy, at 13 it is an ATOMIC increment
plus a decrement when the `Value` drops. So a one-byte difference in the DATA flips the allocation
class, which makes the fixture the experiment: `s12 = format!("{i:012}")` against
`s13 = format!("{i:013}")`, one byte apart, so the length-proportional work is within 8% while the
clone's cost changes completely. (Comparing 8 bytes against 40 would have confounded the two.)

The atomics are real and small: `char_length` cost 30.33 ns a row on `s12` and 35.90 on `s13`,
so **~5.6 ns is the heap clone**. `upper` showed +15.3, but that one also ALLOCATES its result, and
a 13-byte result is heap where a 12-byte one is inline, so its gap is two effects and not one.

### The bigger number in the same table, and the refutation on the way to it

`count(abs(a.n))` — vectorized, and producing the IDENTICAL `Col::Gen` output column — cost
**4.14 ns a row** against `char_length`'s 30.33. The output is the same, the dispatch was refuted
at 759, so the ~26 ns is the INPUT boxing: `value_at` clones the `GStr` into a `Value` that the arm
immediately derefs and drops.

**Refuted first, and recorded next to the code:** an ASCII fast path in `utf16_len`
(`if s.is_ascii() { return s.len(); }`, exactly equal because one ASCII byte is one UTF-16 unit).
It measured **30.33 -> 30.09 ns a row**, which is noise. A panic probe confirms `utf16_len` IS on
this path, so this is a real refutation and not an unreachability null — `encode_utf16().count()`
over a short ASCII string is already cheap and the counting was never the cost.

### The change

`unary_str_fn(name) -> Option<fn(&str) -> Value>` and `eval_unary_str`, the string twins of item
459's `unary_num_fn`/`eval_unary_num`, reading `&str` straight out of a `Col::Str`. A `Col::Str`
holds no null and no non-string — a column with nulls is a `Col::Gen` — so the fast arm needs
neither a null check nor an error path, and every other column kind falls through to a general loop
that keeps `call_scalar_checked` as the single definition of the NULL-versus-`E_INVALID_VALUE`
decision.

Three ALTERNATED rounds, two saved binaries so no rebuild sits between arms (200,000 rows):

| shape                                | before | after |     ratio |
| ------------------------------------ | -----: | ----: | --------: |
| `count(char_length(a.s12))` INLINE   |  30.63 | 12.40 | **2.47x** |
| `count(char_length(a.s13))` HEAP     |  35.94 | 14.98 | **2.40x** |
| `count(upper(a.s12))` INLINE         |  44.38 | 23.42 | **1.89x** |
| `count(upper(a.s13))` HEAP           |  59.47 | 36.45 | **1.63x** |
| CONTROL `count(a.n)` numeric floor   |   0.46 |  0.46 | **1.00x** |
| CONTROL `count(abs(a.n))` vectorized |   4.12 |  4.12 | **1.00x** |
| CONTROL `count(a.s12)` projection    |   0.46 |  0.46 | **1.00x** |
| CONTROL `count(a.s13)` projection    |   0.46 |  0.46 | **1.00x** |

All four controls are 1.00x to two decimals.

**One control is worth a warning rather than trust.** The bare projections read 0.46 ns a row,
which is not "a string column read is free" — it is the count-over-projection SHORTCUT, which never
materializes a value at all. As a baseline for "what a per-row string read costs" it is useless; it
earns its place only as a row the change must not move.

### Teeth, and a coverage fact about the fuzzers

| mutant                                       | predicted | Rust suite                  | fuzzers  |                          |
| -------------------------------------------- | --------- | --------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------ |
| `char_length` counts BYTES, not UTF-16 units | FAIL      | **FAIL** (`corpus_tests_b`) | **pass** | as predicted             |
| `upper`/`lower` swapped                      | FAIL      | FAIL (3 tests)              | FAIL     | as predicted             |
| the typed fast arm deleted                   | SURVIVE   | pass                        | pass     | as predicted, EQUIVALENT |

**The first row is a coverage fact worth keeping: the byte-identity fuzzers do NOT catch a
UTF-16-versus-bytes error, because they do not generate non-ASCII strings.** The two lengths agree
for every ASCII input, so only the corpus test — which has non-ASCII data — pins the UTF-16 string
model that `CLAUDE.md` calls a standing rule. Anyone changing a length or an index path should know
the fuzzer is not the guard there.

### An instrument slip, twice now

The mutation run was piped through `tail -8`, which cut the first mutant's verdict line — the exact
mistake item 764 recorded one tick earlier for the spelling probe. And the third mutant's first
reading was a FUZZ FAILURE where SURVIVE was predicted; re-run in isolation it survives, which is
the documented run-many flake (`sync-test-flake-is-timing`: re-run isolated before believing an
exit 1). Both of those would have been reported as findings if read once and trusted. The fuzzers
were then run TWICE on the real tree: 13 pass, 0 fail, both times.

### Not done

`upper`'s remaining cost is its own allocation: it builds a new `String` via `to_uppercase` and
converts it to a `GStr` per row, which for a result over 12 bytes is a heap block. An in-place
ASCII uppercase into a stack buffer would avoid both, but it is only correct for ASCII and the
non-ASCII path must stay — so it is a second fast path with a fixture-dependent payoff, not a
simplification.

The two-argument string family (`starts_with`, `ends_with`, `contains`, `split`, `substring`,
`left`, `right`, `replace`) still boxes both arguments per row. The same pair of functions would
extend to it, keyed on two `Col::Str` columns, which is the native twin of what the TS side has
open at item 761.

## 766 — the two-argument string PREDICATES vectorized, with a `Col::Bool` output: `starts_with` 4.49x, `ends_with` 4.19x, `contains` 3.61x

**SHIPPED (Rust).** Item 765 vectorized the one-argument string family and left the two-argument
one boxing both arguments per row. This takes the three PREDICATES, which get a second saving the
other vectorized arms cannot have.

### Pricing the family first, which changed what I built

| shape                                                    | ns/row |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -----: |
| CONTROL `count(a.n)` numeric floor                       |   0.47 |
| CONTROL `count(abs(a.n))`                                |   4.18 |
| CONTROL `count(char_length(a.s))` — item 765's new floor |  12.31 |
| `starts_with(a.s, '0')`                                  |  38.00 |
| `starts_with(a.s, a.t)` TWO SLOTS                        |  40.22 |
| `contains(a.s, '7')`                                     |  36.40 |
| `ends_with(a.s, '1')`                                    |  39.25 |
| `replace(a.s, '0', 'x')` 3 args                          |  69.06 |
| `left(a.s, 3)` str+num                                   | 101.82 |
| `substring(a.s, 2)` str+num                              | 118.88 |

**The two biggest numbers are NOT the target.** `substring` at 119 and `left` at 102 are dominated

be a 1.2x there. Item 765 already refuted the UTF-16 DECODE as a cost (an exactly-equal ASCII fast
path in `utf16_len` measured 30.33 -> 30.09), so what is left in those two is the allocation, and
pricing it needs its own diagnosis rather than this fix.

**The literal's BROADCAST was measured and is not the cost either.** `Expr::Lit` becomes
`broadcast(v, n)`, and for a string that is `Col::Str(vec![s; n])` — 200,000 `GStr` clones built
once per call before any row runs, which looks like an obvious target. The two-slot form prices it:
40.22 against the literal form's 38.00, so about 2 ns a row. Not worth a special case, and now
recorded so it is not chased again.

### The change, and the saving only a predicate gets

`binary_str_pred_fn(name) -> Option<fn(&str, &str) -> bool>` and `eval_binary_str_pred`, reading
`&str` out of each `Col::Str`. `regex_match` is deliberately excluded — it compiles or caches a
regex rather than scanning, so it has a different cost profile.

The second saving is the OUTPUT column. Every other vectorized arm in `scalar.rs` must return
`Col::Gen` because its function can produce a null, a NaN or an infinity — item 459's comment says
so explicitly. **A predicate over two `Col::Str` columns cannot:** a `Col::Str` holds no null and
no non-string, so every row yields a real bool and the result is a `Col::Bool`, one byte a row
instead of a `Value`. That is why these three go to 4.5x where item 765's family went to 2.5x.

Three ALTERNATED rounds, two saved binaries:

| `count(ends_with(a.s, '1'))`             |  38.19 |   9.12 | **4.19x** |
| `count(starts_with(a.s, a.t))` two slots |  39.91 |   9.62 | **4.15x** |
| `count(contains(a.s, '7'))`              |  36.38 |  10.09 | **3.61x** |
| CONTROL `count(abs(a.n))`                |   4.09 |   4.10 |     1.00x |

**A flag retracted:** the single-run probe read `substring` at **+15%** — a row this change cannot
