Mutant 3's FIRST reading was `fuzz=FAIL(1)` where SURVIVE was predicted. Re-run in isolation it
passes — and item 765's mutant 3 did exactly the same thing one tick earlier. So: **an unexpected
fuzz failure inside a mutation loop is UNCONFIRMED until it is re-run on its own.** Both times the
mutant was answer-equivalent and the in-loop failure was the documented run-many flake
(`sync-test-flake-is-timing`). Had either been believed, it would have been reported as a

## 767 — `utf16_slice` allocated twice a row: `substring` 2.53x, `left`/`right` 2.10x. And item 765's refutation DIED, because its denominator shrank

**SHIPPED (Rust), two fast paths, one of them a refutation I had to reverse.** Item 766 left
`substring` (119 ns a row), `left` (102) and `replace` (68) as the expensive string shapes and said
their cost was an allocation rather than argument boxing. It was.

### What `utf16_slice` was doing per row

```rust
let units: Vec<u16> = s.encode_utf16().collect();   // one heap allocation
String::from_utf16_lossy(&units[start..end])        // a second
```

and the caller then converted that `String` into a `GStr` — so a one-row `substring` was up to
three heap allocations. For ASCII none of them are needed: one ASCII byte is exactly one UTF-16
unit, so a unit index IS a byte index, the slice is already valid UTF-8, and the `GStr` can be
built straight from it (inline, with no allocation at all, when the result is ≤ 12 bytes).

### The control is INSIDE the function, which is stronger than one beside it

A non-ASCII column cannot take the fast path — `é` is two UTF-8 bytes and one UTF-16 unit, so the
indices diverge and the guard declines. So `substring(a.u, …)` over a column of `é…` strings is a
control that exercises the same function, the same call site and the same arms, and must not move.
That caught a real regression that a function-level control would have missed (below).

Three ALTERNATED rounds, two saved binaries:

| shape                                 | before |  after |     ratio |
| ------------------------------------- | -----: | -----: | --------: |
| `substring(a.s, 2)` ASCII             | 114.21 |  45.09 | **2.53x** |
| `substring(a.s, 2, 5)` ASCII bounded  | 111.33 |  51.78 | **2.15x** |
| `left(a.s, 3)` ASCII                  | 101.85 |  48.34 | **2.11x** |
| `right(a.s, 3)` ASCII                 | 108.75 |  51.79 | **2.10x** |
| CONTROL `substring(a.u, 2)` NON-ASCII | 109.07 | 107.51 |     1.01x |
| CONTROL `left(a.u, 3)` NON-ASCII      |  96.93 | 100.79 |     0.96x |
| CONTROL `replace(a.s, '0', 'x')`      |  68.56 |  67.29 |     1.02x |
| CONTROL `char_length(a.s)` [765]      |  12.14 |  12.36 |     0.98x |
| CONTROL `starts_with(a.s, '0')` [766] |   8.87 |   8.56 |     1.04x |
| CONTROL `count(a.n)` numeric floor    |   0.46 |   0.46 |     1.00x |

**The non-ASCII control caught a regression and changed the implementation.** The first version
returned `Cow<'_, str>` and borrowed on the ASCII arm — elegant, and it cost the NON-ASCII rows
**0.92x and 0.95x** over three alternated rounds: an enum discriminant and a failed `is_ascii` on
the one path that cannot use the fast arm. Returning the `GStr` the callers want anyway removes the
wrapper entirely, which took the non-ASCII `substring` back to 1.01x AND improved the ASCII win
from 2.31x to 2.53x. The residual 0.96x on non-ASCII `left`/`right` is two failed `is_ascii` scans
(those arms call both helpers), about 4 ns on a 100 ns row — an accepted, measured trade, stated
rather than buried.

### Item 765's refutation died one tick later, and the mechanism is worth remembering

Item 765 tried an ASCII fast path in `utf16_len` (`if s.is_ascii() { return s.len(); }`) and
REFUTED it at **30.33 -> 30.09 ns a row** — correctly, with a panic probe confirming the function
was on the measured path. This tick the same three lines are worth **1.16x** on `char_length`
(12.16 -> 10.47, four alternated rounds, the series `[12.2, 12.9, 12.9, 12.2]` against
`[10.7, 10.7, 10.5, 10.5]` — non-overlapping).

Nothing about the lever changed. **The denominator did.** The saving was ~1.7 ns all along; when
`char_length` cost 30 ns through the boxed path that was 6% and invisible, and after item 765
vectorized the family to 12 ns the same 1.7 ns is 16%. So: _a refutation is relative to the path it
was measured on, and vectorizing a path can resurrect every small lever inside it._ The audit
already knew prices can die (item 739); this is the mirror image, and it is the second time this
pair of items has had to correct the other.

### Teeth

| mutant                                    | predicted | Rust suite                                                  |                          |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| the ASCII slice arm taken UNCONDITIONALLY | FAIL      | FAIL (`corpus_tests_b`)                                     | as predicted             |
| the ASCII arm ignores `start`             | FAIL      | FAIL (`substring_edges`, `added_string_and_list_functions`) | as predicted             |
| both fast paths removed                   | SURVIVE   | pass                                                        | as predicted, EQUIVALENT |

The first answers a question item 765 left open. 765 found the byte-identity fuzzers do NOT catch a
UTF-16-versus-bytes LENGTH error because they generate no non-ASCII strings; this shows UTF-16
SLICING _is_ pinned — `corpus_tests_b` catches a byte-indexed slice, and here the fuzzers caught it
too.

### A CORRECTION to items 765 and 766, about my own harness

Both of those records say an unexpected in-loop fuzz failure was "the documented run-many flake".
That attribution was too quick. The failure happened a third time here, and with stdout captured
the evidence is specific: **the output stops after `bun test v1.4.0` with no test-result line at
all.** The fuzz process did not get as far as running a test, so its exit code carries NO
information about the mutant — it is a runner-startup failure, not a divergence. It does not
reproduce when the same mutant is run alone, and three consecutive clean runs on the real tree
follow every time.

The real defect is in the harness, and it is worse than a mislabelled flake: **a mutation harness
that reads only an exit code cannot tell "the tests ran and disagreed" from "the tests never
ran"** — so it can report a mutant as CAUGHT when nothing executed, which is invisible precisely
when FAIL is what you predicted. The verdicts in 765/766/767 all stand, because every FAIL was
accompanied by NAMED failing tests from the Rust suite; but that was luck of reporting, not a
check. A mutation verdict needs evidence of EXECUTION, not an exit status.

### Not done

`replace` (67 ns) is the remaining expensive string row and was deliberately left: it allocates a
result per row like `substring` did, but through `str::replace`, so the fix is not the same shape.
`split` (a list result per row) has never been priced. And the non-ASCII arm still pays its failed
`is_ascii`; collapsing `left`/`right` to one check instead of two would recover ~4 ns on that path
at the cost of threading a flag through both helpers.

## 768 — TS: `sanitizeSurrogates` built an ARRAY per row (`substring` 1.85x) and `replace` split into one (1.60x). Two refutations on the way in, and two untested behaviours found

**SHIPPED (TypeScript), with four measurements that each changed what I did next.** Item 767's
lesson was that vectorizing a path resurrects the small levers inside it, so this tick took the
TS string family — where `replace` was the most expensive row in the engine at **249.80 ns a
row**, against **67** for the same function natively.

### Two things refuted before any engine code was written

- **`String.prototype.replaceAll` is not the fix, and my first measurement said the opposite.**
  Over a CONSTANT string, `split('0').join('x')` reads 54.44 ns and `replaceAll('0','x')` 102.62,
  so `replaceAll` looks **1.9x slower**. Over 200,000 VARYING strings the order flips: 118.64
  against 103.28. The constant-string loop lets the JIT cache the split. **A per-row helper has to
  be benchmarked over per-row DATA** — "match the fixture to the claim", in a form that is easy to
  miss because the harness looks right either way.
- **`str()`'s type-check gauntlet costs nothing.** It tries `isRecord`, `isElement`,
  `Array.isArray` and `instanceof Path` before `String(v)`, and `replaceScalar` calls it three
  times a row, so a `typeof v === 'string'` fast path looked free. Measured: **0.202 ns a call
  either way** — the JIT folds the whole chain when the site is monomorphic. Refuted in ten
  seconds, and recorded so it is not re-derived.

### What the cost actually was

`sanitizeSurrogates`, which `substring`, `left` and `right` all call per row:

```ts
fromUtf16UnitsLossy(Array.from({ length: s.length }, (_, i) => s.charCodeAt(i)));
```

**an array with one element per character, built and then re-joined, on every row.** A
module-scope surrogate regex makes it the identity for any string with no surrogate code unit:
**83.17 -> 8.15 ns a call, 10.2x**, checked against the slow path on 200,000 strings, on an astral
character and on a lone surrogate. The equivalence does not depend on what the slow path does with
a surrogate — the guard only SKIPS it when there is none.

And `replace` got an `indexOf` loop instead of `split`/`join` (**60.56 against 118.64, 1.96x** on
the body). NOT `replaceAll`, which is both slower here and semantically different: it expands
`$&`, `$1` and friends in the REPLACEMENT, where `split`/`join` and native's `str::replace` do
not. That would be a silent cross-engine divergence on any replacement containing a `$`.

### The A/B, two reads

One shape per PROCESS, 14 reps, first three dropped, median of the plateau, arms alternated:

| shape                                                     |                       read 1 |                       read 2 |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------: | ---------------------------: |
| `substring(a.s, 2)`                                       |  **1.85x** (166.10 -> 89.70) |  **1.91x** (165.00 -> 86.50) |
| `replace(a.s, '0', 'x')`                                  | **1.60x** (269.80 -> 168.70) | **1.48x** (253.90 -> 172.10) |
| CONTROL `char_length(a.s)` [761]                          |                        1.18x |                        1.09x |
| CONTROL `starts_with(a.s, '0')`                           |                        1.07x |                        0.93x |
| CONTROL `contains` / `ends_with` / two-slot `starts_with` |                   0.98-0.99x |                   0.99-1.00x |
| CONTROL `abs(a.n)` [760]                                  |                        0.96x |                        1.05x |
| CONTROL `count(a.n)`, no Call                             |                        1.01x |                        1.02x |

`char_length` reads 1.18x then 1.09x on a path this change cannot touch; drifting toward 1.0 across
reads is what noise looks like, so it is not claimed as an effect. The predicate rows swing ±7%,
which is this instrument's band for them.

### TWO UNTESTED BEHAVIOURS, found by mutation and now pinned

| mutant                                        | predicted | gql tests | fuzzers  |                          |
| --------------------------------------------- | --------- | --------- | -------- | ------------------------ |
| `sanitizeSurrogates` NEVER sanitizes          | FAIL      | **pass**  | **pass** | **not as predicted**     |
| `replace` advances by 1, not `search.length`  | FAIL      | **pass**  | **pass** | **not as predicted**     |
| `replace` drops the tail after the last match | FAIL      | FAIL      | FAIL     | as predicted             |
| back to `split`/`join`                        | SURVIVE   | pass      | pass     | as predicted, EQUIVALENT |

The first two are real gaps, and **this is the first unexpected mutation result this session that
arrived WITH evidence of execution** — both runs produced full result lines, which is exactly the
distinction item 767 added to `CLAUDE.md` after three startup failures were nearly read as
findings. The rule paid for itself one tick later.

- **`sanitizeSurrogates` had no test at all.** Making it never sanitize passed 2,587 unit tests
  and all seven byte-identity fuzzers — the fuzzers generate no non-ASCII strings, which item 765
  found for `char_length` and which turns out to cover this whole function.
- **No test used a multi-character search in `replace`.** Advancing by one unit instead of
  `search.length` is wrong for every search longer than one character and nothing noticed.

Both behaviours are now what my fast paths depend on, so both are pinned: a surrogate PAIR sliced
in half yields U+FFFD (`substring('a😀b', 2, 1)`, `left(…, 2)`, `right(…, 2)`), an INTACT pair
survives, a string with no surrogate is unchanged, and `replace` is tested with a multi-character
search, an OVERLAPPING one (`replace('aaa', 'aa', 'b')` is `'ba'`, matching once) and a kept tail.
**Teeth verified, not assumed: both surviving mutants now FAIL the unit suite.**

### The sweep

`bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`: **0 groups disagree on the ANSWER**, two
groups over 2x — the pre-existing `label on start` (item 325) and `a product's one-sided predicate`
(item 285). The gql suite is 2,589 tests after the two added here, and the seven byte-identity
fuzzers pass twice.

### Not done

The two-argument string PREDICATES are still on the general path in TS — 59-71 ns a row against
`char_length`'s 24 — and they are what this tick set out to do before the measurements pointed
elsewhere. Natively the same three went 4.5x at item 766, partly from a `Col::Bool` output that has
no TS equivalent, so the TS ceiling is lower. `substring` at 87 ns is still the dearest string row;
what is left there is the general-path machinery item 764 priced at ~35 ns and the `slice` itself.

## 769 — TS: the two-argument string predicates, 1.57-2.43x. `byte_length` was hiding in the PREDICATE dispatcher, and the check ORDER had no test

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** The TS counterpart of item 766, which took the same three predicates
from 36-40 ns a row to 8-10 natively. Item 768 set out to do this and the measurements redirected
it; this finishes it.

### The numbers, and why they are ranges

One shape per PROCESS, 14 reps, first three dropped, median of the plateau, arms alternated, TWO
reads:

| shape                                  |                     read 1 |                     read 2 |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------: | -------------------------: |
| `starts_with(a.s, '0')`                | **2.43x** (64.40 -> 26.50) | **2.00x** (66.50 -> 33.30) |
| `contains(a.s, '7')`                   |                  **2.05x** |                  **1.68x** |
| `ends_with(a.s, '1')`                  |                  **1.93x** |                  **1.87x** |
| `starts_with(a.s, a.t)` two slots      |                  **1.79x** |                  **1.57x** |
| `byte_length(a.s)` now in `UNARY_STR`  |                  **1.49x** |                  **1.76x** |
| CONTROL `split(a.s, '0')` 2-arg string |                      0.95x |                      1.02x |
| CONTROL `char_length(a.s)` [761]       |                      1.09x |                      0.87x |
| CONTROL `substring(a.s, 2)` [768]      |                      1.06x |                      1.06x |
| CONTROL `abs(a.n)` [760]               |                      1.06x |                      1.17x |
| CONTROL `count(a.n)`, no Call          |                      1.09x |                      0.94x |

`split` is the sharpest control: two arguments, the SAME two asserted positions, and not
specialized. The controls span 0.87-1.17x across the two reads, so this instrument's band for
these rows is about ±15% and a single figure would be false precision. The effects clear it.

**As item 766 predicted, the TS win is smaller than the native 4.5x.** A good part of that one was
writing a `Col::Bool` output column instead of a boxed one, and TypeScript has no typed columns to
write into — so what is left here is the per-row argument array, the assert and the dispatch walk.

### `byte_length` was in the wrong dispatcher

`byte_length` and `octet_length` are ONE-argument string functions, but they live in
`callStringPredicateFn` alongside `contains`/`starts_with`/`ends_with` — so item 761's
`unaryStrCall` never covered them even though `SCALAR_ASSERTS_STR0_ONLY` admits them. They are now
in `UNARY_STR`, which routes them through that path: **1.49-1.76x**. Worth noting as a shape, not
just a fix — a function's cost here depends on which TABLE it is in, and the tables are organized
by family rather than by arity.

### The check ORDER is the contract, and nothing pinned it

`assertScalarArgTypes` validates BOTH argument positions before `callStringPredicateFn`
short-circuits on a nullish argument. So:

- `starts_with(null, 5)` THROWS — the null does not excuse the number.
- `starts_with(null, 'a')` is null.

The specialized closure has to reproduce that order. Writing it the other way — nullish check
first — is one branch cheaper and reads more naturally, and **mutation shows it passes all 2,589
tests and all seven byte-identity fuzzers** while silently converting that data exception into a
null. That is the third consecutive tick where a behaviour one of my own fast paths depends on
turned out to have no test at all (768: `sanitizeSurrogates` and multi-character `replace`; 764:
`coalesce`'s value behaviour).

Now pinned, with teeth verified: the mutant FAILS the unit suite after the test, where it passed
before. The test covers both throwing spellings, both null spellings, and a true/false case.

| mutant                                     | predicted | gql tests | fuzzers  |                                   |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------- | --------- | -------- | --------------------------------- |
| nullish check moved BEFORE the type checks | FAIL      | **pass**  | **pass** | **not as predicted** → test added |
| `starts_with`/`ends_with` swapped          | FAIL      | FAIL      | FAIL     | as predicted                      |
| `byte_length` removed from `UNARY_STR`     | SURVIVE   | pass      | pass     | as predicted, EQUIVALENT          |

### One probe error worth recording

The first A/B used `regex_match` as a control and died with
`E_UNKNOWN_FUNCTION: regex_match()` — that name is in `STR_ARG_POSITIONS` and in the scalar
library but is NOT exposed in the GQL surface. `split` replaced it and is a better control anyway.
A probe that names a function the parser rejects fails loudly, which is the good case; the lesson
is that the presence of a name in the scalar tables does not mean the surface accepts it.

### Not done

`split` at 164-180 ns a row is now the most expensive string shape in the TS engine, and its cost
is inherent in part: it returns a LIST per row, so an allocation is unavoidable. Whether the rest
is the general path or the split itself has not been separated. `regex_match` exists in the library
but is unreachable from GQL, which is either a gap or deliberate and is worth a conformance check
rather than a perf one.

## 770 — I stepped out of the scalar seam, re-priced the whole query surface, and came back with three refutations and no change

**NO ENGINE CHANGE. Three things settled, one of them a correction to this tick's own reasoning.**
Ten consecutive ticks (759-769) worked inside the scalar-function path, which is a narrow seam, so
this one re-priced the surface before picking another target.

### The re-pricing, and what it says

`query_bench`, whole corpus. The two rows that dwarf everything else are element projection:
`hop node, NO distinct` at **598,799 us / 1,000,000 rows = 599 ns/row** and `distinct node` at
**119,808 / 198,672 = 603**. For scale, `cmp str prop/prop` is 48 ns/row and `project 3` is 27.
That matches what items 339-342 recorded: element materialization is the largest per-row cost in
the engine, and `CLAUDE.md` calls `RETURN p` the shape that dominates the corpus.

### `regex_match` is Gremlin's, and item 769's open question is closed

Item 769 found the GQL surface rejects `regex_match` even though it is in `STR_ARG_POSITIONS` and
in the scalar library, and left it as a conformance question. Answered in two minutes: the NATIVE
parser rejects both `regex_match` and `_regex_match` too, so the two engines AGREE, and native's
own comment names the owner — _"Compiled-regex cache for the Gremlin `regex()` predicate"_. It is a
Gremlin primitive sharing the scalar library, by design. Not a gap, and not a divergence.

### Item 342's per-key term RE-CONFIRMED, and the ladder is NOT refuted

Element rendering walks every key in the STORE and filters by presence. Holding the PRESENT
properties at three and varying the store's column count:

| fixture          |            `RETURN n` | `RETURN n.a` | `count(*)` |
| ---------------- | --------------------: | -----------: | ---------: |
| 3 store columns  | 375.9 / 381.5 / 383.1 |         2.45 |       0.00 |
| 10 store columns | 393.2 / 396.0 / 398.8 |         2.46 |       0.00 |
| 30 store columns | 439.8 / 444.5 / 443.3 |         2.48 |       0.00 |

**~2.1 ns per extra store key per row**, which CONFIRMS the 1.79 ns/key the record already carries
(items 340/740) about thirty items later. `RETURN n.a` is flat across all three — the scalar path
resolves one column and never walks the key list — and `count(*)` takes the shortcut.

**My first reading of this was wrong and I am recording the correction rather than the conclusion
I nearly wrote.** At three store keys the walk is ~6 ns of 376, so I started writing that item
342's ~130-edit ladder "buys 1.5%". That ignores what the record actually says: the lever is for a
HETEROGENEOUS store — _"a heterogeneous people-graph (50-200 keys, a handful per node) pays on
every rendered element"_. At 100 keys the term is ~180 ns/row and packing it is worth ~2.1x of
THAT. My fixture had 3-30 keys, so it could not speak to the case the ladder exists for. The
ladder stands exactly as priced; what I added is an independent re-measurement of its term.

Also confirmed from the code: `render_nodes` and `render_edges` already hoist the per-key column
resolution out of the row loop (item 340: 1.54 ns/key hoisted against 7.99 without). The ~2.1
ns/key measured here IS the hoisted figure, so there is nothing left to hoist.

### A 65 ns gap that is NOT what it looked like, and the third measurement that says so

The fixture built two stores, one with external ids and one without, because `CLAUDE.md` warns that
omitting them skips a whole path. The gap was large and stable across three runs: **383 ns a row
without external ids against 312 with**, at three store columns.

The obvious explanation is in the renderer: `GStr::from(id.to_string())` — a malloc, the digits, a
copy into the `GStr`, a free, per rendered element, for any node with no external id. A `u32` is at
most ten digits and `GStr` inlines twelve bytes, so the digits can go into a stack buffer and the
allocation becomes impossible. I wrote that.

**It measures 1.00x.** Three alternated rounds, two saved binaries: 1.00x, 1.00x, 0.98x, 1.01x,
0.98x — nothing, on any fixture. Reverted.

So the 65 ns is NOT the id formatting, and the two sides of that comparison differ in more than one
clause: they are two different STORES (one carries a 200,000-entry external-id index), not two code
paths through one store. `CLOSED.md`'s own rule for this is at item 339 — _"say out loud what each
side does, and if the sentences differ in more than one clause the ratio needs a third
measurement, not an explanation"_ — and the zero-allocation A/B WAS that third measurement. The gap
is real, reproducible and **unattributed**; what is settled is that it is not the dense-id render.

One caveat the first draft of this entry stated as a finding and which is now withdrawn: I was
going to write that the corpus's element rows are inflated because `Builder::node` assigns no
external id. The per-row id cost is zero, so they are not.

### Not done

Element rendering's floor is the allocation PER ELEMENT: the id, the labels `Value::List`, the
properties `Value::Map` behind an `Arc`. Item 341 already found the structural answer — the TS
engine does not materialize an element at all, and does the same work in 213 ns/row against
native's 492 — so the lever there is LAZINESS, a representation change, not a micro-fix. That is
the honest next target for this row and it is not tick-sized.

Gates: no engine change. `cargo test --release` 1224 + 13 + 725 pass, 0 fail; `git status` clean;
the probe example was deleted.

## 771 — element rendering decomposed: 1.03-1.04x shipped, and the two inferences that got me there were BOTH wrong

**SHIPPED (Rust), small and honestly attributed.** Item 770 named element rendering the engine's
largest per-row cost (~376-599 ns) and laziness as the structural answer. This decomposes it,
which produced a 1.04x and — more usefully — two corrections to my own reasoning inside one tick.

### The decomposition, which is the durable part

`RETURN p` over 200,000 three-property nodes, by part (different PLANS, so this localizes rather
than partitions):

| shape                             |     ns/row |
| --------------------------------- | ---------: |
| `count(*)`                        |       0.00 |
| `p.a` — one scalar                |       2.70 |
| `p.a, p.b, p.c` — three scalars   |      24.81 |
| `element_id(p)` — the id alone    |       9.54 |
| `labels(p)` — the labels alone    |  **85.91** |
| `element_id(p) + labels(p)`       |     103.85 |
| `element_id + labels + 3 scalars` |     141.48 |
| **`p` — THE ELEMENT**             | **383.46** |

The parts sum to ~141 and the whole is ~383, so **~242 ns is the map ASSEMBLY**, not reading the
values. And `labels(p)` costing 86 ns to render a ONE-element list is its own finding — the path
allocates twice, a `Vec<&str>` to sort and then a `Vec<Value>`.

Then the two scalings, on ONE store with three property columns so the walk is identical on both
sides: a node with **3 of 3 present costs 393.21 ns against 104.23 for a node with 0 of 3**.

### Wrong inference #1: that is ~96 ns per property, so it must be the growth ladder

`collect()` from a `filter` reserves nothing — the iterator's `size_hint` lower bound is 0 — so the
pair `Vec` grows 1, 2, 4 and a three-property node pays three allocations and two copies. 289 ns
for three properties is ~96 each, far more than a column read and two `Value` clones, and the
growth ladder is exactly the shape that would explain it.

**It does not.** With a clean instrument the whole change is worth **1.04x** on the dense node,
i.e. ~15 ns of 384 — not the ~190 the ladder story predicted. So the 289 ns is the property WORK
(the reads, the `Value` clones, the key clones), and the pair `Vec` is a small part of it. The
inference was arithmetically fine and causally wrong.

### Wrong inference #2: the first version regressed sparse nodes 3.2x, and that reading was ALSO wrong

`Vec::with_capacity(cols.len().min(16))` up front allocates even when nothing is present, where
`collect()` from an empty filter allocated nothing — strictly worse, and a heterogeneous store is
mostly sparse, which is the case the cap exists for. The multi-case probe duly showed the sparse
row at **96.76 -> 308.19, a 3.2x regression**, and I nearly recorded that.

But the same probe showed `1 labels, 0 props` — a store with NO property columns, where the
reserve is `min(0, 16) = 0` and the code is unchanged — going **216 -> 91, 2.37x FASTER**. A row
the change cannot reach cannot move 2.37x. **The probe was contaminated**: it builds seven stores
and runs sixteen queries in one process, and a change to the allocation pattern of the early rows
moves the late ones. That is precisely why `strag_421` carries `PROBE_ONLY` — _"which is what
separates a real control movement from allocator contamination by the targets ahead of it"_ — and
I had read that sentence in the README this same session.

Re-measured with ONE case per process, three alternated rounds:

| case                    | before |  after |     ratio |
| ----------------------- | -----: | -----: | --------: |
| dense (3 of 3 present)  | 384.40 | 369.19 | **1.04x** |
| sparse (0 of 3 present) | 214.57 | 208.81 | **1.03x** |
| CONTROL `p.a` scalar    |   2.47 |   2.48 |     1.00x |
| CONTROL `labels(p)`     |  79.29 |  79.88 |     0.99x |

No regression anywhere. The first version's "3.2x regression" was an artifact — though the design
flaw it pointed at was real, so the shipped version **reserves on the first push**, which keeps an
empty node allocation-free and still gives a dense node one allocation instead of a ladder.

### What the 1.04x actually is

Both `dense` AND `sparse` move ~3-4%, and the two controls that do not go through `render_nodes`
are flat. A sparse node reserves nothing and pushes nothing, so the reservation cannot be what
moved it. **The gain is the loop form** — an explicit `for` with an `if` in place of
`.iter().enumerate().filter().map().collect()` — and it applies to every rendered element.

So: the reservation is kept because it is correct and costs nothing (it cannot fire on an empty
node), but it is NOT separately measurable, and the entry says so rather than claiming it. The
honest headline is **1.03-1.04x on the engine's largest per-row cost, from the loop form**, with
the series non-overlapping (dense before 389.8 / 384.4 / 387.5 against after 369.2 / 374.6 / 370.3)
and two flat controls.

### Not done

`labels(p)` at 86 ns for one label is the next bounded thing in this path: `labels_of_refs`
allocates a `Vec<&str>` and sorts it, then the renderer allocates a `Vec<Value>` — two
allocations where one would do. `GStr::cmp` is `as_bytes().cmp()`, the same order as `&str`, so
sorting the `Value`s directly is byte-identical; it needs an iterator accessor on the store, which
is a small addition. Worth ~15 ns of 384 on the same reasoning as above, so it should be measured
with the one-case-per-process harness before being believed.

The structural answer for this row is still item 341's: the TS engine does not materialize an
element at all and does the same work in 213 ns/row against native's 492.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1224 + 13 + 725 pass, 0
fail; the seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail, run twice. Both probe examples deleted.

## 772 — the labels path: one allocation instead of two. 1.07x at ONE label, 0.99x at three — and item 767's execution check earned itself

**SHIPPED (Rust), small, with the trade stated.** Item 771 priced `labels(p)` at 85.91 ns a row to
render a ONE-element list and named the cause: `labels_of_refs` allocates a `Vec<&str>` to sort,
then every caller that wants `Value`s allocates a second `Vec`.

### The change

`Store::label_names_of(id)` yields the names BORROWED and unsorted, with no allocation, and the
three render sites collect the `Value`s once and sort them in place. Byte-identical by
construction: `GStr` orders by `as_bytes().cmp()`, which IS `&str`'s byte order, so sorting either
representation gives the same sequence. The accessor's doc says INTERN ORDER, NOT SORTED, because
the canonical order every consumer relies on is by name (item 724) and a caller that forgets to
sort would be wrong in a way no type can catch.

### The numbers, and the trade

One case per PROCESS, three alternated rounds — item 771's instrument, after a multi-case probe
there faked a 3.2x regression from allocator contamination:

| case                      | before |  after |     ratio |
| ------------------------- | -----: | -----: | --------: |
| `labels(x)`, ONE label    |  87.93 |  82.14 | **1.07x** |
| `labels(x)`, THREE labels | 135.15 | 137.08 | **0.99x** |
| `labels(x)`, ZERO labels  |  43.00 |  42.37 |     1.01x |
| CONTROL `x.a` scalar      |   2.43 |   2.46 |     0.99x |
| `RETURN x` full element   | 352.29 | 343.90 |     1.02x |

**The trade is real and goes both ways.** At one label the saved allocation wins 7% (series
separate: 92.2 / 90.5 / 87.9 against 82.7 / 83.3 / 82.1). At three labels it loses ~1%, because
sorting `Value` enums costs a `match` per comparison where sorting `&str` did not, and that grows
with the count while the saved allocation does not. One label is overwhelmingly the common case and
0.99x is inside the band the untouched controls show (0.99-1.01x), so this ships — but a
multi-label-heavy store does not benefit, and the entry says so rather than quoting only the 1.07x.

The zero-label row is the arm neither form allocates for, and it is flat as it should be.

### Teeth

| mutant                                 | predicted | Rust suite |                          |
| -------------------------------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------------------ |
| the label sort REMOVED (intern order)  | FAIL      | FAIL       | as predicted             |
| the comparison REVERSED                | FAIL      | FAIL       | as predicted             |
| the unreachable non-`Str` arm → `Less` | SURVIVE   | pass       | as predicted, EQUIVALENT |

The first two confirm the sort order is pinned — item 724's canonical-order rule has tests behind
it. The third is unreachable by construction (every element is built as `Value::Str` two lines
above), which is why the arm is `Equal` rather than a panic: a future caller cannot turn a render
into an abort.

### Item 767's execution check earned itself, one tick later

Mutant 3's first reading inside the loop was `fuzz=FAIL(1)` where SURVIVE was predicted — the
FOURTH time this session (765, 766, 767, here). Item 767 added a rule to `CLAUDE.md` after
diagnosing it: **a mutation verdict needs evidence of EXECUTION, not an exit code**, because a
harness reading only the status cannot tell "the tests ran and disagreed" from "the tests never
ran".

So this tick taught the harness to check for a result line. It now prints **`fuzz=DID-NOT-RUN`**,
and the verdict reads SURVIVE as predicted. That is the mechanism confirmed by instrument rather
than inferred: the in-loop fuzz process exits non-zero without running a test. Items 765 and 766
called it "the documented run-many flake", 767 corrected that to a runner-startup failure, and this
is the check that makes the difference visible automatically instead of requiring a re-run.

### One self-inflicted error

The new accessor was spliced into `store.rs` BETWEEN `labels_of_refs`' own `#[must_use]` attribute
and its signature, so the attribute landed on my function — which returns an `Iterator`, already
`#[must_use]` — and clippy failed with `double_must_use`. Same shape as item 733's orphaned doc
block: inserting above a function means inserting above its ATTRIBUTES, not just its doc comment.
Caught by the gate, in its own command, before anything else ran.

### Not done

`labels(p)` at 82 ns for one label is still 30x a scalar read. What remains is the `Value::List`
allocation itself plus a `GStr` construction per label — and for the full element, item 771's
finding stands: ~242 ns is map assembly and the structural answer is item 341's laziness.

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** The last five ticks were native, so this one re-priced the TS surface
before picking a target — and the sweep earned its keep twice: once by ruling a target out, once by

`BENCH_ENGINES=ts bun run bench`, whole corpus, 200,000 nodes. The largest rows are decode:

`split` was the dearest unclosed string shape (item 769 left it at 164-180 ns). One shape per
process:

| shape                                  | ns/row |
| -------------------------------------- | -----: |
| `count(a.s)` floor                     |  15.44 |
| `count(upper(a.s))` specialized at 761 |  31.67 |
| `count(to_list(a.n))` general path     |  49.75 |
| `count(split(a.s, '9'))` no match      |  93.63 |
| `count(split(a.s, '0'))` ~3 elements   | 127.74 |

And the BODY, in a tight loop over the same 200,000 strings: `s.split('0')` 56.06 ns,
`s.split('9')` 31.26. So ~50 ns of the row was machinery — above `to_list`'s ~29, which fits: one
more argument step and one more asserted position.

`split` is a two-argument STRING function with the same `[0, 1]` positions item 769 specialized for
the predicates; it just returns a LIST instead of a bool. So the change is widening that table
(`BINARY_STR_PRED` → `BINARY_STR_FN`, `(s, sub) => boolean` → `=> unknown`) and adding one entry.
The closure is unchanged, which means item 769's check-ORDER test still guards all four names.

Two alternated reads, one shape per process:

| shape                          |    read 1 |    read 2 |
| ------------------------------ | --------: | --------: |
| `count(split(a.s, '0'))`       | **1.36x** | **1.24x** |
| `count(split(a.s, '9'))`       | **1.39x** | **1.54x** |
| CONTROL `starts_with` [769]    |     1.01x |     1.01x |
| CONTROL `to_list(a.n)` general |     1.02x |     1.02x |
| CONTROL `upper(a.s)` [761]     |     0.97x |         — |
| CONTROL `count(a.s)` floor     |     0.97x |     1.00x |

### `split`'s body stays in `splitScalar`, and mutation shows why that is not optional

The table entry is `split: (s, sub) => splitScalar(s, sub)`, not `s.split(sub)`. The two differ on
exactly one input class: an EMPTY delimiter over a surrogate pair. JS `'a😀b'.split('')` keeps the
two lone surrogates; this engine replaces each with U+FFFD, because native's UTF-8 strings cannot
carry one — the same deviation `sanitizeSurrogates` exists for (item 768).

**`split: (s, sub) => s.split(sub)` — the obvious simplification — passed all 2,590 tests.** Now
pinned: `split('ab','')` is `['a','b']`, `split('a😀b','')` is `['a','�','�','b']`, and
the arguments are not interchangeable (`split('-','a-b')` is `['-']`). Teeth verified: the mutant
FAILS the unit suite after the test.

That is the FOURTH consecutive tick where a contract one of my own fast paths depends on had no
test (770 was docs-only; 768 `sanitizeSurrogates` and multi-char `replace`, 769 the predicate check
order, 764 `coalesce`'s values).

### The in-loop fuzzers are running NOTHING, and the check added at 767/772 now says so

All three mutants this tick reported **`fuzz=DID-NOT-RUN`**. Not "failed" — the process produced no
result line at all, which is what item 767 diagnosed and item 772 wired into the harness. Without
that check these would have read as three FAILs, two of them agreeing with my prediction and
therefore invisible.

So the standing position is now sharper than "re-run an unexpected failure": **the in-loop fuzz
step currently contributes no signal at all**, and every mutation verdict this tick rests on the
2,591-test unit suite. The fuzzers were run twice STANDALONE afterwards (13 pass, 0 fail both
times), which is where their signal actually comes from. Worth fixing the in-loop invocation rather
than tolerating it, and that is a harness task rather than an engine one.

The mutation script crashed mid-run on a variable name (`fz` where the harness calls it `f`) AFTER
applying mutant 1 and building it into the dist — so the tree and the artifact both carried a
mutant. `CLAUDE.md`'s rule is "restore before applying the next mutant, never only after the loop",
and its corollary from item 767 is that restoring the SOURCE is not enough here because the dist is
a build step away. Restored from the pristine copy under `target/` and rebuilt, verified by grep,
before anything else ran.

### Not done

TS edge projection at ~22x node projection per row, above. `replace` at ~168 ns (after 768) and
`substring` at ~87 are three- and mixed-arity string functions, so neither fits the two-argument
table this tick widened; each needs its own shape.

## 774 — `bun test` reports to STDERR, so three ticks of mutation diagnostics were reading an empty stream. Items 767, 772 and 773 are all corrected

**NO ENGINE CHANGE. A guard repaired, and three of my own records corrected.** Items 765-773
shipped eleven fast paths whose main guard is mutation. This tick found that the harness's view of
whether the guard RAN has been wrong in two different ways, and fixed it.

### The fact

```
bun test  →  "N pass" / "N fail"  on STDERR, never stdout
cargo test → "test result: ok. …"  on STDOUT
```

Measured directly, on a run that passed and a run that failed:

| invocation                              |  rc | result line in stdout | in stderr |
| --------------------------------------- | --: | --------------------- | --------- |
| `bun run fuzz --no-build`, clean tree   |   0 | **false**             | true      |
| `bun test packages/gql`, mutant applied |   1 | **false**             | true      |

### What that broke, twice, in opposite directions

**Item 767 inferred a runner-startup failure from an empty stdout.** Its words: _"the output stops
after `bun test v1.4.0` with no test-result line at all … the fuzz process did not get as far as
running a test, so its exit code carries NO information about the mutant."_ The process HAD run and
reported normally — to stderr. So the `fuzz=FAIL(1)` readings at items 765, 766, 767 and 772 were
REAL non-zero exits whose reason I never captured, not startup failures. With 20 consecutive clean
standalone runs on the pristine tree, the remaining explanation is the rare-seed residual
`gremlin-fuzz-families` already records, and its message was sitting in the stream I was not
reading.

**Then items 772 and 773 implemented 767's rule against stdout** and printed **`DID-NOT-RUN`** for
runs that passed cleanly. Item 773's entry says _"the in-loop fuzz step currently contributes no
signal at all"_ — that is wrong, and this entry is the correction. The fuzz step was working
throughout; only the label was false.

So the sequence is: a real intermittent failure → misdiagnosed as a startup failure → a rule
written from the misdiagnosis → implemented against the wrong stream → a false "did not run" that
hid a working step. **Four ticks of compounding error from one unexamined assumption about where a
test runner writes.**

### The fix, and its validation

`verdict()` now concatenates stdout and stderr, looks for a result line there, and only then reads
the exit code (with 124/137/-9 still distinguished as timeout/OOM). Re-running item 773's three
mutants with it:

| mutant                         | predicted | tests   | fuzz     |                          |
| ------------------------------ | --------- | ------- | -------- | ------------------------ |
| `split` bypasses `splitScalar` | FAIL      | FAIL(1) | **pass** | as predicted             |
| `split` arguments swapped      | FAIL      | FAIL(1) | **pass** | as predicted             |
| `split` not specialized        | SURVIVE   | pass    | **pass** | as predicted, EQUIVALENT |

Clean verdicts, and the fuzz column now says `pass` where it said `DID-NOT-RUN` an hour ago. It
also confirms a fact item 765 established and 773 relied on: the byte-identity fuzzers do NOT catch
the empty-delimiter contract, because they generate no non-ASCII strings — the unit test added at
773 is the only guard for it.

### `CLAUDE.md` corrected

The rule item 767 added said "require a result line in the output", which is right in spirit and
was unimplementable as written — it never said WHICH stream, and my own implementation of it got
that wrong twice. It now names stderr for `bun`, stdout for `cargo`, says to concatenate, and keeps
the re-run-on-its-own advice for an unexpected verdict with the reason now actually capturable.

### What this does NOT change

Every verdict in items 765-773 still stands. The ones that mattered were all accompanied by NAMED
failing tests from a suite whose stream I was reading correctly (`cargo test` on stdout for the
Rust mutants, and for the TS ones the unit suite's non-zero exit plus the test name). What was lost
was the fuzz column's contribution, and this tick shows it would have read `pass` — so no mutant
was wrongly declared caught by it.

The engine is unaffected: 20 consecutive clean fuzz runs on the pristine tree, plus the standing
two-run checks in every tick since 765.

### Not done

The rare-seed fuzz residual still exists and now has a capture path. Next time an in-loop run
exits non-zero, the stderr will name the fuzzer and the seed, and `bun run fuzz <name> --seed N`
replays it deterministically — which is the first time that has been possible in this session.

Gates: no engine change. `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0. The corrected harness lives in the
scratchpad, which is where every mutation harness in this session has lived.

## 775 — an ANONYMOUS end node costs 4.4x a named one in TS, cause located. And item 773's "edge projection is 22x" is REFUTED by its own decomposition

**NO ENGINE CHANGE; a 4.4x equivalent-spelling gap found, located, and made a probe group.** Item
773's sweep closed with "TS edge projection is ~22x node projection per row" and named it the next
target. Checking that claim before building on it is what produced this item.

### Item 773's claim was an OVER-CLAIM, and the discriminator says so

The two bench rows differ in TWO clauses, not one:

```
query: project the element [ts lazy]   MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n                     1-slot label scan
query: project the edge    [ts lazy]   MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->() RETURN r        3-slot traversal
```

So the 22x conflates rendering an edge with enumerating via a pattern — exactly the "differ in more
than one clause" trap `CLOSED.md` records at item 339. The third measurement settles it: on one
fixture (40,000 Person nodes, 5 KNOWS edges each, 200,000 edges),

| query                                          |    ms | ns/row |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----: | -----: |
| `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n`                    |  2.20 |     55 |
| `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.age`                |  2.28 |     57 |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->() RETURN r`       | 73.80 |    369 |
| `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->() RETURN r.since` | 84.62 |    423 |

**`RETURN r.since` costs MORE than `RETURN r`.** If rendering the edge were the cost, adding a
property read on top of it could not be dearer than the render itself. The lazy edge render is
nearly free; the ~400 ns is the traversal. Item 773's framing is withdrawn.

**Also recorded, because it broke the obvious decomposition:** `count(*)` cannot baseline
enumeration here. Both `MATCH (:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->() RETURN count(*)` and its `->(b)` twin measure
**0.00 ms** — the count shortcut skips enumeration entirely, so "traversal minus count(*)" is not
available as a subtraction.

### What the decomposition DID find, isolated to one clause

| query                                  |    rows |        ms |
| -------------------------------------- | ------: | --------: |
| `MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->() RETURN r.since`  | 200,000 | **83.51** |
| `MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->(b) RETURN r.since` | 200,000 | **19.03** |

Same RETURN, same edges, **identical row counts (asserted, not assumed)**, differing only in
whether the end node is anonymous. **4.4x**, both answers correct — which is the shape
`CLAUDE.md`'s equivalent-spelling section exists for, and which no correctness test can catch.

### The cause, located rather than guessed

`hopEnds` in `packages/gql/src/executor/hop-projection.ts`:

```ts
const farVar = node.variable;
if (… || farVar === undefined || …) {
  return null;
}
```

An anonymous end node has no `variable`, so `hopEnds` refuses, `detectHopProjection` returns null,
and the query falls to the general row pipeline. The machinery for "the projection does not read
the far end" already exists two functions along — `startOnly: readsStart && !vars.includes(farVar)
&& !needsRel` — so the shape is reachable in principle.

**THIRD INSTANCE OF THIS SHAPE IN THIS ONE FILE.** Item 444: `-[e:E]->` against `-[:E]->` at
**3.7x**, from a guard whose own comment read "defensive, not load-bearing". Item 505: a split
`MATCH` spelling at **747.9 ms against 0.0**. Now an anonymous end at 4.4x. A fast path that gates
on the PRESENCE of a name rather than on whether the name is USED produces this every time.

### Not fixed here, deliberately

That file carries two comments refuted by running what they described. Item 444's guard removal
"broke `a REL VARIABLE bound OUTSIDE correlates on that edge, not the degree`" —
`MATCH (p:U)-[r:T]->(q) RETURN COUNT { MATCH (p)-[r:T]->(z) }` must answer 1 and answered `p`'s
degree — because `freePredicateVars` cannot distinguish an inner pattern that CORRELATES on an
already-bound name from one that binds it freshly. Relaxing `farVar === undefined` needs those
cases in front of it, and a fast path admitted at a tick boundary in a file with that history is
how a wrong answer ships.

### What shipped instead

The pair is now a **spelling-probe group**, which is where a 4.4x equivalent-spelling gap belongs —
the probe exists for exactly this class and did not have it. On the probe's own 200,000-row fixture
it flags at **2.88x** (mine measured 4.4x; different fixture, same direction), and the run reports
**0 groups disagree on the ANSWER**, so the two spellings agree. The group's comment carries the
measurement, the located cause, the two sibling items and the reason it is not yet relaxed.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0
(it first read 1 on an unnecessary type assertion in the scratch probe, which is deleted); `bun run
spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9` — 0 answer disagreements, three groups over 2x, the new
one among them by design.

## 776 — an anonymous end node now takes the hop fast path: 4.60-4.88x, the two spellings CONVERGE, and the sentinel that makes it safe was untested

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 775 found the gap, located the cause and deliberately did not fix
it — that file records two guards that looked defensive and were load-bearing. This fixes it with
those cases in front of it.

### The change, and why not the obvious one

`hopEnds` returned `null` for `node.variable === undefined`, so an anonymous end refused
`detectHopProjection` and fell to the general row pipeline.

The obvious fix is `farVar: string | undefined` threaded through. It is the wrong one: `farVar` has
about fifty uses, six of them `binding.set(farVar, far)` inside separate walk implementations, each
of which would need a branch. In a file whose own comments record two relaxations that broke
correctness, a fifty-site refactor is the wrong instrument.

Instead an anonymous end gets a **synthesized binding name**: `const ANON_FAR_VAR =
'\u0000anon_far'`, and `node.variable ?? ANON_FAR_VAR`. The walks are untouched, and nothing can
read the binding because **the parser cannot produce that name** — `MATCH (a)-[:E]->(\u0000anon_far)`
is rejected as an unexpected character, checked rather than assumed. So `vars.includes(farVar)` is
false exactly as it should be and `startOnly` resolves the same way it does for a named-but-unread
end.

### The numbers

One shape per process, two alternated A/B reads, row counts asserted on every run:

| shape                             |                    read 1 |                    read 2 |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------: | ------------------------: |
| `MATCH (:P)-[r:E]->() RETURN r.k` | **4.88x** (82.13 → 16.83) | **4.60x** (75.84 → 16.48) |
| CONTROL `->(b) RETURN r.k`        |                     1.03x |                     1.02x |
| CONTROL `->(b) RETURN b.age`      |                     0.96x |                     1.01x |
| CONTROL node scan `n.age`         |                     0.92x |                     1.00x |

**The ratio is not the point; the convergence is.** The anonymous spelling now costs 16.48 against
the named one's 17.40 — the two spellings of the same question cost the same, which is what
`CLAUDE.md`'s equivalent-spelling section asks for.

**And the probe agrees from its own instrument.** Item 775 added this pair to `spelling-probe.ts`,
where it flagged at **2.88x**. After this change the group is **absent from the >2x list** — only
the two pre-existing groups remain (`label on start`, item 285's product predicate), with 0 groups
disagreeing on the ANSWER. A gap found by hand, recorded as a probe group, then closed and
confirmed by the probe is the cycle that file exists for.

### The sentinel's uniqueness is LOAD-BEARING, and mutation found nothing testing it

| mutant                                            | predicted | gql tests | fuzzers  |                          |
| ------------------------------------------------- | --------- | --------- | -------- | ------------------------ |
| the sentinel replaced by a plausible name (`'b'`) | FAIL      | **pass**  | **pass** | **not as predicted**     |
| an anonymous end refused again                    | SURVIVE   | pass      | pass     | as predicted, EQUIVALENT |

The first is the one that matters. With the sentinel set to `'b'`,
`MATCH (b:P)-[r:E]->() RETURN b.age` binds the FAR node to `b` and reads ITS age — 20 where the
start's is 10. A wrong answer, reachable only by a query that names its start exactly as the
sentinel, and **the entire 2,591-test suite passed it.**

So the safety of this change rested on an untested property. Two tests now pin it: a start named
`b` with an anonymous end still reads the start (and the same query with `x`, and with the end
named), and the two spellings agree on `r.k`, on `a.age` and on `count(*)`. Teeth verified — the
mutant FAILS after the tests where it passed before.

That is the fifth consecutive tick in which a property one of my own changes depends on turned out
to have no test (764 `coalesce`'s values, 768 `sanitizeSurrogates` and multi-char `replace`, 769
the predicate check order, 773 `split`'s empty delimiter, now this). The pattern is consistent
enough to state plainly: **a fast path's admission gate is exactly where this repo's tests are
thinnest**, because every such gate is answer-equivalent when it is right.

### Not done

There is a SECOND `farVar === undefined` refusal in the same file, in a different function (around
line 844, which also rejects `farVar === startVar`). This tick did not touch it, and the
measurement says the main projection path converged without it — so whatever shape it guards is

## 777 — item 776's second gate costs NOTHING (closed by measurement), and an INLINE start property costs 8.4x its clause twin

**NO ENGINE CHANGE. One open question closed with a negative result, one larger gap found,
located and guarded.** Item 776 left a second `farVar === undefined` refusal untouched and said

### Item 776's second gate: priced, nothing there

The second refusal is in the anchor-hop FUSION detector (item 505's two-`MATCH` shape), which also

per process, row counts asserted:

| query                                         |    ms |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----: |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->() RETURN a.age`           | 15.99 |
| `MATCH (a:P) MATCH (a)-[:E]->() RETURN a.age` | 15.62 |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN a.age`          | 15.85 |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[r:E]->() RETURN a.age`          | 15.89 |

All four converge, and both `count(*)` twins take the shortcut at 0.00. **Item 505's fusion rewrite
plus item 776's relaxation already cover these shapes**, so the second gate's refusal has nothing
behind it. Recorded as a negative result for the same reason item 770 recorded one for item 342's
ladder: the next tick should not "fix" this.

### Then the same method on the detector's other gates, and the biggest gap yet in this file

Both pairs below are equivalent spellings with asserted-equal row counts (2,065 each):

| predicate position |    inline `{k: 5}` |     clause `WHERE` |                 |
| ------------------ | -----------------: | -----------------: | --------------- |
| on the **START**   | 8.69 / 8.34 / 8.42 | 1.00 / 1.00 / 0.99 | **8.4x SLOWER** |
| on the **END**     |               8.34 |              14.36 | 1.7x FASTER     |

**Inline predicates are pushed down at one end of the same hop and fatal at the other.** Cause
located: `plainNode` is `(n.properties?.length ?? 0) === 0 && n.where === undefined`, so an inline
property on the START refuses `detectHopProjection` outright, while `closedFarPred` pushes the
far-node equivalent into the walk. The start/end asymmetry is the tell — it is not that inline
predicates are hard, it is that one position has support and the other has a refusal.

**FOURTH instance in `hop-projection.ts` of a gate on whether something is PRESENT rather than
whether it is USED** — item 444 (`-[e:E]->`, 3.7x), item 505 (split `MATCH`, 747.9 ms against 0.0),
item 776 (anonymous end, 4.6-4.9x), and this at 8.4x, the largest of them.

### Not fixed here, with the reason stated precisely

The fix is item 505's shape: a REWRITE lifting the inline property into the `WHERE` clause the fast
path already handles, rather than teaching the fast path a second predicate position. That is the
smaller and better-tested route — but it **must refuse a NULL literal and a PARAM**:

- inline `{k: null}` means **IS NULL** (item 260), where `k = null` is UNKNOWN. Rewriting one into
  the other changes the answer.
- `{k: $p}` cannot be proven non-null at compile time, so it cannot be lifted either.

That guard IS the correctness story for this change, and it deserves a tick with tests rather than
the tail of one. Items 775 → 776 ran exactly this way — find and probe-group, then fix with tests —
and it worked.

### What shipped

The pair is a spelling-probe group carrying the measurement, the located cause, the mirror
asymmetry and the null/param constraint. It flags at **3.80x** on the probe's own fixture (8.4x on
mine; different fixture, same direction and both large), with **0 groups disagreeing on the
ANSWER**.

## 778 — an inline START property lifts into the `WHERE`: 5.31x and the spellings converge. One rung's gate is another rung's disqualifier, and all three refusals were untested

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 777 found the 8.4x, located the cause and stated the constraint the
fix would need. This implements it, and the two things worth reading are what the suite caught and
what mutation caught.

### The change

`liftStartProps`, a clause-list rewrite beside `fuseAnchorThenHop`:
`MATCH (a:L {k: 5})-[:T]->(b)` becomes `MATCH (a:L)-[:T]->(b) WHERE a.k = 5`. Item 505's shape and
for its reason — the rewritten clause is an ordinary pattern, so every rung of the ladder applies
with no rung knowing it happened. It runs OUTSIDE `fuseAnchorThenHop` so a FUSED clause gets the
lift too, since the fused pattern's start is the anchor's.

| shape                                         | before |    after |     ratio |
| --------------------------------------------- | -----: | -------: | --------: |
| `MATCH (a:P {age: 5})-[:E]->(b) RETURN b.age` |   5.04 | **0.95** | **5.31x** |
| CONTROL its clause-`WHERE` twin               |   0.96 |     0.95 |     1.01x |
| CONTROL inline on the END                     |   8.66 |     7.93 |     1.09x |
| CONTROL unfiltered hop                        |   8.49 |     8.45 |     1.00x |
| CONTROL node scan                             |   1.21 |     1.23 |     0.98x |

The target converges with its twin at 0.95 — equal cost for equal questions, which is the point
rather than the ratio. And the spelling probe's item 777 group, which flagged at **3.80x** when it
was added one tick ago, is **absent from the >2x list** after this change, with 0 groups disagreeing
on the ANSWER.

### ONE RUNG'S ADMISSION GATE IS ANOTHER RUNG'S DISQUALIFIER

The first version lifted any non-null literal, including on a QUANTIFIED pattern. Two
`reachability.test.ts` cases turned from passes into ERRORS:

```
LenkeError: Variable-length pattern exceeded the trail budget; add a tighter bound
  ->+ over a 5000-node connected graph completes and returns the reachable set
```

A clause `WHERE` **disqualifies the unbounded var-length BFS rung**, so
`MATCH (a:N {k: 1})-[:E]->+(b) RETURN DISTINCT b` stopped taking it, fell to the general path and
faulted on the trail budget. Opening one gate closed another, and **nothing about the gate being
opened reveals that** — it is only visible from the far side. This is the hazard in rewriting a
clause list that the file's history (items 444, 505, 776) does not name, and it is now recorded in
`liftStartProps`'s own comment with the error text.

Fixed by refusing a quantified segment. Found by the suite, not by reasoning — which is the only
reason the reachability tests being there matters.

### ALL THREE REFUSALS WERE UNTESTED

| mutant                         | predicted | gql tests | fuzzers  |                                           |
| ------------------------------ | --------- | --------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| the NULL refusal dropped       | FAIL      | **pass**  | **pass** | **not as predicted**                      |
| the PARAM refusal dropped      | FAIL      | **pass**  | **pass** | **not as predicted**                      |
| the QUANTIFIER refusal dropped | FAIL      | FAIL      | pass     | as predicted (`reachability.test.ts`)     |
| the rewrite removed            | SURVIVE   | —         | —        | BUILD FAILED — a bad mutant, says nothing |

The first two are the ones that change an ANSWER. Verified against the engine before writing
anything:

```
MATCH (a:P {k: null})-[:E]->(x) RETURN a.tag      [{"v":"has-null"}]
MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(x) WHERE a.k = null RETURN …   []
MATCH (a:P {k: $p})-[:E]->(x)  with $p = null     [{"v":"has-null"}]
```

Inline `{k: null}` is IS NULL and matches a STORED null (null is a present value here); `a.k = null`
is UNKNOWN and matches nothing. So lifting a null silently drops a row, and `{k: $p}` inherits that
because it cannot be shown non-null at compile time. **Both mutants passed the entire 2,593-test
suite.** Three tests now pin all four behaviours (inline null, the clause twin's empty result, a
null param, a non-null param, and the non-null literal agreeing with its twin), teeth verified —
both mutants FAIL after them.

The fourth mutant build-failed on a bad anchor and is recorded as uninformative rather than as a
survival; the route-choice equivalence is covered by the A/B.

### The count, now at six

Items 764, 768, 769, 773, 776 and 778 each depended on a property with no test, found by mutation.
Item 776 stated the pattern — **a fast path's admission gate is where this repo's tests are
thinnest** — and this item is the strongest case for it yet: the gate had THREE conditions, each
load-bearing, and the suite covered exactly one of them (and that one only by accident, via a
reachability test written for another purpose).

## 779 — "grep the pattern elsewhere" applied ACROSS ENGINES: the Rust engine has NO twin of items 776 or 778, and the proof is a plan, not a timing

**NEGATIVE RESULT, NO ENGINE CHANGE.** Two consecutive ticks closed TypeScript fast-path gaps whose
cause was identical in shape — `hopEnds` refused an ANONYMOUS end node (item 776, 4.6-4.9x) and
`plainNode` refused a start carrying INLINE properties (items 777/778, 8.4x, fixed at 5.31x). The
method says to grep the pattern elsewhere before moving on, and "elsewhere" for a two-engine repo
means the other engine. This is that check, and it comes back empty for a reason worth recording.

### Both pairs lower to one plan

The native `spelling_probe` already covered `inline {k:v} vs WHERE equality` on a node **SCAN**, but
neither the anonymous-end pair nor the inline-start pair on a **HOP with a projection** — and the
scan case is exactly the one that gave TypeScript no warning, because its scan rungs accept both
spellings. So both pairs were added one position along, with a projection rather than a count so the
row-building path is exercised:

| group                                             | spelling A | spelling B | verdict                      |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------: | ---------: | ---------------------------- |
| an ANONYMOUS end node vs a named one              |   0.247 ms |   0.246 ms | `✓ identical optimized plan` |
| inline `{k:v}` on a hop START vs `WHERE` equality |   0.664 ms |   0.653 ms | `✓ identical optimized plan` |

Per this repo's own rule the **plan identity is the signal and the timing is only the backstop** —
and here the two agree. The full probe reports `NO PERF CLIFFS: every equivalent spelling converges
on plan or cost`, with no group disagreeing on an answer.

### Why the two engines differ here, which is the point

This is not luck and it is not that the Rust fast paths happen to have wider gates. It is
structural, and naming it is what stops the next tick from looking for a Rust twin of the next TS
gap in this family:

- **TypeScript's fast paths read the PATTERN.** `detectHopProjection` and `hopEnds` inspect the AST
  node — whether a variable is present, whether a property map is present — so a predicate's
  SPELLING decides which rung admits it. A gate written as "is this field absent" is then a gate on
  the surface syntax, which is how items 444, 505, 776 and 777 all happened in one file.
- **This engine canonicalizes BEFORE any routing decision.** Both spellings become the same
  `ir::Plan`, and `exec` sees one shape. There is no position at which a spelling could be refused,
  so the class of bug cannot occur — which is precisely the claim `CLAUDE.md` makes for the
  single-IR design, now checked at the two positions where the other engine was actually caught.

So item 778 needed a clause-list rewrite (`liftStartProps`) and this side needs nothing. **The
asymmetry in the FIXES follows from an asymmetry in the ARCHITECTURES, not from one engine being
better maintained.**

### What shipped

Two probe groups, kept as **guards rather than targets**, each carrying the measurement, the
negative verdict and the reason. Their value is forward-looking: a future change that routed on the
pattern instead of the plan — the tempting shortcut when adding a fast path — would surface here as a
plan mismatch at exactly the two shapes that have already cost two ticks in the other engine.

This is the second negative result in three ticks recorded deliberately so the next pass does not
re-derive it (item 777 did the same for item 776's second gate). The store for that is `CLOSED.md`,
and the line is in this commit.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0 (it covers examples, which is the only
