## 797 — The Gremlin bench (the fourth instrument) found a NEW gap, in the direction nobody was looking: TS **GQL** is 2.24x its own **Gremlin** twin on a filtered node count, and both are on their fast paths

**NO ENGINE CHANGE — a diagnosed, located, novel finding.** `bun run bench:gremlin` is the fourth
committed instrument and was the last one unrun this session. Items 789-796 found six consecutive
candidates already closed; this one is not in that list.

### The hypothesis, and it was WRONG in a useful way

`bench:gremlin` reads three filtered counts with NO HOP at large ts/native ratios —
`V().has(age,gt).count()` **22.4x**, `V().hasLabel().has().count()` **27.4x**,
`V().has().has().count()` **13.1x**. Those are not the multi-hop count family (closed at 617), so
the hypothesis was a missing node-scan-count lowering on the Gremlin side, since GQL has that
family (items 204-209).

**The floor had to be the GQL TWIN, not native** — item 234's lesson, that a big ts/native ratio can
be data layout rather than a missing path, and the only way to tell is to ask the SAME engine the
SAME question in its other surface language. Measured, 200,000 vertices, one shape per process, 14
reps, median of the plateau, answers asserted equal:

| question                       |         GQL |  Gremlin |                      |
| ------------------------------ | ----------: | -------: | -------------------- |
| count vertices with `age > 28` | **4.78 ms** | **2.13** | GQL **2.24x slower** |
| the same with a label          |        2.61 |     2.10 | 1.24x                |
| two predicates                 |        4.52 |     4.06 | 1.11x                |
| CONTROL unfiltered count       |        0.00 |     0.01 | both O(1)            |

So the hypothesis is refuted and **the gap runs the other way**: the Gremlin surface is already the
faster of the two, and native's 22.4x is the data layout item 234 predicted. ~10.6 ns a vertex for
Gremlin against ~24 for GQL, same engine, same fixture, identical answers (140,202 / 70,101 /
10,786).

**That is an equivalent-spelling gap across the two surface languages** — the class this repo is
named for, in the one place its own probes do not look: `spelling-probe.ts` compares GQL spellings
to GQL spellings, and the native `spelling_probe` has cross-language groups but the TS side has
none.

### Diagnosed, not assumed: both paths are on their fast routes

The obvious explanation would be that the GQL shape falls off its shortcut. **It does not.** A throw
inside `buildNodeCount`'s constrained tally — item 751's reachability technique — fires for all
three GQL shapes:

```text
gql-pred         THREW REACHABILITY PROBE: buildNodeCount constrained tally
gql-label-pred   THREW REACHABILITY PROBE: buildNodeCount constrained tally
gql-two-pred     THREW REACHABILITY PROBE: buildNodeCount constrained tally
```

So the clause `WHERE` IS pushed into the node and the tally IS taken. The 2.24x is **inside** the
tally, at the per-vertex predicate call — `inlineHolds` → `satisfies` — against whatever Gremlin's
`has` step does per vertex.

### Why this is a real target and also a careful one

`buildNodeCount`'s own comment states the design: _"The predicate is applied through `inlineHolds`
-> `satisfies`, the general path's own implementation, so the two spellings of a constrained node
count agree by construction rather than by re-deriving inline-pattern semantics here."_

So the 2.24x is the price of sharing one predicate implementation, and the obvious fix — a
specialized per-vertex comparison in the tally — is exactly the re-derivation that comment refuses.
**The next step is therefore a comparison, not a change**: price `satisfies`'s `cmpProps` arm (item
276's lift, which reads the property straight off the element) against the Gremlin `has` closure on
the same vertex set, and find which of the two is doing more work. If `cmpProps` is already the same
shape as `has`, the gap is elsewhere in the tally and the shared implementation is not the cost.

Not started here, because a change to a path whose comment names cross-spelling agreement as its
reason for existing deserves its own tick with the differential fuzzers on it — the same judgement
item 786 made about `nullif`, which paid off at 787.

### A gap in the instruments, worth recording on its own

The TS spelling probe has **no cross-language group**. The native `spelling_probe` does (items 779's
two, plus `grouped count: GQL vs Gremlin` and others), which is why a native GQL/Gremlin divergence
would be caught and a TS one would not. This finding came from a bench, by accident, not from the
probe whose job it is. That is the actionable instrument change, and it is cheap — the groups above
are three lines each.

Gates: `bun test packages/gql` **2621** pass 0 fail; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run build` 0; the
reachability probe restored and the tree verified clean before measuring the suite. No engine change.

## 798 — NEW, and bigger than what I was chasing: a PARAM-valued predicate costs **1.76x** its literal twin per vertex, and the cause is one line called per row

**NO ENGINE CHANGE — a new finding, priced, diagnosed to a single line, with two candidate fixes and
the risk in each named.** Item 797 located its 2.24x inside `buildNodeCount`'s tally and specified
the next step as a comparison: price `satisfies`'s arms against each other. That comparison found
something larger than the gap it was run to explain.

### The decomposition

200,000 vertices, one shape per process, 14 reps, median of the plateau. All rows count; none builds
a row:

| shape                      | ns/vertex | `satisfies` arm        |
| -------------------------- | --------: | ---------------------- |
| CONTROL no predicate       |       0.0 | the bucket size, O(1)  |
| CONTROL `(n:P)` label only |       0.0 | the label bucket, O(1) |
| `{age: 28}` inline         |      19.7 | `props`                |
| `age = 28` clause          |      22.0 | `eqProps`              |
| `age > 28` clause          |      25.2 | `cmpProps`             |
| **`age > $a` clause**      |  **45.4** | `cmpProps`, a PARAM    |
| `age > 28 AND score > 2`   |      29.2 | `cmpProps` x2          |
| `age = 28 AND score = 3`   |      24.3 | `eqProps` x2           |

Two things fall out. **The scaffolding dominates**: the three arms sit within 5.5 ns of each other,
and a SECOND predicate adds only 2.3-4.0 ns — so ~18-20 ns is per-VERTEX cost shared by every arm
(`inlineHolds` writing the bind variable into a `Map`, `satisfies` allocating
`{ binding, params, graph }`, the `value(env)` call) and only 2-4 ns is the predicate itself. That
answers item 797's question: the shared implementation is NOT the cost, the scaffolding around it is.

And then the row that matters: **a param costs 20 ns a vertex more than the identical literal.**

### Confirmed, with disjoint ranges

Three rounds, literal against param:

```text
  age > 28    24.0  26.6  27.0      min 24.0
  age > $a    42.2  42.6  46.6      min 42.2      1.76x, ranges DISJOINT
```

**This is an equivalent-spelling gap on the spelling applications actually write.** `WHERE k > $a`
and `WHERE k > 28` ask the same question; the param form is the injection-safe one, and this repo's
own notes call `IN $names` "the spelling applications actually write" for exactly that reason. It is
also the named defect class — CLAUDE.md lists `k = $a OR k = $b` against `k IN [$a, $b]` among the
four that cost 100-300x each and returned the correct answer.

**Not previously recorded.** `CLOSED.md` has no entry for param-resolution cost, no literal-vs-param
comparison, and no mention of `Object.hasOwn` — checked before claiming novelty, which is the
discipline that caught six already-closed candidates at items 789-796.

### Diagnosed to one line

`compileExpr`'s `param` arm returns this closure, and it runs PER ROW:

```ts
return (env) => {
  if (Object.hasOwn(env.params, name)) {
    return env.params[name];
  }
  return name === '__now' ? null : undefined;
};
```

`Object.hasOwn` plus a dynamic property read, per vertex, to produce a value that **cannot change
during one execution** — `env.params` is the same object for every row. The `hasOwn` is there for a
documented correctness reason (`$__proto__` must read undefined rather than `Object.prototype`, to
match the Rust engine, whose params live in a `HashMap`), and that reason is about WHICH value
resolves, not about resolving it repeatedly.

### Two candidate fixes, and why neither is a line

1. **Memoize inside the closure on the params OBJECT identity.** Tick-sized and the obvious move —
   and it assumes the params object is never mutated mid-execution. Today's code would observe such
   a mutation and a cache would not, so this trades a cost for a behaviour change in a case nobody
   has specified. Item 310's degree memo is the precedent for how such a memo fails review: it was
   refuted by its own unreachable control, not by being wrong.
2. **Normalize `params` once at the entry point**, so the per-row closure is a plain slot read with
   the `hasOwn` semantics already applied. No identity assumption and no mutation hazard, because
   the normalization happens before any row is touched — but it is an entry-point change touching
   every `query`/`exec` caller, so it is a design decision rather than an edit.

Route 2 is the sound one and is the recommendation. Neither is started here: a change to how params
resolve reaches every predicate in both surface languages, and it wants the differential fuzzers and
a mutation pass of its own — the judgement item 786 made about `nullif`, which paid off at 787.

### What this does to item 797's number

797 measured GQL at ~24 ns a vertex against the Gremlin twin's ~10.6 using a LITERAL. With a param
the GQL side is 42-45, so the cross-surface gap on the spelling applications write is roughly
**4x**, not 2.24x. 797's recommendation stands but its magnitude understates the shape that matters.

Gates: `bun test packages/gql` **2621** pass 0 fail (run at item 797, tree unchanged since); the
probe removed and `git status` verified clean. No engine change.

## 799 — TS: the `$param` reader goes compile-time gated — **1.73x / 2.11x**, the param now costs what its literal twin costs, and the proof is code that already runs

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 798 measured a param-valued predicate at **1.76x** its literal twin,
diagnosed it to one line, and named two routes: an identity-keyed memo (tick-sized, unsound) and
normalizing params at the entry point (sound, broad). **Reading the code found a third that is both
tick-sized AND sound**, and it is sound because of a check that already runs.

### The change

`compileExpr`'s `param` arm ran this PER ROW:

```ts
if (Object.hasOwn(env.params, name)) {
  return env.params[name];
}
return name === '__now' ? null : undefined;
```

**The `hasOwn` is redundant, and the proof is in the executor, not in an assumption.** Plan execution
validates every referenced name before any row is touched — `Object.hasOwn(params, name)` and a
`MissingParameter` throw unless present — so at row time the property IS own and the check cannot
fail. Even `$__proto__` unbound never reaches a row: it fails that validation first, which is the
hazard the per-row check was written for.

**TWO names are outside that proof, and both are decided at COMPILE time so the hot closure carries
no test at all:**

- **`__now`**, the one name the eager validation admits as absent (an unsupplied `current_*` reads
  NULL, and `undefined` would be a different value).
- **a name present on `Object.prototype`** — `toString`, `constructor`, `__proto__` — which must read
  undefined rather than the INHERITED value. Not theoretical: **`compileValidator` is exported from
  the package index** and runs these closures with `params: {}` and WITHOUT the eager validation, so
  `$toString` there would resolve to `Object.prototype.toString`, a function.

| shape                      |         before |    after |     ratio |
| -------------------------- | -------------: | -------: | --------: |
| `WHERE n.age > $a` count   | 43.0 ns/vertex | **24.8** | **1.73x** |
| `WHERE n.age = $a` count   |           43.4 | **20.6** | **2.11x** |
| CONTROL `> 28` literal     |           24.0 |     23.4 |     1.03x |
| CONTROL `= 28` literal     |           20.5 |     19.8 |     1.04x |
| CONTROL `{age: 28}` inline |           19.1 |     18.7 |     1.02x |
| CONTROL no predicate       |            0.0 |      0.0 |         — |

Min of three order-alternated rounds, each arm rebuilt into the dist AND grepped there. **The param
now costs what its literal twin costs** (24.8 against 23.4; 20.6 against 19.8) — equal cost for
equal questions, which is the point rather than the ratio, and it closes an instance of the defect
class CLAUDE.md names.

`compileExpr` went over this file's complexity gate (37 against 35) once the two exceptions were in
it, so the arm is extracted as `compileParam` — the same recipe items 781 and 792 used.

### Mutation: both exceptions untested, one INERT and one load-bearing

| mutant                                | predicted                    | result                                             |
| ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| drop the `__now` exception            | WRONG ANSWER                 | **INERT** — `current_date` still answers null      |
| drop the `Object.prototype` exception | WRONG ANSWER, probably a gap | **WRONG ANSWER, and SURVIVED (2621 pass, 0 fail)** |

**The `__now` one is inert and stays anyway.** Under the mutant `current_date` still reads `null`,
because `undefined` and `null` are both nullish everywhere downstream. So the guard has no teeth of
its own — the same shape as items 781's and 782's inert refusals, and the same call: it stays because
it keeps the equivalence LOCAL, rather than resting on downstream nullish coercion that no test pins
either.

**The prototype one is reachable through a public export and had no test.** Three tests now pin it —
the four prototype names reading nullish, ordinary names reading nullish through the FAST closure,
and a bound param still resolving — and two of the three fail under the mutant.

### An anomaly I could not explain and did not chase

`two-param` (`age > $a AND score > $b`) moved only **1.03x** (30.4 → 29.5), and its PLAIN reading of
30.4 is **LOWER than the single-param shape's 43.0** — a two-param query cheaper than a one-param one
on the arm that charges per param. A reachability probe confirms all three shapes DO reach
`buildNodeCount`'s tally, so it is not off-path. I have no explanation and did not pursue one;
recorded as an open question rather than smoothed into the table, because an unexplained ordering is
exactly what items 748 and 749 were built from.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0 — it
caught four `no-unnecessary-type-assertion` findings in the new tests and a stray probe, which
`bun test` does not typecheck and would have missed; `bun test packages/gql` **2624** pass 0 fail;
the seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail, run twice — this changes how every param resolves in
the TS engine, so the TS-vs-Rust differential is the gate that matters; `bun run spelling` at
`SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`.

### The spelling probe flagged a 2.49x that was NOT a regression — and the control is what proved it

The gate's `bun run spelling` run flagged a FOURTH group that had not flagged in any of the nine
earlier runs this session (items 780-794): _"SEEK: a param equality AND a second conjunct — clause vs
inline (item 578)"_, at **2.49x**. A new param-related flag immediately after a param change is the
one thing that must be ruled out before committing, so it was.

**The group's own members located it.** Three of the four got FASTER (9.65 -> 8.88, 8.80 -> 8.28,
9.35 -> 9.18); the fourth — `WHERE n.k >= 0 AND n.s = $s`, the only member with the param equality
SECOND — read **9.22 before and 20.57 after**. On its face a 2.2x regression on a recorded row.

**The first reproduction attempt measured the wrong question**, and that is worth recording: my
isolated fixture used `s: 's' + (i % 997)`, which answers 201 rows and runs in 0.1 ms — every shape
looked identical and nothing showed. The probe's fixture is `k: i % 50`, `s: 's' + (i % 7)`: SEVEN
distinct values, so the seek returns **28,572** candidates. A reproduction that does not reproduce
the answer size is not a reproduction (items 702 and 790's lesson in a fourth form).

**With the real fixture the row's own variability is larger than the flag.** Nine reps, same binary:

```text
  GATE   param-second   7.73 / 11.16 / 22.46   (min / median / max)
  GATE   lit-second    10.03 / 10.64 / 23.57   ← NO param: the gate cannot reach it
  PLAIN  lit-second    10.38 / 11.11 / 20.36
```

`lit-second` contains no parameter, so the change cannot touch it — and it ranges **2.35x within a
single arm**. A 2.49x BETWEEN members is inside that.

**And the isolated A/B reverses the sign.** Min of 9 per shape, on the probe's own fixture:

| shape                                   | PLAIN |     GATE |                       |
| --------------------------------------- | ----: | -------: | --------------------- |
| `param-second` — the "regressed" member | 13.94 | **7.73** | GATE **1.80x FASTER** |
| `param-first`                           | 14.16 |    10.71 | 1.32x faster          |
| CONTROL `lit-second` — no param         | 10.38 |    10.03 | 1.03x                 |

So the member that appeared to regress 2.2x actually **improves 1.80x**, and the control the change
cannot reach is flat. No regression. CLAUDE.md's "know the noise floor — some rows range 2x for the
same binary" and "a per-row question needs a per-row instrument" are both exactly this, and the
control the change cannot reach is what turned a scare into a measurement.

**Two wrong conclusions were available here** and the method excluded both: committing while
assuming the flag was noise, and abandoning a 1.73-2.11x win because a noisy row moved. The flag was
worth chasing precisely because neither could be dismissed without the isolated arm.

## 800 — BUILT AND REVERTED: a cross-language group cannot live in the TS spelling probe, because the GQL side arrives POLLUTED and the Gremlin side arrives clean

**NO ENGINE CHANGE, and the instrument change is reverted.** Item 797 found TS GQL at 2.24x its own
Gremlin twin on a filtered node count, recorded that the TS spelling probe has no cross-language
group where the native one has had them since item 779, and recommended adding them — "three lines
each". This built that, measured it, and **both halves of 797's recommendation are wrong**.

### What was built

A `Member` type (`string | { label, run }`) so a spelling can carry its own runner, the dispatch in
`timed` plus `labelOf` for display, and a `ROWS_MAY_DIFFER` opt-out on the answer check — the two
surfaces return different SHAPES for one answer (`[{"c":N}]` against `[N]`), so without it every
cross-language group reports `ANSWERS DIFFER` forever. Three groups: a filtered node count
unlabelled and labelled, and a one-hop count.

**"Three lines each" was wrong**, and the reason is structural: the TS Gremlin surface has **no text
entry point** — it is a composable builder — so a Gremlin member cannot be a query string the way
every existing member is. The member type, the runner and the answer-shape opt-out are all
load-bearing.

### Why it is reverted: the groups measure the PROBE, not the engines

Run in isolation (`SPELL_ONLY`) and then in the full sweep, same binary, same fixture:

| member              | isolated | in the full sweep |              |
| ------------------- | -------: | ----------------: | ------------ |
| GQL, unlabelled     |  4.51 ms |          **8.84** | **1.96x**    |
| Gremlin, unlabelled |     2.64 |              2.54 | 1.04x        |
| GQL, labelled       |     6.27 |         **14.42** | **2.30x**    |
| Gremlin, labelled   |     4.68 |              3.37 | 1.39x faster |
| GQL, one-hop        |    23.87 |         **54.67** | **2.29x**    |
| Gremlin, one-hop    |    25.10 |             21.81 | 1.15x faster |

**Every Gremlin member is stable and every GQL member roughly doubles.** A fixture effect or a
warm-up effect would move BOTH; only the GQL side moving is the signature of GQL-path pollution. The
probe runs ~40 GQL groups before these, so by the time a cross-language group executes, the GQL
dispatch sites are megamorphic — **item 762's finding**, that in one process every shape funnels
through the same site — while the Gremlin member is the FIRST Gremlin query in the process and
arrives with clean inline caches.

Item 747 already recorded in-sweep inflation on GQL rows at **1.4x** (`count var-length 1-2 hops`
250.7 in-sweep against ~177 isolated). This is 2.0-2.3x, the same phenomenon at a larger size
because a cross-language group sits at the END of the GQL run.

So the full-sweep readings — **3.49x, 4.27x and 2.51x** — are substantially instrument, and they
flagged as three new entries in the >2x summary. Shipping them would have added three permanent
flags whose real content is "this probe runs GQL groups first", which is exactly the
_a flag that means nothing_ failure the opt-out was added to avoid.

### The two fixes that do not work, and the one that does

- **Keep them and document "isolation only."** Rejected: the summary is where a reader arrives with
  the per-group tables scrolled away — the probe's own comment on item 635 says so — and three
  permanently-flagging groups there is worse than no groups.
- **Run them FIRST, before any GQL group.** That makes the pair fair, and moves every other group's
  number, because they would then execute after a Gremlin warm-up. The whole corpus is calibrated
  against recorded figures; invalidating ~40 of them to add 3 is the wrong trade.
- **ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS.** This is what `probe:scalar` does (item 790): the parent re-executes
  itself per shape so nothing pollutes anything. A cross-language comparison needs that isolation by
  construction, and **that is where these groups belong** — not in a single-process sweep.

### What still stands

**Item 797's finding is unaffected and this is why it was trustworthy**: it was measured one shape
per process, which is the only reason its 2.24x was a comparison rather than a position in a run
order. The instrument gap it identified is real — the TS side still cannot catch a cross-language
divergence — but closing it needs the per-process harness, which is its own tick.

Second time this session that a sweep comparison turned out to be contaminated and the stable side
was what proved it: item 799's 2.49x flag was noise shown by an unreachable control, and this is the
same shape with the roles of the two members as the control.

`bun test packages/gql` **2624** pass 0 fail; the full `bun run spelling` at
`SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`, which is the run that produced the table above; `git status` clean
after the revert.

## 801 — `probe:surface`: the cross-language comparison in the harness item 800 said it needed. Item 797's gap CONFIRMED at ~2.1x, and a second gap found running the OTHER way

**SHIPPED (instrument).** Item 797 found TS GQL at 2.24x its own Gremlin twin and named the
instrument gap. Item 800 built the fix in the wrong place, measured that it was the wrong place, and
specified the right one: **one shape per process**. This is that, and it paid for itself on its first
run.

### The instrument

`packages/native/surface-probe.ts`, `bun run probe:surface`. The parent re-executes itself once per
SPELLING — not per pair — so each child times one query in a process that has run no other. That is
item 762's rule and `scalarfn-probe.ts`'s design, and it is the thing item 800's groups could not
have: there, ~40 GQL groups ran first, and every Gremlin member was stable across isolated and
in-sweep runs while every GQL member roughly doubled.

Two details are the fixture's, carried over deliberately: **both edge endpoints are scattered by
different multipliers** (items 164/286/287 — with `from` in creation order and `to` permuted, one
adjacency map is walked sequentially and the other jumped around, which a cross-surface probe would
read as a surface difference), and the answer is summarised and COMPARED, because a pair that
silently measures two different questions is the failure mode that matters most here.

### Item 797's gap, confirmed in a harness that can be trusted

Three runs, median-of-11 per spelling, each spelling in its own process:

| pair                            |          GQL |     Gremlin | verdict                   | across 3 runs              |
| ------------------------------- | -----------: | ----------: | ------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| filtered node count, unlabelled | 4.71-5.18 ms |   2.30-2.52 | **GQL ~2.1x slower**      | 2.06 / 2.05 / 2.12         |
| filtered node count, labelled   |    4.59-4.76 |   2.11-2.18 | **GQL ~2.2x slower**      | 2.12 / 2.18 / 2.25         |
| project one property            |   6.92-10.41 | 18.19-26.41 | **GQL 1.75-3.82x FASTER** | direction stable, size not |
| one-hop count                   |         0.00 |        0.01 | too fast to compare       | —                          |
| CONTROL unfiltered count        |         0.00 |        0.00 | too fast to compare       | —                          |

**~2.1x, against item 797's 2.24x on its own fixture and item 800's isolated 1.71x.** Three
independent measurements of one gap, two fixtures, two harnesses.

### A SECOND gap, the other way — and it is what bounds the first

`values('k')` is **1.75-3.82x slower** than `RETURN n.k AS k`. So the finding is NOT "GQL is slower
than Gremlin": each surface is faster at a different shape — Gremlin at a filtered scan, GQL at a
projection. The direction holds in all three runs; the magnitude ranges 1.75-3.82x and is reported
as unstable rather than averaged, because one number there would be made up.

**That bounding is better than item 800's**, and 800's is now corrected twice over: its one-hop
group claimed "no gap", but on this fixture both surfaces answer that count from a bucket size and
the pair **cannot be compared at all** — it reads 0.00 against 0.01. And 800's in-sweep reading had
the LABELLED pair narrowing the gap to 1.34x; per-process it is 2.2x, slightly WIDER than the
unlabelled 2.1x. Both of 800's secondary readings were instrument, which is the finding 800 itself
reached about its own numbers.

### Two defects in my own probe, found by reading its first output

Neither was in the engine, and both would have shipped a lie:

- **`answerOf` read the single value out of the FIRST row whatever the length**, so a 200,000-row
  projection reported `0` — the first row's `k` — against Gremlin's `200000 rows`, and the pair
  flagged `⚠️ ANSWERS DIFFER` on a difference that was mine. Fixed by taking the row count first. A
  summary that can disagree with itself is worse than none.
- **no FLOOR**, so the two O(1) pairs printed `GQL Infinityx faster` from 0.00 against 0.01. That is
  item 124's exact mistake — a ratio between two sub-millisecond timings is the clock's resolution —
  and `spelling-probe.ts` keeps `FLOOR_MS` for it. Now they say `too fast to compare (raise
SURFACE_N)`.

### What is open

The ~2.1x itself. Item 798 established where it is — not in the shared `satisfies` implementation
but in the ~18-20 ns of per-vertex scaffolding around it (`inlineHolds`'s `Map` write, the
`{ binding, params, graph }` allocation, the `value(env)` call) — and item 799 removed one term of
that for params. The remaining scaffolding is the target, and it is shared by every predicate caller
in the TS engine, so it wants its own tick.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0 — it
caught a shadowed `out` (the imported Gremlin STEP) and a missing blank line; `bun test packages/gql`
**2624** pass 0 fail; `bun run probe:surface` run three times, which is the table above. No engine
change.

## 802 — the `satisfies` scaffolding: BOTH halves REFUTED, and the instrument that said otherwise failed an arithmetic check a part cannot pass

**NO ENGINE CHANGE.** Item 798 located the TS filtered-count cost in "~18-20 ns of per-vertex
scaffolding around `satisfies`" and item 801 made the remaining scaffolding the named open target.
This priced it, built two changes, measured a 2.4x on `satisfies` in isolation, and then found that
2.4x was a property of my own probe. Both halves are refuted and recorded next to the code.

### What was closed before anything was built

The planned change — hoisting `satisfies`'s `{ binding, params, graph }` into a caller-owned env —
is **item 454**, refuted with numbers, in a doc comment on the function itself, ending "do not
re-derive it: the reasoning is correct and the measurement is not." It was re-derived anyway: the
extraction was written, `satisfiesIn` and all, before the comment three lines above the signature
was read. **The seventh already-closed candidate this session** (789, 793, 795, 796 were the others)
and the first where the record was in the SOURCE rather than in `CLOSED.md` — which is the half of
the rule that gets skipped, because "check the list" reads as "check the list".

### The ladder, which is the result worth keeping

A hand-written loop over the same 200,000 vertices, one arm per process, median of 11, three rounds:

```text
  loop floor (iterate, touch nothing)        1.4-2.1 ns/vertex
  CONSTANT-key property read + compare       9.6-11.1
  propOf: DYNAMIC keyed load + 2 ?. + ??     9.8-11.1    <- the SAME as the named load
  + inlineHolds's binding.set                12.8-15.8   (+~4)
  + { binding, params, graph } + value(env)  13.2-15.7   (+~0.5)
  the engine's whole filtered count          21-27       (4.2-5.5 ms / 200k)
```

Three things fall out. **A dynamic keyed load costs what a named one costs here** — `propOf`'s
optional chains and `??` are free, which is not obvious and was not recorded. **The env allocation
is ~0.5 ns**, an independent confirmation of item 454 from a different instrument. And **the
property read is ~10 of the ~24 ns**, so the per-vertex budget is mostly the read itself, not the
dispatch around it. That re-reads item 798: its "~18-20 ns is scaffolding" was inferred from three
predicate arms sitting within 5.5 ns of each other, and agreement across arms is not a floor (item
791's rule, in a new place).

### The arithmetic check an isolated measurement must pass

A sixth arm called the engine's real `satisfies` with a hand-built `cmpProps` predicate and read
**41.4-46.8 ns/vertex** — against a hand loop doing the same work at 13-15. That 31 ns looked like
the finding, and two changes were built to collect it.

**It cannot have been real, and the number says so without any further measurement: the whole
engine query costs 21-27 ns a vertex, and `satisfies` is a PART of it.** A part measured dearer than
the whole is an instrument result. The cause is the hand-built predicate: a literal `{ props: [],
cmpProps: [...] }` is a different hidden class from the one `compilePredicate` emits, so the
destructuring and property sites inside `satisfies` saw a shape they never see in production.

**The rule, which generalises past this file:** when a probe prices a PART, check it against the
measured WHOLE before believing it. If the part exceeds the whole, the argument is the instrument.
This is the same family as "a reproduction that does not reproduce the ANSWER SIZE is not a
reproduction" (702/790/791/794/799) — a cheap check on the number's own plausibility, run before any
conclusion is drawn from it — and the arms here all answered 156,000, so answer size would not have
caught it.

### Both changes, measured on real queries and refuted

1. **A two-number ORDERING fast path at the top of `compareTruth`.** Byte-identical including NaN:
   `isNullish` is `null`/`undefined` only so a NaN is not nullish, a number is not a temporal, and
   `typeof lv === typeof rv === 'number'` IS the `orderable` test; `=` and `<>` are excluded because
   their answer is `structuralEq`'s to give. It skips two `isNullish` calls, two `op` comparisons and
   two `isTemporal` calls per row. **Nothing, on five shapes that reach it**, three alternated rounds
   each, twice over:

```text
  filtered count       4.70/4.75/4.86 -> 4.74/5.13/4.32   and 4.69/5.50/5.08 -> 4.41/4.65/4.22
  two-bound count      6.31/5.97/5.78 -> 5.55/6.17/5.46
  156,000-row project 10.54/11.22/10.30 -> 10.37/10.09/14.11
  general arm (k*1>10) 13.24/12.21/11.04 -> 10.30/11.61/11.24
  per-edge hop        48.11/48.78/48.88 -> 48.00/48.58/47.81
  CONTROL no predicate 10.56/9.99/10.33 -> 11.08/13.30/12.68
```

2. **Indexed loops in place of the three `for...of` + destructuring loops** in `satisfies` and in
   its pre-filter twin (the one whose own doc records 1.89x, which carries the same three loops — a
   grep found the second copy that the first patch attempt had missed). This is a **TRADE**: on an
   `eqProps` count (`WHERE n.s = 's3'`) the indexed form read 5.66/5.49/5.36 against 5.77/6.51/6.14,
   and on a two-bound `cmpProps` count 6.47/7.42/6.14 against 5.93/6.13/5.66 — **slower in all three
   rounds**. With both halves applied the two cancel and every shape is flat.

**One reading looked like a win and the second run took it back.** The string-equality count read
6.69/6.53/6.33 against 5.68/5.69/5.24 in the first full A/B — disjoint, 1.17x — and 5.93/6.23/6.31
against 6.92/5.79/5.49 in the second. Two A/Bs of the same two binaries, three alternated rounds
each; that is the ~10% noise floor CLAUDE.md names, and a single disjoint triple inside it is not a
flag.

**The control was wrong the first time, and the symptom was item 762's.** `WHERE n.s = 's3'` was
chosen as unreachable because the fast path excludes `=` and strings — but it reaches the OTHER half,
the indexed loops, so when it moved 1.17x while every target stayed flat it read as "the control
moved more than the target" when it was simply a target. **A control has to be unreachable by every
change in the arm, not by the one you have in mind.** Replaced with a no-predicate projection, which
runs neither `satisfies` nor the pre-filter and did not move.

### What this leaves open

Item 801's ~2.1x cross-surface gap stands, and the ladder says where it is NOT: not the env, not the
`propOf` chain, not the loop headers, not `compareTruth`'s dispatch. ~10 of the ~24 ns a vertex is
the property read and ~4 is `inlineHolds`'s `Map` write. Gremlin answers the same question at ~10.6
ns, so the gap is roughly the Map write plus the predicate plumbing — and the Map write is the one
term still unpriced, because `satisfies` reads the binding through `env` and a per-element write is
what lets it. That is a structural change to how a per-element predicate reaches its own variable,
not a tick.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0;
`bun test packages/gql` 2624 pass 0 fail; `git status` clean of the engine change (comments only).

## 803 — the per-element `Map` write goes compile-time gated: **1.11-1.34x**, and "alternated rounds" turns out to mean alternating the ORDER

**SHIPPED.** Item 802's ladder left exactly one unpriced term in the TS filtered-count path:
`inlineHolds`'s `binding.set(bindVar, element)`, ~4 of the ~24 ns a vertex. This removes it wherever
nothing can read it back, and the measured effect matches what the ladder predicted.

### The observation

`inlinePredOf` set `bindVar` whenever the node had a variable. The binding is _read_ in exactly one
of the places a predicate's values come from:

- a general compiled `where` — reads it, through `env`. **This** is the case that needs it.
- `eqProps` / `cmpProps` — CLOSED by construction in `directEqProps`, which admits only
  `<ownVar>.<key> <op> <closed value>`.
- `props` — closed only when the caller has proved it, which both props-carrying callers do with
  the same `freePredicateVars(c.value).size > 0` loop.

So for every predicate that lifts ENTIRELY — an inline `WHERE n.k > 10`, a clause `WHERE n.s =
's3'`, an inline `{k: 2}`, which is the common case and the whole point of items 224/230/276 — the
`Map` write stores an entry nothing ever reads, once per element in a filtered walk.

### Ten sites, one helper

`grep -n 'bindVar:'` found **ten** construction sites, nine of them the same four lines written out
again. They now all go through `predFor(pred, ownVar, closedProps)`, and `bindVar:` appears exactly
once in the package. `closedProps` is a REQUIRED argument rather than inferred, because it cannot be
inferred — a compiled value is a closure and nothing can ask it what it reads — so a future caller
with unproven `props` has to answer the question rather than inherit a wrong default.

### Measured end-to-end, 200,000 vertices, one shape per process, order-alternated

```text
                        PRE                  POST                 verdict
  clause 1bound         4.68/4.74/4.89 ms    4.11/4.42/4.24       1.14x, DISJOINT
  inline {k: 2}         3.39/3.47/4.23       2.85/3.26/6.91       1.19x on min (one outlier)
  clause str-eq         7.10/6.16/5.86       5.13/5.99/4.96       1.18x on min
  inline WHERE          4.54/7.52/4.78       3.89/4.63/4.76       1.17x on min
  CONTROL non-lifting  10.19/11.17/11.18    12.57/10.08/13.99     flat
  CONTROL no-pred      13.74/14.58/10.44    10.42/10.60/ 9.88     flat/noisy
```

An earlier A/B of the two-site arm gave the same picture independently: `clause 1bound`
4.90/4.69/5.26 against 4.24/4.58/4.40 (**1.11x**, disjoint) and `inline {k: 2}` 3.57/4.14/3.65
against 2.75/2.67/3.24 (**1.34x**, disjoint).

**Item 802's ladder PREDICTED this magnitude** — it priced the `Map` write at ~4 of ~24 ns, i.e.
~1.2x — which is why 1.11x counts as a result here and not as noise. A number inside the ~10% band
needs a prior reason to be the size it is, and this one had one before it was measured.

**The two controls are unreachable by construction, which is the lesson item 802 just paid for.**
`n.k * 1 > 10` is not a property comparison, so nothing lifts, so `pred.where` survives and
`bindVar` is still set — the `Map` write stays. `MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k` runs no predicate at all.
Neither moved.

### The order confound, which is new and cost two A/Bs

The first two A/Bs ran **PRE first in every round**. Under that order the `non-lifting` control
appeared to improve 10.19-15.10 → 10.08-11.03, consistently, in the change's favour — a control it
cannot reach moving more than some targets, which is item 762's signature and sent me looking for a
redistribution effect that was not there. **With the order alternated (POST,PRE / PRE,POST /
POST,PRE) the control is flat and the targets stay.** The PRE arm was simply absorbing each round's
cold start.

CLAUDE.md says "the min of that across three order-alternated rounds" and I had been reading
"alternated" as "repeated". It means alternating the ORDER. Three rounds in a fixed order are one
observation of an order, not three of a change.

### Teeth: four of four, after the first two survived

- `pred.where !== undefined` → `=== undefined`: **caught**, 147 fail.
- the whole `where` test → `false` (never bind): **caught**, 149 fail.
- `!closedProps` → `false` and `pred.props.length > 0` → `true`: **both SURVIVED the full
  2,624-test suite.** Expected and the reason is structural — every current caller passes
  `closedProps: true`, so that disjunct is unreachable from any query. It is a guard for a caller
  that does not exist yet, which is the shape item 468 records the cost of, and item 475's rule says
  a survivor there can mean "redundant" as easily as "untested".

  It is not redundant — it is the precondition that makes the other nine sites safe — so it was
  given teeth instead: `predFor` is exported and `bindvar-gating.test.ts` pins all three inputs
  directly, including `closedProps: false` with a `props` entry whose value closure THROWS if
  called. Both mutants are now caught.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0 — it
caught a `no-unnecessary-type-assertion` in the new test; `bun test packages/gql` **2634** pass 0
fail; `bun run fuzz` (all seven, random seeds) 13 pass 0 fail, run TWICE; `bun run spelling` — 0
groups disagree on the answer, and the two groups over 2x are both pre-existing and recorded as
correct (`label on start` is deliberate, `item 285`'s product).

**Rust side: NOT checked, and this item does not claim it.** The change is TS-only — the structure
it removes is `inlineHolds`'s, which has no native counterpart by name. Whether `exec` pays an
analogous per-element write is a separate question and a separate tick; asserting it either way
from here would be the kind of unmeasured claim item 802 was about.

## 804 — native `split` is AT THE ALLOCATOR FLOOR: the exact-capacity lever is refuted, and item 783's by-inspection diagnosis was wrong about which allocation

**NO ENGINE CHANGE** (a rejection record and one bench row). `scalarfn_bench` prices 30 scalar
functions and `split` is the outlier by a factor of five — 49.4 ns/row against 9.7-10.3 for every
other string function. This priced it properly, built the obvious lever, refuted it, and then found
by measurement what the cost actually is.

### What 783 said, and why it was a guess

Item 783's refutation of the `unary_str_fn` table ends: "`split` — which returns a LIST — is 49 ns
at 1M, five times the next worst. Its body is already a single `Vec` and one `GStr` a piece, so that
cost is the allocation itself, not waste around it." Correct that there is an allocation; wrong
about which one, and arrived at by reading the body rather than by measuring it.

**`GStr` is inline up to 12 bytes.** The fixture's strings are `"  pad7  "` (9 bytes), `"plain7"`
(7) and `"naïve-7-ßé"` (~14) — and the PARTS of the third are `naïve` (6), `7` (1) and `ßé` (4).
Every part of every row is under the inline cap, so **the part strings allocate nothing at all.**
The only heap allocation in the arm is the `Vec` holding them.

### The lever, built and refuted

`str::Split` is not an `ExactSizeIterator` and its `size_hint` is `(0, None)`, so `collect` starts
at capacity zero and doubles — a three-part split pays two reallocations and two moves of the whole
`Vec` to build three elements. `Vec::with_capacity(s.matches(d).count() + 1)` buys an exact
allocation for one extra scan of a string already in cache.

Three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds at 1,000,000 rows (POST,PRE / PRE,POST / POST,PRE):

```text
  split         PRE 50.04/49.16/49.40 ns/row    POST 51.54/49.05/49.83    NOTHING
  upper             9.85/ 9.79/ 9.75                 10.23/ 9.95/ 9.77    control, flat
  char_length       8.66/ 8.69/ 8.72                  9.04/ 8.74/ 8.72    control, flat
  replace/3        10.11/ 9.83/ 9.83                 10.73/10.40/10.55    control, flat
  CONTROL count(a.s) 0.6                              0.6-0.7            the floor
```

### The discriminator, which is the result worth keeping

Rather than explain the null, one bench row settles it. **`split/1part` splits on `zz`, which occurs
in no fixture string** — so it builds exactly ONE part in one `Vec` of capacity 1, where growth is
impossible by construction. It costs **42.4 ns/row** against this fixture's 49.6.

So, with `replace/3` and `substring/3` at ~10 ns through the same dispatch:

```text
  ~10 ns   the general two-argument scalar dispatch (shared with every other string function)
  ~32 ns   split's OWN per-row list construction and teardown — FLAT in the part count
  ~10 ns   per EXTRA part (the 0.7 parts this fixture averages beyond the first)
```

**Exact capacity can only remove growth, and growth was never the term.** That is why the lever
measured flat, and the null now has a measured cause rather than a plausible one.

### What would remove it, and why it is not a tick

An inline representation for a short `Value::List`, the way `GStr` inlines a short string. That
changes `Value`'s layout — which the cross-engine byte-identity contract runs through — and it pays
only for small lists. Priced, not taken.

### Also recorded: item 803's effect on the cross-surface gap

Rebuilt the dist and re-ran `probe:surface`, three runs, which is the first reading of item 801's
gap since 803 shipped:

```text
  filtered node count, labelled     before 2.12/2.18/2.25x    after 1.73/1.79/1.74x
  filtered node count, unlabelled   before 2.06/2.05/2.12x    after 1.80/1.95/2.63x
```

The LABELLED pair is the clean one and it narrowed from ~2.2x to ~1.75x (GQL's own time 4.59-4.76 ms
to 3.71-4.38), consistent with 803's measured 1.14-1.19x. The unlabelled pair agrees in direction
with one noisy round. **Item 801's ~2.1x is now ~1.75x** and the remaining term is the property read
item 802's ladder priced at ~10 of the ~24 ns a vertex.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 725 + 13 passed, 0 failed, under
`systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`; the engine diff asserted to be comments only
(zero added non-comment lines) plus the one bench row.

## 805 — `probe:elemread`: item 802's ladder MIS-ATTRIBUTED its biggest line. The walk is 2 ns, the read is 2 ns, and together they are 10

**SHIPPED (instrument), no engine change.** Item 802's ladder priced "a property read and compare"
at 9.6-11.1 ns a vertex and item 804 repeated it as the remaining term of item 801's cross-surface
gap. It is wrong, and separating the two halves is all it took.

### What was tested, and the hypothesis it refuted

Item 802's ladder found a CONSTANT-key read and a DYNAMIC keyed read cost the SAME (9.6-11.1
against 9.8-11.1). I read that as the signature of V8 **dictionary mode**: on a fast-mode object a
literal-key load is an inline-cache hit where a computed key goes through the keyed-load stub, so
equality would mean a hash lookup on both.

**It is not.** The two are equal in EVERY arm, including a plain object literal that is certainly
fast-mode (1.1-1.3 ns either way) — because a hoisted `const key = 'k'` is as constant to V8 as the
literal is. **That pair cannot diagnose object shape at all**, and the equality item 802 found
suspicious is nothing. The arms stay in the probe as the record of a refuted reading.

### The decomposition, which is the result

200,000 vertices, one arm per process, objects built OUTSIDE the timed region, median of 11, three
rounds:

```text
  walk map values (NO read)        1.4-2.3 ns/vertex   iterating `verticesById` alone
  walk map + read v.properties.k   9.2-10.0            the engine's own shape
  walk label Set + read            8.8- 9.7            the labelled spelling's collection
  walk ARRAY + read                7.1- 8.2            the SAME vertex objects, dense array
  property bags in a dense array   1.8- 2.2            the read alone, in order
  plain / frozen object literal    1.1- 1.3            the read's floor
  a Map per element                14.9-15.8           the alternative layout
```

**The walk is ~2 ns. The read is ~2 ns. Together they are ~10.** Neither half explains the pair, so
**~6 ns a vertex exists only in the pairing** — the Map yields vertex objects in insertion order and
`v.properties` is then a dependent load into a separately-allocated bag, one cold line per vertex,
which no prefetcher can anticipate. Extract the bags into a contiguous array first and the identical
read costs 1.8-2.2.

Two things fall out immediately:

- **`Map`-per-element is REFUTED as a property layout, 8x worse** (14.9-15.8 against 1.8-2.2). If a
  future tick proposes replacing the property object with a `Map`, this is the number.
- **The label `Set` is slightly cheaper to walk than the id `Map`** (8.8-9.7 against 9.2-10.0),
  which is the right direction for `probe:surface` showing the labelled pair faster than the
  unlabelled one.

### The array-walk lever, priced and DECLINED — and a correction to my own first reading

A dense array of vertices beside the `Map`, walked instead of it: **7.1-8.2 against 9.2-10.0, so
1.2-1.3x of the pair**, which is ~2 ns of the ~24 ns a vertex a filtered count spends — about 1.08x
end to end, under this repo's noise floor, against a structural change to `@lenke/core` and a
second collection to keep correct through deletes. Declined.

**My first version of that arm read 1.5-1.9x, and it was measuring the wrong thing.** It used
`for (let i = 0; i < vs.length; i += 1)` where the `Map` arms use `for...of`, so the comparison
carried the ACCESS FORM as well as the collection. The lint gate flagged the indexed loop
(`prefer-for-of`), and making both sides `for...of` cut the gap roughly in half. A difference
between two arms is only the thing you changed if nothing else differs — the arms here are built in
pairs for that reason, and I still got it wrong once.

### What this leaves, with a number it did not have before

Item 342's packed-presence / columnar direction now has a measured ceiling on this shape: if a
per-element property read were CONTIGUOUS, the walk-plus-read pair would cost ~4 ns instead of ~10,
which is ~6 of the ~24 ns a vertex — **~1.3x on a filtered node count**, and it is the largest
single term left in it. That is a real target where before there was an unexplained 10 ns.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0 —
it caught the indexed loop above and two needless type assertions; no engine change, so the test
suites and fuzzers are unaffected (`bun test packages/gql` 2634 pass 0 fail unchanged).

## 806 — packed presence, ATTEMPTED: item 741's census missed 123 sites, and item 342's ladder has a rung that is already built

**NO ENGINE CHANGE** (attempted, reverted, re-scoped with a real count). Item 342's packed presence
has been the best-priced unbuilt Rust lever for three items (740, 741, 796). Item 740 called it
"multi-tick"; item 741 counted the call sites and corrected that to **"five operations and one real
rewrite"**. I built it on 741's scoping. **741's count was wrong, and its method is why.**

### Two findings before any code

**Rung 1 of the ladder IS ALREADY BUILT, and the ladder's biggest number is not a clean pair.**
`element_render_cost` prints four rows per store width — the baseline, "columns hoisted", and
"PACKED presence" — and the baseline-to-hoisted step looks enormous (at K=200, 1785.7 → 437.7
ns/row, **4.08x**). It is not a candidate:

- The baseline arm calls the real `node_result_value`, which resolves `store.column(k)` per key per
  row. The hoisted arm pre-resolves the columns AND skips the ext-id, the label list and two `Arc`
  `Value::Map` allocations. **It is not the same work**, so the 4.08x is partly the omitted half.
- The apples-to-apples pair for hoisting is elsewhere in the same harness: `props: one lookup per
key` **95.4** against `props: columns hoisted out of the loop` **92.6** — **3%**, at K=4.
- And `render_nodes`, the BATCH renderer, **already hoists both the columns and the key `Value`s**
  (items 390/391). The per-node `node_result_value` cannot: it is called one node at a time from a
  `Gen` cell, a path and the JSON sinks.

**The clean pair is hoisted-against-packed** — both pre-resolve columns, both build the same `Vec` —
and that is the real price of this lever:

```text
  K=  0 extra store keys    92.2 -> 90.4 ns/row   1.02x
  K= 12                    116.4 -> 105.2         1.11x
  K= 60                    168.0 -> 147.7         1.14x
  K=200                    437.7 -> 246.4         1.78x
```

So it pays **in proportion to how WIDE the store is** and is worth nothing on a narrow one. Item
342's recorded "rung 2 1.67x at K=200" is confirmed; what was not recorded is that K=12 and K=60 —
much closer to most graphs — are 1.11x and 1.14x.

### What was built, and the census that was wrong

A `Presence` bitmap (`words: Vec<u64>`, `len`) with `zeros`/`len`/`get`/`set`/`push`/`pop`,
deliberately NOT a drop-in for `Vec<bool>`: a bitmap cannot hand out a `&mut bool`, and an `Index`
impl would have hidden the one site 741 flagged as needing thought. Then `present: Vec<bool>` and
`nulls: Vec<bool>` swapped in all six `Column` variants, and all 33 indexing sites and 25 literals
inside `store.rs` rewritten.

`store.rs` went through almost exactly as 741 predicted. **Then it stopped compiling in seven other
files.**

|                                                             | 741 said    | actually              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | --------------------- |
| `.present` FIELD accesses outside `store.rs`                | 0           | 0 — this part is true |
| `present`/`nulls` INDEXING sites outside `store.rs`         | not counted | **123**               |
| pattern-match bindings that destructure a column's presence | not counted | **84**                |
| `&[bool]` parameters that ARE a presence slice              | not counted | **16**                |
| files with code sites outside `store.rs`                    | 0 implied   | **10**                |

**The method is the error.** 741 counted `.present` — a FIELD ACCESS — and the exec layer never
writes one. It writes `Column::Num { data, present, .. } => …` and then `present[i]`, which is a
pattern-match binding: the same coupling, invisible to that grep. Two of those bindings are even
renamed on the way in (`present: lp`, `present: rp`), so no grep for `present[` finds them either.

**A census is only a scope if it counts the ways the thing is REACHED, not one syntax for reaching
it.** The right query was "what binds a column's presence", and it is four syntaxes.

### Why that is not just more of the same work

The 123 sites are not a rename. Sixteen helper signatures take `&[bool]` and the vectorized scan
loops read presence per row inside a branch-free pass — which is the shape `scan_layout_probe`
identified as "the byte-wide presence gate" and therefore exactly where the win is supposed to come
from. Converting them means rewriting those loops to shift-and-mask word arithmetic, which is a
different and larger piece of work than swapping a field, and it has its own measurement (a packed
gate inside a branch-free loop may be faster or slower than a byte gate — `bitmap_layout_probe`
exists for that family of question and does not answer this one).

**So item 740 was right and item 741's correction of it was wrong**, and the record now says which
by measurement rather than by impression.

### A mistake of my own, same shape as 741's

Before building, I grepped for `present` outside `store.rs` to check 741's claim — and piped it
through `head -15`. The fifteen lines that came back were codec prose and two examples, so I
concluded there were no bindings outside `store.rs`. **The `fastpath.rs` hits were on line 16 and
after.** This repo's own rule (item 319, re-paid at 791 and 796) is about `head` closing a pipe on a
mutation harness; the general form is the one that bit here — **a conclusion drawn from a truncated
listing is a conclusion about the truncation.** `wc -l` first costs nothing.

### State of this lever

Priced (1.02x / 1.11x / 1.14x / 1.78x by store width), scoped for real (10 files, 123 indexing
sites, 84 bindings, 16 signatures, plus the vectorized gates), and **not started**. Its own
precondition is now explicit: it needs the branch-free scan loops converted, and that wants its own
measurement before the field swap, not after.

Gates: `cargo build --release --features capi` 0 on the reverted tree; `git status` clean;
`element_render_cost` is the harness above (`#[ignore]`, measurement-only).

## 807 — `probe:adjlayout`: the widest gap in the bench finally has a layout number — a flat interned index is **3.5-3.8x** on the lookup, and the concat half-measure is **2x WORSE**

**SHIPPED (instrument), no engine change.** TS multi-hop counts are the widest real gap in the
bench — `count 4-hop` 84.58x native, `count 3-hop` 65.61x, `count 2-hop` 39.19x, one row out so no
carrier explains them. The sweep at item 795 traced three components, found two already spent, and
left the third — `edgesFromByLabel.get(nodeId)` then `.get(type)`, "a nested map costs two by
construction" — as the only remaining lever **with no number on it**. It has one now.

### Three ticks of reading first, and what it closed

Before measuring anything this tick checked the three structural levers the repo lists as all that
remains, and two of them turned out to be answered already:

- **`scan_layout_probe`'s "the per-row operator dispatch is real… hoisting the operator out of the
  loop is an independent, much cheaper win"** — that is **items 450/453/459/462**, built. 453 took
  the two-bound range from 1.782 to 0.458 ms (3.9x) with monomorphic arms, and 462 hoisted the two
  `match`es into `arith_step`/`num_pred`. Nothing left there.
- **`scan_layout_probe`'s variant C' (mask + popcount-sized ids, 6.3-9.7x)** needs BOTH the bitset
  gate and the mask output — variant B, memory order with the same byte gate, "barely beats A". So
  C' is downstream of item 806's finding and inherits its precondition; it is not independent of it.
- **Item 617 is mis-cited** in `CLOSED.md`'s own open-set summary, which calls the remaining lever
  "item 617's CSR for TS multi-hop counts". Item 617 is the GQL point-lookup-by-id fix
  (`Plan::NodeSeed`, 1258x). The CSR diagnosis is in item 795's sweep, which 617 is referenced BY.
  Corrected below.

### The measurement

200,000 (node, type) lookups, 8 types, one arm per process, structures built outside the timed
region, median of 11, three rounds:

```text
  nested   Map<string, Map<string, Set>>   52.1 / 54.8 / 55.8 ns/lookup   what the engine has
  concat   Map<string, Set>, key per call 100.2 /113.7 /137.6             2.0-2.5x WORSE
  numeric  Map<number, Set>, ids interned  15.2 / 14.7 / 16.9             3.4-3.7x FASTER
  CONTROL  the inner short-key lookup only  6.3 /  6.5 /  8.4             the floor
```

**The flat interned index is 3.4-3.7x on the lookup.** That is the first number the layout lever has
had on the TypeScript side, and it is the third component of the widest gap in the bench.

**The outer lookup is almost all of it.** The inner short-key `Map.get` is 6.3-8.4 ns, so of the
~52-56 ns a nested lookup costs, roughly 45 belongs to the OUTER `get(nodeId)` on a 200,000-entry
string-keyed map — a multi-megabyte hash table probed in effectively random order, one cache miss
per lookup. The same 200,000 entries under SMI keys cost 14.7-16.9 for the WHOLE lookup, replacing
both levels.

### The half-measure is refuted, with a number

`Map<string, Set>` keyed by `` `${nodeId}\u0000${type}` `` needs no interning and no new index
structure, which makes it the obvious cheap version — and it is **2.0-2.5x worse than the two
lookups it replaces**. The concatenation allocates a fresh string per lookup whose hash has never
been computed, where both nested keys are long-lived strings whose hashes V8 has already cached. I
expected this and said so before running it; **saying so is not measuring it**, and the number is
what stops it being re-proposed.

### What this does and does not license

It prices the LOOKUP, not a query. The hot loop looks up once per middle EDGE rather than once per
node, and `side()` does more than the lookup, so what share of a 3-hop count this reaches is a
separate measurement — the honest claim is "3.4-3.7x on one component of three, two of which are
already spent". The arms are standalone maps, not the engine, and the interning the `numeric` arm
assumes is itself the work: node ids are strings in `@lenke/core`, so a flat index means an id→u32
intern table maintained through inserts and deletes.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0 —
it caught nine needless non-null assertions, and the probe was re-measured after the fix to confirm
the arms were unchanged; `bun test packages/gql` 2634 pass 0 fail (no engine change).

## 808 — the widest bench gap is CLOSED, not open: interning is worth NOTHING, and the one available layout was refuted at item 200

**DONE (no engine change).** Item 807 shipped `probe:adjlayout` and read it as "a flat INTERNED
index is 3.4-3.7x on the lookup". **Two discriminator arms, added one tick later, retract that
framing and close the target.**

**The arms that were missing.** `numeric` changed TWO things at once — two lookups became one AND
the key became an SMI — and 807 credited the win to the interning. Two new arms separate them:
`prekeyed` (ONE lookup, string key, pre-built so nothing is concatenated per call) and `short keys`
(ONE lookup into a 200,000-entry map, short key, still built per call).

```text
  nested       49.6 / 54.2 / 68.3 ns/lookup   two long-lived-key lookups — the engine
  concat      103.2 /107.5 /106.9             one lookup, key concatenated per call
  short keys   83.5 / 83.9 / 90.7             one lookup, SHORT key, still built per call
  prekeyed     14.2 / 14.9 / 14.9             one lookup, string key ALREADY in hand
  numeric      14.2 / 14.6 / 15.6             one lookup, ids and types INTERNED
  CONTROL       6.5 /  8.1 /  8.3             an 8-entry map — NOT a one-lookup floor
```

**1. INTERNING IS WORTH NOTHING.** `prekeyed` 14.2-14.9 against `numeric` 14.2-15.6 — a long-lived
STRING key costs what an SMI costs. **Item 807's "flat INTERNED index" is the wrong name for the
lever**; there is no case here for an id→u32 intern table, which was the expensive half of what 807
said the change would need.

**2. WHAT COSTS IS BUILDING A KEY PER LOOKUP.** `short keys` does ONE lookup where nested does two
and is still **WORSE** (83.5-90.7 against 49.6-68.3). A fresh string is ~70 ns of allocation plus a
hash never computed; a long-lived string carries V8's cached hash. That is `concat`'s mechanism too,
now isolated rather than asserted.

**3. SO THE LEVER IS 3.3-4.5x AT THE LOOKUP AND NOT AVAILABLE.** Three records between it and a
change:

- **Item 590** measured the one-lookup version at the QUERY level: "per-edge `Map.get` on a memoized
  degree map 42.07 — **only 1.5x**", against the per-edge bucket lookup's 61.80. The lookup-level
  3.3-4.5x does not survive the trip to a query.
- **Item 590** also measured a flattened CSR at **37.65 ms to BUILD** on 200k edges — "so no help at
  all" for a per-query index.
- The one layout that gets a single lookup with keys ALREADY IN HAND is the **type-first inversion**
  (`Map<type, Map<vertexId, Set<Edge>>>`): the type string is long-lived and there are ~8 of them, so
  the outer hit is a tiny cache-resident map and the inner is one long-lived-key lookup. **Refuted at
  item 200 and USER-CONFIRMED CLOSED** — it wins the typed lookup 2.2-4.1x (which is what this probe
  re-derives) and **loses get-by-id 1.4x at three edge types and 4.8x at twenty**, with the
  dual-spine variant costing 2.0-2.4x on `indexEdgeLabel`.

**So item 795's "no tick-sized win remains on the widest row" is stronger than it was stated: there
is no win of any size available on that component without the opt-in index item 200 left as the only
surviving direction — a feature with an API, not an optimization.** The target is closed, not open
with a number.

**A correction to item 807's own reading.** Its `CONTROL inner only` is an 8-entry map, and 807 used
its 6.3-8.4 ns as the floor for "one lookup" to attribute ~45 ns to the outer. The arithmetic holds —
the outer IS most of the nested cost — but 6.5 ns is a tiny-cache-resident-map number and does not
generalize; `prekeyed` at 14.2-14.9 is what one lookup into a 200,000-entry map actually costs. Both
arms stay, the control relabelled.

**Eleventh already-closed candidate caught by reading before building this session** (789, 793, 795,
796, 802's item 454, 805's 784, 806's rungs, 807's 450/453/459/462, and now 590 and 200). The two
that found something new (803, and this probe's own discriminators) both came from measuring a pair
that differed in exactly one thing.

## 809 — `nodes(p)` renders each shared prefix element once per path. A per-column memo is **1.14x** — and the 6x the arithmetic predicted did NOT appear, which reframes the row

**DONE (Rust).** `bench_all`'s standout per-row cost is `anchored + nodes(p)`: **241,750 µs for
47,007 rows = 5,143 ns/row**, against `anchored + path` on the SAME rows at 147 ns/row — 35x. Not
previously recorded as a perf target (the only `nodes(p)` entry in this file is a conformance one).

**THE OBSERVATION.** `path_node_values` called `node_result_value(store, id)` per element per ROW
with no memo. `ANY SHORTEST (x)->*(y)` from one anchored source is a **BFS TREE**, so a node at
depth `d` lies on every path into its subtree and was re-rendered once per such path — 47,007 rows
over ≤50,000 distinct nodes.

**This is the shape item 355's rule says YES to** — "a memo helps a REVISITED element and taxes a
VISITED-ONCE one" — and it is why item 591 refused a memo at five of `side()`'s six call sites while
this one takes it: here an element is revisited once per path through it, by construction.

**It also LOWERS peak memory, which is why there is no size cap.** Without the memo every row's list
owns its own rendered copy of each shared element and all rows are live at once in the `Col`; with
it they share one `Arc`, so entries replace duplicates rather than adding to them.

`render::RenderMemo` + `path_node_values_memo` / `path_edge_values_memo`, one memo per COLUMN (not
per row), wired at all four render sites: `Expr::PathAccess` (`Nodes`, `Relationships`, `Elements`),
`Expr::Path` (the `{vertices, edges, length}` value) and Gremlin's `path_nodes`. The two
un-memoized helpers are gone rather than left as a second definition to drift.

**MEASURED — three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds (POST,PRE / PRE,POST / POST,PRE):**

```text
  anchored + nodes(p)   PRE 235735.6 / 237167.2 / 234442.6 us   POST 212008.2 / 210118.2 / 204911.6
                        min-of-three 1.14x, ranges fully DISJOINT
  CONTROL anchored count       6010.7 /  6002.6 /  5957.6        5980.2 /  5918.6 /  5931.8   flat
  CONTROL anchored + y.name    7137.2 /  6313.1 /  6361.2        6838.5 /  6801.3 /  6816.6   PRE min WINS
  CONTROL anchored + path      6387.8 /  7695.6 /  7105.4        6701.8 /  7274.2 /  7237.4   PRE min WINS
  CONTROL varlen control      16105.6 / 17098.9 / 17078.1       15713.9 / 17095.1 / 16687.9   flat
```

**Two controls move AGAINST the change**, which is the strongest control result available — it rules
out the systematic drift item 803 had to go back and re-measure for. `anchored count` reads a path
length with lineage present, so it allocates the memos and never uses them: flat confirms an empty
`HashMap::new()` costs nothing.

### ⚠️ The arithmetic predicted 3-6x and it did not appear — that is the finding

`element p` costs 392.6 ns/row in the same sweep, and with ~6x fewer renders the row should have
roughly halved. It moved 11%. **So the element RENDER is only ~11% of `nodes(p)`'s 5,143 ns/row**,
and the rest is the per-element `Value` and the per-row `List` construction — an OUTPUT-SIZE cost,
the same family as item 289's carrier finding, not a render cost.

That reframes the row: it is not "the element renderer multiplied by path length", and the remaining
~89% is not reachable by anything that makes rendering cheaper. **Recorded so the next pass does not
price the renderer against this row.** Why the render is so much smaller a share than `element p`
suggests is NOT explained here — the social fixture's nodes are narrower than the `perrow` fixture's,
which would account for some of it, and inventing the rest would be the mistake items 804 and 808
were about.

### Teeth: two of three, and the survivor is INHERITED

- memo keyed by a constant (`entry(0)`) — **caught**, 10 failing suites.
- the edge memo rendering through `node_result_value` — **caught**, 29 failing suites.
- the `other => other.clone()` arm → `Value::Null` — **SURVIVED** all 1,963 tests. The arm is
  **unreachable**: a lineage stores node and edge ids as `Value::Num`, so nothing else arrives. It is
  **inherited from the pristine code**, not introduced here, and it is left in place — deleting a
  defensive arm in a render path on the strength of one fixture is its own tick (item 475's rule says
  a survivor can mean "redundant" as easily as "untested"; here it means "unreachable").

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets -- -D warnings` 0 — it caught an empty line after a doc comment left by my own removal
of the dead helpers, the same rule that bit at item 783; `cargo test --release` 1225 + 13 + 725
passed, 0 failed, under `systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`; `rewrite_fuzz` 10 passed;
`bun run fuzz` (all seven, random seeds) 13 pass 0 fail, run TWICE.

## 811 — item 809's memo hits **90.6%**, which CONFIRMS its inference and reconciles the one thing it left unexplained: the render is ~65 ns on this fixture, not 392

**VERIFICATION, no engine change** (a temporary counter, measured, reverted). Item 809 shipped the
`nodes(p)` render memo for 1.14x and concluded from that 1.14x that "the element render is only ~11%
of `nodes(p)`'s 5,143 ns/row". **That inference is only valid if the memo HITS** — a memo that never
fires buys nothing for a completely different reason, and the two are the same null (item 339's
rule). It was recorded as an inference, so it got checked.

### Measured directly

A counter in `path_node_values_memo`, on the bench's own row (`ANY SHORTEST (x:Person)-[:KNOWS]->*(y)
WHERE x.name = 'name1' RETURN nodes(p)`, 50,000 nodes, 47,007 rows):

```text
  memo calls (Value::Num)   498,969
  memo MISSES (a render)     47,007
  non-Num elements                0
  hit rate                     90.6%      elements per row 10.61
```

**The memo works as designed and the miss count is exactly the distinct-element count** — 47,007
misses for 47,007 reachable targets plus the source, i.e. one render per distinct node and not one
more. The eight other shortest-path rows in that table print `calls=0`, confirming they do not reach
this path at all (so they are controls by construction, which is what item 809 measured them as).

**`other` is 0**, which independently confirms item 809's surviving mutant: the
`other => other.clone()` arm is unreachable because a lineage holds every element id as a
`Value::Num`. The mutation survivor and this counter are the same fact from two directions.

### The arithmetic now closes, and it reconciles 809's open question

451,962 renders removed for a measured 30,000 µs saving (235,000 → 205,000) prices the render at
**~65 ns per element on this fixture**. Item 809 recorded that it could not explain why the render
was so much smaller a share than `element p`'s **392.6 ns/row** suggested, and declined to invent a
reason. The reason is fixture WIDTH, and item 806's ladder predicts it precisely:

```text
  element render, 4 props + 0 extra store keys   169.8 ns   (item 806's ladder)
  element render, 4 props + 200 extra keys      1785.7
  `element p` in query/perrow                    392.6      a wider fixture again
  social_store, ONE property per node              ~65      THIS fixture, derived here
```

So **both numbers are right and they are not the same measurement**: `element p` renders a
multi-property node from a store with many distinct keys, and `nodes(p)` here renders a one-property
node. 809's "the render is only ~11%" stands, for a reason it can now state.

### What is still unattributed, stated as such

205,000 µs remain over 498,969 elements = **~411 ns per element** that is NOT the render. The
search and lineage are accounted for separately — `anchored + path` runs the identical query
projecting `path_length(p)` for **6,700 µs**, so the BFS plus lineage is ~3% of the row and cannot be
it. What remains is the per-element `Arc` clone, the per-row `Vec<Value>` and `Value::List`, the
`Col::Gen` entry, and the drop of 498,969 `Arc`s at the end — none of which plausibly costs 411 ns
each, so **the dominant term here is still unidentified and is NOT being guessed at.** It is the
largest unexplained per-element cost in the native corpus and the natural next target; items 804 and
808 are both records of what happens when a mechanism is asserted rather than measured.

**Fourteen already-closed candidates were checked and set aside before this** (789, 793, 795, 796,
454, 784, 806's rungs, 450/453/459/462, 590, 200, 339's `algo/call` ratio, 359/382's `map field`
20x, and the bench's own `size(b)` note on `repeat-group control`). The native sweep's every
remaining outlier has a record; this is the one fresh number in it.
