--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` **1,238** passed 0 failed; `bun run fuzz` all
seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0. Every measurement
and every mutant under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p
MemorySwapMax=0`.

## 868 — the TS engine had the SAME sorted-LIMIT spelling gap as native, in the OPPOSITE direction: 1.45x taken, and the gap narrowed 6.6x -> 4.6x rather than closed

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).**

Items 865/866 found that a sorted LIMIT's two spellings reached different native code. Item 843's
rule says whether the TS engine shares a defect is a MEASUREMENT and never an inference, so the
spelling probe got three new groups — statement vs clause position, ascending, descending, and on a
low-cardinality key. All three flagged on the first run:

```text
  7.0x  sorted LIMIT: ORDER BY in STATEMENT vs CLAUSE position
  6.9x  sorted LIMIT DESC: statement vs clause position
  6.1x  sorted LIMIT on a LOW-CARDINALITY key: statement vs clause
```

**And the direction is the opposite of native's.** In TS the STATEMENT position is the slow one —
62.36 ms against 9.49 for the clause spelling of the same query — where natively the clause form was
slow. Same gap, mirrored, which is item 843 twice over: neither engine's version was inferable from
the other's.

The cause is specific. The statement-position `<order by and page statement>` materializes the
working binding table, allocates a `{b, keys}` wrapper per row, **full-sorts all 200,000** and
slices ten. The projection's `ORDER BY` has had a bounded heap since item 701; this clause never
got one. The three new probe groups are kept, since this is the axis that was unmeasured.

### What shipped, and what it is worth

`boundedTopKeyed` — the keyed-sequence twin of `boundedTopRows`, for a caller holding opaque items
plus a key function rather than rows with resolved columns — admitted by the same measured `* 16`
gate. Two costs go: the sort becomes O(n log cap), and a loser is discarded the moment it is
compared, so only `cap` key arrays are retained instead of one per row.

ISOLATED A/B, one shape per process, arm selected OUTSIDE the measured loop, min of three
order-alternated rounds at 200,000 nodes:

```text
  shape       heap ON    heap OFF
  stmt          46.12       67.08   1.45x   DISJOINT (46/48/52 against 67/67/74)
  stmt DESC     50.27       71.62   1.42x   DISJOINT
  clause        10.49       12.44   ranges OVERLAP — cannot be reached by the switch
  stmt WIDE     80.86       83.34   flat    — the gate DECLINES at LIMIT 50,000
  count(*)       0.00        0.00   reads no key
```

Two controls, chosen for different reasons. `clause` routes through the projection and so cannot be
reached by this switch at all — it is the NULL control, and it moved 1.19x, which is this
instrument's noise floor on this shape. That is why the target's claim rests on DISJOINTNESS rather
than on the ratio. `stmt WIDE` is the admission gate's own control: at `LIMIT 50,000` the `* 16`
test fails (800,000 > 200,000), both arms full-sort, and they are flat — so the gate is not
regressing the wide window it declines.

### The gap narrowed but did NOT close, and that is the honest result

The probe re-run reads 4.6x where it read 6.6x. **The sort was only part of the cost**: at 43-46 ms
against the clause spelling's 9.5, most of what is left is materializing the binding table and
evaluating the key through a per-row context object — the heap cannot touch either, because keys
must be evaluated for every row and nothing here knows which will win. Recorded as still open rather
than filed as a win, with the remaining 4.6x pointing at binding materialization.

### Mutation: four caught, two provably EQUIVALENT

```text
  heap: arrival tiebreak dropped                  CAUGHT
  heap: final sort of survivors removed           CAUGHT
  heap: siftDown after root replacement removed   CAUGHT
  heap: comparator ignores keys after the first    CAUGHT
  heap: evicts on a TIE as well as a loss         SURVIVED - equivalent
  heap: keeps cap+1 items                         SURVIVED - equivalent
```

Both survivors are no-ops, not coverage gaps, and the reasons are checkable rather than asserted.
`cmp` carries the arrival index as its last term, so it is a TOTAL order: `cmp(a, b) == 0` only when
`a.at == b.at`, i.e. the same item, so `<= 0` and `< 0` cannot differ for two distinct candidates.
And a heap holding `cap + 1` items still has the true `cap` smallest in its first `cap` after the
final sort, which the caller's existing `slice(start, start + take)` is what reads — so the extra
item is trimmed downstream. Worth distinguishing: a survivor that is an equivalent mutant says
nothing about the tests, and reporting it as a gap would send the next reader hunting for a hole
that is not there.

The fixture is deliberately tie-heavy (`k = i % 5`, 400 rows per key at N = 2000) because a heap
that loses the arrival tiebreak returns a correctly-SORTED window containing the WRONG rows, which
no "is it ordered?" assertion catches. One test runs the same query either side of the `* 16`
admission gate — `LIMIT 10` is admitted, `LIMIT 500` is not — so the full sort is the heap's oracle
inside the suite.

### Two of my own expectations were wrong, and the engine was right both times

`ORDER BY q.d` over `r0/r777/r1554` is `r0 < r1554 < r777`: STRING order, where `'1' < '7'`. I wrote
the numeric reading. And `SKIP` is rejected in statement position — `parsePageClause` accepts
`OFFSET` only, while the clause position takes both. That asymmetry is pre-existing and I am
recording it as an OPEN CONFORMANCE QUESTION rather than asserting either way: ISO's
`<offset clause>` admits both spellings, so the statement-position restriction may be a gap, but
that needs checking against the BNF artifact before anyone acts on it.

0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0; `bun test packages/gql
packages/gremlin packages/core` **3,830** pass 0 fail; `bun run fuzz` all seven byte-identity
fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail. Every measurement and every mutant under `timeout`/`systemd-run` with
`MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`; the temporary A/B switch and its probe removed.

## 869 — a KEYLESS statement LIMIT materialized the whole working table: **941x**, and it was the larger half of item 868's remaining gap

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).**

Item 868 took the sort out of the statement-position page clause (67 -> 46 ms) and left 4.6x against
the clause spelling, attributed to "materializing the binding table and evaluating keys". That was a
guess with two terms in it, so this separated them — and the answer was neither key evaluation nor
the sorted path.

### The diagnostic, which found something bigger than the thing it was aimed at

```text
  shape                                              before
  sorted         MATCH (n:P) ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10    46.99 ms
  keyless        MATCH (n:P) LIMIT 10                 36.68
  keylessOffset  MATCH (n:P) OFFSET 5 LIMIT 10        32.82
  clauseKeyless  MATCH (n:P) RETURN … LIMIT 10         0.04   <- 917x
  count(*)                                             0.00
```

**A keyless LIMIT — no ORDER BY, no key, nothing to sort — cost 36.68 ms to return ten rows.** The
clause calls `toArray(bindings)` BEFORE it looks at whether there is an `orderBy` at all, so it
forced 200,000 `Binding` maps and sliced ten off the end. The clause position had always taken
lazily. 917x for the same query written the other way, and it accounts for most of the 46.99 the
sorted shape pays as well.

### The fix, and what it is worth

`slice` from `@lenke/fp` is lazy and BREAKS at its end, so the upstream generator chain produces
only the window. Measured by A/B in one binary, arm selected outside the measured loop, min of
three order-alternated rounds:

```text
  shape                lazy ON   lazy OFF
  keyless                 0.04      37.63   941x   DISJOINT (0.04/0.04/0.06 vs 37.6/39.3/44.6)
  CONTROL sorted         49.08      52.71   ranges OVERLAP — the switch cannot reach it
```

`sorted` is the null control: the branch is gated on `orderBy.length === 0`, so a sorted page runs
identical code either way, and it is flat. The keyless shape now measures 0.04 ms — **the same as
the clause spelling, to the printed digit**, so that spelling pair is converged rather than merely
improved. Both pairs are added to the spelling probe, where they now read 0.01 ms on both members.
A group whose members are both beneath the probe's floor is skipped, which sounds like losing the
guard and is not: a regression would make ONE member measurable, and the group is then compared and
flagged.

Item 868's remaining 4.6x is therefore mostly this, and the sorted path still pays it because it
must see every row to find the top K. What is left for the sorted shape is the per-row key
evaluation through a context object, which is the smaller term and is still open.

### Mutation: four caught, one survivor that corrected my own comment

```text
  keyless: OFFSET ignored (window starts at 0)                CAUGHT
  keyless: end is take, not start+take                        CAUGHT
  keyless: OFFSET with no LIMIT goes through slice (NaN end)   CAUGHT
  keyless: break removed, falls through to the sorted path     CAUGHT
  keyless: toArray dropped, a one-shot generator escapes      SURVIVED
```

The survivor matters because it refuted a justification I had already written. The comment said
`toArray` is applied because "a later clause may iterate `bindings` more than once, which an array
survives and a spent generator does not". Dropping it passes **all 3,838 TS tests** — so no covered
path double-iterates, and quite possibly none exists. The `toArray` stays, because it costs
O(limit) — ten rows for a `LIMIT 10` — and it removes a hazard nobody adding a clause below should
have to re-derive. But the comment now says it is DEFENSIVE and unexercised rather than asserting a
reason the suite does not support. A justification that reads like a measurement and is not is worse
than no comment.

### The hazard of making a clause lazy, asserted

Stopping the pull early must not stop a side effect upstream of it. Mutating clauses force their own
evaluation, so `MATCH (r:R) SET r.touched = 1 LIMIT 3` still writes every row while returning three
— now a test, because the entire change is that the page no longer forces the chain on everyone
else's behalf. Also covered: a `LIMIT` wider than the input, an `OFFSET` past the end, `LIMIT 0`,
`OFFSET` with no `LIMIT`, and a `FILTER` after the page seeing the window and only the window.

## 870 — the native engine does NOT have item 869's keyless-LIMIT defect, at any of seven shapes

**MEASUREMENT (Rust + TypeScript), a probe added to the corpus; no engine change.**

Item 869 found a TS keyless statement `LIMIT` forcing the whole working table — 36.68 ms against
0.04 for the clause spelling of the same query. The native engine has a `pull_capped` for keyless
pages, so the defect "probably" is not there, and "probably" is exactly what item 843's rule exists
to refuse. The two engines have now mirrored each other on sorted-LIMIT spellings twice (865/866
against 868), so this got measured rather than reasoned about.

### Native, 200,000 nodes, min of 9

```text
  floor  count(*)                      0.0003 ms      reads no property
  stmt   LIMIT 10                       0.0002        clause 0.0002
  stmt   OFFSET 5 LIMIT 10              0.0002        clause 0.0002
  stmt   LIMIT 10 (str key)             0.0003        clause 0.0003
  stmt   WHERE + LIMIT 10               0.0145        clause 0.0146
  stmt   hop + LIMIT 10                 0.0143        clause 0.0144
  stmt   SELECTIVE WHERE + LIMIT 10     0.1253        clause 0.1236
  ceil   no LIMIT                       0.2617                   200,000 rows
  ceil   hop no LIMIT                   1.8637                   400,000 rows
```

**All seven pairs within 1.5%**, and the bare pairs sit ~1000x below the ceiling, so a cap really is
applying rather than the query being cheap for some other reason. That is why the ceilings are in
the table: "0.0002 ms" on its own says nothing about whether the page capped anything.

The last three pairs are the interesting ones. `pull_capped` only admits a row-PRESERVING
Scan/Seek/Project chain — a `FILTER` or an `EXPAND` needs more input rows than it yields, so those
fall to `pull_capped_stream`, a different mechanism. Both mechanisms converge on both spellings.

### And item 869's TS fix extends to those shapes, also measured

869 fixed the BARE keyless page and measured only that. A filter or a hop ahead of the page is a
separate question, because the lazy `slice` has to pull THROUGH them:

```text
  keyless LIMIT after a WHERE   statement 0.01 ms   clause 0.01
  keyless LIMIT after a hop     statement 0.01      clause 0.02
```

Converged. Four new groups are now permanent in the TS spelling probe (bare, `OFFSET`, after a
`WHERE`, after a hop) — all reading 0.01-0.02 ms on both members, which puts them under the probe's
floor and therefore "not compared". That is not a lost guard: the floor skips a group only when
BOTH members are tiny, so a regression making one member measurable gets the group compared and
flagged, which is precisely when it matters.

### A stale binary nearly reported the result

The extended probe failed to compile — an array-length annotation I did not update — and the shell
ran the PREVIOUS binary, which printed a clean table of the original eight cases. The giveaway was
the row count, not an error: the output looked entirely plausible and simply answered an older
question. `grep -cE 'Compiling|^error'` on the build is what distinguishes them, and it is the same
trap item 847 recorded for `cargo test` (a `Finished` line with no `Compiling` line means the binary
under test is the previous one).

**Nothing to ship, and that is the result.** Recorded so the symmetry argument — "TS had a 917x
keyless gap, therefore look for one natively" — is answered by a measurement rather than re-derived,
and so the third data point on item 843's rule is written down: this time the engines DIVERGED, with
the defect in TS only.

## 871 — censusing the FILTER family by column representation: a DATE predicate cost MORE than `WHERE true`, now **11.2x** streamed and **6.4x** seeked

**SHIPPED (Rust).** The census move applied to a fourth enum, and it needed two separate fixes
because the diagnosis moved the target.

### The census

`fastpath.rs` names numeric, dictionary and string predicates in its function list
(`try_stream_num_count`, `try_stream_range_count`, `try_stream_dict_pred_count`,
`try_stream_membership_count`, `try_filter_keep_dict`, `try_filtered_scan_{num,str}_agg`) and names
BOOL and TEMPORAL nowhere. One fixture, five columns differing ONLY in representation, each
predicate selecting the same 1/50 — 200,000 nodes, min of 9:

```text
  floor  count(*)            0.3 us       reads no property
  Num   = 7                131.8         the reference
  Num   WHERE true         655.5         the filter machinery with NO column read
  Num   > 25                91.1
  Dict  = 'd7'             125.7
  Str   = 's00007'         406.3
  Bool  = true             125.7
  Bool  bare (p.bul)       312.2         2.3x its own `= true` spelling
  Date  = DATE '...'     2,506.2         19x the numeric, and 3.8x WHERE TRUE
  Date  >= DATE '...'    1,159.4         12.7x the numeric `>`
```

**Costing more than `WHERE true` is the tell.** `WHERE true` reads no property at all, so a
predicate that exceeds it is not merely un-specialized — it is paying something the generic
boolean path does not. Two controls per row, answering different questions, is what makes that
visible; one control would have shown "Date is 19x Num" and left the cause open.

### The diagnosis moved the target, and the first fix only covered half

A `try_stream_date_count` mirroring the numeric sweep took `Date >=` from 1,159.4 to 103.3 us —
and left `Date =` **completely unchanged**. Same column, same literal type, different operator.
Dumping the plans:

```text
  p.dat =  DATE '...'   ->  IndexSeek { key: "dat", value: Temporal(Date(...)) }
  p.dat >= DATE '...'   ->  Filter { pred: Compare { op: Ge, ... } }
  p.num =  7            ->  IndexSeek { key: "num", value: Num(7.0) }
```

**Equality lowers to `IndexSeek` and never reaches the filter family at all** — on a fixture with
no index on either column, so this is the seek's no-index fallback. `Num = 7` takes the same route
and costs 131.8, so the 2,506 was that fallback's TEMPORAL case. Its code says so itself: a comment
there lists `accepts`-but-untyped cases as "`Gen` and … a same-kind `Temporal` — the two the typed
arms below do not cover and which must stay on the boxed path". So the second fix is a
`Column::Temporal` arm beside the existing Str/Dict/Num/Bool ones.

Had I taken the first measurement at face value, the headline would have been "Date filters are 19x"
and half the family would still be slow.

### Measured, min of three order-alternated rounds, separate binaries

```text
  shape                  PRE        POST
  Date  = DATE '...'   2,506.2     391.1    6.4x   DISJOINT (2506-2747 vs 391-428)
  Date  >= DATE '...'  1,159.4     103.3   11.2x   DISJOINT
  CONTROL Num  = 7       131.8     132.8   flat
  CONTROL Dict = 'd7'    125.7     125.5   flat
  CONTROL Str  = 's…'    406.3     405.9   flat
  CONTROL Bool = true    125.7     126.8   flat
```

Four controls, each a representation the change cannot reach, all flat. Row counts identical in
both arms on every case.

**An honest residual:** `Date =` lands at 391 us against the numeric arm's 132. A `Temporal` is a
wider value than an `f64` and the sweep is correspondingly less cache-friendly, so parity was never
the expectation — but 3x the numeric is where this now sits, not at parity, and the entry says so.

### Mutation: six caught, one equivalent, one not test-detectable

```text
  stream: route off (always declines)              CAUGHT
  stream: Ge mapped to a strict >                  CAUGHT
  stream: present[] check dropped                  CAUGHT
  stream: flipped spelling no longer flips the op  CAUGHT
  stream: kind check dropped                       EQUIVALENT (see below)
  seek: temporal arm compares != instead of ==     CAUGHT
  seek: temporal arm drops present[]               CAUGHT (only after a new assertion)
  seek: temporal arm removed entirely              SURVIVED - not test-detectable
```

Two of these are worth the detail.

**The `present[]` check in the seek arm survived at first**, and the reason is a fixture gap rather
than a dead check: a packed column still stores something at an absent row, which for a date column
is day 0. Nothing asked about day 0, so skipping the presence check changed no answer. `WHERE t.d =
DATE '1970-01-01'` is the query that distinguishes "skipped because absent" from "happened not to
equal the literal", and with it the mutant dies.

**The `kind` bail is equivalent, and I checked rather than reasoned.** My first instinct was that it
was load-bearing — if a cross-KIND comparison FAULTED on the general path, a fast path returning 0
would be a wrong answer. So I measured what the general path does: a Date column against `DATETIME`,
against `TIME`, and against a bare string all return **0 rows and no fault**, incomparable operands
being UNKNOWN. With the bail gone the sweep's `if let Temporal::Date` simply never matches and
returns the same 0. The comment now says "a bail, not a correctness guard" with that evidence,
instead of the correctness-sounding justification I first wrote.

The surviving mutant is honest: removing the seek's temporal arm is answer-equivalent and, unlike
items 866/867, there is no route PREDICATE to extract — the route _is_ a match arm. Its correctness
is covered by the answers and its existence only by the probe's timing. Recorded rather than papered
over.

### Left open, both now priced

- **`WHERE p.bul` costs 2.3x `WHERE p.bul = true`** (312.2 against 125.7) — two spellings of one
  predicate, which is the class this repo refuses to ship. Not touched here because it is a
  different mechanism (a bare property as a boolean context) and deserves its own item.
- The two-bound DATE range has no arm. Deliberately: item 451 measured the numeric range sweep at
  3.9x its single-bound twin and traced it to lost VECTORIZATION, not the extra compare, so a range
  arm here needs its own measurement rather than inheriting this one's.

## 872 — a BARE property in boolean context had no typed path: `WHERE p.flag` 1.95x, `WHERE NOT p.flag` **4.51x**, and the spelling spread closes 6.6x -> 1.47x

**SHIPPED (Rust).** Item 871 priced this and deliberately left it; this is that item.

### Three spellings of one question, 6.6x apart

```text
  WHERE p.bul = true    127.7 us     IndexSeek, whose no-index fallback has a typed Bool arm
  WHERE p.bul           283.4        2.2x
  WHERE NOT p.bul       837.9        6.6x
```

The plans say why, and the plan dump is what made it a two-line diagnosis rather than a guess:
`= true` is rewritten to `IndexSeek { key: "bul", value: Bool(true) }`, while a bare property stays
`Filter { pred: Prop { slot: 0, key: "bul" } }` — and `try_filter_keep`'s chain of specialized arms
has no case for a bare `Expr::Prop`, so it fell to the boxed general eval.

### Measured, min of three order-alternated rounds, separate binaries

```text
  shape                PRE      POST
  WHERE p.bul         283.4    145.2   1.95x   DISJOINT (283-312 vs 145.2-145.3)
  WHERE NOT p.bul     837.9    185.9   4.51x   DISJOINT (838-926 vs 185.9-186.8)
  CONTROL  = true     126.2    126.2   flat    (IndexSeek — a different path entirely)
  CONTROL Num = 7     132.9    131.0   flat
  CONTROL Dict = 'd7' 126.3    123.3   flat
  CONTROL Date = …    387.3    390.7   flat
```

Four controls, all flat, and `= true` is the most useful of them: it is the spelling this item is
converging TOWARDS, so it has to stay put while the other two come down. The spread across the three
spellings goes from 6.6x to **1.47x**.

### The correctness condition is the typed column, not conservatism

Restricted to `Column::Bool`. Every present cell of a typed bool column IS a boolean, so there is no
value a boolean context could reject; a `Gen` column can hold anything, and a non-boolean in boolean
position is the general path's business and its static check's. An absent or NULL cell is UNKNOWN,
which a keep-TRUE filter drops, and **`NOT UNKNOWN` is UNKNOWN rather than TRUE** — which is why the
negation keeps the presence test instead of inverting the whole condition.

### Mutation: six caught, but only after TWO fixture defects

```text
  mutant                                          first fixture   final
  route off (never claimed)                       CAUGHT          CAUGHT
  presence test inverted along with the value     CAUGHT          CAUGHT
  present[] dropped (UNKNOWN kept)                CAUGHT          CAUGHT
  claims a Gen column too                         CAUGHT          CAUGHT
  negation ignored (NOT behaves as bare)          SURVIVED        CAUGHT
  optional-miss sentinel not skipped              SURVIVED        CAUGHT
```

**The negation mutant survived because my true and false groups were the same size.** 100 each, so
keeping the TRUE rows for `NOT f` returns 100 — the correct COUNT, with the wrong rows. A count over
a symmetric fixture cannot see a negation bug at all. The groups are now 150 and 50.

**The sentinel guard was unreachable.** An optional miss carries `u32::MAX` in the node slot, and
indexing a column by it is out of bounds — but no plain scan produces one, so nothing asked. It took
an `OPTIONAL MATCH`, and the obvious spelling does not parse: `WHERE` inside `OPTIONAL MATCH` is
`E_NOT_IMPLEMENTED`, so the case is written as a statement-position `FILTER` after it. With that, the
mutant panics and is caught.

### A storage asymmetry found on the way, and measured rather than assumed

My first fixture used a stored `Value::Null` for the UNKNOWN cells and the column assertion failed:
**a null written through `Builder::node` promotes the column to `Gen`**, where `store.rs`'s "the
column NEVER de-opts to `Gen` on a null" describes the `SET` path. Since `Gen` stores a null with
`present = true`, that raised a correctness question — does `IS NOT NULL` then count it? Measured on
both representations: 4 true, 4 `NOT`, 4 `IS NULL`, 8 `IS NOT NULL`, **identical**. So the asymmetry
is representational only and carries no answer consequence. Both fixtures are now in the test, with
the `Gen` one asserting the typed arm DECLINES and the answers still agree.

**1,240** passed 0 failed; `bun run fuzz` all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail; `bun run
fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0. Every measurement and every mutant under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user

## 873 — the TS engine HAS item 872's bare-bool gap (2.02x) and does NOT have item 871's temporal one; the cause is still open, and three candidates are ruled out

**MEASUREMENT (TypeScript), a probe added; no engine change.**

Items 871 and 872 found two native filter gaps. Item 843's rule says whether the TS engine shares
either is a measurement, and this session already has all three possible answers on record — same
gap different cause (843), same gap mirrored direction (868), gap in one engine only (870) — so
inference was never available.

### The census, 200,000 nodes, one shape per process, median of 11

```text
  floor   count(*)           0.002 ms      reads no property
  WHERE true                 2.134         the filter machinery with NO property read
  num = 7                    3.520
  num > 25                   3.847
  str = 's00007'             4.282         8,000 distinct
  low = 'd7'                 4.343         50 distinct (a dictionary column natively)
  bul = true                 3.526
  bul (bare)                 7.499         2.13x its own `= true` spelling
  NOT bul                    5.020         1.34x `= false`
  bul = false                3.749
  dat = DATE '...'           4.050         1.15x the numeric — NO temporal gap
  dat >= DATE '...'          4.271
```

**Item 871's temporal gap is not here.** Natively a date predicate cost 19x the numeric one and
3.8x `WHERE true`, because it boxed a `Value::Temporal` per row; the TS engine has no typed columns
to box out of and lands at 1.15x. **Item 872's bare-bool gap IS here**, at 2.13x — the same shape,
and close to native's 2.2x before the fix.

### A fixture bug of mine, caught by the row count

The first run reported **0 rows for every date shape**. I had stored the dates as ISO STRINGS, and a
string against a `DATE` literal is a cross-type comparison, which is a documented no-match. The
timings looked perfectly reasonable — only the row column gave it away, which is why the probe
prints it. Fixed with real `parseDate` values, and the comment says so where the next reader would
make the same mistake.

### The cause is NOT yet established, and that is the honest state

Three candidates ruled out, each by a measurement or by reading the code that would have to be
responsible:

- **Not the count shortcut.** The gap persists when the projection is a value rather than a count:
  `WHERE p.bul RETURN p.num` 7.489 ms against `WHERE p.bul = true RETURN p.num` 3.703. No count
  shortcut applies to either, so it is the predicate.
- **Not a different evaluation COUNT.** `pushWhereIntoNode` pushes subquery-free conjuncts of a
  single-node pattern's `WHERE` into the node predicate, which both of these are, and its own
  comment records that "the evaluation COUNT is unchanged either way".
- **Not `asTruth`.** It is `isNullish`, a `typeof` and a return — three branches. The gap is ~20 ns
  a row against ~7 for a read-and-compare, which three branches do not explain.

And the arithmetic says something stronger than "unexplained": `compileExpr`'s `prop` arm is
`(env) => propOf(env.binding.get(variable), key)`, and the comparison arm compiles THAT SAME closure
plus a compare — so the comparison does strictly more work per row and should be SLOWER. It is 2x
faster. The leading hypothesis is therefore that the comparison is not evaluated through that
closure at all, but reaches the `collectHints`/`seedHints` inline-gate route that a bare property
has no shape for. **Not confirmed**, and the next step is to instrument which route each takes
rather than reason about it further.

### The hazard any fix has to respect, recorded before attempting one

A property in boolean context is classified **DYNAMIC** by the static boolean-context check, i.e.
it stays a per-row `asTruth` that RAISES on a non-boolean. So a fix may not turn `WHERE p.b` into a
seed or an inline constraint that silently drops a non-boolean row — that would change which
queries error. The adjacent attempt (extending the static check to inline pattern positions) was
tried twice and made things worse, turning ~1 divergence per 20,000 queries into 7. Any
specialization here has to be an implementation change under an unchanged per-row raise.

**Nothing shipped, and that is the result for this tick.** The gap is real, reproducible and 2.02x;
the cause is open with three candidates eliminated, which is a better starting point than the guess
I would have committed.

## 874 — item 873's open cause, CLOSED by instrumentation: a comparison never reaches `compileExpr` at all

**DIAGNOSIS (TypeScript), no engine change.** Item 873 measured the bare-bool gap at 2.02x,
eliminated three candidates and named the next step as "instrument which route each takes". This is
that, and the answer is unambiguous.

### Per-row closure invocations, counted

Temporary counters in `compileExpr`'s `prop` arm (per call) and `compare` arm (per COMPILE and per
call), at 20,000 vertices, divided by the rep count:

```text
  shape        prop reads   compare compiles   compare calls
  bul (bare)       20,000                  0               0
  bul = true            0                  0               0
  num = 7               0                  0               0
  WHERE true            0                  0               0
```

**A comparison predicate never reaches `compileExpr` — not even its compile arm.** The bare
property is evaluated once per scanned vertex through
`(env) => propOf(env.binding.get(variable), key)`: a binding `Map` lookup plus a closure call, per
vertex. The comparison is rewritten BEFORE compilation into a lifted property constraint that
`satisfies` reads straight off the element.

That also resolves item 873's arithmetic puzzle. The comparison arm compiles the `prop` arm's
closure PLUS a compare, so it should be strictly slower; it is 2x faster because it is not that
code at all.

### The mechanism, and exactly why a bare property cannot use it

`directEqProps` lifts a node's `WHERE` conjuncts into `eqProps` (equalities) or `cmpProps` (ordering
comparisons), both read off the element instead of through the binding. Its loop opens with:

```text
  if (conjunct.kind !== 'compare') { return null; }
```

**A bare `prop` conjunct is not a `compare`, so it declines the WHOLE chain** and the predicate
lands on the generic evaluator. The gap is that one line's consequence, and the per-vertex cost
difference is already documented in the file for the comparison case: item 276 measured `k = <lit>`
at 30.5 ns a vertex against `k > <lit>` at 49.9 before `cmpProps` existed, and item 780 measured an
inline node `WHERE` as the SLOWEST of three spellings of one question (20.55 ms against 13.83 for
`{age: 5}`) for exactly this reason — "admitted, then evaluated generically".

### What the fix has to be, and why it is not in this commit

A third lifted category — `truthProps`, keys that must be TRUE in boolean context — following
`cmpProps`'s own stated precedent ("a separate list rather than an `op` field on `CProp`, because
`eqProps` is the already-tuned equality path and a per-entry operator dispatch would make it pay for
a generality only this list needs").

It may NOT be lifted as `eqProps` with value `true`. A property in boolean context is DYNAMIC under
the static boolean-context check: a non-boolean must RAISE, where a lifted equality would silently
not match. So the new loop has to apply `asTruth` and keep that raise — an implementation change
under unchanged semantics, which is the only shape allowed here.

Deliberately not rushed into this commit. `hasPredicate`'s own doc records that `CPredicate` carries
constraints in three places and **six of the seven checks that asked "is this predicate empty?"
listed only two — a WRONG ANSWER**, because a skipped predicate filter returns a SUPERSET and no
correctness test on a fixture lacking that spelling can see it. A fourth field walks into exactly
that trap, so it wants its own item with the `hasPredicate` update, tests, and mutation covering
the superset case.

**Nothing shipped; the open question from item 873 is closed.** The gap, its cause and its fix are
now all written down, which is the state the next tick needs.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint`
0; `bun run build` 0; `bun test packages/gql packages/core` **3,025** pass 0 fail. The counters and
the probe's route block were temporary and are reverted — `git status` clean before the entry was
written.

## 875 — the `truthProps` lift: `WHERE n.flag` **2.25x**, converged with `= true`, and the one survivor is a line I verified unreachable rather than claimed tested

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 874 specified this; this builds it.

### What changed

`directEqProps` lifts a node's `WHERE` conjuncts to be read off the element. Its loop declined its
whole chain on the first conjunct that was not a `compare`, so a bare property — `WHERE n.flag` —
never lifted. It now admits one into a third list, `truthProps`, following `cmpProps`'s own stated
precedent for being the second ("a separate list rather than an `op` field on `CProp`, because
`eqProps` is the already-tuned equality path").

**Not `eqProps` with a `true` right-hand side, and that is a correctness condition.** A property in
boolean context is DYNAMIC under the static boolean-context check, so a non-boolean must RAISE
where a lifted equality would silently fail to match. The gate loop therefore applies `asTruth` —
the same function the generic evaluator used — so this is a cheaper route to an identical answer,
raise included.

### Measured: min of three order-alternated rounds, 200,000 vertices

```text
  shape                 lift ON   lift OFF
  WHERE p.bul             3.315      7.467   2.25x   DISJOINT (3.3-3.4 vs 7.5-7.7)
  CONTROL p.bul = true    3.501      3.410   flat
  CONTROL p.num = 7       3.515      3.455   flat
  CONTROL WHERE true      1.834      1.821   flat
```

Three controls, none reachable by the switch, all flat. And the point of the item is the
convergence rather than the ratio: `WHERE p.bul` now measures 3.315 against `= true`'s 3.501 — the
two spellings of one question agree, where they were 2.25x apart.

### Equivalence checked against the pre-lift build, including both raises

Seven shapes run under both arms and compared as text — the bare property, a number in boolean
position, a string in boolean position, an absent key, a conjunction in both written orders, and
the inline-`WHERE` spelling. **Identical on all seven**, the two `E_INVALID_VALUE` raises included.
That is what licenses the claim that this is a route change and not a semantics change.

### Mutation: six caught, one survivor that is a verified-unreachable line

```text
  lift: route off (bare prop declines as before)            CAUGHT
  lift: variable check dropped (any variable lifts)          CAUGHT
  gate: asTruth result inverted                              CAUGHT
  gate: structuralEq against true (the RAISE disappears)     CAUGHT
  gate: the truthProps loop removed entirely                 CAUGHT
  hasPredicate: truthProps not counted                       CAUGHT
  mergeFarPreds: truthProps DROPPED (silent superset)       SURVIVED
```

The first two are caught only by the route assertions — the lift is answer-equivalent, so with it
off every answer above is still right, which is items 866/867's lesson applied before it could bite
a third time. `hasPredicate` is in the list deliberately: its own doc records six of seven emptiness
checks once listing two of three fields and producing a WRONG ANSWER.

**The survivor took three attempts and the third was the useful one.** `mergeFarPreds` joins a far
node's inline predicate with a lifted clause predicate, and dropping `truthProps` from it should be
a silent SUPERSET. My first hop fixture used a selective inline `{ok: true}`, which filtered to the
right answer by itself — so I made the inline constraint non-selective (`{tag: 1}` on both
neighbours) so the answer rested entirely on the clause predicate surviving the merge. **It still
survived.** So I instrumented the function instead of guessing at a fourth spelling, and it is
simply not reached with a `truthProps` on either side:

- The CLAUSE side cannot carry one. `splitFarConjuncts` admits a conjunct only if
  `truthCannotRaise`, and a bare property can raise — so it never enters the hoisted bucket. That
  is correct behaviour, not an oversight: a raising conjunct must not be hoisted ahead of others.
- The INLINE side can in principle, but the spellings that would exercise it are intercepted
  upstream. Instrumented, `mergeFarPreds` is entered **4 times across the whole GQL suite with
  `clause.truthProps` undefined every time**, and three hand-built inline spellings did not enter
  it at all.

So the merge line stays, as the correctness precondition for when the lift widens, and its comment
says it is unreachable BY MEASUREMENT rather than implying a test covers it. Same treatment as item
865's `nulls_first` guard and item 871's seek arm: a survivor that is explained is worth more than
one quietly deleted or quietly believed.

## 876 — a VACUOUS label cost **2340x** on a hop count, in both front ends, and the TS engine already had the elision

**SHIPPED (Rust).** Found by reading the Gremlin bench's NATIVE column rather than its ratio.

### How it surfaced

`bun run bench:gremlin` prints a ts/native ratio per shape, and the eye goes to the big ones. The
useful row was one where native was the SLOW side:

```text
  V().out().count()                 ts 0.0   native 0.00
  V().hasLabel().out().count()      ts 0.0   native 0.50     <- 50x slower than TS
```

Every vertex in that fixture is a `Person`, so `hasLabel('Person')` is vacuous and the two rows are
the same question. TS answers both at 0.0 because it HAS this elision (`vacuousLabel` in
`shortcuts.ts`); native did not.

### Priced, both front ends, with the selective label as the control

```text
  G no label    out.count       0.0003 ms   1,000,000 rows
  G VACUOUS     out.count       0.5380      1,000,000        1793x
  G SELECTIVE   out.count       0.0113         20,001        the degree-sum, appropriate
  Q no label    hop count       0.0003      1,000,000
  Q VACUOUS     hop count       0.5373      1,000,000        1791x
  Q SELECTIVE   hop count       0.0113         20,001
  plain count(), all three      0.0003                        the elision ALREADY existed here
```

The last row is what made this worth chasing: a bare `count()` already answered a vacuous label in
O(1), so the gap was one shortcut's precondition rather than a missing capability.

### The cause was one line, and its own doc argued for the fix

`typed_hop_count_from_size` answers `()-[:T]->()` from the length of `T`'s CSR partition, gated on

```text
  if !matches!(**src, Plan::Scan { label: None }) { return None; }
```

and its doc gives the reason as "an unlabelled whole-graph `Scan` source — **a label would restrict
the sources**; the partition spans all of them". A label every vertex carries restricts nothing, so
the condition wanted was "whole-graph", not "unlabelled". Now `whole_graph_scan`.

```text
  shape                      PRE       POST
  G VACUOUS   out.count    0.4677     0.0002    ~2340x   DISJOINT
  Q VACUOUS   hop count    0.4971     0.0003    ~1650x
  CONTROL G SELECTIVE      0.0105     0.0096    flat, still 20,001 rows
  CONTROL no label         0.0002     0.0002    flat
```

Row counts identical on every row, in both front ends.

### GREP THE PATTERN ELSEWHERE — clean, and that is worth recording

Four other sites gate on `Scan { label: None }`. All four already carry a labelled arm with its own
O(1) answer (`try_scan_count`'s own `Some(l) => nodes_with_label(l).len()`, `product_of_counts`'s,
`cost.rs`'s estimator, and two lowering decisions that are not perf gates). So the gap was unique
to this function — checked rather than assumed, because "it is probably everywhere" and "it is
probably nowhere" are equally cheap to say.

### My first predicate was wrong twice, and a mutant made me check

I copied `scan_visit`'s `whole` test — `live_node_count == node_count && nodes_with_label(l).len()
== node_count` — and wrote a comment claiming a label list can hold a deleted id, so the live-count
conjunct was load-bearing. Two mutants survived: dropping that conjunct, and loosening the
comparison. So I measured what a delete actually does (`TOMB=1` in the probe):

```text
  before: node_count=100  live=100  person_list=100
  after : node_count=100  live=99   person_list=99
```

**`delete_node` removes the id from the label's list.** So the conjunct was redundant, AND comparing
coverage against `node_count` was over-conservative: a graph with one tombstone declined a label
that genuinely covered every live vertex. The predicate is now
`nodes_with_label(l).len() == live_node_count()`, which is both correct and precise, and the comment
says why this is NOT `scan_visit`'s question — `whole` justifies iterating the dense range
`0..node_count`, which needs no tombstones at all; this needs only "every live vertex carries the
label", which is weaker.

(Deletes are safe for a second reason outside the predicate: `out_typed_flat` returns `None` once
the CSR overlay is stale, and an adjacency write invalidates it.)

### Mutation: 5 of 5, after the route mutant forced a better assertion

```text
  elision: route off (literal label:None again)                      CAUGHT
  elision: ANY label accepted (a selective label elided too)         CAUGHT
  elision: coverage loosened to <=                                   CAUGHT
  elision: coverage compared to node_count (over-conservative)       CAUGHT
  whole_graph_scan: claims a non-Scan plan                           CAUGHT
```

The route mutant survived at first and the reason is instructive: my assertions tested the
PREDICATE, and reverting the CALL SITE to its old literal check leaves the predicate intact and
true. Asking `try_scan_count` directly — does it CLAIM this hop? — is the assertion that sees it.

**And the harness itself failed first.** I derived the mutation script from item 871's and its
`MUTANTS` splice silently did not apply (an escaping slip in a slice bound), so it ran the PREVIOUS
item's mutants against this item's test filter and printed SURVIVED for three of them — verdicts
for nothing, the same class of error item 866 recorded. The rewrite asserts its own mutant count
and anchors before running.

## 877 — `E().hasLabel(T).count()` was **89,800x** its own GQL spelling, and an untyped hop count 18.2x

**SHIPPED (Rust).** Item 876's lens again — the bench row where native was the slow side — and it
led somewhere much larger than the row itself.

### Starting from the one row that was left

After 876, `E().count()` was the last Gremlin bench row with native behind TS (0.04 ms against
0.0). Item 412 says it is answered from `live_edge_count`, "that length by construction", so 40 µs
needed explaining. Printing every spelling of "how many edges are there" WITH ITS PLAN found two
gaps that the bench corpus had no row for at all:

```text
  shape                                    time        rows      plan
  g.E().count()                          0.0337 ms  1,000,000   Aggregate{EdgeScan}
  g.E().hasLabel('KNOWS').count()       18.4327        750,000   Aggregate{Filter{EdgeScan, IsLabeled}}
  MATCH ()-[:KNOWS]->() RETURN count(*)  0.0003        750,000   Aggregate{Expand{Scan, ["KNOWS"]}}
  MATCH ()-[]->()      RETURN count(*)   0.6070      1,000,000   Aggregate{Expand{Scan, []}}
  g.V().count()                          0.0002        200,000
```

**The same question, 61,000x apart**, because the two front ends lower it to different plans and
only one had a shortcut. And the UNTYPED hop was 2,000x its own typed sibling, because
`typed_hop_count_from_size` required exactly ONE edge type and an empty list fell through to a
degree sum — though an out-expansion from every vertex is just the edge count.

### Two arms, measured min of three order-alternated rounds

```text
  shape                         PRE       POST
  g.E().hasLabel('KNOWS')   17.9617     0.0002   ~89,800x   DISJOINT
  g.E().hasLabel(K,L)       19.1772     0.0002   ~95,900x
  g.E().hasLabel('NOPE')    14.4374     0.0002   ~72,000x
  MATCH ()-[]->()            0.5902     0.0325      18.2x
  CONTROL g.V().count()      0.0002     0.0002   flat
  CONTROL ()-[:KNOWS]->()    0.0003     0.0003   flat
  CONTROL g.E().count()      0.0324     0.0323   flat
```

Row counts identical on every row. Note `hasLabel('NOPE')` — a label matching nothing took 14 ms
to answer 0, because it still built the edge id vector first.

### The semantics a label-set count rests on were measured, not assumed

A sum of partition lengths is only right if `hasLabel(A, B)` means A **or** B. Checked before
relying on it: on a fixture carrying only `KNOWS` and `LIKES`, `hasLabel('KNOWS','LIKES').count()`
returns every edge, and `hasLabel('NOPE')` returns 0. Both are now pinned in the test, along with
the two shapes that follow from it — a duplicate label must count one partition (`hasLabel('K','K')`
is 450, not 900) and an unknown label must contribute 0 without forfeiting the path for the known
ones.

### What the untyped arm did NOT reach, and why

It lands at 0.0325 rather than the 0.0003 of its typed sibling, and the reason is one line in the
store: **`live_edge_count()` is `out_adj.iter().map(Vec::len).sum()` — O(V)**, summing 200,000 `Vec`
lengths. So item 412's "that length by construction" is not a stored length at all. `edge_count()`
IS O(1) but counts edges ever created (`next_eid`, monotonic), and there is no deleted-edge tally to
subtract. Making it O(1) means a maintained counter on every edge write and delete path — the store
already keeps one for nodes AND an invariant test for it, because a cached counter is wrong the
moment a write path forgets it. That is a separate item with its own risk, priced here at ~100x on
these two rows and left open rather than bundled in.

### Mutation: 7 of 7, after two survivors that each needed a different kind of test

```text
  label count: route off (never claimed)                       CAUGHT
  label count: duplicate labels counted twice                  CAUGHT
  label count: claims a NODE scan too                          CAUGHT
  label count: an unknown type DECLINES instead of giving 0     CAUGHT  (route assertion)
  label count: multi-label-edge guard dropped                   CAUGHT  (NDJSON fixture)
  untyped hop: answers the node count instead of the edge count CAUGHT
  untyped hop: arm removed (falls back to the degree sum)       CAUGHT
```

Both survivors are worth the detail.

**The unknown-type mutant is answer-equivalent.** Declining on `hasLabel('NOPE')` still answers 0 —
the general path walks every edge and finds none — so only an assertion that the path CLAIMED the
shape can see it. Route assertion added.

**The multi-label guard was unconstructible with the fixture I had.** `Builder::edge` takes a single
label, so `has_multi_label_edges()` was false and the guard never ran. It is reachable through
`ndjson::from_ndjson`, which is how the test now builds an edge carrying `["EXTRA","KNOWS"]` — and
it asserts the fixture really has the property (`has_multi_label_edges()`) before asserting the
decline, because a fixture that quietly lacks the shape is how a guard ends up believed rather than
tested. The guard matters: `Adj.etype` holds an edge's PRIMARY type only, so a partition sum would
UNDERCOUNT an edge whose secondary type is the one asked for.

### The bench corpus gained the row that was missing

`E().hasLabel().count()` is now a `bench:gremlin` row. Its absence is the whole reason an 89,800x
gap sat unmeasured next to an `E().count()` row that looked fine — the unlabelled spelling cannot
see it.

## 878 — `live_edge_count` O(1) RETRACTED on cost/benefit, and the TS `order()` row decomposed: ~212 ms of the 300 is not the sort

**MEASUREMENT + a retraction, no engine change.**

### Item 877's open target, retracted

877 left `live_edge_count()`'s O(V) sum as "~100x on two rows", and that framing was too rosy. Priced
properly:

- The win is **32 µs once per query** (0.0325 ms -> ~0.0003), on `MATCH ()-[]->() RETURN count(*)`
  and `g.E().count()`. **Two callers, both once per query** — it is not a per-row cost.
- The cost is correctness-critical cached state. There is NO edge tombstone bitmap: the adjacency IS
  the edge set, so an O(1) count needs either a maintained counter or a cached sum. A counter would
  have to be right across `mem::take(out_adj[i])` plus a per-neighbour `remove` loop plus the
  undo/restore pushes, with self-loops appearing in both lists — six sites, and "a cached counter is
  wrong the moment a write path forgets it" is exactly why the node equivalent has an invariant test.
  A version-keyed lazy cache needs only ONE hook (`touch()`), but `Store` is shared across threads
  for the parallel algorithms, so it needs atomics.

**32 µs on two rare shapes does not buy that.** Retracted, with the numbers, so the next reader
prices it the same way instead of seeing "~100x" and starting work.

### The TS `order()` row, decomposed

The two largest ABSOLUTE numbers in the Gremlin bench's TS column are a pair:
`V().out().values(age)` at 166.8 ms and the same with `.order()` at 507.2. So `.order()` adds ~340
ms to sort 1,000,000 numbers, and nothing had measured what sorting a million numbers costs.

All arms on the same 1,000,000 values, median of 7 after 2 warm-up:

```text
  copyOnly         2.57 ms    spread the array and nothing else
  rawSort         70.94       default (lexicographic) sort — a floor, not a peer
  rawSortNum      88.36       numeric comparator: THE floor for sorting 1M numbers
  rawSortTotal    87.05       the engine's NaN-total order — FREE against a plain compare
  engineCount      0.01       the count shortcut, reads no value
  engineValues   174.30       the pipeline WITHOUT order()
  engineOrdered  474.30       the row being explained
```

**`.order()` adds 300 ms where the sort itself is 88. ~212 ms is overhead around it.** And
`rawSortTotal` matters as much as the floor: the engine's total order (NaN last, NaN == NaN), which
byte-identity requires, costs nothing against `a - b`. So the overhead is NOT the ordering contract.

### Where it is, read off `sortByBys`

```text
  keyed = items.map(item => ({ item, keys: bys.map(...) }))   1M wrapper objects, each with an ARRAY
  keyed.some(k => k.keys.some(isElement))                      a full pass before sorting
  keyed.filter(k => !k.keys.some(k => k === NO_VALUE))         a second pass + a second 1M array
  live.sort((a, b) => { for (i<bys.length) …                   per comparison: a loop,
      compareTotal(a.keys[i], b.keys[i]) * (dirs[i] === 'desc' ? -1 : 1) … })
```

Per comparison that is a loop, two array indexes, a general `compareTotal`, **a string comparison
for the direction**, and a multiply — over ~20M comparisons for 1M items, which is where ~212 ms of
~10 ns each goes. The allocation side is 2M objects/arrays before a comparison even runs.

**The fix has a precedent in this repo**: `sortRowsByColumns` already notes "ONE sort key, which is
the common case, gets a comparator with NO LOOP and no per-call property reads", and records that
hoisting the spec out of the MULTI-key loop as well measured 1.00-1.02x and was reverted. So the
shape to build is the single-`by` specialization — keys in a parallel array rather than wrapper
objects, the direction resolved to a sign before the sort, no loop and no indexing in the
comparator — and NOT a general hoist.

Not attempted in this commit: it has to stay byte-identical on ties, NaN, mixed types, the
`NO_VALUE` filter and the `isElement` fault, and that is a full item with its own mutation run
rather than a tail-end change.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint`
0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0. No engine change — a probe and two
documents.

## 879 — the single-`by` `order()` specialization: **1.19x** on the row, 1.33x on the step, and a fault test that proved nothing until it used the right stream

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 878 decomposed the row and specified this; this builds it.

### What changed

`sortByBys` allocated a wrapper object AND a `keys` array per item, then compared through a loop
that indexed both arrays and re-tested `dirs[i] === 'desc'` — a STRING comparison — on every
comparison. With one `by` (the common case) it now carries a SCALAR key and picks one of two
loop-free comparators before the sort.

Equivalence was built in point by point, not checked afterwards:

- **Every key is evaluated before the element check**, so an `evalBy` that throws still wins over
  the element fault exactly as it did when `items.map` ran first. Fusing the two passes would have
  reordered those errors.
- **`desc` negates the same comparison** (`-compareTotal(a, b)`) rather than swapping arguments, so
  nothing rests on `compareTotal` being antisymmetric.
- **Still one object per item and still `Array.prototype.sort`**, so the sort is STABLE and ties
  keep arrival order — which is observable and compared against native by the byte-identity fuzzer.

Deliberately NOT a hoist of the multi-key loop as well: `sortRowsByColumns` records that exact
attempt measuring 1.00-1.02x and being reverted at the cost of three allocations per call.

### Measured: min of three order-alternated rounds, 1,000,000 values

```text
  arm                      spec ON   spec OFF
  engineOrdered             389.52     464.54   1.19x   DISJOINT (389-398 vs 464-476)
  CONTROL engineValues      170.69     172.61   flat    (no order step for the switch to reach)
  CONTROL rawSortNum         88.06      87.35   flat    (pure JS, unreachable)
```

The `order()` STEP is 291.9 ms -> 218.8, a **1.33x**, which is the honest figure for what changed;
1.19x is the whole row including the 170 ms pipeline underneath it. The `bench:gremlin` sweep agrees
and is the regression view: **507.2 -> 398.6 ms**, ts/native 6.5 -> 5.1, answers `same`.

### What is still there, and why I am not claiming it

The floor is 88.36 ms (sorting a million numbers with a numeric comparator), so ~131 ms of overhead
remains: three full passes over 1M wrapper objects (key evaluation, the element check, the
`NO_VALUE` filter) plus the final `map` back to items, and 1M allocations. Closing that means
sorting an index permutation with an explicit arrival tiebreak instead of relying on
`Array.prototype.sort`'s stability — which changes the stability argument rather than inheriting it,
so it is its own item with its own fuzzer run.

### My first element-fault test proved nothing, and the mutant said so

I asserted `V().order()` throws. It does — but from `checkStep` at PARSE time, which rejects a
pure-element `order()` before any of this code runs. So the runtime fault's mutant **survived**:
nothing in the test reached it. `sortByBys`' own comment names the shape that does — a stream whose
frontier is no longer "element" — so the test now uses `V().inject(1).order()`, a MIXED stream, and
the mutant dies. The pure-element case is kept as a separate assertion that says it is the parser's
job, so the two cannot be confused again.

```text
  single-by: route off (general path again)                    SURVIVED - see below
  single-by: desc ignored                                      CAUGHT
  single-by: desc reverses the ARRAY instead of the comparison  CAUGHT
  single-by: NO_VALUE items kept instead of filtered            CAUGHT
  single-by: element fault dropped                              CAUGHT (only via the mixed stream)
```

The desc mutant that reverses the ARRAY is the one worth having: it produces a correctly-sorted
result with the TIE GROUPS flipped, which is wrong in a way only an arrival-order assertion sees.
That is why the fixture gives every vertex a distinct `tag` recording its arrival position and the
assertions compare tag sequences rather than age sets.

**The route survivor is honest.** Turning the arm off falls back to the general path and returns
identical rows, and unlike items 866/867 there is no predicate worth extracting — the condition is
`bys.length === 1`. Its value is measured, not asserted, and the comment says so rather than
implying a test covers it.

## 880 — adding a step makes a Gremlin hop **1.9x FASTER**: `out()` and `out().id()` have no fused walk, and my own decomposition arm was invalid

**MEASUREMENT (TypeScript), no engine change.**

Item 879 left the 170 ms `values(age)` pipeline under the `order()` row unexplained, so I tried to
split it into "the hop" and "the values step". The attempt failed in a way worth recording, and the
failure is the finding.

### The arm I added was not a subset, and the numbers said so

```text
  engineScanOnly       7.37 ms     200,000 traversers, no hop
  engineScanValues    22.84        200,000 property reads
  engineValues       175.41      1,000,000 property values  (V().out(T).values(k))
  engineHop          331.45      1,000,000 landing vertices (V().out(T))
```

**`V().out(T)` costs 331 ms and `V().out(T).values(k)` costs 175** — adding a step makes the query
1.9x faster. So "engineValues − engineHop is what `values()` costs" is meaningless, and the negative
is what said so. The two are a subset in PIPELINE terms and not in COST terms, which is item 839's
rule arriving from a direction I had not seen it from: a ladder can be invalid because the
containment I assumed is about the wrong quantity.

The scan pair IS valid — same 200,000 inputs, one extra property read — and gives 77 ns a value for
`values()`. That is **not a new finding**: item 234 already records ~40-50 ns a vertex PER STEP for
"a traverser allocated per vertex to be filtered and discarded", and item 537 closed a filter chain
on it. Checked before pricing, not after.

### The real finding: `id()` costs what the bare hop costs, and `values()` costs half

```text
  V().out(T)              325.21 ms
  V().out(T).id()         322.60        the same, within noise
  V().out(T).values(age)  169.93        HALF
```

So it is not vertex materialization — `id()` also reduces each traverser to a scalar and is just as
slow. `values()` is the odd one out because it has a FUSED WALK and the others do not:
`executor/hop-values.ts` answers `V().out(T).values(k)` with one walk instead of the traverser
pipeline, and its own header prices that at 539 ns/row for the pipeline against 251 fused — 288 ns
of which is "pipeline machinery".

**So `V().out(T)` — give me the neighbours, about as common a traversal as exists — pays the full
pipeline, and so does `.id()`.** The machinery to fix it is already in place: that file walks with
`adjacentEdges`/`otherEndpoint`, the engine's OWN helpers, which is what makes the row order
identical by construction, and item 608 gave it a residual so a trailing step rides the shortcut
rather than defeating it.

**Not attempted here.** A new fused arm has to respect the same preconditions the existing one does
(path tracking, sack, and anything else carried on a traverser rather than derivable from the edge),
and "yield the far vertex" is a different output contract from "yield its property" — so it is its
own item with its own fuzzer run, not a tail-end change. Named, priced at ~1.9x on two shapes, and
left.

### What this tick is really worth

An invalid arm caught by its own sign, a known cost not re-derived (234/537), and a named target
with its machinery identified. The probe keeps all five arms, including the invalid pair, with the
comment saying why `engineHop` is not a floor for `engineValues` — a reader who removes it will
re-derive the same mistake.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint`
0; `bun run fmt` 0. No engine change — a probe and two documents.

## 881 — the fused walk now claims a BARE hop and `id()`: **2.23x** and **2.12x** — and the new bench rows show NATIVE is now the slow side

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Item 880 priced this and identified the machinery; this builds it.

### What changed

`hopValuesShortcut` gated on `steps.length < 3` and an exactly-`values(k)` third step, so the two
commonest hops in the language went down the traverser pipeline while the projected form rode a
fused walk. The gate is now `< 2`, and the third step may be absent (yield the far VERTEX) or `id()`
(yield its id). The walk itself is untouched — it still goes through the engine's own
`adjacentEdges`/`otherEndpoint`, which is what makes the row order identical by construction rather
than by a second derivation.

Measured, min of three order-alternated rounds, 1,000,000 edges:

```text
  shape                  fuse ON   fuse OFF
  V().out(T)              141.53     315.54   2.23x   DISJOINT (141-144 vs 315-327)
  V().out(T).id()         160.60     341.20   2.12x   DISJOINT (160-164 vs 341-348)
  CONTROL .values(age)    172.39     171.93   flat    — already fused, must not move
  CONTROL V() alone         7.08       7.08   flat    — no hop to fuse
```

`values(age)` is the control that matters: it was already on this path, so the refactor had to leave
it where it was.

**Any other third step still declines the whole shortcut**, deliberately. Treating an unrecognised
step as a residual over a bare hop would re-route a large family of plans nothing has measured —
that is a different change, and its mutant is in the list below so the decision cannot erode.

### Mutation: 6 of 6, after the fixture missed a whole branch

```text
  bare hop: not claimed (the old steps.length < 3 gate)          CAUGHT
  bare hop: yields the SOURCE vertex instead of the far one       CAUGHT
  id(): yields the vertex instead of its id                       CAUGHT
  id(): consumes 2 steps, so id() becomes a RESIDUAL              CAUGHT
  an unrecognised third step claimed as bare hop + residual       CAUGHT
  values(): the absent-key DROP is lost                           CAUGHT (only after a `both` test)
```

The last one is the lesson. `hopValuesShortcut` has TWO walks — a tuned one for a single named type
on `out`/`in`, and a general one through the helpers for `both` and for label SETS — and the
existing fixture only ever used `out('K')`. So a mutant deleting the absent-key drop from the
general walk survived. The file now has a `both('K')` case over a far vertex with no `age`, which
reaches it. **A function with two implementations of one contract needs a fixture that visits both**,
and a single-label fixture cannot.

### An existing test had pinned the old contract, and updating it was the point

`a plan below three steps is not claimed at all` asserted exactly what this item changes. I replaced
it with the claims that are now true — a bare hop IS claimed, `id()` IS claimed, any other third step
is NOT — plus the one it was really protecting (`V().values(age)` has no hop to fuse; `V(id)`
enumerates a given set). Deleting it would have removed the decline assertions with it.

### THE A/B SWITCH ITSELF CRASHED, and the shipped code is why it did not

Adding `&& process.env.LENKE_881 !== 'off'` to the `proj === undefined` branch made `fuse=off` throw
a TypeError: with that branch skipped, control fell to `proj.kind === 'id'` on an undefined `proj`.
The shipped ordering is safe precisely because the undefined check comes first — the switch broke
the invariant it was measuring. Re-expressed as an early return INSIDE the branch, the arm measures
cleanly. An instrumented arm has to preserve the control flow it is instrumenting.

### The new bench rows, and what they immediately showed

The corpus had no bare-hop row — the nearest was `V().out().count()`, which a shortcut answers — so
this gap sat next to rows that looked fine. Added, and item 877's lesson applies twice now. The
first sweep with them in:

```text
  V().out() [bare]       ts 185.4   native 329.61   ratio 0.6   same
  V().out().id()         ts 203.5   native  72.81         2.8   same
  V().out().values(age)  ts 169.3   native  30.71         5.5   same
```

**Native is now the SLOW side on the bare hop** — 329.61 against TS's 185.4 — and native's own bare
hop is 4.5x its `id()` (329.61 against 72.81), the same inversion this item just fixed in TS. That
is item 876's lens pointing at the engine, and it is the next target rather than a remark: the sweep
column that matters is the absolute one, not the ratio.

(The sweep's TS figures run above the isolated ones — 185.4 against 141.53 — which is the in-sweep
inflation the bench notes already record. The isolated A/B is the measurement; the sweep is the
regression view.)

## 882 — native's "slow" bare hop RETRACTED: it is not FFI, it is an owned element per row, and that loop was already worked twice

**MEASUREMENT (Rust), a probe added; no engine change.** Item 881's new bench rows showed
`V().out('KNOWS')` at native 329.61 ms against TS's 185.4 and I named it the next target. It is not
one, and this is the evidence.

### First: it is not the FFI boundary

The bench runs native through `createFfiEngineBackend`, so 1,000,000 FULL ELEMENTS crossing that
boundary against 1,000,000 id strings could have been the whole gap. Run IN PROCESS through
`exec::try_run`, with no serialization at all:

```text
  G V().out() [bare]            266.980 ms   1,000,000 rows
  G V().out().id()               20.639       1,000,000
  G V().out().values(age)         4.954       1,000,000
  G V() [bare]                   15.805         200,000
  G V().out().count()             0.000               1
  Q MATCH ()-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN b AS x      266.745  1,000,000
  Q MATCH ()-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN b.age AS x    5.817  1,000,000
```

**267 ms in process, so the cost is the engine.** And the GQL spelling agrees to within 0.1%, which
is the cross-front-end check this repo asks for.

### What it actually is: 46x between returning an ELEMENT and returning a property

The same 1,000,000 rows cost 266.98 ms as elements and 4.95 as a property — 54x — because
`render_nodes` builds an OWNED element value per row: the external id, a sorted labels list, and a
map of every present property. That is the contract for returning an element, not an avoidable step.

**And that loop has already been worked twice.** Its own comments cite the items: 391 hoisted the
property-key `Value`s out of the per-cell path (+24 ns per property once a key stops being inline),
and **828** rewrote it COLUMN-MAJOR after 806's ladder measured `element p` going 169.8 ns/row at
K=0 to 1785.7 at K=200. Then **829** grepped the shape elsewhere and REFUTED a further hoist at
1.00-1.04x, recording that `render_edges` cannot take the same reorder at all. At K=1 this fixture's
267 ns/row sits where that ladder says it should.

### So the 881 comparison was not like-for-like, and the bench row now says so

TS reads 185.4 ms because it hands back REFERENCES to vertices already in its graph; native reads
267 because it materializes owned values. Those are different amounts of work for the same query
text, so the ts/native ratio on that row (~0.6) is a category difference and not a verdict. The row
stays — it is a real regression guard for the TS column, which is what item 881 added it for — but
it now carries a warning saying exactly that, because a future reader scanning for ratios below 1.0
would otherwise re-derive this whole item.

**Retracted.** Second retraction this session (item 878 was the first), and both came from pricing a
target I had named a tick earlier. Naming one is cheap; the check is what makes it a decision.
