--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0. No engine
change — a probe, a bench comment and two documents. Probe run under `timeout 900 systemd-run --user
--scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, indexed by question in `examples/README.md`.

## 883 — the TS parser is **4.5x** native's and its planner **12.6x**, measured from both sides; and the exported `parse()` bypasses the cache

**MEASUREMENT (both engines), two probes added; no engine change.** A fresh area — the parser and
planner rather than the executor — reached by running `bun run bench:usage`, the serving counterpart
this session had not touched.

### The row that pointed at it, and the note that explained it away

```text
  write: append node           ts(-) 130.6k ops/s   engine(-) 459.4k
  write: append node [params]  ts(-) 579.1k         engine(-) 446.6k
```

TS is 4.4x apart on two spellings of one write where native is FLAT. The bench's own comment says
why — the unparameterized row interpolates `i`, so every call is a new text and misses the parse+plan
cache (item 662) — so that part is known and arguably correct: a changing text SHOULD miss.

**The question it leaves is the one worth asking.** Per operation, TS is 7.66 us on a miss and 1.73
on a hit; native is 2.18-2.24 either way. So TS with a HIT is faster than native, and TS's MISS costs
~5.9 us more — and dynamically-built query text is ordinary application code, not a benchmark
artifact.

### Decomposed, same statement, both engines

```text
                    TS        native     ratio
  textOnly        0.022      0.046        —      (the control: formatting is not the cost)
  parse           2.962      0.653       4.5x
  parse + plan    3.979      0.734       5.4x
  full HIT        2.269        —                 cached parse+plan AND execute
  full MISS       8.935        —
```

Two targets, and they are different shapes. **The TS parser is 4.5x native's** (2.962 against 0.653
for a ~50-character `INSERT`, i.e. ~59 ns a character), which is the bigger ABSOLUTE number. **The TS
planner adds ~1.02 us against native's 0.081 — 12.6x**, which is the bigger RATIO on a smaller base.

A cached TS query (2.269 us, parse + plan + execute) costs less than ONE raw TS parse (2.962). The
cache is doing a great deal of work, which is exactly why the miss hurts.

### The exported `parse()` does not consult the cache, and a misnamed arm found it

I wrote an arm called `parseCached` — one fixed text, expecting the cache to serve it — and it
measured 2.969 against the fresh-text arm's 3.486. Nearly identical, so the cache was not involved:
the exported `parse()` is the raw parser and the memoization lives inside `query()`. The arm is
renamed `parseOneText` and carries that correction, because a reader comparing a "cached" arm
against a "miss" arm would conclude the cache is worth 15% when it is worth more than a whole parse.

Worth stating as a rule: **an arm named for the mechanism it is supposed to exercise is a claim, and
the measurement is what checks it.** The 0.5 us between those two arms is one text's worth of
`format!` plus allocator noise, not a cache.

### Not attempted here

Both targets are inside a parser and a planner, and "the parser is slow" is not yet a diagnosis —
the next step is to find where in it, which wants its own tick and its own instrument. Named, priced
from both sides, and left. The pair of probes is the thing that makes a future number meaningful: a
TS parse figure alone cannot say whether 3 us is a lot.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0. No engine
change — two probes and two documents, both indexed by question.

## 884 — the closure hypothesis REFUTED: the TS parser is ~3x native's at EVERY size, so the gap is per-character work

**MEASUREMENT (both engines), no engine change.** Item 883 priced the TS parser at 4.5x native's and
said "find where inside it". This localises it, and the first answer was wrong.

### The hypothesis, and why it looked good

`parse()` declares its helpers as closures in its own body, and they are allocated on EVERY call.
Counted: **96 closures at depth 1**, before a single token is consumed, to parse a statement of
perhaps twenty tokens. At ~10-20 ns each that is 1-2 us of the 2.96 — a tidy explanation.

### The test that killed it

If fixed setup dominates, parse cost is nearly FLAT in input size. Three sizes, fresh text each call
so no cache can serve any of them:

```text
  statement          chars    TS us/op    native us/op
  tiny                  24       1.886           0.638
  the INSERT            47       3.515           0.678
  big (hop + filter)   158      10.487           3.634
```

**It scales.** Fitting the two ends:

```text
                 fixed      marginal        ratio TS/native
  TS            ~0.35 us    64.2 ns/char    —
  native        ~0.10       22.4            —
  at  24 chars                              3.0x
  at 158 chars                              2.9x
```

So the TS parser is **~3x native's at every size**, the gap is proportional, and the fixed term —
which is where the 96 closures live — is only ~0.35 us, at most 10% of a 3.5 us parse. Removing
every closure could not buy more than that. **Hypothesis refuted, and by a measurement that cost one
probe arm rather than a refactor.**

### What the target actually is

~64 ns a character, against native's 22.4. That is roughly 200 CPU cycles per character of query
text, for work that is tokenizing plus a recursive-descent parse. The shape of a fix is a tokenizer
question (what is allocated per token, and whether the scan is a charCode loop or something costlier)
rather than a parser-structure question — which is a different investigation from the one I started,
and the reason to record this rather than carry on guessing.

### Why three sizes and not two

Item 883's figure was a single point, and a single point cannot distinguish "3x slower per character"
from "a large fixed setup". Those have opposite fixes — one is the tokenizer, the other is the 96
closures — so the slope is what makes the next tick's work well-aimed. Both probes now take three
sizes and print the character counts next to the times.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
fmt:check` 0. No engine change — two probe arms and two documents.

## Item 885 — the TS tokenizer allocated two objects and a string PER CHARACTER: 1.46x

Item 884 localised the TS parser's gap to ~64 ns a character and said the shape of the fix was a
tokenizer question. It was, and the per-character work was visible by reading the loop.

### Three costs, all inside the per-character `while`

`tokenize` is one long scan over source characters. Three things happened on every iteration,
regardless of what the character was:

- `const twoChar: Record<string, TokenType> = { … }` — an **8-key object literal**, allocated fresh
  per character.
- `const single: Record<string, TokenType> = { … }` — a **20-key object literal**, likewise.
- `const two = src.slice(i, i + 2)` — a **2-character string**, allocated per character, consumed
  only by the comment openers and the two-char table.

Plus `src.slice(i, i + 3) === '<->'` — a third string, built for every character, to compare against
one spelling that can only begin with `<`.

So tokenizing an N-character query allocated roughly 2N objects and 2N short strings, for tables
that are pure data with no capture. Both tables hoist to module scope unchanged.

### The lookahead is now gated

The 2- and 3-character slices only matter when the current character can BEGIN a multi-character
token. That is six characters — `/ - < > ~ |` — covering the three comment openers (`//`, `--`,
`/*`), all eight `TWO_CHAR` keys, and `<->`:

```ts
const startsMulti = (c: string): boolean =>
  c === '/' || c === '-' || c === '<' || c === '>' || c === '~' || c === '|';
```

Letters, digits and whitespace are most of a query, and none of them allocate a lookahead now.

### Measured: min of three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, 20k ops

| arm                  | chars | pre    | post  | ratio     |
| -------------------- | ----- | ------ | ----- | --------- |
| `parseTiny`          | 24    | 1.781  | 1.546 | 1.15x     |
| `parseOnly`          | 47    | 3.393  | 2.433 | **1.39x** |
| `parseBig`           | 158   | 10.547 | 7.230 | **1.46x** |
| `textOnly` (control) | —     | 0.023  | 0.023 | flat      |

**The win grows with input size**, which is the signature a per-character fix should have — and the
reason item 884's slope was worth measuring before changing anything. The control never calls
`parse()` and does not move.

Refitting the slope: **64.2 → 42.4 ns/char** marginal, ~0.53 us fixed. The gap to native's 22.4
ns/char closes from 2.9x to **1.9x**. The remaining ~20 ns a character is still open.

### Each arm asserted it was the code it claimed, two ways

Identifiers are minified in the built bundle, so a source grep alone cannot tell whether the BUILD
picked the change up — and the probe imports from `dist`. So each arm checked both: the source's
`TWO_CHAR` count (pre 0, post 4), and the bundle's sha256, which had to **differ between the arms
and match within one**. It did (`dec2e0a43289` / `ee70b285c19f`).

### The by-eye claim got a test, and the test got mutated

"`startsMulti` covers every table key's first character" is true by inspection and is exactly the
kind of claim that rots when someone adds a table entry. A hole in it is not an error — it is a
silently wrong token stream: `a <> b` tokenizes as `a < > b`, and a missing `/` turns a `//` comment
into a `slash` token followed by the comment body parsed as real tokens.

`packages/gql/src/lexer-multichar-tokens.test.ts` enumerates all eight `TWO_CHAR` spellings, `<->`,
the three comment openers, and each gated character standing alone. Mutation, restoring BEFORE each
mutant and reading the verdict from the EXIT CODE after proving a result line on either stream:

```
baseline rc=0 13 pass
CAUGHT rc=1 2 fail drop [c === '/' || ]
CAUGHT rc=1 2 fail drop [c === '-' || ]
CAUGHT rc=1 4 fail drop [c === '<' || ]
CAUGHT rc=1 1 fail drop [c === '>' || ]
CAUGHT rc=1 1 fail drop [c === '~' || ]
CAUGHT rc=1 1 fail drop [|| c === '|']
```

Six for six, 1-4 failures each, tree restored byte-identical afterwards.

### A lint trap worth naming

`tokenize` carries `// eslint-disable-next-line complexity, max-statements`. My first edit inserted
the table block BETWEEN that comment and the function, so the suppression applied to a `const` and
`tokenize` went un-suppressed — `bun run lint` failed with a complexity of 60 against a max of 35,
which reads like the change caused it. **`-next-line` suppressions are positional**; inserting
anything above a function moves its suppression off it.

### Verification

`bun test packages/gql` 2679 pass; gremlin 826, core 370, sync 176, all 0 fail. All seven
byte-identity fuzzers pass at random seeds. A whole-repo `bun test` shows 68 failures in the
documented run-many timing families (`@lenke/sync`, the React hooks, Playwright files swept up by
the runner); every one of them passes isolated, and none touches the lexer.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `bun run typecheck` 0;
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 886 — the tokenizer's two biggest character paths: 1.22x and 1.18x

Item 885 took the TS parser from 64.2 to 42.4 ns a character by removing the allocations that ran
for EVERY character, and left ~20 ns over native's 22.4 sitting inside the individual scanners. The
scanners are not equal, so the first move was to find out which one carries the characters.

### Price the paths before changing one

`packages/native/lexer-census-probe.ts` censuses the characters of the real fixture texts by the
scanner that consumes them. It is a static count, not a timing — the question is only which target
is worth having.

| text     | chars | ident     | strlit    | ws    | punct | digit | multi | comment |
| -------- | ----- | --------- | --------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ------- |
| tiny     | 25    | 52.0%     | 0.0%      | 16.0% | 8.0%  | 0.0%  | 0.0%  | 24.0%   |
| insert   | 50    | 46.0%     | 12.0%     | 14.0% | 20.0% | 8.0%  | 0.0%  | 0.0%    |
| big      | 160   | **60.0%** | 3.1%      | 18.1% | 11.9% | 3.1%  | 3.8%  | 0.0%    |
| strheavy | 155   | 32.9%     | **49.7%** | 11.0% | 6.5%  | 0.0%  | 0.0%  | 0.0%    |

Every row re-sums to its own length (the probe throws otherwise), so no class is dropped or
double-counted. Two answers:

- **Identifier characters are the biggest path in every text, 46-60%.** That loop carries more
  characters than anything else in the tokenizer.
- **String-literal characters are FIXTURE-DEPENDENT**: 3-12% of the arms items 884/885 measured, but
  **49.7% of ordinary string-heavy application query text**. Measuring only the existing arms would
  have priced that path at near zero, and it is the one path that was doing per-character string
  concatenation.

### The two changes

**Identifier and parameter scanning moved to character codes.** The inner loop called
`isIdentPart(src[i])`, which takes a one-character STRING — so `src[i]` materialized a
single-character string per character and then did up to four string range comparisons.
`isIdentPartCode(src.charCodeAt(i))` compares integers and allocates nothing. `isIdentStart` and
`isDigit` keep their string form: they are called once per TOKEN on a character the dispatch already
holds, not once per character.

**A string literal with no escape in it is now one slice.** The old loop did `str += src[i]` per
character, so a 20-character literal did 20 concatenations and built 20 single-character strings.
Now the scan runs to the first quote-or-backslash and takes the span in one `slice`; only a literal
that actually contains an escape enters the per-character path, and only from the first backslash
onwards.

### Measured: min of three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, 20k ops

| arm                  | ident% | str% | pre   | post  | ratio     |
| -------------------- | ------ | ---- | ----- | ----- | --------- |
| `parseTiny`          | 52     | 0    | 1.578 | 1.415 | 1.12x     |
| `parseOnly`          | 46     | 12   | 2.432 | 2.196 | 1.11x     |
| `parseBig`           | 60     | 3.1  | 7.337 | 6.232 | **1.18x** |
| `parseStrHeavy`      | 33     | 49.7 | 4.071 | 3.332 | **1.22x** |
| `textOnly` (control) | —      | —    | 0.022 | 0.022 | 1.00x     |

**The two arms move for different reasons, which is what makes this two findings rather than one.**
`parseStrHeavy` has the LEAST identifier share and gains the MOST — that is the string change.
`parseBig` is 60% identifier characters and 3.1% string, so its 1.18x is the scanner. The control
never calls `parse()` and does not move.

Slope refits **42.4 → 35.9 ns/char**. Cumulatively since 884: **64.2 → 35.9**, with `parseBig` down
10.547 → 6.232, **1.69x**. The gap to native's 22.4 ns/char is now **1.6x**, from 2.9x.

The `pre` arm's bundle hash (`ee70b285c19f`) is byte-identical to item 885's `post` hash from that
A/B — an independent confirmation that this item's baseline really is the shipped code and not some
other build.

### Mutation: 5 of 5, and two of them by the memory cap

| mutant                                      | verdict                |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `k === CC_UNDERSCORE` → `k === CC_0`        | CAUGHT rc=137 (OOM)    |
| drop the digit range from `isIdentPartCode` | CAUGHT rc=1, 2 fail    |
| fast span ignores the backslash             | CAUGHT rc=1, 4 fail    |
| `src.slice(bodyStart, i)` → `''`            | CAUGHT rc=1, 4 fail    |
| ident scan reads `charCodeAt(i + 1)`        | CAUGHT rc=-9 (SIGKILL) |

**Two of these do not fail a test — they fail to terminate**, which is the case CLAUDE.md names: a
loop condition is where an off-by-one stops being a wrong answer. Dropping `_` from the identifier
class means the scanner matches ZERO characters at a leading `_`, `i` never advances, and the outer
`while` re-enters at the same index forever, pushing a token per iteration until the cgroup kills
it. The cap is what turned that into a one-second verdict.

### A kill arrives as a NEGATIVE signal when you invoke it through a process API

The last mutant came back as **rc=-9, not 137**. Run under a shell, a cgroup OOM kill surfaces as
exit 137; run through `subprocess.run` (no shell), the same kill surfaces as the negative signal
number. A verdict check that looks only for `124` and `137` classifies it as `DID-NOT-RUN` — a
mutant the cap actually caught, reported as a harness failure. This is the same shape as the
stdout-vs-stderr trap at items 767/772-773: **the verdict check has to match how the runner was
invoked.** Treat a negative return as the signal class it is.

### Verification

`bun test packages/gql` 2697 pass; gremlin 826, core 370, all 0 fail. All seven byte-identity
fuzzers pass at random seeds.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint`
0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 887 — the denominator was wrong: parse cost tracks TOKENS, not characters

MEASUREMENT (both engines), one probe added and one extended; no engine change. Items 884, 885 and
886 all reasoned in **nanoseconds per character**, and 886 left the remaining gap explicitly
unpriced. Two questions turned out to be open, and the second corrects the unit the previous three
items used.

### First: the tokenizer is not most of the parser

Items 885 and 886 both changed the tokenizer, on the reasoning that per-character cost must live in
a per-character loop. Both won — but neither measured how much of the total the tokenizer IS, so
"keep going in the tokenizer" had been an assumption for two ticks. `lexer-split-probe.ts` splits
it (`parseFull` CONTAINS `tokenizeOnly`, so the descent's share is the DIFFERENCE — a pipeline
prefix is not a cost floor, item 880):

| shape    | chars | tokens | tokenize | descent | tokenize share |
| -------- | ----- | ------ | -------- | ------- | -------------- |
| tiny     | 24    | 7      | 0.390    | 1.009   | 27.9%          |
| insert   | 47    | 19     | 0.976    | 1.260   | 43.7%          |
| big      | 158   | 60     | 3.440    | 2.930   | **54.0%**      |
| strheavy | 156   | 31     | 1.476    | 1.791   | 45.2%          |

So the tokenizer is between a quarter and a half, and **the recursive descent is the larger half on
three of the four shapes.** 885 and 886 were worth doing and they were not aimed at the whole cost.

### Second, and the reason to write this up: ns/char is the wrong denominator

`strheavy` is the same LENGTH as `big` and costs half as much per character. That is not noise — it
is the unit being wrong. `big` is 158 characters in 60 tokens; `strheavy` is 156 characters in 31,
because most of its characters sit inside string literals, which item 886 made nearly free (one
slice) while every identifier and punctuation character still becomes a TOKEN.

**The length-matched pair is the controlled comparison**, and both engines agree:

| engine | shape    | chars | tokens | ns/char | ns/token  |
| ------ | -------- | ----- | ------ | ------- | --------- |
| TS     | big      | 158   | 60     | 40.3    | 106.2     |
| TS     | strheavy | 156   | 31     | 20.9    | **105.4** |
| native | big      | 158   | 60     | 23.1    | 60.8      |
| native | strheavy | 156   | 31     | 13.4    | **67.3**  |

At matched length, `ns/char` spans **1.93x in TS and 1.72x in native**, while `ns/token` is flat to
**1.01x and 1.11x**. The native half needed a new arm to check this at all — `parseplan_883` had
only `tiny` and `big`, which vary length and token count TOGETHER and therefore cannot separate the
two. That is why the tiny/big pair looked like a clean per-character slope at item 884.

**What this does and does not retract.** It does NOT touch items 885 or 886: those were pre-vs-post
A/Bs on the same fixtures, where the denominator cancels, and their ratios stand. What it retracts
is the _cross-shape model_ — 884's "64.2 ns/char marginal with ~0.35 us fixed", and the 42.4 and
35.9 restatements of it. That fit was regressing cost on the wrong x, and it only looked clean
because the two fixtures it was fitted to happened to have similar token density. Restated in the
unit that holds: **TS is ~106 ns/token against native's ~61, 1.75x**, where before it read 1.6x per
character.

The denominator is a free choice and it changed the apparent target by a factor of nearly two
between shapes. One length-matched pair settled it, and neither probe had one until now.

### Where that leaves the target

~45 ns/token, split roughly half tokenizer and half descent on a token-dense statement. Both halves
are now priced, so the next change can be aimed rather than assumed. Candidates inside the
tokenizer are what remains per TOKEN rather than per character — `toLowerCase()` on every
identifier for the keyword lookup, and the token objects themselves (4 fields, `num` usually
`undefined`). The descent is unexamined.

--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0. No engine change: one probe added, one example extended, two
documents.

## Item 888 — keywords resolve without normalizing every identifier: 1.08-1.14x

Item 887 priced the parser's two halves and named two remaining per-TOKEN candidates inside the
tokenizer. This prices both with an ablation, kills one of them on the numbers, and ships the other.

### A ceiling ablation, before writing anything correct

Both candidates are awkward to implement correctly, so both were first measured as deliberately
WRONG code — not candidate implementations, but upper bounds on what any correct version could buy.

- `noLower` — `text.toLowerCase()` becomes `text`. Wrong: lowercase-spelled keywords stop being
  recognized. Bounds removing the per-identifier normalization.
- `flatToken` — `push` stops building an object and pushes one shared constant. Very wrong: every
  token becomes the same token. Bounds what the token allocation costs.

Measured on a tokenize-only instrument (min of three alternated rounds, 20k ops):

| arm         | big   | strheavy | ceiling on the tokenizer |
| ----------- | ----- | -------- | ------------------------ |
| base        | 3.488 | 1.434    | —                        |
| `noLower`   | 2.810 | 1.140    | **1.24x / 1.26x**        |
| `flatToken` | 3.255 | 1.390    | 1.07x / 1.03x            |

**The token object is dead on these numbers.** At most 1.03-1.07x of a half of parse, for a change
that would make the token shape polymorphic — the one thing this codebase has repeatedly measured as
a loss. Rejected without a correct implementation being written, which is the point of ablating
first. (Recorded next to `push` in `lexer.ts`.)

### The correct version of the one that survived

Proving a word IS a keyword is a set lookup; proving it is NOT requires normalizing it, which is why
`toLowerCase()` ran on EVERY identifier — 33 of the 60 tokens in the `big` statement. Two
observations make it avoidable:

- An identifier with **no uppercase letter already IS its own lowercasing**, so `KEYWORDS.has(text)`
  is the complete answer.
- One written in **ALL CAPS** — the conventional keyword spelling — is settled by a map keyed on the
  uppercase form.

Only a MIXED-case word (`MaTcH`, `userName`) normalizes. Detecting "contains an uppercase letter"
costs one `&` per character and no branch, because **within the identifier class the test is exact**:
ASCII bit 0x20 is clear for `A`-`Z` and set for `a`-`z`, `0`-`9` and `_`, and the class is only
`[A-Za-z0-9_]`. ANDing every code together and testing that one bit answers it. That is not a general
case test and the code says so.

### Measured end to end: min of three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds

| arm                  | pre   | post  | ratio     |
| -------------------- | ----- | ----- | --------- |
| `parseTiny`          | 1.514 | 1.329 | 1.14x     |
| `parseOnly`          | 2.279 | 2.108 | 1.08x     |
| `parseBig`           | 6.301 | 5.712 | **1.10x** |
| `parseStrHeavy`      | 3.334 | 2.999 | **1.11x** |
| `textOnly` (control) | 0.022 | 0.022 | 1.00x     |

The `pre` arm's bundle hash (`23a5a59f6e60`) is byte-identical to item 886's `post` hash, confirming
the baseline is the shipped code.

On the tokenizer's own instrument: 3.488 → 3.162 (big) and 1.434 → 1.254 (strheavy), so **about half
the ablation's ceiling was captured.** The residual is the per-character `&`, a Map lookup where
there used to be a Set lookup, and the mixed-case fallback. Those two instruments are different
compilations (item 887) so their figures are not mixed — the capture fraction is computed within the
tokenize-only instrument alone.

### The route needed its own test, and this is the proof

All three lookup branches return the same answer. That makes the change a ROUTE choice, and a
mutant that forces one branch for everything is **answer-equivalent** — it is only slower. So the
route got its own assertion: a test that stubs `String.prototype.toLowerCase`, counts the calls, and
asserts **zero** for an all-lowercase statement, **zero** for a conventional UPPERCASE one, and
**exactly two** for a statement containing one mixed-case keyword and one mixed-case identifier.

Mutation, restoring before each mutant, verdict from the exit code:

| mutant                                             | verdict                                                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| invert the case test                               | CAUGHT rc=1, 6 fail                                                                               |
| lowercase branch calls everything a keyword        | CAUGHT rc=1, 1 fail                                                                               |
| stop accumulating the case bit                     | CAUGHT rc=1, 5 fail                                                                               |
| wrong case bit (`0x20` → `0x40`)                   | CAUGHT rc=1, 5 fail                                                                               |
| drop the mixed-case fallback                       | CAUGHT rc=1, 4 fail                                                                               |
| **force the uppercase branch (answer-equivalent)** | correctness tests only: **SURVIVED (23 pass)**; with the route assertion: **CAUGHT rc=1, 3 fail** |

The last row is the whole argument for the rule, run rather than asserted: that mutant is invisible
to all 23 correctness tests and only the route assertion holds it.

### One self-inflicted trap worth recording

The first attempt at the route test captured the original `toLowerCase` as an arrow that
dereferenced `String.prototype.toLowerCase` at CALL time — which by then is the stub it installed,
so it recursed forever and the test run had to be killed. **Capture the function value eagerly; a
lazy reference to the thing you are replacing is a loop.** It was a linter suggestion
(`unbound-method`) taken too literally; the honest fix is a narrow disable with a reason.

### Verification

`bun test packages/gql` 2706 pass; gremlin 826, core 370, all 0 fail. All seven byte-identity
fuzzers pass at random seeds.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint`
0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 889 — the same pattern in the parser is NOT worth fixing: refuted at 1.015x

Item 888 removed `toLowerCase()` from the lexer's keyword lookup for 1.08-1.14x. The pattern repeats
all over the parser, so the obvious next move was to do it again there. It is not worth doing, and
this is the evidence — a refutation that cost one probe instead of a refactor.

### The pattern really does repeat

`peek().value.toLowerCase() === word` appears in several descent predicates, and `isReserved` is
`RESERVED.has(word.toLowerCase())`. Attributing the calls one `big` parse makes, with a stub that
records its caller:

| calls  | site                                                                    |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **15** | `isReserved` (`lexer.ts`)                                               |
| 7      | `parser.ts:2177`                                                        |
| 7      | `parser.ts:2318`                                                        |
| 7      | `parser.ts:512` (`valueSubqueryAhead`)                                  |
| 3      | `tokenize` (the mixed/all-caps non-keyword identifiers 888 left paying) |
| 1      | `parser.ts:2553`                                                        |
| **40** | total, **37 of them in the descent**                                    |

40 calls, against the 33 the lexer was making before 888. On call count alone this looks like the
same target.

### The ceiling says the cost does not repeat

Both arms install a stub of the same shape and the same call cost — `through` calls the original,
`identity` returns the receiver — so the stub's overhead cancels and the only difference is whether
the lowercasing work happens. `identity` is deliberately wrong: every case-insensitive comparison
becomes case-sensitive. A **dose-response ladder** rather than one arm, because an effect this small
is only believable if it scales with the dose:

| shape              | calls | through | identity | ceiling    |
| ------------------ | ----- | ------- | -------- | ---------- |
| zero (the control) | 0     | 0.893   | 0.941    | **0.949x** |
| nine               | 9     | 1.835   | 1.855    | 0.990x     |
| forty              | 40    | 5.783   | 5.697    | 1.015x     |

The direction is monotonic in the dose, which is the only encouraging thing about it. **The
zero-call control swings 5.1% while the 40-call target moves 1.5%** — the control moving MORE than
the target is the giveaway this repo already records. And a first screening run of the same question
read 1.070x, disagreeing with 1.015x by 5.5 points. So the noise floor on this instrument is ≥5% and
the effect sits inside it.

**Refuted.** Item 888 captured about half its own ceiling; half of something under 1.5% is not worth
a change to five call sites in a recursive-descent parser. Recorded next to `isReserved`, which is
where the biggest share would have been removed.

### Two instrument errors caught by the instrument

**The first control was not one.** The screening run labelled a 9-call shape as making zero calls.
The probe PRINTS its call counts, which is the only reason that was visible; the final version has a
genuine zero-call shape (`RETURN 1` normalizes nothing) found by testing candidates rather than
assuming. A control asserted rather than measured is not a control.

**A micro-benchmark of `toLowerCase` itself was invalid.** Trying to explain why the lexer's calls
cost ~20.5 ns each and the parser's ~9.8, I timed `'score'.toLowerCase()` against
`'SCORE'.toLowerCase()` in a loop: every variant came back at 0.27-0.37 ns, i.e. the loop was
constant-folded away — the trap this repo already records for libm constants. **The mechanism behind
that difference is therefore still unexplained, and this item does not claim one.**

### Verification

No engine change: one probe added, one rejection comment, two documents. `bun run typecheck` 0;
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0 — each its own command
with its exit code read UNPIPED.

## Item 890 — the index-permutation sort is refuted, and item 879's ATTRIBUTION with it

Item 879 specialized `order()`'s single-`by` comparator for 1.19x, priced the remaining ~131 ms
above the 88 ms sort floor, and attributed it to the scaffolding: one `{item, key}` object per item,
an element-check pass, a `filter` pass allocating a second array, and a `map` pass allocating a
third. It named the fix — sort an index permutation instead — and said it needed its own item
because it rests on a different stability argument. This is that item. The fix does not work.

### What was built

Keys in one flat array, the sort permuting indexes into it, two passes instead of four, no wrapper
objects at all. Two passes rather than one deliberately: the phase order is observable, because an
`evalBy` that throws must win over the element fault, exactly as it did when `items.map` ran to
completion before the check loop. Fusing them would let an element at index 3 fault before index 4's
key is evaluated, changing which error a caller sees.

A second variant (`post2`) drops the explicit arrival tiebreak and inherits arrival order from the
sort's stability — which ES2019 _requires_ of `Array.prototype.sort`, so it is a spec guarantee and
not an implementation detail, and it is what the pre-890 code already relied on.

### Measured: min of three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, 200k vertices x degree 5

| arm                                    | pre    | post   | post2  | post/pre  |
| -------------------------------------- | ------ | ------ | ------ | --------- |
| `engineOrdered` (the target)           | 387.30 | 373.30 | 370.67 | 1.04x     |
| `engineValues` (control, no `order()`) | 171.61 | 170.63 | 173.80 | 1.01x     |
| `rawSortNum` (the floor, unreachable)  | 88.47  | 87.98  | 87.57  | 1.01x     |
| **`engineHop` (control, unreachable)** | 144.80 | 139.82 | 144.00 | **1.04x** |

**The target moved 1.04x and an unreachable control moved 1.04x in the same rounds.** Nothing was
measured. The tiebreak question is moot too: `post` and `post2` are indistinguishable, so the design
choice that made this "its own item" has no cost either way.

Reverted. The tree is byte-identical to before the attempt.

### The useful part is the refuted attribution

`engineOrdered - engineValues` is ~216 ms and `rawSortNum` is ~88, so the residual above the floor is
~127 ms — item 879's ~131 ms, reproduced. Removing the wrapper objects and two of the four passes
recovers **~14 ms of it, about 11%**. So 879's attribution was wrong: the allocations and the passes
are a tenth of the residual, not the whole of it.

That makes the remaining ~89% the open question, and it has candidates nobody has priced:

- `evalBy(by, project(items[i]), …)` — 1M `evalBy` calls through a `switch`, plus 1M `project`
  closure calls, 2M in total.
- `[...stream]` — materializing 1,000,000 traversers into an array before anything is sorted.
- `compareTotal` over two `unknown` values, ~20M times. Note item 878 measured `rawSortTotal` (the
  same comparator over a raw number array) at 87.05, i.e. the same as a numeric comparator — so the
  comparator is cheap on monomorphic numbers and whatever it costs here is about how it is REACHED,
  not the function.

Recorded next to the code in `aggregation.ts` and in `order-cost-probe.ts`, both saying do not
re-attempt the rewrite and price those three first.

### Mutation, including two deliberate survivors

Before the measurement killed it, the change was mutation-tested. Worth keeping because the survivor
analysis is about the suite, not the change:

| mutant                                         | verdict                            |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| negate the arrival tiebreak under `desc`       | CAUGHT rc=1, 1 fail                |
| swap the asc key comparison                    | CAUGHT rc=1, 22 fail               |
| drop the `NO_VALUE` filter                     | CAUGHT rc=1, 1 fail                |
| drop the element check                         | CAUGHT rc=1, 1 fail                |
| ignore the permutation when materializing      | CAUGHT rc=1, 26 fail               |
| drop the explicit tiebreak (answer-equivalent) | SURVIVED, as predicted             |
| fuse the element check into pass 1             | SURVIVED, as predicted — see below |

The `desc` tiebreak mutant being caught by exactly one test is item 879's arrival-order assertion
earning itself: it returns a correctly-sorted result with tie groups flipped, which only a tag-
sequence comparison can see.

**A mutant that changes two things measures neither.** The fusion mutant first came back CAUGHT, and
it was a false catch: my mutant fused the passes AND threw with a different message, and the
element-fault test matches on message text. Re-run with the real message preserved, it SURVIVES — so
the two-pass phase order is guarded by construction and reasoning only, not by any test. Said plainly
rather than left implied.

### Verification

`bun test packages/gremlin` 826 pass, 0 fail, on the reverted tree. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run
lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0 — each its own command with its exit code read
UNPIPED.

## Item 891 — the `order()` residual DECOMPOSED, and closed: 86% of it is the sort's floor plus the step existing

Item 878 priced this row, item 879 took 1.19x off it, item 890 failed to take the rest and refuted
879's attribution. Three items have now attacked a residual nobody had decomposed. This decomposes
it, and the answer is that the row is at its floor.

### A stage-removal ladder

Four arms, each deleting one stage, every ablated arm deliberately WRONG and existing only to
subtract a cost:

- `base` — as shipped.
- `noSort` — `live1.sort(...)` removed. Keys still evaluated, element-checked, filtered,
  materialized and re-yielded; only the comparator never runs.
- `noKeys` — `sortByBys` returns `items` immediately: no `evalBy`, no `project`, no element check,
  no filter, no wrapper objects, no sort. `[...stream]` and the re-yield remain.
- `passthru` — `orderStep` yields the stream straight through, so even `[...stream]` is gone and the
  step is inert.

`engineValues`, `rawSortTotal` and `engineHop` are controls no arm touches; their spreads across all
four arms were 1.091x, 1.018x and 1.039x, so the ladder is measuring stages and not drift.

### The decomposition, medians of three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds

| stage                                   | subtraction               | ms        | share                    |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------- | ------------------------ |
| the sort itself                         | `base - noSort`           | 98.02     | 43.5%                    |
| **an INERT `order()` step**             | `passthru - engineValues` | **95.73** | **42.4%**                |
| keys + check + filter + wrapper objects | `noSort - noKeys`         | 26.89     | 11.9%                    |
| `[...stream]` of 1M traversers          | `noKeys - passthru`       | 4.92      | 2.2%                     |
|                                         | sums to                   | 225.56    | against a measured 225.6 |

It reconciles to within 0.1 ms, which is the check that no stage is double-counted or missing.

### What this settles

**Two of item 890's three named candidates are dead.** `[...stream]` materializing a million
traversers is **2.2%** — it had looked like an obvious cost and is not one. And the sort runs at
**1.13x its own floor** (`rawSortTotal`, 86.94 ms to sort 1M numbers with the engine's total-order
comparator), so the comparator and the sort together have ~12 ms in them, not 98.

**The finding is the inert step.** An `order()` that sorts NOTHING — `yield* stream`, no keys, no
comparator, no materialization — still costs **95.73 ms, about 96 ns an item, 42% of the total.**
That is the step boundary existing at all. It is not anything `sortByBys` does, and no change to
`sortByBys` can reach it. It is consistent with items 234 and 537, which measured ~40-50 ns a vertex
per step and recorded "a traverser allocated per vertex to be filtered and discarded", concluding
that attacking it generally means restructuring the pipeline.

So: **86% of what `order()` costs is the sort at its floor plus the step's own existence.** The only
remaining tractable slice is the 26.89 ms of keying, and item 890 measured that yielding ~14 ms and
losing it in the noise. **The row is closed as a target.** Recorded in `order-cost-probe.ts` next to
the arms that measured it.

### Two instrument notes, one of which nearly produced a wrong finding

**`min`-of-three picked IDENTICAL minima for two different arms, by coincidence.** `noKeys` and
`passthru` both reported exactly 266.17 ms, which reads like one arm that failed to apply. The raw
per-round series is what settled it — `noKeys` 275.02/266.17/283.18 against `passthru`
266.17/270.71/270.10 — so the arms are distinct and the estimator was the problem. On this path the
spread within an arm reaches 6%, and the repo already records that medians beat `min` for the TS
per-row path. Switching to medians moved that stage from a flat 0.00 ms to 4.92. **Print the series;
a summary statistic coinciding across arms is not evidence that they are the same code.**

**An arm assertion that counts a SHARED marker cannot distinguish arms.** All three ablated arms
carried `ABLATION-891`, so the count proved only "some ablation was applied", never WHICH one. It
would have passed if two arms had been swapped. Assert something arm-specific — the thing the arm
uniquely contains — not a family marker.

### Verification

No engine change: the ladder's wrong code never left its harness (pristine restore before each arm,
byte-identity confirmed after, zero markers left in the tree), and what remains is one probe comment
and two documents. `bun test packages/gremlin` 826 pass, 0 fail. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run
lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0 — each its own command, exit code read UNPIPED.

## Item 892 — removing `orderStep`'s generator layer is refuted, and it corrects 891's attribution

Item 891 decomposed what `order()` costs and found the largest single slice was an **inert** step:
`yield* stream`, no keys, no comparator, no sorting, still 95.73 ms over 1,000,000 items — 42% of
the total, ~96 ns an item. It read that as one extra generator layer whose only job is to forward a
value already sitting in an array, and that reading is wrong.

### What was tried

`sortByBys` returns an array, so what the consumer should be pulling is an array iterator rather
than resuming a generator frame per item. Returning the array directly would do that — and would
also make the step EAGER, running the sort and raising the element fault at `applyStep` time instead
of on the first pull. This engine has a recorded lazy-vs-eager deviation on `limit(0)`-shaped plans,
so eagerness is a real behaviour change, not an implementation detail.

So the change was a lazy `Iterable` whose `[Symbol.iterator]` does the work on first call: nothing
runs until iteration begins, exactly as with the generator, but the iterator handed back is the
array's.

### Measured: three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, both estimators

| arm                      | pre (min) | post (min) | ratio | pre (median) | post (median) | ratio     |
| ------------------------ | --------- | ---------- | ----- | ------------ | ------------- | --------- |
| `engineOrdered` (target) | 388.10    | 370.92     | 1.05x | 388.70       | 383.14        | **1.01x** |
| `engineValues` (control) | 174.47    | 172.24     | 1.01x | 180.12       | 173.46        | **1.04x** |
| `rawSortTotal` (control) | 85.49     | 86.16      | 0.99x | 86.18        | 86.75         | 0.99x     |
| `engineHop` (control)    | 138.12    | 138.97     | 0.99x | 140.73       | 140.03        | 1.00x     |

On medians the target moves 1.01x while a control the change cannot reach moves 1.04x. Both
estimators are reported because they disagree, and the honest summary is the one that does not
flatter the change. Refuted; reverted, and `aggregation.ts` is byte-identical to before the attempt.

### The attribution was the error, and that is the finding

Item 891 obtained the 95.73 ms by comparing a plan WITH an order step against a plan WITHOUT one.
That difference is the cost of the pipeline having one more STEP — dispatch, the consumer's
iteration machinery, whatever the executor wraps each step's output in — and **not** the cost of
`orderStep`'s own `yield*`. Removing this one generator layer leaves the rest of that in place,
which is exactly why it measures nothing.

So 891's conclusion stands and its attribution does not: the row is still closed as a target, and
the reason is now better stated. The inert-step cost is the per-step pipeline as a whole, consistent
with items 234 and 537, and **no single step can fix it** — which is a stronger statement than 891
made, and it rules out the obvious follow-up for every other boundary step as well.

### Mutation, and a perf route with no test

| mutant                                              | verdict                |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| EAGER: `return sortByBys(...)` directly             | CAUGHT rc=1, 2 fail    |
| back to a generator layer (lazy, answer-equivalent) | SURVIVED, as predicted |

The second is a pure PERF route — identical answers, identical laziness — so no test can hold it and
the A/B is its only guard. Which is just as well, since the A/B is what rejected it.

### The tests outlived the change

`packages/gremlin/src/order-step-laziness.test.ts` is kept. The contract it pins — constructing the
step consumes nothing and raises nothing; the first pull does both — holds for the generator too,
and the mutation above shows what it catches: an eager rewrite fails two of its assertions while all
826 other gremlin tests stay green. That rewrite is the simplest thing a future change would reach
for, and until now nothing stopped it. A refuted optimization that leaves a real guard behind is
worth the tick.

### Verification

`bun test packages/gremlin` 828 pass, 0 fail (826 plus the two kept assertions). `bun run typecheck`
0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0 — each its own
command with its exit code read UNPIPED.

## Item 893 — a nested path cloned its base record once per row: 1.17x on the native engine

First Rust-side change since item 359, and found by running `bench_all` as a target finder rather
than a regression pass. The sweep's largest unexplained ratio was `value/maps`: **`map field
meta.city` 5030.6 us against the matched `string city (flat)` 244.1** — 20.6x for the same data,
one level nested.

### Not a new row, and not a new bug — the third item in a family

That row is already worked. Item 359 cut it 2.44x (12145 → 4985) by splitting the dotted key once
per QUERY instead of once per row, and the sweep's 5030.6 is that post-fix state. It also added the
matched flat comparison, which is why the 20.6x is a sound ratio rather than the 33x the unmatched
row used to invite.

What was left is a different per-row cost in the same function. `prop_path_parts` reads its base
with `prop(node, parts[0])`, which returns an **owned** `Value`. A record property lives in a `Gen`
column, and `Value::Record` is `Arc<[(GStr, Value)]>` — so the clone is not a deep copy but it IS an
atomic refcount **bump and a matching drop, per row**, to hand back a record the function
immediately throws away after reading one field out of it.

`prop_ref` already exists for exactly this: item 641 added it after measuring the analogous list case
(`n.tags[0]` cloning a whole list to read one element) at **191x** a plain property read. Using it
here leaves the field clone as the only one.

So this is the third item in a family the audit already names — item 331's property write allocated
its key three times, 332's staging parser allocated a `String` per JSON key, 359 split the path per
row — and the second in this one function.

### Measured: two binaries, ALTERNATED, min of three

| row                                        | pre    | post   | ratio               |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------ | ------ | ------------------- |
| `map field meta.city`                      | 4977.3 | 4267.3 | **1.17x, DISJOINT** |
| `string city (flat)` — the matched control | 245.9  | 245.4  | 1.00x               |
| `scalar age (flat)`                        | 92.4   | 92.1   | 1.00x               |
| `scalar age (map graph)`                   | 92.4   | 92.0   | 1.00x               |

Disjoint: every `pre` reading (4977.3-5027.3) is above every `post` reading (4267.3-4345.1). 24.9 →
21.3 ns/row, which is the size one atomic pair should be. `bench_all`'s own row agrees
independently: **5030.6 → 4300.8**.

**A note on the controls, against item 359's.** That item recorded an honest caveat: its two
flat-NUMERIC control rows moved ~1.11x although the change could not reach them, which it attributed
to code layout (precedent: `pull`'s alignment is load-bearing) and concluded the noise floor there
was ~1.11x rather than 1.00x. **This run does not show that** — all three controls sit at 1.00x
across six readings. So the floor is not inherently 1.11x on this bench; 359 hit layout drift, and
1.17x here clears a floor that was actually measured rather than assumed.

The remaining gap to the matched flat row goes from 20.2x to **17.4x**. Still large, and still the
unindexed `IndexSeek` fallback doing a per-row record lookup against a columnar compare.

### Mutation: 2 caught, a REAL GAP found, and an equivalence control

| mutant                                                      | verdict                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| resolve from segment 0 (look the base up inside itself)     | CAUGHT, 4 failed            |
| return the whole base record instead of the field           | CAUGHT, 3 failed            |
| **fallback yields `Value::Null`**                           | **SURVIVED all 1980 tests** |
| CONTROL: delete the fast arm, everything takes the fallback | SURVIVED, as predicted      |

The control surviving is the point of including it: both routes must agree, and its survival is that
assertion. Item 359 made the same observation about its own control — "a control that only shows the
suite runs is worth less than one that proves an equivalence the change depends on."

**The third mutant is a genuine hole, not an answer-equivalence.** Replacing the owned-read fallback
with `Null` passes everything, because the fallback's only _live_ job inside the engine is producing
`Null`. Checked rather than assumed: `prop_path_parts` has exactly ONE caller in the engine (the
unindexed `IndexSeek` fallback filter) and it always passes a dotted key of two or more segments;
`Store::prop_path` has **no internal caller at all** — it is public API for a host. So the
single-segment case its own doc comment specifies ("`parts[0]` is the base property and the rest are
record sub-fields") is unreachable from GQL and was never tested.

`prop_path_contract` closes it with unit-level assertions, deliberately not routed through a query
because a query cannot reach the shape: one segment on a typed base must return the SCALAR; one
segment on a record base returns the record; a sub-field of a typed base, of an absent base, and an
absent sub-field of a present record are all `Null`; and a record column that is NULL at a node
declines `prop_ref` so the fallback answers, while its typed siblings still read through it. With
that test in, the surviving mutant is **CAUGHT**.

A second test, `dotted_path_base_kinds`, covers the same three base kinds through GQL, plus a
THREE-segment path — the one shape that still takes `resolve_path`'s general loop rather than the
one-segment arm item 359 added.

(One self-inflicted detour: the first draft of that test keyed rows on `n.id`, which is the external
id and not a property, so it read `Null`. Rekeyed onto a property the fixture sets, and the node
indices it uses are now ASSERTED to be the nodes intended rather than assumed from document order.)

### Verification

`cargo test --release` 1243 + 13 + 725 pass, 0 failed. `rewrite_fuzz` 10 passed. All seven
byte-identity fuzzers pass at random seeds. `bench_all` shows no regression anywhere else — ingest,

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun
run check` 0.

## Item 894 — the same scan HASHED its constant key once per row: 1.65x, and 1.92x cumulative

Item 893 left a named residual: "the unindexed `IndexSeek` fallback doing a per-row record lookup
against a columnar compare", 17.4x against the matched flat row. This is the next layer of it, and
it is the same bug for the fourth time.

### A key is constant across a scan — and this one was being HASHED per row

`prop_path_parts` begins with `self.props.get(key)`, a `HashMap` lookup that **hashes the key
string**. It is called from inside the scan's filter closure, so a 200,000-node scan for `meta.city`
hashed the constant `"meta"` 200,000 times.

The audit already names this family, and the earlier three were all in or around this same path:

- item 331 — a property write allocated its key three times and stored one
- item 332 — a staging parser allocated a `String` per JSON key to compare against a literal
- item 359 — this very closure SPLIT the dotted key once per node (the fix hoisted the split out)
- item 894 — and it still HASHED the base segment once per node

Item 359's own summary said it: _"A key is constant across a scan; splitting, parsing or owning it
per row is the recurring bug."_ Hashing belongs on that list.

The fix is `Store::gen_column(key) -> Option<(&[Value], &[bool])>`: resolve the boxed column once
before the loop, then index it per row. A typed or absent base keeps the general path, where a
sub-field still resolves to `Null` exactly as before.

### Measured: two binaries, ALTERNATED, min of three

| row                                        | pre    | post   | ratio               |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------ | ------ | ------------------- |
| `map field meta.city`                      | 4272.5 | 2592.1 | **1.65x, DISJOINT** |
| `string city (flat)` — the matched control | 245.8  | 246.5  | 1.00x               |
| `scalar age (flat)`                        | 92.0   | 92.5   | 1.00x               |
| `scalar age (map graph)`                   | 92.4   | 92.0   | 1.00x               |

Disjoint: `pre` spans 4272.5-4291.9 and `post` 2592.1-2595.0. **21.4 → 13.0 ns/row**, so 8.4 ns
came out — the size of a short-string hash and map probe. `bench_all`'s own row reads 2578-2633
across three separate sweeps.

**Cumulative with item 893: 4977.3 → 2592.1, 1.92x**, and against the pre-359 state (12145) the row
is now **4.7x** faster. The gap to the matched flat row goes **20.2x → 10.5x**.

### Mutation found a WRONG-ANSWER bug that the suite could not see

| mutant                                     | verdict                      |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
| **drop the `present[]` guard**             | **SURVIVED the whole suite** |
| resolve from segment 0 in the hoisted path | CAUGHT, 4 failed             |
| every row reads node 0's record            | CAUGHT, 4 failed             |
| CONTROL: delete the hoisted path entirely  | SURVIVED, as predicted       |

The control's survival is again the equivalence assertion (items 359, 893).

**The first one is not an answer-equivalence.** It survived even after I added a null-at-this-node
case, and the reason is structural: `Column::push_absent` for a `Gen` column stores `Value::Null`,
so a never-set slot reads `Null` whether or not the guard runs. But **`Column::set_absent` clears
`present[i]` and leaves `data[i]` UNTOUCHED** — so after a property REMOVAL the old record is still
physically sitting in the column. With the guard dropped, a dotted-path scan matches a value the
node no longer has: a wrong ROW, not an error.

Checked in the source rather than assumed, and then pinned:
`removed_record_prop_does_not_match_stale_value` sets up two matching nodes, `remove_prop`s one, and
asserts it disappears from the result and reads `Null` through the path. With that in, the mutant is
**CAUGHT**.

Worth stating plainly: the pre-894 code read through `prop_ref`, which checks `present` itself, so
the guard is something this change had to CARRY rather than a new idea — and carrying it correctly
was unverified until the mutant asked. A hoist that moves a read out of an accessor inherits every
check that accessor was doing, and `present`/tombstone checks are the ones easiest to leave behind.

### Verification

`cargo test --release` 1245 + 13 + 725 pass, 0 failed. `rewrite_fuzz` 10 passed, and again at
`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000`. All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass at random seeds. `bench_all`
shows no regression: ingest, codec, algo, parallel, neighboragg, call and scale rows all within
noise across three sweeps.
