--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun
run check` 0.

## Item 895 — an index on a dotted key makes the query 4.1x SLOWER, and the planner is right

MEASUREMENT (native), two bench arms and one probe added; no engine change. Item 894 left the
dotted-path scan at 2594.8 us against a matched flat 253.9, 10.5x, and I went looking for whether
that gap is something a user should care about or something they should index away. It is neither.

### The missing rows

Every row in `value/maps` was the UNINDEXED path, and the scan items 359/893/894 optimized is
explicitly described in the source as "the scan-fallback twin of a dotted `index_lookup`" — so the
section could not say what indexing the key does. Two arms added, both indexed so the comparison
stays matched (item 359's rule: a dotted index against a FLAT index, not against an unindexed scan):

| query                           | us                            |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `string city (flat)`            | 253.9                         |
| `map field meta.city`           | 2594.8                        |
| `string city (flat, INDEXED)`   | **306.0** — 1.2x slower       |
| `map field meta.city (INDEXED)` | **10699.5** — **4.1x slower** |

**Creating an index makes both queries slower.** That is the kind of result that gets attributed to
a planner bug, so the next step was a plan rather than a theory.

### The planner is behaving correctly

`dottedindex_895` prints whether an `IndexSeek` survives optimization:

```
dotted  no index  IndexSeek x1  has_hash_index=false  distinct=None
dotted  indexed   IndexSeek x0  has_hash_index=true   distinct=Some(4)
flat    no index  IndexSeek x1  has_hash_index=false  distinct=None
flat    indexed   IndexSeek x0  has_hash_index=true   distinct=Some(4)
```

With 4 distinct cities over 200,000 nodes the predicate matches ~25% of rows, well above the 15%
`SEEK_MAX_FRACTION` cap, so `seek_beats_scan` **correctly rejects the seek**. Item 407 tuned that
threshold and it is doing its job.

### The finding: two unindexed paths for one predicate, 4.1x apart

The seek is rejected either way; what differs is the plan it is rejected INTO.

- **Without an index**, the plan keeps an `IndexSeek` node, which at execution finds no index and
  runs the no-index fallback filter — the path item 359 (per-row key split), item 893 (per-row base
  clone) and item 894 (per-row key hash) successively optimized, now 2594.8 us.
- **With an index**, the rule rewrites it to `Scan` + `Filter`, and `Filter` evaluates
  `Expr::Field { base: Prop{slot,"meta"}, key:"city" }` by `eval(base)` FIRST — materializing an
  intermediate column holding the whole `meta` record for every row — and only then projecting
  `city` out of it. 10699.5 us.

So the engine has two unindexed implementations of one predicate, they differ by 4.1x, and the cost
model chooses between them on seek-versus-scan grounds that do not model the difference. **Item
894's 1.65x on the fallback widened this gap rather than closing it** — which is worth saying out
loud, because three consecutive items optimized one of two sibling paths without anyone checking the
other.

That is the loop's own "grep the pattern elsewhere" step, not done at 359, 893 or 894. The flat twin
shows the same structure at 1.2x, so this is not specific to dotted keys — it is specific to
`Filter` materializing a base column where the fallback borrows per row.

### Why this is recorded rather than fixed in the same tick

The fix is a fused evaluation of `Field { base: Prop }` that reads the field directly instead of
building the base column, and the evaluator is on the byte-identity path shared with the TS engine.
A fused arm has to produce identical values for every base kind — element, record, map, list, null,
absent — so it wants its own item, its own mutants and the full fuzzer sweep, not the tail of a
measurement. Named, priced from both sides, and left.

### Verification

No engine change: two bench arms, one probe (indexed by question in `examples/README.md`), two
documents. `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` 0; `bun run typecheck` 0;
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0 — each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED.

## Item 896 — the fused `n.rec.field` read: 2.27x, and the first draft regressed a control 1.09x

Item 895 named this fix and left it: `Filter` evaluated `Expr::Field { base: Prop, key }` by
evaluating the base to a COLUMN first — one cloned `Value::Record` per row — and only then
projecting a field out of it. That made a query with an INDEX on the dotted key 4.1x slower than the
same query without one, because the index makes the planner correctly choose `Scan` + `Filter` and
`Filter` took this path.

### Equivalent by construction, not by hope

The fused arm handles exactly the shape `Field { base: Prop{slot, base_key}, key }` where the slot
is a `Col::Nodes` and `base_key`'s column is BOXED (`Gen`). For that shape the two-step does
precisely this, in this order:

- a `u32::MAX` OPTIONAL sentinel — the base read yields `Null`, and `boxed_value_prop(&Null, key)`
  is `Null`
- absent at this node — `Column::read` yields `Null`, likewise
- present — the base cell, then `boxed_value_prop(cell, key)`, **the same function** the fused arm
  calls

So every base kind — record, map, list, scalar, null — resolves through the one function it already
resolved through; only the intermediate column disappears. Anything else (a typed or absent base, an
edge slot, a base that is not a plain `Prop`) returns `None` and takes the general path unchanged.

### Measured: three arms, ALTERNATED, min of three

| row                                                                                   | pre     | post (inline) | post2 (extracted) | post/pre  | post2/pre |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ------------- | ----------------- | --------- | --------- |
| `map field meta.city (INDEXED)` — target                                              | 10331.8 | 4621.1        | 4546.2            | 2.24x     | **2.27x** |
| `map field meta.city` — control (unindexed: `IndexSeek`, never reaches the evaluator) | 2568.6  | 2570.5        | 2576.5            | 1.00x     | 1.00x     |
| `string city (flat, INDEXED)` — control (`Str`/`Dict` column, so the arm declines)    | 297.6   | **324.9**     | 298.6             | **0.92x** | **1.00x** |
| `scalar age (flat)` — control                                                         | 93.7    | 93.8          | 92.8              | 1.00x     | 1.01x     |
| `scalar age (map graph)` — control                                                    | 92.8    | 92.8          | 92.8              | 1.00x     | 1.00x     |
| `string city (flat)` — control                                                        | 246.1   | 246.5         | 247.7             | 1.00x     | 0.99x     |

`bench_all` in situ: the indexed dotted row **10699.5 → 4859.6**, the flat indexed row unchanged at
297.5.

### The first draft regressed a control, and the fix was to move the code out of line

The inline version (`post`) won 2.24x on the target and made `string city (flat, INDEXED)` — a plain
`Expr::Prop` that the new code **cannot reach** — 1.09x SLOWER. That was not noise: four more rounds
at 9 reps each gave pre 298.6-298.9 against post 324.9-326.4, stable and disjoint.

`Expr::Prop` and `Expr::Field` are arms of the same `match` in `eval`, so growing one perturbs the
other's codegen. This is the phenomenon the audit already records for `exec::pull`, whose alignment
is load-bearing. Extracting the fused body into its own `fused_prop_field` function keeps the match
arm small, and `post2` gets the same win with **every control back at 1.00x**.

Worth keeping as a rule: **a control that moves on a change it cannot reach is not automatically
noise — check whether it is stable, and if it is, it is probably layout.** Here it was reproducible
to three significant figures, and the remedy was a code move rather than a tolerance.

### Mutation: 3 caught, one of them only after closing a gap

| mutant                                                 | verdict                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
| **drop the `u32::MAX` sentinel guard**                 | **SURVIVED the whole suite** |
| drop the `present[]` guard                             | CAUGHT, 1 failed             |
| return the whole base record instead of the field      | CAUGHT, 5 failed             |
| CONTROL: never fuse, everything takes the general path | SURVIVED, as predicted       |

The `present[]` guard is caught by item 894's stale-value test, which reaches this path too.

**The sentinel guard was unverified, and dropping it is a CRASH.** An OPTIONAL hop that matches
nothing binds `u32::MAX`, so `present[u32::MAX as usize]` is an out-of-bounds slice index — and Rust
bounds-checks slice indexing in release too. Nothing in the suite combined an OPTIONAL hop with a
nested-path read. `optional_miss_then_dotted_path_is_null` pins it: a miss projects `Null`, and a hit
through the same arm still reads `nyc` so the test is not merely asserting that everything is null.
With it in, the mutant panics exactly as predicted — `index out of bounds: the len is 2 but the index
is 4294967295`.

That is the **second** check in two items that a hoist had to CARRY rather than invent: item 894
carried `present`, this one carries the sentinel. `read_property`, the function being fused, handles
both explicitly. **Fusing a path inherits every guard the path it replaced was applying, and the
guards worth checking are the ones for values that do not occur in an ordinary fixture.**

(One detour: the test's first draft also asserted the predicate form, which is `E_NOT_IMPLEMENTED` —
a `WHERE` inside `OPTIONAL MATCH` is unsupported in this engine. The projection form is the
reachable one and it is the one that indexes `present`.)

### Verification

`cargo test --release` 1246 + 13 + 725 pass, 0 failed. `rewrite_fuzz` 10 passed at
`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000`. **All seven byte-identity fuzzers pass at random seeds** — the one
that matters most here, since this changes a shared evaluator. `bench_all` shows no regression
anywhere else across the ingest, codec, algo, parallel, neighboragg, call and scale groups.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 897 — the TS engine does NOT have item 895's bug, and my first measurement of that was wrong

MEASUREMENT (TS), one probe added; no engine change. Item 895 found that natively, an index on a
dotted key made a query **4.1x slower** — two unindexed implementations of one predicate, 4.1x
apart, with the cost model choosing between them on grounds that do not include the difference. It
also recorded that items 359, 893 and 894 each optimized one of those two sibling paths without
checking the other. So the cross-ENGINE sibling gets checked rather than reasoned about.

### The answer: no

In one process and one graph, querying an INDEXED key costs the same as querying an unindexed TWIN
of the same type and cardinality, and the materializing seek is never reached:

| case                    | ms (min of 3 alternated rounds) | `equals()` calls |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| flat INDEXED            | 4.34                            | 0                |
| flat unindexed (twin)   | 4.68                            | 0                |
| nested INDEXED          | 17.05                           | 0                |
| nested unindexed (twin) | 14.98                           | 0                |

Every seek count is **zero**, for the clause-`WHERE` and the inline `{k: v}` spelling alike, because
`SEEK_MAX_FRACTION` is 1/8 and this predicate matches 25% of the label bucket — item 409's gate
declines, exactly as native's `seek_beats_scan` does. The flat pair has the indexed side marginally
FASTER; the nested pair's 1.14x sits inside that arm's own round-to-round spread (17.05-23.49).

The mechanism is architectural: the TS engine evaluates row-at-a-time through a compiled closure —
`executor.ts`'s `'field'` arm is `baseF(env)` then `recordGet`/`propOf` — so there is no intermediate
column to materialize and no second path to disagree with. **Item 895's bug is specific to the
native columnar evaluator.**

### My first measurement said 1.98x, and it was an artifact

The first version of this probe put each arm in its own process — the repo's usual ONE SHAPE PER
PROCESS rule — and reported, reproducibly across two runs:

```
flat            4.94 / 4.74 ms
flatIndexed     8.14 / 9.41 ms     <- 1.65x to 1.98x "slower with an index"
```

That is not a query cost. **Creating an index over 200,000 vertices changes the HEAP**, so two
processes differ in allocation history, live-set size and GC behaviour, and that difference lands in
the query timing looking exactly like query cost. Run in ONE process against ONE graph, the effect
disappears entirely.

So: **when the thing under test changes the heap, separate processes are not comparable** — the arms
have to share one. That is a real exception to a rule this repo otherwise relies on (one shape per
process, from item 762), and the two are in tension: one shape per process protects against
inline-cache pollution, one process protects against heap divergence. Which matters depends on
whether the change allocates.

**And my discriminator was broken on the same axis.** I added an `indexedOther` arm — an index on a
key the query never names — reasoning that if it were also slow the cost would be "an index exists"
rather than "this key's index". It came back FAST (4.68), which looked like proof the cost was
key-specific. It was not proof of anything: it is still a different process. **A discriminator built
on the broken axis does not fix the axis**, and it produced a confident wrong conclusion that
survived until the one-process run contradicted it.

### A silent fixture corruption, caught by an assert

While isolating this, an inline `bun -e` under `systemd-run` reported `count=1` on a 200,000-node
graph. The cause: **`systemd-run` performs `${...}` expansion on the command it runs**, so
`id: `v${i}`` became `v` for every vertex and the graph collapsed to ONE node. File-based probes are
unaffected; only inline `-e` is.

The timings looked entirely plausible — a fast query over a one-node graph — and the only thing that
caught it was asserting the fixture's own statistic (the row count) on every rep. That is the rule
this repo already records as "check the fixture's own statistics, not just its output", and it paid
for itself here. The probe keeps that assert, with the reason.

### Verification

No engine change: one probe and this entry. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt`
0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0 — each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED.

## Item 898 — collapsing `recordGet`'s two Map probes into one: refuted at 0.96x

Item 897 established that the TS engine does not have item 895's bug, and left a number on the way
past: a TS nested-path read costs ~3.4x a flat property read on the same scan (15.3 ms against 4.99
over 200,000 rows). `recordGet` is what a nested read calls once per row, and it was
`rec.has(key) ? rec.get(key) : null` — **two hash probes for every read**.

### The change, and why it was answer-equivalent

`get` first, and `has` only to disambiguate the one return value that is ambiguous:

| case                     | returns     | probes |
| ------------------------ | ----------- | ------ |
| present, not `undefined` | the value   | 1      |
| ABSENT                   | `null`      | 2      |
| present as `undefined`   | `undefined` | 2      |

`LenkeRecord` stores values as-is and leaves normalization to its callers, so a stored `undefined`
is not assumed impossible — it is handled, which is what keeps absent and stored-undefined
distinguishable.

### Measured: three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds, one process, one graph

| case               | pre   | post  | ratio     | reach                     |
| ------------------ | ----- | ----- | --------- | ------------------------- |
| `nested INDEXED`   | 17.75 | 18.41 | **0.96x** | calls `recordGet` per row |
| `nested unindexed` | 15.31 | 15.34 | **1.00x** | calls `recordGet` per row |
| `flat INDEXED`     | 4.99  | 4.83  | 1.03x     | control                   |
| `flat unindexed`   | 5.23  | 5.23  | 1.00x     | control                   |

Nothing. A `Map` probe on a small record is too cheap to matter, or the JIT already fuses the pair.
**Refuted and reverted**, with the numbers recorded next to `recordGet` so the idea is not
re-proposed from the shape of the code — "two lookups where one would do" reads like a defect and
measures like nothing.

The ~3.4x nested-vs-flat gap is therefore still unattributed. What this rules out is the record
lookup itself; `propOf`'s `?.properties?.[key]` chain, the extra closure dispatch for the nested
`'field'` arm, and whatever `addVertex` does to normalize a nested object into a `LenkeRecord` are
all still unpriced.

### Mutation, and the test that outlived the change

| mutant                                                                  | verdict                |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| drop the `has()` fallback (absent and stored-undefined collapse)        | CAUGHT, 1 fail         |
| coalesce at the `get` (loses stored-undefined)                          | CAUGHT, 1 fail         |
| treat a stored NULL as needing the fallback too (slower, still correct) | SURVIVED, as predicted |
| CONTROL: revert to the two-probe form                                   | SURVIVED, as predicted |

The control surviving is what made the revert safe: it is the assertion that both forms answer
identically, run before the revert rather than assumed after it.

`packages/gql/src/record-get-probes.test.ts` is kept. It pins the three-valued contract — present,
absent, and **present with the value `undefined`**, which must read back as `undefined` and not as
the `null` an absent key gives. Nothing tested that row before, both forms satisfy it, and any
future attempt to collapse the probes has to keep the two cases distinguishable. Second time in this
window that a refuted optimization left a real guard behind (item 892 was the first).

### Verification

`bun test packages/gql` 2711 pass, 0 fail on the reverted tree. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run
lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 899 — the TS nested read decomposed: the FIELD step is all of it, and two suspects are refuted

MEASUREMENT (TS), one probe added; no engine change. Items 897 and 898 measured the gap — a TS
nested read is ~3.4x a flat property read on the same scan — and 898 ruled out one cause. This
decomposes the rest.

### A ladder of QUERIES, with no wrong arms

Every rung reads one stage more than the rung below it, so the differences are the stages. No engine
code is modified and no arm is deliberately wrong, which is why this needed no pristine-restore
harness:

| rung             | query                        | ns/row    | rows   |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------- | --------- | ------ |
| `scalarProp`     | `p.tier = 'NYC'`             | 26.5      | 50,000 |
| `recordProp`     | `p.meta = 'NYC'`             | 25.7      | 0      |
| `nestedField`    | `p.meta.other = 'NYC'`       | **101.5** | 50,000 |
| `scalarPropNull` | `p.nosuch = 'NYC'` (control) | 22.3      | 0      |

`recordProp` is the rung that makes this work: it READS a record-valued property and compares it,
with the same read machinery and the same comparison shape as `scalarProp`, and **no field step**. It
matches nothing — a record never equals a string — which is the point: the per-row work happened
anyway. `scalarPropNull` is the control for that zero-match shape, and it is 4.2 ns/row CHEAPER than
the matching scalar, so "matches nothing" is not what `recordProp` is measuring.

**Reading a record-valued property costs the same as reading a scalar one: −0.8 ns/row.** So
`propOf`, the optional-property chain, and the mere presence of a nested record are all free. **The
field step is 75.8 ns/row — 100% of the gap.**

### Inside the field step: two suspects refuted, one priced

| representation            | ns/read  |
| ------------------------- | -------- |
| plain `Map.get`           | 17.7     |
| **`Map` SUBCLASS `.get`** | **17.5** |
| plain object `[k]`        | **4.3**  |
| subclass `has` + `get`    | 16.0     |

- **`LenkeRecord extends Map` is NOT the cause.** A subclassed `Map` can lose an engine's Map fast
  path — a real JS engine behaviour and the obvious suspect — and here it costs **nothing** (17.5
  against 17.7).
- **`has` + `get` costs no more than `get` alone** (16.0 against 17.5), which independently confirms
  item 898's null result from a completely different instrument. Two measurements agreeing by
  different routes is worth more than either.
- **What IS large is Map-versus-plain-object: 17.7 against 4.3 ns, 4-7x across runs.** That prices
  the representation choice at roughly **13 of the 75.8 ns**, leaving ~63 ns as expression plumbing
  — the extra closure invocation for the nested `'field'` arm, the `instanceof LenkeRecord` test, and
  the two-level dispatch.

(The micro-arms use varying keys and a live sink on purpose: item 889 timed `'score'.toLowerCase()`
at 0.27 ns because a constant-input loop folds away and measures nothing.)

### Not attempted, and why

The ~13 ns is a representation change, and `LenkeRecord` is load-bearing well beyond performance: it
is a `Map` subclass _specifically_ so a record is distinguishable from a graph element and from a
plain object, it keeps keys sorted for canonical JSON, and it is shared by the GQL engine, the
Gremlin engine and every serialization codec — where byte-identity with the native `Value::Map` is a
hard invariant. Trading that for ~13 ns a row on nested reads is not a perf decision made in a perf
tick. Named, priced, and left.

The ~63 ns of plumbing is the larger half and is the better target, but it is a question about how
the expression compiler nests closures rather than about records, so it wants its own item.

### Verification

No engine change: one probe (indexed by question in `examples/README.md`) and two documents. `bun run
typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0 — each its own command with
its exit code read UNPIPED.

## Item 900 — the dotted-path lift measured 0.96x because it NEVER RAN, and a null A/B could not tell me that

Item 899 localised the TS nested read's 75.8 ns/row to the field step and named the expression
plumbing as the better half. The mechanism looked clear: `asPropCompare` matches a plain `prop`
only, so a dotted conjunct makes `directEqProps` decline and takes **the whole predicate** to the
generic evaluator — a route item 874 already priced at 2.02x for a flat property. A fourth lift
beside `eqProps`/`cmpProps`/`truthProps` is the obvious fix.

### It was built completely

A `pathProps` list carrying `{path, op, value}`; a module-scope `pathOf` reader walking
`propOf` then `recordGet` exactly as the compiled `'field'` closures do (at module scope because the
audit records that a walk INLINE in a returned closure gave unrelated queries a new 4x slow mode);
an `asPathCompare` taking BOTH operand orders; the application loop through `compareTruth` — the
generic `compare` arm's own function, so the lift could not change an answer; `hasPredicate`
counting it, which is the list this codebase has a named bug class about; and the `hop-projection`
merge, added with the list rather than left for a later reader.

All 2711 GQL tests, 828 Gremlin and 370 core passed.

### Measured 0.96x — and the number was meaningless

| arm           | pre  | post | ratio     |         |
| ------------- | ---- | ---- | --------- | ------- |
| `nestedField` | 90.9 | 95.1 | **0.96x** | TARGET  |
| `scalarProp`  | 25.0 | 24.7 | 1.01x     | control |
| `recordProp`  | 23.1 | 24.9 | 0.93x     | control |

Read on its own, that is "refuted". It is not: **the code never executed.** Instrumented with two
counters — one where a conjunct is lifted, one where the list is applied:

```
lifted at compile: 3     applied at runtime: 0     answer still correct (c=1250)
```

The conjunct lifts three times during compilation, and **0 of 5,000 runtime predicates carry the
list.** The predicate that reaches the scan comes from a `compilePredicate` call where `ownVar` is
undefined, so `direct` is null and the `WHERE` stays generic; the lifted copies belong to other
compile calls. The answer stayed right throughout precisely because the generic `where` was never
displaced — had the lift also removed the conjunct from `where`, this would have been a silent
SUPERSET instead of a null result.

### A null A/B cannot distinguish "does not help" from "did not run"

That is the finding, and it is the same distinction this window kept hitting in mutation — where a
`DID-NOT-RUN` verdict must be separated from a `CAUGHT` one by looking for a result line before
reading the exit code (items 866, 886). **An A/B needs the same discipline: an execution counter,
not just a timing.** Without it I would have recorded "the dotted lift is worth nothing", and the
next person would have believed a measurement of code that was never reached.

### The diagnostic worth reusing

**Count `matchesPredicate` entries.** For the dotted query it ran **5,000 times — once per SCANNED
vertex**; for the flat query **1,250 — once per MATCHING vertex**, because a lifted predicate filters
before `matchesPredicate` is reached. That asymmetry is a direct read of whether a predicate was
lifted, needs no timing, and is stable. It is how the 0.96x got explained in one run.

Also learned from the same instrumentation: `rejectedByElementDirect` was entered **0** times for
both queries, so the two `preFilter` gates in `matching.ts` — which enumerate the lifted lists BY
NAME (`pre.eqProps !== undefined || pre.cmpProps !== undefined`) — are not the active path for this
shape either. **A new predicate list has more consumers than the three I wired**, and they are not
discoverable from the list's own definition.

(Worth flagging while here: those gates do not mention `truthProps` either. That is a missed
optimization rather than a bug — `matchesPredicate` does carry a `truthProps` loop, so the filtering
happens, just later than it could.)

### Reverted, with the numbers recorded next to `asPropCompare`

Not in CLOSED.md as "refuted": the idea is **unmeasured**, which is a different state and a worse
one to leave implied. The next step is a planner question — which compile call feeds the scan, and
why it has no `ownVar` — and the rejection comment says so, so the list is not rebuilt before that
is answered.

`bun test packages/gql` 2711 pass, gremlin 828, core 370, all 0 fail on the reverted tree. `bun run
typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 901 — correcting item 900: the predicate IS built with the lift, and the lift is NOT additive

Item 900 reverted a dotted-path predicate lift that measured 0.96x because it never ran, and
concluded "the next step is a planner question — which compile call feeds the scan, and why it has
no `ownVar`". That attribution is wrong, and the real answer is more dangerous than the one I wrote.

### `ownVar` is not the problem

Instrumenting `compileNode`'s one `compilePredicate` call site:

```
dotted [var=p where=compare]
flat   [var=p where=compare]
dotIn  [var=p where=compare]
```

`compileNode` is reached with `node.variable = 'p'` and `node.where` set for every spelling. And
`freePredicateVars` handles a `field` node correctly — it walks the base to the `prop` and reports
`{p}` — so the element-local proof holds too. **The predicate is built with an `ownVar` and does
carry the lift.** The gap is entirely on the CONSUMER side.

`shortcuts.ts` builds its OWN `CPredicate` for a filtered count —
`compilePredicate(undefined, where, nodeVar)` — and its `InlinePred` contract spells out the
consumers it knows: "there are exactly three places a value can come from: a general compiled
`where`; `eqProps`/`cmpProps`; `props`". A fourth list is invisible to it. Add
`rejectedByElementDirect` and the two `preFilter` gates in `matching.ts`, which enumerate the lists
by NAME, and the count of consumers a new list must reach is at least five — none of them
discoverable from the list's own definition.

### The hazard item 900 did not state: a lift MOVES a constraint

```ts
const generic = direct === null ? where : direct.residual; // residual is ALWAYS undefined
```

So a successful lift **empties `where`**. A new list is not an additional fast path alongside the
general evaluator — it is the ONLY remaining carrier of that conjunct. Any consumer that enumerates
the lists by name and misses the new one therefore returns a silent **SUPERSET**.

That is precisely `hasPredicate`'s named bug class (item 277), which this codebase has a whole doc
comment about, reappearing one level up: I wired `hasPredicate` itself — the thing that doc warns
about — and still left four other consumers unwired.

**And the attempted change passed all 2,711 GQL tests, 828 Gremlin and 370 core while in that
state.** Not because it was safe, but because no fixture combines a dotted conjunct with the
un-wired consumer. The 0.96x and the green suite together looked like "a harmless no-op"; it was a
latent wrong-answer waiting for a fixture.

### What this changes about re-attempting it

Item 900's next step was "find which compile call feeds the scan". The actual next step is **an
audit of every consumer before writing the list**: `matchesPredicate`, `rejectedByElementDirect`,
both `preFilter` gates, and `shortcuts.ts`' `InlinePred`. A grep for `eqProps` finds some of them and
not all, because the gates name the lists individually and the `InlinePred` contract names them in
prose. The rejection comment next to `asPropCompare` now says this instead of the planner story.

### The general lesson

**A performance list that REPLACES a general path is a correctness surface, not an optimization.**
The tell is whether the general carrier is emptied on success. When it is, "add a fourth list beside
the other three" is not a local change however local it looks — and a green suite is evidence about
the fixtures, not about the wiring.

### Verification

No engine change: the revert stands, and this corrects a comment and two documents. `bun test
packages/gql` 2711 pass, 0 fail. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
check` 0.

## Item 902 — the dotted lift declines a LONE conjunct and admits one in an AND-chain; and item 901's hazard is not demonstrated

Items 900 and 901 both attributed a null A/B to the wrong thing. This asks the public API directly
instead of reading the code, which settles it — and corrects both.

### Twelve route tests, which is coverage that did not exist

`packages/gql/src/dotted-predicate-routes.test.ts` runs a dotted predicate through every route that
carries a node predicate: the count shortcut (clause and inline), a PROJECTION (so the rows are
checked and not a tally), AND-chains in both orders, a three-segment path, the FAR node of a hop
(`hop-projection`'s merge route), both operand orders, an ordering comparison, an absent final
segment, an absent BASE, and a no-predicate control so a "4" is a filter that ran rather than a
coincidence of the fixture. All twelve pass; the expectations are what the engine answers today.

### Item 901's superset hazard is NOT demonstrated

901 claimed the attempted lift was "a latent wrong answer waiting for a fixture". Tested rather than
asserted: **re-applying the exact un-wired lift leaves all twelve cases passing.** Two reasons, one
per shape — in the AND shape `matchesPredicate` DOES apply the list, and in the lone shape nothing
lifts, so nothing is emptied. The structural risk 901 described is real (a successful lift does empty
`where`), but **no shape reaches it today, and the claim as written was too strong.** Softened in the
rejection comment.

### What is actually happening, from three calls to `compilePredicate`

| predicate                       | `where`  | `eqProps` | `pathProps` |
| ------------------------------- | -------- | --------- | ----------- |
| `n.meta.city = 'x'`             | **kept** | 0         | **0**       |
| `n.k = 1`                       | emptied  | 1         | 0           |
| `n.meta.city = 'x' AND n.k = 1` | emptied  | 1         | **1**       |

**A lone dotted conjunct declines; the same conjunct inside an AND-chain lifts.** There is no
lone-conjunct guard in `directEqProps` — `conjuncts` is `where.kind === 'and' ? where.items :
[where]` and nothing else distinguishes them — so this is unexplained, and I am not going to guess
at it.

It does explain item 900's 0.96x completely: the benchmark predicate is
`p.meta.other = 'NYC'`, a LONE dotted conjunct, so **the A/B measured the one shape that never
lifts.** 900's "the code never ran" was right about that shape; 901's "the predicate IS built with
the lift" was right only about the AND shape. Each of us was describing a different half.

And the asymmetry is itself the finding worth having: two spellings of one question —
`WHERE p.meta.city = 'x'` and `WHERE p.meta.city = 'x' AND p.n >= 0` — would take different routes
once the lift works. That is the equivalent-spelling class this engine is named for, sitting in the
admission rule rather than in the planner.

### Three successive corrections of my own attribution, and what they have in common

892 corrected 891, 901 corrected 900, and this corrects 901. The common cause is the same each time:
**an attribution reasoned from reading the code plus ONE instrumented shape, then generalized.** 891
read a stage difference as a generator layer; 900 read a null A/B as a missing `ownVar`; 901 read
`residual: undefined` as a live superset risk. Every one was a plausible reading of real code.

What finally worked was calling the exported function directly across THREE spellings and printing a
table. Not a cleverer instrument — a wider one. **An attribution from a single shape is a
hypothesis; a table across spellings is a finding**, and in an engine whose named bug class is
"equivalent spellings cost differently", the table is the minimum.

### Verification

`bun test packages/gql` 2723 pass (2711 plus the twelve new), 0 fail. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun
run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0 — each its own command with its exit code read
UNPIPED.

## Item 903 — the dotted lift SHIPS at 1.31x, and item 902's "unexplained asymmetry" was my own missing guard

Items 900, 901 and 902 are three attributions for one null measurement, each corrected by the next.
This one closes it, and the cause is smaller and more embarrassing than any of the three:

```ts
if (eq.length === 0 && cmp.length === 0 && truth.length === 0) {
  return null; // ← `path.length` is missing
}
```

`directEqProps` asks "did anything lift?" after its loop. I added a fourth list and did not add it
to that question, so a LONE dotted conjunct accumulated into `path` and was then **discarded** —
lifting only when some OTHER conjunct lifted beside it. Item 900's benchmark predicate is a lone
dotted compare, so the A/B measured the one shape the change could not reach.

**Item 902 called that an unexplained engine asymmetry and filed it in `CLOSED.md` as the real open
question. It was neither unexplained nor the engine's.** Corrected there and in the code comment: a
false open question in the index is exactly the failure that index exists to prevent.

With the guard fixed, through the exported `compilePredicate`:

| predicate                       | `where` | `eqProps` | `pathProps` |
| ------------------------------- | ------- | --------- | ----------- |
| `n.meta.city = 'x'`             | EMPTIED | 0         | **1**       |
| `n.k = 1`                       | EMPTIED | 1         | 0           |
| `n.meta.city = 'x' AND n.k = 1` | EMPTIED | 1         | 1           |
| `n.meta.deep.z > 1`             | EMPTIED | 0         | **1**       |

### Verified to RUN before being measured

Item 900's lesson, applied: a counter in the application loop reports **5,000 entries for 5,000
vertices**, with the answer correct (1,250 of 5,000). Only then was it timed.

| arm           | pre  | post     | ratio     |                                                   |
| ------------- | ---- | -------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `nestedField` | 98.7 | **75.4** | **1.31x** | TARGET, DISJOINT (pre 98.7-124.6, post 75.4-77.7) |
| `scalarProp`  | 25.0 | 24.6     | 1.02x     | control                                           |
| `recordProp`  | 23.5 | 24.0     | 0.98x     | control                                           |

### The superset mutant is CAUGHT — by the tests item 902 could not demonstrate

Item 901 predicted a silent superset if a consumer were unwired; item 902 could not reproduce it,
because with the broken guard the lone shape never lifted and so never emptied `where`. With the
guard fixed the hazard is live, and the guard against it works:

| mutant                                                                        | verdict                |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| **delete the application loop** (`where` is emptied → the predicate VANISHES) | **CAUGHT, 9 fail**     |
| `pathOf` stops using `recordGet` for a `LenkeRecord`                          | CAUGHT, 8 fail         |
| `hasPredicate` stops counting `pathProps`                                     | SURVIVED               |
| the hop merge drops `pathProps`                                               | SURVIVED               |
| `pathOf` resolves from segment 0                                              | SURVIVED               |
| CONTROL: item 900's guard (lone dotted stops lifting)                         | SURVIVED, as predicted |

The first row is `dotted-predicate-routes.test.ts` earning its place exactly as designed — nine of
its twelve cases fail. The control surviving is the whole story of item 900 in one line: that guard
makes the engine slower and never wrong.

**The three survivors, honestly:**

- `pathOf` **from segment 0 is answer-equivalent and my mutant was wrong**, not the code. The loop
  body's `propOf` fallback handles a vertex exactly as the pre-loop line did, so starting at 0 is a
  refactor. A mutant has to be checked for equivalence like anything else.
- `hasPredicate` and the hop merge survive because they are **unreachable for current shapes**. The
  predicate is still applied by `matchesPredicate` either way, so neither is load-bearing today.
  That is the same status the codebase already documents for `truthProps`' merge ("a correctness
  precondition kept live for when the lift widens, not a line any current query depends on"), and
  it means item 901's claim that these are correctness-critical **for this list** is not
  demonstrated. They stay, for the reason `truthProps`' line stays.

### Verification

`bun test packages/gql` 2723 pass, gremlin 828, core 370, all 0 fail. **All seven byte-identity
fuzzers pass at random seeds** — the net that matters for a shared-executor change.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint`
0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

### The lesson across 900-903

Four items for one one-line omission. The attributions failed in the same way each time — a reading
of real code plus one instrumented shape, generalized — and each was plausible. What ended it was
printing a TABLE from the exported function across four spellings, which made the shape-dependence
impossible to miss. **When a change measures nothing, the first question is not "why is it slow"
but "did it run, for THIS shape"**, and the cheapest way to answer it is to call the thing directly
and tabulate, before reaching for an instrument.

## Item 904 — the TS nested read is at its floor: the arithmetic now accounts for all of it

Closing the thread items 897-903 ran. With the lift shipped, the ladder re-reads:

| rung                                         | ns/row   | then (item 899) |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------- | --------------- |
| `scalarProp`                                 | 24.6     | 26.5            |
| `recordProp` (reads a record, no field step) | 24.2     | 25.7            |
| `nestedField`                                | **75.6** | 101.5           |
| the FIELD step                               | **52.0** | 75.8            |

So item 903's lift took **~24 ns off the field step**, and 52 remain.

### Those 52 ns are now fully accounted for, which is the point

- `propOf` on the element — **~17 ns**, and the flat rung pays it too
- a SECOND read, `recordGet` into the `LenkeRecord` — **~17 ns**, measured directly at item 899
  (a `Map.get` is 17.1 ns where a plain-object read is 3.4)
- `instanceof LenkeRecord`, the segment loop, two array indexes, and `compareTruth`'s own overhead —
  the remainder

Against the flat rung's 24.6 (its own `propOf` plus `structuralEq` plus the closure), that adds up.
**There is no unexplained residual left**, which is the difference between "still open" and "at its
floor", and the reason to stop rather than keep probing.

### One hypothesis refuted on inspection, before it cost a build

`eqProps` compares with `structuralEq` where `pathProps` goes through `compareTruth` with an op-table
dispatch, so the comparison route looked like the missing 35 ns. It is not: for `op === '='`,
`compareTruth` is a nullish check, two string compares on the op, and then **`structuralEq` itself**
— the same function. A few nanoseconds, not thirty-five. Reading the function was enough; no arm was
built. (A stand-in micro-benchmark of the two _shapes_ read 1.2 against 1.5 ns, which agreed — but
that is a stand-in, not the functions, so it is reported as corroboration and not as the reason.)

### What is left, and why it is not being taken

The only remaining lever of size is the **representation**: records are a `Map` subclass, and a
plain-object read is 4-7x cheaper (item 899). That is priced and deliberately not attempted —
`LenkeRecord` is a `Map` subclass _specifically_ so a record is distinguishable from a graph element
and a plain object, it keeps keys sorted for canonical JSON, and it is shared by both engines and
every codec where byte-identity with the native `Value::Map` is a hard invariant.

A 2-segment specialization of `pathOf` (no loop, no array indexing) would be worth perhaps 5-8 ns of
the 52 — about 1.1x, which this repo's own rule puts at the boundary where a change "needs its own
isolated harness". Not worth a bespoke harness against a thread that is otherwise closed. Named here
so the next reader does not re-derive it.

### Verification

No engine change: one audit entry and two CLOSED lines. Numbers from
`packages/native/nested-read-ladder-probe.ts`, unchanged.

## Item 905 — equivalent spellings do NOT cost the same to PLAN: 4.4x for one predicate

MEASUREMENT (TS), one probe added; no engine change. This engine is named for a defect class —
equivalent spellings costing differently — and has a probe for it (`bun run spelling`, which has
earned itself twice). That probe measures RUNTIME only. Nothing had looked at planning cost, and
item 883's one figure for "the TS planner" (~1.02 us) was taken on a single INSERT.

### First: the planner is not one number, it is a shape

| shape                | chars | parse us | compile us | compile share |
| -------------------- | ----- | -------- | ---------- | ------------- |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN n` | 18    | 1.162    | **2.653**  | 70%           |
| the INSERT           | 47    | 2.184    | 0.531      | 20%           |
| the big MATCH        | 158   | 7.030    | **9.500**  | 57%           |

**A MATCH plans for 18x what a longer INSERT does**, and the simplest possible MATCH plans for 2.65
us — so this is shape, not size. Item 883's figure was the INSERT, which is the cheap case; it
understated the MATCH case by that factor. (Exactly the lesson item 902 had just recorded about
single-shape attributions, arriving again two items later.)

### Then: three spellings of ONE predicate, 4.4x apart

Against a shared no-predicate control, median of 11 with the warm-up dropped, min of three
ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds:

| spelling               | compile us | over control |
| ---------------------- | ---------- | ------------ |
| control, no predicate  | 2.641      | —            |
| inline `{k: 1}`        | 3.050      | **+0.409**   |
| inline `WHERE n.k = 1` | 3.662      | **+1.021**   |
| clause `WHERE n.k = 1` | 4.434      | **+1.793**   |

And with two predicates: inline `{k: 1, j: 2}` +0.822, clause `WHERE … AND …` **+3.124**, i.e. 3.8x.

Disjoint: the clause arm's fastest round (4.43) is above the inline arm's slowest (3.52).

**The third spelling is what makes this a decomposition rather than a complaint.** The cost splits
in two:

- expressing the predicate as an EXPRESSION rather than a property constraint — inline `{k: 1}` to
  inline `WHERE`, **+0.61 us**
- then putting that expression in CLAUSE position — inline `WHERE` to clause `WHERE`, **+0.77 us**

So neither half dominates, and a fix aimed only at `pushWhereIntoNode` would address about half of
it.

### Why it matters, in the units that reach a user

Item 883 measured a parse+plan cache MISS at ~5.9 us more than a hit. About **2 us of that — a
third — is the clause spelling's extra planning for a single predicate**, and dynamically-built
query text misses every time. Item 231 closed the RUNTIME gap for this exact pair (9.64 ms against
6.78 on a filtered projection); the compile gap sat unmeasured behind it.

### Not fixed here

The two halves point at different code — one at how a property constraint is represented against a
compiled expression, the other at `pushWhereIntoNode` and the clause compiler — and the planner is
on the path every query takes, so each wants its own item with its own controls. Named, priced from
three spellings, and left. `compile-spelling-probe.ts` makes it reproducible and is indexed by
question in `examples/README.md`.

A note on what the probe is: like `spelling-probe.ts`, time is its only signal, so a threshold in CI
would be flaky. It is a probe to run when touching `pushWhereIntoNode`, `directEqProps` or the clause
compiler — and the place to add any new spelling pair.

### Verification

No engine change: one probe and two documents. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run
fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0 — each its own command with its exit code read
UNPIPED.

## Item 906 — `pushWhereIntoNode` is NOT the clause spelling's compile cost: disabling it is 1.20x WORSE

Item 905 split the clause-vs-inline planning gap in two and named the clause half (+0.77 us, inline
`WHERE` to clause `WHERE`) as its own item. The obvious suspect is `pushWhereIntoNode`: it runs for
the clause spelling and has nothing to do for the inline one. It is the wrong suspect.

Ablated to `return clause` immediately — **answer-equivalent**, since the predicate then stays a
clause filter and is applied there, only later and more often at run time:

| spelling              | with the push | push DISABLED |
| --------------------- | ------------- | ------------- |
| control, no predicate | 2.641         | 2.728         |
| inline `{k: 1}`       | 3.050         | 3.036         |
| inline `WHERE`        | 3.662         | 3.474         |
| **clause `WHERE`**    | **4.434**     | **5.336**     |

**Disabling it makes the clause spelling 1.20x worse to compile.** Pushing a predicate into the node
is cheaper to PLAN than leaving it as a clause filter — on top of being much cheaper to RUN, which is
what the function was added for (items 127/128/285 record 1.44x and 15.8x there). So it is part of
the mitigation, not the cost.

That leaves item 905's +0.77 us as the clause-level handling itself — `checkLinearScope` over the
clause, the clause's own `where` plumbing, and the push — rather than any one function worth
attacking. Recorded next to `pushWhereIntoNode` so the obvious attack is not re-attempted.

### A note on the ablation's own validity

The arm is wrong code only in the performance sense: `return clause` preserves the answer, because a
clause filter and a node predicate differ in WHEN the predicate runs and not in what it decides
(item 128's comment makes the same argument for the free-variable case). So this is one of the rare
ablations whose arm could ship — which is exactly why its result is trustworthy as a cost
attribution rather than only as a ceiling.

### Verification

No engine change: one rejection comment and two documents. The ablated tree was restored and
verified byte-identical before anything else ran.

## Item 907 — the planner's bulk is ONE node pattern: 1.714 us of a 2.35 us simplest MATCH

Item 905 found the TS planner is a shape rather than a number (a MATCH plans for 18x a longer
INSERT) and split the clause-vs-inline gap; item 906 refuted the obvious suspect for the clause
half. Neither asked the larger question: what does the 2.35 us of the SIMPLEST possible MATCH
consist of? A stage ladder answers it, each rung adding one stage, min of three ORDER-ALTERNATED
rounds:

| case                           | compile us |
| ------------------------------ | ---------- |
| `RETURN 1`                     | 0.637      |
| `RETURN 1 + 2`                 | 0.887      |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN 1`           | **2.352**  |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN n`           | 2.693      |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN n.k`         | 2.995      |
| `MATCH (n) MATCH (m) RETURN 1` | 3.197      |

| stage                     | us             |
| ------------------------- | -------------- |
| **one bare node pattern** | **+1.714**     |
| projecting the variable   | +0.341         |
| a SECOND match clause     | +0.43 to +0.85 |

**Compiling one bare node pattern is 1.714 us — 73% of the simplest MATCH's total, and larger than
either half of item 905's clause-vs-inline gap (+0.61 and +0.77).** It is the planner's dominant
cost and nothing had isolated it.

### The second pattern costs half the first

`MATCH (n) MATCH (m) RETURN 1` adds only **+0.43 to +0.85 us** over `MATCH (n) RETURN 1` across two
runs of the ladder — between a half and a quarter of what the first pattern cost (+1.71 to +1.88 over
the same runs). The RANGE is quoted rather than one run's figure because the two runs disagree on the
size while agreeing on the direction, and the direction is the finding. A bare node carries no properties, no `WHERE` and no label, so
`compilePredicate` returns an empty predicate either way and there is no per-pattern work that
could differ. That asymmetry therefore points at **per-query setup inside the first `match`
compile** rather than at per-pattern work — and it is the thread to pull, because a one-time cost
paid per compile is exactly what a cache miss pays.

### Not attributed further here, deliberately

Naming the next step precisely rather than guessing at it: the candidates are what `compileMatch`
builds around the pattern (the matcher closure, any `orient`-related precomputation) and
`checkLinearScope`, and separating them needs instrumentation inside `compileMatch` rather than more
query shapes — the query ladder has given all it can. Three items this window went wrong by
attributing from a reading plus one shape (900, 901, 902), so this one stops at the measurement and
says what instrument the next tick needs.

The rungs are now in `compile-spelling-probe.ts`, so the numbers are reproducible rather than
quoted.

### Verification

No engine change: probe rungs and two documents. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run
fmt` 0.

## Item 908 — the planner, attributed: `checkLinearScope` is 15-19% of every compile, and the match arm is only 25% of a node pattern

Item 907 localised the planner's bulk to one node pattern (+1.7-1.9 us, 73% of the simplest MATCH)
and said the next instrument had to be inside `compileMatch` rather than more query shapes. It is,
and it moves the answer twice.

### The match-clause arm is NOT where a node pattern's cost goes

Accumulating time inside each stage (one `performance.now()` pair per compile, small against 1.7 us):

| stage                                               | `MATCH (n) RETURN 1` |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| total                                               | 2.489                |
| the WHOLE `case 'match'` arm (patterns + prefilter) | **0.466**            |
| of which `compilePath`                              | 0.342                |
| of which `seedPrefilter`                            | 0.026                |
| `compileNode` (measured separately)                 | 0.148                |
| `patternVarSets`                                    | 0.152                |

Adding `MATCH (n)` costs ~1.83 us and **the entire match-clause arm is 0.466 of it — 25%.**
`compileNode` is 0.148, i.e. **9%**. So three-quarters of what item 907 called "one node pattern" is
not the pattern compiler, and the two obvious suspects are both small. Had I attributed from the
ladder plus a reading, I would have aimed at `compileNode` and found nothing — which is the trap
items 900-902 fell into three times.

### Where it does go: a consistent 15-19% is eager VALIDATION

| query                                  | total | `checkLinearScope` | `compileLinear` | other |
| -------------------------------------- | ----- | ------------------ | --------------- | ----- |
| `RETURN 1`                             | 0.708 | 0.109 (15%)        | 0.509           | 0.091 |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN 1`                   | 2.313 | 0.428 (18%)        | 1.792           | 0.093 |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN n`                   | 2.702 | 0.507 (19%)        | 2.062           | 0.133 |
| big (hop + 3 predicates + ORDER/LIMIT) | 8.453 | **1.428 (17%)**    | 6.812           | 0.214 |

`compile`'s first act is `for (const part of query.parts) checkLinearScope(part.clauses, new Set())`
— an eager pass that faults on a reference to an unbound variable at COMPILE time rather than
returning a silent null at run time (matching the native engine and ISO). It is **15-19% of planning
across every shape**, 1.43 us on the big query, and it is a SECOND walk over the clause list that
`compileLinear` then walks again.

That is the target: not "make validation cheaper" — it has to happen — but **one walk instead of
two**. The share is remarkably flat across shapes, which is what makes it worth having rather than a
single-fixture artifact.

Within `compileLinear`, the residual is also not the pattern: for `MATCH (n) RETURN 1` it is 1.792
against `RETURN 1`'s 0.509, and only 0.466 of that increase is the match arm. The rest is the
clause-list machinery and the RETURN side compiling with a variable in scope — named, not yet
attributed, and deliberately not guessed at.

### Not fixed here

Fusing validation into the compile walk changes when a scope error is raised relative to other
compile-time faults (`compile` also raises `E_UNKNOWN_FUNCTION` eagerly, after `compileLinear`), and
this engine's error ORDER is observable and compared against native. So it needs its own item, with
the fault-ordering question settled first and a test that pins which error wins when a query has
both. Named, priced at 15-19%, and left.

### A trap that bit again, two items after it was recorded

Item 897 recorded that **`systemd-run` performs `${...}` expansion on the command it runs**, so an
inline `bun -e` using `${…}` is corrupted. It bit again here — the percentage columns of the first
run came back blank, with a warning naming the expression it had eaten. Harmless this time (the raw
numbers were in other columns) but the same shape as 897's silent 200,000-node fixture collapsing to
one node. **The lesson that recording a trap does not stop it: put the code in a FILE.**

### Verification

No engine change: all instrumentation was applied to a scratch copy, the tree restored and verified
byte-identical, and the dist rebuilt from the restored source. One audit entry and two CLOSED lines.

## Item 909 — `checkLinearScope` copied the whole scope per MATCH clause: 1.48x at 48 clauses, and my first fixture hid it

Item 908 priced `checkLinearScope` at 15-19% of every compile and proposed fusing it with
`compileLinear` — one walk instead of two. Before restructuring a central function, I looked inside
it, which is the method's own order (diagnose before assuming). The waste was smaller and more
local than a fused walk:

```ts
case 'match': {
  const withPat = new Set(scope);                        // a full COPY of the visible scope
  for (const v of patternVars(clause.patterns)) withPat.add(v);
  if (clause.where) checkExprScope(clause.where, withPat);
  for (const v of withPat) scope.add(v);                 // iterate the WHOLE copy back in
}
```

**The copy bought nothing.** `scope` ends up as `scope ∪ patternVars` either way — that is what the
copy-back did — and the clause `WHERE` has to see exactly that set, so adding the pattern's
variables to `scope` directly and checking against `scope` is the same two facts without the
allocation or the second pass. (The one behavioural difference is unobservable: if `checkExprScope`
throws, the old code left `scope` without the pattern's variables. A throw aborts the compile, so
nothing reads it.)

### My first A/B said 1.01x, and the fixture was the problem

| case                        | pre   | post  | ratio  |
| --------------------------- | ----- | ----- | ------ |
| `RETURN 1` (control)        | 0.662 | 0.709 | 0.934x |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN 1`        | 2.243 | 2.214 | 1.013x |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.k = 1` | 4.390 | 4.347 | 1.010x |
| big                         | 7.181 | 7.278 | 0.987x |

Every arm inside the noise, with the control moving more than any target — a textbook refutation.
**It was wrong, and for a reason this repo already has a rule about.** The removed work is a Set copy
whose cost scales with SCOPE SIZE, and every one of those fixtures has one to three variables. "Match
the fixture to the claim": a per-edge cost scales with the edge:node ratio and a per-node cost does
not, and here a per-scope-entry cost was measured against an empty scope.

### With a fixture whose scope is big enough

`n` MATCH clauses each binding one variable, so clause `i` copies an `(i-1)`-element scope:

| case                 | pre    | post   | ratio                                                |
| -------------------- | ------ | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `RETURN 1` (control) | 0.733  | 0.839  | 0.874x (noisy — a 0.8 us measurement)                |
| chain 1              | 2.857  | 2.794  | 1.023x                                               |
| chain 8              | 7.813  | 7.189  | 1.087x                                               |
| chain 24             | 24.420 | 19.905 | **1.227x**                                           |
| chain 48             | 53.169 | 35.888 | **1.482x, DISJOINT** (pre 53.2-56.3, post 35.9-38.2) |

**And the saving is quadratic in the clause count, as the mechanism requires.** The delta is 4.52 ms
at 24 clauses and 17.28 at 48 — a factor of **3.8 for twice the clauses**, against the 4.0 that a
`Σi` copy predicts. That agreement is what makes this an attribution rather than a number: the shape
of the curve matches the shape of the removed work.

So the honest claim is conditional: **nothing at 1-3 variables (1.01-1.02x), 1.09x at 8 clauses,
1.23x at 24, 1.48x at 48.** A 48-clause query is rare; 8-24 is ordinary for generated query text, and
the change is strictly less work at every size.

### Teeth

Two mutants, both CAUGHT decisively by the existing suite:

| mutant                                                    | verdict               |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| check the clause `WHERE` BEFORE adding the pattern's vars | CAUGHT, **813** fail  |
| never add the pattern's vars to `scope`                   | CAUGHT, **1814** fail |

The scope checker's semantics are the most-exercised thing in the GQL suite, which is why the
failure counts are in the hundreds — and why the equivalence argument above is worth more than a new
test would be.

### The probe keeps the fixture that found it

`compile-spelling-probe.ts` gains a `scope SIZE` group, so the next change to the scope checker is
measured against a scope large enough to see one. A null result from a fixture that cannot express
the cost is worse than no measurement, because it reads as a refutation.

### Item 908's fusion proposal is NOT what shipped

Fusing the two walks is still open and still wants the fault-ordering question settled. This is the
cheaper half, taken first because it needed no restructuring and no decision about which error wins.

### Verification

`bun test packages/gql` 2723 pass, gremlin 828, core 370, all 0 fail. All seven byte-identity
fuzzers pass. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun
run check` 0.

## Item 910 — 41% of planning is plan-shape DETECTION and REWRITING, not compilation

MEASUREMENT (TS); no engine change. Item 908 attributed `checkLinearScope` (15-19%) and found the
match-clause arm was only 25% of a node pattern, leaving most of `compileLinear` unexplained. This
splits `compileLinear` three ways.

| query                                  | total | rewrite pipeline | `compileClause` | **19 detectors** |
| -------------------------------------- | ----- | ---------------- | --------------- | ---------------- |
| `RETURN 1`                             | 0.827 | 0.131            | 0.362           | 0.080            |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN 1`                   | 2.429 | 0.436            | 0.918           | **0.414 (17%)**  |
| `MATCH (n) RETURN n`                   | 2.621 | 0.541            | 0.989           | 0.452            |
| big (hop + 3 predicates + ORDER/LIMIT) | 7.779 | **1.259 (16%)**  | 2.909           | **1.955 (25%)**  |

### The 19 detectors are a quarter of planning the big query

`compileLinear` ends by running **nineteen independent compile-time probes** —
`detectVarLengthCount`, `detectCountShortcut`, … `detectGroupedHopAggregate` — and its own comment
is explicit that this is not a ladder: _"EVERY detector RUNS … nineteen independent compile-time
probes, not a ladder."_ They are what let the executor answer a recognised shape with a fast path
instead of the general pipeline, and they are measured here for the first time: **1.955 us, 25% of
planning the big query**, and 0.414 (17%) for the simplest MATCH.

Several open with a cheap `clauses.length` guard and bail — but the big query is a 2-clause
`MATCH … RETURN`, which is exactly the length those guards admit, so most proceed to real shape
inspection.

### And the rewrite pipeline is another 16%

`compileLinear` opens with ten nested clause-list transformations —
`dropVacuousQuantifier` → `dropVacuousPage` → `dropUnreadGroupBinds` → `unoptionalizeForAggregate`
→ `inlineTrailingFilter` → `inlineAggregateCall` → `inlineTrailingLet` → `inlineCorrelatedCall`
→ `fuseAnchorThenHop` → `liftStartProps` — each walking the list it is handed. **1.259 us, 16%.**

That is the same shape as item 909's finding and item 908's fusion proposal: **N separate walks over
one small clause list.** Three independent measurements now point at it — `checkLinearScope`'s second
walk (908), the scope copy per clause (909, fixed), and ten rewrite walks plus nineteen detector
walks here.

So: **~41% of planning the big query is shape detection and rewriting**, with `compileClause` — the
thing that actually builds the plan — at 37%.

### Why no change in this tick

The obvious fix is a precomputed shape summary the detectors consult instead of each re-walking. It
is a refactor across nineteen functions in a 7,000-line file, and the failure mode is the one this
repo warns about most sharply: **a wrong summary silently DISABLES a shortcut.** That is
answer-equivalent — right answer, slow route — so no correctness test can see it, and only a route
assertion at the call site has teeth (items 866/867/876, and item 888's `toLowerCase`-counting
assertion is the pattern to copy).

So the prerequisite is a route assertion per detector — "this query shape still takes this
shortcut" — before any sharing is introduced. That is its own item, and a bigger one than the
measurement. Named, priced at 25%, and left with the instrument that found it.

The rewrite pipeline has the same prerequisite for a different reason: the ten transformations
compose in a documented order (`inlineAggregateCall` runs INSIDE `inlineTrailingLet` so the `LET` it
produces is itself inlined), so fusing walks means preserving a fixed-point order that the current
nesting expresses structurally.

### Verification

No engine change: all instrumentation was applied to a scratch copy, the tree restored and verified
byte-identical, and the dist rebuilt from the restored source. One audit entry and two CLOSED lines.

## Item 911 — route assertions for all nineteen detectors, and the pre-existing coverage was UNEVEN

Item 910 priced the nineteen compile-time detectors at 25% of planning the big query and named "a
route assertion per detector" as the prerequisite for sharing work between them — because the
failure mode of that refactor is a shape summary that silently stops a shortcut firing. This is that
prerequisite, and building it corrected my own claim about why it was needed.

### The instrument

`compileLinear` is now exported from `executor.ts` — **not** from `index.ts`, so the package's public
surface is unchanged. That is the pattern three existing tests already use (`predFor`,
`selectiveFirst`, `invertedHopBudget` are all imported from internal modules). `routes-fired.test.ts`
calls it and reads which of the nineteen detector fields came back non-null; that list IS the route.

### A firing spelling for all nineteen, four of which had to be read rather than guessed

Thirteen fell out of obvious shapes. The rest needed their guards read:

- `varLengthCount` wants a BOUNDED quantifier — `->{1,3}` fires it, `->*` does not.
- `forCount` / `forProjection` want ≥3 clauses with the `FOR` second-to-last over a **property**
  list; `FOR x IN [1,2,3]` fires nothing.
- `multiNodeAggregate` / `multiHopAggregate` want ≥2 projection items — one aggregate goes to
  `nodeAggregate`/`hopAggregate` instead.
- `groupHopShortcut` fires only on the FAR key (`RETURN b.k, count(*)`); the NEAR key gets
  `groupedHopAggregate` alone.

27 tests, including a meta-assertion that the covered set equals all nineteen fields — so a detector
added later without a route case fails here rather than going unguarded. Five negative cases pin the
other direction, because a detector that starts firing on a shape it does not handle answers it with
the wrong closure: a wrong ANSWER, not a slow one.

### My reason for building it was overstated, and the measured answer is more useful

I wrote that no correctness test can see a disabled detector. Measured — each detector disabled in
turn, the gql suite run with this file REMOVED:

| disabled               | pre-existing suite     |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `detectCountShortcut`  | **CAUGHT, 4 failures** |
| `detectNodeProjection` | **SURVIVED**           |

So the coverage was **partial and incidental**, not absent. Two tests ("a both-ends-constrained count
seeds its tally", "the sweep is BOUNDED in the path count") happen to assert something only the count
shortcut produces; a dead `detectNodeProjection` was invisible to all 2,723 tests.

**The unevenness is the real hazard**, and it is worse than uniform absence would be: a refactor that
disables three detectors might fail loudly for one and silently for the other two, which reads as
"the suite caught my mistake" when it caught a third of it.

### An invalid comparison I had to redo

My first attempt compared "routes-fired" against "the whole gql suite" — but the suite INCLUDES the
new file, so the second number contained the first and the comparison was worthless (it reported
4 and 4 for `detectNodeProjection`, which looked like "the suite already covers this"). The honest
run removes the file and runs the rest. **A before/after over a suite that contains the "after" is
not a comparison**, and it is the same error shape as item 897's two-process arms: the thing under
test leaking into the baseline.

### Verification

`bun test packages/gql` 2750 pass (2723 plus the 27 new), 0 fail. `bun run typecheck` 0; `bun run
lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0. The mutation script restored `shortcuts.ts` and the tree
was verified to carry zero mutant markers before anything was committed.

## Item 912 — item 910's "detectors are 25% of planning" target is RETRACTED: 87% of it is one detector BUILDING the plan

Item 910 measured the nineteen compile-time detectors at 1.955 us — 25% of planning the big query —
and named a shared shape summary as the fix, with item 911's route assertions as the prerequisite.
The prerequisite is built. The target is not real, and pricing the variants is what showed it.

### Per detector, and it is not nineteen things

| detector                  | us               | share of the 19 |
| ------------------------- | ---------------- | --------------- |
| **`detectHopProjection`** | **1.7547**       | **70.8%**       |
| `detectVarLengthCount`    | 0.0589           | 2.4%            |
| `detectCountShortcut`     | 0.0490           | 2.0%            |
| …the other 16             | 0.032-0.047 each | 1.3-1.9% each   |

One detector is the whole thing; the other eighteen are a call plus a guard.

### And that one detector is not declining — it is FIRING

`hopProjection` **fires** for the big query (`routes-fired.test.ts`'s instrument says so directly).
So its cost is not expensive analysis that comes to nothing: it is the detector **building the
fast-path closure for the route it selected** — compiling the predicates, planning the order,
resolving the ends. That is plan construction, work `compileClause` would otherwise have to do, and
calling it "planning spent on detection" was wrong.

Re-measured with TWO timer pairs rather than nineteen, so the instrument is not most of what it
reports:

| query                                            | total | all 19 | `hopProjection` | **the other 18** |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----- | ------ | --------------- | ---------------- |
| big (`hopProjection` FIRES)                      | 7.703 | 2.098  | **1.823 (87%)** | **0.275**        |
| `MATCH (a:L)-[:R]->(b:L) RETURN b.k` (fires)     | 3.433 | 0.571  | 0.244           | 0.326            |
| `MATCH (n:L) RETURN count(*)` (hopProj DECLINES) | 3.001 | 0.472  | **0.042**       | 0.430            |
| `RETURN 1` (nothing fires)                       | 1.168 | 0.150  | 0.030           | 0.120            |

**The shareable part is 0.275-0.430 us — 3.6% to 14% of a compile, not 25%.** And `detectHopProjection`
declines for **0.042 us** when it does not apply, so it is already well guarded; there is no
expensive-and-fruitless probe to fix.

### So the refactor is refuted before it was written

A shape summary shared across nineteen functions in a 7,000-line file, whose failure mode is a
silently disabled shortcut, for a ceiling of 3.6-14% — and the realistic capture is a fraction of
that, since each of the eighteen still has to be called and still has to decide. Not worth it.
**Item 910's target is withdrawn**, and `CLOSED.md` says so where the target was recorded.

Item 911 is not wasted by this: the route assertions guard nineteen answer-equivalent routes that
were unevenly covered (one of the two mutants I tried survived the whole pre-existing suite), and
that is worth having whether or not anyone refactors the detectors.

### The method note

910 priced the detectors **as a block** and reasoned about the block. Pricing the VARIANTS — the
loop's own first instruction — showed 87% of the block is one member, and that member is productive.
**A block measurement invites a block-shaped fix.** Same lesson as item 902's table-across-spellings,
one level up: the unit you measure in determines the fix you reach for.

### Verification

No engine change: all instrumentation was applied to a scratch copy, the tree restored and verified
byte-identical, and the dist rebuilt from the restored source. `bun test packages/gql` 2750 pass,
0 fail.

## Item 913 — five "open" targets in the index were already superseded by later items

Housekeeping, no engine change — but the kind this repo treats as load-bearing. `CLOSED.md` exists
to answer "what is genuinely open", and its own rule is that **a list that lags is the failure it
exists to prevent.** Reading the open entries end to end, five of them were stated in units or
framings that later items in this same window retracted:

| entry                                                                  | superseded by | why                                                                                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 883 — "the TS parser is 4.5x native's and the planner 12.6x"           | 887, 905      | both halves restated: the per-character denominator was wrong, and "the planner" is a SHAPE — 883's figure is the INSERT, and a MATCH plans for 18x it |
| 884 — "~3x native's PER CHARACTER"                                     | 887           | the per-character MODEL was retracted; `ns/char` spans 1.93x on a length-matched pair where `ns/token` is flat to 1.01x                                |
| 885 — "remaining ~20 ns a character"                                   | 887           | stated in the retracted unit                                                                                                                           |
| 886 — "remaining ~13 ns a character"                                   | 887           | same                                                                                                                                                   |
| 907 — "the planner's bulk is ONE node pattern, look in `compileMatch`" | 908, 910, 912 | 908 showed the match ARM is 25% of that figure and `compileNode` 9%; 912 retracted the detector target                                                 |

Each is now marked `SUPERSEDED` or `REFINED` with a pointer to the item that moved it, **and the
original note is kept** — the measurements are still valid, it is the framing that moved. The
distinction matters: 884's numbers are good data in a bad denominator, and deleting them would lose
the data to fix the denominator.

### Why this is worth a tick

This window alone produced three mis-attributions (900→901→902) and one retracted target (910→912).
Every one of them left a line in the index that reads as a live target to the next reader. **The
index decays fastest exactly when the work is going well**, because each tick that corrects a
framing leaves the superseded framing behind it. Reading the whole open list after a run of items —
rather than only appending to it — is the maintenance that keeps "check the list before measuring"
worth doing.

Concretely: a reader picking a target from this index before this tick would have found four entries
telling them to optimize the TS parser per CHARACTER, a unit item 887 refuted.

### Verification

Doc-only. `bun run fmt:check` 0.

## Item 915 — a regression check that came back clean, and a bench whose "best recorded" is an outlier

This window shipped eight engine changes, three of them in the GQL executor (903's `pathProps`,
909's scope copy, 911's export). The instruction asks for regression checking, and `bench:usage`
appeared to show one.

### What looked like a regression

`read: point lookup` ts(+) read **885.4k ops/s**, against values recorded in this file of 956.0k →
1.08M, 1.15M, and **1.29M "best recorded"**. Below the whole range. And 903 added a
`pred.pathProps !== undefined` check to `matchesPredicate`, which is on exactly that path — a
plausible mechanism, which is what makes a number like this worth taking seriously rather than
shrugging at.

### It is the bench's own noise

Three consecutive runs of the SAME build: **885.4k, 1.04M, 890.4k** — a 1.17x spread. `write: 100
updates in one statement` in the same three runs: 969.7k, 774.8k, 973.6k — **1.26x**. So this bench
cannot resolve a 1.2x question about itself, and its highest figures are labelled "best recorded",
i.e. the top of a noisy distribution.

### The isolated A/B, which can resolve it

`pre` is item 902's tree (before `pathProps`, the scope change and the export), `post` is current.
The arm assertion is on the **application loop** rather than the word `pathProps`, because 902's
rejection comment mentions the word four times and would not distinguish the arms:

| arm  | three ORDER-ALTERNATED rounds | best       | median | spread |
| ---- | ----------------------------- | ---------- | ------ | ------ |
| pre  | 1842019 / 1839484 / 1842823   | 1.843M     | 1.842M | 1.002x |
| post | 1943773 / 1774637 / 1808282   | **1.944M** | 1.808M | 1.095x |

**No regression.** `post`'s best exceeds `pre`'s best and its median is within 2%; the post arm is
simply noisier in this run. 903's extra check does not show.

### The thing worth keeping

**This probe reads ~1.8M ops/s where `bench:usage` reads ~0.9-1.0M for the same operation.** The
difference is that bench's own per-operation harness. So its numbers are comparable to ITSELF and
are not an engine figure — and quoting its "best recorded" as a baseline is how a noisy instrument
manufactures a regression. `point-lookup-probe.ts` is kept with all of that written down, because I
nearly drew the wrong conclusion from the bench and the next reader will have the same numbers in
front of them.

### An assertion that earned itself immediately

The probe asserts its own row count, and the first run failed it: `got 28000 rows, expected 2000`.
My expectation was wrong, not the fixture — `sink` accumulates across all fourteen reps, so the
total is `OPS * REPS`. Worth noting because the assert was doing precisely its job: a point lookup
