## Item 930 — a SECOND `has()` after a hop fell off the count shortcut: **4.73-4.85x** on the Gremlin surface, and this file's own ORACLE had to be rebuilt to see it

**SHIPPED** (`executor/count-shortcut.ts`), plus two probes and a test-oracle repair that matters
more than the speedup. Item 929 closed with a named next step: its 1.71x cross-surface gap on the
filtered hop is "GQL's per-row filter path generally", and that is a LOCATION, not a mechanism. This
decomposes it.

### The decomposition, and why the obvious one was unavailable

The natural instrument is `hop + filter` minus `hop alone`. **It does not exist:** item 929 measured
that an unfiltered edge count is answered O(1) on BOTH surfaces — 0.00 vs 0.01 ms at 200k/600k and
again at 800k/2,400,000 — so there is no hop-alone reading to subtract. Item 926 hit the same wall on
the node scan and solved it with a `WHERE true` floor; the Gremlin surface has no `WHERE true`, so
that fix does not carry.

So instead: **hold the hop constant and vary the number of conjuncts.** The per-conjunct slope is the
per-row predicate cost and the residual is everything else, which makes "filter or hop?" two
distinguishable outcomes rather than one ratio. Every conjunct is TRUE for every row (`k = i % 50`
against `> -1`, `> -2`, …) for two reasons, both load-bearing: AND short-circuits on FALSE in written
order (items 258/259), so a ladder of RESTRICTIVE conjuncts would measure selectivity rather than
predicate cost; and the bounds are DISTINCT so neither planner can dedupe the ladder to one test and
report a free filter. Both are asserted — every arm must answer 600,000 rows, and a mutant that made
the bounds restrictive was confirmed to fail that assertion (`kept 456000 rows, expected 600000`).

### It is a CLIFF, not a slope — `hop-filter-ladder-probe.ts`, 4 order-alternated rounds

| conj | gql med |    grm med |     ratio | gql rounds / grm rounds           |
| ---: | ------: | ---------: | --------: | --------------------------------- |
|    1 |   57.24 |      26.74 |     2.14x | [57 58 57 55] / [27 27 26 27]     |
|    2 |   62.13 | **247.36** | **0.25x** | [62 64 62 61] / [248 243 247 269] |
|    3 |   66.97 |     249.99 |     0.27x | [64 67 67 68] / [257 252 247 248] |
|    4 |   70.21 |     264.22 |     0.27x | [70 68 74 71] / [264 265 261 264] |

**The gap INVERTS.** GQL is 2.14x slower at one conjunct and 4x FASTER at two, because Gremlin pays a
**+220.62 ms step** between one and two filters (then +8.43 ms/conjunct) where GQL pays **+4.89 ms**
(then +4.04). A step that large with a flat floor on both sides of it is a ROUTE being lost, not a
cost being added — so the thing to find was which rung, not which instruction.

### Diagnosis by reading, then confirmed by measuring — `hop-filter-route-map-probe.ts`

`countShortcut` strips the source and terminal `count`, leaving `mid`, and tries rungs in order;
the hop+filter rung sat behind `if (mid.length !== 2) return undefined;`. For
`V().hasLabel(P).out(E).has(k,p)` that is reachable only if `hasLabel` is folded into the source,
leaving `[out, has]` — and a second `has` makes it three and falls off the end of every rung.

| shape                                              |        ms | what it decides                  |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------: | -------------------------------- |
| `V().hasLabel(P).out(E).has(k,>-1)`                |      25.6 | the fast arm                     |
| `V().hasLabel(P).out(E).has(k,>-1).has(k,>-2)`     | **285.4** | **11.15x** — off the cliff       |
| `V().out(E).has(k,>-1)`                            |      28.2 | `hasLabel` IS folded away        |
| `V().hasLabel(P).has(k,>-1).has(k,>-2)`            |       6.0 | a 2-chain with no hop stays fast |
| `V().hasLabel(P).has(k,>-1).has(k,>-2).has(k,>-3)` |       6.7 | and any length, likewise         |

**So the arity limit was the whole cause and there was no semantic obstacle:** `filterChainCount`
had been folding an arbitrary-length chain for the no-hop shape since it was written. Grepping the
siblings says the same from the other side — `startFilteredHopCount` already folds an arbitrary
chain of filters BEFORE the hop (`mid.slice(0, -1)`). Only the post-hop side was gated. Fixed by
teaching `filteredHopCount` a chain and letting the call site pass `mid.slice(1)`; it returns
`undefined` unless every step after the hop is a `has`, so `dedupe` still reaches `distinctHopCount`.

### THE ORACLE THIS FILE RESTS ON WAS SILENTLY DESTROYED BY THE FIX

This is the part worth keeping. `count-shortcut.test.ts` tests a route CHOICE, which is
answer-equivalent, so its whole design is a **forced decline**: run the same question with a step the
shortcut does not recognise and compare. For the hop rungs it forced that decline by **duplicating
the filter** — `out('E'), has('k', gt(1)), has('k', gt(1))` — answer-equivalent because the predicate
is idempotent, and effective because it pushed `mid.length` past the arity gate.

**That is exactly the shape this item taught the rung to absorb.** After the change, all **10**
`declined(...)` comparisons in the file were the shortcut against ITSELF, and the suite stayed green
at 828 pass — because both sides had moved to the same route. Nothing failed; the oracle just stopped
being one. Found by reading the helper, not by any test going red.

Repaired with `identity()`, a step `countShortcut` does not model at all and so cannot be absorbed by
a future widening of which FILTERS are foldable. **RULE: an oracle built from a shape the optimizer is
allowed to learn will eventually stop being an oracle, and it fails SILENTLY — green, comparing one
route to itself.** Items 921 and 923 are the same failure from the other side (a corpus that does not
construct the dangerous case; a size gate that hid the code it guarded). This is the third instance
this session and the first where the optimization itself was what disarmed the test.

### A stale claim in the code, corrected by the mutation run

The comment above `filteredHopCount` justified its raise-parity argument with "`matches` can throw (a
cross-type comparison, mirroring TinkerPop's `ClassCastException`)". **It cannot.** Every ordering
predicate in `predicates.ts` reads `value != null && predCmp(...) > 0` and `predCmp` returns `NaN`
for a cross-type pair, so an incomparable value is FILTERED. The test file had already discovered
this and says so in a comment — "two tests were written asserting a throw, both failed" — so the
source and the tests had disagreed for some time. Corrected in place; the evaluated-set argument it
invoked the throw for is the real content and stands on its own.

This changed the change: my first version of `allMatch` claimed its written-order short-circuit was
load-bearing for raise parity. It is not observable at all here, and the mutation run was made to
prove that rather than assert it.

### Mutation, under `timeout 600` + `MemoryMax=16G` + `MemorySwapMax=0`

Harness proven to kill first: an allocator bomb exits 137 and a bare `for(;;)` exits 124. Pristine
copy under `target/`, restored BEFORE each mutant and verified byte-identical after.

```text
  m1-always-true         CAUGHT (17 fail)      the fold does nothing
  m2-first-only          CAUGHT  (4 fail)      pre-change behaviour smuggled back in
  m3-last-only           CAUGHT  (1 fail)      only the last filter applies
  m4-or-not-and          CAUGHT  (4 fail)      OR instead of AND
  m5-wrong-key           CAUGHT  (1 fail)      every predicate read against filters[0].key
  m6-accept-any-step     CAUGHT (21 fail)      has-only guard removed, dedupe loses its rung
  m7-no-short-circuit    SURVIVED (835 pass)   [PREDICTED — matches cannot throw]
```

m3 and m5 are caught by **1 failure each**, and both of those are tests added here — the
reversed-pair case and the two-different-keys case. Without them the fold could keep one filter and
pass. m7 surviving is the documented outcome, not a gap: with no predicate able to fault, evaluating
every filter is answer- AND fault-equivalent. A KILL there would have meant the comment was wrong.

| ------- | ---: | ------: | -------: | ---------: | ----------- |

and the arms share the process, fixture and machine. It held at 0.99-1.06x against a worst arm

**ARM ASSERTIONS EARNED THEMSELVES IMMEDIATELY.** The first A/B compared two bundles that turned out

null-A/B CLAUDE.md requires that check for.

### The single-filter REGRESSION, chased down to under the noise

The first POST read conj=1 at **0.88x — a real 1.14x regression** on the shape that matters most,
PRE [28 28 27 29] against POST [31 31 30 31], non-overlapping. Routing the common case through
`allMatch` cost it. Two attempts:

- **A `filters.length === 1` early return INSIDE `allMatch`** recovered almost nothing, 0.88x →
  0.91x. That **refuted the iterator-allocation guess** and left the per-vertex CALL as the cause.
- **Hoisting the branch out of the loop** — decide once, read `pred`/`key` from locals in the loop

The ladder cannot settle the residue: its conj≥2 arms are 250 ms and its conj=1 arms are 27 ms, so

independent A/B runs all put PRE ahead (0.88, 0.91, 0.93, 0.956), so it is probably a real small
cost rather than zero — but it is below what this instrument can resolve.

**REJECTED, with numbers: splitting `filteredHopCount` into a single-filter copy and a chain
sibling** to drive the residue to zero by construction. It would duplicate both the vertex-driven
and edge-driven loops (~60 lines) to chase an effect that cannot be measured even on a purpose-built

correct so it must be faster is not evidence" rule is about. The trade shipped instead: **4.7-4.9x on
two or more filters for an unresolvable ≤5% on one.**

### What this leaves open

- **Filters on BOTH sides of a hop still decline.** `V().has(x,p).out(E).has(k,q)` gives
  `mid = [has, out, has]`: `filteredHopCount` needs `mid[0]` to be the hop,
  `startFilteredHopCount` needs the hop LAST, and `filterChainCount` rejects the `out`. Neither
  half's chain-folding helps because the hop is in the middle. Named, not priced.
- **The Rust engine is unmeasured for this shape.** This item moved the TS Gremlin surface only. The
  native engine lowers both surfaces to one `ir::Plan`, so the question there is whether its own

## Item 931 — the RUST engine does NOT have item 930's hop+filter-chain cliff, and the `can_raise` merge decline costs nothing measurable

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change** (one probe added, `native-hop-filter-chain-probe.ts`). Item 930
fixed an 11.15x cliff on the TS Gremlin surface and named the obvious follow-up: the native engine
lowers both surfaces to one `ir::Plan`, so does its count fast-path carry a comparable arity gate?

### The hypothesis, which was specific enough to be wrong

The native engine cannot have 930's bug in 930's form — it dispatches on a `Plan`, not a step list.
But `peel_endpoint_filter` matches **exactly one** `Plan::Filter` whose predicate reads only the
endpoint slot, so two stacked filters would leave an inner one behind. What normally prevents that
is the optimizer's filter-merge rule, `Filter(Filter(x, p_inner), p_outer)` →
`Filter(x, p_outer AND p_inner)` — and **that merge is DECLINED when the OUTER predicate
`can_raise`**, because merged, both predicates are evaluated on every row arriving at the filter
(the `AND` is a vectorized three-valued fold, not control flow), so a raising outer predicate would
fault on rows the inner filter had removed.

`can_raise` is true for `Expr::Arith`, `Expr::Call`, `Expr::Cast` and anything containing one. So the
prediction was sharp: two ordinary endpoint conjuncts keep the fast path, and the same count with an
ARITHMETIC conjunct loses it — same answer, same work, different cost, which is the
equivalent-spelling shape this repo is named for.

**`b.j + b.k`, not `b.j + 0`**, deliberately: a foldable arithmetic expression is constant folded,
the `Arith` vanishes, and the probe would measure the merge happening rather than being declined.
Two slot reads cannot fold, and both properties are non-negative so every conjunct is true for every
row — each arm's answer is asserted (600,000 for the hop arms, 200,000 for the node arms).

### The result: 4 order-alternated rounds, 200,000 vertices / 600,000 edges

| arm                 | med ms | self-var | what it is                              |
| ------------------- | -----: | -------: | --------------------------------------- |
| `one`               |   0.81 |    1.02x | one endpoint filter                     |
| `two`               |   1.89 |    1.12x | two ordinary conjuncts (merge expected) |
| `three`             |   2.78 |    1.17x | three ordinary conjuncts                |
| `arith`             |   7.94 |    1.06x | arithmetic conjunct + ordinary          |
| `arithRev`          |   8.67 |    1.11x | the same pair, written the other way    |
| `arithOnly`         |   7.38 |    1.08x | the arithmetic conjunct ALONE           |
| `nodeTwo` CONTROL   |   0.72 |    1.12x | node scan, two ordinary conjuncts       |
| `nodeArith` CONTROL |   2.74 |    1.02x | node scan, arithmetic conjunct          |

**REFUTED, and the `arithOnly` control is what refutes it.** A single arithmetic filter involves no
merge at all, so it prices the arithmetic with the route held fixed:

```text
  ordinary conjunct                +1.08 ms   (two - one)
  the next ordinary conjunct       +0.89 ms   (three - two)
  arithmetic conjunct ALONE        +6.56 ms   (arithOnly - one)

  if no route is lost, arith ~= arithOnly + one conjunct =  8.45 ms
                       arith  measured                   =  7.94 ms   0.94x of prediction
                       arithRev measured                 =  8.67 ms   1.03x of prediction
```

Both land on the prediction, inside the 1.17x worst arm self-variance. **The arithmetic conjunct
costs what arithmetic costs and nothing extra is lost**, in either conjunct order — so the
`can_raise` decline, although real in the plan, has no measurable consequence for this shape. There
is no native twin of item 930's cliff.

**And the cost is the same on a path with no hop fast path to lose**, which is the second way of
seeing it: the arithmetic conjunct is **10.9 ns a row** on the hop (6.56 ms / 600,000) and
**10.1 ns a row** on the node control (2.02 ms / 200,000). Equal per row across two different
routes says the cost is the expression, not the route.

### Which re-derives item 437, and the record already says what to do about it

The by-product figure — an arithmetic conjunct at ~6.1x an ordinary one — is **not a new target.**
`CLOSED.md` has it twice:

- **Item 437** priced exactly this: one arithmetic node in a filter costs **5.7x** at identical
  selectivity, and diagnosed it as **MATERIALIZATION** — one column per expression node, four passes
  and three allocations against the fast path's one pass and none. It records two wrong guesses
  (**not** a per-row tree walk, since `eval` is columnar, and **not** boxing, since `Col` is typed
  and arith has a raw-f64 arm) and names the fix as expression **FUSION**.
- **Item 438** then built `try_filter_keep_arith` for `<prop> <arith> <lit> <cmp> <lit>` at 5.0x,
  and closes with "**still open and NOT more arm additions** — the answer there is fusion, per 437".

`b.j + b.k` is `<prop> <arith> <prop>`, which 438's arm does not admit, so it falls to the general
materializing path — which is why it reads 6.1x rather than landing on the plain comparison. **So
this adds one datum to 437 and opens nothing:** its 5.7x was measured on the NODE path with a
literal operand, and this shows the same cost, per row, on the HOP path with two property operands.
437's materialization diagnosis generalises; its fix is still fusion; and widening 438's pattern list
to admit a second property is exactly the arm addition 438 declined.

Recorded against the code it would have changed, per the standing rule, because the 6.1x is
genuinely tempting in isolation and this is the third time the arithmetic predicate has been
re-priced from a different direction (437 from the node path, 441 from the TS side, this from the
hop path).

### What this iteration spent and what it bought

One hypothesis refuted with its own control, one closed finding independently confirmed on a new
path, and one target correctly NOT re-opened. The cost of the re-derivation was real but small: the
arithmetic number fell out of a probe built for the merge question, and `CLOSED.md` was checked
before anything was priced off it rather than after — which is the order items 172/200 were got
wrong in.

### Verification

No engine change: one probe and its `package.json` script. Gates each its own command with its exit
code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0. Every arm asserts its
own row count (600,000 / 200,000) before a time is printed, and the analysis asserts 32 of 32
expected readings across 8 shapes and 4 rounds before computing any difference.

## Item 932 — a GENERATED cross-surface matrix over filter ARITY and POSITION: moving one of two filters across the hop costs **5.06x** (Gremlin) / **2.33x** (GQL)

**SCREEN + TOOLING, no engine change** (one probe added, `cross-surface-arity-probe.ts`,
`bun run probe:arity`). Item 930's 11.15x cliff was found by accident — item 929 had added an
edge-walking pair to `probe:surface` for an unrelated reason — and its cause is a shape a generator
can enumerate. This enumerates it.

### Why this axis, and why a generator at all

The TS engines are **two independent implementations over one `@lenke/core` Graph.**
`@lenke/gremlin` and `@lenke/gql` are siblings; neither depends on the other; there is no shared
plan module. Each hand-builds its own fast-path table — `countShortcut`'s rungs against
`shortcuts.ts`'s `tallyHopCount` family — so **in TS the claim that equivalent spellings cost the
same has no structural guarantee, only measurement.** (The native engine lowers both surfaces to one
`ir::Plan` and `spelling_probe` checks the canonicalized plans agree, which is why every
cross-surface item in this file — 797, 801, 929, 930 — is TS-only.)

Item 930's cause was specifically an **arity gate on a step list**: `mid.length !== 2`. That is
enumerable. The matrix is four positions × arity, both surfaces, one shape per process, every filter
TRUE for every row on three distinct keys so arity and position are the only things that vary, with
each arm's row count asserted (200,000 node / 600,000 hop).

### The screen — 200,000 vertices / 600,000 edges, median of 11, ONE round

| cell       |    gql |    grm | gql/grm | winner        |
| ---------- | -----: | -----: | ------: | ------------- |
| `node:1`   |   9.08 |   2.92 |   3.12x | grm 3.12x     |
| `node:2`   |  13.88 |   7.23 |   1.92x | grm 1.92x     |
| `node:3`   |  16.31 |   7.67 |   2.13x | grm 2.13x     |
| `pre:1`    |  54.55 |  36.21 |   1.51x | grm 1.51x     |
| `pre:2`    |  65.36 |  59.98 |   1.09x | grm 1.09x     |
| `pre:3`    |  65.55 |  60.58 |   1.08x | grm 1.08x     |
| `post:1`   |  59.58 |  28.49 |   2.09x | grm 2.09x     |
| `post:2`   |  64.55 |  54.81 |   1.18x | grm 1.18x     |
| `post:3`   |  65.48 |  55.11 |   1.19x | grm 1.19x     |
| `both:1+1` | 150.27 | 277.41 |   0.54x | **GQL 1.85x** |
| `both:2+1` | 243.61 | 289.11 |   0.84x | **GQL 1.19x** |
| `both:1+2` | 167.10 | 279.52 |   0.60x | **GQL 1.67x** |

**THIS IS A SCREEN, NOT A MEASUREMENT** (item 737's distinction). One round, one process per arm, to
find cells worth isolating. Every number below gets its own alternated-round A/B before it is
believed — item 924's rule, and item 928 is what happens without it.

### Finding 1 — `both` is the worst cell on BOTH surfaces, and it is item 930's named open gap

The right comparison holds the predicate COUNT fixed and moves one across the hop. Same answer, same
number of tests, and only the position differs:

```text
  gql   post:2  64.55 ms  ->  both:1+1  150.27 ms    2.33x
  grm   post:2  54.81     ->  both:1+1  277.41       5.06x
```

Item 930 named this and said why, for Gremlin: `V().has(x,p).out(E).has(k,q)` gives
`mid = [has, out, has]`, and `filteredHopCount` needs the hop FIRST, `startFilteredHopCount` needs
it LAST, and `filterChainCount` rejects the `out` — **the hop sits in the middle where no rung
reaches it**, so the whole shape falls to the general traversal. The prediction was that this would
be the matrix's worst cell. It is, and GQL has the same class of miss at 2.33x through a separate
implementation.

**And GQL is asymmetric in WHICH side carries more:** `both:2+1` 243.61 against `both:1+2` 167.10,
**1.46x** for the same three predicates redistributed. Two spellings of one question, and the cost
depends on which end you write them at.

Priced for the next attempt: if Gremlin's `both:1+1` reached the cost of its own two-filter
one-sided twin it would be ~55 ms instead of 277 — about **5x, or ~220 ms on this fixture.** That is
the largest single cell in the matrix and the next target.

### Finding 2 — the arity STEP is a ROUTE CHANGE, not a predicate cost, and then it is flat

| position | surface | 1 → 2 filters               | 2 → 3 filters          |
| -------- | ------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `post`   | grm     | **+26.33 ms (43.9 ns/row)** | +0.29 ms (0.5 ns/row)  |
| `pre`    | grm     | **+23.77 ms (39.6 ns/row)** | +0.60 ms (1.0 ns/row)  |
| `node`   | grm     | +4.32 ms (21.6 ns/row)      | +0.44 ms (2.2 ns/row)  |
| `post`   | gql     | +4.98 ms (8.3 ns/row)       | +0.92 ms (1.5 ns/row)  |
| `pre`    | gql     | +10.81 ms (18.0 ns/row)     | +0.19 ms (0.3 ns/row)  |
| `node`   | gql     | +4.80 ms (24.0 ns/row)      | +2.43 ms (12.1 ns/row) |

**A step then a plateau is a route boundary.** The second filter costs 40-88x what the third costs
on every Gremlin row of the table, which no amount of extra predicate work explains — one more

**This is partly mine, from item 930.** Arity 1 takes the hoisted inline test that item 930 added to

55, about **1.8x** — real but an order of magnitude smaller than Finding 1, so it is second in line.

Gremlin wins all nine one-sided cells; GQL wins all three `both` cells. The margin also narrows with
arity on one side (`post` 2.09x → 1.18x → 1.19x) and inverts across the hop. **That is the signature
of two tables with different coverage, not of one surface being lowered badly** — a uniformly worse
path would lose everywhere. It is the structural reason this matrix is worth keeping rather than a
one-off.

`node:1` at **3.12x** is also the widest one-sided gap here, wider than item 929's 1.80-1.85x on a
filtered node count — but 929's predicate kept 156,000 of 200,000 rows where every row survives
here, so the two are not the same question and this is a screen reading to isolate, not a
contradiction of 929.

## Item 933 — filters on BOTH sides of a hop now have a rung: **1.70-2.06x**, and item 932's 5x estimate was wrong for a structural reason

**SHIPPED** (`executor/count-shortcut.ts`: `bothFilteredHopCount` plus three extracted helpers),
nine tests, eight mutants. Item 932's matrix made this the largest open cell and item 930 had named
the mechanism; this builds the rung and measures what it is actually worth.

### The missing rung

`V().has(x,p).out(T).has(k,q).count()` gives `mid = [has, out, has]`, and the hop sits in the MIDDLE
where none of the three existing rungs can reach it: `filteredHopCount` needs the hop FIRST,
`startFilteredHopCount` needs it LAST, `filterChainCount` rejects the `out` outright. So the shape
fell to the general traversal, and moving ONE of two filters across the hop — same answer, same
predicate count — cost **5.06x** (item 932).

The new rung is disjoint from its siblings by construction: it requires at least one step on each
side of exactly one hop, where one sibling requires the hop first and the other requires it last, so
the dispatch order among the three cannot change which shapes they answer.

### Why it is EDGE-driven, which is the design and also why the prize was smaller than priced

`filteredHopCount` tests each far VERTEX once and adds its whole degree, which is sound only because
with no start filter every edge of the type reaches it. **Here a far vertex's contribution depends on
which of its in-edges start at a SURVIVING vertex**, so a per-vertex test multiplied by degree would
count edges from rejected starts. The rung therefore visits each qualifying EDGE once — 600,000
predicate evaluations on this fixture against the far-driven arm's 200,000.

**That is exactly why item 932's estimate was wrong.** 932 priced the prize as "if Gremlin's
`both:1+1` reached the cost of its own two-filter one-sided twin it would be ~55 ms against 277,
about 5x" — which silently assumed the far-driven walk was available. It is not. Recorded as a
mis-pricing rather than quietly replaced: **the achievable win is 1.70-2.06x, and the residual 2.6x
against `post:2` is structural, not a missing optimization.**

### The A/B: PRE vs POST by swapping the BUILT BUNDLE, 3 alternated rounds

| cell       | surf | PRE min | POST min |     ratio |         |
| ---------- | ---- | ------: | -------: | --------: | ------- |
| `both:1+1` | grm  |  268.21 |   138.48 | **1.94x** | TARGET  |
| `both:2+1` | grm  |  288.83 |   140.47 | **2.06x** | TARGET  |
| `both:1+2` | grm  |  278.52 |   163.44 | **1.70x** | TARGET  |
| `post:2`   | grm  |   53.31 |    53.01 |     1.01x | CONTROL |
| `pre:2`    | grm  |   59.18 |    57.78 |     1.02x | CONTROL |
| `node:2`   | grm  |    6.81 |     6.80 |     1.00x | CONTROL |
| `both:1+1` | gql  |  156.63 |   160.04 |     0.98x | CONTROL |

Worst arm self-variance across all 14 arm-cells: **1.10x**, which every target clears and no control
approaches. The three grm controls are the strong ones — same package, same process, same fixture,
different rung — and the gql control catches harness or machine drift from a different package
entirely. Arms asserted: `bothFilteredHopCount` absent from PRE and present in POST, with the
installed file's sha256 compared to the arm's.

### A fixture fact that decides whether this rung is reachable at all

`dropVacuousLabels` (item 540) removes a `hasLabel` that EVERY element carries before
`countShortcut` sees the plan, because the fast paths match a plan PREFIX from the source and one
vacuous step in front of the hop makes them all decline. Item 932's probe labels every vertex `:P`,
so `V().hasLabel(P).out(E).has(k,p)` arrives as `[out, has]` — the far-driven rung's shape, not this
one. Confirmed by measurement: that shape reads 27.9 ms after this change against 28.2 before, so
**the commonest labelled hop is untouched.**

Two consequences, both acted on:

- The `both` cells use a `has` pre-filter, which is never vacuous, so they do reach the rung.
- **The tests must use a NON-vacuous label or a `has` pre-filter.** The unit fixture has `P` on 4 of
  6 vertices and `Q` on 3, so both survive — a test written against an all-`:P` fixture would have
  exercised `filteredHopCount` while appearing to test this rung.

This was checked by reading the call site rather than inferred from the flat timing, which was
inside the noise and would have supported either conclusion.

### Mutation, under `timeout 600` + `MemoryMax=16G` + `MemorySwapMax=0`

Harness proven to kill first (allocator bomb 137, bare `for(;;)` 124). Pristine under `target/`,
restored BEFORE each mutant, verified byte-identical after. **For a brand-new rung this run also
verifies DISPATCH** — item 439's rule that checking the code fires comes before the A/B, which it
paid three alternated rounds to learn.

```text
  m1-far-filter-ignored        CAUGHT  (3 fail)
  m2-far-end-swapped           CAUGHT  (4 fail)
  m3-direction-flipped         CAUGHT  (4 fail)
  m4-start-filters-ignored     CAUGHT  (4 fail)
  m5-both-admitted             CAUGHT  (1 fail)
  m6-multitype-guard-dropped   CAUGHT  (1 fail)
  m7-multi-hop-admitted        SURVIVED (844 pass)   [expected]
  m8-position-guard-dropped    CAUGHT (20 fail)
```

Six independent kills are what establish the rung is reached; a new route whose mutants all survived
would be dead code with a green suite.

**m7 SURVIVES BY CONSTRUCTION, and the run is what established that rather than a comment claiming
it.** With `soleHopAt`'s multi-hop refusal dropped it returns the FIRST of two hops — and everything
after that first hop still contains the SECOND, which `collectHasFilters` refuses because a hop is
never a `has`. So the rung declines either way and the refusal is **defence in depth, not
load-bearing.** It is kept because it makes the helper's contract true for any future caller that
does not validate the tail, and it is marked expected-to-survive so the survivor is never read as a
missing test. Note this is NOT the failure `pushable`'s doc warns about — that is one rule split
across two places; these are two different rules that happen to overlap on this input.

The discriminating test is `a far vertex reached from a REJECTED start contributes nothing`: vertex 2
is the far end of two `E` edges, the start filter keeps only one of their starts, and the far-driven
mistake would report 2 where the answer is 1. It is what kills m4.

## Item 934 — the 1→2 filter arity step was the per-row CALL **and** the LOOP, ~65 ns each: **1.81x** on a two-filter hop count

**SHIPPED** (`executor/count-shortcut.ts`: `allMatch` deleted, three per-row test sites rewritten),
one test, eight mutants. Item 932's Finding 2 named this and priced it at ~1.8x; this diagnoses and
takes it. The measured win is 1.81x, which is the first time this session an estimate landed.

### The anomaly, which ruled out the obvious cause before any change

Over 200,000 vertices on the far-driven arm: the SECOND filter cost **+132 ns a vertex** and the
THIRD cost **+1.5 ns**. A step followed by a plateau is not a marginal predicate cost — one more
property read and one more `matches` is a few ns. So the step was the route into `allMatch`, and the
question was which part of it.

**Item 930's refutation did NOT transfer, and reusing it would have been wrong.** 930 guessed
iterator allocation, tested it by adding a `filters.length === 1` fast path INSIDE `allMatch`, saw
0.88x → 0.91x and concluded the per-row CALL was the cause. But that test was on the arity-1 case,
where the hoist means `allMatch` is never entered at all. For arity 2 it genuinely is. Diagnosed
fresh, in situ — this file's own rule, from item 593: "a micro-probe mispriced a ratio; take ratios
from an A/B of the real thing."

### The decomposition, measured by four in-situ variants of `post:2`

```text
  allMatch CALL, `Step` property loads inside it     54.81 ms
  inline indexed loop, `Step` property loads         41.79      the CALL was ~13 ms
  the same loop over keys/preds in dense arrays      43.82      extraction bought NOTHING
  unrolled straight-line pair over captured locals   30.25      the LOOP was ~12 ms
  (the one-filter twin, for reference)               28.49
```

**Two costs of ~65 ns a row each, and only removing BOTH recovers the step.** The unrolled variant
lands on the one-filter twin.

**A HYPOTHESIS OF MINE REFUTED IN THE MIDDLE OF THIS.** Seeing that the loop was slower than the
unrolled pair, I reasoned the cost was reading `f.pred` / `f.key` off a `Step` — a wide discriminated
union, so polymorphic loads at a site that runs per row — and extracted them into dense arrays of a
string and a `Predicate`. **It bought nothing: 43.82 against the loop's 41.79.** So the cost is the
loop machinery itself (bounds check, the `hit` carry, a dynamic trip count V8 cannot unroll), not the
property loads. Recorded because it is a plausible-sounding mechanism that measurement killed, and
because the arrays were kept — they make the loop arm read cleanly and cost nothing either way.

### What shipped: straight-line at widths 1 and 2, loop above

Three sites — the far-driven arm, the multi-type edge-driven arm, and `tallyFarEnds` (item 933's
per-EDGE walk). `allMatch` is deleted; nothing calls it. Widths above 2 keep the loop deliberately:
the third filter costs ~1.5 ns a row, so there is nothing there to unroll for, and an unroll per
arity is the kind of unbounded special-casing item 438 declined.

## Item 935 — `n.k > -1` cost **1.93x** its own twin `n.k >= 0` because a negated literal was never folded; folding it also CLOSES a cross-engine divergence and CORRECTS item 932's matrix

**SHIPPED** (`gql/src/parser.ts`, one guarded fold), three tests, three mutants. Item 932's screen
left `node:1` at **3.12x** as the widest one-sided cross-surface gap and flagged it for isolation.
It is not an engine gap; it is a spelling cliff in my own probe's query text, and it was inflating
every GQL cell of that matrix.

### The diagnosis, three candidates eliminated before any change

`node:1` read GQL 9.08 ms against Gremlin 2.92 over 200,000 vertices — **45 ns a vertex**, where
item 926 measured a comparison at **17.52**. Something differed from 926's fixture, and the method
was to vary one thing at a time:

- **EDGES — ruled out.** 932's fixture carries 600,000 edges and 926's none. At `A_DEG=0` the GQL
  arm reads 9.12 against 10.34 at `A_DEG=3`; the cost survives with no edges at all.
- **SELECTIVITY — ruled out, and item 926's claim independently CONFIRMED.** 932 keeps all 200,000
  rows where 926's predicate kept 2,222. Re-running 926's own probe, three order-alternated rounds:
  `cmpsel` (2,222 rows) 18.85 / 20.09 / 19.29 against `cmpall` (200,000 rows) 19.55 / 18.52 / 20.17.
  Fully interleaved. Selectivity is not a confound for a filtered count, exactly as 926 recorded.
- **THE LITERAL — this was it.** 932 writes every GQL bound as `> -1`. Added `cmpneg`
  (`n.k > -1`) beside `cmpall` (`n.k >= 0`) — over `k = i % 90` these are the same predicate, same
  survivors, same operator family, differing only in a minus sign:

```text
  n.k >= 0    20.04 / 18.44 / 19.00  ns a vertex
  n.k > -1    44.13 / 43.12 / 41.63  ns a vertex      2.2x
```

### The mechanism

`parseUnary` built `{ kind: 'neg', expr: { kind: 'lit', value: 1 } }` and **nothing folded it.** The
downstream predicate fast paths require a LITERAL operand, so a `neg` node made every one of them
decline and the general evaluator ran the row. The Gremlin surface never had this cliff because
`gt(-1)` is built programmatically with the value already negative — which is the whole of
`node:1`'s "cross-surface gap".

**The fold CONVERGES the two engines rather than diverging them**, and the codebase already said so:
`valueCannotRaise` in the executor carries a `neg`-of-numeric-literal arm whose comment records that
the native engine folds this to `Lit(Num(-1.0))`, and that the mismatch caused **four of five**
divergences in a 20,000-query differential run. TS now folds it the same way.

Numeric literals ONLY. `-n.s` must still fault, `-$p` must still read the param at run time, `-0`
folds to `-0` (which is what evaluating `neg` on `0` produces anyway), and `- -1` folds twice through
the recursion to `1`.

### The A/B: PRE vs POST by swapping the BUILT bundle, 3 alternated rounds

| shape       |   rows | PRE min | POST min |     ratio |             |
| ----------- | -----: | ------: | -------: | --------: | ----------- |
| `cmpneg`    | 200000 |   35.57 |    18.46 | **1.93x** | TARGET      |
| `cmpall`    | 200000 |   18.69 |    18.96 |     0.99x | **CONTROL** |
| `wheretrue` | 200000 |    9.09 |     9.12 |     1.00x | CONTROL     |
| `cmpsel`    |   2222 |   17.19 |    17.94 |     0.96x | CONTROL     |

**`cmpall` is the control that matters** — the identical predicate with a positive bound, already on
the fast route, in the same probe and process. It did not move. And the strongest evidence is not
the ratio but the convergence: **POST `cmpneg` 18.46 lands on `cmpall` 18.96.** The two spellings now
cost the same, which is the claim, and it does not depend on the noise floor (1.27x here).

### A CONFORMANCE divergence closed as a side effect, and the suite caught it

The gql suite failed one test — `percentile_cont(n.age, -1)` returned 10 where the test asserted a
throw. That test was not wrong; it **documented an open divergence**, in its own words: _"`-1` is a
unary-minus expression rather than a literal token, so `compileAggregate` raises before any value is
read. Native accepts it and clamps to the minimum — an open cross-engine divergence on an input ISO
does not define, recorded rather than papered over."_

Folding the literal removes the cause. **Verified against the real native engine rather than
trusting the comment** — 9 of 9 value cases now agree, where three disagreed before:

```text
  percentile_cont(n.age, -1)     ts 10        native 10      (was: ts THREW)
  percentile_disc(n.age, -1)     ts 10        native 10      (was: ts THREW)
  percentile_cont(n.age, -0.5)   ts 10        native 10      (was: ts THREW)
  WHERE n.age > -1 → count       ts 4         native 4
  RETURN -n.age                  ts -40       native -40
  RETURN - -1                    ts 1         native 1
  RETURN -0                      ts 0         native 0
  RETURN -'abc' / -true          both THROW                  (message text differs — known)
```

The test is updated to the converged behaviour with the verification recorded beside it.

### A STALE DIST caught by two instruments contradicting each other

Mid-diagnosis the gql suite (which runs `src`) said `percentile_cont(-1)` returns 10 while my
differential probe (which imports `@lenke/gql`, resolving to `dist`) said it threw. **Both were
right about different code**: I had not rebuilt. The contradiction is what surfaced it — a single
instrument would have been believed. Rebuilt, re-verified, and the arm assertions on the A/B
bundles exist for the same reason.

```text
  m2-sign-dropped          CAUGHT (12 fail)
  m3-non-numeric-folded    CAUGHT  (1 fail)   — after the boundary tests below
```

**`m3` SURVIVED all 2,760 tests at first.** Dropping the `typeof` guard folds `-'abc'` to

Three route-equality tests were added too, asserting that a negative bound takes the **same route**

## Item 936 — the corrected matrix's widest gap DIAGNOSED: GQL's filtered hop tally is EDGE-driven where Gremlin's is FAR-VERTEX-driven, ~2x. PRICED, NOT BUILT

> **RETRACTED at item 937 — the central claim is FALSE.** GQL does NOT edge-drive this shape:
> `farOnlyHopCount` exists and the measured query already takes it, proven by route markers in all
> three walks. Both engines far-drive, so the "opposite directions" cause and the fault-order
> obstacle below both fall. **This item inferred the route from reading two functions instead of
> verifying it.** Item 937 re-locates the gap: the far walk costs 18 ns a vertex and its PREDICATE
> costs 272 on top, against ~10 on a node scan. Read 937 and not this.

**DIAGNOSIS, no engine change.** After item 935 corrected the GQL column, `post:1` and `post:2` are
the widest one-sided cells left in `probe:arity` — GQL **60.26** and **62.42** ms against Gremlin
**29.09** and **30.23**, i.e. **2.07x** and **2.06x** over 200,000 vertices / 600,000 edges. Unlike
`node:*`, these did not move when the negative-literal fold landed (`post:1` 59.58 → 60.26), which
already said the cause was not the per-row predicate.

### The cause, read off both implementations

The two surfaces answer the same question by walking in **opposite directions**:

- **Gremlin's `filteredHopCount` drives the FAR VERTEX.** It tests each far vertex's predicate ONCE
  and adds that vertex's whole degree of the queried type, skipping `deg === 0` so the evaluated set
  stays exactly the edge walk's far endpoints. **200,000 predicate evaluations.**
- **GQL's `tallyHopCount` drives the EDGE.** `for (const edge of tallyEdges(scan, env))`, resolving
  `far` per edge and testing `inFar` on it. **600,000 predicate evaluations**, plus a far-vertex
  pointer chase per edge in edge order.

At degree 3 that is 3x the far-end work, and the measured 2.07x is what that comes to once the shared
costs are included. The direction is not an accident of this fixture: it is written into each
function, and item 930's own comment already noted the asymmetry — _"The GQL surface answers its
spelling of this question the same way (`tallyHopCount`, items 112/125)"_ — which is true of the
ROUTE and not of the drive direction.

### GQL already has the far-driven walk, and it declines every filter

`farDrivenHopWalk` in `executor/hop-projection.ts` is the same idea, measured at **2.3x** (item 167),
and its header names the two causes — the larger being LOCALITY, _"the start-driven walk reads a far
vertex per EDGE, in edge order, which is random with respect to how vertices sit in memory … ~180ns,
which is most of the 266ns a row took"_. Both causes apply to the tally.

**But its selection is gated on having NO predicate at all:**

```ts
if (farPred === undefined && gate === undefined && !needsStart) {
```

So the far-driven drive is available in GQL only for an unfiltered projection. **The raise-parity
question on a far-driven FILTER has never been solved on this path — it was avoided.** That is the
whole of why this is unbuilt rather than a port.

### The obstacle, stated precisely enough to design against

Driving the far vertex changes **neither the answer nor the fault SET**:

- The answer is a degree sum, and skipping `deg === 0` keeps the evaluated set identical to the
  edge walk's far endpoints — the argument Gremlin's rung already relies on.
- A predicate that faults for far vertex X faults in both walks; one that does not, does not. So no
  fault appears or disappears.

What changes is the fault **ORDER**. Only the first fault escapes, and the walks reach far vertices
in different orders, so a query with two faulting far vertices can surface a different message.
**This matters in GQL and does not in Gremlin, and item 930 is why:** Gremlin's `matches` CANNOT
throw — every ordering predicate filters an incomparable value out via a `NaN` from `predCmp` — so
Gremlin's rung gets raise parity for free. GQL's predicates CAN raise (`compareValues` throws on a
cross-type compare), this path carries bespoke raise-parity handling (items 139/142/144/145), and
`fault-precedence.test.ts` exists to pin orderings.

**Two designs, and the second is the one to price first:**

1. **Gate the far-driven arm on a raise-free far predicate.** Fully sound, needs no fault reasoning
   — but `b.k > -1` can raise in general (a string `k`), so the guard would decline the very shape
   measured here. Likely to buy little.
2. **Admit a raising predicate and establish that the fault order is not observable for a COUNT.**
   A count emits one row, so the only observable is which message escapes. This needs a real answer
   about what `fault-precedence.test.ts` pins and what the differential fuzzers compare for a
   faulting query — memory already records "a faulting PER-REP pred (TS raises, native fails the
   rep)" as an open cross-engine divergence, so the ground truth there is not obvious.

### Price

~**2x** on a filtered hop count — the largest one-sided cell in the corrected matrix, and a common
shape. Not larger than that: the far-driven arm cannot help a rel-reading or start-reading shape
(CLOSED.md's item 167 line already records that its 2.3x _is_ the `projectRow` hoist to once per far
vertex, so a rel-reading query takes the start-driven walk by necessity).

**NOT BUILT this tick, deliberately.** The change is small; the fault-order argument is not, and it
is the kind of reasoning this file records going wrong when it was done at the end of a long pass.
Recorded with the mechanism, the precedent, the exact guard that blocks it and the two candidate
designs, so the next attempt starts from the obstacle rather than re-finding the cause.

### Verification

No engine change: two documents. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED:
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0. The 2.07x/2.06x figures are the corrected
`probe:arity` run recorded at item 935, not a fresh single reading, and both are SCREEN readings — a
build against them owes its own alternated-round A/B.

**MEASUREMENT + RETRACTION, no engine change.** Item 936, written one tick earlier, said GQL's
filtered hop tally is edge-driven where Gremlin's is far-vertex-driven, priced the fix at ~2x and
recorded a fault-order obstacle. **The central claim is false.** Starting from 936's own named next
step — the obstacle — turned up the route trace that disproves its premise.

### What 936 got wrong, and how

936 read `tallyHopCount` (which IS edge-driven), found `farDrivenHopWalk` gated on
`farPred === undefined`, and concluded no far-driven filter route existed. It never checked which
walk the measured query actually takes. Three temporary markers in the three walks, rebuilt, answer
it in one line each:

```text
  MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) WHERE b.k > -1 RETURN count(*)   ->  ROUTE farOnlyHopCount
  MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b)   WHERE b.k > -1 RETURN count(*)   ->  ROUTE farOnlyHopCount
  MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) WHERE a.k > -1 RETURN count(*)   ->  ROUTE startOnlyHopCount
  MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b {k: 2})         RETURN count(*)   ->  ROUTE farOnlyHopCount
```

**`farOnlyHopCount` exists, is the far mirror of `startOnlyHopCount`, and the measured shape already
takes it.** It even reads the vertex's own `adjTo`/`adjFrom` box rather than hashing an id into the
graph's map, so item 591's lesson is applied here too. Both engines far-drive; 936's "opposite
directions" is wrong.

**The method failure is specific and worth naming: 936 read two functions and inferred the route
instead of verifying it.** Items 371 and 439 already say to verify the dispatch reaches the
function, and 439 paid three alternated rounds to learn it — but both are written about verifying
before measuring a CHANGE. This was a diagnosis with no change, and the rule applies identically: a
claim about which code runs is a claim to verify, not to derive. Cost: one tick, no engine damage,
because the item shipped as PRICED-NOT-BUILT rather than as a change.

### Where the 2x actually is, decomposed

Same fixture, 200,000 vertices / 600,000 edges, median of 11, one shape per measurement:

| shape                                |    ms | ns a far vertex |
| ------------------------------------ | ----: | --------------: |
| `WHERE b.k > -1` (the far predicate) | 58.03 |         **290** |
| `WHERE true` (the walk's own floor)  |  3.69 |          **18** |
| no `WHERE` at all                    |  0.01 |     O(1) bucket |
| far label only, `(b:P)`              |  0.00 |     O(1) bucket |

**The far-driven walk costs 18 ns a vertex. The predicate costs 272 ns a vertex on top of it.**

And that is the number that matters, because item 926 measured the SAME operator class on a node
scan at **19-20 ns a vertex** over a `WHERE true` floor of 9.16 — so the predicate term there is
~10 ns. Here it is 272. **A ~27x discrepancy in the predicate term between two walks in the same
engine**, which is a far better-located target than the ~2x cross-surface ratio that led here. The
cross-surface gap is merely where it became visible; Gremlin's rung calls `matches(pred, props[key])`
directly.

**Fixture statistics checked, which killed the other candidate.** Reading the two functions showed a
real asymmetry — GQL evaluates the predicate and calls `degreeOfTypes` AFTER, where Gremlin computes
the degree first and skips `deg === 0` vertices before testing anything. In this fixture it cannot
matter: the in-degree histogram is `deg3=200000`, every vertex has in-degree exactly 3 and there are
no degree-0 vertices. Item 702's rule — check the fixture's own statistics, not just its output —
and it retired a candidate that reading alone made look promising. The asymmetry is still real for a
graph with many vertices carrying no edge of the queried type (the `:S` shape `startWalkFits`'
comment celebrates at 7684x), just not here.

### The candidate cause, named as a hypothesis and NOT measured

`farOnlyHopCount` evaluates `asTruth(pred.fn(env))` per far vertex, having written
`binding.set(farVar, v)` first, inside a `try` whose `catch` re-throws only when
`degreeOfTypes(boxOf(v), types) > 0`. The node scan reaches the same predicate through the lifted
`satisfies`/`eqProps`/`cmpProps` family (items 224/230/798/799/803), which items 798-803 and 926
spent several ticks reducing to ~10 ns. So the hypothesis is that this walk takes the GENERIC bare
predicate and none of those lifts, and that the 272 ns is the binding `Map` write, the `EvalEnv`
indirection, the closure call and the `try` frame rather than the comparison.

**That is a guess, and this file's record of guesses about this exact cost is poor** — item 437
recorded two wrong ones (not a tree walk, not boxing) and item 934 one more (not the polymorphic
property load). So it is written down to be tested, not acted on: the next attempt decomposes the
272 ns before changing anything, and the obvious first cut is `WHERE true` (18 ns, no `pred.fn` at
all) against a predicate that is trivially true, which separates the call scaffolding from the
comparison.

### Price

If the predicate term on this walk could reach the node scan's ~10 ns, the measured shape goes from
58.03 ms to roughly 6 ms — about **9x**, and far larger than the 2x item 936 advertised. Treat that
as an upper bound on an unverified mechanism, not a forecast.

### Verification

No engine change: two documents. The route markers were temporary, the pristine copy was restored
from `target/` and the restore verified by grepping the markers back out. Gates each its own command
with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

per-edge. So "18 ns" was never that walk's floor, and the 272 ns subtraction has no basis.

## Item 939 — item 938's 2.7x mirror asymmetry is REFUTED (1.48x, under a 2.20x noise floor), and the hop-predicate chain is CLOSED without a change

**MEASUREMENT + REFUTATION, no engine change.** Item 938 ended with one specific, unexplained claim:
the far walk's predicate costs 98 ns a candidate against the start walk's 36, a 2.7x asymmetry
between two functions written as mirrors. It does not survive alternated rounds.

### The refutation

Four arms, four alternated rounds, each arm divided by its own 20,000 candidates and asserted to
answer 60,000:

| arm          | min ns/cand | rounds                | self-variance |
| ------------ | ----------: | --------------------- | ------------: |
| `farFloor`   |          86 | 86 / 97 / 117 / 94    |         1.37x |
| `farPred`    |         117 | 126 / 117 / 118 / 188 |         1.60x |
| `startFloor` |          84 | 101 / 184 / 95 / 84   |     **2.20x** |
| `startPred`  |         105 | 119 / 112 / 127 / 105 |         1.21x |

```text
  far   predicate share  32 ns/cand
  start predicate share  21 ns/cand
  ratio                1.48x      (item 938 claimed 2.7x)
  worst arm self-variance 2.20x
```

**1.48x against a 2.20x noise floor is not a reading**, and the single round 938 relied on is simply
a bad sample — every absolute number moved (938's 119/217/121/157 against 86/117/84/105 here).

**The specific methodological error, and it is mine twice over.** 938 derived the asymmetry as a
DIFFERENCE OF DIFFERENCES — `(farPred − farFloor)` against `(startPred − startFloor)` — which
compounds the noise of four readings into two deltas, and then compares those. The arms are 84-117
ns and the effect sought is 20-30 ns, so the question was never resolvable this way. Worse: **938
alternated the conjunct-slope measurement over three rounds and did NOT alternate the floor pair,
in the same item.** The discipline was applied to one half of the item and not the other, and the
unalternated half is the one that produced the headline.

### Why both engines were symmetric all along

Reading settles what the timings could not. `startOnlyHopCount` and `farOnlyHopCount` are
structurally identical — same `hopSeek ?? candidateVertexSource` source, same `matchesLabel`, the
same `try` holding `inlineHolds` / `binding.set` / `asTruth(pred.fn(env))`, the same `catch` that
re-throws only when `degreeOfTypes(boxOf(v), types) > 0`, the same single `degreeOfTypes` on the
happy path. The only differences are which adjacency box is read and which side's names are used.

And the boxes are symmetric too, in `@lenke/core`'s `Vertex`:

```ts
  get adjFrom() { this.#adjFrom ??= this.#graph?.edgesFromByLabel.get(this.id); return this.#adjFrom; }
  get adjTo()   { this.#adjTo   ??= this.#graph?.edgesToByLabel.get(this.id);   return this.#adjTo; }
```

Both cache on first read, both hash the same id into a sibling index. **There is no mechanism for a
2.7x, which is the reading that should have made the number suspect before a fifth item was spent
on it.**

### THE CHAIN IS CLOSED. What is solid, what is not, and why to stop

Four items, no engine change, and the target has not survived three attempts at attribution:

| item | claim                          | verdict                                  |
| ---- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| 936  | GQL is edge-driven here        | **FALSE** (937)                          |
| 937  | walk 18 ns, predicate 272 ns   | **INVALID** (938) — two walks, two units |
| 938  | far predicate 2.7x the start's | **REFUTED** (this) — 1.48x, under noise  |
| 939  | —                              | the chain stops                          |

**SOLID, because they were alternated and clear their own floors:**

- The two hop walks cost **290-305 ns a vertex** with a one-conjunct predicate at 200,000
  candidates, and the two mirrors agree (far 290/292/300, start 305/291/304).
- The **marginal conjunct is ~30 ns** for the second and ~0 for the third, so most of the per-vertex
  cost is fixed and independent of predicate complexity.
- The cross-surface ratio that started this is real on the screen (`post:1` GQL 60.26 against
  Gremlin 29.09), and `farOnlyHopCount` is the route GQL takes.

**NOT ESTABLISHED, and not worth another timing subtraction:** which component of the ~270 ns fixed
cost dominates. Three attributions have failed, and this instrument cannot resolve 20-60 ns effects
against arms that self-vary 1.2-2.2x. **A fourth attempt by subtraction would be the same mistake a
fourth time.**

What a future attempt needs instead, stated so it does not start by re-deriving: either a profiler
on the real query (which no item in this chain used), or a microbenchmark that isolates ONE
component — the `try` frame, the `binding.set`, the `pred.fn` call, the `degreeOfTypes` — rather
than inferring it from a difference of end-to-end timings. The repo's own warning applies and was
ignored here: _"Anything under ~10% needs its own isolated harness, and 'obviously correct so it
must be faster' is not evidence."_

### What this chain cost and what it bought

Four ticks, no engine change, no regression, no wrong code shipped. Every item was cheap **because
each shipped as measurement rather than as a change** — the errors were in the explanations, and
explanations are free to retract. The measured facts above accumulated regardless, and three
specific wrong attributions are now recorded so a fifth attempt does not re-derive them.

It is still four ticks on a target that produced nothing, and the loop moves on.

### Verification

No engine change: two documents. Every arm asserts its own row count (60,000) before a time is read,
and the analysis prints each arm's rounds and self-variance beside the derived deltas, so a delta
smaller than its inputs' spread is visible rather than implied. Gates each its own command with its
exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 940 — the spelling probe run this session's changes owed: CLEAN. And the two groups added for item 935's form were REVERTED, because mutation proved them toothless

**CHECK + REVERTED ADDITION, no engine change.** CLAUDE.md requires `bun run spelling` when the TS
planner is touched or a predicate form is added. This session did both — items 930/933/934 changed
Gremlin count routes and item 935 added a predicate form — and the gate had not been run. Running it
is this item; what it found about the probe itself is the interesting half.

### The regression run: clean

`SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`, the settings the probe's own notes record (single runs are bimodal).

**0 groups disagree on the ANSWER.** Seven groups exceed 2x and clear the nearest null control, and
**every one is pre-existing and already recorded**:

| group                                                             | ratio | recorded at                                        |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `label on start: redundant vs absent`                             | 5386x | item 325 — and the probe file says not to quiet it |
| `sorted LIMIT: ORDER BY in STATEMENT vs CLAUSE position`          | 4.71x | item 868                                           |
| `sorted LIMIT DESC: statement vs clause`                          | 4.72x | item 868                                           |
| `sorted LIMIT on a LOW-CARDINALITY key`                           | 3.53x | item 868                                           |
| `SEEK: a param equality AND a second conjunct — clause vs inline` | 2.70x | item 578                                           |
| `a product's one-sided predicate: comma vs MATCH MATCH`           | 2.22x | item 285                                           |
| `one end labelled, the other free: four spellings`                | 2.06x | item 286                                           |

**So this session's parser and route changes introduced no new spelling cliff**, which is the
assurance the gate exists to give. Checking `CLOSED.md` before chasing the 5386x is what kept this
from becoming a re-derivation of item 325.

### The addition, and why it was reverted

CLAUDE.md's rule has a second half — _"add the new form's spellings to it"_ — so two groups were
added for item 935's negative-literal fold, pairing `n.k > -1` against `n.k >= 0` (over `k = i % 50`
these are the same predicate, same survivors, same answer) on both the node scan and the far hop.

They were quiet, as they should be after 935:

```text
  node scan    9.08 ms  vs   9.39 ms     1.03x
  far hop    209.25     vs 207.43        1.01x
```

**Then the teeth check, which they failed.** With item 935's fold disabled in the parser and the
tree rebuilt:

```text
  node scan   12.26 ms  vs   9.51 ms     1.29x   — the probe's threshold is 2x, so NO FLAG
  far hop    190.17     vs 187.54        1.01x   — no effect whatever
```

**A guard that cannot fail is worse than no guard, because it is believed** — the repo's own rule
about generative tests, applied to a probe group. Both were removed rather than left as decoration.

### What the failed teeth check revealed, which is the useful part

**The fold's benefit is NODE-SCAN-ONLY. The far-hop route is insensitive to it** — 1.01x with the
fold off, so `farOnlyHopCount` never took the lifted path the fold unlocks and never will by this
route. That is consistent with item 935's own matrix re-run, where the hop cells did not move
(`post:1` 59.58 → 60.26) while the node cells improved 1.9-2.6x; **935 showed it implicitly and this
measures it directly.** Item 935's claim is therefore correctly scoped as written, and the scope is
now explicit rather than inferable.

**And the two probes disagree about the same query text**, which is why this one cannot discriminate
the form: the folded node scan reads ~47 ns a vertex here against ~19 in `predicate-scaffold-probe`
at the same `N`. The probes are not measuring the same route — `spelling-probe`'s fixture carries an
index and params (a seek pass, item 579). **Not attributed further**: the cause was not measured,
and this file's record on unmeasured attributions in the last four items is poor.

### The form IS guarded, which is why removing the groups costs nothing

Item 935 added four route-equality tests to `routes-fired.test.ts` asserting a negative bound takes
the SAME route as its positive twin, plus the guard's boundary cases. **Those have proven teeth**:
935's `m1-fold-removed` mutant was CAUGHT, and `m3-non-numeric-folded` was caught only after the
boundary tests were added. A route assertion is the right instrument for a route change; a timing
probe over a differently-routed fixture is not.

## Item 941 — FIVE consecutive stale `OPEN` headers in CLOSED.md, found by bouncing off four of them in one tick

**DOCUMENTATION FIX, no engine change.** CLAUDE.md says to read `CLOSED.md` before pricing a target,
and that _"a list that lags is the failure it exists to prevent."_ This tick went looking for a
shippable Rust lever, worked down the list's priced `OPEN` entries, and found the first four already
dead. That is the failure, observed directly.

### What happened, in order

Looking for the next target, the priced-and-open bullets read as the obvious shortlist. Taken in
turn:

```text
  877  live_edge_count() is O(V), not O(1), ~100x on two rows   -> RETRACTED at 878 on cost/benefit
  881  NATIVE's bare hop is now the slow side                   -> RETRACTED at 882 (a category difference)
  878  the TS order() row is ~212 ms around an 88 ms sort       -> BUILT at 879 (1.19x / 1.33x)
  880  V().out(T) has no fused walk, ~1.9x                      -> BUILT at 881 (2.23x and 2.12x)
```

Four reads, four dead ends, before a live target. Each resolution was already in the file — this is
not missing information, it is **information the headers contradict.**

### The audit

All 30 `OPEN` bullets scanned for a later line naming the same item alongside
RETRACTED/WITHDRAWN/SUPERSEDED/revising/BUILT/SHIPPED. Eleven matched; **the scan over-matches badly
and every candidate had to be read**, which is the method note worth keeping:

- **Six rejected on reading.** Several matched a coincidental mention of the number (item 926's
  bullet against a later line that merely cites 926's param "residual"), and one matched a line that
  is _itself_ an OPEN bullet. Item **910** is the sharpest: a later line says _"RETRACTED — item
  910's '19 detectors are 25% of planning' target"_, but 910's own bullet claims something else
  entirely — the rewrite pipeline at 16% — so **910 stays open** and striking it would have been a
  worse error than leaving it.
- **Five confirmed stale, and corrected in place**: 877 (retracted at 878), 878 (built at 879, its
  residual then refuted at 890), 879 (refuted at 890 — 1.04x, matched exactly by an unreachable
  control, reverted), 880 (built at 881), 881 (retracted at 882).

Each header now carries its resolution in the first clause, so a reader scanning headers — which is
how the list is used — cannot act on a dead lever.

### Why the lag happens, and it is structural rather than careless

**A retraction is written as a NEW bullet and the old one is left standing.** Items 878, 881, 882
and 890 each recorded their correction properly, immediately below or near the entry they overturned
— the information was never lost. What none of them did was go back and strike the header.

Two of the five were genuinely hard to spot: 879's refutation sits ~200 lines later at item 890, and
878's resolution is split across two items (built at 879, residual refuted at 890). The other three
sit within a bullet or two of their retraction, which is exactly why they are easy to leave — the
correction _looks_ adjacent enough to be seen, and a header scan does not see it.

**This session has now corrected nine stale headers** — five here, 797 and 801 at item 935, and the
two items 925 and 926 each fixed — on top of the five item 913 corrected. The pattern is consistent
enough to be worth naming: **the same commit that records a retraction should strike the header it
overturns**, which is the same-commit discipline CLAUDE.md already requires for adding a line.

### What this cost and what it is worth

The cost is measurable in this tick: four reads spent on dead leads before reaching a live one, and
those four were the _highest-priced_ entries on the list, so they are exactly the ones a future
attempt reaches for first. The same four would have cost the next attempt the same.

**Not a perf change, and this item claims none.** It is maintenance of the instrument the method
depends on — the same category as item 932's probe or the route markers at 937, and the direct
reason items 877 and 881 did not become a fifth and sixth re-derivation this session.

### Verification

No engine change: one document. Every correction was verified by READING the resolving item, not by
