## Item 957 — the 1.85x `Expr::Index` gap diagnosed and a working fix REJECTED: it wins 1.62x on the bracket arm and costs the dotted arm 1.07x, so the fix belongs in the optimizer

**DIAGNOSIS + a rejected optimization, recorded next to the code it would change.** Item 956
closed the SEEDING half of item 955 and left the second finding open: on the identical
`Filter { Scan }` route, `p.meta['city']` costs 1.85x `p.meta.city`.

### The cause, read off the evaluator

`Expr::Index` already has a fused fast path — but its pre-scan is

```rust
let all_lists = ids.iter().all(|&id| {
    id != u32::MAX && matches!(store.prop_ref(id, key), Some(Value::List(_)))
});
```

**A RECORD-valued property fails it**, so `p.meta['city']` falls to the general path, where
`eval(base)` materializes a cloned `Value::Record` per row and `bcol.value_at(i)` clones the whole
record AGAIN to project one field. `Expr::Field` has no such problem: item 896 gave it
`fused_prop_field`, which reads the boxed column directly.

### The fix that works, and the control that killed it

Four lines calling the same `fused_prop_field`. It closes the gap:

```text
  with-index route   dotted   bracket   ratio
  PRE                4786.9   8864.9    1.85x
  POST               5574.0   5648.3    1.01x
```

The bracket arm wins **1.62x**. But the **dotted** arm — which this change cannot logically reach,
since it adds a branch to a different match arm — regressed. Alternated POST/PRE rounds on that
control:

```text
  POST  5013.0  5166.6        PRE  4695.0  4786.0        1.07x, DISJOINT
```

**This is `fused_prop_field`'s own documented hazard, from the other side.** Its note records a
**1.09x regression on a NEIGHBOURING arm** when its body was inlined into `Expr::Field`; merely
_growing_ the `Expr::Index` arm costs the same toll. The audit already carries this for
`exec::pull`, whose alignment is load-bearing and charges 1.08–1.24x for any edit.

**And the first measurement overstated it.** Three POST rounds then three PRE rounds read
5407.6/4680.6 = **1.16x**; alternating them put it at **1.07x**. The blocked form inflated a real
regression by half again — the same lesson as item 953's estimator, one layer up: it is not only
_which_ summary you take but _in what order you collect the rounds_.

### Why it is rejected rather than shipped with a caveat

The dotted spelling is the common one and the bracket spelling is rare. Trading 1.07x on the
common path for 1.62x on the rare one is a bad bargain even before the maintenance cost of a
second fused path.

### The right fix, named for the next pass

**Canonicalize in the optimizer**: rewrite `Index { base, Lit(Str(k)), elem: Plain }` to
`Field { base, key: k }`. Three things recommend it over a second fused path:

1. **Sound by a measurement already taken** — item 956 ran both spellings over every base kind a
   segment can meet (record, scalar, absent, number, list) and they agree everywhere.
2. **It adds nothing to the evaluator**, so it cannot perturb alignment — the exact failure above.
3. **The two spellings then produce the IDENTICAL plan**, which is this repo's own standard:
   _two spellings that optimize to the same plan cannot differ._ It also means the bracket form
   inherits every future `Field` improvement for free, instead of needing its own copy.

### Verification

No engine change ships: the diff is a 30-line rejection note in the arm it would have changed,
which is what CLAUDE.md asks for ("Record rejected optimizations with their numbers, next to the
code they would have changed. Several have been re-attempted otherwise."). Gates each its own
command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0;
`bun run check` 0.

## Item 958 — SHIPPED: canonicalize a constant string subscript to `Field` at the IR builder, closing item 957's 1.85x without the regression that rejected its evaluator twin

**SHIPPED.** Item 957 diagnosed the gap, built a working evaluator fusion, and rejected it for a
1.07x disjoint regression on the dotted control — then named the right shape. This is that shape.

### The change, at the one place the IR is built

In the GQL postfix parser, where `base[index]` is constructed:

```rust
base = match (&elem, &index) {
    (ElemKind::Plain, Expr::Lit(Value::Str(k))) => Expr::Field { base: Box::new(base), key: k.to_string() },
    _ => Expr::Index { base: Box::new(base), index: Box::new(index), elem },
};
```

Sound by a measurement already taken: item 956 ran both spellings over every base kind a segment
can meet — record `Str("hit")`/`Str("hit")`, scalar, absent, number and list all `Null`/`Null`.

### The result: the plans are now IDENTICAL, which is the point

```text
  dotted   Filter { Scan, Compare { Eq, Field { base: Prop { slot: 0, key: "meta" }, key: "city" }, Lit(Str("NYC")) } }
  bracket  Filter { Scan, Compare { Eq, Field { base: Prop { slot: 0, key: "meta" }, key: "city" }, Lit(Str("NYC")) } }
```

Byte-identical, so the 1.85x cannot come back: _two spellings that optimize to the same plan
cannot differ._ Both routes measure 1.00x, and the bracket form now inherits `fused_prop_field`,
`prop_path` seeding and every future `Field` improvement for free rather than needing its own copy.

### The control, and why it passes where item 957's did not

The dotted arm executes byte-identical IR in both builds — this change is in the parser, and the
probe times only `exec::try_run`. Any movement is binary layout. Four alternated pairs:

```text
  POST  5182.9  4913.8  5082.9  4910.9
  PRE   4721.8  4804.4  4709.7  5594.5
```

**PRE's worst run exceeds every POST run**, so the distributions overlap and there is no
reliable regression — unlike item 957's clean disjoint 1.07x, where the change added a branch
_inside_ the hot evaluator arm. Four pairs were taken rather than two precisely because the first
single round read 5231.8 and would have looked like a repeat of 957.

### A mutant SURVIVED, and it was right to

```text
  M1  drop the `elem: ElemKind::Plain` guard        SURVIVED all 1,251 tests
  M2  fold ANY literal subscript, not just a string CAUGHT — 3 failures
```

M1 is the same guard whose `prop_path` twin item 956 found **load-bearing for correctness**, so
the survival demanded an explanation rather than a shrug. Constructing the shape it protects —
a group variable from `( (x)-[e:R]->(y) ){1,1}`, where a full-depth subscript yields a typed
ELEMENT — gives:

```text
  x['id'] = Null      x.id = Null
```

**They already agree**, so folding is answer-preserving here and the mutant is genuinely
equivalent. The asymmetry with item 956 is precise and worth keeping: in `prop_path` the fold
changed the SEEK KEY while the evaluator still ran an `Index`, so the two halves disagreed and the
rows changed; at the IR builder both halves move together. The guard is kept as conservatism —
same status item 903 records for `truthProps`' merge, a precondition kept live for when the fold
widens — and `a_group_variable_string_subscript_is_not_a_field_read` pins the behaviour. **That
test documents the shape; it does not give the guard teeth, and saying otherwise would be the
"believed generative test" CLAUDE.md warns about.**

### Verification

Engine suite **1,251** passed / 0 failed (up 2). `rewrite_fuzz` at
`LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` 10 passed / 0 failed. All **7 byte-identity fuzzers** pass, 13
tests — run because this changes the IR the native engine builds while TS builds its own, so the
engines could in principle move apart. Gates each its own command with its exit code read
UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0;
`bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

**Item 956's `prop_path` `Expr::Index` arm is now unreachable from GQL** and is deliberately kept:
it still covers IR built by other means (Gremlin lowering, direct construction, the opt tests),
and its own mutants proved it load-bearing for those.

## Item 959 — SHIPPED in TS: the same canonicalization as item 958, worth 1.27x in a PROJECTION, which is the half item 954's lift could not reach

**SHIPPED, both engines now agree on one AST shape.** Item 954 taught TS's `fieldChain` the
bracket form, which fixed PREDICATES — they lift either way. A **projection never lifts**, so
`compileExpr`'s `case 'index'` arm still ran: an inner closure for the index, an `instanceof`, a
`typeof`, `Array.isArray` and bounds, against `case 'field'`'s single `instanceof`.

### Priced BEFORE building, because "native did it" is not a price

Item 950 recorded exactly that mistake — porting item 896's native fusion to TS on the strength
of its 2.27x and getting a null. So `bracket-projection-probe.ts` measured it first, 100,000
rows, median of 5 alternated rounds, with the full row set fingerprinted (not a count: a
projection that silently returned nulls would otherwise look like a win):

```text
  BEFORE                                            AFTER
  CONTROL flat   18.2 ns/row  0.23x dotted          22.9  0.25x
  dotted         77.9         1.00x                 91.0  1.00x
  bracket        99.1         1.27x                 89.4  0.98x
  rows identical: YES                               YES
```

**1.27x → 0.98x.** The whole process drifted up ~17% between the runs — the CONTROL, a flat
`p.tier` read that the parser canonicalization cannot plausibly reach, moved 18.2 → 22.9 — so the
**ratio within a process is the result and the absolutes are not**. Both arms are alternated
inside each run, which is what makes that ratio trustworthy.

### The change

In the TS parser's postfix loop, mirroring item 958's arm in the Rust IR builder:

```ts
e =
  idx.kind === 'lit' && typeof idx.value === 'string'
    ? { kind: 'field', base: e, key: idx.value }
    : { kind: 'index', base: e, index: idx };
```

Sound by item 954's measurement across every base kind — record `"hit"`/`"hit"`, scalar, absent,
number and list all `null`/`null`.

### Teeth

```text
  M1  fold ANY literal, not just a string   CAUGHT — 2 failures
  M2  remove the canonicalization           CAUGHT — "builds the SAME ast as the dotted spelling"
```

Both under `timeout` + cgroup cap with a restore before each. The assertion is on the **AST**, and
it has to be: both spellings always returned the same rows, so no correctness test can see the
difference — the same reason item 958 asserts the plan natively.

### What this leaves

The two engines now canonicalize identically, so `p.meta['city']` and `p.meta.city` are one shape
in both and cannot drift apart again. `fieldChain`'s `kind: 'index'` arm (item 954) is now
unreachable from the TS parser; it is kept as the native twin is, because it costs nothing and is
the safety net if the canonicalization is ever narrowed.

### Verification

Suites: gql **2,776** pass / 0 fail (up 3), gremlin 845/0, core 370/0, native 933/0. All **7
byte-identity fuzzers** pass, 13 tests — run because an AST-shape change in one engine is exactly
what could move the two apart. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED:
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 960 — the spelling guards items 954-959 owed: both probes now carry the dotted/bracket group, and both say it is one question

**Discharging an obligation, not a new finding.** CLAUDE.md: _"When adding a predicate form to the
planner, add its spellings there."_ Items 954-959 added one — a constant string subscript — across
four changes and never did. This is that.

### Native `spelling_probe`

The shared fixture gained a record-valued `meta`, since no existing node had a nested cell to
read. The group asks the dotted form, the bracket form and the flipped-operand bracket form:

```text
=== a dotted path vs a constant string subscript ===
  GQL  0.950ms  MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.meta.city = 'NYC' RETURN count(*) AS c
  GQL  0.950ms  MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.meta['city'] = 'NYC' RETURN count(*) AS c
  GQL  0.951ms  MATCH (n:Person) WHERE 'NYC' = n.meta['city'] RETURN count(*) AS c
  ✓ identical optimized plan → identical exec (perf guaranteed)
```

**The strongest verdict the probe gives.** Not "close on the clock" — one canonical plan, which is
what item 958's canonicalization bought and what stops the 3.47x returning by drift.

### TS `spelling-probe`

Same group, same fixture addition (a nested `meta` on every node), `SPELL_N=200000
SPELL_REPS=9` because single runs there are bimodal:

```text
  a dotted path vs a constant string subscript
    7.44ms  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.meta.s = 's3' RETURN count(*) AS c
    7.50ms  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.meta['s'] = 's3' RETURN count(*) AS c
    7.47ms  MATCH (n:P) WHERE 's3' = n.meta['s'] RETURN count(*) AS c
```

**1.01x spread**, far under the 2x flag, and the group does not appear in the probe's over-2x
list. TS has no plan to canonicalize against, so time is the only signal available there — which
is exactly why the native plan check matters more.

### On the fixture change, because it touches every other group

Adding `meta` to every node changes the graph all ~30 groups run against. The full run reports
**"0 group(s) disagree on the ANSWER"**, and the seven groups over 2x are all named for
pre-existing items — 868 (ORDER BY statement vs clause, three of them), 286, 285 and 578 — i.e.
the known-open list, with nothing new. The addition is also UNIFORM across nodes, and the probe
compares spellings WITHIN a group over one graph, so a uniform fixture change moves a group's
absolute cost but not its spread.

**Stated as a limitation rather than a claim**: no before-the-change run of the TS probe was taken
this session, so "nothing new is flagged" rests on the flag names matching known items, not on a
diffed baseline.

### Verification

No engine change: two probes. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED:
`cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0;
`bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 961 — the `DISTINCT vs dedup` cliff points the OTHER way: `Distinct` costs 2.07x `DistinctBy` on identical input, and the probe's 1.78x was a semantic filter

**DIAGNOSIS, no engine change.** `spelling_probe` has long flagged
`MATCH (n:Person) RETURN DISTINCT n.dept` against
`g.V().hasLabel('Person').values('dept').dedup()` as a perf cliff — 0.086 ms against 0.152, both
five rows — which reads as Gremlin lowering worse than GQL. Dumping the plans says otherwise.

### The two plans differ in TWO ways, so the probe's ratio can attribute neither

```text
GQL  Distinct   { Project { Scan { Person } } }
GRM  DistinctBy { Project { Filter { Scan { Person }, PropertyExists{dept} } }, key_slots: [0] }
```

1. Gremlin carries a `Filter { PropertyExists }` that GQL does not — and **this is required, not
   waste**: `values('dept')` yields nothing for a vertex lacking the key where `RETURN n.dept`
   yields null. The two spellings are therefore **not the same question**, which alone makes the
   probe's pairing suspect.
2. `DistinctBy { key_slots: [0] }` where GQL emits `Distinct`.

### The third arm makes the pair row-matched, and inverts the finding

`MATCH (n:Person) WHERE PROPERTY_EXISTS(n, dept) RETURN DISTINCT n.dept` gives GQL the same
filter, so the only remaining difference is the dedup operator. 200,000 nodes, min of 9, four
runs — the arms are unusually stable:

```text
  GQL DISTINCT    164.0  164.1  165.9  165.1 us   Distinct,   no filter
  GRM dedup       292.8  295.3  295.4  300.8 us   DistinctBy, filtered
  GQL +exists     608.6  610.8  612.4  650.1 us   Distinct,   filtered
```

**On identical input, `Distinct` costs 2.07x `DistinctBy`** (610 against 295). The probe said
Gremlin was 1.78x slow; the row-matched comparison says **GQL's operator is 2.07x slow**, and the
appearance of a Gremlin penalty came entirely from the filter its semantics require.

### Why this is worth recording beyond the number

The cliff has stood in `spelling_probe`'s output as a GQL-versus-Gremlin lowering question. It is
not one — here Gremlin's lowering is the **better** of the two and GQL inherits the slower
operator. A pair that differs in two ways cannot be read as evidence about either, and the fix is
a third arm, not a tie-breaker argument.

### The target this names, and what must be checked first

`Distinct` keys the WHOLE row; `DistinctBy` keys named slots. For a single-column row those are
the same operation, so lowering `RETURN DISTINCT` over a one-column projection to
`DistinctBy { key_slots: [0] }` — or making `Distinct` take the typed-slot path when the row is
narrow — should recover the 2.07x. **Not built here**, and the preconditions are the usual ones:

- **Read the mechanism first** (items 947-949). Why `Distinct` is dearer is unmeasured — a generic
  whole-row hash against typed slot keys is the hypothesis, not the finding.
- **It is answer-equivalent**, so every mutant survives the differential tests (item 585): it
  needs a plan assertion, and this probe as the before/after.
- **Check the row width where they must diverge.** `Distinct` over a multi-column row is not
  `DistinctBy` over one slot, and a fix that forgets the width is a wrong answer, not a slow one.

### Verification

No engine change: one example added. Both plans are dumped before any timing, and every arm
prints its row count (all 5) so a ratio between arms answering different questions would be
visible. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0;
`bun run check` 0.

## Item 962 — correcting item 961: the cause is a DISQUALIFIED FAST PATH, not an operator choice, and the dedup STEP differs by ~15x, not 2.07x

**CORRECTION + apportionment, no engine change.** Item 961 measured `Distinct` at 2.07x
`DistinctBy` "on identical input" and named the target as _lower a one-column `RETURN DISTINCT` to
`DistinctBy`_. The measurement stands; the attribution does not, and the magnitude was understated.

### Reading the mechanism, which item 961 did not do

```rust
pub(super) fn try_distinct_scan_prop(input: &Plan, store: &Store) -> Option<Batch> {
    let Plan::Project { input: scan, items } = input else { return None };
    let [(_, Expr::Prop { slot: 0, key })] = items.as_slice() else { return None };
    let Plan::Scan { label } = scan.as_ref() else { return None };
```

`Distinct` has a **columnar fast path**, and it requires `Project { Scan }` with **no filter
between them**. Item 961's third arm inserted a `Filter { PropertyExists }`, which disqualifies
it — so that arm is the GENERAL `Distinct` path, not the operator arm 1 runs. **"Distinct costs
2.07x DistinctBy" compares two different code paths wearing one name.** Reading the forty lines
under the name would have caught it; this is the same failure as items 947/948 (corrected at 949)
and 951 (corrected at 952), three times in one session.

### Apportioned, with the filter measured on its own

Two arms added — the filter and scan with no dedup, and the unfiltered count as the floor. Three
runs:

```text
  GQL DISTINCT    164.4  173.8  182.2 us   Distinct fast path, unfiltered
  GRM dedup       296.5  296.7  324.9 us   filter + DistinctBy
  GQL +exists     570.8  574.1  630.8 us   filter + Distinct (general)
  GQL filt cnt    277.4  278.5  305.4 us   filter + scan, NO dedup
  GQL bare cnt      0.3    0.3    0.3 us   label count, O(1) — the floor
```

Subtracting the filtered scan from each dedup arm:

```text
  DistinctBy step   296.5 - 277.4 =   19 us
  Distinct  step    570.8 - 277.4 =  293 us      ~15x
```

**The dedup step itself differs by ~15x, not 2.07x.** The end-to-end 2.07x understated it, because
both arms carry a 277 us filter that has nothing to do with the operator. A ratio of totals is a
ratio of the thing you care about only when the common part is small; here it is half.

### What this changes about the target

Item 961 proposed lowering a one-column `RETURN DISTINCT` to `DistinctBy { key_slots: [0] }`. That
is now **better** motivated, not worse: `DistinctBy`'s general path costs 19 us where `Distinct`'s
costs 293, so the switch does not merely sidestep a missing fast path, it lands on a path that is
already good. The alternative — teaching `try_distinct_scan_prop` to see through a `Filter` —
fixes one shape; routing to `DistinctBy` fixes every shape whose fast path declines.

Still **not built**, and the preconditions from 961 stand with one added:

- **Row width.** `Distinct` keys the whole row; `DistinctBy` keys named slots. Equivalent only
  when the slots cover the row, and forgetting that is a wrong answer rather than a slow one.
- **Answer-equivalent**, so every mutant survives the differential tests (item 585): it needs a
  plan assertion and `dedupplan_961` as the before/after.
- **NEW: check the unfiltered case does not regress.** `Distinct`'s fast path at 164 us beats
  `DistinctBy`'s 19 us step plus a scan only because it fuses both; routing unconditionally to
  `DistinctBy` could lose the fast path where it currently fires. The route must be
  _when the fast path declines_, which means the decision cannot be made in the optimizer without
  knowing what exec will do — the real design question, and the reason this is still a diagnosis.

### Verification

No engine change: two arms added to `dedupplan_961`. Every arm prints its row count, and the two
new arms return 1 row by construction (a count) so they are deliberately NOT compared as
row-matched against the dedup arms — they are subtrahends, not alternatives, which is why the
subtraction is written out rather than printed as a ratio. Gates each its own command with its
exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0;
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 963 — correcting item 962's "~15x": no valid subtrahend exists, and the defensible figure is the DIFFERENCE between the two dedup arms, not a ratio of steps

**CORRECTION, no engine change.** Item 962 apportioned item 961's 2.07x by subtracting a
"filter + scan, no dedup" arm from each dedup arm and reported the dedup STEP at ~19 us against
~293 us, "~15x". The subtraction is invalid, and so is the 15x.

### Why the subtrahend was wrong

The arm subtracted was `… RETURN count(*)`. **A `count(*)` never materializes `dept`**, while both
dedup arms project it. So the subtraction charged the dedup step with the projection's cost in
both arms — unequally, because the two arms build that column through different code.

### The obvious repair also fails, and that is the finding

`RETURN count(n.dept)` forces the column to be built and still returns one row, which looks like
the right "everything but the dedup". Three runs:

```text
  GRM dedup        295.4  298.5  291.7 us    filter + project + DistinctBy
  GQL +exists      575.4  566.0  539.5 us    filter + project + Distinct
  GQL filt proj   1273.3 1239.6 1230.5 us    filter + project + count(expr)   <- the subtrahend
```

**The subtrahend costs more than either whole.** `count(<expr>)` brings its own aggregate
machinery, so it over-subtracts by an unknown amount instead of isolating the projection. Both
candidate subtrahends fail in opposite directions — one omits work the arms do, the other adds
work they do not — and the query surface offers no third.

### What IS defensible

Both dedup arms pay the identical filter, scan and projection, so **their difference isolates the
operator exactly, with no subtrahend needed**:

```text
  575.4 - 295.4 = 280     566.0 - 298.5 = 268     539.5 - 291.7 = 248 us
```

**`Distinct`'s general path costs ~265 us more than `DistinctBy` over 200,000 rows — about
1.3 ns/row.** That is the honest form of the finding. Expressing it as a _ratio of the dedup
steps_ requires knowing the common base, which is exactly what cannot be measured here, so item
962's "~15x" is withdrawn. Item 961's end-to-end 1.9-2.07x stands, because a ratio of totals is a
real statement about two whole queries even when it is not a statement about one operator.

### The rule this earns

**A decomposition by subtraction needs a subtrahend that differs from the whole by EXACTLY the
part being removed.** When no such query exists, the difference between two arms sharing
everything else is available and a per-step ratio is not — report the absolute difference and say
why the ratio is unavailable. The audit already carries the neighbouring rule from item 943 (one
walk, one denominator, a sum check that refuses to print when parts ≠ whole); this is the case
where the sum check cannot even be constructed, and the tell was that a "part" priced at 1239 us
exceeded the 566 us whole it was supposedly part of.

**An impossible number caught it again** — item 942 found a units bug because 4972% cannot be a
percentage; here a component cannot cost more than the thing containing it. That check is free and
has now paid twice.

### Verification

No engine change: one arm added to `dedupplan_961`, which now prints all six so the failed
subtrahends stay visible rather than being quietly dropped. Gates each its own command with its
exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0;
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 964 — the planner DOES reach the shape for an ordinary predicate, so `Distinct` under a `Filter` is a real target; specified, priced and NOT built, with the hazard named

**PLAN VERIFICATION + a specified target, no engine change.** Items 961-963 measured
`Distinct` under a `Filter` using `PROPERTY_EXISTS`, chosen to match Gremlin's `values()`
semantics — **not because it is what anyone writes**. If a plain comparison were seeded or fused
instead, the whole target would be an artifact of my own construction. The loop's own step says
verify the planner reaches the shape, so:

```text
  GQL ord pred   593.0 us   rows=5
    Distinct { Project { Filter { Scan { Person }, Compare { Gt, Prop{0,"dept"}, Lit("a") } },
               items: [("d", Prop { slot: 0, key: "dept" })] } }
```

`MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.dept > 'a' RETURN DISTINCT n.dept` — an entirely ordinary query —
produces **exactly the same shape at the same cost** as the `PROPERTY_EXISTS` arm (566-575 us).
The unfiltered twin is 164 us. So the target is the common shape, and item 961's construction was
representative rather than contrived.

### The mechanism, and the fix it implies

`try_distinct_scan_prop` requires `Project { Scan }` and its `Dict` arm dedups on **dictionary
codes through a dense `vec![false; dict.len()]` bitset** — no hashing. A `Filter` between
`Project` and `Scan` disqualifies it, so the row falls to `distinct_batch`, where a materialized
`Col::Str` takes a hash per row. The fix is to let the fast path accept `Filter { Scan }`,
computing a mask first — and **the mechanism already exists in this file**:
`distinct_chain_endpoints`' own `Plan::Filter` arm builds a `Batch` of candidate ids and calls
`eval_mask(pred, store, &batch)` rather than duplicating filter logic.

### Why it is NOT built here, which is a risk judgement and not a size one

The function has **five column-type arms**, each calling `scan_visit(store, label, |i| …)`, so a
mask must thread through all of them. The `Dict` arm — the one that matters — carries this note:

> _with the body in a closure the compiler keeps neither the `seen` bitset nor the bounds checks
> in hand, and `RETURN DISTINCT n.dept` over 100k nodes measured 148.1us against 85.8us for the
> identical loop written out (E79)._

So the obvious tidy implementation (wrap `scan_visit` in a mask-aware closure) is **the exact
shape E79 measured at 1.7x worse**, and two further tidyings of `scan_visit` were tried and
rejected there. This session has already paid that toll once: item 957 built a correct, working
evaluator fusion and had to reject it because merely growing a neighbouring match arm regressed
the untouched twin by 1.07x, disjoint.

**The risk is therefore specific and known: a widening that regresses the 164 us unfiltered fast
path to buy the 593 us filtered one.** That is a bad trade in the same direction item 957 refused,
and it cannot be ruled out by reading — only by building both arms and alternating them.

### What a future pass needs, so it does not re-derive this

1. Accept `Plan::Filter { input: Scan, pred }` in `try_distinct_scan_prop`, masking via
   `eval_mask` as `distinct_chain_endpoints` already does.
2. Keep the `Dict` whole-graph loop WRITTEN OUT with the mask as a plain index — do not route it
   through a closure (E79).
3. The **control is the unfiltered arm** (164 us), measured in alternated rounds. It is what the
   change must not touch, and it is what item 957's twin failed.
4. First-seen order is the correctness surface: the `Dict` arm pushes on first observation during
   the scan precisely because dict order can differ from scan order under deletes or a label
   subset. A mask must not change which occurrence is first.

### Verification

No engine change: one arm added to `dedupplan_961`, which now prints seven so the plan dump for
the ordinary predicate stays visible. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED:
`cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0;
`bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 965 — SHIPPED: one context object for the whole sorted page, 1.09x disjoint — and the alternation rule that nearly hid it behind a 1.13x phantom

**SHIPPED, and the method note is the larger half.** Item 868 left the TS sorted-LIMIT statement
spelling open at 4.6-5.25x the clause spelling, with the remainder recorded as _"materializing the
binding table and evaluating keys through a per-row context object"_. This takes the second half
of that.

### The isolated baseline, because the sweep is the wrong instrument

Item 737's rule: a per-row question needs a per-row instrument. `sorted-page-probe.ts` runs only
the three flagged shapes plus controls, one process, median of 5 alternated rounds:

```text
  stmt asc          42.16 ms  4.31x clause
  stmt desc         42.75 ms  4.37x
  stmt lowcard      42.11 ms  4.30x
  clause asc         9.79 ms  1.00x
  CONTROL keyless     0.01 ms            item 869's lazy window, untouched by the sorted branch
  stmt asc and clause asc return identical rows: YES
```

### The change

`case 'page'` built `{ binding: b, params, graph }` **inside** the `.map`, so a 200,000-row table
with one sort key made 200,000 context objects plus 200,000 one-element arrays — and this clause
must key every row, since finding the top K requires seeing them all. Now one context, reassigned
per row, with the single-key case specialized out of the `.map` (item 934's arity step, same
reason). Safe because a compiled sort key reads `env.binding` during the call and returns a value;
it does not retain `env`.

### THE METHOD FINDING: alternating PRE/POST is not enough if PRE always runs FIRST

The first alternation said the change won 1.11x on the target — and **1.34x on `clause asc`, and
1.13x on a control with no sort and no page clause at all**. A change confined to `case 'page'`
cannot reach a `count(*)`. Running the same pairs with the within-pair order **reversed** (POST
first, PRE second) made the control's movement vanish.

Pooling all four pairs across both orders:

```text
  stmt asc        POST  37.21  37.44  37.91  37.56      PRE  40.28  40.42  42.78  39.62
  CONTROL count   POST   3.50   3.83   3.89   4.20      PRE   4.31   4.01   4.08   3.51
```

**Every POST is below every PRE on the target — disjoint, 1.09x. The control overlaps, 3.86
against 3.98.** The 1.13x was an artifact of PRE always being measured first in each pair.

**The rule: alternate the ARMS and the ORDER WITHIN each pair.** `PRE,POST,PRE,POST` is still a
biased design if every pair runs PRE first — any warming trend across a pair is credited to POST.
This is the neighbour of item 957's blocked-rounds finding (three POST then three PRE read 1.16x
where alternating read 1.07x); that one was about blocking, this one is about _ordering inside the
alternation_, which looks correct and is not.

**`clause asc` is NOT a control and was wrongly used as one.** It moved 1.31x in the PRE-first
pairs; whether it genuinely benefits is unresolved and **not claimed here**. The real control is
an arm with no `ORDER BY`, no `LIMIT` and no page clause.

### Teeth

```text
  M1  multi-key branch returns nulls    CAUGHT — 1 failure
  M2  single-key branch returns null    CAUGHT — 9 failures
```

Both under `timeout` + cgroup cap with a restore before each, which also proves the new
specialization's **else** branch is covered — a one-armed test would have left it dark.

### What remains of item 868

**The gap is narrowed from 4.31x to ~3.9x, not closed.** The remainder is structural rather than
allocational: the clause spelling sorts rows whose key is already a projected column, while the
statement spelling evaluates the key through a compiled closure over a `Binding` for every row and
then projects again. No amount of context hoisting reaches that.

### Verification

Suites: gql 2,776 pass / 0 fail, gremlin 845/0, core 370/0, native 933/0. All 7 byte-identity
fuzzers pass, 13 tests. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED:
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

**VERIFICATION, no engine change.** Five changes shipped since the last broad sweep — 954 and 959

`bench_all` (native): 231 lines, **zero panics or errors**. `bun run bench` (ts/ffi/wasm): 67

## Item 967 — item 868's remaining 4.4x decomposes into 1.43x × 3.09x, and the product reconstructs the whole exactly

**DIAGNOSIS, no engine change.** Item 965 narrowed the TS sorted-LIMIT statement gap to ~3.9-4.4x
and named the remainder "structural". This says which structure, with two row-matched pairs
instead of a subtraction.

### The hypothesis, read off the code, and PARTIALLY WRONG

`detectNodeProjection` opens with `if (clauses.length !== 2) return null`. The clause spelling
`MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10` is match+return (**2**) and reaches it; the
statement spelling `MATCH (n:P) ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10 RETURN n.k AS c` is match+**page**+return
(**3**) and cannot. That reads like the whole answer.

It is not. A no-op third clause — `FILTER true`, which keeps every row and changes no answer —
added to the CLAUSE spelling costs it **1.43x, not 4.4x**:

```text
  clause asc       8.74 ms  1.00x      2 clauses, sort in RETURN
  clause +3rd     12.54 ms  1.43x      3 clauses, sort in RETURN
  stmt asc        38.76 ms  4.43x      3 clauses, sort in the PAGE clause
```

**Losing the shortcut explains about a third of the gap in log terms, not all of it.** Writing the
reading up as the cause — which items 947/948, 951 and 961 all did and all had to retract — would
have been wrong again; one arm cost one minute and caught it.

### The decomposition, and why this one is valid where item 963's was not

Each ratio is between two arms differing in **exactly one** property:

```text
  clause asc  -> clause +3rd     the 2-clause shortcut, lost        1.43x
  clause +3rd -> stmt asc        WHERE the sort happens             3.09x
  product                                                           4.43x
  observed stmt / clause                                            4.43x
```

**The product reconstructs the whole exactly.** That is item 943's sum check in multiplicative
form, and it is available here precisely because these are differences between row-matched pairs
rather than subtractions of a separately-measured part — the thing item 963 could not construct
when `count(n.dept)` priced a "part" at more than its whole.

So the gap is **two causes, not one**: a third clause disqualifies the whole shortcut family
(1.43x), and sorting in the page clause over `Binding` maps rather than in the projection over
already-materialized columns costs a further 3.09x.

### What each half implies, and why neither is built here

- **The 1.43x is not specific to a page clause.** Any third clause costs it — `FILTER true` does.
  So it is the shortcut family's `clauses.length !== 2` guard, and widening that is a change to
  nineteen detectors' shared precondition, with `routes-fired.test.ts` as the surface. Large, and
  item 910 already priced the detectors at 25% of planning the big query.
- **The 3.09x is the real prize and the harder question.** Folding a trailing page clause into
  the following `RETURN`'s own `ORDER BY`/`LIMIT` would turn 3 clauses into 2 and move the sort
  onto projected columns, collecting both halves at once. But the two are NOT the same operation
  in general: a statement `ORDER BY` sorts the working table and may key on anything in scope,
  while `RETURN … ORDER BY` sorts output rows. **Whether ISO permits the fold, and under exactly
  which condition on the keys, is a specification question** — and per CLAUDE.md that goes to the
  BNF artifact and the session notes, not to a guess made while optimizing.

### Verification

No engine change: one arm added to `sorted-page-probe`. The new arm is row-matched with
`clause asc` by construction — `FILTER true` is ISO §14.6 and keeps every row — and the probe
asserts the statement and clause spellings return identical rows. Gates each its own command with
its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0;
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 968 — the fold is worth 3.72x and the precondition HOLDS: a projection's `ORDER BY` can key on an input variable, and the folded form costs what the clause spelling costs

**PRICING + precondition check, no engine change.** Item 967 named the fold — rewrite a trailing
page clause into the following `RETURN`'s own `ORDER BY`/`LIMIT` — and called whether ISO permits
it a specification question. Two checks settle whether it is worth asking.

### Precondition: can a projection's `ORDER BY` key on an INPUT variable?

If it can only sort by output columns, the fold is impossible whenever the sort key is not
projected. Six-node fixture, `k` descending against `other` ascending so a wrong order is visible:

```text
  statement ORDER BY       MATCH (n:P) ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 3 RETURN n.other AS o   -> [50,40,30]
  clause, output col       MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS o ORDER BY o LIMIT 3         -> [0,1,2]
  clause, INPUT var        MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.other AS o ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 3   -> [50,40,30]
  clause, input var DESC   MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.other AS o ORDER BY n.k DESC …    -> [0,10,20]
```

**It can, and the folded spelling returns the IDENTICAL rows as the statement spelling** — the
first and third lines agree exactly, including on a key the projection does not emit. So the fold
is expressible in this engine, not merely conceivable.

### Price: what the folded form costs

```text
  stmt asc        38.01 ms  3.87x    the shape being replaced
  clause +3rd     12.36 ms  1.26x    3 clauses, sort in RETURN
  folded form     10.22 ms  1.04x    MATCH … RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10
  clause asc       9.83 ms  1.00x
```

**The folded form costs what the clause spelling costs.** So the rewrite is worth
**38.01 → 10.22, a 3.72x** — and it collects BOTH halves of item 967's decomposition at once,
because folding removes the third clause (the 1.43x) and moves the sort into the projection (the
3.09x).

### It has a home and a precedent

`dropVacuousPage` already rewrites a page clause away, composed in `compileLinear` ahead of the
other rewrites (item 549, which took `MATCH … ORDER BY n.age RETURN count(*)` from 126.60 ms to
0.00). This fold is its sibling: the vacuous case drops the clause, this one moves it.

### NOT built here, and the refusal list is the work

A planner rewrite is only as good as what it declines, and these are the cases where folding
changes an answer rather than the cost. Each needs its own test before the rewrite ships:

- **Aggregation in the `RETURN`.** `ORDER BY k LIMIT 10 RETURN count(*)` takes ten rows then
  counts; the folded form counts everything then pages one row. Different answers.
- **`DISTINCT` / `GROUP BY` in the `RETURN`** — both change the row set the `LIMIT` applies to.
- **A key the projection cannot see.** The check above shows an input variable works; a key
  reading something dropped before the `RETURN` would not.
- **`SKIP`/`OFFSET` as well as `LIMIT`**, and more than one page clause in sequence.
- **The page clause not immediately before the `RETURN`** — anything between them observes the
  paged table.

It is also **answer-equivalent where it is legal**, so every mutant of the rewrite survives the
differential tests (item 585): it needs a route assertion on the clause count, plus this probe as
the before/after.

### Verification

No engine change: one arm added to `sorted-page-probe`, and a scratch check of the four ORDER BY
spellings whose output is quoted above. The probe asserts the statement and clause spellings
return identical rows. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED:
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 969 — SHIPPED: `foldPageIntoReturn`, 3.79x, closing the larger half of item 868 — and a mutant proved one of my own refusals inert

**SHIPPED.** Item 968 priced the fold at 3.72x and verified the precondition. This builds it, in
`compileLinear` beside `dropVacuousPage` (item 549) and `inlineTrailingFilter` (item 548), whose
shape it copies: a clause the ladder cannot see, folded back into one it can.

### The measurement, with four controls

```text
                    BEFORE    AFTER
  stmt asc          38.01     10.02   3.79x      key IS projected
  stmt desc         37.93     10.32   3.68x
  stmt lowcard      38.28     36.36   1.05x      key NOT projected
  clause asc         9.83     10.44              CONTROL
  clause +3rd       12.36     12.50              CONTROL
  folded form       10.22     10.23              CONTROL
  CONTROL count      4.63      4.43              CONTROL
```

**All four controls flat.** The statement spelling now costs what the clause spelling costs.

### The arm that did NOT move, and what it proves

`stmt lowcard` keys on `n.lo`, which the projection does not emit. It stayed at ~36. Two readings
were available — the fold declined, or it fired and the folded shape is just as dear — so I
measured the hand-folded query: **`folded lowcard` 36.89 against `stmt lowcard` 34.33.** The fold
**fired**; sorting on a key that is not an output column simply cannot use the materialized
column. So the rewrite is 3.7x where the key is projected and neutral where it is not, which is
the honest characterization and not a caveat discovered later.

### A MUTANT PROVED ONE OF MY OWN REFUSALS INERT

```text
  M1  drop the aggregate refusal       CAUGHT — 3 failures
  M2  drop the alias-shadowing guard   SURVIVED all 2,786 tests
```

M2 surviving was not a hole in the suite. Inspecting it: my "shadowing" test used `ORDER BY
n.other` with alias `other` — a **property** expression whose only free variable is `n`, so the
guard never fired for it either. The real shape needs a bare-variable key, and constructing it
settles the question:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) LET x = n.other ORDER BY x LIMIT 3 RETURN n.k AS x  -> [5,4,3]
  MATCH (n:P) LET x = n.other RETURN n.k AS x ORDER BY x LIMIT 3  -> [5,4,3]
```

**A clause `ORDER BY x` resolves `x` in the INPUT scope, not to the output column of the same
name** — if it resolved to the alias, the second would sort by `n.k` and return `[0,1,2]`. So
this engine is not vulnerable to the hazard and **the guard protects nothing today**. It is kept
the way item 869's `toArray` and item 865's `nulls_first` guard are kept — cheap, and
load-bearing the moment that resolution rule changes — and the test now asserts the resolution
rule itself, so it would notice.

**The test was wrong before the mutant ran.** It claimed to cover shadowing and passed either
way: a test that cannot fail for its stated reason is the "believed generative test" CLAUDE.md
warns about, and only mutation exposed it.

### The refusal list, each case asserting an ANSWER

`page-fold.test.ts`, 11 cases. Aggregation (`LIMIT 3 RETURN count(*)` is 3, not 6), `GROUP BY`
(the two smallest `k` fall in DIFFERENT groups — my first expectation was wrong and the test
caught me), `DISTINCT`, a projection that already pages (two pages compose: 4 then the last 2),
`RETURN *`, and a clause between the page and the `RETURN` (which observes the paged table).

## Item 970 — the native engine has NO page-statement gap: three spellings within 1.00x, so item 969 has no Rust twin

**NEGATIVE RESULT, no engine change.** Item 969 closed a 3.79x in TS by folding a trailing page
statement onto the `RETURN`. "Grep the pattern elsewhere" is the loop's own step, and item 868
recorded that the two engines had this gap in **opposite directions** — _"native: clause slow,
items 865/866; TS: statement slow"_. That note describes a state a hundred items ago, which is a
reason to measure rather than a reason to skip.

### Measured, three rounds, 200,000 nodes, min of 9

```text
            round 1   round 2   round 3
  stmt        998.0    1090.9    1092.3 us     MATCH … ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10 RETURN n.k AS c
  clause     1008.4    1088.3    1091.3        MATCH … RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10
  folded     1009.1    1088.3    1092.7        MATCH … RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10
  stmt lowc  1072.7    1155.3    1154.0        a different key, not compared
```

**All three within 1.00x, and the first three return identical rows** (asserted, not assumed —
the probe prints `rows match` or voids the comparison). **There is no Rust twin to build.**

### The plans DIFFER while the costs do not, and that is the finding

```text
  stmt     Project   { OrderPage { Scan } }
  clause   OrderPage { Project   { Scan } }
  folded   OrderPage { Project   { Scan } }
```

The native engine has the same **plan asymmetry** as TS and none of the **cost asymmetry**,
because a page statement lowers to an `OrderPage` operator over a `Scan` rather than to a
materialized binding table that a later clause sorts. The TS defect was never about where the
sort sits in the plan; it was about what the sort sits on.

**So this is a case where identical plans are NOT required for identical cost**, which cuts
against the reflex the subscript thread (items 956-959) built up, where making the plans
byte-identical was exactly the fix. Both are true: one canonical plan GUARANTEES equal cost, but
two plans can still cost the same, and assuming the converse would have sent a future pass
rewriting native lowering for nothing.

### Why this is worth an item at all

Because the alternative is a future pass seeing "TS 3.79x" and porting it on symmetry, which is
item 950's mistake in the other direction — there, "native did it" was treated as a price for TS;
here, "TS needed it" would be treated as a price for native. Item 843's rule is that neither
engine's version is inferable from the other's, and this is the measurement that says so for this
gap rather than the assumption.

### Verification

No engine change: one example added (`pagefold_970`). The probe asserts the first three arms
return identical rows and prints each plan beside its time. Gates each its own command with its
exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0;
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 972 — the native spelling probe reports NO PERF CLIFFS, by tagging the one flag items 961-964 proved is not a defect

**PROBE CHANGE, no engine change.** `spelling_probe` had flagged `DISTINCT vs dedup` as a cliff
on every run. Items 961-964 established by plan dump that it is **not a defect**: the two
spellings are not the same question, because `values('dept')` yields nothing for a vertex lacking
the key where `RETURN n.dept` yields null, so the Gremlin side carries a
`Filter { PropertyExists }` the GQL side does not — a semantic requirement worth ~277 us of the
~300 measured. Row-matching the pair **inverts** the finding: `Distinct` then costs ~2x
`DistinctBy`, so Gremlin's lowering is the better of the two.

A gate that reports a settled non-defect every run is the failure `CLOSED.md` exists to prevent,
happening inside the probe's own output — and it had already been re-derived once.

### The tag, and why not the existing one

`ROWS_MAY_DIFFER` already exists for `groupCount`, where the same answer comes back in a
different CONTAINER. That is not this case: **the rows match (5 and 5) and the WORK does not.**
Overloading it would have made both tags mean "ignore this", which is how a tag stops carrying
information. So `WORK_DIFFERS` is its own tag with its own message:

```text
=== DISTINCT vs dedup [WORK_DIFFERS] ===
  GQL    0.086ms  rows=5       MATCH (n:Person) RETURN DISTINCT n.dept AS d
  GRM    0.152ms  rows=5       g.V().hasLabel('Person').values('dept').dedup()
  ✓ same rows; one spelling is semantically obliged to do more (see note)
```

### What the tag does NOT suppress

**Both arms are still measured and both times and row counts are still printed** — only the
automatic cliff classification is skipped. A future regression in either arm stays visible to a
reader, and the row-count check still runs. That is the whole difference between annotating a
result and hiding one, and it is why the group was tagged rather than deleted or its fixture
quietened.

The comment at the group carries the four item numbers and the inverted finding, so the next
reader gets the conclusion at the site rather than having to find it in a 27,000-line index.

### The state this leaves

```text
  native spelling_probe   NO PERF CLIFFS: every equivalent spelling converges on plan or cost
  TS spelling-probe       2 groups over 2x, both settled (item 971: 325 correct, 285 closed at 644)
```

**Both spelling gates are now at their floor.** Every remaining flag on either side is recorded
as correct-by-design or closed-with-a-reason, which is the state they are supposed to be in and
have not been for some time.

### Verification

No engine change: one tag, one group comment, one verdict arm in `spelling_probe`. The tagged
group was re-run to confirm it still prints both arms rather than being skipped. Gates each its
own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0;
`bun run check` 0.

## Item 973 — four closed targets declined in one tick, and a 1000x UNIT ERROR found in the record by its own internal inconsistency

**INDEX WORK + a correction, no engine change.** Items 971 and 972 left both spelling gates at
their floor, so this tick needed a target from a different source — the TS bench's `ts/ffi`
column. Every candidate it offered was already closed, and checking cost one grep each.

### The four declines

1. **`project 3 columns`, ffi 10x SLOWER than ts (5.6 against 57.2).** A striking inversion, and
   **item 289 had already decomposed it**: `JSON.parse` 48%, render + FFI call 33%, row shaping
   12% — **~80% carrier, no engine change touches it**, and `queryArrowIpc` is the answer. Its
   note records that it stopped three earlier passes (789, 793, and its own). **This is the
   fourth.**
2. **The other inverted rows** (`project the element`, `project the edge`, `ordered projection
[no window]`) are the same carrier cost, by item 289's rule: **read the table's SHAPE before
   its ratios** — native loses every row with 200k-1M rows out and wins 29-88x every row with one.
3. **`count 4-hop`, the sweep's 88x.** My hypothesis was that `longChainCount`'s forward sweep is
   gated at FIVE segments and 4-hop falls just under it. **Wrong: the gate is already FOUR**, and
   item 301 measured which side each depth belongs on — 3 hops product 250.1 ms against sweep
   374.9 (product wins 1.50x), 4 hops product 980.2 against sweep 512.4 (sweep wins 1.91x). The
   crossover sits where a product stops being linear in the edges, and `fourSegmentCount` was
   deleted rather than left unreachable.
4. **`label on start` 5239x and `a product's one-sided predicate`** — declined last tick (971).

### The unit error, and how it surfaced

Item 810's block records the absolutes for the multi-hop count rows:

```text
  count 4-hop            TS 598.6-639.6 ms   ffi 6.6-6.7 us   <- WRONG UNIT
```

`bench.ts` computes `ms = Math.min(ms, (Bun.nanoseconds() - t) / 1e6)`, so its columns are
**milliseconds**; `bench_all` independently prints native `4-hop` at **6506.4 us = 6.5 ms**. The
figure is right and the unit is off by 1000x. Corrected in place.

**It surfaced from the entry contradicting itself.** Two lines above the table, the same item
reports the ratio as **91-97x**. With `6.6 us` the ratio would be **90,600x**. A reader taking the
absolutes at face value would price this row as a 90,000x algorithmic hole rather than the 88x
constant-factor gap it is — a different kind of target entirely, and the kind someone would spend
a session on.

That is the **impossible-number check** paying a third time: item 942 caught a units bug because
4972% cannot be a percentage, item 963 caught a bad subtrahend because a part cannot exceed its
whole, and here a stated ratio cannot disagree with its own operands by 1000x.

### The irony worth recording rather than enjoying

Item 810's entire argument is _"record the ABSOLUTES alongside the ratio… storing only the
quotient makes a later re-derivation impossible in principle."_ It was right, it acted on it, and
the absolute it stored carried the wrong unit — so the re-derivation it enabled is the one that
caught it. **The lesson is not that the rule failed; it is that an absolute needs its unit checked
against the instrument that produced it, which a ratio never needed.**

### Verification

No engine change: one character in `CLOSED.md` (`us` → `ms`) plus this entry. The correction is
cross-checked against two independent instruments — `bench.ts`'s own arithmetic and `bench_all`'s
`best_us` column. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0;
`bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 974 — item 964's specified fix BUILT and REJECTED: it is 2.9x SLOWER, and the hazard that bit was not the one two items had warned about

**BUILT AND REVERTED, recorded next to the code.** Item 964 specified widening
`try_distinct_scan_prop` to accept `Filter { Scan }`, verified the planner reaches the shape, and
named the risk: regressing the UNFILTERED fast path, because the function's `Dict` arm records
E79 (moving its loop into a closure costs 1.7x) and item 957 had already rejected a change for
regressing an untouched neighbour.

I built it as a **separate sibling** precisely to dodge that: the existing function's body was not
touched by a single byte. The named hazard never arrived. A different one did.

```text
  arm                                   PRE        POST
  WHERE PROPERTY_EXISTS … DISTINCT     571.4     1674.6 us    2.9x SLOWER
  WHERE n.dept > 'a'      DISTINCT     585.3     1181.4       2.0x SLOWER
```

**The replacement is slower than the general route it replaces.** Reverted.

### Why, which is the part worth keeping

**The per-step figures below are an INFERENCE and are corrected at item 975** — they subtract
item 962's filter-and-scan arm, which does not do this route's projection, which is the same
unverified-subtrahend defect item 963 withdrew. What is measured is the end-to-end pair above.
The general route pays `Filter` ~277 us plus ~293 for
the generic dedup. The replacement pays ~1400 for its mask step alone: `eval_mask` over a
synthesized `Col::Nodes` batch reads the property per row through the generic evaluator, where
the `Filter` **operator** in the pipeline has a vectorized path over the typed column.

So the trade was _a vectorized filter swapped for a generic one, in order to save hashing_ — and
the filter is the larger half. The dedup saving was real and irrelevant.

### The transferable lesson

`distinct_chain_endpoints` uses exactly this `eval_mask`-over-`Col::Nodes` device, and is right
to: there the candidate set is a hop frontier, already materialized and usually small. Over a
whole-label scan it is 200,000 rows and the comparison is against a vectorized operator.
**The device is not portable from a frontier to a scan.** Item 964 cited that existing use as
evidence the mechanism was available — which it was — but availability is not suitability, and
the two differ by the size of the set it runs over.

This is also the third time this session a _specified, well-motivated_ fix failed on contact
(947/948 at 949, the evaluator fusion at 957, this). Each was specified from a correct reading.
What they have in common is that the reading establishes a mechanism EXISTS and the measurement
establishes what it COSTS, and only the second one decides.

### A negative result worth one line

Auditing the record for more of item 973's unit error found none: `grep -nE "ffi [0-9.]+ ?(us|µs)"`
over both documents matches only item 973's own quotation of it. **The defect was isolated, not
systemic.**

### Verification

changed, which is what CLAUDE.md asks for ("Record rejected optimizations with their numbers,

## Item 975 — correcting item 974's own per-step figure: I repeated the unverified-subtrahend defect ONE ITEM after recording it

**CORRECTION, no engine change.** Item 974 rejected a change on a measured end-to-end pair and
then explained it with a decomposition:

> _"the general route pays `Filter` ~277 us … plus ~293 for the generic dedup. The replacement
> pays **~1400 for its mask step ALONE**."_

**That ~1400 is an inference, not a measurement**, and it was produced the exact way item 963
withdrew a figure for: by subtracting item 962's filter-and-scan arm, which **does not do this
route's projection**. Item 963's rule is that a decomposition by subtraction needs a subtrahend
differing from the whole by exactly the part being removed, and that when no such query exists
the honest output is the difference between two row-matched arms and no per-step ratio.

I wrote that rule down and then broke it one item later, in the same file, on the same question.

### What actually stands

```text
  WHERE PROPERTY_EXISTS … DISTINCT     571.4 → 1674.6 us    2.9x    MEASURED, both arms
  WHERE n.dept > 'a'      DISTINCT     585.3 → 1181.4       2.0x    MEASURED, both arms
```

The **rejection is unaffected** — it rests entirely on those two pairs, each measured on both
sides of the same change. What does not stand is the claim about _which step inside the route_
spent the difference.

The structural statement survives on its own terms: `eval_mask` over a synthesized `Col::Nodes`
batch reads the property per row through the generic evaluator, while the `Filter` operator has a
vectorized path over the typed column. That is a real difference in mechanism and the only
candidate large enough to explain a 2.9x. **How much it costs is unmeasured**, and the three
places that said otherwise now say so.

### Why this matters beyond tidiness

The inferred ~1400 looked like a new, independent finding — _"`eval_mask` on a Nodes batch is 5x
the Filter operator"_ — and that reading was my first candidate target for this tick. It would
have been a target derived from a number I had invented by subtraction. The correction is
therefore not bookkeeping; it is what stopped the next item being built on it.

947/948 priced a fix against observed behaviour without reading the mechanism (corrected at 949).
951 attributed a gap to a route without verifying it (corrected at 952). 962 decomposed with a
subtrahend that omitted work (withdrawn at 963). 974 decomposed with a subtrahend that omitted
different work (corrected here). **Recording a rule does not install it** — three of these four

## Item 976 — the mask step MEASURED at ~690 us, not the inferred ~1400, and the rejected sibling was wrong in TWO ways rather than one

**MEASUREMENT, no engine change.** Item 975 withdrew item 974's per-step figure as an inference
and said the honest next step was to measure it. `eval_mask` is `pub(super)`, so no example can
call it; the measurement is temporary instrumentation inside the rejected sibling — restored,
timed, read, reverted — the same device item 952 used for the `pathProps` counter.

### The three steps, on the `n.dept > 'a'` arm

```text
  INSTRUMENT ids=86.4us   mask=1200.0us  dedup=414.0us     <- first rep, cold
  INSTRUMENT ids=87.6us   mask=1191.3us  dedup=406.8us
  INSTRUMENT ids=92.5us   mask= 698.9us  dedup=405.5us     <- steady state from here
  INSTRUMENT ids=95.5us   mask= 688.2us  dedup=405.1us
  INSTRUMENT ids=94.8us   mask= 692.7us  dedup=408.0us
  INSTRUMENT ids=95.2us   mask= 688.2us  dedup=404.5us
```

~95 + ~690 + ~405 = **1190 us, matching the 1194.7 the arm reports** — so the parts account for
the whole, which is the check item 943 asks for and item 963 could not construct by subtraction.
Here it is available because the instrument is _inside_ the route rather than beside it.

**The inferred ~1400 was about 2x high.** Item 975 was right to withdraw it.

### Two defects, not one

The correction that matters is not the magnitude but the shape. Item 974 named a single cause; the
instrument shows two:

1. **`eval_mask` alone (~690) exceeds the ENTIRE general route (~585).** It reads the property per
   row through the generic evaluator where the `Filter` operator has a vectorized path over the
   typed column. This half was correctly identified, just mispriced.
2. **The dedup is ~405 us**, not the near-free dense-bitset pass it looks like. A per-row
   `mask.get(row)` compare plus an id indirection loses the sequential locality `scan_visit` has
   — so the part of the design that was supposed to be the WIN is itself slower than the general
   route's dedup.

So the trade was a vectorized filter swapped for a generic one **and** a sequential walk swapped
for an indirected one, in order to save hashing that was not the cost. Item 974 would have been
rejected on either half alone.

### What this closes and what it opens

**Closes**: the ~1400 is retired and replaced with measured numbers at the code, so the next
reader gets `690 / 405` rather than a figure produced by subtraction.

**Opens, narrowly**: `eval_mask` over a `Col::Nodes` batch costs ~3.45 ns/row at 200,000 rows
where the `Filter` operator is materially cheaper on the same predicate. That is a real asymmetry
and it is now a measured one — but it is **not** pursued here, because every caller that uses the
device today (`distinct_chain_endpoints`) runs it over a hop frontier, where the set is small and
the asymmetry is not worth the cost of a second code path (item 974's own transferable lesson).

### Verification

No engine change: the instrumentation was reverted and the arm re-measured at **572.1 / 581.3 us**,
matching its pre-instrumentation 571.4 / 585.3. The committed diff is the rejection note at
`try_distinct_scan_prop`, upgraded from inference to measurement. Engine suite **1,251** passed /
0 failed. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0;
`bun run check` 0.

## Item 977 — the `Clause` enum priced variant by variant: every read-path clause already has a fold, and a vacuous `WITH` costs NOTHING

**NEGATIVE RESULT, no engine change.** The method's first step is _price an enum's variants, pick
the biggest MISSING path_. Item 969 folded `page`; items 548 and 549 had folded `filter` and the
vacuous `page` before it. So: which variant is left?

### The enum, priced

`Clause` has fourteen variants. Between `MATCH` and `RETURN` on the read path, these can stand:

```text
  Filter       → inlineTrailingFilter           item 548, 7.7-10.9x
  Page         → foldPageIntoReturn             item 969, 3.79x
  Page (vacuous) → dropVacuousPage              item 549, 126.60 → 0.00
  Let          → inlineTrailingLet
  With         → boundExprs / inlineTrailingLet  ← the one I thought was missing
  Call (named) → inlineAggregateCall
  Call (inline)→ inlineCorrelatedCall
  For          → detectForCount rung
```

I read the list, saw no fold NAMED for `WITH`, and predicted it would cost the shortcut family
what item 967 measured for a no-op third clause (1.43x) or what item 548 found for `FILTER`
(7.7-10.9x). **Wrong, and the probe is why I know in one run rather than after building
something.**

```text
  A count, no WITH        0.00 ms   1.00x
  B count, WITH n         0.00 ms   1.09x     (both below timer resolution)
  C filtered, no WITH     3.22 ms             the meaningful pair
  D filtered, WITH n      3.19 ms   1.00x
  E WITH that projects    0.00 ms             non-vacuous, shown for the line
  A and B agree: YES      C and D agree: YES
```

**A vacuous `WITH` costs nothing.** The C/D pair is the one worth reading — A, B and E are all
under the timer's resolution, so their ratios are noise and are not claimed.

### Why, which is the part worth keeping

`boundExprs` handles it: a `WITH` whose projection is a simple renaming becomes a binding map and
is substituted away by the same rewrite that inlines a trailing `LET`. Its own comment states the
distinction precisely — _"`LET` ADDS a binding and `WITH` REPLACES the row… A `WITH` that
FILTERS, aggregates, dedupes, groups, orders or pages is a row boundary rather than a renaming,
and declines."_

So the fold exists; it is simply not named after the clause, which is why reading the rewrite
list did not reveal it. **A fold found by grepping for clause names would have missed this one** —
the lesson for the next enumeration is to check behaviour per variant, not the index of rewrite
names.

### What this settles

**There is no missing read-path fold.** Every variant that can stand between `MATCH` and `RETURN`
either folds, inlines, or is a genuine row boundary that must not. Item 967's remaining 1.43x is
therefore not reachable by "fold one more clause" — it is the shortcut family's
`clauses.length !== 2` precondition itself, on shapes where the intervening clause is real work.

Recording this so the enumeration is not repeated: the next pass asking "which clause has no
fold?" has its answer here, with the probe to re-run.

### Verification

No engine change: one probe added (`with-clause-probe.ts`). It asserts A/B and C/D return
identical rows and prints every round, and it deliberately labels the sub-millisecond rows as
unmeasurable rather than reporting their ratios as results. Gates each its own command with its
exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 978 — the INDEXED curve item 949 said was missing, and it finds something bigger: `p.b = true` costs ~5x `p.b` on the SAME plan shape

**MEASUREMENT + an instrument fix, no engine change.** Item 949 withdrew item 948's proposal to
widen `scan_is_cheap` to `Column::Bool` and said exactly why: `scan_is_cheap` governs the
**indexed** path (all four call sites are behind an index check), while 948's sweep measured the
**un-indexed degraded** seek — _"Whether a bool column's INDEXED seek breaks even at 3% or 15% is
a real question and this session has no measurement of it."_ `INDEXED=1` on `seekcross_948` is
that measurement.

### The curve, with the route each row actually took

```text
  true%   seek(= true)   filter(bare)   ratio    rows    route
      2         61.2         145.6      0.42x    4000    [seek  ]  seek wins 2.4x
     10        284.0         151.2      1.88x   20000    [seek  ]  seek LOSES
     20        919.2         161.0      5.71x   40000    [filter]
     40        931.2         169.1      5.51x   80000    [filter]
     60        940.0         178.3      5.27x  120000    [filter]
     80        951.6         187.4      5.08x  160000    [filter]
     98        955.4         195.4      4.89x  196000    [filter]
```

### Finding A — the cap IS too permissive for a Bool column, and now there is a curve for it

With a real hash index the seek wins at 2% and **already loses 1.88x at 10%**.
`SEEK_MAX_FRACTION = 0.154` admits seeks to 15.4%, so a 10%-selective Bool key gets a seek that
costs it nearly double. The break-even sits in the neighbourhood of
`SEEK_MAX_FRACTION_CHEAP_SCAN = 0.031`, which is the constant item 948 proposed applying and item
949 retracted **only** for want of this curve. **948's part (1) is now supported by the right
measurement**; it is still not built here, because changing a planner constant is a route change
needing its own before/after and a mutation pass.

### Finding B — larger, and it is not about seeking at all

From 20% up the gate **correctly declines** and both arms are `Filter { Scan }`. So the two
columns stop comparing seek-against-scan and start comparing two spellings of one predicate on
one plan shape over identical rows:

```text
  WHERE p.b20 = true    Filter { Scan, Compare { Eq, Prop, Lit(Bool(true)) } }    919.2 us
  WHERE p.b20           Filter { Scan, Prop }                                      161.0 us
```

**~5x, same plan shape, same 40,000 rows.** That is an equivalent-spelling cliff in the
EVALUATOR, and it is the same family as item 946's `= false` at 3.18x `NOT` — which until now
read as a seeding artifact. It is not: it survives with the seek gone.

### The instrument defect I had to fix first, which is the methodological point

Adding `INDEXED=1` silently made the `seek(= true)` column **change meaning halfway down the
table** — a seek for the first two rows, a filter for the rest. A reader would have taken 5.71x
at 20% as "the seek is 5.71x worse" when the seek is not running. That is precisely the defect
item 973 found in a stored absolute, reproduced live in my own new output.

Each row now prints the route it took, read off the optimized plan rather than inferred from the
spelling. **A sweep that gains a new mode needs its labels re-checked against that mode**, not
only its numbers.

### Verification

No engine change: `INDEXED=1` and per-row route labelling on `seekcross_948`. Both plan shapes
were dumped and confirmed before any ratio was read; the probe still refuses to print a ratio
unless the two arms' row counts agree. **`cargo clippy` CAUGHT an identity `.map` in the first
version of the labelling** (exit 101) — the gates are separate commands precisely so that shows
up as a failure rather than as a passing pipe. Gates each its own command with its exit code read
UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0;
`bun run fmt:check` 0; `bun run check` 0.

## Item 979 — the `Value`-variant gap is real but `typed_bool_mask` is the WRONG LAYER: zero firings, and the 1.10x I nearly credited to it was noise

**BUILT, VERIFIED NOT REACHED, REVERTED.** Item 978 measured `WHERE p.b = true` at ~5x the bare
`WHERE p.b` on an identical `Filter { Scan }` plan. Reading the dispatch found a clean enum gap:

```text
  Expr::Compare → typed_num_mask   (Prop vs Lit(Num))   ✓
                → typed_str_mask   (Prop vs Lit(Str))   ✓
                → (nothing)        (Prop vs Lit(Bool))  ✗  ← looked like the whole answer
                → as_truth(&eval(…))                        the boxed general path
```

So I wrote `typed_bool_mask` mirroring the two siblings, Eq/Ne only, and dispatched it.

### The measurement, and the trap inside it

```text
  20% arm    PRE 919.2 us    POST 839.1 us    1.10x
```

A 1.10x improvement on exactly the arm I was targeting. **That is what it looks like when a
change works a little**, and it is the most dangerous reading available — a small win on the
right row invites you to ship it and call the rest future work.

A counter in the new function says otherwise:

```text
  TYPED_BOOL_MASK FIRED   ×0
```

**Zero. It never ran.** The 1.10x was run-to-run noise on a row whose cost the change could not
touch, and I would have attributed it to a function that did not execute. Item 900's null A/B is
the same failure with the sign flipped; item 937 is the diagnosis version. This is the third
shape of it: a change that does not run, measured as a small win.

### Where the path actually goes

`MATCH (p:P) WHERE p.b = true RETURN count(*)` is `Aggregate { Filter { Scan } }` over `count(*)`,
and that is `try_filtered_count` — a fast path in its own right, not `eval_mask`'s `Compare` arm.
`try_filtered_scan_num_agg`'s own comment says so in passing: _"count(_) is try_filtered_count;
only a prop agg here."*

And the enum gap **recurs one layer up**: the filtered-scan aggregate family has
`try_filtered_scan_num_agg` and `try_filtered_scan_str_agg` and **no bool twin**. So the shape of
the diagnosis survives; only its address was wrong.

### Why the change was reverted rather than kept

`typed_bool_mask` is not dead in general — `eval_mask`'s `Compare` arm is live for shapes that do
not reach `try_filtered_count`, such as a filtered projection. But it is **unmeasured** on any of
them, and the session's standing rule is not to ship what has not been measured. Keeping it
because it "must help somewhere" is precisely the reasoning items 947, 951, 964 and 974 each had
to withdraw.

### The next step, addressed correctly this time

Price `WHERE p.b = true` against `WHERE p.b` through `try_filtered_count`, confirm the Num/Str
arms are what make the bare spelling 161 us, and add the bool twin there — **with a dispatch
counter before the timing, not after it.**

### Verification

No engine change ships: `git checkout` on `exec.rs`, rebuilt clean. Gates each its own command
with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0;
`bun run check` 0.

## Item 980 — the 5x bool-comparison fix WORKS (919.2 → 158.5) and is NOT shipped: a polarity mutant survives the suite and my 3VL probe never reached the route

**BUILT, MEASURED, HELD BACK.** Item 979 pointed at `try_filtered_count`; the route counters say
every bool arm lands in its `fallback_pull_filter`, and that calls `try_filter_keep`, which opens
with `try_filter_keep_bool_prop` — a fast path for a **bare** bool prop with no equivalent for
`Compare { Eq, Prop, Lit(Bool) }`. Widening that one pattern:

```text
  true%   = true    bare     ratio        BEFORE
     20   158.5    160.7     0.99x   tie   (was 919.2 / 160.2 — 5.71x)
     40   171.2    169.2     1.01x   tie
     98   195.2    195.6     1.00x   tie
```

**~5.8x, and the two spellings converge** across the whole sweep. Engine suite 1,251/0,
`rewrite_fuzz` at 200k seeds 10/0, all 7 byte-identity fuzzers pass.

### Why it is not shipped

**A polarity mutant — `!=` for `==`, which inverts which rows match — passes all 1,251 tests.**
That is not an equivalent mutant; it returns the complement. So nothing in the suite covers
`WHERE p.b = true` over a `Column::Bool` on this route, and the change would ship with its
central decision untested.

### And the evidence I thought I had was from the WRONG ROUTE

`bool3vl_980` compares `p.b = true` against `p.b` over TRUE, FALSE, a stored NULL and an ABSENT
key, and reported SAME on all four. **It reports SAME with the polarity mutant applied too** —
twice, once on a 4-node fixture and again after padding it to 404 nodes to push the selectivity
past the seek gate. A probe that cannot distinguish the change from its inverse is measuring
something else: the 4-node version seeds an `IndexSeek`, and the padded version projects `p.tag`,
which is `Project { Filter { Scan } }` — a different filter path from the `count(*)` shape the
5.8x was measured on.

**So I had equivalence evidence for a route the change does not touch**, which is item 936's
error committed about a TEST rather than about a diagnosis. The only answer-evidence that does
cover the changed route is `seekcross_948`'s per-row count assertion (4,000 / 20,000 / 40,000 …
all agreeing), and that fixture contains no NULLs, so the 3VL question is genuinely open on the
path that matters.

### The hazard the design already handles, and why it belongs in exec

`p.tag = true` on a **string** column returns no rows while the bare `p.tag` **raises
`E_INVALID_VALUE`** — verified, and the one row of the probe that correctly says DIFFER. The two
spellings are therefore _not_ interchangeable in general, which rules out doing this in the
optimizer: `normalize_pred` has no store and cannot check the column type.
`try_filter_keep_bool_prop` already requires `Column::Bool` and declines otherwise, so the
rewrite is safe exactly where it sits. That reasoning survives; only the coverage does not.

### What has to happen before this ships

1. A test that reaches the **count** route with a Bool column and asserts the row count for
   `= true`, `= false`, `<> true`, `<> false` and both operand orders.
2. The same over a **stored NULL** and an **absent** cell, on that route.
3. The polarity mutant re-run against those tests — it must fail.
4. The string-column case asserted to still raise.

### Verification
