## Item 1003 — the multi-label edge demotion is now ~1200x, not 1.5x: the single-label side gained an O(1) route and the record's "not a new target" is stale

**MEASUREMENT, no change.** Found by sweeping the three corpora item 1002 had not run.

### The reading

`storage_bench`, `storage/multilabel`, 100,000 edges, query
`MATCH (p:P)-[:KNOWS]->() RETURN count(*) AS c` — the SAME nodes and endpoints in both arms, only
the edge label set differing:

```text
  single [KNOWS]       1hop    0.3 us
  double [KNOWS,X]     1hop  368.6 us        ~1200x
```

### Why the record says this is settled, and why that is now stale

The corpus entry reads: _"a second label on every edge costs 2.5 → 9.3 bytes/edge and **242.9 →
369.2 µs** on a one-hop. Already recorded, as the limitation item 682 calls 'state 3'… **Not a new
target.**"_ At a 1.5x gap that disposition was right.

**The double arm has not moved (369.2 → 368.6). The single arm has: 242.9 → 0.3, about 800x.** It
now answers from a per-type count in O(1) while the multi-label arm still walks. So the gap grew
from 1.5x to ~1200x without anyone touching the multi-label path — the same shape as item 993,
where item 934's own unroll moved a cliff and left its justification pinned to the old location,
and the same shape as item 941's stale headers. **A disposition is only as current as the numbers
underneath it.**

### The mechanism, and why the obvious fix is not the TS one

Native and TS differ here. TS gates its fast path narrowly — `labels.length === 1 ||
multiTypeEdgeCount === 0` — so naming ONE type is enough to keep it, since one named type cannot
double-count. Native cannot use that escape as written: `Adj.etype` holds only the edge's PRIMARY
label and secondaries live in `edge_extra`, so answering `:KNOWS` must also find edges carrying
`KNOWS` as a SECONDARY. The per-type bucket count does not include those, so it is unusable
rather than merely unsafe.

What would make it usable is a per-type edge count maintained over ALL of an edge's labels, not
just the primary — O(1) to keep on insert and delete, and then the count shortcut applies whatever
the label multiplicity.

### Priced, NOT built, and deliberately so

This is a store-state change (a new maintained counter) on a session where the user is actively
weighing which architectural work to take. It is recorded as a candidate with its number so the
decision is theirs, not a rider on a sweep. Two things a future attempt should check first:
**how common multi-label edges are in the intended workload** — the entire 1200x is zero on a
single-label graph — and whether the counter can be kept byte-identical across the two engines.

### Verification

No code changed. The RSS columns of this row are NOT usable (mine read 11.8 → 3.9 bytes/edge,
i.e. the two-label arm resident SMALLER, which is nonsense); only the `1hop_us` column is read
here.

## Item 1004 — the multi-label guard asked the GLOBAL question where only a PER-TYPE one was needed: 368.6 → 0.3 us, ~1200x

**SHIPPED.** Item 1003 priced this and sketched the wrong fix; reading the code found a far
smaller one.

### What 1003 got wrong

Item 1003 inferred from the store's field comments that native "cannot reuse TS's escape" and
that the fix was a per-type edge count maintained over all labels — a new counter, store state, an
architectural call. Reading `typed_hop_count_from_size` instead:

```rust
  [ty] => {
      if store.has_multi_label_edges() { return None; }
      let t = store.etype_id(ty)?;
      store.out_typed_flat(t).map(<[_]>::len)
  }
```

The guard's own comment gives the reason — _"a partition holds an edge's PRIMARY type only"_ —
and that reason is **per type**. A partition for `t` is incomplete exactly when some edge carries
`t` BEHIND its primary. Whether an unrelated type is doubled up says nothing about `t`. In the
measured fixture every edge is `["KNOWS","X"]`, so `KNOWS` is the primary everywhere and its
partition was complete the whole time — the fast path was refused for no reason.

**Verifying the mechanism at the source rather than inferring it is what found this**, and the
session had already produced three wrong mechanisms from plausible inference (999, 1000, and the
`dlopen` capi guess).

### The change

A MONOTONE `secondary_etypes` set, populated at `set_edge_extra_labels` — the single choke point
for secondaries — and a `type_ever_secondary(t)` check replacing the global guard at both count
sites (`typed_hop_count_from_size` and `try_edge_label_count`).

Monotone matters: deleting the last edge that carried `t` secondarily leaves `t` gated, which is
conservative, never wrong, and keeps this change **entirely out of the delete and rollback paths**.
No new counter, no storage-layout change, nothing on the write hot path but one set insert per
multi-label edge.

```text
  storage/multilabel 1hop      before     after
    single [KNOWS]              0.3 us    0.3 us     control, flat
    double [KNOWS,X]          368.6 us    0.3 us     ~1200x
  storage/write (control)      25.92 ms   26.20      flat
```

### Teeth, and where they are

Both directions asserted, and the SECOND is the load-bearing one: a type carried ONLY as a
secondary is in no partition, so reading its length returns **0 instead of 3**. A mutant dropping
the gate passes the first assertion and fails that one. Plus a mixed graph where `X` is primary on
one edge and secondary on another, so the partition holds exactly one of two.

```text
  M1 BOTH gates removed            CAUGHT
  M3 secondary set never populated CAUGHT
  M4 BOTH gates inverted           CAUGHT
```

M1's verdict was missing from the first run's output (a `tail` cut it) and was re-run alone rather
than assumed — the same truncation that cost items 996 and 998.

### Verification

Engine suite 1,255/0; `rewrite_fuzz` 10/0 at `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` — load-bearing here,
because its "state 3" deliberately generates multi-label edges; all seven byte-identity fuzzers
13/0; `spelling_probe` NO PERF CLIFFS. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED.

## Item 1005 — a transaction-created RANGE index survived rollback; the user called it a bug and it is fixed

**SHIPPED — a correctness fix, not a perf one.** Item 922 found this by accident and deliberately
left it: _"reverting them is a semantics change needing its own decision, not a rider on a perf
commit."_ The decision was asked for and given — _"not rolling back an index in a transaction
feels like a bug. fix it."_

### What was wrong

`SchemaSnapshot` carried `index_paths`, `interval_keys` and `edge_type_index` and **nothing for
range indexes**, so `restore_schema` reverted a tx-created HASH index and left a tx-created RANGE
index standing. Pre-existing — the field had never existed.

`SchemaSnapshot` now carries `range_keys`, and `restore_schema` handles the same three cases its
hash sibling always had: keep what predates the tx, drop what the tx created, rebuild what the tx
dropped. `refresh_index_key_sets` already derived `range_keys` from `ranges`, so the cached sets
follow for free.

### The pinned test was written for this moment

Item 922 did not quietly assert the bug away — it pinned the behaviour that actually held and
said which line to flip: _"If rollback is later taught to revert range indexes, this line is the
one to flip."_ Flipped, with the comment rewritten to describe the decided semantics rather than
the accident. **That is what a pin is for**, and it is worth noting the alternative: had 922
asserted the ASPIRATIONAL behaviour, the suite would have been red for 83 items.

### Teeth, and the case with real content

The pinned line covers only "tx-created is reverted", so a dedicated test covers all three. The
DROPPED case is the substantive one: `create_range_index` rebuilds the `BTreeMap` from the
RESTORED column data rather than by replaying undos into it, so "the index exists again" is not
the claim worth asserting — the test requires it to **answer**, with a `range_lookup` over
`score > 5` finding exactly two of eight rows.

```text
  M1 retain removed (a tx-created index survives)      CAUGHT
  M2 rebuild loop removed (a tx-dropped index stays)   CAUGHT
  M3 snapshot records nothing                          CAUGHT
```

M3 is the one to keep in mind: with the snapshot empty, every rollback would drop every
PRE-EXISTING range index — a worse failure than the bug being fixed, and the reason the "keep"
case is asserted alongside the two that change.

### Verification

Engine suite **1,257/0**; `rewrite_fuzz` 10/0 at `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000`; all seven
byte-identity fuzzers 13/0 — load-bearing here because this is transaction restore, not a query
path. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED.

## Item 1006 — item 908's fusion is BLOCKED by a hazard it did not identify: fusing LOSES scope faults, it does not merely reorder them

**MEASUREMENT, no change.** The user settled the fault-ordering question item 908 was waiting on
("moving ts to native's behavior is fine… whatever is fastest as long as it's reproducible"), so
this went to build it. It is not buildable as framed.

### What 908 knew, and what it missed

908 priced the pre-pass at 15-19% of every compile and named the obstacle as ORDERING: _"fusing
it changes WHEN a scope error is raised relative to the other eager compile-time fault…
Needs its own item with the fault-ordering question settled first."_

It missed that `compileLinear` does not walk the clause list `checkLinearScope` validates. Its
first act is a chain of REWRITES — `dropVacuousQuantifier`, `dropVacuousPage`,
`dropUnreadGroupBinds`, `foldPageIntoReturn`, `unoptionalizeForAggregate`, `inlineTrailingFilter`,
`inlineAggregateCall`, `inlineTrailingLet`, `inlineCorrelatedCall`, `fuseAnchorThenHop`,
`liftStartProps` — and only then compiles. **A clause a rewrite DROPS takes its scope fault with
it.**

### Measured, not reasoned

The pre-pass was disabled and the check moved onto the rewritten list, then six shapes compared:

```text
  shape                      before            after the move
  control: plain unbound     faults            faults
  vacuous quantifier {1,1}   faults            faults
  trailing filter            faults            faults
  unread LET                 faults            **NO FAULT**
  unread LET, grouped        faults            **NO FAULT**
```

So `MATCH (n:P) LET x = nosuchvar.k RETURN n.k AS a` stops erroring and quietly returns rows.

**That is fault LOSS, not fault ORDER**, and the approval given covers the second, not the first.
"Whatever is fastest as long as it's reproducible" is satisfied by losing the error — reproducibly
— which is exactly why the distinction is worth drawing rather than treating the approval as
blanket.

### What remains available, and what it costs

- Moving the pre-pass INSIDE `compileLinear`, before the rewrites, is sound — it checks the same
  clauses — but it is still two walks, so it buys **nothing**. The 15-19% is the second walk.
- Having every clause-dropping rewrite scope-check what it discards would work and is fragile in
  the way that matters: the obligation is spread across eleven rewrites and a twelfth added later
  reopens the hole silently.
- So the 15-19% is **not available at acceptable risk**, and item 908's disposition should read
  blocked-on-correctness rather than blocked-on-a-decision.

### The general point

The approval unblocked the question 908 asked. It did not make the change correct, and a settled
decision is not a licence to skip the diagnosis — the obstacle that actually stopped this was one
nobody had written down. **Ask what the code does before asking whether you are allowed to change
it.**

### Verification

No change ships: the experiment was reverted, `git status` clean of `packages/gql`, the dist
rebuilt from reverted source, GQL suite 2,787/0. The temporary probe was removed.

## Item 1007 — the same guard pattern sits at nine more sites; the traversal ones are UNMEASURED here, and the fixture is why

**MEASUREMENT + one probe column, no engine change.** Item 1004 narrowed two COUNT sites from the
global `has_multi_label_edges()` to a per-type check. The method's own next step is to grep the
pattern elsewhere, so: nine more uses, in `exec.rs` and `algo.rs`.

### Two of them are the identical shape

```text
  exec.rs:4324  for_each_nbr   if let [w] = want { if !store.has_multi_label_edges() { …per-type CSR… } }
  exec.rs:4479  degree reader  let [w] = want else …; if store.has_multi_label_edges() { return None }
```

Both ask the GLOBAL question about a SINGLE wanted type `w`, and both would narrow to
`type_ever_secondary(*w)` by exactly item 1004's argument. These are the TRAVERSAL path, which is
reached far more often than the count shortcut — so on the face of it a bigger target.

### They do not measure, and the fixture is the reason

`storage/multilabel` gained a row-returning column (`walk_us`) so the traversal path is reached at
all; the count column is answered by a partition length and never touches these guards.

```text
  edges                 1hop_us    walk_us
  single [KNOWS]            0.3      690.4
  double [KNOWS,X]          0.4      666.3
```

**No penalty to find** — the two-label arm is marginally FASTER. The reason is degree: this
fixture gives every node exactly ONE out-edge, so seeking a per-type bucket and scanning a
one-element adjacency are the same work. **A degree-1 fixture cannot price an
adjacency-filtering guard**, which is CLAUDE.md's "match the fixture to the claim" and the exact
caution `expand_bench`'s header already carries — _the win is confined to high-degree, many-type
nodes_.

### So the change is NOT made

Narrowing two hot traversal guards on the strength of an argument, with an instrument that
provably cannot see the effect, is what items 947, 951, 964 and 974 each had to withdraw. The
sites are recorded with the measurement that does not reach them and the instrument that would
(`expand_bench`, extended with a multi-label arm).

**Why the count sites DID pay and these may not:** a guard costs what it DENIES. Denying the count
path denies an O(1) partition-length read, so the whole query falls to a walk — 1200x. Denying the
per-type structure on a traversal that walks the adjacency either way costs only the difference
between a bucket seek and a filtered scan, which is zero at degree 1 and grows with degree and
type count. The two sites are the same code shape and a completely different prize.

### Verification

No engine change. One probe column added, with the degree limitation written at it so the row is
not later read as evidence of absence. Clippy 0, `cargo fmt --check` 0.

## Item 1008 — ONE multi-label edge demoted EVERY typed hop: 27.27x at degree 256 / 64 types, now 1.12x

**SHIPPED.** Item 1007 found these two sites and refused to change them, because the only fixture
that reached them could not see the effect. Building the fixture that can turned a 1.1x
non-result into a measured 24x.

### The instrument item 1007 named

`multilabel_taint_1008`: the degree x type shape `expand_bench`'s header says the per-type
structures need, a ROW-RETURNING hop (a count is answered from a partition length and never
reaches these gates — item 1007's distinction), and **exactly ONE edge tainted** with a second
label. One is the right number: the guard was global, so one edge out of `nodes * degree` is
enough to demote the whole graph, while tainting half would measure the secondary-probe cost
instead and confound the question.

```text
  degree  types     clean_us    tainted_us      ratio        after
       4      1        313.3         347.2       1.11x       1.09x
      32      1       2741.4        3070.9       1.12x       1.03x
      32      8        317.5        1233.6       3.88x       1.10x
     256      8       2718.6        9829.3       3.62x       1.03x
     256     64        291.8        7957.2      27.27x       1.12x
```

Row counts identical in every arm — the taint changes no answers, only the guard's verdict.

**The shape confirms the model item 1007 proposed from the count sites: a guard costs what it
DENIES.** At one type the per-type structure saves nothing because every edge matches, so ~1.1x.
At 64 types it is the difference between a selective bucket and a full adjacency scan, so 27x.
The same code, the same change, two orders of magnitude apart in value depending on the fixture —
which is the whole argument for not sweeping a pattern on sight.

### The suite caught a ROUTE assertion, and the shape of the failure is what identified it

`a_degree_read_agrees_with_walking_the_adjacency` failed on one line:
`assert_eq!(taken, !multi_label)` — the GLOBAL rule written down. **Every ANSWER assertion in that
test passed** (`read == walked` across all wants, both directions, 40 nodes, both loop modes),
which is what distinguished a route change from a correctness change without having to guess. The
fixture taints with `EXTRA` and never with `R`, so `R`'s per-type structures are genuinely
complete and taking the slice is right.

The pin was updated to the per-type rule and **strengthened rather than relaxed**: the slice must
be taken for a never-secondary type AND a hop on `EXTRA` — carried only as a secondary — must
still decline. Relaxing it alone would have left the gate untested in the direction that matters,
which is the failure mode item 940 removed two probe groups for.

### Verification

Mutants: `for_each_nbr` gate removed **CAUGHT**, degree-reader gate removed **CAUGHT**. Engine
suite 1,257/0; `rewrite_fuzz` 10/0 at `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` (its "state 3" generates
multi-label edges, so it is the load-bearing fuzzer here); all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0;
`spelling_probe` NO PERF CLIFFS. Gates each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED.

## Item 1009 — the DISJUNCTION taint penalty is real (2.3x, stable) and the obvious narrowing FAILS: a hash lookup costs more than the probe it skips

**MEASUREMENT, change written and REVERTED.** After item 1008, a single-type hop takes the
per-type CSR and never reaches the flat scan, so the remaining `has_multi_label_edges()` sites
serve a disjunction want, a stale CSR, or a secondary-carried type. The probe gained a
disjunction arm (`-[:T0|T1]->`) to price the first.

### The penalty is real and stable

Three rounds, 20,000 nodes, degree 256 across 64 types, ONE tainted edge:

```text
  clean 6470.7 / 6446.8 / 6482.9      tainted 14695.2 / 15161.8 / 14806.9      2.27 / 2.35 / 2.28x
```

Not noise — the clean arm varies 0.6% across rounds. The mechanism is visible in the arithmetic:
a 2-type want over a degree-256 node matches ~8 edges and rejects ~248, and each rejection costs
`edge_has_label` TWICE (once per wanted type), where a clean graph short-circuits on
`has_multi_label_edges()` and pays nothing.

### The narrowing that should have worked, and why it did not

`edge_carries_wanted`'s test became
`has_multi_label_edges() && type_ever_secondary(w) && edge_has_label(…)`, which provably skips
the probe for a type never carried behind a primary — exactly item 1008's argument. **The
tainted arm did not improve** (15113.9 against a ~14900 baseline).

Reading `edge_has_label` says why:

```rust
  self.edge_etype.get(eid).is_some_and(|&t| t == tid)
      || (self.edge_has_extra.get(eid).copied().unwrap_or(false) && …)
```

For an edge with no extras that is **two Vec index reads and a bool test**. `type_ever_secondary`
is a `FnvSet<u32>` hash lookup. The change swapped two cheap indexed reads for one more expensive
hash probe, PER EDGE PER TYPE — a wash, which is what the measurement said.

**The same narrowing was worth 24x one item ago and is worth nothing here**, because there it
replaced a whole adjacency scan and here it replaces two array reads. Item 1008's model — a guard
costs what it DENIES — applies to the FIX as much as to the guard: a check is worth what it skips.

### What the fix would have to be

Hoist the per-type decision OUT of the per-edge loop: decide once per hop which wanted types can
possibly be secondary and pass that in, rather than asking per edge. `edge_carries_wanted` has
six-plus call sites across `exec`, `varlen`, `nested` and `fastpath`, so that is a signature
change, not a one-line gate. Priced at **2.3x on a disjunction hop over a tainted many-type
graph** — narrow, real, and recorded rather than attempted at the end of a long session.

### A near-miss worth recording

The narrowed build's single run read **3.05x** — worse than baseline — because its CLEAN arm came
in at 4958 against a 6470 baseline, a 1.3x improvement a `&&` term after a false short-circuit
cannot cause. Almost certainly an inlining perturbation, and had I read that one sample as "the
change made clean faster" it would have been this session's fifth wrong mechanism. Three
alternated rounds on the reverted build is what gave the stable 2.3x to compare against.

### Verification

No change ships: `git diff` on `crates/lenke-engine/src/exec.rs` empty, rebuilt and re-measured
from reverted source. The probe keeps its disjunction arm — it is the instrument that prices this.

## Item 1010 — the disjunction taint penalty is NOT the probe, and a 1.3x "win" from dead code is an inlining artifact

**MEASUREMENT, two changes written and both REVERTED.** Item 1009 blamed the 2.3x disjunction
penalty on `edge_carries_wanted`'s per-edge probe and blamed its own failed narrowing on the
lookup being a hash. Both halves tested here; the first is wrong.

### Making the lookup cheap did not help the thing it was for

`secondary_etypes` went from `FnvSet<u32>` to a dense `Vec<bool>` indexed by etype id — ids are
interned sequentially, so the lookup becomes ONE index read, cheaper than the two reads of the
`edge_has_label` it skips. That removes item 1009's stated objection entirely. Three rounds,
degree 256 / 64 types:

```text
  tainted   14961.6 / 15080.9 / 15000.1      baseline ~14900      UNCHANGED
  clean      5397.5 /  4994.8 /  4915.6      baseline ~6470       1.3x FASTER
```

**The tainted arm — the one the gate exists for — did not move at all.** In this fixture only
`UNRELATED` is secondary, so `type_ever_secondary(T0)` is false and the probe IS being skipped.
If skipping it changes nothing, the probe was never the 2.3x. **Item 1009's attribution is
withdrawn**: the penalty is real and stable but its cause is unidentified, and the arithmetic
that made the probe look guilty (248 rejections x 2 types per node) was a plausible story, not
evidence.

### And the "win" is dead code

On a clean graph `has_multi_label_edges()` is false, so the added terms never execute — yet the
clean arm improved 1.3x, reproducibly across three rounds. Dead code cannot make a path faster
except by changing how the function compiles. That is `pull-alignment-is-load-bearing`'s shape:
an edit to a hot function moves unrelated costs.

**It is not a justification and it was not shipped.** A reproducible number whose mechanism is
"the optimiser laid the function out differently this time" is one edit away from reversing, and
banking it would attach a 1.3x claim to a change that provably does not do what its comment says.

### What this leaves

- The disjunction taint penalty: **2.3x, stable, LOCATED but NOT ATTRIBUTED.** Not the probe.
- Item 1009's "the fix is a hoist" conclusion also falls, since it rested on the same
  attribution — hoisting a check that changes nothing would change nothing.
- The next attempt needs a profiler on the tainted disjunction arm, the way item 994 settled the
  hop-predicate chain after four failed subtraction-based attributions. The harness exists.

### The pattern across 1008-1010

1008 narrowed a guard and got 24x. 1009 applied the same narrowing one site over and got nothing,
blaming the lookup's cost. 1010 removed that objection and still got nothing — so the lesson is
not "use a cheaper lookup" but **the same code shape can have an entirely different cause at a
neighbouring site**, and three items in a row have now confirmed that the only way to tell is to
measure the specific site rather than reason from the one next door.

### Verification

No change ships: `git status` clean of `crates/`, suite 1,257/0 on the reverted tree. The probe
keeps its disjunction arm.

## Item 1011 — the THIRD site of 1008's shape declines a whole ROUTE, and it is a 1.8x

Item 1008 narrowed two traversal guards from the global `has_multi_label_edges()` to a per-type
`type_ever_secondary(*w)` and measured up to 27.27x. Items 1009/1010 applied the identical
narrowing to `edge_carries_wanted` and measured **flat**, then withdrew the attribution that tried
to explain why. That pair left an obvious question unanswered: which of the remaining sites are
1008-shaped and which are 1009-shaped?

**The discriminator is what the guard DENIES, and it is visible in the code without measuring
first.** `edge_carries_wanted` runs PER EDGE and denies a per-edge probe — the guard's own lookup
is the same order of magnitude as the work it skips, which is why it measured flat. The site found
here, `fused_hop_shape` in `exec.rs`, runs **ONCE PER QUERY** and denies an entire fast ROUTE. That
is 1008's kind, not 1009's, and the prediction was made before the fixture was built.

### The shape

`fused_hop_shape` gates the fused single-hop fast paths for `Filter(<pred>, Expand{single-type,
Out}(Scan))`. It extracts a SINGLE wanted etype and then declined the whole route when the graph
held any multi-label edge anywhere:

```rust
let want = want_etypes(store, edge_label).ok()?;
let [w] = want.as_slice() else { return None; };
if store.type_ever_secondary(*w) { return None; }   // was: has_multi_label_edges()
Some((label, *w, pred, exp.as_ref()))
```

Neither arm of `multilabel_taint_1008` reached it: the single-type arm has no filter, and the
disjunction arm has two types. A third arm was added — `MATCH (n:V)-[:T0]->(m) WHERE m.k > 50
RETURN m.k AS k` — which is the first query in the probe to carry a filter over a single type.

### Measured

20,000 nodes, ONE edge tainted with a second, unrelated label, min of 7:

```text
  degree  types    filt_clean   filt_taint   before    after
       4      1         228.7        391.5    1.71x    1.00x
      32      1        1837.2       2732.0    1.49x    0.99x
      32      8         227.2        412.7    1.82x    1.00x
     256      8        3084.5       3000.8    0.97x    1.00x   (route not taken at this degree)
     256     64         429.5        434.0    1.01x    1.01x   (route not taken at this degree)
```

**The control the change cannot reach is the clean column itself**, measured in the same process:
228.2/1840.0/227.6/3014.4/428.9 after, against 228.7/1837.2/227.2/3084.5/429.5 before — flat. The
other two arms are also controls and also unmoved: the single-type arm stays 1.01–1.09x (1008's fix
still holding) and the disjunction arm stays 2.13/1.86/3.05x, correctly untouched, since 1010
withdrew the attribution that would have had this change fix it.

**The profile is the inverse of 1008's and that is the point.** 1008 paid most at high degree with
many types; this pays at LOW degree and nothing at 256, because the fused route is itself only
chosen for small adjacencies. Two sites, the same guard, the same narrowing, opposite fixtures —
which is why item 1007's refusal to sweep the pattern on sight keeps being right.

### Teeth

Three mutants on the new gate, each built uncapped then run under
`timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, with the pristine
copy kept under `target/` and restored BEFORE each one:

| mutant                                        | effect                                   | verdict                          |
| --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `if false` — never decline                    | `:X` filtered hop returns 0 rows, want 3 | **CAUGHT**                       |
| `!type_ever_secondary` — inverted             | `:X` route taken, 0 rows                 | **CAUGHT**                       |
| `has_multi_label_edges()` — revert the change | **no answer changes at all**             | **CAUGHT by the route pin only** |

The third is the one that matters. Reverting this change is answer-equivalent — it is a route
CHOICE, exactly the hazard CLAUDE.md records as _"a perf gate needs its own test"_ — so every
differential and answer assertion in the repo survives it. It is caught because the test now asks
the selector directly:

```rust
assert!(fused_route_taken("MATCH ()-[:KNOWS]->(m) WHERE m.k >= 0 RETURN m AS m", &store));
assert!(!fused_route_taken("MATCH ()-[:X]->(m) WHERE m.k >= 0 RETURN m AS m", &store));
```

The walk matches only `Project` and `Filter` deliberately: a generic walk would turn a future
plan-shape change into a `false` that reads like a route decision.

### Verification

Engine suite 1,257/0; `rewrite_fuzz` 10/0 at `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000` (its "state 3" generates
multi-label edges, so it is the load-bearing fuzzer for this change); all seven byte-identity
fuzzers 13/0; `spelling_probe` NO PERF CLIFFS.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets -D warnings` 0; `cargo test` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1012 — the fix item 1009 named WORKS at 3x, and its cost is DEAD CODE in a hot function

Item 1009 priced the disjunction taint penalty at 2.3x, refuted the per-edge narrowing, and named
the fix: _"hoist the per-type decision out of the per-edge loop, deciding once per hop which wanted
types can be secondary."_ It declined to build it because `edge_carries_wanted` has 6+ call sites.

**It was looking at the wrong function.** `exec.rs` has FOUR sites where the decision is _already_
hoisted — `let has_extra = store.has_multi_label_edges();` in `for_each_nbr`,
`node_has_num_nbr`, `node_has_matching_nbr` and `node_has_nbr`, each computed once per node and
read by a per-edge closure, each with `want` already in scope. There the hoist 1009 described is a
one-line change per site, with no signature change at all.

### The win is large and reproducible

`has_extra` became `want.iter().any(|&w| store.type_ever_secondary(w))` at those four sites. Three
alternated PRE/POST rounds on `multilabel_taint_1008`, 20,000 nodes, ONE tainted edge whose extra
label is wanted by nothing. Each arm asserted itself before building (`grep -c` of the new symbol,
compared against an expected count per arm) — and that assertion **fired once**, on a wrong
expected count of mine, which is the only reason the round was not scored against the wrong binary.

```text
  disjunction hop        PRE                  POST
  degree 32,  types 8    2.15 / 2.13 / 2.05   1.12 / 1.01 / 1.08
  degree 256, types 8    1.76 / 1.82 / 1.88   0.95 / 1.04 / 1.02
  degree 256, types 64   2.76 / 2.86 / 2.84   0.98 / 0.98 / 1.18

  semijoin               PRE                  POST
  degree 32,  types 8    1.19 / 1.21 / 1.19   1.01 / 1.00 / 0.99
  degree 256, types 8    1.22 / 1.23 / 1.22   1.01 / 1.01 / 1.01
  degree 256, types 64   1.62 / 1.60 / 1.59   1.34 / 0.60 / 0.95  (this row is bimodal)
```

Ranges disjoint on the first five. In absolute terms the tainted degree-256 / 64-type disjunction
goes 15107/15775/15771 → 5439/5529/6413 µs.

**A semijoin arm was added to the probe** for this, because the three existing arms all walk an
adjacency and emit rows and none reaches the three `node_has_*` functions, which early-stop on the
first matching neighbour. Its PRE column shows the taint was demoting semijoins too, which nothing
had measured: 1.59–1.64x at degree 256 / 64 types.

### The cost is a 4–8% regression on the CLEAN semijoin, and it is NOT what it looks like

The same arm's clean column is the control for the change's own cost — a semijoin decides once per
node and may stop after one edge, so it amortizes the per-node work over the fewest edges of any
shape here. It regressed, with disjoint ranges, every round:

```text
  semijoin CLEAN      PRE                    POST
  degree 4,  types 1  269.6 / 271.0 / 270.8  285.8 / 285.5 / 286.8
  degree 32, types 1  273.0 / 281.3 / 274.6  284.6 / 289.4 / 286.8
  degree 32, types 8  359.5 / 362.1 / 358.9  373.7 / 383.0 / 375.9
```

**Three hypotheses, all refuted by experiment, in this order:**

1. ~~The per-want loop costs more than the bool read it replaced~~ — **refuted by a short-circuit.**
   `has_multi_label_edges() && want.iter().any(...)` makes a clean graph short-circuit on the exact
   `is_empty()` call the old code ran inline, so the loop never executes. The regression was
   unchanged (282.2 / 282.1 / 284.3).
2. ~~`Store`'s layout changed~~ — `secondary_etypes` had been converted from an `FnvSet` to a dense
   `Vec<bool>`, which moves every later field. **Refuted by reverting only that**: the regression
   survived with the set restored (289.3 / 284.9 / 285.7). (The conversion did help the _tainted_
   semijoin, 1.04–1.11x against 1.00–1.01x, and is worth keeping on its own merits.)
3. ~~The extracted helper costs a call~~ — **refuted by `#[inline(always)]`**, unchanged
   (286.8 / 285.5 / 285.8).

**And the toll hypothesis is refuted by its own null control.** The repo records that any edit to
`exec::pull` costs the filtered-count cluster 1.08–1.24x and never gains — so "this is just the
toll for editing a hot function" was the obvious last explanation. It is wrong. A **semantically
identical** edit to the same four functions — `has_multi_label_edges() && !want.is_empty()`, which
cannot change an answer because `has_extra` is only ever read inside
`want.is_empty() || want.iter().any(...)` — costs nothing:

```text
  semijoin CLEAN      PRE                    NULL CONTROL
  degree 4,  types 1  269.6 / 271.0 / 270.8  278.9 / 268.7 / 262.4   (overlapping)
  degree 32, types 8  359.5 / 362.1 / 358.9  357.6 / 357.7 / 358.6   (flat)
```

So the cost is attributable to this change specifically, and the mechanism is the one item 1009
withdrew a conclusion to: **code that never executes still costs.** On a clean graph the short-
circuit means the `type_ever_secondary` loop is dead, and a _cheap_ dead term is free while an
_expensive_ dead term is not — register pressure in the enclosing per-edge closure, not
instructions retired.

### Disposition: the lever is right, the placement is one level off

Not shipped. The win is 3x on tainted graphs; the cost is 4–8% with disjoint ranges on clean
semijoins, which are the common case, and the standing instruction is _without regressions_.

The mechanism says exactly where to put it instead: **pass the decision in as a parameter.** The
four functions are private and compute `has_extra` from arguments they already hold, so the
expensive term can move into their (cold) callers and the hot bodies gain no new code at all —
they read a `bool` they are handed. That is 1009's hoist taken one level further out, and it is the
next item rather than this one, because it is a signature change across the call graph and the
evidence for it was only just assembled.

What ships here is the probe's semijoin arm and this entry. The arm is worth keeping on its own:
it is the only case in the corpus that reaches the early-stopping `node_has_*` family, and its
clean column is what caught the regression three times running.

### Verification

No engine change ships: `git diff` on `crates/lenke-engine/src/` is empty apart from the example,
suite 1,257/0 on the reverted tree.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo clippy --all-targets -D
warnings` 0; `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo test` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1013 — five mechanisms refuted for a 4–7%, and two controls that come back free

Item 1012 measured the disjunction-taint fix at 3x, found it cost the clean semijoin 4–8%, and
blamed register pressure from an expensive term inlined into a hot closure. **That blame was
wrong.** This item tried the fix the diagnosis implied and three more besides; all four cost the
same 4–7%, and two controls designed to isolate the cause both come back free.

### What was tried, in order, each as three alternated PRE/POST rounds

Every arm asserted itself before building (`grep -c` of the new symbol against an expected count).
**That assertion fired twice this item, both times on a wrong count of mine** — once expecting 6
where the answer was 5, once 3 where it was 2 — so two of these rounds would otherwise have been
scored against the previous arm's binary. It is the cheapest check in the harness and it has now
caught more than it has cost.

The figure in each cell is the semijoin's CLEAN column (degree 4, types 1), the shape that decides
once per node and may stop after one edge, so it amortizes per-node work over the fewest edges.

| variant                                                             | the idea                                   | clean semijoin, PRE → POST            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| inline `any()` over the want (item 1012)                            | the hoist item 1009 named                  | 269.6/271.0/270.8 → 285.8/285.5/286.8 |
| `+ has_multi_label_edges() &&` short-circuit                        | make the loop DEAD on a clean graph        | → 282.2/282.1/284.3                   |
| `+ Store` layout restored to `FnvSet`                               | undo the moved field offsets               | → 289.3/284.9/285.7                   |
| `+ #[inline(always)]`                                               | remove the call                            | → 286.8/285.5/285.8                   |
| `#[inline(never)] #[cold]` helper                                   | remove the INLINED body (1012's diagnosis) | 275.3/270.7/266.5 → 283.4/283.4/282.9 |
| leaf-preserving: `Vec<bool>` + indexed `while`, no call, no closure | keep the four functions LEAF               | 273.1/263.6/265.0 → 279.2/283.4/285.7 |

Six measurements, one effect, no mechanism.

### The two controls, which are the actual contribution

**A semantic no-op in the same four functions is free.** `has_multi_label_edges() &&
!want.is_empty()` cannot change an answer, because `has_extra` is only ever read inside
`want.is_empty() || want.iter().any(...)`:

```text
  clean semijoin   PRE 269.6 / 271.0 / 270.8   NULL CONTROL 278.9 / 268.7 / 262.4   (overlapping)
  degree 32x8      PRE 359.5 / 362.1 / 358.9   NULL CONTROL 357.6 / 357.7 / 358.6   (flat)
```

**A new function that is DEFINED but never called is also free.** This one was written to test
binary layout — a new function shifts the addresses of everything after it, and a layout bias is
systematic per binary, so no amount of repetition detects it:

```text
  clean semijoin   PRE 264.5 / 276.1 / 258.7   LAYOUT ONLY 273.7 / 266.9 / 268.9  (overlapping)
```

So the effect is not generic hot-function toll (the null control refutes that, and with it the
tempting generalization from `exec::pull`), and it is not binary layout (the layout control
refutes that). It appears if and only if the four functions actually compute the per-want answer,
by any means tried — inlined or out-of-line, hot or cold, hashed or indexed, leaf or non-leaf,
executed or short-circuited away.

### Disposition

**Not shipped, and NOT diagnosed.** The honest statement is that the narrowing is worth 3x on a
tainted graph (disjunction 2.76/2.86/2.84 → 0.98/0.98/1.18; semijoin 1.62/1.60/1.59 → ~1.01) and
costs 4–7% on the clean semijoin for reasons six experiments have not reached. "Obviously correct
so it must be faster" is not evidence here, and neither is "obviously free so it must be free" —
that second one is what each of these six variants assumed in turn.

What remains untried is the signature change item 1012 pointed at: compute the flag in the
CALLERS and pass a `bool`, so the four functions gain no expression at all. That is 34 call sites
for `for_each_nbr` alone, and most are inside per-node loops, so it is only a win if the flag is
hoisted above each loop — 34 edits with a correctness obligation each, to buy a 3x on a feature
(multi-label edges) that most graphs do not use, against a 4–7% cost on one that they all do.
**That trade is the user's call, not a measurement**, and it is recorded here rather than taken.

### Verification

No change ships: `git status --porcelain` empty before the documents were written, suite 1,257/0.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo clippy --all-targets -D
warnings` 0; `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo test` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1014 — the kinds item 850 set aside: `LocalDateTime` and `LocalTime` raw-keyed, 3.3–5.6x, and three mutants that survived first

Item 843 gave TS's `valueKey` a temporal arm; item 850 went further for ONE kind, raw-keying a
`LocalDate` on its `days` count so `valueSet` / `groupIndex` build **no string at all** — 4.15x.
Its note says where it stopped:

> Only `LocalDate`. The kinds carrying a sub-second or zone part have more than one field and no
> single raw key, so they keep `valueKey`.

That is true of the FIELDS and not of the VALUE, and the stop was never priced. `temporal-key-probe`
prices it, one kind per process (the arms differ only in which container the key lands in, so
sharing a process lets the first warm the dispatch for the rest):

```text
  N=100,000, 1,000 distinct values     count(DISTINCT t)   RETURN DISTINCT t
  num        (raw-keyed, control)              1.3-1.4 ms          1.0-1.2
  date       (raw-keyed, item 850)             1.5-1.7             1.2-1.6
  str        (one string, no object)           2.6                 2.5
  localtime                                    6.9-8.3             8.4-8.5
  datetime                                     8.9-11.0           11.0-12.2
  zoned                                       12.8                 8.5
  duration                                    11.3                 6.5
```

So a temporal key costs 5–9x a date and 3–5x a plain string — a `JSON.stringify`-free but still
per-row string, exactly the cost item 850 removed for one kind.

### What shipped, and what the packing argument is

`LocalTime` gets a SINGLE number key: `secs` is bounded by 86,400 and `nanos` by 1e9, so
`secs * 1e9 + nanos` is at most 8.64e13 — inside the exactly-representable integers, so the
packing is a bijection. `LocalDateTime`'s `secs` is unbounded, so the same packing leaves that
range after ~104 days; it gets a two-level `Map` (`secs` outer, `nanos` inner) instead, which
still builds no string. One container PER KIND, never shared, because the tagged `valueKey`
strings keep the kinds apart and raw keying has to as well.

Three alternated PRE/POST rounds, each arm asserted by `grep -c` before building:

```text
                              PRE                   POST              ratio
  datetime count(DISTINCT)    8.9 /  9.2 / 11.0     2.5 / 2.4 / 2.6   3.6-4.2x
  datetime RETURN DISTINCT   12.2 / 11.0 / 11.8     2.1 / 2.2 / 2.5   4.7-5.6x
  localtime count(DISTINCT)   7.6 /  8.3 /  6.9     2.1 / 2.2 / 2.1   3.3-4.0x
  localtime RETURN DISTINCT   8.5 /  8.4 /  8.4     1.9 / 1.8 / 1.7   4.5-4.9x
  CONTROL date count           1.6 /  1.7 /  1.5    1.5 / 1.7 / 1.5   flat
  CONTROL num  count           1.3 /  1.3 /  1.7    1.4 / 1.3 / 1.2   flat
```

**The controls the change CAN reach are the object ones**, and they are the reason the probe grew
two more arms. Every non-temporal object — a list, an element — now walks past two extra
`instanceof` checks before reaching the structural path it used before. Measured, three rounds:

```text
  list  count(DISTINCT)        14.9 / 14.9 / 15.5  ->  15.3 / 15.4 / 15.3
  DISTINCT the element (list)  13.6 / 12.7 / 13.5  ->  13.8 / 13.7 / 13.2
  DISTINCT the element (num)   12.3 / 14.1 / 14.6  ->  13.4 / 14.4 / 15.5
```

Overlapping; two `instanceof` do not register against a row that still builds a string per row.
This is the control item 1012 had to add late and 1013 leaned on — a change that adds work to a
path it cannot speed up needs that path measured, not reasoned about.

### Three mutants SURVIVED, and each named a real hole in the suite

The file they ran against opens by saying a temporal arm had shipped into a suite gap three times
in four items. It happened again, in three different ways:

| mutant                                      | first verdict | the hole                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `groupIndex`'s datetime key drops `nanos`   | **SURVIVED**  | every case tested `count(DISTINCT)` — `valueSet` — and nothing tested the GROUP BY tally, a _separate_ container with its own per-kind branch                        |
| the time map aliased to the DATE map        | **SURVIVED**  | the cross-kind cases all used small numbers; a `LocalTime`'s key is `secs * 1e9 + nanos`, so the date that collides with `LocalTime(5, 0)` is day **5e9**, not day 5 |
| `Number.isFinite` dropped from the time key | **SURVIVED**  | nothing paired a non-finite field with a finite one that still has to separate the values                                                                            |

The same dropped-`nanos` mutation in `valueSet` failed two tests immediately. One shape, two
implementations, only one of them covered — which is the lesson worth more than the speedup.

Four tests were added (tally splitting, tally cross-kind, raw-key collision, the finite guard in
both directions) and all eight mutants are now caught. The last of them, `dateTimeKeyable` stubbed
to `true`, is caught only by a pair of **non-finite** datetimes that must COLLAPSE into one group:
`JSON.stringify` renders `NaN` and `Infinity` both as `null`, item 843 pinned that collapse
rather than "improving" it inside a speedup, and raw keying would separate them.

**A pre-existing asymmetry, recorded and not touched:** that same pair of `LocalTime`s answers 2
today, through a path neither item changed. It is noted in the test rather than altered, because
changing it inside a performance item is exactly what 843 declined to do.

### Still on the string path, deliberately rather than arbitrarily

`ZonedDateTime` (12.8 / 8.5), `ZonedTime` and `Duration` (11.3 / 6.5) keep `valueKey`. Three and
four fields need a deeper nesting than the two here, and the packing argument that makes
`LocalTime` a single number does not survive an unbounded `offset` or `months`. The machinery and
the probe now exist, so this is a measured stop with its numbers attached — not item 850's.

### Verification

## Item 1015 — the Rust twin of 1014: `RETURN DISTINCT <temporal>` up to 33.8x, and the surviving mutant was a design flaw

Item 1014 found the TS engine raw-keying only `LocalDate` for DISTINCT and extended it. Grepping
the pattern across engines: `distinct.rs`'s `ColKeyer` has the identical shape — a `Date` arm from
item 847 and `_ => None` for every other temporal kind.

**But the Rust reason is not the TS reason, and that distinction decided the item.** Item 850's TS
note was about convenience ("more than one field and no single raw key"). Item 840's Rust note is
about SEMANTICS:

> the general path's equivalence is `group_key`'s, which keys a temporal by `t.format()` — RENDER
> equality — while a field is STRUCTURAL. The two coincide where `format` is injective, which for
> `Date` is demonstrable. The kinds carrying a sub-second or zone part keep the general path.

That is a correctness constraint, not a shortcut: substituting a structural key for a render key
splits groups wherever two distinct field tuples render alike. So this item had to establish
injectivity before measuring anything, and `temporal.rs` is where it is read off rather than
assumed:

- `fmt_frac` zero-pads `nanos` to nine digits then trims trailing zeros — `""` for 0, distinct for
  everything else, so no two `nanos` share a rendering.
- `fmt_year` pads to four digits and widens past it; `civil_from_days` is a bijection on `days`,
  and time-of-day splits by division. A `DateTime`'s `(secs, nanos)` is recoverable.
- `fmt_offset` renders whole minutes as `Z` or `±HH:MM` with `{:02}`, widening rather than
  truncating. A zoned kind renders its LOCAL value plus the offset, and the instant is the local
  value minus the offset — `(secs, nanos, offset)` is recoverable.

`Duration` is not admitted: its four fields are not independent under rendering in the same way,
and nothing here needed it enough to prove.

### Priced first

`temporal` is publicly re-exported). 200,000 rows, 1,000 distinct values, min of 9:

Every row answers exactly 1,000 groups in both arms, and the probe CHECKS that rather than

unchanged in both arms — a fourth control, and a finding: **the aggregate path has its own
Date-only gate elsewhere**, so this item's 24x on the scan form leaves `count(DISTINCT <datetime>)`
at 38 ms. That is the next item, not this one.

**The `date` control is flat only because the first attempt wasn't.** Generalizing its arm to the
shared `(i64, u32, i16)` tuple cost that column **813.5 → 1,633.4 us, 2.0x** — a 14-byte hash key
where 4 bytes carry the whole value. `Date` keeps its own narrower arm. The control existed to
catch exactly that and did, on the first run.

### Teeth, and a survivor worth more than the four that failed

Five mutants, each built uncapped then run under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p
MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, pristine copy under `target/`, restored before each:

| mutant                                       | verdict      |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| `DateTime` drops `nanos`                     | CAUGHT       |
| `ZonedDateTime` drops `offset`               | CAUGHT       |
| `Time` drops `nanos`                         | CAUGHT       |
| `ZonedTime` drops `secs`                     | CAUGHT       |
| `Duration` admitted to `temporal_struct_key` | **SURVIVED** |

The survivor was not a missing test — it was **dead code**. `temporal_kind_keyable` was written as
its own `matches!(k, K::Duration)`, so one decision lived in two places: admitting `Duration` to
the key left the column-kind gate still rejecting it, and the arm was unreachable. The fix is to
derive the gate from the key itself — `temporal_struct_key(k.zero()).is_some()` — after which the
two agree by construction and the mutant is reachable and **CAUGHT**. A surviving mutant can mean
the code is wrong rather than the test is missing, and this is that case.

The new test's oracle is the general path itself: every shape is asserted against its own
`WHERE true` twin (item 570), so it states the actual claim — substituting a structural key
changes no answer — rather than restating the keyer's arithmetic. A non-injective kind would show
up as the fast path splitting a group the general path merges. `Duration`, though declined, is
asserted anyway, so if it is ever admitted those assertions are what say the admission was sound.

## Item 1017 — the TS Gremlin dedup, up to 8.0x; and the key decision finally lives in ONE place

The temporal-key family has three sites per engine, and this item is the TS engine's third:

| site                           | engine     | raw-keyed for        | by        |
| ------------------------------ | ---------- | -------------------- | --------- |
| `valueSet` (`count(DISTINCT)`) | TS GQL     | Date, Time, DateTime | 850, 1014 |
| `groupIndex` (`GROUP BY`)      | TS GQL     | Date, Time, DateTime | 850, 1014 |
| `dispatch.ts`'s `dedup()`      | TS Gremlin | **Date only**        | 857       |
| `ColKeyer` (`RETURN DISTINCT`) | Rust       | all but Duration     | 847, 1015 |
| `try_scan_distinct_count`      | Rust       | all but Duration     | 840, 1016 |
| `values(k).dedup()`            | Rust       | all but Duration     | 1016      |

Item 857 fixed the Gremlin dedup for dates and measured why it was worth 23.5x: a non-date temporal
pays a `WeakSet` insert that **can never hit** (every vertex carries its own instance, so a repeated
reference does not occur), plus a `tupleKey` string build, plus a string-`Set` probe — per row.

### Priced, then measured

`temporal-key-probe` gained a Gremlin arm, for the same reason item 1016 gave on the Rust side:
`values(k).dedup()` is a different implementation and carrying one surface's number to another is
an assumption. 100,000 rows, 1,000 distinct values, median of the warm reps, three alternated
rounds:

```text
  kind         PRE                     POST                  ratio
  datetime     77.2 / 64.1 / 82.2      15.7 / 16.3 / 15.3    4.2-5.4x
  localtime    50.1 / 51.4 / 49.2      16.7 / 16.1 / 16.1    3.0-3.2x
  zoned        73.8 / 72.3 / 72.4       9.2 /  9.6 /  9.6    7.5-8.0x
  CONTROL duration  40.1 / 44.5 / 45.8  40.5 / 43.7 / 42.9   unchanged (declined kind)
  CONTROL date      11.8 / 12.0 / 11.6  11.5 / 11.8 / 12.0   flat
  CONTROL num       11.5 / 11.9 / 11.4  11.9 / 12.5 / 12.1   flat
```

`Duration` is the best control available here: it is a temporal, it reaches the same branch, and
it is the one kind the change declines — so it isolates "temporal" from "raw-keyable". `Date`
keeps its own flat `Set` for the reason item 1015 measured in Rust: folding the narrow key into
the wide container cost that column 2.0x on its own.

### The real content: one definition instead of six

Four items in a row tripped over the same structural fault, so the key decision moved to
`@lenke/core`:

- 1014: `valueSet` and `groupIndex` are two implementations of one shape and **only one was
  tested** — a dropped-`nanos` mutant passed everything in the untested twin.
- 1015: `temporal_kind_keyable` and `temporal_struct_key` held one decision in two places, making
  one arm dead code; the surviving mutant was a design flaw, not a missing test.
- 1016: I **reintroduced that exact shape within the hour** at the Rust Gremlin gate.
- And the kinds themselves had been extended site-by-site: 850 did one site, 857 another, 1014
  two more.

`temporalKeyFields(v)` now names the keyable kinds and their fields once, and
`temporalKeyAdd` / `temporalKeySlot` walk a nested container; callers choose only a container.
**The kind rank leads the field list**, so one container holds every kind — without it a
`LocalTime(5, 7)` and a `LocalDateTime(5, 7)` share a key, which is the collision 1014 hit in the
GQL twin and solved with a container per kind. Nested rather than packed into one number because a
`LocalTime`'s `secs * 1e9 + nanos` fits the exact-integer range while a `LocalDateTime`'s `secs`
is unbounded and the same packing silently collides after ~104 days.

### Teeth

Five mutants on the shared helpers, all **CAUGHT**: `LocalDateTime` drops `nanos`; the kind rank
shared between `LocalTime` and `LocalDateTime`; `ZonedDateTime` drops its finite guard;
`ZonedDateTime` drops `offset`; `temporalKeyAdd` always reports NEW.

**One assertion I wrote was wrong, and the engine said so.** Two `ZonedDateTime`s with a non-finite
`offset` and differing `secs` are ONE group, not two: the composite path renders a non-finite
offset in a form that swallows the rest. I expected 2. Checked against the PRE build — 1 there too
— so it is pre-existing behaviour that the guard preserves by sending the value to that path
untouched, and the test now pins it with that note. Raw keying would have SPLIT them, which is
why the guard is load-bearing in this direction as well.

Every new test passes on the PRE build too. That is the point rather than a weakness: the change is
answer-preserving, so the answer tests must pass both ways, and mutation is what shows they have
teeth.

### Still on the string path

`Duration`, in both engines, at a measured 40–46 ms here against a raw-keyed date's 11.8. Its four
fields are not independent under rendering the way the others are. The GQL sites are also not yet
extended to the zoned kinds — `temporalKeyFields` admits them, so that is now a container change
at two call sites rather than a key question. Next item.

## Item 1018 — the zoned kinds in TS GQL, 3.8–5.3x; the shared abstraction REFUTED three ways; and a bimodal row that faked a regression

Item 1017 moved the temporal key decision into `@lenke/core` and noted the two TS GQL sites still
declined the zoned kinds — _"a container change rather than a key question"_. That was wrong in an
instructive way: the container is the whole question.

### What shipped

`valueSet` and `groupIndex` gain a zoned arm each, with `zonedTailKey` packing `(nanos, offset)`
into one number — `nanos < 1e9` and an offset is whole minutes, so `nanos * 2**21 + (offset +
2**20)` is at most ~2.1e15, inside the exactly-representable integers, making a zoned key nest
only TWO levels like `LocalDateTime`'s. Three alternated PRE/POST rounds, 100,000 rows, 1,000
distinct values:

```text
                             PRE                   POST               ratio
  zoned count(DISTINCT)      12.6 / 9.1 / 12.8     2.6 / 2.5 / 2.4    3.8-5.3x
  zoned GROUP BY              9.0 / 9.3 / 11.3     3.3 / 3.0 / 2.8    2.9-4.0x
  CONTROL datetime count      2.5 / 2.3 /  2.6     2.6 / 2.6 / 2.5    flat
  CONTROL datetime GROUP BY   2.9 / 2.6 /  2.7     2.8 / 2.9 / 2.8    flat
  CONTROL localtime           2.2 / 2.1 /  2.2     2.1 / 2.3 / 2.1    flat
  CONTROL date / num                      flat                        flat
  CONTROL duration GROUP BY  11.4 / 11.0 / 11.4    7.1 / 6.8 / 7.3    1.5x FASTER
```

### The shared abstraction was refuted three times, by measurement

Item 1017's conclusion was that the kinds and fields belong in one place. For the Gremlin dedup
path that holds. For these two sites it does not, and each attempt failed for its own reason:

1. **`temporalKeyFields` (returns an array)** — one allocation per row. Noise against the Gremlin
   path's 50–77 ms; fatal at 2 ms: `count(DISTINCT <localtime>)` **2.1 → 4.8**,
   `GROUP BY <datetime>` **2.7 → 5.2**.
2. **`temporalKeyInto` (writes into scratch)** — fixed the first and not the second, because the
   tally needs a SLOT per key and `temporalKeySlot` returned `{ slot, created }` and took a
   closure: two more allocations per row, `GROUP BY` **8.0**.
3. **One dispatch on the `kind` tag with a shared `bumpNested`** — `bumpNested` is a closure built
   per row. `GROUP BY <datetime>` **7.1**.

So the sites keep direct field reads, and `temporalKeyInto` / `temporalKeySlot` were **deleted
rather than left unused** — items 1015 and 1016 were both about a second definition becoming dead
code, and leaving two unused helpers behind would have been the same mistake a third time. This is
item 1015's "a narrow key beats a general one" for the third and fourth time, now with the
mechanism named: **the abstraction is right where the key is cheap relative to the work, and wrong
where the key IS the work.**

### A bimodal row faked a regression, and nearly cost the win

Mid-item I read `GROUP BY <duration>` at **7.2 ms** on one build and **11.1** after the change,
and spent three attempts chasing that "regression" — the `kind` dispatch above was written to fix
it. The alternated A/B then measured PRE at **11.4 / 11.0 / 11.4** and POST at **7.1 / 6.8 / 7.3**:
POST is 1.5x FASTER, and the 7.2 I had been comparing against was the same HEAD code in a
different process. The row is bimodal across processes, which is exactly what `CLOSED.md` says
repetition cannot detect and alternation can. Two readings from different builds are not a
comparison, however carefully each was taken.

### Teeth

Five mutants, all **CAUGHT**: `zonedTailKey` drops `offset`; drops `nanos`; the two zoned kinds
share a container; the finite+bound guard stubbed to `true`; **the packing bound widened from
2^20 to 2^40**.

The last two each needed a case the others could not supply:

- The guard: two `ZonedDateTime`s with a non-finite OFFSET are ONE group — the fallback renders a
  non-finite offset in a form that swallows the rest (the asymmetry item 1017 found on the Gremlin
  path, re-measured here). Raw keying SPLITS them, so the guard is load-bearing in that direction.
  A non-finite `nanos` goes the other way: the finite `secs` still separates, so two.
- The bound: the first huge-offset pair used `nanos = 0`, so there was nothing for a widened
  offset to carry into and the mutant survived. The pair that catches it differs in `nanos` AND in
  an `offset` past the bound — packed under a widened bound, they collide; declined under the real
  one, they reach the fallback and stay apart.

### Verification

GQL suite 2,793/0; Gremlin 852/0; core 370/0; all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0.

`bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1019 — `ORDER BY <temporal> LIMIT k` misses the streaming top-K: ~6,000 µs against `num`'s 1,239 and a dictionary key's 70

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. The temporal-key family (847/840/1015/1016 in Rust, 850/857/1014/
1017/1018 in TS) is closed except `Duration`, so the method's next step is to look for the same
shape in a DIFFERENT code path. `order.rs` mentions `Temporal` **zero times**.

### Where it bails, and why the prior refutation does not transfer

`try_scan_top_k` takes a `Num` column; everything else goes to `try_scan_top_k_wide`, which has a
`Dict` arm and then `_ => return None`. So a temporal key falls to `order_page`: materialize the
frontier, build a key column and an index array, partial-sort.

**`try_scan_top_k_wide` has no `Str` arm, and that is a measured refusal rather than an omission**
— item 864 wrote one and dropped it, because streaming a string key means the surviving buffer
carries row INDICES and every comparison loads `data[idx]` at random (1.22x the wrong way on ASC).
That argument does not reach a temporal: a `Column::Temporal` is a packed vector of fixed-size
`Copy` values, so its loads are the numeric path's loads, not a string's. The reason the `Str` arm
failed is exactly the reason a temporal arm should not.

### Priced

`temporal_distinct_1015` gained a `topk` column and a ceiling column. **The statement-position
spelling** (`MATCH … ORDER BY k LIMIT n RETURN x`), because item 865's correction records that the
clause-position spelling never enters `try_scan_top_k` at all — measuring the wrong spelling here
would have priced `order_page` against itself. 200,000 rows, 1,000 distinct values, min of 9:

```text
  kind              topk_us    unlimited ceiling    topk / num
  num   (control)    1,239.3             43,264          1.00x
  str   (control)       70.2             49,433          0.06x   <- dictionary-encoded, rank-bounded early exit
  date               5,962.5             56,760          4.81x
  time               6,178.8             56,491          4.99x
  datetime           6,012.6             56,268          4.85x
  zoned              6,033.2             56,456          4.87x
  zonedtime          5,980.2             56,725          4.82x
```

Two controls, read in opposite directions. `num` is the path a temporal arm would copy, so it is
the floor to aim at. `str` is the representation that was tried and refused, and at 70 µs it shows
why the DICTIONARY arm is the one worth having: 1,000 distinct values over 200,000 rows is inside
`dict_max_distinct`, so that column is dictionary-encoded and gets the rank-bounded early exit.
Every temporal kind lands within 4% of the others, ~4.8x `num` and ~9x under the full-sort
ceiling — so `order_page` is doing something for them, and the streaming arm is doing nothing.

### Not implemented this item, deliberately

This is an ORDERING change, which is byte-identity territory: the streaming buffer needs a key the
comparator can rank, and it has to induce **exactly** the order `order_page` produces, per kind,
including how a zoned value orders against its own offset. Getting that subtly wrong is a wrong
ANSWER, not a slow one, and the fuzzers compare ordered output. A sorted-LIMIT key is also where
item 844 shipped a 1.6x regression on an unrelated `min` control by giving two arms a shared live
range, and item 866's lift was a 1.28x regression for a numeric key — this file's history is
mostly refuted attempts, so it earns a careful item rather than the tail of a long one.

Recorded with the number, the bail site, and the argument for why item 864's refusal does not
cover it. `topk2_864`'s header now points here, since its fixture has no temporal column and that
is why this went unmeasured.

### Verification

No engine change: `git diff` touches two example files and three documents. Engine suite 1,259/0.

warnings` 0; `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo test` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1020 — the temporal streaming top-K, 3.5–4.5x; and the tiebreak mutant took THREE test fixes

Item 1019 priced `ORDER BY <temporal> LIMIT k` at ~6,000 µs against `num`'s 1,239 and deferred the
build, because it is an ordering change and `order.rs`'s history is mostly refuted attempts. Built
here.

### How the ordering risk was removed rather than managed

The obvious implementation maps a temporal to a wide integer the existing buffer can rank. That is
a **re-derivation** of `Temporal::cmp_total`, and a sort key that is subtly not the general path's
order is a wrong ANSWER, not a slow one. So the buffer carries the `Temporal` itself (`Copy`, at
most 24 bytes) and compares with `cmp_total` directly — the function `value::cmp_total` dispatches
to for a temporal, so the order is identical **by construction** and there is nothing to get
wrong.

It is a separate function rather than an arm of `try_scan_top_k_wide` for two reasons, one of them
the repo's own scar tissue: that function's buffer is `(u32, u32, u32)` and a temporal has no
bounded `u32` rank, and item 844 shipped a 1.6x regression on an unrelated `min` control by giving
two arms a shared live range — item 864's numeric path carries a note asking to be left
byte-for-byte alone. A new function shares nothing, and the numeric destructure is untouched.

No early exit, unlike the dictionary arm: that one knows the extreme rank from the dict, and a
temporal column has no such bound, exactly as the numeric path has none. What it gets is the same
stream-and-trim.

### Measured

Three alternated PRE/POST rounds (arm count derived by `grep -c`, not guessed), 200,000 rows,
1,000 distinct values:

```text
  kind              PRE                        POST                     ratio
  date              5,996 / 6,102 / 6,182      1,704 / 1,481 / 1,643    3.5-4.1x
  time              6,629 / 6,109 / 5,935      1,475 / 1,477 / 1,496    4.0-4.5x
  datetime          6,041 / 6,011 / 5,970      1,723 / 1,517 / 1,656    3.5-4.0x
  datetime_nanos    6,128 / 6,190 / 6,163      1,684 / 1,519 / 1,574    3.6-4.1x
  zoned             6,320 / 6,184 / 6,010      1,512 / 1,545 / 1,441    3.9-4.2x
  zonedtime         6,649 / 6,198 / 6,113      1,467 / 1,685 / 1,451    3.7-4.5x
  CONTROL num topk  1,223 / 1,267 / 1,240      1,221 / 1,218 / 1,229    flat
  CONTROL str topk     70.3 /  71.5 /  70.9       70.6 /  70.0 /  70.4  flat
  CONTROL ceilings                     ~56-59k unchanged in both arms
  CONTROL the DISTINCT / count / dedup columns          unchanged
```

Every kind lands near `num`'s 1,220 — which is the floor this arm was copied from, so landing on
it is the result. The `str` control at 70 µs stays 18x faster than all of them, because a
dictionary column has the rank-bounded early exit this arm cannot have.

### Five mutants, and the one that needed three test fixes

| mutant                                      | verdict                      |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| direction ignored (`desc` treated as `asc`) | CAUGHT                       |
| nulls counted as a value                    | CAUGHT                       |
| nulls-inside-window bail removed            | CAUGHT                       |
| `skip` ignored                              | CAUGHT                       |
| **arrival tiebreak dropped**                | CAUGHT, on the third attempt |

The tiebreak mutant is the instructive one, because each failure to catch it was a different flaw
in the test:

1. **Distinct keys.** The window is then determined by the keys alone, so dropping the tiebreak
   permutes nothing. Added a total-tie fixture.
2. **40 rows.** The buffer only partitions at `max(kcap * 4, 1024)`, so below that
   `select_nth_unstable_by` and `sort_unstable_by` are handed an already-ordered slice and move
   nothing. Raised the tie fixture to 1,100 rows.
3. **Projecting only the temporal.** Every tied row then prints the same string, so the assertion
   could not see WHICH rows the window kept. Added a `seq` property, carried to the output but not
   part of the sort key.

Only with all three does an unstable comparator become visible. "The mutant survived" meant "the
fixture cannot express the difference" three times over, and none of the three was obvious before
it failed.

**Two mutant runs in this item were NULLS and were nearly read as verdicts.** `cargo fmt`
reformatted the anchors between steps, so two `python` edits raised instead of applying and the
suite then passed as the PRISTINE build. The fix is the one CLAUDE.md already states — assert the
anchor matched exactly once and make a miss loud — now applied as `assert ... f"ANCHOR MATCHED {n}
— NOT APPLIED"` rather than a bare assert whose traceback scrolls past.

### Oracles

Every shape is asserted against its `WHERE true` twin (item 570, the general fold), ASC and DESC,
at three `(skip, limit)` windows, over six kinds plus the tie fixture, comparing the SEQUENCE
rather than a sorted multiset. `Duration` is included deliberately: `cmp_total` orders it by
`total_key()`, which is NOT its predicate order, so it is the kind most likely to diverge had the
arm invented a key.

## Item 1021 — item 1020 does NOT transfer to the TS engine, and the negative result is the point

MEASUREMENT, no change beyond a probe arm. Item 1020 gave the Rust engine a temporal streaming
top-K worth 3.5–4.5x. The method's next step is to grep the pattern in the other engine, and the
last four items have all found the gap there — so the prior is that this one does too.

**It does not, and reading the code said so before measuring.** The Rust sorted LIMIT dispatches on
COLUMN REPRESENTATION (`Column::Num` → streaming, `Dict` → streaming with a rank-bounded early
exit, everything else → `order_page`), which is exactly the shape that leaves a representation
behind. The TS engine has no columnar store to dispatch on: `ordered-rows.ts` keeps top-k over
INPUT BINDINGS with a value comparator and no per-type branch at all, so there is no arm for a
temporal to be missing from.

### Measured anyway, because "no gap" is a claim

`temporal-key-probe` gained a sorted-LIMIT arm and its own full-sort ceiling. 100,000 rows, 1,000
distinct values, median of the warm reps:

```text
  kind        ORDER BY t LIMIT 10    ceiling (no LIMIT)    LIMIT / ceiling
  num                      3.4 ms                6.6 ms             1.9x
  date                     3.9                   8.6                2.2x
  str                      4.9                  18.2                3.7x
  datetime                 5.6                  20.2                3.6x
  duration                 6.2                  25.3                4.1x
  zoned                    7.9                  16.8                2.1x
```

Every kind is well under its own ceiling, so **the top-k is firing for temporals** — the thing
item 1020 had to add in Rust. `num` and `date` are the controls: in Rust the pre-fix gap was 4.8x
against `num`; here the whole spread from `num` to `zoned` is 2.3x, and it tracks how many fields
a kind's comparator reads (date 1, datetime 2, zoned 3) rather than a declined route.

### What is left, priced and not built

The 2.3x spread and the 3x ceiling spread are COMPARATOR cost: a temporal is compared as an
object, per comparison, through a kind dispatch. A decorate-sort-undecorate would pay that once
per row instead of once per comparison, and it would help the no-LIMIT ceiling too, which is the
larger number.

It is not attempted here, for a reason this session measured three times in one item: item 1018
found that at these magnitudes an allocation per row dominates, and a decorated key for a
multi-field kind cannot be one number (`LocalDateTime`'s `secs` is unbounded). So the design
question is the same one that refuted 1017's shared helper at the GQL sites, and it deserves the
measurement rather than the assumption.

**The negative result is worth its own item.** Four consecutive items found the TS twin of a Rust
gap, which makes "check the other engine" feel like a reliable generator of work. This is the case
where the structural difference — representation dispatch versus a value comparator — means the
pattern genuinely stops at one engine, and recording that with numbers is what stops a later pass
re-deriving it.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe. GQL suite 2,793/0.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run check` 0;
`bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1022 — `GROUP BY <temporal>` over a FRONTIER, up to 18.9x; and single-sourcing the key cost 12–20%, measured

The fifth site in this family and the last large one. Item 848 gave the SCAN grouping a `Date` arm;
the FRONTIER grouping is a different function, and its `Col::Gen` dispatch had a `Date` arm (packing
`days` into a `u64`) and nothing else. Its own comment named the blocker: _"Only `Date`: the kinds
carrying a sub-second or zone part have not had their field-vs-render injectivity established."_
Item 1015 established it; this is that argument's fifth consumer.

### Priced, then measured

`temporal_distinct_1015` gained a frontier column and a one-source fixture — `frontier_group_by`
cannot be reached without edges, so the gap was unreachable from the existing fixture. Three
alternated PRE/POST rounds, 200,000 rows, 1,000 distinct:

```text
  kind              PRE                           POST                     ratio
  time              19,672 / 19,375 / 18,651      3,248 / 3,060 / 3,201    6.0-6.1x
  datetime          41,221 / 40,622 / 40,659      3,220 / 3,072 / 3,073    12.8-13.2x
  datetime_nanos    52,765 / 50,924 / 51,783      3,062 / 3,068 / 3,053    16.6-17.0x
  zoned             59,274 / 58,615 / 57,404      3,256 / 3,148 / 3,092    18.2-18.9x
  zonedtime         30,569 / 30,688 / 30,996      3,290 / 3,127 / 3,106    9.3-9.9x
  CONTROL date       2,243 /  2,407 /  2,394      2,306 / 2,312 / 2,311    within range
  CONTROL num        1,818 /  1,814 /  1,804      1,882 / 1,853 / 1,852    +2.6%
  CONTROL str        1,026 /  1,029 /  1,020      1,053 / 1,071 / 1,064    +3.5%
  CONTROL the DISTINCT / count / dedup / topk columns                      flat
```

**The `num` and `str` controls are up ~3%, and that is stated rather than rounded to "flat."** The
new arm cannot execute on either — both return at their own `Col::Num`/`Col::Str` arm before the
`Col::Gen` match is reached — so this is the dead-code/layout toll items 1012/1013 spent two items
characterizing, at a magnitude below the ~10% CLOSED.md names as needing an isolated harness. The
ranges are only just separated. It is recorded as a cost, not dismissed.

### Single-sourcing the key was tried, measured, and SPLIT

A `Col::Gen` can MIX kinds across rows where a packed column holds exactly one, so the grouping key
needs a kind discriminant that the column paths do not. The tidy answer is one function: widen
`temporal_struct_key` to lead with a rank and let every caller carry it.

**Measured: that cost the paths items 1015/1016 shipped 12–20%** — `count(DISTINCT <time>)`
1,383 → 1,663 µs, `<datetime>` 1,378 → 1,576, the Gremlin dedup 1,560 → 1,755. A u8 on the front of
a hash key is not free at 1.4 ms.

So there are two functions: `temporal_struct_key` (narrow, for packed columns) and
`temporal_group_key`, which CALLS it and prepends the rank. The FIELDS — the part that must be
right — stay single-sourced; the rank is a discriminant whose only job is separation. This is the
fifth time in this family that a general form lost to a narrow one on measurement (1015's Date arm,
1018's three attempts, now this), and the first time the general form was tried _because_ 1017
argued for single-sourcing. Both lessons are real; the deciding evidence is which side of the
key-cost-vs-work line the site sits on.

### Teeth

| mutant                                                         | verdict        |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| kind rank made to collide (`Time` and `DateTime` share 3)      | CAUGHT         |
| the guard admits `Duration` (`Value::Temporal(_) => true`)     | CAUGHT         |
| the Null group keyed as `Some((0, 0, 0, 0))` instead of `None` | **EQUIVALENT** |

The third is not a test gap: kind ranks start at 1, so no real temporal can produce rank 0 and a
zero-rank sentinel cannot collide. `None` is still the form to keep — it cannot be invalidated by a
later kind taking rank 0 — and the code now says so, rather than a test asserting a difference that
does not exist.

The mixed-kind cases are the ones the packed-column tests could not reach: `Time(5, 7)` beside
`DateTime(5, 7)`, `ZonedTime` beside `ZonedDateTime`, a `Date` beside another kind (which forces
the column out of the narrow `Date` arm and into this one), a `Duration` beside a keyable kind
(which must decline the whole column, testing the guard's `all()`), and an absent property as the
one Null group. Every shape is asserted against its `WHERE true` twin.
