## Item 1023 — the spelling probe was blind to its own headline case: the equality groups had no index

MEASUREMENT + a probe fix, no engine change. The temporal family is exhausted, so this went looking
for a fresh enum — which predicate FORMS can seed an index (`seek_target` admits only
`Compare{Eq}` against a literal) — and found something smaller and worse on the way there.

### The defect

`spelling_probe`'s fixture creates one index:

```rust
// The far-side / seed-side groups are about whether a predicate reaches an INDEX,
// which needs one to exist. Without it those groups silently measured something
// else (pool size before the hop), and read as cliffs that indexing would fix.
store.create_range_index("age");
```

That line was added because an unindexed fixture made those groups measure the wrong thing. **The
same defect was left in the equality and inline groups.** They key on `name` and `dept`, neither
indexed, so:

- `n.name = 'name500'` vs `'name500' = n.name`
- `(n:Person {dept: 'eng'})` vs `WHERE n.dept = 'eng'`

were comparing two SCANS. Those are the first two shapes CLAUDE.md lists among the historical
100–300x index-seeding bugs — _"`$x = u.k` vs `u.k = $x`"_ and _"a clause `WHERE` vs an inline
`{k: $x}`"_ — so the probe built to catch that class could not see it on a seeked key, which is the
only arrangement where the class exists.

### Fixed, and the seek is demonstrated rather than assumed

`create_index("name")` and `create_index("dept")`. The proof the index is now REACHED is the
equality group's own number:

```text
  equality operand order (name = lit vs lit = name)
    before   a scan
    after    0.001 ms both spellings — below the timer's resolution
```

A group that drops to the resolution floor is one whose predicate stopped scanning 100,000 nodes.
Both operand orders seek, so that spelling pair converges — which is the answer the probe existed
to give and had never actually given.

### No cliff found, and one group's 0.162 ms is the SELECTIVITY GATE working

`dept` reads 0.162 ms for both spellings with **identical optimized plans**. That is not a missed
seek: `dept` has five distinct values over 100,000 nodes, so a seek would read a fifth of them and
`seek_cap` (items 989/997) correctly declines. The two spellings still converge, which is what the
group asserts.

Whole probe: **NO PERF CLIFFS**, including the `IN`-vs-OR groups now that `dept` is hash-indexed.

### What this is worth

A negative result on the engine and a positive one on the instrument. The probe's own header says
_"a plan mismatch is the real signal; the time is the backstop"_ — but a backstop measuring the
wrong path is not a backstop, and the groups covering this file's headline bug class were the ones
measuring it. Three items ago (1021) the finding was that a pattern stops at one engine; this one
is that an instrument can be blind in exactly the place it was built to watch, and that the fix is
cheap once looked at.

`seek_target`'s form coverage — the question this tick set out to price — remains open and is
recorded as such: `IN` past `normalize_pred`'s 32-term gate is covered by an existing group and
converges, but `STARTS WITH`, `BETWEEN` and `IS NULL` as seed forms are unexamined.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe. Engine suite 1,261/0.

warnings` 0; `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo test` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1024 — a two-sided range NEVER seeds on a scan: the `And` is the blocker, not the selectivity

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Item 1023 indexed the probe's equality keys and left
`seek_target`'s FORM coverage open: it admits only `Compare{Eq}` against a literal. This went after
the prefix form and found something bigger behind it.

### The hypothesis, and its refutation

`STARTS WITH` lowers to a scalar `Call`, and both `seek_target` and `range_seek_target` admit only
`Expr::Compare` — so a prefix predicate cannot seed an index. The prediction was therefore that the
prefix spelling LOSES to the explicit range it implies, since every string starting with `name500`
is exactly `['name500', 'name501')`.

**Backwards.** With a range index on `name` (added this item, alongside 1023's hash indexes), three
runs put the prefix at **0.280 ms** and the explicit range at **0.458** — 1.64x, with the
_seekable_ spelling losing.

### The plans, which say the cliff is not what the group was written to catch

All four spellings optimize to `Filter { Scan }`:

```text
  STARTS WITH 'name500'                        Filter { Call starts_with } over Scan
  name >= 'name500' AND name < 'name501'       Filter { And(Ge, Lt) }      over Scan
  age >= 30 AND age < 40                       Filter { And(Ge, Lt) }      over Scan
  name >= 'name500'                            Filter { Ge }               over Scan
```

So the 1.64x is FILTER cost — one `starts_with` call per row against two string compares — and the
fast numeric range (0.047 ms) is a columnar filter fast path, not an index seek. Both facts would
have been invisible without printing the plans, and both contradict the natural reading of the
times.

### The real finding, proved directly

The reason the range does not seed is the **`And`**. At the scan site `range_seek_target` is handed
the whole predicate and matches a single `Compare`:

```text
  n.name >= 'name99998'                       ->  RangeSeek          (one row, SINGLE-sided)
  n.name >= 'name5000' AND n.name < 'name5001' ->  Filter { Scan }   (eleven rows, MORE selective)
```

The more selective query gets the worse plan. **The blocker is the shape, not the selectivity** —
so a bounded interval, which is the natural way to write one and what a `BETWEEN` would lower to,
cannot reach a range index on a scan while its own one-sided half can. That is the first entry in
CLAUDE.md's list of historical 100–300x index-seeding bugs, in a shape nothing had measured.

The machinery to fix it already exists: the conjunct path (`opt.rs:1683`/`1734`) extracts a seed
from one conjunct of an `And` and re-`AND`s the rest as a residual, for a different plan shape. The
scan site does not use it.

### Not fixed in the same breath, deliberately

A planner change that gives a selective interval a seek has byte-identity reach (seek order against
scan order) and lands in the file whose history is mostly refuted attempts. Items 1019→1020 went
exactly this way — price and diagnose in one item, build carefully in the next — and that worked,
so this follows it rather than rushing a rewrite at the end of a long tick.

### The probe group FLAGS, and that is intended

`spelling_probe` now reports `1 PERF CLIFF`. The group's own comment carries the diagnosis above so
a later run reads it as a recorded open finding rather than a regression to chase. This is the first
cliff the probe has flagged since it was given indexes — which is the point of having given them.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe; the scratch example used for the
plan dump was removed.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo clippy --all-targets -D
warnings` 0; `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo test` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1025 — item 1024's headline was WRONG: the `And` is not the blocker, per-BOUND pricing is

MEASUREMENT + a correction, no engine change. Item 1024 concluded that a two-sided range never
seeds on a scan because `range_seek_target` is handed the whole `And` and matches a single
`Compare`. This item set out to build the fix and found the diagnosis was wrong.

### What 1024 got wrong, and how

**The conjunct picker already has a range rung.** `opt.rs`'s `seed_from_conjuncts` ranks candidates
by selectivity across four rungs — id, indexed equality, **indexed range (`range_cand`)**,
multi-value — and the scan site calls it as its last `else if`. So an `And` of two range conjuncts
_is_ reached, and 1024's stated mechanism does not exist.

1024's evidence looked conclusive and was not: the single-sided query seeded and the two-sided one
did not, so the `And` was the visible difference. But the two queries differed in a second way that
I did not control — `n.name >= 'name99998'` has an individually selective bound, and
`n.name >= 'name5000' AND n.name < 'name5001'` has two individually unselective ones (every name
beginning 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 is `>= 'name5000'`, about half the keys).

### The controlled experiment

Varying only the bounds' individual selectivity, holding the shape fixed:

```text
  both bounds unselective, interval ~11 rows   ->  Filter { Scan }
  lower bound selective,   interval  ~5 rows   ->  RangeSeek
  lower bound selective,   single-sided        ->  RangeSeek
```

The two-sided form seeds whenever ONE of its bounds is selective on its own. So the shape is not
the blocker; **each bound is priced independently, and a tight interval whose halves are each
unselective is never recognized as tight.**

### The finding that survives, which is better than the one it replaces

A bounded interval's selectivity is the INTERSECTION of its bounds, and nothing computes that.
`seek_beats_scan` asks `seed_fraction(key, op, value)` per conjunct, so `>= lo` and `< hi` are each
~50% and both decline — correctly, in isolation — while their conjunction is 11 rows of 100,000.

That is a sharper statement than 1024's, and it names what a fix needs: a TWO-SIDED seek.
`Plan::RangeSeek` carries one `op` and one `value`, and seeding on either unselective bound alone
is exactly what `seek_beats_scan` is right to refuse — walking half the index and filtering loses
to the columnar scan. So this is a plan-shape change (a bounded range node, or a `RangeSeek` with
an optional upper bound) plus an interval estimate, not a gate tweak.

The prize, for whoever takes it: the two-sided scan measured **0.458 ms** where the same interval
through the index should be nearer the equality seek's 0.001 ms.

### Method

**The difference I could see was not the only difference there was.** 1024 compared two queries
that differed in shape AND in per-bound selectivity, attributed the result to the shape, and wrote
it into `CLOSED.md` and the probe. One experiment holding shape fixed refuted it. This is the trap
items 900–902 and 912/917 are recorded for — _finding a mechanism is easy and finding the one is
not_ — and the specific guard against it is to vary one axis at a time, which a "proved directly"
plan dump feels like but is not.

Both records are corrected in this commit rather than left for a reader to reconcile: the probe
group's comment and `CLOSED.md`'s 1024 entries now carry the per-bound mechanism and say that the
`And` claim was withdrawn.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows the probe and the two documents; the scratch
example used for the experiment was removed. Engine suite 1,261/0.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo clippy --all-targets -D
warnings` 0; `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo test` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1026 — the INTERVAL seek: 153x on a selective bounded range, a 3x regression caught and fixed, and the fuzzer caught a PANIC

SHIPPED (Rust). Item 1025 identified the mechanism — each bound is priced alone, so a tight interval
whose halves are each unselective never seeds — and said the fix needs a two-sided seek rather than
a gate tweak. Built here.

### What shipped

`Plan::RangeSeek` gains `upper: Option<(CompareOp, Value)>`, `Store::range_lookup` closes its
`BTreeMap` bound with it, and `seed_from_conjuncts` gains an INTERVAL rung above the equality one:
two conjuncts bounding one range-indexed key from opposite sides, priced by a new
`interval_fraction` oracle (`range_count_in_capped`), seeded as one `RangeSeek` with both
conjuncts removed from the residual. The rung sits first because a qualifying interval is the most
selective candidate by construction — it is strictly narrower than either of its own bounds, both
of which already lost. An interval that does not qualify falls through and every existing plan is
unchanged, which is what keeps the change additive.

Landed in two stages on purpose: the field and its plumbing first, verified as a **true no-op**
(suite 1,261/0, unchanged), then the planner rung. A behaviour change on top of an unverified
refactor would have left two suspects for any failure.

### Measured

`spelling_probe`'s new group, which item 1024 added for exactly this:

```text
  n.name >= 'name500' AND n.name < 'name501'     0.458 ms  ->  0.003 ms     153x
```

**And the first attempt shipped a 3x REGRESSION, caught by a control.** Under the existing
`SEEK_MAX_FRACTION` (15.4%, measured for a ONE-sided seek against a one-conjunct scan) the probe's
`range AND` group — `30 <= age < 40`, a 10% interval — went **0.047 → 0.142 ms**. An interval
competes against a two-conjunct vectorized filter and materializes the interval's ids, so its
curve is its own:

```text
  width   fraction   filter      interval     ratio
      1      0.1%    222.4 us       3.9 us    57x   better
      2      0.2%    226.3          7.2       31x
      5      0.5%    235.5         16.7       14x
     10      1.0%    247.6         32.6      7.6x
     20      2.0%    275.6         64.4      4.3x
     50      5.0%    358.2        160.1      2.2x
    100     10.0%     94.1        319.0      3.4x   WORSE
```

So `INTERVAL_SEEK_MAX_FRACTION = 0.05` — the widest point measured to win, not an extrapolated
crossover. The filter column is NOT monotone above 5% (94.1 µs at 10% against 358.2 at 5%, so
something else serves the wider shapes), and a threshold placed inside an unexplained region is
one nobody can defend. With it, `range AND` is back to 0.047 ms and the 153x stands.

### The fuzzer caught a panic on its first run

`rewrite_fuzz` failed immediately with a panic inside `BTreeMap`'s search: **`range` panics when
the start bound exceeds the end**, which `k >= 10 AND k < 5` produces — and so does
`k >= 5 AND k < 5`, whose bounds are `Included(5)..Excluded(5)`. Generated plans reach
`range_lookup` directly, so "the planner only emits sane pairs" is not the guarantee this needed.
Both walks (the lookup and the interval count) now return empty for an inverted or empty interval,
with equal endpoints kept only when BOTH bounds are inclusive.

This is the fuzzer earning its place on a change that the unit suite passed.

### Teeth

| mutant                                                    | verdict                             |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| bounds not ordered (written order decides which is lower) | CAUGHT                              |
| the panic guard removed                                   | CAUGHT                              |
| the interval cap widened to the one-sided ceiling         | CAUGHT, after a test fix            |
| the upper bound dropped from the seed                     | CAUGHT                              |
| the interval count ignores its cap                        | EQUIVALENT (a perf-only early exit) |
| `both_inclusive` forced false in `range_lookup`           | **SURVIVED — unexplained**          |

The cap mutant needed a case **inside the band the two ceilings disagree on**: my first "must not
seek" assertion used a 30% interval, which exceeds both, so the mutant passed it. A 10% interval —
under 15.4%, over 5% — is the one that separates them.

**The last row is recorded as an open survivor rather than written up as teeth.** Forcing
`range_lookup`'s equal-endpoint branch to report "empty" changes no answer, through three
successive attempts to reach it: `count(*)` assertions do not reach the walk at all (a count over a
seek is answered without materializing ids — items 1007/1008's lesson, and the row-returning cases
were added because of it), and the row-returning form provably DOES take the interval seek and
provably returns the right rows. I could not construct the input that distinguishes it in the time
this item had. The guard itself is not in doubt — the panic mutant above fails loudly without it —
but that one branch of it is untested and is labelled so.

### Known consequence, not a regression: the prefix spelling is now 95x behind

`STARTS WITH 'name500'` lowers to a scalar `Call`, so it cannot seed, and it now sits at 0.287 ms
against the explicit range's 0.003 — the probe reports it as one cliff. **No query got slower**; one
got 153x faster and the gap between two spellings of one question widened from 1.64x to 95x. By
this repo's spelling doctrine that gap is itself the defect, and the fix is to lower a prefix to the
interval it denotes (`>= p AND < succ(p)`, with the `starts_with` filter kept as the residual so
correctness never depends on `succ`). That is the next item, and the probe carries the number until
it lands.

order**; `spelling_probe` reports the one known cliff above and no others.

## Item 1027 — `STARTS WITH` seeds the interval it denotes: 72x, and the 95x gap item 1026 opened is closed

SHIPPED (Rust). Item 1026 gave a bounded interval a seek, which took `>= p AND < succ(p)` from
0.458 ms to 0.003 and left its own prefix twin at 0.287 — **95x apart, for one question**. No query
had got slower, but by this repo's doctrine that gap is itself the defect, so 1026 named the fix
and this item is it.

### What shipped

`prefix_seek_target` reads the key and literal out of `starts_with(n.k, 'p')` — the scalar `Call`
that `seek_target` and `range_seek_target` cannot see, which is why the predicate could never reach
a range index. `prefix_upper` computes the first string NOT prefixed by `p`, and the scan site
seeds `RangeSeek { op: Ge, value: p, upper: Some((Lt, succ)) }` — item 1026's interval node,
reached from one predicate instead of two, gated on the same `INTERVAL_SEEK_MAX_FRACTION`.

**The `starts_with` filter is KEPT above the seek.** `[p, succ(p))` is in fact exactly the prefix
set, so the residual is not needed for correctness — it is insurance against `prefix_upper` being
wrong, in a family that has shipped two wrong-answer bugs from clever bound arithmetic. The
candidate set it filters is tiny by construction, since the gate only admitted a selective prefix.

`prefix_upper` increments the last CHARACTER, not the last byte: a byte increment can land
mid-sequence and produce invalid UTF-8. It declines an empty prefix (every string starts with it,
so there is no upper bound) and one ending at `char::MAX` (nothing sorts above it).

### Measured

```text
  n.name STARTS WITH 'name500'                  0.287 ms  ->  0.004 ms     72x
  n.name >= 'name500' AND n.name < 'name501'    (1026's)      0.003        unchanged
  the group's spread                            95x       ->  1.23x
```

`spelling_probe` reports **NO PERF CLIFFS** on three consecutive runs — the state item 1026 left
broken. (1026's final run had reported one cliff; three runs here show that was variance on a
different group, not a standing finding.)

### Teeth

| mutant                                                    | verdict                   |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| bump the last BYTE instead of the last character          | CAUGHT                    |
| `char::MAX` not declined (wrap instead of bail)           | CAUGHT                    |
| a prefix with no bound seeds a degenerate interval anyway | CAUGHT                    |
| the upper bound made INCLUSIVE                            | **EQUIVALENT, by design** |

The inclusive-bound mutant is the residual filter doing its job: `[p, succ(p)]` admits rows exactly
equal to `succ(p)`, and the kept `starts_with` removes them. That is the insurance being
demonstrated rather than a coverage hole — and it is why the residual stays even though the bounds
are exact without it.

The Unicode cases are what gave the byte-increment mutant teeth: an ASCII-only fixture cannot tell
a byte increment from a character one. `é`/`éa`/`éb` and `日`/`日本`/`日本語` are in the fixture
for that, with exact counts asserted (3 and 2 — `日本` must not match `日`), plus a
`char::MAX`-terminated value for the decline path.

### Verification

Engine suite 1,263/0; `rewrite_fuzz` 10/0 at `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000`; all seven byte-identity
fuzzers 13/0; `spelling_probe` NO PERF CLIFFS on three runs.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo clippy --all-targets -D
warnings` 0 (after factoring the return into `type PrefixInterval` — the same lint item 1026 hit,
so the shape was predictable and I still walked into it); `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo test` 0;
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1028 — the TS engine had HALF of the Rust gap: `STARTS WITH` 65x, and the interval was already right

SHIPPED (TypeScript). Items 1026/1027 closed two seeding gaps in Rust. Grepping the pattern across
engines, the TS planner **splits**:

- the INTERVAL gap does **not** exist. `coalesceRangeHints` already folds `n.k >= lo AND n.k < hi`
  into one tight bound, with a comment saying exactly why — which is what item 1026 had to add to
  Rust. **TS had this right first**, and that is the first time in this run of cross-engine
  transfers that the TS engine was the one ahead.
- the PREFIX gap **does** exist, for the same reason it did in Rust: `STARTS WITH` parses to a
  `func`, so no compare arm can see it and nothing turns it into a range hint.

### Why the existing probe could not answer this

`spelling-probe.ts` has the exact blindness item 1023 found in the Rust probe's equality groups:
its string key holds SEVEN distinct values (so no prefix over it is selective) and it declares only
HASH indexes. Its own header says the indexes are created after the unindexed groups so their
numbers stay comparable with every recorded figure — so widening that fixture would invalidate
them. Hence `prefix-seek-probe.ts`, with its own fixture and a range index.

### Measured

Three alternated PRE/POST rounds, 100,000 rows, median of the warm reps:

```text
                                PRE                      POST                  ratio
  STARTS WITH (prefix)          4.465 / 5.021 / 5.163    0.080 / 0.082 / 0.077  56-65x
  CONTROL explicit range        0.110 / 0.114 / 0.098    0.090 / 0.088 / 0.090  flat
  CONTROL equality seek         0.004 / 0.004 / 0.004    0.004 / 0.003 / 0.003  flat
  CONTROL one-sided range       0.018 / 0.011 / 0.014    0.010 / 0.008 / 0.009  flat
  CONTROL unselective interval  3.096 / 1.273 / 1.766    1.968 / 2.151 / 1.901  overlapping
```

The prefix now lands on the explicit range it is equivalent to — 0.080 against 0.090, where it was
50x behind.

**The unselective-interval control looked like a +52% regression on the first single-pair reading
(1.402 → 2.129) and is not one**: PRE spans 1.27–3.10 and POST 1.90–2.15, overlapping. Second time
in this session a bimodal row has impersonated a regression (item 1022 was the first), and
alternation is what settles it both times.

### Teeth, and what the residual filter costs the mutation score

Six mutants. Two were caught end-to-end — **the maximum code point not declined** and **an empty
prefix seeding anyway** — because those change which rows the seek can return at all.

**Three were answer-equivalent, and that is the residual filter's doing.** The residual WHERE
re-applies `starts_with`, so a bound that is merely too WIDE changes no answer: a UTF-16 slice
instead of a code-point walk, an inclusive upper bound, and `+2` instead of `+1` all passed every
end-to-end case. For `😀` the UTF-16 slice produces a _lone surrogate_ bound — which still orders
above `😀`, so the interval is a superset and the filter cleans up after it.

That is CLAUDE.md's rule arriving exactly on cue: **an answer-equivalent choice needs the
arithmetic extracted and unit-tested.** `prefixUpper` is now exported and asserted directly —
surrogate pairs advance as one code point (`😀` → `😁`), the untouched prefix is preserved
(`az` → `a{`, not `b`), the result is always the same number of code points as the input, and the
two no-successor cases return `undefined`. With those, all three width mutants fail.

So the residual stays (it is the insurance that makes a bound error a perf bug instead of a wrong
answer) and the arithmetic is tested where errors are visible.

### Verification

GQL suite 2,800/0; core 370/0; Gremlin 852/0; all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0; `bun run
spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9` flags the same two pre-existing groups as before and no
new ones.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run check` 0;
`bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

### Recorded, not built

A PARAM prefix (`STARTS WITH $p`) still scans. The hint's bound is a compiled EXPRESSION, so the
successor would need a compiled "successor of" form rather than a literal computed at compile time.
The literal spelling is the one `STARTS WITH` is written in, so this is noted rather than built.

## Item 1029 — the PARAM prefix, ~100x; item 1028's reason for skipping it was wrong, and the obvious degradation was a pessimization

SHIPPED (TypeScript). Item 1028 handled a LITERAL prefix and left the param spelling scanning, on
the grounds that _"the literal spelling is the one `STARTS WITH` is written in"_.

**That reason contradicts the same file's own note on `IN $names`**, which records that binding is
the INJECTION-SAFE form and inline literals are the rare one. The same argument applies to a
prefix, so the param is likely the commoner spelling and 1028 dismissed it too quickly — on a
plausible-sounding claim that one glance at the neighbouring comment refutes.

### What it needed, which was less than 1028 assumed

1028 said a param would need "a compiled 'successor of' form". It does not: a `CompiledExpr` is a
closure `(env) => value`, so the bound computes the successor at EVALUATION time by wrapping the
prefix's own closure. No new compiled form, no change to `CRangeBound`.

```text
                                PRE                      POST                   ratio
  STARTS WITH $p (param)        4.733 / 4.788 / 4.967    0.051 / 0.049 / 0.049  93-101x
  CONTROL literal prefix        0.076 / 0.076 / 0.074    0.075 / 0.077 / 0.080  flat
  CONTROL param, no successor   5.261 / 3.142 / 3.363    4.739 / 4.834 / 4.848  overlapping
```

### The obvious degradation was a 3x PESSIMIZATION, and a control caught it

A param's value is unknown at compile time, so "no successor" can only be discovered during
evaluation. The natural handling is to drop the upper side and keep the lower — and that is wrong:
for an empty prefix the lower bound is `>= ''`, so the seek materializes EVERY id through the index
and then filters. Measured **3.6 → 11.3 ms** against the plain scan, on the control added for
exactly this shape.

So both sides are tied: present together, or neither. `prefixBound` returns the pair or
`undefined`, both closures read it, and when it declines they return a non-scalar — which
`evalBound` already treats as "no usable endpoint", declining the seek.

**That also removed a change I had already made.** I first taught `evalBound` to distinguish "this
side does not apply" from "this endpoint is unusable". Once both sides are tied, nothing reaches
that branch — it is the dead-guard shape items 1015/1016 are about — so `matching.ts` is reverted
and the file is untouched.

### Two answer-equivalent mutants, and the fix for them

| mutant                                                       | verdict                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| a non-string param still seeds (coerced through `String(v)`) | CAUGHT                                          |
| the no-successor case seeks on the LOWER bound alone         | EQUIVALENT → caught after extraction            |
| `evalBound` nulls the whole bound again                      | EQUIVALENT → change reverted, branch now absent |

The residual `starts_with` re-validates whatever the seek returns, so seeking the wrong SHAPE
changes no answer — only the speed. CLAUDE.md's rule for an answer-equivalent choice is to extract
the decision and test it directly, so `prefixBound` is exported and asserted: both sides or
neither, `''` and the top of the code-point range decline, and a non-string declines. The
lower-bound-only mutant then fails two cases.

A third assertion earns its place by being about the ERROR path: `STARTS WITH $p` with `p: 5`
throws (the scalar's own contract), and it must throw for the same reason with and without the
index — a seed built from `5` would have changed which rows reached the thrower.

### Verification

GQL suite 2,803/0; core 370/0; Gremlin 852/0; all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run check` 0;
`bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

### Still open

The Rust engine's prefix seed (item 1027) takes a literal only, for the same reason 1028 gave — and
the same correction applies. Rust's bounds are `Value`s computed at plan time rather than closures,
so the param case there is a genuine plan-shape question rather than a wrapper. Recorded with that
distinction, since 1028's mistake was assuming the two engines' "needs a new form" costs were the
same.

## Item 1030 — the Rust param prefix was ALREADY covered; item 1029's "still open" is withdrawn, and the ordering it depends on is now pinned

MEASUREMENT + a test, no engine change. Item 1029 closed the TS param prefix and recorded the Rust
one as still open, reasoning that _"Rust's bounds are `Value`s computed at plan time, not closures,
so a param there is a genuine plan-shape question rather than a wrapper."_

**Wrong, and `bind.rs`'s own module doc says so in the opposite direction:**

> Binding before `opt` keeps the value typed (never spliced into query text) and **lets the planner
> seed indexes on the now-literal predicate**, exactly as a direct parameterized query does.

`$p` becomes an `Expr::Lit` before the optimizer runs, so item 1027's literal path covers the param
spelling with no new work at all. Verified rather than read off the comment:

```text
  $p = "name500"  ->  INTERVAL seek     111 rows
  $p = ""         ->  Filter { Scan }   100,000 rows   (no successor — correctly declines)
  $p = "zzz"      ->  INTERVAL seek     0 rows
```

Including the decline. The param spelling optimizes to the _same plan_ as the literal one, so item
1027's 72x carries by construction and there is nothing to re-measure.

### The symmetry worth naming

Two items in a row got this wrong in OPPOSITE directions, both by reasoning about a neighbouring
engine instead of reading the one in front of me:

- 1028 assumed the TS param needed a new compiled form. It needed a closure wrapper (1029).
- 1029 assumed the Rust param needed a new plan shape. It needed **nothing** (this item).

The common error is treating "what would this cost in the engine I just worked in" as evidence
about the other. Both engines answered in one grep of their own binding code.

### What actually ships: the pin

The property is an ORDERING, not a local rule — it holds only while binding precedes optimization —
and nothing tested it. Moving binding after `opt`, or adding a path that optimizes a still-
parameterized plan, would silently drop the seek and leave a 72x-slower query **that still answers
correctly**, which is this repo's definition of the dangerous kind of change.

So `a_param_prefix_seeds_like_a_literal_one` asserts the param and literal spellings optimize to
the SAME plan (not merely to the same answer), that a selective prefix seeds through both, and that
the empty-prefix decline carries through both. Two mutants confirm it has teeth: the prefix arm
declining the test's value, and prefix seeding removed outright — each fails two tests.

### Verification

Engine suite 1,264/0; `rewrite_fuzz` 10/0 at `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=200000`; all seven byte-identity
fuzzers 13/0.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo clippy --all-targets -D
warnings` 0; `cargo fmt --check` 0; `cargo test` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run
fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1031 — an EDGE property index is unreachable from GQL: 38–150x against the Gremlin spelling of the same question

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Items 1023–1030 were all about VERTEX key seeding. Grepping the
pattern elsewhere: `graph.edgePropertyIndex` exists, and `@lenke/gremlin`'s
`executor/index-seed.ts` seeds from it — while **nothing in `@lenke/gql` references it at all.**

So in the TS engine, a declared edge index serves one surface and is invisible to the other.

### Measured

100,000 edges over 200 vertices, 1,000 distinct `amount` values (one value = 0.1% of the edges),
`createIndex({ on: 'edge', kind: 'hash', keys: ['amount'] })` declared. Median of the warm reps,
three runs:

```text
  CONTROL gremlin E().has('amount', 500)      0.030 / 0.030 / 0.031 ms   <- seeds the edge index
  GQL inline  -[e:PAID {amount: 500}]->       1.088 / 1.153 / 1.164
  GQL clause  WHERE e.amount = 500            3.190 / 2.855 / 4.543
  CONTROL GQL on an UNINDEXED edge key        3.787 / 3.311 / 3.530
```

All four answer identically (100 edges; the unindexed control answers 0 by construction, on a key
no edge carries).

- **Gremlin against GQL: 36–39x on the inline spelling, 95–150x on the clause one.**
- The clause spelling lands ON the unindexed control — it is a pure scan, and the declared index
  does nothing for it.
- The inline spelling is ~3x faster than that control but still 38x off the index, so it is a
  cheaper scan rather than a seek: `flatAdj` pushes an inline rel predicate into the adjacency
  walk, which avoids materializing the rest of each bucket.

The Gremlin arm is the control that makes this readable: without it, 1.1 ms for 100 edges out of
100,000 looks respectable rather than 38x off.

### Two separate findings, and only one of them is expensive

**(1) GQL cannot seed an edge index.** This is not a filter that could be cheaper — it is a missing
SEED. `MATCH ()-[e:PAID {amount: 500}]->()` enumerates every vertex and walks each adjacency; the
index would let the query START from the matching edges, which is exactly what `E().has(…)` does.
That is a new plan path with its own qualifying-shape question (both ends unbound, or bound FROM
the edge's endpoints), so it is feature-sized rather than a tick.

**(2) Within GQL, the clause spelling is 2.5–3.9x the inline one**, and that is a contained fix.
`pushWhereIntoNode` pushes a clause `WHERE` into the **start node only** — `path.start.variable` —
and has no relationship twin, so `WHERE e.amount = 500` stays a clause filter (evaluated once per
SURVIVING BINDING) while `{amount: 500}` becomes an inline rel predicate (evaluated inside the
adjacency walk). That is the same mechanism the function's own comment records as a 15.8x for the
multi-pattern case, in a position nobody extended it to.

(2) is the next item. It is worth noting that it does not need (1): pushing the conjunct down makes
the clause spelling as fast as the inline one, which closes a spelling gap that exists today
regardless of whether an index is ever reachable.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the new probe.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run check` 0;
`bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1032 — the rel push-down is WRONG (16 tests), and item 1031's gap is specific to the COUNT shape

MEASUREMENT + an attempted fix REVERTED, no engine change. Item 1031 priced a 2.5–3.9x gap between
`WHERE e.amount = 500` and `-[e:PAID {amount: 500}]->` and named the fix: `pushWhereIntoNode` has
no relationship twin, so push the conjunct into the rel's inline predicate.

### The fix was built and it returns wrong answers

Sixteen GQL tests failed, and not as route assertions — as **wrong rows**:

```text
  MATCH (p:U)-[r:T]->(q) WHERE r.w = 1 RETURN r.w AS w, q.n AS n
    expected  [{ w: 1, … }]
    got       [{ w: 1, … }, { w: 2, n: 9 }]
```

`WHERE r.w = 1` returned a row with `w: 2`, so the pushed predicate is DROPPED on at least one
route rather than merely moved. Reverted; the suite is 2,803/0 again.

**Native had said the two spellings are one question**, and that is still true —
`MATCH ()-[e:T]->() WHERE e.k = v` and the inline spelling optimize to byte-identical
`Filter { Expand { Scan } }` plans in Rust. What I inferred from that was that TS could reach the
same place by rewriting the AST, and the tests say the TS pipeline does not read a pushed
`rel.where` on every route it reads a parsed one. Plan equivalence in one engine is not a recipe
for the other.

### And item 1031's gap is narrower than I reported

1031 presented the clause-vs-inline gap as a property of the spellings. It is a property of the
**result shape**. Three runs each:

```text
  count(*)      inline 1.132 / 1.012 / 1.366 ms    clause 3.032 / 2.810 / 2.864   2.1-2.8x
  projection    inline 8.382 / 9.015 / 9.848       clause 9.611 / 8.184 / 10.184  OVERLAPPING
```

The projection spellings converge, and the reason is in the code: item 447 built
`relBoundFilteredHopWalk` precisely to CARRY a rel-reading clause `WHERE`, and it lives in
`hop-projection.ts` — it serves a projection, not a bare `count(*)`. So the mechanism already
exists and the count path does not use it.

That reframes the target: not "give `pushWhereIntoNode` a rel twin" but "carry the rel predicate in
the COUNT path, as item 447 did for projections". Narrower, and it starts from a route that is
already correct rather than from an AST rewrite that is not.

1031's headline figure is corrected to **2.1–2.8x on the count shape**, and its claim that the gap
is about clause position is withdrawn.

### What stands from 1031

The edge-index finding is untouched: `graph.edgePropertyIndex` is seeded by Gremlin's
`index-seed.ts` and referenced nowhere in `@lenke/gql`, so the Gremlin spelling is 36–39x the GQL
inline one and 95–150x the clause one. That remains the larger, feature-sized item.

### Method

**An attempted fix that fails loudly is a cheaper outcome than one that passes quietly.** The 16
failures arrived on the first run of the suite, before any measurement was taken — so the cost of
the wrong approach was one build, not a shipped wrong answer. The same tests also contain the
reason: they are items 446/447's, which means the shape I was rewriting had already been given a
purpose-built route, and reading those tests first would have found it.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe (two projection arms added). GQL
suite 2,803/0 after the revert.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run check` 0;
`bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1033 — the diagnosis is exact and the fix is refuted: a branch in the hot loop cost three controls 2x

MEASUREMENT + an attempted fix REVERTED, no engine change. Item 1032 reframed the target as "carry
the rel predicate in the COUNT path". This item located it precisely, built the obvious fix, and
the controls refused it.

### The diagnosis, which is now exact

Four readings narrowed it, each ruling something out rather than confirming a guess:

1. **The shortcut is not declining.** A one-segment clause `WHERE` already builds a `HopPred` with
   `relVar: reads(seg.rel.variable)` — item 633 gave it that. So the rel predicate IS carried.
2. **It is not the anonymous ends.** Naming them changes nothing: clause 2.946 against 2.871
   anonymous.
3. **The pushdown machinery works where a lift exists.** A clause conjunct on a NODE key reads
   **0.027 ms** on the same fixture, against the rel conjunct's 2.9.
4. **What differs is the per-edge path.** For a rel-only predicate the generic walk does
   `binding.set(pred.relVar, edge)` and then a general `pred.fn(env)`, where the inline spelling is
   checked as an `InlinePred` directly on the edge. `HopPred` carries `farLifted` and `startLifted`
   (items 995/996) and **no `relLifted`** — the edge is the third position of the same shape, left
   out.

So the gap is not a missing route but a missing LIFT, in machinery I added for the other two
positions.

### The fix, and why it cannot ship

`relLifted: liftedOwnPred(where, free, seg.rel.variable)` plus a branch in `tallyHopCount` applying
it to the edge. All 2,803 GQL tests pass — no wrong answers this time — and the target improves:

```text
  NAMED ends, clause   PRE 3.041 / 3.154 / 2.967    POST 2.069 / 1.178 / 1.265
```

**But three controls the change cannot reach got ~2x WORSE, with disjoint ranges:**

```text
  NAMED ends, inline          0.946 / 0.848 / 0.845  ->  2.062 / 1.965 / 2.067   2.3x worse
  CONTROL unindexed edge key  3.103 / 3.137 / 3.322  ->  5.973 / 7.092 / 5.602   1.8-2.2x worse
  clause on a NODE key        0.033 / 0.024 / 0.022  ->  0.048 / 0.047 / 0.051   2x worse
```

`relLifted` is set only when the predicate reads exactly the rel variable, so none of those three
can execute the new code. What they share is the LOOP: a branch added inside `tallyHopCount`'s
per-edge body changes its shape for every predicate kind that flows through it. That is the hazard
this very file records five times over — `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` — and the reason the far
and start lifts were given **dedicated module-scope walks** (`startOnlyHopCount`, and
`farOnlyHopCount`, whose own comment says "kept at module scope, like `startOnlyHopCount`, so the
closure…").

A 2.4x win on one shape against a 2x loss on three others is a net regression. Reverted; suite
2,803/0.

### What the next attempt should build

A `relOnlyHopCount` at module scope, mirroring `startOnlyHopCount`, routed to when the predicate
reads only the rel variable — so the generic loop is byte-for-byte unchanged and only the new shape
takes the new path. That is what items 995/996 did for the other two positions, and the precedent
is explicit in the code; I reached for the cheaper branch instead and the controls priced it.

### Method

**Second consecutive tick where my fix was refused, and both times by the instrument rather than by
review.** Item 1032's was caught by 16 tests as wrong rows; this one by three controls as a 2x
regression on paths it cannot reach. The controls are doing the job they exist for — but the
pattern in both failures is the same: I took the cheapest edit that looked sufficient instead of
the shape the surrounding code had already established for the identical problem one position over.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe (three named-end arms added). GQL
suite 2,803/0 after the revert.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run check` 0;
`bun run fmt` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

## Item 1034 — the REL lift, as a module-scope walk: 1.8x, and the clause/inline spelling gap is closed

SHIPPED. Item 1031 priced `MATCH ()-[e:PAID]->() WHERE e.amount = 500 RETURN count(*)` at 2.1–2.8x
its inline twin `-[e:PAID {amount: 500}]->` (figure as corrected by item 1032). Item 1033 located
the cause exactly — `HopPred` carries `farLifted` and `startLifted` (items 995/996) and no
`relLifted`, so the edge was the one position of the three left on `binding.set(relVar, edge)` plus
a general `pred.fn(env)` per edge — and then had its fix refused by the controls. This item builds
the shape those controls demanded.

### The change

`relLifted: liftedOwnPred(where, free, seg.rel.variable)` on `HopPred`, consumed by a new
module-scope `relOnlyHopCount`. Routed after `startWalkFits`/`farWalkFits` and before
`tallyHopCount`, with no `relWalkFits` predicate: the lift IS the fit rule, because it is set only
when `freePredicateVars(where)` is exactly the rel's own variable. The two endpoint walks need an
extra condition the rel walk does not — the OTHER side unconstrained, so they can sum degrees —
and this walk cannot trade O(E) for O(V) at all, because a predicate on the edge needs the edge.
Its win is the per-edge constant alone: the same `tallyEdges` source, with `satisfies` reading the
edge directly.

**`tallyHopCount` is byte-for-byte unchanged.** That is the whole lesson of item 1033 and it is
`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` for the fifth time in this file (items 119, 141, 159, 1033).

### The measurement, and why the first reading was wrong

Item 1033's numbers came from `edge-index-probe.ts`: nine shapes in one process, median of six warm
reps. On that instrument this change read as a 2.6x win on the target against ~2x REGRESSIONS on
two other arms — including the anonymous-ends spelling of the target's own query, which is the same
question. One question giving two opposite answers is the instrument, not the engine, and CLAUDE.md
records both halves of why: a two-dist in-process A/B flatters whatever REDISTRIBUTES call sites,
and some TS shapes are outright bimodal inside one process.

So the reading was redone on `rel-lift-probe.ts` — **one shape per PROCESS**, 14 reps, the whole
series printed, median of reps 4+, three alternated rounds with a per-arm `grep -c relOnlyHopCount`
assertion (0 for PRE, 2 for POST). 100,000 `PAID` edges over 200 vertices, 1,000 distinct amounts:

```text
                              PRE                      POST                 ratio
  anon-clause   reached   2.013 1.911 2.185     1.029 1.376 1.072        1.8x faster
  named-clause  reached   1.943 1.889 2.044     1.060 1.066 1.070        1.8x faster
  unindexed     reached   1.721 1.724 2.573     0.973 1.077 0.983        1.8x faster
  named-inline  CONTROL   1.063 1.042 0.962     1.031 0.988 1.000        FLAT
  node-key      CONTROL   0.036 0.041 0.035     0.041 0.041 0.039        FLAT
```

Three reached shapes improve with disjoint ranges; **both controls are flat**, which is what item
1033's branch could not manage. `named-inline` is the inline spelling on the tally and `node-key`
routes to the start walk, so neither can execute the new code.

And the spelling gap is closed on its own terms: the clause spelling now lands at 1.06–1.07 against
the inline spelling's 0.99–1.03, where it was 1.9–2.0 against 1.0. The in-sweep figures (2.9
against 0.85) were inflated on both sides by the same residual CLAUDE.md names.

### Teeth — and a survivor that was a missing test, not dead code

Three mutants, each restored before the next, under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p
MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, each verdict read from stdout AND stderr before the exit code:

```text
  drop the rel's inline gate      rc=1   2802 pass  1 fail     caught
  drop the endpoint label gate    rc=1   2802 pass  1 fail     caught
  needsBind = false               rc=0   2803 pass  0 fail     SURVIVED
```

`needsBind` is `lifted.where !== undefined` — it binds the rel variable for a predicate that does
NOT lift completely, so a RESIDUAL expression can still read the edge through the binding. Setting
it `false` survived all 2,803 tests. Item 1015's rule says a survivor can mean the code is wrong
rather than the test missing, so that was checked first: `liftedOwnPred` returns a `CPredicate`
whatever `directEqProps` leaves behind, so a residual `where` is reachable, and the suite simply
had no `count(*)` over a rel-only clause `WHERE` that leaves one.

`rel-lift-count.test.ts` is that coverage — 13 tests, with a `residualBlock` of four shapes that do
not lift (arithmetic `e.w + 1 = 2`, a disjunction, a negation over an ABSENT cell, and `upper(e.tag)`).
Every count is also checked against the same question as a PROJECTION, which takes item 447's
different route, so a wrong count cannot be confirmed by a wrong expectation. Re-run against the
mutant: **4 fail**, all four residual cases. The survivor is now caught.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,816 (13 new), gremlin 852, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity fuzzers, 13/0.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED, `fmt` first: `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run lint` 0; `bun run check` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0. (Run in the other order, `check` fails
on the new probe's formatting — `fmt` is not idempotent with `fmt:check` for a file it has not yet
touched.)

## Item 1035 — a declared EDGE index now seeds a GQL hop: 27x, and the feature-sized item was a 40-line function

SHIPPED. Item 1031 found `graph.edgePropertyIndex` seeded by `@lenke/gremlin`'s
`executor/index-seed.ts` and referenced NOWHERE in `@lenke/gql`, priced the consequence at 36–150x,
and called it "feature-sized rather than a tick" — a new plan path with its own qualifying-shape
question. That estimate was wrong, and it was wrong for a specific reason worth keeping: between
1031 and now, item 1034 gave the one-hop walks a lifted rel predicate, so by the time the seed was
built BOTH spellings of the predicate were already sitting in the scan descriptor. The feature was
large when it would have had to extract the predicate itself; once something else had, it was a
chooser.

### The change

`edgeSeek(graph, inRel, relLifted, types, env)` — plain arguments, EXPORTED, for `hopSeek`'s
reason (below). It offers one candidate per indexed equality, takes the narrowest, and admits it
only if `count * TALLY_SEEK_MARGIN < bucket`. `tallyEdges` tries it before its two vertex seeds,
and `edgesOfTypesIn` re-applies the edge type the index bucket cannot know about.

Three decisions, each recorded where it is made:

- **Both spellings' keys are read** — the clause `WHERE e.k = v` arrives as `relLifted.eqProps`
  (item 1034), the inline `-[e:T {k: v}]->` as `inRel.pred.props`. They are one question, and this
  file's recurring defect is serving one of them.
- **The denominator is the EDGE TYPE bucket**, so `seekIsWorthIt` is the wrong oracle — its
  `candidateCount` counts vertices. Same rule, right denominator, and `TALLY_SEEK_MARGIN` reused
  rather than a fifth constant invented.
- **A NULL value declines.** `{k: null}` matches a stored null AND an absent key, where the index
  bucket holds only edges that store one — so seeding it would DROP rows. Declining a seed is
  always sound; admitting a narrow one is not.

### The measurement

`rel-lift-probe.ts`, one shape per process, 14 reps, median of reps 4+, three alternated rounds,
per-arm `grep -c edgeSeek` assertion (0 PRE, 2 POST). 100,000 `PAID` edges, 1,000 distinct amounts
so one value is 100 edges:

```text
                              PRE                      POST                 ratio
  CEILING gremlin         0.025 0.023 0.024     0.026 0.027 0.028        —
  anon-clause             1.055 1.089 1.072     0.035 0.038 0.036        29x faster
  named-clause            1.114 1.085 1.060     0.039 0.035 0.041        27x faster
  named-inline            1.045 1.073 0.967     0.038 0.043 0.039        26x faster
  CONTROL unindexed key   0.976 1.010 0.957     1.010 1.029 0.994        FLAT
  CONTROL node-key        0.036 0.040 0.043     0.042 0.040 0.035        FLAT
```

The Gremlin arm is what makes this readable, and it is the arm item 1031 added for that purpose:
GQL now lands within **1.4x** of the surface that has had the index all along, where it was 40x off.
`unindexed` is the control that says the win is the INDEX and not "edge filters got faster" — `other`
is not an indexed key, the seed declines, and the arm does not move.

### Teeth — and a survivor that was a fixture too small to reach the code

Six mutants, each restored before the next, under the cgroup cap:

```text
  never-seed              rc=1   2826 pass  2 fail    caught (by the exported decision)
  always-seed             rc=1   2827 pass  1 fail    caught (by the exported decision)
  widest-candidate        rc=1   2827 pass  1 fail    caught
  admit-null              rc=1   2826 pass  2 fail    caught
  drop-type-residual      rc=0   2828 pass  0 fail    SURVIVED
  wrong-index (vertex)    rc=1   2826 pass  2 fail    caught
```

The first two are the reason `edgeSeek` is exported at all: seeding is answer-preserving, so a
mutant that never seeds — or always does — returns every correct answer. `hopSeek` carries the same
note from items 172/173, and `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test` is the rule.

**`drop-type-residual`'s survival was not a missing test — it was a fixture that could not reach
the code.** The `answers` block used a four-edge graph, where `count * TALLY_SEEK_MARGIN < bucket`
is FALSE and the seed declines, so every assertion in it passed while measuring the old scan. The
block now builds 8,001 `T` edges plus a `U` edge carrying the same `w`, and its FIRST test asserts
`edgeSeek(…)?.size === 9` — the fixture's own premise, checked rather than assumed, which is
CLAUDE.md's "check the fixture's own statistics, not just its output". Against the corrected
fixture the mutant fails 3.

### Not done, and why it is not a side effect

`spelling-probe.ts` cannot see this route: it declares only VERTEX indexes, and its one edge
property is `w = e % 5` — a fifth of 600,000 edges, which the margin correctly declines. Giving it
a selective edge key means adding a property to a SHARED fixture, and items 287/471 are both about
what that does to every group already measured against it. That is its own re-baseline pass, not a
line added while shipping something else. Recorded in `CLOSED.md` as open.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,830 (14 new), gremlin 852, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0. `bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000
SPELL_REPS=9`: 0 groups disagree on the answer, and the three groups over 2x are pre-existing and
structurally unreachable by this change (no edge index in that fixture, so `isIndexed` is false and
`edgeSeek` returns `undefined` for every group in it).

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED, **after the documents were written**:
`bun run fmt` 0; `bun run lint` 0; `bun run check` 0; `bun run fmt:check` 0.

**AND THAT ORDER IS WHY ITEM 1034's CI WENT RED.** Its gates ran BEFORE the audit entry and the
`CLOSED.md` lines were appended, so `oxfmt` never saw them and CI's `oxfmt --check` found one
over-long line in `CLOSED.md`. Everything else in that run was green. The fix ships here; the rule
is that the documents are part of the change and the gates come after them, not after the code.

## Item 1036 — the Rust engine has NO edge property index, and that is worth far less than item 1035 implied

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. One probe, two documents.

Item 1035 gave the TS engine's GQL surface an edge-index seed, 27x. The obvious next move is the
same thing in Rust. Grepping the pattern there first, as the method says:

`crates/lenke-engine/src/schema_op.rs` matches `("vertex", "hash")`, `("vertex", "range")`,
`("edge", "interval")` and `("edge", "type")`, and nothing else — so `on: 'edge', kind: 'hash'`
has **no engine arm at all**. `packages/native/src/graph.ts` says so in as many words: its
`IndexSpec` union omits the cross product deliberately, "a compile error here rather than a runtime
throw". Confirmed at the boundary too — `createIndex({ on: 'edge', kind: 'hash', … })` through the
FFI backend raises `schemaApply: unsupported index: on=edge kind=hash`, which the probe asserts so
that the premise fails loudly if the feature ever lands.

So item 1035 has nothing to port. The Rust engine does not have a slower seed; it has no seed, and
giving it one is a FEATURE — store structure, write maintenance, the undo log, the snapshot codec,
and byte-identity across the FFI and wasm backends.

### What it would be worth — and the answer is not 27x

100,000 `PAID` edges over 200 vertices, 1,000 distinct amounts so one value is 0.1%, both engines
holding the same generated rows (the native side through NDJSON, edge ids included because
`encode` emits them). Median of reps 4+, three rounds:

```text
  native  EDGE predicate, NO index exists     0.113  0.101  0.105 ms   (100 rows)
  ts      EDGE predicate + edge index (1035)  0.037  0.035  0.041      (100 rows)
  CONTROL native VERTEX key + vertex index    0.004  0.003  0.003      (500 rows)
  CONTROL ts     VERTEX key + vertex index    0.025  0.024  0.033      (500 rows)
```

**Native's un-indexed SCAN is 2.9x FASTER than the TS engine's indexed seek.** 100,000 edges in
0.105 ms is ~1.05 ns an edge, which is at the scan floor `simd_index_probe`'s E64 measured
independently (1.88 ns a node). There is nothing to shave inside the scan; the only lever is not
scanning.

That reframes the item. In TS the missing index cost **1.07 ms against 0.036** — a 27x ratio on a
millisecond base, which is why item 1035 was worth 40 lines. In Rust the same gap is ~25-30x in
ratio but **0.10 ms in absolute**, and buying it costs a feature across three backends rather than
a chooser. The vertex control is the arm that keeps that honest: the Rust engine DOES have a hash
index, and the same question asked where the index exists runs in 0.003 ms — so "native is slow at
this shape" is excluded, and what remains is only the absolute size of the prize.

The vertex control also re-measures the layout ceiling in passing: native 0.003-0.004 against TS
0.024-0.033, ~8x, consistent with what item 573 recorded.

### The reading that matters for the loop

**After item 1035's 27x, native still answers this question faster by scanning than TS does by
seeking.** That is the calibration a cross-engine arm exists to produce, and it is the opposite of
what a TS-only reading of 1035 would suggest. A 27x in one engine is not evidence of a gap in the
other; the two engines' scan floors differ by ~10x, so the same missing index is a millisecond
problem in one and a microsecond problem in the other.

Recorded as OPEN and PRICED rather than built. It is a real feature with a real number, and the
number says it is not the next thing to build.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the new probe.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED, after the documents: see the commit.

## Item 1037 — the PROJECTION form of item 1035's question is 130-180x off, and it is a SCAN

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. One probe (four new arms), two documents.

Item 1035 seeded the edge index from `tallyEdges`, which serves the COUNT walks. Grepping the
pattern in the other result shape: `hop-projection.ts` imports `hopSeek` and `edgesOfTypes` and
references `edgeSeek` nowhere, and `relBoundFilteredHopWalk` drives
`candidateVertexSource(graph, startLabel)` and iterates each vertex's adjacency bucket. So the
projection form of the same question still enumerates every vertex and every edge.

### Priced, three rounds, each shape in its own process

```text
  proj-gremlin   E().has('amount',500).values('amount')   0.061  0.049  0.055 ms   CEILING
  proj-inline    MATCH ()-[e:PAID {amount: 500}]->()      7.198  7.871  8.723
  proj-clause    MATCH ()-[e:PAID]->() WHERE e.amount=500 9.952  7.613  9.065
  proj-zero      the same clause, a value NO edge carries 6.718  5.846  7.785   (0 rows)
  named-clause   the COUNT form, seeded since item 1035   0.047  0.044  0.040
```

**130-180x off the Gremlin ceiling**, and 180-200x the count form of the same question on the same
fixture.

**And it is the SCAN, not row construction — `proj-zero` is the arm that settles it.** The same
projection on a value no edge carries returns ZERO rows and still costs 5.8-7.8 ms, so roughly
6-7 ms of the 7-9 is invariant to how many rows come back. 100,000 edges visited to produce 100
rows; row construction is the remaining ~1-2 ms. An answer invariant to the property varied cannot
validate a fixture (CLAUDE.md), and here that invariance is exactly the finding.

### A claim of mine retracted by repetition

A single run read `proj-clause` 11.356 against `proj-inline` 6.071 and I wrote down "the two
projection spellings are 2.2x apart". Three rounds refute it: inline 7.198/7.871/8.723 against
clause 9.952/7.613/9.065 — **overlapping**. The spellings CONVERGE, which is what item 1032 found
independently when it corrected item 1031. The 2x was one noisy pair, and this family's series
spans 6-17 ms inside one process, so a single pair cannot support a ratio at all.

That retraction changes the build, not just the record: if one spelling were already 2x better
there would be a route to copy, and there is not. Both scan.

### What the build needs, and why it is two halves

`relBoundFilteredHopWalk` takes `relPred: CPredicate | undefined` (the rel's INLINE constraint,
closed by `relInlineOf`) and `gate: CompiledExpr | undefined` (the clause `WHERE`) as SEPARATE
parameters, and the call site at `hop-projection.ts:1520` shows them staying separate.

- The INLINE spelling can seed today: `relPred` carries `props`/`eqProps`, which is exactly what
  `edgeSeek` reads.
- The CLAUSE spelling cannot: it arrives as a compiled expression with no `eqProps` to offer. It
  needs the lift item 1034 gave the COUNT path, here.

Doing only the first would take one spelling to ~0.06 ms and leave its twin at ~8 — turning a
shared 130x into a 130x BETWEEN SPELLINGS, which is this engine's named defect class. So both
halves land together or neither does.

The walk itself must be edge-driven and its own closure, not a branch: `startVar`, `farVar` and
the rel binding are all reachable from an edge (`edge.from`/`edge.to`), so an edge seed can drive
it — and items 159 and 1033 both measured what a branch in one of these inner loops costs
(1.6x and ~2x on three controls respectively).

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe. Gates after the documents; see the
commit.

## Item 1038 — the edge-seeded PROJECTION walk: 100-190x, and both spellings together

SHIPPED. Item 1037 priced the projection form of item 1035's question at 130-180x the Gremlin
spelling and showed by a zero-row arm that the cost was the SCAN. This builds the walk, with the
`relSeekedHopWalk` / `narrowerSeed` pair and the clause lift the projection path was missing.

### The change

`relSeekedHopWalk` — an EDGE-DRIVEN closure, routed after `relBoundHopWalk` and before
`relBoundFilteredHopWalk`, which seeds from the edge index and reads both endpoints off each edge
(`edge.from` / `edge.to`). `relBoundFilteredHopWalk` is byte-for-byte unchanged and is the control.

Three things it had to get right that the count side did not:

- **BOTH endpoint labels.** The vertex-driven twin walks the START label's bucket, so it only ever
  needed the far check. An edge-driven walk gets neither for free.
- **BOTH spellings.** `relPred` (the inline constraint) and a new `relLifted` — the projection's
  twin of item 1034's lift, since `gate` is a compiled expression with no `eqProps` to offer — are
  both handed to `edgeSeek`. Seeding one and not the other would have converted a gap SHARED by
  two spellings into a gap BETWEEN them, which is the defect class CLAUDE.md names.
  `edgeSeek` also gained a `props` loop: the count path only ever hands it a LIFTED predicate
  (equalities in `eqProps`), where the projection path hands a bare inline `CPredicate` (`props`).
- **Delegate, do not `return null`, when the index declines.** A runtime `null` from a `RowsFn`
  hands the query to the GENERAL row pipeline, so declining that way would have turned an
  unselective indexed key — the case `edgeSeek`'s margin exists to refuse — into a pessimization
  against the very walk this is an alternative to. The scanning twin is built once and captured as
  `fallback`.

Row order changes (index order rather than vertex-creation order). That is sound: row order without
`ORDER BY` is unspecified and the differential fuzzer compares row MULTISETS for exactly this
reason. No test in any package asserted otherwise.

### The measurement

One shape per process, 14 reps, median of reps 4+, three alternated rounds, per-arm
`grep -c relSeekedHopWalk` assertion (0 PRE, 3 POST):

```text
                              PRE                      POST                   ratio
  proj-inline             4.478 3.844 6.935     0.044 0.046 0.048          ~100x
  proj-clause             7.535 6.736 8.891     0.038 0.044 0.033          ~190x
  proj-zero (0 rows)      5.608 6.238 10.199    0.003 0.003 0.003          ~2000x
  CONTROL proj-unindexed  2.889 6.987 6.211     3.713 2.390 3.321          overlapping
  CONTROL named-clause    0.040 0.056 0.045     0.040 0.054 0.035          FLAT
  CONTROL node-key        0.041 0.048 0.040     0.035 0.036 0.045          FLAT
  CEILING proj-gremlin    0.054 0.047 0.050     0.059 0.059 0.059          see below
```

The two spellings now land within 1.4x of each other and within 1.2x of the Gremlin ceiling.
`proj-zero` is 0.003 ms because an empty seed has nothing to walk — the case that cost 5.8-10.2 ms
before.

**The Gremlin arm read 0.059 three times in POST against 0.047-0.054 in PRE — disjoint, 1.18x — and
it is the sweep, not the engine.** Re-measured alone, nine readings an arm: PRE 0.038-0.071, POST
0.039-0.057, fully overlapping. That is the second time this session an in-sweep reading
manufactured a disjoint range on a control (item 1034 was the first), and the isolated instrument
settled both.

### Teeth

Seven mutants, each restored before the next, under the cgroup cap:

```text
  drop-type-residual     rc=1  2836 pass  4 fail   caught
  drop-near-label        rc=1  2838 pass  2 fail   caught
  drop-far-label         rc=1  2839 pass  1 fail   caught
  drop-relpred-reapply   rc=1  2839 pass  1 fail   caught
  drop-gate-reapply      rc=1  2839 pass  1 fail   caught
  swap-near-far          rc=1  2838 pass  2 fail   caught
  widest-of-two          rc=0  2840 pass  0 fail   SURVIVED
```

`widest-of-two` is answer-equivalent BY CONSTRUCTION: both candidate seeds are supersets and every
predicate is re-applied afterwards, so picking the wider one is slower and never wrong. So the
choice was extracted as `narrowerSeed`, a pure exported function, and unit-tested — five tests
including the tie (deterministic) and an EMPTY seed, which must beat a non-empty alternative rather
than read as "no seed". Against the mutant: **2 fail**. All seven caught.

`edge-seeded-projection.test.ts` carries the rest: 15 tests over a fixture of 8,002 edges, sized to
CLEAR the seek guard — item 1035's `drop-type-residual` survived because its fixture was four edges
and the seed declined, so the first test asserts nine seeded rows before anything else relies on
the route being taken.

### A pre-existing WRONG ANSWER found on the way

Writing an `ORDER BY` arm for the tests turned up a defect that is not this item's. On the
rel-bound hop projection, an `ORDER BY` whose key is a REL property is silently DROPPED, and so is

```text

  MATCH ()-[e:T]->() RETURN e.tag AS a ORDER BY e.tag ASC           ["b","a","c"]   identical
  MATCH ()-[e:T]->() RETURN e.tag AS a ORDER BY a DESC              ["b","a","c"]   the ALIAS too
  MATCH ()-[e:T]->() RETURN e.tag AS a ORDER BY e.tag DESC LIMIT 2  ["b","a","c"]   THREE rows
```

It reproduces identically on the commit before this one, and the neighbouring shapes are correct —
a node scan sorts both directions, and the same hop sorting on a FAR property sorts correctly. So
it is specific to a rel-property sort key on this path. Recorded as item 1039, OPEN; the test file
carries no `ORDER BY` arm, with a comment saying why, because the only two available assertions are
the correct order (red) and the broken one (a wrong answer pinned as a contract).

Suites: core 370, gql 2,845 (15 new), gremlin 852, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.

## Item 1039 — a WRONG ANSWER: the rel-bound hop projection dropped its `ORDER BY` and its `LIMIT`

FIXED. Found while writing item 1038's tests, and it is not item 1038's: it reproduces identically
on every commit before it.

### The defect

`detectHopProjection` wraps every return in `sorted(...)` — except the rel-bound route, which
returned unwrapped. So the sort was computed, admitted by `outputColumnSorts`, and then thrown
away, along with any `LIMIT` or `OFFSET` riding on it. Against the native engine on the same
fixture:

```text
  RETURN e.tag AS a ORDER BY e.tag DESC          ts ["b","a","c"]  native ["c","b","a"]
  RETURN e.tag AS a ORDER BY e.tag ASC           ts ["b","a","c"]  native ["a","b","c"]
  RETURN e.tag AS a ORDER BY a DESC              ts ["b","a","c"]  native ["c","b","a"]
  RETURN e.tag AS a ORDER BY e.tag DESC LIMIT 2  ts ["b","a","c"]  native ["c","b"]
```

Four for four. ASC and DESC returned the SAME order, which is the tell — and the `LIMIT` case
returned THREE rows where two were asked for, so this was a wrong CARDINALITY as well as a wrong
order. All four now agree with native.

The neighbours were already correct — a node scan sorts both directions, and the same hop sorting
on a FAR property sorts correctly — so the defect was specific to this one route.

### Why the differential fuzzers could not see it

Two independent reasons, and neither is a broken invariant:

- They compare row MULTISETS for unordered results, which is correct (row order without `ORDER BY`
  is unspecified), and **a dropped `ORDER BY` is invisible to a multiset comparison.**
- The `LIMIT` half is not invisible — but it only rides along on this route, and the generated hop
  shapes do not read the REL variable, so `itemsReadRel` is false and the route is never reached.

Both halves are coverage. `rel-hop-order.test.ts` is the coverage: 21 tests, every expectation read
off the FFI engine before being written down, because the defect WAS a cross-engine divergence and
a TS-only expectation would have been guesswork about the broken thing.

### The second half: the tie guard, and three fixtures to see it

Item 1038's seeded walk arrives in INDEX order. `Array.prototype.sort` is stable, so a sort pins
the sorted order and leaves TIES on arrival order — and tie order is observable between the engines
(item 605 measured TS and native agreeing over a fixture with 20 ties per group). So wrapping the
route in `sorted(...)` without more would have traded a dropped sort for a diverging tie order.
`relBoundRoute` therefore takes a `sortedQuery` flag and skips the seeded walk under a sort, which
is exactly what `hopOrderPlan` already does to the far-driven walk and for the same reason.

**Proving that guard load-bearing took three fixtures, and the first two each hid it.** Three things
must hold at once:

1. The seed must be ADMITTED — a selective indexed key. `w` with two values is HALF the bucket,
   which `edgeSeek`'s margin correctly refuses, so fixture one never seeded.
2. The sort key must be a PROJECTED OUTPUT COLUMN, or `outputColumnSorts` declines and the whole
   query leaves for the general path where neither walk runs. Fixture two sorted on `e.w` while
   projecting `e.t`, so it measured the general path twice and read "AGREE" both times.
3. The matching edges must be INTERLEAVED against vertex creation order. In fixture two all eight
   `k = 7` edges shared one source vertex, so index order and vertex-driven order coincided.

Fixture three satisfies all three — `m1` from v9, `m2` from v2, `m3` from v9, inserted in that
order, all tied on `w` — and it is decisive:

```text
                                      WITH the guard        WITHOUT
  … ORDER BY w DESC                   m2 m1 m3  = native    m1 m2 m3   DIVERGE
  … ORDER BY w ASC (inline spelling)  m2 m1 m3  = native    m1 m2 m3   DIVERGE
  … ORDER BY w DESC LIMIT 2           m2 m1     = native    m1 m2      DIFFERENT ROWS
```

The `LIMIT` arm is the sharpest: without the guard it returns different ROWS, not a different
order. **A guard whose first two test fixtures cannot reach it is indistinguishable from a guard
that does nothing**, and two of the three readings came back "AGREE" while proving nothing.

### An unordered divergence item 1038 introduced, disclosed rather than fixed

The same fixture shows it: `MATCH ()-[e:T]->() WHERE e.k = 7 RETURN e.t AS a`, with NO `ORDER BY`,
returns `m1 m2 m3` in TS and `m2 m1 m3` in native. That is item 1038's seeded walk arriving in
index order, and it is permitted — row order without `ORDER BY` is unspecified, the policy is
explicit that this is WON'T-FIX rather than something to sort away, and the fuzzers compare
multisets. Recording it because it is a NEW such difference on this shape and nothing else would
say so.

### Teeth

```text
  unwrap-sorted    (the defect re-introduced)   rc=1  2853 pass  13 fail   caught
  seed-under-sort  (the tie guard removed)      rc=1  2863 pass   3 fail   caught
```

`seed-under-sort` SURVIVED on the first two fixtures and is caught on the third. That is the whole
reason this section exists.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,866 (21 new), gremlin 852, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0. Item 1038's win is intact — proj-inline
0.048, proj-clause 0.038, proj-zero 0.003, CONTROL proj-unindexed 3.597.

Gates after the documents; see the commit.

## Item 1040 — the fuzzer now asks the ORDERED question about a rel-key sort, and item 1039's reason is corrected

INSTRUMENT. No engine change. The differential fuzzer gains one generator band and one counter, and
the band is verified against the real historical bug rather than against a hand-written mutant.

### Item 1039's stated reason was WRONG, and the correction matters

Item 1039 said the fuzzer missed the dropped `ORDER BY` because "the generated hop shapes do not
read the REL variable, so `itemsReadRel` is false and the route is never reached". **That is
false.** `genHopProjection` emits `RETURN {v: e} AS x` and `RETURN CAST([e] AS STRING) AS x`, both
of which read the rel — so the rel-bound route has been generated all along.

The real reason is the other half, which 1039 also gave and which stands on its own: those queries
carry no `ORDER BY`, so they are compared as row MULTISETS, and **a dropped sort is invisible to a
multiset comparison.** The comparison is not the thing to change — an unordered result's order is
genuinely unspecified, and `resultsEqual` is the correct invariant for it. What was missing is a
band that asks the ORDERED question.

Worth separating because the two diagnoses imply different fixes: "the route is never generated"
would mean widening the pattern generator, which was already wide enough.

### The band

```text
  MATCH (n:T)-[e:E]->(b:T) RETURN <e.w | e.w + 1 | n.n | b.n> AS x, n.n AS t
    ORDER BY x[ ASC| DESC], t[ LIMIT 1..3]
```

The sort key is the REL's own property — the position that was broken, where a sort on a NODE key
reached `sorted(...)` through a different return and was always correct. `n.n AS t` last makes the
order TOTAL, which is this file's own rule: without it a tie would flag a non-bug.

### Two self-inflicted nulls the counter caught, and it caught them in that order

`relSort=<generated>/<compared in order>` is printed on every run, and both numbers earned
themselves immediately.

**First: the band could never fire.** Bands are checked in sequence, and the first draft sat AFTER
`if (p < 0.68)`, which already owns every `p` below it. A dead band passes exactly like a working
one. Caught by reading the thresholds before trusting the run — moved ahead of it, taking
`[0.64, 0.655)`.

**Second, and this is the one a reading alone would have missed: `relSort=298/0`.** 298 queries
generated and ZERO compared in order. `totallyOrdered` recognises the sentinel as the literal
substring `n.n AS t`, and the band named its start variable `a`, so it emitted `a.n AS t`, failed
that test, and every one of its 298 queries was compared as a multiset after all — asking exactly
the question that had already missed the bug. Renaming the start variable to `n` gives
`relSort=322/322`.

**A band that generates the right text and is then compared the wrong way is worse than no band,
because it looks like coverage.** The generated-vs-compared pair is what distinguishes them, and
one number alone would have reported 298 and looked healthy.

### Teeth — against the real bug, not a mutant

The band was run against the engine as it stood BEFORE item 1039's fix (`git checkout bfe99880 --
hop-projection.ts`), which is the strongest available test: a mutant is a guess at the defect,
where this is the defect.

```text
  [seed …466517] MATCH (n:T)-[e:E]->(b:T) RETURN e.w + 1 AS x, n.n AS t ORDER BY x ASC, t
      ts:     [{"x":3,…},{"x":10,…},{"x":6,…},{"x":8,…},{"x":2,…}]
      native: [{"x":2,…},{"x":3,…},{"x":6,…},{"x":8,…},{"x":10,…}]
  … and the DESC and plain spellings, four divergences before the report cap
```

Red, with TS in insertion order and native sorted — item 1039 exactly. Restored, the whole suite is
green and `bun run fuzz` is 13/0.

### A near-miss worth recording: `git checkout <sha> -- <path>` STAGES the old version

Reverting the fix for that test left the file `MM` — the INDEX holding the pre-1039 version while
the working tree held the fixed one. A `git commit` from there would have **shipped the wrong
answer back in**, under a commit message about adding fuzzer coverage for it. `git status
--porcelain` showed `MM` rather than ` M`, and `git show :<path>` confirmed the staged copy had
`sortedQuery` zero times against the worktree's one. Cleared with `git reset`.

The general rule: **`git checkout <sha> -- <path>` is not symmetric with a `cp` back.** It writes
the index as well as the tree, so restoring the file by copy leaves the index holding the revert.
Check `git diff --stat <path>` against HEAD is empty before committing, not just that the file
looks right.

### Verification

No engine change: `git diff` against HEAD for `hop-projection.ts` is EMPTY; the only modified file
is the fuzzer. Suites: gql 2,866, native 933 — 0 fail. `bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity
fuzzers 13/0, with `relSort=280/280`.

Gates after the documents; see the commit.
