## Item 1041 — the opt-in edge-type index does NOT rescue the stale-CSR cliff, and that says why item 680's named fix is the right one

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. One probe, two documents. Item 680 diagnosed the stale-CSR penalty
in full and named the fix; this adds the one fact it did not have, and the fact turns out to be the
argument for that fix.

### What reading the code suggests, and what it actually does

`out_typed`/`in_typed` — the opt-in edge-type index, maintained incrementally on every `add_edge`
— have exactly ONE non-test consumer in the engine, `for_each_nbr` at `exec.rs:4417`, under the
comment "the CSR overlay is stale (an adjacency write since the last rebuild); the
incrementally-maintained index still answers." A reader would reasonably conclude that declaring
`createIndex({ on: 'edge', kind: 'type' })` cancels the post-write penalty.

**It does not, for the typed-count shape.** 50,000 nodes, 150,000 edges, 1 in 50 carrying the
queried type, `MATCH ()-[:WANTED]->(b) RETURN count(*)`, median of reps 4+, three rounds:

```text
                                   FRESH                    STALE (after ONE write)
  no index                  0.003  0.004  0.004       0.381  0.351  0.352      ~90x
  edge-type index DECLARED  0.008  0.006  0.007       0.413  0.386  0.392      ~55x
```

The stale column does not improve — 0.386-0.413 against 0.351-0.381, if anything marginally worse,
which is what paying the index's write-side maintenance for no read-side benefit looks like.

**~90x, sharper than item 680's 24.07x, and for an identifiable reason**: this shape is answered
from a LENGTH when fresh (`typed_hop_count_from_size` → `out_typed_flat(t).map(<[_]>::len)`, O(1)),
where item 680's fixture measured a walk. So the cliff here is O(1) degrading to O(E), not 2x
degrading to 24x.

### Why the index cannot help, which is the useful part

`typed_hop_count_from_size` and `try_edge_label_count` both end in `store.out_typed_flat(t)?` — the
`?` DECLINES the whole fast path when the CSR is stale, and neither consults `out_typed`. That
could be wired up, but it would not fix much: **the opt-in index is PER NODE, and the count wants a
GLOBAL per-type total.** Summing `out_typed(node, t).len()` over 50,000 nodes trades 150,000 edge
visits for 50,000 hash lookups — a constant-factor improvement on a question whose fresh answer is
a single `len()`.

That is precisely the shape item 680 named: _"the selective-type scan needs only a GLOBAL per-type
edge list, not the whole CSR — appendable O(1) on `add_edge` … that would make the fresh/stale
distinction vanish for this shape without any rebuild policy. Not costed yet."_ This measurement
turns that from the tidier-looking option into the only one that reaches the O(1) answer, and it
also rules out the cheap alternative of pointing the existing fast paths at the existing index.

### An unexplained observation, labelled as such

Declaring the index costs the FRESH path about 2x — 0.003/0.004/0.004 against 0.006/0.008/0.007,
disjoint across three rounds, though only 3-4 µs absolute on an O(1) path. **It is not staleness**:
`create_edge_type_index` sets a flag, allocates two `U32Map` vectors and calls
`reindex_node_etypes` per node, and touches nothing CSR-related — a structural rule-out, not an
inference from the numbers. The remaining candidate is the 2 × 50,000 maps' memory and cache cost,
which cannot be attributed without a profiler this box does not have. Recorded unattributed rather
than guessed, and it is a reason not to recommend the index as a mitigation even where it does
help.

### Next

Cost the maintenance price of a global per-type edge list, which is the step item 680 left open and
the one this item argues is the only route to keeping the O(1) answer across a write. It needs the
`add_edge` and delete sides measured before it is proposed, not after.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the new probe. Answers identical in all four
arms (3,000), so the arms are the same question.

Gates after the documents; see the commit.

## Item 1042 — after ONE write the TS engine is 168x FASTER than native on a typed count, and TS already holds the fix

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. The ratio runs the wrong way round, which is why it is worth its own
entry: item 573's rule is that a big TS/native ratio may be ALGORITHMIC rather than the layout
ceiling, and this is that rule in reverse.

### The 2x2, both engines, same graph, same query

50,000 nodes, 150,000 edges, 1 in 50 carrying the queried type,
`MATCH ()-[:WANTED]->(b) RETURN count(*)`, median of reps 4+:

```text
  ts     BEFORE a write     0.0019 ms      ts     AFTER a write     0.0021 ms    FLAT
  native BEFORE a write     0.0032 ms      native AFTER a write     0.3523 ms    110x WORSE
```

Both answer 3,000. **After a single unrelated write the TS engine is 168x faster than native on
this shape** (0.0021 against 0.3523), where before the write native is slightly ahead.

### Why — and the TS engine is the existence proof of the fix

- **TS** keeps `edgesByLabel: Map<string, Set<Edge>>`, maintained incrementally: `byLabel.add(edge)`
  on insert, `edgesByLabel.get(label)?.delete(edge)` on removal. So
  `edgesByLabel.get(t)?.size` is an O(1) count that is ALWAYS current — the count comes free from a
  structure the engine keeps anyway, and `buildOneHopCount` reads exactly that.
- **native** keeps a CSR partition (a packed adjacency array with per-node offsets, partitioned by
  edge type) built once at load by `rebuild_csr`. Every adjacency write calls `invalidate_csr`,
  which clears a flag; **nothing re-arms it** (item 680). `typed_hop_count_from_size` then gets
  `None` from `out_typed_flat(t)` and the whole fast path declines, so the query falls to an O(E)
  walk for the rest of the session.

So this is not a layout or constant-factor gap. The two engines answer the same question with
different ALGORITHMS once a write has happened: O(1) against O(E).

### The asymmetry that makes the native fix harder than it looks

TS maintains `edgesByLabel` at exactly two places because it has one insert path and one remove
path. Native has more, and the extra ones are the reason item 680's "maintain a counter" was never
costed: `Undo::RestoreEdge` and `Undo::RestoreNode` push entries back onto `out_adj`/`in_adj`
DIRECTLY rather than through `add_edge` — deliberately, because item 676 measured rebuilding a
touched node's whole map at 1136x the O(1) push. So a maintained integer needs
`add_edge`, `add_edge_with_id`, `delete_edge`, `delete_node`, both restore arms and the load/clear
paths, and a desync in any of them is a WRONG ANSWER rather than a slow one.

That is the trade-off to settle before building, and it is a design question rather than a
measurement one, so it is raised rather than decided here.

### What this does NOT say

It does not say native is slower in general — before the write it is ahead (0.0032 against 0.0019
is TS ahead, but both are microseconds and this shape is TS's best case: an O(1) `Set.size`). It
says the native engine has one shape where a single write costs it two orders of magnitude, and the
TS engine does not have that shape at all.

### Verification

No engine change. Both arms answer 3,000 on every reading, so the two engines are being asked the
same question.

## Item 1043 — Gremlin's edge-index seed fires only at the SOURCE: 550-650x, and TinkerPop says why the fix must be narrow

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. One probe, two documents, and the ordering question settled against a
real TinkerPop console before any code was written.

### The gap

`seedFromIndex` destructures `const [source, ...rest] = plan.steps` and fires only when
`source.kind` is `'V'` or `'E'`. So an edge predicate reached THROUGH A HOP never sees the edge
index: by then the source step is `V`, whose seed consults the VERTEX index. 100,000 `PAID` edges
over 200 vertices, 1,000 distinct amounts (one value = 0.1%), edge hash index declared, median of
reps 4+, three rounds:

```text
  CEILING  E().has(amount, 500).count()                0.028  0.025  0.025 ms
  CEILING  E().hasLabel(PAID).has(amount).count()      0.019  0.017  0.017
  SUBJECT  V().outE(PAID).has(amount).count()         16.145 13.787 14.471
  CONTROL  V().outE(PAID).has(other).count()          15.789 16.315 16.464
```

All four correct (100, 100, 100, 0). **550-650x between two spellings of one question**, and the
SUBJECT overlaps the CONTROL — an unindexed key costs the same, so the declared index is not merely
less effective through the hop, it is unreachable. That is the defect class CLAUDE.md names, and
items 1035/1038 closed its GQL twin.

### Why the fix must be scoped — TinkerPop 3.7.3, not reasoning

The seed would make the hop spelling enumerate the edge index, i.e. `E()`'s order. Whether that is
a deviation is a question about TinkerPop, so it was asked of TinkerPop
(`podman run -i docker.io/tinkerpop/gremlin-console:3.7.3`), on a fixture where edge insertion order
and vertex-driven order deliberately differ (`e1` from c, `e2` from a, `e3` from c, `e4` from b):

```text
  TinkerPop  E()            [e1, e2, e3, e4]      <- edge insertion order
  TinkerPop  V().outE()     [e2, e4, e1, e3]      <- vertex order, then out-edges
  TinkerPop  E().hasLabel   [e1, e2, e3, e4]
  TinkerPop  V().outE(T)    [e2, e4, e1, e3]
```

**The two spellings have DIFFERENT orders in real TinkerPop**, and lenke reproduces both exactly:

```text
  lenke      E()            [e1, e2, e3, e4]
  lenke      V().outE(T)    [e2, e4, e1, e3]
```

So the ordering is something this engine currently gets RIGHT, and a seed applied to an
order-visible result would replace vertex-driven order with `E()` order — introducing a TinkerPop
deviation in exchange for speed. That settles the scope: **the seed may serve only an
order-insensitive terminal**, `count()` being the clear case and the one measured above at 550x.

Worth noting what this cost: one container run, before writing any code. The alternative was
building the general rewrite, having the ordering caught by a test or (worse) not caught, and
retracting it — which is the shape of items 1032 and 1033 in this same session.

### What is NOT established

Whether `V()` must be unfiltered for the rewrite to be sound. `V().hasLabel('Q').outE().has(…)`
does NOT cover every edge, so the seed would have to re-apply the start label per edge — reachable
from `edge.from`, as item 1038's walk does, but unmeasured and unimplemented. The narrow version
(`V()` with no ids and no leading filters, then `outE`, then commuting filters, then an
order-insensitive terminal) is what the number above describes.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the new probe. Answers identical across the
three CEILING/SUBJECT arms (100) and 0 for the unindexed control by construction.

## Item 1044 — the Gremlin edge-hop count now seeds the edge index: 660x, and both spellings converge

SHIPPED. Item 1043 priced the gap at 550-650x and settled its scope against a TinkerPop console
before any code existed. This builds the rung.

### The gap, located exactly

`filteredHopCount` opens with `if (hop.kind !== 'out' && hop.kind !== 'in') return undefined` — it
serves VERTEX hops, where the filter applies to the far vertex. So an EDGE hop followed by edge
filters (`V().outE(T).has(k, v).count()`) matched NO rung in `countShortcut` and fell through to the
general traversal, while `E().hasLabel(T).has(k, v).count()` — the same question, the other spelling
— was seeded by `seedFromIndex` and answered in microseconds.

### The change

`edgeHopSeededCount`, routed before its vertex-hop sibling (disjoint by construction: that one takes
`out`/`in`, this one `outE`/`inE`, so the order is readability rather than precedence).

**SEED OR DECLINE, deliberately.** When no filter offers an indexed seek the rung returns
`undefined` and the existing path takes the query unchanged. So it cannot be slower than today for
any shape, and there is no second scanning implementation to keep in step with the first — which is
what the unindexed CONTROL arm below verifies rather than assumes.

The hop's labels are re-applied per edge (an index bucket is keyed by the property and knows nothing
about the type), and each edge is tested once and counted once — so a multi-label edge matching two
wanted labels is not double-counted, which is why this needs no `multiTypeEdgeCount` guard where
SUMMING buckets (`adjacentCount`) does.

### The measurement

One shape per process, median of reps 4+, three alternated rounds, per-arm
`grep -c edgeHopSeededCount` assertion (0 PRE, 3 POST):

```text
                                      PRE                      POST                  ratio
  SUBJECT  V().outE().has(amount)  15.203 15.709 14.550   0.022 0.025 0.020        ~660x
  CONTROL  V().outE().has(OTHER)   14.092 15.298 14.076   12.600 14.537 17.108     overlapping
  CEILING  E().has(amount)          0.026  0.022  0.027   0.027 0.025 0.024        FLAT
  CEILING  E().hasLabel().has()     0.018  0.014  0.017   0.016 0.018 0.015        FLAT
```

The subject now lands ON the ceiling (0.020-0.025 against 0.022-0.027), so the two spellings of the
question cost the same — which was the point. The unindexed control does not move, because the rung
declines it.

### Semantics, from TinkerPop 3.7.3 rather than derived

Every non-obvious expectation in `edge-hop-seeded-count.test.ts` was read off a real console on a
fixture of 4 `T` edges including a SELF-LOOP plus one `U`:

```text
  E().count() 5            E().hasLabel(T).count() 4      V().outE().count() 5
  V().outE(T).count() 4    V().inE(T).count() 4           V().bothE(T).count() 8
  V().outE(T,U).count() 5
  V().outE(T).has(w,1) 3   V().inE(T).has(w,1) 3          E().hasLabel(T).has(w,1) 3
```

So `outE`/`inE` visit each edge exactly ONCE, the self-loop included — which is what makes the
answer "the number of matching edges" — and `bothE` visits it TWICE. `bothE` is therefore EXCLUDED
from the rung rather than served by it, and the test asserts 6 for the `bothE` spelling against 3
for `outE`, so a rung that ever claimed it would go red.

### Teeth

```text
  claim-bothE             rc=1  867 pass  1 fail   caught
  drop-label-residual     rc=1  863 pass  5 fail   caught
  drop-residual-filters   rc=1  866 pass  2 fail   caught
  widest-candidate        rc=1  866 pass  2 fail   caught (after extraction, below)
  always-removable        rc=0  868 pass  0 fail   SURVIVED — see below
```

`widest-candidate` survived its first run for item 1038's reason — the choice is answer-equivalent,
every candidate's bucket being a SUPERSET with the labels and residuals re-applied after. Extracted
as `beats`, a pure exported function, and unit-tested (four tests: the tie keeps the incumbent, and
an EMPTY bucket beats a non-empty one rather than reading as "no seed"). The mutant then fails 2.

**`always-removable` is answer-equivalent BY CONSTRUCTION, and the reason is worth the line.**
A residual filter can only REMOVE members of the seeded bucket, never add one, and
`seedForPred` maps each predicate to an EXACT bound — `inside` to `{gt, lt}`, `between` to
`{gte, lt}`, `startsWith` to `[prefix, succ(prefix))`. So the bucket already equals the predicate's
match set for same-typed data, and re-testing the winner cannot change the count. The flag is
honoured anyway because it is the index's own contract and `seedFromIndex` honours it, so diverging
would make the two seeds disagree about their own invariant. Labelled rather than left as an
apparent gap in the tests.

### A self-inflicted null, caught by its own assertion

The first mutation run reported `ANCHOR-NOT-UNIQUE mutant=always-removable hits=0 >>> THIS RUN IS A
NULL` — the anchor was written with six spaces of indent where the file has four. That is the guard
doing its job: without it the run would have built unmutated code, passed, and been read as "caught".
A second, separate null happened in the test file: a `python` replace added the `beats` import
against a single-line form that `fmt` had already split across lines, so it silently did nothing and
the tests failed with `beats is not defined`. **Both are the same lesson — every replace needs an
assertion on its hit count**, and the one that had it reported itself while the one that did not
had to be debugged.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,866, gremlin 868 (16 new), native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0.

Gates after the documents; see the commit.

## Item 1045 — the START-FILTERED edge hop is 250-370x off, and a VACUOUS label hid it twice

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Item 1043 recorded "whether `V()` must be UNFILTERED" as not
established; this establishes it, and the way the first two readings went wrong is the more useful
half.

### The shape, and why item 1044's rung does not serve it

`countShortcut` hands each rung `mid[0]`. For `V().hasLabel(Q).outE(T).has(k, v).count()` that is
the `hasLabel`, not the hop, so `edgeHopSeededCount` declines and the query falls through — exactly
as the bare hop did before item 1044. And this is the spelling the realistic people-graph question
takes: `g.V().hasLabel('Person').outE('APPLIED_TO').has('stage', 'offer').count()`.

### Priced

100,000 `PAID` edges over 200 vertices, 1,000 distinct amounts, edge hash index declared, median of
reps 4+:

```text
  CEILING  E().has(amount).count()                     0.022 ms
  CEILING  E().hasLabel(PAID).has(amount).count()      0.014
  SUBJECT  V().outE(PAID).has(amount).count()          0.018   <- item 1044's rung
  CONTROL  V().outE(PAID).has(other).count()          16.551   <- unindexed, declines
  CONTROL  V().hasLabel(P).outE(PAID).has(amount)       0.012   <- VACUOUS label, elided
  OPEN     V().hasLabel(Q).outE(PAID).has(amount)       5.206   <- 250-370x off the ceiling
```

All the indexed arms answer 100.

### THE FIXTURE HID IT, TWICE, AND BOTH WERE MINE

**First:** every vertex in the probe carried label `P`, so `hasLabel('P')` is VACUOUS — elided
before any rung looks at `mid`, leaving exactly the `[outE, has]` shape item 1044 already serves.
The arm read **0.022 ms** and I had written down that there was nothing left to fix. The fixture now
puts `Q` on half the vertices, so `hasLabel('Q')` cannot be elided, and the same arm reads 5.206.

**Second:** in the same edit I wrote the two "open" arms as the SAME traversal, labelling one of
them `[vacuous]` as though it differed. Two arms, one query, and the pair looked like a comparison.

Both are the trap CLAUDE.md names from the other direction: _check the fixture's own statistics, not
just its output_. The vacuous-label arm is kept as a CONTROL precisely because it is the thing that
fooled the first reading — at 0.012 ms it now documents that an elidable label costs nothing, which
is the fact that makes the 5.206 attributable to the label being SELECTIVE rather than to the extra
step.

### The fix, with its soundness argument

Seed on the indexed edge key, then re-apply per edge: the hop's types, the residual filters, and
**the START vertex's label** — `edge.from.labels` for `outE`, `edge.to.labels` for `inE`, since the
constrained endpoint is the one the hop departs from. That is precisely what item 1038's GQL walk
does with `edge.from`, so the device is not new here.

`hasLabel(L1, L2)` keeps a vertex carrying ANY of them, and each edge is still tested once and
counted once, so no bucket is summed and no `multiTypeEdgeCount` guard is needed — the same
reasoning item 1044 records.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe. Every indexed arm answers 100, so
the arms are the same question.

Gates after the documents; see the commit.

## Item 1046 — the START-FILTERED edge hop now seeds too: 320x, and three fixtures were needed to prove it

SHIPPED. Item 1045 priced the shape at 250-370x and specified the fix; this builds it. The teeth
took three tries, and each failure was the fixture rather than the code.

### The change

`edgeHopSeededCount` gains an optional `startLabels`, and a rung peels a leading `hasLabel` from
`[hasLabel, outE/inE, …has]`. Per edge the walk now re-applies the hop's types, the residual
filters, and **the start vertex's label off the edge itself** — `edge.from` for `outE`,
`edge.to` for `inE`. That is item 1038's device: an edge-driven walk gets its endpoints from the
edge, so a constraint on the vertex the hop departs from costs one label test rather than a
vertex-side drive.

Disjoint from `bothFilteredHopCount` and `startFilteredHopCount` by construction — both require
`out`/`in` where this requires `outE`/`inE`.

### Which endpoint, from TinkerPop rather than reasoning

Person->Co (x2), Co->Person, and a Person SELF-LOOP, `w: 1` throughout:

```text
  E(T).has(w,1)                        4
  hasLabel(Person).outE(T).has(w,1)    3      hasLabel(Co).outE(T).has(w,1)   1
  hasLabel(Person).inE(T).has(w,1)     2      hasLabel(Co).inE(T).has(w,1)    2
```

`outE` partitions by the edge's SOURCE (3+1), `inE` by its TARGET (2+2), the self-loop counted once
by each. A separate run established the multi-label case is the union and a leading `has` filters
the start vertices (`has(n,1).outE(T).has(w,1)` = 2, `has(n,2)…` = 1).

### The measurement

One shape per process, median of reps 4+, three alternated rounds, per-arm `grep -c startLabels`
assertion (0 PRE, 4 POST):

```text
  V().hasLabel(Q).outE(PAID).has(amount).count()   5.334 5.468 5.233  →  0.017 0.016 0.017   ~320x
```

Answer 100 throughout. In the same builds every other arm is flat or overlapping: both CEILINGs
0.024-0.027 / 0.017-0.019, item 1044's bare hop 0.021-0.027, the unindexed CONTROL 12.4-16.4, and
the VACUOUS-label control 0.013-0.017.

### Teeth — three fixtures, and the first two proved nothing

```text
  drop-start-label   rc=1  872 pass  4 fail   caught
  wrong-endpoint     rc=1  873 pass  3 fail   caught — only on the THIRD fixture
  peel-any-step      rc=1  875 pass  1 fail   caught — only after a test was added
```

**`wrong-endpoint` survived its first run, and the fixture was why.** The first version had one
`Person -> Co` and one `Co -> Person`, which makes the source-split and the target-split BOTH 3/1 —
so reading `edge.to` where `edge.from` belongs gives the IDENTICAL answers. A test comment of mine
called that pair "the sharpest pair: reading the wrong endpoint swaps these", which was simply
false for that fixture. Two `Person -> Co` against one `Co -> Person` makes the splits 3/1 and 2/2,
and only then does direction show. **Both splits still sum to 4, so the totals prove nothing and
the SHAPE of the split is the whole signal.**

**`peel-any-step` survived because nothing exercised a leading `has`.** The rung peels `mid[0]` as a
label constraint; peeling any leading step instead drops it silently and answers 4 where TinkerPop
answers 2. Reachable, not dead — so it is a missing test, and the console supplied the three
expectations.

**`widen-arity` was retired rather than kept.** `mid.length >= 3` survived mutation because
`hasChain` already refuses an empty rest, so `[hasLabel, outE]` declines inside the rung either way.
Item 1016's rule is that a gate nothing can observe comes out rather than staying untested, so the
guard is now `>= 2` — the real requirement, that `mid[1]` exist.

### The pattern across items 1045 and 1046

Four fixture errors in two items, all mine, every one of them making a broken thing look correct: a
VACUOUS label that got elided (1045), two probe arms written as the same query (1045), a SYMMETRIC
edge layout (1046), and a missing leading-`has` case (1046). Three were caught by a mutant or a
control and one by re-reading. The through-line is CLAUDE.md's rule from the other side: an answer
that is INVARIANT to the property you varied cannot validate the fixture — and a fixture whose
splits coincide is invariant to the thing under test.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,866, gremlin 876 (8 new), native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0.

Gates after the documents; see the commit.

## Item 1047 — the GQL AGGREGATE over an edge key is the third result shape that cannot seed: 270-290x

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Items 1035 and 1038 wired `edgeSeek` into `tallyEdges` (the COUNT
walks) and `relSeekedHopWalk` (the PROJECTION). Grepping the pattern one level on: `edgeSeek` is
referenced in `shortcuts.ts` (its definition) and `hop-projection.ts` (two calls inside the
projection walk) and NOWHERE in the aggregate path — `detectHopAggregate` and
`detectMultiHopAggregate` never see it.

### Priced, three rounds

100,000 `PAID` edges over 200 vertices, 1,000 distinct amounts (one value = 0.1%), edge hash index
declared, median of reps 4+:

```text
  count(*)  — seeded since item 1035        0.034  0.035  0.041 ms   answer 100
  sum(e.amount)                             9.955  9.668 10.804      answer 50000
  count(DISTINCT e.amount)                 25.160                    answer 1
  GROUP BY on the edge key                 27.337                    answer 500
```

**270-290x** between the count form and `sum` of the same question, and ~740x for the GROUP BY.

### The zero-match diagnostic says it is the SCAN, and it also corrects a tempting mis-reading

```text
  sum over an INDEXED key, ZERO matches     9.768  9.415  9.211 ms
  sum over an UNINDEXED key, ZERO matches   5.767  5.596  6.136
  sum over an INDEXED key, 100 matches      9.955  9.668 10.804
```

The indexed-key arm costs **9.2-9.8 ms with nothing to aggregate**. A seeded route would walk an
empty bucket and cost ~nothing, so the index is not reached. And the cost is invariant to the match
count (9.2-9.8 at zero against 9.7-10.8 at 100), which is the signature of a scan rather than of
per-row work.

**The tempting mis-reading, recorded because it is the obvious one:** the indexed zero-match arm
(9.2-9.8) costs 1.6x the unindexed zero-match arm (5.6-6.1), and that gap is NOT about seeding —
both scan. It is the predicate: `e.amount = 99999` tests a property every edge CARRIES, while
`e.other = 500` tests one that is ABSENT, and a null comparison settles sooner. Attributing that
1.6x to the index would have been wrong in a way no timing alone reveals.

### Next

Wire `edgeSeek` into the aggregate path, as items 1035/1038 did for the other two result shapes.
Three sub-shapes to check separately rather than assume: a plain `sum`/`min`/`max`, a
`count(DISTINCT …)`, and a `GROUP BY` on the edge key — the last is the most expensive here and may
want the group map built from the seed rather than filtered into.

An aggregate is order-insensitive, so item 1043's ordering constraint does not bind: unlike the
Gremlin value-returning shapes, there is no TinkerPop order to preserve and no reason to restrict
the route to one terminal.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe. Every arm's answer is the expected
one (100, 50000, 1, 500, 0), so the arms are the same question asked four ways.

## Item 1048 — RETRACTING item 1047: `min`/`max` already seed, `sum` is a DELIBERATE refusal, and the real target is narrower

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Item 1047, one tick old, said the GQL aggregate was "the third
result shape that cannot seed" and headlined `sum(e.amount)` at 270-290x. **Two of its claims are
wrong and the second one would have had me break byte-identity.**

### What re-measurement says

Same fixture, three rounds, median of reps 4+:

```text
  max(e.amount)                            0.073 0.075 0.048 ms   answer 500
  min(e.amount)                            0.044 0.077 0.049       answer 500
  max over an INDEXED key, ZERO matches     0.004 0.004 0.003       answer null
  sum(e.amount)                            9.955 9.668 10.804      answer 50000
  sum over an INDEXED key, ZERO matches     9.768 9.415 9.211
  count(DISTINCT e.amount)                26.447 24.312 25.646      answer 1
```

**`min`/`max` ALREADY SEED**, and the zero-match pair proves it: `max` over an indexed key with
nothing to aggregate costs 0.003-0.004 ms where `sum` over the IDENTICAL predicate costs 9.2-9.8.
Same question, same zero rows, 2,500x apart.

The reason is structural: `detectHopAggregate` delegates to `detectHopProjection` with a SYNTHETIC
projection (`hop-projection.ts:3507/3516/3521`), so item 1038's `relSeekedHopWalk` serves it. The
aggregate path got the edge seed for free when the projection did. Item 1047 grepped for `edgeSeek`
and found it absent from the aggregate code, and concluded the route was absent — **a symbol search
answered a question about reachability, which it cannot do.**

### And `sum` is a DELIBERATE refusal, not a gap

`foldFor` accepts exactly `count`, `min` and `max`, and refuses `distinct || star`. `sum` is not in
that switch, so `foldedAggs` is empty and `detectHopAggregate` declines — and its header says why in
as many words: the walk may be FAR-DRIVEN, so only an ORDER-INDEPENDENT aggregate may ride it, while
"`sum`/`avg` and the two `stddev`s are order-sensitive in the last ulp (float addition is not
associative)". Item 532 priced that rather than guessing it.

**An edge seed reorders too** — index order rather than vertex-creation order, which is item 1046's
whole subject. So seeding `sum` would change which ulp it lands on and break byte-identity against
native, for a shape the engine already refuses on purpose. Item 1047's closing note said "an
aggregate is order-insensitive, so item 1043's ordering constraint does not bind" — that is exactly
backwards for `sum`/`avg`/`stddev`, and acting on it was the next tick's plan.

### The real target, narrowed

```text
  count(DISTINCT e.amount)   26.447 24.312 25.646 ms     against count(*)'s 0.034-0.041
  GROUP BY on the edge key   27.337                       (item 1047's reading)
```

Both genuinely open, both ~700x, and each refused for its own reason:

- `count(DISTINCT …)` — `foldFor` refuses `distinct` because "DISTINCT needs every value", i.e. it
  cannot be a left fold with O(1) state. **That is a refusal about FOLDING, not about seeding.** A
  DISTINCT over a seeded edge set is well-defined and order-independent (it is a Set), so this one
  is reachable without touching the ordering rule.
- `GROUP BY` on the edge key — refused outright by `proj.groupKeys.length !== 0`, so it needs its
  own rung rather than a relaxation of this one.

### Method

**A symbol grep cannot answer "is this route reached".** `edgeSeek` appears nowhere in the aggregate
code and the aggregate nevertheless seeds, because the path runs through a delegation. The
zero-match arm — one extra probe arm — settles reachability directly and would have prevented the
whole wrong item. Item 1037 used exactly that diagnostic, two days of items ago, on this same
question.

And **a documented refusal looks identical to a missing optimization from the outside**: both are
"the fast path declines and the query is slow". Only reading why it declines tells them apart, and
here the reason was a correctness one with a measured item behind it.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe. Every arm answers its expected
value (500, 500, null, 50000, 0, 1).

## Item 1049 — `count(DISTINCT x)` becomes a left fold: 550x, and the route test caught the side door

SHIPPED. Item 1048 narrowed the aggregate target to `count(DISTINCT e.k)` (24-26 ms against
`count(*)`'s 0.034-0.041) and said why it was refused: `foldFor` rejects `distinct` because
"DISTINCT needs every value" — true of an O(1) accumulator — and `stepFolded`'s comment says the
same from the other side, that the array path dedups AFTER its `nonNull` filter so a fold had
nowhere to do it.

### The change

`distinctCountFold`: the accumulator is a `Set<string>` of `valueKey(v)`, `step` adds, `finish`
returns `size`. State is O(distinct) rather than O(1) — the same order the array path already pays
to materialize the group. `foldFor` now returns it for `count` with `distinct`, and keeps refusing
every other distinct aggregate (`sum`/`avg` are order-sensitive in the last ulp whether or not they
dedup, `collect`'s order IS its answer, and the extremums gain nothing from dedup).

**Order-independent, which is the precondition that makes this reachable where `sum` is not**: a
Set's `size` does not depend on insertion order. Item 1048 is where believing otherwise about `sum`
was caught, one tick before it would have shipped.

**ONE DEFINITION OF "DISTINCT", and it is `valueKey`.** The {@link AggFold} contract warns that an
accumulator which does not also drive the array path becomes a second definition that can drift.
The array path's `distinctByValueKey` and this fold both key by `valueKey`, so value-equal
temporals, lists and records collapse identically. What is expressed twice is only "count them" — a
pre-dedup plus `COUNT_FOLD` on one path, a set size on the other — which is the same arithmetic.

### The measurement

One shape per process, median of reps 4+, three alternated rounds, per-arm `grep -c
distinctCountFold` assertion (0 PRE, 3 POST):

```text
  count(DISTINCT e.amount)      25.194 25.197 27.694  →  0.051 0.049 0.043   ~550x
  CONTROL node-distinct          0.021  0.020  0.021  →  0.022 0.023 0.022   FLAT
  CONTROL node count(*)          0.002 ×3            →  0.002 ×3            FLAT
  CONTROL max(e.amount)          0.040  0.047  0.059  →  0.068 0.047 0.041   overlapping
  CONTROL count(*) hop           0.059  0.038  0.037  →  0.036 0.037 0.059   overlapping
  CONTROL projection             0.037  0.036  0.041  →  0.032 0.030 0.032   overlapping
```

### The route test caught a side door, which is what it is for

`routes-fired.test.ts` went red: `MATCH (n:L) RETURN count(DISTINCT n.k)` now compiles
`nodeAggregate` as well as `distinctCount`. Making `foldedAggs` non-empty for a distinct count
opened a rung on a completely different shape — **item 778's hazard verbatim** ("opening one gate
can disqualify another rung, and nothing about the gate being opened reveals it"), and nothing but
that table would have said so.

The route TAKEN is unchanged: `clauses.ts` consults `distinctCount` at 1458 and `nodeAggregate` only
at 1474, so the second one compiles and never runs. Rather than assert that is free, the
`node-distinct` arm above measures it — 0.020-0.021 → 0.022-0.023, a microsecond on a 21 µs shape,
and no route change. The expectation is updated with that reasoning rather than merely widened.

### Teeth — and a survivor that was a ROUTE gap in the covering test

```text
  raw-value-key      rc=1  2870 pass   3 fail   caught — after a test was added
  step-noop          rc=1  2843 pass  30 fail   caught
  finish-plus-one    rc=1  2843 pass  30 fail   caught
  any-distinct-name  rc=1  2862 pass  11 fail   caught
```

**`raw-value-key` survived all 2,866 tests**: dedup by REFERENCE IDENTITY instead of `valueKey`, so
two value-equal temporals stop collapsing — a wrong answer. And `temporal-group-key.test.ts` already
covers exactly that hazard, with a comment saying a mutant collapsing `LocalDate`'s key passed 2,635
tests before it was written. It did not catch this one because it asks through
`MATCH (p:P) RETURN count(DISTINCT p.t)`, which takes the dedicated `distinctCount` route and never
reaches a fold at all.

**A covering test on a different ROUTE to the same-looking question is not coverage.** The GROUPED
spelling (`LET gk = p.g … GROUP BY gk`) is what reaches `stepFolded`;
`distinct-count-fold.test.ts` asks it that way, in both failure directions (equal values must
collapse, distinct values must not), over `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime` and a LIST, plus nulls
excluded, an all-null group counting 0, and numbers against strings in disjoint key spaces.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,873 (7 new), gremlin 876, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0 — the one `stepFolded` names as pinning this
("the DISTINCT differential pins it").

Gates after the documents; see the commit.

## Item 1050 — the GROUP BY is confirmed unseeded (600x), and the reason I keep finding result shapes one at a time is structural

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Two documents and one probe arm.

### Confirmed BEFORE building, which is item 1048's lesson applied

Item 1047 read the GROUP BY once at 27.337 ms. Item 1048 then showed that a slow reading does NOT
establish a missing route — `min`/`max` looked unseeded and were already seeded through a
delegation. So the reachability question was asked directly first:

```text
  GROUP BY on the edge key, 100 matches     25.427 25.215 24.523 ms
  GROUP BY on the edge key, ZERO matches    24.858 26.118 24.491      <- INVARIANT
  count(*) on the same predicate             0.053  0.039  0.039
```

The zero-match arm is **invariant to the match count**, so it is a full scan and the index is
genuinely not reached. ~600x, and this time established rather than inferred.

### Why this is the fifth result shape and not the last

`edgeSeek` lives in the SHORTCUT layer. Tracing where each result shape gets its edges:

| result shape           | seeded?            | how                                                                    |
| ---------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `count(*)`             | ✅ item 1035       | `tallyEdges` calls `edgeSeek`                                          |
| projection             | ✅ item 1038       | `relSeekedHopWalk` calls `edgeSeek`                                    |
| `min`/`max`/percentile | ✅ item 1038, free | `detectHopAggregate` DELEGATES to `detectHopProjection`                |
| `count(DISTINCT …)`    | ✅ item 1049       | `foldFor` gained a fold, which opened the same delegation              |
| `sum`/`avg`/`stddev`   | ❌ by design       | order-sensitive in the last ulp (items 532, 1048)                      |
| `GROUP BY`             | ❌                 | refused by `proj.groupKeys.length !== 0`; falls to the general matcher |

And the general matcher cannot seed at all, structurally: its edge source is
`expand(graph, v, rel)` in `graph-queries.ts`, which takes a **VERTEX** and yields that vertex's
incident edges. It is vertex-driven by construction, so there is nowhere to hand it an edge seed —
an edge-driven source would have to derive the endpoints from each edge instead, which is what
items 1038 and 1046 do inside their own walks.

**So the shape of the work so far is not a coincidence.** Every result shape with its own shortcut
needed its own wiring, and every shape that falls through to the general matcher can never seed,
however selective the predicate. A sixth and seventh shape would behave the same way.

### The choice, which is architectural and therefore raised rather than taken

- **A fourth rung** — a `detectHopGroupAggregate` that seeds, mirroring the three that exist.
  Contained, measurable, and it closes this 600x. It also leaves the next shape to be found the
  same way.
- **An edge-driven source at the PATTERN level** — one place to seed, serving the GROUP BY, the
  general pipeline, and every shape not yet enumerated. Much larger: it changes binding order for
  unordered results (permitted — row order without `ORDER BY` is unspecified, and the differential
  fuzzers compare multisets — but item 1039 is a reminder that "permitted" and "nothing observes
  it" are different claims), and the order rule from items 532/1048 means an order-SENSITIVE
  aggregate must still refuse it.

The second is the one that stops this recurring, and it is a change to the matcher rather than an
addition beside it. Raised with the user rather than decided here, alongside item 1042's open CSR
question.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the probe. The zero-match arm answers `none`
(no groups) and the 100-match arm answers its group key, so the pair is the same question at two
selectivities.

## Item 1051 — the Rust spelling probe compared 15 of 38 groups; now 20. And my first verification of that was invalid

INSTRUMENT. No engine change. The Rust engine is CLEAN on every newly-visible group — the value here
is in the instrument, and in a self-check that refuted my own explanation.

### What was wrong with the instrument

`spelling_probe` is the Rust half of the repo's named defect class: for each group of queries that
must be equivalent it compares the canonicalized plan and the measured time. Run as it stood:
**38 groups, 8 of them reporting "all variants below the timer's resolution — no cost to compare",
15 compared on cost.** So a fifth of the instrument built to catch equivalent-spelling cliffs was
permanently unable to see one, and there was no way to change that: the fixture was hardcoded
`fixture(100_000, 5)` with no env knob, where the TS twin has had `SPELL_N`/`SPELL_REPS` all along.

### Three changes, and only one of them is the one that mattered

- **`SPELL_N` / `SPELL_DEG` knobs**, defaults unchanged so every recorded figure stays comparable.
  **They do not fix the blind groups**: raising `SPELL_N` from 100,000 to 1,000,000 left all eight
  blind, which is the answer rather than a disappointment — those queries are answered in CONSTANT
  time (a bucket size, an index point lookup), so no fixture size makes a single run resolvable.
- **Batch timing below `RESOLVE_FLOOR_MS`**: re-time 1,000 runs and divide, printed at six decimals
  with a `b` marker. It fires on 20 lines and turns `0.000ms` into real figures — `0.000322 ms` for
  `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN count(*)`, `0.000259` for `g.V('12345').values('age')`.
- **Replacing the blanket `tmax < 0.001` floor** with a rule that refuses only a group whose
  variants were measured by DIFFERENT estimators. **This is the change that does the work**: 8 blind
  groups → 0, and 15 compared → 20.

Result: `blind=0 mixed=0 compared=20`, and `NO PERF CLIFFS` still — so the engine genuinely
converges on the five groups that had never been checked.

### 🛑 MY FIRST TEETH CHECK WAS INVALID, AND THE SECOND REFUTED MY EXPLANATION

I claimed the batching was what made the eight groups comparable. The causal check — set
`RESOLVE_FLOOR_MS = 0.0` so nothing is ever batched, and expect the eight to go blind again —
reported `blind=0 mixed=0 compared=20`, **identical to the shipping build**.

Because I had DELETED the `println!` that says "below the timer's resolution" when I replaced the
floor. `grep -c 'below the timer'` was counting a string that no longer exists in the program. **The
8 → 0 I had written down was measuring the removal of a log line, not an improvement in
resolution.**

So the claim was re-tested properly, on the only thing that matters — whether the RATIOS are stable
— three runs per arm, all 20 ratios per run:

```text
  batched    1.01 1.01 1.22 1.28 1.00 1.08 1.06 1.34 1.31 1.00 1.00 1.00 1.18 1.18 1.24 1.25 1.27 …
  unbatched  1.00 1.01 1.26 1.17 1.00 1.00 1.04 1.25 1.27 1.00 1.00 1.01 1.18 1.18 1.23 1.21 1.26 …
```

**Indistinguishable, and stable across runs in both arms.** So the honest statement is narrower than
the one I was about to make: batching makes the fast groups' figures READABLE and auditable
(0.000322 rather than 0.000), and it does NOT change a single verdict or ratio. The hypothesis that
sub-microsecond readings were too noisy to compare on this box is **not established** — the floor's
original 1.57x false cliff is a documented historical fact, but it did not reproduce in six runs
here.

### What that leaves honestly unproven

- The **mixed-estimator guard** has never been observed to fire: `mixed=0` in the shipping build and
  also at a deliberately splitting `RESOLVE_FLOOR_MS = 0.06`, because no group's variants straddle
  either floor. It is kept because it guards a real hazard — `min`-of-7 is an optimistic estimator
  and a batch average is not, so one of each in a ratio biases toward the batched side — but by this
  repo's own standard an unobservable gate is a liability, so it is flagged here rather than left to
  look verified.
- Removing the floor could in principle re-expose the 1.57x false positive it was added for. Six
  runs show a maximum ratio of 1.34 at the same positions every time, which is evidence and not a
  proof.

### Verification

`cargo clippy --release --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0. No engine change: the only modified file is
the example. Probe output: `blind=0 mixed=0 compared=20`, `NO PERF CLIFFS`.

```text
  IN list vs OR chain, 33 terms (past the 32 gate)               1.28    1.37      1.34
  range AND (two spellings of 30<=age<40)                        1.01    1.00      1.01
  negative literal (four spellings of "every row")               1.00    1.00      1.00
  negative literal on a traversal frontier                       1.01    1.00      1.02
  far-side predicate: forwards vs backwards                      1.18    1.29      1.19
  seed-side predicate with BOTH ends labelled                    1.18    1.28      1.19
  1-hop projection: GQL vs Gremlin                               1.26    1.43      1.47
  one-hop count: GQL vs Gremlin                                  1.30    1.29      1.27
  one-hop count, start unlabelled: GQL vs Gremlin                1.34    1.27      1.26
  filtered count: GQL vs Gremlin                                 1.04    1.07      1.08
  point lookup by property equality: GQL vs Gremlin              1.23    1.30      1.19
  ordered top-k: GQL LIMIT vs Gremlin range                      1.30    1.28      1.26
```

**No group grows.** Every ratio sits between 1.00 and 1.47 across a 10x change in node count and a
5x change in degree, and no group's ratio moves by 1.5x between configurations. `NO PERF CLIFFS` at
all three.

### What this does and does not establish

It establishes that the Rust engine's equivalent spellings converge at three points in the size ×
degree plane, including the FIVE groups that were never comparable before item 1051 removed the
blanket timer floor. Previously the same claim rested on one configuration with a fifth of the
groups unmeasured.

It does not establish that no cliff exists anywhere — three points are three points, and the degree
axis in particular was swept once. The honest form of the claim is the one above: at these
configurations, with these groups, nothing diverges.

### The one thing with a trend worth naming

`1-hop projection: GQL vs Gremlin` reads 1.26 → 1.43 → 1.47, the only group that moves consistently
upward on both axes. It is well inside the probe's tolerance and well short of the 1.5x I flagged
on, so it is not a finding — but it is the single most likely place for one to appear if the sweep is
ever widened, and it is recorded so a later run has something to compare against rather than
starting from scratch.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the documents. Probe reports `NO PERF CLIFFS`
at 100k d5, 1M d5 and 100k d25, with `blind=0 mixed=0 compared=20` at each.

## Item 1053 — the TS spelling probe can now see the edge-seed routes, and the new group catches a 2229x single-spelling break

INSTRUMENT. No engine change. Item 1035 recorded that `spelling-probe.ts` "CANNOT SEE the edge-seed
route" and deferred it because adding a selective key to a SHARED fixture risked every group's
numbers. Since then this session shipped FIVE routes that make an edge index reachable — items 1035
(GQL count), 1038 (GQL projection), 1044 (Gremlin edge hop), 1046 (start-filtered Gremlin hop) and
1049 (`count(DISTINCT)`) — with no coverage at all in the instrument whose entire purpose is to
catch one spelling reaching an index while its twin does not. All five were verified by hand, one at
a time.

### The fixture worry was avoidable

A NEW property `ew = e % 1000` alongside the existing `w = e % 5`, and a hash index on **`ew`
alone**. Every existing group keys on `w` — a fifth of the edges, which `edgeSeek`'s margin
correctly refuses — so those groups keep scanning exactly as they did and every figure recorded
against them stays comparable. The `indexed EDGE keys:` line is printed next to the vertex one, for
item 576's reason: a seek group that silently measures a SCAN looks fine.

### The groups, and what they measure

Two groups over `ew`, each with the clause and inline spellings, because "one spelling seeds and its
twin scans" is the precise defect and items 1031/1038 priced that gap at 100-190x. Measured at
`SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9 SPELL_FLOOR=0.005`, three runs:

```text
  count, three spellings        0.08  0.10  0.10 ms      (run 2: 0.08 0.09 0.10)
  projection, two spellings     0.09  0.11              (stable across runs)
  the UNINDEXED `w` group       241-244 ms               <- the scan, for contrast
```

All spellings converge within 1.25x, and the seeded route is ~2,400x the unindexed one — so the
probe now distinguishes the two and shows each one's spellings agreeing.

### ⚠️ They were invisible at first, which is the Rust twin's lesson arriving on time

Both groups initially reported "too fast, not compared": the TS probe's `FLOOR_MS` is 1 ms and the
seeded route is 0.08-0.11. **A group below the floor guards nothing**, which is exactly what item
1051 found in the Rust probe one tick earlier. `SPELL_FLOOR` already exists as an env knob, and
these readings are tens of microseconds — well above this timer's resolution, unlike the Rust
probe's nanosecond case — so lowering the floor is sufficient and no batching is needed.

The probe's own advice was also wrong for this class and is corrected: it said "raise `SPELL_N` to
measure them", but raising the fixture raises the match count proportionally and a seeded route stays
fast. Item 1051 established that empirically on the Rust twin — 10x the fixture left all eight blind
groups blind — so the message now names `SPELL_FLOOR` for a group that is fast because it SEEKS.

### Teeth — and the mutant reaches ONE of the two guards, not both

A group that is present but cannot flag anything is the failure this repo keeps recording, so the
seed was broken for ONE spelling only: `edgeSeek`'s `relLifted?.props` loop, which item 1038 added to
serve the inline form.

```text
  projection group   0.09 ms  vs  202.07 ms   ⚠ FLAGGED at 2229.7x
  count group        0.08 / 0.10 / 0.10       no flag
```

**The projection group works**: one spelling lost the seed, its twin kept it, and the probe reported
2229.7x — a regression that would otherwise have needed hand-verification to notice.

**The count group correctly did NOT flag, and the reason is worth recording rather than reading as a
gap.** The count path calls `edgeSeek(graph, scan.inRel, scan.pred.relLifted, …)`, so its inline
spelling is served by the `inRel?.pred.props` loop — a DIFFERENT loop from the `relLifted?.props` one
this mutant removed, which exists for the projection path's bare `CPredicate`. So this single mutant
reaches one of the two guards. The count group's teeth are not established by this run, and saying
otherwise would be the "a covering test on a different route is not coverage" error of item 1049.

### Verification

Suites: gql 2,873, gremlin 876, native 933 — 0 fail (the probe is not in a suite; this confirms the
mutant was fully restored). `git status --porcelain` shows only `spelling-probe.ts`. Probe at the

## Item 1054 — a REAL cross-engine divergence surfaced in CI: deterministic repro, and four hypotheses refuted

OPEN WRONG ANSWER. No engine change yet. Item 1052's CI went red on the differential fuzzer with a
random seed, which is the fuzzer doing its job — this is a genuine byte-identity divergence, not
flake.

### The repro, which is deterministic

```text
  FUZZ_SEED=3076589914 bun test src/differential-fuzz.test.ts

  [seed 3076599143772567]
  MATCH (n:T) ORDER BY (-0.0 < cot((-1.0 * 0.0))) DESC, n.n OFFSET 1
  RETURN ((-0.0 <> cot(0.0)) + (n.nu * n.nan)) AS x, n.n AS t

    ts:     err E_INVALID_VALUE
    native: ok [{"x":null,"t":5},{"x":null,"t":7},{"x":null,"t":11},{"x":null,"t":13},{"x":null,"t":17}]
```

Reproduced locally outside CI, so it is a property of the engines and not of the runner.

**Native returns five rows with `x: null`; TS raises.** Which engine is right is a conformance
question — null propagating through arithmetic says native, and an eager operand type-check says TS
— and `divergence-registry.ts` deliberately does NOT excuse it: its declared
boolean-context/dynamic-operand residual is narrow, "an `E_INVALID_VALUE` against an EMPTY result,
never against rows", and here native returns rows. The registry refusing to cover this is the
registry working.

### FOUR hypotheses, each tested and REFUTED

Recorded because each looked right and the narrowing is what the next attempt starts from:

1. **`boolean + number` is rejected by one engine only.** No — `(1 < 2) + 1` raises on BOTH.
2. **The comparison evaluates to null, so it is really `null + null`.** No —
   `-0.0 <> cot(0.0)` is `true` on both engines (`cot(0.0)` is null, and `<>` against null gives…
   `true` here, which is itself worth a second look).
3. **`boolean + null` diverges on operand eagerness.** No — `(1 < 2) + null`, `null + (1 < 2)`,
   `(1 < 2) + n.missing`, `(1 < 2) * null` and `(1 < 2) - null` all return `null` on both.
4. **An `ORDER BY` whose sort key is a BOOLEAN, or one that evaluates to null.** No —
   `ORDER BY (1 < 2) DESC, n.n`, the `cot` form, and the same with `OFFSET 1` all agree.

Also established: **`nan` is not a property of the fixture at all** (`grep -c '"nan"'` is 0), so
`n.nan` is an absent key and therefore null; `nu` is 5, 9 or null. So the right-hand operand is
`5 * null` or `null * null`, both of which agree in isolation.

So the divergence needs something the reductions dropped — most likely the fixture's full row set
interacting with `OFFSET 1`, or an interaction between the statement-position `ORDER BY`/`OFFSET`
and the projection. **The next attempt should bisect by removing one CLAUSE at a time from the
original query against the original fuzz fixture**, rather than rebuilding a minimal fixture, which
is what each refuted hypothesis above did.

### Why it surfaced now

The fuzzer draws RANDOM seeds in CI, so a latent divergence appears whenever its seed is drawn. Item
1040 added a generator band, which shifts every subsequent draw — so the sampled population changed
and may have surfaced this sooner. That does not create a divergence: the query and fixture are
deterministic and both engines disagree on them outside CI. Recorded so the two facts are not
conflated.

### Status

**Main is intermittently red until this is fixed**, which is the correct state for a byte-identity
divergence rather than something to silence. It must not be added to the registry to make CI green:
the registry's own rule is that a VALUE difference is refused whatever the list says, and native
returning rows against a TS error is exactly that.

## Item 1055 — item 1054 DIAGNOSED: a statement-position OFFSET must skip rows BEFORE the projection, and TS evaluates it anyway

DIAGNOSIS, no engine change yet. Item 1054 recorded the divergence with four refuted hypotheses and
said the next attempt should bisect by CLAUSE against the ORIGINAL fuzz fixture. That is what this
did, and it localized the bug exactly.

### The missing piece was the fixture, not the query

The first bisect built the fixture from the fuzzer's NDJSON and **the full query AGREED** — which was
the clue. The fuzzer runs two statements before fuzzing:

```text
  MATCH (n:T) WHERE n.n = 3 SET n.nan = sin(1e400) RETURN count(*) AS c
  MATCH (n:T) WHERE n.n = 7 SET n.nan = ln(-1)     RETURN count(*) AS c
```

A **stored NaN**, which its own comment explains cannot come from NDJSON: "ingest coerces NaN and
the infinities to null, so the only way to get one into a property is to COMPUTE it with `SET`". So
`n.nan` is not an absent key at all — item 1054's `grep -c '"nan"'` was right about the file and
wrong about the graph.

### The mechanism

Only node `n = 3` carries BOTH `nu = 5` and a stored NaN, so only that row makes
`(-0.0 <> cot(0.0)) + (n.nu * n.nan)` fail: `5 * NaN` is NaN, and `true + NaN` is not valid
arithmetic. Node `n = 7` also has the NaN but `nu` is null, so `null * NaN` is null and
`true + null` is null — no error. **The whole divergence rests on one row.**

`ORDER BY … DESC, n.n OFFSET 1` sorts on a key that is null for every row, so the `n.n` tiebreak
orders ascending and `OFFSET 1` drops exactly `n = 3` — the only faulting row.

```text
                                                      ts        native
  STATEMENT position, OFFSET 1 drops the row        raises     5 rows     ← DIVERGES
  CLAUSE position (projection first)                raises     raises
  STATEMENT, OFFSET 0 (keeps the row)               raises     raises
  STATEMENT, no OFFSET                              raises     raises
  STATEMENT, OFFSET 1, the faulting node ALONE      raises     []         ← DIVERGES, minimal
```

**The rule the engines disagree about: a statement-position `OFFSET` must skip rows BEFORE the
`RETURN` projection is evaluated.** Native does; TS evaluates the projection for rows the offset
has already discarded, and so raises on a row that is not in the result.

Every arm that keeps the faulting row agrees, and the CLAUSE-position form agrees — correctly, since
there the projection genuinely precedes the paging. The one-row case is the sharpest statement of it:
`MATCH (n:T) WHERE n.n = 3 ORDER BY … OFFSET 1 RETURN <faulting expr> AS x` returns `[]` in native
and raises in TS.

### Which engine is right

Native. In ISO GQL an `ORDER BY … OFFSET` in STATEMENT position is an ordering-and-paging statement
that transforms the binding table, and the following `RETURN` projects whatever survives it. A row
that was skipped cannot contribute a value, and therefore cannot contribute an error either. This is
the same class as the recorded "faulting PER-REP predicate" divergence — TS evaluating eagerly where
native does not — but here the ISO ordering of the two statements settles it rather than leaving it
a judgment call.

### What this also corrects

Item 1054 listed "`nan` is not a property of the fixture at all" as established. It is not: the
property exists, created by `SET` at runtime. The grep was over the FILE, and the fixture is the
file PLUS two setup statements. **A fixture is what the code builds, not what the literal says** —
which is why the first bisect's "AGREE" on the full query was information rather than a dead end.

### Next

Make the TS statement-position paging skip rows before the projection is evaluated. The CLAUSE-position
path is already correct and is the control: it must keep raising. The one-row query above is the
regression test, and `FUZZ_SEED=3076589914` is the integration check.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the documents. Every arm above was run against
the original fuzz fixture WITH its two `SET` statements applied.

## Item 1056 — the divergence FIXED: `foldPageIntoReturn` must refuse when the page drops rows and the projection can fault

FIXED. Item 1055 diagnosed it; this confirms the mechanism by experiment and lands the narrow fix.

### The cause, confirmed rather than inferred

`foldPageIntoReturn` (item 969) rewrites `MATCH … ORDER BY k OFFSET n RETURN items` into
`MATCH … RETURN items ORDER BY k OFFSET n`, and its own justification is that "a row-wise
projection preserves row identity", so sorting-then-projecting and projecting-then-sorting give the
same ordered rows. **True of the ORDER, and not of FAULTS.** When the page DROPS rows, the unfolded
form evaluates the projection only for survivors; the folded form evaluates it for every row and
pages afterwards, so a row the `OFFSET` discarded can raise.

Its refusal list already covered aggregation, an existing page, alias shadowing, `RETURN *` and
non-adjacency — every one of them a wrong-ANSWER refusal. This is another, and it was missing.

**Confirmed by disabling the fold**, which turned all three real divergences into agreement:

```text
                                                   fold ON    fold OFF
  FULL (the fuzzer's query)                        DIVERGE     AGREE
  STATEMENT, OFFSET 1 drops the faulting row       DIVERGE     AGREE
  STATEMENT, OFFSET 1, the faulting node ALONE     DIVERGE     AGREE
```

(The three remaining "DIVERGE" rows in that table are the recorded error-MESSAGE-TEXT difference,
where both engines raise.)

### The fix, narrow on BOTH conditions

```ts
if (
  (page.skip !== undefined || page.limit !== undefined) &&
  !proj.items.every((it) => cannotFault(it.expr))
)
  return clauses;
```

`cannotFault` is a WHITELIST of three kinds — `lit`, `var`, `prop` — deliberately, so a kind added
later is assumed to fault: that refuses a fold which might have been sound rather than admitting one
that is not.

Both conditions matter. With no `skip`/`limit` no row is dropped, so the two forms fault
identically and the fold stays. And item 969's measured case projects a plain property read, which
cannot fault, so **the 3.72x survives** — verified rather than asserted:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10 RETURN n.k AS c        13.86 ms   <- still folds
  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10        13.05      (1.06x, as item 969 had it)
  MATCH (n:P) ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10 RETURN n.k + 1 AS c    52.36      <- now REFUSED
  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10      36.01
```

### The cost, stated plainly

**A statement-position page over an ARITHMETIC projection now pays 1.45x** (52.36 against the clause
form's 36.01) because it no longer folds. That is the price of the fix and it is real. It buys a
query that returned a spurious error returning rows instead, which is not a trade worth agonising
over — but it is a cost, not a free win, and the shape that pays it is named here so a later reader
does not rediscover it as a regression.

### Teeth

```text
  no-refusal          rc=1  2878 pass  2 fail   caught — the original bug
  limit-only          rc=1  2878 pass  2 fail   caught — the OFFSET half returns
  arith-cannot-fault  rc=1  2878 pass  2 fail   caught — the whitelist leaking
  always-refuse       rc=0  2880 pass  0 fail   SURVIVED — answer-equivalent
```

`always-refuse` (refuse the fold unconditionally) is CORRECT and only loses speed, so no
result-based test can see it — `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`, and the perf table above is what
guards it. The first run of `arith-cannot-fault` was a NULL (`ANCHOR-NOT-UNIQUE … hits=0`, the
anchor written against a pre-`fmt` line shape) and is re-run above; the guard reporting itself is
why that is visible rather than a silent pass.

`page-fold-fault.test.ts` carries seven tests: the minimal repro (`OFFSET 1` past the only faulting
row answers `[]`), the survivors' values, a `LIMIT` form that excludes the faulting row, and four
CONTROLS that must keep raising — `OFFSET 0`, no page, CLAUSE position, and the fold still applying
to a non-faulting projection. The CLAUSE-position control is the one a too-broad fix would have
broken: there the projection genuinely precedes the paging, so raising is correct and native agrees.

### Verification

`FUZZ_SEED=3076589914`: **1 pass, 0 fail** — the seed that was red. Suites: core 370, gql 2,880
(7 new), gremlin 876, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail. `bun run fuzz`: all seven
byte-identity fuzzers 13/0.

Gates after the documents; see the commit.

## Item 1057 — item 1056's bug class is BOUNDED: eight sibling rewrites tested, all clean

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. A targeted negative result.

Item 1056 fixed a rewrite whose justification ("a row-wise projection preserves row identity") held
for the ORDER and not for FAULTS. The obvious question is whether its siblings share the hazard —
any rewrite that changes WHICH rows are evaluated, or WHETHER an expression is evaluated at all, can
turn a raising query into a succeeding one or the reverse. `executor.ts` has seven others:
`dropVacuousPage`, `dropVacuousQuantifier`, `dropUnreadGroupBinds`, `liftStartProps`,
`pushWhereIntoNode`, `pushWhereAcrossPatterns` and `foldedGroupView`.

### All clean, against native, on a fixture built to fault

Two nodes where only `n = 0` can fault (`nu = 5` AND a stored NaN; the other has `nu` null), two
edges, and the same faulting projection `(1 < 2) + (n.nu * n.nan)` throughout:

```text
  dropUnreadGroupBinds        — an unread LET whose expr faults   both raise
    …and one that IS read                                          both raise
  dropVacuousPage  OFFSET 0   — a page that drops nothing          both raise
  dropVacuousQuantifier       — `->{1,1}` elided to a plain hop    both raise
  pushWhereIntoNode           — a WHERE gating earlier             both ok [{"x":null}]
  quantifier + page                                                both ok
  liftStartProps              — an inline start property           both ok
  hop + page drops faulting                                        both ok
  CONTROL the fixed page fold                                      both ok
```

Nine arms, nine agreements. **`dropUnreadGroupBinds` was the one I most expected to fail** — dropping
a `LET` nobody reads would make a faulting query succeed — and both engines raise, so the bind is
not elided in a fault-visible way.

### 🛑 The quantifier arm proved NOTHING on the first run

The first fixture had **no edges**, so `MATCH (n:T)-[:E]->{1,1}(m)` returned `[]` on both engines
without ever reaching the projection — and printed `AGREE`. Adding two edges turned it into "both
raise", which is a real agreement.

That is **the third fixture of this session that could not reach the code under test and read as a
clean result** — after item 1045's vacuous label and item 1046's symmetric edge layout. The pattern
is consistent enough to state as a rule: **when an arm agrees, check that it EXECUTED the thing
being compared**, because an arm that returns empty agrees with everything.

### What this establishes, and what it does not

It establishes that the fault-order hazard does not appear at eight other rewrite sites on these
shapes. It does not prove them sound in general — one faulting expression, one fixture, nine queries
— and a rewrite not on that list, or a shape not among those nine, is untested. The value is
narrower and real: item 1056 was a single-site bug, not the first instance of a systemic one, so the
next reader of that refusal list does not have to wonder.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the documents. Every arm ran against both
engines with the stored NaN applied to both.

## Item 1058 — REFUTED: sorting on an output ALIAS does not refuse the top-k. The gap is the KEY's cost

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. A hypothesis formed from reading the code and refuted by measuring
it.

### The hypothesis

The top-k path (`ORDER BY … LIMIT n` keeping only the top-k INPUT bindings) is gated on
`!proj.orderNeedsOutput`. So `RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10` — sorting on an OUTPUT alias
— looked like it must refuse the top-k that `ORDER BY n.k + 1 LIMIT 10` reaches, making two
spellings of one question diverge. That is this repo's named defect class, so it looked like a
target.

### Refuted

200,000 nodes, median of the warm reps of 9:

```text
  input key, plain          MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10          11.00 ms
  ALIAS key, plain          MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10             8.39
  input key, arithmetic     … RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY n.k + 1 LIMIT 10            36.88
  ALIAS key, arithmetic     … RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10                  35.44
  CONTROL no LIMIT          … RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY n.k                             25.75
  CONTROL alias, no LIMIT   … RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c                               25.39
```

**The spellings CONVERGE.** The alias form is not slower — it is marginally FASTER in both pairs
(8.39 against 11.00; 35.44 against 36.88). So `orderNeedsOutput` is not refusing these, and there is
no spelling gap here. The two controls confirm the instrument: with no `LIMIT` there is no top-k to
win or lose and both spellings land together at ~25.5 ms.

### What the numbers actually say

The discriminator is not the SPELLING, it is the sort KEY's cost: a plain property key takes the
top-k to 8-11 ms, an arithmetic key to 35-37 ms, both spellings alike — **about 3.3x**. And both
beat the no-LIMIT control only in the plain case: the arithmetic top-k at 35-37 ms is SLOWER than
sorting all 200,000 rows on a plain key (25.75).

That is a legitimate separate target — the key is evaluated per row inside the heap, so an
arithmetic key pays its closure 200,000 times — but it is a cost question, not the equivalent-
spelling defect I went looking for, and it is recorded as such rather than renamed to fit.

### Why the hypothesis was wrong

Reading `orderNeedsOutput`'s gate told me what the flag means, not when it is SET. An alias whose
defining expression reads only the input evidently does not count as "needs output" — which is the
right behaviour and is presumably why someone implemented it that way. **A gate's existence is not
evidence that it fires**, which is the same mistake as item 1048's (a symbol grep answering a
reachability question), one day apart.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the documents.

## Item 1059 — `FUZZ_ITERATIONS`, and 150,000 queries clean: there is no backlog of latent divergences

INSTRUMENT. No engine change. Prompted by a fair question — why has CI failed, and are the checks
being run before pushing?

### The honest accounting first

**Two failures in 39 completed runs**, with opposite causes:

- **`40609792604` (item 1034) — a process error of mine.** `oxfmt --check` rejected a long line in
  `CLOSED.md`, because the gates ran BEFORE the audit entry and `CLOSED.md` lines were appended, so
  the formatter never saw them. Everything else in that run was green. Diagnosed at item 1035 and
  the order changed to gates-AFTER-the-documents; it has not recurred in the ~20 pushes since.
- **`40625821878` (item 1052) — not a skipped check.** The differential fuzzer, drawing a RANDOM
  seed, generated a query no local run had. All seven fuzzers, all five suites and all four gates
  DO run before every push — but a 20,000-query sample with a fresh seed makes "local green" and
  "CI green" different claims. It found a genuine pre-existing wrong answer, fixed at item 1056.

### The knob

`ITERATIONS` was hardcoded at 20,000, so a deeper pre-push sweep was not expressible. It is now
`FUZZ_ITERATIONS`, **default unchanged**, so CI and every recorded figure stay as they were.

**UPWARD ONLY**, and the comment says so, because two readings in this item were nearly reported as
findings and were not:

- `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=500` reports `0 pass 1 fail` — on the COVERAGE FLOORS (`pageGenerated > 200` and
  a dozen more), which are calibrated for the default. 500 queries cannot exercise twenty bands.
  **Not a divergence.**
- `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=500000` also fails — it **TIMED OUT** at bun's 30 s per-test limit, after
  generating 118,190 predicates. **Also not a divergence**, and it had already exercised the one
  declared divergence three times with nothing undeclared.

Both are the same lesson as item 1051's deleted log line: **a red test is not automatically the
thing you are hunting.** Read the diff before concluding.

### The result that answers the question

```text
  FUZZ_ITERATIONS=150000   →   1 pass, 0 fail
  DECLARED static-bool-check-misses-inline-pattern-predicates=4
```

**7.5x the default depth, clean**, with only the single declared divergence used and nothing
undeclared. So after item 1056's fix there is no queue of latent divergences waiting to redden CI
one seed at a time — which is evidence rather than a reassurance, and it is the useful form of an
answer to "why is CI failing".

### What is still true, and not promised away

A random fuzzer will find things again, and that is what it is for: item 1052's failure was the
system working, not the process failing. What changed here is that a deliberate deeper sweep is now
one env var, so the next time a push is worth extra confidence it can have it. Whether CI should
also pin a fixed seed SET alongside its random one — making regressions deterministic while new
discoveries still happen — is a policy question raised with the user rather than decided here.

### Verification

Suites: gql 2,880, native 933 — 0 fail. `bun run fuzz` at the DEFAULT depth: all seven
byte-identity fuzzers 13/0, confirming the knob changed nothing for the standard run.
