## Item 1060 — the top-k's 3x is a ROUTE BOUNDARY at "the projection is a bare property read", and my prediction was wrong

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Item 1058 found that a top-10 costs 8-11 ms with a plain sort key and
35-37 with an arithmetic one, and recorded it as a cost question. This locates the cost, and it is
not where I said it was.

### The 2x2, which refuted the prediction

The top-k path's own comment says "only the top-k INPUT bindings are kept and just those are
projected", so I predicted an arithmetic PROJECTION would be invisible — ten evaluations — and the
whole gap would be the KEY, evaluated 200,000 times. 200,000 nodes, median of the warm reps of 9:

```text
  plain key,  plain proj     14.18 ms
  ARITH key,  plain proj     36.53
  plain key,  ARITH proj     32.52     ← predicted ~14
  ARITH key,  ARITH proj     34.15
  CONTROL no sort, plain      0.03     (no key evaluated, LIMIT is lazy)
  CONTROL no sort, arith      0.01
```

An arithmetic projection costs 32.52 ms **with a plain key**. So either the projection runs per row
after all, or something else decides the route.

### Which — settled by scaling the projection's own cost

Key PLAIN throughout, only the projection's arithmetic widened:

```text
  proj: n.k                                      11.30 ms
  proj: n.k + 1                                  34.11
  proj: n.k + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6              33.07
  proj: n.k + 1 + … + 12  (12x the arithmetic)   33.22
```

**FLAT.** Twelve additions cost what one does. So the projection is NOT running per row — the top-k
is working exactly as documented, keeping and projecting ten rows. What the 11.30 → 34 step is, is a
**ROUTE BOUNDARY**: a bare property read takes one route, ANYTHING else takes a ~3x slower one, and
the expression's complexity is irrelevant once you are on the slow side.

That is a far better target than "arithmetic keys are expensive", which is what item 1058 left and
what I set out to confirm. The cost is a cliff, not a slope.

### The route is NOT identified yet, and one candidate is ruled out

`plainRowProjection` is the obvious suspect and it is **not** this: it refuses any `ORDER BY`
(`(proj.orderBy?.length ?? 0) === 0`), so the shape under test never reaches it. The route that the
plain-property form takes and the arithmetic form does not is still unlocated — named here as the
next step rather than guessed at, because item 1058's wrong hypothesis came from reading a gate and
inferring when it fires.

### Method

**A prediction stated before the measurement is what makes the measurement worth running.** I
predicted ~14 for the plain-key/arith-projection cell; it read 32.52, and that single disagreement
is what turned a vague "arithmetic is slower" into a located route cliff. The scaling run then
settled it in one reading: a cost that does not grow with the work cannot be the work.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the documents. Both no-sort controls at
0.01-0.03 ms confirm the `LIMIT` is lazy without an `ORDER BY`, so the grid's costs are the sort
path's and not the scan's.

---

## Item 1061 — the route is `nodeProjection`, and the boundary is PAGING + a non-plain item (not arithmetic)

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Item 1060 located a ~3x route cliff and named finding the route as
the next step, explicitly rather than guessing because item 1058's wrong hypothesis came from
reading a gate and inferring when it fires. So this used the repo's own instrument — the `routes()`
helper from `routes-fired.test.ts`, which compiles a query and lists the detectors that return
non-null.

### The route

```text
  ["nodeProjection"]   MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10     11-14 ms
  []                   MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10 ~34 ms
  []                   MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY n.k + 1 LIMIT 10 ~36
```

`detectNodeProjection` fires for the fast shape and nothing fires for the slow ones, which land in
the general pipeline. That is the cliff, named.

### The boundary is NOT "arithmetic", and NOT "the key must be an output column"

Both were plausible and both are wrong — tested rather than reasoned:

```text
  ["nodeProjection"]   RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10          key IS an output column
  []                   RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10      key IS an output column too
  []                   RETURN n.k AS c, n.k + 1 AS d ORDER BY c …   sort key plain; ANOTHER item is not
  ["nodeProjection"]   RETURN n.k + 1 AS c                          arithmetic item, NO paging
  ["nodeProjection"]   RETURN upper(n.s) AS c                       a FUNCTION CALL, no paging
  []                   RETURN n.k + 1 AS c LIMIT 10                 arithmetic item + paging
```

So the route handles arithmetic and function-call items perfectly well — `itemLocal` admits any
row-local expression recursively, excluding aggregates. **What it refuses is PAGING combined with an
item that is not a bare property read**, and one such item anywhere disqualifies the whole
projection even when the sort key is plain and is an output column.

That reading explains every row above, where "arithmetic is refused" explains none of the three that
fire and "the key must be an output column" explains neither of the two output-column refusals.

### Why that boundary exists, and the extension it points at

The paging arm builds its heap from property COLUMNS directly (`directKeys`), which needs the item
to BE a property. An arithmetic item has no column to read.

But the top-k emits only `cap` rows, so a compiled expression could be applied to THOSE — `cap`
evaluations, not N. The column still serves the sort key; only the emitted rows need the
expression. That is the shape of the fix and it is worth ~3x on this family:
34 → the 11-14 the plain form already gets.

**Not built here.** The arm reads columns and writes rows in one pass, so threading a per-row
expression through it is a real change to that code rather than a gate relaxation, and item 1060's
whole lesson was that this family punishes assumptions. It is specified, priced, and left for a
tick that can verify it with controls.

### Method

Three measurements, each refuting the hypothesis I held going in: the cost is not the key (1060),
not arithmetic, and not the output-column rule. **The `routes()` helper answered in one run what two
rounds of reading gates had got wrong** — the instrument for "which route does this take" already
existed, and I reached for code-reading twice before using it.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the documents. Every route listing above came
from `compileLinear` on the parsed query, not from reading a condition.

---

## Item 1062 — the deferred-projection arm: 2.0-2.6x, and the spelling probe caught the first cut creating a 3.8x gap

Item 1061 specified an extension and left it unbuilt. This builds it, and the shape of the fix is
not the one that entry described.

### What the refusal actually was

`outputColumnSorts` refuses a window whenever any projected item can fault, because
`detectNodeProjection` projects every row and slices — which would raise on a row the query never
emits. Item 1061 read that as the paging arm needing the item to BE a property because its heap
reads property columns. The heap is `boundedTopRows`, which reads whatever columns the rows carry,
so the obstacle was never the column: it was projecting too often.

So the arm does what the general path does after `aliasDefinition` substitutes the alias, and what
native does: evaluate the SORT KEYS per row, rank those, then project the full width for the `cap`
survivors only. A non-key item that faults on a discarded row is never evaluated; a KEY item that
faults still raises, because the general path evaluates every key per row too.

### The measurement

200,000 nodes, ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS (`defer-sort-probe.ts`), 14 reps, median of reps 4+,
alternated POST / PRE / POST with each arm asserted by symbol count before its build:

```text
  arith            RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10          33.21 → 16.20   2.05x
  arith-expr       … ORDER BY n.k + 1 LIMIT 10                      33.61 → 15.81   2.13x
  unprojected-key  … ORDER BY n.s LIMIT 10                          37.45 → 15.01   2.50x
  fn               RETURN upper(n.s) AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10        45.10 → 21.26   2.12x
  mixed            RETURN n.k AS c, n.k + 1 AS d ORDER BY c LIMIT 10 31.42 → 12.13   2.59x
  CONTROL plain    RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10               13.09 → 12.95   1.01x
  CONTROL nolimit  … ORDER BY c  (no window)                         34.10 → 34.19   1.00x
  CONTROL limit0   … ORDER BY c LIMIT 0                              0.00 → 0.00
  CONTROL unsorted RETURN n.k + 1 AS c LIMIT 10                      0.03 → 0.04
```

### 🛑 The first cut created a 3.8x equivalent-spelling gap

It took the lazy route to "which column do I rank on": a second ask of `outputColumnSorts` with the
fault test relaxed. That function requires every key to NAME an output column and substitutes only
a `prop` alias — deliberately, so "the same expression" stays an exact comparison rather than an
AST deep-equal. So `RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c` resolved and `… ORDER BY n.k + 1` did not, and
`bun run spelling` read the `ORDER BY alias vs its expression` group at

```text
  11.30ms  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10
  43.13ms  MATCH (n:P) RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY n.k + 1 LIMIT 10        3.8x
```

where PRE both spellings sat converged at ~34 ms. **I made a converged pair diverge 3.8x, in the
exact defect class this repo names first** — and the probe that exists for it found it in one run,
before the change shipped. That is the second time this session a dedicated instrument caught
something a full test suite could not see (items 1053, 1062).

The fix was NOT a wider alias match. It was to change what the ranking ranks on: **compile the key
expression and evaluate it into a synthetic column** (`\u0000k<i>`, which no output column can
collide with because the key rows are discarded). With no alias to match there is no asymmetry to
have. It also admits a key that is not projected at all — `ORDER BY n.s`, which the general path
takes the same way — and that arm measures 2.50x.

After the rework the pair reads 10.30 against 12.08 (1.17x, inside this group's own noise) and the
group no longer appears in the probe's flagged list; the two groups that remain are the
long-standing `label on start` and item 285's.

### The window rules, each load-bearing for a different reason

- **`limit === undefined` declines.** A `SKIP` with no `LIMIT` is not a top-k: with no cap the
  general path sorts and projects EVERY row and then drops the skipped ones. Verified against
  native in both directions — `… ORDER BY c SKIP 1` raises on both engines while
  `… ORDER BY c SKIP 1 LIMIT 2` returns rows on both.
- **`limit === 0` declines, and here that is CORRECTNESS rather than speed.** `applyProjection`
  returns `[]` before ranking or projecting anything, so evaluating keys to emit nothing would
  raise where the query does not. In `outputColumnSorts` the identical guard is only a speed guard
  — the same clause meaning different things in two places, so it is documented in both.
- **A key whose free name is also an OUTPUT name declines.** The sort scope overlays output columns
  on the binding, so `RETURN n.k AS n, n.k + 1 AS d ORDER BY d` would read `n` as a number.
  `aliasDefinition` declines for exactly this; native agrees with the general path's answer.
- **A SUBQUERY key declines.** Neither of the neighbouring tests can be what refuses it:
  `freePredicateVars` returns the EMPTY set for a subquery and `itemLocal` returns TRUE for one.
- **A parameterized window declines**, because the route is chosen once at compile time while the
  value lives in `params`, which the plan cache is shared across.

### Teeth

`page-fold-fault.test.ts`'s existing CLAUSE-position control — item 1056's own test, one item
earlier — **caught the first cut admitting `SKIP` with no `LIMIT`**. That is the differential
discipline paying off on the first try, and it is why that control was written to be the arm "a
too-broad fix would break".

Nine mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`,
each with its anchor's hit count asserted, restored before each one, verdict read from stdout AND
stderr concatenated:

```text
  limit0-admitted          2 fail      skip-no-limit-admitted   2 fail
  alias-not-resolved       4 fail      shadow-allowed           1 fail
  subquery-key-allowed     2 fail      nonlocal-key-allowed     1 fail
  stale-binding            7 fail      window-dropped           7 fail
  desc-dropped             1 fail
```

`subquery-key-allowed` SURVIVED the first run, and item 475's rule says a survivor means
"redundant" as readily as "untested" with opposite fixes. Here it was untested: `itemLocal` admits
a subquery, so the guard is load-bearing. It got a correlated-`COUNT` fixture (out-degrees 2/1/0)
and two tests, and the mutant now dies.

30 tests in `deferred-sorted-projection.test.ts`; every expected value confirmed against NATIVE
first, across three cross-engine probes totalling 34 arms, all agreeing — including tie orders on a
duplicated key, `NULLS` placement on a key absent from every row, a faulting key, the shadowing
pair, and both subquery spellings.

### 🛑 Piping the mutation loop into `head` leaves the mutant in the tree

`target/defer-1062/mutants.sh 2>&1 | head -8` SIGPIPEs the loop after the eighth line, so the final
`restore` never runs. The next two readings — a suite at `2908 pass 2 fail` and a spelling run —
were taken against `subquery-key-allowed` before a `grep` on the live file found it, and the suite's
two failures looked like a real regression in the shape I had just changed. Restore-before-each
contained the damage (the earlier mutants were clean) and `git diff --stat` was the only reason it
could not reach a commit. The lesson is narrow and worth having: **do not pipe that loop into
`head`** — print it whole.

### One more thing the gates demanded

Inlining the compile-time half put `detectNodeProjection` at a complexity of **42 against a ceiling
of 35**, so it is extracted as `deferredRoute` — the same move item 1038 made with `relBoundRoute`
for the same reason. `bun run check` then caught two narrowing slips the extraction introduced (a
`k.expr.name` read inside a callback, and `label?.name` on the un-narrowed `LabelExpr` union), which
is the gate doing the job `lint` and `fmt` cannot: `check` is in neither.

### What this does not claim

The arm is `detectNodeProjection`'s only. `hop-projection.ts`'s windowed sorts refuse on the same
rule and are untouched: that rung drives per vertex through `expand`, so the key/projection split
has to be built there separately — the same per-result-shape structure item 1050 recorded.

### ➡️ A PRE-EXISTING divergence the deep sweep found, with a replaying seed

To price the fuzzer's reach I ran `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=120000` 27 times on the POST arm (clean) and 27
times on the PRE arm, which failed **twice**:

```text
  MATCH (t:T) OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE (n.nu AND (n.x IN ['1e3', ''])))
    RETURN t.n AS x, n.n AS y ORDER BY x, y
      ts:     err E_INVALID_VALUE
      native: ok [{"x":3,"y":null},{"x":5,"y":null},…]
  FUZZ_SEED=3728333688      (and FUZZ_SEED=2059721365, a `ln(-1)` in the same position)
```

Both seeds replay on BOTH arms, so this is not item 1062's. It is the inline-pattern-predicate
boolean-context family inside an `OPTIONAL MATCH`, and the declared
`static-bool-check-misses-inline-pattern-predicates` entry does not cover the shape.

**It corrects item 1059.** That item concluded from one clean 150,000-query run that there is no
backlog of latent divergences. 27 runs of 120,000 say otherwise — about 1 in 14 at that depth, which
is consistent with CI having seen one in 39. A single deep run and a repeated one answer different
questions, and the repeated one is the one that matches what CI does.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,910, gremlin 876, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0. `bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000`:
0 groups disagree on the answer, and the `ORDER BY` group no longer flags.

## Item 1063 — the HOP rung's deferred order: 2.7-8.9x across all five walk variants, with no walk changed

Item 1062 fixed the single-node twin of this and recorded the hop rung as untouched, "the same
per-result-shape structure item 1050 recorded". That structure turned out to be avoidable.

### The cliff, priced first

`hopOrderPlan` refuses a WINDOW whenever any projected item could fault, because the walks project
every row and `sortedRows` slices after. 50,000 edges, every shape's plain twin beside it:

```text
  plain directed hop        10.34 ms plain → 51.05 with `b.k + 1`      4.94x
  clause-WHERE filtered     16.96            53.85                     3.17x
  undirected                33.83           121.91                     3.60x
  seeded start (`{k: 7}`)    1.23             5.44                     4.42x
  rel-bound (`e.w`)         11.89            57.42                     4.83x
  CONTROL, the same item with NO window          18.52  (takes the rung)
```

**Uniform across every variant, and the no-window control is what says it is the window rule and
not the item.** Bigger than the node rung's 2.0-2.6x, because a hop has more rows to project.

### Why it needed no change to any walk — the thing that made it affordable

The walks are the hottest loops in the engine and this file records the cost of touching them: item
159 measured that adding even a BRANCH to one costs the hot shape 1.6x. So the arm does not teach
them to defer. It hands them a **reduced projection**: one item per sort key (the already-compiled
`proj.orderBy[i].fn`), plus one item per ENDPOINT the real items read, each a bare
`binding.get(v)`. The walk's code is untouched — the same `projectRow` call — it just builds a
two-or-three column row carrying the keys and the raw elements. The wrapper then sorts, applies the
window, rebuilds a binding from the carried elements and projects the real items for the `cap`
survivors.

Threading it is five construction sites and one `projectRow` call inside the inline start-driven
walk, all taking `proj: walkProj` where `walkProj` is `proj` itself on every path but this one.

**That serves ALL FIVE variants at once, which matters for more than coverage.** A partial build
would make a filtered hop and an unfiltered one take different routes for the same question — the
equivalent-spelling gap item 1062's first cut created, which is the one defect class this repo
names first.

`proj.orderNeedsOutput` is the whole of the key check, and it is better than item 1062's hand-rolled
one: it is the flag the general path already sets for "a key reads an output column", it mirrors the
Rust `CProjection::order_needs_output`, and it subsumes the shadowing hazard. No alias matching, no
AST walking.

### The measurement

ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS (`defer-hop-probe.ts`), 14 reps, median of reps 4+, alternated POST/PRE/POST,
each arm asserted by symbol count before its build. POST is the min of the two rounds:

```text
  SUBJECTS
    directed-arith      RETURN b.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10        49.61 →  12.76   3.89x
    directed-expr-key   … ORDER BY b.k + 1 LIMIT 10                    48.06 →  12.45   3.86x
    filtered-arith      WHERE b.k > 10 … ORDER BY c LIMIT 10           57.55 →  14.19   4.06x
    undirected-arith    (a)-[:E]-(b) … ORDER BY c LIMIT 10            112.37 →  41.89   2.68x
    relbound-arith      RETURN e.w + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10        60.29 →  13.88   4.34x
    seeded-arith        (a:P {k: 7})-… ORDER BY c LIMIT 10              8.94 →   1.00   8.94x
    fn                  RETURN upper(b.s) AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10     62.29 →  13.66   4.56x
    both-ends           RETURN a.k AS x, b.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY x …     44.43 →  12.44   3.57x
  CONTROLS
    directed-plain      RETURN b.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10            11.60 →  11.52   1.01x
    filtered-plain                                                     11.96 →  11.91   1.00x
    undirected-plain                                                   39.91 →  37.90   1.05x
    relbound-plain                                                     12.61 →  12.30   1.03x
    nolimit             … ORDER BY c  (no window)                      15.95 →  16.32   0.98x
    plain-hop           RETURN b.k AS c  (no sort, no window)          11.86 →  10.30   1.15x
    limit0 / unsorted                                                  0.00-0.06, flat
```

Six controls, all flat. And the subjects now sit beside their own plain twins — 12.76 against 11.52
directed, 14.19 against 11.91 filtered — so the spellings have converged rather than one of them
getting a private fast path.

### 🛑 The in-process sweep manufactured a 1.5x regression on an unreachable control, for the third

### time this session

The first reading was a single process running all fourteen shapes in sequence, and it had
`undirected-plain` at **33.83 before and 50.99 after** — a 1.5x regression on an arm whose route
does not change and whose only difference is being handed `walkProj`, which IS `proj` on that path.
Isolated, one shape per process, it reads **39.91 → 37.90 (1.05x)**.

That is the third phantom of this shape in this session (items 1034, 1038, and now this), and the
giveaway each time was the same: the arm that "regressed" is one the change provably cannot execute
for. CLAUDE.md's rule earned itself again — **one shape per process, and a control the change
cannot reach**.

### Teeth

Nine mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`,
each anchor's hit count asserted, restored before each one, the verdict read from stdout AND stderr
concatenated. **All nine caught — but two survived the first run and both were genuinely untested:**

- **`order-needs-output-admitted`** survived because no case had a key reading an output column.
  Added `RETURN b.k AS b, b.k + 1 AS d ORDER BY d LIMIT 3`, where `d`'s expression reads `b` — also
  an output NAME — so `aliasDefinition` refuses the substitution and the sort scope resolves `b` to
  the column. Both engines agree on the general path's answer.
- **`far-driven-allowed`** (setting `startDriven: false`) survived because the main fixture's ties
  did not discriminate between the two walk orders. Added a fixture where they do: three starts
  wired `s0 → f0,f3,f6`, `s1 → f1,f4,f7`, `s2 → f2,f5,f8`, with all nine far vertices tying on the
  key. Start-driven gives `51,54,57,52,…`; far-driven would give `51,52,53,…`. **Native gives the
  start-driven order**, which is item 605's rule holding on a shape nobody had measured.

Both are item 475's lesson again: a surviving mutant means "redundant" as readily as "untested",
and the two have opposite fixes. Here both were untested.

33 tests in `deferred-hop-order.test.ts`, every expected value confirmed against NATIVE first — 24
cross-engine arms including each of the five variants, every raise, the three-element carry, the tie
fixture and both shadowing spellings.

**🛑 One fixture caught itself, for the fourth time this session.** The first cross-engine fixture
had `MATCH (a:P {t: 1})` where `t` holds `'a'`/`'b'`, so that arm returned `[]` and printed AGREE;
and it had TWO faulting vertices, one at each end of the key order, so every window included one
and every faulting case raised — proving the arm raises but never that it defers. Fixed to one
faulting vertex at one extreme, and now `ORDER BY c LIMIT 2` returns rows while `ORDER BY c DESC
LIMIT 2` raises. **When an arm agrees, check it executed the thing being compared.**

### The spelling probe gained the pair, and one group I wrote was not a spelling group

`bun run spelling` has `hop ORDER BY alias vs its expression, windowed` and its FILTERED twin. The
first attempt also had a "walk variants" group — and the probe correctly reported `ANSWERS DIFFER`,
because a filtered hop and an unfiltered one are not two spellings of one question. That comparison
belongs in `defer-hop-probe.ts`, where each variant is measured against its own plain twin. Worth
recording: the probe compares answers as well as times, so it rejects a group that is not actually
an equivalence.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,943, gremlin 876, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0. **Nine runs of `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=120000` all
clean** — deliberately repeated rather than run once, which is item 1062's correction to item 1059.
`bun run spelling` at `SPELL_N=200000`: 0 groups disagree on the answer, and the two flagged groups
are the long-standing `label on start` and item 285's.

## Item 1064 — select the top `cap` DURING the scan: 2.7x on `ORDER BY … LIMIT n`, and `boundedTopKeyed` de-boxed

Item 1063 finished the deferral family, so this tick asked the same question of the RUST engine and
then of the arm neither 1062 nor 1063 touched: the one that was already "fast".

### The Rust engine has no cliff here — measured, so it is not re-derived

```text
  node plain    ORDER BY c LIMIT 10          1.10 ms      hop plain       0.88 ms
  node arith    ORDER BY c LIMIT 10          1.29         hop arith       0.91
  node expr-key ORDER BY n.k + 1 LIMIT 10    1.27         hop fn          1.43
  node fn       upper(n.s)                   2.83         hop relbound    0.95
  node nolimit  (no window)                 29.27
```

1.17x between the plain and arithmetic spellings, against TS's 3-4x before items 1062/1063. Native
already keeps the top-k over input bindings and projects only survivors, which is what those items
taught TS. **Nothing to build in Rust on this axis**, and the numbers are here so the next reader
does not re-measure it.

### What the comparison exposed instead

Native does `RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10` over 200,000 nodes in **1.10 ms**; TS, after item
1062, in **12.9**. The full sort is 29.27 against 34.6 — only 1.18x apart. So the gap is specific to
the WINDOWED case, and it is TS's, not the layout's.

Locating it took three measurements and refuted two hypotheses of mine:

```text
  count(*)                                    0.00 ms
  min(n.k)       scan + one property read      4.63     ← the FLOOR for this shape in TS
  RETURN n.k AS c   + a row per vertex         8.42
  … ORDER BY c LIMIT 10                       12.9      ← 4.5 ms on top is the selection
```

- **Routing it through item 1062's deferred arm measured 14.25 — SLOWER.** That arm allocates a key
  row per candidate, so it trades one object for another.
- **A flat key array plus a full index sort measured 27.60 — much slower.** Avoiding the row object
  is not the win; the O(n log n) is.

What works is both at once: collect the surviving VERTICES (one array push, no object), select `cap`
with `boundedTopKeyed`, project only those.

### `boundedTopKeyed` was boxing every candidate, and that was most of it

The first version reused the helper as it stood and measured **11.97** — the heap was right and the
allocation was not. Its signature was `keysOf: (item) => readonly unknown[]`, so every candidate
allocated an array, and the loop boxed every candidate into a `Kept` as well: `n` allocations to
keep `cap`.

Two changes, both inside the shared helper, so **both callers benefit**:

- `keyAt: (item, i) => unknown` — one key at a time, no array. A LOSER is now compared against the
  root without being boxed at all; only a winner is materialized. `keyAt` is still called at most
  once per sort level per candidate, exactly as `keysOf` was. **11.97 → 8.82.**
- The candidate comparison uses an INDEXED loop, not `sorts.entries()`. That runs once per
  candidate where `cmp` runs O(cap log cap) times, and `entries()` allocates an iterator and a
  tuple per call. **8.82 → 5.26.**

The hand-rolled prototype that motivated this read 6.65, so the shared helper now **beats** the
one-off — which is the argument for fixing the helper rather than writing a second heap.

### The measurement

ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS, 14 reps, median of reps 4+, alternated POST/PRE/POST, each arm asserted by
symbol count before its build. POST is the min of the two rounds:

```text
  SUBJECTS
    topk-plain      RETURN n.k AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10              13.02 →  4.84   2.69x
    stmt-topk       ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10 RETURN n.k AS c            12.76 →  4.75   2.69x
    topk-two-keys   RETURN n.s AS d, n.k AS c ORDER BY d, c LIMIT 10 15.56 →  8.61   1.81x
    stmt-two-keys   ORDER BY n.s, n.k LIMIT 10 …                     18.82 → 17.68   1.06x
  CONTROLS
    big-cap         … ORDER BY c LIMIT 10000  (above the crossover)  34.40 → 26.60   1.29x
    stmt-big-cap    ORDER BY n.k LIMIT 10000 …                       33.82 → 27.24   1.24x
    arith           RETURN n.k + 1 AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10          16.95 → 16.09   1.05x
    fn              RETURN upper(n.s) AS c ORDER BY c LIMIT 10       22.32 → 22.43   1.00x
    nolimit         … ORDER BY c  (no window)                        34.60 → 35.40   0.98x
    unsorted        … LIMIT 10  (no sort)                             0.03 →  0.04
```

4.84 ms is within **1.05x of the 4.63 ms scan floor** the `min(n.k)` row establishes, so almost all
of what remains on this shape is the scan itself — and closing that is the layout question, not this
one. Native's 1.10 is BELOW the TS floor, which is the honest statement of where the rest of the gap
lives.

The two `big-cap` controls came out 1.24-1.29x FASTER, which this item does not claim as a win: that
branch does what the plain arm did plus one array, so a gain there is this family's documented
bimodality rather than an effect. They are reported as NOT REGRESSED.

`stmt-two-keys` moved 1.06x and is honest about it: with two keys the per-candidate work is two
compiled-closure calls either way, so the de-boxing saves proportionally less.

### Teeth, and a fixture mutation caught that agreement could not

Ten mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`,
each anchor's hit count asserted, restored before each one.

**The first run had SIX survivors, and the cause was the FIXTURE.** `heapBeatsSort` admits the
selection only while `cap * 16 <= rows`, so at 30 vertices a `LIMIT 5` took the sort-and-slice
branch and **the heap was never executed** — 23 tests passed, the cross-engine probe agreed on all
20 arms, and the arrival tiebreak, the multi-key comparison, the DESC handling and the NULLS
placement were all untested. Widening to 320 vertices (so `LIMIT 5` and `SKIP 3 LIMIT 4` both clear
the crossover) killed five of the six.

This is the SIXTH fixture this session that could not reach the code under test — and the first that
neither a vacuous answer nor an empty result made visible. **Mutation is what found it.** The rule
that has been accumulating all session ("when an arm agrees, check it executed the thing being
compared") now has a sharper corollary: a route guard whose threshold depends on the INPUT SIZE
makes every small fixture a vacuous one, silently.

```text
  admits-no-limit      2 fail     admits-nondirect-key  2 fail     key-by-position   1 fail
  skip-dropped         1 fail     crossover-inverted    1 fail     crossover-always  3 fail
  first-key-only       1 fail     root-cmp-asc-only     4 fail     root-cmp-nulls    3 fail
  tiebreak-dropped     SURVIVED — and redundant, see below
```

`tiebreak-dropped` survived and is the other horn of item 475's rule: it is REDUNDANT, provably.
Candidates arrive in increasing `at` and every kept item was seen earlier, so a candidate's arrival
index is always greater than the root's and that comparison can never be true. It stays as the
statement of intent and as the thing that fails loudly if the helper is ever fed items out of
arrival order; the tiebreak is load-bearing in `cmp`, which orders the KEPT items — and
`first-key-only`, `root-cmp-asc-only` and `root-cmp-nulls` all dying is that comparison being
exercised.

Both route gates are PURE FUNCTIONS with their own unit tests (`topKPlan`, `heapBeatsSort`), because
the choice is answer-equivalent and no differential test can see it — `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`,
items 1038 and 1044. `key-by-position` is the one that makes `topKPlan`'s tests worth having: reading
`directKeys` positionally instead of by the key's own column is a WRONG ANSWER whenever the sort
order differs from the projection order, and no timing shows it.

27 tests in `topk-node-scan.test.ts`; every expected value confirmed against NATIVE first — 20
cross-engine arms covering each tie group's membership and order, all four NULLS placements, both
key directions, a gate, an inline property, and both the clause and statement spellings.

### One probe artifact, noted rather than chased

`bun run spelling` flagged `a trailing FILTER vs a clause WHERE: node count` at 2.71x while printing
its two members at **7.91 and 8.14 ms — 1.03x apart**. The two numbers cannot both describe the same
run, so it is the instrument (this family is documented bimodal, and the flagged SET shifts with
where the null control lands). It is also unrelated to this item, which touches no count route.
Recorded so it is not read as a new gap.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,970, gremlin 876, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: all seven byte-identity fuzzers 13/0. Six runs of `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=120000`, all

## Item 1065 — the hop's cost is PER START VERTEX, paid even for vertices with no edges; and the hop top-k is already at its floor

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Item 1064 took a node-scan top-k from 13.02 ms to 4.84 by selecting
during the scan. The obvious next move was the same lever on the HOP rung, which item 1063 left
projecting every row. **That target is refuted, and the measurement that refutes it locates a much
larger one.**

### ❌ The hop top-k is ALREADY at its scan floor

50,000 edges, degree 1, median of the warm reps of 9, TS and native side by side:

```text
                                               ts        native
  hop count(*)                               0.00 ms     0.05 ms
  hop min(b.k)    scan + one property read   11.87        0.27     ← the FLOOR for a hop in TS
  hop all rows    + a row per edge           15.47        5.02
  hop top-10                                 11.91        0.63
  hop full sort                              14.81        6.34
  hop top-10, two columns                    10.91        0.56
```

**`min(b.k)` costs 11.87 and the top-10 costs 11.91.** The aggregate materializes no rows and
selects nothing, so the rows AND the selection together cost about zero on this shape — there is
nothing for item 1064's lever to remove. Applying it would have been a day's work for 0%.

(Native's `min` at 0.27 ms is not a fair floor for native: `min` over a hop is `min` over the SET of
far endpoints, so multiplicity does not matter and it can read a column directly. The TS number is
a valid TS floor, because TS gets there by walking.)

### 🔑 So where does a hop's time go? PER START VERTEX — and the sweep says so twice

**First sweep: hold `|E|` at 50,000 and vary the degree.** Three rounds:

```text
  degree  1   50,000 starts   hop-min 13.54 / 13.47 / 16.07 ms   (271 ns per EDGE)
  degree  2   25,000 starts            3.03 /  3.09 /  3.06      ( 61)
  degree  5   10,000 starts            1.53 /  1.34 /  1.46      ( 29)
  degree 10    5,000 starts            0.97 /  1.07 /  0.93      ( 19)
  degree 50    1,000 starts            1.89 /  1.76 /  1.97      ( 38)
```

**4.4x less time for the SAME 50,000 edges**, purely by having fewer start vertices. A per-edge cost
cannot do that. (CLAUDE.md's rule, from the other side: "per-edge costs scale with the edge:node
ratio, per-node costs do not" — here it is the diagnosis rather than a trap.)

**Second sweep, which isolates it properly.** The first sweep also shrank the vertex count, so it
confounds "fewer starts" with "a shorter scan". This one holds the scan at 50,000 vertices and
50,000 edges and varies only how many vertices HOLD an adjacency map:

```text
  sources 50,000 (degree  1)   hop-min 15.67   hop-proj 11.73   hop-top10 10.36   node-min 0.92
  sources 10,000 (degree  5)           11.88            12.48             18.17            0.69
  sources  1,000 (degree 50)           10.42            13.73             16.98            0.95
```

**Flat.** Whether 50,000 vertices have out-edges or 1,000 do, the hop costs 10-16 ms — and the NODE
scan over the same 50,000 vertices costs **0.92**. So it is not the adjacency maps, not the degree
and not the edge count: it is **~210-320 ns of hop-specific overhead per START VERTEX, charged even
for the 49,000 vertices that have no matching edge at all.**

All three hop rungs pay it — the aggregate, the projection and the top-k alike — so it is in the
shared walk rather than in any one rung.

### ➡️ What names the fix: `count(*)` does not pay it

`hop count(*)` is **0.00 ms** on every arm. It answers the same pattern without touching a start
vertex, because `tallyHopCount` reads the EDGE-TYPE BUCKET (item 1035's structure) instead of
walking vertices. So the overhead is not intrinsic to needing the edges — one rung already avoids
it entirely.

**The lever is an EDGE-DRIVEN walk for a whole-graph typed hop**: iterate the type bucket and
resolve both endpoints off each edge, instead of iterating vertices and asking each for its
adjacency. The precedent is in the file already — `relSeekedHopWalk` (item 1038) is edge-driven, and
the start-driven/far-driven choice is already a per-call decision with a `vacuousLabel` test.

Priced from the floors above: a hop projection still has to build a row per result (the node rung's
`RETURN n.k AS c` runs ~42 ns a row, so ~2 ms for 50,000), and an aggregate builds none. So the
ceiling is roughly **11.73 → 2-3 ms for the projection and 15.67 → under 1 ms for the aggregate**,
4-5x and 10x+.

**Two constraints it must respect**, both already written down in `hop-projection.ts`:

- **ORDER is unspecified only for unordered results.** An edge-driven walk emits rows in a different
  order from the start-driven one, and tie order under `ORDER BY` is observable between the engines
  (item 605) — which is why `hopOrderPlan` forces the start-driven walk whenever there is a sort.
  So this applies to UNORDERED shapes, exactly as `farDrivenHopWalk` already does.
- **A START LABEL cannot be applied edge-first** without re-checking it per edge, which is what the
  existing far-driven walk's `vacuousLabel` guard is about.

### Method

Three measurements, and the first one killed the plan I started the tick with. The `min` row is what
did it: **an aggregate that materializes no rows and selects nothing is the cleanest floor available
for a walk**, and comparing the top-k against it answered "is there anything here to win" before any
code was written. The two sweeps then separated three candidate causes — degree, adjacency-map count,
scan length — by holding each fixed in turn, and only the third survived.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the documents. Every figure is a median of the
warm reps of 9; the degree sweep was run three times and the arms it compares differ by more than
4x, well clear of this family's noise.

## Item 1066 — a VACUOUS far label costs a hop 2.8x, and item 1065's attribution was wrong

### 🛑 First, the correction to item 1065

That item concluded the hop's cost is "~210-320 ns per START VERTEX, charged even for the 49,000
vertices that have no matching edge". **Two things in it are wrong.**

1. **It called `min(b.k)` a row-free floor.** It is not: `detectHopAggregate` delegates to the hop
   PROJECTION walks and folds over `row[VALUE_COL]`, so the aggregate materializes a row per edge
   like everything else. The narrow fact that survives is the one the refutation rested on —
   top-10 (11.91), `min` (11.87) and all-rows (15.47) are within noise of each other, so the
   SELECTION costs nothing and item 1064's lever has nothing to remove on a hop. **That
   refutation stands.** The explanation given for it does not.
2. **Its second sweep held the actual cause constant.** That sweep varied how many vertices hold an
   adjacency map while keeping `V = 50,000` and `to: vs[(e * 13 + 1) % V]` — so the FAR POOL was
   50,000 wide in every arm. It read flat, and I attributed the flatness to "the cost is per start
   vertex" when it in fact says "the cost does not depend on the adjacency distribution". The sweep
   I built to isolate the cause could not see it.

I varied two things and credited the one I was thinking about. The fix is the experiment below,
which holds everything fixed but the one variable.

### The experiment that locates it

50,000 vertices scanned, 50,000 edges, one edge per start vertex, 50,000 rows — **identical in
every arm**. The only difference is how many DISTINCT vertices those edges point into:

```text
  far pool 50,000   min(b.k) 15.88 ms   min(a.k) LABELLED 20.38   min(a.k) BARE  8.14   rows 10.72
  far pool 10,000             4.25                       10.33                  5.09         3.59
  far pool  1,000             1.33                        7.64                  5.30         1.03
  far pool    100             1.06                        5.90                  5.48         1.48
```

**9.3-15x on `rows` and `min(b.k)` from nothing but where the edges point.** The cost of a hop is
DEREFERENCING THE FAR VERTEX, and it scales with how scattered the far set is — a cache-residency
effect, which is CLAUDE.md's first rule arriving as the answer rather than as a trap.

And the micro-timing says that deref is not the data structure's fault. Iterating the label bucket,
asking each vertex for `adjFrom.get('E')` and walking every bucket — the walk's own primitives —
costs **0.76-1.36 ms**, against the engine's 9.93-13.86 for the same traversal.

### 🔑 What is fixable: a label that cannot fail still pays for the deref

`min(a.k)` reads ONLY the start, and it cost **20.38 ms with `->(b:P)` against 8.14 with `->(b)`** —
two spellings of one question over a graph where every vertex carries `P`. The far vertex was being
dereferenced solely to test a label that cannot reject anything.

So `matchesLabel(far, farLabel)` is now hoisted: `const fl = vacuousLabel(graph, farLabel) ?
undefined : farLabel`, **once per call**, in the inline start-driven walk and in
`filteredHopWalk`'s general loop. It replaces a variable rather than adding a branch, so the inner
loop is otherwise untouched — item 159's 1.6x is the reason that matters.

**The decision already existed in this file for the DEDUP walk** (`planFor`, items 215/217, where
the far label test alone measured 189 ns a vertex). This is that decision applied to the walks that
project, which is also why it is not a new idea needing a new justification.

Per CALL, not per compile: vacuity is a runtime property of the graph, the same reason the
far-driven choice is made there (items 195/198).

### The measurement

ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS (`vacuous-far-probe.ts`), 14 reps, median of reps 4+, alternated
POST/PRE/POST, each arm asserted by symbol count. POST is the min of the two rounds:

```text
  SUBJECTS
    start-only-labelled   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P) RETURN min(a.k)   18.06 →  6.46   2.80x
    start-proj-labelled   … RETURN a.k AS c                         17.13 →  6.12   2.80x
  CONTROLS
    start-only-bare       … ->(b) RETURN min(a.k)   the SPELLING TWIN  6.43 →  7.59
    start-proj-bare       … ->(b) RETURN a.k                           6.71 →  6.51   1.03x
    far-read              … RETURN min(b.k)   far dereferenced anyway 14.65 → 14.11   1.04x
    far-rows              … RETURN b.k                               13.09 → 12.71   1.03x
    selective-far         … ->(b:Q)   the label MUST still be tested   1.15 →  1.15   1.00x
    node-min              MATCH (n:P) RETURN min(n.k)   not a hop      0.86 →  0.85   1.01x
```

**The result is the CONVERGENCE, not the ratio.** Before: 18.06 labelled against 6.43 bare. After:
6.46 against 7.59 — the same question now costs the same either way. `selective-far` is the control
that matters most: a label on a tenth of the vertices must still be tested, and it did not move.

### Teeth

Four mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`,
each anchor's hit count asserted, restored before each one:

```text
  always-drop              4 fail    (the label dropped whether vacuous or not)
  vacuous-means-nonempty   6 fail    (vacuity mis-read as "the bucket is non-empty")
  vacuous-off-by-one       6 fail    (`>= vertexCount - 1`, one vertex short admitted)
  hoist-only-inline        SURVIVED — answer-equivalent, see below
```

`hoist-only-inline` reverts one of the two hoists, which loses speed and changes no answer, so no
test can see it; the probe's two spelling-convergence rows are its guard
(`perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`). It is in the harness so the next reader does not mistake its
survival for a gap.

17 tests in `vacuous-far-label.test.ts`, built as PAIRS of fixtures differing in one vertex —
`:P` on all 8, or on 7 of 8 — because `vacuousLabel` is a size comparison and the boundary is one
vertex wide. The 7-of-8 fixture asserts the two spellings answer DIFFERENTLY, which is the wrong
answer `always-drop` produces. Every value confirmed against native first (32 arms across both
fixtures).

**Compared as MULTISETS, deliberately.** Two shapes in that fixture emit the same rows in a
different order on the two engines — and they do so on the PRE arm too, which is how I know they
are pre-existing and not this item's. Row order for an unordered result is unspecified, which is
why the byte-identity fuzzers compare multisets as well.

### ➡️ The same bug class on the START label is worth 5783x, and the probe has been printing it

`bun run spelling` flags `label on start: redundant vs absent` — a long-standing group — at:

```text
  57.83ms   MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(*) AS c
   0.00ms   MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b) RETURN count(*) AS c
```

Two spellings of one question over the probe's fixture, where every vertex carries `P`. The
unlabelled form takes the O(1) edge-bucket count; the labelled form walks 200,000 vertices.
`shortcuts.ts` already drops vacuous endpoint labels in the UNDIRECTED hop count (`vacuousLabel` on
both ends) — the DIRECTED count does not. Named, priced and left for the next tick rather than
bundled here.

### Verification

Suites: core 370, gql 2,987, gremlin 876, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: 13/0. Six runs of `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=120000`, all clean. `bun run spelling`: 0 groups
disagree on the answer, and the four flagged groups are the long-standing ones.

## Item 1067 — the bare degree sum: 1.6-1.7x on `MATCH (a:L)-[:T]->(b) RETURN count(*)`, and the 5783x was two instruments lying in the same direction

Item 1066 ended by naming `bun run spelling`'s `label on start: redundant vs absent` group at
**5783x** — 57.83 ms against 0.00 — as the next target. Both halves of that framing needed
correcting before anything could be built.

### 🛑 What the 5783x actually was

```text
  4 extra edge-less `:S` vertices (so `:P` is NOT vacuous)
    labelled  (a:P)-[:E]->(b)     56.02 ms      bare  (a)-[:E]->(b)   0.00 ms
    both ends (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P)  105.22          far only (a)-[:E]->(b:P)  44.64
  0 extra vertices (so `:P` IS vacuous)
    every one of those four        0.00 ms
```

So it is **not** a missed vacuous-label elision: `shortcuts.ts` already drops a vacuous endpoint
label and takes the O(1) bucket count, and with the four extras removed it does exactly that. The
spelling probe's own fixture carries four edge-less `:S` vertices for an unrelated group, and those
four — out of 200,004, changing no answer — are what make `:P` non-vacuous and send the query to a
walk. **The engine is being correctly conservative, and the group has been printing a fixture
artifact as a 5783x gap.**

### 🛑 And the 56 ms was an in-process reading

The isolated instrument puts the PRE cost of that query at **25.59 ms**, not 56. Both my ad-hoc
probes ran several shapes per process, and so did the ladder below. **Two instruments inflating in
the same direction is how a 1.7x becomes a 3.6x**, and the only thing that caught it was building
the one-shape-per-process probe before believing either.

### The ladder, which is still what located the cost

200,000 vertices at degree 3, the degree-sum walk's loop body step by step (in-process, so read the
DELTAS, not the totals):

```text
  iterate the P bucket                                   0.32 ms
    + labels.has('P')                                    3.47      +3.2
    + adjFrom.get('E').size                             20.32     +16.9   ← the irreducible part
    + a types loop, as `degreeOfTypes`                  24.66      +4.3
    + try/catch and a predicate call                    26.83      +2.2
```

`adjFrom.get('E').size` is 85 ns a vertex here against ~9 ns at 50,000 vertices — the same
cache-residency story as item 1066, and CLAUDE.md's "sweep the size" rule for the third time this
session. What is left over is per-vertex call overhead on a shape that has nothing for any of it to
do.

### The change

`bareDegreeSum` sums bucket sizes with none of it: no label re-check, no `try`/`catch`, no
predicate call, no `degreeOfTypes`. It is asked at the top of `startOnlyHopCount` and
`farOnlyHopCount` — BOTH, so `(a:L)-[:T]->(b)` and `(a)-[:T]->(b:L)` cannot diverge — and returns
`null` to hand the query back.

What it drops and why each is sound:

- **the label re-check** — `candidateVertexSource` returns the label's own bucket for a plain `:L`,
  so every candidate carries it by construction; a SEEK would hand back a superset, which is why
  one declines;
- **the predicate call** — reached only with `alwaysTrue`;
- **the `try`/`catch`** — it exists for the raise-parity rule (items 139-145), and with no
  predicate nothing can fault;
- **`degreeOfTypes`'s loop** — for a single relationship type.

### The measurement

ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS (`bare-degree-probe.ts`), 14 reps, median of reps 4+, alternated
POST/PRE/POST/PRE, each arm asserted by symbol count. POST is the min of three POST rounds, PRE of
two:

```text
  SUBJECTS
    start-labelled     (a:P)-[:E]->(b)      25.59 → 14.75   1.74x
    far-labelled       (a)-[:E]->(b:P)      25.76 → 15.88   1.62x
    start-labelled-in  (a:P)<-[:E]-(b)      26.98 → 15.92   1.69x
    far-labelled-in    (a)<-[:E]-(b:P)      26.01 → 15.38   1.69x
  CONTROLS
    both-ends          (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P)   105.56 → 106.5   0.99x  ← see below
    bare               (a)-[:E]->(b)         0.00 → 0.00    the O(1) count, untouched
    filtered           … WHERE a.k > 10     48.85 → 48.12   1.02x
    inline             (a:P {k: 7})-…        7.16 → 6.94    1.03x
    two-types          (a:P)-[:E|F]->(b)   230.17 → 227.76  1.01x
    rows               … RETURN a.k AS c   144.30 → 143.85  1.00x
```

And the spelling group it came from: **5783x → 1521x**. It still flags, and must: while `:P` is not
vacuous the labelled form has to touch every `P` vertex, where the bare form reads one bucket size.
`one end labelled, the other free` (item 286) dropped off the flagged list entirely.

**🛑 The `both-ends` control read 98.85 before against 106.5 after, and that was an outlier.** It
looked exactly like item 119's closure-growth effect — I had added the dispatch at the two call
sites inside the closure `buildOneHopCount` returns — so I moved it into the two module-scope
walks. **That did not change the control** (106.6), and a SECOND PRE round read 105.56. There was
never a regression. The move is kept because it is the right shape by this file's own rule, not
because it fixed anything, and the comment on it says so.

### Teeth, and what mutation actually told me

Eight mutants under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`.
**The first run had SEVEN survivors against 19 passing tests**, which is the same lesson as item
1064's one item later: the fixture could not tell the guards apart.

Rather than guess which, I INSTRUMENTED the fast path with a counter and printed which shapes reach
it — the "verify the planner reaches the shape" step of the method, which I had skipped:

```text
  FIRES   (a:P)-[:E]->(b) / (a)-[:E]->(b:P) / (a:P)<-[:E]-(b) / (a:Z)-[:E]->(b)
  skips   WHERE true · WHERE a.k > 1 · (a:P {k: 0}) · [:E|F] · [:E {w: 1}] · (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P)
          · both indexed seeks
```

Three of my "declines" were answer-equivalent fixtures rather than tests: every edge had `w: 1`, so
a rel constraint ignored read the same; `WHERE true` is item 570's control and is answer-equivalent
BY DESIGN; and the multi-type edge made the alternation's right answer equal the naive sum. The
discriminators that replaced them:

- **`WHERE 1 = 0`** — no free variables, so it is not refused upstream for reading the start, and it
  changes the answer where `WHERE true` cannot. Kills `ignores-predicate`.
- **`[:E|F]` on a fixture with NO multi-type edge** — there the CALLER admits many types and only
  the fast path's single-type guard refuses. Kills `admits-many-types`.
- **`-[:E {w: 2}]->` over alternating `w`.**
- **`(a:P&S)`** — a label expression nothing satisfies, where `candidateVertexSource` hands back
  every vertex, so admitting it counts the whole graph instead of none. Kills `admits-label-expr`.

Final: **4 caught** (`admits-label-expr`, `admits-many-types`, `ignores-predicate`,
`wrong-adjacency`), **4 survive and each is explained by the instrumentation**:

- `ignores-inline` and `admits-seek` — the inline branch's `cstart` carries a seed hint, so the
  seek guard refuses first; neither guard is individually observable and the PAIR is still
  necessary.
- `ignores-rel-inline` — `startWalkFits` already requires `inRel === undefined`, so the shape never
  arrives.
- `wrong-end-label` — using `pa` for the far side makes the path DECLINE rather than answer wrongly
  (the label is undefined there), which is answer-equivalent.

They are kept as the statement of intent, the way this file keeps `variable === nodeVar`, and item
475's rule is why each one says WHICH condition masks it.

21 tests in `bare-degree-sum.test.ts`, run against two fixtures differing only in whether one edge
carries two types. Every number read off BOTH engines first — 46 arms, all agreeing — after three of
my hand-derived counts in the first version turned out wrong and the engines right.

Suites: core 370, gql 3,008, gremlin 876, native 933, serialization 144 — 0 fail.
`bun run fuzz`: 13/0. Six runs of `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=120000`, all clean. `bun run spelling`:

## Item 1068 — RUST: hoist the LABEL name `Value`s out of the element render, the half item 391 left

A Rust tick. The previous four items were all TypeScript, and item 1064 established the native
engine has no cliff on the sorted-page axis — so this starts from the Rust corpus instead of from a
TS gap.

### Where the corpus says the money is

`query_bench -- perrow` answers "what does a row cost, by what is returned?":

```text
  count(*)           0.3 us         1 row     320.0 ns/row
  scalar p.age     537.2       200,000          2.7
  string p.name   1461.9       200,000          7.3
  element p      69804.0       200,000        349.0
  element r     300486.2     1,000,000        300.5
```

**Element materialization is 129x a scalar read**, and `CLOSED.md` already calls it "the largest
per-row cost in the engine… next target, and unlike the 69x it is a real one" (item 338). Item 390
ablated it: **47% in the property loop, 37% in two `Value::Map` allocations, 12% in labels, ~0 in
the external-id lookup.** Item 391 then hoisted the property KEYS out of the row loop (1.09x on the
corpus, 1.32x on a realistic schema) and item 392 refuted pre-sizing the property vector.

### The labels were the same defect, one field over

Item 391's note says it took four sites and "the two single-element renders are deliberately left".
What it did NOT say is that the LABELS inside those same row loops were never hoisted:

```rust
store.label_names_of(id).map(|l| Value::Str(l.into()))   // per label, PER ROW
```

`Value::Str` on a `&str` runs `GStr::new`, which **copies the bytes** — inline to `INLINE_CAP` = 12,
and a **heap allocation with a refcount header above it**. So a label name longer than twelve
characters allocated once per node per label, for a name every node in the bucket shares. Exactly
the thing item 391 removed for keys.

The fix is its twin: one `Value` per LABEL ID, built once per call, cloned per row — a relaxed
`fetch_add` for a heap string, a 16-byte copy for an inline one. Two new crate-private accessors
(`label_ids_of`, `label_names_table`) so the render can go through the ids.

### Why the corpus cannot show it, and what can

`query_bench`'s fixture labels are `Person` and `Company`, both inline, so it reads the flat part of
the curve — `element p` **349.0 → 345.3 ns/row (1.01x)**, `element r` 300.5 → 304.7 (untouched).
**That is the predicted result, not a disappointment**: item 391 recorded the identical situation for
keys ("the bench cannot show the real win… its fixture keys are all inline"), and its own earlier
probe had hidden the effect by using keys `"a".."d"`.

So the axis is NAME LENGTH, and `labelhoist_1068` sweeps it. 100,000 nodes, four properties each,
min of 5, two alternated rounds:

```text
  label chars      PRE r1   PRE r2     POST r1  POST r2
   6 (Person)       225.1    223.6       223.0    221.5     ← in-arm control: inline, unchanged
  12 (boundary)     227.3    226.5       221.3    223.5     ← in-arm control
  14                239.3    240.9       227.5    222.5       1.07x
  17                240.7    250.7       221.9    223.2       1.09x
  39                245.2    253.0       224.1    223.5       1.09x
  CONTROL scalar      1.3      1.3         1.3      1.3     (no element rendered)
```

**PRE steps at the inline boundary and rises; POST is flat at every length.** That the step lands at
12-to-14 and not earlier is what identifies it as the copy rather than something else, and the two
short rows are controls INSIDE the subject arm — the same fixture, the same code, the only
difference being whether `GStr` touches the heap.

So the claim is not "1.09x on element render": it is **the length dependence is gone**, worth
1.07-1.09x at 14-39 characters on this fixture and nothing below 12. One label per node here; a node
with two or three long labels pays proportionally more.

### Teeth

Behaviour-preserving, so the existing suite is the right instrument and the question is whether it
has teeth on this code. Two mutants under
`timeout 900 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`:

```text
  wrong-label-index  (every row gets `label_vals[0]`)    2 failed  — CAUGHT
  labels-unsorted    (the per-row sort removed)          1 failed  — CAUGHT
```

Both by the existing 1,264-test suite, which is what licenses this as a hoist rather than a
rewrite. Byte identity against the TS engine: `bun run fuzz` 13/0, plus three runs of
`FUZZ_ITERATIONS=120000`, all clean.

### ➡️ The EDGE mirror is next, and it may be worth more

`render_edges` has the same copy, plus one more allocation on top:

```rust
let mut labels = store.edge_labels_of_refs(eid);   // a Vec<&str> PER ROW
labels.sort_unstable();
Value::List(labels.into_iter().map(|t| Value::Str(t.into())).collect())
```

So an edge pays a `Vec` allocation per row that a node does not, and `element r` is the corpus's
largest single row (1,000,000 rows, 300 ms). It needs its own accessors (`edge_etype`, `edge_extra`)
and its own length sweep, so it is NOT bundled here — one measured change per commit, and the edge
half has not been measured.

### Verification

Rust: 1,264 + 13 + 725 tests, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0,
`cargo fmt` applied. Byte identity: `bun run fuzz` 13/0 and three deep differential runs clean.
Corpus controls: `scalar p.age` 2.7 → 2.4 ns/row, `string p.name` 7.3 → 7.0, `element r` flat.

## Item 1069 — RUST: the EDGE-label hoist, 1.11-1.31x — and the first cut of it measured SLOWER than what it replaced

Item 1068's named next step. The edge side pays THREE costs per row where the node side paid one:

```rust
let mut labels = store.edge_labels_of_refs(eid);   // 1. a Vec<&str> PER ROW
labels.sort_unstable();                            // 2. each id through `etype_name_ref`,
Value::List(labels.into_iter()                     //    a LINEAR SCAN of `etype_ids`
    .map(|t| Value::Str(t.into())).collect())      // 3. and then COPIES the bytes
```

So the axes are edge-type COUNT (how long the scanned table is) and name LENGTH (whether the copy
heap-allocates). `query_bench -- perrow`'s `element r` — the corpus's largest single row, 1,000,000
rows at ~300 ms — holds both at their flat corner: one short edge type. `edgelabel_1069` sweeps them.

### 🛑 The first cut was a REGRESSION, and nearly got the idea retracted

Replacing all three with a hoisted `Vec<Option<Value>>` indexed by type id, built once per call and
read per row through `primary.into_iter().chain(extra.iter().copied()).filter_map(|t|
etype_vals.get(t as usize).and_then(Option::clone)).collect()`:

```text
  arm              PRE     POST (iterator chain)
  T=1  len=6     222.9  →  241.6     0.92x  SLOWER
  T=8  len=6     219.3  →  240.2     0.91x  SLOWER
  T=64 len=6     222.4  →  238.3     0.93x  SLOWER
  T=1  len=20    236.3  →  242.8     0.97x
  T=8  len=20    235.5  →  240.6     0.98x
  T=64 len=20    258.0  →  241.3     1.07x  faster — the only arm that improved
```

Both axes went flat, which is what the hoist is for — and the FLOOR rose from ~220 to ~240, so it
lost everywhere except the extreme corner. On those numbers the honest call is to revert, and I was
about to.

**What stopped me was that the mechanism did not fit.** The hoist removes an allocation, a linear
scan and a byte copy; a net loss means the REPLACEMENT costs more than all three, and
`chain`/`filter_map`/`collect` over an `Option` is the only thing it added. So: same hoist, written
as the node twin writes it — `Vec::with_capacity(1 + extra.len())` and two indexed pushes, no
iterator machinery.

```text
  arm              PRE     POST (indexed)
  T=1  len=6     218.6  →  196.5     1.11x
  T=1  len=20    231.7  →  196.6     1.18x
  T=8  len=6     218.5  →  195.1     1.12x
  T=8  len=20    235.5  →  196.5     1.20x
  T=64 len=6     222.4  →  196.4     1.13x
  T=64 len=20    258.0  →  196.2     1.31x
  CONTROL scalar   7.5  →    7.4     (no element rendered)
```

**Flat at ~196 on every arm, and below the PRE floor everywhere.** PRE is the min of three rounds,
POST of two, alternated.

So the lesson is not "the mirror pays" or "it does not" — it is that **the iterator chain cost more
than the three things the hoist removed (~45 ns/row), and a measurement that only says SLOWER cannot
tell you which of those it was.** The mechanism check is what separated them: if removing three
costs makes a loop slower, suspect what you added, not the premise.

### The corpus CAN see this one

Unlike item 1068's node hoist (1.01x on the corpus, because its labels are inline), `element r`
reads **304.7 → 287.3 ns/row (1.06x)** — the per-row `Vec` and the resolver scan are paid at T=1 and
six characters too, where only the byte copy needed a long name. `element p` 345.3 → 338.4 (untouched
path), `scalar p.age` 2.4, `string p.name` 7.0 — controls flat.

### Teeth

Behaviour-preserving, so the existing suite is the instrument and the question is whether it has
teeth here. Three mutants under
`timeout 900 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`:

```text
  edge-wrong-type-index   (every row gets `etype_vals[0]`)   1 failed  — CAUGHT
  edge-extras-dropped     (secondary labels skipped)         1 failed  — CAUGHT
  edge-labels-unsorted    (the per-row sort removed)         1 failed  — CAUGHT
```

All by the existing 1,264-test suite. Byte identity against the TS engine: `bun run fuzz` 13/0 plus
three runs of `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=120000`, all clean.

### Where this leaves the element-render target

Items 338/390 put element materialization at 129x a scalar read and ablated it as 47% property
loop, 37% two `Value::Map` allocations, 12% labels, ~0 external id. The labels are now hoisted on
both sides (1068, 1069). **The 37% is the remaining named target**, and item 392 already refuted the
obvious attack on it (pre-sizing the property vector measured 1.25x SLOWER) — so the next attempt
there needs a different idea, not a retry.

### Verification

Rust: 1,264 + 13 + 725 tests, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0, `cargo fmt`
applied. Byte identity: `bun run fuzz` 13/0, three deep differential runs clean.

## Item 1070 — REFUTED: `Value::Map(Arc<[(Value, Value)]>)` is SLOWER than `Arc<Vec<_>>`, in both halves

MEASUREMENT, no engine change. Items 338/390 ablated element materialization — the engine's largest
per-row cost, 129x a scalar read — as **47% property loop, 37% two `Value::Map` allocations, 12%
labels, ~0 external id.** The labels are now hoisted on both sides (1068, 1069), so the 37% is the
remaining named sub-target, and item 392 already refuted the obvious attack on it (pre-sizing the
property vector measured 1.25x SLOWER).

### The idea, and why it looked right

`Map(Arc<Vec<(Value, Value)>>)` is TWO allocations — the `Vec`'s buffer and the `Arc`'s box — and
`Value::Record` **in the same enum already uses the single-allocation `Arc<[(GStr, Value)]>` form.**
An element render builds two maps per row, so the floor looked like 2 allocations where it pays 4.

That is a cross-crate refactor of every `Value::Map` construction and match site, so it gets priced
first. `mapalloc_1070` times the four shapes at the sizes a render actually uses, three rounds:

```text
  outer 3-pair: Arc::new(vec![..])   (today)    29.7 / 29.1 / 26.7     min 26.7
  outer 3-pair: Arc::from_iter([..])            41.8 / 42.9 / 39.0     min 39.0   +12.3  SLOWER
  props: pushes -> Arc::new(v)       (today)    45.0 / 44.6 / 45.7     min 44.6
  props: pushes -> Arc::from_iter(v)            55.5 / 55.2 / 55.3     min 55.2   +10.6  SLOWER
  CONTROL props: pushes only, no map            30.1 / 30.1 / 30.3     min 30.1
```

**+22.9 ns/row in total, the wrong way.** The refactor would be a regression, and it is refuted
before the work rather than after it.

### Why — and the half I predicted versus the half I did not

`Arc<[T]>` is one allocation only when built from an `ExactSizeIterator`, where `Arc::from_iter`
writes in place; `Arc::<[T]>::from(vec)` COPIES into a fresh allocation instead. So the PROPERTY
map's +10.6 was predicted in the probe's own header: its length is not known up front (which
properties are present varies per row), so converting the accumulated `Vec` costs the `Vec` plus the
`Arc` plus a memcpy — the same count, plus the copy.

**The outer map's +12.3 was NOT predicted.** Three pairs with a length known at the construction
site is exactly the case `Arc::from_iter` should win, and it loses by more than the props map does.
`vec![a, b, c]` compiles to one sized allocation and three moves; `Arc::from_iter` over an array
goes through the iterator protocol and a `RcInnerPtr` layout computation, and at three elements that
machinery costs more than the allocation it removes. Item 1069's lesson one item earlier, in the
same shape: **iterator machinery is not free, and at small N it can exceed what it saves.**

### What the control bought, and the fixture mistake that nearly cost it

`props: pushes only` at 30.1 ns/row against `pushes -> Arc::new(v)` at 44.6 prices the thing item
390 named: **the props map's `Arc` box is 14.5 ns/row**, and the pair construction plus the `Vec` is
the other 30. So "37% in two map allocations" is better read as ~15 ns of `Arc` boxing and ~60 ns of
`Vec` + pair building across the two maps — of ~338 ns/row today.

**🛑 The first cut of this probe could not have said that.** Its `pair()` built the key with
`format!`, so every row allocated a `String` per pair and the control read **107.1 ns/row** — the
differences were still valid (both arms paid it) but the absolute numbers were my fixture's
allocation, not the map's, and the 14.5 ns figure was invisible underneath it. The engine does not
build keys that way either — items 391/1068/1069 hoisted exactly those — so cloning a pre-built
`Value` is both the faithful shape and the one that makes the control mean something. **A control is
only useful if the thing being measured is above the fixture's own floor.**

### Where this leaves the element-render target

- 12% labels: **done** (1068, 1069).
- 37% map allocations: **two attacks now refuted** — pre-sizing the property vector (392, 1.25x
  slower) and the `Arc<[_]>` representation (this item, +22.9 ns/row). What is left inside it is
  ~15 ns of `Arc` boxing per row and the `Vec` allocations, and nothing cheap removes either while
  each row's map is independently owned.
- 47% property loop: **the largest share and the one nobody has attacked.** `present_at` +
  `read` per present cell, column-major since item 828.

So the honest statement is that the 37% is close to its floor for this data shape, and the next
attempt on element render should go at the 47%.

### Verification

No engine change: `git status --porcelain` shows only the new example and the documents. Three
rounds, min-of-three, every arm built from the same allocation-free pair constructor.

## Item 1071 — RUST: specialize the property loop per COLUMN, 1.08x at K=4 and 1.18x at K=64 — and the corpus could not adjudicate it

The 47% share item 1070 left: item 390's ablation put **47% of an element render in the property
loop**, the largest piece and the one both map-allocation attacks (392, 1070) left untouched.

### What the loop was paying per CELL

```rust
if c.present_at(id as usize) {                       // matches the variant, reads present||nulls
    props.push((key_vals[j].clone(), c.read(id)));   // matches the variant AGAIN, reads present
}
```

Two variant matches and three bitmap reads per present cell — where the variant is **fixed for the
whole inner loop** (the loop is per column) and one presence read suffices. So: match once per
column, then run a specialized row loop per variant that indexes `data`/`present`/`nulls` directly.

**Byte-identical by construction**, which is why this is a specialization and not a rewrite: the
generic path pushes when `present[i] || nulls[i]` with the value from `read`, which yields the datum
when `present[i]` and `Value::Null` otherwise. Each arm is exactly that pair of conditions inlined,
so a STORED null (`SET k = null`, which is `present=false, nulls=true`) still pushes a
`Value::Null` pair and an absent cell still pushes nothing. `Gen` keeps the generic path — it has no
`nulls` bitset, storing `Value::Null` in `data` directly, so an arm for it would be a near-duplicate
with different semantics.

### 🛑 The corpus cannot adjudicate this, and said so out loud

`query_bench -- perrow` renders FOUR properties, so a per-cell saving arrives diluted by the
~250 ns/row the rest of the render pays. Alternated POST/PRE/POST:

```text
  element p  (the row this changes)   PRE 341.9  →  POST 335.4 / 332.3    1.03x
  element r  (render_edges — UNREACHABLE from this change)
                                      PRE 267.2  →  POST 282.5 / 277.3    0.95x
  scalar p.age  CONTROL                   2.4         2.4 / 2.5           flat
```

**The subject moved 1.03x and an unreachable control moved 1.04x the OTHER way.** Same magnitude, so
the instrument cannot separate the change from build-to-build drift on those rows — CLAUDE.md's
"anything under ~10% needs its own isolated harness", arriving as a verdict rather than a warning.

### The isolated instrument: sweep the axis the change acts on

A per-CELL saving scales with cells per row. `propcells_1071` sweeps K, properties per node, every
one present, half numeric and half string so both specialized arms run. Mins across rounds:

```text
  K          PRE      POST     ratio
   1       162.1     160.4     1.01x   ← the control at the bottom of the curve: one cell a row
   4       231.2     214.1     1.08x   ← the corpus's width
  16       549.2     482.4     (not claimed — see below)
  64      2667.8    2254.1     1.18x
  CONTROL scalar at K=64       1.4 → 1.3, flat (no element rendered, so no cell materialized)
```

**The ratio grows with K, which is the signature of a per-cell saving** — 1.01x where there is one
cell a row, 1.18x where there are 64. A change that moved the fixed per-row cost instead would show
the opposite shape.

**K=16 is NOT claimed**: its POST readings were 482.4 / 635.2 / 717.7 across three rounds, a 1.5x
spread, against a stable PRE (549.2 / 564.7). Three readings that disagree by more than the effect
are not evidence, and the monotone drift across rounds says machine rather than arm. The K=1, K=4
and K=64 rows were each stable within ~3%.

### Teeth, and the arm mutation found UNTESTED

Five mutants under `timeout 900 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`:

```text
  present-ignored   (push every cell, absent or not)   2 failed  — CAUGHT
  nulls-dropped     (stored nulls lost)                1 failed  — CAUGHT
  num-arm-zero                                         2 failed  — CAUGHT
  str-arm-first     (every row reads data[0])          2 failed  — CAUGHT
  dict-code-zero    (every row reads dict[0])          SURVIVED  ← no test reached that arm
```

**`dict-code-zero` surviving means no fixture in 1,264 tests rendered an element off a
DICTIONARY-encoded column** — an arm I had just written, with no coverage at all. `dict_encode` takes
a string column only when values repeat (distinct × 2 ≤ rows), and the element-render fixtures in
this file are four nodes wide, which cannot qualify. `an_element_renders_a_dict_encoded_column` is
ten nodes over three departments (3 × 2 ≤ 10), asserts `scan_is_cheap("dept")` so the fixture is
proved to dict-encode before anything else is checked, and then asserts each row decodes **its own**
code — `dict[0]` makes three of the ten legitimately right, so the assertion is the whole sequence.
With it, all five mutants die.

That is the second time in three items that mutation found a fixture which could not reach the code
under test (1067's guards, 1064's heap), and the first where the untested arm was brand new.

### Verification

Rust: 1,265 + 13 + 725 tests, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0, `cargo fmt`
applied. Byte identity: `bun run fuzz` 13/0 plus three runs of `FUZZ_ITERATIONS=120000`, all clean.
