## Item 1117 — the maintained per-type count's site list is LONGER than item 1042 recorded: two sites move a whole `Vec`, not an entry, and one of them is a restore

Item 1116 reproduced the stale-CSR typed count at 85x and named the one undisproven fix: a global
per-type edge count, maintained O(1) per write, which is what the TS engine already has. This tick
enumerated the sites against the code rather than against the prior note, because the failure mode
is a WRONG ANSWER and not a slow one.

### What the count has to be

`Adj { nbr, etype, eid }` carries the edge's PRIMARY type, and `rebuild_csr`'s partition builder is

```rust
  for a in adj { if let Some(t) = typed.get_mut(a.etype as usize) { t.1.push(*a); } }
```

so partition `t` holds every adjacency entry whose `etype == t`, and `out_typed_flat(t)?.len()` is
the number of OUT entries with primary type `t` — one per live edge. So the counter is
`counts[t] = |{ live out_adj entries with etype == t }|`, and one counter serves both directions.

### The sites, found by searching for `out_adj` MUTATIONS rather than for function names

Item 1042 named seven: `add_edge`, `add_edge_with_id`, `delete_edge`, `delete_node`, both `Undo`
restore arms, and load/clear. Searching the code for structural changes to `out_adj` finds those and
**two more that are not per-entry at all**:

```text
  +1  store.rs:3705   add_edge / add_edge_with_id — the ordinary push
  +1  store.rs:6087   Undo::RestoreEdge — pushes the entry back (guarded by `is_out`)
  +1  store.rs:6126   Undo::RestoreNode — rebuilds each NEIGHBOUR's mirror entry
  +N  store.rs:6130   Undo::RestoreNode — `self.out_adj[i] = out;` assigns a WHOLE Vec back
  +N  store.rs:6297   the Builder's load path — pushes every edge, then rebuilds anyway
  -1  store.rs:5244   delete_edge — `adj.remove(at)`, with `dropped_etype` already captured
  -N  store.rs:5616   delete_node_inner — `std::mem::take(&mut self.out_adj[i])` empties a WHOLE Vec
  -1  store.rs:5629   delete_node_inner — removes this node's mirror from each neighbour's out list
  -0  store.rs:6203   `out_adj.pop()` — the node's list is already empty by then
```

**The two `Vec`-granularity sites are the ones a per-entry hook misses**, and one of them is a
RESTORE: `Undo::RestoreNode` puts a deleted node's entire out list back with an assignment, so a
counter updated only at `push` call sites would under-count after a rolled-back `delete_node`, and
every later typed count would be WRONG — silently, and only on the undo path. `delete_node_inner`'s
`mem::take` is the mirror of it.

That is why the existing `push_etype_entry` hook cannot simply be copied: it maintains the OPT-IN
edge-type index and is called beside the per-entry pushes, where this counter must also track two
whole-`Vec` moves and must be unconditional.

### The shape the implementation needs

- a `Vec<usize>` indexed by etype, grown when a type is interned, cloned with the store;
- deltas at the seven live sites above, with the two `Vec` moves iterating the moved entries;
- **a `debug_assert` that recomputes the counts from `out_adj` and compares**, so a missed site
  fails loudly in the 1,267-test suite and in the fuzzers rather than returning a wrong count. This
  is the part that makes the change safe to make at all, and it is why the counter goes in before
  any consumer is wired to it;
- then the two consumers — `fastpath::typed_hop_count_from_size` and
  `fastpath::try_edge_label_count` — which today end in `out_typed_flat(t)?` and so decline whenever
  the overlay is stale.

**Not implemented this tick, deliberately.** Nine sites with two of them at `Vec` granularity, where
a miss is a wrong answer on an undo path, is not a change to half-land with the remaining budget —
and the previous tick's lesson is that the expensive mistake in this area is acting on a
site list read from a note rather than from the code. The list is now from the code.

No engine change; `bun run fmt` and `bun run check` clean.

## Item 1118 — the maintained per-type edge count: the stale-CSR typed count cliff is GONE, **0.347 → 0.003 ms**

Items 680/851/852 priced this cliff and refused both automatic repairs; item 1116 re-reproduced it at
85x on today's build; item 1117 enumerated the nine mutation sites from the code. This builds the one
design those items leave standing — a per-type live-edge count maintained O(1) per write, which is
what the TS engine has had all along in `edgesByLabel`.

### The numbers, alternated min-of-three, with the fresh path as the control

```text
                 fresh    stale (after ONE add_edge)
  PRE            0.003         0.347 / 0.350 / 0.352      116x cliff
  POST           0.003         0.003 / 0.003 / 0.003      GONE
```

**The fresh arm IS the control** and it does not move: this change cannot make a fresh count faster
(it was already a `len()`), and the thing to watch is that it does not make it slower. 0.003-0.004
in both arms across six builds. Answers are 3000 in every arm.

### The design

`Store::etype_counts: Vec<usize>`, indexed by type id, grown on demand by `bump_etype_count` — which
is what keeps the three type-interning sites out of this change entirely, since a type id is
`etype_ids.len()` when it is minted. Ten call sites, from item 1117's enumeration:

- `+1` the ordinary push in `add_edge`/`add_edge_with_id` — which is also how the ndjson and codec
  LOAD paths are covered, since both call it rather than building adjacency directly;
- the Builder tallies `edge_etypes` directly, every builder edge being live and laid down once;
- `-1` in `delete_edge`, ONE per edge rather than one per endpoint (`dropped_etype` is already
  captured there, and a live edge has exactly one `out_adj` entry);
- `-N` for `delete_node_inner`'s `mem::take` of the node's own OUT list, and `-1` per neighbour
  mirror it removes — guarded on the removal actually happening, because a SELF-LOOP is in both
  `out` and `inc` and its entry left with the take;
- `+1` on `Undo::RestoreEdge`'s out arm and on `Undo::RestoreNode`'s neighbour mirrors, and `+N`
  for `RestoreNode`'s whole-`Vec` assignment of the node's own OUT list.

Consumers: `typed_hop_count_from_size` and `try_edge_label_count` now read `live_etype_count(t)`
where they read `out_typed_flat(t)?.len()` — the `?` that declined the whole fast path for the rest
of the session after one write.

**The staleness was doing correctness work, and that argument is replaced rather than dropped.** The
old doc said the fresh-overlay requirement "is also what keeps this correct across deletes: an
adjacency write invalidates the overlay, so a fresh partition can never contain a detached edge".
The maintained count has to carry that itself, which is exactly what the oracle test below exists
for, and the doc now says so instead of the old reasoning.

### The oracle, which is why this was safe to build at all

`recomputed_etype_counts` tallies `out_adj` — not a second implementation but the invariant itself,
since every live edge has exactly one out entry. `the_maintained_etype_counts_match_a_recount_after_
every_mutation_kind` compares against it after: the builder's load, an ordinary add, an add that
INTERNS A NEW TYPE (the grow path), a parallel add, `delete_edge`, `delete_node` over a node with
in-edges, out-edges and a self-loop, and then the three rollbacks — of `delete_node` (the whole-`Vec`
restore), of `delete_edge`, and of `add_node` (`pop_last_node`). It finishes by rebuilding the CSR
and asserting `out_typed_flat(t).len() == live_etype_count(t)` for every type, which is the claim the
consumers actually rely on.

### Teeth, under `timeout 900 systemd-run … MemoryMax=16G MemorySwapMax=0`

| mutant                              | verdict                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `add-never-counts`                  | CAUGHT (`edge_label_and_untyped_counts`)            |
| `delete-edge-no-decrement`          | CAUGHT (the oracle)                                 |
| `delete-node-out-take-missed`       | CAUGHT (the oracle)                                 |
| **`restore-node-whole-vec-missed`** | **CAUGHT (the oracle)** — item 1117's headline risk |
| `restore-edge-missed`               | CAUGHT (the oracle)                                 |
| `selfloop-double-decrement`         | CAUGHT at compile time                              |
| `pop-last-node-missed`              | **SURVIVED**                                        |

**Six of seven caught, and the survivor is reported rather than papered over.** Removing the
`pop_last_node` decrement leaves the whole suite green, which says that on every path the tests
reach, the node's OUT list is already empty when it is popped — a delete detaches first, and rolling
back an `add_node` unwinds the edge entries before the node. So that arm is INSURANCE against a
future caller that pops an attached node, not a load-bearing site, and its comment now says exactly
that with the mutation result as the evidence. The alternative — leaving it to read as though a test
pinned it — is the failure item 1110 cost a whole verdict set to learn.

Suites: Rust **1268 + 13 + 725 pass, 0 fail**; native 933, gql 3117, gremlin 918, all 0 fail.
Fuzzers **13 pass, 0 fail**. `query_bench -- counts` and the `gql` group flat (`1-hop` 0.3,
`label scan` 0.3, `hop prop` 444, `scan prop` 49.8).

Four gates, each its own command: `cargo fmt` 0, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` 0,
`bun run fmt` 0, `bun run check` 0.

## Item 1119 — the maintained count's REACH, mapped: one more consumer could use it and deliberately does not, because its staleness may be load-bearing

Item 1118 shipped `live_etype_count` and converted the two consumers that were declining on CSR
staleness. "Grep the pattern elsewhere" asks whether there are more. There are exactly three other
sites that read a per-type partition, and they split three ways.

### The three remaining sites

```text
  exec.rs:4382/4390/4401/4545   out_typed_csr / in_typed_csr — PER-NODE slices
  exec.rs:5084                  for_each_typed_out — `out_typed_flat(w)?` as a freshness gate
  exec/reverse.rs:203           `filter_map(|&t| out_typed_flat(t).map(len))` — a LENGTH
```

- **The per-node slices cannot use it.** `live_etype_count` is a GLOBAL per-type total; a per-node
  typed degree needs per-node data. `slice_degree`'s three O(1) cases are the per-node analogue and
  they are a separate question (item 1101 read them).
- **`for_each_typed_out` legitimately needs the ENTRIES**, not a count — it visits each neighbour.
  Its `?` is a real freshness gate and stays one.
- **`reverse.rs:203` reads a LENGTH, and is the one that could.**

### Why the one that could, does not

That site computes `fwd`, the endpoint type's forward edge count, to decide whether reverse-seeding
a predicate beats sweeping the type's edges forward. After ANY adjacency write `out_typed_flat`
returns `None`, so `filter_map` drops every type, `fwd` sums to **0**, and the guard `fwd > 0 && …`
skips the decline entirely. A route choice that stops working for the rest of the session — the same
staleness defect item 1118 just fixed, in a different dress, and answer-equivalent so no test can
see it.

`live_etype_count(t)` would restore it in one line. **It is not used, and the reason is the thing
worth recording:** the estimate prices a forward alternative that is ALSO gated on freshness —
`for_each_typed_out` returns `None` when the overlay is stale. So after a write the cheap forward
sweep this guard would decline _in favour of_ may not be available at all, and a correct `fwd` could
decline the reverse seed into the GENERAL path instead, which may be slower than the reverse seed it
replaced. The current `fwd = 0` behaviour might therefore be accidentally right.

Which way it lands is a measurement on the shape this function's own comment already names — a
non-selective range on a sparse type, "`age >= 77` = 92k seeds vs 80k forward F edges" — and not
something to settle by argument. A one-line change that looks obviously correct, on a route choice
no test can police, is exactly the shape this corpus keeps records for.

**So the site is ANNOTATED and the behaviour is unchanged.** The annotation states the staleness,
names the fix, and says why it is not applied — because the risk now is the opposite one: with
`live_etype_count` in the codebase, the next reader has a one-line "fix" available and no reason
written down to stop and measure first.

Comment-only change in the engine. Gates: `cargo fmt` 0, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` 0.

## Item 1120 — the `fwd`-estimate fix is MEASURED NEUTRAL, and the same probe prices what item 1118 did NOT fix: a FILTERED typed count still pays **6x** after one write

Item 1119 found that `reverse_seed_decide`'s `fwd` estimate silently becomes 0 after any adjacency
write, named the one-line fix (`live_etype_count`, from item 1118), and deliberately withheld it
because the forward route the estimate prices is itself freshness-gated — so a correct `fwd` might
decline the reverse seed into something slower. This measures it.

### The fixture, and the answer

A temporary example (removed in this item, the pattern items 851/852 used), on the shape
`reverse_seed_decide`'s own comment names — a non-selective range on a SPARSE type. 200,000 nodes,
80,000 `F` edges, `MATCH (a)-[:F]->(b) WHERE b.age >= 77 RETURN count(*)`, min of 5:

```text
  FRESH (just loaded)                 257.9 us
  STALE (after one add_edge)         1556.9        6.0x
  STALE then rebuild_csr              207.2        the reference
```

Then the one-liner, alternated:

```text
            PRE (fwd broken)     POST (fwd correct)
  stale       1530.6 / 1536.8      1535.6 / 1525.1
```

**Identical.** And the reason is not that the estimate does not matter but that both of its branches
cost the same once the overlay is stale: with `fwd = 0` the guard is skipped and the reverse seed is
kept; with `fwd` correct the guard fires and declines it — and the forward sweep it declines in
favour of is ALSO freshness-gated, so the plan falls to the general path, which costs what the
reverse seed did.

**Not shipped.** A route choice no test can police, with no measured benefit, is not a change — and
item 1119's refusal to apply it on the reasoning alone was the right call for the right reason, even
though the reasoning's specific worry (that it might be WORSE) also did not materialize.

### What the probe found that was not the question

The 6x in the first table is the finding. **Item 1118's maintained count does not reach this
shape**: `typed_hop_count_from_size` requires an unfiltered whole-graph hop, and this query filters
the endpoint, so it goes through the walk — which loses `out_typed_flat`/`out_typed_csr` the moment
the overlay is stale. The rebuilt reference at 207.2 us against 1556.9 stale is the cost of exactly
that.

So the cliff is now split cleanly in two, which is worth having explicitly:

- **the GLOBAL per-type count** — fixed at item 1118, 0.347 → 0.003 ms, by maintaining one integer
  per type;
- **the PER-NODE typed adjacency** — still 6x on a filtered shape, and NOT reachable by a global
  count. This is the incremental per-type CSR maintenance item 852 calls "the only undisproven
  design", with the cost model it has to beat: `O(E + types × N)` amortized over fewer than 6 reads.

Item 1118's win was the half that a single integer per type could carry. The other half needs the
per-node structure, and now has a 6x price on a named shape rather than a general claim.

Comment-only change in the engine: the annotation item 1119 left now carries this measurement, so
the next reader finds the one-liner already tried and priced rather than merely cautioned against.

## Item 1121 — item 852's "6 to 27 stale reads" is a property of the QUERY it used, and that query no longer has a penalty: on the shape that does, the break-even is **~2 reads**, stable across a 10x fixture range

Item 852 refused an unconditional rebuild-at-commit hook because "a rebuild costs between 6 and 27
stale reads", measured with `MATCH (a:P)-[:T0]->(b) RETURN count(*)` — whose stale penalty was
~134 µs (295 against 161). Two things have changed since, and together they invalidate the basis of
that refusal rather than its caution.

### 852's own shape has NO penalty left

```text
  unfiltered count (852's shape)   fresh 0.3 us   stale 0.3 us   penalty 0.0
```

Item **1118** answers it from the maintained per-type count, so there is nothing left to amortize a
rebuild against on that query. **852's number is now being quoted for a shape that cannot produce
it.** That is exactly what CLOSED.md exists to prevent, and it took a measurement rather than a
reading to notice — the entry is still correct about what it measured.

### On the shape that still has one, the break-even is ~2 reads

The filtered endpoint predicate item 1120 priced, swept over fixture size (rebuild and both query
arms on ONE store each, min of 5, break-even = `rebuild / (stale − fresh)`):

```text
  nodes    edges    rebuild_csr    fresh    stale   penalty   BREAK-EVEN
  200,000   80,000     2757.0       232.0   1548.9   1316.9     2.09 reads
  200,000  400,000     5254.6      1380.6   3811.4   2430.9     2.16
  400,000  400,000     8686.2      1462.2   5359.4   3897.2     2.23
  800,000  800,000    17189.3      2905.4  11626.8   8721.4     1.97
```

**1.97 to 2.23 reads across a 10x range of both axes.** The stability is the useful part: the
rebuild and the stale penalty are both roughly O(E) here, so the ratio barely moves, and the number
is a property of the SHAPE rather than of the fixture — which is precisely what 852's single row
could not show.

### What this does and does not license

It does **not** ship a commit hook. 852's policy objection survives in form — "the policy it would
need depends on a future read count the store does not have" — and a rebuild per commit still loses
on a write-only workload.

What it changes is the size of the bet. At 6-27 reads, an unconditional hook is a gamble; at **2**,
any serving workload that reads at all after a write has already paid for it. And 852's objection
has an answer it did not consider: the store does not know the FUTURE read count, but it can know
the PAST one — reads served since the last rebuild is a cheap counter and a standard proxy. A hook
that rebuilds at commit only once the store has served a couple of reads since the last rebuild
costs nothing on a write-only workload and converges on the right answer for a serving one. That is
a new design, with a measured break-even to size it against, and it is the next thing to try.

### A measurement error worth recording, because its tell was the numbers

The first sweep reported IDENTICAL figures at three different fixture sizes (rebuild 2634/2659/2678,
filtered 1554/1547/1550). That is impossible for a 5x edge count, and the cause was
`for cfg in "200000 80000" …; set -- $cfg` — **zsh does not word-split an unquoted parameter**, so
`$1` was the whole string, `PROBE_NODES` failed to parse and both arms fell back to the same
defaults. CLAUDE.md records that zsh behaviour; what is worth adding is the tell: **three fixtures
that disagree by 5x producing numbers that agree to 1% is the instrument, not the result.** Re-run
with `${pair%%:*}` / `${pair##*:}`, the sizes moved and so did every figure.

The temporary probe is removed (items 851/852/1120's pattern) with its numbers here.

## Item 1122 — the CSR re-arms at the QUERY BOUNDARY after 4 stale reads: **1.68x at ten reads per write, 2.74x at twenty**, and nothing measurable below five

Three items closed the automatic designs and one re-opened the arithmetic. Item 851 excluded a LAZY
rebuild structurally. Item 852 refused an UNCONDITIONAL commit hook, with the objection that mattered:
"the policy it would need depends on a future read count the store does not have". Item 1121 found
852's break-even belonged to a query that no longer has a penalty, and measured the real one at
**1.97-2.23 reads**. This builds the design that objection leaves open — **the store cannot know the
future read count, but it can know the PAST one.**

### Why the query boundary is available where the accessors were not

Item 851's exclusion is specific: `out_typed_csr`/`out_typed_flat` take `&self` and return borrows
into the very `Vec`s a rebuild replaces. `lnk_query` already holds `store_mut` — a mutable borrow,
taken before any accessor has lent anything out — so `store.rearm_if_warranted()` there is not the
rebuild 851 excluded, it is one at a different point in the call stack.

### The threshold is MEASURED, and it is the whole change

One write then `k` reads, swept over `k`, min of 5 (`rearm-probe.ts`):

```text
   k     PRE      T=2      T=3      T=4
   1     1.5      1.6      1.5      1.5
   2     3.0      4.3      3.0      3.0
   3     4.5      4.6      5.8      4.5
   5     7.5      5.1      6.4      7.6
  10    14.9      6.3      7.6      8.9
  20    29.6      8.4      9.4     10.9
```

Every threshold wins on a read-heavy cycle and every one of them has a LOSS BAND where the rebuild
fires and is not amortized — T=2 costs 1.43x at k=2, T=3 costs 1.29x at k=3. **T=4 is the smallest
with no loss band above the noise floor**, and it is what ships. Alternated min-of-three on T=4:

```text
   k     PRE    POST
   1     1.5     1.5      flat
   2     3.1     3.0      flat
   3     4.5     4.5      flat
   5     7.4     7.6      +2.7%  ← consistent in sign, inside the ~10% floor, and REPORTED
  10    14.8     8.8      1.68x
  20    29.6    10.8      2.74x
```

The +2.7% at k=5 is break-even by construction (three stale reads, the rebuild, one fresh) and is
stated rather than rounded to "flat" — it was 7.7/7.7/7.6 against 7.5/7.5/7.4, consistent in sign.

A write RESETS the count, so a steady stream of small write batches never accumulates its way to a
rebuild — which is the other half of protecting the write-heavy workload, and `k = 1` flat is that
protection measured.

### Teeth, and two survivors that got two DIFFERENT answers

First sweep: 3 of 5 caught. The two survivors were not both test gaps.

- **`no-reset-after-rebuild` SURVIVED because the line was REDUNDANT.** `rebuild_csr` sets
  `csr_fresh`, so the guard returns early on every later call, and the only route back to stale is
  `invalidate_csr`, which resets the count itself. **The line is deleted**, not tested — a mutant
  surviving is sometimes the measurement telling you the code cannot matter, and a line no test can
  justify reads as load-bearing when it is not.
- **`ignores-fresh` SURVIVED because it is a PERF GATE.** Dropping the `csr_fresh` guard rebuilds
  every fourth query on a store that needs no rebuild — answer-neutral, so no result-based test can
  see it, and `csr_fresh` cannot either since it is true both ways. The gate's only observable is
  the COUNT, so a `#[cfg(test)]` `stale_reads()` accessor exists and the test asserts it stays 0 on
  a fresh overlay. The audit's own rule: a perf gate needs its own test.

After both: **4 of 4 caught** (`never-rearms`, `rearms-immediately`, `write-does-not-reset`,
`ignores-fresh`), with the fifth deleted as code rather than covered as behaviour.

### Scope, stated plainly

The hook is at `lnk_query`, so it reaches both TS engines and every FFI consumer — the product
surface — and NOT the in-process Rust API that `query_bench` uses. That is why this item's numbers
come from a TS probe and the bench groups show no change.

Suites: Rust **1269 + 13 + 725 pass, 0 fail**; native 933, gql 3117, gremlin 918, all 0 fail.
Fuzzers **13 pass, 0 fail**. Four gates each its own command: `cargo fmt` 0, `cargo clippy
--all-targets --features capi -D warnings` 0, `bun run fmt` 0, `bun run check` 0.

## Item 1123 — item 292's blocker on caching the OPTIMIZED plan is avoidable: the optimizer already plans `Prop <op> Param`, so optimize-then-bind still seeds

Reading CLOSED.md's open-and-priced list for a target rather than inventing one. The entry that
matters is `bench:usage`'s indexed read rows, where native loses to pure TS — my own run of that
bench reproduces it: `read: point lookup` **ts(+) 977.1k ops/s against engine(+) 455.4k**, the most
common serving shape.

Item 291 accounted for that call completely (and exonerated the FFI boundary at 8 ns), and item 292
split the residual. Two avoidable items were named, and this verifies the first against the code
rather than the note.

### Both query paths still optimize on EVERY call — verified in the code

```text
  ffi.rs:626-630   lnk_query:     optimize_indexed(parse_cache::parse_for_run(q, &params, …), store)
  ffi.rs:1127      prepared_run:  let plan = crate::opt::optimize_indexed(plan, store);
```

So the parse is cached (items 228/229's `parse_cache`, which stores a PREPARED plan and binds per
call) and the OPTIMIZE is not — 295-330 ns of a ~3000 ns call by 292's split, and ~11% of the
prepared path's 2648 ns.

### 292's blocker, and why it does not hold

292 recorded the obstacle as the plan depending on param VALUES: `gql::parse_with_params`
substitutes params during parse so the planner sees literals and can still seed an index, and the
serving shape is `WHERE u.name = $n` with a different value every call — so a text-keyed cache of
the optimized plan would miss every time.

That is true of bind-THEN-optimize, which is what both paths do today. It is not true of the
optimizer:

```rust
  opt.rs:3805    (Expr::Prop { key, .. }, Expr::Lit(_) | Expr::Param(_))
  opt.rs:3806  | (Expr::Lit(_) | Expr::Param(_), Expr::Prop { key, .. }) => key,
```

**It recognises `Prop <op> Param` alongside `Prop <op> Lit`.** So optimizing the PREPARED plan —
params still params — and binding AFTERWARDS still produces the seeking plan, and that plan is
param-independent and therefore cacheable by text. Which is how a prepared statement is supposed to
work, and what `prepared_run`'s own comment claims it does ("the plan is graph-agnostic, so one
prepared statement serves any store") while in fact re-optimizing each call.

### What the change needs, and the one thing to measure before believing it

- **A STORE VERSION in the key**, which 292 already identified and which exists:
  `Store::version()` at `store.rs:1771`. `optimize_indexed` reads the store, and a cached plan that
  seeks a dropped index is a wrong answer rather than a slow one.
- **A behaviour trade that is NOT free, and is the reason this is not obviously right:** an
  optimized-once plan is no longer VALUE-specific. For index seeding that costs nothing — the seek
  is the same shape whatever the needle. For a selectivity-dependent route choice it is classic
  parameter sniffing: `reverse_seed_decide` and `cost::estimate` both read values, so a plan chosen
  for `age >= 77` can be served to `age >= 0`. **That is the measurement this target needs first** —
  a fixture where two param values want different plans, and the cost of giving them one.

Priced at ~11% of the prepared serving call, located to two lines, with its correctness key and its
one real risk named. Not built this tick.

### The serving A/B for item 1122 is still running, with one row to watch

`bench:usage`, engine(+), alternated: `read: point lookup` reads PRE 490.0k / 491.4k against POST
452.0k so far — an 8% drop on a PURE READ row that item 1122 cannot reach, since with no write the
overlay stays fresh and `rearm_if_warranted` is two boolean checks. The row's own spread across runs
is 452-491k, so variance is the likely reading, but the second POST arm is not in yet and this is
recorded as PENDING rather than resolved. If it reproduces it is a real regression and 1122's
threshold is not the issue — an unconditional call per query would be.
